ramayan::33.translation_literal: सः (he) / कामम् (desire, wish) / अनवाप्य (not having obtained) / एव (indeed) / राम-पादौ (Rama's feet/sandals) / उपस्पृशन् (touching, worshipping) / नन्दिग्रामे (in Nandigrama) / अकरोत् (he did) / राज्यम् (the kingdom, rule) / राम-आगमन-काङ्क्षया (with longing for Rama's return)
ramayan::33.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::33.essence: Loyalty can rule without claiming what it protects.
ramayan::33.simple_meaning: Bharata did not get Rama back. He honoured Rama's sandals, governed from Nandigrama, and kept waiting for Rama to return.
ramayan::33.simple_insight: Real loyalty keeps working even when the person you love is absent.
ramayan::33.detailed_meaning: Rama has gone to the forest, and Bharata has failed to bring him home. Rather than seize power for himself, he places Rama's sandals on the throne and rules from Nandigrama, treating the kingdom as a trust until Rama returns.
ramayan::33.modern_relevance: You keep a project alive after the founder leaves, not because you own it, but because you promised to guard it. Bharata knows how to hold responsibility without pretending it belongs to him.
ramayan::33.insight: It teaches you to carry authority as a stewardship, not a possession.

ramayan::34.verse_sanskrit: गते तु भरते श्रीमान् सत्यसन्धो जितेन्द्रिय: । । 1139 । । रामस्तु पुनरालक्ष्य नागरस्य जनस्य च । तत्रागमनमेकाग्रो दण्डकान्प्रविवेश ह । । 1140 । ।
ramayan::34.verse_hindi: When Bharata departed, Sri Rama, a man of good fortune and steadfast in vows  one who had conquered under control perceiving that the citizens from Ayodhya would arrive there, entered the Dandaka forest with single minded determination (so that there would not be breach of his promise).
ramayan::34.english_translation: When Bharata had gone, noble Rama, steadfast in vows and master of his senses, looked again toward the people of the city and, intent on keeping his promise, entered the Dandaka forest with single-minded resolve.
ramayan::34.translation_literal: गते (having gone) / तु (but) / भरते (when Bharata) / श्रीमान् (the glorious one) / सत्यसन्धः (steadfast in vows) / जितेन्द्रियः (master of his senses) / रामः (Rama) / तु (then) / पुनः (again) / आलक्ष्य (seeing) / नागरस्य (of the city-dwellers) / जनस्य (of the people) / च (and) / तत्र (there) / आगमनम् (arrival) / एकाग्रः (one-pointed) / दण्डकान् (to Dandaka) / प्रविवेश (entered) / ह (indeed)
ramayan::34.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::34.essence: A vow becomes real only when you keep it after longing returns.
ramayan::34.simple_meaning: Rama leaves for the forest once Bharata is gone. He stays focused on his promise and does not let the pull of the city change his path.
ramayan::34.simple_insight: Keeping your word can mean choosing the harder road without looking back.
ramayan::34.detailed_meaning: Bharata has already failed to bring Rama back and now rules from Nandigrama. With that last pull toward Ayodhya gone, Rama turns fully toward exile and enters Dandaka. The moment shows a man locking himself into his vow.
ramayan::34.modern_relevance: You’ve said yes to something painful and now every part of you wants to renegotiate. Rama’s example is the harder move: stop circling the exit and walk the path your word created.
ramayan::34.insight: It shifts attention from comfort to commitment, showing that a vow matters most when it hurts.

ramayan::35.verse_sanskrit: प्रविश्य तु महारण्यं रामो राजीवलोचनः । विराधं राक्षसं हत्वा शरभङ्गं ददर्श ह । । 1141 । । सुतीक्ष्णं चाप्यगस्त्यं च अगस्त्यभ्रातरं तथा ।
ramayan::35.verse_hindi: Having entered the dense forest Dandaka, Rama slew the demon Viradha and saw the sages Sarabhanga, Sutikshna and Agastya with his brother.
ramayan::35.english_translation: Having entered the dense forest of Dandaka, Rama slew the demon Viradha and saw Sarabhanga, Sutikshna, Agastya, and Agastya's brother.
ramayan::35.translation_literal: प्रविश्य (having entered) / तु (indeed) / महारण्यं (the great forest) / रामः (Rama) / राजीवलोचनः (lotus-eyed) / विराधं (Viradha) / राक्षसं (the demon) / हत्वा (having killed) / शरभङ्गं (Sarabhanga) / ददर्श (saw) / ह (indeed) / सुतीक्ष्णं (Sutikshna) / च (and) / अपि (also) / अगस्त्यं (Agastya) / च (and) / अगस्त्यभ्रातरं (Agastya's brother) / तथा (likewise)
ramayan::35.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::35.essence: The exile deepens as danger and guidance meet in the forest.
ramayan::35.simple_meaning: Rama enters the forest, kills Viradha, and meets several sages there.
ramayan::35.simple_insight: Not every turning point is philosophical; sometimes the story simply moves forward, and the next task appears.
ramayan::35.detailed_meaning: Rama has left the city and entered Dandaka Forest, where exile becomes real. He kills Viradha and then meets holy sages like Sarabhanga, Sutikshna, and Agastya. The verse sets the scene for the forest journey, not a teaching by itself.
ramayan::35.modern_relevance: You arrive in a new place and immediately have to deal with what it contains: one problem, then the next, before you can even settle.
ramayan::35.insight: It keeps attention on sequence and movement rather than extracting a lesson from the scene.

ramayan::36.verse_sanskrit: अगस्त्यवचनाच्चैव जग्राहैन्द्रं शरासनम् । । 1142 । । खड्गं च परमप्रीतस्तूणी चाक्षयसायकौ ।
ramayan::36.verse_hindi: As directed by sage Agastya, Rama received with extreme delight a bow, a sword and quivers with inexhaustible arrows, given by Indra to Agastya (to be passed on to
ramayan::36.english_translation: As directed by sage Agastya, Rama gladly received Indra’s bow, sword, and two quivers of inexhaustible arrows.
ramayan::36.translation_literal: अगस्त्यवचनात् (by Agastya's words) / च (and) एव (indeed) / जग्राह (he received) / ऐन्द्रम् (of Indra) / शरासनम् (bow) / खड्गम् (sword) / च (and) / परमप्रीतः (greatly pleased) / तूणी (quivers) / च (and) / अक्षयसायकौ (with inexhaustible arrows)
ramayan::36.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::36.essence: Rama is armed for the trials ahead, not for comfort.
ramayan::36.simple_meaning: Rama accepts divine weapons from Agastya: a bow, a sword, and quivers that never run empty.
ramayan::36.simple_insight: Preparation matters. The right tools arrive when the journey turns dangerous.
ramayan::36.detailed_meaning: Rama has entered Dandaka, met Agastya, and now receives weapons that will matter as the forest exile turns more perilous. This verse is a handoff, not a teaching: it prepares the next stage of the story.
ramayan::36.modern_relevance: You finally get the equipment you needed after the hard part has already begun. The timing feels late, but it is exactly right for what comes next.
ramayan::36.insight: It shifts attention from instruction to preparation before the next trial.

ramayan::37.verse_sanskrit: वसतस्तस्य रामस्य वने वनचरैस्सह । ऋषयोऽभ्यागमन्सर्वे वधायासुररक्षसाम् । । 1143 । ।
ramayan::37.verse_hindi: While Rama was dwelling in the forest (in the hermitage of sage Sarabhanga), all the ascetics along with others (sages) inhabiting the forest approached Rama requesting for the destruction of the asuras and rakshasas seizing upon their lives.
ramayan::37.english_translation: While Rama was dwelling in the forest, all the ascetics and forest-dwellers approached him, asking him to destroy the asuras and rakshasas who were tormenting their lives.
ramayan::37.translation_literal: वसतस्तस्य (while he was dwelling) / रामस्य (of Rama) / वने (in the forest) / वनचरैः (with forest-dwellers) / सह (together) / ऋषयः (the sages) / अभ्यागमन् (approached) / सर्वे (all) / वधाय (for the destruction) / असुर-रक्षसाम् (of asuras and rakshasas)
ramayan::37.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::37.essence: Their suffering turns Rama's exile into a duty.
ramayan::37.simple_meaning: The forest sages came to Rama and asked him to protect them by defeating the beings attacking their lives.
ramayan::37.simple_insight: Some calls for help are really calls to step into responsibility.
ramayan::37.detailed_meaning: Rama is deep in the Dandaka forest after meeting Agastya. The sages of the forest, worn down by violent beings, come to him together and ask for protection. This verse sets up the promise Rama makes in the next line.
ramayan::37.modern_relevance: A neighbourhood keeps reporting the same threat, and everyone is waiting for someone steady to act. Before the solution, there is always the moment when people finally come asking for help.
ramayan::37.insight: It shifts attention from private travel to public responsibility.

ramayan::38.verse_sanskrit: स तेषां प्रतिशुश्राव राक्षसानां तथा वने । । 1144 । । प्रतिज्ञातश्च रामेण वधस्संयति रक्षसाम् । ऋषीणामग्निकल्पानां दण्डकारण्यवासिनाम् । । 1145 । ।
ramayan::38.verse_hindi: Rama promised those ascetics, who resembled flaming fire in lustre living in Dandakaranya inhabited by rakshasas to slay them.
ramayan::38.english_translation: Rama promised those ascetics, who shone like fire and lived in Dandakaranya among the rakshasas, that he would slay the rakshasas in battle.
ramayan::38.translation_literal: स (he) / तेषां (to them) / प्रतिशुश्राव (promised in return) / राक्षसानां (of the rakshasas) / तथा (thus) / वने (in the forest) / प्रतिज्ञातः (having pledged) / च (and) / रामेण (by Rama) / वधः (slaying) / संयति (in battle) / रक्षसाम् (of the rakshasas) / ऋषीणाम् (of the sages) / अग्निकल्पानाम् (fire-like) / दण्डकारण्यवासिनाम् (of those dwelling in Dandakaranya)
ramayan::38.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::38.essence: Protection begins when your word becomes a shield for others.
ramayan::38.simple_meaning: Rama gives the forest sages his word that he will destroy the rakshasas threatening them.
ramayan::38.simple_insight: A serious promise can become protection for people who have none.
ramayan::38.detailed_meaning: In Dandakaranya, Rama is living among sages who are being harassed by rakshasas. They come to him for safety, and he answers not with sympathy alone but with a binding vow: he will kill the demons. This is the moment his protection becomes personal duty.
ramayan::38.modern_relevance: A neighbour texts you at midnight because someone is threatening their family. You do not just comfort them. You decide what you will do, and your word starts carrying weight.
ramayan::38.insight: It shifts duty from abstract goodness to a concrete promise that must be kept.

ramayan::39.verse_sanskrit: तेन तत्रैव वसता जनस्थाननिवासिनी । विरूपिता शूर्पणखा राक्षसी कामरूपिणी । । 1146 । ।
ramayan::39.verse_hindi: During his stay there a demon called Surpanakha living in Janasthana (resting place for the army of Ravana in Dandakaranya) and capable of assuming any form at will was rendered deformed by Lakshmana.
ramayan::39.english_translation: During his stay there, Lakshmana disfigured Surpanakha, the shapeshifting rakshasi who lived in Janasthana.
ramayan::39.translation_literal: तेन (by that) / तत्रैव (there itself) / वसता (while dwelling) / जनस्थाननिवासिनी (inhabitant of Janasthana) / विरूपिता (was disfigured) / शूर्पणखा (Surpanakha) / राक्षसी (rakshasi) / कामरूपिणी (one who can assume any form at will)
ramayan::39.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::39.essence: One sharp act in the forest sets the war in motion.
ramayan::39.simple_meaning: Surpanakha, who could change her form, was disfigured by Lakshmana while Rama stayed in the forest.
ramayan::39.simple_insight: A single violent act can turn a quiet forest exile into a turning point.
ramayan::39.detailed_meaning: Rama is living in Dandaka forest among sages he has vowed to protect. In that setting, Surpanakha appears and is disfigured by Lakshmana. The verse is a plot detail that sets up the larger conflict to follow.
ramayan::39.modern_relevance: A small humiliation in a tense room can ignite consequences no one planned for.
ramayan::39.insight: It marks the moment a local insult begins a much larger chain of violence.

ramayan::40.verse_sanskrit: ततश्शूर्पणखावाक्यादुद्युक्तान्सर्वराक्षसान् । खरं त्रिशिरसं चैव दूषणं चैव राक्षसम् । । 1147 । । निजघान वने रामस्तेषां चैव पदानुगान् ।
ramayan::40.verse_hindi: Thereafter Rama killed in the fight all the rakshasas, Khara, Trisira, and Dushana with their followers in a battle who were instigated by  Surpanakhas words.
ramayan::40.english_translation: Then, provoked by Surpanakha's words, Rama killed in the forest the rakshasa Khara, Trisira, Dushana, and their followers.
ramayan::40.translation_literal: तत्श्शूर्पणखा-वाक्यात् (from Surpanakha's words) / उद्युक्तान् (aroused) / सर्व-राक्षसान् (all the rakshasas) / खरम् (Khara) / त्रिशिरसम् (Trisira) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / दूषणम् (Dushana) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / राक्षसम् (the rakshasa) / निजघान (slew) / वने (in the forest) / रामः (Rama) / तेषाम् (their) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / पद-अनुगान् (followers)
ramayan::40.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::40.essence: One provocation turns into a massacre.
ramayan::40.simple_meaning: Rama killed Khara, Trisira, Dushana, and their followers in the forest after Surpanakha stirred them up.
ramayan::40.simple_insight: Violence here is a consequence, not a triumph.
ramayan::40.detailed_meaning: In Dandaka forest, Surpanakha's humiliation has turned into retaliation. Khara, Trisira, Dushana, and their forces rush at Rama, and he destroys them in battle. The verse is a combat detail, not a teaching moment.
ramayan::40.modern_relevance: A small insult can spiral into a much larger conflict. One sharp reaction pulls in allies, pride, and retaliation until nobody remembers the original wound.
ramayan::40.insight: It shows how quickly provocation can escalate into irreversible conflict.

ramayan::41.verse_sanskrit: वने तस्मिन्निवसता जनस्थाननिवासिनाम् । । 1148 । । रक्षसां निहतान्यासन्सहस्राणि चतुर्दश ।
ramayan::41.verse_hindi: During his stay in that forest Rama killed fourteen thousand rakshasas who were inhabitants of Janasthana.
ramayan::41.english_translation: During his stay in that forest, Rama killed fourteen thousand rakshasas who lived in Janasthana.
ramayan::41.translation_literal: वने (in the forest) / तस्मिन् (in that) / निवसता (while dwelling) / जनस्थाननिवासिनाम् (of the inhabitants of Janasthana) / रक्षसाम् (of the rakshasas) / निहतानि (were slain) / आसन् (were) / चतुर्दश (fourteen) / सहस्राणि (thousands)
ramayan::41.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::41.essence: The forest clash left thousands dead before Ravana even entered the story.
ramayan::41.simple_meaning: While Rama stayed in the forest, fourteen thousand rakshasas of Janasthana were slain.
ramayan::41.simple_insight: The verse marks the scale of the conflict, not a moral teaching.
ramayan::41.detailed_meaning: Rama has already destroyed Khara, Trisira, and Dushana after Surpanakha's provocation. This line adds the toll of that wider battle: fourteen thousand rakshasas of Janasthana fell while he stayed in the forest, setting up Ravana's furious response.
ramayan::41.modern_relevance: No modern parallel is needed here; the verse mainly counts the cost of an unfolding war.
ramayan::41.insight: It shifts the scene from a duel to a massacre, showing how quickly one conflict expands.

ramayan::42.verse_sanskrit: ततो ज्ञातिवधं श्रुत्वा रावणः क्रोधमूर्छितः । । 1149 । । सहायं वरयामास मारीचं नाम राक्षसम् ।
ramayan::42.verse_hindi: Having heard the slaughter of fellow rakshasa, Ravana became violent with anger and sought the help of a rakshasa named Maricha.
ramayan::42.english_translation: Then, hearing of the slaughter of his kin, Ravana was seized by rage and sought the help of a rakshasa named Maricha.
ramayan::42.translation_literal: ततः (then) / ज्ञातिवधम् (slaughter of kin) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / रावणः (Ravana) / क्रोधमूर्छितः (overcome by anger) / सहायम् (help / ally) / वरयामास (sought / chose) / मारीचम् (Maricha) / नाम (named) / राक्षसम् (rakshasa)
ramayan::42.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::42.essence: Rage makes a powerful mind choose poor help.
ramayan::42.simple_meaning: Ravana hears that his kin have been killed, loses his temper, and turns to Maricha for support.
ramayan::42.simple_insight: Anger can make even a powerful person reach for the wrong ally.
ramayan::42.detailed_meaning: After Rama destroys Khara, Trisira, Dushana, and thousands of rakshasas in Janasthana, Ravana hears of the loss and burns with rage. Instead of pausing, he immediately seeks out Maricha, setting the next part of the conflict in motion.
ramayan::42.modern_relevance: You get one furious message about a family member, and your first move is to call the one person who always makes things worse. Rage loves bad company.
ramayan::42.insight: It shows how anger narrows judgment and pushes you toward dangerous alliances.

ramayan::43.verse_sanskrit: वार्यमाणस्सुबहुशो मारीचेन स रावणः । । 1150 । । न विरोधो बलवता क्षमो रावण तेन ते ।
ramayan::43.verse_hindi: Maricha repeatedly dissuaded him saying, O Ravana It  is not proper for you to enter into hostility with the  mighty and powerful Rama.
ramayan::43.english_translation: Maricha repeatedly dissuaded him, saying, "O Ravana, it is not proper for you to enter into hostility with the mighty Rama."
ramayan::43.translation_literal: वार्यमाणः (being restrained) / सुबहुशः (again and again) / मारीचेन (by Maricha) / सः (he) / रावणः (Ravana) / न (not) / विरोधः (hostility) / बलवता (with the powerful one) / क्षमः (proper/fit) / रावण (O Ravana) / तेन (with that one) / ते (for you)
ramayan::43.speaker: Maricha
ramayan::43.essence: Clear warning means little when anger has already chosen the path.
ramayan::43.simple_meaning: Maricha warns Ravana not to pick a fight with Rama, who is stronger than he is.
ramayan::43.simple_insight: Pride can ignore good counsel even when the danger is obvious.
ramayan::43.detailed_meaning: Ravana has already set his anger in motion after hearing of the rakshasas killed in Janasthana. He turns to Maricha for help, but Maricha sees the danger clearly and tries to stop him. This verse is the warning before Ravana chooses disaster.
ramayan::43.modern_relevance: You know the plan is reckless, and someone wiser says so out loud. The danger is clear, but your anger wants the last word.
ramayan::43.insight: It shows how self-will can override clear warning and push a person toward avoidable ruin.

ramayan::44.verse_sanskrit: अनादृत्य तु तद्वाक्यं रावण: कालचोदित: । । 1151 । । जगाम सह मारीचस्तस्याश्रमपदं तदा ।
ramayan::44.verse_hindi: Disregarding his words Ravana incited by fate left for the hermitage of Rama along with Maricha.
ramayan::44.english_translation: Disregarding his words, Ravana, driven on by fate, went then with Maricha to Rama's hermitage.
ramayan::44.translation_literal: अनादृत्य (disregarding) / तु (but) / तत्-वाक्यं (that advice) / रावणः (Ravana) / काल-चोदितः (driven by fate) / जगाम (went) / सह (with) / मारीचः (Maricha) / तस्य (his) / आश्रम-पदं (hermitage) / तदा (then)
ramayan::44.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::44.essence: Pride keeps moving even after wisdom has spoken.
ramayan::44.simple_meaning: Ravana ignored Maricha's warning and went with him toward Rama's hermitage.
ramayan::44.simple_insight: Ignoring wise counsel can carry you straight into ruin.
ramayan::44.detailed_meaning: Maricha has already warned Ravana against provoking Rama. Ravana refuses to listen and goes with Maricha toward the hermitage, setting in motion the abduction of Sita. The verse is a bridge, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::44.modern_relevance: You hear the warning in the room, but your pride keeps moving. By the time the damage is visible, the choice was made earlier.
ramayan::44.insight: It shows how a mind bent on desire keeps walking past clear warning.

ramayan::45.verse_sanskrit: तेन मायाविना दूरमपवाह्य नृपात्मजौ । । 1152 । । जहार भार्यां रामस्य गृध्रं हत्वा जटायुषम् ।
ramayan::45.verse_hindi: He with the help of deceitful Maricha drew the princes (Rama and Lakshmana) far away from their hermitage abducted Sita the wife of Rama and  slaughtered vulture Jatayu,
ramayan::45.english_translation: Using the deceitful Maricha, he drew the two princes far away, abducted Rama's wife, and killed Jatayu the vulture.
ramayan::45.translation_literal: तेन (by that one) / मायाविना (by the deceitful one) / दूरम् (far away) / अपवाह्य (having drawn away) / नृपात्मजौ (the two princes) / जहार (abducted) / भार्याम् (the wife) / रामस्य (of Rama) / गृध्रम् (the vulture) / हत्वा (having killed) / जटायुषम् (Jatayu)
ramayan::45.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::45.essence: Deceit creates the opening that violence needs.
ramayan::45.simple_meaning: Ravana used deception to lure Rama and Lakshmana away, then seized Sita and killed Jatayu.
ramayan::45.simple_insight: A single act of deceit can unravel an entire life in moments.
ramayan::45.detailed_meaning: After Maricha has lured Rama and Lakshmana away, Ravana seizes the opening he came for. He abducts Sita from the hermitage and kills Jatayu, the bird who tries to resist. The verse is a grim link in the chain leading to Rama's grief.
ramayan::45.modern_relevance: Someone distracts you with a fake emergency, and while your attention is elsewhere, the real damage is done. The harm often begins with misdirection.
ramayan::45.insight: It shows how deception works best when it splits attention and strikes at the unguarded moment.

ramayan::46.verse_sanskrit: गृध्रं च निहतं दृष्ट्वा हृतां श्रुत्वा च मैथिलीम् । । 1153 । । राघवश्शोकसन्तप्तो विललापाकुलेन्द्रिय: ।
ramayan::46.verse_hindi: Having seen and heard from the eagle Jatayu struck down by Ravana that Sita had been abducted Rama bewailed, choked with tears his senses dulled by distress.
ramayan::46.english_translation: Having seen Jatayu slain and hearing that Sita had been carried off, Rama, overwhelmed with grief, wept aloud with his senses clouded by anguish.
ramayan::46.translation_literal: गृध्रम् (the eagle) / च (and) / निहतम् (killed) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / हृताम् (abducted) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / च (and) / मैथिलीम् (Maithili, Sita) / राघवः (Raghava, Rama) / शोकसन्तप्तः (burned by grief) / विललाप (lamented) / आकुलेन्द्रियः (with senses agitated)
ramayan::46.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::46.essence: Loss strikes first as grief, before it becomes a search.
ramayan::46.simple_meaning: Rama sees that Jatayu is dead and learns that Sita has been taken. Grief overwhelms him, and he breaks into lamentation.
ramayan::46.simple_insight: Some losses hit so hard that even the strongest person is briefly undone.
ramayan::46.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana return to find the forest emptied of Sita’s presence. Jatayu lies slain after trying to save her. The news lands all at once: she is gone, and the one who resisted was killed. This verse captures Rama’s first wave of collapse before action returns.
ramayan::46.modern_relevance: You open a message and realise something precious is gone, and someone else paid the price trying to protect it. For a moment, your body knows before your mind can.
ramayan::46.insight: It shows that grief can suspend action before duty resumes.

ramayan::47.verse_sanskrit: ततस्तेनैव शोकेन गृध्रं दग्ध्वा जटायुषम् । । 1154 । । मार्गमाणो वने सीतां राक्षसं सन्ददर्श ह । कबन्धन्नाम रूपेण विकृतं घोरदर्शनम् । । 1155 । ।
ramayan::47.verse_hindi: Then he performed in the midst of tears the funeral rites of the vulture Jatayu. Wandering in search of Sita, he beheld a rakshasa named Kabandha who was dreadful, in deformed in appearance.
ramayan::47.english_translation: Then, still grieving, he performed the funeral rites for Jatayu. Searching for Sita in the forest, he saw a terrible rakshasa named Kabandha, deformed in form.
ramayan::47.translation_literal: ततः (then) / तेनैव (by that very) / शोकेन (with grief) / गृध्रम् (the vulture) / दग्ध्वा (having burned) / जटायुषम् (Jatayu) / मार्गमाणः (searching) / वने (in the forest) / सीताम् (Sita) / राक्षसम् (a rakshasa) / सन्ददर्श (saw) / ह (indeed) / कबन्धम् (Kabandha) / नाम (named) / रूपेण (by form) / विकृतम् (deformed) / घोरदर्शनम् (terrifying to behold)
ramayan::47.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::47.essence: Even in grief, Rama keeps the duty of action alive.
ramayan::47.simple_meaning: Rama honors Jatayu with funeral rites, then keeps searching for Sita and comes upon the monstrous Kabandha.
ramayan::47.simple_insight: Grief does not stop him. He buries the fallen and keeps moving.
ramayan::47.detailed_meaning: After hearing of Sita’s abduction and seeing Jatayu dead, Rama gives the bird funeral rites even while drowning in sorrow. He does not collapse into grief; he turns back into the search and, in that same forest, encounters Kabandha.
ramayan::47.modern_relevance: You get bad news, do the hard thing, and still have to keep moving. First you tend the loss; then you face what comes next.
ramayan::47.insight: It shows grief without paralysis: honour the loss, then continue the search.

ramayan::48.verse_sanskrit: तं निहत्य महाबाहुर्ददाह स्वर्गतश्च स: । स चास्य कथयामास शबरीं धर्मचारिणीम् । । 1156 । । श्रमणीं धर्मनिपुणामभिगच्छेति राघव । 1151
ramayan::48.verse_hindi: Mightyarmed Rama, having killed Kabandha, consigned his body to flames. While leaving for heavens he informed him saying, O Raghava, there is a female ascetic in Sabara community, performing religious duties and proficient in practising austerities. You may visit her.
ramayan::48.english_translation: Mighty-armed Rama, having killed Kabandha, consigned his body to flames. While leaving for the higher realm, Kabandha told Raghava: "Visit the ascetic woman Sabari, who is skilled in dharma and austerity."
ramayan::48.translation_literal: तम् (him) / निहत्य (having killed) / महाबाहुः (mighty-armed one) / ददाह (burned) / स्वर्गतः (gone to the higher realm) / च (and) / सः (he) / सः (he) / च (and) / अस्य (to him) / कथयामास (told) / शबरीम् (Sabari) / धर्मचारिणीम् (the one who practices dharma) / श्रमणीम् (female ascetic) / धर्मनिपुणाम् (skilled in dharma) / अभिगच्छेति (go and meet) / राघव (O Raghava)
ramayan::48.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::48.essence: A defeated figure becomes the guide to the next meeting.
ramayan::48.simple_meaning: Rama burns Kabandha’s body after killing him. Kabandha, before departing, directs Rama to meet Sabari, a devoted ascetic.
ramayan::48.simple_insight: Even in the middle of loss and battle, the path forward appears through a wise, humble guide.
ramayan::48.detailed_meaning: After Jatayu’s death and Sita’s abduction, Rama is still moving through grief and search. He kills Kabandha, gives him funeral rites, and receives the clue that will lead him to Sabari. The verse keeps the story moving, not the teaching.
ramayan::48.modern_relevance: You are still processing one painful event when the next clue arrives. Sometimes the way forward comes from a stranger who appears only after the worst moment.
ramayan::48.insight: It shifts attention from reflection to the next necessary step in the search.

ramayan::49.verse_hindi: Rama son of Dasaratha, destroyer of enemies and possessing great splendour approached Sabari who duly worshipped him৷৷
ramayan::49.english_translation: Rama, son of Dasharatha, destroyer of enemies and of great splendour, approached Sabari, who honoured him properly.
ramayan::49.translation_literal: सः (he) / अभ्यगच्छत् (approached) / महातेजाः (great splendour) / शबरीम् (Sabari) / शत्रुसूदनः (destroyer of enemies) / शबर्या (by Sabari) / पूजितः (honoured, worshipped) / सम्यक् (properly) / रामः (Rama) / दशरथात्मजः (son of Dasharatha)
ramayan::49.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::49.essence: A reverent welcome turns a search into a meeting.
ramayan::49.simple_meaning: Rama went to meet Sabari after she had welcomed him with reverence.
ramayan::49.simple_insight: Respect opens the way to meeting what you are searching for.
ramayan::49.detailed_meaning: After Jatayu’s death and Kabandha’s fall, Rama’s search leads him deeper into the forest. He now reaches Sabari, the devoted ascetic who has prepared for his arrival. The moment is a quiet pause before the next alliance forms.
ramayan::49.modern_relevance: You finally arrive at the house of someone who has been waiting for you all day, and their welcome changes the whole mood of the visit.
ramayan::49.insight: It shows that devotion can create a meeting long before words are spoken.

ramayan::50.verse_sanskrit: पम्पातीरे हनुमता सङ्गतो वानरेण ह । । 1158 । । हनुमद्वचनाच्चैव सुग्रीवेण समागत: ।
ramayan::50.verse_hindi: On the bank of Pampa he met a monkey named Hanuman on whose advice he made friendship with Sugriva.
ramayan::50.english_translation: On the bank of Pampa, he met Hanuman, the monkey, and through Hanuman's counsel he came to meet Sugriva.
ramayan::50.translation_literal: पम्पातीरे (on the bank of Pampa) / हनुमता (with Hanuman) / सङ्गतः (met together) / वानरेण (with the monkey) / ह (indeed) / हनुमद्वचनात् (from Hanuman's words) / च एव (and indeed) / सुग्रीवेण (with Sugriva) / समागतः (came together / met)
ramayan::50.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::50.essence: A single meeting opens the path to alliance.
ramayan::50.simple_meaning: Rama meets Hanuman on the bank of Pampa, and Hanuman's guidance leads him to Sugriva.
ramayan::50.simple_insight: Right help can arrive as a meeting, not a miracle.
ramayan::50.detailed_meaning: After Sabari's blessing, Rama reaches Pampa and meets Hanuman. That meeting becomes the bridge to Sugriva, the ally he needs to continue the search for Sita. The verse is a linking step, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::50.modern_relevance: You are standing at the edge of a new phase, and one conversation changes everything. The right person does not solve the whole problem — they connect you to the next needed step.
ramayan::50.insight: It shows how progress often depends on a timely meeting and a trusted introduction.

ramayan::51.verse_sanskrit: सुग्रीवाय च तत्सर्वं शंसद्रामो महाबल: । । 1159 । । आदितस्तद्यथावृत्तं सीतायाश्च विशेषत: ।
ramayan::51.verse_hindi: Mighty  Rama related to Sugriva all that had happened right from the beginning, more importantly Sitas abduction and also to Hanuman.
ramayan::51.english_translation: Mighty Rama related to Sugriva all that had happened from the beginning, especially Sita's abduction.
ramayan::51.translation_literal: सुग्रीवाय (to Sugriva) / च (and) / तत्सर्वं (all that) / शंसत् (related, told) / रामः (Rama) / महाबलः (mighty) / आदितः (from the beginning) / तद् (that) / यथावृत्तं (as it happened) / सीतायाः (of Sita) / च (and) / विशेषत: (especially)
ramayan::51.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::51.essence: Shared purpose begins when the whole wound is spoken aloud.
ramayan::51.simple_meaning: Rama tells Sugriva the full story, beginning at the start and focusing on Sita's abduction.
ramayan::51.simple_insight: Trust grows when the whole truth is spoken plainly.
ramayan::51.detailed_meaning: After meeting Hanuman and coming into Sugriva's circle, Rama gives a full account of events, especially Sita's abduction. This is not a teaching verse but a bridge: it prepares the alliance that will follow.
ramayan::51.modern_relevance: You finally sit down with someone who can help, and you tell the whole story from the beginning. The breakthrough starts when nothing important is left out.
ramayan::51.insight: It shows that alliance begins with honest disclosure, not half-truths.

ramayan::52.verse_sanskrit: सुग्रीवश्चापि तत्सर्वं श्रुत्वा रामस्य वानर: । । 1160 । । चकार सख्यं रामेण प्रीतश्चैवाग्निसाक्षिकम् ।
ramayan::52.verse_hindi: Hearing everything that story from Rama, Sugriva was very pleased and made a pact with Rama in the presence of Agni as witness.
ramayan::52.english_translation: Hearing everything from Rama, Sugriva was pleased and made a pact with Rama in the presence of Agni as witness.
ramayan::52.translation_literal: सुग्रीवः (Sugriva) / च (and) / अपि (also) / तत् सर्वम् (all that) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / रामस्य (of Rama) / वानरः (the monkey king) / चकार (made) / सख्यम् (friendship/pact) / रामेण (with Rama) / प्रीतः (pleased) / च एव (and indeed) / अग्नि-साक्षिकम् (with Agni as witness)
ramayan::52.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::52.essence: Trust becomes real when sympathy turns into a witnessed promise.
ramayan::52.simple_meaning: Sugriva hears Rama's account, feels pleased, and seals their friendship with a formal pact before Agni.
ramayan::52.simple_insight: Trust becomes solid when it is openly chosen, not just privately felt.
ramayan::52.detailed_meaning: After Rama tells Sugriva everything, including Sita's abduction, the monkey king responds not with hesitation but with commitment. Their friendship is sealed before Agni, turning sympathy into alliance at the exact moment both men need each other.
ramayan::52.modern_relevance: You finally tell someone the full story — the part you usually hide. They hear it, believe you, and the relationship changes shape in that moment.
ramayan::52.insight: It shifts trust from emotion to commitment, showing that a bond deepens when it is formally chosen.

ramayan::53.verse_sanskrit: ततो वानरराजेन वैरानुकथनं प्रति । । 1161 । । रामायावेदितं सर्वं प्रणयाद्दु:खितेन च ।
ramayan::53.verse_hindi: Thereafter Sugriva, king of monkeys filled with sorrow narrated to Rama out of friendship the entire account of his hostilities (with Vali).
ramayan::53.english_translation: Thereafter Sugriva, the king of monkeys, sorrowful and out of friendship, related to Rama the whole account of his enmity.
ramayan::53.translation_literal: ततः (thereafter) / वानर-राजेन (by the monkey-king) / वैर-अनुकथनं (the recounting of enmity) / प्रति (regarding) / रामाय (to Rama) / आवेदितं (was told) / सर्वं (everything) / प्रणयात् (out of friendship) / दुःखितेन (by the sorrowful one) / च (and)
ramayan::53.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::53.essence: Friendship deepens when grief is spoken plainly.
ramayan::53.simple_meaning: Sugriva, still hurt by his own past, tells Rama everything about the conflict that drove him into exile.
ramayan::53.simple_insight: Trust begins with telling the whole story, even the painful parts.
ramayan::53.detailed_meaning: After Rama has explained Sita’s abduction, Sugriva responds with his own wound. He speaks as a friend, but also as a man carrying grief and grievance against Vali. This is the moment alliance becomes personal truth.
ramayan::53.modern_relevance: You finally sit down with someone you trust and tell the part you usually skip — the betrayal, the shame, the old anger. That honesty is how real alliance begins.
ramayan::53.insight: It shifts connection from formal agreement to truthful sharing.

ramayan::54.verse_sanskrit: प्रतिज्ञातं च रामेण तदा वालिवधं प्रति । । 1162 । । वालिनश्च बलं तत्र कथयामास वानर: ।
ramayan::54.verse_hindi: Then Rama vowed to slay Vali. The monkey (Sugriva) described about Valis prowess to Rama.
ramayan::54.english_translation: Then Rama vowed to kill Vali, and Sugriva described Vali's strength to him.
ramayan::54.translation_literal: प्रतिज्ञातं (vowed) / च (and) / रामेण (by Rama) / तदा (then) / वालिवधं (the killing of Vali) / प्रति (regarding) / वालिनः (of Vali) / च (and) / बलं (strength) / तत्र (there) / कथयामास (described) / वानरः (the monkey)
ramayan::54.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::54.essence: Rama commits before the danger is fully measured.
ramayan::54.simple_meaning: Rama makes a vow to kill Vali, and Sugriva explains how strong Vali is.
ramayan::54.simple_insight: A promise is made, but the danger is still real.
ramayan::54.detailed_meaning: After Sugriva tells Rama the full story of his suffering, Rama commits himself to killing Vali. Sugriva then answers with a sober account of Vali's strength, reminding Rama that this is no small task.
ramayan::54.modern_relevance: You agree to help someone, then hear how hard the problem really is. The promise stands, but now the cost is clear.
ramayan::54.insight: It shifts commitment from sympathy to a concrete vow backed by full knowledge of the risk.

ramayan::55.verse_sanskrit: सुग्रीवश्शङ्कितश्चासीन्नित्यं वीर्येण राघवे । । 1163 । । राघवप्रत्ययार्थं तु दुन्दुभे: कायमुत्तमम् । दर्शयामास सुग्रीवो महापर्वतसन्निभम् । । 1164 । ।
ramayan::55.verse_hindi: Doubtful of the prowess Sugriva of Rama Sugriva inorder to get convinced showed him the huge (dead) body of Dundubhi resembling a big mountain.
ramayan::55.english_translation: Sugriva, still doubtful of Rama's strength, showed Rama the huge body of Dundubhi, which looked like a great mountain, to convince him.
ramayan::55.translation_literal: सुग्रीवः (Sugriva) / शङ्कितः (doubtful) / च (and) / आसीत् (was) / नित्यम् (always) / वीर्येण (by strength) / राघवे (in Rama) / राघव-प्रत्यय-अर्थम् (for the sake of convincing Rama) / तु (indeed) / दुन्दुभेः (of Dundubhi) / कायम् (body) / उत्तमम् (huge/excellent) / दर्शयामास (showed) / सुग्रीवः (Sugriva) / महा-पर्वत-सन्निभम् (resembling a great mountain)
ramayan::55.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::55.essence: Trust is earned here by proof, not assertion.
ramayan::55.simple_meaning: Sugriva still isn't sure of Rama's strength, so he shows Rama Dundubhi's enormous body as proof.
ramayan::55.simple_insight: Doubt asks for evidence before trust can open.
ramayan::55.detailed_meaning: After promising to kill Vali, Rama is still only a claim to Sugriva. To win his confidence, Sugriva points to Dundubhi's massive corpse like a mountain, using visible proof to test whether Rama truly has the strength he claims.
ramayan::55.modern_relevance: You say you can handle it, but the other person still needs proof. In hard moments, trust often begins with something visible and undeniable.
ramayan::55.insight: It shows how trust can be built through clear evidence, not just promises.

ramayan::56.verse_sanskrit: उत्स्मयित्वा महाबाहु: प्रेक्ष्य चास्थि महाबल: । पादाङ्गुष्ठेन चिक्षेप सम्पूर्णं दशयोजनम् । । 1165 । ।
ramayan::56.verse_hindi: The strongarmed Rama, who was endowed with great strength looked at the skeleton and smiled within himself for a while. He kicked off the skeleton with the great toe of his foot completely to a full distance of ten yojanas (eighty miles).
ramayan::56.english_translation: The strong-armed Rama looked at the skeleton and smiled, then kicked it away with the big toe of his foot for a full ten yojanas.
ramayan::56.translation_literal: उत्स्मयित्वा (having smiled) / महाबाहु: (the strong-armed one) / प्रेक्ष्य (having looked at) / च (and) / अस्थि (the skeleton) / महाबल: (the very strong one) / पादाङ्गुष्ठेन (with the big toe of the foot) / चिक्षेप (threw/kicked) / सम्पूर्णं (completely) / दशयोजनम् (ten yojanas)
ramayan::56.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::56.essence: Power needs no announcement; one effortless act settles doubt.
ramayan::56.simple_meaning: Rama casually proves his strength by kicking a giant skeleton ten yojanas away with his big toe.
ramayan::56.simple_insight: Real confidence does not need to boast; it shows itself in one effortless act.
ramayan::56.detailed_meaning: Sugriva is still testing Rama before trusting him with the alliance. To prove his power, Rama looks at Dundubhi's huge remains, smiles, and sends them flying with a toe. It is a display, not a teaching.
ramayan::56.modern_relevance: A room goes quiet while everyone waits to see whether you can really handle the task. You answer once, cleanly, and the doubt disappears.
ramayan::56.insight: It shows strength through effortless action, not through explanation or self-praise.

ramayan::57.verse_sanskrit: बिभेद च पुनस्सालान्सप्तैकेन महेषुणा । गिरिं रसातलं चैव जनयन्प्रत्ययं तथा । । 1166 । ।
ramayan::57.verse_hindi: Again inorder to create confidence (in Sugriva), he released a single mighty shaft which penetrated seven palmyra trees, a mountain and the Rasatala.
ramayan::57.english_translation: Again, to create confidence in Sugriva, he released a single mighty shaft that pierced seven palmyra trees, a mountain, and the lower depths of the earth.
ramayan::57.translation_literal: बिभेद (pierced) / च (and) / पुनः (again) / सालान् (palmyra trees) / सप्त (seven) / एकेन (with one) / महेषुणा (mighty shaft) / गिरिम् (mountain) / रसातलम् (lower depths) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / जनयन् (creating) / प्रत्ययम् (confidence) / तथा (thus)
ramayan::57.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::57.essence: One impossible shot turns hesitation into trust.
ramayan::57.simple_meaning: Rama fired one arrow that cut through seven palmyra trees, a mountain, and the lower depths of the earth to prove his power to Sugriva.
ramayan::57.simple_insight: Sometimes trust is built by unmistakable proof, not promises.
ramayan::57.detailed_meaning: Sugriva still doubts Rama’s strength. To remove that doubt, Rama shows his power in a single impossible shot: one arrow passes through seven palmyra trees, a mountain, and the lower depths. This is not the climax, but the proof that seals their alliance.
ramayan::57.modern_relevance: You can talk about your capability all day. The moment that matters is when your work makes someone stop doubting you.
ramayan::57.insight: It shifts trust from explanation to demonstration.

ramayan::58.verse_sanskrit: तत: प्रीतमनास्तेन विश्वस्तस्स महाकपि: । किष्किन्धां रामसहितो जगाम च गुहां तदा । । 1167 । ।
ramayan::58.verse_hindi: Pleased with Ramas action and convinced of his prowess he left thereafter with Rama he left for Kishkindha which was like a cave.
ramayan::58.english_translation: Pleased by Rama's display and now convinced of his strength, the great monkey set out with Rama for Kishkindha, which looked like a cave.
ramayan::58.translation_literal: तत: (then) / प्रीतमनाः (pleased in mind) / तेन (by that) / विश्वस्तः (confident, reassured) / सः (that) / महाकपिः (great monkey) / किष्किन्धाम् (to Kishkindha) / रामसहितः (together with Rama) / जगाम (went) / च (and) / गुहाम् (cave) / तदा (then)
ramayan::58.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::58.essence: Trust grows when strength becomes visible.
ramayan::58.simple_meaning: Sugriva feels reassured by Rama's strength and goes with him toward Kishkindha.
ramayan::58.simple_insight: Trust can begin with proof, not promises.
ramayan::58.detailed_meaning: After Rama proves his strength by hurling the skeleton and splitting the trees, Sugriva finally believes him. The fearful exile-king stops hesitating and walks with Rama toward Kishkindha, ready to act on the alliance.
ramayan::58.modern_relevance: You only followed after seeing real proof. One clear demonstration can end weeks of doubt.
ramayan::58.insight: It shows how confidence turns into movement once fear is replaced by evidence.

ramayan::59.verse_sanskrit: ततोऽगर्जद्धरिवर: सुग्रीवो हेमपिङ्गल: । तेन नादेन महता निर्जगाम हरीश्वर: । । 1168 । ।
ramayan::59.verse_hindi: On entering the city of Kishkindha, Sugriva the best of monkeys of reddish yellow hue roared with a great voice. There upon Vali, the lord of monkeys came out (of the cave).
ramayan::59.english_translation: Sugriva, the best of monkeys, with a golden-yellow body, then roared. At that great sound, Vali, lord of the monkeys, came out.
ramayan::59.translation_literal: तत: (then) / अगर्जत् (roared) / हरिवर: (best of monkeys) / सुग्रीवो (Sugriva) / हेमपिङ्गल: (golden-yellow) / तेन (by that) / नादेन (sound) / महता (great) / निर्जगाम (came out) / हरीश्वर: (lord of monkeys)
ramayan::59.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::59.essence: A single roar brings the hidden rival into the open.
ramayan::59.simple_meaning: Sugriva let out a huge roar to draw Vali out of the cave, and Vali emerged in response.
ramayan::59.simple_insight: The moment is tactical, not teaching: a shout pulls the hidden opponent into the open.
ramayan::59.detailed_meaning: Rama has already proved his strength to Sugriva. Now, at the mouth of Kishkindha, Sugriva roars to summon Vali from the cave. The verse only moves the action forward; the real turning point comes in the next line.
ramayan::59.modern_relevance: You call out from the edge of a hard conversation, hoping the other person finally steps forward. The real confrontation has not started yet.
ramayan::59.insight: It advances the scene by showing the bait worked and the hidden rival surfaced.

ramayan::60.verse_sanskrit: अनुमान्य तदा तारां सुग्रीवेण समागत: । निजघान च तत्रैनं शरेणैकेन राघव: । । 1169 । ।
ramayan::60.verse_hindi: After convincing his wife Tara, who was dissuading from this, Vali entered into a combat with Sugriva. There, Rama killed Vali with a single shaft.
ramayan::60.english_translation: After convincing his wife Tara, who was dissuading him, Vali entered combat with Sugriva. There, Rama killed Vali with a single shaft.
ramayan::60.translation_literal: अनुमान्य (having persuaded) / तदा (then) / तारां (Tara) / सुग्रीवेण (with Sugriva) / समागतः (having met in combat) / निजघान (struck down) / च (and) / तत्र (there) / एनं (him) / शरेण (with an arrow) / एकेन (one) / राघवः (Raghava/Rama)
ramayan::60.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::60.essence: One arrow changes the fate of a kingdom.
ramayan::60.simple_meaning: Rama shot Vali with one arrow while Vali was fighting Sugriva.
ramayan::60.simple_insight: A single decisive act can end a conflict that words could not.
ramayan::60.detailed_meaning: Vali has entered battle with Sugriva after Tara's warning. In that charged moment, Rama intervenes from the side of Sugriva and kills Vali with one arrow. The verse is a turning point in the Kishkindha alliance, not a teaching by itself.
ramayan::60.modern_relevance: You watch a conflict finally tip after weeks of buildup. One clear decision ends what endless arguing could not.
ramayan::60.insight: It shifts attention from the duel itself to the irreversible consequence of intervention.

ramayan::61.verse_sanskrit: ततस्सुग्रीववचनाद्धत्वा वालिनमाहवे । सुग्रीवमेव तद्राज्ये राघव: प्रत्यपादयत् । । 1170 । ।
ramayan::61.verse_hindi: After he killed Vali in the combat in compliance with the words of Sugriva, Rama installed Sugriva as  king.
ramayan::61.english_translation: After he killed Vali in the combat in compliance with the words of Sugriva, Rama installed Sugriva as king.
ramayan::61.translation_literal: ततस् (then) / सुग्रीव-वचनात् (from Sugriva's words) / हत्वा (having killed) / वालिनम् (Valin) / आहवे (in battle) / सुग्रीवम् एव (Sugriva himself) / तद्-राज्ये (in that kingdom) / राघवः (Rama) / प्रत्यपादयत् (installed, restored)
ramayan::61.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::61.essence: Victory is incomplete until you restore what was promised.
ramayan::61.simple_meaning: Rama kept his promise to Sugriva: he defeated Vali and placed Sugriva on the throne.
ramayan::61.simple_insight: A promise matters most when keeping it costs you something.
ramayan::61.detailed_meaning: Vali has fallen, and the alliance that began in need now turns into kingship. Rama does not stop at victory; he restores the rightful throne to Sugriva, completing the bargain that made the war possible.
ramayan::61.modern_relevance: You backed someone when they had nothing and promised you would stand by them. The real test comes after the crisis, when you still have power and could quietly walk away.
ramayan::61.insight: It shifts duty from winning a fight to completing responsibility after the fight.

ramayan::62.verse_sanskrit: स च सर्वान्समानीय वानरान्वानरर्षभ: । दिश: प्रस्थापयामास दिदृक्षुर्जनकात्मजाम् । । 1171 । ।
ramayan::62.verse_hindi: The best of monkeys (Sugriva) gathered his monkey forces and despatched them in various directions in search of Janakas daughter (Sita).
ramayan::62.english_translation: Sugriva gathered all the monkeys and sent them in every direction, eager to see Janaka's daughter Sita.
ramayan::62.translation_literal: स (he) / च (and) / सर्वान् (all) / समानीय (having gathered) / वानरान् (the monkeys) / वानरर्षभः (the best of monkeys) / दिशः (directions) / प्रस्थापयामास (sent forth) / दिदृक्षुः (wishing to see) / जनकात्मजाम् (Janaka's daughter)
ramayan::62.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::62.essence: Urgency turns scattered strength into a search.
ramayan::62.simple_meaning: Sugriva gathers the monkey army and sends search parties in every direction to find Sita.
ramayan::62.simple_insight: When the goal is urgent, everyone moves with one purpose.
ramayan::62.detailed_meaning: After Vali's death and Sugriva's restoration, the search for Sita begins in earnest. Sugriva gathers the monkey leaders and sends them out in all directions. This is the moment the rescue becomes an organised mission.
ramayan::62.modern_relevance: A missing phone, a lost child, a vanished contact, and suddenly every friend is searching at once. This verse carries that feeling of urgent, coordinated effort.
ramayan::62.insight: It shifts attention from grief to organised action.

ramayan::63.verse_sanskrit: ततो गृध्रस्य वचनात्सम्पातेर्हनुमान्बली । शतयोजनविस्तीर्णं पुप्लुवे लवणार्णवम् । । 1172 । ।
ramayan::63.verse_hindi: At the suggestion of the vulture, Sampathi mighty Hanuman leapt over the saltocean extending over a hundred yojanas.
ramayan::63.english_translation: At the suggestion of the vulture, Sampati, mighty Hanuman leapt over the salt ocean extending over a hundred yojanas.
ramayan::63.translation_literal: ततः (then) / गृध्रस्य (of the vulture) / वचनात् (from the word) / सम्पातेः (of Sampati) / हनुमान् (Hanuman) / बली (mighty) / शतयोजनविस्तीर्णम् (spreading a hundred yojanas wide) / पुप्लुवे (leapt across) / लवणार्णवम् (the salt ocean)
ramayan::63.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::63.essence: Certainty turns a vast obstacle into one leap.
ramayan::63.simple_meaning: Hanuman, guided by Sampati's advice, crossed the vast ocean in one leap.
ramayan::63.simple_insight: A single clear direction can unlock what once felt impossible.
ramayan::63.detailed_meaning: After Sugriva sends the search parties out, Hanuman reaches the edge of the sea. Sampati's guidance gives him the final certainty he needs, and he launches himself across the hundred-yojana expanse toward Lanka.
ramayan::63.modern_relevance: You have the plan, but not the courage to start. Then one trusted voice says, 'Go now,' and the impossible becomes a single move.
ramayan::63.insight: It shifts hesitation into decisive action by showing that the right counsel can turn fear into motion.

ramayan::64.verse_sanskrit: तत्र लङ्कां समासाद्य पुरीं रावणपालिताम् । ददर्श सीतां ध्यायन्तीमशोकवनिकां गताम् । । 1173 । ।
ramayan::64.verse_hindi: Hanuman arrived at the city of Lanka ruled by Ravana and found Sita in the Ashoka garden meditating on Rama.
ramayan::64.english_translation: Hanuman arrived at the city of Lanka ruled by Ravana and found Sita in the Ashoka garden meditating on Rama.
ramayan::64.translation_literal: तत्र (there) / लङ्काम् (to Lanka) / समासाद्य (having reached) / पुरीम् (the city) / रावणपालिताम् (ruled by Ravana) / ददर्श (he saw) / सीताम् (Sita) / ध्यायन्तीम् (meditating) / अशोकवनिकाम् (the Ashoka grove) / गताम् (gone to)
ramayan::64.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::64.essence: After the hardest crossing, he found her still holding on.
ramayan::64.simple_meaning: Hanuman reaches Lanka and sees Sita sitting in the Ashoka grove, absorbed in thoughts of Rama.
ramayan::64.simple_insight: The search ends in a single sighting, and hope becomes real.
ramayan::64.detailed_meaning: Hanuman has crossed the ocean and entered Ravana's city alone. In the Ashoka grove, he finally sees Sita, not broken, but inwardly fixed on Rama. This is the moment the search turns into proof.
ramayan::64.modern_relevance: You keep looking through one more message, one more room, one more night. Then you finally see the person you were searching for, still holding on.
ramayan::64.insight: It turns searching into witnessing: the mission becomes real when the seeker sees the one sought.

ramayan::65.verse_sanskrit: निवेदयित्वाऽऽभिज्ञानं प्रवृत्तिं च निवेद्य च । समाश्वास्य च वैदेहीं मर्दयामास तोरणम् । । 1174 । ।
ramayan::65.verse_hindi: Hanuman delivered Ramas ring to Sita as a token of recognition, related the whole story and consoled her. He then crushed the arch (of the outer gate of the garden) before leaving.
ramayan::65.english_translation: Hanuman delivered Rama's token of recognition, told Sita the whole story, consoled her, and then smashed the archway before leaving.
ramayan::65.translation_literal: निवेदयित्वा (having delivered) / अभिज्ञानम् (the token of recognition) / प्रवृत्तिम् (the news, account) / च (and) / निवेद्य (having reported) / च (and) / समाश्वास्य (having consoled) / च (and) / वैदेहीम् (Sita, daughter of Videha) / मर्दयामास (crushed, smashed) / तोरणम् (the archway, gate)
ramayan::65.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::65.essence: Proof, comfort, and force arrive together.
ramayan::65.simple_meaning: Hanuman shows Sita Rama's sign, gives her the news, comforts her, and breaks the garden gate as he leaves.
ramayan::65.simple_insight: A messenger can carry comfort and force in the same breath.
ramayan::65.detailed_meaning: Hanuman has found Sita in Lanka's Ashoka garden. Before he leaves, he gives her Rama's ring, tells her what has happened, and steadies her heart. Then he smashes the gate, turning a quiet meeting into the opening of conflict.
ramayan::65.modern_relevance: You finally send the message that proves you're telling the truth, then you stay long enough to calm the other person before walking away changed.
ramayan::65.insight: It shows how reassurance and decisive action can belong to the same moment.

ramayan::66.verse_sanskrit: पञ्च सेनाग्रगान्हत्वा सप्तमन्त्रिसुतानपि । शूरमक्षं च निष्पिष्य ग्रहणं समुपागमत् । । 1175 । ।
ramayan::66.verse_hindi: After killing five commanders, seven sons of the counsellors, stamping out valiant Akshayakumara, the son of Ravana, Hanuman got himself captured (to be taken as captive).
ramayan::66.english_translation: After killing five commanders, seven sons of the counsellors, and the valiant Akshayakumara, Hanuman allowed himself to be captured.
ramayan::66.translation_literal: पञ्च (five) / सेनाग्रान् (army leaders) / हत्वा (having killed) / सप्त (seven) / मन्त्रि-सुतान् (sons of the counsellors) / अपि (also) / शूरम् (the brave) / अक्षम् (Aksha) / च (and) / निष्पिष्य (having crushed) / ग्रहणम् (capture) / समुपागमत् (came upon)
ramayan::66.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::66.essence: He wins by force, then chooses capture for the larger purpose.
ramayan::66.simple_meaning: Hanuman destroys Ravana’s defenders and then lets himself be taken prisoner.
ramayan::66.simple_insight: Power is not always shown by escaping; sometimes it is shown by choosing the next move.
ramayan::66.detailed_meaning: Inside Lanka, Hanuman has already found Sita and torn through Ravana’s defenders. After killing the guards and Akshayakumara, he does not flee. He allows capture, because the larger mission is still unfolding.
ramayan::66.modern_relevance: You could walk away after proving your point, but you stay long enough to finish what matters.
ramayan::66.insight: It shifts the mind from raw victory to strategic restraint.

ramayan::67.verse_sanskrit: अस्त्रेणोन्मुक्तमात्मानं ज्ञात्वा पैतामहाद्वरात् । मर्षयन्राक्षसान्वीरो यन्त्रिणस्तान्यदृच्छया । । 1176 । । ततो दग्ध्वा पुरीं लङ्कामृते सीतां च मैथिलीम् । रामाय प्रियमाख्यातुं पुनरायान्महाकपि: । । 1177 । ।
ramayan::67.verse_hindi: The heroic Hanuman came to know that he could be released from the entanglements of the weapon granted to him through a boon by Brahma. He allowed himself to be restrained by the rakshasas with the ropes for the sake of achieving his other objective of seeing Ravana. Thereafter, he burnt the whole of Lanka except the place where Sita was and returned to deliver the good news to Rama.
ramayan::67.english_translation: The heroic Hanuman knew he could break free from the Brahma-given weapon. He let the rakshasas bind him for the sake of another aim, then burned Lanka except Sita's place and returned to bring Rama the welcome news.
ramayan::67.translation_literal: अस्त्रेण (by the weapon) / उन्मुक्तम् (released) / आत्मानम् (himself) / ज्ञात्वा (knowing) / पैतामहात् (from Brahma) / वरात् (from the boon) / मर्षयन् (enduring) / राक्षसान् (the rakshasas) / वीरः (the hero) / यन्त्रिणः (those who bound) / तान् (them) / यदृच्छया (of his own accord) / ततः (then) / दग्ध्वा (having burned) / पुरीम् (the city) / लङ्काम् (Lanka) / अमृते (except) / सीताम् (Sita) / च (and) / मैथिलीम् (daughter of Mithila) / रामाय (to Rama) / प्रियम् (pleasant) / आख्यातुम् (to tell) / पुनः (again) / आयात् (returned) / महाकपिः (the great monkey)
ramayan::67.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::67.essence: Constraint does not stop him; it only reveals his focus.
ramayan::67.simple_meaning: Hanuman knows he can escape the weapon, allows himself to be bound, burns Lanka while sparing Sita, and returns to Rama with the news.
ramayan::67.simple_insight: Steady purpose can absorb restraint without losing direction.
ramayan::67.detailed_meaning: In Lanka, Hanuman has already found Sita and destroyed the enemy's confidence. Even when bound, he stays clear-minded, uses the moment to advance his mission, and leaves the city in flames except for Sita's place before returning to Rama.
ramayan::67.modern_relevance: You get cornered in a meeting, blamed for a problem, and still keep your larger aim intact. Not every restraint stops you; some only test whether you can stay clear.
ramayan::67.insight: It teaches you to endure temporary constraint without abandoning the larger mission.

ramayan::68.verse_sanskrit: सोऽधिगम्य महात्मानं कृत्वा रामं प्रदक्षिणम् । न्यवेदयदमेयात्मा दृष्टा सीतेति तत्त्वत: । । 1178 । ।
ramayan::68.verse_hindi: Reaching Rama the great Hanuman gifted with boundless intellect circumambulated him and infact informed him that he had seen Sita.
ramayan::68.english_translation: Reaching Rama, the great Hanuman, endowed with boundless intellect, circumambulated him and reported truthfully that he had seen Sita.
ramayan::68.translation_literal: सोऽधिगम्य (having reached) / महात्मानं (the great one) / कृत्वा (having done) / रामं (Rama) / प्रदक्षिणम् (circumambulation) / न्यवेदयत् (reported) / अमेयात्मा (one of immeasurable mind) / दृष्टा (seen) / सीता (Sita) / इति (thus) / तत्त्वत: (in truth)
ramayan::68.speaker: Hanuman
ramayan::68.essence: The search ends in one clean report: Sita has been found.
ramayan::68.simple_meaning: Hanuman returns to Rama, bows around him, and tells him plainly that he has found Sita.
ramayan::68.simple_insight: Relief arrives through clear reporting, not dramatic flourish.
ramayan::68.detailed_meaning: Hanuman has crossed Lanka, found Sita, and now comes back to Rama after a mission that could have cost him everything. This verse is the delivery of the message, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::68.modern_relevance: You finally get the answer after a long search, and the first thing you do is tell the person who was waiting.
ramayan::68.insight: It shows the value of returning with facts intact, especially after a high-stakes search.

ramayan::69.verse_sanskrit: ततस्सुग्रीवसहितो गत्वा तीरं महोदधे: । समुद्रं क्षोभयामास शरैरादित्यसन्निभै: । । 1179 । ।
ramayan::69.verse_hindi: Thereafter, Rama reached the shore of the ocean together with Sugriva and saw the ocean agitated with shafts burning like the Sun.
ramayan::69.english_translation: Thereafter, Rama reached the shore of the ocean together with Sugriva and shook the sea with arrows blazing like the sun.
ramayan::69.translation_literal: ततस् (thereafter) / सुग्रीवसहितो (together with Sugriva) / गत्वा (having gone) / तीरं (to the shore) / महोदधेः (of the great ocean) / समुद्रं (the ocean) / क्षोभयामास (shook up, agitated) / शरैः (with arrows) / आदित्यसन्निभैः (sun-like)
ramayan::69.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::69.essence: The journey stops being a search and becomes a confrontation.
ramayan::69.simple_meaning: Rama and Sugriva reach the ocean shore and strike the sea with glowing arrows.
ramayan::69.simple_insight: Sometimes the next step begins with force, not hesitation.
ramayan::69.detailed_meaning: Rama and Sugriva stand before the vast ocean on the way to Lanka. After Hanuman's report, the march has reached its next hard limit: the sea itself. Rama lashes it with sun-like arrows, forcing the ocean to respond.
ramayan::69.modern_relevance: You hit a wall after every option has failed, and now the problem is bigger than patience. The moment calls for decisive pressure, not another round of waiting.
ramayan::69.insight: It shifts the mind from passive delay to forceful action when a barrier must answer.

ramayan::70.verse_sanskrit: दर्शयामास चात्मानं समुद्रस्सरितां पति: । समुद्रवचनाच्चैव नलं सेतुमकारयत् । । 1180 । ।
ramayan::70.verse_hindi: Samudra, lord of rivers, (afraid of Ramas anger) and having appeared in his own form, and on his advice got a bridge built with the help of Nala.
ramayan::70.english_translation: The lord of rivers revealed himself, and at his advice Nala built the bridge.
ramayan::70.translation_literal: दर्शयामास (showed/revealed) / च (and) / आत्मानं (himself) / समुद्रः (the ocean) / सरितां (of rivers) / पति: (lord) / समुद्र-वचनात् (from the ocean's words/advice) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / नलं (Nala) / सेतुं (bridge) / अकारयत् (caused to be built)
ramayan::70.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::70.essence: Even resistance can yield when met with the right force.
ramayan::70.simple_meaning: The ocean appears in person and allows a bridge to be built across it.
ramayan::70.simple_insight: What once blocked your way can become part of the crossing.
ramayan::70.detailed_meaning: Rama has already reached the shore with Sugriva and is forcing the ocean to respond. In the pressure of that moment, the ocean reveals itself and Nala is set to build the bridge that will carry the army to Lanka.
ramayan::70.modern_relevance: You hit a wall after weeks of trying, and then the right person finally answers. The obstacle doesn't vanish, but it starts cooperating.
ramayan::70.insight: It shows that force alone is not the whole answer; the crossing also needs response and skill.

ramayan::71.verse_sanskrit: तेन गत्वा पुरीं लङ्कां हत्वा रावणमाहवे । राम: सीतामनुप्राप्य परां व्रीडामुपागमत् । । 1181 । ।
ramayan::71.verse_hindi: Rama entered the city of Lanka by means of that bridge, killed Ravana in the battle
ramayan::71.english_translation: Rama entered the city of Lanka by means of that bridge, killed Ravana in the battle, and then, having regained Sita, fell into deep shame.
ramayan::71.translation_literal: तेन (by that) / गत्वा (having gone) / पुरीं लङ्कां (the city of Lanka) / हत्वा (having killed) / रावणम् (Ravana) / आहवे (in battle) / रामः (Rama) / सीताम् (Sita) / अनुप्राप्य (having regained) / पराम् (deep) / व्रीडाम् (shame) / उपागमत् (came upon)
ramayan::71.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::71.essence: Winning the battle does not erase the shame left behind.
ramayan::71.simple_meaning: Rama crossed into Lanka, defeated Ravana, regained Sita, and was overcome by shame.
ramayan::71.simple_insight: Victory can still feel heavy when what you lost has already changed you.
ramayan::71.detailed_meaning: The bridge is complete, Lanka is breached, and Ravana falls. Yet the victory is not clean triumph. Rama reaches Sita, and the moment that should end the war instead brings a deep, painful shame before the next crisis begins.
ramayan::71.modern_relevance: You finally finish the project, win the case, or make it through the hardest season. Instead of relief, you feel the cost of everything it took to get there.
ramayan::71.insight: It frames success as morally incomplete when the human cost is still unresolved.

ramayan::72.verse_sanskrit: तामुवाच ततो राम: परुषं जनसंसदि । अमृष्यमाणा सा सीता विवेश ज्वलनं सती । । 1182 । ।
ramayan::72.verse_hindi: Rama spoke harsh words about Sita in the assembly. Sita, incapable of enduring such words, entered fire.
ramayan::72.english_translation: Rama spoke harsh words about Sita in the assembly. Sita, unable to bear such words, entered the fire.
ramayan::72.translation_literal: ताम् (her) / उवाच (spoke) / ततः (then) / रामः (Rama) / परुषम् (harsh) / जनसंसदि (in the public assembly) / अमृष्यमाणा (unable to endure) / सा (she) / सीता (Sita) / विवेश (entered) / ज्वलनम् (fire) / सती (as a chaste woman)
ramayan::72.speaker: Rama
ramayan::72.essence: She answered humiliation with a choice no crowd could soften.
ramayan::72.simple_meaning: Rama publicly spoke harshly about Sita, and she responded by entering the fire rather than living under that humiliation.
ramayan::72.simple_insight: There is fierce dignity in refusing to survive public doubt at any cost.
ramayan::72.detailed_meaning: After Ravana’s defeat, Rama stands before the crowd and speaks to Sita in words that wound her honor. Sita does not plead or collapse. She walks into the fire, placing her truth before the whole assembly.
ramayan::72.modern_relevance: You’re accused in front of everyone, and the room goes quiet. In that moment, you decide whether to defend yourself endlessly or stand in the only way that still feels clean.
ramayan::72.insight: It shifts the mind from self-protection to unflinching self-respect under public judgment.

ramayan::73.verse_sanskrit: ततोऽग्निवचनात्सीतां ज्ञात्वा विगतकल्मषाम् । बभौ रामस्सम्प्रहृष्ट: पूजितस्सर्वदैवतै: । । 1183 । ।
ramayan::73.verse_hindi: With the of testimony of the firegod, Rama was exceedingly pleased to know that Sita was sinless. All the gods adored him.
ramayan::73.english_translation: With the firegod's testimony, Rama was greatly pleased to know that Sita was free from stain. All the radiant beings honored him.
ramayan::73.translation_literal: ततः (then) / अग्निवचनात् (from the fire's testimony) / सीताम् (Sita) / ज्ञात्वा (having known) / विगतकल्मषाम् (free from stain) / बभौ (shone) / रामः (Rama) / सम्प्रहृष्टः (greatly pleased) / पूजितः (honored) / सर्वदैवतैः (by all radiant beings)
ramayan::73.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::73.essence: Truth ends the torment of public doubt.
ramayan::73.simple_meaning: The fire's witness clears Sita, and Rama's grief turns to relief. The gods honor the moment because the truth has been publicly restored.
ramayan::73.simple_insight: There is relief when truth is finally seen without distortion.
ramayan::73.detailed_meaning: After Sita steps into fire, the firegod's testimony confirms her purity. Rama, who has been forced into unbearable public doubt, is relieved. The scene restores moral order, and even the divine beings honor what has been vindicated.
ramayan::73.modern_relevance: A false accusation has hung over you for weeks, and then one clear message, one verified fact, changes everything. The relief is not just personal — it is the return of dignity.
ramayan::73.insight: It shifts the mind from suspicion to verified trust, and from private anguish to restored order.

ramayan::74.verse_sanskrit: कर्मणा तेन महता त्रैलोक्यं सचराचरम् । सदेवर्षिगणं तुष्टं राघवस्य महात्मन: । । 1184 । ।
ramayan::74.verse_hindi: All the animate and inanimate beings, gods and sages in the three worlds were very pleased at this noble deed of the great Rama.
ramayan::74.english_translation: All the animate and inanimate beings, gods and sages in the three worlds were very pleased at this noble deed of the great Rama.
ramayan::74.translation_literal: कर्मणा (by the deed) / तेन (by that) / महता (great) / त्रैलोक्यं (the three worlds) / सचराचरम् (with the moving and unmoving) / सदेवर्षिगणं (with the hosts of gods and sages) / तुष्टं (pleased) / राघवस्य (of Rama) / महात्मनः (of the great-souled one)
ramayan::74.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::74.essence: A costly act can calm an entire world.
ramayan::74.simple_meaning: Rama's great act satisfied everyone across the three worlds, from living beings to gods and sages.
ramayan::74.simple_insight: A right action can restore harmony far beyond the moment it was made.
ramayan::74.detailed_meaning: Sita has passed through fire, and Rama has accepted the fire's witness. The tension of the trial breaks at once: the three worlds, from creatures to sages, are satisfied by this act. The verse marks the moral release after a painful public ordeal.
ramayan::74.modern_relevance: You make a hard decision in public, and the room goes quiet. Then the tension lifts because everyone can see you chose what was right, not what was easy.
ramayan::74.insight: It shifts attention from personal vindication to the wider harmony restored by a difficult act.

ramayan::75.verse_sanskrit: अभिषिच्य च लङ्कायां राक्षसेन्द्रं विभीषणम् । कृतकृत्यस्तदा रामो विज्वर: प्रमुमोद ह । । 1185 । ।
ramayan::75.verse_hindi: After coronating the rakshasa chief Vibhishana in the city of Lanka, Rama free from distress, exceedingly rejoiced after having accomplished his objective.
ramayan::75.english_translation: After coronating the rakshasa chief Vibhishana in the city of Lanka, Rama, free from distress, greatly rejoiced after accomplishing his purpose.
ramayan::75.translation_literal: अभिषिच्य (having anointed/crowned) / च (and) / लङ्कायाम् (in Lanka) / राक्षसेन्द्रम् (the chief of the rakshasas) / विभीषणम् (Vibhishana) / कृतकृत्यः (having accomplished what had to be done) / तदा (then) / रामः (Rama) / विज्वरः (free from distress) / प्रमुमोद (rejoiced greatly) / ह (indeed)
ramayan::75.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::75.essence: He rejoices not at victory, but at having done what was required.
ramayan::75.simple_meaning: Rama crowns Vibhishana in Lanka and feels relief and joy after completing the task.
ramayan::75.simple_insight: Doing the right thing can bring relief, not just victory.
ramayan::75.detailed_meaning: After the war in Lanka, Rama installs Vibhishana as king, sealing the restoration of order. The fighting is over, the burden is lifted, and Rama rejoices because the task that dharma required has finally been completed.
ramayan::75.modern_relevance: You finally send the message, make the hard call, and close the loop. The relief comes not from winning, but from doing what had to be done.
ramayan::75.insight: It shifts attention from conquest to rightful completion.

ramayan::76.verse_sanskrit: देवताभ्यो वरं प्राप्य समुत्थाप्य च वानरान् । अयोध्यां प्रस्थितो राम: पुष्पकेण सुहृद्वृत: । । 1186 । ।
ramayan::76.verse_hindi: Having obtained a boon from the devatas (who had come to see him) Rama, revived all monkeys (fallen in the battle) and set out for Ayodhya accompanied by friends in the  pushpaka (aerial car).
ramayan::76.english_translation: Having obtained a boon from the devas who had come to see him, Rama revived all the monkeys and set out for Ayodhya in the Pushpaka, surrounded by friends.
ramayan::76.translation_literal: देवताभ्यो (from the devas) / वरं (a boon) / प्राप्य (having obtained) / समुत्थाप्य (having raised up, revived) / च (and) / वानरान् (the monkeys) / अयोध्यां (to Ayodhya) / प्रस्थितः (set out) / रामः (Rama) / पुष्पकेण (by the Pushpaka) / सुहृद्वृतः (surrounded by friends)
ramayan::76.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::76.essence: He leaves as a victor, but only after restoring those who fell.
ramayan::76.simple_meaning: Rama is ready to leave Lanka. After the devas bless him, he revives the fallen monkeys and travels home with his friends.
ramayan::76.simple_insight: Victory is complete only when you lift others with you.
ramayan::76.detailed_meaning: The war is over, Vibhishana has been crowned, and Rama stands in Lanka no longer as a fighter but as a victor preparing to return. Before leaving, he restores the fallen monkey army and departs for Ayodhya in the Pushpaka with his companions.
ramayan::76.modern_relevance: You finally finish the hardest stretch of a project, but before celebrating, you check on the teammates who were drained by it. Real completion includes everyone who carried the burden.
ramayan::76.insight: It shifts victory from personal triumph to shared restoration.

ramayan::77.verse_sanskrit: भरद्वाजाश्रमं गत्वा रामस्सत्यपराक्रम: । भरतस्यान्तिकं रामो हनूमन्तं व्यसर्जयत् । । 1187 । ।
ramayan::77.verse_hindi: Rama who was a delight of all whose strength lies in truth went to the hermitage of Bharadwaja (as promised) and  despatched Hanuman to Bharata as his messenger.
ramayan::77.english_translation: Rama, whose strength lies in truth, went to Bharadwaja's hermitage and sent Hanuman ahead to Bharata as his messenger.
ramayan::77.translation_literal: भरद्वाजाश्रमं (to Bharadwaja's hermitage) / गत्वा (having gone) / रामः (Rama) / सत्यपराक्रमः (whose valor is truth-based) / भरतस्य (of Bharata) / अन्तिकं (near) / रामः (Rama) / हनूमन्तं (Hanuman) / व्यसर्जयत् (sent forth)
ramayan::77.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::77.essence: Even after victory, Rama still finishes the promise properly.
ramayan::77.simple_meaning: Rama reaches Bharadwaja's hermitage and sends Hanuman to Bharata with a message.
ramayan::77.simple_insight: A promise kept is not just remembered; it is carried all the way through.
ramayan::77.detailed_meaning: After the war ends and Lanka is secured, Rama travels back toward home. At Bharadwaja's hermitage, he pauses and sends Hanuman ahead to Bharata, fulfilling the next step of his return with the same steadiness that carried him through exile and battle.
ramayan::77.modern_relevance: You finally have the chance to go home, but there is still one message to send, one person to reassure, one promise to complete.
ramayan::77.insight: It shifts attention from finishing the big ordeal to completing the final obligation cleanly.

ramayan::78.verse_sanskrit: पुनराख्यायिकां जल्पन्सुग्रीवसहितश्च स: । पुष्पकं तत्समारुह्य नन्दिग्रामं ययौ तदा । । 1188 । ।
ramayan::78.verse_hindi: Again accompanied by Sugriva and recalling earlier incidents and after both of them discussed with each other, Rama departed to Nandigrama riding that pushpaka chariot.
ramayan::78.english_translation: Again, while talking over old events with Sugriva beside him, Rama boarded that Pushpaka chariot and set out for Nandigrama.
ramayan::78.translation_literal: पुनः (again) / आख्यायिकाम् (old story, account) / जल्पन् (speaking) / सुग्रीव-सहितः (together with Sugriva) / सः (he) / पुष्पकम् (the Pushpaka) / तत् (that) / समारुह्य (having mounted) / नन्दिग्रामम् (to Nandigrama) / ययौ (went) / तदा (then)
ramayan::78.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::78.essence: Coming home can begin before you arrive.
ramayan::78.simple_meaning: Rama and Sugriva keep talking about past events as Rama rides the Pushpaka toward Nandigrama.
ramayan::78.simple_insight: Some returns are marked not by triumph, but by quiet conversation after hardship.
ramayan::78.detailed_meaning: After the war, Rama is no longer in battle but in motion toward home. He rides the Pushpaka with Sugriva, speaking of earlier events as they go. This verse is a transition, not the emotional peak.
ramayan::78.modern_relevance: You leave a hard season and keep replaying what happened with the one person who lived it with you. The journey home is already part memory.
ramayan::78.insight: It shifts attention from victory to the long return that follows it.

ramayan::79.verse_sanskrit: नन्दिग्रामे जटां हित्वा भ्रातृभिस्सहितोऽनघ: । रामस्सीतामनुप्राप्य राज्यं पुनरवाप्तवान् । । 1189 । ।
ramayan::79.verse_hindi: At Nandigrama sinless Rama arrived, met his brothers. They shed their  matted locks. With  Sita  restored  he regained his kingdom.
ramayan::79.english_translation: At Nandigrama, sinless Rama met his brothers, cast off his matted locks, and with Sita restored, regained his kingdom.
ramayan::79.translation_literal: नन्दिग्रामे (at Nandigrama) / जटां (matted locks) / हित्वा (having abandoned) / भ्रातृभिस्सहितोऽनघ: (the sinless one, together with his brothers) / रामः (Rama) / सीताम् (Sita) / अनुप्राप्य (having regained) / राज्यं (the kingdom) / पुनरवाप्तवान् (regained again)
ramayan::79.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::79.essence: Exile ends, but only after everything costly has been lived through.
ramayan::79.simple_meaning: Rama returns to Nandigrama, removes the signs of exile, reunites with his brothers, and regains the kingdom with Sita restored.
ramayan::79.simple_insight: The long loss is over, and what was taken from them is finally made whole again.
ramayan::79.detailed_meaning: After the exile and the war, Rama reaches Nandigrama with his brothers. He sheds the matted hair of forest life, Sita is back, and the royal order is restored. The verse marks the end of suffering and the formal return of kingship.
ramayan::79.modern_relevance: You finally come home after a season that changed you. The old marker of struggle comes off, but the cost of the journey still remains in your body.
ramayan::79.insight: It marks the closing of exile and the return from hardship to rightful order.

ramayan::80.verse_sanskrit: प्रहृष्टमुदितो लोकस्तुष्ट: पुष्टस्सुधार्मिक: । निरामयो ह्यरोगश्च दुर्भिक्षभयवर्जित: । । 1190 । ।
ramayan::80.verse_hindi: The entire world rejoiced with happiness with their desire fulfilled they were content.  All people were following the path of righteousness. There was no fear of sufferings or agonies, diseases or famine.
ramayan::80.english_translation: The whole world was joyful and fulfilled; everyone lived by righteousness. There was no illness, fear, famine, or suffering.
ramayan::80.translation_literal: प्रहृष्टमुदित: (filled with joy) / लोक: (the world) / तुष्ट: (content) / पुष्ट: (prosperous) / सुदार्मिक: (very righteous) / निरामय: (free from affliction) / हि (indeed) / अरोग: (free from disease) / च (and) / दुर्भिक्षभयवर्जित: (devoid of fear of famine)
ramayan::80.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::80.essence: Rightful rule makes an entire world breathe easier.
ramayan::80.simple_meaning: Rama's return brings a world at peace: people are happy, prosperous, moral, and free from fear, disease, and famine.
ramayan::80.simple_insight: A just life ripples outward until even ordinary fear begins to disappear.
ramayan::80.detailed_meaning: After Rama returns to Nandigrama, the kingdom begins to feel whole again. Valmiki pauses to show the effect of rightful rule: people are content, healthy, safe, and living in harmony. This is the first sign of Rama's restored reign.
ramayan::80.modern_relevance: A home after months of strain can feel like this: arguments stop, everyone eats properly again, and the air itself seems lighter. Good leadership changes the atmosphere before it changes the headlines.
ramayan::80.insight: It shifts attention from personal victory to the social health that follows right conduct.

ramayan::81.verse_sanskrit: न पुत्रमरणं किञ्चिद्द्रक्ष्यन्ति पुरुषा: क्वचित् । नार्यश्चाविधवा नित्यं भविष्यन्ति पतिव्रता: । । 1191 । ।
ramayan::81.verse_hindi: During the period of Ramas rule, no where  would men witness the death of their sons or women widowed. They would ever remain chaste and devoted to their husbands.
ramayan::81.english_translation: No man would ever see the death of a son, and women would remain ever-widowed. Devoted wives would remain faithful to their husbands.
ramayan::81.translation_literal: न (not) / पुत्र-मरणम् (death of a son) / किञ्चित् (at all) / द्रक्ष्यन्ति (will see) / पुरुषाः (men) / क्वचित् (anywhere) / नार्यः (women) / च (and) / अविधवाः (not widowed) / नित्यम् (always) / भविष्यन्ति (will become) / पतिव्रताः (devoted to their husbands)
ramayan::81.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::81.essence: Good rule is measured by the grief it prevents.
ramayan::81.simple_meaning: Rama's rule was so just and protective that families were safe from the sorrow of losing sons or husbands.
ramayan::81.simple_insight: A life governed well does not just look noble — it keeps ordinary people from unbearable grief.
ramayan::81.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Rama's reign after the return to Ayodhya. The city is at peace, and the blessing of good rule reaches into private homes: fathers do not lose sons, and wives are not left widowed. This is the human measure of Rama's kingship.
ramayan::81.modern_relevance: A neighborhood where children come home safely, elders are cared for, and families are not shattered by preventable harm — that is what good leadership feels like. This verse measures power by the suffering it prevents.
ramayan::81.insight: It shifts the mind from praising authority to asking whether your actions make life safer for others.

ramayan::82.verse_sanskrit: न चाग्निजं भयं किञ्चिन्नाप्सु मज्जन्ति जन्तव: । न वातजं भयं किञ्चिन्नापि ज्वरकृतं तथा । । 1192 । । न चापि क्षुद्भयं तत्र न तस्करभयं तथा ।
ramayan::82.verse_hindi: There (in the kingdom of Rama) was no fear of fire, water, wind, disease, hunger and also theft.
ramayan::82.english_translation: There, in Rama's kingdom, there was no fear of fire, water, wind, disease, hunger, or theft.
