ramayan::82.translation_literal: न (not) / च (also not) / अग्नि-जं (born from fire) / भयम् (fear) / किञ्चित् (any) / न (not) / अप्सु (in waters) / मज्जन्ति (sink) / जन्तवः (living beings) / न (not) / वात-जं (born from wind) / भयम् (fear) / किञ्चित् (any) / न (not) / अपि (also) / ज्वर-कृतं (caused by fever) / तथा (likewise) / न (not) / च (and) / अपि (also) / क्षुद्-भयम् (fear of hunger) / तत्र (there) / न (not) / तस्कर-भयम् (fear of thieves) / तथा (likewise)
ramayan::82.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::82.essence: Good rule is measured by the fears it removes.
ramayan::82.simple_meaning: Rama's kingdom is described as a place where people are safe from fire, floods, storms, illness, hunger, and theft.
ramayan::82.simple_insight: A just world is one where ordinary fears stop ruling daily life.
ramayan::82.detailed_meaning: The poem is describing Rama's reign after his return to rule Ayodhya. The previous verses already said the people were happy, healthy, and free from grief. This line adds the practical proof: even the basic terrors of life no longer disturb the land.
ramayan::82.modern_relevance: A night fire alarm, a flooded street, a doctor’s warning, an empty fridge, a break-in — real safety is when these fears no longer define daily life.
ramayan::82.insight: It shifts the idea of good leadership from prestige to protection of ordinary life.

ramayan::83.verse_sanskrit: नगराणि च राष्ट्राणि धनधान्ययुतानि च । । 1193 । । नित्यं प्रमुदितास्सर्वे यथा कृतयुगे तथा ।
ramayan::83.verse_hindi: All the cities and villages were affluent with wealth and food grains. People lived
ramayan::83.english_translation: The cities and kingdoms were rich in wealth and grain, and everyone was always delighted, just as in the golden age.
ramayan::83.translation_literal: नगराणि (cities) / च (and) / राष्ट्राणि (kingdoms) / धनधान्ययुतानि (endowed with wealth and grain) / च (and) / नित्यं (always) / प्रमुदिताः (delighted) / सर्वे (all) / यथा (as) / कृतयुगे (in the golden age) / तथा (so)
ramayan::83.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::83.essence: Right rule makes abundance and joy feel normal.
ramayan::83.simple_meaning: Rama's kingdom was so prosperous that cities and regions overflowed with wealth and food, and people stayed happy all the time.
ramayan::83.simple_insight: A just order can make ordinary life feel abundant and safe.
ramayan::83.detailed_meaning: The verse continues the picture of Rama's reign in Ayodhya. After describing the absence of fear, illness, hunger, and loss, it adds that towns and kingdoms were full of wealth and grain, and everyone remained joyful, as if the age itself had become golden.
ramayan::83.modern_relevance: A neighborhood where the shops are full, the streets feel safe, and people are not living in constant strain can feel almost unreal. This verse imagines that kind of shared ease as the mark of right rule.
ramayan::83.insight: It shifts attention from private success to the conditions that let whole communities thrive.

ramayan::84.verse_sanskrit: अश्वमेधशतैरिष्ट्वा तथा बहुसुवर्णकै: । । 1194 । । गवां कोट्ययुतं दत्वा ब्रह्मलोकं प्रयास्यति । असंख्येयं धनं दत्वा ब्राह्मणेभ्यो महायशा: । । 1195 । ।
ramayan::84.verse_hindi: Highly renowned Rama, having satisfied the gods with the performance of a hundred of aswamedhas and many suvarnakas  bestowing hundreds of thousands of cows and immense wealth on the brahmins, will return to Brahmaloka.
ramayan::84.english_translation: Highly renowned Rama, having satisfied the gods with the performance of a hundred horse sacrifices and many golden gifts, giving hundreds of thousands of cows and immense wealth to the brahmins, will return to Brahmaloka.
ramayan::84.translation_literal: अश्वमेधशतैः (with hundreds of horse sacrifices) / इष्ट्वा (having worshipped) / तथा (and also) / बहुसुवर्णकैः (with many gold gifts) / गवां (of cows) / कोट्ययुतम् (hundreds of thousands) / दत्वा (having given) / ब्रह्मलोकम् (to Brahmaloka) / प्रयास्यति (will go) / असंख्येयम् (countless) / धनम् (wealth) / दत्वा (having given) / ब्राह्मणेभ्यः (to the brahmins) / महायशाः (highly renowned one)
ramayan::84.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::84.essence: Rama's greatness is measured by what his rule gives away.
ramayan::84.simple_meaning: Rama is praised as a ruler whose reign will be so prosperous and righteous that he will complete great sacrifices, give vast gifts, and ascend to Brahmaloka.
ramayan::84.simple_insight: Great rule is measured by generosity, order, and the good it leaves behind.
ramayan::84.detailed_meaning: The poem is describing Rama's future reign in glowing terms. After peace, abundance, and safety have filled the land, the speaker says Rama's fame will be sealed by grand sacrifices, charity to brahmins, and a final ascent beyond the earthly world.
ramayan::84.modern_relevance: People remember the leader who leaves behind safety, generosity, and a society that works. Titles fade; the world you made for others stays.
ramayan::84.insight: It shifts attention from power itself to the moral legacy power creates.

ramayan::85.verse_sanskrit: राजवंशान्शतगुणान्स्थापयिष्यति राघव: । चातुर्वर्ण्यं च लोकेऽस्मिन् स्वे स्वे धर्मे नियोक्ष्यति । । 1196 । ।
ramayan::85.verse_hindi: Rama will establish hundredfold royal dynasties and employ the four castes to do their respective duties, in this world.
ramayan::85.english_translation: Rama will establish royal dynasties a hundredfold and place the four social orders in their proper duties in this world.
ramayan::85.translation_literal: राजवंशान् (royal dynasties) / शतगुणान् (hundredfold) / स्थापयिष्यति (will establish) / राघवः (Rama) / चातुर्वर्ण्यम् (the four social orders) / च (and) / लोकेऽस्मिन् (in this world) / स्वे स्वे (their own) / धर्मे (in duty) / नियोक्ष्यति (will appoint/place)
ramayan::85.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::85.essence: True rule is measured by the order it restores.
ramayan::85.simple_meaning: Rama will create lasting order by strengthening kingdoms and assigning each social group to its proper role and duty.
ramayan::85.simple_insight: There is dignity in building a world where everyone can do what fits them best.
ramayan::85.detailed_meaning: In this praise of Rama’s future reign, the speaker imagines a kingdom so well governed that royal lines multiply and society itself becomes orderly. Rama is not only victorious; he restores structure, stability, and rightful function.
ramayan::85.modern_relevance: A team is collapsing because everyone is doing everyone else’s job, and no one knows who decides what. Good leadership doesn’t just win the day — it clarifies roles so the whole system can breathe.
ramayan::85.insight: It shifts attention from personal glory to the harder work of creating a just order.

ramayan::86.verse_sanskrit: दशवर्षसहस्राणि दशवर्षशतानि च । रामो राज्यमुपासित्वा ब्रह्मलोकं प्रयास्यति । । 1197 । ।
ramayan::86.verse_hindi: Rama, reigning the kingdom for eleven thousand years, will attain Brahmaloka.
ramayan::86.english_translation: Rama, reigning the kingdom for eleven thousand years, will attain Brahmaloka.
ramayan::86.translation_literal: दशवर्षसहस्राणि (ten-thousand years) / दशवर्षशतानि (and one hundred years) / च (and) / रामः (Rama) / राज्यम् (the kingdom) / उपासित्वा (having ruled) / ब्रह्मलोकम् (Brahmaloka) / प्रयास्यति (will go)
ramayan::86.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::86.essence: Even the best reign is only a passage beyond itself.
ramayan::86.simple_meaning: Rama rules for a vast span of time, then moves on to the highest realm. Even the ideal king does not remain forever in worldly rule.
ramayan::86.simple_insight: A life can be fully fulfilled and still point beyond itself.
ramayan::86.detailed_meaning: Valmiki closes the royal vision of Rama's reign with a cosmic horizon. After eleven thousand years of just rule, Rama does not end in power or fame; he moves on from the kingdom to Brahmaloka, showing that even perfect rule is not the final destination.
ramayan::86.modern_relevance: You finally built the career, the home, the reputation you once chased. Then you feel the quiet question: is this all there is? This verse answers by widening the frame.
ramayan::86.insight: It shifts success from possession to transcendence, reminding you that even the best worldly achievement is not ultimate.

ramayan::87.verse_sanskrit: इदं पवित्रं पापघ्नं पुण्यं वेदैश्च सम्मितम् । य: पठेद्रामचरितं सर्वपापै: प्रमुच्यते । । 1198 । ।
ramayan::87.verse_hindi: This story of Rama is sacred and holy. It destroys sins and is equal to the Vedas. Whosoever reads it will be freed from all sins.
ramayan::87.english_translation: This story of Rama is sacred and holy. It destroys sins and is equal to the Vedas. Whoever reads Rama's story is freed from all sins.
ramayan::87.translation_literal: इदम् (this) / पवित्रम् (sacred) / पापघ्नम् (destroyer of sins) / पुण्यम् (holy/meritorious) / वेदैः (with the Vedas) / च (and) / सम्मितम् (equal) / यः (whoever) / पठेत् (reads) / रामचरितम् (Rama's story) / सर्वपापैः (from all sins) / प्रमुच्यते (is freed)
ramayan::87.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::87.essence: Rama's story is meant to cleanse, not merely to be read.
ramayan::87.simple_meaning: Rama's story is presented as deeply sacred and powerful. Reading it is said to clear away all wrongdoing and inner burden.
ramayan::87.simple_insight: There is comfort in trusting that sacred stories can purify and renew you.
ramayan::87.detailed_meaning: Valmiki closes this section by praising the Ramayana itself. After describing Rama's long reign and final ascent, he says the story is holy, Veda-like, and capable of freeing the reader from all wrongdoing.
ramayan::87.modern_relevance: You open a story when you are tired of carrying yourself. Some narratives entertain; some rearrange you. This one is offered as a cleansing force, not just a tale.
ramayan::87.insight: It shifts reading from entertainment to purification and reverence.

ramayan::88.verse_sanskrit: एतदाख्यानमायुष्यं पठन्रामायणं नर: । सपुत्रपौत्रस्सगण: प्रेत्य स्वर्गे महीयते । । 1199 । ।
ramayan::88.verse_hindi: This story of Ramayana enhances longevity of those who read it and recite it. They will be worshipped in heavens after their death along with their sons and grandsons, servants and relations.
ramayan::88.english_translation: This story of Ramayana increases lifespan. Those who read or recite it will be honored in heaven after death, together with their sons, grandsons, servants, and relatives.
ramayan::88.translation_literal: एतत् (this) / आख्यानम् (story, account) / आयुष्यम् (life-giving, increasing longevity) / पठन् (reading) / रामायणम् (the Ramayana) / नरः (a man, a person) / सपुत्रपौत्रः (together with sons and grandsons) / सगणः (with attendants and relations) / प्रेत्य (after dying, having gone beyond) / स्वर्गे (in heaven) / महीयते (is honored, is celebrated)
ramayan::88.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::88.essence: Your devotion to sacred reading can bless more than your own life.
ramayan::88.simple_meaning: Reading or reciting the Ramayana is said to bring long life and lasting honor after death, not only to you but to your family and relations.
ramayan::88.simple_insight: Sacred reading is not private — it blesses your whole line, past and future.
ramayan::88.detailed_meaning: Valmiki closes this praise of the Ramayana by promising a worldly and posthumous reward for reading it. The verse says the text extends life now and brings honor after death, not just to the reader but to the whole family line.
ramayan::88.modern_relevance: You open a book at night after everyone else has gone to sleep, not knowing if it will change anything. Some acts of reading quietly reshape the life around you, and long after you are gone.
ramayan::88.insight: It shifts reading from information-gathering to an act that nourishes family, memory, and continuity.

ramayan::89.verse_sanskrit: पठन्द्विजो वागृषभत्वमीयात्स्यात्क्षत्रियो भूमिपतित्वमीयात् । वणिग्जन: पण्यफलत्वमीयात्जनश्च शूद्रोऽपि महत्वमीयात् । । 11100 । ।
ramayan::89.verse_hindi: A brahmin becomes proficient in the eighteen branches of learning a kshatriya gets lordship over landed possessions a vaisya gets the fruits of his business and sudra also attains greatness  by reading Ramayana.
ramayan::89.english_translation: By reading the Ramayana, a Brahmin becomes skilled in the eighteen branches of learning, a Kshatriya gains lordship over lands, a merchant gains the fruits of trade, and even a Shudra attains greatness.
ramayan::89.translation_literal: पठन् (reading) / द्विजः (a twice-born one, a Brahmin) / वागृषभत्वम् (mastery in speech and learning) / ईयात् (may attain) / स्यात् (may become) / क्षत्रियः (a Kshatriya) / भूमिपतित्वम् (lordship over land) / ईयात् (may attain) / वणिग्जनः (merchant class) / पण्यफलत्वम् (the fruits of trade) / ईयात् (may attain) / जनः (a person) / च (and) / शूद्रः अपि (even a Shudra) / महत्वम् (greatness) / ईयात् (may attain)
ramayan::89.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::89.essence: One true story can elevate every kind of person in its own way.
ramayan::89.simple_meaning: Reading the Ramayana benefits every kind of person. Each person gains something fitting their role and capacity.
ramayan::89.simple_insight: Sacred reading is not narrow or exclusive; it can refine anyone, wherever they begin.
ramayan::89.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is praising his own epic after Narada's prompting. He says the Ramayana does not belong to one class alone: the learned, the ruler, the व्यापारी, and even the servant all gain something real from it.
ramayan::89.modern_relevance: You open a book at midnight after a hard day, not expecting much, and one page steadies you. Different people need different things, but a true work can still meet each of them.
ramayan::89.insight: It shifts the mind from status to transformation: the same reading can mature different people in different ways.

ramayan::90.verse_sanskrit: नारदस्य तु तद्वाक्यं श्रुत्वा वाक्यविशारद: । पूजयामास धर्मात्मा सहशिष्यो महामुनि: । । 121 । ।
ramayan::90.verse_hindi: On hearing the words of Narada the distinguished and righteous sage Valmiki, proficient in composing slokas worshipped him along with his disciples.
ramayan::90.english_translation: On hearing Narada's words, the righteous great sage Valmiki, skilled in speech, honoured him together with his disciples.
ramayan::90.translation_literal: नारदस्य (of Narada) / तु (indeed) / तत् (that) / वाक्यम् (speech) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / वाक्य-विशारदः (skilled in speech) / पूजयामास (honoured) / धर्मात्मा (righteous in nature) / सह-शिष्यः (with disciples) / महामुनिः (great sage)
ramayan::90.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::90.essence: The first act of wisdom is respectful reception.
ramayan::90.simple_meaning: Valmiki hears Narada and responds with respect, honouring him together with his students.
ramayan::90.simple_insight: Respect opens the door before any teaching can begin.
ramayan::90.detailed_meaning: Narada has just arrived and spoken to Valmiki. Before any epic or philosophy unfolds, Valmiki receives the visitor properly, along with his disciples. The scene establishes humility, reverence, and the right setting for sacred instruction.
ramayan::90.modern_relevance: A mentor messages you with feedback that could change your work. Before defending yourself, you pause, listen fully, and respond with respect.
ramayan::90.insight: It shows that wisdom begins with honouring the one who brings it.

ramayan::91.verse_hindi: The divine sage Narada after having been worshipped by Valmiki in a befitting manner sought his leave and went to heaven.
ramayan::91.english_translation: The divine sage Narada, after being duly honored by Valmiki, took leave and went away through the sky.
ramayan::91.translation_literal: यथावत् (duly) / पूजितः (honored) / तेन (by him) / देवर्षिः (divine sage) / नारदः (Narada) / तदा (then) / आपृष्ट्वा (having taken leave) / एव (indeed) / अभ्यनुज्ञातः (having been permitted) / सः (he) / जगाम (went) / विहायसम् (through the sky)
ramayan::91.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::91.essence: A complete exchange ends in mutual respect, not lingering.
ramayan::91.simple_meaning: Valmiki honors Narada properly, and Narada leaves after giving permission to depart.
ramayan::91.simple_insight: Even sacred meetings end cleanly when respect is complete.
ramayan::91.detailed_meaning: Narada has just guided Valmiki, and Valmiki responds with proper reverence. Once the exchange is complete, Narada takes leave and departs through the sky. The verse simply closes that encounter before the next step begins.
ramayan::91.modern_relevance: A mentor finishes the conversation, you thank them fully, and they walk out. Some moments end best when nothing is left hanging.
ramayan::91.insight: It marks the respectful close of one meeting before the next stage begins.

ramayan::92.verse_sanskrit: स मुहूर्तं गते तस्मिन्देवलोकं मुनिस्तदा । जगाम तमसातीरं जाह्नव्यास्त्वविदूरत: । । 123 । ।
ramayan::92.verse_hindi: After Narada had gone to devaloka, sage Valmiki reached the bank of river Tamasa which is not very far from the Ganges for morning ablutions.
ramayan::92.english_translation: After Narada had gone to the higher realm, the sage then went to the bank of the Tamasa, not far from the Ganges.
ramayan::92.translation_literal: स (he) / मुहूर्तं (for a moment) / गते (having gone) / तस्मिन् (that one) / देवलोकं (to the divine realm) / मुनिः (the sage) / तदा (then) / जगाम (went) / तमसातीरं (to the bank of the Tamasa) / जाह्नव्याः (of the Ganges) / अविदूरतः (not far)
ramayan::92.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::92.essence: A quiet departure opens the way for revelation.
ramayan::92.simple_meaning: After Narada leaves, Valmiki goes to the Tamasa riverbank near the Ganges.
ramayan::92.simple_insight: Sometimes the next turning point begins with a simple walk away from conversation.
ramayan::92.detailed_meaning: Narada has just departed after speaking with Valmiki. The sage leaves the hermitage and walks to the Tamasa riverbank near the Ganges. This is a quiet transition scene that prepares the setting for the next revelation.
ramayan::92.modern_relevance: You finish a conversation that stirs something in you, then step outside without fully knowing why. The body moves first; the mind catches up later.
ramayan::92.insight: It marks a shift from listening to observation, setting up the next act of discovery.

ramayan::93.verse_sanskrit: स तु तीरं समासाद्य तमसाया महामुनि: । शिष्यमाह स्थितं पार्श्वे दृष्ट्वा तीर्थमकर्दमम् । । 124 । ।
ramayan::93.verse_hindi: The eminent sage Valmiki reached the bank of Tamasa and seen a descent into the river with pellucid waters, spoke to the disciple standing by the side.
ramayan::93.english_translation: The great sage Valmiki reached the bank of the Tamasa River and, seeing the holy place with clear, unstained water, spoke to the disciple standing beside him.
ramayan::93.translation_literal: सः (he) / तु (indeed) / तीरम् (bank) / समासाद्य (having reached) / तमसाया (of Tamasa) / महामुनिः (great sage) / शिष्यम् (to the disciple) / आह (said) / स्थितम् (standing) / पार्श्वे (beside) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / तीर्थम् (holy place) / अकर्दमम् (without mud, unstained)
ramayan::93.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::93.essence: A clear place can make speech itself begin.
ramayan::93.simple_meaning: Valmiki reaches the riverbank and notices the water is clear and pure. He turns to the disciple beside him and speaks.
ramayan::93.simple_insight: Sometimes a clean place can open a clean thought.
ramayan::93.detailed_meaning: Valmiki has just sent Narada away and walked to the Tamasa river with Bharadwaja beside him. Seeing the clear, unstained water, he pauses and speaks. This is the quiet moment before the first verse of the Ramayana takes shape.
ramayan::93.modern_relevance: You step out after a noisy day and find a quiet river path, a clean window, a room that finally feels still. Something in you settles before you even know why.
ramayan::93.insight: It sets the scene for reflection by showing how outer clarity can invite inner expression.

ramayan::94.verse_sanskrit: अकर्दममिदं तीर्थं भरद्वाज निशामय । रमणीयं प्रसन्नाम्बु सन्मनुष्यमनो यथा । । 125 । ।
ramayan::94.verse_hindi: O Bharadwaja, behold the beautiful and pleasant waters of this river. This holy spot  is as clear and pure as the mind of a virtuous man.
ramayan::94.english_translation: O Bharadwaja, behold the beautiful and pleasant waters of this river. This holy spot is as clear and pure as the mind of a virtuous man.
ramayan::94.translation_literal: अकर्दमम् (free from mud) / इदम् (this) / तीर्थम् (holy ford) / भरद्वाज (Bharadwaja) / निशामय (look, behold) / रमणीयम् (beautiful) / प्रसन्नाम्बु (clear-watered) / सत्-मनुष्य (virtuous man) / मनः (mind) / यथा (as)
ramayan::94.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::94.essence: A clear place reflects the clarity a good mind can hold.
ramayan::94.simple_meaning: The riverbank is clean, beautiful, and calm, like the mind of a good person.
ramayan::94.simple_insight: Purity can be seen in both water and character.
ramayan::94.detailed_meaning: Valmiki has reached the Tamasa riverbank with his pupil Bharadwaja. Seeing the clear water and spotless shore, he points out its beauty by comparing it to the mind of a virtuous person. The line prepares for his next act of bathing there.
ramayan::94.modern_relevance: You step outside after rain and notice how everything looks washed clean. Sometimes the world gives you a glimpse of the calm you wish your own mind could have.
ramayan::94.insight: It links outer cleanliness with inner character, turning a simple sight into a moral mirror.

ramayan::95.verse_sanskrit: न्यस्यतां कलशस्तात दीयतां वल्कलं मम । इदमेवावगाहिष्ये तमसातीर्थमुत्तमम् । । 126 । ।
ramayan::95.verse_hindi: O dear one Put down the pitcher on the ground. Give me my garment. I shall take a dip in Tamasa, the holiest of places.
ramayan::95.english_translation: O dear one, put down the pitcher. Give me my garment. I shall bathe in this excellent sacred place on the Tamasa.
ramayan::95.translation_literal: न्यस्यताम् (let it be laid down) / कलशः (pitcher) / तात (dear one) / दीयताम् (let it be given) / वल्कलम् (bark garment) / मम (my) / इदम् (this) / एव (indeed) / अवगाहिष्ये (I shall bathe) / तमसा-तीर्थम् (Tamasa holy place) / उत्तमम् (excellent)
ramayan::95.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::95.essence: A quiet ritual can become the threshold to revelation.
ramayan::95.simple_meaning: Valmiki asks his companion to set down the water pot and hand over his bark garment so he can bathe in the Tamasa river.
ramayan::95.simple_insight: A simple act of bathing can mark the beginning of a life-changing moment.
ramayan::95.detailed_meaning: Valmiki has reached the bank of the Tamasa with Bharadwaja beside him. Seeing the clear river, he pauses only to put down his pitcher and change his garment before entering the water. The moment is ordinary on the surface, but it leads directly into the birth of the Ramayana itself.
ramayan::95.modern_relevance: You stop at a quiet riverbank, set your bag down, and feel something in you loosen. A small pause can open the door to a new beginning.
ramayan::95.insight: It shifts attention from motion to readiness, showing that transition often begins with a deliberate pause.

ramayan::96.verse_sanskrit: एवमुक्तो भरद्वाजो वाल्मीकेन महात्मना । प्रायच्छत मुनेस्तस्य वल्कलं नियतो गुरो: । । 127 । ।
ramayan::96.verse_hindi: Asked thus by the nobleminded master Valmiki, Bharadwaja, ever obedient to his spiritual master, gave the sage the bark garment.
ramayan::96.english_translation: Thus addressed by the noble Valmiki, Bharadwaja, ever obedient to his teacher, gave the sage the bark garment.
ramayan::96.translation_literal: एवमुक्तः (thus addressed) / भरद्वाजः (Bharadwaja) / वाल्मीकेन (by Valmiki) / महात्मना (by the noble-minded) / प्रायच्छत् (gave) / मुनेः (of the sage) / तस्य (to him) / वल्कलम् (bark garment) / नियतः (disciplined, obedient) / गुरोः (to the teacher)
ramayan::96.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::96.essence: A disciple’s quick response lets the larger moment continue.
ramayan::96.simple_meaning: Bharadwaja, faithful to his teacher, handed Valmiki the bark garment he had asked for.
ramayan::96.simple_insight: Small acts of obedience can keep a sacred moment moving forward.
ramayan::96.detailed_meaning: Valmiki asks Bharadwaja for the bark cloth before entering the Tamasa. Bharadwaja, a disciplined disciple, immediately hands it over. The verse simply marks that exchange, keeping the scene flowing toward Valmiki's bath and movement into the forest.
ramayan::96.modern_relevance: You ask a colleague for one missing item before a big presentation, and they hand it over without fuss. The moment is small, but it keeps everything from stalling.
ramayan::96.insight: It shows how readiness and obedience support the next step without drama.

ramayan::97.verse_sanskrit: स शिष्यहस्तादादाय वल्कलं नियतेन्द्रिय: । विचचार ह पश्यंस्तत्सर्वतो विपुलं वनम् । । 128 । ।
ramayan::97.verse_hindi: Valmiki who had his senses under his command received the barkgarment from the hands of his disciple and wandered about in that extensive forest, looking all around.
ramayan::97.english_translation: Valmiki, with his senses under control, took the bark garment from his disciple's hands and wandered through that vast forest, looking all around.
ramayan::97.translation_literal: स (he) / शिष्य-हस्तात् (from the disciple's hand) / आदाय (taking) / वल्कलम् (the bark garment) / नियत-इन्द्रियः (one whose senses are controlled) / विचचार (wandered) / ह (indeed) / पश्यन् (looking) / तत् (that) / सर्वतः (all around) / विपुलम् (vast) / वनम् (forest)
ramayan::97.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::97.essence: Controlled attention prepares the mind for revelation.
ramayan::97.simple_meaning: Valmiki takes the bark garment and walks through the forest with calm self-control, looking around him.
ramayan::97.simple_insight: Quiet discipline lets the mind stay open to what the world is about to reveal.
ramayan::97.detailed_meaning: After asking for the bark garment, Valmiki receives it from his disciple Bharadwaja. He walks on through the vast forest with his senses restrained, and that calm, alert wandering leads directly into the moment that will birth the first poem.
ramayan::97.modern_relevance: You step outside after a long day, still carrying the noise of your phone and your thoughts. The world only becomes visible when you stop gripping it so tightly.
ramayan::97.insight: It shifts attention from inner chatter to alert, disciplined presence.

ramayan::98.verse_sanskrit: तस्याभ्याशे तु मिथुनं चरन्तमनपायिनम् । ददर्श भगवांस्तत्र क्रौञ्चयोश्चारुनिस्वनम् । । 129 । ।
ramayan::98.verse_hindi: Sage Valmiki espied a pair of melodious kraunchas. Flying about in each others in separable company there in its vicinity.
ramayan::98.english_translation: Near him, the blessed sage saw a pair of krauncha birds moving together in inseparable company, with a lovely cry.
ramayan::98.translation_literal: तस्याभ्याशे (near him) / तु (indeed) / मिथुनं (a pair) / चरन्तम् (moving about) / अनपायिनम् (inseparable) / ददर्श (saw) / भगवान् (the blessed one) / तत्र (there) / क्रौञ्चयोः (of the two krauncha birds) / चारु-निस्वनम् (lovely cry)
ramayan::98.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::98.essence: A beautiful pair is seen just before loss tears it apart.
ramayan::98.simple_meaning: Valmiki sees two krauncha birds moving together, their call beautiful and inseparable.
ramayan::98.simple_insight: Some moments of beauty are fragile enough to break your heart.
ramayan::98.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is wandering in the forest after receiving his bark garment. Near him, he notices a pair of krauncha birds moving together and calling softly to each other. The scene is calm, intimate, and about to be shattered.
ramayan::98.modern_relevance: You notice two people walking home together, laughing like nothing can touch them. Then one sudden act breaks the whole mood.
ramayan::98.insight: It prepares the emotional ground for grief to turn into speech.

ramayan::99.verse_sanskrit: तस्मात्तु मिथुनादेकं पुमांसं पापनिश्चय: । जघान वैरनिलयो निषादस्तस्य पश्यत: । । 1210 । ।
ramayan::99.verse_hindi: A sinful and cruelhearted hunter struck down the male bird of the pair in his very  presence.
ramayan::99.english_translation: A sinful and cruelhearted hunter struck down the male bird of the pair in his very presence.
ramayan::99.translation_literal: तस्मात् (from that) / तु (indeed) / मिथुनात् (from the pair) / एकम् (one) / पुमांसम् (male) / पापनिश्चयः (one fixed in wrongdoing) / जघान (struck down) / वैरनिलयः (dwelling in enmity) / निषादः (the hunter) / तस्य (of that one) / पश्यतः (while seeing)
ramayan::99.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::99.essence: Cruelty seen clearly becomes unforgettable grief.
ramayan::99.simple_meaning: A hunter kills one bird from a loving pair while Valmiki watches helplessly.
ramayan::99.simple_insight: Some violence is shocking because it breaks something innocent right in front of you.
ramayan::99.detailed_meaning: Valmiki has just seen two krauncha birds moving together in the forest. In that peaceful moment, a hunter strikes the male bird down before his eyes. The sudden cruelty becomes the wound that turns grief into verse.
ramayan::99.modern_relevance: You watch a small cruelty happen in a place that was supposed to be safe. The shock stays with you because innocence was broken in plain sight.
ramayan::99.insight: It turns a moment of witnessing into the birth of lament.

ramayan::100.verse_sanskrit: तं शोणितपरीताङ्गं वेष्टमानं महीतले । भार्या तु निहतं दृष्ट्वा रुराव करुणां गिरम् । । 1211 । । वियुक्ता पतिना तेन द्विजेन सहचारिणा । ताम्रशीर्षेण मत्तेन पत्रिणा सहितेन वै । । 1212 । ।
ramayan::100.verse_hindi: The female companion saw the male bird struck down by the hunter and rolling on the earth, drenched in blood. Separated from her winged comparion with coppercrested head intoxicated with her love, the female companion lifted a piteous wail.
ramayan::100.english_translation: The female companion saw the male bird struck down by the hunter and rolling on the earth, drenched in blood. Separated from her winged companion with copper-crested head, intoxicated with love, she lifted a pitiful wail.
ramayan::100.translation_literal: तं (that) / शोणितपरीताङ्गं (whose body was covered in blood) / वेष्टमानं (writhing, rolling) / महीतले (on the earth) / भार्या (the mate, female companion) / तु (then) / निहतम् (struck down, slain) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / रुराव (cried out) / करुणां (pitiful) / गिरम् (voice) / वियुक्ता (separated) / पतिना (from her mate) / तेन (that) / द्विजेन (winged one, bird) / सहचारिणा (companion) / ताम्रशीर्षेण (with copper-colored head) / मत्तेन (intoxicated, enamored) / पत्रिणा (winged one) / सहितेन (together with) / वै (indeed)
ramayan::100.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::100.essence: A lover’s cry turns violence into verse.
ramayan::100.simple_meaning: The female bird sees her mate dying on the ground and cries out in grief. The scene is about raw loss, not instruction.
ramayan::100.simple_insight: Grief becomes unmistakable when you witness love being torn apart.
ramayan::100.detailed_meaning: Valmiki has just watched a hunter kill one bird of a loving pair. The surviving bird sees her companion rolling in blood and cries out in anguish. That cry, born from innocent suffering, becomes the emotional spark for the poem itself.
ramayan::100.modern_relevance: You see someone you love collapse after a sudden betrayal, and the room changes shape. The pain is not abstract anymore; it has a voice.
ramayan::100.insight: It turns private shock into the emotional origin of the epic.

ramayan::101.verse_sanskrit: तदा तु तं द्विजं दृष्ट्वा निषादेन निपातितम् । ऋषेर्धर्मात्मनस्तस्य कारुण्यं समपद्यत । । 1213 । ।
ramayan::101.verse_hindi: Then, having seen the bird struck down by the fowler, the pious sage Valmiki was filled with compassion.
ramayan::101.english_translation: Then, having seen the bird struck down by the fowler, the pious sage Valmiki was filled with compassion.
ramayan::101.translation_literal: तदा (then) / तु (indeed) / तं (that) / द्विजं (bird) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / निषादेन (by the fowler) / निपातितम् (struck down) / ऋषेः (of the sage) / धर्मात्मनः (righteous) / तस्य (of him) / कारुण्यम् (compassion) / समपद्यत (arose)
ramayan::101.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::101.essence: Compassion begins the moment cruelty becomes unbearable to witness.
ramayan::101.simple_meaning: Seeing the bird struck down, Valmiki's heart moved into compassion. Pain in front of him awakened care, not indifference.
ramayan::101.simple_insight: A sharp heart can still be a tender one.
ramayan::101.detailed_meaning: Valmiki watches the male bird fall to a hunter's arrow, while its mate cries beside it. The sight does not harden him; it breaks open compassion. That inner response becomes the first spark of the Ramayana itself.
ramayan::101.modern_relevance: You scroll past a cruel clip, then stop because something in you refuses to stay numb. That pause, that ache, is where compassion begins.
ramayan::101.insight: It trains you to notice suffering and respond before hardness takes over.

ramayan::102.verse_sanskrit: तत: करुणवेदित्वादधर्मोऽयमिति द्विज: । निशाम्य रुदतीं क्रौञ्चीमिदं वचनमब्रवीत् । । 1214 । ।
ramayan::102.verse_hindi: Having heard the wailing of the female bird, the sage (Valmiki) moved to pity at this irreligious act uttered the following words.
ramayan::102.english_translation: Having heard the wailing of the female bird, the sage Valmiki, moved to pity by this wrongful act, spoke these words.
ramayan::102.translation_literal: तत: (then) / करुणवेदित्वात् (because of feeling compassion) / अधर्मः (wrongdoing) / अयम् (this) / इति (thus) / द्विजः (the twice-born sage) / निशाम्य (having heard) / रुदतीम् (weeping) / क्रौञ्चीम् (the female krauncha) / इदम् (this) / वचनम् (word) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::102.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::102.simple_meaning: Valmiki hears the crying bird, feels compassion, sees the act as wrongful, and speaks in response.
ramayan::102.simple_insight: Compassion can turn grief into a moral response instead of numbness.
ramayan::102.detailed_meaning: A hunter has struck down one bird of a pair, and the female bird cries over the body. Valmiki, watching this loss, is pierced by compassion. His reaction becomes the opening movement of the epic, because pain here is not ignored — it is answered.
ramayan::102.modern_relevance: You hear a child crying in the next room after a hard fall. Something in you tightens before you even think. That first movement of care is where moral speech begins.
ramayan::102.insight: It teaches you to let compassion become a clear response, not just a feeling.

ramayan::103.verse_sanskrit: मा निषाद प्रतिष्ठां त्वमगमश्शाश्वतीस्समा: । यत्क्रौञ्चमिथुनादेकमवधी: काममोहितम् । । 1215 । । 15
ramayan::103.verse_hindi: O fowler, since you have killed one of the pair of infatuated kraunchas you will be permanently deprived of your position.
ramayan::103.english_translation: O fowler, since you have killed one of the pair of infatuated kraunchas, you will be permanently deprived of your standing.
ramayan::103.translation_literal: मा (not) / निषाद (fowler) / प्रतिष्ठाम् (standing) / त्वम् (you) / अगमः (have attained) / शाश्वतीः (permanent) / समाः (years) / यत् (because) / क्रौञ्च-मिथुनात् (from the krauncha pair) / एकम् (one) / अवधीः (you killed) / काम-मोहितम् (infatuated)
ramayan::103.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::103.essence: Pain at innocent loss becomes the first line of poetry.
ramayan::103.simple_meaning: Valmiki curses the fowler for killing one bird of a loving pair, saying the act has destroyed his standing for good.
ramayan::103.simple_insight: Cruelty spoken against in grief can become a turning point.
ramayan::103.detailed_meaning: After seeing one krauncha bird killed and hearing the mate cry out, Valmiki is overwhelmed by compassion. In that surge of pain, he speaks this spontaneous curse to the fowler, and the moment becomes the birth of poetic speech.
ramayan::103.modern_relevance: You watch someone hurt a loyal pair — a friend, a partner, a family bond — and something in you refuses to stay silent.
ramayan::103.insight: It shows how grief can break into language and turn raw feeling into verse.

ramayan::104.verse_sanskrit: तस्यैवं ब्रुवतश्चिन्ता बभूव हृदि वीक्षतः । शोकार्तेनास्य शकुने: किमिदं व्याहृतं मया । । 1216 । ।
ramayan::104.verse_hindi: Brooding over his utterances, he reflected, What is this that I uttered in reaction to the grief of this bird?
ramayan::104.english_translation: Brooding over his utterances, he reflected, "What is this that I uttered in reaction to the grief of this bird?"
ramayan::104.translation_literal: तस्य (of that) / एवम् (thus) / ब्रुवतः (speaking) / चिन्ता (thought) / बभूव (arose) / हृदि (in the heart) / वीक्षतः (while seeing) / शोकार्तेन (by one afflicted with grief) / अस्य (of this) / शकुनेः (bird) / किम् (what) / इदम् (this) / व्याहृतम् (spoken) / मया (by me)
ramayan::104.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::104.essence: Grief spoke first; awareness arrived a moment later.
ramayan::104.simple_meaning: After speaking in grief, Valmiki stops and questions what he has just said. The moment turns spontaneous emotion into self-reflection.
ramayan::104.simple_insight: A passing reaction can become the start of clear seeing.
ramayan::104.detailed_meaning: Valmiki has just spoken in sorrow after seeing the wounded bird. Now he turns inward and asks what came out of him. That pause matters, because the epic begins not with certainty, but with a mind examining its own words.
ramayan::104.modern_relevance: You send a message in anger, then stare at the screen and feel the sting of your own tone. That tiny pause — the moment you ask, 'What did I just say?' — can change everything.
ramayan::104.insight: It trains you to examine your own speech before it hardens into action.

ramayan::105.verse_sanskrit: चिन्तयन्स महाप्राज्ञश्चकार मतिमान्मतिम् । शिष्यं चैवाऽब्रवीद्वाक्यमिदं स मुनिपुङ्गव: । । 1217 । ।
ramayan::105.verse_hindi: Very wise and learned, he (Valmiki), preeminent among sages, pondered over it (for a while) and spoke these words to his disciple.
ramayan::105.english_translation: Very wise and learned, Valmiki pondered for a while and then spoke these words to his disciple.
ramayan::105.translation_literal: चिन्तयन् (pondering) / सः (he) / महाप्राज्ञः (very wise) / चकार (made) / मतिमान् (intelligent) / मतिम् (a thought) / शिष्यं (to the disciple) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / अब्रवीत् (said) / वाक्यम् (a statement) / इदम् (this) / सः (he) / मुनिपुङ्गवः (best among sages)
ramayan::105.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::105.essence: Grief becomes poetry only after thought gives it form.
ramayan::105.simple_meaning: Valmiki pauses, thinks deeply, and then turns to his disciple to speak.
ramayan::105.simple_insight: A true insight is not rushed; it ripens in silence before it is spoken.
ramayan::105.detailed_meaning: After the grief of the krauncha bird and the sudden curse-like outburst, Valmiki stands in thought. The first poem has not yet fully formed, but something irreversible has begun. He turns to his disciple, ready to give shape to what grief has awakened.
ramayan::105.modern_relevance: You hear or see something painful, and for a moment you do not speak. You let the meaning settle before you answer, because not every reaction deserves to become your voice.
ramayan::105.insight: It teaches you to let reflection come before expression, so your words carry more than impulse.

ramayan::106.verse_sanskrit: पादबद्धोऽक्षरसमस्तन्त्रीलयसमन्वित: । शोकार्तस्य प्रवृत्तो मे श्लोको भवतु नान्यथा । । 1218 । ।
ramayan::106.verse_hindi: Occasioned by the griefstricken (state of the bird) and composed in rhymed lines each of equal number of syllables tuned to the accompaniment of stringed instruments, let it be known as a sloka and not by any other name.
ramayan::106.english_translation: Occasioned by the grief-stricken state of the bird and composed in rhymed lines with equal syllables and musical cadence, let it be known as a sloka and by no other name.
ramayan::106.translation_literal: पादबद्धो (set in feet) / अक्षरसम (with equal syllables) / तन्त्रीलयसमन्वितः (joined with musical rhythm) / शोकार्तस्य (of the grief-stricken one) / प्रवृत्तः (arisen) / मे (by me) / श्लोकः (verse) / भवतु (let it be) / न अन्यथा (not otherwise)
ramayan::106.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::106.essence: Grief became poetry because it found its proper form.
ramayan::106.simple_meaning: Valmiki defines the verse he has just spoken: it arose from grief and has the structure of a true metrical line.
ramayan::106.simple_insight: Even sorrow can become form, rhythm, and language.
ramayan::106.detailed_meaning: Valmiki has just spoken in response to the grief of the bird and paused to examine what came out of him. Here he names that spontaneous utterance a true poetic meter, marking the birth of the first sloka in the epic.
ramayan::106.modern_relevance: You stare at a message you typed in anger, then realize it came out cleaner than you expected. Pain can still be shaped into something precise.
ramayan::106.insight: It turns raw feeling into disciplined expression, showing that form can hold grief without denying it.

ramayan::107.verse_sanskrit: शिष्यस्तु तस्य ब्रुवतो मुनेर्वाक्यमनुत्तमम् । प्रतिजग्राह संहृष्टस्तस्य तुष्टोऽभवद्गुरु: । । 1219 । ।
ramayan::107.verse_hindi: His disciple, delighted by the excellent verse composed by the sage, committed it to memory which left his spiritual preceptor pleased.
ramayan::107.english_translation: His disciple, delighted by the sage's excellent verse, committed it to memory, and the guru was pleased.
ramayan::107.translation_literal: शिष्यः (the disciple) / तु (indeed) / तस्य (his) / ब्रुवतः (while speaking) / मुनेः (of the sage) / वाक्यम् (statement/verse) / अनुत्तमम् (excellent) / प्रतिजग्राह (received, took up) / संहृष्टः (delighted) / तस्य (his) / तुष्टः (pleased) / अभवत् (became) / गुरुः (the teacher)
ramayan::107.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::107.essence: A true verse lives when another heart receives it.
ramayan::107.simple_meaning: The disciple memorized the sage's beautiful verse, and the teacher felt satisfied.
ramayan::107.simple_insight: Good words are not only heard; they are received, kept, and honoured.
ramayan::107.detailed_meaning: Valmiki has just created the first measured verse from grief. His disciple hears it, remembers it gladly, and the teacher sees that the new form has landed. The moment confirms the birth of poetry, not a teaching about conduct.
ramayan::107.modern_relevance: You say something with care, and someone beside you quietly holds onto it. That small moment of being understood can feel larger than praise.
ramayan::107.insight: It shifts attention from performance to reception: the right words find a home in another mind.

ramayan::108.verse_sanskrit: सोऽभिषेकं तत: कृत्वा तीर्थे तस्मिन्यथाविधि । तमेव चिन्तयन्नर्थमुपावर्तत वै मुनि: । । 1220 । ।
ramayan::108.verse_hindi: After having performed his ablution at that holy spot according to the prescribed ritual, the sage (Valmiki) returned (to his hermitage), pondering over the matter.
ramayan::108.english_translation: After performing his ablution at that holy place according to the proper rite, the sage returned, still thinking about that same matter.
ramayan::108.translation_literal: सोऽभिषेकं (then ablution) / ततः (after that) / कृत्वा (having done) / तीर्थे (at the sacred place) / तस्मिन् (there) / यथाविधि (according to the proper rite) / तम् एव (that very) / चिन्तयन् (thinking) / अर्थम् (matter) / उपावर्तत (returned) / वै (indeed) / मुनिः (the sage)
ramayan::108.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::108.essence: Ritual ends, but the mind stays with the wound.
ramayan::108.simple_meaning: Valmiki finishes a ritual bath at the sacred spot and goes back to his hermitage, still absorbed in the same thought.
ramayan::108.simple_insight: Even after the ritual is done, the mind keeps returning to what wounded it.
ramayan::108.detailed_meaning: After hearing the bird’s pained cry and shaping the first verse, Valmiki completes his ritual bath at the holy riverbank. He returns to his hermitage, but his attention stays fixed on the sorrow that sparked the poem.
ramayan::108.modern_relevance: You finish the meeting, wash your face, and walk back to your desk — but one hard moment still follows you. Some experiences keep asking to be understood.
ramayan::108.insight: It shows how a single painful event can keep shaping thought even after the outward action is complete.

ramayan::109.verse_sanskrit: भरद्वाजस्ततश्शिष्यो विनीतश्श्रुतवान्मुनेः । कलशं पूर्णमादाय पृष्ठतोऽनुजगाम ह । । 1221 । ।
ramayan::109.verse_hindi: Then saint Bharadwaja, his disciple humble and learned in scriptures, followed him with a pitcher full (of water).
ramayan::109.english_translation: Then saint Bharadwaja, humble and learned, followed him behind with a pitcher full of water.
ramayan::109.translation_literal: भरद्वाजः (Bharadvaja) / ततः (then) / शिष्यः (disciple) / विनीतः (humble) / श्रुतवान् (learned) / मुनेः (of the sage) / कलशम् (pitcher) / पूर्णम् (full) / आदाय (having taken) / पृष्ठतः (from behind) / अनुजगाम (followed) / ह (indeed)
ramayan::109.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::109.essence: Humility is shown by carrying what the teacher needs.
ramayan::109.simple_meaning: Bharadvaja, the sage's humble and learned disciple, followed behind carrying a full water pitcher.
ramayan::109.simple_insight: Respect is shown in action, not just in words.
ramayan::109.detailed_meaning: Valmiki has finished bathing and is returning toward the hermitage. Bharadvaja, his disciple, walks behind him carrying water in a pitcher. The verse simply shows the disciple's humility and service before the larger act of storytelling begins.
ramayan::109.modern_relevance: You walk behind someone who has taught you, carrying the small thing they no longer need to lift. That quiet service says more than praise.
ramayan::109.insight: It shifts attention from status to service, showing reverence through practical support.

ramayan::110.verse_sanskrit: स प्रविश्याश्रमपदं शिष्येण सह धर्मवित् । उपविष्ट: कथाश्चान्याश्चकार ध्यानमास्थित: । । 1222 । ।
ramayan::110.verse_hindi: Valmiki who knows dharma entered the hermitage along with his disciple and sat in meditation and composed other stories.
ramayan::110.english_translation: Valmiki, who knows dharma, entered the hermitage with his disciple. Seated in meditation, he composed other stories.
ramayan::110.translation_literal: स (he) / प्रविश्य (having entered) / आश्रमपदम् (the hermitage) / शिष्येण (with the disciple) / सह (together) / धर्मवित् (knower of dharma) / उपविष्टः (seated) / कथाः (stories) / च (and) / अन्याः (other) / चकार (made/composed) / ध्यानम् (meditation) / आस्थितः (established in)
ramayan::110.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::110.essence: Quiet meditation becomes the doorway to new creation.
ramayan::110.simple_meaning: Valmiki returns to his hermitage with his disciple, sits in meditation, and begins composing more stories.
ramayan::110.simple_insight: Creative work can rise from quiet attention, not just effort and noise.
ramayan::110.detailed_meaning: Valmiki has finished his ritual bathing and returned to his hermitage with Bharadvaja. In the stillness of that place, he sits in meditation and begins composing stories. The scene sets up the moment before Brahma arrives.
ramayan::110.modern_relevance: You come home after a long walk, put your phone aside, and sit in silence. The next clear idea often arrives only after you stop chasing it.
ramayan::110.insight: It shifts attention from outward activity to the quiet state where insight and composition can emerge.

ramayan::111.verse_sanskrit: आजगाम ततो ब्रह्मा लोककर्ता स्वयं प्रभु: । चतुर्मुखो महातेजा द्रष्टुं तं मुनिपुङ्गवम् । । 1223 । ।
ramayan::111.verse_hindi: At that moment, the effulgent, fourfaced Brahma, creator and lord of the world, himself, desirous of seeing him (Valmiki), the best among sages, arrived.
ramayan::111.english_translation: At that moment, the effulgent, fourfaced Brahma, creator and lord of the world, himself, desirous of seeing him, the best among sages, arrived.
ramayan::111.translation_literal: आजगाम (arrived) / ततः (then) / ब्रह्मा (Brahma) / लोककर्ता (creator of the world) / स्वयं (himself) / प्रभुः (lord) / चतुर्मुखः (four-faced) / महातेजाः (greatly effulgent) / द्रष्टुम् (to see) / तम् (him) / मुनिपुङ्गवम् (best among sages)
ramayan::111.speaker: Brahma
ramayan::111.essence: Quiet devotion can draw the highest attention.
ramayan::111.simple_meaning: Brahma himself comes to see Valmiki, showing that the sage's meditation and words have drawn cosmic attention.
ramayan::111.simple_insight: Deep practice can become so complete that even greatness comes to your door.
ramayan::111.detailed_meaning: Valmiki has entered his hermitage with his disciple and settled into meditation. In that quiet, Brahma, the four-faced creator, arrives personally to see the sage. The moment marks a divine response to Valmiki's disciplined stillness.
ramayan::111.modern_relevance: You sit alone after a long stretch of work, not chasing attention, just doing the thing properly. Then the right person notices. Some effort changes the room without asking to.
ramayan::111.insight: It shifts attention from seeking recognition to becoming so steady that recognition finds you.

ramayan::112.verse_sanskrit: वाल्मीकिरथ तं दृष्ट्वा सहसोत्थाय वाग्यत: । प्राञ्जलि: प्रयतो भूत्वा तस्थौ परमविस्मित: । । 1224 । ।
ramayan::112.verse_hindi: Greatly surprised to see him, Valmiki, purified by austerities and disciplined in speech, immediately got up and with folded palms stood before him.
ramayan::112.english_translation: Greatly surprised to see him, Valmiki, purified by austerities and disciplined in speech, immediately got up and with folded palms stood before him.
ramayan::112.translation_literal: वाल्मीकिः (Valmiki) / अथ (then) / तम् (him) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / सहसा (suddenly) / उत्थाय (having risen) / वाग्यतः (restrained in speech) / प्राञ्जलिः (with folded palms) / प्रयतः (purified, disciplined) / भूत्वा (having become) / तस्थौ (stood) / परमविस्मितः (greatly amazed)
ramayan::112.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::112.essence: A silent mind rises first into reverence.
ramayan::112.simple_meaning: Valmiki is startled by Brahma's arrival, rises at once, and stands with folded hands in reverence.
ramayan::112.simple_insight: True reverence shows itself before words do.
ramayan::112.detailed_meaning: Brahma has just arrived to see Valmiki in the hermitage. Valmiki, absorbed in meditation and silence, is overwhelmed by the visitor's presence. He rises immediately, folds his hands, and stands in awe before the creator.
ramayan::112.modern_relevance: You look up from your work and realize someone important has entered the room. Before you say anything, your body already knows how to meet the moment.
ramayan::112.insight: It shifts attention from self-possession to humble readiness in the presence of greatness.

ramayan::113.verse_sanskrit: पूजयामास तं देवं पाद्यार्घ्यासनवन्दनै: । प्रणम्य विधिवच्चैनं पृष्ट्वाऽनामयमव्ययम् । । 1225 । ।
ramayan::113.verse_hindi: Bowing with reverence as enjoined by tradition and having enquired of his well being,
ramayan::113.english_translation: He honored that radiant being with water for the feet, offerings, a seat, and reverent bows, then asked after his well-being in the proper way.
ramayan::113.translation_literal: पूजयामास (he honored) / तं (that) / देवं (radiant being) / पाद्य (water for the feet) / अर्घ्य (offering) / आसन (seat) / वन्दनैः (with bows) / प्रणम्य (having bowed) / विधिवत् (according to proper rule) / च (and) / एनम् (him) / पृष्ट्वा (having asked) / अनामयम् (about well-being) / अव्ययम् (the imperishable)
ramayan::113.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::113.essence: Honor comes before speech when greatness arrives.
ramayan::113.simple_meaning: Valmiki greets Brahma with full ritual respect and asks about his well-being.
ramayan::113.simple_insight: Respect begins with how you receive someone, not just what you say.
ramayan::113.detailed_meaning: Brahma has arrived to see Valmiki. Startled, Valmiki rises at once, bows, offers the traditional honors, and asks after Brahma's well-being. The moment shows reverence before any teaching begins.
ramayan::113.modern_relevance: A respected elder walks into your home unannounced, and you stop everything to welcome them properly. Before any conversation, you let your conduct show recognition.
ramayan::113.insight: It shifts attention from casual familiarity to disciplined reverence in the presence of greatness.

ramayan::114.verse_sanskrit: अथोपविश्य भगवानासने परमार्चिते । वाल्मीकये महर्षये सन्दिदेशासनं तत: । । 1226 । ।
ramayan::114.verse_hindi: Lord Brahma sat down on a highly worshipful seat and showed a seat for the  ascetic Valmiki to be seated.
ramayan::114.english_translation: Then Lord Brahma sat on a highly honored seat and directed that a seat be offered to the great sage Valmiki.
ramayan::114.translation_literal: अथ (then) / उपविश्य (having sat down) / भगवान् (the Lord) / आसने (on a seat) / परमार्चिते (highly honored) / वाल्मीकये (for Valmiki) / महर्षये (for the great sage) / सन्दिदेश (directed) / आसनं (a seat) / ततः (then)
ramayan::114.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::114.essence: Honor is shown first through the way you make space.
ramayan::114.simple_meaning: Brahma takes an honored seat and has another seat arranged for Valmiki.
ramayan::114.simple_insight: Respect is shown before words are spoken.
ramayan::114.detailed_meaning: After Valmiki welcomes the visitor with reverence, Brahma sits on a specially honored seat and has another seat arranged for the sage. The moment is ceremonial, not teaching-focused; it simply prepares for the divine message that follows.
ramayan::114.modern_relevance: Someone important walks into your room, and you stop what you're doing to make space for them. The gesture matters before any conversation begins.
ramayan::114.insight: It shifts attention from the message itself to the dignity of the meeting.

ramayan::115.verse_sanskrit: ब्रह्मणा समनुज्ञातस्सोऽप्युपाविशदासने । उपविष्टे तदा तस्मिन्सर्वलोकपितामहे । तद्गतेनैव मनसा वाल्मीकिर्ध्यानमास्थित: । । 1227 । ।
ramayan::115.verse_hindi: Having been ordered by Brahma, he also sat down on a seat. Although seated in the presence of the lord of the worlds, he was absorbed in the thought of events (leading to the death of the krauncha ).
ramayan::115.english_translation: Having been permitted by Brahma, he also sat down on a seat. Though seated before the grandfather of all worlds, Valmiki remained absorbed in the thought of the krauncha's death.
ramayan::115.translation_literal: ब्रह्मणा (by Brahma) / समनुज्ञातः (having been permitted) / सः (he) / अपि (also) / उपाविशत् (sat down) / आसने (on a seat) / उपविष्टे (having been seated) / तदा (then) / तस्मिन् (in that) / सर्वलोकपितामहे (in the grandfather of all worlds) / तद्गतेन (with thought fixed on that) / एव (indeed) / मनसा (with mind) / वाल्मीकिः (Valmiki) / ध्यानम् (meditation) / आस्थितः (engaged in)
ramayan::115.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::115.essence: A wounded mind can sit still while remaining elsewhere.
ramayan::115.simple_meaning: Brahma gives Valmiki permission to sit, but Valmiki's mind stays fixed on the grief and violence he has just witnessed.
ramayan::115.simple_insight: Even in a sacred presence, grief can keep your mind elsewhere.
ramayan::115.detailed_meaning: Brahma has received Valmiki with honour and offered him a seat. Yet Valmiki cannot fully enter the moment. His attention stays with the cruel death of the krauncha, and that wound becomes the seed of his meditation and poetry.
ramayan::115.modern_relevance: You can be sitting in a calm room, nodding politely, while your mind is still trapped in the thing that hurt you an hour ago.
ramayan::115.insight: It shows how a disturbing event can dominate attention and become the starting point for reflection.

ramayan::116.verse_sanskrit: पापात्मना कृतं कष्टं वैरग्रहणबुद्धिना । यस्तादृशं चारुरवं क्रौञ्चं हन्यादकारणात् । । 1228 । ।
ramayan::116.verse_hindi: The hunter killed the sweetvoiced krauncha without any cause. That sinfulminded one with hostile feeling of capturing it, had perpetrated this cruel act, he thought.
ramayan::116.english_translation: The hunter killed the sweet-voiced krauncha without any cause. That cruel, hostile-minded man committed this sinful act.
ramayan::116.translation_literal: पापात्मना (by a sinful-minded one) / कृतं (done) / कष्टं (cruelly) / वैरग्रहणबुद्धिना (with a mind holding hostility) / यः (who) / तादृशं (such) / चारुरवं (sweet-voiced) / क्रौञ्चं (krauncha) / हन्यात् (would kill) / अकारणात् (without cause)
ramayan::116.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::116.essence: Needless cruelty can become the birth of poetry.
ramayan::116.simple_meaning: A hunter cruelly kills a sweet-voiced bird for no reason at all. Valmiki sees the act as hostile, senseless, and deeply wrong.
ramayan::116.simple_insight: Random cruelty can strike so hard that it changes a life.
ramayan::116.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is seated before Brahma, already in a heightened state of attention. Then he sees a hunter kill a krauncha bird without cause. The violence shocks him so deeply that it becomes the seed of his grief and his first verse.
ramayan::116.modern_relevance: You watch a small act of cruelty unfold in front of you — a careless insult, a needless blow, a moment of bullying — and something in you breaks open and refuses to stay silent.
ramayan::116.insight: It shows how witnessing needless harm can awaken grief into speech.

ramayan::117.verse_sanskrit: शोचन्नेव मुहु: क्रौञ्चीमुपश्लोकमिमं पुन: । जगावन्तर्गतमना भूत्वा शोकपरायण: । । 1229 । ।
ramayan::117.verse_hindi: Griefstricken, Valmiki having become introspective and lamenting the plight of the female krauncha  again and again, recited this sloka.
ramayan::117.english_translation: Grief-stricken, Valmiki became inwardly absorbed and, lamenting the female krauncha again and again, recited this verse.
ramayan::117.translation_literal: शोचन् (grieving) / एव (indeed) / मुहु: (again and again) / क्रौञ्चीम् (the female krauncha) / उपश्लोकम् (this verse) / इमम् (this) / पुन: (again) / जगौ (he recited) / अन्तर्गतमना (with inwardly turned mind) / भूत्वा (having become) / शोकपरायण: (devoted to grief)
ramayan::117.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::117.essence: Grief became the first line of a great poem.
ramayan::117.simple_meaning: Valmiki, filled with grief, turned inward and recited the verse again and again while mourning the female bird.
ramayan::117.simple_insight: Deep feeling can become the doorway to creation.
ramayan::117.detailed_meaning: After seeing the hunter kill the krauncha bird, Valmiki is overcome with sorrow. He keeps mourning the female bird and, with his mind turned inward, spontaneously gives voice to the first poetic verse of the Ramayana.
ramayan::117.modern_relevance: You hear something cruel and cannot shake it all day. The mind keeps circling the hurt until, unexpectedly, it finds words.
ramayan::117.insight: It shows how grief can be transformed into expression instead of remaining raw pain.

ramayan::118.verse_sanskrit: तमुवाच ततो ब्रह्मा प्रहसन्मुनिपुङ्गवम् । श्लोक एव त्वया बद्धो नात्र कार्या विचारणा । । 1230 । ।
ramayan::118.verse_hindi: Thereafter lord Brahma smilingly addressed Valmiki, the preeminent among sages, saying, You have indeed composed a sloka.There is no doubt about it.
ramayan::118.english_translation: Then Brahma smiled and said to the great sage Valmiki, 'You have indeed composed a verse. There is no doubt about it.'
ramayan::118.translation_literal: तम् (to him) / उवाच (said) / ततः (then) / ब्रह्मा (Brahma) / प्रहसन् (smiling) / मुनिपुङ्गवम् (to the foremost of sages) / श्लोकः (a verse) / एव (indeed) / त्वया (by you) / बद्धः (composed) / न (not) / अत्र (here) / कार्या (to be done) / विचारणा (doubt)
ramayan::118.speaker: Brahma
ramayan::118.essence: Grief becomes verse when it is seen clearly.
ramayan::118.simple_meaning: Brahma tells Valmiki that his grief has turned into poetry. The words have already taken shape as a verse.
ramayan::118.simple_insight: What hurts you can become something precise, beautiful, and lasting.
ramayan::118.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is mourning the slain krauncha when Brahma appears and confirms that the cry has become poetry. This moment marks the birth of the Ramayana itself: suffering is not erased, but transformed into sacred speech.
ramayan::118.modern_relevance: You write the message you wish you didn't have to send. Hours later, you realize the raw honesty of it said exactly what needed saying.
ramayan::118.insight: It reframes pain as material for creation, not just something to endure.

ramayan::119.verse_sanskrit: मच्छन्दादेव ते ब्रह्मन् प्रवृत्तेयं सरस्वती । रामस्य चरितं सर्वं कुरु त्वमृषिसत्तम । । 1231 । ।
ramayan::119.verse_hindi: OBrahmarshi, at my will, this speech had originated from you. Most excellent ascetic, compose the history of Rama in its entirety (in this metre).
ramayan::119.english_translation: O Brahmarshi, this speech arose from me by my will. Most excellent sage, compose the entire history of Rama in this metre.
ramayan::119.translation_literal: मच्छन्दात् (by my will) / एव (indeed) / ते (from you) / ब्रह्मन् (O Brahmarshi) / प्रवृत्ता (arisen) / इयम् (this) / सरस्वती (speech) / रामस्य (of Rama) / चरितम् (history) / सर्वम् (entire) / कुरु (compose) / त्वम् (you) / ऋषिसत्तम (O best of sages)
ramayan::119.speaker: Brahma
ramayan::119.essence: The first true verse becomes a command to tell Rama's whole life.
ramayan::119.simple_meaning: Brahma tells Valmiki that the verses came to him by divine prompting and instructs him to narrate Rama's full story.
ramayan::119.simple_insight: When the right work arrives, your voice can become larger than your own effort.
ramayan::119.detailed_meaning: After Valmiki's grief turns into the first verse, Brahma appears and blesses that spontaneous speech. He tells the sage that the metre came through divine will and asks him to shape the complete life of Rama into poetry.
ramayan::119.modern_relevance: You sit before a blank page and suddenly the right words arrive. The task is no longer to force them, but to honour what came through you and finish it with care.
ramayan::119.insight: It shifts attention from self-conscious invention to faithful transmission of a larger truth.

ramayan::120.verse_sanskrit: धर्मात्मनो गुणवतो लोके रामस्य धीमत: । वृत्तं कथय धीरस्य यथा ते नारदाच्छ्रुतम् । । 1232 । ।
ramayan::120.verse_hindi: Narrate the history of Rama who is renowned for righteousness, virtues, wisdom and steadfastness in the manner you have heard it from sage Narada.
ramayan::120.english_translation: Narrate the history of Rama who is renowned for righteousness, virtues, wisdom and steadfastness in the manner you have heard it from sage Narada.
ramayan::120.translation_literal: धर्मात्मनो (of the righteous one) / गुणवतो (of the virtuous one) / लोके (in the world) / रामस्य (of Rama) / धीमतः (of the wise) / वृत्तं (the history) / कथय (tell) / धीरस्य (of the steadfast one) / यथा (as) / ते (by you) / नारदात् (from Narada) / श्रुतम् (heard)
ramayan::120.speaker: Brahma
ramayan::120.essence: Rama’s story must be told as it truly was.
ramayan::120.simple_meaning: Brahma asks Valmiki to tell Rama’s life exactly as he heard it from Narada, highlighting Rama’s righteousness, wisdom, and steadiness.
ramayan::120.simple_insight: There is dignity in telling a noble life faithfully, without adding or subtracting anything.
ramayan::120.detailed_meaning: Brahma has just blessed Valmiki’s spontaneous verse and instructed him to compose Rama’s life. Now he names the qualities that define Rama: righteous, virtuous, wise, and steadfast. The command is not to invent, but to preserve truth with care.
ramayan::120.modern_relevance: A senior asks you to write the story of someone who changed your life, and you feel the pressure to exaggerate or soften it. This verse asks for something harder: faithful telling, with respect intact.
ramayan::120.insight: It shifts you from creative distortion to exact, reverent testimony.

ramayan::121.verse_sanskrit: रहस्यं च प्रकाशं च यद्वृत्तं तस्य धीमत: । रामस्य सहसौमित्रेः राक्षसानां च सर्वश: । । 1233 । । वैदेह्याश्चैव यद्वृत्तं प्रकाशं यदि वा रह: । तच्चाप्यविदितं सर्वं विदितं ते भविष्यति । । 1234 । ।
ramayan::121.verse_hindi: The incidents pertaining to sagacious Rama together with Lakshmana, Sita, Bharata, etc. and the rakshasas  their deeds, thoughts, unknown or known to everybody and even not known to you, will be revealed to you by my grace.
ramayan::121.english_translation: The hidden and open deeds of wise Rama, of Lakshmana, of Sita, and of the rakshasas, known and unknown, will all become known to you by my grace.
ramayan::121.translation_literal: रहस्यं (hidden) / च (and) / प्रकाशं (open) / च (and) / यत् (whatever) / वृत्तं (deeds, events) / तस्य (of that) / धीमतः (of the wise) / रामस्य (of Rama) / सहसौमित्रेः (together with Lakshmana) / राक्षसानाम् (of the rakshasas) / च (and) / सर्वशः (in every way) / वैदेह्याः (of Vaidehi/Sita) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / यत् (whatever) / वृत्तं (deeds, events) / प्रकाशं (open) / यदि वा (or if) / रहः (secret) / तत् (that) / च अपि (and also) / अविदितं (unknown) / सर्वं (all) / विदितं (known) / ते (to you) / भविष्यति (will become)
ramayan::121.speaker: Brahma
ramayan::121.essence: Nothing in Rama's story will remain hidden from the poet.
ramayan::121.simple_meaning: Brahma promises that Valmiki will learn every deed and secret of Rama, Lakshmana, Sita, and the rakshasas, whether known or hidden.
ramayan::121.simple_insight: Some stories are so complete that even what is hidden becomes clear.
ramayan::121.detailed_meaning: Brahma is answering Valmiki's request to tell Rama's story. He promises that nothing about Rama, Lakshmana, Sita, or the rakshasas will remain unknown to the poet, whether public or secret. This is part of the divine authorization of the epic.
ramayan::121.modern_relevance: You keep trying to understand a person from fragments — one message, one rumor, one moment. Some lives only make sense when the hidden and the visible are both allowed to speak.
ramayan::121.insight: It frames the epic as complete revelation, not partial biography.

ramayan::122.verse_sanskrit: न ते वागनृता काव्ये काचिदत्र भविष्यति । कुरु रामकथां पुण्यां श्लोकबद्धां मनोरमाम् । । 1235 । ।
ramayan::122.verse_hindi: Not even a single word of yours in this epic will ever prove untruthful. Compose this sacred, delightful story of Rama, set in the form of slokas.
ramayan::122.english_translation: Not even a single word of yours in this epic will ever prove untruthful. Compose this sacred, delightful story of Rama, set in the form of slokas.
ramayan::122.translation_literal: न (not) / ते (your) / वाग् (speech) / अनृता (untrue) / काव्ये (in the poem) / काचिद् (any) / अत्र (here) / भविष्यति (will be) / कुरु (compose) / रामकथाम् (the story of Rama) / पुण्याम् (sacred) / श्लोकबद्धाम् (bound in verses) / मनोरमाम् (delightful)
ramayan::122.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::122.essence: A true story can be beautiful without losing a single fact.
ramayan::122.simple_meaning: The speaker asks for Rama's sacred story to be composed in beautiful verse, and says nothing in it will be untrue.
ramayan::122.simple_insight: Truth does not need to be plain to be faithful.
ramayan::122.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is being asked to tell Rama's story after hearing the earlier outline from Narada. He answers with confidence that the poem will remain truthful and worthy, turning memory into sacred art.
ramayan::122.modern_relevance: You want to tell a hard story without flattening it or dressing it up. This verse says you can hold truth and beauty together without betraying either.
ramayan::122.insight: It teaches you to shape meaningful truth with care, not just accuracy.

ramayan::123.verse_sanskrit: यावत् स्थास्यन्ति गिरयस्सरितश्च महीतले । तावद्रामायणकथा लोकेषु प्रचरिष्यति । । 1236 । ।
ramayan::123.verse_hindi: As long as the mountains and rivers exist on this earth, the story of Ramayana will prevail among the people.
ramayan::123.english_translation: As long as mountains and rivers exist on this earth, the story of Ramayana will prevail among people.
ramayan::123.translation_literal: यावत् (as long as) / स्थास्यन्ति (will stand) / गिरयस्सरितश्च (mountains and rivers also) / महीतले (on the earth's surface) / तावत् (so long) / रामायणकथा (the Ramayana story) / लोकेषु (among the people) / प्रचरिष्यति (will spread / prevail)
ramayan::123.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::123.essence: What is rooted in truth outlives the age that first heard it.
ramayan::123.simple_meaning: Valmiki says Rama's story will last as long as the natural world itself lasts. Its reach will not fade with time.
ramayan::123.simple_insight: What is rooted in truth can outlive kingdoms, generations, and memory.
ramayan::123.detailed_meaning: At the close of the epic, Valmiki is not just ending a poem. He is claiming that Rama's story has become part of the world's lasting order, as enduring as mountains and rivers. The poem itself is being sealed as something time cannot erase.
ramayan::123.modern_relevance: You pour years into something that may never trend, never go viral, never get applause. Then one day you realise it changed the people who touched it, and that is what lasts.
ramayan::123.insight: It shifts attention from immediate recognition to lasting cultural and moral impact.

ramayan::124.verse_sanskrit: यावद्रामायणकथा त्वत्कृता प्रचरिष्यति । तावदूर्ध्वमधश्च त्वं मल्लोकेषु निवत्स्यसि । । 1237 । ।
ramayan::124.verse_hindi: So long as the story of the Ramayana composed by you is remembered in this world, you will live in the upper world, the nether world and Brahmaloka.
ramayan::124.english_translation: So long as the story of the Ramayana composed by you is remembered in this world, you will live in the upper world, the nether world and Brahmaloka.
ramayan::124.translation_literal: यावत् (so long as) / रामायणकथा (the Ramayana story) / त्वत्कृता (composed by you) / प्रचरिष्यति (will continue to spread) / तावत् (so long) / ऊर्ध्वम् (in the upper world) / अधः (in the lower world) / च (and) / त्वम् (you) / मल्लोकेषु (in my worlds) / निवत्स्यसि (will dwell)
ramayan::124.speaker: Brahma
ramayan::124.essence: What you create with truth can outlive your own lifetime.
ramayan::124.simple_meaning: Brahma says Valmiki's Ramayana will endure, and Valmiki himself will dwell in exalted realms as long as it is remembered.
ramayan::124.simple_insight: There is comfort in knowing a true work can carry your name beyond a single lifetime.
ramayan::124.detailed_meaning: Brahma has just praised Valmiki's flawless verse and the sacred story of Rama. Now he gives the poet a blessing: as long as this epic is sung, Valmiki will remain present in higher and lower realms and in Brahma's own world.
ramayan::124.modern_relevance: You finish something honest and beautiful, then wonder if it mattered. Years later, someone still quotes it, still returns to it, and your voice is not gone.
ramayan::124.insight: It shifts attention from temporary achievement to lasting contribution through art, memory, and truth.

ramayan::125.verse_hindi: Having spoken these words, lord Brahma vanished. At this he and his disciples were astonished.
ramayan::125.english_translation: Having spoken these words, Lord Brahma vanished. At this, Valmiki and his disciples were astonished.
ramayan::125.translation_literal: इत्युक्त्वा (having spoken thus) / भगवान् (the lord) / ब्रह्मा (Brahma) / तत्र (there) / एव (indeed) / अन्तरधीयत (vanished) / ततस् (then) / सः (he) / शिष्यः (with disciples) / भगवान् (the venerable one) / मुनिः (sage) / विस्मयम् (astonishment) / आययौ (came upon)
ramayan::125.speaker: Brahma
ramayan::125.essence: The blessing ends, but its force remains.
ramayan::125.simple_meaning: Brahma disappears after blessing Valmiki, and Valmiki with his disciples are left astonished.
ramayan::125.simple_insight: Some moments end so fully that all you can do is stand in wonder.
ramayan::125.detailed_meaning: Brahma has just blessed Valmiki’s Ramayana and foretold its lasting fame. The speech ends, the creator vanishes, and Valmiki is left with his disciples stunned by what they have heard.
ramayan::125.modern_relevance: You finish something important and sit in silence for a second, realizing it landed deeper than you expected. Some words keep echoing after the speaker is gone.
ramayan::125.insight: It closes a divine blessing with silence, leaving the teaching to live through memory.

ramayan::126.verse_sanskrit: तस्य शिष्यास्ततस्सर्वे जगुश्श्लोकमिमं पुन: । मुहुर्मुहु: प्रीयमाणा: प्राहुश्च भृशविस्मिता: । । 1239 । ।
ramayan::126.verse_hindi: Thereafter, the disciples of Valmiki chanted this sloka again and again in delight. They were greatly astonished and spoke about it often.
ramayan::126.english_translation: Thereafter, all of Valmiki's disciples chanted this verse again and again in delight. Deeply astonished, they kept speaking of it often.
ramayan::126.translation_literal: तस्य (his) / शिष्याः (disciples) / ततः (then) / सर्वे (all) / जगुः (chanted) / श्लोकम् (verse) / इमम् (this) / पुनः (again) / मुहुः मुहुः (again and again) / प्रीयमाणाः (being delighted) / प्राहुः च (and spoke) / भृशविस्मिताः (greatly astonished)
ramayan::126.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::126.essence: A verse becomes alive when astonished listeners keep repeating it.
ramayan::126.simple_meaning: Valmiki's disciples kept repeating the verse with delight and wonder. Their amazement made them speak of it over and over.
ramayan::126.simple_insight: Some lines are so fitting that people return to them without being told.
ramayan::126.detailed_meaning: After Brahma's blessing, Valmiki's students respond with delight and astonishment. They repeat the new verse again and again, showing that the moment is about the birth of poetry itself, not a teaching meant to stand alone.
ramayan::126.modern_relevance: You hear a line and keep sending it to friends because it lands too perfectly. Some words spread because they name something everyone felt but never said.
ramayan::126.insight: It shows how a memorable line becomes shared through repetition and delight, not argument.

ramayan::127.verse_hindi: This sloka of four lines, each consisting of equal number of syllables, was recited by the maharshi. Constant recitation (by others) elicited admiration (from the listeners).
ramayan::127.english_translation: This four-line verse, with equal syllables in each line, was sung by the great sage. Through repeated recitation, it came to be known as a true verse.
ramayan::127.translation_literal: समाक्षरैः (with equal syllables) / चतुर्भिः (four) / यः (which) / पादैः (with lines) / गीतः (sung) / महर्षिणा (by the great sage) / सः (that) / अनुव्याहरणात् (through repeated recitation) / भूयः (again) / श्लोकः (verse) / श्लोकत्वम् (the state of being a verse) / आगत: (came to)
ramayan::127.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::127.essence: Repetition and balance turn speech into a lasting form.
ramayan::127.simple_meaning: A verse with four equal lines was sung by Valmiki, and repeated recitation made it famous as a true poetic form.
ramayan::127.simple_insight: Great form becomes lasting through repetition and shared appreciation.
ramayan::127.detailed_meaning: After Brahma vanishes and Valmiki's disciples marvel at the newly heard verse, the poem pauses to explain why it matters. The four balanced lines Valmiki sang are now being recognised as the first true shloka, setting the form for the epic that follows.
ramayan::127.modern_relevance: A line you hear once in a workshop can feel ordinary. Then people repeat it, quote it, and it starts shaping the way they speak. Some ideas become lasting because they are easy to carry and hard to forget.
ramayan::127.insight: It shows how a memorable form can turn a single utterance into a lasting tradition.

ramayan::128.verse_sanskrit: तस्य बुद्धिरियं जाता वाल्मीकेर्भावितात्मन: । कृत्स्नं रामायणं काव्यमीदृशै: करवाण्यहम् । । 1241 । ।
ramayan::128.verse_hindi: A thought occurred to Valmiki, who is capable of putting thoughts into action I shall  compose the epic named Ramayana entirely in this metre.
ramayan::128.english_translation: A thought arose in Valmiki, a man of disciplined mind: 'I will compose the entire Ramayana in this meter.'
ramayan::128.translation_literal: तस्य (of him) / बुद्धिः (thought) / इयम् (this) / जाता (arose) / वाल्मीकेः (of Valmiki) / भावितात्मनः (of the disciplined-minded one) / कृत्स्नम् (entire) / रामायणम् (Ramayana) / काव्यम् (poem) / ईदृशैः (in such) / करवाणि (I shall make) / अहम् (I)
ramayan::128.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::128.essence: A clear mind does not stop at admiration; it begins the work.
ramayan::128.simple_meaning: Valmiki decides to turn the inspired meter into a full epic. His disciplined mind does not just admire beauty; it immediately moves to create.
ramayan::128.simple_insight: Inspiration becomes powerful when you give it form.
ramayan::128.detailed_meaning: After hearing the first perfect verse, Valmiki is struck by a creative certainty. The moment is not just admiration — it is commitment. He decides to build the entire Ramayana in that same meter, turning insight into a vast poem.
ramayan::128.modern_relevance: You catch one sentence in a notebook, and suddenly the whole book appears in your mind. The difference between a passing idea and a real project is the moment you decide to build it.
ramayan::128.insight: It shifts you from receiving inspiration to committing to a full creation.

ramayan::129.verse_sanskrit: उदारवृत्तार्थपदैर्मनोरमैःतदास्य रामस्य चकारकीर्तिमान् । समाक्षरैश्श्लोकशतैर्यशस्विनो यशस्करं काव्यमुदारधीर्मुनि: । । 1242 । ।
ramayan::129.verse_hindi: The renowned and sagacious sage composed a kavya with hundreds of charming verses, each containing equal number of syllables and excellent meaningful words set in metre, conferring glory on celebrated Rama.
ramayan::129.english_translation: The renowned and sagacious sage composed a kavya with hundreds of charming verses, each containing equal number of syllables and excellent meaningful words set in metre, conferring glory on celebrated Rama.
ramayan::129.translation_literal: उदारवृत्तार्थपदैः (with noble metre, meaning, and words) / मनोरमैः (charming) / तदा (then) / अस्य (of this) / रामस्य (of Rama) / चकार (made) / कीर्तिमान् (the renowned one) / समाक्षरैः (with equal syllables) / श्लोकशतैः (with hundreds of verses) / यशस्विनः (of the celebrated one) / यशस्करम् (glory-giving) / काव्यम् (poem) / उदारधीः (the sagacious one) / मुनिः (sage)
ramayan::129.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::129.essence: Beautiful form can preserve greatness long after the moment has passed.
ramayan::129.simple_meaning: Valmiki composed the Ramayana in polished, rhythmic verses that give Rama lasting glory.
ramayan::129.simple_insight: Great stories endure when form and meaning carry the same weight.
ramayan::129.detailed_meaning: After hearing the first seed of the Ramayana, Valmiki turns insight into art. He shapes hundreds of balanced, beautiful verses into a poem that will preserve Rama’s fame and make the story fit for remembrance.
ramayan::129.modern_relevance: You finish a piece of work and realize the form matters as much as the message. A clear structure can carry someone’s name, effort, or truth farther than raw emotion ever could.
ramayan::129.insight: It shifts attention from inspiration alone to disciplined craft that makes meaning memorable.

ramayan::130.verse_hindi: This story of Rama and the killing of Ravana composed by the sage consists of compound words, melodious sandhis and lines composed in lucid, melodious and meaningful  phrases. Listen to it.
