ramayan::130.english_translation: Listen to the story of the noble Rama, composed by the sage, and to the killing of the ten-headed Ravana. It is woven with smooth compounds, graceful sandhi, and words of clear, sweet, meaningful phrasing.
ramayan::130.translation_literal: तत् (that) / उपगत (arrived at, fitted with) / समास (compounds) / सन्धि-योगम् (joining of euphonic combinations) / सम (even, balanced) / मधुर (sweet) / उपनत (well-formed) / अर्थ-वाक्य-बद्धम् (bound in meaningful phrases) / रघु-वर-चरितम् (the conduct/story of the best of the Raghu line) / मुनि-प्रणीतम् (composed by the sage) / दश-शिरसः (of the ten-headed one) / च (and) / वधम् (slaying) / निशामयध्वम् (listen)
ramayan::130.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::130.essence: Good form can carry grave meaning without weakening it.
ramayan::130.simple_meaning: Valmiki invites listeners to hear his poem about Rama and Ravana. He praises its graceful language, smooth structure, and clear meaning.
ramayan::130.simple_insight: Beautiful form can carry serious meaning without losing clarity.
ramayan::130.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is presenting his own poem to the listener. After announcing that he has composed the Ramayana, he describes its style: tightly linked compounds, smooth sound, and meaningful phrasing. This is a literary self-introduction, not a teaching on conduct.
ramayan::130.modern_relevance: You open a book or a podcast and know within seconds whether it was shaped with care. This line is that quiet confidence: form, rhythm, and meaning can all belong together.
ramayan::130.insight: It shifts attention from just content to the craft that makes content memorable.

ramayan::131.verse_sanskrit: श्रुत्वा वस्तु समग्रं तद्धर्मात्मा धर्मसंहितम् । व्यक्तमन्वेषते भूयो यद्वृत्तं तस्य धीमत: । । 131 । ।
ramayan::131.verse_hindi: Hearing the entire story of Rama from the intellecual Narada, the righteous (Valmiki) sought to know clearly more about the history of Rama endowed  with wisdom.
ramayan::131.english_translation: Hearing the full story, the righteous sage sought to understand more clearly the deeds of that wise one.
ramayan::131.translation_literal: श्रुत्वा (having heard) / वस्तु (the whole matter) / समग्रं (complete) / तद् (that) / धर्मात्मा (righteous one) / धर्मसंहितम् (joined with dharma) / व्यक्तम् (clearly) / अन्वेषते (seeks out) / भूयः (again, further) / यत् (what) / वृत्तम् (happened) / तस्य (of that one) / धीमतः (of the wise one)
ramayan::131.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::131.essence: Listening well can awaken the need to understand even more deeply.
ramayan::131.simple_meaning: After hearing the full account, the righteous sage wanted a clearer understanding of Rama's story.
ramayan::131.simple_insight: Curiosity can be a form of reverence, not doubt.
ramayan::131.detailed_meaning: Valmiki has just heard Narada's full account of Rama. Instead of stopping at the summary, he wants the events made fully clear. That desire to understand becomes the beginning of the epic.
ramayan::131.modern_relevance: You hear a half-told story about someone you care about, and you feel the pull to check the facts yourself. Real understanding starts when you refuse to settle for the first version.
ramayan::131.insight: It shifts you from passive hearing to active investigation.

ramayan::132.verse_sanskrit: उपस्पृश्योदकं सम्यग्मुनिस्स्थित्वा कृताञ्जलि: । प्राचीनाग्रेषु दर्भेषु धर्मेणान्वेषते गतिम् । । 132 । ।
ramayan::132.verse_hindi: Having performed achamana, Valmiki seated on kusha grass with folded palms, searched for the course of past events in the history of Rama by his power of penance.
ramayan::132.english_translation: Having purified himself with water, the sage stood in stillness, palms joined, and sought the path of events by dharma.
ramayan::132.translation_literal: उपस्पृश्योदकम् (having touched water / purified with water) / सम्यक् (properly) / मुनिः (the sage) / स्थित्वा (having stood) / कृताञ्जलिः (with folded palms) / प्राचीनाग्रेषु (on grass with tips pointing east) / दर्भेषु (on kusa grass) / धर्मेण (by dharma / rightly) / अन्वेषते (seeks, searches) / गतिम् (the course, path)
ramayan::132.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::132.essence: Clear seeing begins with a prepared and questioning mind.
ramayan::132.simple_meaning: Valmiki prepares himself ritually, sits in a disciplined posture, and begins searching for the true sequence of Rama's story.
ramayan::132.simple_insight: Real understanding begins with stillness, preparation, and a sincere search.
ramayan::132.detailed_meaning: After hearing Narada's account, Valmiki does not rush to write. He purifies himself, sits on kusa grass, folds his hands, and turns inward to investigate Rama's story more deeply. This verse marks the start of his search for exact truth.
ramayan::132.modern_relevance: You close the laptop, wash your face, and sit down before the blank page. Before insight comes, you make space for it and begin asking carefully.
ramayan::132.insight: It shifts the mind from passive hearing to disciplined investigation.

ramayan::133.verse_sanskrit: रामलक्ष्मणसीताभी राज्ञा दशरथेन च । सभार्येण सराष्ट्रेण यत्प्राप्तं तत्र तत्त्वत: । । 133 । । हसितं भाषितं चैव गतिर्या यच्च चेष्टितम् । तत्सर्वं धर्मवीर्येण यथावत्सम्प्रपश्यति । । 134 । ।
ramayan::133.verse_hindi: By the power of his penance, the holy sage visualised clearly Rama, Lakshmana and Sita, king Dasaratha, his wives and his kingdom and all that they had observed,
ramayan::133.english_translation: By the power of his penance, the holy sage clearly saw Rama, Lakshmana, Sita, King Dasharatha, his wives, and his kingdom, along with everything they had experienced. He also saw their laughter, speech, movements, and actions exactly as they had happened.
ramayan::133.translation_literal: रामलक्ष्मणसीताभी (Rama, Lakshmana, and Sita) / राज्ञा (by the king) / दशरथेन (by Dasharatha) / च (and) / सभार्येण (with his wives) / सराष्ट्रेण (with his kingdom) / यत्प्राप्तं (whatever was experienced) / तत्र (there) / तत्त्वत: (in truth, clearly) / हसितं (laughter) / भाषितं (speech) / चैव (and also) / गतिर्या (movement that) / यच्च (and whatever) / चेष्टितम् (actions) / तत्सर्वं (all that) / धर्मवीर्येण (by the power of penance) / यथावत् (exactly as it was) / सम्प्रपश्यति (he clearly saw)
ramayan::133.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::133.essence: Penance sharpens vision until even ordinary actions become fully visible.
ramayan::133.simple_meaning: Valmiki’s penance gives him a clear vision of Rama, Lakshmana, Sita, Dasharatha, and everything around them — even their speech, movement, and actions.
ramayan::133.simple_insight: Deep attention can reveal a whole life, not just isolated moments.
ramayan::133.detailed_meaning: The sage Valmiki is not merely hearing a story anymore. Through disciplined insight, he sees the royal family, their world, and the smallest details of their lives exactly as they unfolded. This is a scene of poetic vision, not teaching.
ramayan::133.modern_relevance: You replay a conversation for the tenth time and suddenly see the whole pattern — not just what was said, but how everyone moved, paused, and revealed themselves.
ramayan::133.insight: It shifts attention from fragments to the full shape of a life or event.

ramayan::134.verse_sanskrit: स्त्रीतृतीयेन च तदा यत्प्राप्तं चरता वने । सत्यसन्धेन रामेण तत्सर्वं चान्ववेक्षितम् । । 135 । ।
ramayan::134.verse_hindi: All that was acquired by truthful Rama, Lakshmana and wife Sita as the third person when they were moving in the Dandakaranya forest, was visualised.
ramayan::134.english_translation: Everything that happened to truthful Rama, Lakshmana, and Sita while they wandered in the forest was clearly seen.
ramayan::134.translation_literal: स्त्रीतृतीयेन (with Sita as the third) / च (and) / तदा (then) / यत् (whatever) / प्राप्तम् (was experienced, obtained) / चरता (while moving, wandering) / वने (in the forest) / सत्यसन्धेन (by the truth-bound) / रामेण (by Rama) / तत् (that) / सर्वम् (all) / च (and) / अन्ववेक्षितम् (was observed, clearly seen)
ramayan::134.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::134.essence: The forest exile is seen whole, without distortion.
ramayan::134.simple_meaning: Valmiki, in meditation, clearly saw everything that happened to Rama, Lakshmana, and Sita during their forest exile.
ramayan::134.simple_insight: Some events are so important that they demand to be seen with complete honesty.
ramayan::134.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is not telling a story casually here. He sits in disciplined stillness and, through yogic sight, watches Rama, Lakshmana, and Sita in the forest. This verse continues that visionary act, showing that the epic is being recovered in full.
ramayan::134.modern_relevance: You replay a hard season in your mind and finally see it clearly — not as fragments, but as one complete, painful whole.
ramayan::134.insight: It shifts attention from scattered memory to complete witnessing.

ramayan::135.verse_sanskrit: तत: पश्यति धर्मात्मा तत्सर्वं योगमास्थित: । पुरा यत्तत्र निर्वृत्तं पाणावामलकं यथा । । 136 । ।
ramayan::135.verse_hindi: With the power of yoga, the righteous (Valmiki) saw clearly, like an amalaka fruit in the
ramayan::135.english_translation: Then the righteous sage, absorbed in yoga, saw everything that had happened there in the past as clearly as an amalaka fruit in his hand.
ramayan::135.translation_literal: तत: (then) / पश्यति (sees) / धर्मात्मा (the righteous one) / तत् सर्वम् (all that) / योगम् आस्थितः (established in yoga) / पुरा (formerly, in the past) / यत् तत्र (what there) / निर्वृत्तम् (had occurred) / पाणौ (in the hand) / आमलकम् इव (like an amalaka fruit)
ramayan::135.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::135.essence: A settled mind can see the whole past without distortion.
ramayan::135.simple_meaning: A disciplined, steady mind can see past events with complete clarity, as if they were right in front of the hand.
ramayan::135.simple_insight: Clarity is possible when the mind is settled enough to stop distorting what happened.
ramayan::135.detailed_meaning: Valmiki, deep in contemplation, is not guessing at Rama's story. He sees the whole sequence of events in Dandaka clearly, as though it were an amalaka fruit resting in his palm. That inner clarity becomes the basis for the epic itself.
ramayan::135.modern_relevance: You replay a painful conversation for days, and each time it changes shape. Then, in a quiet moment, you see what actually happened without the blur of emotion. That is the kind of seeing this verse points to.
ramayan::135.insight: It shifts you from mental fog to clear, settled observation of events.

ramayan::136.verse_sanskrit: तत्सर्वं तत्त्वतो दृष्ट्वा धर्मेण स महाद्युति: । अभिरामस्य रामस्य चरितं कर्तुमुद्यत: । । 137 । । कामार्थगुणसंयुक्तं धर्मार्थगुणविस्तरम् । समुद्रमिव रत्नाढ्यं सर्वश्रुतिमनोहरम् । । 138 । ।
ramayan::136.verse_hindi: Highly resplendent Valmiki, having visualised the story (of Rama), with his power of penance and blending the merits of attainment of worldly prosperity and pleasures together with the detailed description of the merit of righteousness as an end and aim, like an ocean filled with gems, got ready to compose the story of delightful Rama which regales everybodys ears.
ramayan::136.english_translation: Having seen all that exactly as it was, the radiant sage, established in righteousness, prepared to compose the story of delightful Rama—rich with worldly aims and pleasures, and expansive with righteousness—like an ocean filled with gems, pleasing to every ear.
ramayan::136.translation_literal: तत्सर्वं (all that) / तत्त्वतो (exactly as it was) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / धर्मेण (with righteousness) / स (he) / महाद्युति: (greatly radiant) / अभिरामस्य (of delightful) / रामस्य (of Rama) / चरितं (the story / conduct) / कर्तुम् (to make / compose) / उद्यत: (prepared) / कामार्थगुणसंयुक्तं (joined with qualities of desire and worldly aims) / धर्मार्थगुणविस्तरम् (expansive with the qualities of righteousness and purpose) / समुद्रमिव (like an ocean) / रत्नाढ्यं (rich with gems) / सर्वश्रुतिमनोहरम् (delighting to all who hear)
ramayan::136.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::136.essence: A true telling holds both human desire and righteousness together.
ramayan::136.simple_meaning: Valmiki sees Rama’s life clearly and prepares to tell it as a rich story that includes both worldly life and righteousness.
ramayan::136.simple_insight: A great story can hold pleasure, purpose, and duty without losing its depth.
ramayan::136.detailed_meaning: After seeing Rama’s life exactly as it unfolded, Valmiki turns to compose the epic. The poem is not just praise; it is meant to hold human desire, duty, and beauty together, just as the ocean holds gems.
ramayan::136.modern_relevance: You finally understand a life-changing event, and the story you tell yourself becomes richer than blame or praise. What happened can carry both pain and meaning.
ramayan::136.insight: It teaches you to see a life whole, not in fragments of success or suffering.

ramayan::137.verse_sanskrit: स यथा कथितं पूर्वं नारदेन महर्षिणा । रघुवंशस्य चरितं चकार भगवानृषिः । । 139 । ।
ramayan::137.verse_hindi: The divine sage, composed the history of Rama born in the race of Raghu, just as it was related by the illustrious sage Narada in the past.
ramayan::137.english_translation: The divine sage composed the history of Rama born in the race of Raghu, just as it was related by the illustrious sage Narada in the past.
ramayan::137.translation_literal: स (he) / यथा (as) / कथितं (spoken) / पूर्वं (earlier) / नारदेन (by Narada) / महर्षिणा (by the great sage) / रघुवंशस्य (of the Raghu line) / चरितं (the deeds/history) / चकार (composed) / भगवान् (the venerable/divine) / ऋषिः (sage)
ramayan::137.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::137.essence: True composition begins with faithful remembering, not invention.
ramayan::137.simple_meaning: Valmiki says he composed Rama’s story exactly as Narada had described it before.
ramayan::137.simple_insight: Great stories are often shaped by faithful listening before they are shaped by writing.
ramayan::137.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is explaining his own work. After seeing Rama’s story clearly, he says he composed the account of the Raghu line exactly as Narada had earlier narrated it. The verse is about authorship and faithful transmission, not a teaching on conduct.
ramayan::137.modern_relevance: You rewrite a family story, a company history, or a friend’s pain, and the temptation is to make it clever. This verse honors the harder task: telling it as it was received.
ramayan::137.insight: It shifts you from inventing a version to preserving what was truly seen and heard.

ramayan::138.verse_sanskrit: जन्म रामस्य सुमहद्वीर्यं सर्वानुकूलताम् । लोकस्य प्रियतां क्षान्तिं सौम्यतां सत्यशीलताम् । । 1310 । ।
ramayan::138.verse_hindi: (He described) the birth of Rama, his great prowess, benevolence, pleasant disposition, forbearance, handsome looks and his adherence to truth.
ramayan::138.english_translation: He described Rama's birth, his great prowess, his universal goodwill, his popularity with the people, his forbearance, gentleness, and truthfulness.
ramayan::138.translation_literal: जन्म (birth) / रामस्य (of Rama) / सुमहद्वीर्यं (great prowess) / सर्वानुकूलताम् (universal goodwill) / लोकस्य (of the people) / प्रियताम् (popularity, being dear) / क्षान्तिं (forbearance) / सौम्यतां (gentleness) / सत्यशीलताम् (truthful conduct)
ramayan::138.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::138.essence: Rama’s power mattered because it was joined to gentleness and truth.
ramayan::138.simple_meaning: Rama is described as powerful, kind, patient, gentle, and truthful. His greatness is shown as a full human character, not just one heroic trait.
ramayan::138.simple_insight: Real strength includes warmth, restraint, and honesty.
ramayan::138.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is laying out the qualities that make Rama worth singing about: his birth, force, popularity, patience, gentleness, and truthfulness. This is the portrait the whole epic will keep testing under pressure.
ramayan::138.modern_relevance: A leader wins applause by being sharp, but people trust the one who is steady, kind, and honest when pressure rises.
ramayan::138.insight: It teaches you to measure greatness by character, not just achievement.

ramayan::139.verse_sanskrit: नानाचित्रकथाश्चान्या विश्वामित्रसमागमे । जानक्याश्च विवाहं च धनुषश्च विभेदनम् । । 1311 । ।
ramayan::139.verse_hindi: (He described) Ramas association with Viswamitra, a variety of wonderful stories, the breaking of the great bow and his (Ramas) marriage with Janaki.
ramayan::139.english_translation: He described Rama's association with Vishvamitra, many wonderful stories, the breaking of the great bow, and Janaki's marriage.
ramayan::139.translation_literal: नानाचित्रकथाः (many wonderful stories) / च (and) / अन्याः (other) / विश्वामित्रसमागमे (in the meeting with Vishvamitra) / जानक्याः (of Janaki) / च (and) / विवाहम् (marriage) / च (and) / धनुषः (of the bow) / च (and) / विभेदनम् (breaking)
ramayan::139.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::139.essence: Rama's story turns on a few irreversible moments.
ramayan::139.simple_meaning: The verse lists key events from Rama's life: his meeting with Vishvamitra, the bow-breaking, and his marriage to Janaki.
ramayan::139.simple_insight: Great lives are remembered through the moments that changed everything.
ramayan::139.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is summarising the epic's early turning points: Rama meets Vishvamitra, performs wondrous deeds, breaks Shiva's bow, and wins Janaki in marriage. It is a catalogue of the story's major milestones, not a separate teaching.
ramayan::139.modern_relevance: A biography often feels like a list until you reach the few moments that changed a whole life: the mentor, the test, the marriage, the turning point. This verse gathers those turning points together.
ramayan::139.insight: It shifts attention from continuous life to the decisive events that define a person.

ramayan::140.verse_sanskrit: रामरामविवादं च गुणान्दाशरथेस्तथा । तथाऽभिषेकं रामस्य कैकेय्या दुष्टभावताम् । । 1312 । ।
ramayan::140.verse_hindi: (He described) Ramas altercation with Parasurama, his noble qualities, the preparations for his coronation and the wicked nature of Kaikeyi.
ramayan::140.english_translation: (He described) Rama's altercation with Parashurama, his noble qualities, the preparations for his coronation, and the wicked nature of Kaikeyi.
ramayan::140.translation_literal: रामरामविवादं (the dispute between Rama and Rama) / च (and) / गुणान् (qualities) / दाशरथेः (of Dasharatha's son) / तथा (also) / तथा (and so) / अभिषेकं (coronation) / रामस्य (of Rama) / कैकेय्याः (of Kaikeyi) / दुष्टभावताम् (wicked nature)
ramayan::140.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::140.essence: A king's rise, and the betrayal waiting behind it, are both named at once.
ramayan::140.simple_meaning: The verse lists events and traits already being narrated: Rama's clash with Parashurama, his virtues, the planned coronation, and Kaikeyi's malicious turn.
ramayan::140.simple_insight: It is a bridge in the story, not a teaching on its own.
ramayan::140.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is summarizing the span of events he has covered: Rama's meeting with Parashurama, his admirable qualities, the hope of coronation, and the first shadow of Kaikeyi's betrayal. It functions as a catalog inside the larger narration.
ramayan::140.insight: It keeps the story moving by naming the key turns before the exile begins.

ramayan::141.verse_sanskrit: विघातं चाभिषेकस्य राघवस्य विवासनम् । राज्ञश्शोकविलापं च परलोकस्य चाश्रयम् । । 1313 । ।
ramayan::141.verse_hindi: (He described) the obstacles to the coronation of Rama, his departure to the forest, the wailing and death of king Dasaratha with sorrow.
ramayan::141.english_translation: He described the obstacles to Rama's coronation, his exile to the forest, the king's sorrowful lamentation and death, and his departure for the next world.
ramayan::141.translation_literal: विघातं (obstacles) / च (and) / अभिषेकस्य (of the coronation) / राघवस्य (of Rama) / विवासनम् (exile) / राज्ञः (of the king) / शोकविलापं (sorrowful lamentation) / च (and) / परलोकस्य (of the other world) / च (and) / आश्रयम् (departure)
ramayan::141.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::141.essence: One blocked coronation leads straight into exile, grief, and death.
ramayan::141.simple_meaning: The verse lists the disasters that followed the blocked coronation: Rama went to the forest, Dasharatha grieved, and the king died.
ramayan::141.simple_insight: A single broken promise can unravel an entire kingdom.
ramayan::141.detailed_meaning: In Ayodhya, the promised coronation collapses. Rama is sent into exile, Dasharatha is crushed by grief, and the royal house begins to break apart. This verse is one link in a larger summary of the tragedy.
ramayan::141.modern_relevance: A family message arrives at midnight and changes everything: one decision has undone months of careful plans. The shock is not only the loss, but how quickly grief spreads through everyone connected to it.
ramayan::141.insight: It turns attention to the chain reaction that follows one unjust decision.

ramayan::142.verse_sanskrit: प्रकृतीनां विषादं च प्रकृतीनां विसर्जनम् । निषादाधिपसंवादं सूतोपावर्तनं तथा । । 1314 । ।
ramayan::142.verse_hindi: (He described) the grief of people of Ayodhya and his (Ramas) abandoning them and his (Ramas) conversation with Guha, the ruler of nishadas, the charioteer (Sumantra)s return (after leaving Rama in the forest).
ramayan::142.english_translation: (He described) the grief of Ayodhya's people, Rama's leaving them, his conversation with Guha, the ruler of the Nishadas, and the charioteer Sumantra's return after leaving Rama in the forest.
ramayan::142.translation_literal: प्रकृतीनां (of the people) / विषादं (grief) / च (and) / प्रकृतीनां (of the people) / विसर्जनम् (abandoning) / निषादाधिपसंवादं (conversation with the ruler of the Nishadas) / सूतोपावर्तनं (the charioteer's return) / तथा (and also)
ramayan::142.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::142.essence: Exile has already begun to separate everyone who loves him.
ramayan::142.simple_meaning: Ayodhya grieves as Rama leaves, meets Guha, and Sumantra returns alone after taking him to the forest.
ramayan::142.simple_insight: A departure can wound an entire city, not just the one who leaves.
ramayan::142.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is listing the next movements of the exile: Ayodhya's people sink into grief, Rama parts from them, meets Guha the Nishada chief, and Sumantra returns after leaving him in the forest. It is a bridge verse, not a teaching.
ramayan::142.modern_relevance: The train pulls away and the platform stays behind in silence. One decision has just split a family, a routine, and a whole sense of home.
ramayan::142.insight: It marks the emotional cost of exile and the first human bonds formed outside Ayodhya.

ramayan::143.verse_sanskrit: गङ्गायाश्चापि सन्तारं भरद्वाजस्य दर्शनम् । भरद्वाजाभ्यनुज्ञानाच्चित्रकूटस्य दर्शनम् । । 1315 । ।
ramayan::143.verse_hindi: (He described) Rama, Lakshmana and Sita ferrying the river Ganges, the visit to holy sage Bharadwaja and the departure to Chitrakuta mountain.
ramayan::143.english_translation: He described Rama, Lakshmana, and Sita crossing the Ganges, meeting the sage Bharadwaja, and reaching Chitrakuta with Bharadwaja's blessing.
ramayan::143.translation_literal: गङ्गायाः (of the Ganges) / च अपि (and also) / सन्तारम् (crossing over) / भरद्वाजस्य (of Bharadwaja) / दर्शनम् (meeting/seeing) / भरद्वाज-अभ्यनुज्ञानात् (with Bharadwaja's permission/blessing) / चित्रकूटस्य (of Chitrakuta) / दर्शनम् (seeing/reaching)
ramayan::143.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::143.essence: The journey continues under blessing, not ease.
ramayan::143.simple_meaning: Rama, Lakshmana, and Sita cross the Ganges, meet Bharadwaja, and continue toward Chitrakuta with his blessing.
ramayan::143.simple_insight: The exile keeps moving forward, step by step, with no turning back.
ramayan::143.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is still listing the stages of Rama's exile: the river crossing, the visit to sage Bharadwaja, and the move toward Chitrakuta. It is a connective verse, not a teaching verse, carrying the story from one place to the next.
ramayan::143.insight: It marks the next turn in Rama's exile, not a separate lesson.

ramayan::144.verse_sanskrit: वास्तुकर्म निवेशं च भरतागमनं तथा । प्रसादनं च रामस्य पितुश्च सलिलक्रियाम् । । 1316 । ।
ramayan::144.verse_hindi: (He described) the making of, and dwelling in, a hut, the arrival of Bharata, Bharatas persuasion to Rama (to return to the kingdom), and Ramas performance the funeral ablution for his father.
ramayan::144.english_translation: (He described) the making of, and dwelling in, a hut, the arrival of Bharata, Bharata's persuasion to Rama to return to the kingdom, and Rama's performance of the funeral ablution for his father.
ramayan::144.translation_literal: वास्तु-कर्‍म (making of a dwelling) / निवेशं (settling, dwelling) / च (and) / भरत-आगमनं (Bharata's arrival) / तथा (and also) / प्रसादनं (persuasion, appeasement) / च (and) / रामस्य (of Rama) / पितुः (of the father) / च (and) / सलिल-क्रियाम् (funeral water-rite, ablution)
ramayan::144.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::144.essence: Grief, duty, and family loyalty meet in one brief stretch of exile.
ramayan::144.simple_meaning: The verse lists the next events: building a hut, Bharata arriving, Bharata asking Rama to return, and Rama performing his father's funeral rites.
ramayan::144.simple_insight: Some moments in exile are not dramatic battles, but the heavy duties that follow loss.
ramayan::144.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is summarizing the exile episode around Chitrakuta. Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana live in a hut when Bharata arrives to plead for Rama's return. The verse also marks Rama's duty to honor Dasharatha with funeral rites, binding grief, loyalty, and kingship together.
ramayan::144.modern_relevance: You are unpacking boxes in a temporary room when family news arrives, and grief suddenly shares space with practical duties. Some seasons ask you to keep moving while your heart is still elsewhere.
ramayan::144.insight: It shifts attention from grand conflict to the obligations that remain after a loss.

ramayan::145.verse_sanskrit: पादुकाग्र्याभिषेकं च नन्दिग्रामनिवासनम् । दण्डकारण्यगमनं विराधस्य वधं तथा । । 1317 । ।
ramayan::145.verse_hindi: (He described) the installation of sandals (of Rama as the symbol of authority),  Bharata is residing at Nandigrama (and his ruling the kingdom from there), Ramas departure for Dandakaranya, and the killing of Viradha.
ramayan::145.english_translation: The installation of Rama's sandals, Bharata's stay at Nandigrama, Rama's departure for Dandakaranya, and the killing of Viradha.
ramayan::145.translation_literal: पादुकाग्र्याभिषेकं (the installation of the foremost sandals) / च (and) / नन्दिग्रामनिवासनम् (dwelling at Nandigrama) / दण्डकारण्यगमनं (going to Dandakaranya) / विराधस्य (of Viradha) / वधं (killing) / तथा (and also)
ramayan::145.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::145.essence: The exile deepens as Rama's authority and danger both take shape.
ramayan::145.simple_meaning: This is a summary of events: Bharata keeps Rama's sandals as the sign of rule, Rama goes to Dandaka forest, and Viradha is slain.
ramayan::145.simple_insight: The story moves forward through duty, exile, and danger.
ramayan::145.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is listing the next turning points in the exile narrative: Bharata rules from Nandigrama through Rama's sandals, while Rama enters Dandakaranya and meets violent resistance in Viradha. It is scene-setting, not a teaching verse.
ramayan::145.insight: It marks the transition from separation into the forest's harsher trials.

ramayan::146.verse_sanskrit: दर्शनं शरभङ्गस्य सुतीक्ष्णेन समागमम् । अनसूयासहास्यामप्यङ्गरागस्य चार्पणम् । । 1318 । ।
ramayan::146.verse_hindi: (He described) Ramas meeting with (sage) Sarabhanga and his arrival at Sutikshnas, Sitas companionship with Anasuya and anointing of fragrant unguents to her body.
ramayan::146.english_translation: He described Rama's meeting with Sarabhanga, his arrival at Sutikshna's hermitage, Sita's meeting with Anasuya, and Anasuya's application of fragrant unguents to Sita's body.
ramayan::146.translation_literal: दर्शनं (meeting/seeing) / शरभङ्गस्य (of Sarabhanga) / सुतीक्ष्णेन (with Sutikshna) / समागमम् (meeting/arrival) / अनसूया-सहास्याम् (with Anasuya, smiling) / अपि (also) / अङ्गरागस्य (of fragrant unguent) / च (and) / अर्पणम् (application/offering)
ramayan::146.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::146.essence: The forest journey unfolds through a series of remembered encounters.
ramayan::146.simple_meaning: The verse lists several encounters from Rama and Sita's forest journey: meetings with sages, and Anasuya gently adorning Sita.
ramayan::146.simple_insight: A journey is also made of the people who receive you along the way.
ramayan::146.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is summarizing the forest chapter's sequence of sacred encounters: Rama meets Sarabhanga and Sutikshna, while Sita meets Anasuya, who honors her with fragrant unguents. It is a transition verse, not a teaching.
ramayan::146.modern_relevance: A long trip can feel like one blur until you remember the faces that marked it — the host who welcomed you, the elder who blessed you, the person who made you feel seen.
ramayan::146.insight: It organizes the narrative as a chain of meetings, not a single lesson.

ramayan::147.verse_sanskrit: अगस्त्यदर्शनं चैव जटायोरभिसङ्गमम् । पञ्चवट्याश्च गमनं शूर्पणख्याश्च दर्शनम् । । 1319 । ।
ramayan::147.verse_hindi: (He described) the departure of Rama for Panchavati, the interview with sage Agastya, the  meeting with Jatayu and the appearance of Surpanakha.
ramayan::147.english_translation: (He described) Rama's departure for Panchavati, the meeting with sage Agastya, the encounter with Jatayu, and the sighting of Surpanakha.
ramayan::147.translation_literal: अगस्त्यदर्शनं (meeting with Agastya) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / जटायोः (of Jatayu) / अभिसङ्गमम् (meeting, encounter) / पञ्चवट्याः (to Panchavati) / च (and) / गमनं (going, departure) / शूर्पणख्याः (of Surpanakha) / च (and) / दर्शनम् (sighting, appearance)
ramayan::147.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::147.essence: A journey can look like a list until one encounter changes everything.
ramayan::147.simple_meaning: The verse lists key events in Rama's journey: he goes to Panchavati, meets Agastya, meets Jatayu, and sees Surpanakha.
ramayan::147.simple_insight: Some verses simply move the story forward, marking the turning points that lead to later conflict.
ramayan::147.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is summarizing the middle of Rama's forest exile: the move to Panchavati, Agastya's blessing, Jatayu's later meeting, and Surpanakha's appearance. It is a bridge verse, not a teaching verse, preparing for the events that follow.
ramayan::147.modern_relevance: A chapter in your life can be remembered as a sequence of encounters: one move, one meeting, one stranger, and then everything changes.
ramayan::147.insight: It marks the transition from exile into the events that will trigger the war in Lanka.

ramayan::148.verse_sanskrit: शूर्पणख्याश्च संवादं विरूपकरणं तथा । वधं खरत्रिशिरसोरुत्थानं रावणस्य च । । 1320 । ।
ramayan::148.verse_hindi: (He described) Ramas dialogue with Surpanakha, her disfigurement, the slaughter of Khara and Trisira, and the beginning of efforts by Ravana (to harm Rama).
ramayan::148.english_translation: (He described) Rama's dialogue with Surpanakha, her disfigurement, the slaughter of Khara and Trisira, and the beginning of Ravana's hostile efforts.
ramayan::148.translation_literal: शूर्पणख्याः (of Surpanakha) / च (and) / संवादम् (dialogue) / विरूपकरणम् (disfigurement) / तथा (and so) / वधम् (slaughter) / खरत्रिशिरसोः (of Khara and Trisira) / उत्थानम् (arising/beginning) / रावणस्य (of Ravana) / च (and)
ramayan::148.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::148.essence: A single insult can set off an entire war of retaliation.
ramayan::148.simple_meaning: The verse lists the chain of events that follows Surpanakha's encounter: insult, violence, and Ravana's hostile response.
ramayan::148.simple_insight: A small provocation can trigger a larger collapse when pride answers pain.
ramayan::148.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is summarizing the turning points of the Aranya Kanda: Rama's exchange with Surpanakha, her mutilation, the killing of Khara and Trisira, and Ravana's reaction. It is a bridge verse, not a teaching verse.
ramayan::148.modern_relevance: A sharp comment in a family argument can turn into weeks of silence, then a bigger fight nobody wanted. One wound, left to pride, keeps multiplying.
ramayan::148.insight: It marks the escalation from insult to retaliation, showing how quickly wounded ego turns into conflict.

ramayan::149.verse_sanskrit: मारीचस्य वधं चैव वैदेह्या हरणं तथा । राघवस्य विलापं च गृध्रराजनिबर्हणम् । । 1321 । ।
ramayan::149.verse_hindi: (He described) the killing of Maricha, the abduction of Sita, Ramas lamentation (over his separation from Sita), and the death of Jatayu.
ramayan::149.english_translation: (He described) the killing of Maricha, the abduction of Sita, Rama's lamentation over separation from Sita, and the death of Jatayu.
ramayan::149.translation_literal: मारीचस्य (of Maricha) / वधं (killing) / चैव (and also) / वैदेह्या (of Vaidehi, Sita) / हरणं (abduction) / तथा (and) / राघवस्य (of Rama) / विलापं (lamentation) / च (and) / गृध्रराजनिबर्हणम् (the killing of the king of vultures, Jatayu)
ramayan::149.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::149.essence: One abduction turns a forest exile into irreversible grief.
ramayan::149.simple_meaning: The verse lists key events in the forest exile: Maricha is killed, Sita is taken away, Rama grieves, and Jatayu dies.
ramayan::149.simple_insight: A chain of loss begins here, and each event deepens the wound.
ramayan::149.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is reciting the sequence of the forest crisis: Maricha is slain, Sita is carried off, Rama breaks into grief, and Jatayu falls. It is not a teaching verse, but a compact summary of the turning point that drives the exile deeper into tragedy.
ramayan::149.modern_relevance: A day can split open like this: one wrong move, then the fallout, then the grief, then the damage you cannot undo.
ramayan::149.insight: It helps you see how one act of violence can trigger a whole chain of irreversible consequences.

ramayan::150.verse_sanskrit: कबन्धदर्शनं चापि पम्पायाश्चापि दर्शनम् । शबर्या: दर्शनं चैव हनूमद्दर्शनं तथा । । 1322 । ।
ramayan::150.verse_hindi: (He described) Ramas encounter with Kabandha, the viewing of river Pampa, the meeting with Sabari and Hanuman.
ramayan::150.english_translation: (He described) Rama's encounter with Kabandha, the sight of Pampa, the meeting with Sabari, and the meeting with Hanuman.
ramayan::150.translation_literal: कबन्धदर्शनं (the sight of Kabandha) / चापि (and also) / पम्पायाः (of Pampa) / चापि (and also) / दर्शनम् (sight) / शबर्याः (of Sabari) / दर्शनं (sight) / चैव (and also) / हनूमद्दर्शनं (meeting with Hanuman) / तथा (likewise)
ramayan::150.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::150.essence: The road to rescue is built from unexpected meetings.
ramayan::150.simple_meaning: The verse lists key moments from Rama's journey: Kabandha, Pampa, Sabari, and Hanuman.
ramayan::150.simple_insight: Some journeys are marked by the people you meet along the way.
ramayan::150.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is summarizing the middle stretch of Rama's exile: the strange encounter with Kabandha, the arrival at Pampa, the blessing of Sabari, and the first meeting with Hanuman. Each meeting moves the story toward alliance and rescue.
ramayan::150.modern_relevance: A difficult season can feel like random stops and detours, until later you see they were the turning points. The people you meet on the way can change the whole direction of your life.
ramayan::150.insight: It frames the exile as a chain of encounters that prepare Rama for the larger mission ahead.

ramayan::151.verse_sanskrit: ऋश्यमूकस्य गमनं सुग्रीवेण समागमम् । प्रत्ययोत्पादनं सख्यं वालिसुग्रीवविग्रहम् । । 1323 । ।
ramayan::151.verse_hindi: (He described) Ramas departure for Rishyamuka mountain, his meeting with Sugriva
ramayan::151.english_translation: (He described) Rama's departure for Rishyamuka mountain, his meeting with Sugriva, the building of trust, the friendship, and the conflict between Vali and Sugriva.
ramayan::151.translation_literal: ऋश्यमूकस्य (of Rishyamuka) / गमनं (going) / सुग्रीवेण (with Sugriva) / समागमम् (meeting) / प्रत्ययोत्पादनं (the producing of trust) / सख्यं (friendship) / वालिसुग्रीवविग्रहम् (the conflict of Vali and Sugriva)
ramayan::151.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::151.essence: Trust turns strangers into allies before the real conflict begins.
ramayan::151.simple_meaning: Rama goes to Rishyamuka, meets Sugriva, and begins the trust and friendship that will shape the alliance against Vali.
ramayan::151.simple_insight: A life-changing alliance often begins with one meeting and a small act of trust.
ramayan::151.detailed_meaning: The story has moved from Hanuman's search to the meeting on Rishyamuka mountain. Rama and Sugriva come together, trust begins to form, and the long conflict with Vali enters the center of the epic. This line is a scene marker, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::151.modern_relevance: You take one careful meeting with someone you barely know, and suddenly a larger struggle has a shape. Trust starts there.
ramayan::151.insight: It frames alliance as the turning point that makes action possible.

ramayan::152.verse_sanskrit: वालिप्रमथनं चैव सुग्रीवप्रतिपादनम् । ताराविलापं समयं वर्षरात्रनिवासनम् । । 1324 । ।
ramayan::152.verse_hindi: (He described) the killing of Vali (by Rama), the installation of Sugriva, the mourning of Tara, the waiting (for the search of Sita as per the pact of friendship with Sugriva), and the sojourn on the mountain during the rainy season.
ramayan::152.english_translation: (He described) the killing of Vali by Rama, the installation of Sugriva, the mourning of Tara, the waiting period under the pact of friendship, and the stay on the mountain during the rainy season.
ramayan::152.translation_literal: वालिप्रमथनं (the slaying of Vali) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / सुग्रीवप्रतिपादनम् (the establishing of Sugriva) / ताराविलापं (the lament of Tara) / समयं (the pact / agreed time) / वर्षरात्रनिवासनम् (dwelling through the rainy season on the mountain)
ramayan::152.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::152.essence: A chain of events is being recounted, not a teaching offered.
ramayan::152.simple_meaning: This is a scene list, not a teaching: Vali is killed, Sugriva is installed, Tara grieves, and the agreed waiting period passes during the rains.
ramayan::152.simple_insight: Some verses simply move the story forward without pausing to teach.
ramayan::152.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is summarizing the Kishkindha sequence: Rama kills Vali, Sugriva takes the throne, Tara mourns, and the allies wait through the rainy season under their pact. The verse functions as a bridge between events, not a standalone reflection.
ramayan::152.insight: It marks a transition in the story rather than a principle to apply.

ramayan::153.verse_sanskrit: कोपं राघवसिंहस्य बलानामुपसङ्ग्रहम् । दिश: प्रस्थापनं चैव पृथिव्याश्च निवेदनम् । । 1325 । ।
ramayan::153.verse_hindi: (He described) the anger of Rama, the lion in the race of the Raghus (over the delay by Sugriva), the consolidation of the monkey forces, the despatch of envoys to different directions, the report (about the different places) on earth.
ramayan::153.english_translation: (He described) the anger of Rama, the lion of the Raghu race, over Sugriva's delay; the gathering of the monkey forces; the sending of envoys in all directions; and the report about the lands of the earth.
ramayan::153.translation_literal: कोपम् (anger) / राघवसिंहस्य (of Rama, the lion among the Raghus) / बलानाम् (of the forces) / उपसङ्ग्रहम् (gathering, consolidation) / दिशः (to the directions) / प्रस्थापनम् (sending forth) / च एव (and indeed) / पृथिव्याः (of the earth) / च (and) / निवेदनम् (reporting, informing)
ramayan::153.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::153.essence: Urgency turns a promise into a coordinated search.
ramayan::153.simple_meaning: Rama grows impatient with Sugriva, the monkey army is assembled, messengers are sent out, and the search begins across the land.
ramayan::153.simple_insight: Big goals still need coordination, urgency, and follow-through.
ramayan::153.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is summarizing the next stage after Rama's alliance with Sugriva. Rama's anger over delay pushes the plan forward, the monkey forces are gathered, and search parties are sent across the world. The rescue of Sita is now becoming an organised campaign.
ramayan::153.modern_relevance: You promised to help, but the deadline keeps slipping. Frustration rises, people are mobilised, and suddenly everyone is checking maps, calls, and contacts to make the plan real.
ramayan::153.insight: It shifts attention from intention alone to organised action under pressure.

ramayan::154.verse_sanskrit: अङ्गुलीयकदानं च ऋक्षस्य बिलदर्शनम् । प्रायोपवेशनं चापि सम्पातेश्चापि दर्शनम् । । 1326 । ।
ramayan::154.verse_hindi: (He described) the delivery of  the ring (to Hanuman by Rama), the entry into the cave of the riksha, the preparations for their fast unto death, and the meeting with Sampati.
ramayan::154.english_translation: He described the giving of the ring to Hanuman, the entry into the cave, the decision to fast unto death, and the meeting with Sampati.
ramayan::154.translation_literal: अङ्गुलीयकदानं (giving of the ring) / च (and) / ऋक्षस्य (of the bear) / बिलदर्शनम् (seeing the cave) / प्रायोपवेशनं (fast unto death) / चापि (and also) / सम्पातेः (of Sampati) / चापि (and also) / दर्शनम् (seeing)
ramayan::154.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::154.essence: A chain of events pushes the search toward revelation.
ramayan::154.simple_meaning: A list of events is being recounted: the ring is given to Hanuman, the cave is found, a fast unto death is begun, and Sampati is seen.
ramayan::154.simple_insight: Some moments matter because they move the story forward, not because they teach a lesson.
ramayan::154.detailed_meaning: This is part of a summary of Hanuman's search in the Kishkindha episode. The verse strings together key plot steps: Rama's ring, the cave, the vow of fasting, and Sampati's appearance. It advances the rescue story rather than offering a standalone teaching.
ramayan::154.insight: It functions as narrative bridge, linking one rescue step to the next.

ramayan::155.verse_sanskrit: पर्वतारोहणं चापि सागरस्यापि लङ्घनम् । समुद्रवचनाच्चैव मैनाकस्य च दर्शनम् । । 1327 । ।
ramayan::155.verse_hindi: (He described) the climbing of Mahendra mountain (by Hanuman), crossing the sea  emergence of Mainaka hill at the command of the lord of ocean.
ramayan::155.english_translation: (He described) the climbing of Mahendra mountain by Hanuman, the crossing of the sea, and the sight of Mainaka at the command of the lord of the ocean.
ramayan::155.translation_literal: पर्वतारोहणम् (mountain-climbing) / च (and) / अपि (also) / सागरस्य (of the sea) / अपि (also) / लङ्घनम् (crossing) / समुद्रवचनात् (at the ocean's command) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / मैनाकस्य (of Mainaka) / च (and) / दर्शनम् (sight)
ramayan::155.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::155.essence: Hanuman's journey is measured by impossible distances crossed, not comfort preserved.
ramayan::155.simple_meaning: Hanuman climbs a mountain, crosses the sea, and sees Mainaka rise before him.
ramayan::155.simple_insight: Great effort can meet unexpected help along the way.
ramayan::155.detailed_meaning: Hanuman is already in motion toward Lanka. This line is part of a rapid inventory of his feats: the mountain climb, the sea crossing, and Mainaka's appearance. It supports the larger account of his journey rather than offering a separate teaching.
ramayan::155.modern_relevance: You finally start the hard thing, and the route keeps changing under you — stairs, ferry, detour, surprise help. The work is still yours to cross.
ramayan::155.insight: It frames progress as a sequence of obstacles met one by one.

ramayan::156.verse_sanskrit: सिंहिकायाश्च निधनं लङ्कामलयदर्शनम् । रात्रौ लङ्काप्रवेशं च एकस्याथ विचिन्तनम् । । 1328 । ।
ramayan::156.verse_hindi: (He described) the slaughter of (the female demon) Simhika, the viewing of in Lanka
ramayan::156.english_translation: (He described) the slaying of Simhika, the sight of Lanka and Malaya, the entry into Lanka at night, and the solitary contemplation.
ramayan::156.translation_literal: सिंहिकायाः (of Simhika) / च (and) / निधनम् (slaying) / लङ्का-मलय-दर्शनम् (seeing Lanka and Malaya) / रात्रौ (at night) / लङ्का-प्रवेशम् (entry into Lanka) / च (and) / एकस्य (of one alone) / अथ (then) / विचिन्तनम् (contemplation)
ramayan::156.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::156.essence: Hanuman's courage is shown in quiet, exact steps.
ramayan::156.simple_meaning: Hanuman kills Simhika, sees Lanka, enters the city at night, and moves forward alone, thinking carefully.
ramayan::156.simple_insight: Great courage is often quiet: one person, one night, one impossible task.
ramayan::156.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is listing Hanuman's successive feats as he reaches Lanka: defeating Simhika, seeing the city and its surroundings, slipping in after dark, and thinking alone before the next step. The verse is a link in the larger account, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::156.modern_relevance: You step into a new place after dark, alone, with no backup and no room for noise. The next move matters more than the fear.
ramayan::156.insight: It shifts attention from spectacle to disciplined, solitary action under pressure.

ramayan::157.verse_sanskrit: दर्शनं रावणस्यापि पुष्पकस्य च दर्शनम् । आपानभूमिगमनमवरोधस्य दर्शनम् । । 1329 । ।
ramayan::157.verse_hindi: (He described) the view of Ravana and the (aerial chariot), Pushpaka, (by Hanuman),
ramayan::157.english_translation: He described the sight of Ravana, the sight of Pushpaka, and the sight of the women’s quarters.
ramayan::157.translation_literal: दर्शनम् (sight) / रावणस्य (of Ravana) / अपि (also) / पुष्पकस्य (of Pushpaka) / च (and) / दर्शनम् (sight) / आपानभूमि-गमनम् (going to the drinking-hall area) / अवरोधस्य (of the women’s quarters) / दर्शनम् (sight)
ramayan::157.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::157.essence: The search is still unfolding; the key meeting has not happened yet.
ramayan::157.simple_meaning: Hanuman sees Ravana, Pushpaka, and the women’s quarters while moving through Lanka. The verse is part of a sequence listing what he observed.
ramayan::157.simple_insight: Not every step is a lesson; some verses simply carry the journey forward.
ramayan::157.detailed_meaning: Hanuman is moving alone through Lanka at night, taking in every crucial sight: Ravana, the Pushpaka chariot, and the women’s quarters. The poem is still building the scene before Sita is found, so this verse functions as a link in the larger search.
ramayan::157.modern_relevance: You can be in the middle of something important and still only be gathering details. Not every moment carries the main revelation yet.
ramayan::157.insight: It marks a stage in the search, not the discovery itself.

ramayan::158.verse_sanskrit: अशोकवनिकायानं सीतायाश्चपि दर्शनम् । अभिज्ञानप्रदानं च रावणस्य च दर्शनम् । । 1330 । ।
ramayan::158.verse_hindi: (He described) the entry (of Hanuman) into the Ashoka garden, the finding of Sita, the  presentation of the ring (as token of recognition by Hanuman) and the sight of Ravana.
ramayan::158.english_translation: He described Hanuman's entry into the Ashoka grove, the sight of Sita, the presentation of the ring as a token of recognition, and the sight of Ravana.
ramayan::158.translation_literal: अशोकवनिकायानम् (entry into the Ashoka grove) / सीतायाः (of Sita) / च अपि (and also) / दर्शनम् (sight) / अभिज्ञान-प्रदानम् (presentation of the token of recognition) / च (and) / रावणस्य (of Ravana) / च (and) / दर्शनम् (sight)
ramayan::158.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::158.essence: Hanuman's search becomes proof, and proof becomes danger.
ramayan::158.simple_meaning: Hanuman enters the Ashoka grove, finds Sita, gives her the ring, and sees Ravana.
ramayan::158.simple_insight: The mission reaches its turning point: proof is given, and the enemy is finally seen.
ramayan::158.detailed_meaning: In Lanka, Hanuman has already crossed the sea and slipped past danger. Now he enters the Ashoka grove, finds Sita, shows her Rama's ring, and also sees Ravana. This is part of the unfolding reconnaissance, not a standalone teaching.
ramayan::158.modern_relevance: You finally reach the person you came to help, and the proof you carried matters more than any speech. The real test is still ahead.
ramayan::158.insight: It shows how a mission moves from searching to confirmation to confrontation.

ramayan::159.verse_sanskrit: राक्षसीतर्जनं चैव त्रिजटास्वप्नदर्शनम् । मणिप्रदानं सीताया वृक्षभङ्गं तथैव च । । 1331 । ।
ramayan::159.verse_hindi: (He described) threatenings of the demonesses, (the narration of) dream by Trijata,
ramayan::159.english_translation: (He described) the threats of the demonesses, the narration of Trijata's dream, the giving of the jewel to Sita, and the breaking of the tree.
ramayan::159.translation_literal: राक्षसीतर्जनं (threatening of demonesses) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / त्रिजटास्वप्नदर्शनम् (seeing of Trijata's dream) / मणिप्रदानं (giving of the jewel) / सीतायाः (of Sita) / वृक्षभङ्गं (breaking of the tree) / तथा (also) / एव (indeed) / च (and)
ramayan::159.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::159.essence: A scene is being cataloged, not interpreted.
ramayan::159.simple_meaning: Hanuman's visit to Ashoka grove is being summarized: the demonesses threatened Sita, Trijata had a dream, Sita received a jewel, and a tree was broken.
ramayan::159.simple_insight: The scene is being recounted in pieces, not teaching a lesson.
ramayan::159.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is listing the events Hanuman saw in Lanka's Ashoka grove: the demonesses' threats, Trijata's dream, Sita receiving the token, and the tree being broken. It is a chain of dramatic details inside Hanuman's report, not a complete teaching on its own.
ramayan::159.insight: It functions as a narrative link in a larger sequence, not a standalone reflection.

ramayan::160.verse_sanskrit: राक्षसीविद्रवं चैव किङ्कराणां निबर्हणम् । ग्रहणं वायुसूनोश्च लङ्कादाहाभिगर्जनम् । । 1332 । ।
ramayan::160.verse_hindi: (He described) the flight of the female demons, the killing of the servants (of Ravana),
ramayan::160.english_translation: (He described) the flight of the female demons, the killing of the servants of Ravana, the capture of the son of the Wind, and the roaring of Lanka's burning.
ramayan::160.translation_literal: राक्षसीविद्रवम् (the flight of the female demons) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / किङ्कराणाम् (of the servants) / निबर्हणम् (the killing) / ग्रहणम् (the capture) / वायुसूनोः (of the son of the Wind) / च (and) / लङ्कादाहाभिगर्जनम् (the roaring of Lanka's burning)
ramayan::160.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::160.essence: Hanuman's presence turns Lanka's confidence into panic.
ramayan::160.simple_meaning: Hanuman's rampage in Lanka is being described: the female demons flee, Ravana's servants are killed, Hanuman is seized, and Lanka burns as he roars.
ramayan::160.simple_insight: Some victories are so complete that even the enemy's fear becomes part of the story.
ramayan::160.detailed_meaning: In the Sundara Kanda, the narration is still moving through Hanuman's night inside Lanka. The Ashoka grove, Sita, Trijata, and Ravana have already been mentioned. This verse adds the next burst of action: panic among the demons, dead guards, Hanuman's capture, and the roar of a city in flames.
ramayan::160.modern_relevance: A crisis spirals in seconds: security rushes in, alarms blare, messages flood your phone, and the room that felt controlled a minute ago is suddenly chaos.
ramayan::160.insight: It keeps the focus on unstoppable momentum rather than a single isolated act.

ramayan::161.verse_sanskrit: प्रतिप्लवनमेवाथ मधूनां हरणं तथा । राघवाश्वासनं चापि मणिनिर्यातनं तथा । । 1333 । ।
ramayan::161.verse_hindi: (He described) Hanuman crossing the ocean back, forcibly seizing the Madhu forest and enjoying honey, informing Rama about Sita and consoling him and delivering the gem.
ramayan::161.english_translation: (He described) Hanuman crossing the ocean back, forcibly seizing the Madhu forest and enjoying honey, informing Rama about Sita and consoling him and delivering the gem.
ramayan::161.translation_literal: प्रतिप्लवनम् (crossing back) / एव (indeed) / अथ (then) / मधूनाम् (of the honey-sweet grove) / हरणम् (seizing) / तथा (and) / राघवाश्वासनम् (consoling Rama) / च (and) / अपि (also) / मणिनिर्यातनम् (delivering the gem) / तथा (and)
ramayan::161.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::161.essence: Hanuman’s return mattered as much as his crossing.
ramayan::161.simple_meaning: Hanuman returns after his mission, raids the Madhu grove, brings back honey, comforts Rama with news of Sita, and hands over the gem.
ramayan::161.simple_insight: Even a finished mission still carries the weight of what was found, lost, and brought back.
ramayan::161.detailed_meaning: In the Sundara Kanda, Hanuman has already found Sita in Lanka and now returns to Rama. This verse is one item in a longer list of what he did on the way back: crossing the sea, taking honey from Madhuvana, reassuring Rama, and delivering Sita’s token.
ramayan::161.modern_relevance: You come back from a hard errand with the message, the proof, and the emotional fallout. The task may be done, but the impact is still landing.
ramayan::161.insight: It shifts attention from heroic action alone to the full aftermath of service: report, reassurance, and responsibility.

ramayan::162.verse_sanskrit: सङ्गमं च समुद्रेण नलसेतोश्च बन्धनम् । प्रतारं च समुद्रस्य रात्रौ लङ्कावरोधनम् । । 1334 । ।
ramayan::162.verse_hindi: (He described) the meeting with the (lord of the) seas, the construction of bridge by
ramayan::162.english_translation: The meeting with the sea, the building of Nala's bridge, the crossing of the ocean, and the night siege of Lanka.
ramayan::162.translation_literal: सङ्गमम् (meeting) / च (and) / समुद्रेण (with the sea) / नलसेतोः (of Nala's bridge) / च (and) / बन्धनम् (building) / प्रतारम् (crossing) / च (and) / समुद्रस्य (of the sea) / रात्रौ (at night) / लङ्कावरोधनम् (the siege/blockade of Lanka)
ramayan::162.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::162.essence: A sequence of war actions is being recounted, not a separate teaching.
ramayan::162.simple_meaning: Hanuman's return journey is being described in a list of actions: reaching the sea, building the bridge, crossing it, and surrounding Lanka at night.
ramayan::162.simple_insight: The verse is part of a larger summary, not a complete teaching on its own.
ramayan::162.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is listing the major events of the war's closing movement: the sea is confronted, Nala's bridge is built, the ocean is crossed, and Lanka is surrounded at night. It reads like a catalog of deeds, not a standalone reflection.
ramayan::162.insight: It records events rather than offering a distinct lesson.

ramayan::163.verse_sanskrit: विभीषणेन संसर्गं वधोपायनिवेदनम् । कुम्भकर्णस्य निधनं मेघनादनिबर्हणम् । । 1335 । ।
ramayan::163.verse_hindi: (He described) the association with Vibhisana, disclosure of the means of destruction (of Ravana), the death of Kumbhakarna, and the killing of Meghanada.
ramayan::163.english_translation: He described the association with Vibhishana, the disclosure of the means of Ravana's destruction, the death of Kumbhakarna, and the killing of Meghanada.
ramayan::163.translation_literal: विभीषणेन (with Vibhishana) / संसर्गं (association) / वधोपायनिवेदनम् (disclosure of the means of destruction) / कुम्भकर्णस्य (of Kumbhakarna) / निधनं (death) / मेघनादनिबर्हणम् (the killing of Meghanada)
ramayan::163.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::163.essence: Ravana's fall begins when his own side starts breaking apart.
ramayan::163.simple_meaning: This is a scene summary: Vibhishana joins Rama, the way to defeat Ravana is revealed, and Ravana's key warriors fall.
ramayan::163.simple_insight: The verse moves the war forward by listing the turning points that break Ravana's side.
ramayan::163.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is summarizing the final stretch of the war. Vibhishana joins Rama, the strategy to end Ravana's rule is disclosed, and Kumbhakarna and Meghanada are killed. It is part of a larger sequence of victory, not a teaching on its own.
ramayan::163.modern_relevance: A project reaches the stage where one trusted ally, one clear plan, and two decisive setbacks change everything. The real shift is already underway before anyone announces the result.
ramayan::163.insight: It frames victory as a chain of turning points, not a single dramatic moment.

ramayan::164.verse_sanskrit: रावणस्य विनाशं च सीतावाप्तिमरे: पुरे । विभीषणाभिषेकं च पुष्पकस्य च दर्शनम् । । 1336 । ।
ramayan::164.verse_hindi: (He described) Ravanas destruction, the reunion with Sita in the enemycity, the coronation of Vibhishana and the sighting of Pushpaka.
ramayan::164.english_translation: Ravana's destruction, the reunion with Sita in the enemy city, the coronation of Vibhishana, and the sight of Pushpaka.
ramayan::164.translation_literal: रावणस्य (of Ravana) / विनाशं (destruction) / च (and) / सीतावाप्तिम् (the obtaining of Sita; reunion with Sita) / अरेः पुरे (in the enemy's city) / विभीषणाभिषेकं (the coronation of Vibhishana) / च (and) / पुष्पकस्य (of Pushpaka) / च (and) / दर्शनम् (sighting)
ramayan::164.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::164.essence: The war ends by restoring what was broken, not just by defeating Ravana.
ramayan::164.simple_meaning: The verse lists the major outcomes of the war: Ravana falls, Sita is found, Vibhishana is crowned, and Pushpaka is seen.
ramayan::164.simple_insight: Victory is not just defeat of the enemy; it also restores right order.
ramayan::164.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is summarizing the end of the war: Ravana is destroyed, Sita is recovered in Lanka, Vibhishana is installed as king, and Pushpaka appears. It is a catalogue of triumphs, not a teaching verse.
ramayan::164.modern_relevance: You finish the hardest project of your life, then discover the real reward is not applause but repair: the broken trust, the lost bond, the rightful next step.
ramayan::164.insight: It shifts attention from one victory to the full restoration that follows it.

ramayan::165.verse_sanskrit: अयोध्यायाश्च गमनं भरतेन समागमम् । रामाभिषेकाभ्युदयं सर्वसैन्यविसर्जनम् । स्वराष्ट्ररञ्जनं चैव वैदेह्याश्च विसर्जनम् । । 1337 । ।
ramayan::165.verse_hindi: (He described) Ramas return to Ayodhya, the reunion with Bharata, the festive occasion of Ramas coronation disbanding the entire forces, keeping his subjects happy and banishing Sita (in the forest).
ramayan::165.english_translation: Rama's return to Ayodhya, his reunion with Bharata, his coronation, the disbanding of the entire army, the delight of his kingdom, and the banishment of Sita.
ramayan::165.translation_literal: अयोध्यायाः (of Ayodhya) / च (and) / गमनम् (going/return) / भरतेन (with Bharata) / समागमम् (meeting) / रामाभिषेकाभ्युदयम् (the auspicious coronation of Rama) / सर्वसैन्यविसर्जनम् (disbanding of all the army) / स्वराष्ट्ररञ्जनम् (delighting his own kingdom) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / वैदेह्याः (of Sita, daughter of Videha) / च (and) / विसर्जनम् (sending away/banishment)
ramayan::165.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::165.essence: Rama's triumph is inseparable from the wound that follows it.
ramayan::165.simple_meaning: The verse lists the later events of Rama's story: his return, reunion, coronation, the army's dismissal, the joy of the kingdom, and Sita's exile.
ramayan::165.simple_insight: Some victories arrive with a wound still open.
ramayan::165.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is closing the arc of Rama's story by listing the great events still to be sung in the later book: the return to Ayodhya, Bharata's reunion, the coronation, the army's dismissal, the kingdom's joy, and Sita's banishment. It is a summary, not a teaching.
ramayan::165.modern_relevance: A project finally succeeds, the team celebrates, and one painful decision still sits in the background. The public ending looks complete, but the private cost remains.
ramayan::165.insight: It frames victory and loss as part of the same historical moment, not separate stories.

ramayan::166.verse_sanskrit: अनागतं च यत्किञ्चिद्रामस्य वसुधातले । तच्चकारोत्तरे काव्ये वाल्मीकिर्भगवानृषि: । । 1338 । ।
ramayan::166.verse_hindi: Divine sage Valmiki composed events yet to happen on this earth in the history of Rama in Uttarakanda.
ramayan::166.english_translation: Divine sage Valmiki composed in the later book whatever had not yet happened on earth in Rama's story.
ramayan::166.translation_literal: अनागतं (not yet come) / च (and) / यत्किञ्चिद् (whatever) / रामस्य (of Rama) / वसुधातले (on the earth) / तत् (that) / चकार (composed) / उत्तरे (in the later) / काव्ये (poem) / वाल्मीकिः (Valmiki) / भगवान् (divine) / ऋषिः (sage)
ramayan::166.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::166.essence: Valmiki presents Rama's whole story as already complete.
ramayan::166.simple_meaning: Valmiki says he composed, in the later book, the events in Rama's story that had not yet happened on earth.
ramayan::166.simple_insight: The epic is being told as a complete vision, not just a record of what already occurred.
ramayan::166.detailed_meaning: The poem has reached its own self-description. Valmiki, speaking as the sage-poet, says that in the later book he also composed the future events of Rama's earthly story. It is a literary closing note, not a teaching verse.
ramayan::166.modern_relevance: A writer finishes the final chapter and realizes the whole arc was already alive in the first page. This line is that kind of backward-looking completion.
ramayan::166.insight: It frames the Ramayana as a single, fully held narrative from beginning to end.

ramayan::167.verse_sanskrit: 24000 प्राप्तराज्यस्य रामस्य वाल्मीकिर्भगवानृषि: । चकार चरितं कृत्स्नं विचित्रपदमात्मवान् । । 141 । ।
ramayan::167.verse_hindi: The divine sage Valmiki, composed in wonderful lines the entire lifestory of Rama who regained his kingdom.
ramayan::167.english_translation: The divine sage Valmiki composed the complete life story of Rama, who had regained his kingdom, in wondrous verses.
ramayan::167.translation_literal: चतुर्विंशत्सहस्राणि (twenty-four thousand) / प्राप्तराज्यस्य (of the one who regained the kingdom) / रामस्य (of Rama) / वाल्मीकिः (Valmiki) / भगवान् ऋषिः (the divine sage) / चकार (composed) / चरितं (the life story) / कृत्स्नं (complete) / विचित्रपदम् (in varied/wondrous lines) / आत्मवान् (self-possessed)
ramayan::167.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::167.essence: Valmiki turns Rama’s restored life into enduring form.
ramayan::167.simple_meaning: Valmiki composed the full story of Rama in beautiful, varied verses after Rama regained his kingdom.
ramayan::167.simple_insight: Great lives become lasting only when someone can shape them into words.
ramayan::167.detailed_meaning: The poem is closing its own frame. After the return to Ayodhya and Rama’s restoration, Valmiki steps back in as poet and records the whole life of Rama in crafted verse. This line is about the making of the epic itself, not a teaching inside the story.
ramayan::167.modern_relevance: You finish a long project and realize the real work was not only living it, but giving it shape so others can remember it.
ramayan::167.insight: It shifts attention from event to narration: meaning deepens when experience is carefully preserved.

ramayan::168.verse_sanskrit: चतुर्विंशत्सहस्राणि श्लोकानामुक्तवानृषि: । तथा सर्गशतान्पञ्च षट्काण्डानि तथोत्तरम् । । 142 । ।
ramayan::168.verse_hindi: Sage Valmiki composed the Ramayanam in twentyfour thousand verses in six kandas and also Uttarakanda (consisting of five hundred cantos).
ramayan::168.english_translation: Sage Valmiki composed the Ramayana in twenty-four thousand verses, six kandas, and also Uttarakanda.
ramayan::168.translation_literal: चतुर्विंशत् (twenty-four) / सहस्राणि (thousands) / श्लोकानाम् (of verses) / उक्तवान् (composed/spoke) / ऋषिः (sage) / तथा (also) / सर्गशतान् (hundreds of cantos) / पञ्च (five) / षट्काण्डानि (six kandas) / तथा (and) / उत्तरम् (Uttarakanda)
ramayan::168.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::168.essence: The epic’s grandeur begins with its vast, deliberate form.
ramayan::168.simple_meaning: Valmiki’s Ramayana is being described by its size and structure: 24,000 verses, six kandas, and Uttarakanda.
ramayan::168.simple_insight: Great works can be measured by their scope, not just their story.
ramayan::168.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is being praised as the poet who shaped Rama’s story into a vast, ordered epic. This verse gives the scale of the work itself — how many verses it contains and how it is divided — rather than offering a teaching or emotional turning point.
ramayan::168.modern_relevance: You open a manuscript and realize the project was never small. Before the meaning lands, you feel the sheer discipline it took to build something this large.
ramayan::168.insight: It shifts attention from the story’s events to the craft and scale of its composition.

ramayan::169.verse_sanskrit: कृत्वापि तन्महाप्राज्ञस्सभविष्यं सहोत्तरम् । चिन्तयामास कोन्वेतत्प्रयुञ्जीयादिति प्रभु: । । 143 । ।
ramayan::169.verse_hindi: The great intellectual and competent Valmiki having composed the Ramayanam including the events of Uttarakanda as well as future events, reflected as to who could translate into performance the epic.
ramayan::169.english_translation: The great, wise Valmiki composed the Ramayana, including the events of Uttara Kanda and future events, and then wondered who could perform it.
ramayan::169.translation_literal: कृत्वापि (having composed) / तत् (that) / महाप्राज्ञः (greatly wise one) / सः (he) / भविष्यं (future) / सहोत्तरम् (along with Uttara Kanda) / चिन्तयामास (thought) / कः (who) / नु (indeed) / एतत् (this) / प्रयुञ्जीयात् (could perform) / इति (thus) / प्रभुः (the capable one)
ramayan::169.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::169.essence: A finished work still needs the right voice to awaken it.
ramayan::169.simple_meaning: Valmiki finished composing the epic, including later events, and then wondered who could bring it to life in performance.
ramayan::169.simple_insight: Even a completed work can still wait for the right voice to carry it.
ramayan::169.detailed_meaning: Valmiki has already composed the full Ramayana, including Uttara Kanda and events yet to unfold. But completion is not enough for him; he now pauses to ask who could sing or perform this vast work so others can hear it.
ramayan::169.modern_relevance: You finish something large and beautiful, then stare at it wondering who can present it well. Writing it was only half the task; finding the right voice is the other half.
ramayan::169.insight: It shifts attention from creating the work to finding the right medium to carry it forward.

ramayan::170.verse_sanskrit: तस्य चिन्तयमानस्य महर्षेर्भावितात्मन: । अगृह्णीतां तत: पादौ मुनिवेषौ कुशीलवौ । । 144 । ।
ramayan::170.verse_hindi: While the highly honoured sage Valmiki was thus pondering over, Kusa and Lava came to him in the garb of ascetics and bowed at his feet.
ramayan::170.english_translation: While the highly honoured sage Valmiki was thus pondering over, Kusa and Lava came to him in the garb of ascetics and bowed at his feet.
ramayan::170.translation_literal: तस्य (his) / चिन्तयमानस्य (while pondering) / महर्षेः (of the great sage) / भावितात्मनः (of the self-realized one) / अगृह्णीताम् (seized) / ततः (then) / पादौ (the feet) / मुनिवेषौ (in ascetic disguise) / कुशीलवौ (Kusha and Lava)
ramayan::170.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::170.essence: The story pauses just long enough for recognition to begin.
ramayan::170.simple_meaning: Valmiki was deep in thought when Kusha and Lava, dressed as ascetics, came and bowed at his feet.
ramayan::170.simple_insight: The scene is about recognition and arrival, not teaching. Something important is about to be revealed.
ramayan::170.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is absorbed in thought after composing the epic. At that moment, Kusha and Lava arrive disguised as ascetics and bow before him. The verse simply moves the story into the meeting that will reveal who they are.
ramayan::170.modern_relevance: You can be lost in your own thoughts when life quietly brings the next meeting to your feet.
ramayan::170.insight: It sets up a recognition scene, preparing the reader for revelation rather than instruction.

ramayan::171.verse_sanskrit: कुशीलवौ तु धर्मज्ञौ राजपुत्रौ यशस्विनौ । भ्रातरौ स्वरसम्पन्नौ ददर्शाश्रमवासिनौ । । 145 । ।
ramayan::171.verse_hindi: The sage saw the two illustrious princely brothers, wellversed in dharma and endowed with a sweet voice living in the hermitage.
ramayan::171.english_translation: The sage saw the two illustrious princely brothers, well-versed in dharma and endowed with a sweet voice, living in the hermitage.
ramayan::171.translation_literal: कुशीलवौ (Kusha and Lava) / तु (indeed) / धर्मज्ञौ (knowers of dharma) / राजपुत्रौ (two princes) / यशस्विनौ (glorious) / भ्रातरौ (brothers) / स्वरसम्पन्नौ (endowed with sweet voice) / ददर्श (saw) / आश्रमवासिनौ (dwelling in the hermitage)
ramayan::171.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::171.essence: Their bearing alone shows they are ready for a greater task.
ramayan::171.simple_meaning: Valmiki notices Kusha and Lava in the hermitage: two noble princes, skilled in right conduct, and gifted with beautiful voices.
ramayan::171.simple_insight: Even quiet presence can reveal greatness before any formal teaching begins.
ramayan::171.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is still considering what to do with his new composition when he sees Kusha and Lava, the two boys who have come to his hermitage in disguise. Their noble bearing, knowledge of right conduct, and musical gift make them stand out immediately.
ramayan::171.modern_relevance: You meet two young people in a quiet place, and before they speak, their manner tells you they are ready for something larger than the room they’re in.
ramayan::171.insight: It sets up the moment when Valmiki recognises the boys as suitable students for his poem and teaching.

ramayan::172.verse_sanskrit: स तु मेधाविनौ दृष्ट्वा वेदेषु परिनिष्ठितौ । वेदोपबृंहणार्थाय तावग्राहयत प्रभु: । । 146 । ।
ramayan::172.verse_hindi: Valmiki, the master, having found both Kusa and Lava endowed with intellect and accomplished in the Vedas initiated them into the Ramayana composed by him for the purpose of nourishing the Vedas.
ramayan::172.english_translation: Valmiki, the master, having found both Kusa and Lava endowed with intellect and accomplished in the Vedas initiated them into the Ramayana composed by him for the purpose of nourishing the Vedas.
ramayan::172.translation_literal: सः (he) / तु (indeed) / मेधाविनौ (the intelligent ones) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / वेदेषु (in the Vedas) / परिनिष्ठितौ (fully established) / वेदोपबृंहणार्थाय (for the purpose of expanding the Vedas) / तौ (those two) / अग्राहयत (had him teach) / प्रभुः (the master)
ramayan::172.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::172.essence: True instruction enlarges what the student already knows.
ramayan::172.simple_meaning: Valmiki sees Kusa and Lava are intelligent and well-grounded in the Vedas, so he teaches them the Ramayana to deepen their learning.
ramayan::172.simple_insight: Real teaching builds on what a student already knows and then stretches it further.
ramayan::172.detailed_meaning: Valmiki has just welcomed the two royal boys in ascetic clothing. Seeing their sharp minds and Vedic training, he recognizes they are ready for something larger. He begins teaching them the Ramayana so the epic can enrich and extend their understanding.
ramayan::172.modern_relevance: A teacher notices two students who already know the basics and gives them something bigger than memorisation. Good learning does not stop at information; it widens the mind.
ramayan::172.insight: It shifts teaching from repetition to enlargement: start with what is established, then deepen it.

ramayan::173.verse_sanskrit: काव्यं रामायणं कृत्स्नं सीतायाश्चरितं महत् । पौलस्त्यवधमित्येव चकार चरितव्रत: । । 147 । ।
ramayan::173.verse_hindi: Valmiki who practised religious austerities composed this entire epic named the Ramayana which constitutes the great history of Sita and the killing of Paulastya (Ravana).
ramayan::173.english_translation: Valmiki, who practised austerity, composed this entire epic called the Ramayana, the great account of Sita and the slaying of Paulastya.
ramayan::173.translation_literal: काव्यं (poem/epic) / रामायणं (Ramayana) / कृत्स्नं (entire) / सीतायाः (of Sita) / चरितं (account/life-story) / महत् (great) / पौलस्त्यवधम् (slaying of Paulastya) / इति (thus) / एव (indeed) / चकार (made/composed) / चरितव्रत: (one who kept a vow of austerity)
ramayan::173.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::173.essence: The poet names the whole story as Sita's life and Ravana's fall.
ramayan::173.simple_meaning: Valmiki composed the whole Ramayana as the great story of Sita and Ravana's defeat.
ramayan::173.simple_insight: A great work can hold both tenderness and ruin without shrinking either.
ramayan::173.detailed_meaning: After seeing Kusa and Lava and training them in sacred learning, Valmiki explains what he has created. This verse steps back from the lesson to name the whole work: the Ramayana, centered on Sita's story and Ravana's destruction.
ramayan::173.modern_relevance: You finish something enormous and realise it was never just a project. It was a whole world of loss, courage, and memory that needed a voice.
ramayan::173.insight: It frames the epic as a crafted whole, not a loose collection of episodes.

ramayan::174.verse_sanskrit: पाठ्ये गेये च मधुरं प्रमाणैस्त्रिभिरन्वितम् । जातिभिस्सप्तभिर्बद्धं तन्त्रीलयसमन्वितम् । । 148 । । रसैश्शृङ्गारकारुण्यहास्यवीरभयानकै: । रौद्रादिभिश्च संयुक्तं काव्यमेतदगायताम् । । 149 । । तौ तु गान्धर्वतत्त्वज्ञौ मूर्छनास्थानकोविदौ । भ्रातरौ स्वरसम्पन्नौ गन्धर्वाविव रूपिणौ । । 1410 । । रूपलक्षणसम्पन्नौ मधुरस्वरभाषिणौ । बिम्बादिवोद्धृतौ बिम्बौ रामदेहात्तथाऽपरौ । । 1411 । ।
ramayan::174.verse_hindi: The twin brothers Kusa and Lava, endowed with a melodious voice,  possessed auspicious form and beauty. They were gandharvas in human form. They looked like the two reflected images of Rama. The contents of this epic, apart from being memorable are sweet and suitable for verbal recitation as well as singing. This charming and attractive kavya is fit to be adapted to the three measures of time and to stringed instruments. It possesses seven notes together with various moodsamorous, compassionate, humorous, heroic, fearful and also violent.
ramayan::174.english_translation: The twin brothers Kusa and Lava, endowed with a melodious voice, possessed auspicious form and beauty. They were gandharvas in human form. They looked like the two reflected images of Rama. This charming and attractive poem is fit for recitation and singing, shaped by three measures of time and seven notes, and joined with many moods: love, compassion, humor, heroism, fear, and violence.
ramayan::174.translation_literal: पाठ्ये (fit for recitation) / गेये (fit for singing) / च (and) / मधुरम् (sweet) / प्रमाणैः (by measures) / त्रिभिः (three) / अन्वितम् (joined) / जातिभिः (with modes) / सप्तभिः (seven) / बद्धम् (composed) / तन्त्री-लय-समन्वितम् (joined with stringed-instrument rhythm) / रसैः (with moods) / शृङ्गार-कारुण्य-हास्य-वीर-भयानकैः (with love, compassion, humor, heroism, and fear) / रौद्र-आदिभिः (with violence and others) / च (and) / संयुक्तम् (combined) / काव्यम् (poem) / एतत् (this) / अगायताम् (let it be sung)
ramayan::174.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::174.essence: A great poem can hold every mood and still sing as one.
ramayan::174.simple_meaning: The poem is praising the Ramayana itself: it can be recited or sung, and it contains many moods, rhythms, and musical forms. Kusa and Lava are described as beautiful, gifted singers who resemble Rama.
ramayan::174.simple_insight: Great art holds many emotions at once and still feels whole.
ramayan::174.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is introducing the poem as a work meant to be performed, not just read. Kusa and Lava, Rama’s sons, are shown as gifted singers who can carry the whole epic aloud, while the poem itself is praised for its musical structure and emotional range.
ramayan::174.modern_relevance: You hear a story sung aloud and realise it can carry grief, courage, tenderness, and fury without falling apart. Some works are strong enough to hold your whole emotional life.
ramayan::174.insight: It frames the epic as a living performance, not a static text, and highlights its emotional range and musical form.

ramayan::175.verse_sanskrit: तौ राजपुत्रौ कार्त्स्न्येन धर्म्यमाख्यानमुत्तमम् । वाचोविधेयं तत्सर्वं कृत्वा काव्यमनिन्दितौ । । 1412 । । ऋषीणां च द्विजातीनां साधूनां च समागमे । यथोपदेशं तत्त्वज्ञौ जगतुस्सुसमाहितौ । । 1413 । ।
ramayan::175.verse_hindi: These two princes blameless, disciplined and wellversed, committed to memory the whole epic and chanted as instructed in the assembly of rishis, brahmins and saints.
ramayan::175.english_translation: These two princes, blameless and disciplined, learned the entire noble poem and sang it exactly as instructed before the gathering of sages, brahmins, and saints.
ramayan::175.translation_literal: तौ (those two) / राजपुत्रौ (princes) / कार्त्स्न्येन (completely) / धर्म्यम् (righteous) / आख्यानम् (narrative) / उत्तमम् (excellent) / वाचोविधेयम् (to be followed in speech) / तत् सर्वम् (all that) / कृत्वा (having made) / काव्यम् (poem) / अनिन्दितौ (blameless ones) / ऋषीणाम् (of sages) / च (and) / द्विजातीनाम् (of twice-born) / च (and) / साधूनाम् (of the virtuous) / समागमे (in the gathering) / यथोपदेशम् (according to instruction) / तत्त्वज्ञौ (knowers of reality) / जगतुः (they sang) / सुसमाहितौ (deeply focused)
ramayan::175.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::175.essence: True mastery can sound like perfect obedience.
ramayan::175.simple_meaning: Kusha and Lava learned the whole poem and recited it exactly as they had been taught, with calm focus, before an assembly of sages and holy men.
ramayan::175.simple_insight: Careful learning matters when you are carrying something sacred or important.
ramayan::175.detailed_meaning: Valmiki has finished shaping his epic, and the two princes he has raised now stand before an assembly of sages, brahmins, and saints. Their role here is not argument or revelation, but faithful recitation: they hold the poem whole and deliver it with discipline.
ramayan::175.modern_relevance: You rehearse the speech until every line lands cleanly, then step onto the stage and trust the preparation. Some moments ask for exactness, not improvisation.
ramayan::175.insight: It shifts attention from personal performance to faithful transmission.

ramayan::176.verse_sanskrit: महात्मानौ महाभागौ सर्वलक्षणलक्षितौ । तौ कदाचित्समेतानामृषीणां भावितात्मनाम् । आसीनानां समीपस्थाविदं काव्यमगायताम् । । 1414 । ।
ramayan::176.verse_hindi: On a particular occasion both the great princes who were dignified and endowed with good features, chanted this great epic in the presence of honoured ascetics who assembled at one place.
ramayan::176.english_translation: On a particular occasion, both great princes, dignified and marked by every auspicious sign, sang this great epic before the assembled honoured ascetics.
ramayan::176.translation_literal: महात्मानौ (great-souled) / महाभागौ (highly fortunate) / सर्वलक्षणलक्षितौ (marked with all signs) / तौ (those two) / कदाचित् (on a certain occasion) / समेतानाम् (assembled) / ऋषीणाम् (of sages) / भावितात्मनाम् (of disciplined minds) / आसीनानाम् (sitting) / समीपस्थौ (standing near) / इदम् (this) / काव्यम् (poem/epic) / अगायताम् (they sang)
ramayan::176.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::176.essence: The twins sing the epic before the gathered sages.
