ramayan::176.simple_meaning: Kusa and Lava sang the epic before a gathering of respected sages. The verse simply describes the scene, not a teaching.
ramayan::176.simple_insight: Some moments matter because they are witnessed by the right ears.
ramayan::176.detailed_meaning: Kusa and Lava, the twin sons of Rama and Sita, stand near a gathering of ascetics and sing Valmiki’s epic. The verse prepares the scene for the sages’ emotional response in the next line, so it functions as narrative setup.
ramayan::176.modern_relevance: You finish a performance and look up to see the room still. The real test is not the singing — it is who heard it, and how deeply.
ramayan::176.insight: It frames the recital as a public event, not a teaching. The focus is on setting up the sages’ reaction.

ramayan::177.verse_sanskrit: तच्छ्रुत्वा मुनयस्सर्वे बाष्पपर्याकुलेक्षणा: । साधुसाध्विति तावूचु: परं विस्मयमागता: । । 1415 । ।
ramayan::177.verse_hindi: All the sages having heard the chanting (of that glorious kavya), experienced great
ramayan::177.english_translation: Hearing that, all the sages, their eyes brimming with tears, cried, "Excellent, excellent!" and were filled with wonder.
ramayan::177.translation_literal: तत् (that) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / मुनयः (the sages) / सर्वे (all) / बाष्प-पर्याकुल-ईक्षणाः (with eyes overwhelmed by tears) / साधु साधु इति ("excellent, excellent" thus) / तौ (to them) / ऊचुः (said) / परम् (great) / विस्मयम् (wonder) / आगताः (having come to)
ramayan::177.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::177.essence: The sages are so moved they can only praise in tears.
ramayan::177.simple_meaning: The sages are moved to tears and praise the princes' singing with wonder.
ramayan::177.simple_insight: Beautiful truth can move even the most disciplined hearts to tears.
ramayan::177.detailed_meaning: Kusha and Lava have been singing Valmiki's epic before an assembly of sages. When the chanting reaches its end, the listeners are overwhelmed, tearful, and astonished. This verse records their spontaneous praise, not a new teaching.
ramayan::177.modern_relevance: A room goes silent after a performance that lands too deeply to explain. People look at each other with wet eyes and know they have just heard something rare.
ramayan::177.insight: It shows the power of sacred poetry to soften even learned listeners into awe.

ramayan::178.verse_sanskrit: ते प्रीतमनसस्सर्वे मुनयो धर्मवत्सला: । प्रशशंसु: प्रशस्तव्यौ गायमानौ कुशीलवौ । । 1416 । ।
ramayan::178.verse_hindi: All the sages steeped in dharma, pleased with them, praised the admirable Kusa and Lava as they sang.
ramayan::178.english_translation: All the sages, devoted to dharma and pleased, praised the admirable Kusha and Lava as they sang.
ramayan::178.translation_literal: ते (they) / प्रीतमनसः (with pleased minds) / सर्वे (all) / मुनयः (sages) / धर्मवत्सलाः (fond of dharma) / प्रशशंसुः (praised) / प्रशस्तव्यौ (worthy of praise) / गायमानौ (the two singing) / कुशीलवौ (Kusha and Lava)
ramayan::178.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::178.essence: The sages responded with praise to the boys' singing.
ramayan::178.simple_meaning: The sages were delighted by Kusha and Lava's singing and praised them warmly.
ramayan::178.simple_insight: Good work earns recognition when it is sincere and skillful.
ramayan::178.detailed_meaning: In Valmiki's assembly, Kusha and Lava have just sung the epic before a circle of sages. The listeners are moved, but this line only records their praise; it supports the larger scene rather than delivering a teaching of its own.
ramayan::178.modern_relevance: You finish a recital, presentation, or performance and the room goes quiet before applause starts. That first wave of appreciation tells you the work landed.
ramayan::178.insight: It simply shows the audience's approval after the performance, not a separate lesson.

ramayan::179.verse_sanskrit: अहो गीतस्य माधुर्यं श्लोकानां च विशेषत: । चिरनिर्वृत्तमप्येतत्प्रत्यक्षमिव दर्शितम् । । 1417 । ।
ramayan::179.verse_hindi: How melodious is this chanting, especially the verses Though it (the events) had happened long ago, it is described as if it is happening at the present moment, exclaimed the audience.
ramayan::179.english_translation: How melodious is this chanting, especially the verses! Though these events happened long ago, they are shown as if happening right now.
ramayan::179.translation_literal: अहो (ah, how) / गीतस्य (of the chanting) / माधुर्यम् (sweetness, melody) / श्लोकानाम् (of the verses) / च (and) / विशेषत: (especially) / चिरनिर्वृत्तम् (happened long ago) / अपि (even though) / एतत् (this) / प्रत्यक्षम् इव (as if before the eyes) / दर्शितम् (has been shown)
ramayan::179.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::179.essence: True poetry makes the past feel present.
ramayan::179.simple_meaning: The listeners are amazed by how beautiful the singing is, and by how vividly it makes ancient events feel present.
ramayan::179.simple_insight: Great art can make the distant feel immediate and alive.
ramayan::179.detailed_meaning: The sages have just heard Kusa and Lava sing Valmiki's poem. Moved by the beauty of the melody and the vividness of the telling, they marvel that events from long ago seem to stand before them.
ramayan::179.modern_relevance: You hear a story and suddenly feel it in your chest, as if it happened yesterday. That is the power of language that makes the distant undeniable.
ramayan::179.insight: It highlights how powerful telling can turn memory into living presence.

ramayan::180.verse_sanskrit: प्रविश्य तावुभौ सुष्ठु भावं सम्यगगायताम् । सहितौ मधुरं रक्तं सम्पन्नं स्वरसम्पदा । । 1418 । ।
ramayan::180.verse_hindi: They both chanted in perfect unison in theme and passion, with their charming
ramayan::180.english_translation: They both chanted in perfect unison, with matching feeling and flawless musical skill.
ramayan::180.translation_literal: प्रविश्य (having entered) / तौ उभौ (those two both) / सुष्ठु (well) / भावं (feeling, mood) / सम्यक् (properly, perfectly) / अगायताम् (sang) / सहितौ (together) / मधुरं (sweetly) / रक्तं (colored, infused) / सम्पन्नं (endowed, complete) / स्वरसम्पदा (with wealth of melody, musical skill)
ramayan::180.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::180.essence: Their singing was so unified it sounded effortless.
ramayan::180.simple_meaning: Kusha and Lava sang together with perfect harmony, matching both the emotion and the music.
ramayan::180.simple_insight: True skill shows when feeling and form move together without strain.
ramayan::180.detailed_meaning: The two boys have entered the gathering and begun their recitation. The sages are already delighted by their singing, and this verse adds that their voices blend perfectly in mood, sweetness, and musical mastery.
ramayan::180.modern_relevance: Two performers step onto a stage and lock into the same rhythm so completely that the room goes quiet. You can feel when skill and feeling finally meet.
ramayan::180.insight: It highlights harmony so complete that technique and emotion seem to become one.

ramayan::181.verse_sanskrit: एवं प्रशस्यमानौ तौ तपश्श्लाघ्यैर्महात्मभि: । संरक्ततरमत्यर्थं मधुरं तावगायताम् । । 1419 । ।
ramayan::181.verse_hindi: Praised in this manner by the great sages commendable for their austerities, they chanted even with greater charm and sweetness.
ramayan::181.english_translation: Praised in this manner by the great sages, who were noble through austerity, the two sang with even greater sweetness and charm.
ramayan::181.translation_literal: एवं (thus) / प्रशस्यमानौ (being praised) / तौ (those two) / तपश्श्लाघ्यैः (by those praiseworthy for austerity) / महात्मभिः (by the great-souled ones) / संरक्ततरम् (even more deeply) / अत्यर्थम् (greatly) / मधुरम् (sweetly) / तौ (those two) / अगायताम् (sang)
ramayan::181.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::181.essence: True praise can make sincere speech even more beautiful.
ramayan::181.simple_meaning: The two singers received praise from holy sages, and their singing became even sweeter and more moving.
ramayan::181.simple_insight: Praise can deepen sincere expression instead of making it less true.
ramayan::181.detailed_meaning: In the hermitage gathering, two gifted singers have already impressed the sages with their Ramayana recitation. The holy men, themselves known for austerity, praise them openly. Encouraged by that response, the two sing with even greater sweetness.
ramayan::181.modern_relevance: You’re presenting something you care about in front of people who truly understand it. Their approval doesn’t inflate you — it steadies your voice and lets you give more.
ramayan::181.insight: It shows how recognition from the right audience can refine effort rather than distract from it.

ramayan::182.verse_sanskrit: प्रीत: कश्चिन्मुनिस्ताभ्यां संस्थित: कलशं ददौ । प्रसन्नो वल्कलं कश्चिद्ददौ ताभ्यां महायशा: । । 1420 । ।
ramayan::182.verse_hindi: Pleased with the singing, one of the sages seated in the assembly presented them a pitcher. Another sage of renown got so delighted that he gave them garments.
ramayan::182.english_translation: Pleased with the singing, one of the sages seated in the assembly presented them a pitcher. Another sage of renown got so delighted that he gave them garments.
ramayan::182.translation_literal: प्रीत: (pleased) / कश्चिन्मुनि: (one sage) / ताभ्याम् (to those two) / संस्थित: (seated) / कलशम् (a pitcher) / ददौ (gave) / प्रसन्न: (delighted) / वल्कलम् (bark-cloth garments) / कश्चित् (another) / ददौ (gave) / ताभ्याम् (to those two) / महायशा: (the greatly renowned one)
ramayan::182.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::182.essence: Sincere art invites gifts before it asks for praise.
ramayan::182.simple_meaning: The sages listening to the singing were so pleased that they offered gifts to the two singers.
ramayan::182.simple_insight: True skill draws generosity without asking for it.
ramayan::182.detailed_meaning: Valmiki and his companion have just finished singing before the sages. The assembly responds not with argument, but with gratitude: one sage offers a pitcher, another offers garments. The moment shows the poem winning its first audience.
ramayan::182.modern_relevance: You finish something with care, and the room goes quiet. Then someone simply hands you water, or thanks you, because they felt the beauty of what you gave.
ramayan::182.insight: It shifts attention from performance to the natural recognition that follows sincere expression.

ramayan::183.verse_sanskrit: आश्चर्यमिदमाख्यानं मुनिना सम्प्रकीर्तितम् । परं कवीनामाधारं समाप्तं च यथाक्रमम् । । 1421 । ।
ramayan::183.verse_hindi: This wonderful epic chronologically composed and completed by the sage (Valmiki),  is the supreme source for poetry.
ramayan::183.english_translation: This wonderful epic, chronologically composed and completed by the sage, is the supreme source for poetry.
ramayan::183.translation_literal: आश्चर्यम् (wonderful) / इदम् (this) / आख्यानम् (epic tale) / मुनिना (by the sage) / सम्प्रकीर्तितम् (fully composed and recited) / परम् (supreme) / कवीनाम् (of poets) / आधारम् (foundation) / समाप्तम् (completed) / च (and) / यथाक्रमम् (in proper order)
ramayan::183.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::183.essence: A finished work can become the ground beneath future creators.
ramayan::183.simple_meaning: Valmiki says this epic is a remarkable, fully ordered work and the highest foundation for poets.
ramayan::183.simple_insight: What you create with care can become a gift for generations.
ramayan::183.detailed_meaning: After the sages praise the singing, the poem turns inward and names itself. Valmiki presents his finished work as a complete, orderly epic and claims it will stand as the great source for later poets.
ramayan::183.modern_relevance: You finish a project, close the laptop, and think it is done. Years later, someone else learns how to write, speak, or build from what you made. Careful work can become a foundation.
ramayan::183.insight: It shifts attention from finishing for applause to finishing as an offering that can guide others.

ramayan::184.verse_sanskrit: अभिगीतमिदं गीतं सर्वगीतेषु कोविदौ । आयुष्यं पुष्टिजनकं सर्वश्रुतिमनोहरम् । । 1422 । । प्रशस्यमानौ सर्वत्र कदाचित्तत्र गायकौ । रथ्यासु राजमार्गेषु ददर्श भरताग्रज: । । 1423 । ।
ramayan::184.verse_hindi: The two singers, proficient in all kinds of notes recited the epic in the streets and on the principal roads. It was pleasing to hear for all. It gave long life and prosperity to the listeners. People admired them. Once Rama happened to see them.
ramayan::184.english_translation: The two singers, proficient in all kinds of notes, recited the epic in the streets and on the principal roads. It was pleasing to hear for all. It gave long life and prosperity to the listeners. People admired them. Once Rama happened to see them.
ramayan::184.translation_literal: अभिगीतम् (sung/recited) / इदम् (this) / गीतम् (song) / सर्वगीतेषु (among all songs) / कोविदौ (skilled) / आयुष्यम् (life-giving) / पुष्टिजनकम् (prosperity-producing) / सर्वश्रुतिमनोहरम् (pleasing to all hearing) / प्रशस्यमानौ (being praised) / सर्वत्र (everywhere) / कदाचित् (once) / तत्-रथ्यासु (in those streets) / राजमार्गेषु (on royal roads) / ददर्श (saw) / भरताग्रजः (Rama, elder brother of Bharata)
ramayan::184.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::184.essence: Public praise brings hidden excellence into the king's sight.
ramayan::184.simple_meaning: Kusa and Lava sang the Ramayana beautifully in public, and everyone loved hearing them. Their song was praised everywhere, and Rama saw them there.
ramayan::184.simple_insight: Recognition often begins in public, where excellence can be heard before it is understood.
ramayan::184.detailed_meaning: In Ayodhya, the twin singers Kusa and Lava perform Valmiki's poem in the streets and royal roads. Their mastery wins praise from everyone who hears them, and that public acclaim finally brings them into Rama's sight.
ramayan::184.modern_relevance: You post something raw and honest, and it starts getting shared before you know why. The right work can travel farther than you ever planned.
ramayan::184.insight: It sets up the public recognition that leads Rama to notice the boys and draw them into the court.

ramayan::185.verse_sanskrit: स्ववेश्म चानीय तदा भ्रातरौ स कुशीलवौ । पूजयामास पूजार्हौ रामश्शत्रुनिबर्हण: । । 1424 । ।
ramayan::185.verse_hindi: Thereafter, Rama, the destroyer of enemies, having invited the two brothers Kusa and Lava who deserved honour. He brought them to his royal palace and extended respectful hospitality.
ramayan::185.english_translation: Thereafter, Rama, the destroyer of enemies, invited the two brothers Kusa and Lava, who deserved honour, and brought them to his royal palace. He received them with respectful hospitality.
ramayan::185.translation_literal: स्ववेश्म (to his own house/palace) / च (and) / आनीय (having brought) / तदा (then) / भ्रातरौ (the two brothers) / स (he) / कुशीलवौ (Kusa and Lava) / पूजयामास (honoured) / पूजार्हौ (worthy of honour) / रामः (Rama) / शत्रुनिबर्हणः (destroyer of enemies)
ramayan::185.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::185.essence: Respect comes first, even before recognition.
ramayan::185.simple_meaning: Rama brings Kusa and Lava into his palace and treats them with honour. The moment is about respectful reception, not teaching or debate.
ramayan::185.simple_insight: True strength can look like hospitality, not force.
ramayan::185.detailed_meaning: Kusa and Lava have been singing the Ramayana in public. Rama hears of them, brings the two boys into his palace, and honours them properly. The verse sets up a formal meeting, showing Rama’s royal courtesy before the larger recognition unfolds.
ramayan::185.modern_relevance: Two children arrive at a house where no one knows their story, and the person in charge chooses welcome before questions. That first act of respect changes everything that follows.
ramayan::185.insight: It shifts attention from status or suspicion to dignified reception.

ramayan::186.verse_sanskrit: आसीन: काञ्चने दिव्ये स च सिंहासने प्रभु: । उपोपविष्टस्सचिवैर्भ्रातृभिश्च परन्तप: । । 1425 । ।
ramayan::186.verse_hindi: Rama, the tormentor of enemies, surrounded by his ministers and brothers occupied the splendid golden throne.
ramayan::186.english_translation: Rama, the tormentor of enemies, surrounded by his ministers and brothers occupied the splendid golden throne.
ramayan::186.translation_literal: आसीनः (seated) / काञ्चने (golden) / दिव्ये (splendid, divine) / सः (he) / सिंहासने (on the throne) / प्रभुः (the lord) / उपोपविष्टः (seated around) / सचिवैः (with ministers) / भ्रातृभिः (with brothers) / च (and) / परन्तपः (the tormentor of enemies)
ramayan::186.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::186.essence: Rama sits in full kingship, quietly held by his circle.
ramayan::186.simple_meaning: Rama sits on a splendid golden throne, with his ministers and brothers gathered around him.
ramayan::186.simple_insight: Power here is shown through order, not noise.
ramayan::186.detailed_meaning: In Ayodhya, Rama has returned to the royal seat after exile. He is surrounded by his ministers and brothers, and the scene settles into formal kingship. This verse simply places him in the throne room before the arrival of Kusa and Lava.
ramayan::186.modern_relevance: You walk into a room where the decision-makers are already seated, and you can feel the hierarchy before anyone speaks.
ramayan::186.insight: It frames authority as composed presence, not display.

ramayan::187.verse_sanskrit: दृष्ट्वा तु रूपसम्पन्नौ तावुभौ नियतस्तथा । उवाच लक्ष्मणं रामश्शत्रुघ्नं भरतं तदा । । 1426 । ।
ramayan::187.verse_hindi: Then selfpossessed Rama, having seen those very handsome brothers (Kusa and Lava), addressed Lakshmana, Satrughna and Bharata, saying:
ramayan::187.english_translation: Then selfpossessed Rama, having seen those very handsome brothers Kusa and Lava, addressed Lakshmana, Shatrughna, and Bharata, saying:
ramayan::187.translation_literal: दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / तु (indeed) / रूपसम्पन्नौ (endowed with beauty) / तौ (those two) / उभौ (both) / नियतस्तथा (self-possessed thus) / उवाच (said) / लक्ष्मणं (to Lakshmana) / रामः (Rama) / शत्रुघ्नं (to Shatrughna) / भरतम् (to Bharata) / तदा (then)
ramayan::187.speaker: Rama
ramayan::187.essence: He sees them first, then chooses his words.
ramayan::187.simple_meaning: Rama sees the two handsome boys and turns to Lakshmana, Shatrughna, and Bharata to speak.
ramayan::187.simple_insight: A calm leader notices before he speaks.
ramayan::187.detailed_meaning: In Ayodhya, Rama sits in state with his brothers and ministers while Kusa and Lava stand before him. Their beauty catches his attention, and he is about to introduce the story they sing. This line simply sets up that moment.
ramayan::187.modern_relevance: You notice someone’s presence before you decide what to say. That quiet pause changes the whole tone of the room.
ramayan::187.insight: It shows attentive presence before speech, not impulsive reaction.

ramayan::188.verse_hindi: Listen to this story sung by both of them, portraying excellent sense and words. Having said this, Rama urged the singers with the lustre of devatas to commence.
ramayan::188.english_translation: Listen to this story sung by both of them, rich in meaning and graceful words. Having said this, Rama urged the singers to begin.
ramayan::188.translation_literal: श्रूयताम् (let it be heard) / इदम् (this) / आख्यानम् (story) / अनयोः (of these two) / देववर्चसोः (of radiant splendor) / विचित्रार्थपदम् (with varied meanings and words) / सम्यक् (properly) / गायकौ (the two singers) / तौ (them) / अचोदयत् (he urged)
ramayan::188.speaker: Rama
ramayan::188.essence: The story begins when Rama gives it permission to be heard.
ramayan::188.simple_meaning: Rama asks everyone to listen and tells the two singers to begin their story.
ramayan::188.simple_insight: The moment is about listening first, not speaking first.
ramayan::188.detailed_meaning: Rama, seated in royal splendour, sees the two beautiful young singers and invites the court to hear their story. He then urges the pair to begin. The verse sets up the recitation that follows, rather than offering a teaching of its own.
ramayan::188.modern_relevance: A room goes quiet before a presentation begins, and everyone turns toward the person who has been asked to speak. This verse lives in that opening breath.
ramayan::188.insight: It marks the start of a public telling, not the lesson itself.

ramayan::189.verse_sanskrit: तौ चापि मधुरं रक्तं स्वञ्चितायतनिस्वनम् । तन्त्रीलयवदत्यर्थं विश्रुतार्थमगायताम् । । 1428 । ।
ramayan::189.verse_hindi: Both of them, with good and ample voice, chanted the kavya in a distinctly meaningful way. Tuning their stringed instruments, they sang melodiously and engagingly.
ramayan::189.english_translation: Both of them sang the poem with a sweet, resonant voice, in perfect rhythm and with clear meaning.
ramayan::189.translation_literal: तौ (those two) / चापि (also) / मधुरम् (sweetly) / रक्तम् (resonant) / स्वञ्चितायतनिस्वनम् (with a well-stretched, broad voice) / तन्त्रीलयवत् (with stringed-instrument rhythm) / अत्यर्थम् (very much) / विश्रुतार्थम् (with well-known meaning) / अगायताम् (they sang)
ramayan::189.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::189.essence: Beauty and meaning arrive together in their song.
ramayan::189.simple_meaning: The two boys sang beautifully, with clear rhythm and words that carried real meaning.
ramayan::189.simple_insight: Skill becomes memorable when beauty and meaning move together.
ramayan::189.detailed_meaning: In Rama's court, the two young singers have begun reciting the poem before a gathered audience. This verse focuses on how they sing: polished, musical, and intelligible. It is a descriptive step in the larger scene, not the main teaching.
ramayan::189.modern_relevance: A song sounds polished, but it only lands when the words are clear and the rhythm feels alive.
ramayan::189.insight: It shifts attention from performance alone to the union of form, feeling, and meaning.

ramayan::190.verse_sanskrit: ह्लादयत्सर्वगात्राणि मनांसि हृदयानि च । श्रोत्राश्रयसुखं गेयं तद्बभौ जनसंसदि । । 1429 । ।
ramayan::190.verse_hindi: The chanting of the kavya in the assembly of men comforted the sense of hearing. The listeners rejoiced in their mind, heart and the whole being.
ramayan::190.english_translation: The chanting of the kavya comforted the ears; the listeners rejoiced in mind, heart, and whole body in the assembly.
ramayan::190.translation_literal: ह्लादयत् (delighting) / सर्वगात्राणि (all limbs) / मनांसि (minds) / हृदयानि (hearts) / च (and) / श्रोत्राश्रयसुखम् (pleasure resting in the ear) / गेयं (the song) / तत् (that) / बभौ (shone) / जनसंसदि (in the assembly of people)
ramayan::190.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::190.essence: True song reaches the whole body, not just the ear.
ramayan::190.simple_meaning: The song was so beautiful that everyone in the crowd felt it in their ears, minds, hearts, and bodies.
ramayan::190.simple_insight: Beautiful speech can move people beyond thought into full-bodied delight.
ramayan::190.detailed_meaning: Rama has asked the twin singers to begin. As their song fills the royal assembly, the effect is immediate: the crowd is not merely listening, but visibly moved in mind, heart, and body. This verse lingers on that shared response before the story continues.
ramayan::190.modern_relevance: A room goes quiet when a voice, a poem, or a performance lands exactly right. Everyone stops scrolling, stops shifting, and feels the same thing at once.
ramayan::190.insight: It shows how art can gather scattered attention and create one shared emotional field.

ramayan::191.verse_sanskrit: इमौ मुनी पार्थिवलक्षणान्वितौकुशीलवौ चैव महातपस्विनौ । ममापि तद्भूतिकरं प्रवक्ष्यतेमहानुभावं चरितं निबोधत । । 1430 । ।
ramayan::191.verse_hindi: Addressing the assembly of men Rama said Both Kusa and Lava, even though ascetics, are endowed with the attributes of royalty. Eventhough they are singers, they are ascetics. This is even conducive to my wellbeing. Listen to the meaningful story with concentration.
ramayan::191.english_translation: Rama said: These two ascetics, Kusha and Lava, are marked by royal qualities too. Their singing is a blessing to me. Listen closely to this noble story.
ramayan::191.translation_literal: इमौ (these two) / मुनी (ascetics) / पार्थिव-लक्षण-अन्वितौ (endowed with royal marks) / कुशीलवौ (Kusha and Lava) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / महा-तपस्विनौ (great ascetics) / मम (to me) / अपि (also) / तत् (that) / भूति-करम् (conducive to wellbeing) / प्रवक्ष्यते (will be spoken) / महानुभावम् (great-souled) / चरितम् (story / conduct) / निबोधत (listen closely)
ramayan::191.speaker: Rama
ramayan::191.essence: Their song matters because their identity carries hidden weight.
ramayan::191.simple_meaning: Rama introduces Kusha and Lava as both ascetics and noble-born boys, then asks the assembly to listen closely to their story.
ramayan::191.simple_insight: Respect can recognize greatness before the full story is told.
ramayan::191.detailed_meaning: In Valmiki's court, the singing has already drawn everyone in. Rama now identifies the two boy-singers, Kusha and Lava, as both disciplined ascetics and children marked by royal bearing. He invites the assembly to hear their meaningful story with full attention.
ramayan::191.modern_relevance: A room goes quiet when someone finally names what everyone has felt but not yet understood. Before the facts are complete, respect can already be present.
ramayan::191.insight: It frames the boys with dignity before revealing their true identity, preparing the listener for recognition.

ramayan::192.verse_sanskrit: ततस्तु तौ रामवच:प्रचोदितावगायतां मार्गविधानसम्पदा । स चापि राम: परिषद्गतः शनैर्बुभूषयासक्तमना बभूव । । 1431 । ।
ramayan::192.verse_hindi: Encouraged by the words of Rama, the two brothers chanted according to marga
ramayan::192.english_translation: Then, encouraged by Rama's words, the two brothers sang with perfect musical skill. Rama, seated in the assembly, listened slowly, his mind absorbed with pleasure.
ramayan::192.translation_literal: ततस्तु (then) / तौ (those two) / रामवचःप्रचोदितौ (prompted by Rama's words) / अगायताम् (sang) / मार्गविधानसम्पदा (with the wealth of musical method) / सः (he) / च (and) / अपि (also) / रामः (Rama) / परिषद्गतः (gone to the assembly) / शनैः (slowly) / बुभूषयासक्तमनाः (with mind attached to the desire to hear) / बभूव (became)
ramayan::192.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::192.essence: Skillful song and open listening turn an assembly into stillness.
ramayan::192.simple_meaning: Rama listens as the two brothers sing beautifully, and the assembly is filled with delight.
ramayan::192.simple_insight: Sometimes true listening is its own kind of grace.
ramayan::192.detailed_meaning: In the royal assembly, Kusa and Lava sing under Rama's encouragement. Their performance is so skillful that Rama settles into attentive listening, and the court is held by the music itself. The verse simply shows the atmosphere taking shape.
ramayan::192.modern_relevance: You walk into a room where someone finally speaks with real skill, and everyone stops scrolling. The whole space changes because one person is fully present.
ramayan::192.insight: It shifts attention from action to receptive presence, showing how listening can deepen a shared moment.

ramayan::193.verse_sanskrit: सर्वा पूर्वमियं येषामासीत्कृत्स्ना वसुन्धरा । प्रजापतिमुपादाय नृपाणां जयशालिनाम् । । 151 । ।
ramayan::193.verse_hindi: Formerly, this entire earth belonged to  those victorious kings starting from Prajapati (Manu).
ramayan::193.english_translation: Formerly, this entire earth belonged to the victorious kings beginning with Prajapati Manu.
ramayan::193.translation_literal: सर्वा (all) / पूर्वम् (formerly) / इयम् (this) / येषाम् (whose) / आसीत् (was) / कृत्स्ना (entire) / वसुन्धरा (earth) / प्रजापतिम् (Prajapati Manu) / उपादाय (beginning with) / नृपाणाम् (of kings) / जयशालिनाम् (victorious)
ramayan::193.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::193.essence: Even the widest kingdom was only borrowed for a time.
ramayan::193.simple_meaning: The whole earth once belonged to a line of victorious kings, starting with Manu.
ramayan::193.simple_insight: Power changes hands. Even the greatest reigns become part of history.
ramayan::193.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is listing the ancient kings from whom Rama’s line descends. This verse is not a teaching in itself; it is part of a royal genealogy that builds the scale and legitimacy of the Ikshvaku lineage before naming figures like Sagara.
ramayan::193.modern_relevance: A family tree on a faded certificate can feel impressive for a moment, then suddenly small. This verse works like that: it reminds you that even vast power is inherited, counted, and eventually passed on.
ramayan::193.insight: It shifts attention from possession to lineage, showing that rule is temporary and remembered, not owned forever.

ramayan::194.verse_sanskrit: येषां स सगरो नाम सागरो येन खानित: । षष्टि: पुत्रसहस्राणि यं यान्तं पर्यवारयन् । । 152 । ।
ramayan::194.verse_hindi: Among them a king named Sagara got the ocean dug and his sixty thousand sons surrounded him whenever he went (to battle).
ramayan::194.english_translation: Among them a king named Sagara got the ocean dug and his sixty thousand sons surrounded him whenever he went to battle.
ramayan::194.translation_literal: येषाम् (of whom) / स (that) / सगरः (Sagara) / नाम (by name) / सागरः (the ocean) / येन (by whom) / खानितः (dug) / षष्टिः (sixty) / पुत्रसहस्राणि (thousand sons) / यम् (whom) / यान्तम् (going) / पर्यवारयन् (surrounded)
ramayan::194.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::194.essence: Power once looked like a king surrounded by thousands of loyal sons.
ramayan::194.simple_meaning: Sagara was a powerful king known for digging up the ocean, and his sixty thousand sons protected him in battle.
ramayan::194.simple_insight: Greatness here is measured by force, reach, and the scale of a ruler's household.
ramayan::194.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is listing the ancient kings of Rama's line before the story proper begins. Sagara stands out as a legendary ancestor: a ruler so mighty that the ocean bears his name, and so surrounded by his sons that he never moved alone into battle.
ramayan::194.modern_relevance: A family name, a reputation, or a team can make one person feel untouchable. This verse points to the old dream of power backed by many hands.
ramayan::194.insight: It shifts attention from personal heroism to dynastic power and inherited force.

ramayan::195.verse_sanskrit: इक्ष्वाकूणामिदं तेषां राज्ञां वंशे महात्मनाम् । महदुत्पन्नमाख्यानं रामायणमिति श्रुतम् । । 153 । ।
ramayan::195.verse_hindi: It was from the family of mighty monarchs with Ikshvaku as its founder and the kings born in that race, the celebrated epic known as the Ramayanam arose.
ramayan::195.english_translation: It was from the line of mighty kings, with Ikshvaku as its founder, that the celebrated story known as the Ramayana arose.
ramayan::195.translation_literal: इक्ष्वाकूणाम् (of the Ikshvaku line) / इदम् (this) / तेषाम् (of them) / राज्ञाम् (of kings) / वंशे (in the lineage) / महात्मनाम् (of the great-souled) / महत् (great) / उत्पन्नम् (arisen) / आख्यानम् (story) / रामायणम् (Ramayana) / इति (thus) / श्रुतम् (heard of)
ramayan::195.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::195.essence: The Ramayana rises from a royal line already heavy with greatness.
ramayan::195.simple_meaning: The Ramayana comes from the noble line of Ikshvaku kings. Valmiki is placing the story inside a real royal lineage before beginning the full telling.
ramayan::195.simple_insight: Great stories grow from great lineages, but they are carried forward by memory and narration.
ramayan::195.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is opening the epic by grounding it in the ancient Ikshvaku dynasty, the royal line of Rama. After mentioning earlier kings and Sagara, he now identifies the Ramayana as a famous account born from that lineage, preparing to tell the story in full.
ramayan::195.modern_relevance: Before a family story becomes a legend, someone has to remember where it began. A name, a lineage, a past worth carrying — that is how meaning survives time.
ramayan::195.insight: It frames the epic as inherited memory, not random invention, and prepares the listener to hear it as a serious lineage story.

ramayan::196.verse_sanskrit: तदिदं वर्तयिष्यामि सर्वं निखिलमादित: । धर्मकामार्थसहितं श्रोतव्यमनसूयया । । 154 । ।
ramayan::196.verse_hindi: I shall propagate this Ramayanam, incorporating the merits of dharma, artha and kama, and complete in all respects. It deserves to be heard right from the start without prejudice.
ramayan::196.english_translation: I shall tell this Ramayana fully, from the beginning, complete with dharma, artha, and kama. It should be heard without prejudice.
ramayan::196.translation_literal: तत् (that) / इदम् (this) / वर्तयिष्यामि (I shall narrate) / सर्वम् (all) / निखिलम् (completely) / आदितः (from the beginning) / धर्मकामार्थसहितम् (endowed with dharma, kama, and artha) / श्रोतव्यम् (to be heard) / अनसूयया (without prejudice)
ramayan::196.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::196.essence: The whole story can only be heard by a mind without bias.
ramayan::196.simple_meaning: Valmiki says he will tell the whole Ramayana from the beginning, and it should be listened to openly and fairly.
ramayan::196.simple_insight: Real understanding begins when you stop filtering the story before it reaches you.
ramayan::196.detailed_meaning: Valmiki has just introduced the royal line of Ikshvaku and Sagara. Now he turns to his own telling, promising to present the whole Ramayana from the start, with its full range of duty, desire, and worldly life, and asking the listener to receive it without bias.
ramayan::196.modern_relevance: You open a book, podcast, or conversation already deciding what counts as true. Then you miss the shape of the whole thing. Valmiki asks for a cleaner mind: hear the full story before you judge it.
ramayan::196.insight: It trains you to receive a teaching before sorting it into likes and dislikes.

ramayan::197.verse_sanskrit: कोसलो नाम मुदितस्स्फीतो जनपदो महान् । निविष्टस्सरयूतीरे प्रभूतधनधान्यवान् । । 155 । ।
ramayan::197.verse_hindi: On the banks of river Sarayu, a great and prosperous country named Kosala, abundant in foodgrains and wealth and inhabited by contended people, was situated.
ramayan::197.english_translation: A great, prosperous country named Kosala lay on the banks of the Sarayu, rich in grain and wealth, and full of contented people.
ramayan::197.translation_literal: कोसलः (Kosala) / नाम (named) / मुदितः (joyful, contented) / स्फीतः (flourishing, abundant) / जनपदः (country) / महान् (great) / निविष्टः (situated) / सरयू-तीरे (on the bank of the Sarayu) / प्रभूत (plentiful) / धन-धान्यवान् (rich in wealth and grain)
ramayan::197.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::197.essence: Peaceful abundance makes the coming fracture feel tragic.
ramayan::197.simple_meaning: Kosala is introduced as a large, prosperous land on the Sarayu, rich in grain, wealth, and happy people.
ramayan::197.simple_insight: A kingdom's greatness begins with abundance that reaches ordinary people, not just its rulers.
ramayan::197.detailed_meaning: Valmiki begins by grounding the epic in a real, flourishing land before any royal drama starts. Kosala is shown as prosperous, peaceful, and well-fed, setting the stage for Ayodhya and the house of Rama.
ramayan::197.modern_relevance: Before the family conflict, the city, or the exile, there is a world that feels stable and well-ordered. You can almost see the river, the fields, and the ordinary life that makes the coming rupture more painful.
ramayan::197.insight: It frames the story in a world of visible prosperity, so the coming loss feels larger.

ramayan::198.verse_sanskrit: अयोध्या नाम नगरी तत्रासील्लोकविश्रुता । मनुना मानवेन्द्रेण या पुरी निर्मिता स्वयम् । । 156 । ।
ramayan::198.verse_hindi: In the country called Kosala was the famous capital city of Ayodhya built by the lord of men, Manu .
ramayan::198.english_translation: In the country called Kosala was the famous city of Ayodhya, built by Manu himself, the lord of men.
ramayan::198.translation_literal: अयोध्या (Ayodhya) / नाम (called) / नगरी (city) / तत्र (there) / आसीत् (was) / लोकविश्रुता (famous among the people) / मनुना (by Manu) / मानवेन्द्रेण (by the lord of men) / या (which) / पुरी (city) / निर्मिता (built) / स्वयम् (himself)
ramayan::198.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::198.essence: Ayodhya is introduced as an ancient city with inherited authority.
ramayan::198.simple_meaning: Ayodhya was a renowned city in Kosala, and tradition says Manu himself founded it.
ramayan::198.simple_insight: A place can carry a whole lineage of meaning before any story begins.
ramayan::198.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is opening the world of the epic by naming Ayodhya, the celebrated capital of Kosala. He traces its origin to Manu, giving the city ancient authority and setting up the royal household where the coming tragedy and duty will unfold.
ramayan::198.modern_relevance: A city sign flashes by on a train ride, and you barely notice it. Later you learn that place has shaped generations. Some settings are not background — they are inheritance.
ramayan::198.insight: It grounds the story in a sacred royal lineage before the action begins.

ramayan::199.verse_sanskrit: आयता दश च द्वे च योजनानि महापुरी । श्रीमती त्रीणि विस्तीर्णा सुविभक्तमहापथा । । 157 । ।
ramayan::199.verse_hindi: With welllaid out thoroughfares, the beautiful and prosperous city of Ayodhya extended for twelve yojanas in length and three yojanas in breadth.
ramayan::199.english_translation: With welllaid out thoroughfares, the beautiful and prosperous city of Ayodhya extended for twelve yojanas in length and three yojanas in breadth.
ramayan::199.translation_literal: आयता (extended in length) / दश (ten) / च (and) / द्वे (two) / च (and) / योजनानि (yojanas) / महापुरी (great city) / श्रीमती (prosperous, beautiful) / त्रीणि (three) / विस्तीर्णा (spread out in breadth) / सुविभक्तमहापथा (with well-divided great roads)
ramayan::199.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::199.essence: Beauty here comes from order, not ornament.
ramayan::199.simple_meaning: Ayodhya is described as a large, prosperous city with broad, well-planned roads and fixed dimensions.
ramayan::199.simple_insight: Some places are built to reflect order, beauty, and care before anyone speaks a word.
ramayan::199.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is painting Ayodhya before the story’s pain begins. He gives its size, its wealth, and its orderly roads so the reader feels the loss later when this perfect city is shaken by exile and grief.
ramayan::199.modern_relevance: You walk into a city where the streets are clean, the lanes are planned, and nothing feels accidental. Before the drama begins, you can already sense the discipline behind the beauty.
ramayan::199.insight: It shifts attention from spectacle to the quiet order that makes a city feel alive.

ramayan::200.verse_sanskrit: राजमार्गेण महता सुविभक्तेन शोभिता । मुक्तपुष्पावकीर्णेन जलसिक्तेन नित्यश: । । 158 । ।
ramayan::200.verse_hindi: It looked splendid with its welllaid out and broad highway strewn with flowers and regularly sprinkled with water.
ramayan::200.english_translation: It looked splendid with its well-laid out and broad highway strewn with flowers and regularly sprinkled with water.
ramayan::200.translation_literal: राजमार्गेण (with the royal road) / महता (great, broad) / सुविभक्तेन (well-divided, well-laid out) / शोभिता (adorned, splendid) / मुक्तपुष्पावकीर्णेन (strewn with fallen flowers) / जलसिक्तेन (sprinkled with water) / नित्यश: (always, regularly)
ramayan::200.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::200.essence: Beauty here comes from care, order, and daily maintenance.
ramayan::200.simple_meaning: Ayodhya is described as a beautiful city, made even more splendid by its broad, orderly road, flowers, and regular watering.
ramayan::200.simple_insight: The verse is about outward splendour, not inner teaching.
ramayan::200.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Ayodhya before the main drama begins. The city’s broad, orderly royal road is covered with flowers and kept fresh with water, showing the prosperity and care that define Rama’s kingdom before exile and loss enter the story.
ramayan::200.modern_relevance: A city street after a festival cleanup, petals still stuck to the pavement and water glinting in the morning light — the verse simply lingers on beauty made by care.
ramayan::200.insight: It shifts attention from drama to the visible order of a well-kept place.

ramayan::201.verse_sanskrit: तां तु राजा दशरथो महाराष्ट्रविवर्धन: । पुरीमावासयामास दिवं देवपतिर्यथा । । 159 । ।
ramayan::201.verse_hindi: King Dasartha, augmenting the prosperity of the great kingdom, lived in the city of Ayodhya like Indra in heaven.
ramayan::201.english_translation: King Dasharatha, increasing the prosperity of the great kingdom, lived in the city of Ayodhya like Indra in heaven.
ramayan::201.translation_literal: तां (that) / तु (but) / राजा (king) / दशरथो (Dasharatha) / महाराष्ट्रविवर्धन: (increasing the great kingdom's prosperity) / पुरीम् (city) / आवासयामास (made his abode / lived) / दिवं (in heaven) / देवपतिः (the lord of the devas, Indra) / यथा (like)
ramayan::201.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::201.essence: A true ruler makes the whole kingdom flourish around him.
ramayan::201.simple_meaning: Dasharatha lived in Ayodhya with the splendour of Indra in heaven, and his rule made the kingdom prosper.
ramayan::201.simple_insight: Greatness is not only personal power; it is the ability to make a place flourish.
ramayan::201.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is still describing Ayodhya before the exile begins. Dasharatha sits at the center of a prosperous, orderly kingdom, and the comparison to Indra shows the scale of his royal stature. It is a scene of calm before loss.
ramayan::201.modern_relevance: A city feels alive when its leader is steady, visible, and worthy of trust. Before the crisis arrives, everyone can sense whether the center of power is strengthening the place or merely occupying it.
ramayan::201.insight: It frames leadership as the power to nourish a whole world around you.

ramayan::202.verse_hindi: The city where all kinds of artificers lived had arched outer gateways, wellarranged local markets and all kinds of instruments and weapons.
ramayan::202.english_translation: The city where all kinds of artificers lived had arched outer gateways, well-arranged local markets and all kinds of instruments and weapons.
ramayan::202.translation_literal: कवाटतोरणवतीम् (having arched gateways) / सुविभक्तान्तरापणाम् (with well-divided inner markets) / सर्वयन्त्रायुधवतीम् (possessing all kinds of machines and weapons) / उपेताम् (endowed with) / सर्वशिल्पिभिः (with all artisans)
ramayan::202.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::202.essence: Ayodhya's greatness is shown through its order, craft, and abundance.
ramayan::202.simple_meaning: Ayodhya is described as a beautifully organized city full of craftsmen, markets, gateways, tools, and weapons.
ramayan::202.simple_insight: Order, skill, and prosperity are part of what makes a place truly flourish.
ramayan::202.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is still painting Ayodhya before the exile begins. The city is shown as prosperous, orderly, and fully equipped, with artisans, markets, gateways, tools, and weapons. This is scene-setting, not a teaching verse.
ramayan::202.modern_relevance: A city block with repaired roads, busy shops, and workshops humming at dawn can feel alive before anyone speaks. The verse simply lingers on that visible prosperity.
ramayan::202.insight: It shifts attention from grand claims to the everyday structures that make a city strong.

ramayan::203.verse_hindi: With matchless splendour, it abounded in eulogists and genealogists. It contained stately edifices decorated with flags and hundreds of sataghnis (missiles).
ramayan::203.english_translation: With matchless splendour, it abounded in eulogists and genealogists. It contained stately edifices decorated with flags and hundreds of sataghnis (missiles).
ramayan::203.translation_literal: सूत-मागध-सम्बाधाम् (crowded with bards and genealogists) / श्रीमतीम् (splendid) / अतुल-प्रभाम् (of unmatched radiance) / उच्चाट्टाल-ध्वजवतीम् (having lofty towers and flags) / शतघ्नी-शत-सङ्कुलाम् (filled with hundreds of sataghnis)
ramayan::203.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::203.essence: Ayodhya stands as a brilliant, fortified capital at the height of order.
ramayan::203.simple_meaning: The city is described as rich, bright, and heavily fortified, with bards, genealogists, towers, flags, and weapons everywhere.
ramayan::203.simple_insight: The verse builds a vivid picture of a powerful capital before the story turns.
ramayan::203.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is still describing Ayodhya, the royal city of Dasharatha. After naming its walls and markets, he adds its splendour, its courtly singers and historians, and its defensive strength. It is a scene-setting verse, not a teaching.
ramayan::203.insight: It establishes the city as glorious, crowded, and secure before any conflict begins.

ramayan::204.verse_sanskrit: वधूनाटकसङ्घैश्च संयुक्तां सर्वत: पुरीम् । उद्यानाम्रवणोपेतां महतीं सालमेखलाम् । । 1512 । ।
ramayan::204.verse_hindi: The city with suburban towns on all sides had several female dancers and actors.It was filled with gardens and mangogroves. And girdled by sal trees.
ramayan::204.english_translation: The city on every side was joined with suburbs, full of troupes of women dancers and actors, and filled with gardens, mango groves, and a belt of sal trees.
ramayan::204.translation_literal: वधू-नाटक-सङ्घैः (with troupes of women dancers and actors) / च (and) / संयुक्ताम् (joined with) / सर्वतः (on every side) / पुरीम् (the city) / उद्यान-अम्र-वण-उपेताम् (endowed with gardens and mango groves) / महतीम् (great) / साल-मेखलाम् (girdled by sal trees)
ramayan::204.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::204.essence: The city is shown as rich, ordered, and alive.
ramayan::204.simple_meaning: The city was large, lively, and beautifully surrounded by suburbs, gardens, mango groves, and sal trees.
ramayan::204.simple_insight: A place can feel alive before any action begins.
ramayan::204.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is still describing the city before the story moves into its tensions. He lists its suburbs, entertainment troupes, gardens, mango groves, and sal-tree boundary to show a prosperous, ordered capital. The verse is scenery, not a teaching.
ramayan::204.insight: It builds the setting before the plot tightens, giving the city a living, inhabited texture.

ramayan::205.verse_hindi: It was enclosed by strong fortifications and a deep moat. No enemy can ever enter and occupy that city. It abounded with several elephants and horses, cattle, camels and mules.
ramayan::205.english_translation: It was enclosed by strong fortifications and a deep moat. No enemy can ever enter and occupy that city. It abounded with elephants and horses, cattle, camels, and mules.
ramayan::205.translation_literal: दुर्ग (fortress) / गम्भीर (deep) / परिघाम् (moat) / दुर्गाम् (hard to enter) / अन्यैः (by others) / दुरासदाम् (hard to approach) / वाजि (horses) / वारण (elephants) / सम्पूर्णाम् (full of) / गोभिः (with cattle) / उष्ट्रैः (with camels) / खरैः (with mules) / तथा (and)
ramayan::205.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::205.essence: A city is truly strong when protection and abundance support each other.
ramayan::205.simple_meaning: The city was heavily protected, impossible for enemies to enter, and rich in animals and supplies.
ramayan::205.simple_insight: Strength is not only walls; it is the abundance that lets a city endure.
ramayan::205.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is still describing the splendour of Ayodhya before the exile begins. After listing its crowds, banners, and gardens, he adds its defenses and wealth: deep moats, strong walls, and plenty of animals. The point is the city’s complete security and prosperity.
ramayan::205.modern_relevance: You walk past a gated apartment complex, security cameras, and stocked stores, and still feel uneasy. Real safety is not just barriers — it is the stability and abundance that make a place truly livable.
ramayan::205.insight: It shifts attention from mere defense to the fuller conditions that make security real.

ramayan::206.verse_hindi: It was embellished with a host of tributary kings who used to pay tributes and with  merchants from different countries.
ramayan::206.english_translation: It was embellished with a host of tributary kings who paid tribute, and with merchants from many countries.
ramayan::206.translation_literal: सामन्त-राज-सङ्घैः (with groups of subordinate kings) / च (and) / बलि-कर्मभिः (with tribute-giving duties) / आवृताम् (surrounded) / नाना-देश-निवासैः (by residents from many regions) / च (and) / वणिग्भिः (by merchants) / उपशोभिताम् (adorned)
ramayan::206.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::206.essence: Ayodhya’s greatness showed in the people and powers drawn to it.
ramayan::206.simple_meaning: The city was crowded with tribute-paying kings and merchants from many lands. It was prosperous, busy, and politically powerful.
ramayan::206.simple_insight: Power is visible not only in walls, but in who gathers around a place.
ramayan::206.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Ayodhya before Rama's exile: a thriving capital ringed by fortifications, livestock, and trade. This line adds the political and commercial life around the city, showing its reach and wealth rather than offering a teaching of its own.
ramayan::206.modern_relevance: A city square packed with traders, officials, and visitors tells you more than a headline ever could. Real strength shows up in the networks a place can hold together.
ramayan::206.insight: It shifts attention from spectacle to structure: a kingdom’s health is reflected in its alliances and trade.

ramayan::207.verse_hindi: Like Indras Amaravati, it was adorned by mountains and mansions with precious stones.
ramayan::207.english_translation: Like Indra's Amaravati, it was adorned with mansions made of precious stones and with lofty towers.
ramayan::207.translation_literal: प्रासादैः (with mansions) / रत्नविकृतैः (made of precious stones) / पर्वतैः (with mountains) / उपशोभिताम् (adorned) / कूटागारैः (with lofty towers) / च (and) / सम्पूर्णाम् (filled) / इन्द्रस्य (of Indra) / इव (like) / अमरावतीम् (Amaravati)
ramayan::207.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::207.essence: Beauty and scale prepare the stage, not the argument.
ramayan::207.simple_meaning: The city looked splendid, with jewel-like palaces and high towers, like Indra's heavenly city.
ramayan::207.simple_insight: The scene is meant to impress you with grandeur before the story moves on.
ramayan::207.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is still describing the great city in all its splendor: jewel-studded palaces, towering structures, and a richness that makes it resemble Amaravati, Indra's city. This is part of the larger scenic buildup, not a teaching on its own.
ramayan::207.modern_relevance: You walk into a place built to overwhelm: shining glass, polished stone, towers, and lights. The verse lingers on first impressions before anything happens.
ramayan::207.insight: It frames the setting as majestic so the reader feels the scale of what is about to unfold.

ramayan::208.verse_hindi: With groups of men and women and adorned with sevenstoried palaces, it looked wonderful like a board where the game of ashtapada, is played. It was rich in all kinds of gems.
ramayan::208.english_translation: With groups of men and women and adorned with seven-storied palaces, it looked wonderful like a board where the game of ashtapada is played. It was rich in all kinds of gems.
ramayan::208.translation_literal: चित्राम् (wonderful) / अष्टापदाकाराम् (shaped like an ashtapada board) / नरनारीगणैः (with groups of men and women) / युताम् (filled with) / सर्वरत्नसमाकीर्णाम् (filled with all gems) / विमानगृहशोभिताम् (adorned with palaces)
ramayan::208.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::208.essence: Splendor is being built up, detail by detail.
ramayan::208.simple_meaning: The city is described as crowded, jewel-filled, and beautiful, with tall palaces and orderly streets.
ramayan::208.simple_insight: Some places are so carefully built that even their beauty feels deliberate.
ramayan::208.detailed_meaning: Valmiki continues describing a grand city before the story turns to action. He piles up images of people, gems, and palaces to show its splendor. This verse is part of a larger scene-setting passage, not a teaching on its own.
ramayan::208.modern_relevance: You walk into a city at dusk and notice the lights, the crowds, the polished towers. The scene matters here more than any lesson.
ramayan::208.insight: It keeps attention on setting, not principle, so the mind can enter the epic world.

ramayan::209.verse_hindi: Its dwellings were constructed on levelled ground with no space left unutilised it was abundant stocked with fialgrained rice and water which fasted sweet like sugarcane juice.
ramayan::209.english_translation: Its dwellings were built on level ground with no space left unused; it was full of fine rice and water sweet like sugarcane juice.
ramayan::209.translation_literal: गृहगाढाम् (packed with houses) / अविच्छिद्राम् (unbroken, with no gaps) / समभूमौ (on level ground) / निवेशिताम् (placed, built) / शालितण्डुलसम्पूर्णाम् (filled with fine rice) / इक्षुकाण्डरसोदकाम् (with water sweet like sugarcane juice)
ramayan::209.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::209.essence: Order and abundance make a city feel alive.
ramayan::209.simple_meaning: The city is described as tightly built, perfectly laid out, and richly supplied with food and sweet water.
ramayan::209.simple_insight: A place feels secure when it is orderly, full, and cared for.
ramayan::209.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is still painting Ayodhya before the story turns inward. After comparing the city to a jeweled, heavenly capital, he adds practical details: packed houses, level streets, grain, and sweet water. The point is the city's abundance and completeness, not a teaching.
ramayan::209.modern_relevance: You walk into a neighbourhood where every lane is clean, every home is lived in, and even the water tastes fresh. Before anyone speaks, you can feel that this place has been cared for.
ramayan::209.insight: It shifts attention from glamour to the quiet signs of a well-run home or city.

ramayan::210.verse_sanskrit: दुन्दुभीभिर्मृदङ्गैश्च वीणाभि: पणवैस्तथा । नादितां भृशमत्यर्थं पृथिव्यां तामनुत्तमाम् । । 1518 । ।
ramayan::210.verse_hindi: The city echoed with the sounds of trumpets, mrudangas, vinas and panavas. There was no city on earth superior to Ayodhya.
ramayan::210.english_translation: The city echoed with the sounds of trumpets, mridangas, vinas, and panavas. There was no city on earth superior to Ayodhya.
ramayan::210.translation_literal: दुन्दुभीभिः (with trumpets) / मृदङ्गैः (with mridangas) / च (and) / वीणाभिः (with vinas) / पणवैः (with panavas) / तथा (also) / नादिताम् (resounded) / भृशम् (greatly) / अत्यर्थम् (exceedingly) / पृथिव्याम् (on earth) / ताम् (that) / अनुत्तमाम् (unsurpassed)
ramayan::210.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::210.essence: Ayodhya is so complete that even its sound feels royal.
ramayan::210.simple_meaning: Ayodhya is described as a magnificent city filled with music and unmatched on earth.
ramayan::210.simple_insight: Some places feel alive before anyone speaks there.
ramayan::210.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is still painting Ayodhya before the exile begins. The city is full of music, beauty, and abundance, setting up the emotional loss that follows when Rama leaves it behind.
ramayan::210.modern_relevance: You walk through a festival street at dusk, music spilling from every doorway, and realise the place itself feels like a living being.
ramayan::210.insight: It turns a city into a presence, making the coming loss feel personal.

ramayan::211.verse_sanskrit: विमानमिव सिद्धानां तपसाधिगतं दिवि । सुनिवेशितवेश्मान्तां नरोत्तमसमावृताम् । । 1519 । ।
ramayan::211.verse_hindi: Like an aerial car acquired by the siddhas in heaven through their austerities, the palaces were perfectly constructed in rows and inhabited by the noblest of men.
ramayan::211.english_translation: Like an aerial car acquired by the siddhas in heaven through their austerities, the palaces were perfectly constructed in rows and inhabited by the noblest of men.
ramayan::211.translation_literal: विमानमिव (like an aerial car) / सिद्धानाम् (of the siddhas) / तपसाधिगतम् (acquired through austerity) / दिवि (in heaven) / सुनिवेशित-वेश्म-अन्ताम् (with well-arranged house-rows) / नरोत्तम-समावृताम् (surrounded by the noblest of men)
ramayan::211.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::211.essence: Order and nobility make a city feel almost heavenly.
ramayan::211.simple_meaning: Ayodhya was laid out with beautifully arranged palaces and filled with noble people, like a heavenly city earned through discipline.
ramayan::211.simple_insight: A well-ordered life can make a whole city feel elevated and secure.
ramayan::211.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Ayodhya before the story turns darker. The city’s palaces stand in perfect rows, and the people who live there are noble and disciplined. The image lifts the city to a heavenly standard, showing what Rama is about to lose.
ramayan::211.modern_relevance: You walk through a neighborhood where every home is cared for, every street feels settled, and the whole place seems to hold itself with dignity.
ramayan::211.insight: It shifts attention from mere wealth to the moral order that makes a place beautiful.

ramayan::212.verse_sanskrit: ये च बाणैर्न विध्यन्ति विविक्तमपरापरम् । शब्दवेध्यं च विततं लघुहस्ता विशारदा: । । 1520 । । सिंहव्याघ्रवराहाणां मत्तानां नर्दतां वने । हन्तारो निशितैश्शस्त्रैर्बलाद्बाहुबलैरपि । । 1521 । । तादृशानां सहस्रैस्तामभिपूर्णां महारथै: । पुरीमावासयामास राजा दशरथस्तदा । । 1522 । ।
ramayan::212.verse_hindi: The city was inhabited by thousands of warriors known as maharathas. They were skilled archers and sharphanded. They would not pierce with arrows, solitary persons, persons without defence, fleeing foes who could be tracked down through hints from sound. With sharp arrows or with the strength of their arms, they would kill
ramayan::212.english_translation: The city was inhabited by thousands of mighty warriors, skilled archers who would not shoot at solitary men, the unarmed, or fleeing foes tracked by sound. With sharp weapons and strong arms, they could kill even fierce beasts in the forest. King Dasharatha had filled the city with such thousands of great chariot-warriors.
ramayan::212.translation_literal: ये (these) / च (and) / बाणैः (with arrows) / न (not) / विध्यन्ति (pierce, shoot) / विविक्तम् (solitary) / अपरापरम् (one after another, unprotected) / शब्दवेध्यम् (trackable by sound) / च (and) / विततम् (spread out, fleeing) / लघुहस्ताः (light-handed, quick-handed) / विशारदाः (skilled) / सिंहव्याघ्रवराहाणाम् (of lions, tigers, boars) / मत्तानाम् (of the intoxicated, enraged) / नर्दताम् (roaring) / वने (in the forest) / हन्तारः (killers) / निशितैः (with sharp) / शस्त्रैः (weapons) / बलात् (by force) / बाहुबलैः (with arm-strength) / अपि (also) / तादृशानाम् (of such) / सहस्रैः (by thousands) / ताम् (that) / अभिपूर्णाम् (filled) / महारथैः (by great chariot-warriors) / पुरीम् (city) / आवासयामास (caused to dwell, populated) / राजा (king) / दशरथः (Dasharatha) / तदा (then)
ramayan::212.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::212.essence: True strength includes restraint; the strong do not strike the helpless.
ramayan::212.simple_meaning: Ayodhya was filled with thousands of elite warriors, but they followed a code: they did not attack the helpless, the solitary, or a fleeing enemy.
ramayan::212.simple_insight: Strength feels nobler when it knows restraint.
ramayan::212.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Ayodhya under Dasharatha’s rule. The city is not just wealthy and bright; it is protected by thousands of disciplined maharathas. Their skill is measured by restraint as much as by force, showing the moral order of Rama’s world before exile begins.
ramayan::212.modern_relevance: A team can be powerful in the wrong way — always ready to crush, never ready to restrain. The harder test is having strength and still refusing to use it on the vulnerable.
ramayan::212.insight: It shifts respect from raw force to disciplined conduct under power.

ramayan::213.verse_hindi: That city (of Ayodhya) was filled with excellent dwijas (brahmana, kshatriya and vaisyas) performing rituals of sacrificial fire, virtuous and wellversed in the Vedas and Vedangas. They were generous, truthful and dignified. They were almost equal to rishis and maharshis.
ramayan::213.english_translation: That city was filled with excellent twice-born people who kept sacrificial fire, were virtuous, knew the Vedas and the six auxiliaries, gave generously, spoke truth, and were great-souled, almost like sages and great sages.
ramayan::213.translation_literal: ताम् (that) / अग्निमद्भिः (with sacrificial fires) / गुणवद्भिः (with virtues) / आवृताम् (filled) / द्विजोत्तमैः (by the best of the twice-born) / वेदषडङ्गपारगैः (by those who had crossed over into the Vedas and the six auxiliaries) / सहस्रदैः (by givers of thousands) / सत्यरतैः (devoted to truth) / महात्मभिः (by great-souled ones) / महर्षिकल्पैः (resembling great sages) / ऋषिभिः (by sages) / च (and) / केवलैः (pure, alone)
ramayan::213.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::213.essence: Ayodhya's greatness came from the character of its people.
ramayan::213.simple_meaning: Ayodhya was full of learned, generous, truthful, and noble people who lived close to the ideals of sages.
ramayan::213.simple_insight: A city becomes great when its people live with learning, generosity, and truth.
ramayan::213.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Ayodhya before the exile crisis, building a picture of a city at its height. It is not a teaching verse but a scene-setting detail: the capital is prosperous because its people are disciplined, learned, generous, and morally refined.
ramayan::213.modern_relevance: A neighborhood where people know how to keep promises, share freely, and speak plainly feels different the moment you enter. That atmosphere is built, not accidental.
ramayan::213.insight: It shifts attention from buildings and wealth to the character of the people who make a place worthy of trust.

ramayan::214.verse_sanskrit: तस्यां पुर्यामयोध्यायां वेदवित्सर्वसङ्ग्रह: । दीर्घदर्शी महातेजा: पौरजानपदप्रिय: । । 161 । । इक्ष्वाकूणामतिरथो यज्वा धर्मरतो वशी । महर्षिकल्पो राजर्षिस्त्रिषु लोकेषु विश्रुत: । । 162 । । बलवान्निहतामित्रो मित्रवान्विजितेन्द्रिय: । धनैश्च सङ्ग्रहैश्चान्यैश्शक्रवैश्रवणोपम: । । 163 । । यथा मनुर्महातेजा लोकस्य परिरक्षिता । तथा दशरथो राजा वसञ्जगदपालयत् । । 164 । ।
ramayan::214.verse_hindi: From that city of Ayodhya, king Dasaratha ruled the entire world, following the tradition of Manu who was a highly powerful protector of the people. Dasaratha was
ramayan::214.english_translation: In Ayodhya, Dasaratha was learned in the Vedas, far-seeing, radiant, beloved by the people, and the best of the Ikshvakus. He was a great warrior, devoted to sacrifice, steady in dharma, self-controlled, like a great sage and a royal sage famed in all three worlds. Strong, victorious over enemies, surrounded by loyal friends, and rich in wealth, he ruled the world like Manu, the great protector of people.
ramayan::214.translation_literal: तस्यां (in that) / पुर्याम् (city) / अयोध्यायाम् (in Ayodhya) / वेदवित् (knower of the Vedas) / सर्वसङ्ग्रहः (all-embracing) / दीर्घदर्शी (far-seeing) / महातेजाः (highly radiant) / पौरजानपदप्रियः (dear to the townspeople and country people) / इक्ष्वाकूणाम् (of the Ikshvakus) / अतिरथः (great warrior) / यज्वा (sacrificer) / धर्मरतः (devoted to dharma) / वशी (self-controlled) / महर्षिकल्पः (like a great sage) / राजर्षिः (royal sage) / त्रिषु लोकेषु (in the three worlds) / विश्रुतः (famed) / बलवान् (strong) / निहतामित्रः (one whose enemies were slain) / मित्रवान् (possessing friends) / विजितेन्द्रियः (one who has conquered the senses) / धनैः (with wealth) / च (and) / सङ्ग्रहैः (with accumulations) / च (and) / अन्यैः (other) / शक्रवैश्रवणोपमः (like Shakra and Vaishravana) / यथा (as) / मनुः (Manu) / महातेजाः (highly powerful) / लोकस्य (of the people) / परिरक्षिता (protector) / तथा (thus) / दशरथः (Dasaratha) / राजा (king) / वसन् (dwelling/ruling) / जगत् (the world) / अपालयत् (protected/rule)
ramayan::214.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::214.essence: Dasaratha’s greatness came from restraint, learning, and public trust.
ramayan::214.simple_meaning: Dasaratha is praised as a wise, disciplined, and powerful king who protected his people well and ruled with great dignity.
ramayan::214.simple_insight: Great leadership is not just power; it is steadiness, self-control, and care for the people you serve.
ramayan::214.detailed_meaning: Valmiki pauses in Ayodhya to describe Dasaratha before the exile crisis begins. The king is shown as learned, generous, disciplined, and admired by all. This is background, not a teaching verse in itself.
ramayan::214.modern_relevance: A city trusts the leader who is calm under pressure, fair in private, and respected without needing to demand it. That kind of authority is built long before a crisis arrives.
ramayan::214.insight: It frames leadership as earned through self-mastery and public trust, not just rank or force.

ramayan::215.verse_sanskrit: तेन सत्याभिसन्धेन त्रिवर्गमनुतिष्ठता । पालिता सा पुरी श्रेष्ठा इन्द्रेणेवामरावती । । 165 । ।
ramayan::215.verse_hindi: King Dasaratha, who always kept his word and followed dharma, attained prosperity and pleasure in equal measure by righteous means ruled that best of the cities as Indra ruled Amaravati.
ramayan::215.english_translation: King Dasaratha, who always kept his word and followed dharma, attained prosperity and pleasure in equal measure by righteous means, and ruled that best of cities as Indra ruled Amaravati.
ramayan::215.translation_literal: तेन (by him) / सत्याभिसन्धेन (by one whose resolve is truth-bound) / त्रिवर्गम् (the three aims of life) / अनुतिष्ठता (being duly pursued) / पालिता (was protected) / सा (that) / पुरी (city) / श्रेष्ठा (best) / इन्द्रेण (by Indra) / इव (like) / अमरावती (Amaravati)
ramayan::215.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::215.essence: A ruler's truthfulness protects more than his own honour.
ramayan::215.simple_meaning: Dasaratha protected Ayodhya because he lived by truth and dharma. His rule was prosperous because his life was governed by righteousness, not selfish desire.
ramayan::215.simple_insight: Integrity is not just personal; it stabilises everything around you.
ramayan::215.detailed_meaning: Valmiki describes Ayodhya at its peak under Dasaratha. The king is not merely powerful; he is truth-bound and balanced in the three aims of life. Because he rules rightly, the city stands secure and radiant like Indra's Amaravati.
ramayan::215.modern_relevance: You sign a contract, keep your promise, and people begin to trust the whole team again. One person's truthfulness can steady an entire system.
ramayan::215.insight: It shifts leadership from control and image to truth-bound responsibility.

ramayan::216.verse_sanskrit: तस्मिन्पुरवरे हृष्टा धर्मात्मानो बहुश्रुता: । नरास्तुष्टा धनैस्स्वैस्स्वैरलुब्धास्सत्यवादिन: । । 166 । ।
ramayan::216.verse_hindi: The people living in that excellent city were happy, virtuous, wellread (in the Vedas and the sastras) and content with the possessions of their own. They were free from avarice. And always spoke the truth.
ramayan::216.english_translation: The people living in that excellent city were happy, virtuous, learned, content with their own possessions, free from greed, and always truthful.
ramayan::216.translation_literal: तस्मिन् (in that) / पुरवरे (in the excellent city) / हृष्टा (joyful) / धर्मात्मानः (righteous-minded) / बहुश्रुताः (well-read) / नराः (men) / तुष्टाः (content) / धनैः स्वैः स्वैः (with their own possessions) / अलुब्धाः (free from greed) / सत्यवादिनः (truth-speakers)
ramayan::216.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::216.essence: A truly prosperous city is made of truthful, content people.
ramayan::216.simple_meaning: Ayodhya was full of people who were happy, disciplined, content, free from greed, and committed to truth.
ramayan::216.simple_insight: A good society begins with people who want less and speak honestly.
ramayan::216.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Ayodhya before Rama's exile: a city ruled well by Dasharatha, where the citizens themselves reflect the order around them. Their learning, contentment, and truthfulness show what a flourishing kingdom looks like from the inside.
ramayan::216.modern_relevance: A neighborhood where no one is scrambling to outdo the next house, and people still keep their word, feels almost unreal now. Valmiki points to that kind of ordinary integrity as the mark of a healthy world.
ramayan::216.insight: It shifts attention from public power to the moral character of everyday life.

ramayan::217.verse_sanskrit: नाल्पसन्निचय: कश्चिदासीत्तस्मिन् पुरोत्तमे । कुटुम्बी यो ह्यसिद्धार्थोऽगवाश्वधनधान्यवान् । । 167 । ।
ramayan::217.verse_hindi: In that best of cities, there was not even a single householder who had not adequate wealth or who had not achieved dharma, artha and kama or who did not possess the wealth of foodgrains, cattle and horses.
ramayan::217.english_translation: In that best of cities, there was not even a single householder who had not adequate wealth or who had not achieved dharma, artha and kama or who did not possess the wealth of foodgrains, cattle and horses.
ramayan::217.translation_literal: न-अल्पसन्निचयः (not having small accumulation) / कश्चित् (anyone) / आसीत् (was) / तस्मिन् (in that) / पुरोत्तमे (best of cities) / कुटुम्बी (householder) / यः (who) / हि (indeed) / असिद्धार्थः (without fulfilled aims) / अगवाश्वधनधान्यवान् (possessed of cattle, horses, wealth, and grain)
ramayan::217.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::217.essence: Good rule is measured by the security of ordinary homes.
ramayan::217.simple_meaning: Ayodhya was so prosperous that every householder had enough wealth, food, cattle, and horses, and had fulfilled life’s aims.
ramayan::217.simple_insight: A truly ordered society leaves ordinary families secure, not scrambling for survival.
ramayan::217.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Ayodhya at its height under Dasharatha: a city so well-governed that no householder lacked wealth or basic abundance. This is part of a larger portrait of a kingdom where prosperity, virtue, and contentment all coexist.
ramayan::217.modern_relevance: A neighborhood where families can pay rent, buy food, and still breathe is not a luxury — it is the sign of real governance.
ramayan::217.insight: It shifts attention from elite success to whether ordinary households are secure and complete.

ramayan::218.verse_sanskrit: कामी वा न कदर्यो वा नृशंस: पुरुष: क्वचित् । द्रष्टुं शक्यमयोध्यायान्नाविद्वान्न च नास्तिक: । । 168 । ।
ramayan::218.verse_hindi: The lustful, the miserly, the unscholarly and atheists were not to be seen anywhere in the city of Ayodhya.
ramayan::218.english_translation: The lustful, the miserly, the cruel, the ignorant, and the unbelieving could not be seen anywhere in Ayodhya.
ramayan::218.translation_literal: कामी (lustful) / वा (or) / न (not) / कदर्यः (miserly) / वा (or) / नृशंसः (cruel) / पुरुषः (person) / क्वचित् (anywhere) / द्रष्टुम् (to see) / शक्यः (possible) / अयोध्यायाम् (in Ayodhya) / न (not) / अविद्वान् (ignorant) / न (not) / च (and) / नास्तिकः (unbelieving)
ramayan::218.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::218.essence: A righteous city makes vice feel out of place.
ramayan::218.simple_meaning: Ayodhya was so upright that you could not find lust, greed, cruelty, ignorance, or disbelief there.
ramayan::218.simple_insight: A whole city can be shaped by what it refuses to tolerate.
ramayan::218.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Ayodhya before the exile begins: a city so orderly that even vice seems absent. This verse continues the portrait of a society held together by discipline, learning, and moral restraint.
ramayan::218.modern_relevance: You walk into a room where cruelty is treated as normal, and everyone stays quiet. Ayodhya feels different: a place where the whole atmosphere makes vice harder to hide.
ramayan::218.insight: It shifts attention from individual virtue to the moral climate a community creates.

ramayan::219.verse_sanskrit: सर्वे नराश्च नार्यश्च धर्मशीलास्सुसंयता: । उदिताश्शीलवृत्ताभ्यां महर्षय इवामला: । । 169 । ।
ramayan::219.verse_hindi: All men and women (in the city) were of righteous conduct, fully selfcontrolled and prosperous with good conduct and behaviour. They were pure like maharshis.
ramayan::219.english_translation: All men and women in the city were righteous in conduct, fully self-controlled, and radiant with good character and behavior. They were pure like great sages.
ramayan::219.translation_literal: सर्वे (all) / नराः (men) / च (and) / नार्यः (women) / च (and) / धर्मशीलाः (righteous in conduct) / सुसंयताः (fully self-controlled) / उदिताः (raised, shining) / शीलवृत्ताभ्याम् (by character and conduct) / महर्षयः इव (like great sages) / अमलाः (pure, spotless)
ramayan::219.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::219.essence: A righteous city makes purity feel ordinary.
ramayan::219.simple_meaning: Everyone in Ayodhya lived with discipline, purity, and self-control. The city was so orderly that its people seemed as pure as sages.
ramayan::219.simple_insight: A whole society can be shaped by inner discipline, not just laws.
ramayan::219.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Ayodhya before the exile begins: a city where men and women alike are disciplined, pure, and steady in conduct. This is not a side detail but part of the larger portrait of a kingdom worthy of Rama.
ramayan::219.modern_relevance: Walk through a neighborhood where people still greet each other, keep promises, and raise children with care. The atmosphere feels different because character has become public life.
ramayan::219.insight: It shifts attention from private virtue alone to the moral climate created by an entire community.

ramayan::220.verse_sanskrit: नाकुण्डली नामकुटी नास्रग्वी नाल्पभोगवान् । नामृष्टो नानुलिप्ताङ्गो नासुगन्धश्च विद्यते । । 1610 । ।
ramayan::220.verse_hindi: In the city, there was none without earornaments, without coronet, without wearing garlands and none unclean. And none without the anointment of fragrants on the body.
ramayan::220.english_translation: In the city, there was no one without ear ornaments, without a crown, without garlands, unclean, or without fragrant anointing on the body.
ramayan::220.translation_literal: न (not) / अकुण्डली (wearing no ear ornaments) / नामकुटी (wearing no crown) / न (not) / अस्रग्वी (wearing no garlands) / न (not) / अल्पभोगवान् (having little enjoyment) / न (not) / अमृष्टः (unclean) / न (not) / अनुलिप्ताङ्गः (with an un-anointed body) / न (not) / असुगन्धः (without fragrance) / च (and) / विद्यते (is found)
ramayan::220.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::220.essence: Ayodhya’s harmony appears even in how its people present themselves.
ramayan::220.simple_meaning: Ayodhya is described as a city where everyone is adorned, clean, and fragrant. The verse adds to the picture of a prosperous, orderly kingdom.
ramayan::220.simple_insight: A well-ruled life shows up in small outward details.
ramayan::220.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is still painting Ayodhya’s golden age. After saying the people are righteous and restrained, he adds another layer: everyone is decorated, clean, and pleasant to the senses. It is not a teaching verse on its own, but part of the larger portrait of a flourishing city.
ramayan::220.modern_relevance: You walk through a neighborhood where every house is kept with care, every doorway swept, every face composed. The verse notices how order in a society appears even in appearance.
ramayan::220.insight: It shifts attention from abstract prosperity to the visible signs of a cared-for community.

ramayan::221.verse_sanskrit: नामृष्टभोजी नादाता नाप्यनङ्गदनिष्कधृक् । नाहस्ताभरणो वाऽपि दृश्यते नाप्यनात्मवान् । । 1611 । ।
ramayan::221.verse_hindi: (In the city of Ayodhya) there was no one who did not eat food to full satisfaction and was not charitable. None was found without wearing ornaments on the hands and bracelets on the upper arms and around the neck. Also no one could be seen who had not restrained his passions and emotions.
ramayan::221.english_translation: (In the city of Ayodhya) there was no one who did not eat food to full satisfaction and was not charitable. None was found without wearing ornaments on the hands and bracelets on the upper arms and around the neck. Also no one could be seen who had not restrained his passions and emotions.
ramayan::221.translation_literal: नामृष्टभोजी (not eating without satisfaction) / नादाता (not a giver) / न अपि (and not even) / अनङ्गद-निष्कधृक् (wearing no armlet or necklace) / न अहस्ताभरणः (not without hand-ornaments) / वा अपि (or also) / दृश्यते (is seen) / न अपि (and not even) / अनात्मवान् (without self-restraint)
ramayan::221.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::221.essence: True prosperity shows itself in generosity and restraint.
ramayan::221.simple_meaning: Ayodhya was so prosperous and well-ordered that everyone ate well, gave freely, wore ornaments, and kept their desires under control.
ramayan::221.simple_insight: A thriving society shows up in ordinary people living with dignity, generosity, and self-restraint.
ramayan::221.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Ayodhya at its height: a city where material comfort, generosity, and disciplined conduct all coexist. This is one more brushstroke in a larger portrait of a kingdom so orderly that even its smallest details reflect abundance and restraint.
ramayan::221.modern_relevance: A neighborhood where people feel safe enough to be generous, well-kept, and calm after dinner tells you more than any slogan ever could.
ramayan::221.insight: It shifts attention from private wealth to public character: prosperity is real when it produces generosity and self-control.

ramayan::222.verse_sanskrit: नानाहिताग्निर्नायज्वा न क्षुद्रो वा न तस्कर: । कश्चिदासीदयोध्यायान्न च निर्वृत्तसङ्कर: । । 1612 । ।
ramayan::222.verse_hindi: In the city of Ayodhya there was none who did not kindle the sacrificial fire. There was none who did not perform a sacrifice. There were no thieves or meanminded persons or persons of improper descent of mixed castes.
ramayan::222.english_translation: In the city of Ayodhya, there was no one who did not maintain the sacred fire or perform sacrifice. There were no thieves, no mean-minded people, and no one of mixed or confused lineage.
ramayan::222.translation_literal: नानाहिताग्निः (not one who has not maintained the sacred fire) / नायज्वा (not one who performs sacrifice) / न (not) / क्षुद्रः (mean-minded) / वा (or) / न (not) / तस्करः (thief) / कश्चित् (anyone) / आसीत् (was) / अयोध्यायाम् (in Ayodhya) / न (not) / च (and) / निर्वृत्तसङ्करः (one of mixed or confused lineage)
ramayan::222.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::222.essence: A righteous city is one where wrongdoing has nowhere to settle.
ramayan::222.simple_meaning: Ayodhya is described as a place where ritual duty was kept, wrongdoing was absent, and social order was intact.
ramayan::222.simple_insight: A society stays whole when people guard both conduct and conscience.
ramayan::222.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Ayodhya at its height, before the exile begins. The city is so orderly that even basic moral failures are absent: no theft, no cruelty, no neglect of sacred duty. This is part of a larger portrait of a kingdom fit for Rama.
ramayan::222.modern_relevance: A neighborhood where doors stay unlocked, children walk home safely, and no one is afraid of being cheated feels almost unreal. This verse points to that kind of shared moral climate.
ramayan::222.insight: It shifts attention from individual virtue alone to the social fabric that protects it.
