ramayan::223.verse_sanskrit: स्वकर्मनिरता नित्यं ब्राह्मणा विजितेन्द्रिया: । दानाध्ययनशीलाश्च संयताश्च परिग्रहे । । 1613 । ।
ramayan::223.verse_hindi: The brahmins were always interested in the performance of their duties. They had control over their senses. They were charitable and studious. They were selfcontrolled  while accepting charity and maintaining marital relations.
ramayan::223.english_translation: The brahmins were always devoted to their duties. They had conquered their senses, and were generous, studious, and self-controlled in accepting gifts and in marriage.
ramayan::223.translation_literal: स्वकर्मनिरता (devoted to their own duties) / नित्यम् (always) / ब्राह्मणा: (the brahmins) / विजितेन्द्रिया: (those who have conquered their senses) / दानाध्ययनशीलाः (inclined to giving and study) / च (and) / संयताः (restrained) / च (and) / परिग्रहे (in accepting gifts / household relations)
ramayan::223.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::223.essence: A righteous society begins with disciplined, self-governed people.
ramayan::223.simple_meaning: Ayodhya’s brahmins lived with discipline: devoted to duty, self-controlled, generous, and committed to study.
ramayan::223.simple_insight: A well-ordered society begins with people who can govern themselves.
ramayan::223.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Ayodhya’s moral order in broad strokes. After noting the city’s purity in daily life, he adds that even the brahmins were steady in duty, disciplined in the senses, and careful in both giving and receiving.
ramayan::223.modern_relevance: A home where everyone is distracted, reactive, and always grasping starts to feel unstable. This verse points to a quieter foundation: people who can control themselves before they try to guide others.
ramayan::223.insight: It shifts attention from status to character: learning, restraint, and generosity make a community fit to flourish.

ramayan::224.verse_sanskrit: न नास्तिको नानृतको न कश्चिदबहुश्रुत: । नासूयको न चाऽशक्तो नाविद्वान्विद्यते तदा । । 1614 । ।
ramayan::224.verse_hindi: That time there was no atheist, no liar and none ignorant of the sastras. There was no one who was jealous, incompetent or illiterate.
ramayan::224.english_translation: At that time, there was no atheist, no liar, and no one ignorant of the scriptures. There was no one who was jealous, incapable, or unlearned.
ramayan::224.translation_literal: न (not) / नास्तिकः (atheist) / न (not) / अनृतकः (liar) / न (not) / कश्चित् (anyone) / अबहुश्रुतः (unlearned in many teachings) / न (not) / असूयकः (jealous) / न (not) / च (and) / अशक्तः (incapable) / न (not) / अविद्वान् (unlearned) / विद्यते (exists) / तदा (then/at that time)
ramayan::224.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::224.essence: A great city begins with honest, capable people.
ramayan::224.simple_meaning: Ayodhya was so well-ordered that people were truthful, learned, capable, and free from envy.
ramayan::224.simple_insight: A healthy society is built from character, not just wealth or power.
ramayan::224.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Ayodhya at its peak before exile and collapse begin. The city is not just rich or powerful; its people are morally and intellectually refined. This verse adds another layer to that ideal order.
ramayan::224.modern_relevance: A neighborhood where people keep their word, study seriously, and do not envy each other feels almost unreal now. This verse remembers what a well-ordered community looks like before it decays.
ramayan::224.insight: It shifts attention from external prosperity to the inner quality of the people who hold a society together.

ramayan::225.verse_sanskrit: नाषडङ्गविदत्रासीन्नाव्रतो नासहस्रद: । न दीन: क्षिप्तचित्तो वा व्यथितो वाऽपि कश्चन । । 1615 । ।
ramayan::225.verse_hindi: There was no brahmin who was not well versed in the Vedangas or who did not perform religious vows. There was not even one  who would not donate in thousands. There was no one distracted or depressed.
ramayan::225.english_translation: There was no brahmin who was not well versed in the Vedangas or who did not perform vows. No one failed to donate generously in thousands. No one was distracted, poor in spirit, or distressed.
ramayan::225.translation_literal: न अषडङ्गविद् (not versed in the six auxiliaries) / अत्रासीत् (there was not) / न अव्रतः (not one without vows) / न असहस्रदः (not one who gives thousands) / न दीनः (not dejected) / क्षिप्तचित्तः (mind thrown about) / वा (or) / व्यथितः (distressed) / वा अपि (or even) / कश्चन (anyone)
ramayan::225.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::225.essence: A strong city is built by disciplined, generous, steady people.
ramayan::225.simple_meaning: Ayodhya’s learned men were disciplined, generous, and steady-minded. No one was careless, miserly, or emotionally shaken.
ramayan::225.simple_insight: A healthy society begins when people are trained, generous, and inwardly steady.
ramayan::225.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Ayodhya at its best before the exile crisis. The city’s brahmins are learned, vow-bound, and generous in thousands, and no one is mentally scattered or distressed. It is a portrait of order before the kingdom’s moral collapse begins.
ramayan::225.modern_relevance: A family, team, or school can look successful on the outside and still be inwardly frayed. This verse points to a deeper standard: learning, restraint, generosity, and a steady mind.
ramayan::225.insight: It shifts attention from outer success to the character that quietly holds a community together.

ramayan::226.verse_sanskrit: कश्चिन्नरो वा नारी वा नाश्रीमान्नाप्यरूपवान् । द्रष्टुं शक्यमयोध्यायां नापि राजन्यभक्तिमान् । । 1616 । ।
ramayan::226.verse_hindi: In Ayodhya, there was no man or woman who was not endowed with wealth or beauty. It was not possible to see any one who had no devotion for the king.
ramayan::226.english_translation: In Ayodhya, there was no man or woman who was not wealthy or beautiful. It was impossible to find anyone who lacked devotion to the king.
ramayan::226.translation_literal: कश्चित् (anyone) / नरः (man) / वा (or) / नारी (woman) / वा (or) / न (not) / अश्रीमान् (without wealth) / न अपि (nor even) / अरूपवान् (without beauty) / द्रष्टुम् (to see) / शक्यः (possible) / अयोध्यायाम् (in Ayodhya) / न अपि (nor even) / राजनि (for the king) / अभक्तिमान् (without devotion)
ramayan::226.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::226.essence: A just city makes prosperity and loyalty visible in everyone.
ramayan::226.simple_meaning: Ayodhya was so prosperous and orderly that everyone seemed prosperous and attractive, and everyone respected the king.
ramayan::226.simple_insight: A healthy society shows itself in how naturally people respect good leadership.
ramayan::226.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Ayodhya at its height, before exile and loss. The city is not just rich; its people are dignified, content, and loyal to Rama and Dasharatha. This verse is one brushstroke in a larger portrait of an ideal kingdom.
ramayan::226.modern_relevance: Walk through a neighborhood where people still greet the local elder with respect, and children feel safe in the streets. You can tell something is working there before anyone explains it.
ramayan::226.insight: It frames good rule as something visible in everyday life, not just in palace politics.

ramayan::227.verse_sanskrit: वर्णेष्वग्र्यचतुर्थेषु देवतातिथिपूजका: । कृतज्ञाश्च वदान्याश्च शूरा विक्रमसंयुता: । । 1617 । । दीर्घायुषो नरास्सर्वे धर्मं सत्यं च संश्रिता: । सहिता: पुत्रपौत्रैश्च नित्यं स्त्रीभि: पुरोत्तमे । । 1618 । ।
ramayan::227.verse_hindi: There in Ayodhya the best of cities, the first of the four castes (brahmins) used to worship gods and guests. They had the sense of gratitude. They were munificient, heroic and possessed prowess. They lived long. They were righteous and truthful. And they lived together with their sons, grandsons and wives.
ramayan::227.english_translation: In Ayodhya, the best of cities, the leading caste served the divine and honored guests. People were grateful, generous, brave, and full of courage. They lived long, upheld righteousness and truth, and stayed together with sons, grandsons, and wives.
ramayan::227.translation_literal: वर्णेषु (among the classes) / अग्र्यचतुर्थेषु (among the foremost four) / देवतातिथिपूजका: (worshippers of the divine and guests) । कृतज्ञा: (grateful) / च (and) / वदान्या: (generous) / च (and) / शूरा: (brave) / विक्रमसंयुता: (endowed with prowess) । दीर्घायुष: (long-lived) / नरा: (men) / सर्वे (all) / धर्मं (righteousness) / सत्यम् (truth) / च (and) / संश्रिता: (established in) । सहिता: (together) / पुत्रपौत्रै: (with sons and grandsons) / च (and) / नित्यम् (always) / स्त्रीभि: (with wives) / पुरोत्तमे (in the best of cities)
ramayan::227.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::227.essence: A great city is built by virtue, gratitude, and family bonds.
ramayan::227.simple_meaning: Ayodhya is described as a city where people are virtuous, generous, brave, grateful, long-lived, and closely bonded with family.
ramayan::227.simple_insight: It paints a world where character, not status, holds a city together.
ramayan::227.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Ayodhya before the exile tears it apart. The city is full of people who honor guests, repay kindness, speak truth, and live in stable family households. This is the moral order Rama is about to lose.
ramayan::227.modern_relevance: You can feel when a home or community has become thin and transactional. This verse remembers a place where gratitude, truth, and family life still held people together.
ramayan::227.insight: It shifts attention from wealth alone to the moral fabric that makes a society strong.

ramayan::228.verse_hindi: The kshatriyas were obedient to brahmins and vaisyas followed kshatriyas. Sudras assisted the three castes and all were fully occupied in their respective professions.
ramayan::228.english_translation: The kshatriyas were obedient to brahmins, the vaisyas followed the kshatriyas, and the sudras remained devoted to their own duties, serving the three higher orders.
ramayan::228.translation_literal: क्षत्रम् (kshatriyas) / ब्रह्ममुखम् (obedient to brahmins) / च (and) / आसीत् (were) / वैश्याः (vaisyas) / क्षत्रम् (kshatriyas) / अनुव्रताः (following) / शूद्राः (sudras) / स्वधर्मनिरताः (devoted to their own duties) / त्रीन् (three) / वर्णान् (orders) / उपचारिणः (serving)
ramayan::228.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::228.essence: A city’s order can be complete and still leave everyone in their assigned place.
ramayan::228.simple_meaning: Ayodhya's social order was orderly and hierarchical: each group stayed within its role, and the lower groups served the higher ones.
ramayan::228.simple_insight: Order can shape a city, but it also shows how completely people accepted their place.
ramayan::228.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Ayodhya before the exile begins, painting it as a city where social duties are tightly arranged. Kshatriyas defer to brahmins, vaishyas follow kshatriyas, and sudras serve the three groups, setting up a picture of disciplined but rigid civic order.
ramayan::228.modern_relevance: You walk into a workplace where everyone knows exactly who answers to whom, who speaks first, and who stays invisible. The system runs smoothly — and you can feel how much of each person it asks them to surrender.
ramayan::228.insight: It shifts attention from individual will to the structure that organizes behavior and rank.

ramayan::229.verse_sanskrit: सा तेनेक्ष्वाकुनाथेन पुरी सुपरिरक्षिता । यथा पुरस्तान्मनुना मानवेन्द्रेण धीमता । । 1620 । ।
ramayan::229.verse_hindi: That city was ably governed by Dasaratha, scion of the Ikshvakus, in the same way as it was  previously administered by (Manu), the foremost among men and and the most intelligent.
ramayan::229.english_translation: That city was ably governed by Dasaratha, scion of the Ikshvakus, in the same way as it was previously administered by Manu, the foremost among men and the most intelligent.
ramayan::229.translation_literal: सा (that) / तेनेक्ष्वाकुनाथेन (by that lord of the Ikshvakus) / पुरी (city) / सुपरिरक्षिता (well-protected, well-governed) / यथा (as) / पुरस्तात् (formerly) / मनुना (by Manu) / मानवेन्द्रेण (by the lord among men) / धीमता (by the wise one)
ramayan::229.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::229.essence: A ruler is measured by the safety his rule creates.
ramayan::229.simple_meaning: Ayodhya was ruled well by Dasharatha, just as it had once been ruled by Manu.
ramayan::229.simple_insight: Good rule is remembered by the safety and order it leaves behind.
ramayan::229.detailed_meaning: Valmiki pauses over Ayodhya before the exile begins. He shows Dasharatha’s city as carefully protected and orderly, linking the present king to Manu, the ancient model of wise rule. The praise sets up how much is about to be lost.
ramayan::229.modern_relevance: A city, team, or family feels different when leadership is steady. You notice it most when that steadiness is gone.
ramayan::229.insight: It shifts attention from power itself to the quality of care that power leaves in its wake.

ramayan::230.verse_sanskrit: योधानामग्निकल्पानां पेशलानाममर्षिणाम् । सम्पूर्णा कृतविद्यानां गुहा केसरिणामिव । । 1621 । ।
ramayan::230.verse_hindi: It abounded with warriors, like a cave with lions. They were almost like flaming fire, the most determined among experts and accomplished in learning (the science of arms).
ramayan::230.english_translation: It abounded with warriors, like a cave with lions. They were like flaming fire, fierce, skilled, and fully trained in the science of arms.
ramayan::230.translation_literal: योधानाम् (of warriors) / अग्निकल्पानाम् (like fire) / पेशलानाम् (skilled, polished) / अमर्षिणाम् (fierce, intolerant of insult) / सम्पूर्णा (full, abundant) / कृतविद्यानाम् (of those who have completed their training) / गुहा (cave) / केसरिणाम् (of lions) / इव (like)
ramayan::230.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::230.essence: True strength lies in trained force, not mere abundance.
ramayan::230.simple_meaning: The city was packed with fierce, highly trained warriors, as crowded and powerful as a lion's cave.
ramayan::230.simple_insight: Strength is not just numbers; it is trained force held in readiness.
ramayan::230.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Ayodhya’s strength before the story turns toward succession and exile. The city is not fragile or undefended — it is full of disciplined warriors, so the coming crisis will be moral, not military.
ramayan::230.modern_relevance: A company can look unstoppable on paper: skilled people, sharp systems, strong numbers. But when the real crisis comes, all that strength still has to answer to character.
ramayan::230.insight: It shifts attention from raw force to trained, disciplined readiness.

ramayan::231.verse_sanskrit: काम्भोजविषये जातैर्बाह्लीकैश्च हयोत्तमै: । वनायुजैर्नदीजैश्च पूर्णा हरिहयोत्तमै: । । 1622 । ।
ramayan::231.verse_hindi: The city was full of excellent horses born in the regions of Kambhoja, Bahlika, Vanayu and Sindhu, similar to that of Indras horse (called Ucchaisrava).
ramayan::231.english_translation: The city was full of excellent horses born in Kambhoja, Bahlika, Vanayu, and Sindhu, like Indra's horse Ucchaihshrava.
ramayan::231.translation_literal: काम्भोजविषये (in the Kambhoja region) / जातैः (born) / बाह्लीकैः (from Bahlika) / च (and) / हयोत्तमैः (excellent horses) / वनायुजैः (from Vanayu) / नदीजैः (from Sindhu-river lands) / च (and) / पूर्णा (filled) / हरिहयोत्तमैः (with Indra's finest horses)
ramayan::231.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::231.essence: Ayodhya's greatness is shown through the abundance it can command.
ramayan::231.simple_meaning: Ayodhya was stocked with superb horses from famous breeding regions, so many that the city seemed overflowing with them.
ramayan::231.simple_insight: The verse builds a picture of abundance and royal splendour before the story turns.
ramayan::231.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Ayodhya's wealth and strength under Dasharatha. After mentioning its careful governance and fierce warriors, he lists its prized horses from distant regions. The point is not teaching but scene-setting: this is a city rich enough to support a kingly world.
ramayan::231.modern_relevance: A city block lined with parked luxury cars, delivery trucks, and private stables of polished machines can feel like this verse: prosperity made visible in what a place can gather.
ramayan::231.insight: It shifts attention from plot to atmosphere, showing the scale of the kingdom before conflict begins.

ramayan::232.verse_sanskrit: विन्ध्यपर्वतजैर्मत्तै: पूर्णा हैमवतैरपि । मदान्वितैरतिबलैर्मातङ्गै: पर्वतोपमै: । । 1623 । । ऐरावतकुलीनैश्च महापद्मकुलैस्तथा । अञ्जनादपि निष्पन्नैर्वामनादपि च द्विपैः । । 1624 । ।
ramayan::232.verse_hindi: It was full of intoxicated elephants born in Vindhya mountains, elephants of enormous
ramayan::232.english_translation: It was full of intoxicated elephants born in Vindhya mountains, elephants of enormous strength, mountain-like in size; and also elephants of the lines of Airavata, Mahapadma, and those born from Anjana and Vamana.
ramayan::232.translation_literal: विन्ध्यपर्वतजैः (born in the Vindhya mountains) / मत्तैः (intoxicated) / पूर्णा (filled) / हैमवतैः (from the Himalaya) / अपि (also) / मदान्वितैः (endowed with intoxication) / अतिबलैः (very strong) / मातङ्गैः (elephants) / पर्वतोपमैः (mountain-like) / ऐरावतकुलीनैः (of the Airavata lineage) / च (and) / महापद्मकुलैः (of the Mahapadma lineage) / तथा (and also) / अञ्जनात् (from Anjana) / अपि (also) / निष्पन्नैः (produced) / वामनात् (from Vamana) / अपि (also) / च (and) / द्विपैः (elephants)
ramayan::232.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::232.essence: Ayodhya's grandeur is measured in the living strength it shelters.
ramayan::232.simple_meaning: Ayodhya is described as overflowing with powerful elephants from many famous lineages, huge as mountains and full of energy.
ramayan::232.simple_insight: The city's wealth is shown through scale, abundance, and living power.
ramayan::232.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Ayodhya's splendor before the exile begins. The city is packed with mighty elephants from celebrated breeds, each one huge, strong, and well-kept. The point is not a lesson but a vivid picture of royal abundance.
ramayan::232.insight: It builds the sense of a prosperous capital through concrete detail, not abstraction.

ramayan::233.verse_sanskrit: भद्रैर्मन्द्रैर्मृगैश्चैव भद्रमन्द्रमृगैस्तथा । भद्रमन्द्रैर्भद्रमृगैर्मृगमन्द्रैश्च सा पुरी । नित्यमत्तैस्सदा पूर्णा नागैरचलसन्निभै: । । 1625 । ।
ramayan::233.verse_hindi: The city (of Ayodhya) was always full of intoxicated elephants resembling mountains belonging to the races of Bhadra, Mandra, Mriga and interbreed of these three races, interbreed of races of Bhadra and Mandra, Bhadra and Mriga, Mriga and Mandra.
ramayan::233.english_translation: The city of Ayodhya was always full of intoxicated elephants, like mountains, from the Bhadra, Mandra, Mriga, and mixed breeds.
ramayan::233.translation_literal: भद्रैः (of the Bhadra breed) / मन्द्रैः (of the Mandra breed) / मृगैः (of the Mriga breed) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / भद्रमन्द्रमृगैः (of mixed Bhadra-Mandra-Mriga breeds) / तथा (likewise) / भद्रमन्द्रैः (of mixed Bhadra-Mandra breeds) / भद्रमृगैः (of mixed Bhadra-Mriga breeds) / मृगमन्द्रैः (of mixed Mriga-Mandra breeds) / च (and) / सा (that) / पुरी (city) / नित्यमत्तैः (always intoxicated) / सदा (always) / पूर्णा (full) / नागैः (with elephants) / अचलसन्निभैः (mountain-like)
ramayan::233.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::233.essence: Ayodhya is shown in its full magnificence before the fall begins.
ramayan::233.simple_meaning: Ayodhya is described as a city overflowing with powerful elephants of many prized breeds, always lively and grand.
ramayan::233.simple_insight: The picture is abundance, not struggle — a royal city at full strength.
ramayan::233.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Ayodhya before the exile begins: a prosperous capital packed with mountain-like elephants of prized breeds. The detail builds the scale and splendour of Dasharatha’s kingdom, setting up the loss that follows.
ramayan::233.insight: It frames the city as a place of wealth, order, and royal power before everything changes.

ramayan::234.verse_sanskrit: सा योजने च द्वे भूय: सत्यनामा प्रकाशते । यस्यां दशरथो राजा वसन् जगदपालयत् । । 1626 । ।
ramayan::234.verse_hindi: The city where king Dasaratha lived and ruled, spread over a distance of sixteen miles. And it was worthy of its name.
ramayan::234.english_translation: The city where king Dasaratha lived and ruled spread over sixteen miles, and it was true to its name.
ramayan::234.translation_literal: सा (that) / योजने (in yojanas) / च (and) / द्वे (two) / भूय: (more) / सत्यनामा (truly named) / प्रकाशते (shines forth) / यस्यां (in which) / दशरथो (Dasharatha) / राजा (king) / वसन् (dwelling) / जगदपालयत् (protected the world)
ramayan::234.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::234.essence: A city's greatness is reflected in the king who protects it.
ramayan::234.simple_meaning: Ayodhya was about sixteen miles wide, and it truly deserved its name because Dasharatha lived there and protected the realm from it.
ramayan::234.simple_insight: A ruler's presence can make a city feel worthy of its name.
ramayan::234.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Ayodhya before the exile begins: a grand city, measured and praised, with Dasharatha at its center. The verse is a supporting detail in the larger portrait of royal splendor, not a separate teaching.
ramayan::234.modern_relevance: A neighborhood feels different when a steady, responsible leader is present. The place itself seems to hold its dignity more easily.
ramayan::234.insight: It grounds the scene in royal order before the coming collapse.

ramayan::235.verse_sanskrit: तां पुरीं स महातेजा राजा दशरथो महान् । शशास शमितामित्रो नक्षत्राणीव चन्द्रमा: । । 1627 । ।
ramayan::235.verse_hindi: Mighty king Dasaratha, of great brilliance vanquished his foes and ruled the city like the Moon over the  stars.
ramayan::235.english_translation: Mighty king Dasaratha, of great brilliance, vanquished his foes and ruled the city like the Moon over the stars.
ramayan::235.translation_literal: तां (that) / पुरीं (city) / सः (he) / महातेजाः (of great brilliance) / राजा (king) / दशरथः (Dasaratha) / महान् (great) / शशास (ruled) / शमित-अमित्रः (one who had subdued enemies) / नक्षत्राणीव (like the stars) / चन्द्रमाः (the Moon)
ramayan::235.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::235.essence: Power can look serene right before it begins to fail.
ramayan::235.simple_meaning: Dasaratha ruled Ayodhya with power and brilliance, keeping enemies subdued, like the moon shining over the stars.
ramayan::235.simple_insight: A steady ruler brings order without needing to shout for it.
ramayan::235.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Ayodhya before exile and collapse. Dasaratha still sits secure on the throne, brilliant and unchallenged, ruling the city with the calm dominance of the moon over the night sky. The line builds the world that will soon be broken.
ramayan::235.modern_relevance: You walk into a room where everything looks settled: the leader is confident, the system is working, and no one expects the crack that is coming next.
ramayan::235.insight: It frames authority as quiet, luminous control rather than loud force.

ramayan::236.verse_sanskrit: तां सत्यनामां दृढतोरणार्गलांगृहैर्विचित्रैरुपशोभितां शिवाम् । पुरीमयोध्यां नृसहस्रसङ्कुलांशशास वै शक्रसमो महीपति: । । 1628 । ।
ramayan::236.verse_hindi: The king who equalled Indra (in splendour) ruled the invincible city of Ayodhya true to its name with its strong gates and solid locks. It was adorned with wonderful edifices teeming with thousands of men.
ramayan::236.english_translation: The king who equalled Indra in splendour ruled Ayodhya, a true-to-name city with strong gates, firm bolts, beautiful buildings, and thousands of inhabitants.
ramayan::236.translation_literal: तां (that) / सत्यनामाम् (true to its name) / दृढतोरणार्गलांगृहैः (with strong gates and bolts and houses) / विचित्रैः (with wonderful) / उपशोभिताम् (adorned) / शिवाम् (auspicious) / पुरीम् (city) / अयोध्याम् (Ayodhya) / नृसहस्रसङ्कुलाम् (crowded with thousands of men) / शशास (ruled) / वै (indeed) / शक्रसमः (equal to Indra) / महीपतिः (king)
ramayan::236.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::236.essence: Ayodhya stands secure and splendid under Dasaratha's rule.
ramayan::236.simple_meaning: Ayodhya is described as a secure, beautiful city full of people, and Dasaratha rules it with great splendour.
ramayan::236.simple_insight: Great rule is not only power; it also creates order, safety, and a city people can live in.
ramayan::236.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is still painting Ayodhya before the exile begins. Dasaratha sits at the height of power, ruling a prosperous capital with strong defenses, fine buildings, and a dense population. The verse adds grandeur to the setting, not a new teaching.
ramayan::236.modern_relevance: A city skyline at dusk, lit offices, locked apartment gates, crowded streets, and a leader whose name barely reaches the people below. This verse simply frames that world before the real crisis begins.
ramayan::236.insight: It shifts attention from drama to context: before the fall, there was order, wealth, and visible strength.

ramayan::237.verse_sanskrit: तस्यामात्या गुणैरासन्निक्ष्वाकोस्तु महात्मन: । मन्त्रज्ञाश्चेङ्गितज्ञाश्च नित्यं प्रियहिते रता: । । 171 । ।
ramayan::237.verse_hindi: The ministers of the great descendent of the Ikshvakus were endowed with all virtues. They were competent counsellors, skilled in judging motives from facial features and were always intent on doing good and all that was dear and helpful to the king.
ramayan::237.english_translation: The ministers of the great descendent of the Ikshvakus were endowed with all virtues. They were competent counsellors, skilled in judging motives from facial features and were always intent on doing good and all that was dear and helpful to the king.
ramayan::237.translation_literal: तस्य (his) / अमात्याः (ministers) / गुणैः (with virtues) / आसन् (were) / इक्ष्वाकोः (of Ikshvaku) / तु (indeed) / महात्मनः (of the great-souled one) / मन्त्रज्ञाः (skilled in counsel) / च (and) / ईङ्गितज्ञाः (knowers of gestures / motives) / च (and) / नित्यं (always) / प्रियहिते (in what is pleasing and beneficial) / रताः (devoted)
ramayan::237.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::237.essence: A king’s strength depends on ministers who can read people and serve wisely.
ramayan::237.simple_meaning: Dasharatha’s ministers were wise, loyal, and good at reading people. They always worked for what was helpful and pleasing to the king.
ramayan::237.simple_insight: Good leadership is surrounded by people who can tell the truth, not just flatter it.
ramayan::237.detailed_meaning: Ayodhya is being described in its strength and order under Dasharatha. His ministers are not random attendants but skilled advisers, sensitive to motives and devoted to the king’s welfare. The verse sets up a court that should have been stable.
ramayan::237.modern_relevance: A team meeting where everyone nods too quickly can hide disaster. Real support means people who can read the room, speak honestly, and still care about the person in charge.
ramayan::237.insight: It shifts attention from royal power alone to the quality of counsel that sustains it.

ramayan::238.verse_sanskrit: अष्टौ बभूवुर्वीरस्य तस्यामात्या यशस्विन: । शुचयश्चानुरक्ताश्च राजकृत्येषु नित्यश: । । 172 । ।
ramayan::238.verse_hindi: The mighty and glorious (king Dasaratha) had eight ministers who were free from blemish in their dealings and ever devoted to royal duties.
ramayan::238.english_translation: The mighty and glorious king Dasharatha had eight ministers who were pure in conduct and always devoted to royal duties.
ramayan::238.translation_literal: अष्टौ (eight) / बभूवुः (there were) / वीरस्य (of the heroic) / तस्य (his) / अमात्याḥ (ministers) / यशस्विनः (of the glorious) / शुचयः (pure) / च (and) / अनुरक्ताः (devoted) / च (and) / राजकृत्येषु (in royal duties) / नित्यशः (always)
ramayan::238.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::238.essence: A kingdom stands on ministers who are clean and loyal.
ramayan::238.simple_meaning: Dasharatha had eight ministers. They were clean in conduct and always loyal to the work of the kingdom.
ramayan::238.simple_insight: Good leadership depends on people who are steady, loyal, and free from corruption.
ramayan::238.detailed_meaning: In Ayodhya, Valmiki pauses to show the strength of Dasharatha’s court before the crisis begins. The king is surrounded by eight ministers who are morally clean and devoted to state duty, setting up the royal order that will soon be tested.
ramayan::238.modern_relevance: A team meeting runs smoothly because the people in the room are dependable, not dramatic. The real strength is invisible: clean conduct, loyalty, and habits that hold under pressure.
ramayan::238.insight: It shifts attention from charisma to the quality of the people carrying responsibility.

ramayan::239.verse_sanskrit: धृष्टिर्जयन्तो विजयस्सिद्धार्थो ह्यर्थसाधक: । अशोको मन्त्रपालश्च सुमन्त्रश्चाष्टमोऽभवत् । । 173 । ।
ramayan::239.verse_hindi: The eight ministers were Dhrishti, Jayanta,Vijaya, Siddhartha, Arthasadhaka, Ashoka, Mantrapala and Sumantra.
ramayan::239.english_translation: The eight ministers were Dhrishti, Jayanta, Vijaya, Siddhartha, Arthasadhaka, Ashoka, Mantrapala, and Sumantra.
ramayan::239.translation_literal: धृष्टिः (Dhrishti) / जयन्तः (Jayanta) / विजयः (Vijaya) / सिद्धार्थः (Siddhartha) / हि (indeed) / अर्थसाधकः (one who accomplishes tasks) / अशोकः (Ashoka) / मन्त्रपालः (protector of counsel) / च (and) / सुमन्त्रः (Sumantra) / च (and) / अष्टमः (the eighth) / अभवत् (was)
ramayan::239.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::239.essence: A king's court is defined by the people closest to his decisions.
ramayan::239.simple_meaning: Dasaratha's eight ministers are named here. The verse is a roster, not a teaching.
ramayan::239.simple_insight: Sometimes a story pauses just to show the weight of a court.
ramayan::239.detailed_meaning: In Ayodhya, Valmiki is introducing Dasharatha's inner circle before the exile crisis begins. This verse simply lists the eight ministers, including Sumantra, so the reader knows who stands around the king when the coming decisions start to break the kingdom.
ramayan::239.modern_relevance: You walk into a meeting and learn who actually has influence before anyone speaks. This verse works the same way: it names the people around the king before the real trouble begins.
ramayan::239.insight: It sets the scene by naming the court’s key voices before the story turns.

ramayan::240.verse_sanskrit: ऋत्विजौ द्वावभिमतौ तस्याऽऽस्तामृषिसत्तमौ । वसिष्ठो वामदेवश्च मन्त्रिणश्च तथापरे । । 174 । ।
ramayan::240.verse_hindi: He had two wellchosen excellent rishis, Vasishta and Vamadeva, as family priests besides some other counsellors.
ramayan::240.english_translation: He had two well-chosen excellent rishis, Vasishta and Vamadeva, as family priests, besides other counsellors.
ramayan::240.translation_literal: ऋत्विजौ (family priests) / द्वौ (two) / अभिमतौ (well-chosen) / तस्य (his) / आस्ताम् (were) / ऋषि-सत्तमौ (best among sages) / वसिष्ठः (Vasishta) / वामदेवः (Vamadeva) / च (and) / मन्त्रिणः (counsellors) / च (and) / तथा (also) / अपरे (others)
ramayan::240.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::240.essence: Good rule depends on wise counsel, not strength alone.
ramayan::240.simple_meaning: Dasharatha had Vasishta and Vamadeva as his respected family priests, along with other advisers.
ramayan::240.simple_insight: A ruler is steadied by wise counsel, not by power alone.
ramayan::240.detailed_meaning: The verse continues the portrait of Dasharatha’s court in Ayodhya. After naming his ministers, Valmiki adds that two great sages, Vasishta and Vamadeva, served as his priests and advisers, showing that the king’s rule rested on sacred and practical guidance.
ramayan::240.modern_relevance: A founder is about to make a decision that could shake the whole team. The smartest move is not to trust impulse, but to keep wise, steady counsel close.
ramayan::240.insight: It shifts attention from personal authority to the value of trusted guidance in rule and decision-making.

ramayan::241.verse_sanskrit: विद्याविनीता ह्रीमन्त: कुशला नियतेन्द्रिया: । श्रीमन्तश्च महात्मानश्शास्त्रज्ञा दृढविक्रमा: । । 175 । । कीर्तिमन्त: प्रणिहिता: यथावचनकारिण: । तेज: क्षमायश:प्राप्ता स्मितपूर्वाभिभाषिण: । । 176 । ।
ramayan::241.verse_hindi: They were welleducated in all branches of knowledge and deemed unjust acts shameful. They were renowned, proficient, versed in sastras, wealthy and magnanimous. They had their senses restrained and their deeds were in accordance with their words. They acted with determination. They were brilliant, forgiving and reputed. And always spoke with a smile.
ramayan::241.english_translation: They were well educated in all branches of knowledge and considered shameful any unjust act. They were renowned, proficient, versed in the scriptures, wealthy, magnanimous, self-controlled, and steadfast. They were famous, composed, true to their word, radiant, forgiving, honorable, and always spoke with a smile.
ramayan::241.translation_literal: विद्याविनीता (well-educated and disciplined by learning) / ह्रीमन्त: (possessed of shame) / कुशला (skilled) / नियतेन्द्रिया: (with restrained senses) / श्रीमन्तश्च (and endowed with prosperity) / महात्मानश्शास्त्रज्ञा (great-souled, knowers of the scriptures) / दृढविक्रमा: (firm in valor) / कीर्तिमन्त: (famous) / प्रणिहिता: (composed, dedicated) / यथावचनकारिण: (doers according to their word) / तेज: (radiance) / क्षमायश:प्राप्ता (obtained through forgiveness and fame) / स्मितपूर्वाभिभाषिण: (speaking first with a smile)
ramayan::241.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::241.essence: True distinction is calm conduct that matches your words.
ramayan::241.simple_meaning: These men were educated, self-controlled, brave, honest, and gracious. Their conduct matched their words, and they carried themselves with dignity and forgiveness.
ramayan::241.simple_insight: You can measure character by calm speech, kept promises, and controlled impulses.
ramayan::241.detailed_meaning: In Ayodhya, Valmiki pauses to describe the king's trusted ministers and advisers. They are not merely capable; they are disciplined, honorable men whose learning, restraint, and consistency make the court stable. This verse shows the kind of people around a righteous ruler.
ramayan::241.modern_relevance: At a tense family dinner, the person who speaks softly, keeps promises, and does not lash out changes the whole room. That steadiness is not weakness; it is authority.
ramayan::241.insight: It shifts attention from status to character: learning matters only when it becomes restraint, honesty, and steady conduct.

ramayan::242.verse_sanskrit: क्रोधात्कामार्थहेतोर्वा न ब्रूयुरनृतं वच: । तेषामविदितं किञ्चित्स्वेषु नास्ति परेषु वा । क्रियमाणं कृतं वापि चारेणापि चिकीर्षितम् । । 177 । ।
ramayan::242.verse_hindi: Either in anger or for pecuniary gains or for fulfilment of desire, they never uttered an untrue or unjust word. In the midst of their own people or among their enemies, they knew, through spies everything being done or had been done or intended to be done in future.
ramayan::242.english_translation: Either in anger or for gain or for desire, they never spoke an untrue or unjust word. Through spies, they knew everything being done, already done, or intended among their own people and among their enemies.
ramayan::242.translation_literal: क्रोधात् (from anger) / कामार्थहेतोः (for the sake of desire and gain) / वा (or) / न (not) / ब्रूयुः (they would speak) / अनृतम् (false, untrue) / वचः (speech) / तेषाम् (of them) / अविदितम् (unknown) / किञ्चित् (anything) / स्वेषु (among their own) / न अस्ति (there is not) / परेषु (among others) / वा (or) / क्रियमाणम् (being done) / कृतम् (done) / वा अपि (or even) / चारेण अपि (even by spies) / चिकीर्षितम् (intended to be done)
ramayan::242.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::242.essence: Clean speech and clear awareness are marks of disciplined character.
ramayan::242.simple_meaning: Good people do not lie for anger, profit, or desire. They also stay alert to what is happening around them, whether among allies or enemies.
ramayan::242.simple_insight: Integrity is strongest when emotions and incentives both push you off course.
ramayan::242.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing the king's trusted men and ministers: disciplined, intelligent, and hard to deceive. They do not let anger, greed, or desire corrupt their speech, and they remain fully aware of events through careful observation and intelligence.
ramayan::242.modern_relevance: You are in a tense meeting, and one sharp reply could protect your ego but damage trust. This verse points to the harder victory: keeping your speech clean even when pressure, profit, or desire tempts you otherwise.
ramayan::242.insight: It teaches you to guard speech from emotional distortion and to stay aware of what is really happening around you.

ramayan::243.verse_sanskrit: कुशला व्यवहारेषु सौहृदेषु परीक्षिता: । प्राप्तकालं तु ते दण्डं धारयेयुस्सुतेष्वपि । । 178 । ।
ramayan::243.verse_hindi: They knew how to deal (with people). They were true to their friends. They used to impose appropriate punishment even on their own sons.
ramayan::243.english_translation: They knew how to deal with people. They were true to their friends. They imposed the right punishment even on their own sons.
ramayan::243.translation_literal: कुशलाः (skilled) / व्यवहारेषु (in dealings) / सौहृदेषु (in friendships) / परीक्षिताः (tested) / प्राप्तकालम् (at the proper time) / तु (but) / ते (they) / दण्डम् (punishment) / धारयेयुः (would apply) / सुतेषु (to sons) / अपि (even)
ramayan::243.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::243.essence: True fairness does not stop at family ties.
ramayan::243.simple_meaning: A good ruler or person handles people wisely, stays loyal to friends, and corrects wrongdoing fairly even when it hurts personally.
ramayan::243.simple_insight: Real care is not softness alone; it includes the courage to correct what is wrong.
ramayan::243.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing the ideal men of Ayodhya, the kind of people a kingdom can trust. They are socially skilled, loyal in friendship, and never let family affection stop them from enforcing justice when the time comes.
ramayan::243.modern_relevance: Your child breaks a rule, and everyone around you expects you to excuse it. You feel the pull to protect them, but you also know that mercy without correction teaches the wrong lesson.
ramayan::243.insight: It teaches you to balance affection with accountability, so love does not become favoritism.

ramayan::244.verse_sanskrit: कोशसङ्ग्रहणे युक्ता बलस्य च परिग्रहे । अहितं चापि पुरुषं न विहिंस्युरदूषकम् । । 179 । ।
ramayan::244.verse_hindi: They were experts in replenishing the exchequer and in collecting the army. They never inflicted any punishment even on those who were not their wellwishers, if they did not commit any offence.
ramayan::244.english_translation: They were skilled in collecting revenue and in assembling the army. They never harmed even an unfriendly person who had done no wrong.
ramayan::244.translation_literal: कोशसङ्ग्रहणे (in collecting the treasury) / युक्ता (skilled, engaged) / बलस्य (of the army) / च (and) / परिग्रहे (in gathering, assembling) / अहितं (an unfriendly person) / चापि (and also) / पुरुषं (a person) / न (not) / विहिंस्युः (they would harm) / अदूषकम् (one who is not guilty)
ramayan::244.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::244.essence: Power is measured by restraint, not by how much damage it can do.
ramayan::244.simple_meaning: A ruler should raise resources and strength carefully, but never harm someone who has done no wrong, even if that person is unfriendly.
ramayan::244.simple_insight: Real strength feels controlled, not cruel.
ramayan::244.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing the kind of kings Rama’s line produced: capable in revenue, military, and punishment, yet restrained by justice. Power is not for venting anger; it is for protecting order without harming the innocent.
ramayan::244.modern_relevance: You have the power to approve, deny, promote, or punish. The clean use of that power is not softness — it is restraint, especially when someone irritates you but has done nothing wrong.
ramayan::244.insight: It teaches you to separate capability from cruelty, and authority from impulse.

ramayan::245.verse_sanskrit: वीराश्च नियतोत्साहा राजशास्त्रमनुष्ठिता: । शुचीनां रक्षितारश्च नित्यं विषयवासिनाम् । । 1710 । ।
ramayan::245.verse_hindi: They were heroic. They possessed steady perseverance. They followed the state policy and always protected the virtuous people living in the state.
ramayan::245.english_translation: They were heroic, steady in effort, versed in statecraft, and always protectors of the virtuous people living in the realm.
ramayan::245.translation_literal: वीराः (heroic) / च (and) / नियतोत्साहाः (steady in effort) / राजशास्त्रम् (state policy) / अनुष्ठिताः (practised) / शुचीनाम् (of the virtuous) / रक्षितारः (protectors) / च (and) / नित्यम् (always) / विषयवासिनाम् (of those living in the realm)
ramayan::245.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::245.essence: True power is measured by how faithfully it protects the good.
ramayan::245.simple_meaning: A ruler should be brave, disciplined, skilled in governance, and always protect good people in the kingdom.
ramayan::245.simple_insight: Real strength is not just force; it is reliable protection.
ramayan::245.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing the kind of rulers an ideal kingdom needs: brave, consistent, trained in governance, and committed to shielding decent people. The passage builds a standard for power before showing how it should be used.
ramayan::245.modern_relevance: You lead a team, a home, or a project, and people depend on your steadiness more than your charisma. What matters is whether your strength makes life safer for others.
ramayan::245.insight: It shifts leadership from display to dependable protection.

ramayan::246.verse_sanskrit: ब्रह्म क्षत्रमहिंसन्तस्ते कोशं समपूरयन् । सुतीक्ष्णदण्डास्संप्रेक्ष्य पुरुषस्य बलाबलम् । । 1711 । ।
ramayan::246.verse_hindi: While ensuring that they did not cause pain to brahmanas and kshatriyas (in thought, word and deed), they filled the treasury. They inflicted stringent punishments on a man after examining his strength and weakness.
ramayan::246.english_translation: While ensuring that they did not cause pain to brahmanas and kshatriyas in thought, word, and deed, they filled the treasury. They imposed severe punishments only after judging a man's strength and weakness.
ramayan::246.translation_literal: ब्रह्म (brahmanas) / क्षत्र (kshatriyas) / महिंसन्तः (not harming) / ते (they) / कोशम् (treasury) / समपूरयन् (filled) / सुतीक्ष्णदण्डाः (having very severe punishments) / संप्रेक्ष्य (after examining) / पुरुषस्य (a man's) / बल (strength) / अबलम् (weakness)
ramayan::246.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::246.essence: Justice stays clean when punishment follows careful seeing.
ramayan::246.simple_meaning: Good rulers protect the respected classes, build up the treasury, and punish only after careful judgment.
ramayan::246.simple_insight: Power stays just when it is restrained by clear judgment.
ramayan::246.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing the ministers and rulers of Ayodhya, not a single dramatic turn. They manage wealth, protect social order, and punish only after weighing a person's strength and weakness. It is a portrait of careful governance, not a standalone teaching.
ramayan::246.modern_relevance: A manager is about to fire someone in a meeting, but pauses to check the full story first. Fairness is not softness; it is judgment that sees before it strikes.
ramayan::246.insight: It shifts authority from impulse to measured discernment.

ramayan::247.verse_sanskrit: शुचीनामेकबुद्धीनां सर्वेषां सम्प्रजानताम् । नासीत्पुरे वा राष्ट्रे वा मृषावादी नर: क्वचित् । । 1712 । ।
ramayan::247.verse_hindi: While the ministers of chaste conduct administered the kingdom with unanimous decisions, there was no one who was a liar, either in the city or in the kingdom.
ramayan::247.english_translation: Among the pure-minded and unanimous ministers, there was not a single liar anywhere in the city or the kingdom.
ramayan::247.translation_literal: शुचीनाम् (of the pure-minded) / एकबुद्धीनाम् (of one mind) / सर्वेषाम् (of all) / सम्प्रजानताम् (of the fully aware) / न (not) / आसीत् (there was) / पुरे (in the city) / वा (or) / राष्ट्रे (in the kingdom) / वा (or) / मृषावादी (a liar) / नरः (man) / क्वचित् (anywhere)
ramayan::247.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::247.essence: A truthful leadership culture makes lying unnecessary and unsafe.
ramayan::247.simple_meaning: A kingdom led by pure, united ministers becomes so orderly that no one dares to lie in city or country.
ramayan::247.simple_insight: Integrity at the top changes the moral climate for everyone below.
ramayan::247.detailed_meaning: In Rama’s kingdom, the ministers are described as pure, single-minded, and fully aware. Their shared integrity is so strong that false speech disappears from both the city and the wider realm.
ramayan::247.modern_relevance: A team meeting where everyone knows the boss rewards honesty changes the room instantly. People stop performing and start speaking plainly because the culture no longer protects deception.
ramayan::247.insight: It shows that ethical leadership creates an environment where dishonesty cannot easily survive.

ramayan::248.verse_sanskrit: कश्चिन्न दुष्टस्तत्रासीत्परदाररतो नर: । प्रशान्तं सर्वमेवासीद्राष्ट्रं पुरवरं च तत् । । 1713 । ।
ramayan::248.verse_hindi: In that kingdom no one was wicked or enamoured of others wives. Serenity prevailed over the entire kingdom including the city of excellence.
ramayan::248.english_translation: In that kingdom no one was wicked or enamoured of others' wives. Serenity prevailed over the entire kingdom, including the city of excellence.
ramayan::248.translation_literal: कश्चित् (anyone) / न (not) / दुष्टः (wicked) / तत्र (there) / आसीत् (was) / परदाररतः (attached to another's wife) / नरः (man) / प्रशान्तम् (peaceful) / सर्वम् (all) / एव (indeed) / आसीत् (was) / राष्ट्रम् (kingdom) / पुरवरम् (best of cities) / च (and) / तत् (that)
ramayan::248.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::248.essence: Peace becomes possible when desire and wickedness lose their grip.
ramayan::248.simple_meaning: No one in that kingdom was wicked or lustful, and the whole land was peaceful.
ramayan::248.simple_insight: A society feels safe when desire and cruelty no longer rule people.
ramayan::248.detailed_meaning: Ayodhya is being described in its best state, before exile and fracture. The people are disciplined, honest, and orderly; even moral corruption is absent. This verse adds the final seal: the whole kingdom rests in peace.
ramayan::248.modern_relevance: A neighborhood where doors stay unlocked and gossip never turns cruel feels almost unreal. This verse points to that kind of collective trust — rare, fragile, and worth protecting.
ramayan::248.insight: It shifts attention from private virtue to the peace a whole society creates together.

ramayan::249.verse_sanskrit: सुवाससस्सुवेषाश्च ते च सर्वे सुशीलिन: । हितार्थं च नरेन्द्रस्य जाग्रतो नयचक्षुषा । । 1714 । ।
ramayan::249.verse_hindi: They all were welldressed in fine clothes. They possessed good character with an eye on justice and vigilant about the kings welfare.
ramayan::249.english_translation: They all were well-dressed in fine clothes. They possessed good character, with an eye on justice, and stayed vigilant for the king's welfare.
ramayan::249.translation_literal: सुवाससः (well-clothed) / सुवेषाः (well-adorned) / च (and) / ते (they) / च (and) / सर्वे (all) / सुशीलिनः (well-mannered, virtuous) / हितार्थम् (for the welfare) / च (and) / नरेन्द्रस्य (of the king) / जाग्रतः (awake, vigilant) / नयचक्षुषा (with the eye of policy/justice)
ramayan::249.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::249.essence: A healthy kingdom is held together by vigilant, virtuous people.
ramayan::249.simple_meaning: The ministers and attendants were dignified, virtuous, and alert. They kept the king's welfare in view and acted with sound judgment.
ramayan::249.simple_insight: Good leadership depends on people who stay alert, decent, and loyal to the common good.
ramayan::249.detailed_meaning: Ayodhya is being described at its best: orderly, moral, and carefully governed. The people around the king are refined in dress and conduct, and they watch over his welfare with disciplined judgment. This is part of a larger portrait of a kingdom where corruption has no foothold.
ramayan::249.modern_relevance: A team room before a major launch feels calm because everyone knows their role, stays sharp, and keeps the bigger mission in view.
ramayan::249.insight: It shifts attention from flashy appearance to steady character and alert responsibility.

ramayan::250.verse_sanskrit: गुरोर्गुणगृहीताश्च प्रख्याताश्च पराक्रमे । विदेशेष्वपि विज्ञातास्सर्वतो बुद्धिनिश्चयात् । । 1715 । ।
ramayan::250.verse_hindi: They imbibed virtues from the elderlies. They were renowned in prowess. They were guided by their intellect in all affairs. They were wellknown everywhere.
ramayan::250.english_translation: They had learned virtue from their elders, were famed for prowess, and were known everywhere for firm intelligence and clear judgment.
ramayan::250.translation_literal: गुरोः (from the elders/teacher) / गुण-गृहीताः (having taken in virtues) / च (and) / प्रख्याताः (well-known, famed) / च (and) / पराक्रमे (in prowess) / विदेशेषु अपि (even in foreign lands) / विज्ञाताः (recognized, known) / सर्वतः (everywhere) / बुद्धि-निश्चयात् (from firm intelligence and resolve)
ramayan::250.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::250.essence: Character and judgment make a person known far beyond their own circle.
ramayan::250.simple_meaning: These people were shaped by good teachers, known for courage, and trusted for sound judgment wherever they went.
ramayan::250.simple_insight: Real respect comes from character, competence, and steady judgment.
ramayan::250.detailed_meaning: The verse continues describing the king’s ministers and attendants. They are not merely well-dressed; they have absorbed good qualities from their elders, earned fame through courage, and built a reputation for clear judgment even beyond their own land.
ramayan::250.modern_relevance: In a team where everyone is watching who can be trusted, your reputation comes from judgment, not just talk. People remember who stays steady when decisions get hard.
ramayan::250.insight: It shifts attention from appearance to the qualities that make trust possible.

ramayan::251.verse_sanskrit: सन्धिविग्रहतत्त्वज्ञा: प्रकृत्या सम्पदान्विता: । । 1716 । । मन्त्रसंवरणे शक्ताश्श्लक्ष्णास्सूक्ष्मासु बुद्धिषु । नीतिशास्त्रविशेषज्ञास्सततं प्रियवादिन: । । 1717 । ।
ramayan::251.verse_hindi: The ministers were inherently well aware of the real nature of peace or war. They were affluent, adept in keeping secrecy and sharp in comprehending the points (before making any decision). They were experts in the science of ethics and morality. They always spoke  pleasing words.
ramayan::251.english_translation: The ministers were naturally skilled in the realities of peace and conflict. They were prosperous, able to keep counsel secret, sharp in subtle judgment, expert in ethics, and always spoke pleasing words.
ramayan::251.translation_literal: सन्धि-विग्रह-तत्त्व-ज्ञा: (knowers of the truth of peace and conflict) / प्रकृत्या (by nature) / सम्पदा-अन्विता: (endowed with wealth) / मन्त्र-संवरणे (in keeping counsel secret) / शक्ताः (capable) / श्लक्ष्णाः (smooth-gifted) / सूक्ष्मासु बुद्धिषु (in subtle minds) / नीतिशास्त्र-विशेष-ज्ञाः (experts in the special science of ethics) / सततं (always) / प्रिय-वादिन: (speaking pleasing words)
ramayan::251.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::251.essence: Wise rule depends on ministers who can judge, restrain, and advise well.
ramayan::251.simple_meaning: Dasharatha's ministers were wise, discreet, politically skilled, and careful in speech. They knew how to judge conflict and peace, and they helped govern with intelligence.
ramayan::251.simple_insight: Good leadership depends on people who can think clearly, keep counsel, and speak with restraint.
ramayan::251.detailed_meaning: These lines continue the portrait of Dasharatha's court. Valmiki lists the qualities of the king's ministers: they understand diplomacy and conflict, guard secrets, think with subtle intelligence, know ethics, and speak pleasantly. The verse supports the larger point that Dasaratha ruled with capable advisers.
ramayan::251.modern_relevance: A leadership meeting where everyone talks loudly, leaks half-formed ideas, and rushes to conclusions can collapse fast. This verse points to the opposite: counsel that is discreet, thoughtful, and ethically grounded.
ramayan::251.insight: It shifts attention from charisma to judgment: the right advisers make rule stable.

ramayan::252.verse_hindi: The faultless king Dasaratha, with the assistance of such ministers endowed with virtues, ruled the earth.
ramayan::252.english_translation: The faultless king Dasaratha, supported by such virtuous ministers, ruled the earth.
ramayan::252.translation_literal: ईदृशैः (with such) / तैः (by them) / अमात्यैः (with ministers) / तु (indeed) / राजा (king) / दशरथः (Dasharatha) / अनघः (faultless) / उपपन्नः (supported) / गुणोपेतैः (endowed with virtues) / अन्वशासत् (ruled) / वसुन्धराम् (the earth)
ramayan::252.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::252.essence: A ruler's strength rests on the virtue of those who advise him.
ramayan::252.simple_meaning: Dasharatha ruled well because he was surrounded by capable, virtuous ministers.
ramayan::252.simple_insight: Good leadership is never solitary; wise support makes rule steady.
ramayan::252.detailed_meaning: Valmiki pauses to describe Ayodhya before the crisis begins. Dasharatha is not yet the broken father of exile, but a faultless king whose rule stands on the strength of ministers skilled in judgment, secrecy, and statecraft.
ramayan::252.modern_relevance: A manager is only as steady as the team around them. When the people close to you are sharp, trustworthy, and disciplined, your decisions can actually hold.
ramayan::252.insight: It shifts attention from lone authority to the quality of the counsel around power.

ramayan::253.verse_sanskrit: अवेक्षमाणश्चारेण प्रजा धर्मेण रञ्जयन् । प्रजानां पालनं कुर्वन्नधर्मान्परिवर्जयन् । । 1719 । । विश्रुतस्त्रिषु लोकेषु वदान्यस्सत्यसङ्गर: । स तत्र पुरुषव्याघ्रश्शशास पृथिवीमिमाम् । । 1720 । ।
ramayan::253.verse_hindi: In the three worlds he (Dasaratha) was acclaimed in the three words as munificient and upholder of truth, a tiger among men, who ruled protecting and guarding the people through spies. He. ruled the kingdom with righteousness by deserting irreligious and keeping the subjects happy.
ramayan::253.english_translation: Dasaratha, the faultless king, ruled the earth with ministers skilled in peace and war. He watched through spies, protected his people, delighted them through righteousness, avoided unrighteousness, and was famed in all three worlds as generous and true to his word. That tiger among men governed this land.
ramayan::253.translation_literal: अवेक्षमाणः (watching closely) / चारेण (through spies) / प्रजा (the people) / धर्मेण (by righteousness) / रञ्जयन् (delighting) / प्रजानाम् (of the people) / पालनम् (protection) / कुर्वन् (doing) / अधर्मान् (unrighteousness) / परिवर्जयन् (avoiding) / विश्रुतः (famed) / त्रिषु लोकेषु (in the three worlds) / वदान्यः (generous) / सत्यसङ्गरः (true to his word) / सः (he) / तत्र (there) / पुरुषव्याघ्रः (tiger among men) / शशास (ruled) / पृथिवीम् इमाम् (this earth)
ramayan::253.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::253.essence: True rule protects people and stays clean of wrongdoing.
ramayan::253.simple_meaning: Dasaratha was a just ruler who protected his people, avoided wrongdoing, and was known for generosity and truthfulness.
ramayan::253.simple_insight: Real authority feels safe to the people it governs.
ramayan::253.detailed_meaning: Valmiki describes Dasaratha at the height of his rule. With capable ministers and spies, he keeps watch, protects his subjects, and avoids harmful action. His fame rests not on force alone, but on generosity, truth, and righteous rule.
ramayan::253.modern_relevance: You manage a team, a household, or a classroom, and people feel safer when your rules are clear and your word is reliable. Leadership is not domination; it is protection with integrity.
ramayan::253.insight: It shifts leadership from control to responsible care.

ramayan::254.verse_sanskrit: नाध्यगच्छद्विशिष्टं वा तुल्यं वा शत्रुमात्मन: । मित्रवान्नतसामन्त: प्रतापहतकण्टक: । । 1721 । । स शशास जगद्राजा दिवं देवपतिर्यथा ।
ramayan::254.verse_hindi: The king (Dasaratha) had many friends. All the tributary kings were obedient to him. He killed his enemies with his might. There was no foe who was either superior to or equal to him. He ruled the world as Indra ruled the heaven.
ramayan::254.english_translation: The king Dasaratha had no foe superior or equal to him. His allies were loyal, his enemies were crushed, and he ruled the world like Indra rules heaven.
ramayan::254.translation_literal: नाध्यगच्छत् (did not find) / विशिष्टम् (superior) / वा (or) / तुल्यम् (equal) / वा (or) / शत्रुम् (enemy) / आत्मनः (of himself) / मित्रवान् (having friends) / नतसामन्तः (with bowed tributary kings) / प्रतापहतकण्टकः (with thorns of enemies destroyed by might) / सः (he) / शशास (ruled) / जगत् (the world) / राजा (the king) / दिवम् (heaven) / देवपतिः (lord of the gods) / यथा (as)
ramayan::254.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::254.essence: Even the strongest reign can hide the seed of ruin.
ramayan::254.simple_meaning: Dasaratha had no rival, many allies, and a kingdom secured by strength and obedience.
ramayan::254.simple_insight: Power feels complete until the story shows how quickly it can still be undone.
ramayan::254.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Dasaratha at the height of his rule: respected, unmatched, and surrounded by obedient tributary kings and loyal friends. This is not a teaching verse but a scene-setting portrait of a king whose outward greatness makes the coming fracture feel sharper.
ramayan::254.modern_relevance: You can be surrounded by loyal people, strong systems, and public praise — and still be one decision away from collapse.
ramayan::254.insight: It frames Dasaratha’s later tragedy against the background of total political strength.

ramayan::255.verse_sanskrit: तैर्मन्त्रिभिर्मन्त्रहिते नियुक्तैर्वृतोऽनुरक्तै: कुशलैस्समर्थै: । स पार्थिवो दीप्तिमवाप युक्तस्तेजोमयैर्गोभिरिवोदितोऽर्क: । । 1722 । ।
ramayan::255.verse_hindi: Accompanied by the ministers who were devoted to his welfare, adept in counselling, skilful, capable and loyal towards him, the king acquired glory like the rising Sun with luminous rays.
ramayan::255.english_translation: Accompanied by the ministers who were devoted to his welfare, adept in counselling, skilful, capable and loyal towards him, the king acquired glory like the rising Sun with luminous rays.
ramayan::255.translation_literal: तैः (by those) / मन्त्रिभिः (with ministers) / मन्त्रहिते (in counsel and welfare) / नियुक्तैः (appointed) / वृतः (surrounded) / अनुरक्तैः (devoted) / कुशलैः (skilled) / समर्थैः (capable) / सः (that) / पार्थिवः (king) / दीप्तिम् (splendour) / अवाप (obtained) / युक्तः (joined) / तेजोमयैः (luminous) / गोभिः (with rays) / इव (like) / उदितः (risen) / अर्कः (sun)
ramayan::255.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::255.essence: His glory came from wise, loyal counsel around him.
ramayan::255.simple_meaning: The king shone because he was surrounded by loyal, skilled ministers who served his welfare well.
ramayan::255.simple_insight: Good leadership is not solo brilliance; it also depends on the quality of people around you.
ramayan::255.detailed_meaning: This is still the opening portrait of Dasharatha. The poet is showing why his rule looked radiant: he is backed by ministers who are loyal, competent, and committed to his good. It is a supporting detail before the deeper problem of his lack of an heir appears.
ramayan::255.modern_relevance: A team meeting runs smoothly because the people around the table actually care, know their work, and speak honestly. The leader looks strong, but the real strength is the circle he has built.
ramayan::255.insight: It shifts attention from personal authority to the supporting network that makes authority effective.

ramayan::256.verse_sanskrit: तस्य त्वेवं प्रभावस्य धर्मज्ञस्य महात्मन: । सुतार्थं तप्यमानस्य नासीद्वंशकरस्सुत: । । 181 । ।
ramayan::256.verse_hindi: Such a majestic, righteous, and magnaninous king had no son to perpetuate the race even though he performed austerities for one.
ramayan::256.english_translation: Such a majestic, righteous, and magnanimous king had no son to perpetuate the line, even though he performed austerities for one.
ramayan::256.translation_literal: तस्य (of him) / तु (indeed) / एवम् (thus) / प्रभावस्य (of the mighty one) / धर्मज्ञस्य (of the righteous-knowing) / महात्मनः (of the great-souled one) / सुतार्थम् (for the sake of a son) / तप्यमानस्य (of the one performing austerity) / न (not) / आसीत् (there was) / वंशकरः (lineage-continuing) / सुतः (son)
ramayan::256.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::256.essence: Power and virtue cannot force what the heart most wants.
ramayan::256.simple_meaning: Dasharatha was a powerful, righteous king, but he still had no son. Even his austerities had not yet brought the heir he longed for.
ramayan::256.simple_insight: Sometimes sincere effort meets silence before it meets reward.
ramayan::256.detailed_meaning: King Dasharatha rules Ayodhya with strength, justice, and honor, but one ache remains: he has no son to carry forward his line. He has already tried austerity for this, and the absence still stands.
ramayan::256.modern_relevance: You do the work, keep your promises, and still hear nothing back. The promotion, the child, the answer, the relief — none of it arrives on schedule.
ramayan::256.insight: It shifts attention from achievement to the deeper human longing that drives action.

ramayan::257.verse_sanskrit: चिन्तयानस्य तस्यैवं बुद्धिरासीन्महात्मन: । सुतार्थं हयमेधेन किमर्थं न यजाम्यहम् । । 182 । ।
ramayan::257.verse_hindi: While reflecting over the matter, a thought struck the magnanimous king: Why not invoke gods by performing a horsesacrifice for a son.
ramayan::257.english_translation: While reflecting over the matter, a thought struck the magnanimous king: Why not perform a horse sacrifice for a son?
ramayan::257.translation_literal: चिन्तयानस्य (while reflecting) / तस्य (to him) / एवम् (thus) / बुद्धिः (thought) / आसीत् (arose) / महात्मनः (of the magnanimous one) / सुतार्थम् (for a son) / हयमेधेन (by horse-sacrifice) / किमर्थम् (why) / न (not) / यजामि (shall I sacrifice) / अहम् (I)
ramayan::257.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::257.essence: Clear need can turn sorrow into decisive action.
ramayan::257.simple_meaning: The king, troubled by having no son, decides to seek a son through a horse sacrifice.
ramayan::257.simple_insight: When a real need is seen clearly, hesitation gives way to decisive action.
ramayan::257.detailed_meaning: King Dasharatha has everything except an heir, and the absence cuts deep. As he reflects, he turns from grief to action and considers the horse sacrifice as the path that may answer his longing.
ramayan::257.modern_relevance: You keep circling the same empty place in your life, until the need becomes impossible to ignore. Then you stop wishing and finally choose a serious step.
ramayan::257.insight: It shifts the mind from passive longing to purposeful response.

ramayan::258.verse_sanskrit: स निश्चितां मतिं कृत्वा यष्टव्यमिति बुद्धिमान् । मन्त्रिभिस्सह धर्मात्मा सर्वैरेव कृतात्मभि: । । 183 । । ततोऽब्रवीदिदं राजा सुमन्त्रं मन्त्रिसत्तमम् । शीघ्रमानय मे सर्वान्गुरूंस्तान् सपुरोहितान् । । 184 । ।
ramayan::258.verse_hindi: Having made up his mind to perform the sacrifice, that sagacious and pious king, in consultation with his wise ministers, issued the following command to Sumantra, the best of ministers Bring all my spritual preceptors along with family priests.
ramayan::258.english_translation: Having made up his mind to perform the sacrifice, that sagacious and pious king, in consultation with his wise ministers, issued the following command to Sumantra, the best of ministers: Bring all my spiritual preceptors along with the family priests.
ramayan::258.translation_literal: स (that) / निश्चितां (decided) / मतिं (mind) / कृत्वा (having made) / यष्टव्यमिति (to be performed as sacrifice) / बुद्धिमान् (the wise one) / मन्त्रिभिः (with ministers) / सह (together) / धर्मात्मा (righteous) / सर्वैः (with all) / एव (indeed) / कृतात्मभिः (with disciplined-minded ones) / ततः (then) / अब्रवीत् (spoke) / इदम् (this) / राजा (king) / सुमन्त्रम् (to Sumantra) / मन्त्रिसत्तमम् (best of ministers) / शीघ्रम् (quickly) / आनय (bring) / मे (for me) / सर्वान् (all) / गुरून् (teachers) / तान् (those) / सपुरोहितान् (with family priests)
ramayan::258.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::258.essence: A resolved mind turns longing into action.
ramayan::258.simple_meaning: Dasharatha decides to perform a sacrifice and orders Sumantra to bring the royal teachers and priests.
ramayan::258.simple_insight: Big changes begin with a clear decision, not hesitation.
ramayan::258.detailed_meaning: King Dasharatha has been grieving over his lack of an heir. After consulting his ministers, he settles on a horse sacrifice and immediately sends Sumantra to gather the royal teachers and priests. This is the practical step that sets the larger event in motion.
ramayan::258.modern_relevance: You stop circling the same problem and finally call the people who can help. The decision is made; now the work begins.
ramayan::258.insight: It shifts the mind from private worry to decisive action with wise counsel.

ramayan::259.verse_sanskrit: तान्पूजयित्वा धर्मात्मा राजा दशरथस्तदा । इदं धर्मार्थसहितं श्लक्ष्णंवचनमब्रवीत् । । 187 । ।
ramayan::259.verse_hindi: Virtuous king Dasaratha paid homage to them (the ministers) and uttered these gracious, righteous and meaningful words.
ramayan::259.english_translation: Virtuous king Dasaratha paid homage to them and then spoke these gentle, righteous, and meaningful words.
ramayan::259.translation_literal: तान् (them) / पूजयित्वा (having honoured) / धर्मात्मा (righteous-minded) / राजा (king) / दशरथः (Dasharatha) / तदा (then) / इदम् (this) / धर्मार्थसहितम् (joined with righteousness and purpose) / श्लक्ष्णम् (gentle) / वचनम् (speech) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::259.speaker: Dasharatha
ramayan::259.essence: Respect comes before the hard truth.
ramayan::259.simple_meaning: Dasharatha respectfully addresses his ministers and begins speaking with care and seriousness.
ramayan::259.simple_insight: Even a king pauses to honour counsel before speaking from the heart.
ramayan::259.detailed_meaning: Dasharatha has already begun turning over his painful problem: he wants a son and is considering sacrifice. After consulting his ministers, he honours them first, then speaks. This verse is the respectful opening to a decision that will change Ayodhya.
ramayan::259.modern_relevance: You gather the people who know the situation best, listen fully, and only then speak from the place that matters.
ramayan::259.insight: It shows that serious decisions begin with respect, not impulse.

ramayan::260.verse_sanskrit: मम लालप्यमानस्य पुत्रार्थन्नास्ति वै सुखम् । तदर्थं हयमेधेन यक्ष्यामीति मतिर्मम । । 188 । ।
ramayan::260.verse_hindi: There is no happiness for one who has no son. This is the cause of my intense suffering. Therefore, I have made up my mind to perform a horsesacrifice.
ramayan::260.english_translation: There is no happiness for one who has no son. This is the cause of my intense suffering. Therefore, I have made up my mind to perform a horse sacrifice.
ramayan::260.translation_literal: मम (for me) / लालप्यमानस्य (for one who is grieving) / पुत्रार्थम् (for the sake of a son) / न अस्ति (there is not) / वै (indeed) / सुखम् (happiness) / तत्-अर्थम् (for that reason) / हयमेधेन (with the horse sacrifice) / यक्ष्यामि (I will sacrifice) / इति (thus) / मतिः मम (my resolve)
ramayan::260.speaker: Dasharatha
ramayan::260.essence: Deep longing can be redirected into a decisive vow.
ramayan::260.simple_meaning: Dasharatha says his lack of a son has left him deeply unhappy, so he decides to perform a horse sacrifice to seek one.
ramayan::260.simple_insight: Longing can become a disciplined response instead of helpless despair.
ramayan::260.detailed_meaning: In Ayodhya, King Dasharatha has gathered his ministers and admitted a private wound: he has no son, and that emptiness has become unbearable. He decides to seek help through the horse sacrifice, turning grief into action.
ramayan::260.modern_relevance: You sit with a painful absence that keeps showing up in every quiet moment. Instead of collapsing into it, you finally choose a concrete step that can answer it.
ramayan::260.insight: It shifts grief from passive suffering into purposeful action.

ramayan::261.verse_sanskrit: तदहं यष्टुमिच्छामि शास्त्रदृष्टेन कर्मणा । कथं प्राप्स्याम्यहं कामं बुद्धिरत्रविचार्यताम् । । 189 । ।
ramayan::261.verse_hindi: Therefore, I intend to perform a horsesacrifice in accordance with the scriptures. How  can I fulfil my desire in this regard? You may deliberate and find a solution.
ramayan::261.english_translation: Therefore, I intend to perform a horse sacrifice in accordance with the scriptures. How can I fulfil my desire in this regard? You may deliberate and find a solution.
ramayan::261.translation_literal: तद् (therefore) / अहम् (I) / यष्टुम् (to sacrifice) / इच्छामि (wish) / शास्त्र-दृष्टेन (seen in the scriptures) / कर्मणा (by action) / कथम् (how) / प्राप्स्यामि (shall I obtain) / अहम् (I) / कामम् (desire) / बुद्धिः (intelligence / judgment) / अत्र (here) / विचार्यताम् (let it be considered)
ramayan::261.speaker: Dasharatha
ramayan::261.essence: Wanting something is not enough; you still need the right way to pursue it.
ramayan::261.simple_meaning: Dasharatha wants to perform the horse sacrifice according to scripture and asks his ministers to think through how it can be done.
ramayan::261.simple_insight: Even a powerful desire must pass through wise, proper action.
ramayan::261.detailed_meaning: King Dasharatha has confessed his sorrow over having no son and now turns that longing into a formal plan. He asks the ministers to deliberate on the scripturally proper way to perform the horse sacrifice, because the wish is urgent but the method must be right.
ramayan::261.modern_relevance: You want something badly enough to rush, but you still pause to ask: what is the proper way to do this? The pressure is real, yet the method matters too.
ramayan::261.insight: It shifts desire into disciplined planning instead of impulsive action.

ramayan::262.verse_sanskrit: ततस्साध्विति तद्वाक्यं ब्राह्मणा: प्रत्यपूजयन् । वसिष्ठप्रमुखास्सर्वे पार्थिवस्य मुखाच्च्युतम् । । 1810 । ।
ramayan::262.verse_hindi: The brahmins along with Vasishta in the forefront extolled the kings decision,
ramayan::262.english_translation: Then the brahmins, with Vasishta at their head, praised the king's words, spoken from his own mouth.
ramayan::262.translation_literal: ततस् (then) / साधु (well done) / इति (thus) / तत्-वाक्यम् (that speech) / ब्राह्मणाः (the brahmins) / प्रत्यपूजयन् (praised in return) / वसिष्ठ-प्रमुखाः (with Vasishta foremost) / सर्वे (all) / पार्थिवस्य (of the king) / मुखात्-च्युतम् (fallen from the mouth)
ramayan::262.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::262.essence: His resolve is accepted, and action can now begin.
ramayan::262.simple_meaning: The priests, led by Vasishta, approved Dasharatha's decision and welcomed his words.
ramayan::262.simple_insight: Approval can turn a private resolve into an accepted course of action.
ramayan::262.detailed_meaning: Dasharatha has just spoken of performing the horse sacrifice to gain a son. Vasishta and the other brahmins respond with approval, showing that the king's plan has been accepted by the sacred authorities. This verse is a brief bridge to the practical arrangements that follow.
ramayan::262.modern_relevance: You finally say out loud the plan you've been carrying alone, and the room quietly gives you permission to begin.
ramayan::262.insight: It shows how a serious intention becomes real when wise people endorse it and the next steps are set in motion.

ramayan::263.verse_sanskrit: ऊचुश्च परमप्रीतास्सर्वे दशरथं वच: । सम्भारास्सम्भ्रियन्तां ते तुरगश्च विमुच्यताम् । । 1811 । ।
ramayan::263.verse_hindi: Highly pleased, they all said to king Dasaratha, Requisite articles be collected for the sacrifice and the  horse be released.
ramayan::263.english_translation: Highly pleased, they all said to King Dasaratha, 'Let the necessary materials for the sacrifice be gathered, and let the horse be released.'
ramayan::263.translation_literal: ऊचुः (said) / च (and) / परमप्रीताः (highly pleased) / सर्वे (all) / दशरथं (to Dasaratha) / वचः (words) / सम्भाराः (sacrificial materials) / सम्भ्रियन्ताम् (let be gathered) / ते (your) / तुरगः (horse) / च (and) / विमुच्यताम् (let be released)
ramayan::263.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::263.essence: A sacred decision becomes real only when preparation begins.
ramayan::263.simple_meaning: The priests welcome Dasaratha's decision and tell him to prepare the sacrificial items and release the horse.
ramayan::263.simple_insight: Big vows begin with practical preparation.
ramayan::263.detailed_meaning: Dasaratha has just announced his wish to perform the horse sacrifice. The assembled priests, led by Vasishta, are pleased and immediately instruct him to gather the ritual materials and free the horse, moving the decision from intention into action.
ramayan::263.modern_relevance: You finally commit to the thing you've been postponing, and the next step is not drama — it's logistics, preparation, and follow-through.
ramayan::263.insight: It shifts you from wishing to organizing the exact steps that make a vow real.

ramayan::264.verse_sanskrit: सर्वथा प्राप्स्यसे पुत्रानभिप्रेतांश्च पार्थिव । यस्य ते धार्मिकी बुद्धिरियं पुत्रार्थमागता । । 1812 । ।
ramayan::264.verse_hindi: O king, the wish that arose in your mind is just and right. You will definitely obtain sons as desired by you.
ramayan::264.english_translation: O king, the wish that arose in your mind is just and right. You will definitely obtain sons as desired by you.
ramayan::264.translation_literal: सर्वथा (in every way) / प्राप्स्यसे (you will obtain) / पुत्रान् (sons) / अभिप्रेतान् (desired) / च (and) / पार्थिव (O king) / यस्य (whose) / ते (your) / धार्मिकी (righteous) / बुद्धिः (intention) / इयम् (this) / पुत्रार्थम् (for sons) / आगता (has arisen)
ramayan::264.speaker: Brahmins
ramayan::264.essence: A righteous desire can carry its own assurance.
ramayan::264.simple_meaning: The priests reassure King Dasharatha that his wish for sons is righteous and will be fulfilled.
ramayan::264.simple_insight: A sincere, dharmic intention can steady you when you cannot yet see the result.
ramayan::264.detailed_meaning: Dasharatha has just accepted the priests' counsel and prepared for the sacrifice that may end his childlessness. The brahmins, led by Vasishta, reassure him that the desire for sons is righteous and will succeed, giving him hope before the ritual begins.
ramayan::264.modern_relevance: You finally commit to something frightening — a surgery, a move, a long-delayed attempt to have a child — and need to hear that your choice is not foolish.
ramayan::264.insight: It shifts the mind from doubt about desire to confidence in a rightful aim.

ramayan::265.verse_sanskrit: तत: प्रीतोऽभवद्राजा श्रुत्वा तद्विजभाषितम् । अमात्यांश्चाब्रवीद्राजा हर्षपर्याकुलेक्षण: । । 1813 । ।
ramayan::265.verse_hindi: On hearing the words of the brahmins, the king was pleased and said to his ministers with eyes excited with delight.
ramayan::265.english_translation: On hearing the words of the brahmins, the king was pleased and said to his ministers with eyes excited with delight.
ramayan::265.translation_literal: तत: (then) / प्रीतः (pleased) / अभवत् (became) / राजा (the king) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / तत् (that) / विजभाषितम् (words of the brahmins) / अमात्यान् (to the ministers) / च (and) / अब्रवीत् (spoke) / राजा (the king) / हर्ष-पर्याकुल-ईक्षणः (with eyes agitated by joy)
ramayan::265.speaker: Dasharatha
ramayan::265.essence: Joy at approval immediately becomes preparation.
ramayan::265.simple_meaning: Dasharatha feels joy after hearing the brahmins’ words and immediately speaks to his ministers.
ramayan::265.simple_insight: Relief can arrive the moment hope is confirmed.
ramayan::265.detailed_meaning: At Ayodhya, the brahmins have just approved Dasharatha’s wish for sons through sacrifice. Hearing their words, the king’s face lights up and he turns at once to his ministers, ready to begin the preparations that will reshape his house.
ramayan::265.modern_relevance: You wait for one message that can change everything. When it finally arrives, your whole body reacts before your mind catches up.
ramayan::265.insight: It shows how quickly hope turns into action once doubt is lifted.

ramayan::266.verse_sanskrit: सम्भारास्सम्भ्रियन्तां मे गुरूणां वचनादिह । समर्थाधिष्ठितश्चाश्वस्सोपाध्यायो विमुच्यताम् । । 1814 । ।
ramayan::266.verse_hindi: Let the  articles required (for performing the sacrifice) be procured in accordance with the words of my spiritual preceptors and the horse be released under the protection of able men.
ramayan::266.english_translation: Let the articles required for the sacrifice be procured according to the words of my teachers, and let the horse, guarded by capable men, be released.
ramayan::266.translation_literal: सम्भाराः (materials/provisions) / सम्भ्रियन्ताम् (let be gathered) / मे (my) / गुरूणाम् (of the teachers) / वचनात् (by the word) / इह (here) / समर्थ-अधिष्ठितः (guarded by capable ones) / च (and) / अश्वः (horse) / सोपाध्यायः (with the preceptor) / विमुच्यताम् (let be released)
ramayan::266.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::266.essence: Dharma moves from approval into precise preparation.
ramayan::266.simple_meaning: The king orders the sacrifice supplies to be gathered and the horse to be released under proper protection, following his teachers’ instructions.
ramayan::266.simple_insight: Right action begins with careful preparation, not impulse.
ramayan::266.detailed_meaning: After hearing the brahmins, the king turns immediately to action. He orders the sacrificial materials to be gathered and the horse to be released under protection. The sacrifice is no longer an idea; it is becoming real through disciplined command.
ramayan::266.modern_relevance: You finally decide to do the hard thing, and the first step is logistics: the forms, the booking, the call, the follow-through.
ramayan::266.insight: It shifts you from intention to organised execution.

ramayan::267.verse_sanskrit: सरय्वाश्चोत्तरे तीरे यज्ञभूमिर्विधीयताम् । शान्तयश्चाभिवर्धन्तां यथाकल्पं यथाविधि । । 1815 । ।
ramayan::267.verse_hindi: On the northern bank of  Sarayu, a sacrificial pavillion be prepared according to the  methods ordained in the Kalpa. Auspicious rites be performed in accordance with the ordinance for its uninterrupted completion.
ramayan::267.english_translation: On the northern bank of the Sarayu, let the sacrificial pavilion be prepared according to the rites laid down in the Kalpa. Let auspicious rites increase in the proper order, exactly as prescribed.
