ramayan::599.simple_insight: Integrity begins when your words become actions, not intentions.
ramayan::599.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has just praised Dasharatha’s noble line and steady speech. Now he presses the king to stop circling the issue: decide the matter of Rama and stand by the promise already given. The request carries the weight of a sacred bargain.
ramayan::599.modern_relevance: You said you'd confirm by evening, and the message is still sitting unsent. The real test is not what you meant — it is whether you will choose and follow through.
ramayan::599.insight: It turns hesitation into a moral test: make the decision, then honour the word.

ramayan::600.verse_sanskrit: अहंनियममातिष्ठे सिध्यर्थं पुरुषर्षभ । तस्य विघ्नकरौ द्वौ तु राक्षसौ कामरूपिणौ । । 1194 । ।
ramayan::600.verse_hindi: O best among men for the successful completion of a sacrifice I took up a selfimposed  religious observance. Two rakshasas, capable of assuming forms at will, are creating impediments to that sacrifice.
ramayan::600.english_translation: O best among men, for the successful completion of a sacrifice I took up a self-imposed observance. Two rakshasas, capable of assuming forms at will, are creating impediments to that sacrifice.
ramayan::600.translation_literal: अहम् (I) / नियमम् (observance, vow) / आतिष्ठे (took up, undertook) / सिध्यर्थम् (for the sake of success, for completion) / पुरुषर्षभ (best among men) / तस्य (of that) / विघ्नकरौ (causing obstacles, hindering) / द्वौ (two) / तु (indeed, but) / राक्षसौ (rakshasas) / कामरूपिणौ (able to assume forms at will)
ramayan::600.speaker: Vishvamitra
ramayan::600.essence: A sacred task can fail unless you defend it from disruption.
ramayan::600.simple_meaning: Vishvamitra says he undertook a vow to complete a sacrifice, but two shape-shifting rakshasas keep blocking it.
ramayan::600.simple_insight: Some duties are sacred enough to demand protection, not just intention.
ramayan::600.detailed_meaning: Vishvamitra is speaking to Rama and Lakshmana in the forest. He has begun a long sacrificial rite, but Maricha and Subahu keep disrupting it. This is the moment he explains why he needs Rama's help.
ramayan::600.modern_relevance: You finally sit down to finish something that matters, and the same two interruptions keep returning. The work is not hard because it is unclear; it is hard because something keeps trying to break your focus.
ramayan::600.insight: It shifts attention from the ritual itself to the obstacles that threaten its completion.

ramayan::601.verse_sanskrit: व्रते मे बहुशश्चीर्णे समाप्त्यां राक्षसाविमौ । मारीचश्च सुबाहुश्च वीर्यवन्तौ सुशिक्षितौ । । 1195 । । समांसरुधिरौघेण वेदिं तामभ्यवर्षताम् ।
ramayan::601.verse_hindi: When my sacrifice generally speaking, is nearing completion the powerful and welltrained Maricha and Subahu who are raining streams of blood and flesh upon the altar.
ramayan::601.english_translation: When my sacrifice was nearing completion, the powerful and well-trained Maricha and Subahu showered the altar with streams of flesh and blood.
ramayan::601.translation_literal: व्रते (in the vow / sacrificial observance) / मे (of mine) / बहुशः (repeatedly / many times) / चीर्णे (having been performed / having been carried out) / समाप्त्यां (at the completion) / राक्षसौ (the two demons) / इमौ (these two) / मारीचः (Maricha) / च (and) / सुबाहुः (Subahu) / च (and) / वीर्यवन्तौ (powerful) / सुशिक्षितौ (well-trained) / समांसरुधिरौघेण (with streams of flesh and blood) / वेदिम् (the sacrificial altar) / ताम् (that) / अभ्यवर्षताम् (were showering)
ramayan::601.speaker: Vishvamitra
ramayan::601.essence: Violence can ruin years of disciplined effort in a single moment.
ramayan::601.simple_meaning: Vishvamitra says his long ritual was almost complete when Maricha and Subahu attacked the altar with blood and flesh, ruining the sacrifice.
ramayan::601.simple_insight: A sacred effort can be undone by violence in a moment.
ramayan::601.detailed_meaning: Vishvamitra is explaining why he has come to Dasharatha. After long discipline and ritual observance, two powerful rakshasas keep assaulting his altar at the very moment the sacrifice should finish. The interruption creates the crisis that leads him to ask for Rama and Lakshmana.
ramayan::601.modern_relevance: You spend weeks building something carefully, then one reckless intrusion ruins the whole stretch. The pain is not just loss — it is seeing disciplined effort treated like nothing.
ramayan::601.insight: It frames violence as the destruction of disciplined sacred work, setting up the need for protection.

ramayan::602.verse_hindi: The (solemn) vow for observance of religious rites being thus interrupted, I left that country as an exerted and discouraged man.
ramayan::602.english_translation: The solemn vow for the ritual was interrupted, and I left that place exhausted and disheartened.
ramayan::602.translation_literal: अवधूते (being disturbed) / तथाभूते (in such a state) / तस्मिन् (that) / नियमनिश्चये (firm vow of observance) / कृतश्रमः (having exerted myself) / निरुत्साहः (without enthusiasm) / तस्मात् (from that) / देशात् (place) / अपाक्रमे (I departed)
ramayan::602.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::602.essence: A broken vow can leave even disciplined effort exhausted.
ramayan::602.simple_meaning: The interruption of the ritual left him worn out and discouraged, so he left that place.
ramayan::602.simple_insight: Even a righteous effort can leave you drained when it is violently disrupted.
ramayan::602.detailed_meaning: Vishvamitra is explaining to Rama why he left the place where his sacrifice was being protected. The rite had been broken by the attack of Maricha and Subahu, and the disruption left him exhausted, disappointed, and forced to withdraw before the larger teaching continues.
ramayan::602.modern_relevance: You spend weeks preparing something sacred to you, and one sudden interruption ruins the whole rhythm. The frustration is not just inconvenience — it is the ache of seeing careful effort broken.
ramayan::602.insight: It shows how disruption can break momentum and force a retreat before the task is complete.

ramayan::603.verse_sanskrit: न च मे क्रोधमुत्स्रष्टुं बुद्धिर्भवति पार्थिव । । 1197 । । तथा भूता हि सा चर्या न शापस्तत्र मुच्यते ।
ramayan::603.verse_hindi: O King my mind does not permit me to vent my wrath. The nature of sacrifice is such that I refrain from cursing them.
ramayan::603.english_translation: O King, my mind does not permit me to vent my wrath. The nature of sacrifice is such that I refrain from cursing them.
ramayan::603.translation_literal: न च (not) / मे (my) / क्रोधम् (anger) / उत्स्रष्टुम् (to release) / बुद्धिः (mind) / भवति (becomes) / पार्थिव (O king) / तथा (thus) / भूता (being) / हि (indeed) / सा (that) / चर्या (conduct / observance) / न (not) / शापः (curse) / तत्र (there) / मुच्यते (is released)
ramayan::603.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::603.essence: Anger may be natural, but discipline decides your response.
ramayan::603.simple_meaning: Even when anger is justified, the speaker refuses to lash out. The discipline of the ritual matters more than revenge.
ramayan::603.simple_insight: Self-control can protect what anger would damage.
ramayan::603.detailed_meaning: The sage is speaking to King Janaka about a sacrifice that was interrupted by Maricha and Subahu. Instead of answering harm with a curse, he explains that the discipline of the rite itself forbids that release of anger.
ramayan::603.modern_relevance: You get cut off in the middle of something important, and the first reply on your tongue is sharp. This verse reminds you that not every insult deserves your full force.
ramayan::603.insight: It teaches you to let form and discipline govern your reaction, especially when provoked.

ramayan::604.verse_sanskrit: स्वपुत्रं राजशार्दूल रामं सत्यपराक्रमम् । । 1198 । । काकपक्षधरं शूरं ज्येष्ठं मे दातुमर्हसि ।
ramayan::604.verse_hindi: O tiger among kings it is befitting of you to entrust your eldest son Rama to me who is valiant, young (having sidelocks of hair) and true to his prowess.
ramayan::604.english_translation: O tiger among kings, it is fitting that you entrust your eldest son Rama to me — valiant, young, with matted hair, and true to his prowess.
ramayan::604.translation_literal: स्वपुत्रम् (your own son) / राजशार्दूल (tiger among kings) / रामम् (Rama) / सत्यपराक्रमम् (true in prowess) / काकपक्षधरम् (wearing crow-like side-locks) / शूरम् (brave) / ज्येष्ठम् (eldest) / मे (to me) / दातुम् (to give) / अर्हसि (you ought)
ramayan::604.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::604.essence: Rama is being chosen because courage has already made him fit.
ramayan::604.simple_meaning: The speaker asks the king to hand over his eldest son Rama, praising his courage, youth, and proven strength.
ramayan::604.simple_insight: Real worth is recognized by action, not age or title.
ramayan::604.detailed_meaning: A serious request is being made to a king: send Rama, your eldest son, to me. The speaker is not flattering casually; he is identifying Rama as brave, capable, and ready for a task that will test him.
ramayan::604.modern_relevance: A mentor asks for the one person everyone else still wants to keep close. The request lands because the young person has already shown the steadiness needed for the next challenge.
ramayan::604.insight: It shifts attention from family protection to earned readiness.

ramayan::605.verse_sanskrit: शक्तो ह्येष मया गुप्तो दिव्येन स्वेन तेजसा । । 1199 । । राक्षसा ये विकर्तारस्तेषामपि विनाशने ।
ramayan::605.verse_hindi: Protected by me and by his own divine power, Rama is capable of destroying even those demons causing impediments to the sacrifice.
ramayan::605.english_translation: Protected by me and by his own divine power, Rama is capable of destroying even those demons causing impediments to the sacrifice.
ramayan::605.translation_literal: शक्तः (capable) / हि (indeed) / एषः (this one) / मया (by me) / गुप्तः (protected) / दिव्येन (divine) / स्वेन (his own) / तेजसा (by power) / राक्षसाः (demons) / ये (who) / विकर्तारः (causing harm) / तेषाम् (of those) / अपि (even) / विनाशने (in destruction)
ramayan::605.speaker: Brahma
ramayan::605.essence: True power proves itself by defending what should not be broken.
ramayan::605.simple_meaning: Rama has been protected by Brahma and by his own divine power, so he can destroy the beings who obstruct the sacrifice.
ramayan::605.simple_insight: Protection and strength can serve a larger purpose when they are placed in the service of right action.
ramayan::605.detailed_meaning: Brahma is speaking about Rama in the middle of a sacrificial crisis. The sages need the rite protected, and Brahma declares that Rama has both divine backing and his own power to destroy the beings disrupting it.
ramayan::605.modern_relevance: A team is trying to finish important work while one hostile person keeps derailing everything. Real strength is not just having power — it is using it to protect what matters.
ramayan::605.insight: It shifts strength from self-display to protection of a worthy task.

ramayan::606.verse_sanskrit: श्रेयश्चास्मै प्रदास्यामि बहुरूपं न संशय: । । 11910 । । त्रयाणामपि लोकानां येन ख्यातिं गमिष्यति ।
ramayan::606.verse_hindi: I will confer upon him, without doubt, a lot of blessings for his wellbeing by which he will attain fame in all the three worlds.
ramayan::606.english_translation: I will confer upon him, without doubt, many blessings for his wellbeing, by which he will attain fame in all the three worlds.
ramayan::606.translation_literal: श्रेयः (wellbeing / blessing) च (and) अस्मै (to him) प्रदास्यामि (I will give) बहुरूपम् (manyfold / of many forms) न (not) संशयः (doubt) त्रयाणाम् (of three) अपि (even) लोकानाम् (worlds) येन (by which) ख्यातिम् (fame) गमिष्यति (he will attain)
ramayan::606.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::606.essence: A true blessing can make greatness visible everywhere.
ramayan::606.simple_meaning: A blessing can be so complete that it brings lasting fame across all worlds.
ramayan::606.simple_insight: What you give with full intent can shape a life far beyond the moment.
ramayan::606.detailed_meaning: A sage is speaking about Rama and the power of his blessing. He promises not just protection, but lasting greatness for Rama, because Rama is worthy of a destiny that will be known everywhere.
ramayan::606.modern_relevance: You mentor someone before a big leap, and your encouragement changes how they carry themselves for years. A real blessing is not praise — it enlarges what the other person believes is possible.
ramayan::606.insight: It shifts support from short-term help to life-shaping affirmation.

ramayan::607.verse_sanskrit: न च तौ राममासाद्य शक्तौ स्थातुं कथञ्चन । । 11911 । । न च तौ राघवादन्यो हन्तुमुत्सहते पुमान् ।
ramayan::607.verse_hindi: Both of them (Maricha and Subahu) will not be able to withstand Rama in any way. Rama, and Rama alone, is capable of destroying them.
ramayan::607.english_translation: Both of them will not be able to withstand Rama in any way. No man other than Rama can destroy them.
ramayan::607.translation_literal: न (not) / च (and not) / तौ (those two) / रामम् (Rama) / आसाद्य (approaching, confronting) / शक्तौ (able) / स्थातुम् (to stand) / कथञ्चन (in any way) / न (not) / च (and not) / तौ (those two) / राघवात् (than Rama) / अन्यः (another) / हन्तुम् (to kill) / उत्सहते (is able, dares) / पुमान् (man)
ramayan::607.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::607.essence: Only Rama can end what keeps defeating others.
ramayan::607.simple_meaning: Maricha and Subahu cannot stand against Rama, and no other man can kill them.
ramayan::607.simple_insight: Some threats are already finished the moment they meet the right force.
ramayan::607.detailed_meaning: Vishvamitra is describing the two demons who have been tormenting his sacrificial rites. He makes the stakes plain to Rama: these enemies are not ordinary foes, and no one but Rama has the strength to stop them.
ramayan::607.modern_relevance: A problem has been circling for weeks, and everyone keeps treating it like a normal fix. Then the one person who can handle it walks in, and the whole room changes.
ramayan::607.insight: It narrows the field of action to the one who can truly resolve the threat.

ramayan::608.verse_sanskrit: वीर्योत्सिक्तौ हि तौ पापौ कालपाशवशं गतौ । । 11912 । । रामस्य राजशार्दूल न पर्याप्तौ महात्मन: ।
ramayan::608.verse_hindi: Proud of their strength, the two wicked demons have been noosed by Yama, the god of death. O tiger among kings they are no match for the magnanimous Rama.
ramayan::608.english_translation: Proud of their strength, the two wicked demons have already fallen into death's noose. O tiger among kings, they are no match for the magnanimous Rama.
ramayan::608.translation_literal: वीर्योत्सिक्तौ (proud of strength) / हि (indeed) / तौ (those two) / पापौ (wicked ones) / कालपाशवशं (under death's noose) / गतौ (gone) / रामस्य (for Rama's) / राजशार्दूल (tiger among kings) / न (not) / पर्याप्तौ (a match) / महात्मनः (of the magnanimous one)
ramayan::608.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::608.essence: Pride has already tightened the trap before the fight begins.
ramayan::608.simple_meaning: The two demons have become overconfident, but their defeat is already certain. Rama is far beyond their strength.
ramayan::608.simple_insight: Pride can make defeat feel distant, but it often arrives already sealed.
ramayan::608.detailed_meaning: A sage is reassuring a king about Rama's mission. Maricha and Subahu are described as arrogant and already caught by death, so the real point is not their power but Rama's overwhelming superiority. This verse supports the argument, not the climax.
ramayan::608.modern_relevance: You may be dealing with someone loud, confident, and impossible to ignore. But bravado is not the same as strength, and it is not the same as safety.
ramayan::608.insight: It shifts attention from an opponent's display to the actual balance of power.

ramayan::609.verse_sanskrit: न च पुत्रकृतस्नेहं कर्तुमर्हसि पार्थिव । । 11913 । । अहं ते प्रतिजानामि हतौ तौ विद्धि राक्षसौ ।
ramayan::609.verse_hindi: O king it is not proper for you to hesitate because of your paternal affection. You need to know that both the rakshasas will perish. This, I assure you.
ramayan::609.english_translation: O king, it is not proper for you to hesitate because of your paternal affection. I assure you: know that both demons will be slain.
ramayan::609.translation_literal: न च (not) / पुत्रकृतस्नेहं (paternal affection) / कर्तुमर्हसि (you ought to do) / पार्थिव (O king) / अहं (I) / ते (to you) / प्रतिजानामि (promise) / हतौ (slain) / तौ (those two) / विद्धि (know) / राक्षसौ (the two demons)
ramayan::609.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::609.essence: Affection cannot be allowed to weaken a necessary decision.
ramayan::609.simple_meaning: A king should not let fatherly affection weaken his resolve. The speaker assures him that both demons will be killed.
ramayan::609.simple_insight: You can care deeply and still act firmly when the moment demands it.
ramayan::609.detailed_meaning: In the forest, Rama has just been judged too strong for Maricha and Subahu to face. Now the speaker turns to the king and removes doubt: paternal feeling must not cloud judgment, because the demons are already as good as dead.
ramayan::609.modern_relevance: You’re about to excuse someone because you love them, even though you know the pattern is dangerous. This verse asks you to keep your heart open without surrendering your judgment.
ramayan::609.insight: It separates affection from decision, so love does not override what must be done.

ramayan::610.verse_sanskrit: अहं वेद्मि महात्मानं रामं सत्यपराक्रमम् । । 11914 । । वसिष्ठोऽपि महातेजा ये चेमे तपसि स्थिता: ।
ramayan::610.verse_hindi: I know Rama who is a great soul, true to his prowess and also Vasishta of great lustre and these other sages who have been steadfast in asceticism also know.
ramayan::610.english_translation: I know Rama, the great-souled one, true in prowess; Vasishta of great splendour and these sages who stand in austerity know him too.
ramayan::610.translation_literal: अहं (I) / वेद्मि (know) / महात्मानं (the great-souled one) / रामं (Rama) / सत्यपराक्रमम् (true in prowess) / वसिष्ठोऽपि (and Vasishta also) / महातेजा (of great splendour) / ये (who) / चेमे (and these) / तपसि (in austerity) / स्थिता: (are established)
ramayan::610.speaker: Ravana
ramayan::610.essence: Recognition is not surrender; pride can speak the truth and still refuse it.
ramayan::610.simple_meaning: Ravana admits that Rama's greatness is obvious, and that wise sages also recognise it. The problem is not ignorance; it is refusal.
ramayan::610.simple_insight: Knowing the truth is not the same as yielding to it.
ramayan::610.detailed_meaning: Ravana is still trying to justify keeping Sita, but even he cannot pretend Rama is ordinary. He names Rama, Vasishta, and other ascetics as witnesses to Rama's greatness, making his own self-deception more tragic.
ramayan::610.modern_relevance: You know exactly who is right in the meeting, but your pride still wants the last word. The mind can recognise excellence and still choose resistance.
ramayan::610.insight: It shifts the mind from arguing against reality to noticing when ego is doing the arguing.

ramayan::611.verse_sanskrit: यदि ते धर्मलाभं च यशश्च परमं भुवि । । 11915 । । स्थितमिच्छसि राजेन्द्र रामं मे दातुमर्हसि ।
ramayan::611.verse_hindi: O king of kings, if you are seeking the benefits of righteousness, great everlasting
ramayan::611.english_translation: O king of kings, if you seek the rewards of righteousness and the highest fame on earth, you should give Rama to me.
ramayan::611.translation_literal: यदि (if) / ते (you) / धर्मलाभं (gain of righteousness) / च (and) / यशः (fame) / च (and) / परमं (highest) / भुवि (on earth) / स्थितम् (established) / इच्छसि (you wish) / राजेन्द्र (O king of kings) / रामं (Rama) / मे (to me) / दातुम् (to give) / अर्हसि (you ought)
ramayan::611.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::611.essence: Honor comes from releasing what you want most when righteousness demands it.
ramayan::611.simple_meaning: True honor comes from doing what is right, even when it costs you dearly. The speaker urges the king to release Rama rather than cling to him.
ramayan::611.simple_insight: Real greatness is measured by the cost you are willing to bear for what is right.
ramayan::611.detailed_meaning: A tense court appeal is underway. The speaker has already argued that Rama and the sages should be freed, and now presses the king to choose dharma over attachment. The verse makes the moral stakes explicit: fame and righteousness belong to the one who can let go.
ramayan::611.modern_relevance: You are holding onto a decision because it flatters your image, even though you know the fair choice is harder. This verse cuts through that hesitation and asks what kind of name you want to leave behind.
ramayan::611.insight: It shifts the mind from protecting personal attachment to choosing the action that preserves honor.

ramayan::612.verse_sanskrit: यदिह्यनुज्ञां काकुत्स्थ ददते तव मन्त्रिण: । । 11916 । । वसिष्ठप्रमुखा: सर्वे ततो रामं विसर्जय ।
ramayan::612.verse_hindi: O Kakustha if your counsellors and all other sages headed by Vasishta give their consent, then only you may relieve Rama.
ramayan::612.english_translation: O Kakustha, if your counsellors and all the sages led by Vasishta give their consent, then release Rama.
ramayan::612.translation_literal: यदिहि (if indeed) / अनुज्ञाम् (permission) / काकुत्स्थ (O Kakustha) / ददते (they give) / तव (your) / मन्त्रिणः (counsellors) / वसिष्ठ-प्रमुखाः (headed by Vasishta) / सर्वे (all) / ततः (then) / रामम् (Rama) / विसर्जय (release)
ramayan::612.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::612.essence: Release comes after wise consent, not before.
ramayan::612.simple_meaning: Rama should be released only if the king's ministers and sages, led by Vasishta, agree.
ramayan::612.simple_insight: Big choices should not be made in isolation.
ramayan::612.detailed_meaning: In Janaka's court, the discussion has turned to Rama's future. The king is being urged to let him go only after hearing the consent of trusted ministers and sages led by Vasishta. The verse adds a condition to a larger plea, not the final teaching itself.
ramayan::612.modern_relevance: You are about to make a decision that affects everyone in the room. The pressure is real, but so is the need to hear the people who see what you may miss.
ramayan::612.insight: It shifts decision-making from impulse to counsel, reminding you that important action needs wise agreement.

ramayan::613.verse_sanskrit: अभिप्रेतमसंसक्तमात्मजं दातुमर्हसि । । 11917 । । दशरात्रं हि यज्ञस्य रामं राजीवलोचनम् ।
ramayan::613.verse_hindi: You should spare your dear son, the lotuseyed Rama, impartial and detached, for ten nights.
ramayan::613.english_translation: You should spare your dear son, the lotuseyed Rama, impartial and detached, for ten nights.
ramayan::613.translation_literal: अभिप्रेतम् (desired/dear) / असंसक्तम् (unattached) / आत्मजम् (own son) / दातुमर्हसि (you should give) / दशरात्रम् (ten nights) / हि (indeed) / यज्ञस्य (of the sacrifice) / रामम् (Rama) / राजीवलोचनम् (lotus-eyed)
ramayan::613.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::613.essence: Duty can require you to set aside even what you love most.
ramayan::613.simple_meaning: Dasaratha is being asked to keep Rama back for ten days, because the sacrifice must continue and Rama is being treated as too dear to lose.
ramayan::613.simple_insight: Even sacred duty can ask for painful delay.
ramayan::613.detailed_meaning: A sacrifice is underway, and the priestly voice is pressing King Dasaratha to hold back Rama for ten nights. The request is not about affection alone; it is about protecting the ritual's timing while the king faces a choice that weighs love against obligation.
ramayan::613.modern_relevance: Your family wants one answer, your work needs another, and the clock is already moving. Sometimes the hardest thing is not choosing fast, but choosing without breaking what must still be honored.
ramayan::613.insight: It teaches you to respect the timing of a binding duty, even when personal feeling pulls the other way.

ramayan::614.verse_sanskrit: नात्येति कालो यज्ञस्य यथाऽयं मम राघव । । 11918 । । तथा कुरुष्व भद्रं ते मा च शोके मन: कृथा: ।
ramayan::614.verse_hindi: O (Dasaratha), descendant of Raghu act in such a manner that the time for my sacrifice is not delayed. Do not indulge in grief. Prosperity to you
ramayan::614.english_translation: O descendant of Raghu, do not let the time for my sacrifice be delayed. Do what is proper, and do not let your mind dwell on grief. May you prosper.
ramayan::614.translation_literal: नात्येति (does not pass / is not delayed) / कालो (time) / यज्ञस्य (of the sacrifice) / यथाऽयं (as this) / मम (my) / राघव (O descendant of Raghu) / तथा (thus) / कुरुष्व (do / act) / भद्रं ते (well-being to you) / मा (not) / च (and) / शोके (in grief) / मन: (mind) / कृथा: (make)
ramayan::614.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::614.essence: Grief may be real, but it cannot be allowed to block right action.
ramayan::614.simple_meaning: The speaker asks Rama to act quickly so the sacrifice is not delayed, and to keep his mind from sinking into grief.
ramayan::614.simple_insight: You can feel sorrow without letting it stop the work in front of you.
ramayan::614.detailed_meaning: Vishwamitra is pressing Dasharatha to send Rama at once, because the sacrifice cannot wait. The issue is no longer debate but timing: the right action must happen before grief and hesitation take over.
ramayan::614.modern_relevance: You’re staring at a difficult message you need to send before noon. The feeling can stay; the decision still has to be made.
ramayan::614.insight: It shifts attention from emotional delay to timely responsibility.

ramayan::615.verse_sanskrit: इत्येवमुक्त्वा धर्मात्मा धर्मार्थसहितं वच: । । 11919 । । विरराम महातेजा विश्वामित्रो महामुनि: ।
ramayan::615.verse_hindi: After speaking these words charged with dharma and artha the great sage resplendent Viswamitra fell silent.
ramayan::615.english_translation: After speaking these words charged with dharma and artha, the great sage, resplendent Vishvamitra, fell silent.
ramayan::615.translation_literal: इत्येवम् (thus) / उक्त्वा (having spoken) / धर्मात्मा (righteous in nature) / धर्मार्थसहितम् (joined with dharma and artha) / वचः (words) / विरराम (fell silent) / महातेजा (greatly radiant) / विश्वामित्रः (Vishvamitra) / महामुनिः (great sage)
ramayan::615.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::615.essence: Clear words can carry their own final silence.
ramayan::615.simple_meaning: Vishvamitra finishes his appeal and stops speaking. His words have been carefully chosen to serve both moral duty and practical purpose.
ramayan::615.simple_insight: Sometimes the most powerful move is to speak clearly, then stop.
ramayan::615.detailed_meaning: Vishvamitra has just pressed Dasaratha to give up Rama for the sacrifice. He has made his case with moral weight and practical urgency, and now he falls silent, leaving the king alone with the demand and its cost.
ramayan::615.modern_relevance: You’ve said everything you can in a hard conversation. The next moment belongs to silence, not more argument.
ramayan::615.insight: It shows that persuasion has a limit; after clarity, pressure must give way to response.

ramayan::616.verse_sanskrit: स तन्निशम्य राजेन्द्रो विश्वामित्रवचश्शुभम् । । 11920 । । शोकमभ्यगमत्तीव्रं व्यषीदत भयान्वित: ।
ramayan::616.verse_hindi: Having listened to those auspicious words of Viswamitra, the king among kings, (Dasaratha) experienced intense grief out of fear. He became despondent.
ramayan::616.english_translation: Having listened to those auspicious words of Viswamitra, the king among kings, Dasaratha experienced intense grief out of fear. He became despondent.
ramayan::616.translation_literal: स (he) / तत् (those) / निशम्य (having heard) / राजेन्द्रः (king among kings) / विश्वामित्रवचः (Viswamitra's words) / शुभम् (auspicious) / शोकम् (grief) / अभ्यगमत् (he experienced) / तीव्रम् (intense) / व्यषीदत् (he became despondent) / भयान्वितः (filled with fear)
ramayan::616.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::616.essence: Fear hits before the king can answer.
ramayan::616.simple_meaning: Dasaratha hears Viswamitra's words and is overwhelmed by fear and grief.
ramayan::616.simple_insight: Even a powerful king can be shaken when duty and fear collide.
ramayan::616.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has just pressed Dasaratha to send Rama with him for a sacrifice. The request lands like a blow: the king of Ayodhya hears the sage's calm words and collapses inward, gripped by fear for what this means.
ramayan::616.modern_relevance: You get a message that changes everything, and your chest tightens before you even answer. The mind knows the cost before the body does.
ramayan::616.insight: It shows how a single demand can expose fear before any decision is made.

ramayan::617.verse_sanskrit: इति हृदयमनोविदारणंमुनिवचनं तदतीव शुश्रुवान् । नरपतिरभवन्महांस्तदाव्यथितमना: प्रचचाल चासनात् । । 11921 । ।
ramayan::617.verse_hindi: The great king felt shaken off his throne after listening to the words of the sage (Viswamitra) which broke his heart and terribly upset his mind.
ramayan::617.english_translation: The great king was shaken off his throne after hearing the sage's words, which broke his heart and disturbed his mind.
ramayan::617.translation_literal: इति (thus) / हृदय-मनो-विदारणम् (heart-and-mind tearing) / मुनि-वचनम् (sage's words) / तत् (those) / अतीव (greatly) / शुश्रुवान् (having heard) / नरपतिः (the king) / अभवत् (became) / महान् (great) / तत्-आ (then) / व्यथित-मनाः (mind distressed) / प्रचचाल (moved/shook) / च (and) / आसनात् (from the seat)
ramayan::617.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::617.essence: A hard truth can knock even a king off his seat.
ramayan::617.simple_meaning: Dasaratha is devastated by Viswamitra's words and rises in distress from his throne.
ramayan::617.simple_insight: Some words hit so hard they unseat you before you can answer.
ramayan::617.detailed_meaning: In Ayodhya, Viswamitra has just made his demand, and Dasaratha has heard enough to know the cost. The king is stunned, grieved, and physically shaken from his seat before he can speak.
ramayan::617.modern_relevance: You hear one message and feel your stomach drop. Before you reply, you already know your life may have to change.
ramayan::617.insight: It shows the body registering grief before the mind can organize a response.

ramayan::618.verse_sanskrit: तच्छ्रुत्वा राजशार्दूलो विश्वामित्रस्य भाषितम् । मुहूर्तमिव निस्संज्ञस्संज्ञावानिदमब्रवीत् । । 1201 । ।
ramayan::618.verse_hindi: On hearing Viswamitra, words the tiger among kings (Dasaratha) lost his senses for a moment  and  on regaining his consciousness spoke this way.
ramayan::618.english_translation: On hearing Viswamitra's words, the tiger among kings, Dasaratha, lost consciousness for a moment and, regaining it, spoke these words.
ramayan::618.translation_literal: तत् (that) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / राजशार्दूलः (tiger among kings) / विश्वामित्रस्य (of Viswamitra) / भाषितम् (speech) / मुहूर्तम् इव (for a moment) / निस्संज्ञः (unconscious) / संज्ञावान् (regaining consciousness) / इदम् (this) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::618.speaker: Dasaratha
ramayan::618.essence: Even a king can be stunned before he finds his words.
ramayan::618.simple_meaning: Dasaratha is stunned by Viswamitra's request and needs a moment before he can respond.
ramayan::618.simple_insight: Some news hits so hard that even a king has to gather himself before speaking.
ramayan::618.detailed_meaning: In Ayodhya, Viswamitra has asked for Rama's help against the rākṣasas. Dasaratha is struck silent by the demand, briefly overwhelmed before he can answer. This verse shows the shock before his refusal and fear.
ramayan::618.modern_relevance: You hear a request that changes everything, and your mind goes blank for a second. Before you answer, you need that same breath of recovery.
ramayan::618.insight: It captures the pause between shock and response, when emotion briefly overtakes judgment.

ramayan::619.verse_sanskrit: ऊनषोडशवर्षो मे रामो राजीवलोचन: । न युद्धयोग्यतामस्य पश्यामि सह राक्षसै: । । 1202 । ।
ramayan::619.verse_hindi: My lotuseyed son Rama is less than sixteen. I do not think  he has ability to fight with the rakshasas in a battle.
ramayan::619.english_translation: My lotuseyed son Rama is less than sixteen. I do not think he is fit to fight the rakshasas in battle.
ramayan::619.translation_literal: ऊनषोडशवर्षो (less than sixteen years old) / मे (my) / रामो (Rama) / राजीवलोचन: (lotus-eyed) / न (not) / युद्धयोग्यताम् (fitness for battle) / अस्य (of him) / पश्यामि (I see) / सह (with) / राक्षसै: (rakshasas)
ramayan::619.speaker: Dasharatha
ramayan::619.essence: A father sees the cost of duty before the king can answer.
ramayan::619.simple_meaning: Dasharatha says Rama is only fifteen and not ready to fight demons in battle.
ramayan::619.simple_insight: Love can make a ruler admit a hard truth: not every duty should be forced onto the young.
ramayan::619.detailed_meaning: Dasharatha has just heard Viswamitra's demand. His senses return, and the father in him speaks before the king can hide it: Rama is still too young for the battlefield, and the request asks too much of him.
ramayan::619.modern_relevance: You watch your child walk into a room that feels bigger than their age. Your first instinct is not strategy — it is the ache of knowing they should not have to carry this yet.
ramayan::619.insight: It separates protective fear from heroic duty, showing that readiness matters before action.

ramayan::620.verse_sanskrit: इयमक्षौहिणी पूर्णा यस्याहं पतिरीश्वर: । अनया संवृतो गत्वा योद्धाऽहं तैर्निशाचरै: । । 1203 । ।
ramayan::620.verse_hindi: Here is the whole akshauhini (army) of which I am the lord and sustainer.
ramayan::620.english_translation: Here is the full akshauhini army, of which I am the lord and sustainer. With this force surrounding me, I will go and fight those night-roamers.
ramayan::620.translation_literal: इयम् (this) / अक्षौहिणी (akshauhini army) / पूर्णा (complete) / यस्य (of which) / अहम् (I) / पतिरीश्वरः (lord and master) / अनया (with this) / संवृतः (surrounded) / गत्वा (going) / योद्धा (to fight) / अहम् (I) / तैः (with those) / निशाचरैः (night-roamers)
ramayan::620.speaker: Dasharatha
ramayan::620.essence: He offers his army because he cannot bear to offer his son.
ramayan::620.simple_meaning: Dasharatha says he has a full army under his command and can go to battle against the night-roamers.
ramayan::620.simple_insight: Power can still sound like fear when it is spoken by a worried father.
ramayan::620.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has asked for Rama, and Dasharatha recoils at the thought of sending his young son into danger. To resist, he points to his own vast army and offers to go himself, trying to replace a son's risk with a king's force.
ramayan::620.modern_relevance: You want to protect someone you love, so you reach for every resource you have, even when the real issue is fear, not lack of power.
ramayan::620.insight: It shows how attachment can dress itself up as practical strength.

ramayan::621.verse_sanskrit: इमे शूराश्च विक्रान्ता भृत्या मेऽस्त्रविशारदा: । योग्या रक्षोगणैर्योद्धुं न रामं नेतुमर्हसि । । 1204 । ।
ramayan::621.verse_hindi: These servants of mine are warriors, valiant, powerful and courageous, skilled in the
ramayan::621.english_translation: These are my warriors, brave, powerful, and skilled with weapons. You should not take Rama into battle against the rakshasas.
ramayan::621.translation_literal: इमे (these) / शूराः (brave warriors) / च (and) / विक्रान्ताः (powerful) / भृत्याः (servants) / मे (my) / अस्त्रविशारदाः (skilled in weapons) / योग्याः (fit) / रक्षोगणैः (with the rakshasa hosts) / योद्धुम् (to fight) / न (not) / रामम् (Rama) / नेतुम् (to lead) / अर्हसि (you should, you ought)
ramayan::621.speaker: Dasharatha
ramayan::621.essence: A father refuses to let his son be treated as expendable.
ramayan::621.simple_meaning: Dasharatha says his own army is ready, so Rama should not be sent to fight the demons.
ramayan::621.simple_insight: Love can sound like refusal when a father sees danger first.
ramayan::621.detailed_meaning: Dasharatha is still trying to shield Rama. He points to his seasoned warriors and says they are fit for battle, while Rama is not. Beneath the military argument is a father's fear that his son is being pulled toward a war he should never have to face.
ramayan::621.modern_relevance: You see your child, younger colleague, or younger sibling being pushed into something brutal just because they seem capable. The first truth you speak is not strategy — it is protection.
ramayan::621.insight: It shows how concern for someone’s safety can override pride in their ability.

ramayan::622.verse_sanskrit: अहमेव धनुष्पाणिर्गोप्ता समरमूर्धनि । यावत्प्राणान्धरिष्यामि तावद्योत्स्ये निशाचरै: । । 1205 । ।
ramayan::622.verse_hindi: Wielding bow in hand I will protect the sacrifice. As long as my life sustains, I will engage the rakshasas in the battle.
ramayan::622.english_translation: Wielding bow in hand, I will protect the sacrifice. As long as life remains in me, I will fight the rakshasas in battle.
ramayan::622.translation_literal: अहम् (I) / एव (indeed) / धनुष्पाणिः (with bow in hand) / गोप्ता (protector) / समरमूर्धनि (at the front of battle) / यावत् (as long as) / प्राणान् (breaths/life-forces) / धरिष्यामि (I will sustain) / तावत् (until then) / योत्स्ये (I will fight) / निशाचरैः (with the night-walkers/rakshasas)
ramayan::622.speaker: Rama
ramayan::622.essence: He makes his own body the shield until the task is safe.
ramayan::622.simple_meaning: Rama says he will personally guard the sacrifice and keep fighting the rakshasas until his last breath.
ramayan::622.simple_insight: There is dignity in staying at your post even when danger keeps returning.
ramayan::622.detailed_meaning: Visvamitra has brought Rama to protect a sacrifice from rakshasas. Facing a threat that keeps interrupting sacred work, Rama steps forward himself, bow in hand, and promises to keep fighting as long as he lives.
ramayan::622.modern_relevance: You are the one left awake when a family crisis keeps circling back at 3 a.m. No one else can carry it for you right now, so you stay, steady and alert, until the danger passes.
ramayan::622.insight: It shifts you from hoping someone else will handle the threat to taking direct responsibility yourself.

ramayan::623.verse_sanskrit: निर्विघ्ना व्रतचर्या सा भविष्यति सुरक्षिता । अहं तत्रागमिष्यामि न रामं नेतुमर्हसि । । 1206 । ।
ramayan::623.verse_hindi: I shall go there, protect the sacrifice and see that it is conducted without obstacles. It
ramayan::623.english_translation: I shall go there, protect the sacrifice, and ensure it is conducted without obstacles. You must not take Rama away.
ramayan::623.translation_literal: निर्विघ्ना (without obstacles) / व्रतचर्या (the conduct of the sacrifice) / सा (that) / भविष्यति (will become) / सुरक्षिता (well protected) / अहम् (I) / तत्र (there) / आगमिष्यामि (will come) / न (not) / रामम् (Rama) / नेतुम् (to take) / अर्हसि (you should)
ramayan::623.speaker: Vishwamitra
ramayan::623.essence: The sacred task comes first, even when it requires personal intervention.
ramayan::623.simple_meaning: Vishwamitra says he will personally ensure the sacrifice continues safely, and he refuses to let Rama be taken away.
ramayan::623.simple_insight: Sometimes protection means staying with the task yourself, not handing it off.
ramayan::623.detailed_meaning: Vishwamitra is facing the threat around his sacrifice. He tells the king's messenger that he will go himself, guard the ritual, and keep it free of disturbance. The immediate issue is not theory — it is whether Rama stays where he is needed.
ramayan::623.modern_relevance: A project is collapsing because the most important person keeps getting pulled into side demands. You stop the drift, return to the core task, and make sure the work gets finished cleanly.
ramayan::623.insight: It shifts attention from argument to responsibility: protect the essential task first, then deal with everything else.

ramayan::624.verse_sanskrit: बालो ह्यकृतविद्यश्च न च वेत्ति बलाबलम् । न चास्त्रबलसंयुक्तो न च युद्धविशारद: । । 1207 । । न चासौ रक्षसां योग्य: कूटयुद्धा हि ते ध्रुवम् ।
ramayan::624.verse_hindi: Rama is still a child, he is not learned in the science of warfare,he does not know the  strength and weakness of enemies. He has not acquired  as yet the strength of using  weapons and is not proficient in warfare. You know certainly those rakshasas are deceitful in battle. And hence he is not qualified to oppose them in the battle succesfully.
ramayan::624.english_translation: Rama is still a child. He does not know the strength and weakness of enemies, has not yet mastered weapons, and is not skilled in battle. Those rakshasas fight by deceit, so he is not fit to face them successfully.
ramayan::624.translation_literal: बालः (a child) / हि (indeed) / अकृतविद्यः (unlearned) / च (and) / न (not) / वेत्ति (knows) / बलाबलम् (strength and weakness) / न (not) / च (and) / अस्त्रबलसंयुक्तः (equipped with weapon-power) / न (not) / च (and) / युद्धविशारदः (skilled in battle) / न (not) / च (and) / असौ (he) / रक्षसाम् (of rakshasas) / योग्यः (fit) / कूटयुद्धाः (deceitful in battle) / हि (indeed) / ते (they) / ध्रुवम् (certainly)
ramayan::624.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::624.essence: Love sometimes means keeping someone out of a fight they cannot yet win.
ramayan::624.simple_meaning: Rama is too young and untrained for this fight. The enemy uses trickery, so taking him along would put him at risk.
ramayan::624.simple_insight: Love can mean refusing a brave but reckless choice.
ramayan::624.detailed_meaning: In the forest, the sages are pleading for protection. The speaker argues against bringing Rama into danger: he is still young, untrained in weapons, and facing enemies who fight by deceit. The verse strengthens the case that safety, not pride, must decide.
ramayan::624.modern_relevance: You want to bring the inexperienced person into the hardest meeting because they care most. But care alone is not readiness, and courage alone is not enough.
ramayan::624.insight: It shifts judgment from affection to practical protection.

ramayan::625.verse_sanskrit: विप्रयुक्तो हि रामेण मुहूर्तमपि नोत्सहे । । 1208 । । जीवितुं मुनिशार्दूल न रामं नेतुमर्हसि ।
ramayan::625.verse_hindi: Separated from Rama, I do not like to live even for a moment. O tiger among ascetics, it is not proper to take Rama with you.
ramayan::625.english_translation: Separated from Rama, I do not like to live even for a moment. O tiger among ascetics, it is not proper to take Rama with you.
ramayan::625.translation_literal: विप्रयुक्तो (separated) / हि (indeed) / रामेण (from Rama) / मुहूर्तमपि (even for a moment) / न (not) / उत्सहे (I desire) / जीवितुं (to live) / मुनिशार्दूल (tiger among ascetics) / न (not) / रामं (Rama) / नेतुमर्हसि (you ought to take)
ramayan::625.speaker: Rama
ramayan::625.essence: Some bonds make absence feel impossible.
ramayan::625.simple_meaning: Rama says he cannot bear even a moment away from Rama, and asks the sage not to take Rama with him.
ramayan::625.simple_insight: Love can make absence feel physically unbearable.
ramayan::625.detailed_meaning: In the forest, Vishvamitra is trying to take Rama away for a sacred task. Rama interrupts with fierce honesty: being separated from Rama feels unbearable, and he refuses the idea of parting. The moment shows how deeply bonded he is.
ramayan::625.modern_relevance: You stand at a train platform watching someone you depend on disappear into the crowd. The body knows what the mind resists: some separations are felt as pain, not preference.
ramayan::625.insight: It shifts attention from polite attachment to the raw cost of separation.

ramayan::626.verse_sanskrit: यदि वा राघवं ब्रह्मन्नेतुमिच्छसि सुव्रत । । 1209 । । चतुरङ्गसमायुक्तं मया च सहितं नय ।
ramayan::626.verse_hindi: O sage of great vows, O brahman if at all you intend to take Rama with you, take me  also along with my army.
ramayan::626.english_translation: O sage of great vows, O brahman, if you intend to take Rama with you, take me too, along with my army.
ramayan::626.translation_literal: यदि वा (if indeed) / राघवं (Rama) / ब्रह्मन् (O brahman) / नेतुम् इच्छसि (you wish to take) / सुव्रत (O one of great vows) / चतुरङ्ग-समायुक्तम् (together with fourfold forces) / मया (with me) / च सहितम् (along with) / नय (take/lead)
ramayan::626.speaker: Dasharatha
ramayan::626.essence: He would rather go with Rama than endure separation.
ramayan::626.simple_meaning: Dasharatha says that if Vishvamitra takes Rama, he must take Dasharatha and his army as well. He cannot bear Rama being taken away alone.
ramayan::626.simple_insight: Love can make separation feel impossible, even when the request is reasonable.
ramayan::626.detailed_meaning: Vishvamitra has come to take Rama for a dangerous mission. Dasharatha has already resisted, then weakened, then pleaded. Now he offers the impossible: if Rama must go, the father will go too, with his whole force. The verse shows how hard it is to let go.
ramayan::626.modern_relevance: Your child is leaving for a new city, and your first impulse is not advice but attachment. You want to protect, accompany, delay, or somehow stay folded into their path.
ramayan::626.insight: It reveals how attachment can turn even a lawful request into a personal wound.

ramayan::627.verse_sanskrit: षष्टिर्वर्षसहस्राणि जातस्य मम कौशिक । । 12010 । । दु:खेनोत्पादितश्चायं न रामं नेतुमर्हसि ।
ramayan::627.verse_hindi: O scion of of Kusika family, sixty thousand years have passed since I was born.  Rama was born to me after a great deal of suffering. It is not proper to take him with you.
ramayan::627.english_translation: O scion of the Kusika family, sixty thousand years have passed since I was born. Rama was born to me after great suffering. It is not proper to take him with you.
ramayan::627.translation_literal: षष्टिः (sixty) / वर्षसहस्राणि (thousand years) / जातस्य (of the one born) / मम (my) / कौशिक (O Kusika-born) / दुःखेन (with suffering) / उत्पादितः (brought forth, born) / च (and) / अयम् (this one) / न (not) / रामम् (Rama) / नेतुम् (to take) / अर्हसि (you ought, it is proper)
ramayan::627.speaker: Dasharatha
ramayan::627.essence: What costs the most is hardest to release.
ramayan::627.simple_meaning: Dasharatha says Rama was born to him after great hardship, so it is wrong to take Rama away.
ramayan::627.simple_insight: Love deepened by suffering makes separation feel unbearable.
ramayan::627.detailed_meaning: In the palace at Ayodhya, Dasharatha begs Vishvamitra not to take Rama. He reminds the sage that Rama was born after years of anguish and that this son is precious beyond measure. The plea is both fatherly and desperate.
ramayan::627.modern_relevance: You finally got the child, project, or relationship you waited years for, and now someone wants to pull it away. The ache is not possessiveness alone; it is memory.
ramayan::627.insight: It shifts the mind from treating people as transferable to recognising the cost hidden inside attachment.

ramayan::628.verse_sanskrit: चतुर्णामात्मजानां हि प्रीति:परमिका मम । । 12011 । । ज्येष्ठं धर्मप्रधानं च न रामं नेतुमर्हसि ।
ramayan::628.verse_hindi: My love for Rama among all my four sons is supreme.It is not proper for you to take Rama, the eldest son whose prime qualification  is his virtue.
ramayan::628.english_translation: My love for Rama among all my four sons is supreme. It is not proper for you to take Rama, the eldest son whose chief quality is virtue.
ramayan::628.translation_literal: चतुर्णाम् (of the four) / आत्मजानाम् (of my sons) / हि (indeed) / प्रीतिः (affection) / परमिका (highest) / मम (my) / ज्येष्ठम् (the eldest) / धर्मप्रधानम् (with virtue as the foremost quality) / च (and) / न (not) / रामम् (Rama) / नेतुम् (to take away) / अर्हसि (you are fit)
ramayan::628.speaker: Dasharatha
ramayan::628.essence: The heart resists most when virtue and love point to the same person.
ramayan::628.simple_meaning: Dasharatha says Rama is his most beloved son and the eldest, so it is not right to take him away.
ramayan::628.simple_insight: Love and duty can collide most painfully where your heart is strongest.
ramayan::628.detailed_meaning: In Ayodhya, the old king Dasharatha is pleading with Vishwamitra not to take Rama away. He reminds the sage that Rama is not only his eldest son but also the child he loves most, and the one whose virtue makes him especially precious.
ramayan::628.modern_relevance: You know the feeling when someone asks for the one person you most want to protect — your best employee, your eldest child, your most reliable friend. The request is reasonable, but your heart resists.
ramayan::628.insight: It shows how attachment can make even a rightful request feel unbearable.

ramayan::629.verse_sanskrit: किंवीर्या राक्षसास्ते च कस्य पुत्राश्च ते च के । । 12012 । । कथं प्रमाणा: के चैतान्रक्षन्ति मुनिपुङ्गव ।
ramayan::629.verse_hindi: O best of sages, how powerful are those rakshsas? Whose  sons are they? Who are they and how huge is their body? Who are protecting them?
ramayan::629.english_translation: O best of sages, how powerful are those rakshasas? Whose sons are they? Who are they, how large are they, and who protects them?
ramayan::629.translation_literal: किंवीर्या (what power / how powerful) / राक्षसाः (rakshasas) / ते (those) / च (and) / कस्य (whose) / पुत्राः (sons) / च (and) / ते (those) / च (and) / के (who) / कथं (how) / प्रमाणाः (of what size / how large) / के (who) / च (and) / एतान् (these) / रक्षन्ति (protect) / मुनिपुङ्गव (O best of sages)
ramayan::629.speaker: Dasharatha
ramayan::629.essence: He stalls by demanding every detail of the danger.
ramayan::629.simple_meaning: Dasharatha asks Vishvamitra to identify the demons: how strong they are, whose sons they are, what they look like, and who protects them.
ramayan::629.simple_insight: Before facing a threat, you want to know exactly what you're up against.
ramayan::629.detailed_meaning: Dasharatha is resisting Vishvamitra’s request to take Rama away, and he turns to questions about the rakshasas instead. He wants their strength, lineage, size, and protection, hoping to judge whether Rama should be sent at all.
ramayan::629.modern_relevance: Before you agree to a risky request, you ask the hard questions: who is involved, how dangerous is it, and what protection exists?
ramayan::629.insight: It shifts the mind from emotional refusal to practical assessment of the threat.

ramayan::630.verse_sanskrit: कथं च प्रतिकर्तव्यं तेषां रामेण रक्षसाम् । । 12013 । । मामकैर्वा बलैर्ब्रह्मन्मया वा कूटयोधिनाम् । 3
ramayan::630.verse_hindi: O brahman, how to rebuff those deceitful warriors either through Rama or through my army or through me?
ramayan::630.english_translation: O brahman, how can those deceitful warriors be repelled by Rama, by my forces, or by me?
ramayan::630.translation_literal: कथं (how) / च (and) / प्रतिकर्तव्यं (to be repelled) / तेषां (of those) / रामेण (by Rama) / रक्षसाम् (of the rakshasas) / मामकैः (by my own) / वा (or) / बलैः (by forces) / ब्रह्मन् (O brahman) / मया (by me) / वा (or) / कूटयोधिनाम् (of deceitful fighters)
ramayan::630.speaker: Dasharatha
ramayan::630.essence: Deceit cannot always be answered by strength alone.
ramayan::630.simple_meaning: Dasharatha asks how Rama, his army, or he himself should deal with these deceitful enemies.
ramayan::630.simple_insight: Sometimes raw strength is not the real answer; you need clear strategy too.
ramayan::630.detailed_meaning: Dasharatha is speaking to the sage after hearing that Rama must face dangerous rakshasas. He wants to know not just who they are, but how they can possibly be checked in battle. The verse opens the practical problem that follows.
ramayan::630.modern_relevance: You are up against someone who lies, twists facts, and plays dirty in a meeting, a lawsuit, or a family conflict. Brute force alone feels inadequate, and you start asking for a better way to respond.
ramayan::630.insight: It shifts the mind from simple confrontation to strategic response against manipulation.

ramayan::631.verse_sanskrit: सर्वं मे शंस भगवन्कथं तेषां मया रणे । । 12014 । । स्थातव्यं दुष्टभावानां वीर्योत्सिक्ता हि राक्षसा: । 4तस्य तद्वचनं श्रुत्वा विश्वामित्रोऽभ्यभाषत । । 12015 । ।
ramayan::631.verse_hindi: O venerable one, how to fight those wickednatured ones in the battle and stay aginst them? For rakshasas are proud of their prowess. Having heard the words of Dasaratha, Viswamitra said:
ramayan::631.english_translation: O venerable one, how should I stand against those wicked-minded rakshasas in battle? They are proud of their strength. Hearing Dasharatha's words, Vishwamitra then spoke.
ramayan::631.translation_literal: सर्वं (everything) / मे (to me) / शंस (tell) / भगवन् (venerable one) / कथं (how) / तेषाम् (of those) / मया (by me) / रणे (in battle) / स्थातव्यम् (to be stood against) / दुष्टभावानाम् (of wicked-minded ones) / वीर्योत्सिक्ताः (proud of strength) / हि (indeed) / राक्षसाः (rakshasas) / तस्य (of that) / तत् (that) / वचनम् (speech) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / विश्वामित्रः (Vishwamitra) / अभ्यभाषत (spoke)
ramayan::631.speaker: Dasharatha
ramayan::631.essence: The question is not whether danger exists, but how to face it.
ramayan::631.simple_meaning: Dasharatha asks Vishwamitra how anyone can stand against the powerful, wicked rakshasas in battle.
ramayan::631.simple_insight: Fear gets named plainly before action begins.
ramayan::631.detailed_meaning: In the forest, Dasharatha has heard enough to feel the scale of the threat. He asks Vishwamitra how to face these arrogant rakshasas at all. The verse ends by turning the exchange over to Vishwamitra’s reply.
ramayan::631.modern_relevance: You hear the first details about a problem and suddenly it feels larger than you can handle. Before you act, you need the full truth of what you're facing.
ramayan::631.insight: It frames the enemy as a real force, making the coming guidance necessary.

ramayan::632.verse_sanskrit: पौलस्त्यवंशप्रभवो रावणो नाम राक्षस: । स ब्रह्मणा दत्तवरस्त्रैलोक्यं बाधते भृशम् । । 12016 । । महाबलो महावीर्यो राक्षसैर्बहुभिर्वृत: ।
ramayan::632.verse_hindi: पौलस्त्यवंशप्रभवो रावणो नाम राक्षस: । स ब्रह्मणा दत्तवरस्त्रैलोक्यं बाधते भृशम् । । 12016 । । महाबलो महावीर्यो राक्षसैर्बहुभिर्वृत: ।
ramayan::632.english_translation: Ravana, born in the Pulastya line, is a rakshasa. Blessed by Brahma, he greatly troubles the three worlds. He is very powerful, very valiant, and surrounded by many rakshasas.
ramayan::632.translation_literal: पौलस्त्यवंशप्रभवः (born in the Pulastya line) / रावणः (Ravana) / नाम (named) / राक्षसः (a rakshasa) / सः (he) / ब्रह्मणा (by Brahma) / दत्तवरः (granted a boon) / त्रैलोक्यम् (the three worlds) / बाधते (troubles) / भृशम् (greatly) / महाबलः (very powerful) / महावीर्यः (very valiant) / राक्षसैः (by rakshasas) / बहुभिः (many) / वृतः (surrounded)
ramayan::632.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::632.essence: Great power becomes peril when nothing holds it back.
ramayan::632.simple_meaning: Ravana is introduced as a powerful rakshasa from the Pulastya line, blessed by Brahma, and a terror to the three worlds.
ramayan::632.simple_insight: Power without restraint becomes a threat to everyone around it.
ramayan::632.detailed_meaning: A brahman is being told who Ravana is before the battle can be answered. He is not just an enemy warrior but a boon-blessed ruler of rakshasas, backed by force, pride, and numbers. The verse sets up the scale of the danger.
ramayan::632.modern_relevance: Before the meeting starts, someone quietly explains why one person in the room can derail everything. The danger is not just strength — it is strength with no restraint.
ramayan::632.insight: It shifts attention from Ravana's might to the moral danger of unchecked power.

ramayan::633.verse_sanskrit: श्रूयते हि महावीर्यो रावणो राक्षसाधिप: । । 12017 । । साक्षाद्वैश्रवणभ्राता पुत्रो विश्रवसो मुने: ।
ramayan::633.verse_hindi: Ravana, king of rakshasas, is the brother of Kubera and son of ascetic Visravana. He is said to possess great prowess.
ramayan::633.english_translation: Ravana, king of the rakshasas, is said to possess great prowess. He is the brother of Kubera and the son of the sage Vishrava.
ramayan::633.translation_literal: श्रूयते (is said) / हि (indeed) / महावीर्यः (greatly powerful) / रावणः (Ravana) / राक्षसाधिपः (king of the rakshasas) / साक्षात् (directly) / वैश्रवणभ्राता (brother of Vaishravana/Kubera) / पुत्रः (son) / विश्रवसः (of Vishrava) / मुनेः (of the sage)
ramayan::633.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::633.essence: Know the enemy fully before you move.
ramayan::633.simple_meaning: Ravana is introduced as a powerful king with a notable family line: brother of Kubera and son of Vishrava.
ramayan::633.simple_insight: Some dangers are not random; they come with status, strength, and a long backstory.
ramayan::633.detailed_meaning: Rama is asking how to face the enemy in battle, and the reply begins by identifying Ravana. Before any strategy comes, the poem reminds us who Ravana is: powerful, famous, and born into a striking lineage. The threat is real because the opponent is real.
ramayan::633.modern_relevance: You meet someone who seems impossible to challenge: respected, powerful, and backed by a long network. Before you react, it helps to understand exactly what you are facing.
ramayan::633.insight: It shifts attention from panic to clear-eyed recognition of the opponent's scale and background.

ramayan::634.verse_sanskrit: यदा स्वयं न यज्ञस्य विघ्नकर्ता महाबल: । । 12018 । । तेन सञ्चोदितौ द्वौ तु राक्षसौ वै महाबलौ । मारीचश्च सुबाहुश्च यज्ञविघ्नं करिष्यत: । । 12019 । ।
ramayan::634.verse_hindi: Although endowed with great strength, Ravana, by himself, never created impediments to the sacrifice. But two rakshasas by name Maricha and Subahu are incited by him to cause obstacles.
ramayan::634.english_translation: Although endowed with great strength, Ravana, by himself, never created impediments to the sacrifice. But two rakshasas by name Maricha and Subahu are incited by him to cause obstacles.
ramayan::634.translation_literal: यदा (when) / स्वयं (himself) / न (not) / यज्ञस्य (of the sacrifice) / विघ्नकर्ता (obstructor) / महाबलः (very powerful) / तेन (by him) / सञ्चोदितौ (incited) / द्वौ (two) / तु (indeed) / राक्षसौ (rakshasas) / वै (indeed) / महाबलौ (very powerful) / मारीचः (Maricha) / च (and) / सुबाहुः (Subahu) / च (and) / यज्ञविघ्नम् (obstruction to the sacrifice) / करिष्यतः (will do)
ramayan::634.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::634.essence: Power often hides behind the people it sends.
ramayan::634.simple_meaning: Ravana did not attack the sacrifice directly. He used Maricha and Subahu to disrupt it instead.
ramayan::634.simple_insight: Some harm is done through proxies, not open force.
ramayan::634.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra is explaining the threat behind the coming sacrifice. Ravana's power is real, but he does not act openly here; he sends Maricha and Subahu to ruin the ritual. The verse sets up why the king must be warned.
ramayan::634.modern_relevance: A boss never sends the harsh email himself. He asks someone else to do it, then stays out of view. The damage is still his.
ramayan::634.insight: It teaches you to see through indirect harm and recognise the hand behind it.

ramayan::635.verse_sanskrit: इत्युक्तो मुनिना तेन राजोवाच मुनिं तदा । न हि शक्तोऽस्मि सङ्ग्रामे स्थातुं तस्य दुरात्मन: । । 12020 । ।
ramayan::635.verse_hindi: Informed in this manner by sage Viswamitra, king Dasaratha addressed the sage,  saying, I am not competent enough to stand before those evilminded rakshasas in the batlle.
ramayan::635.english_translation: Informed in this manner by sage Viswamitra, King Dasaratha then said to the sage, "I am not strong enough to stand in battle before that evil-minded one."
ramayan::635.translation_literal: इत्युक्तो (having been told thus) / मुनिना (by the sage) / तेन (by that) / राजा (the king) / उवाच (said) / मुनिं (to the sage) / तदा (then) / न (not) / हि (indeed) / शक्तः (able) / अस्मि (I am) / सङ्ग्रामे (in battle) / स्थातुम् (to stand) / तस्य (before that) / दुरात्मनः (evil-minded one)
ramayan::635.speaker: Dasaratha
ramayan::635.essence: Strength begins with admitting where you cannot stand alone.
ramayan::635.simple_meaning: Dasharatha admits he cannot face the demon in battle. The line shows his fear, limits, and the pressure of the moment.
ramayan::635.simple_insight: Honesty about your limits can be the first step toward the right help.
ramayan::635.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has asked for help against the rakshasas troubling his sacrifice. Dasharatha, though king and warrior, openly admits he cannot stand before that enemy. The verse shows the human cost of weakness before a duty he cannot personally fulfil.
ramayan::635.modern_relevance: You’re staring at a task that is bigger than your current strength. Naming that honestly can be wiser than pretending you can carry it alone.
ramayan::635.insight: It teaches you to face limitation without self-deception and to seek the right support.

ramayan::636.verse_sanskrit: स त्वं प्रसादं धर्मज्ञ कुरुष्व मम पुत्रके । मम चैवाल्पभाग्यस्य दैवतं हि भवान्गुरु: । । 12021 । ।
ramayan::636.verse_hindi: You are the knower of righteousness. Extend your favour to my little son and also to me for I am so who is unfortunate. You are verily my spiritual preceptor and god.
ramayan::636.english_translation: You know righteousness. Please show favor to my son and to me, who am unfortunate. You are truly my teacher and my divine guide.
ramayan::636.translation_literal: स (that) / त्वं (you) / प्रसादं (favor) / धर्मज्ञ (knower of righteousness) / कुरुष्व (do) / मम (my) / पुत्रके (little son) / मम (my) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / अल्पभाग्यस्य (of the unfortunate one) / दैवतं (divine guide) / हि (indeed) / भवान् (you) / गुरु: (teacher)
ramayan::636.speaker: Dasharatha
ramayan::636.essence: Real strength can sound like a plea for help.
ramayan::636.simple_meaning: Dasharatha asks Vishwamitra, who knows righteousness, to bless his son and himself. He speaks from helplessness and reverence, calling the sage his teacher and guide.
ramayan::636.simple_insight: There is dignity in asking clearly when you cannot carry the burden alone.
ramayan::636.detailed_meaning: After admitting he cannot face Ravana's power, Dasharatha turns to Vishwamitra. The king, usually commanding, now speaks as a humble father: he asks protection for Rama and for himself, placing trust in the sage's wisdom and power.
ramayan::636.modern_relevance: You sit in a hospital corridor, finally calling the one person who may know what to do. Pride is useless there. Clear trust becomes the only honest move.
ramayan::636.insight: It shifts the mind from self-reliance to humble dependence on trustworthy guidance.

ramayan::637.verse_sanskrit: देवदानवगन्धर्वा यक्षा:पतगपन्नगा: । न शक्ता रावणं सोढुं किं पुनर्मानवा युधि । । 12022 । ।
ramayan::637.verse_hindi: Gods, danavas, gandharvas, yakshas, birds and great serpents cannot withstand Ravana in battle. What are men to him? (They are no match to him).
ramayan::637.english_translation: Gods, danavas, gandharvas, yakshas, birds, and great serpents cannot withstand Ravana in battle. What are men to him?
ramayan::637.translation_literal: देवदानवगन्धर्वा: (gods, danavas, gandharvas) / यक्षा: (yakshas) / पतगपन्नगा: (birds and serpents) / न शक्ता: (not able) / रावणं (Ravana) / सोढुं (to withstand) / किं पुन: (what then) / मानवा: (men) / युधि (in battle)
ramayan::637.speaker: Dasaratha
ramayan::637.essence: Ravana seems so overwhelming that courage itself starts to shrink.
ramayan::637.simple_meaning: Dasaratha says Ravana is so powerful that even gods and other mighty beings cannot face him in war, so humans stand no chance.
ramayan::637.simple_insight: Fear can make a threat feel larger than life.
ramayan::637.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has asked Dasaratha for Rama's help. Dasaratha, shaken by the thought of facing Ravana, admits that even celestial and nonhuman beings cannot withstand the demon king in battle. The line deepens his refusal and shows how overwhelming Ravana seems.
ramayan::637.modern_relevance: You look at one impossible problem and start measuring yourself against everyone who failed before you. The fear grows faster than the facts.
ramayan::637.insight: It shows how fear magnifies an opponent until action feels impossible.

ramayan::638.verse_sanskrit: स हि वीर्यवतां वीर्यमादत्ते युधि राक्षस: । तेन चाहं न शक्तोऽस्मि संयोद्धुं तस्य वा बलै: । । 12023 । । सबलो वा मुनिश्रेष्ठ सहितो वा ममात्मजै: ।
ramayan::638.verse_hindi: That rakshasa pulls out warriors prowess in the battle. O foremost of ascetics Either with forces or with my sons it is not possible for me to engage him or his forces in battle.
ramayan::638.english_translation: That rakshasa strips warriors of their prowess in battle. O foremost of ascetics, I cannot fight him or his forces, even with my army or my sons.
ramayan::638.translation_literal: सः (that one) / हि (indeed) / वीर्यवताम् (of the powerful) / वीर्यम् (prowess) / आदत्ते (takes away) / युधि (in battle) / राक्षसः (the rakshasa) / तेन (therefore) / च (and) / अहम् (I) / न (not) / शक्तः अस्मि (am able) / संयोद्धुम् (to fight) / तस्य (his) / वा (or) / बलैः (with forces) / सबलः (with army) / वा (or) / मुनिश्रेष्ठ (O foremost of ascetics) / सहितः (together) / वा (or) / मम आत्मजैः (with my sons)
ramayan::638.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::638.essence: Pride won’t change a battle you cannot win.
ramayan::638.simple_meaning: Ravana is so powerful that even strong warriors lose their strength against him. The speaker admits he cannot defeat him, even with an army or his sons.
ramayan::638.simple_insight: Sometimes honesty is the first act of wisdom: admit the limit before it becomes a disaster.
ramayan::638.detailed_meaning: A frightened father is speaking to a sage about Ravana’s terrifying strength. He says no army can stand against the rakshasa, and even his own sons would be no match. The line builds the case for why this child must not be sent into danger.
ramayan::638.modern_relevance: You’re weighing whether to send someone into a fight they can’t win — and your stomach already knows the answer. Naming the danger clearly is part of protecting what matters.
ramayan::638.insight: It teaches you to face danger realistically instead of hiding behind pride or hope.

ramayan::639.verse_sanskrit: कथमप्यमरप्रख्यं सङ्ग्रामाणामकोविदम् । बालं मे तनयं ब्रह्मन् नैव दास्यामि पुत्रकम् । । 12024 । ।
ramayan::639.verse_hindi: O brahman although my son resembles the celestials he is not experienced in warfare. On no account shall I spare him.
ramayan::639.english_translation: O brahman, although my son resembles the celestials, he is inexperienced in warfare. On no account shall I spare him.
ramayan::639.translation_literal: कथमपि (somehow / although) / अमरप्रख्यम् (resembling the celestials) / सङ्ग्रामाणाम् (of battles) / अकोविदम् (unskilled) / बालम् (young) / मे (my) / तनयम् (son) / ब्रह्मन् (O brahman) / नैव (never) / दास्यामि (I shall give) / पुत्रकम् (dear son)
ramayan::639.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::639.essence: Promise is not the same as readiness.
ramayan::639.simple_meaning: A father refuses to hand over his young son, even though the boy looks extraordinary, because the boy is not ready for battle.
ramayan::639.simple_insight: Love can mean refusing what others ask, even when the request sounds noble.
ramayan::639.detailed_meaning: A threatened father is weighing whether to offer his son to protect a sacrifice. He praises the boy’s brilliance, but refuses to treat appearance as readiness. The moment turns on a parent’s duty to protect what is still unformed.
ramayan::639.modern_relevance: A coach wants to push a gifted teenager into a harsh competition before the basics are secure. You know the praise is real, but so is the danger of moving too soon.
ramayan::639.insight: It teaches you to separate promise from preparedness before placing someone under pressure.

ramayan::640.verse_sanskrit: अथ कालोपमौ युध्दे सुतौ सुन्दोपसुन्दयो: । । 12025 । । यज्ञविघ्नकरौ तौ ते नैव दास्यामि पुत्रकम् ।
ramayan::640.verse_hindi: Further the sons of Sunda and Upasunda by name Maricha and Subahu are causing obstacles to your sacrifice. They resemble the god of death, Yama. I shall never part with my son.
ramayan::640.english_translation: Maricha and Subahu, the sons of Sunda and Upasunda, are like Yama in battle. They are disturbing your sacrifice, and I will never give you my son.
ramayan::640.translation_literal: अथ (then) / कालोपमौ (like Time/Death) / युद्धे (in battle) / सुतौ (the two sons) / सुन्दोपसुन्दयोः (of Sunda and Upasunda) / यज्ञविघ्नकरौ (makers of obstacles to sacrifice) / तौ (those two) / ते (your) / नैव (never) / दास्यामि (I will give) / पुत्रकम् (son)
ramayan::640.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::640.essence: A parent’s refusal becomes an act of duty, not defiance.
ramayan::640.simple_meaning: The speaker refuses to hand over his son, saying the boy is too young and must not be sent into danger.
ramayan::640.simple_insight: Love can sound like refusal when protection matters more than pride.
ramayan::640.detailed_meaning: A sage is being asked for help against Maricha and Subahu, who are disrupting a sacrifice. He compares them to death itself and insists his son is not to be given up for the fight. The verse continues the argument, not the teaching.
ramayan::640.modern_relevance: You are asked to send someone you love into a situation they are not ready for. Your no is not weakness; it is responsibility.
ramayan::640.insight: It frames protection as a duty stronger than pressure from outside.

ramayan::641.verse_sanskrit: मारीचश्च सुबाहुश्च वीर्यवन्तौ सुशिक्षितौ । तयोरन्यतरेणाहं योध्दा स्यां ससुहृद्गण: । । 12026 । ।
ramayan::641.verse_hindi: Maricha and Subahu not only possess prowess but also are experienced in warfare. Together with my group of friends I can combat with one of the two.
ramayan::641.english_translation: Maricha and Subahu are mighty and well trained. With one of them, I can fight together with my band of friends.
ramayan::641.translation_literal: मारीचः (Maricha) / च (and) / सुबाहुः (Subahu) / च (and) / वीर्यवन्तौ (mighty) / सुशिक्षितौ (well trained) / तयोः (of the two) / अन्यतरेण (with one of them) / अहम् (I) / योध्दा (will fight) / स्याम् (can be) / ससुहृद्गणः (together with my group of friends)
ramayan::641.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::641.essence: Honest limits are not defeat; they are the start of right action.
ramayan::641.simple_meaning: Maricha and Subahu are strong and trained in battle. Viswamitra says he can face one of them with help from his companions.
ramayan::641.simple_insight: Strength matters, but so does knowing the limits of your own side.
ramayan::641.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra is speaking to King Dasharatha about the demons who disturb his sacrifice. He names Maricha and Subahu as dangerous fighters, and explains that even with allies, he can only hope to face one of them. The moment shows the scale of the threat.
ramayan::641.modern_relevance: You look at a problem and know you cannot carry it alone. The honest sentence is not weakness — it is the first step toward the right help.
ramayan::641.insight: It shifts the mind from bravado to clear assessment of capacity and support.

ramayan::642.verse_sanskrit: इति नरपतिजल्पनाद्द्विजेन्द्रं कुशिकसुतं सुमहान्विवेश मन्यु: । सुहुत इव मखेऽग्निराज्यसिक्त स्समभवदुज्ज्वलितो महर्षिवह्नि: । । 12027 । ।
ramayan::642.verse_hindi: Having heard the statements of the king the son of Kusika, Viswamitra who was like Indra among the ascetics was seized by great anger. As though fire in the form of  maharshi blazed like the sacrificial fire into which oblations of clarified butter have been poured.
ramayan::642.english_translation: Having heard the king's words, the son of Kusika was seized by great anger. The great sage blazed like a sacrificial fire fed with clarified butter.
ramayan::642.translation_literal: इति (thus) / नरपतिजल्पनाद् (from the king's speaking) / द्विजेन्द्रं (the foremost among twice-born) / कुशिकसुतं (the son of Kusika) / सुमहान् (very great) / विवेश (entered) / मन्यु: (anger) / सुहुतः (well-offered) / इव (like) / मखे (in the sacrifice) / अग्निः (fire) / आज्यसिक्तः (anointed with clarified butter) / समभवत् (became) / उज्ज्वलितः (blazing) / महर्षिवह्निः (the fire of the great sage)
ramayan::642.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::642.essence: Refusal can turn even a holy meeting into fire.
ramayan::642.simple_meaning: Viswamitra heard the king's refusal and became fiercely angry, blazing like sacrificial fire fed with ghee.
ramayan::642.simple_insight: Some words do not calm a wound; they ignite it.
ramayan::642.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has come to Dasharatha asking for help against the demons who disturb his sacrifice. Instead of receiving support, he hears hesitation and resistance. The sage's anger rises at once, and the verse shows that the meeting has turned tense.
ramayan::642.modern_relevance: You ask for help with something serious, and the reply is polite but evasive. The smile stays on the surface, but the hurt turns hot underneath.
ramayan::642.insight: It shows how a sacred request can turn into conflict when support is withheld.

ramayan::643.verse_sanskrit: तच्छ्रुत्वा वचनं तस्य स्नेहपर्याकुलाक्षरम् । समन्यु: कौशिको वाक्यं प्रत्युवाच महीपतिम् । । 1211 । ।
ramayan::643.verse_hindi: Out of affection towards his son, his (king Dasarathas) plea to Viswamitra was full of contradiction. And on hearing the king, enraged Viswamitra replied:
ramayan::643.english_translation: Hearing the king's plea, full of affection and confusion, the angry Vishvamitra replied to the ruler.
ramayan::643.translation_literal: तत् (that) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / वचनं (the speech) / तस्य (his) / स्नेह-पर्याकुल-अक्षरम् (words troubled by affection) / समन्यु: (angry) / कौशिकः (Kausika/Vishvamitra) / वाक्यं (speech) / प्रत्युवाच (replied) / महीपतिम् (to the king)
ramayan::643.speaker: Vishvamitra
ramayan::643.essence: A wavering promise meets a sage who will not let it soften.
ramayan::643.simple_meaning: Vishvamitra hears Dasharatha's emotional plea and answers in anger. The verse marks the moment the sage rejects the king's attempt to soften his promise.
ramayan::643.simple_insight: A promise loses force when fear starts speaking louder than resolve.
ramayan::643.detailed_meaning: Dasharatha has already agreed to send Rama with Vishvamitra, but now his love for his son makes him hesitate. Vishvamitra hears the wavering and, angered, answers the king directly. The real conflict is no longer about demons in the forest but about whether a royal word can be trusted.
ramayan::643.modern_relevance: You promised something when it was easy. Then the cost became real, and your voice changed. This verse catches that moment before a hard commitment is broken.
ramayan::643.insight: It teaches you to notice when affection or fear is pushing you to undo a clear decision.

ramayan::644.verse_sanskrit: पूर्वमर्थं प्रतिश्रुत्य प्रतिज्ञां हातुमिच्छसि । राघवाणामयुक्तोऽयं कुलस्यास्य विपर्यय: । । 1212 । ।
ramayan::644.verse_hindi: पूर्वमर्थं प्रतिश्रुत्य प्रतिज्ञां हातुमिच्छसि । राघवाणामयुक्तोऽयं कुलस्यास्य विपर्यय: । । 1212 । ।
ramayan::644.english_translation: You promised first, and now you want to abandon your vow. This reversal is not fit for the house of the Raghu line.
ramayan::644.translation_literal: पूर्वम् (first) / अर्थम् (matter, promise) / प्रतिश्रुत्य (having promised) / प्रतिज्ञाम् (vow) / हातुम् (to abandon) / इच्छसि (you wish) / राघवाणाम् (of the Raghu line) / अयुक्तः (unfit) / अयम् (this) / कुलस्य (of the family) / अस्य (of this) / विपर्ययः (reversal, turning upside down)
ramayan::644.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::644.essence: A vow loses its value the moment you treat it as optional.
ramayan::644.simple_meaning: After agreeing to something, you should not back out. Viswamitra says this kind of reversal does not suit Rama's family.
ramayan::644.simple_insight: Broken promises damage trust more than inconvenience ever will.
ramayan::644.detailed_meaning: King Dasharatha has already agreed to send Rama with Viswamitra, then tries to withdraw. Viswamitra answers sharply: a promise made first cannot be abandoned later, especially by a line known for keeping its word.
ramayan::644.modern_relevance: You said yes to a commitment before you knew how hard it would become. Now the pressure is real, and backing out would cost more than the effort itself.
ramayan::644.insight: It shifts you from protecting comfort to protecting credibility.

ramayan::645.verse_sanskrit: यदीदं ते क्षमं राजन् गमिष्यामि यथाऽगतम् । मिथ्याप्रतिज्ञ: काकुत्स्थ सुखीभव सबान्धव: । । 1213 । ।
ramayan::645.verse_hindi: O king, if this act of yours is appropriate to you, I will go back (to the places) where from I came. O scion of the race of kakutstha, you have proved false to your promise. Live happily with your relatives.
ramayan::645.english_translation: O king, if this act of yours is appropriate to you, I will go back to the places where I came from. O scion of the Kakutstha line, you have proved false to your promise. Live happily with your relatives.
ramayan::645.translation_literal: यदि (if) / इदम् (this) / ते (of you) / क्षमम् (proper) / राजन् (O king) / गमिष्यामि (I will go) / यथा (as) / आगतम् (having come) / मिथ्या (false) / प्रतिज्ञः (promise-holder) / काकुत्स्थ (O Kakutstha) / सुखीभव (be happy) / स-बान्धवः (with relatives)
ramayan::645.speaker: Vishwamitra
ramayan::645.essence: A king who breaks his word breaks the ground beneath his own rule.
ramayan::645.simple_meaning: Vishwamitra rejects Dasaratha's wavering and says he will leave if the king cannot keep his promise. A promise once made must be honored.
ramayan::645.simple_insight: Broken words cost trust immediately, even when no one is physically harmed.
ramayan::645.detailed_meaning: Dasaratha has promised Vishwamitra help, then hesitates out of love for his son. The sage, angered by this reversal, stands before the king and demands consistency. The moment turns on whether a king's word means anything at all.
ramayan::645.modern_relevance: You said yes to something before the pressure started. Now, when it becomes costly, you feel the urge to soften it. This verse meets that moment and asks whether your word still stands.
ramayan::645.insight: It teaches you to treat your promise as binding, especially when keeping it becomes inconvenient.

ramayan::646.verse_sanskrit: तस्य रोषपरीतस्य विश्वामित्रस्य धीमत: । चचाल वसुधा कृत्स्ना विवेश च भयं सुरान् । । 1214 । ।
ramayan::646.verse_hindi: At the sight of the wise sage Viswamitra seized of wrath, the entire earth shook and  devatas were gripped in fear.
ramayan::646.english_translation: At the sight of the wise sage Viswamitra seized of wrath, the entire earth shook and the devas were gripped in fear.
ramayan::646.translation_literal: तस्य (of him) / रोषपरीतस्य (surrounded by wrath) / विश्वामित्रस्य (of Vishvamitra) / धीमत: (of the wise one) / चचाल (shook) / वसुधा (the earth) / कृत्स्ना (entire) / विवेश (entered) / च (and) / भयम् (fear) / सुरान् (the devas)
ramayan::646.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::646.essence: Wrath can make even the world seem unstable.
ramayan::646.simple_meaning: Vishvamitra’s anger was so intense that the whole earth trembled and the celestial beings felt fear.
ramayan::646.simple_insight: Powerful emotion can shake the world around you, not just your own mind.
ramayan::646.detailed_meaning: Vishvamitra has just been provoked in the royal court, and his anger is no longer private. Valmiki shows the force of that wrath by making the earth tremble and the devas recoil, turning a human confrontation into a cosmic disturbance.
