ramayan::646.modern_relevance: A room goes silent after one sharp remark, and everyone feels the temperature drop. Some emotions do not stay inside you; they change the whole atmosphere.
ramayan::646.insight: It shows how quickly unchecked anger can spread its force beyond the person feeling it.

ramayan::647.verse_sanskrit: त्रस्तरूपं तु विज्ञाय जगत्सर्वं महानृषि: । नृपतिं सुव्रतो धीरो वसिष्ठो वाक्यमब्रवीत् । । 1215 । ।
ramayan::647.verse_hindi: Great Vasishta, an adherent of ascetic practices and steadfast (to duty), seeing that the entire world frightened addressed the king, saying:
ramayan::647.english_translation: Great Vasishta, an adherent of ascetic practices and steadfast to duty, seeing that the entire world was frightened, addressed the king and said:
ramayan::647.translation_literal: त्रस्तरूपम् (frightened state) / तु (indeed) / विज्ञाय (having known) / जगत्-सर्वम् (all the world) / महानृषिः (the great sage) / नृपतिम् (to the king) / सुव्रतः (firm in vows) / धीरः (steadfast) / वसिष्ठः (Vasishta) / वाक्यम् (words) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::647.speaker: Vasishta
ramayan::647.essence: Vasishta sees fear spreading and steps in to answer it.
ramayan::647.simple_meaning: Seeing that everyone was frightened, Vasishta spoke to the king.
ramayan::647.simple_insight: A steady voice can hold a shaken room together.
ramayan::647.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra's anger has shaken the earth and terrified the gods. In that charged moment, Vasishta, calm and disciplined, turns to the king and begins to speak. The verse is the opening of a response, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::647.modern_relevance: A room goes silent after a harsh email or public clash, and someone grounded finally speaks. This is that moment before the actual words begin.
ramayan::647.insight: It marks the pause before counsel, when steadiness matters more than force.

ramayan::648.verse_sanskrit: इक्ष्वाकूणां कुले जातस्साक्षाद्धर्म इवापर: । धृतिमान् सुव्रत: श्रीमान्नधर्मं हातुमर्हसि । । 1216 । ।
ramayan::648.verse_hindi: Born in the line of Ikshvaku, you are a veritable the second god of righteousness, firm adherent of vows auspicious and virtuous. It is not right on your part to abandon your
ramayan::648.english_translation: Born in the line of Ikshvaku, you are like righteousness itself. Steadfast in vows and glorious, you should not abandon dharma.
ramayan::648.translation_literal: इक्ष्वाकूणां (of the Ikshvakus) / कुले (in the line) / जातः (born) / साक्षात् (directly) / धर्मः (righteousness) / इव (like) / अपरः (another) / धृतिमान् (steadfast) / सुव्रतः (firm in vows) / श्रीमान् (glorious) / न (not) / अधर्मम् (dharma-violation) / हातुम् (to abandon) / अर्हसि (you should)
ramayan::648.speaker: Vasishta
ramayan::648.essence: Your lineage means nothing if you abandon righteousness.
ramayan::648.simple_meaning: Vasishta reminds Dasharatha that his royal lineage and character demand he stay faithful to righteousness instead of turning away from it.
ramayan::648.simple_insight: Your dignity is not in power, but in refusing to betray what you know is right.
ramayan::648.detailed_meaning: Vasishta speaks to Dasharatha after sensing the king's fear and confusion. He reminds him that the Ikshvaku line is known for steadfastness, vows, and righteousness. This is a direct warning: do not let panic or desire push you into adharma.
ramayan::648.modern_relevance: You are about to send a message that will hurt someone because it is easier than facing the truth. In that moment, your history, your promises, and your character all ask the same question: will you stay clean?
ramayan::648.insight: It shifts the mind from emotional pressure to moral consistency.

ramayan::649.verse_sanskrit: त्रिषु लोकेषु विख्यातो धर्मात्मा इति राघव । स्वधर्मं प्रतिपद्यस्व नाधर्मं वोढुमर्हसि । । 1217 । ।
ramayan::649.verse_hindi: O Dasaratha you are reputed in the three worlds as righteousminded. Do your own
ramayan::649.english_translation: O Raghava, you are known in the three worlds as righteous. Take up your own duty; you should not bear unrighteousness.
ramayan::649.translation_literal: त्रिषु लोकेषु (in the three worlds) / विख्यातो (well-known) / धर्मात्मा (righteous-minded) / इति (thus) / राघव (O Raghava) / स्वधर्मं (one's own duty) / प्रतिपद्यस्व (take up) / न (not) / अधर्मं (unrighteousness) / वोढुम् (to bear) / अर्हसि (you should)
ramayan::649.speaker: Vasishta
ramayan::649.essence: Your true standing is measured by whether you keep faith with your duty.
ramayan::649.simple_meaning: A respected person should stay with their own duty and avoid any action that goes against it.
ramayan::649.simple_insight: Your reputation means little if your choices no longer match it.
ramayan::649.detailed_meaning: Vasishta is speaking to Dasaratha after the king has been shaken by the demands of his promise. He reminds him that a ruler known across the world for righteousness cannot now carry out an unrighteous act.
ramayan::649.modern_relevance: You’re about to say yes to something in a room full of pressure, even though your stomach already knows it’s wrong. Your name, your role, and your standards all matter now.
ramayan::649.insight: It shifts you from image-protection to alignment with your actual duty.

ramayan::650.verse_sanskrit: संश्रुत्यैवं करिष्यामीत्यकुर्वाणस्य राघव । इष्टापूर्तवधो भूयात्तस्माद्रामं विसर्जय । । 1218 । ।
ramayan::650.verse_hindi: O Dasaratha, a promise made and not kept amounts to destruction of merits earned through previous pieties. Therefore send Rama (with him).
ramayan::650.english_translation: O Dasaratha, a promise made and not kept amounts to destruction of merits earned through previous pieties. Therefore send Rama.
ramayan::650.translation_literal: संश्रुत्य (having promised) / एवम् (thus) / करिष्यामि (I will do) / इति (so saying) / अकुर्वाणस्य (of one not doing) / राघव (O Dasaratha) / इष्टापूर्तवधः (destruction of merit from sacrifices and charitable works) / भूयात् (may there be) / तस्मात् (therefore) / रामम् (Rama) / विसर्जय (send forth)
ramayan::650.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::650.essence: A broken promise can cancel a lifetime of good.
ramayan::650.simple_meaning: A promise must be honoured. If Dasaratha breaks his word, even good deeds lose their value, so Rama must be sent away.
ramayan::650.simple_insight: Integrity matters more than comfort. Keeping your word protects your character.
ramayan::650.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra presses Dasaratha in Ayodhya after the king hesitates over sending Rama. The issue is no longer politics but moral collapse: a king who breaks a promise destroys the worth of all his past pious acts.
ramayan::650.modern_relevance: You promised your child, your team, or your partner something before you knew the cost. Now the cost is real. This verse asks whether your word still stands when keeping it hurts.
ramayan::650.insight: It shifts the mind from protecting comfort to protecting credibility.

ramayan::651.verse_sanskrit: कृतास्त्रमकृतास्त्रं वा नैनं शक्ष्यन्ति राक्षसा: । गुप्तं कुशिकपुत्रेण ज्वलनेनामृतं यथा । । 1219 । ।
ramayan::651.verse_hindi: Trained or not in the use of arms, as long as Rama is protected by Viswamitra, just as nectar is protected by the flaming firegod rakshasas will not be able to compete with him.
ramayan::651.english_translation: Trained or untrained in arms, the rakshasas will not be able to overcome him while he is protected by the son of Kushika, just as nectar is guarded by the blazing fire.
ramayan::651.translation_literal: कृतास्त्रम् (trained in weapons) / अकृतास्त्रम् (untrained in weapons) / वा (or) / न (not) / एनम् (him) / शक्ष्यन्ति (will be able) / राक्षसाः (rakshasas) / गुप्तम् (protected) / कुशिकपुत्रेण (by the son of Kushika) / ज्वलनेन (by fire) / अमृतम् (nectar) / यथा (as)
ramayan::651.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::651.essence: Safety comes from wise protection, not skill alone.
ramayan::651.simple_meaning: Rama cannot be defeated by the rakshasas while Vishwamitra protects him, whether or not he has learned weapons.
ramayan::651.simple_insight: Protection can matter more than skill when danger is near.
ramayan::651.detailed_meaning: In Vishvamitra's company, Rama is being described as untouchable to the rakshasas. The point is not Rama's weapon training alone, but the strength of the sage's protection, which makes the prince as safe as nectar guarded by fire.
ramayan::651.modern_relevance: You may feel unprepared before a hard situation, but the right mentor or ally can change everything. Skill matters less than being held by someone who knows the terrain.
ramayan::651.insight: It shifts attention from raw ability to the power of wise protection and guidance.

ramayan::652.verse_sanskrit: एष विग्रहवान् धर्म एष वीर्यवतां वर: । एष बुध्याऽधिको लोके तपसश्च परायणम् । । 12110 । ।
ramayan::652.verse_hindi: This (Viswamitra) is an embodiment of righteousness and unsurpassed among the powerful. None can excel him in intellect in this world. He is the supreme refuge in
ramayan::652.english_translation: This is embodied righteousness, the best among the powerful. He surpasses others in worldly intelligence and is the supreme refuge of austerity.
ramayan::652.translation_literal: एष (this) / विग्रहवान् (embodied) / धर्मः (righteousness) / एष (this) / वीर्यवताम् (of the powerful) / वरः (best) / एष (this) / बुध्या (in intellect) / अधिकः (greater) / लोके (in the world) / तपसः (of austerity) / च (and) / परायणम् (supreme refuge)
ramayan::652.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::652.essence: True greatness joins power, intelligence, and righteousness.
ramayan::652.simple_meaning: Viswamitra is described as the living form of righteousness: strong, wise, and devoted to austerity.
ramayan::652.simple_insight: Real strength is not brute force; it is strength held in service of what is right.
ramayan::652.detailed_meaning: At Vishwamitra's side, Rama is being introduced to the kind of teacher who can shape a prince's life. Valmiki pauses the action to praise him as righteous, powerful, intelligent, and grounded in austerity before the journey continues.
ramayan::652.modern_relevance: A mentor walks into the room and everyone feels it: competence, restraint, and moral weight in one person. Some people do not just know more — they carry a standard others can trust.
ramayan::652.insight: It shifts attention from mere talent to the character that makes talent worthy of trust.

ramayan::653.verse_sanskrit: एषोऽस्त्रान् विविधान्वेत्ति त्रैलोक्ये सचराचरे । नैनमन्य: पुमान्वेत्ति न च वेत्स्यन्ति केचन । । 12111 । ।
ramayan::653.verse_hindi: This Viswamitra knows the use of various kinds of weapons which no one knows among the animate and the inanimate in the three worlds. Nor will any one even know in future.
ramayan::653.english_translation: This Viswamitra knows the use of various kinds of weapons which no one knows among the animate and the inanimate in the three worlds. Nor will anyone ever know them in the future.
ramayan::653.translation_literal: एषः (this one) / अस्त्रान् (weapons) / विविधान् (various) / वेत्ति (knows) / त्रैलोक्ये (in the three worlds) / सचराचरे (among the moving and unmoving) / न (not) / एनम् (him) / अन्यः (another) / पुमान् (man) / वेत्ति (knows) / न (not) / च (and) / वेत्स्यन्ति (will know) / केचन (anyone)
ramayan::653.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::653.essence: No one in the three worlds matches his mastery of weapons.
ramayan::653.simple_meaning: Viswamitra is being praised as unmatched in his knowledge of weapons. No one in the three worlds can rival his mastery.
ramayan::653.simple_insight: Great power can be real, but still remain part of a larger moral drama.
ramayan::653.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra is being introduced to Rama and Lakshmana as more than a sage: he is a seer, warrior, and master of divine weapons. The verse builds his stature by saying no being in the worlds can match his knowledge, setting up the authority behind his request for protection.
ramayan::653.modern_relevance: A mentor walks into the room and everyone falls quiet because they know he has seen more, trained longer, and can open doors you cannot yet imagine.
ramayan::653.insight: It frames Viswamitra as a rare authority whose knowledge exceeds ordinary human limits.

ramayan::654.verse_sanskrit: न देवा नर्षय: केचिन्नासुरा न च राक्षसा: । गन्धर्वयक्षप्रवरास्सकिन्नरमहोरगा: । । 12112 । ।
ramayan::654.verse_hindi: No gods nor sages nor asuras in rakshasas nor kinnaras nor mighty serpents nor
ramayan::654.english_translation: No gods, sages, asuras, rakshasas, gandharvas, yakshas, kinnaras, or mighty serpents knew them.
ramayan::654.translation_literal: न (not) / देवा (gods) / न (not) / ऋषयः (sages) / केचिद् (any) / न (not) / असुराः (asuras) / न (not) / च (and) / राक्षसाः (rakshasas) / गन्धर्व-यक्ष-प्रवराः (the foremost gandharvas and yakshas) / स-किन्नर-महोरगाः (together with kinnaras and mighty serpents)
ramayan::654.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::654.essence: His mastery reaches beyond every known order of beings.
ramayan::654.simple_meaning: No one among the celestial, sage, or nonhuman beings knew these weapons.
ramayan::654.simple_insight: Some knowledge is so rare that even the greatest beings do not possess it.
ramayan::654.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has already been praised as unmatched in power, intellect, and mastery of weapons. This line pushes that praise further: even the highest beings in the cosmos do not know these arms. It is a supporting step in the larger description of his extraordinary stature.
ramayan::654.modern_relevance: A room full of experts can still miss the one person who truly understands the problem. Real mastery is often invisible until pressure exposes it.
ramayan::654.insight: It deepens Viswamitra’s stature by showing that his knowledge exceeds every ordinary category.

ramayan::655.verse_sanskrit: सर्वास्त्राणि भृशाश्वस्य पुत्रा: परमधार्मिका: । कौशिकाय पुरा दत्ता यदा राज्यं प्रशासति । । 12113 । ।
ramayan::655.verse_hindi: All these weapons were given to Viswamitra by Bhrisasvas highly virtuous sons while
ramayan::655.english_translation: All the weapons were given to Vishvamitra by the highly righteous sons of Bhrishashva, when he was ruling the kingdom.
ramayan::655.translation_literal: सर्वास्त्राणि (all weapons) / भृशाश्वस्य (of Bhrishashva) / पुत्राः (sons) / परमधार्मिकाः (highly righteous) / कौशिकाय (to Kaushika/Vishvamitra) / पुरा (formerly) / दत्ता (given) / यदा (when) / राज्यं (the kingdom) / प्रशासति (was ruling)
ramayan::655.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::655.essence: His power was not seized; it was entrusted to him.
ramayan::655.simple_meaning: Bhrishashva’s righteous sons once handed over all their weapons to Vishvamitra while he was ruling his kingdom.
ramayan::655.simple_insight: Great power can be passed on through trust and respect, not just force.
ramayan::655.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is explaining Vishvamitra’s extraordinary mastery of weapons. After saying that no being in the three worlds knew these weapons like him, the poem adds their source: they were given to him by the virtuous sons of Bhrishashva during his rule.
ramayan::655.modern_relevance: A senior mentor hands you the tools no one else knows how to use, because they trust your discipline. What you do with that access becomes your real test.
ramayan::655.insight: It shifts attention from raw possession to the moral legitimacy of what you hold.

ramayan::656.verse_sanskrit: तेऽपि पुत्रा भृशाश्वस्य प्रजापतिसुतासुता: । नैकरूपा महावीर्या दीप्तिमन्तो जयावहा: । । 12114 । ।
ramayan::656.verse_hindi: Grandsons (daughters sons) of Prajapati, they (these weapons) are in diverse forms, highly energetic and full of glory they bring victory.
ramayan::656.english_translation: They too are the sons of Bhrishashva, grandsons of Prajapati, diverse in form, mighty in power, radiant, and bring victory.
ramayan::656.translation_literal: तेऽपि (they too) / पुत्रा: (sons) / भृशाश्वस्य (of Bhrishashva) / प्रजापतिसुतासुता: (grandsons of Prajapati) / नैकरूपा: (of many forms) / महावीर्या: (greatly powerful) / दीप्तिमन्तो (radiant) / जयावहा: (bringing victory)
ramayan::656.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::656.essence: Power becomes meaningful when it is tied to rightful inheritance and victory.
ramayan::656.simple_meaning: These weapons are described as powerful, radiant, and varied in form, with a history tied to sacred lineages.
ramayan::656.simple_insight: Some things carry power not just from force, but from the lineage and purpose behind them.
ramayan::656.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is listing the origins and qualities of divine weapons passed through ancient lineages. This verse adds another layer to that catalogue, emphasizing their power, brilliance, and victory-bringing nature rather than offering a separate teaching.
ramayan::656.modern_relevance: A team inherits tools, methods, and standards from people before them. What they carry forward matters as much as what they build themselves.
ramayan::656.insight: It shifts attention from the object itself to the tradition and force behind it.

ramayan::657.verse_sanskrit: जया च सुप्रभा चैव दक्षकन्ये सुमध्यमे । ते सुवातेऽस्त्रशस्त्राणि शतं परमभास्वरम् । । 12115 । ।
ramayan::657.verse_hindi: Jaya and Suprabha of slender waists are the two daughters of Daksha. They gave  birth to one hundred effulgent sons known as astras and shastras.
ramayan::657.english_translation: Jaya and Suprabha, the two daughters of Daksha with slender waists, gave birth to one hundred radiant weapons.
ramayan::657.translation_literal: जया (Jaya) / च (and) / सुप्रभा (Suprabha) / चैव (and indeed) / दक्षकन्ये (daughters of Daksha) / सुमध्यमे (slender-waisted) / ते (they) / सुवाते (gave birth) / अस्त्रशस्त्राणि (weapons and missiles) / शतं (a hundred) / परमभास्वरम् (highly radiant)
ramayan::657.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::657.essence: Their power comes from an ancient lineage, not a sudden creation.
ramayan::657.simple_meaning: Jaya and Suprabha, daughters of Daksha, are named as the mothers of one hundred radiant weapons.
ramayan::657.simple_insight: Some things in epic stories are inherited, not invented in the moment.
ramayan::657.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is tracing the lineage of powerful weapons used in the larger war tradition. After naming their ancestral origin, he identifies Jaya and Suprabha as the mothers of these radiant astras and shastras, continuing a catalog rather than making a teaching point.
ramayan::657.insight: It adds origin and pedigree to the weapons, not a moral lesson.

ramayan::658.verse_sanskrit: पञ्चाशतं सुतान् लेभे जया नाम परान् पुरा । वधायासुरसैन्यानाममेयान् कामरूपिण: । । 12116 । ।
ramayan::658.verse_hindi: Formerly Jaya, for the destruction of the army of asuras gave birth to fifty sons by virtue of a boon. They  possess immeasurable power of changing forms at will.
ramayan::658.english_translation: Formerly Jaya, for the destruction of the army of asuras, gave birth to fifty sons by virtue of a boon. They possess immeasurable power of changing forms at will.
ramayan::658.translation_literal: पञ्चाशतम् (fifty) / सुतान् (sons) / लेभे (obtained / gave birth to) / जया (Jaya) / नाम (named) / परान् (excellent) / पुरा (formerly) / वधाय (for destruction) / असुरसैन्यानाम् (of the armies of asuras) / अमेयान् (immeasurable) / कामरूपिणः (shape-shifters)
ramayan::658.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::658.essence: Another set of boon-born warriors is introduced, not a lesson.
ramayan::658.simple_meaning: Jaya gave birth to fifty powerful sons, created to destroy the armies of the asuras. They could change form at will.
ramayan::658.simple_insight: Some passages simply widen the world: power here is inherited, multiplied, and sent toward war.
ramayan::658.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is listing the strange, boons-born offspring of Jaya and Suprabha as part of a larger genealogy of weapons and powers. The verse adds more names and capacities, but does not yet make a teaching or decision of its own.
ramayan::658.insight: It expands the catalogue of supernatural forces without pausing for reflection.

ramayan::659.verse_sanskrit: सुप्रभाऽजनयच्चापि पुत्रान्पञ्चाशतं पुन: । संहारान्नामदुर्धर्षान् दुराक्रामान् बलीयस: । । 12117 । ।
ramayan::659.verse_hindi: Suprabha gave birth to another fifty sons named Samharas who are unassailable,  invincible and more powerful.
ramayan::659.english_translation: Suprabha gave birth to another fifty sons named Samharas who are unassailable, invincible, and more powerful.
ramayan::659.translation_literal: सुप्रभा (Suprabha) / अजनयत् (gave birth) / च (and) / अपि (also) / पुत्रान् (sons) / पञ्चाशतम् (fifty) / पुनः (again) / संहारान् (Samharas) / नाम (named) / दुर्धर्षान् (unassailable) / दुराक्रामान् (hard to attack) / बलीयसः (more powerful)
ramayan::659.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::659.essence: Another line in the lineage, not a teaching.
ramayan::659.simple_meaning: Suprabha had fifty more sons, called Samharas, and they were described as too strong to overcome.
ramayan::659.simple_insight: No new teaching appears here; the verse simply adds another group of powerful beings to the lineage.
ramayan::659.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is listing the offspring of Daksha's daughters. After Jaya's sons are named, Suprabha's fifty sons are introduced as another formidable set, and the passage moves on to Vishvamitra's knowledge of these weapons.
ramayan::659.modern_relevance: A family tree or company org chart can keep growing with impressive names and titles, but the list itself is not the lesson.
ramayan::659.insight: It keeps the focus on genealogy and scale, not on a moral or philosophical point.

ramayan::660.verse_sanskrit: तानि चास्त्राणि वेत्त्येष यथावत्कुशिकात्मज: । अपूर्वाणां च जनने शक्तो भूयस्स धर्मवित् । । 12118 । ।
ramayan::660.verse_hindi: Viswamitra is well conversant with these weapons. Being virtuous, he is capable of creating new weapons also.
ramayan::660.english_translation: Viswamitra knows these weapons exactly as they are. Being a knower of dharma, he is also able to create new weapons.
ramayan::660.translation_literal: तानि (those) / च (and) / अस्त्राणि (weapons) / वेत्ति (knows) / एषः (this one) / यथावत् (properly, exactly) / कुशिकात्मजः (the son of Kushika) / अपूर्वाणाम् (of new, unprecedented things) / च (and) / जनने (in creating) / शक्तः (able) / भूयः (furthermore) / सः (he) / धर्मवित् (knower of dharma)
ramayan::660.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::660.essence: True mastery can invent what does not yet exist.
ramayan::660.simple_meaning: Viswamitra knows every weapon perfectly, and his understanding is so complete that he can even create new ones.
ramayan::660.simple_insight: Real mastery means you can respond to what already exists and also meet what has never appeared before.
ramayan::660.detailed_meaning: The sages are proving Viswamitra's worth to Dasharatha. This verse adds that he not only knows the existing weapons but can also create new ones because he understands dharma and power deeply. The point is to remove any doubt about sending Rama with him.
ramayan::660.modern_relevance: A senior engineer is asked whether she can handle a problem no one has solved before. She does not just know the old tools — she understands the system so well she can build what is missing.
ramayan::660.insight: It shifts respect from memorized skill to deep adaptability and creative competence.

ramayan::661.verse_sanskrit: एवं वीर्यो महातेजा विश्वामित्रो महायशाः । न रामगमने राजन् संशयं कर्तुमर्हसि । । 12119 । ।
ramayan::661.verse_hindi: Such is the prowess of Viswamitra who is a highly effulgent and highly renowned  sage. O King in sending Rama, you need not entertain any doubt.
ramayan::661.english_translation: Such is the prowess of Viswamitra who is a highly effulgent and highly renowned sage. O King, you need not entertain any doubt about sending Rama.
ramayan::661.translation_literal: एवम् (thus) / वीर्यः (prowess) / महातेजाः (highly effulgent) / विश्वामित्रः (Viswamitra) / महायशाः (highly renowned) / राजन् (O King) / न (not) / रामगमने (about Rama's going) / संशयम् (doubt) / कर्तुम् (to make) / अर्हसि (you ought)
ramayan::661.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::661.essence: A proven guide deserves trust when a child’s safety is at stake.
ramayan::661.simple_meaning: Viswamitra is powerful, wise, and capable, so Dasharatha should not doubt sending Rama with him.
ramayan::661.simple_insight: Trust the one who is asking for your child when his character is already proven.
ramayan::661.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has already been described as a sage with formidable power and mastery over weapons. Now the speaker reassures King Dasharatha that such a man is fully worthy of Rama's company, removing fear before the boy's journey begins.
ramayan::661.modern_relevance: You hesitate before letting your child leave with someone new. Then you remember the person has already earned trust through action, not promises.
ramayan::661.insight: It shifts the mind from suspicion to informed trust based on character.

ramayan::662.verse_sanskrit: तेषां निग्रहणे शक्तस्स्वयं च कुशिकात्मज: । तव पुत्रहितार्थाय त्वामुपेत्याभियाचते । । 12120 । ।
ramayan::662.verse_hindi: Son of Kusika, even though capable of repressing those rakhsasas by himself, it is for the welfare of your son that he is here requesting you to spare him.
ramayan::662.english_translation: Son of Kusika, even though capable of repressing those rakshasas by himself, he has come to you for the welfare of your son and is asking you to grant him this request.
ramayan::662.translation_literal: तेषां (of those) / निग्रहणे (in restraining) / शक्तः (capable) / स्वयं (himself) / च (and) / कुशिकात्मजः (the son of Kusika) / तव (your) / पुत्रहितार्थाय (for the welfare of your son) / त्वाम् (you) / उपेत्य (having approached) / अभियाचते (is requesting earnestly)
ramayan::662.speaker: Vasishta
ramayan::662.essence: Strength becomes noble when it asks for another's good.
ramayan::662.simple_meaning: Viswamitra could defeat the rakshasas himself, but he has come to Dasharatha for Rama's welfare and is requesting him.
ramayan::662.simple_insight: Real strength can be humble enough to ask for help when it serves someone else.
ramayan::662.detailed_meaning: Vasishta is calming Dasharatha's fear. He explains that Viswamitra is no helpless petitioner: he could destroy the rakshasas himself. Yet he has come personally and asked for Rama because he wants the prince's welfare and future growth.
ramayan::662.modern_relevance: Someone capable of fixing a problem alone still comes to you, not because they need rescuing, but because your growth is part of the task. That kind of request deserves trust.
ramayan::662.insight: It shifts you from seeing requests as weakness to seeing them as deliberate, protective action.

ramayan::663.verse_sanskrit: इति मुनिवचनात्प्रसन्नचित्तोरघुवृषभस्तु मुमोद भास्वराङ्ग: । गमनमभिरुरोच राघवस्यप्रथितयशा: कुशिकात्मजाय बुध्या । । 12121 । ।
ramayan::663.verse_hindi: Satisfied in his mind at the words of the sage (Vasishta), the full one among the Raghus (Dasaratha) one with wide reputation, his frame shining gave his cheerful
ramayan::663.english_translation: Then, hearing the sage's words, Dasaratha, bull among the Raghus, became glad in mind and approved Vishvamitra's request with understanding.
ramayan::663.translation_literal: इति (thus) / मुनिवचनात् (from the sage's words) / प्रसन्नचित्तः (glad-minded) / रघुवृषभः (bull among the Raghus) / तु (indeed) / मुमोद (rejoiced) / भास्वराङ्गः (with radiant limbs) / गमनम् (the going) / अभिरुरोच (approved) / राघवस्य (of Rama) / प्रथितयशाः (widely famed) / कुशिकात्मजाय (to the son of Kusika) / बुध्या (with understanding)
ramayan::663.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::663.essence: Clear understanding turns resistance into willing agreement.
ramayan::663.simple_meaning: Dasaratha feels relieved and agrees to let Rama go with Vishvamitra after hearing the sage's words.
ramayan::663.simple_insight: Sometimes peace comes not from getting your way, but from finally seeing the right thing clearly.
ramayan::663.detailed_meaning: Vasishta has just explained why Vishvamitra's request must be honored. Dasaratha, who had been wavering over sending Rama away, now feels his mind settle. He understands, approves, and prepares to call Rama and Lakshmana.
ramayan::663.modern_relevance: You were resisting a decision until someone you trust laid out the full picture. Then the tension eased, and you could finally say yes.
ramayan::663.insight: It shifts the mind from hesitation to clear consent once dharma is understood.

ramayan::664.verse_sanskrit: तथा वसिष्ठे ब्रुवति राजा दशरथस्सुतम प्रहृष्टवदनो राममाजुहाव सलक्ष्मणम् । । 1221 । ।
ramayan::664.verse_hindi: Vasishta having said thus, king Dasaratha, with cheerful countenance summoned Rama and Lakshmana.
ramayan::664.english_translation: When Vasishta had spoken thus, king Dasharatha, with a joyful face, called Rama and Lakshmana to him.
ramayan::664.translation_literal: तथा (thus) / वसिष्ठे (when Vasishta) / ब्रुवति (was speaking) / राजा (king) / दशरथः (Dasharatha) / सुतम् (the son) / प्रहृष्टवदनः (with a joyful face) / रामम् (Rama) / आजुहाव (called) / सलक्ष्मणम् (together with Lakshmana)
ramayan::664.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::664.essence: A king's relief can still lead to a son's exile.
ramayan::664.simple_meaning: After Vasishta speaks, Dasharatha happily calls Rama and Lakshmana to him.
ramayan::664.simple_insight: A hard decision has been made, and the next step begins with a father's call.
ramayan::664.detailed_meaning: Vasishta has just spoken to ease Dasharatha's mind. The king, now cheerful again, summons Rama and Lakshmana. This is the quiet turning point before the farewell that will send Rama into exile.
ramayan::664.modern_relevance: A parent takes a breath after a difficult family decision and calls the children in. The words are ordinary, but everyone in the room feels that life has just changed.
ramayan::664.insight: It marks the moment when private resolve becomes public action.

ramayan::665.verse_sanskrit: कृतस्वस्त्ययनं मात्रा पित्रा दशरथेन च । पुरोधसा वसिष्ठेन मङ्गलैरभिमन्त्रितम् । । 1222 । । स पुत्रं मूर्ध्न्युपाघ्राय राजा दशरथ: प्रियम् । ददौ कुशिकपुत्राय सुप्रीतेनान्तरात्मना । । 1223 । ।
ramayan::665.verse_hindi: Rama was given farewell by his parents with recitation of mantras (for securing prosperity and averting evils). Priest Vasishta sanctified him with mantras Dasaratha kissed his son on the forehead and delivered him to the care of Viswamitra, with a heart full of cheer.
ramayan::665.english_translation: Rama was blessed by his mother, father, and priest with protective rites. Dasaratha kissed his beloved son on the forehead and handed him over to Viswamitra with a joyful heart.
ramayan::665.translation_literal: कृतस्वस्त्ययनम् (with protective rites performed) / मात्रा (by the mother) / पित्रा (by the father) / दशरथेन (by Dasaratha) / च (and) / पुरोधसा (by the family priest) / वसिष्ठेन (by Vasishta) / मङ्गलैः (with auspicious chants) / अभिमन्त्रितम् (consecrated) / सः (he) / पुत्रम् (son) / मूर्ध्नि (on the forehead) / उपाघ्राय (having kissed) / राजा (the king) / दशरथः (Dasaratha) / प्रियम् (beloved) / ददौ (gave) / कुशिकपुत्राय (to the son of Kushika, Viswamitra) / सुप्रीतेन (with great delight) / अन्तरात्मना (in his inner heart)
ramayan::665.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::665.essence: A father’s love is tested by the moment he must let go.
ramayan::665.simple_meaning: Dasaratha prepares Rama with blessings and sacred rites, then lovingly sends him with Viswamitra.
ramayan::665.simple_insight: Love can be shown in release, not only in holding on.
ramayan::665.detailed_meaning: After Vasishta’s approval, Dasaratha has Rama blessed by his mother, father, and priest. The king kisses his son and gives him to Viswamitra. It is a tender handover, but it also begins the exile-like path that will reshape Rama’s life.
ramayan::665.modern_relevance: You packed your child’s bag, fixed their collar, and watched them walk into something bigger than you could control.
ramayan::665.insight: It shifts attention from possession to entrusted duty: loving someone also means letting them go forward.

ramayan::666.verse_sanskrit: ततो वायुस्सुखस्पर्शो नीरजस्को ववौ तदा । विश्वामित्रगतं दृष्ट्वा रामं राजीवलोचनम् । । 1224 । ।
ramayan::666.verse_hindi: At the sight of the lotuseyed Rama accompanying Viswamitra, the wind blew pollenfree with a gentle touch.
ramayan::666.english_translation: At the sight of the lotuseyed Rama accompanying Viswamitra, the wind blew pollenfree with a gentle touch.
ramayan::666.translation_literal: ततः (then) / वायुः (the wind) / सुखस्पर्शः (gentle to touch) / नीरजस्कः (without pollen) / ववौ (blew) / तदा (then) / विश्वामित्रगतं (gone with Viswamitra) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / रामं (Rama) / राजीवलोचनम् (lotuseyed)
ramayan::666.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::666.essence: A great beginning can make even the air feel different.
ramayan::666.simple_meaning: As Rama leaves with Viswamitra, even the wind turns soft and clean, as if nature itself blesses the moment.
ramayan::666.simple_insight: Some departures feel so significant that the world seems to make room for them.
ramayan::666.detailed_meaning: Rama has just been blessed and is setting out with Viswamitra. Valmiki pauses on the moment itself: the prince begins his journey, and the air becomes gentle and pollen-free, as if the world recognises the importance of what is beginning.
ramayan::666.modern_relevance: You leave home for something that will change you, and the room seems to hold its breath. Even ordinary things can feel consecrated when a life is turning.
ramayan::666.insight: It turns a departure into a charged moment, showing how meaning can seem to reshape the world around it.

ramayan::667.verse_hindi: The departure of glorious Viswamitra was greeted with incessant showers of flowers, the beating of celestial drums and the blowing of conches.
ramayan::667.english_translation: The departure of glorious Viswamitra was greeted with incessant showers of flowers, the beating of celestial drums and the blowing of conches.
ramayan::667.translation_literal: पुष्पवृष्टिः (shower of flowers) / महती (great) / आसीत् (was) / देवदुन्दुभिनिस्वनैः (with the sounds of celestial drums) / शङ्खदुन्दुभिनिर्घोषः (blare of conches and drums) / प्रयाते (when departing) / तु (indeed) / महात्मनि (the great-souled one)
ramayan::667.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::667.essence: A great departure is marked as sacred, but the verse itself only sets the scene.
ramayan::667.simple_meaning: As Viswamitra departed with Rama, the sky itself seemed to celebrate with flowers, drums, and conches.
ramayan::667.simple_insight: Some moments feel so significant that even the world seems to mark them.
ramayan::667.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has taken Rama under his guidance, and the journey is about to begin. As the great sage departs with the prince, the scene turns ceremonial: flowers fall, divine drums sound, and conches ring out. It is a grand transition, not a teaching verse.
ramayan::667.modern_relevance: A child leaves home for the first time with a mentor beside him. The room goes quiet, then everyone feels the weight of that departure before the door closes.
ramayan::667.insight: It frames a turning point as something larger than private choice, adding solemnity to the journey ahead.

ramayan::668.verse_sanskrit: विश्वामित्रो ययावग्रे ततो रामो धनुर्धर: । काकपक्षधरो धन्वी तं च सौमित्रिरन्वगात् । । 1226 । ।
ramayan::668.verse_hindi: Viswamitra walked in the forefront. Behind him was Rama, bow in hand, while in the archer, Sumitras son (Lakshmana) with side locks of hair followed.
ramayan::668.english_translation: Viswamitra walked in the forefront. Behind him was Rama, bow in hand, while Lakshmana, son of Sumitra, followed with side locks of hair.
ramayan::668.translation_literal: विश्वामित्रः (Viswamitra) / ययौ (went) / अग्रे (in front) / ततः (then) / रामः (Rama) / धनुर्धरः (bow-bearer) / काकपक्षधरः (wearing side locks) / धन्वी (the archer) / तम् (him) / च (and) / सौमित्रिः (the son of Sumitra) / अन्वगात् (followed)
ramayan::668.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::668.essence: The journey begins with a teacher leading and brothers following.
ramayan::668.simple_meaning: Viswamitra led the way, Rama walked behind him with his bow, and Lakshmana followed close behind.
ramayan::668.simple_insight: Sometimes the whole story turns on who is willing to follow.
ramayan::668.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has taken Rama and Lakshmana under his guidance and is now leading them onward. The verse simply shows their order of movement: the teacher ahead, the prince behind, and Lakshmana following faithfully.
ramayan::668.modern_relevance: You leave with someone you trust, carrying your responsibilities in silence. The real story is not the road itself, but who walks ahead and who stays close.
ramayan::668.insight: It shifts attention from action to arrangement: guidance, readiness, and loyal following.

ramayan::669.verse_sanskrit: कलापिनौ धनुष्पाणी शोभमानौ दिशो दश । विश्वामित्रं महात्मानं त्रिशीर्षाविव पन्नगौ । । 1227 । । अनुजग्मतुरक्षुद्रौ पितामहमिवाश्विनौ ।
ramayan::669.verse_hindi: Rama and Lakshmana equipped with bows and quivers resembled three hooded serpents. Warriors of no less prowess, they illuminated the ten quarters and followed the high souled Viswamitra like twin Aswanikumaras  following the grandsire, Brahma.
ramayan::669.english_translation: Rama and Lakshmana, armed with bows and quivers, shone in all directions as they followed the great Viswamitra, like twin serpents with three hoods, or like the Ashvini twins following Brahma.
ramayan::669.translation_literal: कलापिनौ (with quivers) / धनुष्पाणी (with bows in hand) / शोभमानौ (shining, beautiful) / दिशो दश (the ten directions) / विश्वामित्रं (Viswamitra) / महात्मानं (the great-souled one) / त्रिशीर्षाविव (like three-headed) / पन्नगौ (serpents) / अनुजग्मतुः (followed) / अक्षुद्रौ (the two not-small, mighty ones) / पितामहमिव (like the grandsire) / अश्विनौ (the Ashvins)
ramayan::669.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::669.essence: Their journey begins with strength, radiance, and disciplined companionship.
ramayan::669.simple_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana walk behind Viswamitra, armed and radiant. The verse compares their presence to powerful, divine pairs moving with purpose.
ramayan::669.simple_insight: Some journeys announce themselves before the first step is taken.
ramayan::669.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra leads the two princes into the forest, and the poet lingers on how they look: armed, bright, and formidable. The point is not a teaching, but the visual dignity of their departure and the sense that a major training journey has begun.
ramayan::669.modern_relevance: You leave with the right people, carrying the right tools, and the whole day changes shape before anything happens.
ramayan::669.insight: It frames Rama and Lakshmana as prepared companions entering a serious apprenticeship.

ramayan::670.verse_sanskrit: तदा कुशिकपुत्रं तु धनुष्पाणी स्वलङ्कृतौ । । 1228 । । बद्धगोधाङ्गुलित्राणौ खड्गवन्तौ महाद्युती । कुमारौ चारुवपुषौ भ्रातरौ रामलक्ष्मणौ । । 1229 । । अनुयातौ श्रिया दीप्तौ शोभयेतामनिन्दितौ । स्थाणुं देवमिवाचिन्त्यं कुमाराविव पावकी । । 12210 । ।
ramayan::670.verse_hindi: Then bows in hand, wellattired, their fingers encased in mongrel skin, for protection (against the bowstring) armed with scimitars, resplendent, young, handsome the two brothers, Rama and Lakshmana shone unblemished. As they followed sage Viswamitra spreading radiance, they looked like sons of the god of fire, (Skanda and Visakhu) following the  incomprehensible Siva.
ramayan::670.english_translation: Then the two brothers, Rama and Lakshmana, well-adorned, bow in hand, their fingers protected by leather guards, armed with swords, radiant and handsome, followed the son of Kushika. Unblemished and shining with splendour, the young brothers looked like the sons of the fire god following the incomprehensible Shiva.
ramayan::670.translation_literal: तदा (then) / कुशिकपुत्रं (the son of Kushika) / तु (indeed) / धनुष्पाणी (with bows in hand) / स्वलङ्कृतौ (well-adorned) / बद्धगोधाङ्गुलित्राणौ (with fingers protected by leather guards) / खड्गवन्तौ (armed with swords) / महाद्युती (very radiant) / कुमारौ (the two young princes) / चारुवपुषौ (of handsome bodies) / भ्रातरौ (the two brothers) / रामलक्ष्मणौ (Rama and Lakshmana) / अनुयातौ (following) / श्रिया (with splendour) / दीप्तौ (shining) / शोभयेताम् (shone) / अनिन्दितौ (blameless) / स्थाणुं (Shiva) / देवम् (the deity) / इव (like) / अचिन्त्यम् (incomprehensible) / कुमारौ (the two youths) / इव (like) / पावकी (of Fire)
ramayan::670.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::670.essence: Readiness can be as striking as action itself.
ramayan::670.simple_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana walk behind Vishvamitra, fully armed and shining with youth and beauty. The verse mainly paints their appearance as they travel together.
ramayan::670.simple_insight: Sometimes a verse does not teach a lesson — it simply lets you feel the presence of greatness arriving.
ramayan::670.detailed_meaning: Vishvamitra leads the way while Rama and Lakshmana, still young, follow him with bows, swords, and protective gear. Valmiki lingers on their radiance and beauty, using a simile to lift the scene before Vishvamitra speaks again.
ramayan::670.modern_relevance: You can feel it when two young people walk into a room prepared, alert, and unmistakably ready. Before anyone speaks, their presence has already changed the air.
ramayan::670.insight: It shifts attention from action to atmosphere, showing how readiness itself can be powerful.

ramayan::671.verse_sanskrit: अध्यर्धयोजनं गत्वा सरय्वा दक्षिणे तटे । रामेति मधुरां वाणीं विश्वामित्रोऽभ्यभाषत । । 12211 । ।
ramayan::671.verse_hindi: After crossing a distance of over half a yojana on the southern bank of Sarayu, Viswamitra addressed Rama sweet in a gentle voice.
ramayan::671.english_translation: After crossing more than half a yojana to the southern bank of the Sarayu, Vishvamitra addressed Rama in a gentle, sweet voice.
ramayan::671.translation_literal: अध्यर्धयोजनम् (more than half a yojana) / गत्वा (having gone) / सरय्वा (of the Sarayu) / दक्षिणे तटे (on the southern bank) / रामेति (saying Rama) / मधुराम् (sweet) / वाणीम् (voice) / विश्वामित्रः (Vishvamitra) / अभ्यभाषत (addressed)
ramayan::671.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::671.essence: The journey pauses so the next teaching can begin.
ramayan::671.simple_meaning: Vishvamitra and the princes have reached the riverbank, and he now speaks to Rama.
ramayan::671.simple_insight: Some moments simply move the story forward without carrying the lesson themselves.
ramayan::671.detailed_meaning: Vishvamitra has led Rama and Lakshmana across the Sarayu and now, on the southern bank, turns to Rama with a calm address. The verse is a transition into the next instruction, not the instruction itself.
ramayan::671.modern_relevance: You arrive somewhere after a long walk, and the real conversation begins only after the journey pauses.
ramayan::671.insight: It marks a shift from travel to teaching, preparing the ground for what comes next.

ramayan::672.verse_sanskrit: गृहाण वत्स सलिलं मा भूत्कालस्य पर्यय: । मन्त्रग्रामं गृहाण त्वं बलामतिबलां तथा । । 12212 । ।
ramayan::672.verse_hindi: O child, take this water (in your hands), let there be no delay. You will receive from me a collection of mantras and also bala and atibala.
ramayan::672.english_translation: O child, take this water in your hands; let there be no delay. You will receive from me a collection of mantras, along with Bala and Atibala.
ramayan::672.translation_literal: गृहाण (take) / वत्स (child) / सलिलं (water) / मा (do not) / भूत् (let there be) / कालस्य (of time) / पर्ययः (delay) / मन्त्रग्रामं (collection of mantras) / गृहाण (take) / त्वं (you) / बलाम् (Bala) / अतिबलाम् (Atibala) / तथा (also)
ramayan::672.speaker: Vishwamitra
ramayan::672.essence: The right help matters only if you receive it in time.
ramayan::672.simple_meaning: Vishwamitra tells Rama to accept the ritual water immediately and receive the mantras of Bala and Atibala without delay.
ramayan::672.simple_insight: Some openings only stay open for a moment. When the right help arrives, take it fully.
ramayan::672.detailed_meaning: Vishwamitra has brought Rama and Lakshmana to the riverbank for a decisive initiation. He asks Rama to take the water at once and receive protective mantras, because this training must happen before the journey continues.
ramayan::672.modern_relevance: The coach is finally ready to teach you, but the train leaves in ten minutes. You either step forward now or lose the chance. Some help only works when you receive it immediately.
ramayan::672.insight: It teaches you to respond quickly when guidance or protection is being offered.

ramayan::673.verse_sanskrit: न श्रमो न ज्वरो वा ते न रूपस्य विपर्यय: । न च सुप्तं प्रमत्तं वा धर्षयिष्यन्ति नैऱृता: । । 12213 । ।
ramayan::673.verse_hindi: (If you receive these mantras), you will experience neither fatigue, nor fever nor will there be a change in your appearance. Whether you are asleep or agitated, rakshasas cannot harm you.
ramayan::673.english_translation: (If you receive these mantras), you will experience neither fatigue nor fever, nor will there be any change in your appearance. Whether you are asleep or distracted, the rākshasas cannot harm you.
ramayan::673.translation_literal: न (not) / श्रमो (fatigue) / न (not) / ज्वरो (fever) / वा (or) / ते (to you) / न (not) / रूपस्य (of appearance) / विपर्ययः (change) / न (not) / च (and) / सुप्तम् (asleep) / प्रमत्तम् (heedless) / वा (or) / धर्षयिष्यन्ति (will harm) / नैरृताः (rākshasas)
ramayan::673.speaker: Vishwamitra
ramayan::673.essence: Proper preparation can keep you safe even when you are not fully alert.
ramayan::673.simple_meaning: The mantras Vishwamitra is giving Rama will protect him completely. They will guard him from fatigue, fever, visible change, and attack even when he is asleep or distracted.
ramayan::673.simple_insight: Real protection lets you move through danger without constant strain.
ramayan::673.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has led Rama to the Sarayu and is passing on sacred weapons and mantras. Before the deeper instruction begins, he explains their effect: they will keep Rama steady, unharmed, and beyond the reach of rākshasas even in vulnerable moments.
ramayan::673.modern_relevance: You walk into a hard week already worn down, but still expected to stay sharp. The right preparation does more than help you fight — it keeps you intact when your attention slips.
ramayan::673.insight: It shifts attention from raw effort to the protective power of disciplined preparation.

ramayan::674.verse_sanskrit: न बाह्वोस्सदृशो वीर्ये पृथिव्यामस्ति कश्चन । त्रिषु लोकेषु वै राम न भवेत्सदृशस्तव । । 12214 । ।
ramayan::674.verse_hindi: O Rama, there is none in this world equal to the might of your hands nor does such a person exist in the three worlds.
ramayan::674.english_translation: O Rama, there is none in this world equal to the might of your arms, nor in the three worlds is there anyone like you.
ramayan::674.translation_literal: न (not) / बाह्वोः (of the arms) / सदृशः (equal) / वीर्ये (in might) / पृथिव्याम् (on the earth) / अस्ति (there is) / कश्चन (anyone) / त्रिषु (in the three) / लोकेषु (worlds) / वै (indeed) / राम (Rama) / न (not) / भवेत् (would be) / सदृशः (equal) / तव (to you)
ramayan::674.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::674.essence: Rama’s strength is presented as singular, beyond comparison.
ramayan::674.simple_meaning: Rama is being praised as unmatched in physical strength and heroic power. The speaker says no one on earth or in the three worlds equals him.
ramayan::674.simple_insight: It reminds you that true greatness can be steady, visible, and beyond comparison.
ramayan::674.detailed_meaning: A teacher is arming Rama with sacred knowledge and protection before a dangerous task. In that charged moment, he praises Rama’s unmatched strength, making clear that this is no ordinary youth but a force fit for a world-shaping struggle.
ramayan::674.modern_relevance: You watch someone carry the heaviest box without strain, then quietly take the next one too. Some people are simply built for burden, and everyone in the room knows it.
ramayan::674.insight: It shifts attention from ordinary ability to exceptional capacity, preparing the reader to see Rama as uniquely fit for the task ahead.

ramayan::675.verse_sanskrit: न सौभाग्ये न दाक्षिण्ये न ज्ञाने बुद्धिनिश्चये । नोत्तरे प्रतिवक्तव्ये समो लोके तवाऽनघ । । 12215 । ।
ramayan::675.verse_hindi: O sinless one, there is none in this world equal to you in good fortune, kindness, wisdom, in taking a decsion or giving a reply.
ramayan::675.english_translation: O sinless one, there is none in this world equal to you in good fortune, kindness, wisdom, in taking a decision or giving a reply.
ramayan::675.translation_literal: न (not) / सौभाग्ये (in good fortune) / न (not) / दाक्षिण्ये (in kindness) / न (not) / ज्ञाने (in wisdom) / बुद्धिनिश्चये (in firm decision of the discerning mind) / न (not) / उत्तरे (in reply) / प्रतिवक्तव्ये (to be answered back) / समः (equal) / लोके (in the world) / तव (to you) / अनघ (sinless one)
ramayan::675.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::675.essence: Real excellence shows up in how you decide, speak, and treat others.
ramayan::675.simple_meaning: Rama is praised as unmatched in fortune, kindness, wisdom, clear decision-making, and answering well.
ramayan::675.simple_insight: True strength includes grace, judgment, and the ability to respond well.
ramayan::675.detailed_meaning: A sage is praising Rama after giving him the protective mantras. The praise is not just about power; it names the full shape of an ideal person — fortunate, kind, wise, decisive, and composed in speech.
ramayan::675.modern_relevance: In a tense meeting, someone watches how you answer a hard question. Not just the answer, but the calm behind it — the restraint, clarity, and timing. That is the kind of strength being praised here.
ramayan::675.insight: It shifts respect from raw ability to the whole quality of character and response.

ramayan::676.verse_sanskrit: एतद्विद्याद्वये लब्धे भविता नास्ति ते सम: । बलात्वतिबला चैव सर्वज्ञानस्य मातरौ । । 12216 । ।
ramayan::676.verse_hindi: With these two kinds of knowledge secured, there will be none equal to you, at present or in fututre. Bala and atibala are  mother to all kinds of knowledge .
ramayan::676.english_translation: With these two kinds of knowledge secured, there will be none equal to you, now or in the future. Bala and Atibala are the mothers of all knowledge.
ramayan::676.translation_literal: एतद् (this) / विद्या-द्वये (in the two knowledges) / लब्धे (having been obtained) / भविता (will be) / न अस्ति (there is not) / ते (to you) / समः (equal) / बलातिवला (Bala and Atibala) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / सर्वज्ञानस्य (of all knowledge) / मातरौ (the two mothers)
ramayan::676.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::676.essence: Two rare knowledges can make even great strength complete.
ramayan::676.simple_meaning: Rama is told that mastering Bala and Atibala will make him unmatched now and in the future. These two powers are described as the source of all other knowledge.
ramayan::676.simple_insight: Real strength is not raw force alone; it grows when power is joined with deeper understanding.
ramayan::676.detailed_meaning: Vishvamitra has brought Rama and Lakshmana into sacred training. After praising Rama’s gifts, he reveals the hidden reward of this discipline: two rare knowledges that will protect him and make him unmatched in the world.
ramayan::676.modern_relevance: You finally learn the skill that makes everything else easier — the one that protects your energy, sharpens your judgment, and changes how you move through the day.
ramayan::676.insight: It shifts attention from talent alone to the training that multiplies every other ability.

ramayan::677.verse_sanskrit: क्षुत्पिपासे न ते राम भविष्येते नरोत्तम । बलामतिबलां चैव पठत: पथि राघव । । 12217 । ।
ramayan::677.verse_hindi: O Rama, best among men, scion in the line of Raghu, on your way you will not feel hunger or thirst if you recite bala and atibala.
ramayan::677.english_translation: O Rama, best among men, scion of Raghu, on your way you will not feel hunger or thirst if you recite Bala and Atibala.
ramayan::677.translation_literal: क्षुत्पिपासे (hunger and thirst) / न (not) / ते (to you) / राम (Rama) / भविष्येते (will arise) / नरोत्तम (best among men) / बलामतिबलां (Bala and Atibala) / चैव (and indeed) / पठत: (while reciting) / पथि (on the road) / राघव (scion of Raghu)
ramayan::677.speaker: Vishwamitra
ramayan::677.essence: Preparation can shield you where effort alone cannot.
ramayan::677.simple_meaning: Reciting these two sacred formulas protects Rama from hunger and thirst while traveling.
ramayan::677.simple_insight: Preparation can carry you through conditions that would otherwise drain you.
ramayan::677.detailed_meaning: Vishwamitra is training Rama for a dangerous journey that demands more than courage. He gives him Bala and Atibala, saying that reciting them on the road will keep hunger and thirst away. The lesson is practical power through disciplined learning.
ramayan::677.modern_relevance: You are about to walk into a long day with no margin for error — a flight delay, a missed meal, a meeting that keeps running. What you prepared earlier becomes the thing that keeps you steady.
ramayan::677.insight: It shifts attention from raw willpower to the protective power of learned discipline.

ramayan::678.verse_sanskrit: विद्याद्वयमधीयाने यशश्चाप्यतुलं त्वयि । पितामहसुते ह्येते विद्ये तेजस्समन्विते । । 12218 । । प्रदातुं तव काकुत्स्थ सदृशस्त्वं हि धार्मिक ।
ramayan::678.verse_hindi: O Rama, born in the line Kakutstha and one who is righteous, these two radiant sciences are daughters of the grandsire Brahma. If you pursue these two sciences, you will get unequalled fame. You are a fit person to confer these two sciences.
ramayan::678.english_translation: O Rama, born in the line of Kakutstha and one who is righteous, these two radiant sciences are daughters of the grandsire Brahma. If you pursue these two sciences, you will gain unequalled fame. You are fit to receive these two sciences.
ramayan::678.translation_literal: विद्याद्वयम् (the two sciences) / अधीयाने (to one studying) / यशः (fame) / च अपि (and also) / अतुलम् (unequalled) / त्वयि (in you) / पितामहसुते (daughters of the grandsire) / हि (indeed) / एते (these) / विदे (sciences) / तेजः-समन्विते (endowed with radiance) / प्रदातुम् (to give) / तव (to you) / काकुत्स्थ (O Kakutstha) / सदृशः (fit) / त्वम् (you) / हि (indeed) / धार्मिक (righteous)
ramayan::678.speaker: Vishvamitra
ramayan::678.essence: Powerful knowledge belongs to the person who can carry it rightly.
ramayan::678.simple_meaning: Vishvamitra tells Rama that the two luminous sciences of Bala and Atibala belong to Brahma’s line and suit a righteous person like him. Learning them will bring Rama unmatched fame.
ramayan::678.simple_insight: Real readiness is not just talent; it is the character that can hold power responsibly.
ramayan::678.detailed_meaning: Vishvamitra is preparing Rama for the next stage of his training. After explaining Bala and Atibala, he praises Rama’s righteousness and says these powerful sciences are worthy to be given only to someone like him.
ramayan::678.modern_relevance: A mentor finally trusts you with the hard thing others would misuse. The compliment is not flattery — it is a test of whether your character can carry what your ability can reach.
ramayan::678.insight: It shifts attention from raw ability to moral fitness for knowledge and power.

ramayan::679.verse_sanskrit: कामं बहुगुणास्सर्वे त्वय्येते नात्र संशय: । तपसा सम्भृते चैते बहुरूपे भविष्यत: । । 12219 । ।
ramayan::679.verse_hindi: You possess all these qualities in great measure. There is no doubt that If  these two sciences (mantras) are nourished with austerities they will assume multiple forms (and benefit you).
ramayan::679.english_translation: You possess all these qualities in great measure. There is no doubt that if these two sciences are nourished with austerities, they will assume multiple forms and benefit you.
ramayan::679.translation_literal: कामं (indeed) / बहुगुणाः (many qualities) / सर्वे (all) / त्वयि (in you) / एते (these) / न (not) / अत्र (here) / संशयः (doubt) / तपसा (by austerity) / सम्भृते (nourished, cultivated) / च (and) / एते (these) / बहुरूपे (many-formed, manifold) / भविष्यतः (will become)
ramayan::679.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::679.essence: Talent becomes useful only when it is cultivated.
ramayan::679.simple_meaning: Rama already has the qualities needed. If these two sacred sciences are strengthened through austerity, they will take many forms and serve him well.
ramayan::679.simple_insight: Real power grows when talent is joined with disciplined effort.
ramayan::679.detailed_meaning: The sages are preparing Rama for a greater task. After praising his natural qualities, they explain that these two mantras will only fully bloom through austerity and practice. The verse is a supporting step in that instruction, not the main teaching.
ramayan::679.modern_relevance: You may have the raw ability already. What turns it into real strength is the steady work you keep doing when no one is watching.
ramayan::679.insight: It shifts attention from natural gift alone to the discipline that makes gift fruitful.

ramayan::680.verse_sanskrit: ततो रामो जलं स्पृष्ट्वा प्रहृष्टवदनश्शुचि: । प्रतिजग्राह ते विद्ये महर्षेर्भावितात्मन: । । 12220 । ।
ramayan::680.verse_hindi: Thereafter Rama, touched the water and was sanctified. With a cheerful face he received those two sciences from the maharshi who had perceived the supreme soul.
ramayan::680.english_translation: Thereafter Rama, touched the water and was purified. With a cheerful face he received those two sciences from the maharshi who had perceived the supreme reality.
ramayan::680.translation_literal: ततस् (thereafter) / रामः (Rama) / जलम् (water) / स्पृष्ट्वा (touching) / प्रहृष्टवदनः (with a delighted face) / शुचिः (pure) / प्रतिजग्राह (received) / ते (those) / विद्ये (two sciences) / महर्षेः (of the great sage) / भावितात्मनः (of the one whose inner being was realized)
ramayan::680.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::680.essence: Strength becomes complete when it can still receive instruction.
ramayan::680.simple_meaning: Rama purified himself, then gladly accepted the two sacred sciences from the sage.
ramayan::680.simple_insight: Real readiness begins with humility and receptivity, not just strength.
ramayan::680.detailed_meaning: Vishvamitra has praised Rama’s worth and prepared to give him divine knowledge. Rama responds by touching water, becoming ritually pure, and accepting the teaching with joy. The moment shows a prince ready to be shaped by the teacher.
ramayan::680.modern_relevance: You can be talented and still need to bow your head before learning. The moment you stop defending your image, real training can begin.
ramayan::680.insight: It shifts you from self-assertion to disciplined receptivity before instruction.

ramayan::681.verse_sanskrit: विद्यासमुदितो रामश्शुशुभे भूरिविक्रम: । सहस्ररश्मिर्भगवान् शरदीव दिवाकर: । । 12221 । । गुरुकार्याणि सर्वाणि नियुज्य कुशिकात्मजे । ऊषुस्तां रजनीं तत्र सरय्वां सुसुखं त्रय: । । 12222 । ।
ramayan::681.verse_hindi: Rama, the highly heroic  after acquiring knowledge (of the two sciences) and having rendered all services to preceptor Viswamitra, appeared resplendent like the Sungod in autumn. There the three of them spent the night comfortably on the bank of Sarayu.
ramayan::681.english_translation: Rama, the highly heroic, after acquiring knowledge and completing all services to his teacher Viswamitra, shone like the autumn sun. There the three of them spent that night comfortably on the bank of the Sarayu.
ramayan::681.translation_literal: विद्यासमुदितो (filled with learning) / रामः (Rama) / शुशुभे (shone) / भूरिविक्रमः (of great prowess) / सहस्ररश्मिः (the thousand-rayed one) / भगवान् (the radiant one) / शरदि (in autumn) / इव (like) / दिवाकरः (the sun) / गुरुककार्याणि (the teacher's tasks) / सर्वाणि (all) / नियुज्य (having completed) / कुशिकात्मजे (for the son of Kushika) / ऊषुः (they spent) / ताम् (that) / रजनीम् (night) / तत्र (there) / सरय्वाम् (on the Sarayu) / सुसुखम् (comfortably) / त्रयः (the three)
ramayan::681.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::681.essence: Learning and service together make Rama shine.
ramayan::681.simple_meaning: Rama now shines with learning and strength after serving his teacher well. He, Viswamitra, and Lakshmana then rest comfortably for the night by the Sarayu.
ramayan::681.simple_insight: Real growth shows in how steadily you carry yourself after discipline and service.
ramayan::681.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has finished teaching Rama the secret knowledge he came for. Rama has also completed every task required of a student. In that fulfilled state, he shines with the calm brilliance of a sun after rain, and the three companions rest by the river.
ramayan::681.modern_relevance: You finish a hard apprenticeship, clear the final task, and suddenly your posture changes. People notice the confidence before they know the work behind it.
ramayan::681.insight: It shifts attention from raw talent to the radiance earned through learning and service.

ramayan::682.verse_sanskrit: दशरथनृपसूनुसत्तमाभ्यांतृणशयनेऽनुचिते सहोषिताभ्याम् । कुशिकसुतवचोऽनुलालिताभ्यांसुखमिव सा विबभौ विभावरी च । । 12223 । ।
ramayan::682.verse_hindi: The night was spent as though with comfort  by the two eminent sons of Dasaratha, who shared the unaccustomed bed of grass. They were kept in good humour by the words of Kusikas son.
ramayan::682.english_translation: The night passed as if in comfort for the two best sons of Dasaratha, who lay on an unfit bed of grass. They were soothed by the words of the son of Kushika.
ramayan::682.translation_literal: दशरथ-नृप-सूनु-सत्तमाभ्याम् (by the two best sons of King Dasharatha) / तृण-शयने (on a bed of grass) / अनुचिते (unsuitable) / सहोषिताभ्याम् (having spent the night together) / कुशिक-सुत-वचः (the words of Kushika's son) / अनुलालिताभ्याम् (having been soothed) / सुखम् इव (as if in comfort) / सा विभावरी च (that night also) / विबभौ (shone / passed)
ramayan::682.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::682.essence: Comfort can come from steadiness, not surroundings.
ramayan::682.simple_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana slept on grass, yet the night felt easy because Viswamitra's words comforted them.
ramayan::682.simple_insight: Hard conditions feel lighter when your mind is steady and your company is wise.
ramayan::682.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana have begun life in the forest with Viswamitra. They sleep on grass, far from palace comfort, yet the sage's calm presence and guidance make the harsh night feel almost pleasant. The verse quietly shows their readiness for the path ahead.
ramayan::682.modern_relevance: You crash on a borrowed floor after a long day, but the right company makes the discomfort disappear. Some nights are hard only until trust enters the room.
ramayan::682.insight: It shifts attention from physical ease to the quality of presence around you.

ramayan::683.verse_sanskrit: प्रभातायां तु शर्वर्यां विश्वामित्रो महामुनि: । अभ्यभाषत काकुत्स्थौ शयानौ पर्णसंस्तरे । । 1231 । ।
ramayan::683.verse_hindi: When the night turned into daybreak, the eminent ascetic Viswamitra, addressing the descendants of Kakutstha (Rama and Lakshmana) who were lying on a bed of leaves said:
ramayan::683.english_translation: When night gave way to dawn, the great sage Viswamitra spoke to Rama and Lakshmana, who were lying on a bed of leaves.
ramayan::683.translation_literal: प्रभातायां (at daybreak) / तु (indeed) / शर्वर्याम् (in the night) / विश्वामित्रः (Viswamitra) / महामुनिः (the great sage) / अभ्यभाषत (spoke to) / काकुत्स्थौ (the two descendants of Kakutstha) / शयानौ (lying down) / पर्णसंस्तरे (on a bed of leaves)
ramayan::683.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::683.essence: Dawn interrupts rest because the journey is not finished.
ramayan::683.simple_meaning: At daybreak, Viswamitra addressed Rama and Lakshmana while they were still resting on leaves.
ramayan::683.simple_insight: The next lesson begins the moment rest ends.
ramayan::683.detailed_meaning: After a night of travel and austerity, Rama and Lakshmana lie on a bed of leaves in the forest. At dawn, Viswamitra wakes them and begins the next instruction. The verse mainly sets the scene for what follows.
ramayan::683.modern_relevance: You finally lie down after a long day, and the alarm goes off before your body is ready. The work of the morning does not wait for comfort.
ramayan::683.insight: It shifts attention from the pause of rest to the discipline of responding when duty calls.

ramayan::684.verse_sanskrit: कौसल्या सुप्रजा राम पूर्वा सन्ध्या प्रवर्तते । उत्तिष्ठ नरशार्दूल कर्तव्यं दैवमाह्निकम् । । 1232 । ।
ramayan::684.verse_hindi: O beloved son of Kausalya, O Rama the day dawns. O best among men, awake, oblations to gods and other sacred rites are required to be performed.
ramayan::684.english_translation: O Rama, son of Kausalya, the first dawn is breaking. Rise, tiger among men; the daily rites that must be done are waiting.
ramayan::684.translation_literal: कौसल्या-सुप्रजा (O noble son of Kausalya) / राम (Rama) / पूर्वा सन्ध्या (the first dawn) / प्रवर्तते (is beginning) / उत्तिष्ठ (arise) / नर-शार्दूल (tiger among men) / कर्तव्यम् (to be done) / दैवम् (divine) / आह्निकम् (daily rites)
ramayan::684.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::684.essence: Start the day by doing what your role requires.
ramayan::684.simple_meaning: Morning has arrived, and Rama is told to get up and complete the daily sacred duties before anything else.
ramayan::684.simple_insight: A steady day begins with doing what is required, not with delay or mood.
ramayan::684.detailed_meaning: At dawn in the forest, Viswamitra wakes Rama and Lakshmana after their rough night on grass. Before any journey or teaching can continue, the princes must rise, bathe, and perform the morning rites that keep their lives ordered.
ramayan::684.modern_relevance: Your alarm goes off before sunrise, and your mind wants five more minutes. The verse meets that exact resistance: get up first, then let the day unfold.
ramayan::684.insight: It shifts you from sleepy hesitation to disciplined first action.

ramayan::685.verse_sanskrit: तस्यर्षे: परमोदारं वचश्श्रुत्वा नृपात्मजौ । स्नात्वा कृतोदकौ वीरौ जेपतु: परमं जपम् । । 1233 । ।
ramayan::685.verse_hindi: On hearing the very affectionate call of Viswamitra both the brave princes had their bath and offered oblations to Sungod (standing in the water) and recited the holy name of the Lord.
ramayan::685.english_translation: On hearing the very affectionate call of Viswamitra, both brave princes bathed, offered oblations, and recited the sacred prayer.
ramayan::685.translation_literal: तस्य (his) / ऋषेः (of the sage) / परम-उदारम् (very affectionate, noble) / वचः (words, call) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / नृप-आत्मजौ (the two sons of the king) / स्नात्वा (having bathed) / कृत-उदकौ (having offered water oblations) / वीरौ (the two brave ones) / जेपतुḥ (they recited) / परमम् (supreme) / जपम् (prayer, recitation)
ramayan::685.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::685.essence: Readiness begins with obedience to the morning rite.
ramayan::685.simple_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana obeyed Viswamitra at once: they bathed, made their morning offerings, and prayed.
ramayan::685.simple_insight: A disciplined morning can turn readiness into strength.
ramayan::685.detailed_meaning: At dawn, Viswamitra wakes Rama and Lakshmana for the day’s sacred routine. They do not hesitate or complain. They rise, bathe, offer water, and pray before following him onward into the forest.
ramayan::685.modern_relevance: Your phone is buzzing before sunrise, but you still get up, wash your face, and start the day clean before the chaos begins.
ramayan::685.insight: It teaches you to begin demanding days with ritual, steadiness, and readiness instead of delay.

ramayan::686.verse_sanskrit: कृताह्निकौ महावीर्यौ विश्वामित्रं तपोधनम् । अभिवाद्याभिसंहृष्टौ गमनायाभितस्थतु: । । 1234 । ।
ramayan::686.verse_hindi: On performing the morning rites, the two highly powerful and and energetic princes stood before Viswamitra who was richly endowed with asceticism. They prostrated before him. And stood ready for their onward journey.
ramayan::686.english_translation: After completing the morning rites, the two mighty princes joyfully saluted Viswamitra, the ascetic, and stood ready to depart.
ramayan::686.translation_literal: कृताह्निकौ (having completed the morning rites) / महावीर्यौ (the two greatly powerful ones) / विश्वामित्रं (to Viswamitra) / तपोधनम् (richly endowed with ascetic power) / अभिवाद्य (having saluted) / अभिसंहृष्टौ (filled with joy) / गमनाय (for departure) / अभितस्थतु: (they stood ready)
ramayan::686.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::686.essence: Prepared action begins with reverence and calm.
ramayan::686.simple_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana finish their morning duties, bow to Viswamitra, and prepare to continue the journey.
ramayan::686.simple_insight: Readiness begins with respect and ritual, not with haste.
ramayan::686.detailed_meaning: At dawn, Rama and Lakshmana complete their morning rites after Viswamitra’s call. The princes bow to the sage with joy and stand prepared to move on. The verse simply marks the transition from preparation to travel.
ramayan::686.modern_relevance: You pack your bag, check your phone, and step out the door before sunrise. The day goes better when you begin with order and respect, not rush.
ramayan::686.insight: It teaches you to start action only after finishing what grounds you.

ramayan::687.verse_sanskrit: तौ प्रयातौ महावीर्यौ दिव्यां त्रिपथगां नदीम् । ददृशाते ततस्तत्र सरय्वास्सङ्गमे शुभे । । 1235 । ।
ramayan::687.verse_hindi: Thereafter, having gone a little further both the heroic brothers looked at the confluence of holy  Sarayu with  divine Ganga divided into three branches.
ramayan::687.english_translation: Thereafter, having gone a little further, the two heroic brothers saw the holy confluence where the divine Ganga divides into three streams and meets the Sarayu.
ramayan::687.translation_literal: तौ (they two) / प्रयातौ (having gone) / महावीर्यौ (the highly powerful ones) / दिव्याम् (divine) / त्रिपथगाम् (flowing in three paths) / नदीम् (river) / ददृशाते (saw) / ततस् (then) / तत्र (there) / सरय्वाः (of the Sarayu) / सङ्गमे (at the confluence) / शुभे (auspicious)
ramayan::687.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::687.essence: A sacred crossing appears just before the next stage begins.
ramayan::687.simple_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana travel on and see an auspicious river confluence where the Ganga is described as flowing in three channels.
ramayan::687.simple_insight: Some moments are only a crossing point, but they still feel sacred.
ramayan::687.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana, guided by Vishwamitra, continue their journey and come upon a holy river meeting point. The verse simply marks their arrival at a significant landscape before the deeper forest-and-ashram events begin.
ramayan::687.modern_relevance: You pass a place that seems ordinary to everyone else, but it lands in you as a threshold. Some moments are not decisions yet — they are the quiet edge before one.
ramayan::687.insight: It slows the journey and marks a sacred transition before the next encounter.

ramayan::688.verse_sanskrit: तत्राश्रमपदं पुण्यमृषीणामग्य्रतेजसाम् । बहुवर्षसहस्राणि तप्यतां परमं तप: । । 1236 । ।
ramayan::688.verse_hindi: There they saw a sacred hermitage of anchorites of great vitality performing severe austerities for thousands of years.
ramayan::688.english_translation: There they saw a sacred hermitage of anchorites of great vitality performing severe austerities for thousands of years.
ramayan::688.translation_literal: तत्र (there) / आश्रमपदम् (hermitage-place) / पुण्यम् (sacred) / ऋषीणाम् (of sages) / अग्र्यतेजसाम् (of foremost radiance) / बहुवर्षसहस्राणि (for many thousands of years) / तप्यताम् (of those practicing austerity) / परमम् (supreme) / तपः (austerity)
ramayan::688.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::688.essence: Sacredness is built by years of disciplined endurance.
ramayan::688.simple_meaning: They came upon a sacred hermitage where great sages had been living in severe discipline for thousands of years.
ramayan::688.simple_insight: Some places carry the weight of long effort and quiet devotion.
ramayan::688.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana travel with Vishwamitra and reach a holy hermitage near the Sarayu. Before any teaching begins, Valmiki pauses to show the setting: a place made sacred by sages who have endured years of austerity.
ramayan::688.modern_relevance: You walk into a room where someone has practiced for years before you arrived. The calm you feel is not accidental; it was built by discipline you did not see.
ramayan::688.insight: It trains you to notice the invisible effort that makes a place or person worthy of respect.

ramayan::689.verse_sanskrit: तं दृष्ट्वा परमप्रीतौ राघवौ पुण्यमाश्रमम् । ऊचतुस्तं महात्मानं विश्वामित्रमिदं वच: । । 1237 । ।
ramayan::689.verse_hindi: Exceedingly delighted to see the sacred hermitage, the two princes enquired from the illustrious sage Viswamitra:
ramayan::689.english_translation: Seeing the sacred hermitage, the two princes were greatly pleased and spoke these words to the great-souled Viswamitra.
ramayan::689.translation_literal: तम् (that) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / परमप्रीतौ (greatly delighted) / राघवौ (the two Raghava princes) / पुण्यम् (sacred) / आश्रमम् (hermitage) / ऊचतुः (the two spoke) / तम् (to him) / महात्मानम् (great-souled one) / विश्वामित्रम् (Viswamitra) / इदम् (these) / वचः (words)
ramayan::689.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::689.essence: Wonder makes you ask with respect.
ramayan::689.simple_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana feel joy on reaching the holy hermitage and turn to Viswamitra with questions.
ramayan::689.simple_insight: Curiosity can be pure when it comes from wonder, not impatience.
ramayan::689.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana arrive with Viswamitra at a sacred forest hermitage. The place moves them immediately, and they turn to the sage with respectful questions. This verse sets up the inquiry that follows.
ramayan::689.modern_relevance: You step into a quiet temple courtyard after a long drive and feel your voice soften before you even ask anything. Some places change the way you speak.
ramayan::689.insight: It frames curiosity as reverent attention, not casual information-seeking.

ramayan::690.verse_sanskrit: कस्यायमाश्रम: पुण्य: कोन्वस्मिन्वसते पुमान् । भगवन् श्रोतुमिच्छाव: परं कौतूहलं हि नौ । । 1238 । ।
ramayan::690.verse_hindi: O worshipful one, whose sacred hermitage is this? Who lives here? Indeed, we are curious to know.
ramayan::690.english_translation: O worshipful one, whose sacred hermitage is this? Who lives here? Indeed, we are curious to know.
ramayan::690.translation_literal: कस्य (whose) / अयम् (this) / आश्रमः (hermitage) / पुण्यः (sacred) / कः (who) / नु (indeed) / अस्मिन् (in this) / वसते (lives) / पुमान् (man) / भगवन् (worshipful one) / श्रोतुम् (to hear) / इच्छावः (we wish) / परम् (great) / कौतूहलम् (curiosity) / हि (indeed) / नौ (of us two)
ramayan::690.speaker: Rama
ramayan::690.essence: Respectful curiosity opens the door to the story that follows.
ramayan::690.simple_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana ask Viswamitra whose holy hermitage this is and who lives there.
ramayan::690.simple_insight: Curiosity can be the first step into a new world.
ramayan::690.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana have reached a sacred forest hermitage with Viswamitra. Moved by its holiness, they ask who founded it and who lives there, opening the next story about the place's past.
ramayan::690.modern_relevance: You enter a place that feels charged with meaning and ask, quietly, who built it and what it has held.
ramayan::690.insight: It sets the scene by showing the princes' respectful curiosity before the sage explains the hermitage's history.

ramayan::691.verse_sanskrit: तयोस्तद्वचनं श्रुत्वा प्रहस्य मुनिपुङ्गव: । अब्रवीच्छ्रूयतां राम यस्यायं पूर्व आश्रम: । । 1239 । ।
ramayan::691.verse_hindi: On having heard their words, the foremost of sages gently smiled and said, O Rama listen, who this hermitage belonged to in the past.
ramayan::691.english_translation: On hearing their words, the foremost of sages smiled gently and said, "Listen, Rama, to whom this hermitage belonged in the past."
ramayan::691.translation_literal: तयोः (their two) / तद्वचनम् (that speech) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / प्रहस्य (smiling) / मुनिपुङ्गवः (foremost of sages) / अब्रवीत् (said) / श्रूयताम् (let it be heard) / राम (Rama) / यस्य (whose) / अयम् (this) / पूर्वः (former/past) / आश्रमः (hermitage)
ramayan::691.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::691.essence: A place can look peaceful and still hold an older wound.
ramayan::691.simple_meaning: Viswamitra smiles and begins to explain the hermitage's past to Rama and Lakshmana.
ramayan::691.simple_insight: Curiosity opens the door to a larger story.
ramayan::691.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana ask Viswamitra about a sacred hermitage. The sage smiles at their interest and begins to reveal its hidden history, setting up the story of what happened there before.
ramayan::691.modern_relevance: You ask a simple question about a place, and suddenly a whole buried history starts to open.
ramayan::691.insight: It shifts attention from the present scene to the deeper story behind it.

ramayan::692.verse_sanskrit: कन्दर्पो मूर्तिमानासीत्काम इत्युच्यते बुधै: । तपस्यन्तमिह स्थाणुं नियमेन समाहितम् । । 12310 । । कृतोद्वाहं तु देवेशं गच्छन्तं समरुद्गगणम् । धर्षयामास दुर्मेधा हुङ्कृतश्च महात्मना । । 12311 । ।
ramayan::692.verse_hindi: Kandarpa (the god of love) once lived here in human form. He is called Kama by the learned. The wicked Kama on his way with the maruts (god of wind) insulted Siva, the god of gods, while he was absorbed in austere meditation along with his newly wedded consort. On seeing Kama Lord Siva roared at him (menacingly).
ramayan::692.english_translation: Kama, the god of love, once had a body. The wise call him desire. While Shiva was absorbed in disciplined meditation with his newly married consort, the foolish Kama insulted him. Shiva then roared in anger.
ramayan::692.translation_literal: कन्दर्पः (Kama) / मूर्तिमान् (embodied) / आसीत् (was) / कामः (desire) / इति (thus) / उच्यते (is called) / बुधैः (by the wise) । / तपस्यन्तम् (practising austerity) / इह (here) / स्थाणुम् (Shiva) / नियमेन (with discipline) / समाहितम् (absorbed) । / कृतोद्वाहम् (newly married) / तु (but) / देवेशम् (lord of the gods) / गच्छन्तम् (going) / समरुद्गणम् (with the maruts) । / धर्षयामास (insulted) / दुर्मेधाः (the foolish one) / हुङ्कृतः (roared at) / च (and) / महात्मना (by the great-souled one) ।
ramayan::692.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::692.essence: Desire becomes dangerous when it mocks what is being guarded.
ramayan::692.simple_meaning: Kama once appeared in a body and is identified with desire. He mocked Shiva while Shiva was deep in meditation, and Shiva answered with a fierce roar.
ramayan::692.simple_insight: Unchecked desire can turn reckless fast, and that recklessness meets consequences.
ramayan::692.detailed_meaning: This is part of a larger telling of how Kama came to be burned by Shiva. Valmiki is setting up the cause: Kama, careless and arrogant, interrupts Shiva's austere meditation just after Shiva's marriage. The next verse shows the punishment.
ramayan::692.modern_relevance: A sharp comment sent in the heat of attraction, ego, or impatience can cross a line you cannot uncross. The moment may feel small; the consequence may not be.
ramayan::692.insight: It warns you that desire without restraint becomes self-destructive provocation.

ramayan::693.verse_sanskrit: अवदग्धस्य रौद्रेण चक्षुषा रघुनन्दन । व्यशीर्यन्त शरीरात्स्वात्सर्वगात्राणि दुर्मते: । । 12312 । ।
