ramayan::693.verse_hindi: O descendant of Raghu, burnt down by his fierce (third) eye, all the limbs of the body of that evilminded Kama were consumed.
ramayan::693.english_translation: O descendant of Raghu, burnt down by his fierce eye, all the limbs of that evil-minded Kama were consumed.
ramayan::693.translation_literal: अवदग्धस्य (of the one who was burnt) / रौद्रेण (by the fierce) / चक्षुषा (by the eye) / रघुनन्दन (O descendant of Raghu) / व्यशीर्यन्त (were scattered apart) / शरीरात् (from the body) / स्वात् (own) / सर्वगात्राणि (all limbs) / दुर्मतेः (of the evil-minded one)
ramayan::693.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::693.essence: Desire can be reduced to ashes by a single, fierce glance.
ramayan::693.simple_meaning: Kama's body was destroyed by Shiva's fierce third eye, and his limbs fell apart.
ramayan::693.simple_insight: Unchecked desire can be shattered in an instant by a force greater than it.
ramayan::693.detailed_meaning: The sage is explaining to Rama and Lakshmana why this hermitage carries such weight. After describing Kama's arrogance, he shows the moment Shiva's fierce eye reduced him to ashes. It is a mythic cause-and-effect detail, not the main teaching.
ramayan::693.modern_relevance: A craving you thought was harmless can collapse the moment reality turns against it. What looked powerful can disappear fast when it meets a stronger force.
ramayan::693.insight: It shows desire as fragile when faced with disciplined power.

ramayan::694.verse_sanskrit: तस्य गात्रं हतं तत्र निर्दग्थस्य महात्मना । अशरीर: कृत: काम: क्रोधाद्देवेश्वरेण हि । । 12313 । ।
ramayan::694.verse_hindi: Having been completely burnt down by Lord Siva, Kamas body was destroyed. Mighty angry, Siva, reduced Kama to a disembodied being.
ramayan::694.english_translation: Having been completely burnt down by Lord Siva, Kama's body was destroyed. In anger, Siva reduced Kama to a disembodied being.
ramayan::694.translation_literal: तस्य (his) / गात्रं (body) / हतं (struck down, destroyed) / तत्र (there) / निर्दग्धस्य (of the one completely burnt) / महात्मना (by the great-souled one) / अशरीरः (bodiless) / कृतः (made) / कामः (Kama) / क्रोधात् (out of anger) / देवेश्वरेण (by the lord of the gods) / हि (indeed)
ramayan::694.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::694.essence: Desire can be reduced to nothing when it collides with fierce restraint.
ramayan::694.simple_meaning: Kama was burned completely by Shiva, and his body was destroyed. In anger, Shiva made him bodiless.
ramayan::694.simple_insight: Unchecked desire can be shattered in an instant by force greater than it.
ramayan::694.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing the aftermath of Kama's attempt to disturb Shiva's austerity. Shiva's third eye has already burned him; now the poem states the final result: Kama's body is gone, and only a bodiless existence remains.
ramayan::694.modern_relevance: A craving flares up in you at the worst moment — and one sharp boundary, one hard truth, cuts it down before it takes over.
ramayan::694.insight: It shows how desire loses power when it meets disciplined force and clear seeing.

ramayan::695.verse_sanskrit: अनङ्ग इति विख्यातस्तदाप्रभृति राघव । स चाङ्गविषयश्श्रीमान्यत्राङ्गं प्रमुमोच ह । । 12314 । ।
ramayan::695.verse_hindi: O descendant of the Raghus, from that time onwards, he was known as Ananga (one without form). The  beautiful place where he gave up his body is known as Angadesa.
ramayan::695.english_translation: O descendant of the Raghus, from that time onwards, he was known as Ananga, the formless one. The beautiful place where he gave up his body is known as Angadesa.
ramayan::695.translation_literal: अनङ्गः (the formless one) / इति (thus) / विख्यातः (known) / तदाप्रभृति (from that time onward) / राघव (O descendant of Raghu) / सः (he) / च (and) / अङ्गविषयः (the region of Anga) / श्रीमान् (beautiful) / यत्र (where) / अङ्गम् (his body) / प्रमुमोच (gave up) / ह (indeed)
ramayan::695.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::695.essence: A body can vanish, but the place remembers.
ramayan::695.simple_meaning: Kama became known as the formless one after Shiva burned his body. The place where this happened was later called Angadesa.
ramayan::695.simple_insight: Some names carry the memory of a dramatic loss.
ramayan::695.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is closing the story of Kama's destruction by Shiva. After the burning, Kama is no longer described as embodied, and the sacred place where he fell is given a lasting name. The verse adds a mythic footnote to the larger tale.
ramayan::695.modern_relevance: A place on a map can still carry the memory of one irreversible moment. People keep naming things after what happened there, long after the event itself is gone.
ramayan::695.insight: It shifts attention from the person to the lasting mark left behind.

ramayan::696.verse_sanskrit: तस्यायमाश्रम: पुण्यस्तस्येमे मुनय: पुरा । शिष्या धर्मपरा नित्यं तेषां पापं न विद्यते । । 12315 । ।
ramayan::696.verse_hindi: This holy hermitage belongs to Kama. These ascetics are his disciples. They are  always righteous and are free from sin.
ramayan::696.english_translation: This holy hermitage belongs to Kama. These ascetics are his disciples. They are always righteous and are free from sin.
ramayan::696.translation_literal: तस्य (his) / अयम् (this) / आश्रमः (hermitage) / पुण्यः (holy) / तस्य (his) / इमे (these) / मुनयः (ascetics) / पुरा (formerly/long ago) / शिष्याः (disciples) / धर्मपराः (devoted to righteousness) / नित्यम् (always) / तेषाम् (of them) / पापम् (wrong/sin) / न (not) / विद्यते (exists)
ramayan::696.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::696.essence: A sacred place is defined by the discipline it continues to shelter.
ramayan::696.simple_meaning: This sacred hermitage is linked to Kama, and the sages here live in steady righteousness, untouched by wrongdoing.
ramayan::696.simple_insight: A place can carry the fragrance of discipline long after the person is gone.
ramayan::696.detailed_meaning: The scene is explaining a sacred site tied to Kama’s story. The sages living there are described as his disciples, steady in righteous conduct and free from wrongdoing. It is a brief descriptive detail, not a teaching in itself.
ramayan::696.modern_relevance: You walk into a home where someone kept the same morning routine for years. The room still feels ordered, almost instructed by their presence. Some places inherit the discipline of the people who lived there.
ramayan::696.insight: It frames holiness as something preserved through disciplined living, not just remembered history.

ramayan::697.verse_sanskrit: इहाद्य रजनीं राम वसेम शुभदर्शन । पुण्ययोस्सरितोर्मध्ये श्वस्तरिष्यामहे वयम् । । 12316 । ।
ramayan::697.verse_hindi: O auspiciouslooking Rama, we will stay here tonight at the confluence of both these sacred rivers (Sarayu and Ganga) and cross over Ganga tomorrow.
ramayan::697.english_translation: O auspicious-looking Rama, we will stay here tonight at the confluence of these sacred rivers and cross the Ganga tomorrow.
ramayan::697.translation_literal: इह (here) / अद्य (today, tonight) / रजनीं (the night) / राम (Rama) / वसेम (let us stay) / शुभदर्शन (auspicious-looking) / पुण्ययोः (of the sacred) / सरितोः (rivers) / मध्ये (in the middle, at the confluence) / श्वः (tomorrow) / तरिष्यामहे (we shall cross over) / वयम् (we)
ramayan::697.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::697.essence: Not every crossing should happen at once.
ramayan::697.simple_meaning: Rama and the others plan to rest at the meeting point of two holy rivers and cross the Ganga the next day.
ramayan::697.simple_insight: Sometimes the right move is simple: stop, rest, and continue tomorrow.
ramayan::697.detailed_meaning: Rama is travelling with companions and reaches the sacred meeting of the Sarayu and Ganga. Rather than rush onward, the group decides to spend the night there and cross the river in the morning. The verse mainly marks a pause in the journey.
ramayan::697.modern_relevance: You reach the edge of something important late at night and choose not to force it. You sleep, reset, and cross in the morning with a clearer mind.
ramayan::697.insight: It shifts action from urgency to timing, showing that restraint can be wiser than pushing ahead.

ramayan::698.verse_sanskrit: अभिगच्छामहे सर्वे शुचय: पुण्यमाश्रमम् । स्नाताश्च कृतजप्याश्च हुतहव्या नरोत्तम । । 12317 । ।
ramayan::698.verse_hindi: O best of men, after morning ablutions offering oblations to the sacred fire, all of us sanctified will enter this pious hermitage.
ramayan::698.english_translation: O best of men, after morning ablutions, offering oblations to the sacred fire, all of us purified will enter this pious hermitage.
ramayan::698.translation_literal: अभिगच्छामहे (we will enter) / सर्वे (all) / शुचयः (purified) / पुण्यम् (holy) / आश्रमम् (hermitage) / स्नाताः (having bathed) / च (and) / कृतजप्याः (having done recitation) / च (and) / हुतहव्याḥ (having offered oblations) / नरोत्तम (O best of men)
ramayan::698.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::698.essence: Sacred spaces ask for inner and outer preparation.
ramayan::698.simple_meaning: After bathing, prayer, and fire offerings, everyone will enter the holy hermitage together.
ramayan::698.simple_insight: Ritual preparation comes before entering sacred space.
ramayan::698.detailed_meaning: Rama and the others are resting near a sacred river confluence. Before they step into the hermitage, they first purify themselves with bathing, prayer, and offerings. The verse is a practical step in the journey, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::698.modern_relevance: Before you walk into a place that matters, you pause to wash up, collect yourself, and settle your mind. Some moments deserve more than a rushed arrival.
ramayan::698.insight: It shifts attention from movement alone to the preparation that makes entry fitting.

ramayan::699.verse_sanskrit: तेषां संवदतां तत्र तपोदीर्घेण चक्षुषा । विज्ञाय परमप्रीता मुनयो हर्षमागमन् । । 12318 । ।
ramayan::699.verse_hindi: As they were conversing thus, the ascetics, with their far reaching spiritual vision (beyond the veil of time) recognised them and were immensely pleased.
ramayan::699.english_translation: As they were conversing thus, the ascetics, with their far-reaching spiritual vision, recognised them and were immensely pleased.
ramayan::699.translation_literal: तेषाम् (of them) / संवदताम् (while speaking together) / तत्र (there) / तपोदीर्घेण (with ascetic-long) / चक्षुषा (with the eye) / विज्ञाय (having recognised) / परमप्रीताः (deeply pleased) / मुनयः (the sages) / हर्षम् (joy) / आगमन् (came)
ramayan::699.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::699.essence: The wise saw who had arrived and joy rose instantly.
ramayan::699.simple_meaning: The sages recognised Rama and Lakshmana through their spiritual insight and felt great joy.
ramayan::699.simple_insight: Being seen clearly by the wise can feel like being welcomed before a word is spoken.
ramayan::699.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana have arrived at the sacred hermitage of Vishvamitra. While they speak, the resident sages perceive who they are through ascetic insight and rejoice. This is a recognition scene, not a teaching verse.
ramayan::699.modern_relevance: You walk into a room carrying worry, and someone who truly knows life reads your face before you speak. That kind of recognition lands like relief.
ramayan::699.insight: It shows that quiet presence can be recognised more deeply than words.

ramayan::700.verse_sanskrit: अर्घ्यं पाद्यं तथाऽतिथ्यं निवेद्य कुशिकात्मजे । रामलक्ष्मणयो: पश्चादकुर्वन्नतिथिक्रियाम् । । 12319 । ।
ramayan::700.verse_hindi: After extending hospitality to the son of Kusika (Viswamitra) with respectful offerings, and water for washing feet they played the host to Rama and Lakshmana.
ramayan::700.english_translation: After offering respectful water, foot-washing, and hospitality to the son of Kusika, they then hosted Rama and Lakshmana.
ramayan::700.translation_literal: अर्घ्यम् (respectful offering) / पाद्यम् (water for washing feet) / तथा (and) / अतिथ्यम् (hospitality) / निवेद्य (having offered) / कुशिकात्मजे (to the son of Kusika) / रामलक्ष्मणयोः (for Rama and Lakshmana) / पश्चात् (afterward) / अकुर्वन् (they did) / अतिथिक्रियाम् (the act of receiving a guest)
ramayan::700.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::700.essence: True welcome is shown through careful, ordered acts.
ramayan::700.simple_meaning: The sages first honoured Vishwamitra with formal hospitality, then received Rama and Lakshmana properly as guests.
ramayan::700.simple_insight: Respect is shown in actions first, not words alone.
ramayan::700.detailed_meaning: In Vishwamitra's hermitage, the sages complete the proper rites of hospitality. They honour the son of Kusika, then receive Rama and Lakshmana with the same care. The verse simply marks this orderly welcome before the deeper conversation begins.
ramayan::700.modern_relevance: You arrive at someone’s home carrying stress, and they still set water, a seat, and attention before asking anything of you.
ramayan::700.insight: It shifts attention from casual reception to deliberate respect for the guest.

ramayan::701.verse_sanskrit: सत्कारं समनुप्राप्य कथाभिरभिरञ्जयन् । यथार्हमजपन् सन्ध्यामृषयस्ते समाहिता: । । 12320 । ।
ramayan::701.verse_hindi: Having received due hospitality, they delighted them (ascetics) with their talk. The rishis with composed minds recited their evening prayer as usual.
ramayan::701.english_translation: Having received due hospitality, they delighted the ascetics with their talk. The sages, with composed minds, recited their evening prayer as usual.
ramayan::701.translation_literal: सत्कारम् (hospitality) / समनुप्राप्य (having received) / कथाभिः (with stories, with talk) / अभिरञ्जयन् (delighting) / यथार्हम् (as is fitting) / अजपन् (recited) / सन्ध्याम् (the evening prayer) / ऋषयः (the sages) / ते (those) / समाहिताः (composed, focused)
ramayan::701.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::701.essence: Hospitality and daily practice can sit together without friction.
ramayan::701.simple_meaning: The guests are welcomed properly, the conversation is pleasant, and the sages keep to their evening prayer with calm focus.
ramayan::701.simple_insight: Respect, warmth, and discipline can coexist in the same moment.
ramayan::701.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has brought Rama and Lakshmana to a hermitage where the ascetics receive them with proper hospitality. After the formal welcome, everyone shares gentle conversation, and the sages still pause for their evening rites. The scene shows sacred order and courtesy before the journey continues.
ramayan::701.modern_relevance: You arrive at a home after a long day, and the first thing people offer is care, not questions. The room feels easier because kindness and routine still hold their place.
ramayan::701.insight: It shows that true welcome does not disturb discipline; it deepens it.

ramayan::702.verse_sanskrit: तत्र वासिभिरानीता मुनिभिस्सुव्रतै: सह । न्यवसन् सुसुखं तत्र कामाश्रमपदे तदा । । 12321 । ।
ramayan::702.verse_hindi: The ascetics who resided there, faithful to their vows, took them in. There they staed happily  in Kamas hermitage.
ramayan::702.english_translation: The ascetics who lived there, faithful to their vows, received them. There, in Kama's hermitage, they stayed happily.
ramayan::702.translation_literal: तत्र (there) / वासिभिः (by the residents) / आनीता (brought in) / मुनिभिः (by the ascetics) / सुव्रतैः (faithful to vows) / सह (along with) / न्यवसन् (they stayed) / सुसुखम् (very happily) / तत्र (there) / कामाश्रमपदे (in Kama's hermitage) / तदा (then)
ramayan::702.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::702.essence: Rest can begin when disciplined people make room for you.
ramayan::702.simple_meaning: The sages living there welcomed Rama and Lakshmana, and the princes stayed comfortably in the hermitage.
ramayan::702.simple_insight: A place of discipline can also become a place of welcome.
ramayan::702.detailed_meaning: After Viswamitra’s arrival, the forest hermitage receives Rama and Lakshmana with care. The ascetics, steady in their vows, make space for the princes, and the two sons of Dasharatha rest happily before the next teaching begins.
ramayan::702.modern_relevance: You arrive exhausted at a place where everyone lives by a different rhythm, and instead of being judged, you are quietly received. That kind of welcome changes everything.
ramayan::702.insight: It shifts attention from the journey’s strain to the relief of being safely received.

ramayan::703.verse_sanskrit: कथाभिरभिरामाभिरभिरामौ नृपात्मजौ । रमयामास धर्मात्मा कौशिको मुनिपुङ्गव: । । 12322 । ।
ramayan::703.verse_hindi: Foremost among the ascetics the son of Kusika (Viswamitra) delighted the charming  princes with enchanting tales.
ramayan::703.english_translation: Foremost among the ascetics, the righteous Viswamitra delighted the two princes with charming tales.
ramayan::703.translation_literal: कथाभिः (with tales) / अभिरामाभिः (delightful) / अभिरामौ (the two charming ones) / नृपात्मजौ (the two princes) / रमयामास (delighted) / धर्मात्मा (righteous-minded) / कौशिकः (Kausika) / मुनिपुङ्गवः (foremost among sages)
ramayan::703.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::703.essence: Trust opens the door before instruction can enter.
ramayan::703.simple_meaning: Viswamitra entertained Rama and Lakshmana with pleasant stories while they stayed with him.
ramayan::703.simple_insight: Some guidance begins by winning trust, not by teaching hard truths first.
ramayan::703.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana have reached Viswamitra’s hermitage and are being received with care. Before the journey’s demands begin, the sage first puts them at ease with stories, building trust and setting the tone for the training ahead.
ramayan::703.modern_relevance: A mentor starts with a calm conversation before the hard feedback. That first warmth lowers the guard enough for real learning to begin.
ramayan::703.insight: It shows that instruction lands better when the listener feels welcomed first.

ramayan::704.verse_sanskrit: तत: प्रभाते विमले कृताह्निकमरिन्दमौ । विश्वामित्रं पुरस्कृत्य नद्यास्तीरमुपागतौ । । 1241 । ।
ramayan::704.verse_hindi: Thereafter the destroyers of foes, Rama and Lakshmana offering their morning oblations on that bright dawn arrived at the bank of the river (Ganga) with Viswamitra ahead of them.
ramayan::704.english_translation: Thereafter the destroyers of foes, Rama and Lakshmana, having completed their morning rites, came to the bank of the river with Viswamitra leading them.
ramayan::704.translation_literal: तत: (thereafter) / प्रभाते (at dawn) / विमले (bright, pure) / कृताह्निकौ (having performed the morning rites) / अरिन्दमौ (the two subduers of foes) / विश्वामित्रम् (Viswamitra) / पुरस्कृत्य (placing in front, led by) / नद्याः (of the river) / तीरम् (bank) / उपागतौ (arrived)
ramayan::704.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::704.essence: Right action begins with quiet readiness.
ramayan::704.simple_meaning: At dawn, Rama and Lakshmana finish their morning rites and reach the riverbank with Viswamitra leading them.
ramayan::704.simple_insight: The journey begins with discipline, not drama.
ramayan::704.detailed_meaning: After a peaceful night in Viswamitra’s hermitage, Rama and Lakshmana rise before sunrise, complete their morning rites, and walk to the riverbank under the sage’s guidance. The moment simply moves the story from rest to the next stage of travel.
ramayan::704.modern_relevance: You wake before the house is fully alive, wash your face, and step into the day before anyone asks for anything. Some journeys begin in that quiet order.
ramayan::704.insight: It keeps attention on preparation and movement, not on meaning-making.

ramayan::705.verse_sanskrit: ते च सर्वे महात्मानो मुनयस्संश्रितव्रता: । उपस्थाप्य शुभां नावं विश्वामित्रमथाब्रुवन् । । 1242 । ।
ramayan::705.verse_hindi: All the highminded ascetics and strict followers of vows secured an auspicious boat for them and addressed Viswamitra, saying:
ramayan::705.english_translation: All the high-minded ascetics, steadfast in their vows, brought a good boat and then spoke to Viswamitra:
ramayan::705.translation_literal: ते (those) / च (and) / सर्वे (all) / महात्मानः (high-minded ones) / मुनयः (ascetics) / संश्रितव्रताः (steadfast in vows) / उपस्थाप्य (having brought forward) / शुभाम् (auspicious) / नावम् (boat) / विश्वामित्रम् (to Viswamitra) / अथ (then) / अब्रुवन् (they said)
ramayan::705.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::705.essence: The journey advances because others quietly make room for it.
ramayan::705.simple_meaning: The sages, devoted to their vows, bring a boat so Viswamitra and the princes can continue the journey.
ramayan::705.simple_insight: Small acts of help can keep a righteous journey moving.
ramayan::705.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana have reached the riverbank with Viswamitra at dawn. The local ascetics, known for their vows, arrange a boat for them and speak to the sage so the journey can continue without delay.
ramayan::705.modern_relevance: You arrive at a ferry terminal with two tired children and a friend carrying the paperwork. A stranger quietly points you to the right boat and saves the whole morning.
ramayan::705.insight: It shows how supporting the right journey is itself a form of dharma.

ramayan::706.verse_sanskrit: आरोहतु भवान्नावं राजपुत्रपुरस्कृत: । अरिष्टं गच्छ पन्थानं मा भूत्कालविपर्यय: । । 1243 । ।
ramayan::706.verse_hindi: With the princes ahead of you, board the boat. Tread the safe path. Let there be no loss of time.
ramayan::706.english_translation: With the princes ahead of you, board the boat. Tread the safe path. Let there be no loss of time.
ramayan::706.translation_literal: आरोहतु (let board) / भवान् (you) / नावं (the boat) / राजपुत्र-पुरस्कृतः (with the princes in front) / अरिष्टं (safe) / गच्छ (go) / पन्थानं (path) / मा (do not) / भूत् (let there be) / काल-विपर्ययः (loss of time)
ramayan::706.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::706.essence: The right path is the one you take without delay.
ramayan::706.simple_meaning: Viswamitra is told to board the boat with Rama and Lakshmana ahead, take the safe route, and not waste time.
ramayan::706.simple_insight: The journey begins with urgency and care, not hesitation.
ramayan::706.detailed_meaning: The sages have already secured a boat for Viswamitra, Rama, and Lakshmana. Now they urge him to board at once and cross the river without delay. It is a practical moment of movement, not a teaching verse.
ramayan::706.modern_relevance: You’re at the riverbank with bags in hand, the cab waiting, and everyone ready. This is the moment to move, not overthink.
ramayan::706.insight: It keeps attention on timely action and the safest next step.

ramayan::707.verse_sanskrit: विश्वामित्रस्तथेत्युक्तवा तानृषीनभिपूज्य च । ततार सहितस्ताभ्यां सरितं सागरङ्गमाम् । । 1244 । ।
ramayan::707.verse_hindi: Be it so, said Viswamitra and paid respect to all those sages. And accompanied by them (Rama and Lakshmana), crossed the river flowing towards the sea.
ramayan::707.english_translation: Be it so, said Viswamitra and paid respect to all those sages. Accompanied by Rama and Lakshmana, he crossed the river flowing toward the sea.
ramayan::707.translation_literal: विश्वामित्रः (Viswamitra) / तथा (so) / इति (thus) / उक्त्वा (having said) / तान् (those) / ऋषीन् (sages) / अभिपूज्य (having honored) / च (and) / ततार (crossed) / सहितः (accompanied) / ताभ्याम् (by those two) / सरितम् (the river) / सागरङ्गमाम् (flowing to the sea)
ramayan::707.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::707.essence: Respect and forward motion can happen in the same breath.
ramayan::707.simple_meaning: Viswamitra respectfully accepts the sages' help, then crosses the river with Rama and Lakshmana.
ramayan::707.simple_insight: Sometimes progress is simple: accept help, show respect, and keep moving.
ramayan::707.detailed_meaning: The sages have arranged a boat and urged Viswamitra onward with Rama and Lakshmana. He answers with courtesy, honors them, and continues the journey across the river. It is a brief transition, not the main teaching.
ramayan::707.modern_relevance: You finally get the ride, the ticket, or the opening you needed. The right move is not to linger — say thank you, take the help, and continue.
ramayan::707.insight: It shows steady movement after receiving support, without fuss or delay.

ramayan::708.verse_sanskrit: ततश्शुश्राव वै शब्दमतिसंरम्भवर्धितम् । मध्यमागम्य तोयस्य सह राम:कनीयसा । । 1245 । ।
ramayan::708.verse_hindi: As they reached the midstream, Rama and his younger brother heard a sound greatly  augmented by the speed (of the river).
ramayan::708.english_translation: As they reached the midstream, Rama and his younger brother heard a sound greatly augmented by the speed of the river.
ramayan::708.translation_literal: ततस् (then) / शुश्राव (heard) / वै (indeed) / शब्दम् (sound) / अतिसंरम्भवर्धितम् (greatly increased by speed) / मध्यम् (middle) / आगम्य (having reached) / तोयस्य (of the water) / सह (with) / रामः (Rama) / कनीयसा (with the younger brother)
ramayan::708.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::708.essence: The crossing turns tense the moment the water speaks back.
ramayan::708.simple_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana hear a loud sound as their boat reaches the middle of the river.
ramayan::708.simple_insight: A small moment of travel can turn suddenly serious.
ramayan::708.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has just guided Rama and Lakshmana onto the river. As the boat reaches midstream, a strange, intensified sound rises from the water. The moment is only a scene-setting beat before Rama asks what is happening.
ramayan::708.modern_relevance: You are halfway across something important when a strange noise breaks the calm. Before you name the danger, you first notice that the calm has changed.
ramayan::708.insight: It keeps attention on the immediate sensory shift before the real question is asked.

ramayan::709.verse_sanskrit: अथ रामस्सरिन्मध्ये पप्रच्छ मुनिपुङ्गवम् । वारिणो भिद्यमानस्य किमयं तुमुलो ध्वनि: । । 1246 । ।
ramayan::709.verse_hindi: Rama enquired of Viswamitra, the best of sages, What is this tumultuous sound  bursting out of the waters?
ramayan::709.english_translation: Rama asked Viswamitra, the best of sages, “What is this loud, tumultuous sound breaking through the water?”
ramayan::709.translation_literal: अथ (then) / रामः (Rama) / सरित्-मध्ये (in the middle of the river) / पप्रच्छ (asked) / मुनि-पुङ्गवम् (the best of sages, Viswamitra) / वारिणः (of the water) / भिद्यमानस्य (being broken) / किम् (what) / अयम् (this) / तुमुलः (tumultuous) / ध्वनिः (sound)
ramayan::709.speaker: Rama
ramayan::709.essence: Stay alert enough to ask before you assume.
ramayan::709.simple_meaning: While crossing the river, Rama hears a strange roaring sound and asks Viswamitra what it is.
ramayan::709.simple_insight: Curiosity can be the first step toward understanding what feels threatening.
ramayan::709.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana are crossing a river with Viswamitra when a loud roar rises from the water. Rama, alert and unafraid, turns to the sage and asks what is happening. The verse sets up the explanation that follows.
ramayan::709.modern_relevance: You hear an unfamiliar crash while crossing a flooded road at night. Instead of panicking, you pause long enough to ask what is actually happening.
ramayan::709.insight: It models calm curiosity before reacting to danger.

ramayan::710.verse_sanskrit: राघवस्य वचश्श्रुत्वा कौतूहलसमन्वित: । कथयामास धर्मात्मा तस्य शब्दस्य निश्चयम् । । 1247 । ।
ramayan::710.verse_hindi: At the words of Rama filled with curiosity, the righteous (Viswamitra) narrated the true nature of that sound.
ramayan::710.english_translation: At the words of Rama, filled with curiosity, the righteous Viswamitra narrated the true nature of that sound.
ramayan::710.translation_literal: राघवस्य (of Rama) / वचः (words) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / कौतूहलसमन्वितः (filled with curiosity) / कथयामास (narrated) / धर्मात्मा (the righteous one) / तस्य (of that) / शब्दस्य (sound's) / निश्चयम् (true nature)
ramayan::710.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::710.essence: Curiosity becomes understanding when you ask the right person.
ramayan::710.simple_meaning: Viswamitra answers Rama’s question by explaining what the sound really is.
ramayan::710.simple_insight: Curiosity opens the door to understanding.
ramayan::710.detailed_meaning: Rama hears a strange roar in the river and asks Viswamitra what it is. The sage, pleased by Rama’s attention, explains the sound’s source. This verse is the bridge from wondering to learning.
ramayan::710.modern_relevance: You notice something strange, ask plainly, and get the real answer instead of guessing. That small act of curiosity can change the whole direction of a moment.
ramayan::710.insight: It shifts the mind from passive hearing to active questioning.

ramayan::711.verse_sanskrit: कैलासपर्वते राम मनसा निर्मितं सर: । ब्रह्मणा नरशार्दूल तेनेदं मानसं सर: । । 1248 । ।
ramayan::711.verse_hindi: O tiger among men, Rama. Brahma created out of his mind a lake on mount Kailas and so that lake is called Manasa (Sarovara).
ramayan::711.english_translation: O tiger among men, Rama. Brahma created out of his mind a lake on Mount Kailas, and that lake is called Manasa Sarovara.
ramayan::711.translation_literal: कैलासपर्वते (on Mount Kailasa) / राम (Rama) / मनसा (by mind) / निर्मितं (created) / सरः (lake) / ब्रह्मणा (by Brahma) / नरशार्दूल (O tiger among men) / तेनेदं (therefore this) / मानसं (Manasa) / सरः (lake)
ramayan::711.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::711.essence: A sacred place can be defined by the mind that brought it forth.
ramayan::711.simple_meaning: Brahma created Manasa Sarovara with his mind on Mount Kailash. That is why it is called Manasa Sarovara.
ramayan::711.simple_insight: Some sacred places are remembered not for distance, but for the meaning they carry.
ramayan::711.detailed_meaning: Rama asks Viswamitra about a strange sound coming from the waters. Viswamitra explains the origin of the sacred lake Manasa Sarovara on Mount Kailash. This verse is part of a flowing explanation, not a teaching on its own.
ramayan::711.modern_relevance: You hear a name tied to a place and want its story. The meaning behind a place often matters more than the place itself.
ramayan::711.insight: It shifts attention from the object to the story that gives it significance.

ramayan::712.verse_sanskrit: तस्मात्सुस्राव सरसस्सायोध्यामुपगूहते । सर प्रवृत्ता सरयू: पुण्या ब्रह्मसरश्च्युता । । 1249 । ।
ramayan::712.verse_hindi: This river which flows from Manasa Sarovara is, therefore, known as Sarayu. It
ramayan::712.english_translation: Therefore, the sacred Sarayu flowed from that lake and embraced Ayodhya.
ramayan::712.translation_literal: तस्मात् (therefore) / सुस्राव (flowed forth) / सरसः (from the lake) / सा (that) / अयोध्याम् (to Ayodhya) / उपगूहते (embraces) / सरः (lake) / प्रवृत्ता (set in motion) / सरयूः (Sarayu) / पुण्या (sacred) / ब्रह्मसरः (Brahma-lake) / च्युता (fallen/flowing down from)
ramayan::712.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::712.essence: A river’s holiness is traced back to its source.
ramayan::712.simple_meaning: The sacred Sarayu river is said to have flowed from Brahma's lake and reached Ayodhya. The verse gives the river's origin, not a teaching.
ramayan::712.simple_insight: Even a place becomes sacred through the source it comes from.
ramayan::712.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has just explained the origin of the strange sound Rama heard. He traces the sacred Sarayu back to Manasa Lake on Mount Kailasa, showing how this river came to embrace Ayodhya. The verse is part of that explanation, not a separate lesson.
ramayan::712.modern_relevance: You hear a place called home, but its meaning comes from where it began. A river, a family, a life — each carries its source with it.
ramayan::712.insight: It shifts attention from the visible river to the hidden origin that gives it meaning.

ramayan::713.verse_sanskrit: तस्यायमतुलश्शब्दो जाह्नवीमभिवर्तते । वारिसङ्क्षोभजो राम प्रणामं नियत:कुरु । । 12410 । ।
ramayan::713.verse_hindi: When Ganga approaches this river (Sarayu), there is a clash of waters and this great noise is produced. Rama, offer respectful salutations here, with a calm mind.
ramayan::713.english_translation: When Ganga approaches this river, the clash of waters creates this great sound. Rama, offer respectful salutations here with a composed mind.
ramayan::713.translation_literal: तस्य (of that) / अयम् (this) / अतुलः (matchless) / शब्दः (sound) / जाह्नवीम् (to Ganga) / अभिवर्तते (approaches) / वारि-सङ्क्षोभ-जः (born of the agitation of waters) / राम (Rama) / प्रणामम् (salutation) / नियतः (composed, restrained) / कुरु (do)
ramayan::713.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::713.essence: Respect starts with a calm mind, even before you take the next step.
ramayan::713.simple_meaning: The meeting of these rivers makes a powerful sound, and Rama is told to bow with a calm, disciplined mind.
ramayan::713.simple_insight: Even at a sacred crossing, reverence begins with inner composure.
ramayan::713.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing the confluence where the Sarayu meets the Ganga. The sound of the waters is said to be unmatched. Before Rama and Lakshmana cross, they are instructed to bow respectfully, showing that even movement through a holy place begins with restraint and reverence.
ramayan::713.modern_relevance: You walk into a place that deserves silence — a temple, a memorial, a hospital corridor — and your body knows before your mind does. Pause, steady yourself, and enter with respect.
ramayan::713.insight: It teaches you to meet sacred or serious moments with inward discipline, not casual haste.

ramayan::714.verse_sanskrit: ताभ्यां तु तावुभौ कृत्वा प्रणाममतिधार्मिकौ । तीरं दक्षिणमासाद्य जग्मतुर्लघुविक्रमौ । । 12411 । ।
ramayan::714.verse_hindi: Deeply religious (in nature) they both made obeisance to the two rivers and reached the southern bank and advanced with quick steps.
ramayan::714.english_translation: Then those two deeply righteous men bowed to the rivers and quickly reached the southern bank.
ramayan::714.translation_literal: ताभ्यां (by those two) / तु (then) / तावुभौ (both of them) / कृत्वा (having done) / प्रणामम् (obeisance) / अतिधार्मिकौ (very righteous) / तीरम् (bank) / दक्षिणम् (southern) / आसाद्य (having reached) / जग्मतुः (they went) / लघुविक्रमौ (of quick stride)
ramayan::714.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::714.essence: Even departure can be carried out with reverence.
ramayan::714.simple_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana bowed to the rivers and crossed to the south bank with quick steps.
ramayan::714.simple_insight: Even a crossing can be done with reverence and discipline.
ramayan::714.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana stand by the Sarayu and Ganga before entering the forest. They bow first, then cross to the southern bank. The moment is transitional, marking the end of Ayodhya's safety and the beginning of exile.
ramayan::714.modern_relevance: You leave a familiar place with one last look back, one silent thank-you, and the knowledge that life is about to change.
ramayan::714.insight: It shows how to move into hardship without bitterness or hesitation.

ramayan::715.verse_sanskrit: स वनं घोरसङ्काशं दृष्ट्वा नृपवरात्मज: । अविप्रहतमैक्ष्वाक: पप्रच्छ मुनिपुङ्गवम् । । 12412 । ।
ramayan::715.verse_hindi: He who was a descendent of Ikshvaku and son of the best of kings, (Dasaratha) having seen that untrodden and dreadful forest asked the foremost of the ascetics:
ramayan::715.english_translation: He who was a descendant of Ikshvaku and son of the best of kings, having seen that untrodden and dreadful forest, asked the foremost of the ascetics:
ramayan::715.translation_literal: स (he) / वनं (forest) / घोरसङ्काशं (resembling something dreadful) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / नृपवरात्मजः (son of the best of kings) / अविप्रहतम् (untrodden, untraversed) / ऐक्ष्वाकः (an Ikshvaku descendant) / पप्रच्छ (asked) / मुनिपुङ्गवम् (the foremost of ascetics)
ramayan::715.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::715.essence: A prince faces the unknown by asking before advancing.
ramayan::715.simple_meaning: Rama sees a wild, untouched forest and turns to the sage beside him with a question.
ramayan::715.simple_insight: Even the strongest traveler pauses before the unknown.
ramayan::715.detailed_meaning: Rama, the Ikshvaku prince, stands before a terrible, untouched forest with the sage at his side. The scene is not about teaching yet; it simply shows him noticing danger and seeking guidance before going further.
ramayan::715.modern_relevance: You reach the edge of a new job, a hard conversation, or a risky move. Before rushing in, you stop, look carefully, and ask someone wiser.
ramayan::715.insight: It shows the habit of pausing before entering danger and seeking counsel instead of pride.

ramayan::716.verse_sanskrit: अहो वनमिदं दुर्गं झिल्लिकागणनादितम् । भैरवैश्शपदै: पूर्णं शकुन्तैर्दारुणारुतै: । । 12413 । ।
ramayan::716.verse_hindi: What a wonder This inaccessible forest echoes with the (shrill) chirpings of crickets It is filled with ferocious beasts and birds producing fearful sounds.
ramayan::716.english_translation: What a wonder! This inaccessible forest echoes with the shrill chirping of crickets. It is filled with ferocious beasts and birds making fearful sounds.
ramayan::716.translation_literal: अहो (what a wonder) / वनम् (forest) / इदम् (this) / दुर्गम् (inaccessible, hard to pass) / झिल्लिकागणनादितम् (resounding with the chirping of crickets) / भैरवैः (with fearsome) / शपदैः (beasts) / पूर्णम् (filled) / शकुन्तैः (with birds) / दारुणारुतैः (with terrifying cries)
ramayan::716.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::716.essence: The forest announces hardship before the journey even begins.
ramayan::716.simple_meaning: The forest is wild, hard to cross, and full of unsettling sounds from insects, beasts, and birds.
ramayan::716.simple_insight: Some journeys begin by reminding you how small and exposed you really are.
ramayan::716.detailed_meaning: Rama has entered the forest after leaving the safety of Ayodhya. Looking around, he sees not beauty but danger: thick wilderness, harsh cries, and creatures everywhere. This verse deepens the scene before any teaching begins.
ramayan::716.modern_relevance: You step off a bus at dusk near a forest trail you should not have taken alone. Every sound feels louder than it should. The verse captures that first moment when the world feels untamed.
ramayan::716.insight: It frames the setting as hostile and uncertain, preparing the reader for the hardship ahead.

ramayan::717.verse_hindi: It resounds with the frightful shricks of various kinds of birds. Lions, tigers, boars and elephants prowl about.
ramayan::717.english_translation: It resounds with the frightful cries of various birds. Lions, tigers, boars, and elephants roam there.
ramayan::717.translation_literal: नानाप्रकारैः (of various kinds) / शकुनैः (by birds) / वाश्यद्भिः (crying out) / भैरवस्वनैः (with terrifying sounds) / सिंह-व्याघ्र-वराहैः (with lions, tigers, and boars) / च (and) / वारणैः (with elephants) / च (and) / उपशोभितम् (adorned)
ramayan::717.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::717.essence: The forest announces danger before anyone speaks.
ramayan::717.simple_meaning: The forest is full of terrifying bird calls and dangerous wild animals.
ramayan::717.simple_insight: The place feels hostile before anyone even takes a step inside.
ramayan::717.detailed_meaning: Rama is being led through a terrible forest during exile. He notices not beauty first, but danger: shrieking birds, predators, and elephants roaming freely. The verse adds to the growing sense that this is a place built to test endurance.
ramayan::717.modern_relevance: You walk into a place that feels wrong the moment you arrive — too loud, too sharp, too alert. Your body knows before your mind catches up.
ramayan::717.insight: It trains you to notice when an environment itself is working against calm and safety.

ramayan::718.verse_hindi: This forest jampacked with dhava, ashvakarna, kakubha, bilva, tinduka, patala and badari trees, how frightening this forest could be
ramayan::718.english_translation: This forest, crowded with dhava, ashvakarna, kakubha, bilva, tinduka, patala, and badari trees, is truly frightening.
ramayan::718.translation_literal: धवाश्वकर्णककुभैः (with dhava, ashvakarna, and kakubha trees) / बिल्वतिन्दुकपाटलैः (with bilva, tinduka, and patala trees) / सङ्कीर्णम् (crowded, densely packed) / बदरीभिः (with badari trees) / किन्नु (how indeed) / एतत् (this) / दारुणम् (terrifying, harsh) / वनम् (forest)
ramayan::718.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::718.essence: The forest itself becomes a warning before any enemy appears.
ramayan::718.simple_meaning: The forest is thick with many kinds of trees, and its density makes it feel harsh and frightening.
ramayan::718.simple_insight: Some places feel dangerous before anything even happens there.
ramayan::718.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana are moving through a wild forest with Vishwamitra. The sage points out the dense, harsh terrain around them, building the sense that this is no ordinary woodland but a place of danger and trial.
ramayan::718.modern_relevance: You step off a bus into a place you do not know, with narrow lanes, strange sounds, and no familiar landmark in sight. Your body knows before your mind does: this place asks for caution.
ramayan::718.insight: It frames the forest as a living obstacle, preparing the mind for the danger ahead.

ramayan::719.verse_sanskrit: तमुवाच महातेजा विश्वामित्रो महामुनि: । श्रूयतां वत्स काकुत्स्थ यस्यैतद्दारुणं वनम् । । 12416 । ।
ramayan::719.verse_hindi: Viswamitra, the great sage radiating energy addressing Rama said, O child of kakusthsa dynasty I shall tell you whose dreadful forest this is. Listen
ramayan::719.english_translation: Viswamitra, the great sage radiating energy, said to Rama, “Listen, child of the Kakustha line. I will tell you whose dreadful forest this is.”
ramayan::719.translation_literal: तम् (that one) / उवाच (said) / महातेजा (the greatly radiant one) / विश्वामित्रः (Viswamitra) / महामुनिः (great sage) / श्रूयताम् (let it be heard / listen) / वत्स (child) / काकुत्स्थ (O Kakustha) / यस्य (whose) / एतत् (this) / दारुणम् (dreadful) / वनम् (forest)
ramayan::719.speaker: Vishvamitra
ramayan::719.essence: The sage pauses the journey to reveal the forest’s hidden past.
ramayan::719.simple_meaning: Viswamitra tells Rama to listen, because he is about to explain the story of this frightening forest.
ramayan::719.simple_insight: Not every important moment is a teaching; some verses simply open the door to one.
ramayan::719.detailed_meaning: Rama and Viswamitra stand in a wild, fearsome forest filled with dangerous animals and ominous sounds. Rama has asked what place this is, and the sage begins to answer. This verse is the opening of an explanation, not the explanation itself.
ramayan::719.modern_relevance: You ask why a place feels heavy before you know its history. The answer often comes only after someone who remembers begins to speak.
ramayan::719.insight: It signals a shift from scene-setting to revelation, preparing you to receive the story behind the place.

ramayan::720.verse_sanskrit: एतौ जनपदौ स्फीतौ पूर्वमास्तां नरोत्तम । मलदाश्च करूशाश्च देवनिर्माणनिर्मितौ । । 12417 । ।
ramayan::720.verse_hindi: O best among men, formerly these two large and prosperous cities called Malada and Karusha built by celestial architects existed.
ramayan::720.english_translation: O best among men, formerly these two large and prosperous cities called Malada and Karusha, built by celestial architects, existed.
ramayan::720.translation_literal: एतौ (these two) / जनपदौ (kingdoms, regions) / स्फीतौ (prosperous, flourishing) / पूर्वम् (formerly, in the past) / आस्ताम् (existed) / नरोत्तम (O best among men) / मलदाः (Malada) / च (and) / करूशाः (Karusha) / च (and) / देवनिर्माणनिर्मितौ (made by celestial architects)
ramayan::720.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::720.essence: Even ruined places can carry the memory of former greatness.
ramayan::720.simple_meaning: These two prosperous regions, Malada and Karusha, once existed and were said to have been built by celestial architects.
ramayan::720.simple_insight: Some places are described with almost mythic grandeur before their fall or change.
ramayan::720.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra is leading Rama through a dangerous forest and explaining its earlier history. Before it became frightening and barren, this land held two prosperous regions, Malada and Karusha, said to have been built by celestial architects.
ramayan::720.modern_relevance: You walk through a neighborhood that used to be full of life, and the silence feels heavier because you can still imagine what was there before.
ramayan::720.insight: It shifts attention from the present ruin to the memory of what once made a place whole.

ramayan::721.verse_sanskrit: पुरा वृत्रवधे राम मलेन समभिप्लुतम् । क्षुधा चैव सहस्राक्षं ब्रह्महत्या समाविशत् । । 12418 । ।
ramayan::721.verse_hindi: O Rama, in ancient times after killing Vritrasura, Indra was overpowered by the sin of slaying a brahmin and was affected by impurity and hunger.
ramayan::721.english_translation: O Rama, in ancient times after killing Vritrasura, Indra was overpowered by impurity and hunger, and the burden of brahmahatya entered him.
ramayan::721.translation_literal: पुरा (in ancient times) / वृत्रवधे (in the slaying of Vritra) / राम (O Rama) / मलेन (by impurity) / समभिप्लुतम् (overwhelmed) / क्षुधा (by hunger) / चैव (and indeed) / सहस्राक्षम् (Indra, the thousand-eyed one) / ब्रह्महत्या (brahmahatya) / समाविशत् (entered)
ramayan::721.speaker: Visvamitra
ramayan::721.essence: Victory can still leave you burdened by what it took.
ramayan::721.simple_meaning: After Indra killed Vritra, he was struck by impurity, hunger, and the burden of brahmahatya.
ramayan::721.simple_insight: Even a great victory can leave a hidden stain and a heavy aftertaste.
ramayan::721.detailed_meaning: Visvamitra is explaining to Rama why this land is tainted. He reaches back to Indra’s ancient killing of Vritra and shows how even the king of the radiant beings was not untouched by the moral cost of violence.
ramayan::721.modern_relevance: You win the argument, get the promotion, or crush the competition — and still feel strangely unclean afterward. Some victories carry a residue that success cannot wash away.
ramayan::721.insight: It shifts attention from triumph to consequence, showing that power does not erase moral cost.

ramayan::722.verse_sanskrit: तमिन्द्रं स्नापयन् देवा ऋषयश्च तपोधना: । कलशैस्स्नापयामासुर्मलं चास्य प्रमोचयन् । । 12419 । ।
ramayan::722.verse_hindi: Devas and rishis endowed with the wealth of asceticism bathed Indra with the (consecrated) waters (brought from all rivers) from the pitchers and got him cleansed of impurities.
ramayan::722.english_translation: The devas and ascetics bathed Indra with consecrated water from pitchers and washed away his impurity.
ramayan::722.translation_literal: तम् (that) / इन्द्रम् (Indra) / स्नापयन् (bathing) / देवा: (the devas) / ऋषयः (sages) / च (and) / तपोधना: (wealthy in ascetic power) / कलशैः (with pitchers) / स्नापयामासुः (bathed) / मलम् (impurity) / च (and) / अस्य (his) / प्रमोचयन् (removing)
ramayan::722.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::722.essence: Purification is not symbolic here; it is something done carefully, together.
ramayan::722.simple_meaning: The devas and sages used sacred water to cleanse Indra and remove the impurity from him.
ramayan::722.simple_insight: Even great power can be stained, and cleansing still matters.
ramayan::722.detailed_meaning: The story pauses to describe a ritual act: the devas and ascetics gather sacred waters in pitchers and bathe Indra after his burden of impurity. It is a supporting detail in the larger tale of Malada and Karusha, not a complete teaching on its own.
ramayan::722.modern_relevance: After a long mistake, you may need more than apology — you may need a real cleansing, a reset that others help witness.
ramayan::722.insight: It reminds you that restoration can be communal, deliberate, and sacred in form.

ramayan::723.verse_sanskrit: इह भूम्यां मलं दत्वा दत्वा कारूशमेव च । शरीरजं महेन्द्रस्य ततो हर्षं प्रपेदिरे । । 12420 । ।
ramayan::723.verse_hindi: With the hunger and the taint and impurity from the body of Mahendra removed at this place, the devas rejoiced.
ramayan::723.english_translation: With the bodily impurity and hunger of Mahendra removed here on earth, the devas rejoiced.
ramayan::723.translation_literal: इह (here) / भूम्यां (on the earth) / मलं (impurity) / दत्वा (having given/removed) / दत्वा (having given/removed) / कारूशम् (taint, impurity) / एव (indeed) / च (and) / शरीरजम् (born of the body) / महेन्द्रस्य (of Mahendra/Indra) / ततः (then) / हर्षम् (joy) / प्रपेदिरे (they attained)
ramayan::723.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::723.essence: Restoration brings joy after impurity is removed.
ramayan::723.simple_meaning: The gods were glad after Indra’s bodily impurity and hunger were removed on earth.
ramayan::723.simple_insight: Even the mighty need cleansing before they can be restored.
ramayan::723.detailed_meaning: The story has shifted to Indra’s purification after the burden of brahmin-slaughter and hunger is ritually removed by the devas and sages. This line is a brief result: once his taint is lifted, the heavenly beings rejoice.
ramayan::723.modern_relevance: After a crisis, the room goes quiet and everyone waits to see whether the damage is really gone. Relief arrives only when the stain has been fully cleared.
ramayan::723.insight: It marks the completion of purification, not the struggle itself.

ramayan::724.verse_sanskrit: निर्मलो निष्करूशश्च शुचिरिंन्द्रो यदाभवत् । ददौ देशस्य सुप्रीतो वरं प्रभुरनुत्तमम् । । 12421 । ।
ramayan::724.verse_hindi: Cleansed of his impurities and his hunger gone, Indra once again became pure. Allpowerful Indra highly pleased gave an excellent boon to that region.
ramayan::724.english_translation: Cleansed of his impurities and his hunger gone, Indra once again became pure. All-powerful Indra highly pleased gave an excellent boon to that region.
ramayan::724.translation_literal: निर्मलः (pure, cleansed) / निष्करूशः (without hunger, without impurity) / च (and) / शुचिः (pure) / इन्द्रः (Indra) / यदा (when) / अभवत् (became) / ददौ (gave) / देशस्य (to the region) / सुप्रीतः (highly pleased) / वरम् (boon) / प्रभुः (the powerful one) / अनुत्तमम् (excellent, unsurpassed)
ramayan::724.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::724.simple_meaning: Indra was purified and satisfied, then he blessed the land with an excellent boon.
ramayan::724.simple_insight: Even a moment of cleansing can change what you leave behind for others.
ramayan::724.detailed_meaning: The devas and sages have just bathed Indra and removed the taint from his body. Once purified, Indra is pleased with the place where this happened and grants it a boon. The verse is a bridge in the story, showing the reward that follows the cleansing.
ramayan::724.modern_relevance: You leave a hard conversation lighter than you entered it. The relief in your own body can make you kinder to the room you walk out of.
ramayan::724.insight: It shifts attention from ritual cleansing to the blessing that follows gratitude and relief.

ramayan::725.verse_sanskrit: इमौ जनपदौ स्फीतौ ख्यातिं लोके गमिष्यत: । मलदाश्च करूशाश्च ममाङ्गमलधारिणौ । । 12422 । ।
ramayan::725.verse_hindi: Indra blessed the place saying, Having absorbed impurities of my body, let these places be extremely fertile and prosperous and let this be renowned throughout this world as Malada and Karusha.
ramayan::725.english_translation: Indra blessed the place, saying: 'These two lands will become fertile and famous in the world. They will be known as Malada and Karusha, because they bore the impurities of my body.'
ramayan::725.translation_literal: इमौ (these two) / जनपदौ (lands) / स्फीतौ (prosperous, fertile) / ख्यातिं (fame) / लोके (in the world) / गमिष्यत: (will attain) / मलदाः (Malada) / च (and) / करूशाः (Karusha) / च (and) / मम (my) / अङ्ग-मल-धारिणौ (bearers of the body's impurities)
ramayan::725.speaker: Indra
ramayan::725.essence: What carried the impurity is transformed into a source of abundance.
ramayan::725.simple_meaning: Indra names the two places and blesses them with fertility and fame because they carried away the impurities from his body.
ramayan::725.simple_insight: Even a difficult burden can become the reason a place is remembered with honor.
ramayan::725.detailed_meaning: After Indra is cleansed, he turns to the land that absorbed his bodily impurity. He does not dismiss it; he blesses it. The place is given new names and a future of prosperity, turning pollution into honor.
ramayan::725.modern_relevance: A place that once held your mess can still become the place you remember with gratitude. What felt unwanted may become the reason something new can grow there.
ramayan::725.insight: It shifts the mind from seeing burden as shame to seeing it as the seed of blessing.

ramayan::726.verse_sanskrit: साधु साध्विति तं देवा: पाकशासनमब्रुवन् । देशस्य पूजां तां दृष्ट्वा कृतां शक्रेण धीमता । । 12423 । ।
ramayan::726.verse_hindi: Having seen the honour bestowed on that land by the wise Indra, the gods said to him, Well done, Well done.
ramayan::726.english_translation: Having seen the honour bestowed on that land by the wise Indra, the gods said to him, Well done, Well done.
ramayan::726.translation_literal: साधु (well done) / साधु (well done) / इति (thus) / तम् (to him) / देवाः (the gods) / पाकशासनम् (Indra, slayer of Paka) / अब्रुवन् (said) / देशस्य (of the land) / पूजाम् (honour, reverence) / ताम् (that) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / कृताम् (done) / शक्रेण (by Indra) / धीमता (by the wise)
ramayan::726.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::726.essence: Wise action that blesses others deserves praise.
ramayan::726.simple_meaning: The gods praised Indra after seeing him honour the land and bless it with prosperity.
ramayan::726.simple_insight: Goodness that benefits others is noticed and praised.
ramayan::726.detailed_meaning: Indra has just purified himself and blessed the lands of Malada and Karusha so they may become fertile. Seeing that wise act, the gods applaud him. The verse is a brief reaction, not the main teaching.
ramayan::726.modern_relevance: You fix a place no one else wanted to care for, and the change spreads quietly. The real reward is often the respect of those who understand what you did.
ramayan::726.insight: It highlights that wise, generous action can restore a place and earn recognition.

ramayan::727.verse_sanskrit: एतौ जनपदौ स्फीतौ दीर्घकालमरिन्दम । मलदाश्च करूशाश्च मुदितौ धनधान्यत: । । 12424 । ।
ramayan::727.verse_hindi: O Destroyers of enemies these prosperous townships, Malada and Karusha looked cheerful with (bumper) crops and wealth for a long time.
ramayan::727.english_translation: O destroyer of enemies, the prosperous townships of Malada and Karusha remained cheerful for a long time, rich in crops and wealth.
ramayan::727.translation_literal: एतौ (these two) / जनपदौ (townships, regions) / स्फीतौ (prosperous, flourishing) / दीर्घकालम् (for a long time) / अरिन्दम (O destroyer of enemies) / मलदाः (Maladas) / च (and) / करूशाः (Karushas) / च (and) / मुदितौ (cheerful, delighted) / धनधान्यतः (with wealth and grain)
ramayan::727.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::727.essence: Peace and abundance can last only until disorder enters.
ramayan::727.simple_meaning: Malada and Karusha were prosperous for a long time, full of grain, wealth, and happiness.
ramayan::727.simple_insight: Some places carry a blessing that shows up in daily life: abundance, ease, and visible well-being.
ramayan::727.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing the land before Tataka’s arrival. After Indra’s blessing, Malada and Karusha flourish for years, rich in food and prosperity. This is a quiet setup verse, showing the peace that will soon be disturbed.
ramayan::727.modern_relevance: A neighborhood finally feels safe again: shops open, children play outside, and people start breathing easier. Then you remember how fragile that calm can be.
ramayan::727.insight: It sets up a before-and-after contrast, making the coming disruption feel sharper.

ramayan::728.verse_sanskrit: कस्यचित्त्वथ कालस्य यक्षी वै कामरूपिणी । बलं नागसहस्रस्य धारयन्ती तदा ह्यभूत् । । 12425 । । ताटका नाम भद्रं ते भार्या सुन्दस्य धीमत: । 2मारीचो राक्षस: पुत्रो यस्याश्शक्रपराक्रम: । । 12426 । ।
ramayan::728.verse_hindi: Then, after a lapse of several years, O gentle one a terrible yakshini by name Tataka,
ramayan::728.english_translation: Then, after some time, a yakshini who could take any form, and who bore the strength of a thousand elephants, appeared. A blessed one, she was Tataka, the wife of the wise Sunda, and the mother of the rakshasa Maricha, whose power was like Indra's.
ramayan::728.translation_literal: कस्यचित् (of some) / अथ (then) / कालस्य (of time) / यक्षी (female yaksha) / वै (indeed) / कामरूपिणी (able to assume any form) / बलम् (strength) / नागसहस्रस्य (of a thousand elephants) / धारयन्ती (bearing) / तदा (then) / हि (indeed) / अभूत् (became) / ताटका (Tataka) / नाम (by name) / भद्रम् ते (blessed be you) / भार्या (wife) / सुन्दस्य (of Sunda) / धीमतः (of the wise) / मारीचः (Maricha) / राक्षसः (rakshasa) / पुत्रः (son) / यस्याः (whose) / शक्रपराक्रमः (having Indra-like prowess)
ramayan::728.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::728.essence: The threat is not random; it has a lineage.
ramayan::728.simple_meaning: A powerful shapeshifting being named Tataka is introduced, along with her husband Sunda and their son Maricha. The verse sets up the threat that will soon trouble the land.
ramayan::728.simple_insight: Some dangers are born from old violence and grow into a family legacy.
ramayan::728.detailed_meaning: Valmiki pauses the story to introduce the force behind the coming disturbance: Tataka, a shapeshifting yakshini with immense strength, wife of Sunda and mother of Maricha. This is background, not the main teaching yet; it prepares the reader for Vishwamitra's warning and Rama's next test.
ramayan::728.modern_relevance: A problem shows up at work, but the real issue is the long history underneath it — the family pattern, the old resentment, the inherited habit no one named.
ramayan::728.insight: It shifts attention from the immediate threat to the larger source that created it.

ramayan::729.verse_sanskrit: वृत्तबाहुर्महावीर्यो विपुलास्य तनुर्महान् । राक्षसो भैरवाकारो नित्यं त्रासयते प्रजा: । । 12427 । ।
ramayan::729.verse_hindi: The arms (of Maricha) are round and strong. He is highly energetic. He has a large face and a huge body. In appearance, he is gigantic and possesses a dreadful form. That rakshasa always threatened the inhabitants.
ramayan::729.english_translation: Maricha has round, powerful arms, great energy, a broad face, and a huge body. He looks dreadful, and he always terrifies the people.
ramayan::729.translation_literal: वृत्तबाहुः (round-armed) / महावीर्यः (greatly powerful) / विपुलास्य (broad-faced) / तनुः (bodied) / महान् (great, huge) / राक्षसः (rakshasa) / भैरवाकारः (of dreadful form) / नित्यम् (always) / त्रासयते (terrifies) / प्रजा: (the people)
ramayan::729.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::729.essence: Fear becomes a way of life when a threat never stops.
ramayan::729.simple_meaning: Maricha is being described as a terrifying, powerful demon who constantly frightens the local people.
ramayan::729.simple_insight: Some threats are not dramatic once — they wear people down by being constant.
ramayan::729.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is still setting the scene in the forest regions of Malada and Karusha. Before the real conflict begins, he describes the kind of being Rama and Lakshmana are about to confront: huge, fierce, and a source of fear for the people.
ramayan::729.modern_relevance: A neighborhood starts changing when one intimidating presence makes everyone shorten their walk home and lower their voice. Fear spreads long before any direct attack.
ramayan::729.insight: It frames danger as a continuing pressure on ordinary life, not a single event.

ramayan::730.verse_sanskrit: इमौ जनपदौ नित्यं विनाशयति राघव । मलदांश्च करूशांश्च ताटका दुष्टचारिणी । । 12428 । ।
ramayan::730.verse_hindi: O Rama that wicked than Tataka carried on her depredations at regular intervals in these locations, Malada and Karusha.
ramayan::730.english_translation: O Rama, that wicked Tataka regularly devastates these two regions, Malada and Karusha.
ramayan::730.translation_literal: इमौ (these two) / जनपदौ (regions) / नित्यं (always) / विनाशयति (destroys) / राघव (O Rama) / मलदांश्च (and Malada) / करूशांश्च (and Karusha) / ताटका (Tataka) / दुष्टचारिणी (wicked-doing)
ramayan::730.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::730.essence: Repeated harm turns a local threat into an immediate duty.
ramayan::730.simple_meaning: Tataka is repeatedly destroying the two regions named Malada and Karusha.
ramayan::730.simple_insight: A threat becomes urgent when its damage is repeated and public.
ramayan::730.detailed_meaning: Vishvamitra is describing Tataka to Rama before asking for help. He is not teaching a principle here, only building the case: this being keeps ravaging the countryside, so action is needed now.
ramayan::730.modern_relevance: A neighborhood keeps getting hit by the same vandalism, and everyone knows the pattern. Before anyone talks theory, the damage itself is the warning.
ramayan::730.insight: It frames the danger as ongoing harm that demands intervention, not debate.

ramayan::731.verse_sanskrit: सेयं पन्थानमावृत्य वसत्यध्यर्धयोजने । अत एव न गन्तव्यं ताटकाया वनं यत: । । 12429 । ।
ramayan::731.verse_hindi: Tataka lives at a distance of one and a half yojanas from here obstructing the path.
ramayan::731.english_translation: Tataka lives one and a half yojanas away, blocking the path. So you should not go into Tataka's forest.
ramayan::731.translation_literal: सेयं (this one) / पन्थानम् (the path) / आवृत्य (blocking) / वसति (lives) / अध्यर्धयोजने (at one and a half yojanas) / अतः (therefore) / एव (indeed) / न (not) / गन्तव्यम् (to be gone) / ताटकाया (of Tataka) / वनम् (forest) / यतः (because)
ramayan::731.speaker: Vishwamitra
ramayan::731.essence: A blocked path must be seen clearly before it can be cleared.
ramayan::731.simple_meaning: Tataka lives nearby and blocks the route, so the forest ahead is not safe to enter.
ramayan::731.simple_insight: Some places are dangerous because of the force that claims them.
ramayan::731.detailed_meaning: Vishwamitra is guiding Rama and Lakshmana through a region terrorized by Tataka. He points out that her forest lies close by and that she obstructs the path, setting up the urgent request for Rama to remove the threat.
ramayan::731.modern_relevance: You know that one route home where the streetlights fail and everyone warns you to avoid it after dark. The danger is not abstract — it has a name, a place, and a pattern.
ramayan::731.insight: It frames danger as a real obstacle that must be recognised before action can begin.

ramayan::732.verse_sanskrit: स्वबाहुबलमाश्रित्य जहीमां दुष्टचारिणीम् । मन्नियोगादिमं देशं कुरु निष्कण्टकं पुन: । । 12430 । ।
ramayan::732.verse_hindi: By  the strength of your arms slay this one of wicked deeds. Comply with my orders and make this country safe (and habitable).
ramayan::732.english_translation: By the strength of your arms slay this one of wicked deeds. Comply with my orders and make this country safe and habitable again.
ramayan::732.translation_literal: स्वबाहुबलम् (your own arm-strength) / आश्रित्य (taking refuge in) / जही (slay) / इमाम् (this) / दुष्टचारिणीम् (one of wicked conduct) / मन्नियोगात् (by my command) / इमम् (this) / देशम् (country) / कुरु (make) / निष्कण्टकम् (free of thorns, safe) / पुनः (again)
ramayan::732.speaker: Vishwamitra
ramayan::732.essence: Strength matters when it restores safety, not when it merely proves itself.
ramayan::732.simple_meaning: Vishwamitra asks Rama to rely on his own strength, kill the dangerous woman, and restore the region to safety.
ramayan::732.simple_insight: Real strength is not display; it is the courage to protect what others cannot.
ramayan::732.detailed_meaning: Vishwamitra has shown Rama the danger of Tataka, who has made this region unsafe. Now he stops explaining and gives the first hard command: use your own power, remove the threat, and reclaim the land for ordinary life.
ramayan::732.modern_relevance: A neighborhood has been ruled by one bully for years, and everyone has learned to avoid the street after dark. Someone finally says, 'Enough — use what you have and make this place livable again.'
ramayan::732.insight: It shifts action from caution to decisive protection of the vulnerable.

ramayan::733.verse_sanskrit: न हि कश्चिदिमं देशं शक्नोत्यागन्तुमीदृशम् । यक्षिण्या घोरया राम उत्सादितमसह्यया । । 12431 । ।
ramayan::733.verse_hindi: O Rama none dare approach this country ravaged by such dreadful, intolerable yakshini.
ramayan::733.english_translation: O Rama, no one can enter this land, for it has been ruined by that dreadful, unbearable yakshini.
ramayan::733.translation_literal: न हि (indeed not) / कश्चिद् (anyone) / इमम् (this) / देशम् (land) / शक्नोति (is able) / आगन्तुम् (to come) / ईदृशम् (such) / यक्षिण्या (by the yakshini) / घोरया (dreadful) / राम (Rama) / उत्सादितम् (ruined) / असह्यया (unbearable)
ramayan::733.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::733.essence: A ruined place warns you that danger has already taken root.
ramayan::733.simple_meaning: No one can enter this land because a terrible yakshini has devastated it.
ramayan::733.simple_insight: Some places become dangerous enough that even courage has to pause.
ramayan::733.detailed_meaning: Vishvamitra is explaining the danger of the forest to Rama and Lakshmana. He has already named Tataka as the threat and now shows the scale of her destruction: this land is not merely wild, but made unfit for safe passage.
ramayan::733.modern_relevance: You walk into a place where everyone has learned to stay alert, and you feel the tension before anyone speaks. Some environments carry danger in the air itself.
ramayan::733.insight: It shifts attention from curiosity about the forest to the real cost of leaving a threat unchecked.

ramayan::734.verse_sanskrit: एतत्ते सर्वमाख्यातं यथैतद्दारुणं वनम् । यक्ष्या चोत्सादितं सर्वमद्यापि न निवर्तते । । 12432 । ।
ramayan::734.verse_hindi: You have been told the manner in which this fierce forest is entirely ruined by that cruel yakshini. Tell now she has not left this place.
ramayan::734.english_translation: Everything about this fierce forest has been told to you. It was ruined by that yakshini, and even now she has not gone away.
ramayan::734.translation_literal: एतत् (this) / ते (to you) / सर्वम् (everything) / आख्यातम् (has been told) / यथा (how) / एतत् (this) / दारुणम् (fierce) / वनम् (forest) / यक्ष्या (by the yakshini) / च (and) / उत्सादितम् (destroyed) / सर्वम् (entirely) / अद्यापि (even now) / न (not) / निवर्तते (she departs/withdraws)
ramayan::734.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::734.essence: The danger is still here, so the response cannot wait.
ramayan::734.simple_meaning: The forest has been laid waste by a terrible yakshini, and she still remains here.
ramayan::734.simple_insight: Some dangers do not pass on their own; you have to face them directly.
ramayan::734.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra is explaining the ruined forest to Rama before asking for help. He has already described the threat, and this line adds urgency: the destructive yakshini is still present, so the danger is immediate, not historical.
ramayan::734.modern_relevance: You keep hearing the same warning about a place, a person, or a pattern — and then you see it is still there. The problem was never in the past; it is still active now.
ramayan::734.insight: It sharpens attention to a threat that remains present, not one that has already ended.

ramayan::735.verse_sanskrit: अथ तस्याप्रमेयस्य मुनेर्वचनमुत्तमम् । श्रुत्वा पुरुषशार्दूल: प्रत्युवाच शुभां गिरम् । । 1251 । ।
ramayan::735.verse_hindi: On hearing the excellent words of Viswamitra, a sage with unimaginable faculty. Rama, the tiger among men (Rama) replied in a, gentle voice:
ramayan::735.english_translation: On hearing the excellent words of Viswamitra, a sage with unimaginable faculty, Rama, the tiger among men, replied in a gentle voice:
ramayan::735.translation_literal: अथ (then) / तस्य (his) / अप्रमेयस्य (immeasurable) / मुनेः (of the sage) / वचनम् (words) / उत्तमम् (excellent) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / पुरुषशार्दूलः (tiger among men) / प्रत्युवाच (replied) / शुभाम् (gentle / auspicious) / गिरम् (speech)
ramayan::735.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::735.essence: Strength shows itself first in the way you answer.
ramayan::735.simple_meaning: Rama listens carefully to Viswamitra and answers him calmly and respectfully.
ramayan::735.simple_insight: Real strength can sound gentle when it is secure.
ramayan::735.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has just explained the danger of the ruined forest and the fierce yakshini haunting it. Rama hears the sage's words fully, then answers without arrogance or fear. The moment shows his discipline, respect, and readiness before the real challenge begins.
ramayan::735.modern_relevance: Someone gives you hard feedback, and you do not rush to defend yourself. You listen all the way through, then answer with calm strength instead of pride.
ramayan::735.insight: It teaches you to meet danger with composure before taking action.

ramayan::736.verse_sanskrit: अल्पवीर्या यदा यक्षा श्श्रूयन्ते मुनिपुङ्गव । कथन्नागसहस्रस्य धारयत्यबला बलम् । । 1252 । ।
ramayan::736.verse_hindi: O best of ascetics, I have heard the yakshas possess little prowess. How can a woman who is by gender weak possess the strength of a thousand elephants?
ramayan::736.english_translation: O best of ascetics, I have heard the yakshas possess little prowess. How can a woman who is by gender weak possess the strength of a thousand elephants?
ramayan::736.translation_literal: अल्पवीर्या (of little prowess) / यदा (when) / यक्षा (yakshas) / श्रूयन्ते (are heard of) / मुनिपुङ्गव (O best among sages) / कथम् (how) / नागसहस्रस्य (of a thousand elephants) / धारयति (possesses) / अबला (the weak woman) / बलम् (strength)
ramayan::736.speaker: Rama
ramayan::736.essence: Appearances of weakness can conceal overwhelming force.
ramayan::736.simple_meaning: Rama asks how a woman, who is usually considered weak, could carry the strength of a thousand elephants, especially since yakshas are said to be of little prowess.
ramayan::736.simple_insight: Even a small-seeming threat can hide impossible force.
ramayan::736.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has just described a ruined forest and the danger haunting it. Rama listens carefully and questions the contradiction: if yakshas are usually weak, how can this woman wield such enormous strength? The exchange sets up Viswamitra's explanation of a boon.
ramayan::736.modern_relevance: You hear a warning about someone and still cannot quite believe the scale of harm. Then one detail breaks the pattern, and you realise the threat is larger than it looked.
ramayan::736.insight: It trains the mind to question appearances before assuming power is where it seems to be.

ramayan::737.verse_sanskrit: विश्वामित्रोऽब्रवीद्वाक्यं शृण येन बलोत्तरा । वरदानकृतं वीर्यं धारयत्यबला बलम् । । 1253 । ।
ramayan::737.verse_hindi: Viswamitra said, Listen, how she acquired the prowess and strength by virtue of a boon she received.
ramayan::737.english_translation: Viswamitra said, “Listen, I will tell you how she gained strength greater than her own by a boon.”
ramayan::737.translation_literal: विश्वामित्रः (Viswamitra) / अब्रवीत् (said) / वाक्यम् (speech) / शृणु (listen) / येन (by which) / बलोत्तरा (stronger in strength) / वरदानकृतम् (made by a boon) / वीर्यम् (prowess) / धारयति (possesses) / अबला (a woman) / बलम् (strength)
ramayan::737.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::737.essence: Her strength came from a hidden blessing, not from appearance.
ramayan::737.simple_meaning: Viswamitra begins explaining the source of a woman's unusual strength: it came from a boon, not from ordinary power.
ramayan::737.simple_insight: Strength can come from a cause you cannot see at first.
ramayan::737.detailed_meaning: Rama has asked how a seemingly weak woman could hold such power. Viswamitra answers by opening the story behind her strength, pointing to a boon that changed what she could do. The verse is a bridge into the explanation.
ramayan::737.modern_relevance: You meet someone calm and unshaken, and only later learn what they survived. The visible person is not the whole story; hidden causes often explain visible strength.
ramayan::737.insight: It shifts you from judging by appearance to asking what formed a person’s power.

ramayan::738.verse_sanskrit: पूर्वमासीन्महायक्षस्सुकेतुर्नाम वीर्यवान् । अनपत्यश्शुभाचारस्स च तेपे महत्तप: । । 1254 । ।
ramayan::738.verse_hindi: In the past there was a powerful and great yaksha by name Suketu. He had no  children. So he performed an intense penance following virtuous practices.
ramayan::738.english_translation: In the past there was a powerful great yaksha named Suketu. He had no children, so he performed severe austerities while living by virtuous conduct.
ramayan::738.translation_literal: पूर्वम् (in the past) / आसीत् (there was) / महायक्षः (great yaksha) / सुकेतुः (Suketu) / नाम (by name) / वीर्यवान् (powerful) / अनपत्यः (childless) / शुभाचारः (of virtuous conduct) / सः (he) / च (and) / तेपे (performed austerity) / महत् (great) / तपः (austerity)
ramayan::738.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::738.essence: A hidden ache can become the force behind severe discipline.
ramayan::738.simple_meaning: Suketu was a powerful yaksha who had no children. Because of that, he turned to intense austerity and virtuous living.
ramayan::738.simple_insight: Even longing can become discipline when it is met with restraint and effort.
ramayan::738.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra is explaining Tataka’s origin. Before the boon and the curse, there was Suketu, a strong yaksha grieved by childlessness. His austerity sets up the family line that will soon shape the conflict around Tataka.
ramayan::738.modern_relevance: A person who cannot bear the silence of an empty home or an unanswered hope may throw themselves into work, prayer, or discipline to fill the ache.
ramayan::738.insight: It shows how a private lack can drive a person into sustained self-discipline.

ramayan::739.verse_sanskrit: पितामहस्तु सुप्रीतस्तस्य यक्षपते स्तदा । कन्यारत्नं ददौ राम ताटकां नाम नामत: । । 1255 । ।
ramayan::739.verse_hindi: Rama the grandsire Brahma was highly gratified and granted to the king of yakshas, the gem of a daughter by name known asTataka.
ramayan::739.english_translation: The grandsire Brahma, greatly pleased, gave the king of the yakshas a jewel-like daughter named Tataka.
ramayan::739.translation_literal: पितामहः (the grandsire) / तु (indeed) / सुप्रीतः (greatly pleased) / तस्य (to him) / यक्षपतेः (of the king of the yakshas) / तदा (then) / कन्यारत्नम् (a jewel among daughters) / ददौ (gave) / राम (Rama) / ताटकाम् (Tataka) / नाम (by name) / नामतः (by name)
ramayan::739.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::739.essence: A granted boon can carry the seed of later ruin.
ramayan::739.simple_meaning: Brahma was pleased with Suketu's austerity and granted him a daughter named Tataka.
ramayan::739.simple_insight: A blessing can become a burden when power is given without wisdom.
ramayan::739.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra is explaining Tataka's origin to Rama. Suketu's austerity moved Brahma, who granted him a daughter instead of the son he wanted. This verse is part of the setup for Tataka's later threat, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::739.modern_relevance: You can get exactly what you asked for and still not get what you needed. A gift, a promotion, or a child can arrive carrying a future problem no one foresaw.
ramayan::739.insight: It shifts attention from receiving blessings to understanding their consequences.

ramayan::740.verse_sanskrit: ददौ नागसहस्रस्य बलं चास्या: पितामह: । नत्वेव पुत्रं यक्षाय ददौ ब्रह्मा महायशा: । । 1256 । ।
ramayan::740.verse_hindi: The illustrious grandsire Brahma granted her the strength of a thousand elephants,
ramayan::740.english_translation: The illustrious grandsire Brahma granted her the strength of a thousand elephants, but did not grant the yaksha a son.
ramayan::740.translation_literal: ददौ (granted) / नागसहस्रस्य (of a thousand elephants) / बलम् (strength) / च (and) / अस्याः (to her) / पितामहः (the grandsire) / न (not) / तु (but) / एव (indeed) / पुत्रम् (a son) / यक्षाय (to the yaksha) / ददौ (granted) / ब्रह्मा (Brahma) / महायशाः (the greatly renowned)
ramayan::740.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::740.essence: Strength arrived, but the real longing was left untouched.
ramayan::740.simple_meaning: Brahma gave Tataka enormous strength, but did not give Suketu a son.
ramayan::740.simple_insight: Power can be granted without the blessing you actually wanted.
ramayan::740.detailed_meaning: Suketu has performed severe austerity, and Brahma has already granted his wish in part. He receives a daughter, Tataka, and she is given immense strength. But the deeper longing for a son remains unfulfilled, setting up the family line that follows.
ramayan::740.modern_relevance: You finally get the promotion, the money, or the recognition — and still feel the missing piece. Getting power does not always heal the original ache.
ramayan::740.insight: It separates outward success from the deeper absence that still drives a story forward.

ramayan::741.verse_sanskrit: तां तु जातां विवर्धन्तीं रूपयौवनशालिनीम् । झर्झपुत्राय सुन्दाय ददौ भार्यां यशस्विनीम् । । 1257 । ।
ramayan::741.verse_hindi: As she grew up, glowing with youth and beauty she was given in marriage to Sunda, son of Jharjha.
ramayan::741.english_translation: As she grew up, glowing with youth and beauty, she was given in marriage to Sunda, son of Jharjha.
ramayan::741.translation_literal: ताम् (her) / तु (indeed) / जाताम् (having been born) / विवर्धन्तीम् (growing up) / रूप-यौवन-शालिनीम् (endowed with beauty and youth) / झर्झ-पुत्राय (to the son of Jharjha) / सुन्दाय (to Sunda) / ददौ (gave) / भार्याम् (as wife) / यशस्विनीम् (the illustrious one)
ramayan::741.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::741.essence: A marriage is recorded because the next generation is coming.
ramayan::741.simple_meaning: The girl grew into a beautiful young woman and was married to Sunda.
ramayan::741.simple_insight: Some verses simply move the story forward, showing how one family line continues.
ramayan::741.detailed_meaning: Brahma has just granted a yaksha daughter extraordinary strength and blessing. This verse simply notes her growth and marriage to Sunda, setting up the later birth of Maricha. It is scene-setting, not a teaching.
ramayan::741.modern_relevance: A family story moves ahead quietly: a child grows, marries, and the next generation begins before anyone notices.
ramayan::741.insight: It marks a lineage step that leads into the next event, not a moral statement.

ramayan::742.verse_sanskrit: कस्यचित्त्वथ कालस्य यक्षी पुत्रमजायत । मारीचं नाम दुर्धर्षं यश्शापाद्राक्षसोऽभवत् । । 1258 । ।
ramayan::742.verse_hindi: After some time that yakshini gave birth to an unassailable son by name Maricha. Because of a curse, he became a rakshasa (though born of yaksha parentage).
ramayan::742.english_translation: After some time that yakshini gave birth to an unassailable son named Maricha. Because of a curse, he became a rakshasa despite his yaksha birth.
ramayan::742.translation_literal: कस्यचित् (of some) / अथ (then) / कालस्य (of time) / यक्षी (the yakshini) / पुत्रम् (a son) / अजायत (gave birth) / मारीचम् (Maricha) / नाम (by name) / दुर्धर्षम् (unassailable) / यः (who) / शापात् (from a curse) / राक्षसः (a rakshasa) / अभवत् (became)
ramayan::742.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::742.essence: A cursed beginning can turn strength into menace.
ramayan::742.simple_meaning: A yakshini gives birth to Maricha, and a curse turns him into a rakshasa.
