ramayan::742.simple_insight: Birth does not fix a life; a curse can twist even a noble beginning.
ramayan::742.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is introducing Maricha’s origin after Tataka’s line has already been traced. The verse explains why this powerful figure is not simply a yaksha-born being but a cursed rakshasa, setting up the danger that will soon touch Agastya and Rama’s path.
ramayan::742.modern_relevance: Someone can begin life with every advantage and still become shaped by a wound, a curse, or a bad inheritance. Origins matter, but they do not tell the whole story.
ramayan::742.insight: It shifts attention from pedigree to the forces that deform character.

ramayan::743.verse_sanskrit: सुन्दे तु निहते राम सागस्त्यमृषिसत्तमम् । ताटका सह पुत्रेण प्रधर्षयितुमिच्छति । । 1259 । ।
ramayan::743.verse_hindi: O Rama when Sunda died Tataka along with her son wanted to attack Agastya, the best of sages.
ramayan::743.english_translation: O Rama, when Sunda was killed, Tataka, along with her son, wanted to attack Agastya, the best of sages.
ramayan::743.translation_literal: सुन्दे (when Sunda) / तु (indeed) / निहते (having been killed) / राम (O Rama) / सागस्त्यमृषिसत्तमम् (Agastya, the best of sages) / ताटका (Tataka) / सह (along with) / पुत्रेण (with her son) / प्रधर्षयितुम् (to attack) / इच्छति (wishes)
ramayan::743.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::743.essence: Anger does not end with one loss; it searches for another victim.
ramayan::743.simple_meaning: After Sunda is killed, Tataka and her son turn their anger toward Agastya and plan to attack him.
ramayan::743.simple_insight: Unchecked anger keeps moving until it finds a new target.
ramayan::743.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is setting up the origin of Tataka's hostility. After Sunda's death, she and her son Maricha turn against Agastya, and this chain of violence leads directly to the curse that follows in the next verse.
ramayan::743.modern_relevance: A family argument ends, but the bitterness does not. It looks for a new face, a new message, a new room to enter.
ramayan::743.insight: It shows how resentment survives the original injury and spreads into fresh harm.

ramayan::744.verse_sanskrit: भक्षार्थं जातसंरम्भा गर्जन्ती साभ्यधावत । 0आपतन्तीं तु तां दृष्ट्वा अगस्त्यो भगवानृषि: । । 12510 । । राक्षसत्वं भजस्वेति मारीचं व्याजहार स: । 1
ramayan::744.verse_hindi: Roaring, she rushed with excitement to devour him. The venerable  rishi Agastya saw her approaching him and cursed Maricha to assume form of a demoness.
ramayan::744.english_translation: Roaring, she rushed forward with the intent to devour him. Seeing her charge, the venerable sage Agastya spoke to Maricha: "Assume the form of a demon."
ramayan::744.translation_literal: भक्षार्थम् (for eating) / जातसंरम्भा (aroused with fury) / गर्जन्ती (roaring) / सा (she) / अभ्यधावत (rushed toward) / आपतन्तीम् (approaching) / ताम् (her) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / अगस्त्यः (Agastya) / भगवान् (venerable) / ऋषिः (sage) / राक्षसत्वम् (demonhood) / भजस्व (assume) / इति (thus) / मारीचम् (to Maricha) / व्याजहार (spoke)
ramayan::744.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::744.essence: Rage rushes forward, and the response becomes a curse.
ramayan::744.simple_meaning: Tataka charges at Agastya in a rage, and Agastya responds with a curse that turns Maricha into a demon-form.
ramayan::744.simple_insight: Violence and curse move faster than reason here.
ramayan::744.detailed_meaning: Tataka, furious and hungry for destruction, rushes toward Agastya. The sage does not meet her with debate; he answers with a curse that changes Maricha's fate. This is part of the larger origin story behind the threat Rama will later face.
ramayan::744.modern_relevance: A small insult online can turn into a full-blown attack in minutes. Once rage is in motion, the response often hardens the whole situation instead of cooling it.
ramayan::744.insight: It shows how quickly anger can trigger consequences that shape an entire future conflict.

ramayan::745.verse_sanskrit: अगस्त्य: परमक्रुद्धस्ताटकामपि शप्तवान् । । 12511 । । पुरुषादी महायक्षी विरूपा विकृतानना । इदं रूपं विहायाथ दारुणं रूपमस्तु ते । । 12512 । ।
ramayan::745.verse_hindi: Mighty angry, Agastya cursed Tataka saying, Abandon this form of a great yakshini and assume the terrible figure of a rakshasi, a cannibal with distorted appearance and a hideous countenance.
ramayan::745.english_translation: Mighty angry, Agastya cursed Tataka: abandon this form of a great yakshini and take on a terrible, distorted, hideous form.
ramayan::745.translation_literal: अगस्त्यः (Agastya) / परमक्रुद्धः (greatly enraged) / ताटकाम् (Tataka) / अपि (also) / शप्तवान् (cursed) / पुरुषादी (man-eating) / महायक्षी (great yakshini) / विरूपा (deformed) / विकृतानना (distorted-faced) / इदम् (this) / रूपम् (form) / विहाय (abandoning) / अथ (then) / दारुणम् (terrible) / रूपम् (form) / अस्तु (let it be) / ते (for you)
ramayan::745.speaker: Agastya
ramayan::745.essence: Anger turns a confrontation into a lasting curse.
ramayan::745.simple_meaning: Agastya curses Tataka to lose her beautiful form and become a frightening, deformed man-eater.
ramayan::745.simple_insight: Cruel power can reshape a life into its own ugliness.
ramayan::745.detailed_meaning: Tataka rushes toward Agastya in fury. He does not merely stop her; he curses her transformation, stripping away her yakshini form and fixing her into a monstrous shape. The verse marks the moment her violence turns into a lasting curse.
ramayan::745.modern_relevance: A heated exchange can leave a mark that outlives the argument. One furious decision can harden someone’s life into something harsher than it was before.
ramayan::745.insight: It shows how violence and rage can escalate into irreversible damage, not just immediate conflict.

ramayan::746.verse_sanskrit: सैषा शापकृतामर्षा ताटका क्रोधमूर्छिता । देशमुत्सादयत्येनमगस्त्यचरितं शुभम् । । 12513 । ।
ramayan::746.verse_hindi: Enraged at the curse, senseless, Tataka with anger, has been ravaging this sacred land when Agastya walked.
ramayan::746.english_translation: Enraged by the curse, Tataka, blinded by anger, is destroying this sacred land where Agastya once walked.
ramayan::746.translation_literal: सा एषा (this very one) / शापकृतामर्षा (made furious by the curse) / ताटका (Tataka) / क्रोधमूर्छिता (faint with anger) / देशम् (the land) / उत्सादयति (is destroying) / एनम् (this) / अगस्त्यचरितम् (walked by Agastya) / शुभम् (auspicious)
ramayan::746.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::746.essence: A curse-fed rage begins destroying everything around it.
ramayan::746.simple_meaning: Tataka, furious over Agastya's curse, is now wrecking the sacred region associated with him.
ramayan::746.simple_insight: Unchecked rage turns a wounded being into a force that poisons everything nearby.
ramayan::746.detailed_meaning: Agastya has just cursed Tataka after she rushed at him to devour him. Now the narration shows the result: she does not calm down, but lashes out against the whole sacred region tied to his presence. The verse prepares the case for Rama to intervene.
ramayan::746.modern_relevance: A person gets humiliated in public and starts taking it out on everyone around them. The original injury is real, but the damage spreads far beyond it.
ramayan::746.insight: It shows how anger can expand from one wound into widespread destruction.

ramayan::747.verse_sanskrit: एनां राघव दुर्वृत्तां यक्षीं परमदारुणाम् । गोब्राह्मणहितार्थाय जहि दुष्टपराक्रमाम् । । 12514 । ।
ramayan::747.verse_hindi: O Rama for the welfare of cows and brahmins, slay this yakshini who is wicked, extremely cruel and possessing vile prowess.
ramayan::747.english_translation: O Rama, for the welfare of cows and brahmins, slay this wicked yakshini of terrible cruelty and vile strength.
ramayan::747.translation_literal: एनां (this) / राघव (O Rama) / दुर्वृत्ताम् (wicked) / यक्षीम् (yakshini) / परमदारुणाम् (extremely terrible) / गोब्राह्मणहितार्थाय (for the welfare of cows and brahmins) / जहि (slay) / दुष्टपराक्रमाम् (of vile prowess)
ramayan::747.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::747.essence: Protecting the innocent can require decisive action against cruelty.
ramayan::747.simple_meaning: Rama is urged to kill Tataka because she is harming the land and threatening the protectors of order.
ramayan::747.simple_insight: Some dangers are not personal conflicts; they are duties that must be faced for the sake of others.
ramayan::747.detailed_meaning: Agastya has already shown why Tataka is a menace: cursed, furious, and devastating the sacred region. Now the request turns to Rama alone, asking him to remove the threat for the protection of cows, brahmins, and the land itself.
ramayan::747.modern_relevance: A neighborhood starts changing because one violent person keeps everyone afraid. You do not want a fight, but you also know silence is not kindness.
ramayan::747.insight: It frames intervention as protection of the vulnerable, not a display of force.

ramayan::748.verse_sanskrit: न ह्येनां शापसम्स्पृष्टां कश्चिदुत्सहते पुमान् । निहन्तुं त्रिषु लोकेषु त्वामृते रघुनन्दन । । 12515 । ।
ramayan::748.verse_hindi: O son of Raghus dynasty she is maligned by the curse, and so not a single man in the three worlds except you, is  competent to slay this yakshini.
ramayan::748.english_translation: O son of the Raghu dynasty, except for you, no man in the three worlds is capable of killing her, because she is touched by a curse.
ramayan::748.translation_literal: न हि (indeed not) / एनाम् (her) / शापसम्स्पृष्टाम् (touched by a curse) / कश्चित् (anyone) / उत्सहते (is able) / पुमान् (man) / निहन्तुम् (to kill) / त्रिषु लोकेषु (in the three worlds) / त्वाम् ऋते (except you) / रघुनन्दन (O delight of the Raghu line)
ramayan::748.speaker: Vishvamitra
ramayan::748.essence: Some burdens can only be carried by the one prepared for them.
ramayan::748.simple_meaning: Vishvamitra tells Rama that no one else in the world can kill Tataka because of the curse on her. He is pointing to Rama as the one who must take this burden.
ramayan::748.simple_insight: Sometimes the hardest task is the one only you can carry.
ramayan::748.detailed_meaning: Vishvamitra has brought Rama and Lakshmana into the forest and is explaining why Tataka must be stopped. He says her curse makes her untouchable to ordinary men, and only Rama has the strength and right to end her threat.
ramayan::748.modern_relevance: Everyone else has stepped back from the problem in the group chat, and the deadline is still there. Then it becomes clear: this one cannot be avoided, and it is yours to handle.
ramayan::748.insight: It shifts responsibility from general reluctance to specific obligation: when a task is uniquely yours, hesitation becomes avoidance.

ramayan::749.verse_sanskrit: न हि ते स्त्रीवधकृते घृणा कार्या नरोत्तम । चातुर्वण्यहितार्थाय कर्तव्यं राजसूनुना । । 12516 । ।
ramayan::749.verse_hindi: O best among men you need not hate killing a woman. You are a prince. You should serve the interest of the four orders of the society.
ramayan::749.english_translation: O best among men, you need not shrink from killing a woman. You are a prince, and you must act for the welfare of the four social orders.
ramayan::749.translation_literal: न हि (not indeed) / ते (for you) / स्त्रीवधकृते (for the killing of a woman) / घृणा (hesitation, disgust) / कार्या (to be done) / नरोत्तम (best among men) / चातुर्वण्यहितार्थाय (for the welfare of the four orders) / कर्तव्यं (to be done) / राजसूनुना (by a prince)
ramayan::749.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::749.essence: A ruler’s duty can require a painful act he would rather avoid.
ramayan::749.simple_meaning: A ruler cannot avoid a harsh act just because it feels terrible. If protecting society requires it, he must do it.
ramayan::749.simple_insight: Moral seriousness sometimes means carrying a burden you would rather refuse.
ramayan::749.detailed_meaning: In the forest, Rama is being urged to end a dangerous curse-bound threat. The argument is not about comfort but kingship: a prince must protect the social order even when the act is ugly. This verse sharpens that hard duty.
ramayan::749.modern_relevance: You have to make the call that leaves a knot in your stomach — the one that protects others, even if it stains your comfort.
ramayan::749.insight: It shifts you from personal disgust to responsible action when others depend on your choice.

ramayan::750.verse_sanskrit: नृशंसमनृशंसं वा प्रजारक्षणकारणात् । पातकं वा सदोषं वा कर्तव्यं रक्षता सता । । 12517 । ।
ramayan::750.verse_hindi: Whether cruel or kind, sinful or wrong whatever contributes to the protection of the subjects, should be done by the righteous (king).
ramayan::750.english_translation: Whether cruel or kind, sinful or wrong, whatever contributes to the protection of the subjects should be done by the righteous king.
ramayan::750.translation_literal: नृशंसम् (cruel) / अनृशंसं (kind) / वा (or) / प्रजारक्षणकारणात् (for the reason of protecting the subjects) / पातकं (sinful) / वा (or) / सदोषं (faulty) / वा (or) / कर्तव्यं (to be done) / रक्षता (by the protector) / सता (by the righteous one)
ramayan::750.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::750.essence: A righteous ruler may have to do what feels morally difficult to protect the many.
ramayan::750.simple_meaning: A ruler must do what protects the people, even if the act feels harsh, flawed, or morally troubling.
ramayan::750.simple_insight: Leadership sometimes demands choices you would never choose for yourself.
ramayan::750.detailed_meaning: Ravana's death is being argued in the background, but the real issue is kingship itself. The speaker says that a ruler must act for the safety of the people even when the action seems cruel or blameworthy. The next verse calls this the eternal law of a king.
ramayan::750.modern_relevance: A manager has to cut a failing project that many people loved. A parent has to set a boundary that causes tears. The right choice can still feel ugly when you are responsible for others.
ramayan::750.insight: It shifts you from personal comfort to responsibility for the larger good.

ramayan::751.verse_sanskrit: राज्यभारनियुक्तानामेष धर्मस्सनातन: । अधर्म्यां जहि काकुत्स्थ धर्मोह्यस्या न विद्यते । । 12518 । ।
ramayan::751.verse_hindi: This is the eternal law binding those who are appointed to bear the burden of a kingdom. O Kakutstha kill her. She knows no dharma.
ramayan::751.english_translation: This is the eternal law for those appointed to bear the burden of a kingdom. O Kakutstha, kill her. She has no dharma.
ramayan::751.translation_literal: राज्यभारनियुक्तानाम् (of those appointed to bear the burden of a kingdom) / एषः (this) / धर्मः (law, duty) / सनातनः (eternal) / अधर्म्याम् (the unrighteous one) / जहि (kill) / काकुत्स्थ (O Kakutstha) / धर्मः (dharma) / हि (indeed) / अस्याः (of her) / न (not) / विद्यते (exists)
ramayan::751.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::751.essence: Kingship means acting against personal reluctance when the realm is at risk.
ramayan::751.simple_meaning: A ruler's duty is to protect the kingdom, even if that means making a harsh choice. The speaker says the woman has no moral restraint and must be killed.
ramayan::751.simple_insight: Leadership can demand decisions that feel unbearable, yet still be judged by responsibility rather than comfort.
ramayan::751.detailed_meaning: In the palace debate over whether a threat to the kingdom should be spared, the speaker argues that a ruler's first law is protection. He tells Kakutstha that the woman stands outside dharma and must be killed, because kings are bound to guard the people.
ramayan::751.modern_relevance: You are the one everyone looks to when a situation turns dangerous. The harder choice may not feel kind, but delaying it can leave others exposed.
ramayan::751.insight: It shifts the mind from personal softness to public responsibility when harm threatens the many.

ramayan::752.verse_sanskrit: श्रूयते हि पुरा शक्रो विरोचनसुतां नृप । पृथिवीं हन्तुमिच्छन्तीं मन्थरामभ्यसूदयत् । । 12519 । ।
ramayan::752.verse_hindi: O Prince It is heard that in the past Indra slew Manthara, Virochanas daughter who intended to destroy the earth.
ramayan::752.english_translation: O Prince, it is said that in old times Indra destroyed Manthara, the daughter of Virochana, when she wished to ruin the earth.
ramayan::752.translation_literal: श्रूयते (it is heard) / हि (indeed) / पुरा (in ancient times) / शक्रः (Indra) / विरोचनसुताम् (the daughter of Virochana) / नृप (O king) / पृथिवीम् (the earth) / हन्तुम् (to destroy) / इच्छन्तीम् (desiring) / मन्थराम् (Manthara) / अभ्यसूदयत् (slew)
ramayan::752.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::752.essence: Protection can demand an act that looks cruel from the outside.
ramayan::752.simple_meaning: A king is reminded that rulers may act harshly to protect the people. The verse gives an old example of a powerful being destroying a threat to the world.
ramayan::752.simple_insight: Hard choices can feel severe, yet still serve the larger protection you are responsible for.
ramayan::752.detailed_meaning: In Ayodhya's crisis, the argument has turned brutal: the king must decide whether a dangerous woman should be killed for the safety of the realm. To justify that harsh duty, the speaker recalls an ancient example of Indra destroying a being who meant harm to the earth.
ramayan::752.modern_relevance: A parent blocks a harmful influence from the house and feels cruel for doing it. A leader cuts off a destructive partner and hates the ugliness of the decision. The verse reminds you that protection can demand severity.
ramayan::752.insight: It shifts the mind from softness as virtue to protection as responsibility.

ramayan::753.verse_sanskrit: विष्णुनापि पुरा राम भृगुपत्नी दृढव्रता । अनिन्द्रं लोकमिच्छन्ती काव्यमाता निषूदिता । । 12520 । ।
ramayan::753.verse_hindi: O Rama! In olden times, Kavya, the mother of Sukracharya, the wife of sage Bhrigu, was destroyed by Vishnu determined to destroy Indra.
ramayan::753.english_translation: O Rama! In ancient times, Vishnu destroyed Kavya, the wife of Bhrigu, who was firmly devoted and wished for a world without Indra.
ramayan::753.translation_literal: विष्णुना (by Vishnu) / अपि (also) / पुरा (in ancient times) / राम (O Rama) / भृगुपत्नी (the wife of Bhrigu) / दृढव्रता (firm in vows) / अनिन्द्रम् (without Indra) / लोकम् (world) / इच्छन्ती (desiring) / काव्यमाता (Kavya, mother of Sukracharya) / निषूदिता (was destroyed)
ramayan::753.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::753.essence: Order sometimes requires firm action against what threatens the whole.
ramayan::753.simple_meaning: Vishnu once destroyed a woman who wanted to remove Indra from power. The verse is used as an example of removing a harmful force for the protection of order.
ramayan::753.simple_insight: Sometimes protection of the larger order requires hard action against a destructive threat.
ramayan::753.detailed_meaning: Rama is being urged to act decisively in a kingdom-threatening situation. The speaker cites old examples: Indra once killed Manthara, and Vishnu once destroyed Kavya, Bhrigu's wife, when she opposed the cosmic order. The point is to justify forceful action against adharma.
ramayan::753.modern_relevance: A manager keeps excusing one person whose sabotage is hurting the whole team. Eventually, protecting the group means stopping the damage, not protecting the troublemaker's comfort.
ramayan::753.insight: It shifts the mind from hesitation to lawful intervention when a threat is clearly destructive.

ramayan::754.verse_sanskrit: एतैश्चान्यैश्च बहुभी राजपुत्र महात्मभि: । अधर्मसहिता नार्यो हता: पुरुषसत्तमै: । । 12521 । ।
ramayan::754.verse_hindi: O Prince by these magnanimous persons and by great men several unrighteous women were killed for the common good.
ramayan::754.english_translation: O Prince, by these great royal men and by many other noble men, unrighteous women were killed for the common good.
ramayan::754.translation_literal: एतैः (by these) / च (and) / अन्यैः (by others) / च (and) / बहुभिः (by many) / राजपुत्र (O prince) / महात्मभिः (by great-souled ones) / अधर्म-सहिता (joined with unrighteousness) / नार्यः (women) / हताः (were killed) / पुरुष-सत्तमैः (by the best of men)
ramayan::754.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::754.essence: Severe action can be justified when unrighteousness threatens the whole.
ramayan::754.simple_meaning: Great men have sometimes killed women who were acting against righteousness, for the protection of the larger good.
ramayan::754.simple_insight: It frames a harsh act as something done only under moral necessity.
ramayan::754.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra is explaining to Rama why the sages once used force against dangerous beings. The point is not celebration, but precedent: even noble men have sometimes taken severe action when unrighteousness threatened the world.
ramayan::754.modern_relevance: A leader has to make a hard call that no one will praise in the moment. The question is not whether it feels clean, but whether it protects what must be protected.
ramayan::754.insight: It shifts judgment from personal discomfort to the wider consequences of inaction.

ramayan::755.verse_sanskrit: मुनेर्वचनमक्लीबं श्रुत्वा नरवरात्मज: । राघव: प्राञ्जलिर्भूत्वा प्रत्युवाच दृढव्रत: । । 1261 । ।
ramayan::755.verse_hindi: After listening to the manly command of ascetic Viswamitra, Rama, of the lineage of Raghu, the son of the foremost of men and firm in determination, replied with folded palms:
ramayan::755.english_translation: After listening to the manly command of ascetic Viswamitra, Rama, the son of the foremost of men and firm in determination, replied with folded palms.
ramayan::755.translation_literal: मुनेः (of the sage) / वचनम् (the command) / अक्लीबम् (manly, firm) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / नरवरात्मजः (son of the foremost of men) / राघवः (Rama) / प्राञ्जलिः भूत्वा (having become with folded palms) / प्रत्युवाच (replied) / दृढव्रतः (firm in vow)
ramayan::755.speaker: Rama
ramayan::755.essence: Obedience begins with composure, not hesitation.
ramayan::755.simple_meaning: Rama hears Vishwamitra's firm command and answers respectfully, with folded hands, ready to act.
ramayan::755.simple_insight: Respect can be the first form of readiness.
ramayan::755.detailed_meaning: Vishwamitra has just given Rama a hard command in the forest. Rama does not argue or resist. He folds his hands, listens fully, and answers as a prince who is already learning how to carry duty without flinching.
ramayan::755.modern_relevance: Your manager gives you a task you did not ask for, and you feel the first surge of resistance. The better response begins with steadiness, not defensiveness.
ramayan::755.insight: It teaches you to meet obligation with calm respect before you act.

ramayan::756.english_translation: Because of my father's command and because of the weight of my father's word, I must carry out Vishvamitra's request without hesitation.
ramayan::756.translation_literal: पितुर्वचननिर्देशात् (because of father's command) / पितुर्वचनगौरवात् (because of father's word's weight) / वचनं (the word) / कौशिकस्य (of Kaushika) / इति (thus) / कर्तव्यम् (to be done) / अविशङ्कया (without hesitation)
ramayan::756.speaker: Rama
ramayan::756.essence: A promise from your father becomes your duty, even before you want it.
ramayan::756.simple_meaning: Rama says he must obey Vishvamitra because his father's command is binding and worthy of respect. He will act without doubt or delay.
ramayan::756.simple_insight: Real strength is keeping faith with a promise even when it costs you.
ramayan::756.detailed_meaning: In Ayodhya, Rama has just heard Vishvamitra's request. He does not treat it as a choice to debate. Because Dasharatha's word carries authority, Rama accepts the task at once and with no hesitation.
ramayan::756.modern_relevance: Your parent made a promise for you, and now you feel the weight of it in your chest. The easy escape is to negotiate. Rama shows another way: carry the obligation cleanly.
ramayan::756.insight: It teaches you to treat a binding promise as action, not as a topic for debate.

ramayan::757.verse_sanskrit: अनुशिष्टोऽस्म्ययोध्यायां गुरुमध्ये महात्मना । पित्रा दशरथेनाहं नावज्ञेयं हि तद्वच: । । 1263 । ।
ramayan::757.verse_hindi: In Ayodhya in the presence of elders and spiritual masters (of Dasarathas court), I have been ordered by my magnanimous father to act according to your instructions  and his words cannot be disobeyed.
ramayan::757.english_translation: In Ayodhya, before elders and teachers, my magnanimous father instructed me. His word cannot be disobeyed.
ramayan::757.translation_literal: अनुशिष्टः (instructed) / अस्मि (I am) / अयोध्यायाम् (in Ayodhya) / गुरुमध्ये (among the teachers and elders) / महात्मना (by the great-souled one) / पित्रा (by my father) / दशरथेन (by Dasharatha) / अहम् (I) / न (not) / अवज्ञेयम् (to be disobeyed) / हि (indeed) / तत् (that) / वचः (word)
ramayan::757.speaker: Rama
ramayan::757.essence: A son's freedom ends where his father's word begins.
ramayan::757.simple_meaning: Rama says he was instructed by his father in Ayodhya before respected elders, and that his father's command must be obeyed without hesitation.
ramayan::757.simple_insight: Some obligations are not negotiable; they ask for obedience, not convenience.
ramayan::757.detailed_meaning: In Ayodhya, with teachers and elders listening, Rama answers Vishwamitra. He does not treat his father's command as optional or private. The exile has already begun in his mind: if Dasharatha has spoken, Rama will follow.
ramayan::757.modern_relevance: You promised your family you'd show up, even though the easier plan is to cancel and disappear. The moment gets expensive, but your word still has a shape.
ramayan::757.insight: It shifts you from asking what feels easier to asking what you have already committed to.

ramayan::758.verse_sanskrit: सोऽहं पितुर्वचश्श्रुत्वा शासनाद्ब्रह्मवादिन: । करिष्यामि न सन्देहस्ताटकावधमुत्तमम् । । 1264 । ।
ramayan::758.verse_hindi: As per the words of my father and the command of Viswamitra, who has the knowledge of the Brahman,  I shall execute the welcome act of killing Tataka.
ramayan::758.english_translation: Hearing my father’s word and the command of Viswamitra, I will certainly carry out the excellent killing of Tataka.
ramayan::758.translation_literal: सोऽहम् (so I) / पितुर्वचः (father's word) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / शासनात् (from the command) / ब्रह्मवादिनः (of the knower of Brahman) / करिष्यामि (I will do) / न (no) / सन्देहः (doubt) / ताटकावधम् (the killing of Tataka) / उत्तमम् (excellent)
ramayan::758.speaker: Rama
ramayan::758.essence: Duty is cleanest when you stop arguing with it.
ramayan::758.simple_meaning: Rama says he will not hesitate: he will obey his father and Viswamitra by killing Tataka.
ramayan::758.simple_insight: Clear duty becomes easier when you stop negotiating with it.
ramayan::758.detailed_meaning: Rama has left Ayodhya and stands under Viswamitra’s guidance. He recalls his father’s command and accepts the task before him: Tataka must be killed. The verse shows obedience turning into action without inner resistance.
ramayan::758.modern_relevance: You already know the task you agreed to, even if it is uncomfortable now. The mind may bargain, but the promise is still standing there, waiting for you.
ramayan::758.insight: It shifts you from hesitation to decisive obedience when a rightful command is already clear.

ramayan::759.verse_sanskrit: गोब्राह्मणहितार्थाय देशस्यास्य सुखाय च । तव चैवाप्रमेयस्य वचनं कर्तुमुद्यत: । । 1265 । ।
ramayan::759.verse_hindi: For the welfare of cows and brahmins and also for the good of this country, I am ready to perform such acts as commanded by you of  boundless energy.
ramayan::759.english_translation: For the welfare of cows and brahmins and also for the good of this country, I am ready to perform such acts as commanded by you of boundless energy.
ramayan::759.translation_literal: गोब्राह्मणहितार्थाय (for the welfare of cows and brahmins) / देशस्य (of this country) / अस्य (of this) / सुखाय (for the good) / च (and) / तव (your) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / अप्रमेयस्य (of the immeasurable) / वचनं (command) / कर्तुम् (to do) / उद्यत: (ready)
ramayan::759.speaker: Rama
ramayan::759.essence: Duty becomes noble when it protects more than your own comfort.
ramayan::759.simple_meaning: Rama says he is ready to act for the welfare of cows, learned people, and the kingdom, while also obeying Vishwamitra's command.
ramayan::759.simple_insight: Real duty is bigger than personal preference; it serves what protects and sustains life around you.
ramayan::759.detailed_meaning: In Vishwamitra's presence, Rama has already accepted the task before him. He now names the reason: this act is for the welfare of cows, learned men, and the land itself. The moment shows a prince choosing responsibility over comfort.
ramayan::759.modern_relevance: You take on a hard task at work or at home, not because it flatters you, but because other people depend on it. That is the kind of yes Rama gives here.
ramayan::759.insight: It shifts action away from self-interest and toward what upholds the people and place around you.

ramayan::760.verse_sanskrit: एवमुक्त्वा धनुर्मध्ये बध्वा मुष्टिमरिन्दम: । ज्याशब्दमकरोत्तीव्रं दिशश्शब्देन नादयन् । । 1266 । ।
ramayan::760.verse_hindi: Rama, the destroyer of enemies having said so clinched the middle of the bow with his fist and filled the ten quarters with the resounding twanging of the bowstring.
ramayan::760.english_translation: Rama, the destroyer of enemies, spoke and then gripped the middle of the bow with his fist, making the bowstring thunder and filling all directions with its sound.
ramayan::760.translation_literal: एवमुक्त्वा (having said thus) / धनुर्मध्ये (in the middle of the bow) / बध्वा (binding/gripping) / मुष्टिम् (fist) / अरिन्दमः (enemy-subduer) / ज्याशब्दम् (sound of the bowstring) / अकरोत् (made) / तीव्रम् (loud/forceful) / दिशः (the directions) / शब्देन (with sound) / नादयन् (resounding)
ramayan::760.speaker: Rama
ramayan::760.essence: Resolve becomes real only when your hands move.
ramayan::760.simple_meaning: Rama takes the bow firmly and draws it with such force that its sound fills every direction.
ramayan::760.simple_insight: Some acts speak before the battle begins.
ramayan::760.detailed_meaning: Rama has just declared he will obey his father and Vishwamitra by killing Tataka for the good of the land. Now he grips the great bow and draws it with force. The sound itself announces that the decision has become action.
ramayan::760.modern_relevance: You stop talking, tighten your grip, and do the hard thing in one clean motion. The room changes before anyone says a word.
ramayan::760.insight: It shifts resolve from statement to action, showing that readiness becomes real only when the body commits.

ramayan::761.verse_sanskrit: तेन शब्देन वित्रस्तास्ताटकावनवासिन: । ताटका च सुसंक्रुद्धा तेन शब्देन मोहिता । । 1267 । ।
ramayan::761.verse_hindi: The dwellers of the Tataka forest were terrified by the sound (of the bow). Tataka, was might angry and amazed.
ramayan::761.english_translation: The dwellers of the Tataka forest were terrified by the sound of the bow. Tataka herself was enraged and stunned by that sound.
ramayan::761.translation_literal: तेन (by that) / शब्देन (sound) / वित्रस्ताः (terrified) / ताटकावनवासिनः (the inhabitants of Tataka's forest) / ताटका (Tataka) / च (and) / सुसंक्रुद्धा (very enraged) / तेन (by that) / शब्देन (sound) / मोहिता (bewildered, stunned)
ramayan::761.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::761.essence: The bow's sound exposes fear before the fight even begins.
ramayan::761.simple_meaning: The bowstring's sound frightens the forest's inhabitants and throws Tataka into anger and confusion.
ramayan::761.simple_insight: Even a single decisive act can shake fear into a violent response.
ramayan::761.detailed_meaning: Rama has just gripped Vishvamitra's bow and drawn it with force. The sound rolls through Tataka's forest, startling its inhabitants and jolting Tataka herself. This verse is a reaction shot, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::761.modern_relevance: A room goes quiet after one sharp sentence lands. People who were comfortable a moment ago suddenly feel exposed, and the person challenged turns hot with anger.
ramayan::761.insight: It shows how forceful action can reveal hidden fear and provoke resistance.

ramayan::762.verse_sanskrit: तं शब्दमभिनिध्याय राक्षसी क्रोधमूर्छिता । श्रुत्वा चाभ्यद्रवद्वेगाद्यतश्शब्दो विनिस्सृत: । । 1268 । ।
ramayan::762.verse_hindi: Hearing that sound, the demoness thought for a while and senseless with anger  rushed in the direction where the sound had come from.
ramayan::762.english_translation: Hearing that sound, the demoness thought for a moment and, maddened by anger, rushed toward the place from which the sound had come.
ramayan::762.translation_literal: तं (that) / शब्दम् (sound) / अभिध्याय (having thought upon) / राक्षसी (the demoness) / क्रोधमूर्छिता (fainted/confused by anger) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / च (and) / अभ्यद्रवत् (rushed toward) / वेगात् (swiftly) / यतः (from where) / शब्दः (sound) / विनिस्सृतः (had issued forth)
ramayan::762.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::762.essence: Anger can make you charge before you understand.
ramayan::762.simple_meaning: Tataka hears the sound, loses herself to anger, and charges toward its source.
ramayan::762.simple_insight: Anger narrows your world until you run straight at the trigger.
ramayan::762.detailed_meaning: In the forest near Vishvamitra's sacrificial arena, Rama has just drawn the bow and its thunder has shaken the woods. Tataka, already enraged, hears it, loses steadiness, and rushes toward the sound. The scene is building toward first contact.
ramayan::762.modern_relevance: Your phone buzzes with one sharp message, and your whole body moves before your mind does. That is how anger works: it makes you rush toward what it thinks is the threat.
ramayan::762.insight: It shows how anger can override reflection and pull action into blind momentum.

ramayan::763.verse_sanskrit: तां दृष्ट्वा राघव: क्रुद्धां विकृतां विकृताननाम् । प्रमाणेनातिवृद्धां च लक्ष्मणं सोऽभ्यभाषत । । 1269 । ।
ramayan::763.verse_hindi: Filled with wrath Rama saw Tataka, disfigured with a distorted face and gigantic in
ramayan::763.english_translation: Seeing Tataka enraged, distorted in form and face, and huge beyond measure, Rama spoke to Lakshmana.
ramayan::763.translation_literal: तां (her) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / राघवः (Rama) / क्रुद्धाम् (angry) / विकृताम् (deformed) / विकृताननाम् (distorted-faced) / प्रमाणेन (by measure) / अतिवृद्धाम् (very large) / च (and) / लक्ष्मणम् (to Lakshmana) / सः (he) / अभ्यभाषत (spoke)
ramayan::763.speaker: Rama
ramayan::763.essence: Clear sight comes before the right response.
ramayan::763.simple_meaning: Rama sees Tataka’s terrifying form and turns to Lakshmana to speak. The verse prepares the next warning about her danger.
ramayan::763.simple_insight: Some moments are so stark that even a glance becomes a warning.
ramayan::763.detailed_meaning: Rama has already drawn Tataka’s attention with the sound of the bow. Now the enraged demoness rushes in, and he takes in her monstrous form at once. He turns to Lakshmana to name the danger before the fight begins.
ramayan::763.modern_relevance: You spot the person in the room whose anger has already changed the air. Before the situation explodes, you read the danger clearly and tell someone beside you.
ramayan::763.insight: It trains you to notice threat quickly and respond with clear-eyed speech, not panic.

ramayan::764.verse_sanskrit: पश्य लक्ष्मण यक्षिण्या भैरवं दारुणं वपु: । भिद्येरन् दर्शनादस्या भीरूणां हृदयानि च । । 12610 । ।
ramayan::764.verse_hindi: O Lakshmana, behold, the sight of the dreadful hideous body of this yakshini will break timid hearts.
ramayan::764.english_translation: O Lakshmana, behold the dreadful, terrible body of this yakshini. Even timid hearts would break at the sight of her.
ramayan::764.translation_literal: पश्य (behold) / लक्ष्मण (Lakshmana) / यक्षिण्या (of the yakshini) / भैरवं (dreadful) / दारुणं (terrible) / वपुः (body) / भिद्येरन् (would break) / दर्शनात् (at the sight) / अस्याः (of her) / भीरूणाम् (of timid ones) / हृदयानि (hearts) / च (and)
ramayan::764.speaker: Rama
ramayan::764.essence: Her appearance is meant to frighten you before the real fight begins.
ramayan::764.simple_meaning: Rama points out how terrifying the yakshini looks and says even fearful people would lose heart just seeing her.
ramayan::764.simple_insight: Fear grows fast when the mind focuses on appearance instead of steadiness.
ramayan::764.detailed_meaning: Rama is showing Lakshmana the terrifying form of Tataka, a yakshini whose appearance alone can shake the weak. The line is part of a tense exchange before Rama moves to confront her, not a complete teaching on its own.
ramayan::764.modern_relevance: You see someone enter the room and instantly decide they are too intimidating to face. Sometimes the fear is real, but sometimes the first battle is simply not looking away.
ramayan::764.insight: It trains attention to notice fear without surrendering to it.

ramayan::765.verse_sanskrit: एनां पश्य दुराधर्षां मायाबलसमन्विताम् । विनिवृत्तां करोम्यद्य हृतकर्णाग्रनासिकाम् । । 12611 । ।
ramayan::765.verse_hindi: See, she is unassailable because of the strength gained through black magic. I shall cut off her ears and the tip of her nose and make her turn away.
ramayan::765.english_translation: See, she is unassailable because of the strength gained through black magic. I shall cut off her ears and the tip of her nose and make her turn away.
ramayan::765.translation_literal: एनाम् (her) / पश्य (see) / दुराधर्षाम् (hard to assail) / मायाबलसमन्विताम् (endowed with power gained through illusion) / विनिवृत्ताम् (turned back) / करोमि (I will make) / अद्य (today) / हृतकर्णाग्रनासिकाम् (with ears and tip of nose cut off)
ramayan::765.speaker: Rama
ramayan::765.essence: A dangerous power must be stopped before it can spread further.
ramayan::765.simple_meaning: Rama says this enemy is hard to defeat because of her magical power, and he will disable her by cutting off her ears and nose.
ramayan::765.simple_insight: Force sometimes means stopping a threat before it can keep spreading.
ramayan::765.detailed_meaning: Rama points out Tataka's dangerous, magical strength to Lakshmana and explains his immediate response. This is still the setup before the deeper moral question in the next verse: whether a woman may be killed or only disfigured and driven away.
ramayan::765.modern_relevance: You see a harmful pattern that keeps making itself untouchable, and you have to decide how firmly to stop it before it hurts more people.
ramayan::765.insight: It frames restraint and force as a tactical choice, not a moral slogan.

ramayan::766.verse_sanskrit: न ह्येनामुत्सहे हन्तुं स्त्रीस्वभावेन रक्षिताम् । वीर्यं चास्यां गतिं चापि हनिष्यामीति मे मति: । । 12612 । ।
ramayan::766.verse_hindi: By virtue of being a woman, she is protected. I am not inclined to slay her but take away her prowess and power of motion.
ramayan::766.english_translation: By virtue of being a woman, she is protected. I am not inclined to slay her but take away her prowess and power of motion.
ramayan::766.translation_literal: न (not) / हि (indeed) / एनाम् (her) / उत्सहे (I am willing) / हन्तुम् (to kill) / स्त्री-स्वभावेन (by woman-nature) / रक्षिताम् (protected) / वीर्यम् (prowess) / च (and) / अस्याम् (in her) / गतिम् (movement) / च अपि (and also) / हनिष्यामि (I shall destroy) / इति (thus) / मे (my) / मतिः (thought)
ramayan::766.speaker: Rama
ramayan::766.essence: Power is tested by how little harm it needs.
ramayan::766.simple_meaning: Rama refuses to kill Tataka. He chooses to disable her power instead, because he will not strike down a woman unless absolutely necessary.
ramayan::766.simple_insight: Real strength can protect without losing restraint.
ramayan::766.detailed_meaning: Rama stands before Tataka in the forest while Lakshmana watches. Her violence is real, but so is Rama's refusal to let power become cruelty. In this moment, he chooses a disciplined response that limits harm.
ramayan::766.modern_relevance: You have the chance to shut someone down completely in one message, one decision, one public correction. The harder choice is to stop the damage without becoming the thing you oppose.
ramayan::766.insight: It teaches you to restrain force and choose the least harmful effective response.

ramayan::767.verse_sanskrit: एवं ब्रुवाणे रामे तु ताटका क्रोधमूर्छिता । उद्यम्य बाहू गर्जन्ती राममेवाभ्यधावत । । 12613 । ।
ramayan::767.verse_hindi: While Rama was still speaking, Tataka, incensed with fury rushed with her uplifted arms towards him roaring.
ramayan::767.english_translation: While Rama was still speaking, Tataka, incensed with fury, rushed toward him with her arms raised, roaring.
ramayan::767.translation_literal: एवं (thus) / ब्रुवाणे (while speaking) / रामे (Rama) / तु (but) / ताटका (Tataka) / क्रोध-मूर्छिता (overcome by anger) / उद्यम्य (raising) / बाहू (arms) / गर्जन्ती (roaring) / रामम् (at Rama) / एव (indeed) / अभ्यधावत (rushed)
ramayan::767.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::767.essence: Anger makes the first move before understanding can.
ramayan::767.simple_meaning: Tataka, blinded by rage, charged at Rama with her arms raised while he was still speaking.
ramayan::767.simple_insight: Rage can make a person charge forward before hearing anything at all.
ramayan::767.detailed_meaning: In Vishwamitra's forest lesson, Rama is still speaking with restraint, trying to act by judgment rather than impulse. Tataka, furious and armed with black magic, loses control and rushes him. The verse heightens the clash before Vishwamitra steps in.
ramayan::767.modern_relevance: Someone cuts you off mid-sentence, and the whole room tightens. The moment anger takes over, listening ends and collision begins.
ramayan::767.insight: It shows how fury destroys discernment and turns conversation into attack.

ramayan::768.verse_sanskrit: विश्वामित्रस्तु ब्रह्मर्षिर्हुङ्कारेणाभिभर्त्स्यताम् । स्वस्ति राघवयोरस्तु जयं चैवाभ्यभाषत । । 12614 । ।
ramayan::768.verse_hindi: Brahmarshi Viswamitra threatened her with hunkara (menacing sound), uttering, Auspices to the Raghavas (Rama and Lakshmana) be aupicousness and success victorious.
ramayan::768.english_translation: Brahmarshi Viswamitra rebuked her with a sharp roar and said, "May auspiciousness and victory be with Rama and Lakshmana."
ramayan::768.translation_literal: विश्वामित्रः (Viswamitra) / तु (indeed) / ब्रह्मर्षिः (the great seer) / हुङ्कारेण (with a menacing roar) / अभिभर्त्स्यताम् (having threatened) / स्वस्ति (auspiciousness) / राघवयोः (for the two Raghavas) / अस्तु (may it be) / जयं (victory) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / अभ्यभाषत (he spoke)
ramayan::768.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::768.essence: A true guide shields courage with force and blessing.
ramayan::768.simple_meaning: Viswamitra steps in with a fierce warning and blesses Rama and Lakshmana with victory and safety.
ramayan::768.simple_insight: Right support can be both protective and encouraging.
ramayan::768.detailed_meaning: Tataka has rushed at Rama in fury. Before the clash continues, Viswamitra, the sage guiding the brothers, intervenes with a commanding roar and blesses Rama and Lakshmana. It is a brief moment of protection before the fight resumes.
ramayan::768.modern_relevance: A mentor cuts through the noise in the middle of a tense moment and says, "Stay steady. You've got this." That kind of backing can change how you meet the next second.
ramayan::768.insight: It shows how a trusted guide can steady courage at the exact moment pressure rises.

ramayan::769.verse_sanskrit: उद्धून्वाना रजो घोरं ताटका राघवावुभौ । रजोमोहेन महता मुहूर्तं सा व्यमोहयत् । । 12615 । ।
ramayan::769.verse_hindi: Tataka raising a cloud of frightening dust left the descendants of Raghu bewildered quite for a moment.
ramayan::769.english_translation: Tataka, raising a terrible cloud of dust, bewildered both the descendants of Raghu for a moment.
ramayan::769.translation_literal: उद्धून्वाना (raising) / रजो (dust) / घोरं (terrible) / ताटका (Tataka) / राघवौ (the two descendants of Raghu) / उभौ (both) / रजोमोहेन (by the confusion of dust) / महता (great) / मुहूर्तं (for a moment) / सा (she) / व्यमोहयत् (bewildered)
ramayan::769.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::769.essence: The first shock is disorientation, not defeat.
ramayan::769.simple_meaning: Tataka throws up so much dust that Rama and Lakshmana are briefly confused.
ramayan::769.simple_insight: Even a momentary cloud can shake your footing before the real struggle begins.
ramayan::769.detailed_meaning: Tataka has already charged at Rama while Vishwamitra stands nearby. Now she whips up a terrifying wall of dust that briefly disorients both brothers. The verse is a combat beat, not a teaching moment; it sets up the next attack.
ramayan::769.modern_relevance: A problem hits before you have your bearings — a call, a deadline, a harsh message — and for a second you cannot think straight. The real test comes after that first blur.
ramayan::769.insight: It frames the fight as sudden confusion before direct force, not yet the decisive clash.

ramayan::770.verse_sanskrit: ततो मायां समास्थाय शिलावर्षेण राघवौ । अवाकिरत्सुमहता ततश्चुक्रोध राघव: । । 12616 । ।
ramayan::770.verse_hindi: Then invoking the power of magic, she showered extensive rain of boulders on both the descendants of Raghu. Rama was enraged at this.
ramayan::770.english_translation: Then, using magical power, she showered the two descendants of Raghu with a great rain of rocks, and Rama became enraged.
ramayan::770.translation_literal: ततः (then) / मायाम् (magic, illusion) / समास्थाय (having resorted to) / शिलावर्षेण (with a rain of rocks) / राघवौ (the two Raghavas) / अवाकिरत् (she showered) / सुमहता (very great) / ततः (then) / चुक्रोध (became enraged) / राघवः (Rama)
ramayan::770.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::770.essence: Magic and anger push the encounter into open combat.
ramayan::770.simple_meaning: Tataka turns to magic and attacks Rama and Lakshmana with a storm of rocks. Rama responds with anger.
ramayan::770.simple_insight: Pressure exposes force, and force answers force.
ramayan::770.detailed_meaning: In the forest encounter with Tataka, the fight has already become dangerous. After dust and confusion, she uses illusion and hurls rocks at Rama and Lakshmana. This verse is a beat in the escalation before Rama strikes back.
ramayan::770.modern_relevance: A situation spirals fast: one sharp message, one hostile reply, then everything hardens. Before you know it, the exchange is no longer about the issue — it is about impact.
ramayan::770.insight: It shows conflict intensifying from menace to direct retaliation.

ramayan::771.verse_sanskrit: शिलावर्षं महत्तस्याश्शरवर्षेण राघव: । प्रतिहत्योपधावन्त्या: करौ चिच्छेद पत्रिभि: । । 12617 । ।
ramayan::771.verse_hindi: Rama retaliated that mighty rain of rocks with a volley of arrows. While she was advancing towards him, he cut off her hands.
ramayan::771.english_translation: Rama retaliated that mighty rain of rocks with a volley of arrows. While she was advancing towards him, he cut off her hands.
ramayan::771.translation_literal: शिलावर्षम् (rain of rocks) / महत् (mighty) / तस्याः (her) / शरवर्षेण (with a rain of arrows) / राघवः (Rama) / प्रतिहत्य (having repelled) / उपधावन्त्याः (of her advancing) / करौ (the two hands) / चिच्छेद (cut off) / पत्रिभिः (with arrows)
ramayan::771.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::771.essence: Violence is met here with faster, cleaner force.
ramayan::771.simple_meaning: Rama blocks Tataka's attack with arrows and cuts off her hands as she rushes at him.
ramayan::771.simple_insight: It shows decisive force meeting violent chaos without hesitation.
ramayan::771.detailed_meaning: Tataka has already filled the battlefield with dust and rocks, trying to overwhelm Rama and Lakshmana. Rama answers with arrows and, as she charges again, cuts off her hands. The verse is a combat detail in the middle of a larger fight.
ramayan::771.modern_relevance: A problem keeps escalating and you stop reacting with panic. You answer firmly, cleanly, and without delay.
ramayan::771.insight: It shifts you from being shaken by attack to meeting it with controlled force.

ramayan::772.verse_hindi: When she was tired and roaring in a nearby place with her hands chopped off, Lakshmana cut off her ears and the tip of her nose in indignation.
ramayan::772.english_translation: When she was tired and roaring nearby with her hands cut off, Lakshmana, in anger, cut off her ears and the tip of her nose.
ramayan::772.translation_literal: ततः (then) / छिन्नभुजाम् (with cut-off arms) / श्रान्ताम् (tired) / अभ्याशे (nearby) / परिगर्जतीम् (roaring) / सौमित्रिः (Lakshmana) / अकरोत् (did) / क्रोधात् (from anger) / धृतकर्णाग्रनासिकाम् (with cut ears and nose-tip)
ramayan::772.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::772.essence: Anger makes punishment keep growing after the danger has passed.
ramayan::772.simple_meaning: Lakshmana, angered by the attacking demoness, mutilates her further after Rama has already cut off her arms.
ramayan::772.simple_insight: Violence can keep escalating once anger takes over.
ramayan::772.detailed_meaning: In the forest battle, Rama has already severed the demoness's arms. She still roars and presses close, and Lakshmana reacts in fury by disfiguring her further. The verse is a grim action detail, not a teaching moment.
ramayan::772.modern_relevance: A fight in a family chat can turn ugly fast: one sharp reply becomes three, then ten. Once anger is driving, people stop responding and start striking back.
ramayan::772.insight: It shows how quickly retaliation can exceed the original harm.

ramayan::773.verse_sanskrit: कामरूपधरा सद्य: कृत्वा रूपाण्यनेकश: । अन्तर्धानं गता यक्षी मोहयन्तीव मायया । । 12619 । । अश्मवर्षं विमुञ्चन्ती भैरवं विचचार ह ।
ramayan::773.verse_hindi: Capable of assuming forms at will, that yakshini intending to delude the princes through her power of magic, vanished from the sight. She then assumed various forms and released a rain of rocks. And started moving about frightfully.
ramayan::773.english_translation: Capable of assuming forms at will, that yakshini intending to delude the princes through her power of magic, vanished from sight. She then took many forms, rained down rocks, and moved about fearfully.
ramayan::773.translation_literal: कामरूपधरा (able to assume forms at will) / सद्यः (at once) / कृत्वा (having made) / रूपाणि (forms) / अनेकशः (in many ways) / अन्तर्धानं (disappearance) / गता (went) / यक्षी (the yakshini) / मोहयन्तीव (as if deluding) / मायया (through magic) / अश्मवर्षं (a rain of rocks) / विमुञ्चन्ती (releasing) / भैरवं (fearfully) / विचचार (moved about) / ह (indeed)
ramayan::773.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::773.essence: Threat can keep moving after it is wounded.
ramayan::773.simple_meaning: A shape-shifting yakshini disappears, takes many forms, throws rocks, and terrorizes the princes with magical tricks.
ramayan::773.simple_insight: Some dangers do not meet you openly; they change shape to confuse you.
ramayan::773.detailed_meaning: In the forest, the yakshini has already been wounded, but she does not stop. She vanishes, shifts forms, and keeps attacking with rocks and terror. This is a brief action beat showing the danger still active before Viswamitra speaks.
ramayan::773.modern_relevance: A problem at work changes form after every fix — a new excuse, a new delay, a new face. You are not dealing with one issue, but with something that keeps disguising itself.
ramayan::773.insight: It trains you to recognise confusion tactics and stay alert when resistance becomes evasive.

ramayan::774.verse_sanskrit: ततस्तावश्मवर्षेण कीर्यमाणौ समन्तत: । । 12620 । । दृष्ट्वा गाधिसुतश्श्रीमानिदं वचनमब्रवीत् ।
ramayan::774.verse_hindi: On seeing them hit and thrown about by a rain of stones from all sides, the  auspicious son of Gadhi, (Viswamitra) spoke these words:
ramayan::774.english_translation: On seeing them hit and thrown about by a rain of stones from all sides, the auspicious son of Gadhi, Viswamitra, spoke these words:
ramayan::774.translation_literal: ततस् (then) / तौ (those two) / अश्मवर्षेण (by a rain of stones) / कीर्यमाणौ (being pelted) / समन्ततः (on all sides) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / गाधिसुतः (the son of Gadhi) / श्रीमान् (the glorious one) / इदम् (this) / वचनम् (speech) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::774.speaker: Vishwamitra
ramayan::774.essence: The crisis is visible, and Vishwamitra is about to answer it.
ramayan::774.simple_meaning: Vishwamitra sees Rama and Lakshmana being stoned from every side and is about to respond.
ramayan::774.simple_insight: Pressure reveals who will act next.
ramayan::774.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana are under attack from a yakshini's stone shower in the forest. Vishwamitra watches the danger close in and prepares to intervene. This verse is the turn before his command, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::774.modern_relevance: You see someone being overwhelmed from every side, and the next words matter. This is the split second before leadership becomes real.
ramayan::774.insight: It sets up a response to danger rather than offering a lesson itself.

ramayan::775.verse_sanskrit: अलं ते घृणया राम पापैषा दुष्टचारिणी । । 12621 । । यज्ञविघ्नकरी यक्षी पुरावर्धति मायया ।
ramayan::775.verse_hindi: O Rama she does not deserve any more compassion. This yakshini who is sinful, wicked and obstructor of sacrifice will regain her strength by her magical powers .
ramayan::775.english_translation: O Rama, she does not deserve any more compassion. This yakshini, sinful and wicked, obstructs sacrifice and will regain her strength through magic.
ramayan::775.translation_literal: अलम् (enough) / ते (for you) / घृणया (with compassion) / राम (Rama) / पापैषा (this sinful one) / दुष्टचारिणी (of wicked conduct) / यज्ञविघ्नकरी (obstructing sacrifice) / यक्षी (yakshini) / पुरा (soon) / वर्धति (grows strong) / मायया (by magic)
ramayan::775.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::775.essence: Mercy without discernment can strengthen the very harm you want to stop.
ramayan::775.simple_meaning: Viswamitra tells Rama to stop feeling pity for the yakshini. She is dangerous, blocks the sacrifice, and will only become stronger if left alone.
ramayan::775.simple_insight: Compassion without discernment can prolong harm.
ramayan::775.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has brought Rama and Lakshmana to protect his sacrifice, but a shape-shifting yakshini is attacking them with stones and illusion. Seeing Rama hesitate, Viswamitra warns him that mercy here would only feed the threat.
ramayan::775.modern_relevance: You keep excusing the person who keeps sabotaging the group chat, the plan, and your sleep. Kindness matters, but not when it protects repeated harm.
ramayan::775.insight: It teaches you to separate sympathy from enabling and act before a problem grows stronger.

ramayan::776.verse_sanskrit: वध्यतां तावदेवैषा पुरा सन्ध्या प्रवर्तते । । 12622 । । रक्षांसि सन्ध्याकालेषु दुर्धर्षाणि भवन्ति वै ।
ramayan::776.verse_hindi: Kill her, for dusk is fast approaching. During evening the strength of rakshasas tends to increase and they become unassailable.
ramayan::776.english_translation: Kill her now, before dusk begins. Rakshasas become hard to defeat at evening time.
ramayan::776.translation_literal: वध्यताम् (let her be killed) / तावत् (at once) / एव (indeed) / एषा (this one) / पुरा (before) / सन्ध्या (dusk) / प्रवर्तते (begins) / रक्षांसि (rakshasas) / सन्ध्याकालेषु (at evening times) / दुर्धर्षाणि (hard to overcome) / भवन्ति (become) / वै (indeed)
ramayan::776.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::776.essence: Delay can strengthen what you meant to stop.
ramayan::776.simple_meaning: Viswamitra urges Rama to act immediately, before evening makes the enemy harder to defeat.
ramayan::776.simple_insight: Delaying the right action can make it harder than it needed to be.
ramayan::776.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has already seen the yakshini strike the sages with stones. He now presses Rama to finish the threat before dusk, because the rakshasa's strength rises at evening. The verse is tactical, not reflective: timing itself is part of victory.
ramayan::776.modern_relevance: You already know the problem needs attention, but the day is slipping away. Waiting for a better moment can give the issue more power than it had at noon.
ramayan::776.insight: It teaches you to act before a growing problem gains strength.

ramayan::777.verse_sanskrit: इत्युक्तस्तु तदा यक्षी अश्मवृष्ट्याभिवर्षतीम् । । 12623 । । दर्शयन् शब्दवेधित्वं तां रुरोध स सायकै: ।
ramayan::777.verse_hindi: Addressed thus (by Viswamitra), Rama attacked her exhibiting his skill in targetting her by the sound and prevented with arrows the yakshini from showering  stones.
ramayan::777.english_translation: Addressed thus by Vishwamitra, Rama struck her, showing his skill in aiming by sound, and held back the yakshini with arrows as she showered stones.
ramayan::777.translation_literal: इत्युक्तः (thus addressed) / तु (indeed) / तदा (then) / यक्षी (the yakshini) / अश्मवृष्ट्या (with a rain of stones) / अभिवर्षतीम् (showering) / दर्शयन् (showing) / शब्दवेधित्वं (skill in piercing by sound) / तां (her) / रुरोध (restrained) / सः (he) / सायकैः (with arrows)
ramayan::777.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::777.simple_meaning: Rama quickly stopped the yakshini’s attack with arrows, proving he could aim by sound alone.
ramayan::777.simple_insight: True skill stays calm under pressure and responds without hesitation.
ramayan::777.detailed_meaning: Vishwamitra has just urged Rama to act before dusk makes the enemy stronger. Rama answers at once, using his bow to block the yakshini’s stone attack and displaying his rare precision. The verse is a combat detail in an unfolding scene.
ramayan::777.modern_relevance: A problem hits before you have time to think: a harsh email, a sudden interruption, a room turning tense. You respond cleanly, without panic, because your training is already there.
ramayan::777.insight: It shifts attention from fear to practiced response under pressure.

ramayan::778.verse_sanskrit: सा रुद्धा शरजालेन मायाबलसमन्विता । । 12624 । । अभिदुद्राव काकुत्स्थं लक्ष्मणं च विनेदुषी ।
ramayan::778.verse_hindi: Prevented by a multitude of arrows, she with her magical powers, advanced towards Rama and Lakshmanaroaring.
ramayan::778.english_translation: Prevented by a net of arrows, she, endowed with magical power, rushed toward Rama and Lakshmana, roaring.
ramayan::778.translation_literal: सा (she) / रुद्धा (blocked) / शरजालेन (by a net of arrows) / मायाबलसमन्विता (endowed with magical power) / अभिदुद्राव (rushed toward) / काकुत्स्थं (toward the descendant of Kakutstha, Rama) / लक्ष्मणं (Lakshmana) / च (and) / विनेदुषी (roaring)
ramayan::778.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::778.essence: Stopping a danger is not the same as ending it.
ramayan::778.simple_meaning: Blocked by arrows, the magical attacker still charges straight at Rama and Lakshmana.
ramayan::778.simple_insight: Some threats keep coming even after you think they are stopped.
ramayan::778.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has ordered Rama to stop the night-demon woman before dusk strengthens her further. Even after arrows block her, she powers forward through illusion and force, rushing at Rama and Lakshmana in the middle of the attack.
ramayan::778.modern_relevance: You shut down one problem, and it comes back louder a minute later. The first fix only exposed how determined it was.
ramayan::778.insight: It shows that force alone may restrain a threat briefly, but not end it.

ramayan::779.verse_sanskrit: तामापतन्तीं वेगेन विक्रान्तामशनीमिव । । 12625 । । शरेणोरसि विव्याथ सा पपात ममार च ।
ramayan::779.verse_hindi: Her chest pierced with an arrow, she rushing menacingly towards them like a thunderbolt fell down dead.
ramayan::779.english_translation: Her chest pierced with an arrow, she rushed toward them like a thunderbolt and fell dead.
ramayan::779.translation_literal: ताम् (her) / आपतन्तीम् (rushing toward) / वेगेन (swiftly) / विक्रान्ताम् (fierce) / अशनीम् इव (like a thunderbolt) / शरेण (with an arrow) / उरसि (in the chest) / विव्याथ (pierced) / सा (she) / पपात (fell) / ममार (died) / च (and)
ramayan::779.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::779.essence: A relentless threat is stopped by one decisive strike.
ramayan::779.simple_meaning: Rama pierces the charging yakshini in the chest, and she falls dead.
ramayan::779.simple_insight: Some threats end only when met decisively.
ramayan::779.detailed_meaning: After Vishwamitra commands Rama, the yakshini keeps charging like a thunderbolt despite the arrows. Rama answers with one fatal shot, and the immediate danger ends. The next verse shows the celestial beings praising him.
ramayan::779.modern_relevance: A problem keeps rushing at you even after warnings and boundaries. At some point, you stop negotiating and deal with it cleanly.
ramayan::779.insight: It shows that restraint has a limit; when harm keeps advancing, decisive action becomes necessary.

ramayan::780.verse_sanskrit: तां हतां भीमसङ्काशां दृष्ट्वा सुरपतिस्तदा । । 12626 । । साधु साध्विति काकुत्स्थं सुराश्च समपूजयन् ।
ramayan::780.verse_hindi: Having seen the slain yakshini of terrible appearance, Indra and other celestials worshipped Rama, exclaiming well done, well done .
ramayan::780.english_translation: Having seen the slain yakshini of terrible appearance, Indra and the other celestials worshipped Rama, exclaiming, "Well done, well done."
ramayan::780.translation_literal: तां (her) / हतां (slain) / भीमसङ्काशां (of terrible appearance) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / सुरपतिः (the lord of the celestials) / तदा (then) / साधु साधु इति (well done, well done) / काकुत्स्थम् (to Rama, descendant of Kakutstha) / सुराः (the celestials) / च (and) / समपूजयन् (worshipped, praised)
ramayan::780.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::780.essence: Victory is confirmed when the danger is finally gone.
ramayan::780.simple_meaning: The celestials praise Rama after seeing the fearsome yakshini killed.
ramayan::780.simple_insight: Recognition can arrive instantly when a dangerous force is stopped.
ramayan::780.detailed_meaning: A fearsome yakshini has just fallen before Rama’s arrow. Indra and the other celestials see the danger ended and immediately praise him. The verse is a reaction to the victory, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::780.modern_relevance: The room goes quiet after the threat is removed, and only then do people finally say, "You were right."
ramayan::780.insight: It marks approval after the action, not a principle to apply.

ramayan::781.verse_sanskrit: उवाच परमप्रीत स्सहस्राक्ष: पुरन्दर: । । 12627 । । सुराश्च सर्वे संहृष्टा विश्वामित्रमथाब्रुवन् ।
ramayan::781.verse_hindi: Then exceedingly pleased the thousandeyed Indra and all other delighted celestials  said to Viswamitra:
ramayan::781.english_translation: Then exceedingly pleased the thousand-eyed Indra and all other delighted celestials said to Viswamitra:
ramayan::781.translation_literal: उवाच (said) / परमप्रीत (exceedingly pleased) / सहस्राक्षः (thousand-eyed) / पुरन्दरः (Indra) / सुराः (celestials) / च (and) / सर्वे (all) / संहृष्टाः (delighted) / विश्वामित्रम् (to Viswamitra) / अथ (then) / अब्रुवन् (said)
ramayan::781.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::781.essence: The victory is complete, and the praise begins.
ramayan::781.simple_meaning: Indra and the other celestial beings, filled with delight, spoke to Viswamitra after Rama's victory.
ramayan::781.simple_insight: Recognition often comes after the hard act is already done.
ramayan::781.detailed_meaning: Rama has just killed the terrible yakshini, and the celestials rejoice at the outcome. Indra, pleased by the deed, turns to Viswamitra. This verse only sets up the praise that follows.
ramayan::781.modern_relevance: You finish the difficult thing, and only then do others notice what it took. The acknowledgment comes after the strain, not before it.
ramayan::781.insight: It shifts attention from the action itself to the praise that follows it.

ramayan::782.verse_sanskrit: मुने कौशिक भद्रं ते सेन्द्रास्सर्वे मरुद्गणा: । । 12628 । । तोषिता: कर्मणाऽनेन स्नेहं दर्शय राघवे ।
ramayan::782.verse_hindi: O ascetic Kausika, may prosperity be to you All devatas have been gratified by this act (of Rama) and have expressed their love for Rama.
ramayan::782.english_translation: O ascetic Kausika, may prosperity be to you. All the radiant beings have been gratified by this act and have shown their affection for Rama.
ramayan::782.translation_literal: मुने (O ascetic) / कौशिक (Kausika) / भद्रं ते (may prosperity be to you) / सेन्द्राः (with Indra) / सर्वे (all) / मरुद्गणाः (the hosts of wind-deities) / तोषिताः (gratified) / कर्मणा (by the act) / अनेन (this) / स्नेहम् (affection) / दर्शय (show) / राघवे (toward Rama)
ramayan::782.speaker: Indra
ramayan::782.essence: Right action earns recognition even from those you cannot see.
ramayan::782.simple_meaning: Indra tells Vishwamitra that the radiant beings are pleased by Rama's deed and want their affection for Rama to be shown.
ramayan::782.simple_insight: Good action draws recognition beyond the visible world.
ramayan::782.detailed_meaning: After Rama kills the terrible yakshini, Indra and the other radiant beings rejoice. Speaking to Vishwamitra, Indra praises the deed and asks him to show affection for Rama. The verse links Rama's action to divine approval, but it is part of a longer exchange.
ramayan::782.modern_relevance: You finish a hard, quiet task and only later hear that it mattered more than anyone said. The real approval arrives after the work is already done.
ramayan::782.insight: It shifts attention from public praise to the deeper recognition that follows right action.

ramayan::783.verse_sanskrit: प्रजापतेर्भृशाश्वस्य पुत्रान् सत्यपराक्रमान् । । 12629 । । तपोबलभृतो ब्रह्मन् राघवाय निवेदय ।
ramayan::783.verse_hindi: O Brahmarshi, you may offer to Rama, the sons of  Prajapati Brishasva who are the weapons bestowed with the power that comes from truth and ascetic energy.
ramayan::783.english_translation: O Brahmarshi, offer to Rama the sons of Prajapati Brishasva, endowed with truth and ascetic power.
ramayan::783.translation_literal: प्रजापतेः (of Prajapati) / भृशाश्वस्य (of Brishasva) / पुत्रान् (sons) / सत्यपराक्रमान् (whose power is rooted in truth) / तपोबलभृतः (bearing the strength of austerity) / ब्रह्मन् (O Brahmarshi) / राघवाय (to Rama) / निवेदय (present)
ramayan::783.speaker: Indra
ramayan::783.essence: Power is given only after character has already been proven.
ramayan::783.simple_meaning: The celestial beings ask Vishvamitra to present powerful divine weapons to Rama.
ramayan::783.simple_insight: Great help often arrives only after trust has already been proven.
ramayan::783.detailed_meaning: After Rama's feat has pleased Indra and the celestial hosts, they speak to Vishvamitra. They ask him to hand over the sons of Brishasva—powerful weapons born of truth and austerity—to Rama, because he has shown he is worthy of them.
ramayan::783.modern_relevance: You finally earn the trust to handle something serious: a role, a tool, a responsibility. What comes next is not random reward; it is recognition of readiness.
ramayan::783.insight: It shifts attention from receiving power to becoming fit for it.

ramayan::784.verse_sanskrit: पात्रभूतश्च ते ब्रह्मंस्तवानुगमने धृत: । । 12630 । । कर्तव्यं च महत्कर्म सुराणां राजसूनुना ।
ramayan::784.verse_hindi: O Brahmarshi following you with firmness of mind, Rama is worthy to receive the weapons. He who is a prince has to accomplish many such great tasks for the benefit of the celestials.
ramayan::784.english_translation: O Brahmarshi, Rama is fit to receive the weapons, for he follows you with steadfast mind. A prince must accomplish many great tasks for the good of the celestials.
ramayan::784.translation_literal: पात्रभूतः (fit to receive) / च (and) / ते (your) / ब्रह्मन् (O Brahmarshi) / तव (your) / अनुगमने (in following) / धृतः (steadfast) / कर्तव्यम् (to be done) / च (and) / महत् (great) / कर्म (task) / सुराणाम् (of the celestials) / राजसूनुना (by the prince)
ramayan::784.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::784.essence: You become fit for big work by holding firm in small trials.
ramayan::784.simple_meaning: Rama has shown the steadiness needed for bigger responsibilities. Because of that, he is worthy of the weapons and the larger work ahead.
ramayan::784.simple_insight: Steadiness is what prepares you for larger responsibility.
ramayan::784.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra is preparing Rama for a task beyond ordinary training. The gods have been pleased by Rama's conduct, and now the sage is told to give him weapons, because a prince must be ready for great acts done for the world's good.
ramayan::784.modern_relevance: You handled the small assignment without drama, and now someone trusts you with the harder one. That trust was earned by how you carried yourself before anyone was impressed.
ramayan::784.insight: It shifts attention from entitlement to earned readiness: greater responsibility follows proven steadiness.

ramayan::785.verse_sanskrit: एवमुक्त्वा सुरास्सर्वे हृष्टा जग्मुर्यथागतम् । । 12631 । । विश्वामित्रं पुरस्कृत्य ततस्सन्ध्या प्रवर्तते ।
ramayan::785.verse_hindi: Having said these words, the celestials were pleased. They honoured Viswamitra and returned to their abodes from where they had come. And then dusk set in.
ramayan::785.english_translation: Having said these words, the celestials were pleased. They honoured Viswamitra and returned to their abodes from where they had come. And then dusk set in.
ramayan::785.translation_literal: एवमुक्त्वा (having said thus) / सुराः सर्वे (all the celestials) / हृष्टाः (delighted) / जग्मुः (went) / यथागतम् (as they had come) / विश्वामित्रम् (Viswamitra) / पुरस्कृत्य (placing in front, honouring) / ततः (then) / सन्ध्या (dusk) / प्रवर्तते (began)
ramayan::785.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::785.essence: The appeal is over; the next trial waits in the dusk.
ramayan::785.simple_meaning: The celestials leave in satisfaction after honouring Viswamitra, and evening falls.
ramayan::785.simple_insight: Some victories end quietly, with relief and the return of ordinary time.
ramayan::785.detailed_meaning: The celestials have finished their appeal and depart, satisfied that Rama is ready for the next stage of his training. Viswamitra is honoured, the divine assembly withdraws, and the scene settles into dusk before the next encounter begins.
ramayan::785.modern_relevance: A tense meeting ends, the room empties, and you finally notice the evening light outside the window. The pressure lifts, but the real work is still waiting.
ramayan::785.insight: It marks a pause between one test and the next, not the teaching itself.

ramayan::786.verse_sanskrit: ततो मुनिवर: प्रीतस्ताटकावधतोषित: । । 12632 । । मूर्ध्नि राममुपाघ्राय इदं वचनमब्रवीत् ।
ramayan::786.verse_hindi: Then, the best of ascetics Viswamitra rejoiced over the death of Tataka, kissed the forehead of Rama (fondly) and spoke these words:
ramayan::786.english_translation: Then the best of ascetics, pleased by Tataka's death, kissed Rama on the forehead and said these words.
ramayan::786.translation_literal: ततः (then) / मुनिवरः (best of ascetics) / प्रीतः (pleased) / ताटकावधतोषितः (satisfied by the killing of Tataka) / मूर्ध्नि (on the forehead) / रामम् (Rama) / उपाघ्राय (having kissed) / इदम् (these) / वचनम् (words) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::786.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::786.essence: Approval comes only after courage is proved.
ramayan::786.simple_meaning: Viswamitra is happy that Rama has killed Tataka. He shows affection and then speaks to Rama.
ramayan::786.simple_insight: A hard act can mark the moment when trust turns into approval.
ramayan::786.detailed_meaning: After Rama kills Tataka, Viswamitra is relieved and pleased. He responds not with distance, but with affection, kissing Rama’s forehead before speaking. The moment shows the teacher’s trust deepening after Rama proves himself.
ramayan::786.modern_relevance: You finally handled the difficult thing everyone was circling around. The person who guided you can now see your strength clearly.
ramayan::786.insight: It marks the shift from instruction to recognition after a decisive act.

ramayan::787.verse_sanskrit: इहाद्य रजनीं राम वसेम शुभदर्शन । । 12633 । । श्व: प्रभाते गमिष्यामस्तदाश्रमपदं मम ।
ramayan::787.verse_hindi: O auspiciouslooking Rama tonight we shall stay here. Tomorrow morning we proceed to my hermitage.
ramayan::787.english_translation: O auspicious-looking Rama, tonight we shall stay here. Tomorrow morning we will go to my hermitage.
ramayan::787.translation_literal: इह (here) / अद्य (today, tonight) / रजनीं (the night) / राम (Rama) / वसेम (let us stay) / शुभदर्शन (auspicious-looking one) / श्वः (tomorrow) / प्रभाते (in the morning) / गमिष्यामः (we will go) / तदाश्रमपदम् (that hermitage-place) / मम (my)
ramayan::787.speaker: Vishwamitra
ramayan::787.essence: The journey pauses here; the real work continues at dawn.
ramayan::787.simple_meaning: Viswamitra asks Rama to spend the night there and continue to his hermitage in the morning.
ramayan::787.simple_insight: Sometimes the right move is simply to rest and continue at dawn.
ramayan::787.detailed_meaning: After Tataka is slain, Viswamitra is pleased with Rama and stops for the night in the forest. He tells Rama they will leave at sunrise and continue to his hermitage. The verse mainly moves the journey forward.
ramayan::787.modern_relevance: After a draining day, you stop the drive at a small roadside lodge and finish the trip in the morning. Not every journey should be forced through exhaustion.
ramayan::787.insight: It shifts attention from urgency to timing, showing that even a sacred task can wait for morning.

ramayan::788.verse_sanskrit: विश्वामित्रवच: श्रुत्वा हृष्टो दशरथात्मज: । । 12634 । । उवास रजनीं तत्र ताटकाया वने सुखम् ।
ramayan::788.verse_hindi: Having heard the words of Viswamitra, Rama rejoiced and rested happily that night in the Tataka forest .
ramayan::788.english_translation: Having heard the words of Viswamitra, Rama rejoiced and rested happily that night in the Tataka forest.
ramayan::788.translation_literal: विश्वामित्रवच: (the words of Viswamitra) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / हृष्टो (rejoiced) / दशरथात्मज: (the son of Dasharatha) / उवास (stayed) / रजनीं (the night) / तत्र (there) / ताटकाया (of Tataka) / वने (in the forest) / सुखम् (happily)
ramayan::788.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::788.essence: He had entered danger, and now he could finally rest inside it.
ramayan::788.simple_meaning: Rama heard Viswamitra's words, felt glad, and spent the night peacefully in the forest.
ramayan::788.simple_insight: Sometimes trust is shown not by speech, but by resting without fear in the middle of danger.
ramayan::788.detailed_meaning: After Tataka is killed, Viswamitra asks Rama to remain in the same forest for the night. Rama, Dasharatha's son, accepts without hesitation and sleeps peacefully there. The verse marks the calm after a dangerous first victory, not a new teaching.
ramayan::788.modern_relevance: You finish a hard, tense day and finally sit down in the same room where everything felt sharp an hour ago. Your body knows the danger has passed before your mind catches up.
ramayan::788.insight: It shows settled confidence after action, not restless replaying of what just happened.

ramayan::789.verse_sanskrit: मुक्तशापं वनं तच्च तस्मिन्नेव तदाहनि । । 12635 । । रमणीयं विबभ्राज यथा चैत्ररथं वनम् ।
ramayan::789.verse_hindi: Freed from the curse from that day that forest looked charming and shone like Chitraratha Kuberas (garden).
ramayan::789.english_translation: Freed from the curse, that forest on that very day shone beautifully like the garden of Kubera.
ramayan::789.translation_literal: मुक्तशापं (freed from the curse) / वनं (forest) / तत् (that) / तस्मिन्-एव (in that very) / तद्-अहनि (on that day) / रमणीयं (charming, beautiful) / विबभ्राज (shone) / यथा (like) / चैत्ररथं (Chitraratha) / वनम् (forest, garden)
ramayan::789.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::789.essence: Lifting a curse can make the world look new again.
ramayan::789.simple_meaning: The cursed forest lost its darkness and appeared beautiful again, like Kubera's celestial garden.
ramayan::789.simple_insight: Some places change when a burden is lifted from them.
ramayan::789.detailed_meaning: After Rama hears Vishwamitra and rests in the forest, the land itself is transformed. The curse on Tataka's forest has ended, and the place now shines like Kubera's garden. It is a scene-setting verse, not a teaching.
ramayan::789.modern_relevance: A room feels different after a heavy argument ends and everyone goes quiet. Nothing in the walls changed, but the air did. This verse captures that kind of sudden release.
ramayan::789.insight: It shifts attention from action to atmosphere: one event can restore beauty to a whole place.

ramayan::790.verse_sanskrit: निहत्य तां यक्षसुतां स राम:प्रशस्यमानस्सुरसिद्धसङ्घै: । उवास तस्मिन्मुनिना सहैवप्रभातवेलां प्रतिबोध्यमान: । । 12636 । ।
ramayan::790.verse_hindi: Rama having killed the daughter of yaksha was praised by multitudes of devatas and siddhas. He stayed in the same forest with the sage. At the first glimpse of dawn, he was awakened by the sage (Viswamitra).
ramayan::790.english_translation: Having killed the yaksha's daughter, Rama was praised by hosts of devas and siddhas. He stayed there with the sage, and at dawn the sage awakened him.
ramayan::790.translation_literal: निहत्य (having killed) / ताम् (her) / यक्षसुताम् (the yaksha's daughter) / सः (he) / रामः (Rama) / प्रशस्यमानः (being praised) / सुरसिद्धसङ्घैः (by hosts of devas and siddhas) / उवास (stayed) / तस्मिन् (there) / मुनिना (by the sage) / सह (together) / एव (indeed) / प्रभातवेलाम् (at dawn time) / प्रतिबोध्यमानः (being awakened)
ramayan::790.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::790.essence: The battle ends, and dawn carries Rama onward.
ramayan::790.simple_meaning: Rama killed the yaksha's daughter, was praised by celestial beings, and spent the night with Viswamitra until dawn.
ramayan::790.simple_insight: Some moments are important only because they move the story forward.
ramayan::790.detailed_meaning: After Tataka is slain, the forest is freed and the night settles. Rama receives praise from celestial beings, then rests beside Viswamitra until the sage wakes him at dawn. The verse bridges the battle’s end and the next lesson.
ramayan::790.modern_relevance: A hard task ends, the room goes quiet, and everyone moves on to the next thing. Not every moment carries a lesson; some simply mark the turning of the night.
ramayan::790.insight: It keeps the narrative moving from victory to the next instruction.

ramayan::791.verse_sanskrit: अथ तां रजनीमुष्य विश्वामित्रो महायशाः । प्रहस्य राघवं वाक्यमुवाच मधुराक्षरम् । । 1271 । ।
ramayan::791.verse_hindi: The night over, illustrious Viswamitra called Rama with a sweet smile.
ramayan::791.english_translation: Then, after that night had passed, the illustrious Vishvamitra smiled and spoke to Rama in sweet words.
ramayan::791.translation_literal: अथ (then) / ताम् (that) / रजनीम् (night) / उष्य (having spent) / विश्वामित्रः (Vishvamitra) / महायशाः (greatly renowned) / प्रहस्य (smiling) / राघवम् (to Rama) / वाक्यम् (words) / उवाच (spoke) / मधुराक्षरम् (with sweet words)
ramayan::791.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::791.essence: The quiet after waiting is where the next teaching begins.
ramayan::791.simple_meaning: After the night ended, Vishvamitra smiled and addressed Rama kindly.
ramayan::791.simple_insight: A hard night has passed, and the next step is ready to begin.
ramayan::791.detailed_meaning: After a night in the forest, Vishvamitra turns to Rama with warmth and approval. This is the quiet pause before he reveals his purpose and begins the next stage of Rama's training.
