ramayan::884.detailed_meaning: A guide points Rama toward Mithila, where King Janaka's great bow and sacred sacrifice await. The verse simply prepares the scene for the test that will reveal who can lift the bow and win Sita.
ramayan::884.modern_relevance: You arrive at a place where everything is about to change, but the change has not happened yet. This is the doorway before the decisive moment.
ramayan::884.insight: It sets up the coming trial by naming the place, the bow, and the sacrifice.

ramayan::885.verse_sanskrit: तद्धि यज्ञफलं तेन मैथिलेनोत्तमं धनु: । याचितं नरशार्दूल सुनाभं सर्वदैवतै: । । 13112 । ।
ramayan::885.verse_hindi: O best among men, that excellent bow strong in the middle was offered by king of Mithila, Devarata as well as by all devatas as fruit of the sacrifice.
ramayan::885.english_translation: O best among men, that excellent bow, strong in the middle, was offered by king of Mithila, Devarata, as the fruit of the sacrifice, along with all the radiant beings.
ramayan::885.translation_literal: तद्धि (that indeed) / यज्ञफलं (the fruit of the sacrifice) / तेन (by that) / मैथिलेन (by the Mithila king) / उत्तमं (excellent) / धनु: (bow) / याचितं (offered) / नरशार्दूल (O tiger among men) / सुनाभं (well-naved, strong in the middle) / सर्वदैवतै: (by all the radiant beings)
ramayan::885.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::885.essence: The bow matters because it was born from sacrifice, not ordinary power.
ramayan::885.simple_meaning: The great bow was a sacred reward from a sacrifice, given by the king of Mithila and the radiant beings.
ramayan::885.simple_insight: Some objects carry a history so sacred that touching them changes the moment.
ramayan::885.detailed_meaning: Janaka's court is preparing to reveal the impossible bow that no prince has lifted. Valmiki pauses to explain its sacred origin: it was gained as the result of a sacrifice and honored by the king of Mithila and the radiant beings. The scene builds reverence before Rama is asked to act.
ramayan::885.modern_relevance: You walk into a room and see an object everyone treats with caution — not because it is fragile, but because it carries meaning. Some things are heavier than their weight.
ramayan::885.insight: It frames the bow as a consecrated object, raising the stakes before Rama's test.

ramayan::886.verse_sanskrit: आयागभूतं नृपतेस्तस्य वेश्मनि राघव । अर्चितं विविधैर्गन्धैर्धूपैश्चागरुगन्धिभि: । । 13113 । ।
ramayan::886.verse_hindi: O Rama, that bow is worshipped in the kings palace as principal deity with various kinds of perfumes, sandal paste, incense and fragrant agaru.
ramayan::886.english_translation: O Rama, that bow is worshipped in the king's palace as a principal sacred object, with many kinds of perfumes, sandal paste, incense, and fragrant agaru.
ramayan::886.translation_literal: आयागभूतम् (made into an object of worship) / नृपतेः (of the king) / तस्य (that) / वेश्मनि (in the palace) / राघव (O Rama) / अर्चितम् (worshipped) / विविधैः (with various) / गन्धैः (with perfumes) / धूपैः (with incense) / च (and) / अगरुगन्धिभिः (with agaru-fragrance)
ramayan::886.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::886.essence: The bow's value is shown by the reverence around it.
ramayan::886.simple_meaning: The bow is kept in the king's palace and treated with great reverence, surrounded by perfumes and incense.
ramayan::886.simple_insight: Some things are honoured so much that even their stillness feels sacred.
ramayan::886.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra is guiding Rama and Lakshmana toward the bow of Janaka in Mithila. Before the great test begins, he describes how the bow is preserved in the palace with ritual care. The verse is a vivid detail, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::886.modern_relevance: You walk into a museum room where one object is guarded, lit softly, and never touched. Before anyone explains why it matters, you already feel its weight.
ramayan::886.insight: It sets the scene for the bow's importance, preparing you for the coming test.

ramayan::887.verse_sanskrit: एवमुक्त्वा मुनिवर: प्रस्थानमकरोत्तदा । सर्षिसङ्घ स्सकाकुत्स्थ: आमन्त्र्य वनदेवता: । । 13114 । ।
ramayan::887.verse_hindi: Having spoken thus, Viswamitra,  the best of ascetics commenced the onward journey along with the Kakutshas and rishis, taking leave of the deities of the forest.
ramayan::887.english_translation: Having spoken thus, Viswamitra, the best of ascetics, commenced the onward journey with the descendants of Kakutstha, after taking leave of the forest deities.
ramayan::887.translation_literal: एवम् (thus) / उक्त्वा (having spoken) / मुनिवरः (the best of ascetics) / प्रस्थानम् (departure / onward journey) / अकरोत् (made / commenced) / तदा (then) / सर्षिसङ्घः (with the group of sages) / सकाकुत्स्थः (with the Kakutsthas) / आमन्त्र्य (taking leave of) / वनदेवताः (forest deities)
ramayan::887.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::887.essence: The journey continues only after a respectful farewell.
ramayan::887.simple_meaning: After speaking, Viswamitra set out again with Rama and the sages, first respectfully taking leave of the forest deities.
ramayan::887.simple_insight: Even a holy journey pauses to show respect before moving on.
ramayan::887.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has finished speaking in the forest and now resumes the journey with Rama and the gathered sages. Before leaving, he respectfully takes leave of the forest deities. The verse simply marks the transition to the next stage of travel.
ramayan::887.insight: It signals a clean transition: speak, bow out, and move forward without lingering.

ramayan::888.verse_sanskrit: स्वस्ति वोऽस्तु गमिष्यामि सिद्वस्सिद्धाश्रमादहम् । उत्तरे जाह्नवीतीरे हिमवन्तं शिलोच्चयम् । । 13115 । ।
ramayan::888.verse_hindi: (O ascetics of the forest) May you be safe. My purpose has been achieved in this Siddhaashrama. From here I shall go to the Himavanta mountain situated on the
ramayan::888.english_translation: May you be safe. My purpose has been fulfilled in this Siddhashrama. Now I shall go to Mount Himavanta on the northern bank of the Ganges.
ramayan::888.translation_literal: स्वस्ति (may there be well-being) / वोऽस्तु (to you be) / गमिष्यामि (I shall go) / सिद्धस्सिद्धाश्रमात् (having succeeded from Siddhashrama) / अहम् (I) / उत्तरे (in the northern) / जाह्नवीतीरे (on the bank of the Ganges) / हिमवन्तम् (to Himavanta) / शिलोच्चयम् (the mountain)
ramayan::888.speaker: Vishwamitra
ramayan::888.essence: Fulfilled work can be left behind without regret.
ramayan::888.simple_meaning: Vishwamitra blesses the ascetics, says his aim in Siddhashrama is complete, and prepares to travel onward to Mount Himavanta.
ramayan::888.simple_insight: Completion is not clinging. When a task is fulfilled, moving on is also right.
ramayan::888.detailed_meaning: Vishwamitra has brought Rama and Lakshmana through the Siddhashrama and completed the purpose of his stay there. He bids the forest ascetics well, then turns north toward Mount Himavanta, marking the end of one sacred stage and the beginning of another.
ramayan::888.modern_relevance: You finish the project, thank the people who helped, and close the laptop without reopening the tab. Some chapters end cleanly because their work is done.
ramayan::888.insight: It teaches you to recognise completion and move forward without lingering out of habit.

ramayan::889.verse_sanskrit: प्रदक्षिणं तत: कृत्वा सिद्धाश्रममनुत्तमम् । उत्तरां दिशमुद्दिश्य प्रस्थातुमुपचक्रमे । । 13116 । ।
ramayan::889.verse_hindi: Thereafter, circumambulating the supreme Siddhasrama with reverence, they (Viswamitra and the princes) commenced their journey in the northern direction.
ramayan::889.english_translation: Thereafter, circumambulating the supreme Siddhasrama with reverence, they commenced their journey northward.
ramayan::889.translation_literal: प्रदक्षिणम् (circumambulation) / ततः (then) / कृत्वा (having done) / सिद्धाश्रमम् (the Siddhasrama) / अनुत्तमम् (supreme) / उत्तराम् (northern) / दिशम् (direction) / उद्दिश्य (toward) / प्रस्थातुम् (to set out) / उपचक्रमे (began)
ramayan::889.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::889.simple_meaning: They respectfully circle the sacred hermitage and then continue their journey to the north.
ramayan::889.simple_insight: Even a departure can begin with reverence.
ramayan::889.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has finished his work at Siddhasrama. Before moving on, he and the princes honor the place by walking around it in reverence, then set out again toward the northern mountains. The verse is a transition, not a teaching.
ramayan::889.modern_relevance: You leave a place that changed you, but you do not rush out carelessly. You pause, acknowledge it, and then move on.
ramayan::889.insight: It shows that transitions can be handled with respect, not haste.

ramayan::890.verse_sanskrit: तं प्रयान्तं मुनिवरमन्वयादनुसारिणम् । शकटीशतमात्रं तु प्रायेण ब्रह्मवादिनाम् । । 13117 । ।
ramayan::890.verse_hindi: As Viswamitra, the best of ascetics set out on his journey, expounders of the Vedas followed him, nearly in one hundred carriages.
ramayan::890.english_translation: As Viswamitra, the best of ascetics set out on his journey, expounders of the Vedas followed him, nearly in one hundred carriages.
ramayan::890.translation_literal: तं (him) / प्रयान्तम् (departing) / मुनिवरम् (best of ascetics) / अन्वयात् (followed) / अनुसारिणम् (the followers) / शकटीशतमात्रम् (about one hundred carts) / तु (indeed) / प्रायेण (almost) / ब्रह्मवादिनाम् (of Veda-expounders)
ramayan::890.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::890.essence: A great sage departs, and many follow behind him.
ramayan::890.simple_meaning: As Viswamitra departed, many Vedic scholars followed him in nearly a hundred carriages.
ramayan::890.simple_insight: A revered teacher can draw people after him without asking.
ramayan::890.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has completed his stay at Siddhashrama and now leaves with Rama and Lakshmana. This verse simply shows the scale of the departure: learned Vedic scholars and attendants follow the great sage in a long procession.
ramayan::890.modern_relevance: A respected teacher leaves a retreat center, and the whole lane fills with cars and people seeing him off. The verse is just the procession — a detail in a larger journey.
ramayan::890.insight: It sets the scene with movement and reverence, not a teaching.

ramayan::891.verse_sanskrit: मृगपक्षिगणाश्चैव सिद्धाश्रमनिवासिन: । अनुजग्मुर्महात्मानं विश्वामित्रं महामुनिम् । । 13118 । । निवर्तयामास तत: पक्षिसङ्घान् मृगानपि ।
ramayan::891.verse_hindi: Birds and beasts living in Siddhaashrama also followed the illustrious maharshi
ramayan::891.english_translation: The birds and animals living in Siddhashrama followed the great sage Vishvamitra, and he then sent the flocks of birds and the animals back.
ramayan::891.translation_literal: मृगपक्षिगणाः (groups of deer and birds) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / सिद्धाश्रमनिवासिनः (residents of Siddhashrama) / अनुजग्मुः (followed) / महात्मानम् (the great-souled one) / विश्वामित्रम् (Vishvamitra) / महामुनिम् (the great sage) / निवर्तयामास (sent back) / ततः (then) / पक्षिसङ्घान् (flocks of birds) / मृगान् (deer) / अपि (also)
ramayan::891.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::891.essence: A saint’s departure is so gentle that even the forest follows.
ramayan::891.simple_meaning: The animals and birds of Siddhashrama followed Vishvamitra, and he gently sent them back.
ramayan::891.simple_insight: Even the forest seems to honor a sage who lives in harmony with it.
ramayan::891.detailed_meaning: Vishvamitra leaves Siddhashrama with Rama and Lakshmana. As he departs, the birds and animals of the hermitage follow him like loyal companions, and he turns them back. The verse paints affection, reverence, and the quiet harmony of the sage’s world.
ramayan::891.modern_relevance: When you leave a place where you were deeply respected, even small signs of affection can follow you to the door.
ramayan::891.insight: It shows a presence so steady and kind that even animals respond to it.

ramayan::892.verse_sanskrit: ते गत्वा दूरमध्वानं लम्बमाने दिवाकरे । वासं चक्रुर्मुनिगणाः शोणाकूले समाहिता: । । 13119 । ।
ramayan::892.verse_hindi: The sages travelled a long distance and halted on the bank of  Sona at sunset.
ramayan::892.english_translation: The sages travelled a long distance and halted on the bank of the Sona at sunset.
ramayan::892.translation_literal: ते (they) / गत्वा (having gone) / दूरम् (far) / अध्वानम् (the road/journey) / लम्बमाने (while descending) / दिवाकरे (the sun) / वासम् (resting place) / चक्रुः (made) / मुनिगणाः (the groups of sages) / शोणाकूले (on the bank of the Sona) / समाहिताः (collected, composed)
ramayan::892.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::892.essence: Progress also means knowing when to stop.
ramayan::892.simple_meaning: The sages walked far and stopped for the night by the Sona River as the sun was setting.
ramayan::892.simple_insight: Sometimes the right move is simply to stop, rest, and continue tomorrow.
ramayan::892.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra’s group has already begun its journey, with sages and followers moving together through the landscape. This verse simply marks their long day of travel ending at the Sona River, setting up the next action at dusk.
ramayan::892.modern_relevance: You finally reach the highway rest stop after hours on the road, too tired to keep pushing. The journey continues tomorrow, but tonight, you need a place to land.
ramayan::892.insight: It shifts attention from motion to timing: even a sacred journey needs rest at the right moment.

ramayan::893.verse_sanskrit: तेऽस्तं गते दिनकरे स्नात्वा हुतहुताशना: । विश्वामित्रं पुरस्कृत्य निषेदुरमितौजस: । । 13120 । ।
ramayan::893.verse_hindi: The sages who possessed great splendour bathed and offered oblations to fire at sunset and sat in front of  Viswamitra.
ramayan::893.english_translation: At sunset, the radiant sages bathed, offered oblations to fire, and sat down with Vishvamitra in front.
ramayan::893.translation_literal: ते (those) / अस्तं गते (having set) / दिनकरे (the sun) / स्नात्वा (having bathed) / हुतहुताशना: (having offered oblations to fire) / विश्वामित्रं (Vishvamitra) / पुरस्कृत्य (placing in front) / निषेदुः (sat down) / अमितौजस: (of immense splendour)
ramayan::893.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::893.essence: Even on the road, their discipline does not break.
ramayan::893.simple_meaning: The sages finished their evening rites, then sat together in front of Vishvamitra.
ramayan::893.simple_insight: Daily discipline gives shape to even a long journey.
ramayan::893.detailed_meaning: Vishvamitra and the sages have travelled far and stopped by the Sona at sunset. After bathing and offering fire rites, they settle down in order, with Vishvamitra at the front. The verse simply marks the camp's evening routine before Rama and Lakshmana arrive.
ramayan::893.modern_relevance: After a long day on the road, you still wash up, do what must be done, and sit in order before the night begins.
ramayan::893.insight: It shows how sacred routine continues even in transit, keeping the group steady and orderly.

ramayan::894.verse_sanskrit: रामोऽपि सहसौमित्रिर्मुनीं स्तानभिपूज्य च । अग्रतो निषसादाथ विश्वामित्रस्य धीमत: । । 13121 । ।
ramayan::894.verse_hindi: Rama together with Lakshmana having offered respectful salutations to the sages, sat in front of the sagacious Viswamitra.
ramayan::894.english_translation: Rama together with Lakshmana, having offered respectful salutations to the sages, sat in front of the wise Viswamitra.
ramayan::894.translation_literal: रामोऽपि (Rama also) / सहसौमित्रिः (together with Lakshmana) / मुनीन् (to the sages) / तान् (those) / अभिपूज्य (having honoured) / च (and) / अग्रतः (in front) / निषसाद (sat down) / अथ (then) / विश्वामित्रस्य (of Viswamitra) / धीमतः (of the wise one)
ramayan::894.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::894.essence: Respect comes first; only then can teaching begin.
ramayan::894.simple_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana respectfully greet the sages and sit before Viswamitra.
ramayan::894.simple_insight: Respect opens the way before any teaching begins.
ramayan::894.detailed_meaning: After the sages rest by the Sona at sunset, bathe, and gather around Viswamitra, Rama and Lakshmana arrive, honour the sages, and take their seats before the teacher. The scene sets up the coming instruction, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::894.modern_relevance: You walk into a room where people already carry authority and experience. Before asking for guidance, you first show respect and take your place quietly.
ramayan::894.insight: It teaches you to begin learning with humility, not with your own urgency.

ramayan::895.verse_sanskrit: अथ रामो महातेजाः विश्वामित्रं महामुनिम् । पप्रच्छ नरशार्दूल: कौतूहलसमन्वित: । । 13122 । ।
ramayan::895.verse_hindi: Thereafter highly lustrous Rama, the best among men, filled with curiosity enquired of
ramayan::895.english_translation: Thereafter, radiant Rama, the best among men, asked the great sage Vishwamitra, filled with curiosity.
ramayan::895.translation_literal: अथ (thereafter) / रामः (Rama) / महातेजाः (highly lustrous) / विश्वामित्रम् (Vishwamitra) / महामुनिम् (great sage) / पप्रच्छ (asked) / नरशार्दूलः (best among men) / कौतूहल-समन्वितः (filled with curiosity)
ramayan::895.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::895.essence: Curiosity opens the door to wisdom.
ramayan::895.simple_meaning: Rama turns to Vishwamitra and asks a question out of genuine curiosity.
ramayan::895.simple_insight: Curiosity can be a form of strength, not weakness.
ramayan::895.detailed_meaning: After the sages settle near Vishwamitra at dusk, Rama and Lakshmana sit before the wise teacher. Rama then leans in with curiosity and asks him to explain the land they have entered, beginning the exchange that will reveal its story.
ramayan::895.modern_relevance: You are in a new place, and instead of pretending you understand it, you ask. That honest question can open everything.
ramayan::895.insight: It shifts the mind from passive watching to active questioning.

ramayan::896.verse_sanskrit: भगवन् कोऽन्वयं देशस्समृद्धवनशोभित: । श्रोतुमिच्छामि भद्रं ते वक्तुमर्हसि तत्त्वत: । । 13123 । ।
ramayan::896.verse_hindi: O worshipful one, what could be the reason for this region shining with luxuriant groves?  I wish to hear from you. You can tell me all about this (region). May it be safe for you
ramayan::896.english_translation: O worshipful one, what is the reason this region shines with luxuriant groves? I wish to hear the truth from you. Please tell me all about it, if it is well with you.
ramayan::896.translation_literal: भगवन् (O worshipful one) / कः (what) / अन्वयम् (the reason) / देशः (region) / समृद्ध-वन-शोभितः (shining with luxuriant groves) / श्रोतुम् इच्छामि (I wish to hear) / भद्रम् ते (may it be well with you) / वक्तुम् अर्हसि (you should speak) / तत्त्वतः (truly, in full)
ramayan::896.speaker: Rama
ramayan::896.essence: Respectful curiosity opens the door to real understanding.
ramayan::896.simple_meaning: Rama asks Viswamitra why this land is so beautiful and asks him to explain it fully.
ramayan::896.simple_insight: Good questions can be humble, precise, and open at once.
ramayan::896.detailed_meaning: Rama sits before Viswamitra after greeting the sages. Curious about the forested land around them, he asks the sage to explain why this region is so lush and remarkable. The moment shows the first movement of learning: respectful inquiry.
ramayan::896.modern_relevance: You walk into a new city and notice one street feels alive while another feels empty. Instead of assuming, you ask someone who knows the place and listen all the way through.
ramayan::896.insight: It trains the mind to ask before judging, and to seek explanation directly from a reliable source.

ramayan::897.verse_sanskrit: चोदितो रामवाक्येन कथयामास सुव्रत: । तस्य देशस्य निखिलमृषिमध्ये महातपा: । । 13124 । ।
ramayan::897.verse_hindi: A sage of  excellent vows and rigid austerities, Viswamitra, urged by the words of Rama, described  in the midst of rishis the entire story relating to that region.
ramayan::897.english_translation: Urged by Rama's words, the great ascetic Vishvamitra told the full story of that land among the assembled sages.
ramayan::897.translation_literal: चोदितः (urged) / रामवाक्येन (by Rama's words) / कथयामास (told) / सुव्रतः (of excellent vows) / तस्य (of that) / देशस्य (of the region) / निखिलम् (the whole) / ऋषिमध्ये (among the sages) / महातपाः (the great ascetic)
ramayan::897.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::897.essence: A single question opens the door to the land's hidden story.
ramayan::897.simple_meaning: Vishvamitra responds to Rama's question by narrating the full history of the region to the gathered sages.
ramayan::897.simple_insight: Curiosity opens the door to a larger story.
ramayan::897.detailed_meaning: Rama has asked Vishvamitra why this land is so beautiful and full of groves. Moved by Rama's question, the sage begins explaining the region's complete history before the other sages. The verse simply turns the conversation toward the next story.
ramayan::897.modern_relevance: You ask a question at the right moment, and someone finally tells you the real backstory. The answer changes how you see the whole place.
ramayan::897.insight: It shifts attention from the question itself to the deeper history behind what you see.

ramayan::898.verse_hindi: There was a great ascetic named Kusa, born to Brahma, as ascetic indefatigable in vows, knowldegeable in dharma and a respector of the virtuous.
ramayan::898.english_translation: There was a great ascetic named Kusa, born to Brahma, indefatigable in vows, knowledgeable in dharma, and a respecter of the virtuous.
ramayan::898.translation_literal: ब्रह्मयोनिः (born to Brahma) / महान् (great) / आसीत् (was) / कुशः (Kusa) / नाम (named) / महातपाः (great ascetic) / अक्लिष्टव्रतधर्मज्ञः (unwearied in vows and knowledgeable in dharma) / सज्जनप्रतिपूजकः (one who honors the virtuous)
ramayan::898.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::898.essence: Greatness here is measured by vows, dharma, and respect for the worthy.
ramayan::898.simple_meaning: Kusa is introduced as a noble ascetic: disciplined, devoted to dharma, and respectful toward good people.
ramayan::898.simple_insight: Character is shown by steady vows and respect, not by status alone.
ramayan::898.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra is explaining an old lineage story to Rama. He names Kusa, a great ascetic linked to Brahma, then describes his vows, conduct, and reverence for the virtuous. The verse is a character introduction, not the main teaching.
ramayan::898.modern_relevance: Someone enters the room with impressive credentials, but what you notice later is steadiness, restraint, and how they treat decent people.
ramayan::898.insight: It shifts attention from title to temperament and from fame to conduct.

ramayan::899.verse_sanskrit: स महात्मा कुलीनायां युक्तायां सुगुणोल्बणान् । वैदर्भ्यां जनयामास चतुरस्सदृशान् सुतान् । । 1322 । । कुशाम्बं कुशनाभं च अधूर्तरजसं वसुम् ।
ramayan::899.verse_hindi: That great soul, Kusa, married the princess of Vidarbha  born in a noble family and a match for him. He begot four virtuous sons who resembled him. They were Kusamba, Kusanabha, Adhurtarajas and Vasu.
ramayan::899.english_translation: That great soul, Kusa, married the princess of Vidarbha, born in a noble family and suited to him. He begot four virtuous sons who resembled him: Kusamba, Kusanabha, Adhurtarajas, and Vasu.
ramayan::899.translation_literal: सः (he) / महात्मा (great-souled one) / कुलीनायाम् (in a noble-born woman) / युक्तायाम् (fit/suited) / सुगुणोल्बणान् (abounding in good qualities) / वैदर्भ्याम् (from Vidarbha) / जनयामास (begot) / चतुरस्सदृशान् (four who were like him) / सुतान् (sons) / कुशाम्बम् (Kusamba) / कुशनाभम् च (and Kusanabha) / अधूर्तरजसम् (Adhurtarajas) / वसुम् (Vasu)
ramayan::899.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::899.essence: Virtue here becomes a family line, not a private achievement.
ramayan::899.simple_meaning: Kusa married a noble Vidarbha princess and fathered four sons who matched his virtues.
ramayan::899.simple_insight: A life of character leaves its shape in the next generation.
ramayan::899.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing Kusa's lineage, not teaching a doctrine. After introducing Kusa as a great ascetic, the poem notes his marriage to a fitting noble bride and the birth of four sons. The passage sets up the family line before the next verse turns to their qualities.
ramayan::899.modern_relevance: A family photo, years later, can show what kind of home someone built. The children carry not just a name, but the atmosphere of the life that raised them.
ramayan::899.insight: It shifts attention from individual achievement to the moral texture a person passes on.

ramayan::900.verse_sanskrit: दीप्तियुक्तान् महोत्साहान् क्षत्रधर्मचिकीर्षया । । 1323 । । तानुवाच कुश: पुत्रान् धर्मिष्ठान् सत्यवादिन: ।
ramayan::900.verse_hindi: Kusa addressed his four brilliant sons who were highly enthusiastic, pious, truthful and were wedded to duties of the warrior race:
ramayan::900.english_translation: Kusa addressed his four brilliant sons who were highly enthusiastic, righteous, truthful, and devoted to the duties of the warrior class.
ramayan::900.translation_literal: दीप्तियुक्तान् (endowed with brilliance) / महोत्साहान् (greatly enthusiastic) / क्षत्रधर्मचिकीर्षया (with the desire to perform the duty of the warrior class) / तान् (them) / उवाच (said) / कुशः (Kusa) / पुत्रान् (sons) / धर्मिष्ठान् (righteous) / सत्यवादिनः (truth-speakers)
ramayan::900.speaker: Kusa
ramayan::900.essence: Even noble sons still need direction toward duty.
ramayan::900.simple_meaning: Kusa spoke to his four sons, who were bright, energetic, righteous, and committed to the duties of warriors.
ramayan::900.simple_insight: Good character is not just inherited; it must be directed toward right action.
ramayan::900.detailed_meaning: Kusa, the learned ancestor of a royal line, turns to his four exceptional sons. He praises their brilliance and warrior spirit, then prepares to instruct them in how to rule and uphold their inherited duty.
ramayan::900.modern_relevance: A parent sees a capable child full of drive and knows talent alone is not enough. What matters next is how that energy gets shaped into responsibility.
ramayan::900.insight: It shifts attention from giftedness to the discipline of using gifts well.

ramayan::901.verse_sanskrit: क्रियतां पालनं पुत्रा: धर्मं प्राप्स्यथ पुष्कलम् । । 1324 । । ऋषेस्तु वचनं श्रुत्वा चत्वारो लोकसम्मता: । निवेशं चक्रिरे सर्वे पुराणां नृवरास्तदा । । 1325 । ।
ramayan::901.verse_hindi: O my sons, govern with righteousness so that you will acquire immense merit. Hearing the words of the rishi, the four sons who were the best among men and revered in the world constructed four cities as their abodes.
ramayan::901.english_translation: O my sons, govern with righteousness so that you will acquire immense merit. Hearing the words of the rishi, the four sons who were the best among men and revered in the world constructed four cities as their abodes.
ramayan::901.translation_literal: क्रियताम् (let be done) / पालनम् (governing, protection) / पुत्राः (sons) / धर्मम् (righteousness, duty) / प्राप्स्यथ (you will obtain) / पुष्कलम् (abundant, immense) / ऋषेः (of the rishi) / तु (then) / वचनम् (word, instruction) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / चत्वारः (four) / लोकसम्मताः (approved by the world) / निवेशम् (settlement, abode) / चक्रिरे (they made) / सर्वे (all) / पुराणाम् (of cities) / नृवराः (best among men) / तदा (then)
ramayan::901.speaker: Kusa
ramayan::901.essence: Righteous rule creates the merit that power alone cannot.
ramayan::901.simple_meaning: Kusa tells his sons to rule their cities justly. If they govern with righteousness, they will earn great merit.
ramayan::901.simple_insight: Good leadership is measured by fairness, not force.
ramayan::901.detailed_meaning: Kusa has raised four noble sons and now hands them the burden of rule. He tells them to govern righteously, and they respond by founding four cities. The verse shows succession being anchored in duty, not ambition.
ramayan::901.modern_relevance: You inherit a team, a home, or a project with real consequences. The question is not whether you can control everything, but whether you will lead fairly enough to deserve trust.
ramayan::901.insight: It shifts leadership from control to righteous stewardship.

ramayan::902.verse_sanskrit: कुशाम्बस्तु महातेजा: कौशाम्बीमकरोत्पुरीम् । कुशनाभस्तु धर्मात्मा पुरं चक्रे महोदयम् । । 1326 । ।
ramayan::902.verse_hindi: The brilliant Kushamba and the righteous Kushanabha constructed the cities of
ramayan::902.english_translation: The brilliant Kushamba built the city of Kaushambi, and righteous Kushanabha built the great city of Mahodaya.
ramayan::902.translation_literal: कुशाम्बः (Kushamba) / तु (indeed) / महातेजाः (very brilliant) / कौशाम्बीम् (Kaushambi) / अकरोत् (made) / पुरीम् (city) / कुशनाभः (Kushanabha) / तु (indeed) / धर्मात्मा (righteous in nature) / पुरम् (city) / चक्रे (built) / महोदयम् (Mahodaya)
ramayan::902.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::902.essence: Their names survived because they built cities, not stories.
ramayan::902.simple_meaning: Kushamba founded Kaushambi, and Kushanabha founded Mahodaya. The verse simply names these kings and the cities they built.
ramayan::902.simple_insight: Great rulers leave more than memories; they leave places shaped by their character.
ramayan::902.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is listing the descendants of Kusha and the cities they established. Kushamba, known for brilliance, founded Kaushambi. Kushanabha, known for righteousness, built Mahodaya. The passage is genealogical and descriptive, not a teaching.
ramayan::902.modern_relevance: A family name on a building, a road, or a town still carries someone's choices. Some people are remembered because they built things that outlasted them.
ramayan::902.insight: It shifts attention from heroic action to the quieter legacy of building and founding.

ramayan::903.verse_sanskrit: अधूर्तरजसो राम धर्मारण्यं महीपति: । चक्रे पुरवरं राजा वसुश्चक्रे गिरिव्रजम् । । 1327 । ।
ramayan::903.verse_hindi: O Rama king Adhurtarajasa constructed Dharmaranya, the best of cities and king Vasu, the city of Girivrajam.
ramayan::903.english_translation: O Rama, the righteous king Adhurtarajasa built the excellent city of Dharmaranya, and King Vasu built Girivraja.
ramayan::903.translation_literal: अधूर्तरजसो (of unclouded radiance) / राम (O Rama) / धर्मारण्यं (Dharmaranya) / महीपति: (the king) / चक्रे (made) / पुरवरं (the best city) / राजा (the king) / वसु: (Vasu) / चक्रे (made) / गिरिव्रजम् (Girivraja)
ramayan::903.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::903.essence: True rule leaves behind places people can live well.
ramayan::903.simple_meaning: Kings of old founded great cities and gave them order and shape.
ramayan::903.simple_insight: Greatness is not only won in battle; it is also built into places that can hold people well.
ramayan::903.detailed_meaning: The sage is listing ancient kings and the cities they founded: Dharmaranya by one ruler, Girivraja by Vasu. Rama is being addressed as the listener while the verse continues the genealogy of noble city-building, not a separate teaching.
ramayan::903.modern_relevance: A planner stands over an empty plot, deciding where homes, roads, and water lines will go. The work is invisible now, but it will shape how thousands live later.
ramayan::903.insight: It shifts attention from glory to the quieter work of building what lasts.

ramayan::904.verse_sanskrit: एषा वसुमती राम वसोस्तस्य महात्मन: । एते शैलवरा: पञ्च प्रकाशन्ते समन्तत: । । 1328 ।
ramayan::904.verse_hindi: O Rama this place where we are (called Vasumati) belongs to the magnanimous king Vasu. This is  surrounded by five great shining mountains.
ramayan::904.english_translation: O Rama, this place called Vasumati belongs to the magnanimous king Vasu. These five great mountains shine all around it.
ramayan::904.translation_literal: एषा (this) / वसुमती (Vasumati) / राम (O Rama) / वसोः (of Vasu) / तस्य (of that) / महात्मनः (magnanimous one) / एते (these) / शैलवराḥ (great mountains) / पञ्च (five) / प्रकाशन्ते (shine) / समन्ततः (all around)
ramayan::904.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::904.essence: The poem pauses to map the world before the journey continues.
ramayan::904.simple_meaning: Valmiki points out a region named Vasumati, says it belonged to King Vasu, and notes that five great mountains shine around it.
ramayan::904.simple_insight: Some verses simply place you in the world before the story moves on.
ramayan::904.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is guiding Rama through an ancient landscape, naming the land of Vasu and the five mountains that surround it. The verse is geographic description, part of a broader travel passage that builds the setting rather than offering a teaching.
ramayan::904.modern_relevance: You’re driving through an unfamiliar region and someone keeps naming rivers, hills, and old kingdoms. The details matter because they locate you, but they are not asking anything of you.
ramayan::904.insight: It anchors the scene in place and prepares the ground for the next movement.

ramayan::905.verse_sanskrit: सुमागधी नदी रम्या मगधान् विश्रुताययौ । पञ्चानां शैलमुख्यानां मध्ये मालेव शोभते । । 1329 । ।
ramayan::905.verse_hindi: The delightful and renowned river Sumagadhi (known as Sona), flowing in the country of Magadha, looks beautiful like a garland amidst five great mountains.
ramayan::905.english_translation: The delightful and renowned river Sumagadhi, flowing through Magadha, shines like a garland among five great mountains.
ramayan::905.translation_literal: सुमागधी (Sumagadhi) / नदी (river) / रम्या (delightful) / मगधान् (in Magadha) / विश्रुताययौ (came to be renowned) / पञ्चानां (of five) / शैलमुख्यानां (chief mountains) / मध्ये (in the middle) / मालेव (like a garland) / शोभते (shines)
ramayan::905.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::905.essence: Landscape can be so ordered that it feels like ornament.
ramayan::905.simple_meaning: The river Sumagadhi is beautiful and famous. It runs through Magadha and stands out among five major mountains like a garland.
ramayan::905.simple_insight: A place can feel alive when its river, hills, and land all seem to belong together.
ramayan::905.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing the landscape around Magadha: a famous river, five great mountains, and a city shaped by nature. The verse is not teaching a doctrine; it simply adds vivid beauty to the scene before the story moves on.
ramayan::905.modern_relevance: You pass a roadside overlook at dusk, and the whole valley suddenly makes sense. The river, the hills, and the fields seem arranged with quiet grace.
ramayan::905.insight: It trains the mind to notice how geography itself can carry beauty and harmony.

ramayan::906.verse_sanskrit: सैषा हि मागधी राम वसोस्तस्य महात्मन: । पूर्वाभिचरिता राम सुक्षेत्रा सस्यमालिनी । । 13210 । ।
ramayan::906.verse_hindi: Rama, this Magadhi river, of great Vasu flows from the east surrounded by fertile crops fields like a garland.
ramayan::906.english_translation: Rama, this Magadhi river, belonging to the great king Vasu, flows from the east and is surrounded by fertile fields like a garland.
ramayan::906.translation_literal: सा एषा (this) हि (indeed) मागधी (Magadhi) राम (Rama) वसोः (of Vasu) तस्य (his) महात्मनः (of the great-souled one) पूर्वाभिचरिता (flowing from the east) राम (Rama) सुक्षेत्रा (having fertile fields) सस्यमालिनी (garlanded with crops)
ramayan::906.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::906.essence: Landscape detail deepens the journey, but carries no separate teaching here.
ramayan::906.simple_meaning: The verse describes the Magadhi river as flowing from the east through fertile, crop-filled land.
ramayan::906.simple_insight: It paints the landscape clearly so the journey feels alive and real.
ramayan::906.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is guiding Rama through the geography of the region, naming the Magadhi river and its fertile banks. The verse is part of a larger travel description, adding vivid detail rather than a separate teaching.
ramayan::906.modern_relevance: A road trip where someone keeps naming rivers, fields, and hills can feel slow — until the place starts becoming part of the story.
ramayan::906.insight: It anchors the scene in place, preparing the listener for the next movement.

ramayan::907.verse_sanskrit: कुशनाभस्तु राजर्षि: कन्याशतमनुत्तमम् । जनयामास धर्मात्मा घृताच्यां रघुनन्दन । । 13211 । ।
ramayan::907.verse_hindi: O scion of the Raghu family, the virtuous rajarshi Kusanabha begot one hundred beautiful daughters through a nymph named Ghritachi.
ramayan::907.english_translation: O scion of the Raghu family, the virtuous rajarshi Kusanabha begot one hundred beautiful daughters through a nymph named Ghritachi.
ramayan::907.translation_literal: कुशनाभः (Kusanabha) / तु (indeed) / राजर्षिः (king-sage) / कन्याशतम् (a hundred daughters) / अनुत्तमम् (excellent) / जनयामास (begot) / धर्मात्मा (righteous in nature) / घृताच्याम् (through Ghritachi) / रघुनन्दन (O delight of Raghu)
ramayan::907.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::907.essence: A lineage detail prepares the next turn in the story.
ramayan::907.simple_meaning: Kusanabha, a righteous king-sage, had one hundred beautiful daughters through Ghritachi.
ramayan::907.simple_insight: Some verses simply set the stage for the story that follows.
ramayan::907.detailed_meaning: The journey has reached a new place in the lineage story. After the river is described, Valmiki introduces Kusanabha and his hundred daughters so the next scene can unfold around them.
ramayan::907.modern_relevance: You sometimes meet people only by their role in the next event, not by a lesson they carry. This verse works like that—quietly placing the pieces before the real action begins.
ramayan::907.insight: It marks a transition from landscape to character introduction.

ramayan::908.verse_sanskrit: तास्तु यौवनशालिन्यो रूपवत्य स्स्वलङ्कृता: । उद्यानभूमिमागम्य प्रावृषीव शतह्रदा: । । 13212 । । गायन्त्यो नृत्यमानाश्च वादयन्त्यश्च सर्वश: । आमोदं परमं जग्मुर्वराभरणभूषिता: । । 13213 । ।
ramayan::908.verse_hindi: Those welladorned, beautiful, young maidens in the pleasuregarden looked like lightnings in the rainy season. Bedecked with fine ornaments they were singing, dancing, playing on instruments and moving in all directions in great delight.
ramayan::908.english_translation: Those well-adorned, beautiful, young maidens in the pleasure garden looked like lightning in the rainy season. Bedecked with fine ornaments, they were singing, dancing, playing instruments, and moving everywhere in great delight.
ramayan::908.translation_literal: ताः (those) / तु (indeed) / यौवनशालिन्यः (endowed with youth) / रूपवत्यः (beautiful) / स्वलङ्कृताः (well-adorned) / उद्यानभूमिम् (to the garden ground) / आगम्य (having come) / प्रावृषि (in the rainy season) / इव (like) / शतह्रदाः (lightning flashes) / गायन्त्यः (singing) / नृत्यमानाः (dancing) / च (and) / वादयन्त्यः (playing instruments) / च (and) / सर्वशः (in every way) / आमोदम् (delight) / परमम् (supreme) / जग्मुः (they attained) / वराभरणभूषिताः (adorned with excellent ornaments)
ramayan::908.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::908.essence: A garden full of music and dazzling youth sets the stage.
ramayan::908.simple_meaning: The princesses entered the garden, beautifully dressed and full of joy, singing, dancing, and playing instruments like lightning flashes in the monsoon sky.
ramayan::908.simple_insight: Beauty and joy can fill a space so fully that they seem to brighten the whole scene.
ramayan::908.detailed_meaning: Kusanabha's hundred daughters have come into the garden. Valmiki pauses on their youth, beauty, and movement, comparing them to lightning in the rainy season. The verse is vivid description, not a teaching moment.
ramayan::908.insight: It paints the scene before the next event, giving the story its visual and emotional brightness.

ramayan::909.verse_sanskrit: अथ ताश्चारुसर्वाङ्ग्यो रूपेणाप्रतिमा भुवि । उद्यानभूमिमागम्य तारा इव घनान्तरे । । 13214 । ।
ramayan::909.verse_hindi: With beautiful limbs of unparalleled beauty on earth, they shone in the pleasuregarden like stars in the midst of clouds.
ramayan::909.english_translation: With beautiful limbs of unparalleled beauty on earth, they shone in the pleasure garden like stars in the midst of clouds.
ramayan::909.translation_literal: अथ (then) / ताः (those) / चारु-सर्व-अङ्ग्यः (beautiful-limbed) / रूपेण (in beauty) / अप्रतिमाः (unmatched) / भुवि (on earth) / उद्यान-भूमिम् (to the garden ground) / आगम्य (having come) / ताराः इव (like stars) / घन-अन्तरे (amid clouds)
ramayan::909.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::909.essence: The scene pauses to let their radiance be seen.
ramayan::909.simple_meaning: The princesses entered the garden, and their beauty made them seem like stars shining through clouds.
ramayan::909.simple_insight: Some scenes are meant to be seen, not interpreted.
ramayan::909.detailed_meaning: Kusanabha's hundred daughters have already been introduced, and now Valmiki pauses to paint their appearance as they enter the pleasure garden. The verse is pure description, setting up the moment before Vayu notices them.
ramayan::909.modern_relevance: A room goes quiet when someone unexpectedly beautiful, graceful, or radiant walks in. The moment is about presence, not action.
ramayan::909.insight: It slows the story to let beauty register before the next event begins.

ramayan::910.verse_sanskrit: तास्सर्वगुणसम्पन्ना रूपयौवनसंयुता: । दृष्ट्वा सर्वात्मको वायुरिदं वचनमब्रवीत् । । 13215 । ।
ramayan::910.verse_hindi: At the sight of the maidens embellished with all virtues and youth and beauty, the allpervading Windgod addressed them these words:
ramayan::910.english_translation: At the sight of the maidens endowed with every virtue, beauty, and youth, the all-pervading Windgod spoke these words.
ramayan::910.translation_literal: तास् (those) / सर्वगुणसम्पन्ना (endowed with all virtues) / रूपयौवनसंयुता: (joined with beauty and youth) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / सर्वात्मको (all-pervading) / वायुः (Windgod) / इदम् (this) / वचनम् (speech) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::910.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::910.essence: Beauty is seen first; desire follows immediately after.
ramayan::910.simple_meaning: Seeing the beautiful maidens, the Windgod spoke to them.
ramayan::910.simple_insight: A single glance can turn admiration into desire.
ramayan::910.detailed_meaning: In the pleasure garden, a group of radiant maidens appears. Their beauty is described first, then the Windgod notices them and begins to speak. This verse is the setup for his proposal in the next line, not the full teaching itself.
ramayan::910.modern_relevance: You walk into a room and the atmosphere shifts before anyone speaks. Attraction can arrive instantly, before judgment has time to catch up.
ramayan::910.insight: It sets up the moment when desire moves from seeing to speaking.

ramayan::911.verse_sanskrit: अहं व: कामये सर्वा भार्या मम भविष्यथ । मानुषस्त्यज्यतां भावः दीर्घमायुरवाप्स्यथ । । 13216 । ।
ramayan::911.verse_hindi: I request you all to be my wives. You will leave this feeling of mortality and attain a
ramayan::911.english_translation: I desire all of you. Become my wives, and you will give up mortal nature and attain long life.
ramayan::911.translation_literal: अहम् (I) / वः (you all) / कामये (desire) / सर्वा (all) / भार्या (wives) / मम (my) / भविष्यथ (you will become) / मानुषः (mortal) / त्यज्यताम् (let be cast off) / भावः (nature/state) / दीर्घम् (long) / आयुः (life-span) / अवाप्स्यथ (you will attain)
ramayan::911.speaker: Vayu
ramayan::911.essence: Desire here is wrapped in a promise of escape from human limits.
ramayan::911.simple_meaning: The speaker invites the women to become his wives and promises them freedom from human mortality and a longer life.
ramayan::911.simple_insight: The promise sounds tempting because it offers escape from the limits you already know.
ramayan::911.detailed_meaning: In the garden, the Wind-god is struck by the beauty of the maidens and speaks openly. He offers marriage and a transformed existence: no longer ordinary human life, but a longer, more radiant one. The scene turns desire into a promise of elevation.
ramayan::911.modern_relevance: A stranger offers you a shortcut that sounds like transcendence: less pain, more time, a better version of yourself. The real question is not whether it dazzles you, but what it asks you to become.
ramayan::911.insight: It frames desire as a trade: give up one identity to gain another.

ramayan::912.verse_sanskrit: चलं हि यौवनं नित्यं मानुषेषु विशेषत: । अक्षय्यं यौवनं प्राप्ताः अमर्यश्च भविष्यथ । । 13217 । ।
ramayan::912.verse_hindi: Youth is always unstable, especially in human beings. If you marry me, you will be ever youthful like devatas.
ramayan::912.english_translation: Youth is always unstable, especially in human beings. If you marry me, you will be ever youthful like devas.
ramayan::912.translation_literal: चलं (unstable) / हि (indeed) / यौवनं (youth) / नित्यं (always) / मानुषेषु (among humans) / विशेषत: (especially) / अक्षय्यं (imperishable) / यौवनं (youth) / प्राप्ताः (having obtained) / अमर्यः (deathless) / च (and) / भविष्यथ (you will become)
ramayan::912.speaker: Vayu
ramayan::912.essence: Youth fades; only what you become can endure.
ramayan::912.simple_meaning: Physical youth does not last, especially for human beings. The speaker offers the maidens a way to become deathless and forever young.
ramayan::912.simple_insight: What feels permanent in the body is already moving on. Real security comes from what outlasts appearance.
ramayan::912.detailed_meaning: Vayu has just proposed marriage to a hundred beautiful maidens. To persuade them, he reminds them that human youth always fades. He promises a condition beyond decay if they accept him, turning desire into a claim about impermanence.
ramayan::912.modern_relevance: You catch your reflection and notice the first sign of change — a line, a softness, a thing you can't reverse. The verse asks what you are chasing: fading youth, or something that endures.
ramayan::912.insight: It shifts attention from preserving appearance to seeking what does not decay.

ramayan::913.verse_sanskrit: तस्य तद्वचनं श्रुत्वा वायोरक्लिष्टकर्मण: । अपहास्य ततो वाक्यं कन्याशतमथाब्रवीत् । । 13218 । ।
ramayan::913.verse_hindi: At the works of the untiringly blowing Windgod the lunged maidens laughed and said:
ramayan::913.english_translation: Hearing that speech of the untiring Windgod, the hundred maidens laughed and then spoke.
ramayan::913.translation_literal: तस्य (his) / तद्वचनं (that speech) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / वायोः (of the Windgod) / अक्लिष्टकर्मणः (of the one whose action is never weary) / अपहास्य (laughing at) / ततः (then) / वाक्यं (speech) / कन्याशतम् (the hundred maidens) / अथ (then) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::913.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::913.essence: Their laughter exposes how thin his boast really is.
ramayan::913.simple_meaning: The hundred maidens heard the Windgod's proposal and laughed before replying.
ramayan::913.simple_insight: Not every offer deserves silence; some are answered by clear, immediate refusal.
ramayan::913.detailed_meaning: The Windgod has just boasted to the maidens, promising youth and a life beyond human limits if they accept him. Hearing him, the hundred girls laugh, and the scene turns toward their sharp reply in the next verse. This verse is only the reaction before the refusal.
ramayan::913.modern_relevance: Someone makes an absurd offer with complete confidence, expecting awe. The first response is not debate — it is laughter, because your instincts already know the line has been crossed.
ramayan::913.insight: It shows the moment before rejection: the body recognises arrogance faster than the mouth does.

ramayan::914.verse_sanskrit: अन्तश्चरसि भूतानां सर्वेषां त्वं सुरोत्तम । प्रभावज्ञा: स्म ते सर्वा: किमस्मानवमन्यसे । । 13219 । ।
ramayan::914.verse_hindi: O best among devatas you move within all living beings, we feel your impact. Why do you insult us?
ramayan::914.english_translation: O best among the radiant beings, you move within all living beings. We know your power well, so why do you slight us?
ramayan::914.translation_literal: अन्तः (within) / चरसि (you move) / भूतानाम् (of living beings) / सर्वेषाम् (of all) / त्वम् (you) / सुरोत्तम (best among the radiant beings) / प्रभावज्ञाः (knowers of your power) / स्म (indeed) / ते (your) / सर्वाः (all) / किम् (why) / अस्मान् (us) / अवमन्यसे (do you slight)
ramayan::914.speaker: Apsaras
ramayan::914.essence: Power means little if it comes wrapped in contempt.
ramayan::914.simple_meaning: The celestial women recognize his power and ask why he is treating them with disrespect.
ramayan::914.simple_insight: Even admiration can turn sharp when dignity feels ignored.
ramayan::914.detailed_meaning: The daughters of Kusanabha have just laughed at Vayu's strange proposal. Now they answer him directly, acknowledging his greatness but refusing to be treated lightly. The verse is part of a playful exchange, not a teaching.
ramayan::914.modern_relevance: A message arrives from someone who clearly wants something from you, but their tone feels dismissive. You can respect their competence and still notice the slight.
ramayan::914.insight: It shows how quickly social charm breaks when respect is missing.

ramayan::915.verse_sanskrit: कुशनाभसुतास्सर्वा: समर्थास्त्वां सुरोत्तम । स्थानाच्च्यावयितुं देवं रक्षामस्तु तपो वयम् । । 13220 । ।
ramayan::915.verse_hindi: O best among devatas we are daughters of Kusanabha, We are capable of pulling you down from your position. We are safeguarding our ascetic merit as virgins (we could curse you to save our ascetic merit) of Kusnabha.
ramayan::915.english_translation: O best among the devas, we are the daughters of Kushanabha. We are able to pull you down from your place. We protect our ascetic merit.
ramayan::915.translation_literal: कुशनाभसुताः (daughters of Kushanabha) / सर्वाः (all of us) / समर्थाः (able) / त्वाम् (you) / सुरोत्तम (O best among the devas) / स्थानात् (from place) / च्यावयितुम् (to make fall) / देवं (deva) / रक्षामः (we protect) / तु (indeed) / तपः (ascetic merit) / वयम् (we)
ramayan::915.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::915.essence: Real strength is keeping what anger would make you waste.
ramayan::915.simple_meaning: The daughters of Kushanabha tell the divine visitor that they can force him down, but they choose to guard their ascetic merit instead.
ramayan::915.simple_insight: Power is not the same as wisdom; restraint can be stronger than retaliation.
ramayan::915.detailed_meaning: The wind god has spoken to the daughters of Kushanabha, and they answer with dignity. They remind him of their power, but the real point is their restraint: they will not waste their ascetic merit in anger, even when insulted.
ramayan::915.modern_relevance: Someone cuts you off, then acts offended when you react. You have the power to strike back, but you also know what that reaction would cost you.
ramayan::915.insight: It shifts the mind from proving strength to protecting hard-won discipline.

ramayan::916.verse_sanskrit: माभूत्स कालो दुर्मेध: पितरं सत्यवादिनम् । नावमन्यस्व धर्मेण स्वयं वरमुपास्महे । । 13221 । ।
ramayan::916.verse_hindi: O wicked one, do not dishonour our father who always speaks the truth. He will choose the bridegrooms righteously. Do not invite death (father may be the cause of your death).
ramayan::916.english_translation: O wicked one, do not dishonour our father who always speaks the truth. He will choose the bridegrooms righteously. Do not invite death.
ramayan::916.translation_literal: मा भूत् (may it not be) / सः (that) / कालः (time) / दुर्मेधः (wicked-minded one) / पितरम् (father) / सत्य-वादिनम् (truth-speaking) / न (do not) / अवमन्यस्व (disrespect) / धर्मेण (righteously) / स्वयम् (by himself) / वरम् (bridegroom) / उपास्महे (we shall choose / seek)
ramayan::916.speaker: One of Kusanabha's daughters
ramayan::916.essence: Respect for truth matters more than someone’s impatience.
ramayan::916.simple_meaning: The daughters refuse the insult and insist that their father, who always tells the truth, will choose their husbands properly and fairly.
ramayan::916.simple_insight: There is dignity in trusting a just process instead of forcing your way through.
ramayan::916.detailed_meaning: Kusanabha's daughters are answering a disrespectful challenge. They defend their father’s integrity and remind the speaker that marriage will be decided by righteous conduct, not arrogance. The moment turns on honor, restraint, and trust in their father's judgment.
ramayan::916.modern_relevance: Someone tries to pressure your family into a decision before you're ready. You stay calm and refuse the push, because the right choice does not need intimidation.
ramayan::916.insight: It teaches you to protect dignity without losing self-command.

ramayan::917.verse_sanskrit: पिता हि प्रभुरस्माकं दैवतं परमं हि न: । यस्य नो दास्यति पिता स नो भर्ता भविष्यति । । 13222 । ।
ramayan::917.verse_hindi: Our father is our lord. Our father is god to us. Whomsoever our father offers us shall become our husband.
ramayan::917.english_translation: Our father is our lord. Our father is the highest reverence for us. Whomever our father gives us to will become our husband.
ramayan::917.translation_literal: पिता (father) / हि (indeed) / प्रभुः (lord) / अस्माकम् (of us) / दैवतं (highest reverence) / परमम् (supreme) / हि (indeed) / नः (for us) / यस्य (whom) / नः (to us) / दास्यति (will give) / पिता (father) / सः (that one) / नः (our) / भर्ता (husband) / भविष्यति (will become)
ramayan::917.speaker: Kusnabh's daughters
ramayan::917.essence: A daughter's marriage is placed under her father's lawful choice.
ramayan::917.simple_meaning: The daughters say their father has the right to decide whom they marry, and they will accept his choice.
ramayan::917.simple_insight: There is dignity in trusting a rightful authority without resistance.
ramayan::917.detailed_meaning: Kusnabh's daughters answer the suitors before the scene turns violent. They insist that their father's authority over their marriage is rightful, and that his chosen match alone will be accepted. Their loyalty sets the moral stage for the Wind god's anger.
ramayan::917.modern_relevance: You may not like a decision made by someone responsible for you, but you still have to face what that decision means. Sometimes respect is shown not by winning the argument, but by accepting the structure already in place.
ramayan::917.insight: It shifts attention from personal preference to rightful obligation and family authority.

ramayan::918.verse_sanskrit: तासां तद्वचनं श्रुत्वा वायु: परमकोपन: । प्रविश्य सर्वगात्राणि बभञ्ज भगवान् प्रभु: । । 13223 । ।
ramayan::918.verse_hindi: Having heard the words of those maidens, the most powerful and venerable Windgod became furious. He entered all the limbs of their bodies, twisted and distorted them.
ramayan::918.english_translation: Having heard the words of those maidens, the most powerful and venerable Windgod became furious. He entered all their limbs and twisted and distorted them.
ramayan::918.translation_literal: तासां (of those) / तद्वचनं (that speech) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / वायु: (the Windgod) / परमकोपन: (most furious) / प्रविश्य (having entered) / सर्वगात्राणि (all limbs) / बभञ्ज (broke, twisted) / भगवान् (the venerable one) / प्रभु: (the powerful lord)
ramayan::918.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::918.essence: Unchecked anger turns force into injury.
ramayan::918.simple_meaning: The Windgod grew angry at the maidens' words and violently crippled their bodies.
ramayan::918.simple_insight: Cruel speech can trigger immediate harm when power is unchecked.
ramayan::918.detailed_meaning: The maidens have just insulted their father’s truth and the legitimacy of his choice. In response, the Windgod, who guards their family line, lashes out at once and maims them. The verse is a consequence, not a teaching.
ramayan::918.modern_relevance: A room full of laughing friends can turn silent in a second when someone crosses a line and power answers too fast.
ramayan::918.insight: It shows how quickly anger can become violence when restraint is absent.

ramayan::919.verse_sanskrit: ता: कन्या वायुना भग्ना विविशुर्नृपतेर्गृहम् । प्रापतन् भुवि सम्भ्रान्तास्सलज्जा स्सास्रलोचना: । । 13224 । ।
ramayan::919.verse_hindi: Their bodies disfigured and shattered by the Windgod, the maidens with tears flowing from their eyes entered the palace and fell down on the ground, agitated and overtaken by shame.
ramayan::919.english_translation: Their bodies disfigured and shattered by the Windgod, the maidens with tears flowing from their eyes entered the palace and fell down on the ground, agitated and overtaken by shame.
ramayan::919.translation_literal: ता: (those) / कन्या: (maidens) / वायुना (by the Windgod) / भग्ना: (broken) / विविशु: (entered) / नृपते: (of the king) / गृहम् (palace) / प्रापतन् (fell down) / भुवि (on the ground) / सम्भ्रान्ता: (agitated) / सस्लज्जा: (ashamed) / सास्रलोचना: (with tear-filled eyes)
ramayan::919.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::919.essence: Humiliation follows contempt faster than pride expects.
ramayan::919.simple_meaning: The maidens return to the palace broken, ashamed, and crying after being struck by the Windgod.
ramayan::919.simple_insight: Cruel speech can turn pride into humiliation in a moment.
ramayan::919.detailed_meaning: After insulting the Windgod, the king's daughters are struck and sent back into the palace shaken, ashamed, and weeping. This verse is the visible aftermath of the curse-like punishment, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::919.modern_relevance: A cruel remark in a group chat can leave someone silent, flushed, and unable to meet anyone's eyes. The damage often shows up after the words are already gone.
ramayan::919.insight: It shows the immediate human cost of arrogance and disrespect.

ramayan::920.verse_sanskrit: स च ता दयिता दीना: कन्या: परमशोभना: । दृष्ट्वा भग्नास्तदा राजा सम्भ्रान्त इदमब्रवीत् । । 13225 । ।
ramayan::920.verse_hindi: The king saw his extremely beautiful beloved daughters distressed and shattered and spoke these words with bewilderment.
ramayan::920.english_translation: The king saw his extremely beautiful beloved daughters distressed and shattered and spoke these words with bewilderment.
ramayan::920.translation_literal: स (he) / च (and) / ता: (those) / दयिता: (beloved) / दीना: (distressed) / कन्या: (maidens/daughters) / परमशोभना: (extremely beautiful) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / भग्ना: (broken/shattered) / तदा (then) / राजा (the king) / सम्भ्रान्तः (bewildered/confused) / इदम् (this) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::920.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::920.essence: His shock matters because it leads into the search for who caused the harm.
ramayan::920.simple_meaning: The king sees his daughters hurt and is shocked into speaking. It is a moment of sudden concern, not a teaching.
ramayan::920.simple_insight: Shock can break through pride in an instant.
ramayan::920.detailed_meaning: The king returns to find his beloved daughters disfigured and weeping after the Windgod’s fury. He is startled and speaks in confusion, setting up the question of who has done this and why.
ramayan::920.modern_relevance: You walk into a room and realize something has gone terribly wrong with people you care about. Before anger or blame, there is that stunned second where your mind simply stops.
ramayan::920.insight: It shows a reaction, not a principle: the scene turns the king from observer into a desperate questioner.

ramayan::921.verse_sanskrit: किमिदं कथ्यतां पुत्र्य: को धर्ममवमन्यते । कुब्जा: केन कृता: सर्वा वेष्टन्त्यो नाभिभाषथ । एवं राजा विनिश्श्वस्य समाधिं सन्दधे तत: । । 13226 । ।
ramayan::921.verse_hindi: O daughters What has happened? Who has dishonoured virtue? Say it at once. Who has made you hunchbacked? Standing roud me, why are you dumb? The king heaved a sigh and entered into a state of samadhi.
ramayan::921.english_translation: O daughters, what has happened? Who has dishonoured virtue? Say it at once. Who has made you hunchbacked? Standing around me, why are you silent? The king heaved a sigh and then entered a state of concentration.
ramayan::921.translation_literal: किमिदम् (what is this) / कथ्यताम् (let it be spoken) / पुत्र्यः (daughters) / कः (who) / धर्मम् (virtue) / अवमन्यते (has dishonoured) / कुब्जाः (hunchbacked) / केन (by whom) / कृताḥ (made) / सर्वाḥ (all) / वेष्टन्त्यः (standing around) / नाभिभाषथ (you do not speak) / एवम् (thus) / राजा (the king) / विनिश्श्वस्य (having sighed) / समाधिम् (a state of concentration) / सन्दधे (entered)
ramayan::921.speaker: Kusanabha
ramayan::921.essence: He sees the damage first and only then begins to ask why.
ramayan::921.simple_meaning: The king sees his daughters transformed and asks who has done this, but the scene is still unfolding and no teaching is being delivered yet.
ramayan::921.simple_insight: Shock can stop speech before understanding arrives.
ramayan::921.detailed_meaning: Kusanabha sees his hundred daughters returned in a ruined state and asks who has violated dharma and made them deformed. But this is only his startled reaction, not the lesson of the episode. The real explanation comes later.
ramayan::921.modern_relevance: You walk into a room and instantly know something has gone wrong, but you do not yet know what. The first breath is shock, not understanding.
ramayan::921.insight: It shows the moment before inquiry begins, when grief and surprise briefly silence the mind.

ramayan::922.verse_sanskrit: तस्य तद्वचनं श्रुत्वा कुशनाभस्य धीमत: । शिरोभिश्चरणौ स्पृष्ट्वा कन्याशतमभाषत । । 1331 । ।
ramayan::922.verse_hindi: On hearing the words of sagacious Kusanabha, his hundred daughters touched his feet  with their heads and  said:
ramayan::922.english_translation: On hearing the words of wise Kusanabha, his hundred daughters touched his feet with their heads and said:
ramayan::922.translation_literal: तस्य (his) / तत् (that) / वचनं (speech) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / कुशनाभस्य (of Kusanabha) / धीमतः (of the wise one) / शिरोभिः (with their heads) / चरणौ (the feet) / स्पृष्ट्वा (having touched) / कन्याशतम् (the hundred daughters) / अभाषत (spoke)
ramayan::922.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::922.essence: They answer their father with reverence before they answer his question.
ramayan::922.simple_meaning: After hearing Kusanabha's words, his hundred daughters bowed to him and began to speak.
ramayan::922.simple_insight: Respect comes before speech. Even in distress, they answer their father with humility.
ramayan::922.detailed_meaning: Kusanabha has just seen his daughters transformed and is demanding an explanation. They respond not with defiance, but by bowing first and then speaking. The verse is a bridge into their explanation, not the explanation itself.
ramayan::922.modern_relevance: A tense family conversation pauses for one breath before anyone answers. That small act of respect changes the whole room.
ramayan::922.insight: It shows that even painful truth can be spoken without breaking reverence.

ramayan::923.verse_sanskrit: वायुस्सर्वात्मको राजन् प्रधर्षयितुमिच्छति । अशुभं मार्गमास्थाय न धर्मं प्रत्यवेक्षते । । 1332 । ।
ramayan::923.verse_hindi: O king, the  allpervading Windgod, having taken recourse to foul means intended to outrage our modesty without and moral compunction.
ramayan::923.english_translation: O king, the all-pervading Wind-god, taking a foul path, intended to outrage our modesty without regard for righteousness.
ramayan::923.translation_literal: वायुः (the Wind-god) / सर्वात्मकः (all-pervading) / राजन् (O king) / प्रधर्षयितुम् इच्छति (wished to violate) / अशुभम् मार्गम् आस्थाय (taking a foul path) / न धर्मम् प्रत्यवेक्षते (did not consider righteousness)
ramayan::923.speaker: Kusanabha's daughters
ramayan::923.simple_meaning: The daughters say the Wind-god tried to violate them by acting unrighteously.
ramayan::923.detailed_meaning: Kusanabha's hundred daughters answer their father after he asks who has dishonoured them. They explain that the Wind-god approached them through wrongful means, ignoring righteousness and trying to force them.
ramayan::923.modern_relevance: A person in power uses charm, pressure, or status to cross a line, then acts as if nothing happened. This verse names that abuse plainly.
ramayan::923.insight: It shifts attention from power to conduct: even a mighty being is judged by restraint, not force.

ramayan::924.verse_sanskrit: पितृमत्यस्स्म भद्रं ते स्वच्छन्दे न वयं स्थिता: । पितरं नो वृणीष्व त्वं यदि नो दास्यते तव । । 1333 । ।
ramayan::924.verse_hindi: We have our father who is dear to us. Hence we do not have freedom to choose. You may ask our father if he is willing to give us (in marriage).
ramayan::924.english_translation: We have our father who is dear to us. Hence we do not have freedom to choose. You may ask our father if he is willing to give us in marriage.
ramayan::924.translation_literal: पितृमत्यः (having a father) / स्म (indeed) / भद्रम् ते (good fortune to you) / स्वच्छन्दे (in freedom) / न (not) / वयम् (we) / स्थिता: (situated) / पितरम् (father) / नः (our) / वृणीष्व (choose/ask for) / त्वम् (you) / यदि (if) / नः (us) / दास्यते (will give) / तव (to you)
ramayan::924.speaker: Kusanabha's daughters
ramayan::924.essence: Marriage cannot be claimed by force; rightful consent belongs elsewhere.
ramayan::924.simple_meaning: The daughters say they are under their father's authority and cannot choose for themselves. If the marriage is to happen, the suitor must ask their father.
ramayan::924.simple_insight: Respect for family authority can be a boundary, not a burden.
ramayan::924.detailed_meaning: Kusanabha's hundred daughters answer the Windgod's demand with calm dignity. They remind him that they are not free agents in marriage and direct him to their father, the only proper authority in the matter. Their refusal sets up the violation that follows.
ramayan::924.modern_relevance: A message arrives late at night asking for an answer you cannot give alone. You know some choices are not yours to make in isolation, and saying so is not weakness.
ramayan::924.insight: It distinguishes personal desire from rightful consent and family approval.

ramayan::925.verse_sanskrit: तेन पापानुबन्धेन वचनं न प्रतीच्छता । एवं ब्रुवन्त्यस्सर्वास्स्म वायुना निहता भृशम् । । 1334 । ।
ramayan::925.verse_hindi: As all of us were speaking thus, the sinful Windgod, disregarding our words repeatedly assaulted us.
ramayan::925.english_translation: As all of us were speaking thus, the sinful Windgod, disregarding our words, repeatedly assaulted us.
ramayan::925.translation_literal: तेन (by that) / पापानुबन्धेन (with sinful intent) / वचनं (speech) / न (not) / प्रतीच्छता (accepting) । / एवं (thus) / ब्रुवन्त्यः (speaking) / सर्वाः (all) / स्म (indeed) / वायुना (by the Windgod) / निहताḥ (struck) / भृशम् (severely) ।
ramayan::925.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::925.essence: Force keeps speaking when respect should have begun.
ramayan::925.simple_meaning: While they were speaking, the Windgod ignored their refusal and kept attacking them.
ramayan::925.simple_insight: A refusal means nothing to someone who chooses force over restraint.
ramayan::925.detailed_meaning: The daughters have already said they cannot accept him without their father’s consent. Instead of respecting that boundary, the Windgod keeps pressing them. This verse is a supporting detail in a larger exchange about desire, refusal, and conduct.
ramayan::925.modern_relevance: You say no clearly, and someone keeps pushing anyway. The pressure itself reveals the character of the one who cannot hear your boundary.
ramayan::925.insight: It shows how desire becomes aggression when it refuses to accept limits.

ramayan::926.verse_sanskrit: तासां तद्वचनं श्रुत्वा राजा परमधार्मिक: । प्रत्युवाच महातेजा: कन्याशतमनुत्तमम् । । 1335 । ।
ramayan::926.verse_hindi: The deeply religious and highly powerful king, having heard those words of his one hundred exceptional daughters, replied:
ramayan::926.english_translation: The deeply religious and highly powerful king, having heard those words of his one hundred exceptional daughters, replied:
ramayan::926.translation_literal: तासाम् (of those) / तत्-वचनम् (that speech) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / राजा (the king) / परम-धार्मिकः (most righteous) / प्रत्युवाच (replied) / महा-तेजाः (greatly radiant, powerful) / कन्या-शतम् (hundred daughters) / अनुत्तमम् (unsurpassed)
ramayan::926.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::926.essence: Power becomes meaningful only when it answers with righteousness.
ramayan::926.simple_meaning: The king listens to his daughters and answers them with authority and righteousness.
ramayan::926.simple_insight: Listening well can be the first act of fairness.
ramayan::926.detailed_meaning: A king hears the words of his hundred daughters after they speak together with one voice. He is not just a father here; he is the ruler whose response will shape the family’s next move. This verse sets up his reply in the next line.
ramayan::926.modern_relevance: A parent hears children speak together after a hard family decision. The next sentence will show whether power hardens into control or becomes responsibility.
ramayan::926.insight: It shifts attention from the complaint itself to the quality of the response.

ramayan::927.verse_sanskrit: क्षान्तं क्षमावतां पुत्र्य: कर्तव्यं सुमहत्कृतम् । ऐकमत्यमुपागम्य कुलं चावेक्षितं मम । । 1336 । ।
ramayan::927.verse_hindi: O daughters you have done a great act of forgiveness of which only the tolerant are capable. By taking a united stand, you have protected the honour of my dynasty.
ramayan::927.english_translation: O daughters, you have done a great act of forgiveness, which only the tolerant can do. By standing together, you have protected my lineage.
ramayan::927.translation_literal: क्षान्तं (forgiven / endured) / क्षमावतां (of the tolerant) / पुत्र्य: (daughters) / कर्तव्यं (a deed to be done) / सुमहत् (very great) / कृतम् (done) / ऐकमत्यम् (unity / one-mindedness) / उपागम्य (having come together) / कुलं (lineage / family) / च (and) / अवेक्षितं (protected / looked after) / मम (my)
ramayan::927.speaker: King
ramayan::927.essence: Forgiveness becomes power when it protects the whole family.
ramayan::927.simple_meaning: The king praises his daughters for forgiving together instead of reacting in anger. Their shared restraint protected the family's honour.
ramayan::927.simple_insight: Forgiveness is not weakness; it can be the strongest way to hold a family together.
ramayan::927.detailed_meaning: After the daughters speak of being struck by Vayu, the king answers with admiration instead of blame. He sees their forgiveness and united response as a real protection of his lineage, and as proof of their strength.
ramayan::927.modern_relevance: A family group chat is full of hurt messages, and one person chooses to de-escalate instead of winning. That quiet restraint can preserve relationships that outrage would shatter.
ramayan::927.insight: It shifts you from reacting to injury toward protecting the larger bond through restraint and unity.

ramayan::928.verse_sanskrit: अलङ्कारो हि नारीणां क्षमा तु पुरुषस्य वा । दुष्करं तच्च यत् क्षान्तं त्रिदशेषु विशेषत: । । 1337 । । यादृशी व: क्षमा पुत्र्यस्सर्वासामविशेषत: ।
ramayan::928.verse_hindi: Whether for women or men forgiveness is an ornament. It is difficult even for gods. For you, daughters, to show it without any difference of opinion is especially hard.
ramayan::928.english_translation: Whether for women or men, forgiveness is an ornament. It is difficult even for the highest beings. The forgiveness you daughters have shown, without any difference among you, is especially hard.
ramayan::928.translation_literal: अलङ्कारः (ornament) / हि (indeed) / नारीणाम् (of women) / क्षमा (forgiveness) / तु (indeed) / पुरुषस्य (of a man) / वा (or) / दुष्करम् (difficult) / तत् (that) / च (and) / यत् (which) / क्षान्तम् (forgiveness shown) / त्रिदशेषु (among the gods) / विशेषतः (especially) / यादृशी (such as) / वः (your) / क्षमा (forgiveness) / पुत्र्यः (daughters) / सर्वासाम् (of all) / अविशेषत: (without distinction)
ramayan::928.speaker: King
ramayan::928.essence: Forgiveness becomes rare when everyone must choose it together.
ramayan::928.simple_meaning: Forgiveness is a noble quality for anyone, but it is especially difficult to show it together and without disagreement.
ramayan::928.simple_insight: Real strength can look gentle when you choose forgiveness together.
ramayan::928.detailed_meaning: A king answers his daughters after they have stood together in forgiveness. He praises their unity and says that forgiving without division is hard even for the highest beings. The moment turns their restraint into a royal virtue.
ramayan::928.modern_relevance: A family group chat is full of hurt feelings, and everyone wants to be right first. Choosing to forgive together, without splitting into sides, takes more courage than winning the argument.
ramayan::928.insight: It shifts the mind from treating forgiveness as weakness to seeing it as disciplined strength.

ramayan::929.verse_sanskrit: क्षमा दानं क्षमा यज्ञः क्षमा सत्यं हि पुत्रिका: । । 1338 । । क्षमा यश: क्षमा धर्म: क्षमया निष्ठितं जगत् ।
ramayan::929.verse_hindi: Forbearance is charity, forbearance is sacrifice, forbearance is truth, forbearance is glory and forbearance is virtue. O daughters, the universe is supported by forbearance.
ramayan::929.english_translation: Forbearance is charity, forbearance is sacrifice, forbearance is truth, forbearance is glory and forbearance is virtue. O daughters, the universe is supported by forbearance.
ramayan::929.translation_literal: क्षमा (forbearance/forgiveness) / दानं (charity) / क्षमा (forbearance/forgiveness) / यज्ञः (sacrifice) / क्षमा (forbearance/forgiveness) / सत्यं (truth) / हि (indeed) / पुत्रिका: (daughters) / क्षमा (forbearance/forgiveness) / यश: (glory) / क्षमा (forbearance/forgiveness) / धर्म: (virtue/righteous conduct) / क्षमया (by forbearance) / निष्ठितं (supported/established) / जगत् (world/universe)
ramayan::929.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::929.essence: Forbearance is not passive; it is the force that holds life together.
ramayan::929.simple_meaning: Forbearance is the highest form of giving, sacrifice, truth, honor, and righteous conduct. It is what keeps the world steady.
ramayan::929.simple_insight: You do not become smaller by holding back anger; you become steadier, and everything around you benefits.
ramayan::929.detailed_meaning: A king is praising forgiveness to a group of daughters after they have shown remarkable restraint and unity. He says their forbearance is not weakness but the very force that makes charity, sacrifice, truth, and social order possible.
ramayan::929.modern_relevance: You get the harsh email, the rude reply, the family comment that lands too hard. The strongest response is not always the sharpest one; sometimes it is the one that keeps the whole room from breaking.
ramayan::929.insight: It shifts you from reacting to preserving what matters most.

ramayan::930.verse_sanskrit: विसृज्य कन्या: काकुत्स्थ राजा त्रिदशविक्रम: । । 1339 । । मन्त्रज्ञो मन्त्रयामास प्रदानं सह मन्त्रिभि: । देशकालौ प्रदानस्य सदृशे प्रतिपादनम् । । 13310 । ।
ramayan::930.verse_hindi: O Rama after sending away his daughters, the king endowed with the power of the celestials and wellversed in the art of counselling, consulted his ministers about a suitable person for marriage of his daughters at proper time and place.
ramayan::930.english_translation: O Rama, after sending away his daughters, the king, endowed with the power of the celestials and skilled in counsel, consulted his ministers about a suitable marriage for his daughters at the proper time and place.
ramayan::930.translation_literal: विसृज्य (having sent away) / कन्या: (daughters) / काकुत्स्थ (O descendant of Kakutstha, Rama) / राजा (the king) / त्रिदशविक्रम: (possessing the prowess of the thirty-three gods) / मन्त्रज्ञो (knower of counsel) / मन्त्रयामास (consulted) / प्रदानं (giving in marriage) / सह (with) / मन्त्रिभि: (with ministers) / देशकालौ (time and place) / प्रदानस्य (of the giving in marriage) / सदृशे (suitable) / प्रतिपादनम् (arrangement)
ramayan::930.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::930.essence: Wise decisions honor timing, place, and counsel.
ramayan::930.simple_meaning: The king sends his daughters away and then consults his ministers about arranging their marriages at the right time and place.
ramayan::930.simple_insight: Some decisions need counsel, timing, and care — not haste.
ramayan::930.detailed_meaning: The scene shifts from praise of forgiveness to a practical royal decision. A powerful king, addressed as Rama, has sent his daughters away and now sits with ministers, weighing the right time and place for their marriages. The verse is a brief step in the larger narrative.
ramayan::930.modern_relevance: You have a family decision that cannot be rushed: a move, a wedding, a major commitment. Before acting, you gather the people who can see what you may miss.
ramayan::930.insight: It shifts attention from impulse to thoughtful consultation before a binding choice.

ramayan::931.verse_sanskrit: एतस्मिन्नेव काले तु चूली नाम महातपा: । ऊर्ध्वरेताश्शुभाचारो ब्राह्मं तप उपागमत् । । 13311 । ।
ramayan::931.verse_hindi: At that time a great and virtuous ascetic named Chuli living in celebacy was performing austerities in pursuit of the knowledge of Brahman.
ramayan::931.english_translation: At that time, a great ascetic named Chuli, steadfast in celibacy and virtuous conduct, undertook austerities aimed at Brahman.
ramayan::931.translation_literal: एतस्मिन् (at this) / एव (indeed) / काले (time) / तु (but) / चूली (Chuli) / नाम (named) / महातपा: (great ascetic) / ऊर्ध्वरेताश्शुभाचारो (one of pure conduct and celibacy) / ब्राह्मं (Brahman-related) / तप (austerity) / उपागमत् (undertook)
ramayan::931.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::931.essence: Real transformation begins with disciplined restraint and a single aim.
ramayan::931.simple_meaning: A highly disciplined ascetic named Chuli began severe austerities focused on Brahman.
ramayan::931.simple_insight: Single-minded discipline can shape a life toward something higher.
ramayan::931.detailed_meaning: The story briefly shifts away from the main action to introduce Chuli, a severe ascetic known for celibacy and pure conduct. He is absorbed in austerity, and the next verse will show who comes to serve him.
ramayan::931.modern_relevance: Someone quietly wakes before dawn, turns off the phone, and returns to the same practice again and again. No audience is needed for that kind of seriousness.
ramayan::931.insight: It frames spiritual progress as sustained restraint, not a dramatic moment.

ramayan::932.verse_sanskrit: तप्यन्तं तमृषिं तत्र गन्धर्वी पर्युपासते । सोमदा नाम भद्रं ते ऊर्मिला तनया तदा । । 13312 । ।
ramayan::932.verse_hindi: When he was performing austerities, a nymph named Somada, daughter of Urmila, used to serve him. Prosperity to you
ramayan::932.english_translation: When he was performing austerities, a nymph named Somada, daughter of Urmila, used to serve him. Prosperity to you.
ramayan::932.translation_literal: तप्यन्तं (performing austerities) / तम् (him) / ऋषिम् (sage) / तत्र (there) / गन्धर्वी (nymph) / पर्युपासते (served, attended upon) / सोमदा (Somada) / नाम (named) / भद्रम् ते (prosperity to you) / ऊर्मिला-तनया (daughter of Urmila) / तदा (then)
ramayan::932.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::932.essence: Austerity often draws quiet service from others.
ramayan::932.simple_meaning: A nymph named Somada served the sage while he was deep in austerity.
ramayan::932.simple_insight: Quiet service can surround even the hardest discipline.
ramayan::932.detailed_meaning: The story pauses on Chuli's austerities in the forest. While the sage endures his tapas, Somada, daughter of Urmila, attends him there. The verse is a scene-setting detail, not the teaching itself.
