ramayan::932.modern_relevance: Someone keeps showing up with tea, silence, and steady help while you do the hard work no one sees.
ramayan::932.insight: It shifts attention from the ascetic's effort to the supporting presence around him.

ramayan::933.verse_sanskrit: सा च तं प्रणता भूत्वा शुश्रूषणपरायणा । उवास काले धर्मिष्ठा तस्यास्तुष्टोऽभवद्गुरु: । । 13313 । ।
ramayan::933.verse_hindi: Somada rendered her services with devotion and humility. There she lived a religious life. In the might time her spiritual guide was satisfied with her services.
ramayan::933.english_translation: Somada bowed to him and served him devotedly. She lived there in righteousness, and her teacher was pleased with her conduct.
ramayan::933.translation_literal: सा (she) / च (and) / तं (him) / प्रणता (bowed down) / भूत्वा (having become) / शुश्रूषणपरायणा (devoted to service) / उवास (lived) / काले (for a time) / धर्मिष्ठा (righteous) / तस्याः (of her) / तुष्टः (pleased) / अभवत् (became) / गुरुः (the teacher)
ramayan::933.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::933.essence: Steady service can transform humility into lasting trust.
ramayan::933.simple_meaning: Somada served the ascetic with humility and lived righteously until he was pleased with her conduct.
ramayan::933.simple_insight: Quiet devotion and steady conduct can earn trust over time.
ramayan::933.detailed_meaning: Somada, a celestial maiden, stays with the ascetic Chuli not in pride but in humble service. She lives by discipline and patience, and her teacher grows satisfied with her conduct. The next verse will show the result of that long devotion.
ramayan::933.modern_relevance: You keep showing up for someone day after day, with no applause and no certainty. Over time, your steadiness becomes its own proof.
ramayan::933.insight: It shifts attention from dramatic gestures to patient, consistent service.

ramayan::934.verse_sanskrit: स च तां कालयोगेन प्रोवाच रघुनन्दन । परितुष्टोऽस्मि भद्रं ते किं करोमि तव प्रियम् । । 13314 । ।
ramayan::934.verse_hindi: When her services came to a fruition with the passage of time, maharshi Chuli, spoke to her: I am pleased with you. What favour shall I do for you? May you be prosperous
ramayan::934.english_translation: When her long service had ripened with time, the sage said to her: “I am pleased with you. What good thing can I do for you?”
ramayan::934.translation_literal: स (he) / च (and) / तां (to her) / कालयोगेन (through the coming of time) / प्रोवाच (spoke) / रघुनन्दन (Raghunandana) / परितुष्टोऽस्मि (I am fully pleased) / भद्रं ते (may good be with you) / किं (what) / करोमि (shall I do) / तव (for you) / प्रियम् (a desired/favourable thing)
ramayan::934.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::934.essence: Long devotion is eventually seen and answered.
ramayan::934.simple_meaning: After a long period of devoted service, the sage tells Somada that he is pleased and asks what blessing he can give her.
ramayan::934.simple_insight: Patient service can ripen into recognition, and sincere effort is not forgotten.
ramayan::934.detailed_meaning: Somada has served the sage with humility during his austerities. Now, after time has matured her devotion, the sage turns to her with approval and asks what he can do for her. The verse sets up the exchange that follows.
ramayan::934.modern_relevance: You keep showing up for years, quietly, without applause. Then one day the person you served finally sees the whole of it and asks what they can give back.
ramayan::934.insight: It highlights how steady service can earn recognition when the right moment arrives.

ramayan::935.verse_sanskrit: परितुष्टं मुनिं ज्ञात्वा गन्धर्वी मधुरस्वरा । उवाच परमप्रीता वाक्यज्ञा वाक्यकोविदम् । । 13315 । ।
ramayan::935.verse_hindi: Having perceived that the sage was satisfied, the gandharva who was skilled in speech said exceedingly delighted to the sage in a sweet voice.
ramayan::935.english_translation: Having seen that the sage was pleased, the sweet-voiced gandharva, skilled in speech, spoke with great delight to the sage.
ramayan::935.translation_literal: परितुष्टम् (fully pleased) / मुनिम् (the sage) / ज्ञात्वा (having known) / गन्धर्वी (the gandharva woman) / मधुरस्वरा (sweet-voiced) / उवाच (said) / परमप्रीता (greatly delighted) / वाक्यज्ञा (knowing speech) / वाक्यकोविदम् (skilled in speech)
ramayan::935.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::935.essence: Respectful speech follows when trust has already been earned.
ramayan::935.simple_meaning: The gandharva woman noticed that the sage was pleased, and she responded with joy and respectful speech.
ramayan::935.simple_insight: Courtesy opens the next door. When someone feels seen and respected, honest speech becomes possible.
ramayan::935.detailed_meaning: Somada has served the sage faithfully until his satisfaction is clear. Seeing that moment, the gandharva woman answers with delight and careful words. The verse simply turns the scene from patient service to the beginning of a request.
ramayan::935.modern_relevance: You can feel the shift in a room when someone finally relaxes and listens. That is the moment a real request, apology, or confession can begin.
ramayan::935.insight: It shows how timing and tone matter when you ask for something important.

ramayan::936.verse_sanskrit: लक्ष्म्या समुदितो ब्राह्म्या ब्रह्मभूतो महातपा: । ब्राह्मेण तपसा युक्तं पुत्रमिच्छामि धार्मिक । । 13316 । ।
ramayan::936.verse_hindi: Bestowed with the great asceticism and brilliance of a brahmin, you look like Brahma. O righteous one, I desire a son endowed with the ascetic virtues of a brahmin.
ramayan::936.english_translation: Bestowed with the great asceticism and brilliance of a brahmin, you look like Brahma. O righteous one, I desire a son endowed with the ascetic virtues of a brahmin.
ramayan::936.translation_literal: लक्ष्म्या (with brilliance) / समुदितः (endowed) / ब्राह्म्याः (of brahminical) / ब्रह्मभूतः (like Brahma) / महातपाः (great ascetic) / ब्राह्मेण (with brahminical) / तपसा (asceticism) / युक्तम् (endowed) / पुत्रम् (a son) / इच्छामि (I desire) / धार्मिक (O righteous one)
ramayan::936.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::936.essence: She asks for brilliance to become lineage, not just admiration.
ramayan::936.simple_meaning: A woman, impressed by a sage's radiance and austerity, asks him for a son who will share that same ascetic power.
ramayan::936.simple_insight: A blessing can be asked for with reverence, not greed.
ramayan::936.detailed_meaning: A gandharva woman speaks to a satisfied sage in the forest. Seeing his brahmin-like brilliance and austerity, she asks not for wealth or comfort, but for a son shaped by the same sacred discipline.
ramayan::936.modern_relevance: You meet someone whose calm and discipline feel rare, almost luminous. Instead of asking for advantage, you ask for a life shaped by that same steadiness.
ramayan::936.insight: It shifts desire from possession to the wish for noble qualities to continue.

ramayan::937.verse_sanskrit: अपतिश्चास्मि भद्रं ते भार्या चास्मि न कस्यचित् । ब्राह्मेणोपगतायाश्च दातुमर्हसि मे सुतम् । । 13317 । ।
ramayan::937.verse_hindi: I am without a husband, my sire. I am not a wife to any one. Since I have taken refuge in you, you are competent to bestow on me a son with the power of your penance.
ramayan::937.english_translation: I am without a husband, my sire. I am not a wife to any one. Since I have taken refuge in you, you are competent to bestow on me a son with the power of your penance.
ramayan::937.translation_literal: अपतिः (without a husband) / च (and) / अस्मि (I am) / भद्रं ते (may good be to you) / भार्या (wife) / च (and) / अस्मि (I am) / न (not) / कस्यचित् (of anyone) / ब्राह्मेण (through brahminical) / उपगतायाः (of one who has approached) / च (and) / दातुम् (to give) / अर्हसि (you are fit) / मे (to me) / सुतम् (a son)
ramayan::937.speaker: Gandharvi
ramayan::937.essence: She asks from need and respect, not from entitlement.
ramayan::937.simple_meaning: She tells the sage she has no husband and belongs to no one, so he should grant her a son because she has come seeking refuge.
ramayan::937.simple_insight: A sincere request can be made with dignity, even when it is deeply personal.
ramayan::937.detailed_meaning: A gandharvi has approached a brahmarshi and, seeing him pleased, makes her request plainly: she is unmarried, unattached, and seeking his blessing for a son. The verse is part of a respectful exchange, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::937.modern_relevance: You finally ask for help after carrying something alone for too long. You speak plainly, without apology, because dignity matters even in need.
ramayan::937.insight: It shows how to ask directly when you need support, without hiding your situation or softening the truth.

ramayan::938.verse_sanskrit: तस्या: प्रसन्नो ब्रह्मर्षिर्ददौ पुत्रमनुत्तमम् । ब्रह्मदत्त इति ख्यातं मानसं चूलिनस्सुतम् । । 13318 । ।
ramayan::938.verse_hindi: Pleased with her, brahmarshi Chuli gave her an excellent son to be wellknown as Brahmadatta born through the will of his mind.
ramayan::938.english_translation: Pleased with her, the brahmarshi Chuli gave her an excellent son, known as Brahmadatta, born through the power of his mind.
ramayan::938.translation_literal: तस्याः (of her) / प्रसन्नः (pleased) / ब्रह्मर्षिः (the brahmarshi) / ददौ (gave) / पुत्रम् (a son) / अनुत्तमम् (excellent) / ब्रह्मदत्तः इति (as Brahmadatta) / ख्यातम् (known) / मानसम् (mind-born) / चूलिनः सुतम् (son of Chuli)
ramayan::938.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::938.essence: A son is granted by grace and named for that gift.
ramayan::938.simple_meaning: Chuli grants the woman an excellent son, Brahmadatta, born by the power of thought rather than ordinary birth.
ramayan::938.simple_insight: Some blessings arrive through grace, not effort — and they still become real in the world.
ramayan::938.detailed_meaning: A brahmarshi named Chuli is moved by the woman's request and gives her a son. The child is named Brahmadatta and is said to be born from the mind. The verse simply records the gift, not a teaching.
ramayan::938.modern_relevance: A family story gets retold years later: someone was given a child after a long plea, and the child’s very name still carries that moment of grace.
ramayan::938.insight: It marks a miraculous birth as a narrative detail, not a moral instruction.

ramayan::939.verse_sanskrit: स राजा सौमदेयस्तु पुरीमध्यवसत्तदा । कांपिल्यां परया लक्ष्म्या देवराजो यथा दिवम् । । 13319 । ।
ramayan::939.verse_hindi: Then king Brahmadatta, son of Somada, lived in the city of Kampilya with great
ramayan::939.english_translation: Then king Brahmadatta, son of Somada, lived in the city of Kampilya with great splendour, like Indra in heaven.
ramayan::939.translation_literal: स राजा (that king) / सौमदेयः (son of Somada) / तु (indeed) / पुरी-मध्य-अवसत् (dwelt in the middle of the city) / तदा (then) / कांपिल्यां (in Kampilya) / परया (with supreme) / लक्ष्म्या (splendour) / देवराजः (the king of the devas) / यथा (like) / दिवम् (in heaven)
ramayan::939.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::939.essence: Prosperity fills the city before the next turning point arrives.
ramayan::939.simple_meaning: Brahmadatta lived in Kampilya with great splendour, as Indra lives in heaven.
ramayan::939.simple_insight: Some lines simply set the scene: wealth, status, and a city at its height.
ramayan::939.detailed_meaning: After Chuli blesses the woman with a son, the story moves forward to Brahmadatta’s rule in Kampilya. This verse is a setting detail, showing his royal splendour before the next family decision is made.
ramayan::939.modern_relevance: A story pauses to show you a life that looks complete from the outside: a fine house, public honour, everything in place. Then the next choice arrives and changes the whole picture.
ramayan::939.insight: It frames the next event against a background of royal prosperity and expectation.

ramayan::940.verse_sanskrit: स बुद्धिं कृतवान् राजा कुशनाभस्सुधार्मिक: । ब्रह्मदत्ताय काकुत्स्थ दातुं कन्याशतं तदा । । 13320 । ।
ramayan::940.verse_hindi: O Rama, then the highly righteous king Kusanabha decided to give his hundred daughters to Brahmadatta.
ramayan::940.english_translation: O Rama, then the highly righteous king Kusanabha decided to give his hundred daughters to Brahmadatta.
ramayan::940.translation_literal: स (then/he) / बुद्धिं कृतवान् (made a decision) / राजा (king) / कुशनाभः (Kusanabha) / सुधार्मिकः (highly righteous) / ब्रह्मदत्ताय (to Brahmadatta) / काकुत्स्थ (O Rama) / दातुम् (to give) / कन्याशतम् (a hundred daughters) / तदा (then)
ramayan::940.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::940.essence: Kusanabha decides to unite his daughters with Brahmadatta.
ramayan::940.simple_meaning: King Kusanabha decided to give his hundred daughters in marriage to Brahmadatta.
ramayan::940.simple_insight: A ruler’s decision can shape an entire family’s future.
ramayan::940.detailed_meaning: In the line of Kusanabha and Brahmadatta, the king of Kampilya decides to give his hundred daughters to Brahmadatta. The verse moves the marriage story forward; it is a plot step, not a teaching on its own.
ramayan::940.modern_relevance: A parent makes a major family decision after weighing what will bind two lives together. The choice matters, but the verse is mainly setting up the next event.
ramayan::940.insight: It advances the marriage arrangement by showing Kusanabha’s intention before the formal invitation and gift.

ramayan::941.verse_sanskrit: तमाहूय महातेजा ब्रह्मदत्तं महीपति: । ददौ कन्याशतं राजा सुप्रीतेनान्तरात्मना । । 13321 । ।
ramayan::941.verse_hindi: The lord of the earth, highly powerful king Kusanabha invited Brahmadatta, and gave his hundred daughters in marriage to him with a heart highly pleased.
ramayan::941.english_translation: The mighty king Kusanabha called Brahmadatta and gave him his hundred daughters in marriage with a very pleased heart.
ramayan::941.translation_literal: तम् (him) / आहूय (having called) / महातेजा (highly powerful) / ब्रह्मदत्तम् (Brahmadatta) / महीपति: (lord of the earth) / ददौ (gave) / कन्याशतम् (hundred daughters) / राजा (the king) / सुप्रीतेन (with very pleased) / अन्तरात्मना (inner heart)
ramayan::941.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::941.essence: A generous agreement is sealed when both sides are ready.
ramayan::941.simple_meaning: King Kusanabha invited Brahmadatta and gladly gave him his hundred daughters in marriage.
ramayan::941.simple_insight: A royal decision is made with full goodwill, not hesitation.
ramayan::941.detailed_meaning: In the royal city of Kampilya, Kusanabha has already decided on the marriage alliance. He now formally calls Brahmadatta and gives his hundred daughters with a pleased heart. The verse moves the story forward, but its main role is to complete the setup.
ramayan::941.modern_relevance: A family meeting ends with an agreement everyone has been circling for weeks. The real moment is not drama but final consent — the point where a decision becomes real.
ramayan::941.insight: It shows how a choice becomes complete only when it is openly given and accepted.

ramayan::942.verse_sanskrit: यथाक्रमं तत: पाणीन् जग्राह रघुनन्दन । ब्रह्मदत्तो महीपालस्तासां देवपतिर्यथा । । 13322 । ।
ramayan::942.verse_hindi: O son of Raghus dynasty that king Brahmadatta resembling Indra received the hands of those maidens in due order.
ramayan::942.english_translation: Then, in proper order, the king Brahmadatta, like Indra, received the hands of those maidens.
ramayan::942.translation_literal: यथाक्रमं (in due order) / ततः (then) / पाणीन् (hands) / जग्राह (received) / रघुनन्दन (O delight of the Raghu line) / ब्रह्मदत्तः (Brahmadatta) / महीपालः (king) / तासाम् (of those) / देवपतिर्यथा (like the lord of the gods)
ramayan::942.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::942.essence: The scene advances by ritual detail, not by teaching.
ramayan::942.simple_meaning: Brahmadatta received the brides' hands in the proper order, like Indra receiving a royal wedding honor.
ramayan::942.simple_insight: A marriage is being completed, not a lesson being taught.
ramayan::942.detailed_meaning: Kusanabha has already decided and given his hundred daughters to Brahmadatta. This line simply marks the formal marriage rite: Brahmadatta receives their hands in order, with the dignity of a king compared to Indra.
ramayan::942.modern_relevance: A wedding ceremony moves step by step, with no need for commentary. Some moments are meant to be witnessed, not interpreted.
ramayan::942.insight: It keeps the reader inside the sequence of the marriage rite rather than turning it into instruction.

ramayan::943.verse_sanskrit: स्पृष्टमात्रे तत: पाणौ विकुब्जा विगतज्वरा: । युक्ता: परमया लक्ष्म्या बभु: कन्याशतं तदा । । 13323 । । ृ32
ramayan::943.verse_hindi: Thereafter, with the mere touch of his hand, the hundred daughters were cured of their hump back and freed from anguish. They assumed great beauty.
ramayan::943.english_translation: Thereafter, with the mere touch of his hand, the hundred daughters were cured of their hump back and freed from anguish. They assumed great beauty.
ramayan::943.translation_literal: स्पृष्टमात्रे (with mere touch) / ततः (then) / पाणौ (of the hand) / विकुब्जाः (hump-backed) / विगतज्वराः (freed from anguish) / युक्ताः (endowed) / परमया (with supreme) / लक्ष्म्या (beauty, fortune) / बभूवुः (became) / कन्याशतम् (the hundred daughters) / तदा (then)
ramayan::943.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::943.essence: A single touch restores what suffering had twisted.
ramayan::943.simple_meaning: A single touch from Brahmadatta’s hand restores the hundred daughters to health and beauty.
ramayan::943.simple_insight: Healing can arrive suddenly, and what was broken can be made whole.
ramayan::943.detailed_meaning: King Kusanabha has just given his hundred daughters to Brahmadatta. At the wedding, Brahmadatta touches their hands, and the curse or deformity that had bent them is lifted at once. The verse marks the miracle itself, not a teaching.
ramayan::943.modern_relevance: A doctor’s words, a friend’s call, or one honest conversation can change a life in a moment. Some wounds loosen all at once when the right touch finally comes.
ramayan::943.insight: It shows how relief can come through a single restoring act, not a long struggle.

ramayan::944.verse_sanskrit: स दृष्ट्वा वायुना मुक्ता: कुशनाभो महीपति: । बभूव परमप्रीतो हर्षं लेभे पुन:पुन: । । 13324 । ।
ramayan::944.verse_hindi: King Kusanabha, having seen his daughters released from disfigurement caused by  the Windgod was immensely pleased. He experienced waves of delight.
ramayan::944.english_translation: King Kusanabha, seeing his daughters freed from the Windgod’s disfigurement, was overjoyed again and again.
ramayan::944.translation_literal: स (he) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / वायुना (by the Windgod) / मुक्ताः (freed) / कुशनाभः (Kusanabha) / महीपतिः (king) / बभूव (became) / परमप्रीतः (greatly pleased) / हर्षम् (joy) / लेभे (obtained) / पुनःपुनः (again and again)
ramayan::944.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::944.essence: Healing restores more than the body; it restores a father’s joy.
ramayan::944.simple_meaning: Kusanabha was deeply happy when he saw his daughters restored to normal after their affliction was removed.
ramayan::944.simple_insight: Relief can arrive so fully that joy comes in waves, not once.
ramayan::944.detailed_meaning: The king watches his daughters stand healed after the Windgod’s curse is removed. Their marriage can now proceed without shame or sorrow. This verse lingers on his repeated joy, showing how much the restoration means to the family.
ramayan::944.modern_relevance: You wait outside a clinic while a result is being checked, and the moment relief finally comes, it keeps washing over you. Some joys do not arrive all at once.
ramayan::944.insight: It shifts attention from the cure itself to the father’s repeated relief and gratitude.

ramayan::945.verse_sanskrit: कृतोद्वाहं तु राजानं ब्रह्मदत्तं महीपति: । सदारं प्रेषयामास सोपाध्यायगणं तदा । । 13325 । ।
ramayan::945.verse_hindi: Then the king along with his queens performed the marriage of his daughters in the assembly of priests and sent them with Brahmadatta (to his kingdom).
ramayan::945.english_translation: Then the king, along with his queens, performed the marriage of his daughters in the assembly of priests and sent them with Brahmadatta to his kingdom.
ramayan::945.translation_literal: कृतोद्वाहम् (having completed the marriage) / तु (then) / राजानम् (the king) / ब्रह्मदत्तम् (Brahmadatta) / महीपतिः (the king) / सदारम् (with his wives) / प्रेषयामास (sent away) / सः (he) / उपाध्याय-गणम् (assembly of priests) / तदा (then)
ramayan::945.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::945.essence: Restoration becomes complete when the daughters are sent into their new lives.
ramayan::945.simple_meaning: The king completed his daughters’ marriages and sent them off with Brahmadatta, together with the queens and priests.
ramayan::945.simple_insight: A family’s joy is complete when blessing and release come together.
ramayan::945.detailed_meaning: King Kusanabha’s daughters have been restored and married. In this verse, the household ceremony is completed in the presence of priests, and the brides are sent away with Brahmadatta. It is a closing detail in the larger story of their restoration.
ramayan::945.modern_relevance: A parent watches the wedding rituals end and the car pull away. The house is quieter, but the right thing has been done, and the children are beginning their own lives.
ramayan::945.insight: It marks the transition from restoration to release, where healing leads into a new household order.

ramayan::946.verse_sanskrit: सोमदाऽपि सुसंहृष्टा पुत्रस्य सदृशीं क्रियाम् । यथान्यायं च गन्धर्वी स्नुषास्ता: प्रत्यनन्दत । । 13326 । ।
ramayan::946.verse_hindi: Somada the gandharvi was exeedingly delighted with her daughtersinlaw and praised her son for his right action.
ramayan::946.english_translation: Somada, too, was greatly delighted. She welcomed her daughters-in-law and praised her son for his proper conduct.
ramayan::946.translation_literal: सोमदा (Somada) / अपि (also) / सुसंहृष्टा (greatly delighted) / पुत्रस्य (of the son) / सदृशीं (proper, fitting) / क्रियाम् (action) / यथान्यायं (according to justice, properly) / च (and) / गन्धर्वी (the gandharvi) / स्नुषाः (daughters-in-law) / ताः (those) / प्रत्यनन्दत (welcomed, rejoiced in)
ramayan::946.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::946.essence: Proper action restores joy to the whole family.
ramayan::946.simple_meaning: Somada rejoices at her son’s proper conduct and warmly welcomes her daughters-in-law.
ramayan::946.simple_insight: Right action brings peace not only to the actor, but to the whole family around him.
ramayan::946.detailed_meaning: After the daughters are restored and married, Somada sees that her son has acted rightly. She is filled with joy and receives her new daughters-in-law with affection. The verse closes the family blessing around the marriage.
ramayan::946.modern_relevance: You watch a son do the hard right thing, and the whole house softens. Relief spreads because someone finally acted with decency.
ramayan::946.insight: It shifts attention from private achievement to the harmony created by right conduct.

ramayan::947.verse_sanskrit: कृतोद्वाहे गते तस्मिन् ब्रह्मदत्ते च राघव । अपुत्र: पुत्रलाभाय पौत्रीमिष्टिमकल्पयत् । । 1341 । ।
ramayan::947.verse_hindi: O son of Raghus dynasty (Rama) Brahmadatta got married and left for his kingdom. Now a putreshti was performed by king Kusanabha in order to beget a son.
ramayan::947.english_translation: O Rama, after Brahmadatta had completed his marriage and departed, the childless king then arranged a sacrifice to obtain a son.
ramayan::947.translation_literal: कृतोद्वाहे (after the marriage was completed) / गते (having gone) / तस्मिन् (that one) / ब्रह्मदत्ते (Brahmadatta) / च (and) / राघव (O Rama) / अपुत्रः (childless) / पुत्रलाभाय (for obtaining a son) / पौत्रीम् (a sacrifice for a grandson/descendant) / इष्टिम् (sacrifice) / अकल्पयत् (arranged)
ramayan::947.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::947.essence: A childless king turns to sacrifice when ordinary life has not given him an heir.
ramayan::947.simple_meaning: King Kusanabha had no son, so he arranged a sacrifice to seek one after the marriage was completed and Brahmadatta had left.
ramayan::947.simple_insight: Some wishes are so deep that people turn to ritual when ordinary effort is not enough.
ramayan::947.detailed_meaning: Brahmadatta has finished his marriage and returned home. In the same royal world, King Kusanabha remains childless and prepares a sacrifice to seek a son. The verse sets up the next exchange, not a teaching on its own.
ramayan::947.modern_relevance: A family waits through months of appointments, tests, and prayers, hoping for a child. The ache is private, but the longing is unmistakable.
ramayan::947.insight: It frames the next event by showing a king trying to answer absence with ritual action.

ramayan::948.verse_sanskrit: इष्ट्यां तु वर्तमानायां कुशनाभं महीपतिम् । उवाच परमोदार: कुशो ब्रह्मसुतस्तदा । । 1342 । ।
ramayan::948.verse_hindi: Then, while putreshti was on Kusa the highly generous son of Brahma, said to king Kusanabha :
ramayan::948.english_translation: Then, while the putreshti was in progress, Kusha, the highly generous son of Brahma, said to King Kushanabha:
ramayan::948.translation_literal: इष्ट्यां (in the sacrifice) / तु (then) / वर्तमानायाम् (while being in progress) / कुशनाभम् (to Kushanabha) / महीपतिम् (the king) / उवाच (said) / परम-उदारः (the highly generous) / कुशः (Kusha) / ब्रह्म-सुतः (son of Brahma) / तदा (then)
ramayan::948.speaker: Kusha
ramayan::948.essence: The verse opens the speech; the real claim comes next.
ramayan::948.simple_meaning: During the sacrifice, Kusha speaks to King Kushanabha. The verse only sets up the speech that follows.
ramayan::948.simple_insight: Sometimes the most important line is still just the doorway to the real message.
ramayan::948.detailed_meaning: A royal sacrifice is underway for Kushanabha, and Kusha, the generous son of Brahma, begins speaking. The verse is a bridge into a blessing or prophecy that comes next, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::948.modern_relevance: You are in the room before the real announcement begins. The sentence that matters is still coming, and everyone can feel it.
ramayan::948.insight: It frames the moment as a transition, preparing you for the promise that follows.

ramayan::949.verse_sanskrit: पुत्रस्ते सदृश: पुत्र भविष्यति सुधार्मिक: । गाधिं प्राप्स्यसि तेन त्वं कीर्तिं लोके च शाश्वतीम् । । 1343 । ।
ramayan::949.verse_hindi: O son, a highly virtuous son named Gadhi, similar to you will be born. Because of him you will obtain everlasting fame throughtout this world.
ramayan::949.english_translation: A virtuous son, like you, will be born to you named Gadhi. Through him, you will gain lasting fame throughout the world.
ramayan::949.translation_literal: पुत्रः (son) / ते (to you) / सदृशः (similar) / पुत्रः (son) / भविष्यति (will be) / सुधार्मिकः (highly virtuous) / गाधिम् (Gadhi) / प्राप्स्यसि (you will obtain) / तेन (through him) / त्वम् (you) / कीर्तिम् (fame) / लोके (in the world) / च (and) / शाश्वतीम् (lasting)
ramayan::949.speaker: Kusha
ramayan::949.essence: Virtue can outlive you through the life it shapes next.
ramayan::949.simple_meaning: A noble son will be born to you, and through him your name will live on in the world.
ramayan::949.simple_insight: There is comfort in knowing a life can keep shining through the next generation.
ramayan::949.detailed_meaning: Kusha, the son of Brahma, speaks to King Kushanabha while the sacrificial rite is underway. He blesses the king with a son who will resemble him in virtue and bring him lasting renown, turning a ritual moment into a promise of continuity.
ramayan::949.modern_relevance: You wonder whether any of your effort will matter after you are gone. Then a child repeats your habit, your steadiness, your kindness — and you see how a life continues.
ramayan::949.insight: It shifts attention from immediate reward to the longer arc of what you leave behind.

ramayan::950.verse_sanskrit: एवमुक्त्वा कुशो राम कुशनाभं महीपतिम् । जगामाकाशमाविश्य ब्रह्मलोकं सनातनाम् । । 1344 । ।
ramayan::950.verse_hindi: O Rama so saying to king Kusanabha, Kusa left through space for the eternal   Brahmaloka.
ramayan::950.english_translation: Having spoken thus to King Kusanabha, Kusa entered the sky and went to the eternal Brahmaloka.
ramayan::950.translation_literal: एवमुक्त्वा (having spoken thus) / कुशः (Kusa) / राम (O Rama) / कुशनाभं (to Kusanabha) / महीपतिम् (king) / जगाम (went) / आकाशम् (the sky) / आविश्य (entering) / ब्रह्मलोकं (to Brahmaloka) / सनातनाम् (eternal)
ramayan::950.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::950.essence: A blessing can arrive, change everything, and then vanish.
ramayan::950.simple_meaning: Kusa finishes his blessing, rises into the sky, and departs for Brahmaloka, leaving Kusanabha behind.
ramayan::950.simple_insight: Some encounters end in blessing, not possession.
ramayan::950.detailed_meaning: Kusa has just blessed King Kusanabha with the promise of a righteous son and lasting fame. His task complete, he leaves the mortal world at once, rising through space toward Brahmaloka. The verse closes the brief divine visit and turns the focus back to the king's future.
ramayan::950.modern_relevance: A mentor gives you the one sentence you needed, then disappears from your life. The meeting was never meant to last — only to change what comes next.
ramayan::950.insight: It shows that sacred encounters can be brief and still reshape an entire family line.

ramayan::951.verse_sanskrit: कस्य चित्त्वथ कालस्य कुशनाभस्य धीमत: । जज्ञे परमधर्मिष्ठो गाधिरित्येव नामत: । । 1345 । ।
ramayan::951.verse_hindi: After some time, a supremely righteous son by name Gadhi was born to the sagacious Kusanabha.
ramayan::951.english_translation: After some time, a supremely righteous son named Gadhi was born to the wise Kusanabha.
ramayan::951.translation_literal: कस्यचित् (after some time) / अथ (then) / कालस्य (of time) / कुशनाभस्य (of Kusanabha) / धीमतः (of the wise one) / जज्ञे (was born) / परमधर्मिष्ठः (supremely righteous) / गाधिः (Gadhi) / इति एव (thus indeed) / नामतः (by name)
ramayan::951.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::951.essence: A promised line of virtue is now born.
ramayan::951.simple_meaning: Kusanabha, known for wisdom, had a son named Gadhi, and that son was deeply righteous.
ramayan::951.simple_insight: A family line can carry virtue forward, even across generations.
ramayan::951.detailed_meaning: Kusa has just left Kusanabha with a blessing of future fame. Now the story confirms that promise: Kusanabha later has a son named Gadhi, known for righteousness. It is a genealogical bridge, not a teaching verse.
ramayan::951.modern_relevance: A family photo, a grandfather's story, a name passed down at a funeral — some legacies are carried quietly until they suddenly matter.
ramayan::951.insight: It shifts attention from action to lineage, marking the continuity of a noble family line.

ramayan::952.verse_sanskrit: स पिता मम काकुत्स्थ गाधि: परमधार्मिक: । कुशवंशप्रसूतोऽस्मि कौशिको रघुनन्दन । । 1346 । ।
ramayan::952.verse_hindi: O son of Raghus dynasty the highly virtuous Gadhi is my father. I am known as Kausika being born in the family of Kusa.
ramayan::952.english_translation: O son of the Raghu dynasty, Gadhi, my father, was highly righteous. I am known as Kausika, born in the line of Kusa.
ramayan::952.translation_literal: स (he) / पिता (father) / मम (my) / काकुत्स्थ (O descendant of Kakutstha) / गाधि: (Gadhi) / परमधार्मिक: (highly righteous) / कुशवंशप्रसूतोऽस्मि (I am born in the Kusa line) / कौशिक: (Kausika) / रघुनन्दन (O delight of the Raghu line)
ramayan::952.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::952.essence: He grounds his authority in a lineage of righteousness.
ramayan::952.simple_meaning: Vishvamitra identifies his father and lineage to Rama, saying he comes from the noble line of Kusa and is known as Kausika.
ramayan::952.simple_insight: Lineage matters here because it carries the weight of character, not just blood.
ramayan::952.detailed_meaning: Vishvamitra is speaking to Rama and tracing his own family line back to Gadhi and the Kusa dynasty. He is not teaching a principle yet; he is establishing who he is before the deeper story continues.
ramayan::952.modern_relevance: Someone asks where you come from, and you answer with more than a hometown. You name the values, sacrifices, and family line that shaped you.
ramayan::952.insight: It frames identity as inherited responsibility, not mere personal branding.

ramayan::953.verse_sanskrit: पूर्वजा भगिनी चापि मम राघव सुव्रता । नाम्ना सत्यवती नाम ऋचीके प्रतिपादिता । । 1347 । ।
ramayan::953.verse_hindi: O Raghava adherent of best religious practices, is my elder sister well known by name Satyavati. She was bestowed in marriage to Richika.
ramayan::953.english_translation: O Raghava, my elder sister, known as Satyavati, was a woman of excellent vows. She was given in marriage to Richika.
ramayan::953.translation_literal: पूर्वजा (elder-born sister) / भगिनी (sister) / च (and) / अपि (also) / मम (my) / राघव (O Raghava) / सुव्रता (of excellent vows) / नाम्ना (by name) / सत्यवती (Satyavati) / नाम (named) / ऋचीके (to Richika) / प्रतिपादिता (was given in marriage)
ramayan::953.speaker: Kausika
ramayan::953.essence: A lineage detail links Kausika to an honored family.
ramayan::953.simple_meaning: Kausika tells Rama that his elder sister Satyavati was a woman of firm vows and was married to Richika.
ramayan::953.simple_insight: A family line is being traced, not a teaching being delivered.
ramayan::953.detailed_meaning: Kausika is explaining his own lineage to Rama. He has already named his father Gadhi and his clan, and now he mentions his elder sister Satyavati and her marriage to Richika. The verse simply continues the genealogical account.
ramayan::953.modern_relevance: At a family gathering, someone is naming grandparents, cousins, and old marriages to explain where the family came from. This verse works the same way: it is lineage, not instruction.
ramayan::953.insight: It keeps the narrative moving by placing Kausika within a remembered family line.

ramayan::954.verse_sanskrit: सशरीरा गता स्वर्गं भर्तारमनुवर्तिनी । कौशिकी परमोदारा प्रवृत्ता च महानदी । । 1348 । ।
ramayan::954.verse_hindi: Following her husband my highly generous sister reached heaven with her human body and down assuming the form of a sacred river, flowed Kausiki.
ramayan::954.english_translation: Following her husband, my noble sister reached heaven in her bodily form. Then Kausiki took the form of a great river and flowed on.
ramayan::954.translation_literal: सशरीरा (with the body) / गता (gone) / स्वर्गं (to heaven) / भर्तारमनुवर्तिनी (following her husband) / कौशिकी (Kausiki) / परमोदारा (most generous / noble) / प्रवृत्ता (became active / set forth) / च (and) / महानदी (great river)
ramayan::954.speaker: Vishvamitra
ramayan::954.essence: Her fidelity is remembered as a river that keeps flowing.
ramayan::954.simple_meaning: Vishvamitra is describing how his sister Satyavati remained devoted to her husband, attained a higher realm in her body, and then became the river Kausiki.
ramayan::954.simple_insight: Love and loyalty can outlast a single human life.
ramayan::954.detailed_meaning: Vishvamitra is telling Rama and Lakshmana about his family line. He names his father, his sister Satyavati, and now explains her extraordinary fate: she followed her husband faithfully, reached heaven, and became the river Kausiki. It is family history, not a teaching verse by itself.
ramayan::954.modern_relevance: A family story is being passed down at the dinner table, and someone pauses on the detail that a loved one’s devotion became part of the landscape itself.
ramayan::954.insight: It frames devotion as something that can shape memory, place, and lineage.

ramayan::955.verse_sanskrit: दिव्या पुण्योदका रम्या हिमवन्तमुपाश्रिता । लोकस्य हितकामार्थं प्रवृत्ता भगिनी मम । । 1349 । ।
ramayan::955.verse_hindi: Conferring the benefit of the other world and worldly pleasures on men my sister  Kausiki who is divine and beautiful having sacred waters took resort in Himavat mountain and started flowing from there.
ramayan::955.english_translation: My sister Kausiki is divine, beautiful, and full of sacred water. She took refuge in Himavat and began to flow from there for the welfare of the world.
ramayan::955.translation_literal: दिव्या (divine) / पुण्योदका (having sacred waters) / रम्या (beautiful) / हिमवन्तम् (Himavat) / उपाश्रिता (having taken refuge in) / लोकस्य (of the world) / हितकामार्थम् (for the welfare and benefit) / प्रवृत्ता (began to flow) / भगिनी (sister) / मम (my)
ramayan::955.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::955.essence: A sacred source becomes a blessing by flowing beyond itself.
ramayan::955.simple_meaning: Kausiki is described as a sacred river, beautiful and life-giving, arising from Himavat for the good of the world.
ramayan::955.simple_insight: Some lives nourish others simply by their presence and flow.
ramayan::955.detailed_meaning: Brahma? No—this is the sage speaking of his sister Kausiki, the river born from Satyavati. He praises her as sacred, beautiful, and beneficial to all, linking her origin to Himavat and to the welfare of the world.
ramayan::955.modern_relevance: A mountain spring appears in silence, but it feeds fields, villages, and cities far below. Some sources of care are like that: quiet, beautiful, and necessary before anyone notices them.
ramayan::955.insight: It shifts attention from private identity to the larger good a life can carry into the world.

ramayan::956.verse_sanskrit: ततोऽहं हिमवत्पार्श्वे वसामि निरतस्सुखम् । भगिन्यां स्नेहसंयुक्त: कौशिक्यां रघुनन्दन । । 13410 । ।
ramayan::956.verse_hindi: O son of the Raghus, from then onwards with affection towards my sister Kausiki, I am  living happily in the vicinity of Himavat mountains.
ramayan::956.english_translation: O son of the Raghus, from then onwards, with affection for my sister Kausiki, I have been living happily near Mount Himavat.
ramayan::956.translation_literal: ततः (then) / अहम् (I) / हिमवत्-पार्श्वे (near Mount Himavat) / वसामि (I live) / निरतस् (happily / continually) / सुखम् (in comfort) / भगिन्याम् (towards my sister) / स्नेह-संयुक्तः (joined with affection) / कौशिक्याम् (for Kausiki) / रघुनन्दन (O delight of the Raghu line)
ramayan::956.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::956.essence: Affection for family can make a place feel like home.
ramayan::956.simple_meaning: He says he has lived happily near Mount Himavat because of his loving bond with his sister Kausiki.
ramayan::956.simple_insight: Love for family can shape where you live and how you live.
ramayan::956.detailed_meaning: The river Kausiki is being described through a family memory. The speaker says he has stayed near Himavat, content and affectionate toward his sister Kausiki. It is a supporting detail in a larger praise of the river, not the main teaching.
ramayan::956.modern_relevance: You move closer to the people who matter, and your life quietly reorganizes around that bond.
ramayan::956.insight: It shifts attention from geography to relationship as the real source of contentment.

ramayan::957.verse_sanskrit: सा तु सत्यवती पुण्या सत्ये धर्मे प्रतिष्ठिता । पतिव्रता महाभागा कौशिकी सरितां वरा । । 13411 । ।
ramayan::957.verse_hindi: Satyavati is sacred, firmly established in truth and righteousness. She is chaste holy and best among rivers. She is known as river Kausiki.
ramayan::957.english_translation: Satyavati is sacred, firmly established in truth and righteousness. She is chaste, noble, and the best among rivers. She is known as the river Kausiki.
ramayan::957.translation_literal: सा (she) / तु (indeed) / सत्यवती (Satyavati, the truthful one) / पुण्या (sacred) / सत्ये (in truth) / धर्मे (in righteousness) / प्रतिष्ठिता (firmly established) / पतिव्रता (devoted to her husband) / महाभागा (highly fortunate / noble) / कौशिकी (Kausiki) / सरितां (among rivers) / वरा (the best)
ramayan::957.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::957.essence: A river can be honoured like a righteous presence.
ramayan::957.simple_meaning: The river Kausiki is praised as sacred, truthful, righteous, and devoted, with a noble place among rivers.
ramayan::957.simple_insight: Some places are remembered not just for beauty, but for the purity they carry.
ramayan::957.detailed_meaning: Visvamitra is speaking to Rama about the river linked to his own past. After mentioning his attachment to this place, he names Kausiki with reverence, praising her sacred character before explaining how she shaped his life and penance.
ramayan::957.modern_relevance: A place by the river, a family story, a name spoken with respect — some landscapes carry the weight of memory and moral meaning, not just geography.
ramayan::957.insight: It shifts attention from scenery to the values a place embodies and preserves.

ramayan::958.verse_sanskrit: अहं हि नियमाद्राम हित्वा तां समुपागत: । सिद्धाश्रममनुप्राप्य सिद्धोऽस्मि तव तेजसा । । 13412 । ।
ramayan::958.verse_hindi: Rama, for the sake of  observance of austerity I have come to Siddhaashrama leaving her behind. Having reached here, I have fulfilled my desire through your valour.
ramayan::958.english_translation: Rama, for the sake of observing austerity I came here, leaving her behind. Having reached Siddhashrama, I have fulfilled my purpose through your power.
ramayan::958.translation_literal: अहम् (I) / हि (indeed) / नियमात् (for the sake of observance) / राम (Rama) / हित्वा (having left) / ताम् (her) / समुपागतः (have come here) / सिद्धाश्रमम् (to Siddhashrama) / अनुप्राप्य (having reached) / सिद्धः अस्मि (I am fulfilled) / तव (your) / तेजसा (by power, by valor)
ramayan::958.speaker: Vishvamitra
ramayan::958.essence: A disciplined life can feel complete when the right person arrives.
ramayan::958.simple_meaning: Vishvamitra tells Rama that he left behind a woman to come here for austerity, and Rama's arrival has fulfilled the purpose of that effort.
ramayan::958.simple_insight: Your presence can become the answer to someone else's long discipline.
ramayan::958.detailed_meaning: Vishvamitra is explaining why he came to Siddhashrama and what this sacred place means to him. He has lived apart from attachment for the sake of austerity, and Rama's arrival now makes that effort feel complete.
ramayan::958.modern_relevance: You keep a hard promise for months, maybe years, and then one person shows up who makes all that strain feel worth it. Some arrivals do that — they answer a discipline you have been carrying alone.
ramayan::958.insight: It shifts attention from private effort to the way righteous presence can fulfil another person's striving.

ramayan::959.verse_sanskrit: एषा राम ममोत्पत्तिस्स्वस्य वंशस्य कीर्तिता । देशस्य च महाबाहो यन्मां त्वं परिपृच्छसि । । 13413 । ।
ramayan::959.verse_hindi: O mightyarmed Rama since you asked me I narrated this, my origin, the history of my family and the history of this place.
ramayan::959.english_translation: O mighty-armed Rama, since you asked, I have told you my origin, the history of my family, and the story of this land.
ramayan::959.translation_literal: एषा (this) / राम (Rama) / मम (my) / उत्पत्तिः (origin) / स्वस्य (of one's own) / वंशस्य (of the family) / कीर्तिता (has been told) / देशस्य (of the land) / च (and) / महाबाहो (mighty-armed one) / यत् (what) / माम् (me) / त्वम् (you) / परिपृच्छसि (you ask about)
ramayan::959.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::959.essence: The answer is complete, and the conversation can move on.
ramayan::959.simple_meaning: The speaker says he has answered Rama's question by telling the story of his own origin, family line, and the land.
ramayan::959.simple_insight: Some answers are just the full story, given plainly.
ramayan::959.detailed_meaning: In Siddhashrama, the sage has already begun explaining himself to Rama. He says he has now told the story of his birth, his lineage, and the place Rama asked about. It is a bridge verse, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::959.modern_relevance: Someone finally asks where you come from, and you give the whole background: family, place, and the path that shaped you.
ramayan::959.insight: It marks a transition from explanation to the next part of the conversation.

ramayan::960.verse_sanskrit: गतोऽर्धरात्र: काकुत्स्थ कथा: कथयतो मम । निद्रामभ्येहि भद्रं ते मा भूद्विघ्नोऽध्वनीह न: । । 13414 । ।
ramayan::960.verse_hindi: O son of the Kakusthas while telling my stories, midnight has passed by. Go to sleep now. Prosperity to you. Let there be no obstacles on our way.
ramayan::960.english_translation: O son of the Kakusthas, while I was telling my story, midnight has passed. Go to sleep now. Prosperity to you. Let there be no obstacle on our journey.
ramayan::960.translation_literal: गतः (passed) / अर्धरात्रः (midnight) / काकुत्स्थ (O son of the Kakusthas) / कथााः (stories) / कथयतः (while telling) / मम (my) / निद्राम् (sleep) / अभ्येहि (go to) / भद्रम् (prosperity) / ते (to you) / मा (let not) / भूत् (be) / विघ्नः (obstacle) / अध्वनि (on the journey) / इह (here) / नः (our)
ramayan::960.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::960.essence: A good conversation ends when the night has already won.
ramayan::960.simple_meaning: The speaker notices that midnight has passed and tells Rama to sleep, wishing him well and hoping their journey stays free of trouble.
ramayan::960.simple_insight: Even in the middle of a meaningful conversation, rest matters before the road ahead.
ramayan::960.detailed_meaning: After recounting his lineage and the history of the place, the speaker sees how late it has become. He gently ends the conversation, asks Rama to sleep, and blesses the journey ahead. The verse simply closes the exchange.
ramayan::960.modern_relevance: You realize the conversation has gone past midnight, and the next morning still matters. Sometimes the kindest thing is to stop, sleep, and continue tomorrow.
ramayan::960.insight: It shifts attention from the story being told to the practical need to rest before travel.

ramayan::961.verse_sanskrit: निष्पन्दास्तरवस्सर्वे निलीनमृगपक्षिण: । नैशेन तमसा व्याप्ता दिशश्च रघुनन्दन । । 13415 । ।
ramayan::961.verse_hindi: O son of the Raghus the trees stand motionless, with the beasts and birds calm, all directions are pervaded with darkness.
ramayan::961.english_translation: O son of the Raghus, the trees stand motionless, the beasts and birds are quiet, and all directions are filled with night-darkness.
ramayan::961.translation_literal: निष्पन्दाः (motionless) / तरवः (trees) / सर्वे (all) / निलीन-मृग-पक्षिणः (beasts-and-birds settled) / नैशेन (by night) / तमसा (with darkness) / व्याप्ताः (pervaded) / दिशः (directions) / च (and) / रघुनन्दन (O delight of the Raghu line)
ramayan::961.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::961.essence: Night has taken over the forest completely.
ramayan::961.simple_meaning: Night has settled so deeply that the forest is still, the animals are quiet, and darkness covers every direction.
ramayan::961.simple_insight: The world itself seems to pause when night fully arrives.
ramayan::961.detailed_meaning: As Rama listens to the sage at night, the conversation shifts from story to silence. The forest has gone still: trees unmoving, animals asleep, every direction swallowed by darkness. It is a scene-setting line, not a teaching.
ramayan::961.insight: It marks the passage from conversation into deep night, preparing the next movement of the scene.

ramayan::962.verse_sanskrit: शनैर्वियुज्यते सन्ध्या नभो नेत्रैरिवावृतम् । नक्षत्रतारागहनं ज्योतिर्भिरिव भासते । । 13416 । ।
ramayan::962.verse_hindi: Evening has gradually disappeared. The sky is littered with stars and planets gleaming points of light as though they are the eyes of the skies.
ramayan::962.english_translation: Evening has gradually disappeared. The sky is filled with stars and planets, gleaming like the eyes of the sky.
ramayan::962.translation_literal: शनैः (gradually) / वियुज्यते (is separated, fades away) / सन्ध्या (evening twilight) / नभः (sky) / नेत्रैः इव (like eyes) / आवृतम् (covered) / नक्षत्र-तारा-गहनम् (dense with stars and planets) / ज्योतिर्भिः इव (like with lights) / भासते (shines)
ramayan::962.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::962.essence: Night arrives softly, and the sky begins to watch.
ramayan::962.simple_meaning: Twilight is fading, and the night sky is coming alive with stars.
ramayan::962.simple_insight: A quiet shift is happening, and the world feels hushed and luminous.
ramayan::962.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing the forest night after the long conversation has gone on past midnight. The twilight has thinned, the sky has opened, and stars now stand out like eyes. It is a scene-setting verse, not a teaching.
ramayan::962.modern_relevance: You look up after a long conversation and realize the night has changed around you. The room is the same, but the world outside has quietly turned.
ramayan::962.insight: It slows the mind and places you inside the passing hour.

ramayan::963.verse_sanskrit: उत्तिष्ठति च शीतांशुश्शशी लोकतमोनुद: । ह्लादयन् प्राणिनां लोके मनांसि प्रभया विभो । । 13417 । ।
ramayan::963.verse_hindi: O Lord the Moon with his cool rays, dispelling the darkness of the earth and delighting the minds of all living beings in this world, is rising higher and higher.
ramayan::963.english_translation: O Lord, the moon with his cool rays is rising higher and higher, dispelling the darkness of the earth and delighting the minds of all living beings in this world.
ramayan::963.translation_literal: उत्तिष्ठति (is rising) / च (and) / शीतांशुः (cool-rayed one, the moon) / शशी (the moon) / लोकतमोनुदः (dispeller of the world's darkness) / ह्लादयन् (delighting) / प्राणिनाम् (of living beings) / लोके (in the world) / मनांसि (minds) / प्रभया (with radiance) / विभो (O Lord)
ramayan::963.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::963.essence: A gentle light can change the whole mood of a world.
ramayan::963.simple_meaning: The moon is rising, and its cool light is pushing back darkness while soothing every mind.
ramayan::963.simple_insight: Even darkness can be eased by a quiet, steady light.
ramayan::963.detailed_meaning: The forest evening has deepened into night. Trees, animals, and birds have fallen still, stars have appeared, and now the moon rises over the scene. This is part of a flowing description of night settling in, not a separate teaching.
ramayan::963.modern_relevance: A streetlight comes on after a blackout, and the whole block seems to exhale. Some changes do not shout; they simply soften everything around them.
ramayan::963.insight: It shifts attention from darkness itself to the quiet relief that light brings.

ramayan::964.verse_sanskrit: नैशानि सर्वभूतानि प्रचरन्ति ततस्तत: । यक्षराक्षससङ्घाश्च रौद्राश्च पिशिताशना: । । 13418 । ।
ramayan::964.verse_hindi: All nocturnal creatures groups of yakshas and rakshasas and dreadful eaters of human flesh are moving here and there.
ramayan::964.english_translation: All nocturnal creatures, groups of yakshas and rakshasas, and dreadful flesh-eaters move here and there.
ramayan::964.translation_literal: नैशानि (night-dwelling) / सर्वभूतानि (all beings) / प्रचरन्ति (move about) / ततस्तत: (here and there) / यक्षराक्षससङ्घाश्च (and groups of yakshas and rakshasas) / रौद्राश्च (and the fierce) / पिशिताशना: (flesh-eaters)
ramayan::964.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::964.essence: Night brings out the beings that daylight hides.
ramayan::964.simple_meaning: At night, all kinds of eerie beings roam around, including yakshas, rakshasas, and flesh-eating creatures.
ramayan::964.simple_insight: Night changes the whole world; what is hidden by day comes alive after dark.
ramayan::964.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing the close of day as moonlight rises and the forest-city world wakes into its nocturnal life. The line is atmospheric, not teaching-based: it simply lists the beings that move about in the dark.
ramayan::964.modern_relevance: You step outside after midnight and the street feels different—quieter, stranger, full of movement you would never notice in daylight.
ramayan::964.insight: It shifts attention from the visible daytime world to the hidden activity of night.

ramayan::965.verse_sanskrit: एवमुक्त्वा महातेजा विरराम महामुनि: । साधु साध्विति तं सर्वे ऋषयो ह्यभ्यपूजयन् । । 13419 । ।
ramayan::965.verse_hindi: Having spoken thus the highly lustrous, great ascetic rested. All sages praised him,
ramayan::965.english_translation: Having spoken thus, the highly lustrous great ascetic paused. All the sages praised him, saying, 'Well said, well said.'
ramayan::965.translation_literal: एवम् (thus) / उक्त्वा (having spoken) / महातेजा (highly lustrous) / विरराम (paused) / महामुनिः (great ascetic) / साधु (well) / साधु (well) / इति (thus) / तम् (him) / सर्वे (all) / ऋषयः (sages) / हि (indeed) / अभ्यपूजयन् (praised)
ramayan::965.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::965.essence: A true speech ends in silence and approval.
ramayan::965.simple_meaning: The sage finishes speaking, and the gathered sages respond with praise.
ramayan::965.simple_insight: A truthful speech can leave a room in shared agreement.
ramayan::965.detailed_meaning: Valmiki has just described the moon rising and the strange beings of the night. He then stops speaking, and the assembled sages immediately honour his words with approval. This verse marks the close of a scene, not a teaching.
ramayan::965.modern_relevance: A speaker ends a hard-won explanation in a quiet hall, and the room answers before anyone asks a question. Some words land because they were true, not loud.
ramayan::965.insight: It shows how a scene can close with recognition rather than argument.

ramayan::966.verse_sanskrit: कुशिकानामयं वंशो महान् धर्मपरस्सदा । ब्रह्मोपमा महात्मान: कुशवंश्या नरोत्तमा: । । 13420 । ।
ramayan::966.verse_hindi: This is the family of the Kusas, venerable always devoted to dharma, foremost of men, great like Lord Brahma.
ramayan::966.english_translation: This is the family of the Kusas, always devoted to dharma, great-souled, and foremost among men, like Brahma.
ramayan::966.translation_literal: कुशिकानाम् (of the Kusikas) / अयम् (this) / वंशः (lineage) / महान् (great) / धर्मपरः (devoted to dharma) / सदा (always) / ब्रह्मोपमा (Brahma-like) / महात्मानः (great-souled ones) / कुशवंश्याः (descendants of Kusha) / नरोत्तमाः (foremost among men)
ramayan::966.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::966.essence: A noble lineage is proven by dharma, not by name.
ramayan::966.simple_meaning: The Kusha line is praised as noble, consistently devoted to right conduct, and elevated among people.
ramayan::966.simple_insight: What your family stands for is built by what you repeatedly choose.
ramayan::966.detailed_meaning: After praising Vishwamitra's greatness, the sage turns to his lineage and honors the Kusha family. The point is not blood alone, but a family identity shaped by steady devotion to dharma and a noble standard of conduct.
ramayan::966.modern_relevance: A child hears the family name spoken at a wedding and feels both pride and pressure. What people inherit is only half the story; the other half is what they keep choosing in private.
ramayan::966.insight: It shifts respect from ancestry alone to the character a family repeatedly embodies.

ramayan::967.verse_sanskrit: विशेषेण भवानेव विश्वामित्रो महायशा: । कौशिकी सरितां श्रेष्ठा कुलोद्योतकरी तव । । 13421 । ।
ramayan::967.verse_hindi: Highly illustrious Viswamitra, you  are similar to Brahma. Among the rivers, Kausiki is the best, refurbishing the image of your dynasty.
ramayan::967.english_translation: Highly illustrious Viswamitra, you are like Brahma. Among rivers, Kausiki is the finest, and she brings honor to your line.
ramayan::967.translation_literal: विशेषेण (especially) / भवानेव (you indeed) / विश्वामित्रो (Viswamitra) / महायशाः (highly illustrious) / कौशिकी (Kausiki) / सरिताम् (among rivers) / श्रेष्ठा (the best) / कुलोद्योतकरी (one who brightens the family) / तव (your)
ramayan::967.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::967.essence: His stature makes his whole line shine.
ramayan::967.simple_meaning: Viswamitra is praised as a great sage, compared to Brahma, and his river Kausiki is called the best among rivers because it honors his lineage.
ramayan::967.simple_insight: Honor can flow through a family name when your life reflects greatness.
ramayan::967.detailed_meaning: The sages have just finished praising Viswamitra’s lineage. Now they single him out directly, comparing him to Brahma and linking his family to the sacred Kausiki river. It is part of a formal blessing, not a teaching in itself.
ramayan::967.modern_relevance: At a family gathering, someone finally says the quiet part aloud: your work has lifted the name you carry. The praise feels less like flattery and more like a life being recognized.
ramayan::967.insight: It turns praise into lineage: a person’s greatness can illuminate the family behind them.

ramayan::968.verse_sanskrit: इति तैर्मुनिशार्दूलै: प्रशस्त: कुशिकात्मज: । निद्रामुपागमच्छ्रीमान् अस्तंगत इवांशुमान् । । 13422 । ।
ramayan::968.verse_hindi: In this way, adored by the best of ascetics, the auspicious son of Kusika, went to sleep like the lustrous Sun setting.
ramayan::968.english_translation: In this way, praised by the best of ascetics, the illustrious son of Kusika went to sleep like the setting sun.
ramayan::968.translation_literal: इति (in this way) / तैः (by them) / मुनिशार्दूलैः (by the tiger-like sages) / प्रशस्तः (praised) / कुशिकात्मजः (the son of Kusika) / निद्राम् (sleep) / उपागमत् (went to) / श्रीमान् (the illustrious one) / अस्तंगतः (set) / इव (like) / अंशुमान् (the sun)
ramayan::968.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::968.essence: Honored at last, he rests without strain.
ramayan::968.simple_meaning: The sages finish praising Vishvamitra, and he falls asleep peacefully, like the sun setting at day’s end.
ramayan::968.simple_insight: Even greatness rests when it has been properly honored.
ramayan::968.detailed_meaning: The forest sages have just praised Vishvamitra’s lineage and stature. Hearing their reverence, the illustrious son of Kusika settles into sleep, calm and satisfied, like the sun sinking below the horizon. It is a quiet transition, not a teaching.
ramayan::968.modern_relevance: After a long evening when everyone finally acknowledges the weight you carried, you can feel your body loosen and let sleep come. The moment is simple, but it matters.
ramayan::968.insight: It marks a pause in the scene, not a principle to apply.

ramayan::969.verse_sanskrit: रामोऽपि सहसौमित्रि: किञ्चिदागतविस्मय: । प्रशस्य मुनिशार्दूलं निद्रां समुपसेवते । । 13423 । ।
ramayan::969.verse_hindi: Rama as well as Lakshmana, with a sense of wonder went to sleep full of admiration for the great ascetic.
ramayan::969.english_translation: Rama and Lakshmana, filled with wonder and praise for the great ascetic, went to sleep.
ramayan::969.translation_literal: रामः (Rama) / अपि (also) / सहसौमित्रिः (together with Lakshmana) / किञ्चित् (somewhat) / आगतविस्मयः (having come to wonder) / प्रशस्य (having praised) / मुनिशार्दूलम् (the tiger among ascetics) / निद्राम् (sleep) / समुपसेवते (took to / entered)
ramayan::969.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::969.essence: Wonder gives way to rest when greatness is recognized.
ramayan::969.simple_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana admire Vishvamitra’s greatness, then rest for the night.
ramayan::969.simple_insight: Respect can quiet the mind enough for rest.
ramayan::969.detailed_meaning: After Vishvamitra is praised by the assembled sages, Rama and Lakshmana are struck with wonder at the ascetic’s stature. Their response is not speech or action, but quiet sleep, as the night closes over the camp.
ramayan::969.modern_relevance: You meet someone whose discipline changes the room, and your own noise falls away. Sometimes admiration is the first form of learning.
ramayan::969.insight: It shows that genuine reverence can settle the mind before the next day’s demands.

ramayan::970.verse_sanskrit: उपास्य रात्रिशेषं तु शोणाकूले महर्षिभि: । निशायां सुप्रभातायां विश्वामित्रोऽभ्यभाषत । । 1351 । ।
ramayan::970.verse_hindi: Viswamitra lay on the bank of Sona with the ascetics, for the rest of the night. (Getting up) at daybreak he said:
ramayan::970.english_translation: Having spent the rest of the night on the bank of the Sona with the great ascetics, Viswamitra spoke at daybreak.
ramayan::970.translation_literal: उपास्य (having spent) / रात्रिशेषं (the remainder of the night) / तु (indeed) / शोणाकूले (on the bank of the Sona) / महर्षिभि: (with the great ascetics) / निशायां (in the night) / सुप्रभातायां (at daybreak) / विश्वामित्रो (Viswamitra) / अभ्यभाषत (spoke)
ramayan::970.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::970.essence: Morning ends the pause and starts the next teaching.
ramayan::970.simple_meaning: Viswamitra and the ascetics rested by the river through the night, then he spoke when morning came.
ramayan::970.simple_insight: A quiet pause can prepare the way for the next step.
ramayan::970.detailed_meaning: After a long night on the Sona riverbank, Viswamitra rests with the sages while Rama and Lakshmana sleep nearby. At dawn, he breaks the silence and resumes the journey, so this verse simply turns the scene toward the next movement.
ramayan::970.modern_relevance: You sleep on a train platform after a long journey, then wake before sunrise to catch the first connection. The real shift is not dramatic — it is the moment the waiting ends and action begins.
ramayan::970.insight: It marks the transition from rest to instruction.

ramayan::971.verse_sanskrit: सुप्रभाता निशा राम पूर्वा सन्ध्या प्रवर्तते । उत्तिष्ठोत्तिष्ठ भद्रं ते गमनायाभिरोचय । । 1352 । ।
ramayan::971.verse_hindi: Rama, the night makes way for the dawn. It is time for morning rituals. Arise, arise May the day bring good news Get ready for the onward journey.
ramayan::971.english_translation: Rama, the night makes way for the dawn. It is time for morning rituals. Arise, arise. May the day bring you good fortune. Prepare for the onward journey.
ramayan::971.translation_literal: सुप्रभाता (well-lit / has become bright) / निशा (night) / राम (Rama) / पूर्वा (earlier / first) / सन्ध्या (dawn / twilight) / प्रवर्तते (is beginning / is moving forward) / उत्तिष्ठ (arise) / उत्तिष्ठ (arise) / भद्रं (good fortune) / ते (to you) / गमनाय (for going) / अभिरोचय (prepare / be pleased with)
ramayan::971.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::971.essence: Dawn ends rest and calls you back to duty.
ramayan::971.simple_meaning: The night has ended, so it is time to get up, do the morning rites, and continue the journey.
ramayan::971.simple_insight: A new day can begin with discipline, not delay.
ramayan::971.detailed_meaning: At dawn on the riverbank, Vishwamitra wakes Rama after a night of rest with the ascetics. The journey with the sage is continuing, and the first task is simple: rise, complete the morning rites, and move on.
ramayan::971.modern_relevance: Your alarm goes off before sunrise, and the day already feels heavy. Still, the first clean step is the same: get up, do what must be done, and begin.
ramayan::971.insight: It shifts attention from sleep and hesitation to timely action and readiness.

ramayan::972.verse_sanskrit: तच्छ्रुत्वा वचनं तस्य कृत्वा पौर्वाह्णिकीं क्रियाम् । गमनं रोचयामास वाक्यं चेदमुवाच ह । । 1353 । ।
ramayan::972.verse_hindi: On hearing his words Rama performed morning oblations and getting ready for the
ramayan::972.english_translation: On hearing his words, Rama performed the morning rites and prepared for departure. Then he spoke these words:
ramayan::972.translation_literal: तत् (that) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / वचनं (word/speech) / तस्य (his) / कृत्वा (having done) / पौर्वाह्णिकीं (morning) / क्रियाम् (rite/action) / गमनं (departure) / रोचयामास (he desired/prepared) / वाक्यं (speech) / च (and) / इदम् (this) / उवाच (said) / ह (indeed)
ramayan::972.speaker: Rama
ramayan::972.essence: Rama answers the morning by getting ready to move.
ramayan::972.simple_meaning: Rama hears Vishwamitra, completes his morning rites, and gets ready to continue the journey.
ramayan::972.simple_insight: Readiness begins with doing the next small thing well.
ramayan::972.detailed_meaning: At dawn on the bank of the Sona, Vishwamitra wakes Rama and calls him onward. Rama does his morning rites without delay, prepares to move, and is about to speak. The verse is a transition, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::972.modern_relevance: The alarm goes off before a long travel day, and you still wash, pray, pack, and move. Before the next demand arrives, you make yourself ready.
ramayan::972.insight: It shows disciplined readiness: complete the required rite, then step into the next task without hesitation.

ramayan::973.verse_sanskrit: अयं शोणश्शुभजलोऽगाध: पुलिनमण्डित: । कतरेण पथा ब्रह्मन् सन्तरिष्यामहे वयम् । । 1354 । ।
ramayan::973.verse_hindi: O knower of Brahman Clean waters of this river are adorned with sandbanks. This Sona is deep. Which way shall we cross this river?
ramayan::973.english_translation: O knower of Brahman, this Sona has clean waters, deep channels, and sandbanks. By which path shall we cross it?
ramayan::973.translation_literal: अयम् (this) / शोणः (the Sona river) / शुभजलः (with pure waters) / अगाधः (deep) / पुलिनमण्डितः (adorned with sandbanks) / कतरेण (by which) / पथा (path) / ब्रह्मन् (O knower of Brahman) / सन्तरिष्यामहे (shall we cross) / वयम् (we)
ramayan::973.speaker: Rama
ramayan::973.simple_meaning: Rama asks how they should cross the deep Sona River, since it has clean waters and sandbanks.
ramayan::973.simple_insight: Even a strong journey begins with noticing the obstacle clearly.
ramayan::973.detailed_meaning: Rama and Vishwamitra are travelling through the forest at dawn. They reach the Sona River, broad and deep, and Rama pauses to ask how they will cross. The verse simply sets up the next instruction.
ramayan::973.modern_relevance: You reach a flooded road on a long drive and slow down before forcing it. First see the obstacle clearly; then choose the safe crossing.
ramayan::973.insight: It teaches you to pause and assess the terrain before moving ahead.

ramayan::974.verse_sanskrit: एवमुक्तस्तु रामेण विश्वामित्रोऽब्रवीदिदम् । एष पन्था मयोद्दिष्टो येन यान्ति महर्षय: । । 1355 । ।
ramayan::974.verse_hindi: Having been addressed by Rama thus Viswamitra said, We shall take the way the ascetics have gone before.
ramayan::974.english_translation: Having been addressed by Rama thus, Viswamitra said, "This is the path I have marked out, the one the great sages have taken before."
ramayan::974.translation_literal: एवमुक्तः (thus addressed) / तु (indeed) / रामेण (by Rama) / विश्वामित्रः (Viswamitra) / अब्रवीत् (said) / इदम् (this) / एषः (this) / पन्थाः (path) / मया (by me) / उद्दिष्टः (pointed out) / येन (by which) / यान्ति (go) / महर्षयः (great sages)
ramayan::974.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::974.essence: The way forward is the one the wise have already walked.
ramayan::974.simple_meaning: Viswamitra answers Rama by pointing to the route ahead. He says this is the path followed by great sages before them.
ramayan::974.simple_insight: Sometimes the safest way forward is the one others of integrity have already walked.
ramayan::974.detailed_meaning: Rama asks how they will cross the deep river. Viswamitra replies that he has already marked the route, and it is the same path used by ancient sages. The verse simply moves the party forward through the forest.
ramayan::974.modern_relevance: You are standing at the edge of a choice and want certainty. Sometimes the next step is simply the route that wiser people have already tested.
ramayan::974.insight: It shifts attention from hesitation to guidance already available.

ramayan::975.verse_sanskrit: एवमुक्ता महर्षयो विश्वामित्रेण धीमता । पश्यन्तस्ते प्रयाता वै वनानि विविधानि च । । 1356 । ।
ramayan::975.verse_hindi: With these words of the wise Viswamitra the ascetics moved forward surveying various forests.
ramayan::975.english_translation: With these words of the wise Viswamitra the ascetics moved forward surveying various forests.
ramayan::975.translation_literal: एवमुक्ताः (having been thus spoken to) / महर्षयः (the great sages) / विश्वामित्रेण (by Vishwamitra) / धीमता (the wise one) / पश्यन्तः (seeing) / ते (they) / प्रयाता (set out) / वै (indeed) / वनानि (forests) / विविधानि (various) / च (and)
ramayan::975.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::975.essence: Once the path is chosen, the only task is to keep moving.
ramayan::975.simple_meaning: The sages continue their journey under Vishvamitra's guidance, looking at the many forests around them.
ramayan::975.simple_insight: Progress sometimes looks ordinary: you keep walking, watching, and trusting the guide ahead.
ramayan::975.detailed_meaning: Vishvamitra has chosen the route across the river country, and the sages follow him without argument. This line simply moves the party onward through unfamiliar forests, setting up the next sighting of the river.
ramayan::975.modern_relevance: You follow the person who knows the terrain, even when the path is long and unfamiliar.
ramayan::975.insight: It shifts attention from decision to movement: the route is set, so the group keeps going.

ramayan::976.verse_sanskrit: ते गत्वा दूरमध्वानं गतेऽर्धदिवसे तदा । जाह्नवीं सरितां श्रेष्ठां ददृशुर्मुनिसेविताम् । । 1357 । ।
ramayan::976.verse_hindi: After travelling a long distance for half a day, they saw Jahnavi, the best among rivers  haunted or worshipped by ascetics.
ramayan::976.english_translation: After travelling a long distance for half a day, they saw Jahnavi, the best among rivers, visited by ascetics.
ramayan::976.translation_literal: ते (they) / गत्वा (having gone) / दूरम् (far) / अध्वानम् (the road) / गतेऽर्धदिवसे (when half the day had passed) / तदा (then) / जाह्नवीम् (Jahnavi) / सरिताम् (among rivers) / श्रेष्ठाम् (the best) / ददृशुः (they saw) / मुनिसेविताम् (served by ascetics)
ramayan::976.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::976.essence: The journey pauses at a sacred crossing.
ramayan::976.simple_meaning: After half a day of travel, the group reaches the sacred river Ganga, a place frequented by ascetics.
ramayan::976.simple_insight: Some moments are only about arrival: the road ends, and the next part begins.
ramayan::976.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra leads Rama and the sages onward through the forest. After hours on the road, they finally see the holy river Ganga, a familiar resting place for ascetics. The verse simply marks their arrival before the next sacred moment unfolds.
ramayan::976.modern_relevance: After a long train ride, you finally catch the first sight of the river or city you were aiming for. The real change is not the view itself, but the threshold it marks.
ramayan::976.insight: It marks a transition in the journey, not a teaching about how to live.

ramayan::977.verse_sanskrit: तां दृष्ट्वा पुण्यसलिलां हंससारससेविताम् । बभूवुर्मुदिता स्सर्वे मुनयस्सह राघवा: । । 1358 । ।
ramayan::977.verse_hindi: On seeing the river Ganga with swans and cranes floating on the surface of the  sacred waters, all the sages including the sons of the Raghus (Rama and Lakshmana) were delighted.
ramayan::977.english_translation: On seeing the sacred Ganga, frequented by swans and cranes, all the sages and the sons of the Raghus felt delighted.
ramayan::977.translation_literal: ताम् (that) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / पुण्यसलिलाम् (with sacred waters) / हंससारससेविताम् (frequented by swans and cranes) / बभूवुः (became) / मुदिताः (delighted) / सर्वे (all) / मुनयः (the sages) / सह (together with) / राघवाः (the sons of Raghu)
ramayan::977.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::977.essence: Beauty can restore tired hearts before the work resumes.
ramayan::977.simple_meaning: Everyone feels joy at seeing the sacred river, beautiful with birds and holy water.
ramayan::977.simple_insight: Even a simple sight can soften the heart when the mind is open.
ramayan::977.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has led Rama, Lakshmana, and the sages to the Ganga after a long walk. They see the holy river alive with birds and clean water, and the whole group feels uplifted before the journey continues.
ramayan::977.modern_relevance: After hours on a dusty road, you finally reach a riverbank and the whole group goes quiet. Beauty does that: it resets the mind before anyone says a word.
ramayan::977.insight: It shows how shared wonder can refresh tired minds before the next task.

ramayan::978.verse_sanskrit: तस्यास्तीरे ततश्चक्रुस्त आवासपरिग्रहम् । ततस्स्नात्वा यथान्यायं सन्तर्प्य पितृदेवता: । । 1359 । । हुत्वा चैवाग्निहोत्राणि प्राश्य चामृतवद्धवि: । विविशुर्जाह्नवीतीरे शुचौ मुदितमानसा: । । 13510 । । विश्वामित्रं महात्मानं परिवार्य समन्तत: ।
ramayan::978.verse_hindi: The birds had made the bank of the river their home. They (Rama and Lakshmana) took a dip and offered traditional oblations to ancestors. Thereafter they lighted the sacrificial fire and made customary offerings to the fire and partook of the nectarlike remains. With cheerful hearts they stood round the illustrious Viswamitra and entered the sacred bank of Jahnavi.
ramayan::978.english_translation: The birds had made the riverbank their home. Rama and Lakshmana bathed, offered rites to their ancestors, lit the sacred fire, shared the offering, and stood cheerfully around Viswamitra on the pure bank of the Jahnavi.
ramayan::978.translation_literal: तस्याः (of that) / तीरे (on the bank) / ततः (then) / चक्रुः (they made) / ताः (those) / आवासपरिग्रहम् (a place of dwelling) / ततः (then) / स्नात्वा (having bathed) / यथान्यायम् (properly) / सन्तर्प्य (having satisfied) / पितृदेवताः (ancestors and divine beings) / हुत्वा (having offered) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / अग्निहोत्राणि (fire offerings) / प्राश्य (having partaken) / च (and) / अमृतवत् (like nectar) / हविः (offering) / विविशुः (they entered) / जाह्नवीतीरे (on the bank of Jahnavi) / शुचौ (pure) / मुदितमानसाः (with joyful minds) / विश्वामित्रम् (Viswamitra) / महात्मानम् (the great-souled one) / परिवार्य (surrounding) / समन्ततः (all around)
ramayan::978.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::978.essence: Orderly ritual keeps the journey clean and the mind ready.
ramayan::978.simple_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana pause by the Ganga, complete their rites, and settle joyfully around Viswamitra.
ramayan::978.simple_insight: Even a journey has its sacred rhythm: stop, honor, and continue with a clear mind.
ramayan::978.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana are traveling with Viswamitra along the Ganga. At the riverbank, they make camp, bathe, honor their ancestors, perform the fire rites, and then gather around their teacher in calm, cheerful readiness before the next question begins.
ramayan::978.modern_relevance: You finally reach the hotel after a long train ride, wash your face, call home, and sit down before the next meeting. The body resets; the mind becomes fit to continue.
ramayan::978.insight: It teaches you to restore yourself through ritual before the next demand.

ramayan::979.verse_sanskrit: अथ तत्र तदा रामो विश्वामित्रमथाब्रवीत् । । 13511 । । भगवन् श्रोतुमिच्छामि गङ्गां त्रिपथगां नदीम् । त्रैलोक्यं कथमाक्रम्य गता नदनदीपतिम् । । 13512 । ।
ramayan::979.verse_hindi: Then Rama said to Viswamitra O venerable one I wish to know why Ganga flowing in three directions, occupy (purified) the three worlds before entering the sea, the lord of rivers?
ramayan::979.english_translation: Then Rama said to Vishvamitra, 'O venerable one, I wish to know how Ganga, flowing through the three worlds, reached the lord of rivers.'
ramayan::979.translation_literal: अथ (then) तत्र (there) तदा (at that time) रामः (Rama) विश्वामित्रम् (to Vishvamitra) अथ (then) अब्रवीत् (said) / भगवन् (venerable one) श्रोतुम् (to hear) इच्छामि (I wish) गङ्गाम् (Ganga) त्रिपथगाम् (flowing through three paths) नदीम् (river) / त्रैलोक्यम् (the three worlds) कथम् (how) आक्रम्य (having traversed) गता (gone) नदनदीपतिम् (to the lord of rivers)
ramayan::979.speaker: Rama
ramayan::979.essence: Real understanding begins when you ask how things came to be.
ramayan::979.simple_meaning: Rama asks Vishvamitra to explain the origin and journey of the Ganga river.
ramayan::979.simple_insight: Curiosity is not weakness; it is how deeper understanding begins.
ramayan::979.detailed_meaning: On the bank of the Ganga, Rama has just completed the rites of arrival and bathing. Instead of moving on, he asks Vishvamitra how this river moved through the three worlds before reaching the sea. The journey now turns into a teaching moment.
ramayan::979.modern_relevance: You hear a story everyone else repeats, but you pause and ask where it came from. That one question can turn a passing moment into real learning.
ramayan::979.insight: It shifts the mind from passive listening to active inquiry.

ramayan::980.verse_sanskrit: चोदितो रामवाक्येन विश्वामित्रो महामुनि: । वृद्धिं जन्म च गङ्गाया वक्तुमेवोपचक्रमे । । 13513 । ।
ramayan::980.verse_hindi: Prompted by Ramas words, maharshi Viswamitra started narrating the account of the birth and progress of river Ganga.
ramayan::980.english_translation: Prompted by Rama's words, the great sage Vishwamitra began to narrate the birth and growth of the river Ganga.
ramayan::980.translation_literal: चोदितः (prompted) / रामवाक्येन (by Rama's words) / विश्वामित्रः (Vishvamitra) / महामुनिः (great sage) / वृद्धिं (growth) / जन्म (birth) / च (and) / गङ्गायाः (of Ganga) / वक्तुम् (to speak) / एव (indeed) / उपचक्रमे (began)
ramayan::980.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::980.essence: A single question can open an entire lineage of meaning.
ramayan::980.simple_meaning: Rama asks about Ganga, and Vishvamitra begins telling her origin and development.
ramayan::980.simple_insight: Curiosity opens the door to a larger story.
ramayan::980.detailed_meaning: After bathing and offering rites by the riverbank, Rama asks Vishvamitra about the sacred Ganga. The sage responds by beginning a long account of her birth and course, so this verse simply turns the conversation into a teaching story.
ramayan::980.modern_relevance: You ask one sincere question, and a whole hidden history starts to unfold.
ramayan::980.insight: It shifts the moment from question to explanation, preparing the listener for a larger sacred narrative.

ramayan::981.verse_sanskrit: शैलेन्द्रो हिमवान्नाम धातूनामाकरो महान् । तस्य कन्याद्वयं राम रूपेणाप्रतिमं भुवि । । 13514 । ।
ramayan::981.verse_hindi: O Rama the great mountain named Himavan is a treasuretrove of ores. He is the king of mountains. He had two daughters, unrivalled in beauty in this world.
ramayan::981.english_translation: O Rama, the great mountain named Himavan is a treasure-trove of ores and the king of mountains. He had two daughters, unrivalled in beauty in this world.
ramayan::981.translation_literal: शैलेन्द्रः (king of mountains) / हिमवान् (Himavan) / नाम (named) / धातूनाम् (of ores) / आकरः (treasure-trove) / महान् (great) / तस्य (his) / कन्याद्वयम् (two daughters) / राम (Rama) / रूपेण (in beauty) / अप्रतिमम् (unrivalled) / भुवि (in the world)
ramayan::981.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::981.essence: Greatness is often introduced through the family and place that shaped it.
ramayan::981.simple_meaning: Himavan is described as a mighty mountain rich in minerals, and he has two daughters of unmatched beauty.
ramayan::981.simple_insight: Some stories begin by showing where greatness comes from.
ramayan::981.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra is explaining Ganga’s origin to Rama. He begins with Himavan, the king of mountains, rich and immense, and introduces his two incomparable daughters. This verse is setting up the family line before the main story moves forward.
ramayan::981.modern_relevance: Someone starts telling you a family story by naming the grandparents, the hometown, and the old house before reaching the person you asked about. The details matter because they prepare the ground.
ramayan::981.insight: It teaches you to read the setup before expecting the reveal.

ramayan::982.verse_sanskrit: या मेरुदुहिता राम तयोर्माता सुमध्यमा । नाम्ना मनोरमा नाम पत्नी हिमवत: प्रिया । । 13515 । ।
