ramayan::1127.verse_hindi: Exceedingly valiant Ashuman beheld the elephant of the quarter worshipped by daityas, danavas, rakshasas, pisachas, birds and serpents.
ramayan::1127.english_translation: Exceedingly valiant Ashuman beheld the elephant of the quarter worshipped by daityas, danavas, rakshasas, pisachas, birds and serpents.
ramayan::1127.translation_literal: दैत्यदानवरक्षोभि: (by daityas, danavas, and rakshasas) / पिशाचपतगोरगै: (by pisachas, birds, and serpents) / पूज्यमानं (being worshipped) / महातेजा (the greatly radiant) / दिशागजम् (the elephant of the direction) / अपश्यत (saw)
ramayan::1127.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1127.essence: A hidden world appears before the search can begin.
ramayan::1127.simple_meaning: Ashuman comes upon the guardian elephant of the direction, a being honored by many kinds of creatures.
ramayan::1127.simple_insight: The path opens into a vast, strange world beyond ordinary sight.
ramayan::1127.detailed_meaning: Anshuman has descended into the underworld in search of his ancestors. After following the hidden path, he suddenly sees the mighty elephant that guards the quarter, revered by many beings of the lower and higher worlds. This is a scene-setting detail before the real exchange begins.
ramayan::1127.modern_relevance: You keep going through one more door, one more corridor, and suddenly the place feels larger than your fear.
ramayan::1127.insight: It slows the reader down and prepares the scene before the next encounter.

ramayan::1128.verse_sanskrit: स तं प्रदक्षिणं कृत्वा पृष्ट्वा चापि निरामयम् । पितृ़न् स परिपप्रच्छ वाजिहर्तारमेव च । । 1418 । ।
ramayan::1128.verse_hindi: Having circumambulated the elephant, he (Anshuman) enquired about his wellbeing, the where abouts of his uncles and also about the one who had stolen the sacrificial horse.
ramayan::1128.english_translation: Having circumambulated the elephant, Anshuman asked about its well-being, about the whereabouts of his uncles, and about the one who had stolen the sacrificial horse.
ramayan::1128.translation_literal: स (he) / तम् (that) / प्रदक्षिणम् (circumambulation) / कृत्वा (having done) / पृष्ट्वा (having asked) / च (and) / अपि (also) / निरामयम् (free from illness) / पितृ़न् (his fathers/uncles) / सः (he) / परिपप्रच्छ (asked in detail) / वाजिहर्तारम् (horse-stealer) / एव (indeed) / च (and)
ramayan::1128.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1128.essence: Respect comes first, even when you need urgent answers.
ramayan::1128.simple_meaning: Anshuman respectfully circles the elephant, checks on its welfare, and asks where his uncles are and who stole the horse.
ramayan::1128.simple_insight: Courtesy and purpose can coexist in the same moment.
ramayan::1128.detailed_meaning: Anshuman has descended into the underworld on his grandfather Sagara’s command. After finding the divine elephant, he does not rush in with demands. He first shows respect, then asks the questions that matter: the fate of his uncles and the stolen horse.
ramayan::1128.modern_relevance: You walk into a difficult conversation and begin with respect instead of accusation. That small choice can open a door that force would slam shut.
ramayan::1128.insight: It teaches you to lead with respect before pressing for answers.

ramayan::1129.verse_sanskrit: दिशागजस्तु तच्छ्रुत्वा प्रत्याहांशुमतो वच: । आसमञ्ज कृतार्थस्त्वं सहाश्वश्शीघ्रमेष्यसि । । 1419 । ।
ramayan::1129.verse_hindi: Having listened to the words of Anshuman the elephant of the quarter replied, O
ramayan::1129.english_translation: Having heard Anshuman's words, the elephant of the quarter replied, "O Anshuman, Asamanja has been made successful; you will soon return with the horse."
ramayan::1129.translation_literal: दिशागजः (the elephant of the quarter) / तु (indeed) / तत् (that) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / प्रत्याह (replied) / अंशुमतः (of Anshuman) / वचः (words) / आसमञ्जः (Asamanja) / कृतार्थः (successful, fulfilled) / त्वम् (you) / सहाश्वः (with the horse) / शीघ्रम् (soon) / एष्यसि (you will come)
ramayan::1129.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1129.essence: A single answer turns a wandering search into a path forward.
ramayan::1129.simple_meaning: The guardian elephant answers Anshuman that Asamanja has already succeeded, and Anshuman will soon return with the horse.
ramayan::1129.simple_insight: The search is not over; the answer is finally within reach.
ramayan::1129.detailed_meaning: Anshuman has found the elephant guarding the direction and asked about the lost horse and his ancestors. The elephant replies that Asamanja has already succeeded and that Anshuman will soon return with the horse, moving the search one step forward.
ramayan::1129.modern_relevance: You ask the right person after a long search, and suddenly the path opens. The answer is still partial, but it changes everything.
ramayan::1129.insight: It advances the quest by confirming progress and pointing to the next step.

ramayan::1130.verse_sanskrit: तस्य तद्वचनं श्रुत्वा सर्वानेव दिशागजान् । यथाक्रमं यथान्यायं प्रष्टुं समुपचक्रमे । । 14110 । ।
ramayan::1130.verse_hindi: Having listened to the words of the elephant, Anshuman started enquring the well being of each of the guardians (elephants) of the quarters successively with due respect:
ramayan::1130.english_translation: Having listened to the words of the elephant, Anshuman started enquiring the well being of each of the guardians of the quarters successively with due respect.
ramayan::1130.translation_literal: तस्य (of that) / तद्वचनं (that speech) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / सर्वान् एव (all indeed) / दिशागजान् (elephants of the quarters) / यथाक्रमं (in proper order) / यथान्यायं (according to propriety) / प्रष्टुम् (to ask) / समुपचक्रमे (began)
ramayan::1130.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1130.simple_meaning: Anshuman responds with courtesy, asking after each guardian elephant in the proper order and with respect.
ramayan::1130.simple_insight: Respect is shown in small details, not just grand gestures.
ramayan::1130.detailed_meaning: Anshuman has reached the guardian elephant and is speaking within a formal, sacred setting. Rather than rushing to his own purpose, he follows proper order and asks about each guardian respectfully, showing discipline and courtliness.
ramayan::1130.modern_relevance: You meet someone important and do not barrel into your request. You listen first, answer carefully, and let respect shape the whole exchange.
ramayan::1130.insight: It trains attention to move through a conversation with order, patience, and etiquette.

ramayan::1131.verse_hindi: All those elephants of the quarters were knowers of the essence of words and proficient in the right use of words. Treating him kindly the elephants encouraged him saying, You will go back with the horse.
ramayan::1131.english_translation: All those guardians of the directions, skilled in speech and masters of fitting words, honoured him and encouraged him, saying, 'You will go back with the horse.'
ramayan::1131.translation_literal: तैः (by them) / च (and) / सर्वैः (all) / दिशापालैः (by the guardians of the directions) / वाक्यज्ञैः (knowers of speech) / वाक्यकोविदैः (skilled in words) / पूजितः (honoured) / सहयः (with the horse) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / गन्ता असि (you will go) / इति (thus) / अभिचोदितः (encouraged)
ramayan::1131.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1131.essence: Respectful words can keep a hard journey moving.
ramayan::1131.simple_meaning: The guardians of the directions treated Anshuman kindly and assured him that he would return with the horse.
ramayan::1131.simple_insight: Kind words can steady someone on a difficult mission.
ramayan::1131.detailed_meaning: Anshuman is speaking with the guardians of the directions as he searches for the lost horse. They receive him respectfully, answer him carefully, and give him hope that his quest will succeed. The verse is a brief bridge in the larger search.
ramayan::1131.modern_relevance: You are deep in a difficult task and one calm, respectful reply keeps you moving. Sometimes progress begins with being heard well.
ramayan::1131.insight: It shows how respectful speech can support someone in the middle of uncertainty.

ramayan::1132.verse_sanskrit: तेषां तद्वचनं श्रुत्वा जगाम लघुविक्रम: । भस्मराशीकृता यत्र पितरस्तस्य सागरा: । । 14112 । ।
ramayan::1132.verse_hindi: Hearing their words with a quick pace where he reached the place his uncles, sons of Sagara were reduced to heaps of ashes.
ramayan::1132.english_translation: Hearing their words, he quickly went to the place where his ancestors, the sons of Sagara, had been reduced to ashes.
ramayan::1132.translation_literal: तेषाम् (of them) / तद्वचनम् (that word) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / जगाम (went) / लघुविक्रमः (with quick stride) / भस्मराशी-कृता (made into heaps of ashes) / यत्र (where) / पितरः (ancestors/fathers) / तस्य (his) / सागरा: (the sons of Sagara)
ramayan::1132.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1132.essence: He goes at once to the place where his family was destroyed.
ramayan::1132.simple_meaning: He heard their words and went quickly to the place where the sons of Sagara had been turned to ashes.
ramayan::1132.simple_insight: The journey moves forward because memory and duty still matter.
ramayan::1132.detailed_meaning: Anshuman has just spoken with the guardians of the directions. After hearing them, he sets off at once toward the place where his ancestors, the sons of Sagara, were burned to ashes. The verse simply moves the story from inquiry to action.
ramayan::1132.modern_relevance: You finally hear the full story behind a family wound, and you go straight to the place it began.
ramayan::1132.insight: It shifts attention from explanation to movement, showing that understanding must lead somewhere.

ramayan::1133.verse_sanskrit: स दु:खवशमापन्नस्त्वसमञ्जसुतस्तदा । चुक्रोश परमार्तस्तु वधात्तेषां सुदु:खित: । । 14113 । ।
ramayan::1133.verse_hindi: Then the son of Asamanjasa, overwhelmed with sorrow and deeply distressed at their destruction, bewailed with great grief.
ramayan::1133.english_translation: Then the son of Asamanjasa, overwhelmed with sorrow and deeply distressed at their destruction, bewailed with great grief.
ramayan::1133.translation_literal: स (he) / दुःखवशम् (under the power of sorrow) / आपन्नः (overwhelmed) / तु (indeed) / असमञ्जसुतः (the son of Asamanjasa) / तदा (then) / चुक्रोश (cried out) / परम-आर्तः (deeply distressed) / तु (indeed) / वधात् (at the destruction) / तेषाम् (of them) / सु-दुःखितः (greatly grieved)
ramayan::1133.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1133.essence: Sorrow comes first when you meet irreversible loss.
ramayan::1133.simple_meaning: He saw his ancestors reduced to ashes and cried out in grief. The loss hit him all at once, and he could not bear it.
ramayan::1133.simple_insight: Grief can arrive so fully that even action stops for a moment.
ramayan::1133.detailed_meaning: Anshuman has followed the trail to the ashes of his ancestors, the sons of Sagara. What he finds is not reunion but ruin. Seeing the destruction, he collapses into grief before he can even think of the next step.
ramayan::1133.modern_relevance: You open a message and realize something irreversible has already happened. For a moment, all you can do is feel the full weight of it.
ramayan::1133.insight: It shows grief before strategy: first the heart breaks, then the task begins.

ramayan::1134.verse_sanskrit: यज्ञीयं च हयं तत्र चरन्तमविदूरत: । ददर्श पुरुषव्याघ्रो दु:खशोकसमन्वित: । । 14114 । ।
ramayan::1134.verse_hindi: Possessed by grief and tears, Anshuman, that tiger among men, beheld the sacrificial horse grazing nearby.
ramayan::1134.english_translation: Possessed by grief and tears, Anshuman, that tiger among men, beheld the sacrificial horse grazing nearby.
ramayan::1134.translation_literal: यज्ञीयं (fit for sacrifice) / च (and) / हयं (horse) / तत्र (there) / चरन्तम् (grazing) / अविदूरतः (not far away) / ददर्श (saw) / पुरुषव्याघ्रः (tiger among men) / दुःखशोकसमन्वितः (filled with grief and sorrow)
ramayan::1134.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1134.essence: Grief narrows the world until one necessary thing appears.
ramayan::1134.simple_meaning: Anshuman, still grieving, sees the sacrificial horse grazing nearby.
ramayan::1134.simple_insight: Grief can make the world feel immediate and unreal at once.
ramayan::1134.detailed_meaning: After finding the ashes of his ancestors, Anshuman is overwhelmed with sorrow. In that raw state, he notices the sacrificial horse nearby, the key to completing the rites and restoring honor to his family.
ramayan::1134.modern_relevance: You are already hurting, and then you spot the one thing that could help. In that moment, even small hope feels enormous.
ramayan::1134.insight: It shifts attention from grief alone to the first practical opening inside it.

ramayan::1135.verse_sanskrit: स तेषां राजपुत्राणां कर्तुकामो जलक्रियाम् । सलिलार्थी महातेजा न चापश्यज्जलाशयम् । । 14115 । ।
ramayan::1135.verse_hindi: With the intention of performing traditional funeral rites with water for the deceased princes, highly lustrous Anshuman looked around for water but could not see any
ramayan::1135.english_translation: With the intention of performing funeral rites with water for the deceased princes, highly lustrous Anshuman looked around for water but could not see any.
ramayan::1135.translation_literal: सः (he) / तेषाम् (of those) / राजपुत्राणाम् (of the princes) / कर्तुकामः (wishing to perform) / जलक्रियाम् (water rite) / सलिलार्थी (seeking water) / महातेजाः (highly lustrous) / न (not) / चापश्यत् (saw) / जलाशयम् (a body of water)
ramayan::1135.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1135.essence: He wants to honour the dead, but even water is out of reach.
ramayan::1135.simple_meaning: Anshuman wants to perform the water rites for the dead princes, but he cannot find any water nearby.
ramayan::1135.simple_insight: Grief often begins with one practical problem: you want to honor the dead, but you cannot yet do even that.
ramayan::1135.detailed_meaning: After finding the sacrificial horse, Anshuman is overwhelmed by the loss of his ancestors. He wants to complete the water offering for the dead princes, but the land offers no water at all. The scene stays in motion, carrying him toward the next discovery.
ramayan::1135.modern_relevance: You stand at a funeral with dry hands and no clear next step. The heart wants to honour what was lost, but the practical world has not yet made room for it.
ramayan::1135.insight: It shows how grief first becomes action: seeking the means to honour the dead.

ramayan::1136.verse_sanskrit: विसार्य निपुणां दृष्टिं ततोऽपश्यत्खगाधिपम् । पितृ़णां मातुलं राम सुपर्णमनिलोपमम् । । 14116 । ।
ramayan::1136.verse_hindi: O Rama with his keen eyes, he (Anshuman) marked Suparna, the maternal uncle of his uncles, lord of the eagles (Garuda) bestowed with the swiftness of the wind.
ramayan::1136.english_translation: With his sharp gaze, he then saw Garuda, lord of birds, the wind-swift one, the maternal uncle of his fathers.
ramayan::1136.translation_literal: विसार्य (spreading) / निपुणाम् (keen, sharp) / दृष्टिम् (gaze) / ततः (then) / अपश्यत् (saw) / खगाधिपम् (lord of birds) / पितृणाम् (of fathers/ancestors) / मातुलम् (maternal uncle) / राम (O Rama) / सुपर्णम् (Suparna, Garuda) / अनिलोपमम् (wind-like, wind-swift)
ramayan::1136.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1136.essence: Careful seeing reveals the ally you did not know was near.
ramayan::1136.simple_meaning: Anshuman spots Garuda, the swift lord of birds, after searching carefully.
ramayan::1136.simple_insight: Sometimes help appears only after patient looking.
ramayan::1136.detailed_meaning: Anshuman has found the sacrificial horse and still has no water for the funeral rites of his dead ancestors. While searching the area, he notices Garuda, the mighty bird who is linked to his ancestral line. This sight leads into Garuda's speech.
ramayan::1136.modern_relevance: You keep scanning a crowded station for the one person who can help. After the panic, you finally notice the ally standing right there.
ramayan::1136.insight: It shifts attention from helpless searching to recognizing the unexpected helper already present.

ramayan::1137.verse_sanskrit: स चैवमब्रवीद्वाक्यं वैनतेयो महाबल : । मा शुच: पुरुषव्याघ्र वधोऽयं लोकसम्मत: । । 14117 । ।
ramayan::1137.verse_hindi: Highly powerful Garuda, son of Vinata, addressing Anshuman said O Tiger among men do not grieve. This act of assasination is meant for the welfare of the three worlds.
ramayan::1137.english_translation: Highly powerful Garuda, son of Vinata, addressing Anshuman said, "O tiger among men, do not grieve. This act of destruction is for the welfare of the three worlds."
ramayan::1137.translation_literal: स (he) / च (and) / एवम् (thus) / अब्रवीत् (said) / वाक्यम् (speech) / वैनतेयः (son of Vinata) / महाबलः (very powerful) / मा (do not) / शुचः (grieve) / पुरुषव्याघ्र (tiger among men) / वधः (destruction) / अयम् (this) / लोकसम्मतः (approved by the worlds)
ramayan::1137.speaker: Garuda
ramayan::1137.essence: Some losses belong to a larger order you cannot yet see.
ramayan::1137.simple_meaning: Garuda tells Anshuman not to mourn. The destruction of the princes happened for a larger good.
ramayan::1137.simple_insight: Grief softens when you see that not every loss is meaningless.
ramayan::1137.detailed_meaning: Anshuman has found Garuda while searching for water for the dead princes. Garuda stops his sorrow and explains that the princes were destroyed by a power beyond ordinary harm, for a purpose tied to the welfare of the three worlds.
ramayan::1137.modern_relevance: You lose something precious and immediately want a reason that makes it hurt less. Sometimes the first task is not explanation, but hearing that the loss is larger than your fear.
ramayan::1137.insight: It shifts the mind from personal sorrow to a wider moral frame.

ramayan::1138.verse_sanskrit: कपिलेनाप्रमेयेन दग्धा हीमे महाबला: । सलिलं नार्हसि प्राज्ञ दातुमेषां हि लौकिकम् । । 14118 । ।
ramayan::1138.verse_hindi: Your valiant uncles have been burnt by Kapila of boundless power. O Sagcious one performing traditional rites with ordinary water is not proper.
ramayan::1138.english_translation: Your valiant uncles have been burnt by Kapila of boundless power. O sagacious one, offering ordinary water for their rites is not proper.
ramayan::1138.translation_literal: कपिलेन (by Kapila) / अप्रमेयेन (by the immeasurable one) / दग्धाः (burnt) / हि (indeed) / इमे (these) / महाबलाः (greatly powerful ones) / सलिलम् (water) / न अर्हसि (you do not deserve / it is not proper for you) / प्राज्ञ (wise one) / दातुम् (to give) / एषाम् (for these) / हि (indeed) / लौकिकम् (ordinary / worldly)
ramayan::1138.speaker: Garuda
ramayan::1138.essence: Ordinary remedies fail when the wound itself is extraordinary.
ramayan::1138.simple_meaning: Garuda explains that Anshuman's strong ancestors were burned by Kapila, so ordinary water is not enough for their funeral rites.
ramayan::1138.simple_insight: Some losses need more than routine gestures. The right response must match the scale of what happened.
ramayan::1138.detailed_meaning: Anshuman has found Garuda, who has already softened his grief and explained why his ancestors died. Now Garuda adds the crucial detail: Kapila's fire was extraordinary, so a normal offering will not do. The next step must be different.
ramayan::1138.modern_relevance: You try to fix a family wound with a polite message and a ritual apology. But the hurt was deeper than routine can touch, and you know it.
ramayan::1138.insight: It shifts you from automatic ritual to a response worthy of the actual loss.

ramayan::1139.verse_sanskrit: गङ्गा हिमवतो ज्येष्ठा दुहिता पुरुषर्षभ । तस्यां कुरु महाबाहो पितृ़णां तु जलक्रियाम् । । 14119 । ।
ramayan::1139.verse_hindi: O Best among men O Mightyarmed one perform  the traditional rites of your uncles with water from river Ganga, the eldest daughter of Himavat.
ramayan::1139.english_translation: O best among men, mighty-armed one, perform the water rites for your ancestors with the river Ganga, the eldest daughter of Himavat.
ramayan::1139.translation_literal: गङ्गा (Ganga) / हिमवतो (of Himavat) / ज्येष्ठा (eldest) / दुहिता (daughter) / पुरुषर्षभ (best among men) / तस्यां (in that) / कुरु (do) / महाबाहो (mighty-armed one) / पितृ़णां (of the ancestors) / तु (indeed) / जलक्रियाम् (water rite)
ramayan::1139.speaker: Garuda
ramayan::1139.essence: Grief becomes duty when the dead still need your hands.
ramayan::1139.simple_meaning: Garuda tells Anshuman to use the river Ganga for the funeral water rites of his ancestors.
ramayan::1139.simple_insight: Some duties are urgent because love and respect cannot be postponed.
ramayan::1139.detailed_meaning: Garuda is guiding Anshuman after revealing that his sixty thousand ancestors were burned to ashes. Instead of grief alone, he gives a clear next step: use sacred Ganga water to complete the rites that restore honor to the dead.
ramayan::1139.modern_relevance: You are standing by a hospital bed after the worst phone call of your life, and someone still needs decisions made. Grief does not cancel responsibility.
ramayan::1139.insight: It shifts you from helpless mourning to a concrete act of care and completion.

ramayan::1140.verse_sanskrit: भस्मराशीकृतानेतान् प्लावयेल्लोकपावनी । तया क्लिन्नमिदं भस्म गङ्गया लोककान्तया । । 14120 । । षष्टिं पुत्रसहस्राणि स्वर्गलोकं च नेष्यति ।
ramayan::1140.verse_hindi: Ganga, the purifier of the three worlds, will sanctify your uncles reduced to heaps of ashes. These heaps when inundated by waters of Ganga, beloved of the worlds, will take  all the sixty thousand sons to heaven.
ramayan::1140.english_translation: Ganga, the purifier of the three worlds, will sanctify your uncles reduced to heaps of ashes. These heaps, when drenched by Ganga, beloved of the world, will carry all sixty thousand sons to the higher realm.
ramayan::1140.translation_literal: भस्मराशीकृतान् (made into heaps of ashes) / एतान् (these) / प्लावयेत् (should flood/sanctify) / लोकपावनी (the purifier of the worlds) / तया (by that) / क्लिन्नम् (drenched) / इदम् (this) / भस्म (ash) / गङ्गया (by Ganga) / लोककान्तया (beloved of the world) / षष्टिम् (sixty) / पुत्रसहस्राणि (thousand sons) / स्वर्गलोकम् (the higher realm) / च (and) / नेष्यति (will carry)
ramayan::1140.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1140.essence: Some endings need a cleansing you cannot produce yourself.
ramayan::1140.simple_meaning: Ganga's water can purify the ashes of the dead and help them reach the higher realm. The verse explains why Bhagiratha must bring Ganga to his ancestors.
ramayan::1140.simple_insight: Some burdens can only be lifted by grace beyond your own effort.
ramayan::1140.detailed_meaning: Bhagiratha is being told how to complete the rites for his ancestors, whose bodies were burned by Kapila's power. The sage explains that only Ganga can wash these ashes and free the sixty thousand sons. The verse supports the larger instruction, not a separate teaching.
ramayan::1140.modern_relevance: You can do everything right and still need help that comes from beyond your own hands. Some losses ask for cleansing, not just effort.
ramayan::1140.insight: It shifts the focus from human control to the need for a purifying force greater than you.

ramayan::1141.verse_sanskrit: गच्छ चाश्वं महाभाग तं गृह्य पुरुषर्षभ । । 14121 । । यज्ञं पैतामहं वीर संवर्तयितुमर्हसि ।
ramayan::1141.verse_hindi: O Highly fortunate one O Best among men go back with that horse. O Hero It
ramayan::1141.english_translation: O highly fortunate one, O best among men, go back with that horse. O hero, you should complete the ancestral sacrifice.
ramayan::1141.translation_literal: गच्छ (go) / च (and) / अश्वं (horse) / महाभाग (highly fortunate one) / तं (that) / गृह्य (having taken) / पुरुषर्षभ (best among men) / यज्ञं (sacrifice) / पैतामहं (ancestral) / वीर (hero) / संवर्तयितुम् (to complete) / अर्हसि (you should)
ramayan::1141.speaker: Garuda
ramayan::1141.essence: Finding the missing piece is not enough; you must finish the work it was for.
ramayan::1141.simple_meaning: The horse must be taken back so the ancestral sacrifice can be finished.
ramayan::1141.simple_insight: Some duties are unfinished until you return and complete them.
ramayan::1141.detailed_meaning: Anshuman has reached the point where the lost horse must be recovered. Garuda directs him to return with it and complete the ancestral sacrifice, because the whole quest has meaning only when the ritual is finished.
ramayan::1141.modern_relevance: You found what everyone was waiting for, but the job is still incomplete. The real relief comes only when you bring it back and finish what was started.
ramayan::1141.insight: It shifts attention from recovery alone to completing the responsibility that recovery serves.

ramayan::1142.verse_sanskrit: सुपर्णवचनं श्रुत्वा सोंऽशुमानतिवीर्यवान् । । 14122 । । त्वरितं हयमादाय पुनरायान्महायशा: ।
ramayan::1142.verse_hindi: Exceedingly powerful and highly renowned Anshuman, on hearing the words of Garuda returned quickly to the capital with the horse৷৷
ramayan::1142.english_translation: Hearing Garuda's words, the mighty and glorious Anshuman quickly returned with the horse.
ramayan::1142.translation_literal: सुपर्णवचनं (Garuda's words) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / सः (he) / अंशुमान् (Anshuman) / अतिवीर्यवान् (exceedingly powerful) / त्वरितम् (quickly) / हयम् (the horse) / आदाय (having taken) / पुनः (again) / अयात् (returned) / महायशाः (highly renowned)
ramayan::1142.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1142.essence: Clear instruction met with swift action keeps the larger duty alive.
ramayan::1142.simple_meaning: Anshuman hears Garuda's message, takes the horse, and hurries back without delay.
ramayan::1142.simple_insight: Sometimes the right response is immediate: hear clearly, act quickly, and bring back what must be restored.
ramayan::1142.detailed_meaning: Garuda has just told Anshuman to take the horse and return so the ancestral sacrifice can be completed. Anshuman obeys at once, carrying the horse back with speed. The verse is a brief movement in the larger story, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::1142.modern_relevance: You get the message, stop arguing with it, and do the next necessary thing before hesitation grows teeth.
ramayan::1142.insight: It shifts the mind from delay to prompt obedience when the task is clear.

ramayan::1143.verse_sanskrit: ततो राजानमासाद्य दीक्षितं रघुनन्दन । । 14123 । । न्यवेदयद्यथावृत्तं सुपर्णवचनं तथा ।
ramayan::1143.verse_hindi: O Descendant of the Raghus (Rama), having reached the king who had been initiated into the ceremony, Anshuman communicated faithfully to him all that had happened. He also reported the words Suparna had said.
ramayan::1143.english_translation: O Descendant of the Raghu line, after reaching the king who had been initiated for the rite, Anshuman faithfully reported everything that had happened, including Suparna's words.
ramayan::1143.translation_literal: ततः (then) / राजानम् (to the king) / आसाद्य (having approached) / दीक्षितम् (initiated) / रघुनन्दन (O delight of the Raghus) / न्यवेदयत् (reported) / यथावृत्तम् (all that had happened) / सुपर्णवचनम् (Suparna's words) / तथा (also) /
ramayan::1143.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1143.essence: Truth reaches power before power can respond.
ramayan::1143.simple_meaning: Anshuman reaches the king and repeats exactly what Garuda said and what had happened.
ramayan::1143.simple_insight: Sometimes the most important act is simply telling the truth clearly.
ramayan::1143.detailed_meaning: Anshuman returns to the king after recovering the horse and speaks without distortion. He tells the whole story, including Garuda's warning. The verse is a bridge: the real consequence comes next, when the king responds to what he has heard.
ramayan::1143.modern_relevance: You finally get the call, walk into the room, and tell the whole story without softening it. The next decision depends on whether you were honest.
ramayan::1143.insight: It emphasizes accurate reporting before action changes anything.

ramayan::1144.verse_sanskrit: तच्छ्रुत्वा घोरसङ्काशं वाक्यमंशुमतो नृप: । । 14124 । । यज्ञं निवर्तयामास यथाकल्पं यथाविधि ।
ramayan::1144.verse_hindi: The king heard (was stunned to hear) the awful words of Anshuman, (yet) he
ramayan::1144.english_translation: Hearing Anshuman's terrifying words, the king ended the sacrifice exactly as prescribed.
ramayan::1144.translation_literal: तत् (that) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / घोरसङ्काशं (terrifying) / वाक्यम् (words) / अंशुमतः (of Anshuman) / नृपः (the king) / यज्ञम् (the sacrifice) / निवर्तयामास (caused to stop) / यथाकल्पम् (according to proper procedure) / यथाविधि (according to rule)
ramayan::1144.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1144.essence: Shock does not excuse disorder; he finishes what must be finished.
ramayan::1144.simple_meaning: The king heard Anshuman's terrible report and brought the sacrifice to a proper close.
ramayan::1144.simple_insight: Even in shock, he does not break the ritual order.
ramayan::1144.detailed_meaning: Sagara has just heard Anshuman's account of Garuda's warning and the fate of the sacrifice. The news is grim, but he does not react wildly. He ends the ritual in the proper way, preserving order even in disappointment.
ramayan::1144.modern_relevance: You get a message that ruins the plan, but you still close the meeting cleanly, file the paperwork, and leave no mess behind.
ramayan::1144.insight: It shifts you from emotional reaction to disciplined completion.

ramayan::1145.verse_sanskrit: स्वपुरं चागमच्छ्रीमानिष्टयज्ञोमहीपति: । । 14125 । । गङ्गायाश्चागमे राजा निश्चयं नाध्यगच्छत ।
ramayan::1145.verse_hindi: The great lord of the earth (king Sagara) after performing the sacrifice reached his capital. (But) He could not devise any means to bring Ganga down to the earth.
ramayan::1145.english_translation: The great king Sagara returned to his capital after completing the sacrifice, but he could not find any way to bring the Ganga down to earth.
ramayan::1145.translation_literal: स्वपुरम् (to his own city) / च (and) / अगमत् (went) / श्रीमान् (the glorious one) / इष्टयज्ञः (one who had completed the sacrifice) / महीपतिः (king) / गङ्गायाः (of Ganga) / च (and) / आगमे (in the coming/downbringing) / राजा (the king) / निश्चयम् (a decision / resolution) / न (not) / अध्यगच्छत (found, obtained)
ramayan::1145.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1145.essence: Completion does not always solve the deeper problem.
ramayan::1145.simple_meaning: Sagara returned home after finishing the sacrifice, but he still had no way to bring the Ganga down to earth.
ramayan::1145.simple_insight: Even after success, some tasks remain unresolved and demand patience beyond achievement.
ramayan::1145.detailed_meaning: Sagara has completed the sacrifice and returned to his capital, but the deeper task remains unfinished. His sons need the Ganga brought down from the higher realm, and he still has no plan. The verse marks a pause before the long delay that follows.
ramayan::1145.modern_relevance: You finish the big presentation, close the laptop, and still know the harder problem remains unsolved. The work is done; the real obstacle is still waiting.
ramayan::1145.insight: It shifts attention from completion to the unresolved consequence that still needs a solution.

ramayan::1146.verse_sanskrit: अकृत्वा निश्चयं राजा कालेन महता महान् । त्रिंशद्वर्षसहस्राणि राज्यं कृत्वा दिवं गत: । । 14126 । ।
ramayan::1146.verse_hindi: The mighty king (Sagara), over a long period of time without being able to devise means (to bring Ganga down to the earth), ruled the kingdom for thirty thousand years and ascended to heaven.
ramayan::1146.english_translation: The mighty king Sagara ruled for thirty thousand years, unable to find a way to bring Ganga down to earth, and then he passed on.
ramayan::1146.translation_literal: अकृत्वा (not having made) / निश्चयं (a decision, a plan) / राजा (the king) / कालेन (with time) / महता (great) / महान् (mighty) / त्रिंशत्-वर्ष-सहस्राणि (thirty thousand years) / राज्यं (the kingdom) / कृत्वा (having ruled) / दिवं (to heaven) / गतः (gone)
ramayan::1146.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1146.essence: Great power still cannot outrun unfinished work.
ramayan::1146.simple_meaning: Sagara spent a vast span of time ruling, but he still could not solve the problem before him. In the end, he died and moved on.
ramayan::1146.simple_insight: Some problems outlast even great power and long effort.
ramayan::1146.detailed_meaning: After the failed sacrifice and Anshuman's grim report, Sagara returns to rule his kingdom. The larger task remains unfinished: the descent of Ganga has not been secured. This verse marks the passing of time and the king's death before the matter is resolved.
ramayan::1146.modern_relevance: You keep circling the same unresolved problem for years — the family issue, the stalled project, the apology you never made. Time passes, but unfinished work still waits.
ramayan::1146.insight: It shifts attention from achievement to mortality: even a mighty ruler cannot finish every task before death.

ramayan::1147.verse_sanskrit: कालधर्मं गते राम सगरे प्रकृतीजना: । राजानं रोचयामासुरंशुमन्तं सुधार्मिकम् । । 1421 । ।
ramayan::1147.verse_hindi: O Rama when Sagara died, the subjects installed the highly virtuous Anshuman as king.
ramayan::1147.english_translation: O Rama, when Sagara died, the people chose the highly righteous Anshuman as king.
ramayan::1147.translation_literal: कालधर्मं (having gone to the law of death) / गते (when gone) / राम (O Rama) / सगरे (Sagara) / प्रकृतीजना: (the people) / राजानं (king) / रोचयामासुः (chose) / अंशुमन्तं (Anshuman) / सुधार्मिकम् (highly righteous)
ramayan::1147.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1147.essence: A righteous kingdom survives by naming the next worthy ruler.
ramayan::1147.simple_meaning: After Sagara died, the people chose his righteous son Anshuman to rule.
ramayan::1147.simple_insight: A kingdom continues by choosing the next right ruler, not by clinging to the past.
ramayan::1147.detailed_meaning: Sagara's long reign has ended, and the story moves on to the next generation. The people of the kingdom do not hesitate; they install Anshuman, known for his righteousness, as king. It is a brief transition in the line of rulers.
ramayan::1147.modern_relevance: A family business closes its founder's chapter, and everyone quietly looks to the son who has earned trust. The handover matters more than the loss.
ramayan::1147.insight: It shifts attention from grief over a ruler's death to the responsibility of orderly succession.

ramayan::1148.verse_sanskrit: स राजा सुमहानासीदंशुमान् रघुनन्दन । तस्य पुत्रो महानासीद्दिलीप इति विश्रुत: । । 1422 । ।
ramayan::1148.verse_hindi: O descendnt of the Raghus that Anshuman became a very great monarch. He had a great son, Dilipa who became famous.
ramayan::1148.english_translation: O descendant of the Raghus, Anshuman became a very great monarch. He had a great son, Dilipa, who became famous.
ramayan::1148.translation_literal: सः (he) / राजा (king) / सुमहान् (very great) / आसीत् (was) / अंशुमान् (Anshuman) / रघुनन्दन (O delight of the Raghu line) / तस्य (his) / पुत्रः (son) / महान् (great) / आसीत् (was) / दिलीपः (Dilipa) / इति (thus) / विश्रुतः (famous)
ramayan::1148.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1148.essence: Greatness is inherited as a burden, then proved anew.
ramayan::1148.simple_meaning: Anshuman was a great king, and his son Dilipa was also renowned for greatness.
ramayan::1148.simple_insight: Greatness can continue through a family, but each generation must still earn its own name.
ramayan::1148.detailed_meaning: After Sagara’s line continues through Anshuman, the text briefly marks the next king in the dynasty: Anshuman is great, and his son Dilipa is equally notable. The verse is setting up the royal lineage before the story moves into Dilipa’s reign and austerities.
ramayan::1148.modern_relevance: A family business passes to the next generation, and the name on the door still carries weight. The son inherits reputation, but he still has to become worthy of it.
ramayan::1148.insight: It shifts attention from one celebrated ruler to the continuity of responsibility across generations.

ramayan::1149.verse_sanskrit: तस्मिन् राज्यं समावेश्य दिलीपे रघुनन्दन । हिमवच्छिखरे पुण्ये तपस्तेपे सुदारुणम् । । 1423 । ।
ramayan::1149.verse_hindi: O Delight of the Raghus having vested the kingdom with Dilipa, Anshuman performed rigid penance on the sacred peak of the Himavat mountain.
ramayan::1149.english_translation: O Delight of the Raghus, having vested the kingdom in Dilipa, Anshuman performed severe penance on the sacred peak of Himavat.
ramayan::1149.translation_literal: तस्मिन् (in that) / राज्यं (kingdom) / समावेश्य (having placed) / दिलीपे (in Dilipa) / रघुनन्दन (O delight of the Raghus) / हिमवच्छिखरे (on the peak of Himavat) / पुण्ये (sacred) / तपः (penance) / तेपे (performed) / सुदारुणम् (very severe)
ramayan::1149.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1149.essence: Power is temporary; discipline is what he carried onward.
ramayan::1149.simple_meaning: After giving the kingdom to Dilipa, Anshuman went to the holy peak of Himavat and undertook severe penance.
ramayan::1149.simple_insight: Real strength is shown by what you keep practicing after power is no longer in your hands.
ramayan::1149.detailed_meaning: Anshuman has already secured the royal line by placing Dilipa on the throne. Instead of clinging to rule, he withdraws to the sacred Himalayan peak and takes up harsh penance. The verse marks a king choosing inner discipline over outward power.
ramayan::1149.modern_relevance: You finish the promotion handover, delete the old files, and walk away from the title. What remains is the habit you built when nobody was watching.
ramayan::1149.insight: It shifts attention from holding status to sustaining discipline after status is gone.

ramayan::1150.verse_sanskrit: द्वात्रिंशच्च सहस्राणि वर्षाणि सुमहायशा: । तपोवनं गतो राम स्वर्गं लेभे तपोधन: । । 1424 । ।
ramayan::1150.verse_hindi: O Rama highly renowned Anshuman, having lived for thirtytwo thousand years in the  tapovana, turned an ascetic and attained heaven (without accomplishing his objective).
ramayan::1150.english_translation: O Rama, the highly renowned Anshuman, having gone to the forest of austerity, lived there for thirty-two thousand years. That ascetic attained heaven.
ramayan::1150.translation_literal: द्वात्रिंशत् (thirty-two) / च (and) / सहस्राणि (thousands) / वर्षाणि (years) / सुमहायशाः (highly renowned) / तपोवनं (to the forest of austerity) / गतः (gone) / राम (O Rama) / स्वर्गं (heaven) / लेभे (attained) / तपोधनः (the wealth of austerity; ascetic)
ramayan::1150.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1150.essence: Long discipline can end in grace, not in the result you chased.
ramayan::1150.simple_meaning: Anshuman spent thirty-two thousand years in a place of austerity and eventually attained a higher realm.
ramayan::1150.simple_insight: Great effort can still end without the result you wanted.
ramayan::1150.detailed_meaning: Anshuman has already handed the kingdom to Dilipa and gone into severe austerity on a sacred mountain. This verse closes his arc by saying that even after immense discipline and long years, he attained a higher realm without completing his original aim.
ramayan::1150.modern_relevance: You can pour years into a project, a career, or a promise and still not reach the outcome you hoped for. The effort may be real even when the result is not.
ramayan::1150.insight: It shifts attention from achievement to the moral weight of sustained practice.

ramayan::1151.verse_sanskrit: दिलीपस्तु महातेजाश्श्रुत्वा पैतामहं वधम् । दु:खोपहतया बुद्ध्या निश्चयं नाध्यगच्छत । । 1425 । ।
ramayan::1151.verse_hindi: When exceedingly brilliant Dilipa heard about the death of his grandfathers, he was overtaken by grief but could not arrive at any conclusion with his intellect (regarding means of bringing down the sacred river).
ramayan::1151.english_translation: When exceedingly brilliant Dilipa heard about the death of his grandfathers, he was overtaken by grief but could not arrive at any conclusion with his intellect regarding how to bring down the sacred river.
ramayan::1151.translation_literal: दिलीपः (Dilipa) / तु (but) / महातेजाः (very brilliant) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / पैतामहम् (of the grandfathers) / वधम् (death) / दुःखोपहतया (struck by grief) / बुद्ध्या (with intellect) / निश्चयम् (decision) / न अधिगच्छत (did not arrive at)
ramayan::1151.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1151.essence: Grief can freeze thought, but it can also begin the search.
ramayan::1151.simple_meaning: Dilipa is devastated by news of his ancestors' death and cannot decide how to restore their rites. His mind is blocked by sorrow, so he enters a search for a solution.
ramayan::1151.simple_insight: Grief does not erase the need to think; it can become the start of a deeper search.
ramayan::1151.detailed_meaning: Dilipa hears that his ancestors died without the sacred river's descent, and the loss hits him hard. He is not lazy or indifferent; he is so shaken that his mind cannot settle on a solution. This verse opens the problem that will drive his quest.
ramayan::1151.modern_relevance: You get terrible news and sit there staring at your phone, unable to think straight. The ache is real, but so is the need to ask the next question.
ramayan::1151.insight: It shifts the mind from emotional collapse to purposeful questioning.

ramayan::1152.verse_sanskrit: कथं गङ्गावतरणं कथं तेषां जलक्रिया । तारयेयं कथं चैतानिति चिन्तापरोऽभवत् । । 1426 । ।
ramayan::1152.verse_hindi: How to bring about the descent of Ganga? How to perform funeral rites of the ancestors with Ganga water? How to liberate them Thus Dilipa was constantly engaged in such thoughts.
ramayan::1152.english_translation: How can I bring Ganga down? How can I perform the funeral rites with her water? How can I free my ancestors? Dilipa kept thinking like this.
ramayan::1152.translation_literal: कथम् (how) / गङ्गावतरणम् (the descent of Ganga) / कथम् (how) / तेषाम् (of those) / जलक्रिया (water rites) / तारयेयम् (I may free) / कथम् (how) / चैतान् (these) / इति (thus) / चिन्तापरः (absorbed in thought) / अभवत् (became)
ramayan::1152.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1152.essence: Clear seeing begins with refusing to look away from the hard question.
ramayan::1152.simple_meaning: Dilipa cannot stop thinking about how to bring Ganga down, perform the rites, and free his ancestors.
ramayan::1152.simple_insight: Real progress begins when you stay with the question instead of rushing past it.
ramayan::1152.detailed_meaning: Dilipa has heard the terrible truth about his ancestors and feels no clear way forward. He sits with the problem of Ganga's descent, the rites, and their release. This verse shows the mind turning the question over until a true answer can emerge.
ramayan::1152.modern_relevance: You stare at a hospital bill, a family problem, or a decision that no shortcut can fix. The mind circles the same question because the question matters. That steady looking is where the next step begins.
ramayan::1152.insight: It teaches you to keep investigating until the real solution reveals itself.

ramayan::1153.verse_sanskrit: तस्य चिन्तयतो नित्यं धर्मेण विदितात्मन: । पुत्रो भगीरथो नाम जज्ञे परमधार्मिक: । । 1427 । ।
ramayan::1153.verse_hindi: As Dilipa known for his knowledge of the soul constantly reflected righteously on (this matter of Ganga), a highly virtuous son named Bhagiratha was born to him.
ramayan::1153.english_translation: As Dilipa, righteous and self-aware, kept reflecting on the matter, a highly virtuous son named Bhagiratha was born to him.
ramayan::1153.translation_literal: तस्य (of him) / चिन्तयतो (while reflecting) / नित्यं (constantly) / धर्मेण (righteously) / विदितात्मनः (of one who knows the self) / पुत्रः (son) / भगीरथः (Bhagiratha) / नाम (by name) / जज्ञे (was born) / परमधार्मिकः (highly virtuous)
ramayan::1153.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1153.essence: Faithful concern can call forth the help needed to complete a hard duty.
ramayan::1153.simple_meaning: Dilipa kept thinking about how to fulfill his duty, and Bhagiratha was born to him as a virtuous son.
ramayan::1153.simple_insight: Steady concern for what is right can shape the future in ways you cannot yet see.
ramayan::1153.detailed_meaning: Dilipa has been grieving the loss of his ancestors and searching for a way to honour them through Ganga's descent and proper rites. While he keeps turning that duty over in his mind, Bhagiratha is born — the son who will eventually carry that burden forward.
ramayan::1153.modern_relevance: You keep worrying over a responsibility you cannot solve tonight. Then, slowly, the right person, idea, or opening appears — not by accident, but because you stayed faithful to the task.
ramayan::1153.insight: It shifts attention from immediate frustration to patient moral continuity.

ramayan::1154.verse_sanskrit: दिलीपस्तु महातेजा यज्ञैर्बहुभिरिष्टवान् । त्रिंशद्वर्षसहस्राणि राजा राज्यमकारयत् । । 1428 । ।
ramayan::1154.verse_hindi: Most brilliant king Dilipa ruled the kingdom for thirty thousand years performing many sacrifices.
ramayan::1154.english_translation: Most brilliant king Dilipa ruled the kingdom for thirty thousand years, performing many sacrifices.
ramayan::1154.translation_literal: दिलीपः (Dilipa) / तु (indeed) / महातेजाः (very radiant, brilliant) / यज्ञैः (with sacrifices) / बहुभिः (many) / इष्टवान् (he worshipped, performed) / त्रिंशत्-वर्ष-सहस्राणि (thirty thousand years) / राजा (the king) / राज्यम् (the kingdom) / अकारयत् (ruled, caused to be governed)
ramayan::1154.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1154.essence: Power becomes meaningful only when held in sustained service.
ramayan::1154.simple_meaning: King Dilipa ruled for thirty thousand years and performed many sacrifices.
ramayan::1154.simple_insight: Greatness can be measured by steadiness, not just by moments of brilliance.
ramayan::1154.detailed_meaning: The story pauses on Dilipa, Rama's ancestor, to show the scale of his reign: long rule, ritual duty, and royal splendour. He is praised here as part of the larger chain of ancestors whose unfinished concern for the Ganga will matter next.
ramayan::1154.modern_relevance: A leader who stays in office for years can still be remembered for what he kept offering, not just what he controlled. Long tenure means little without sustained responsibility.
ramayan::1154.insight: It frames legacy as endurance in duty, not short bursts of achievement.

ramayan::1155.verse_sanskrit: अगत्वा निश्चयं राजा तेषामुद्धरणं प्रति । व्याधिना नरशार्दूल कालधर्ममुपेयिवान् । । 1429 । ।
ramayan::1155.verse_hindi: O Tiger among men king Dilipa was unable to arrive at a conclusion regarding the
ramayan::1155.english_translation: O tiger among men, King Dilipa died from illness before reaching a decision about their deliverance.
ramayan::1155.translation_literal: अगत्वा (not having reached) / निश्चयं (a decision) / राजा (the king) / तेषाम् (of them) / उद्धरणं (deliverance, rescue) / प्रति (regarding) / व्याधिना (by illness) / नरशार्दूल (tiger among men) / कालधर्मम् (the law of time, death) / उपेयिवान् (having gone to, died)
ramayan::1155.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1155.essence: He died before finishing what he had set in motion.
ramayan::1155.simple_meaning: Dilipa died before he could decide how to free them.
ramayan::1155.simple_insight: Some tasks outlive the person who meant to finish them.
ramayan::1155.detailed_meaning: Dilipa has spent years in righteous austerity, and a son, Bhagiratha, has already been born. But the problem of bringing the sacred river down to the world is still unresolved. Before the king can settle the plan, illness takes him.
ramayan::1155.modern_relevance: You keep circling a decision for months, telling yourself there will be time. Then life interrupts, and the unfinished thing passes to someone else.
ramayan::1155.insight: It shows how even noble intentions can remain incomplete, forcing the next generation to carry the work forward.

ramayan::1156.verse_sanskrit: इन्द्रलोकं गतो राजा स्वार्जितेनैव कर्मणा । राज्ये भगीरथं पुत्रमभिषिच्य नरर्षभ: । । 14210 । ।
ramayan::1156.verse_hindi: The king (Dilipa) performed the coronation of his son Bhagiratha and reached the region of Indra as a reward for virtuous acts done by him.
ramayan::1156.english_translation: The king crowned his son Bhagiratha and, by the merit of his own deeds, reached Indra's realm.
ramayan::1156.translation_literal: इन्द्रलोकं (to Indra's realm) / गतः (gone) / राजा (the king) / स्वार्जितेनैव (by his own earned) / कर्मणा (by deed) / राज्ये (in the kingdom) / भगीरथं (Bhagiratha) / पुत्रम् (son) / अभिषिच्य (having crowned) / नरर्षभः (bull among men)
ramayan::1156.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1156.essence: Good deeds outlive the king who performs them.
ramayan::1156.simple_meaning: Dilipa crowned Bhagiratha as king and, because of his own virtuous actions, attained a higher realm after death.
ramayan::1156.simple_insight: What you build with integrity can outlast your own life.
ramayan::1156.detailed_meaning: Dilipa's story closes with a final honor: he places Bhagiratha on the throne, then passes on after a life of merit. The verse completes the thought begun in the previous line, showing reward, succession, and the end of a righteous reign.
ramayan::1156.modern_relevance: You hand over your work to the next person and leave the room for the last time. What remains after you are gone is shaped by what you did when no one was watching.
ramayan::1156.insight: It shifts attention from personal gain to the lasting fruit of righteous action.

ramayan::1157.verse_sanskrit: भगीरथस्तु राजर्षिर्धार्मिको रघुनन्दन । अनपत्यो महातेजा: प्रजाकामस्स चाप्रज: । । 14211 । ।
ramayan::1157.verse_hindi: O delight of the Raghus righteous Bhagiratha who was highly lustrous rajarshi was without sons. He was desirous of progeny but did not beget children.
ramayan::1157.english_translation: Bhagiratha, the righteous royal sage and delight of the Raghus, was highly radiant, yet he had no children. He desired offspring but remained childless.
ramayan::1157.translation_literal: भगीरथः (Bhagiratha) / तु (indeed) / राजर्षिः (royal sage) / धार्मिकः (righteous) / रघुनन्दन (delight of the Raghu line) / अनपत्यः (without offspring) / महातेजाः (greatly radiant) / प्रजाकामः (desiring progeny) / सः (he) / च (and) / अप्रजाः (childless)
ramayan::1157.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1157.essence: Radiance does not cancel the pain of being childless.
ramayan::1157.simple_meaning: Bhagiratha was a noble, righteous king, but he had no children and longed for them.
ramayan::1157.simple_insight: Even the most accomplished life can still carry one deep ache.
ramayan::1157.detailed_meaning: After Dilipa's reign is passed on, the poem turns to Bhagiratha. He is praised as righteous, radiant, and worthy of the Raghu line, but the verse pauses on one sorrow: he remains childless. That lack prepares the vow and austerity that follow.
ramayan::1157.modern_relevance: You can have status, virtue, and strength, and still feel the sting of what is missing. The ache may become the very thing that reshapes your life.
ramayan::1157.insight: It shifts attention from achievement to the quiet pressure of unfulfilled longing.

ramayan::1158.verse_sanskrit: मन्त्रिष्वाधाय तद्राज्यं गङ्गावतरणे रत: । स तपो दीर्घमातिष्ठद्गोकर्णे रघुनन्दन । । 14212 । । ऊर्ध्वबाहु: पञ्चतपा मासाहारो जितेन्द्रिय: ।
ramayan::1158.verse_hindi: O son of the Raghus (Rama), Bhagiratha, with a determination to bring down Ganga
ramayan::1158.english_translation: Bhagiratha entrusted the kingdom to his ministers and, devoted to bringing down the Ganga, performed severe austerities at Gokarna. With arms raised, living on a single meal a month, and mastering his senses, he continued his long penance.
ramayan::1158.translation_literal: मन्त्रिषु (to the ministers) / आधाय (having placed) / तत् (that) / राज्यम् (kingdom) / गङ्गावतरणे (in bringing down the Ganga) / रत: (devoted) / सः (he) / तपः (austerity) / दीर्घम् (long) / आस्थित् (undertook) / गोकर्णे (at Gokarna) / रघुनन्दन (O delight of the Raghus) / ऊर्ध्वबाहु: (with raised arms) / पञ्चतपा (practising five-fire austerity) / मासाहारो (eating once a month) / जितेन्द्रिय: (one who has conquered the senses)
ramayan::1158.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1158.essence: A great aim demands a life reorganized around it.
ramayan::1158.simple_meaning: Bhagiratha handed the kingdom to his ministers and devoted himself to severe austerity until he could bring the Ganga down to earth.
ramayan::1158.simple_insight: Real commitment changes your habits, not just your intentions.
ramayan::1158.detailed_meaning: Bhagiratha has no sons and no easy answer. He leaves the kingdom in his ministers' care and goes to Gokarna, standing with raised arms in harsh austerity, eating sparingly and mastering his senses, because he is determined to bring the Ganga down for his ancestors.
ramayan::1158.modern_relevance: You stop checking your phone, change your routine, and build your days around one hard goal. That is what real resolve looks like when you want something enough.
ramayan::1158.insight: It shifts effort from wishing to disciplined, sustained practice.

ramayan::1159.verse_sanskrit: तस्य वर्षसहस्राणि घोरे तपसि तिष्ठत: । । 14213 । । अतीतानि महाबाहो तस्य राज्ञो महात्मन: । सुप्रीतो भगवान् ब्रह्मा प्रजानां पतिरीश्वर: । । 14214 । ।
ramayan::1159.verse_hindi: O mightyarmed, (Rama) Bhagiratha continued in that state for a thousand years amidst rigid austerities. Lord of  all creatures, Brahma was highly pleased with that illustrious king.
ramayan::1159.english_translation: Bhagiratha, the mighty king, remained in that severe austerity for a thousand years. Brahma, lord of all creatures, was greatly pleased with that noble king.
ramayan::1159.translation_literal: तस्य (his) / वर्षसहस्राणि (thousand years) / घोरे (severe, terrible) / तपसि (in austerity) / तिष्ठत: (remaining) / अतीतानि (passed) / महाबाहो (mighty-armed one) / तस्य (of that) / राज्ञो (king) / महात्मन: (of the great-souled one) / सुप्रीतः (greatly pleased) / भगवान् (the venerable one) / ब्रह्मा (Brahma) / प्रजानां (of creatures) / पतिरीश्वर: (lord)
ramayan::1159.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1159.essence: Endurance becomes power when it lasts long enough to be seen.
ramayan::1159.simple_meaning: Bhagiratha kept up severe austerity for a thousand years, and Brahma was pleased by his steadfastness.
ramayan::1159.simple_insight: Long devotion to a hard practice can open doors that quick effort never will.
ramayan::1159.detailed_meaning: Bhagiratha has handed over his kingdom and begun a punishing vow to bring the Ganga down to earth. Years pass in the wilderness, and his endurance finally reaches Brahma, who notices the depth of his resolve.
ramayan::1159.modern_relevance: You keep showing up at dawn to practice when nobody is watching, and the results still feel far away. Bhagiratha’s story says that steady endurance is not wasted.
ramayan::1159.insight: It shifts attention from quick results to sustained practice that reshapes reality over time.

ramayan::1160.verse_hindi: Thereafter, the Grandsire arrived with the gods and spoke to the noble Bhagiratha engaged in austerities.
ramayan::1160.english_translation: Thereafter, the Grandsire arrived with the gods and spoke to the noble Bhagiratha engaged in austerities.
ramayan::1160.translation_literal: ततस् (thereafter) / सुरगणैः (with the hosts of gods) / सार्धम् (together) / उपागम्य (having approached) / पितामहः (the Grandsire) / भगीरथम् (to Bhagiratha) / महात्मानम् (the noble one) / तप्यमानम् (while performing austerities) / अथ (then) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::1160.speaker: Brahma
ramayan::1160.essence: Endurance finally meets a voice that can answer it.
ramayan::1160.simple_meaning: Brahma comes with the gods to Bhagiratha, who is still deep in austerity, and speaks to him.
ramayan::1160.simple_insight: Patient effort can draw even distant help to your side.
ramayan::1160.detailed_meaning: Bhagiratha has endured severe austerity for years to bring the Ganga down to earth. At last, Brahma arrives with the gods and addresses him directly. This verse is the turning point just before the boon is granted.
ramayan::1160.modern_relevance: You keep showing up for the same hard thing, even when nothing seems to move. Then, one day, the answer arrives without warning.
ramayan::1160.insight: It marks the moment persistence begins to yield a response from beyond your own effort.

ramayan::1161.verse_sanskrit: भगीरथ महाभाग प्रीतस्तेऽहं जनेश्वर । तपसा च सुतप्तेन वरं वरय सुव्रत । । 14216 । ।
ramayan::1161.verse_hindi: O distinguished one O mighty monarch O Bhagiratha of excellent vows I am pleased with your  welldisciplined austerities. Ask for a boon.
ramayan::1161.english_translation: O distinguished one, O mighty monarch Bhagiratha, I am pleased with your well-disciplined austerities. Ask for a boon.
ramayan::1161.translation_literal: भगीरथ (Bhagiratha) / महाभाग (distinguished one) / प्रीतः (pleased) / ते (with you) / अहम् (I) / जनेश्वर (O lord of people) / तपसा (by austerity) / च (and) / सुतप्तेन (well-heat, well-disciplined) / वरम् (boon) / वरय (ask) / सुव्रत (O one of good vows)
ramayan::1161.speaker: Brahma
ramayan::1161.essence: Long discipline can turn effort into a granted boon.
ramayan::1161.simple_meaning: Bhagiratha's long austerity has been noticed and rewarded. Brahma is pleased and invites him to ask for a boon.
ramayan::1161.simple_insight: Quiet persistence can open doors you cannot force open.
ramayan::1161.detailed_meaning: After a thousand years of severe austerity, Bhagiratha stands before Brahma with the gods gathered around. The long wait has ended, not because he pushed harder, but because his discipline has ripened into a request being granted.
ramayan::1161.modern_relevance: You kept showing up when no one could measure progress — the training, the drafts, the apology, the long wait. Then one day the door opens because you did not quit.
ramayan::1161.insight: It teaches you that sustained discipline can prepare you to receive what force cannot obtain.

ramayan::1162.verse_sanskrit: तमुवाच महातेजा: सर्वलोकपितामहम् । भगीरथो महाभाग: कृताञ्जलिरुपस्थित: । । 14217 । ।
ramayan::1162.verse_hindi: Brilliant, glorious Bhagiratha, stood before the Grandsire of all the worlds with folded palms and spoke:
ramayan::1162.english_translation: Brilliant, glorious Bhagiratha stood before the Grandsire of all the worlds with folded palms and spoke.
ramayan::1162.translation_literal: तम् (to him) / उवाच (spoke) / महातेजाः (very radiant) / सर्वलोकपितामहम् (the Grandsire of all the worlds) / भगीरथः (Bhagiratha) / महाभागः (highly fortunate) / कृताञ्जलिः (with folded palms) / उपस्थितः (standing before)
ramayan::1162.speaker: Bhagiratha
ramayan::1162.essence: The request matters, but the reverent approach matters first.
ramayan::1162.simple_meaning: Bhagiratha stands respectfully before Brahma and begins to speak.
ramayan::1162.simple_insight: A humble request begins with reverence.
ramayan::1162.detailed_meaning: Bhagiratha has completed severe austerities, and Brahma has come with the gods to grant him audience. Standing with folded hands before the Grandsire, he prepares to ask for the boon that will free his ancestors.
ramayan::1162.modern_relevance: You finally get the meeting, and your first move is not demand but respect. The moment matters because what follows depends on how you enter it.
ramayan::1162.insight: It shows that even power begins with humility and the right posture.

ramayan::1163.verse_sanskrit: यदि मे भगवन् प्रीतो यद्यस्ति तपस: फलम् । सगरस्यात्मजास्सर्वे मत्तस्सलिलमाप्नुयु: । । 14218 । ।
ramayan::1163.verse_hindi: O Lord if you are pleased with my austerities and if they are worthy of a reward, grant me the boon whereby all the sons of Sagara will receive from me funeral rites with the waters (of Ganga).
ramayan::1163.english_translation: O Lord, if you are pleased with my austerities and if they have borne fruit, grant me this boon: let all the sons of Sagara receive funeral rites from me through the waters of the Ganga.
ramayan::1163.translation_literal: यदि (if) / मे (to me) / भगवन् (O Lord) / प्रीतः (pleased) / यद्यस्ति (if there is) / तपसः (of austerity) / फलम् (fruit) / सगरस्य (of Sagara) / आत्मजाः (sons) / सर्वे (all) / मत्तः (from me) / सलिलम् (water) / आप्नुयुः (may receive)
ramayan::1163.speaker: Bhagiratha
ramayan::1163.essence: True asking turns personal merit into relief for others.
ramayan::1163.simple_meaning: Bhagiratha asks for a blessing: if his austerity has pleased the divine, let its fruit help his ancestors receive funeral rites through Ganga's waters.
ramayan::1163.simple_insight: Real devotion wants its reward to heal someone else.
ramayan::1163.detailed_meaning: Bhagiratha stands before Brahma after severe austerity. He does not ask for comfort or power. He asks for one impossible mercy: that Ganga's waters may reach the ashes of Sagara's sons and free his family line from sorrow.
ramayan::1163.modern_relevance: You finally get the chance to ask for something after years of effort. Instead of asking for yourself, you ask for the person your work was really meant to help.
ramayan::1163.insight: It shifts desire from personal gain to redemptive service.

ramayan::1164.verse_sanskrit: गङ्गायास्सलिलक्लिन्ने भस्मन्येषां महात्मनाम् । स्वर्गं गच्छेयुरत्यन्तं सर्वे मे प्रपितामहा: । । 14219 । ।
ramayan::1164.verse_hindi: The ashes of these eminent uncles of my grandfather, immersed by the waters of Ganga may ultimately go to heaven.
ramayan::1164.english_translation: May the ashes of my great-grandfathers, soaked by the waters of the Ganga, finally attain the higher realm.
ramayan::1164.translation_literal: गङ्गायाः (of the Ganga) / सलिल (water) / क्लिन्ने (soaked) / भस्मनि (in the ashes) / एषाम् (of these) / महात्मनाम् (great-souled) / स्वर्गम् (higher realm) / गच्छेयुः (may go) / अत्यन्तम् (finally) / सर्वे (all) / मे (my) / प्रपितामहाः (great-grandfathers)
ramayan::1164.speaker: Bhagiratha
ramayan::1164.essence: Even the dead can be helped by a living act of devotion.
ramayan::1164.simple_meaning: Bhagiratha asks that the ashes of his ancestors, touched by the Ganga, may reach the higher realm at last.
ramayan::1164.simple_insight: Love for the dead can become a sacred act of repair.
ramayan::1164.detailed_meaning: Bhagiratha stands before Brahma after long austerity, pleading not for himself but for his ancestors. He asks that the ashes of his forefathers be washed by Ganga so their suffering may end. This verse is one link in that larger request.
ramayan::1164.modern_relevance: You stand at a river with a handful of ashes, or at a memorial with a name you still cannot let go. Some acts are not about moving on — they are about honoring what came before you.
ramayan::1164.insight: It turns grief into responsibility: you do something for those who can no longer do it themselves.

ramayan::1165.verse_sanskrit: देया च सन्ततिर्देव नावसीदेत्कुलं च न: । इक्ष्वाकूणां कुले देव एष मेऽस्तु वर:पर: । । 14220 । ।
ramayan::1165.verse_hindi: O Lord let the progeny be perpuated in our race of the Ikshvakus. Let not that dynasty be terminated with me. This is another boon I seek.
ramayan::1165.english_translation: O Lord, let our lineage continue. Let the Ikshvaku dynasty not end with me. This is another boon I seek.
ramayan::1165.translation_literal: देया (may be given) / च (and) / सन्ततिः (progeny, lineage) / देव (O divine one) / नावसीदेत् (may not perish, may not be cut off) / कुलम् (family line, dynasty) / च (and) / नः (our) / इक्ष्वाकूणाम् (of the Ikshvakus) / कुले (in the line) / देव (O divine one) / एषः (this) / मे (of me) / अस्तु (may it be) / वरः (boon) / परः (another, supreme)
ramayan::1165.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1165.essence: A life becomes larger when it asks to continue beyond itself.
ramayan::1165.simple_meaning: The king asks that his family line continue and not die out with him.
ramayan::1165.simple_insight: Some prayers are really about refusing to let your life be the last chapter.
ramayan::1165.detailed_meaning: King Sagara's descendant stands before Brahma, asking for one more boon. After the ashes of his ancestors are to be purified, he asks for something larger: that the Ikshvaku line itself not end with him.
ramayan::1165.modern_relevance: You look at a family name, a business, or a tradition and wonder whether it will survive your generation. This verse carries that ache: not just to succeed, but to pass something on intact.
ramayan::1165.insight: It shifts attention from personal gain to the burden of continuity and legacy.

ramayan::1166.verse_sanskrit: उक्तवाक्यं तु राजानं सर्वलोकपितामह: । प्रत्युवाच शुभां वाणीं मधुरां मधुराक्षराम् । । 14221 । ।
ramayan::1166.verse_hindi: To this the Grandsire of all the worlds replied with a sweet voice full of good wishes and sweet words.
ramayan::1166.english_translation: To this the Grandsire of all the worlds replied with a sweet voice full of good wishes and sweet words.
ramayan::1166.translation_literal: उक्तवाक्यम् (to the spoken words) / तु (then) / राजानम् (to the king) / सर्वलोकपितामहः (the Grandsire of all the worlds) / प्रत्युवाच (replied) / शुभाम् (auspicious) / वाणीम् (speech) / मधुराम् (sweet) / मधुराक्षराम् (with sweet syllables)
ramayan::1166.speaker: Brahma
ramayan::1166.essence: Grace answers earnest prayer with kindness.
ramayan::1166.simple_meaning: Brahma answers Bhagiratha kindly and favorably, responding to his request with gracious words.
ramayan::1166.simple_insight: A sincere request can meet a gracious answer.
ramayan::1166.detailed_meaning: Bhagiratha has just begged for the release of his ancestors. The Grandsire of all worlds answers him gently, and that reply opens the way for the river to come down and lift the family line.
ramayan::1166.modern_relevance: You finally ask for help after carrying the burden alone. The answer you hoped for may come in a voice softer than your fear expected.
ramayan::1166.insight: It shifts the moment from pleading to blessing, showing that the request has been heard.

ramayan::1167.verse_sanskrit: मनोरथो महानेष भगीरथ महारथ । एवं भवतु भद्रं ते इक्ष्वाकुकुलवर्धन । । 14222 । ।
ramayan::1167.verse_hindi: O Great charioteer Bhagiratha, your desire is great. O Perpetuator of dynasty of the
ramayan::1167.english_translation: O great charioteer Bhagiratha, your desire is vast. May it come to pass, and may you be well, O enhancer of the Ikshvaku line.
ramayan::1167.translation_literal: मनोरथः (desire / wish) / महान् (great) / एषः (this) / भगीरथ (Bhagiratha) / महारथ (great charioteer) । एवं (thus) / भवतु (may it be) / भद्रम् (well-being / auspicious) / ते (to you) / इक्ष्वाकु-कुल-वर्धन (enhancer of the Ikshvaku lineage) ।
ramayan::1167.speaker: Brahma
ramayan::1167.essence: A great desire becomes worthy when it serves a whole lineage.
ramayan::1167.simple_meaning: Bhagiratha's wish is honoured as noble and vast. The blessing is that his great effort for his family line should succeed.
ramayan::1167.simple_insight: Big aims deserve blessing when they serve something larger than yourself.
ramayan::1167.detailed_meaning: Bhagiratha has asked Brahma for a boon to bring the Ganga down and free his ancestors. Brahma answers with approval, recognising the scale of Bhagiratha's resolve and blessing the wish as worthy of the Ikshvaku line.
ramayan::1167.modern_relevance: You keep pushing for something that helps more than just you — a family, a team, a future. The work feels enormous because it is.
ramayan::1167.insight: It frames ambitious effort as noble when it serves a larger duty beyond personal gain.

ramayan::1168.verse_sanskrit: इयं हैमवती गङ्गा ज्येष्ठा हिमवतस्सुता । तां वै धारयितुं शक्तो हरस्तत्र नियुज्यताम् । । 14223 । ।
ramayan::1168.verse_hindi: This Hymavati (Ganga) is Himavats eldest daughter and only lord Siva is capable to hold (the force of her descent to earth). Therefore let Siva be entreated.
ramayan::1168.english_translation: This is Ganga, daughter of Himavat and the eldest among his daughters. Only Shiva can bear her force, so let Shiva be approached.
ramayan::1168.translation_literal: इयम् (this) / हैमवती (daughter of Himavat) / गङ्गा (Ganga) / ज्येष्ठा (eldest) / हिमवत्-सुता (daughter of Himavat) । / ताम् (her) / वै (indeed) / धारयितुम् (to hold) / शक्तः (able) / हरः (Shiva) / तत्र (there) / नियुज्यताम् (let be requested / let be entreated) ।
ramayan::1168.speaker: Brahma
ramayan::1168.essence: Great gifts need a strength equal to their force.
ramayan::1168.simple_meaning: Ganga is Himavat's eldest daughter, and her descent is so powerful that only Shiva can contain it. The answer is to ask Shiva to receive her.
ramayan::1168.simple_insight: Some forces are too great to meet casually; they need the right vessel.
ramayan::1168.detailed_meaning: Bhagiratha has asked for Ganga to descend and redeem his ancestors. Brahma agrees, but warns that the river's force will shatter the earth. He identifies Shiva as the only one strong enough to bear her fall, so the next step is to invoke him.
ramayan::1168.modern_relevance: You finally get the chance you've prayed for, but it is bigger than your current setup. Before you rush ahead, you need the right support to hold it.
ramayan::1168.insight: It shifts the mind from wanting the goal to preparing the container that can safely receive it.

ramayan::1169.verse_sanskrit: गङ्गाया: पतनं राजन् पृथिवी न सहिष्यति । तां वै धारयितुं वीर नान्यं पश्यामि शूलिन: । । 14224 । ।
ramayan::1169.verse_hindi: O King Gangas descent cannot be sustained by earth. O Hero I do not see any other person to hold her than the wielder of the trident (Siva).
ramayan::1169.english_translation: O King, the earth cannot bear Ganga's descent. O hero, I see no one else able to hold her except the wielder of the trident.
ramayan::1169.translation_literal: गङ्गाया: (of Ganga) / पतनं (descent/fall) / राजन् (O king) / पृथिवी (earth) / न (not) / सहिष्यति (will bear/endure) / तां (her) / वै (indeed) / धारयितुं (to hold) / वीर (O hero) / नान्यं (no other) / पश्यामि (I see) / शूलिन: (of the trident-bearer)
ramayan::1169.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1169.essence: Only Shiva can contain what the earth cannot bear.
ramayan::1169.simple_meaning: The earth cannot withstand Ganga's full descent, so only Shiva can receive her force.
ramayan::1169.simple_insight: Some burdens are too vast for ordinary support; they need a greater holder.
ramayan::1169.detailed_meaning: The Creator is speaking to King Bhagiratha about bringing Ganga down to earth. He warns that the earth itself cannot bear her force, and that only Shiva, the trident-bearing one, can hold her descent safely.
ramayan::1169.modern_relevance: You are trying to carry a flood of emotion, responsibility, or grief alone. Some things cannot be handled by sheer will; they need a stronger vessel than you are right now.
ramayan::1169.insight: It shifts the mind from forcing a problem to finding the right support for it.

ramayan::1170.verse_sanskrit: तमेवमुक्त्वा राजानं गङ्गां चाभाष्य लोककृत् । जगाम त्रिदिवं देवस्सहदेवैर्मरुद्गणै: । । 14225 । ।
ramayan::1170.verse_hindi: The Creator of the worlds having thus addressed the king and conversing with Ganga went towards heaven along with devatas and maruts.
ramayan::1170.english_translation: The Creator of the worlds having thus addressed the king and conversing with Ganga went towards heaven along with the gods and the Maruts.
ramayan::1170.translation_literal: तमेवम् (thus) / उक्त्वा (having spoken) / राजानम् (to the king) / गङ्गाम् (to Ganga) / च (and) / अभाष्य (having addressed) / लोककृत् (the creator of the worlds) / जगाम (went) / त्रिदिवम् (to heaven) / देवः (the god) / सह (along with) / देवैः (the gods) / मरुद्गणैः (with the Maruts)
ramayan::1170.speaker: Brahma
ramayan::1170.essence: Guidance ends here; the burden now falls on others.
ramayan::1170.simple_meaning: Brahma speaks to the king and Ganga, then returns to heaven with the gods and Maruts.
ramayan::1170.simple_insight: Some moments are only a bridge: the real turning point comes after the speaker leaves.
ramayan::1170.detailed_meaning: Brahma has just explained why Ganga’s descent cannot be borne by the earth and why Shiva must receive her force. After giving that instruction to King Bhagiratha and speaking with Ganga, he departs with the gods, leaving the next burden to be carried by Shiva and the king.
ramayan::1170.modern_relevance: A meeting ends, the expert leaves, and you are still standing with the decision. The explanation is over; now the work begins.
ramayan::1170.insight: It marks the close of divine counsel and the start of human and cosmic action.

ramayan::1171.verse_sanskrit: देवदेवे गते तस्मिन् सोऽङ्गुष्ठाग्रनिपीडिताम् । कृत्वा वसुमतीं राम संवत्सरमुपासत । । 1431 । ।
ramayan::1171.verse_hindi: O Rama when that God of the gods (Brahma) departed, Bhagiratha, pressing the earth with the tip of his big toe (standing supported by the big toe) penanced (meditated upon Siva) for one year.
ramayan::1171.english_translation: When that god of gods departed, Bhagiratha, pressing the earth with the tip of his big toe, performed austerity for one year.
ramayan::1171.translation_literal: देवदेवे (the god of gods) / गते (having departed) / तस्मिन् (when he) / सः (he) / अङ्गुष्ठ-अग्र-निपीडिताम् (pressed by the tip of the big toe) / कृत्वा (having made) / वसुमतीम् (the earth) / राम (O Rama) / संवत्सरम् (for a year) / उपासत (performed austerity; worshipped)
ramayan::1171.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1171.essence: He kept the strain alive for a year because the task was not finished.
ramayan::1171.simple_meaning: After Brahma left, Bhagiratha stood in a painful pose and kept up his austerity for a full year.
ramayan::1171.simple_insight: Real resolve is shown by staying with the hard thing long after the first burst of effort fades.
ramayan::1171.detailed_meaning: Brahma has just told Bhagiratha that only Shiva can hold the descending Ganga. After the creator departs, Bhagiratha does not relax or look for an easier way. He keeps one toe pressing into the earth and continues his austerity for a full year.
ramayan::1171.modern_relevance: You finally get the answer you needed, but the real work is still ahead. The waiting, the discipline, the uncomfortable stretch of staying with it — that is where Bhagiratha lives.
ramayan::1171.insight: It shifts you from seeking quick relief to sustaining effort until the larger task is complete.

ramayan::1172.verse_sanskrit: अथ संवत्सरे पूर्णे सर्वलोकनमस्कृत: । उमापति: पशुपती राजानमिदमब्रवीत् । । 1432 । ।
ramayan::1172.verse_hindi: After one full year was completed, Iswara who is worshipped by all in all the worlds said to king Bhagiratha:
ramayan::1172.english_translation: After one full year was completed, Iswara who is worshipped by all in all the worlds said to king Bhagiratha:
ramayan::1172.translation_literal: अथ (then) / संवत्सरे (year) / पूर्णे (completed) / सर्वलोकनमस्कृतः (worshipped by all worlds) / उमापतिः (Lord of Uma) / पशुपतिः (Lord of beings) / राजानम् (to the king) / इदम् (this) / अब्रवीत् (said)
ramayan::1172.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1172.essence: Endurance has its own moment when the answer finally comes.
ramayan::1172.simple_meaning: After Bhagiratha's year of endurance, Shiva finally speaks to him.
ramayan::1172.simple_insight: Patience can ripen into a response you cannot force.
ramayan::1172.detailed_meaning: Bhagiratha has stood in severe penance for a full year, pressing on until the world itself seems to notice. At last, Shiva, honored by all beings, turns to him and speaks. This verse is the pause before the blessing, not the blessing itself.
ramayan::1172.modern_relevance: You keep showing up for a hard thing with no sign it is working. Then, after a long silence, the answer finally arrives.
ramayan::1172.insight: It teaches you that steadfast waiting can prepare the ground for grace.

ramayan::1173.verse_sanskrit: प्रीतस्तेऽहं नरश्रेष्ठ करिष्यामि तव प्रियम् । शिरसा धारयिष्यामि शैलराजसुतामहम् । । 1433 । ।
ramayan::1173.verse_hindi: O Best of men  I am pleased with your devotion. I will hold Ganga on my head, the daughter of the king of mountains (to reduce  the force of her descent). I shall do your wish.
ramayan::1173.english_translation: O best of men, I am pleased with your devotion. I will hold Ganga on my head, the daughter of the king of mountains, to soften her descent. I shall do what you ask.
ramayan::1173.translation_literal: प्रीतः (pleased) / ते (with you) / अहम् (I) / नरश्रेष्ठ (O best of men) / करिष्यामि (I will do) / तव (your) / प्रियम् (what is dear; wish) / शिरसा (with the head) / धारयिष्यामि (I will hold) / शैलराजसुताम् (the daughter of the king of mountains) / अहम् (I)
ramayan::1173.speaker: Shiva
ramayan::1173.essence: Devotion is answered when the greater power agrees to carry the weight.
ramayan::1173.simple_meaning: Shiva tells Bhagiratha that he is pleased and will hold Ganga on his head so her descent will not be destructive.
ramayan::1173.simple_insight: Patient devotion can open a path where force cannot.
ramayan::1173.detailed_meaning: Bhagiratha has stood in austerity for a year, asking Shiva to release Ganga for the sake of his ancestors. Now Shiva answers. He accepts the request and prepares to bear the river's force himself so the descent can happen safely.
ramayan::1173.modern_relevance: You keep showing up for something that matters, even when nothing seems to move. Then, unexpectedly, the pressure shifts because the right support appears at the right time.
ramayan::1173.insight: It teaches you that sincere devotion can meet grace halfway, turning a dangerous descent into a workable one.

ramayan::1174.verse_sanskrit: ततो हैमवती ज्येष्ठा सर्वलोकनमस्कृता । तदा सातिमहद्रूपं कृत्वा वेगं च दुस्सहम् । । 1434 । । आकाशादपतद्राम शिवे शिवशिरस्युत ।
ramayan::1174.verse_hindi: Then Ganga, the eldest daughter of Himavat who is adored by all the worlds, assuming the form of a mighty river descended from the sky with unbearable speed on the auspicious head of Siva.
ramayan::1174.english_translation: Then Ganga, the eldest daughter of Himavat, adored by all the worlds, took on a vast form and descended from the sky with unbearable speed onto the auspicious head of Shiva.
ramayan::1174.translation_literal: ततः (then) / हैमवती (daughter of Himavat) / ज्येष्ठा (the eldest) / सर्वलोकनमस्कृता (worshipped by all worlds) / तदा (then) / सा (she) / अति-महत्-रूपम् (a very great form) / कृत्वा (having made) / वेगम् (speed) / च (and) / दुस्सहम् (unbearable) / आकाशात् (from the sky) / अपतत् (descended) / राम (O Rama) / शिवे (on the auspicious) / शिव-शिरस्य्-उत (on Shiva's head)
ramayan::1174.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1174.essence: Even a force from heaven needs a steady head to meet it.
ramayan::1174.simple_meaning: Ganga descends from the sky in a huge, forceful form and lands on Shiva's head.
ramayan::1174.simple_insight: Some arrivals are so immense they must be received, not resisted.
ramayan::1174.detailed_meaning: Bhagiratha has won Shiva's promise to hold Ganga. Now the river goddess comes down from the sky with overwhelming force, and Shiva receives her on his head so the earth will not be shattered. The verse shows the first moment of that cosmic descent.
ramayan::1174.modern_relevance: A message lands with such force that you have to stop and absorb it before you can respond. Some things cannot be met with speed; they need steadiness first.
ramayan::1174.insight: It shifts attention from the power of the descent to the steadiness required to bear it.

ramayan::1175.verse_sanskrit: अचिन्तयच्च सा देवी गङ्गा परमदुर्धरा । । 1435 । । विशाम्यहं हि पातालं स्रोतसा गृह्य शङ्करम् ।
ramayan::1175.verse_hindi: Goddess Ganga, extremely difficult to contain, thought that seizing Siva with her flow she would enter the lower regions of the earth.
