ramayan::1223.translation_literal: भगीरथः (Bhagiratha) / अपि (also) / राजर्षिः (royal sage) / कृत्वा (having done) / सलिलम् (water) / उत्तमम् (excellent) / यथाक्रमम् (in proper order) / यथान्यायम् (according to proper law) / सागराणाम् (of the sons of Sagara) / महायशाः (greatly renowned) / कृतोदकः (having completed the water rites) / शुचिः (purified) / राजा (the king) / स्वपुरम् (his own city) / प्रविवेश (entered) / ह (indeed) / समृद्धार्थः (one whose aim was fulfilled) / रघुश्रेष्ठ (O best of the Raghus) / स्वराज्यम् (his own kingdom) / प्रशशास (ruled) / ह (indeed)
ramayan::1223.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1223.essence: A fulfilled vow returns you to ordinary rule, but not as the same person.
ramayan::1223.simple_meaning: Bhagiratha completes the rites for his ancestors, returns purified, and resumes ruling his kingdom after fulfilling his mission.
ramayan::1223.simple_insight: Some duties end only when they are fully honoured, not merely when they are finished.
ramayan::1223.detailed_meaning: Bhagiratha has finally brought the Ganga down and given the sons of Sagara their rites. This verse closes that long struggle: the king finishes the sacred task, returns purified, and takes up rule again. It is a completion scene, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::1223.modern_relevance: You finally finish the task that has lived in your chest for years. The relief is real, but so is the return: life asks you to step back into it and keep going.
ramayan::1223.insight: It shifts attention from the achievement itself to the responsibility that follows fulfillment.

ramayan::1224.verse_sanskrit: प्रमुमोद ह लोकस्तं नृपमासाद्य राघव । नष्टशोकस्समृद्धार्थो बभूव विगतज्वर: । । 14419 । ।
ramayan::1224.verse_hindi: O Best of the Raghus the world rejoiced having Bhagiratha as king. With his purpose achieved, he was freed from all mental afflictions and sorrows and thereafter lived happily.
ramayan::1224.english_translation: O best of the Raghus, the people rejoiced when Bhagiratha became king. With his aim fulfilled, he was freed from sorrow and lived free of distress.
ramayan::1224.translation_literal: प्रमुमोद (rejoiced) / ह (indeed) / लोकः (the people) / तम् (that) / नृपम् (king) / आसाद्य (having obtained / having attained) / राघव (O descendant of Raghu) / नष्टशोकः (with sorrow gone) / समृद्धार्थः (with accomplished purpose) / बभूव (became) / विगतज्वरः (free from distress)
ramayan::1224.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1224.essence: A fulfilled purpose can lift grief and restore ease.
ramayan::1224.simple_meaning: Bhagiratha became king, and people were happy. His goal was complete, so his grief and strain fell away.
ramayan::1224.simple_insight: Fulfilment can quiet the mind after a long burden.
ramayan::1224.detailed_meaning: After Bhagiratha completes the sacred rites for his ancestors, the people rejoice at his rule. The verse closes the episode by showing a king whose long effort has ended in relief, not pride.
ramayan::1224.modern_relevance: You finally finish the thing that has haunted you for months. The room feels lighter, your chest unclenches, and you realize the burden was never just the task.
ramayan::1224.insight: It shows how completion can dissolve the sorrow that effort had been carrying.

ramayan::1225.verse_sanskrit: एष ते राम गङ्गाया विस्तरोऽभिहितो मया । स्वस्ति प्राप्नुहि भद्रं ते संध्याकालोऽतिवर्तते । । 14420 । ।
ramayan::1225.verse_hindi: O Rama I have related you the story of Ganga in detail. Evening time is passing by (and we shall perform the ablutions) farewell.
ramayan::1225.english_translation: O Rama, I have related to you the story of the Ganga in detail. Evening is passing; may you be well and auspicious.
ramayan::1225.translation_literal: एष (this) / ते (to you) / राम (Rama) / गङ्गाया (of Ganga) / विस्तरः (full account) / अभिहितः (spoken) / मया (by me) / स्वस्ति (well-being) / प्राप्नुहि (may you attain) / भद्रम् (auspiciousness) / ते (to you) / संध्याकालः (evening time) / अतिवर्तते (is passing beyond)
ramayan::1225.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1225.essence: A story ends, and the speaker lets you go with blessing.
ramayan::1225.simple_meaning: Valmiki tells Rama that the story of Ganga has been fully explained and that evening is now passing, so they should part for the moment.
ramayan::1225.simple_insight: Some teachings end simply: with gratitude, closure, and a gentle release.
ramayan::1225.detailed_meaning: Valmiki finishes recounting the sacred story of Ganga to Rama, then notices that evening has already slipped past. The verse is not a teaching itself, but a closing line that ends the narration and sends Rama onward with a blessing.
ramayan::1225.modern_relevance: A conversation has gone long, the light is fading, and you can feel the moment to stop. Not every meaningful exchange needs to be pushed further; sometimes closure is the right kindness.
ramayan::1225.insight: It marks the end of a spoken account and a graceful return to the day.

ramayan::1226.verse_sanskrit: धन्यं यशस्यमायुष्यं पुत्र्यं स्वर्ग्यमतीव च । यश्श्रावयति विप्रेषु क्षत्रियेष्वितरेषु च । । 14421 । । प्रीयन्ते पितरस्तस्य प्रीयन्ते दैवतानि च ।
ramayan::1226.verse_hindi: He will be blessed with fame, longevity, progeny and (after death) heaven brahmins One who recites this story of Ganga to the kshatriyas and others, the gods and his forefathers would be pleased with him.
ramayan::1226.english_translation: One who recites this story of Ganga to brahmins, kshatriyas, and others is blessed with fame, longevity, children, and even heaven; his ancestors and the radiant beings are pleased.
ramayan::1226.translation_literal: धन्यं (blessed) / यशस्यम् (famous) / आयुष्यम् (long-lived) / पुत्र्यम् (bringing sons) / स्वर्ग्यम् (leading to heaven) / अतीव च (and very much) / यः (who) / श्रावयति (causes to hear) / विप्रेषु (among brahmins) / क्षत्रियेषु (among kshatriyas) / इतरेषु च (and among others) / प्रीयन्ते (are pleased) / पितरः (ancestors) / तस्य (of that one) / प्रीयन्ते (are pleased) / दैवतानि (radiant beings) / च (and)
ramayan::1226.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1226.essence: A story shared with reverence blesses both the teller and the listener.
ramayan::1226.simple_meaning: Sharing this sacred story brings blessings, good name, long life, children, and honor after death. It also delights your ancestors and the radiant beings.
ramayan::1226.simple_insight: What you pass on with reverence can bless more than just you.
ramayan::1226.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is closing the praise of Ganga's descent. After telling Rama the story, he says that anyone who recites it widely gains blessings in this life and after death, and even pleases ancestors and the radiant beings.
ramayan::1226.modern_relevance: You retell a family story at a memorial, and the room softens. Some words do more than inform — they carry blessing, memory, and connection across generations.
ramayan::1226.insight: It shifts attention from private possession to generous transmission of what is sacred and meaningful.

ramayan::1227.verse_sanskrit: इदमाख्यानमव्यग्रो गङ्गावतरणं शुभम् । । 14422 । । यश्शृणोति च काकुत्स्थ सर्वान् कामानवाप्नुयात् । सर्वे पापा: प्रणश्यन्ति आयु: कीर्तिश्च वर्धते । । 14423 । ।
ramayan::1227.verse_hindi: O Son of the Kakusthas whosoever listens to this auspicious story relating to the descent of Ganga with concentration, all his desires will be achieved, his sins will be destroyed and his longevity and fame will increase.
ramayan::1227.english_translation: O Son of the Kakusthas, whoever listens to this auspicious story of Ganga's descent with concentration will obtain all desires; all sins will be destroyed, and longevity and fame will increase.
ramayan::1227.translation_literal: इदम् (this) / आख्यानम् (story) / अव्यग्रः (with concentration) / गङ्गावतरणम् (the descent of Ganga) / शुभम् (auspicious) / यः (whoever) / शृणोति (listens) / च (and) / काकुत्स्थ (O son of the Kakusthas) / सर्वान् (all) / कामान् (desires) / अवाप्नुयात् (may obtain) / सर्वे (all) / पापाः (sins) / प्रणश्यन्ति (are destroyed) / आयुः (longevity) / कीर्तिः (fame) / च (and) / वर्धते (increases)
ramayan::1227.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1227.essence: Full attention turns sacred hearing into lasting gain.
ramayan::1227.simple_meaning: Listening carefully to this sacred story brings fulfillment, clears harmful actions, and increases life and reputation.
ramayan::1227.simple_insight: Attention itself becomes a form of blessing when you receive something sacred fully.
ramayan::1227.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is closing the Ganga descent episode and promising Rama that this telling is not ordinary entertainment. He says that hearing it with full attention brings desire-fulfillment, washes away wrongdoing, and strengthens life and reputation.
ramayan::1227.modern_relevance: You half-listen while checking your phone, and nothing stays with you. But when you give a story your full attention, it changes you — it can steady your mind and reshape what you carry forward.
ramayan::1227.insight: It shifts you from distracted consumption to reverent listening that transforms the listener.

ramayan::1228.verse_sanskrit: विश्वामित्रवचश्श्रुत्वा राघव स्सहलक्ष्मण: । विस्मयं परमं गत्वा विश्वामित्रमथाब्रवीत् । । 1451 । ।
ramayan::1228.verse_hindi: On hearing the words of Viswamitra, Rama along with Lakshmana, filled with astonishment said to him:
ramayan::1228.english_translation: On hearing Vishwamitra's words, Rama, together with Lakshmana, was filled with wonder and then spoke to Vishwamitra:
ramayan::1228.translation_literal: विश्वामित्रवचः (Vishwamitra's words) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / राघवः (Rama) / सहलक्ष्मणः (together with Lakshmana) / विस्मयं (astonishment) / परमम् (great) / गत्वा (having reached) / विश्वामित्रम् (to Vishvamitra) / अथ (then) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::1228.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1228.essence: A great story first leaves you speechless.
ramayan::1228.simple_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana hear Vishwamitra and respond with amazement before speaking to him.
ramayan::1228.simple_insight: Wonder can be the first honest response to a sacred story.
ramayan::1228.detailed_meaning: After Vishwamitra finishes describing the sacred descent of the Ganga, Rama and Lakshmana are stunned. Their response is not debate or resistance, but awe. This verse simply marks the moment before Rama speaks.
ramayan::1228.modern_relevance: You hear a story so vast it stops your usual reactions. For a moment, all you can do is listen in silence before answering.
ramayan::1228.insight: It shows that reverence begins with being genuinely moved before speaking.

ramayan::1229.verse_sanskrit: अत्यद्भुतमिदं ब्रह्मन् कथितं परमं त्वया । गङ्गावतरणं पुण्यं सागरस्यापि पूरणम् । । 1452 । ।
ramayan::1229.verse_hindi: O Knower of the Brahman this story narrated by you relating to the descent of the sacred Ganga and the fullness of the ocean  (due to Gangas fall) is very wonderful.
ramayan::1229.english_translation: O Knower of the Brahman, the sacred story you have told about Ganga's descent is truly wonderful, even to the point of the ocean's fullness.
ramayan::1229.translation_literal: अत्यद्भुतम् (very wonderful) / इदम् (this) / ब्रह्मन् (O knower of Brahman) / कथितम् (told) / परमम् (supreme) / त्वया (by you) / गङ्गावतरणम् (the descent of Ganga) / पुण्यम् (auspicious) / सागरस्य (of the ocean) / अपि (also) / पूरणम् (fullness)
ramayan::1229.speaker: Rama
ramayan::1229.essence: Wonder is the first response to something truly vast.
ramayan::1229.simple_meaning: Rama praises Vishwamitra's account of Ganga's descent as astonishing, sacred, and so vast it seems to fill the ocean.
ramayan::1229.simple_insight: Wonder is a sign that you are meeting something larger than your usual frame.
ramayan::1229.detailed_meaning: After hearing Vishwamitra explain how Ganga descended to earth, Rama and Lakshmana are stunned. Rama responds with reverence and wonder, showing that even before the great war, he is a student who can still be amazed.
ramayan::1229.modern_relevance: You hear a story so alive that you stop checking your phone and just listen. Something in you recognizes that real wisdom does not shrink the world — it enlarges it.
ramayan::1229.insight: It shifts the mind from casual hearing to reverent listening.

ramayan::1230.verse_sanskrit: तस्य सा शर्वरी सर्वा सह सौमित्रिणा तदा । जगाम चिन्तयानस्य विश्वामित्रकथां शुभाम् । । 1453 । ।
ramayan::1230.verse_hindi: Then Rama along with Lakshmana spent the whole night reflecting on the auspicious story narrated by Viswamitra.
ramayan::1230.english_translation: Then Rama along with Lakshmana spent the whole night reflecting on the auspicious story narrated by Viswamitra.
ramayan::1230.translation_literal: तस्य (of that) / सा (that) / शर्वरी (night) / सर्वा (whole) / सह (together with) / सौमित्रिणा (with Saumitri, Lakshmana) / तदा (then) / जगाम (passed) / चिन्तयानस्य (while reflecting) / विश्वामित्रकथां (the story of Viswamitra) / शुभाम् (auspicious)
ramayan::1230.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1230.essence: Real understanding begins when you keep thinking after the words end.
ramayan::1230.simple_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana do not rush past what they heard. They spend the night quietly thinking it over, letting the story sink in.
ramayan::1230.simple_insight: Some truths need time in the mind before they become action.
ramayan::1230.detailed_meaning: After hearing Viswamitra's account, Rama and Lakshmana do not sleep easily or dismiss it. They spend the entire night turning it over in their minds. The scene shows how a great teaching is received: with attention, wonder, and inward reflection before the next step.
ramayan::1230.modern_relevance: You hear something that unsettles your assumptions, then reach for your phone to escape the feeling. Rama does the opposite: he stays with the question until morning.
ramayan::1230.insight: It teaches you to pause and let important information mature before reacting.

ramayan::1231.verse_sanskrit: तत: प्रभाते विमले विश्वामित्रं महामुनिम् । उवाच राघवो वाक्यं कृताह्निकमरिन्दम: । । 1454 । ।
ramayan::1231.verse_hindi: Thereafter, the progeny of the Raghus, the destroyer of enemies (Rama) addressed Viswamitra in the clear early morning after Viswamitra had completed his routine rites:
ramayan::1231.english_translation: Thereafter, Rama spoke to the great sage Vishwamitra in the clear early morning, after Vishwamitra had completed his morning rites.
ramayan::1231.translation_literal: तत: (thereafter) / प्रभाते (in the morning) / विमले (clear, pure) / विश्वामित्रम् (to Vishwamitra) / महामुनिम् (great sage) / उवाच (spoke) / राघवः (Rama, descendant of Raghu) / वाक्यम् (words) / कृताह्निकम् (after completing morning rites) / अरिन्दमः (destroyer of enemies)
ramayan::1231.speaker: Rama
ramayan::1231.essence: The story pauses at dawn before the next reply begins.
ramayan::1231.simple_meaning: After finishing his morning duties, Rama speaks to Vishwamitra.
ramayan::1231.simple_insight: The moment matters, but the verse itself is only a scene bridge.
ramayan::1231.detailed_meaning: The night of listening has ended. Rama and Lakshmana have spent it reflecting on Vishwamitra's account, and now, in the clean light of morning after the sage's rites, Rama begins to speak. The verse sets the stage for the next exchange.
ramayan::1231.modern_relevance: You finish a long, intense conversation and the next morning begins before the real reply has come. This verse is that pause between hearing and responding.
ramayan::1231.insight: It marks a transition from listening to speaking, not a teaching on its own.

ramayan::1232.verse_sanskrit: गता भगवती रात्रिश्श्रोतव्यं परमं श्रुतम् । क्षणभूतेव नौ रात्रि स्सम्वृत्तेयं महातप: । । 1455 । । इमां चिन्तयतस्सर्वां निखिलेन कथां तव ।
ramayan::1232.verse_hindi: O Noble ascetic we have heard this great story worthy to be listened. As we both lay pondering over the entire story (narrated by you), the glorious night passed off just like a moment.
ramayan::1232.english_translation: O noble ascetic, we have heard this great story worthy of being listened to. As we both pondered your whole account, the glorious night passed as if it were only a moment.
ramayan::1232.translation_literal: गता (passed) / भगवती (glorious) / रात्रिः (night) / श्रोतव्यम् (worthy to be heard) / परमम् (supreme) / श्रुतम् (heard) / क्षणभूता इव (as if a moment) / नौ (for us two) / रात्रिः (night) / सम्वृत्ता (became) / इयम् (this) / महातपः (great ascetic) / इमाम् (this) / चिन्तयतः (while pondering) / सर्वाम् (entire) / निखिलेन (completely) / कथाम् (story) / तव (your)
ramayan::1232.speaker: Rama
ramayan::1232.essence: What truly holds your attention can make a whole night vanish.
ramayan::1232.simple_meaning: Rama tells Vishvamitra that listening to his story and reflecting on it made the whole night feel very short.
ramayan::1232.simple_insight: Deep attention can make time feel light and brief.
ramayan::1232.detailed_meaning: At dawn, Rama speaks to Vishvamitra after a night spent listening closely with Lakshmana. The story has absorbed them so fully that the night felt like a moment. The verse marks the transition from listening to readiness for action.
ramayan::1232.modern_relevance: You finish a conversation at 2 a.m. and realize the room has gone silent around you. When something truly matters, your mind stops counting minutes and starts living inside the meaning.
ramayan::1232.insight: It shows how focused listening can dissolve fatigue and prepare the mind for the next step.

ramayan::1233.verse_sanskrit: तराम सरितां श्रेष्ठां पुण्यां त्रिपथगां नदीम् । । 1456 । । नौरेषा हि सुखास्तीर्णा ऋषीणां पुण्यकर्मणाम् । भगवन्तमिह प्राप्तं ज्ञात्वा त्वरितमागता । । 1457 । ।
ramayan::1233.verse_hindi: We will cross over Ganga, the best of rivers, the sacred river that flows in three directions.This boat of pious saints which is well laidout has come here swiftly, having come to know that you, O Venerable one have arrived.
ramayan::1233.english_translation: We will cross over the best of rivers, the sacred Ganga that flows in three directions. This boat of pious sages, well laid out, has come swiftly, having learned that you, O venerable one, have arrived.
ramayan::1233.translation_literal: तराम (we will cross) / सरिताम् (of rivers) / श्रेष्ठाम् (the best) / पुण्याम् (sacred) / त्रिपथगाम् (flowing in three paths) / नदीम् (river) / नौः (boat) / एषा (this) / हि (indeed) / सुखा-स्तीर्णा (well laid out) / ऋषीणाम् (of sages) / पुण्य-कर्मणाम् (of meritorious deeds) / भगवन्तम् (the venerable one) / इह (here) / प्राप्तम् (having arrived) / ज्ञात्वा (having known) / त्वरितम् (quickly) / आगता (has come)
ramayan::1233.speaker: Rama
ramayan::1233.essence: The journey resumes through a sacred crossing, not a speech.
ramayan::1233.simple_meaning: Rama says they will cross the sacred Ganga, and a sages' boat has come quickly because it recognized Viswamitra's arrival.
ramayan::1233.simple_insight: A needed crossing is already waiting for you when the time is right.
ramayan::1233.detailed_meaning: At dawn, Rama speaks to Viswamitra after a night of listening and reflection. The river is ahead, and a boat belonging to holy sages has come to the bank as if summoned by the moment itself. The verse simply sets up the crossing.
ramayan::1233.modern_relevance: You reach the riverbank with your bags in hand, and the ferry is already there. The next step is not a philosophy lesson — it is just the crossing, waiting for you.
ramayan::1233.insight: It shifts attention from reflection to the practical next move: crossing the river and continuing the journey.

ramayan::1234.verse_sanskrit: तस्य तद्वचनं श्रुत्वा राघवस्य महात्मन: । सन्तारं कारयामास सर्षिसङ्घ स्सराघव: । । 1458 । ।
ramayan::1234.verse_hindi: Hearing the words of noble Rama, he (Viswamitra), accompanied by hosts of sages besides Rama and Lakshmana made arrangements to cross (the river).
ramayan::1234.english_translation: Hearing the words of noble Rama, Viswamitra, along with the host of sages and Rama and Lakshmana, arranged for the crossing.
ramayan::1234.translation_literal: तस्य (his) / तत्-वचनम् (that word) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / राघवस्य (of Rama) / महात्मनः (of the great-souled one) / सन्तारम् (crossing) / कारयामास (made happen / arranged) / सर्षि-सङ्घः (with the host of sages) / सराघवः (together with Rama) ।
ramayan::1234.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1234.essence: A wise word becomes action the moment it is heard.
ramayan::1234.simple_meaning: After hearing Rama's words, Viswamitra arranged for everyone to cross the river together.
ramayan::1234.simple_insight: The journey moves forward because someone acts on a wise decision.
ramayan::1234.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has led Rama and Lakshmana to the Ganga with a group of sages. After Rama speaks, the crossing is arranged at once. It is a small but necessary step in the larger movement of the forest journey.
ramayan::1234.modern_relevance: A group chat finally settles on a plan, and one person books the ferry before the moment passes. Progress often depends on that quiet follow-through.
ramayan::1234.insight: It highlights the practical step that turns intention into movement.

ramayan::1235.verse_sanskrit: उत्तरं तीरमासाद्य सम्पूज्यर्षिगणं तदा । गङ्गाकूले निविष्टास्ते विशालां ददृशु: पुरीम् । । 1459 । ।
ramayan::1235.verse_hindi: Having reached the northern bank, they paid homage to the sages encamped on the bank of  Ganga and beheld the city of Vishala.
ramayan::1235.english_translation: Having reached the northern bank, they paid homage to the sages encamped on the bank of Ganga and beheld the city of Vishala.
ramayan::1235.translation_literal: उत्तरं (northern) / तीरम् (bank) / आसाद्य (having reached) / सम्पूज्य (having honored) / ऋषिगणम् (the group of sages) / तदा (then) / गङ्गाकूले (on the bank of Ganga) / निविष्टाः (settled) / ते (they) / विशालाम् (Vishala) / ददृशुः (saw)
ramayan::1235.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1235.essence: Arrival comes with gratitude, then the journey continues.
ramayan::1235.simple_meaning: After crossing the river, Rama and the others honor the sages on the bank and then see the city of Vishala.
ramayan::1235.simple_insight: Some moments simply mark arrival: respect first, then the next place ahead.
ramayan::1235.detailed_meaning: Rama, Lakshmana, and Vishvamitra have crossed Ganga and reached the far bank. Before moving on, they honor the sages resting there, then look out and see Vishala ahead. The verse is a quiet transition, not a teaching.
ramayan::1235.modern_relevance: You finally arrive after a long trip, step out of the train, and pause to thank the people who helped you get there before looking for the next street.
ramayan::1235.insight: It marks a transition from crossing to onward travel, with reverence before movement.

ramayan::1236.verse_sanskrit: ततो मुनिवरस्तूर्णं जगाम सह राघव: । विशालां नगरीं रम्यां दिव्यां स्वर्गोपमां तदा । । 14510 । ।
ramayan::1236.verse_hindi: Thereupon Viswamitra, the best of ascetics, accompanied by Rama and Lakshmana soon proceeded towards the enchanting and splendid city of Vishala comparable to heaven.
ramayan::1236.english_translation: Thereupon Viswamitra, the best of ascetics, accompanied by Rama and Lakshmana soon proceeded towards the enchanting and splendid city of Vishala comparable to heaven.
ramayan::1236.translation_literal: ततः (thereupon) / मुनिवरः (best of ascetics) / तूर्णम् (quickly) / जगाम (went) / सह (with) / राघवः (Rama) / विशालाम् (to Vishala) / नगरीम् (city) / रम्याम् (enchanting) / दिव्याम् (splendid) / स्वर्ग-उपमाम् (comparable to heaven) / तदा (then)
ramayan::1236.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1236.essence: A beautiful place appears, but the story is still in motion.
ramayan::1236.simple_meaning: Viswamitra leads Rama and Lakshmana on to Vishala, a beautiful city described as heavenly.
ramayan::1236.simple_insight: Some moments simply move the story forward; not every step carries a teaching.
ramayan::1236.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra travels onward with Rama and Lakshmana toward Vishala, a city of great beauty. The verse is a scene-setting bridge between their crossing of the Ganga and Rama's curiosity about the city in the next line.
ramayan::1236.modern_relevance: You arrive in a new city and keep walking because the next part of the journey is still ahead. This verse is the movement between moments, not the moment of decision.
ramayan::1236.insight: It keeps attention on the unfolding journey rather than forcing meaning onto a passing scene.

ramayan::1237.verse_sanskrit: अथ रामो महाप्राज्ञो विश्वामित्रं महामुनिम् । पप्रच्छ प्राञ्जलिर्भूत्वा विशालामुत्तमां पुरीम् । । 14511 । ।
ramayan::1237.verse_hindi: Thereafter great intellectual, Rama, with folded palms enquired of eminent ascetic Viswamitra, about the excellent city of Vishala.
ramayan::1237.english_translation: Thereafter the highly wise Rama, with folded palms, asked the great ascetic Vishwamitra about the excellent city of Vishala.
ramayan::1237.translation_literal: अथ (thereafter) / रामः (Rama) / महाप्राज्ञः (highly wise) / विश्वामित्रम् (to Vishwamitra) / महामुनिम् (great ascetic) / पप्रच्छ (asked) / प्राञ्जलिः (with folded palms) / भूत्वा (having become) / विशालाम् (about Vishala) / उत्तमाम् (excellent) / पुरीम् (city)
ramayan::1237.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1237.simple_meaning: Rama respectfully asks Vishwamitra about the city of Vishala.
ramayan::1237.simple_insight: Curiosity can be humble when it bows before wisdom.
ramayan::1237.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana have reached Vishala with Vishwamitra. Seeing the city, Rama does not assume or act on impulse. He first folds his hands and asks the sage what place this is, showing reverence and attentiveness before entering a new world.
ramayan::1237.modern_relevance: You arrive in a new place and do not pretend to know it all. You pause, ask the right person, and learn before you move.
ramayan::1237.insight: It teaches you to meet new situations with humility, not assumption.

ramayan::1238.verse_sanskrit: कतरो राजवंशोऽयं विशालायां महामुने । श्रोतुमिच्छामि भद्रं ते परं कौतूहलं हि मे । । 14512 । ।
ramayan::1238.verse_hindi: O Distinguished ascetic, which royal dynasty is ruling this city of Vishala? Could you tell me? Great is my curiosity. May you prosper
ramayan::1238.english_translation: O distinguished ascetic, which royal dynasty rules this city of Vishala? I wish to hear it, for my curiosity is great. May you prosper.
ramayan::1238.translation_literal: कतरो (which) / राजवंशः (royal dynasty) / अयम् (this) / विशालायाम् (in Vishala) / महामुने (O great ascetic) / श्रोतुम् (to hear) / इच्छामि (I wish) / भद्रम् (prosperity / well-being) / ते (to you) / परम् (great) / कौतूहलम् (curiosity) / हि (indeed) / मे (my)
ramayan::1238.speaker: Rama
ramayan::1238.essence: Clear curiosity is the start of real understanding.
ramayan::1238.simple_meaning: Rama politely asks Viswamitra which royal family rules Vishala, saying he is eager to hear the answer.
ramayan::1238.simple_insight: Real learning begins with a direct question, not vague interest.
ramayan::1238.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana have reached Vishala with Viswamitra. Before the sage begins his story, Rama pauses and asks who rules the city. The moment shows his disciplined curiosity: he does not rush past what he does not know.
ramayan::1238.modern_relevance: You hear a place name in a meeting, a book, or a conversation and feel the urge to nod along. Rama does the opposite: he asks the exact question instead of pretending to know.
ramayan::1238.insight: It teaches you to turn curiosity into a precise question, so understanding can actually begin.

ramayan::1239.verse_sanskrit: तस्य तद्वचनं श्रुत्वा रामस्य मुनिपुङ्गव: । आख्यातुं तत्समारेभे विशालस्य पुरातनम् । । 14513 । ।
ramayan::1239.verse_hindi: Viswamitra, preeminent among ascetics, hearing the words of Rama commenced to relate the history of the ancient city of Vishala.
ramayan::1239.english_translation: Viswamitra, preeminent among ascetics, hearing Rama's words began to relate the ancient history of Vishala.
ramayan::1239.translation_literal: तस्य (of that) / तत् (that) / वचनं (speech) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / रामस्य (of Rama) / मुनिपुङ्गवः (bull among sages) / आख्यातुं (to narrate) / तत् (that) / समारेभे (began) / विशालस्य (of Vishala) / पुरातनम् (ancient)
ramayan::1239.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1239.essence: A question opens the gate to an older story.
ramayan::1239.simple_meaning: After hearing Rama's question, Viswamitra begins telling the old story of Vishala.
ramayan::1239.simple_insight: Curiosity opens the door to a larger story.
ramayan::1239.detailed_meaning: Rama has just asked Viswamitra about the royal line that rules Vishala. The sage answers by starting an old tale, shifting the scene from a simple question to the history behind the city.
ramayan::1239.modern_relevance: You ask one careful question at a family dinner, and suddenly an elder begins telling the story behind everything you thought was random.
ramayan::1239.insight: It signals a transition from inquiry to explanation, not a teaching in itself.

ramayan::1240.verse_sanskrit: श्रूयतां राम शक्रस्य कथां कथयतश्शुभाम् । अस्मिन् देशे तु यद्वृत्तं तदपि शृणु राघव । । 14514 । ।
ramayan::1240.verse_hindi: O Rama hear the auspicious legend of Indra. Listen, too, what had happened to this
ramayan::1240.english_translation: Listen, Rama, to the auspicious story of Indra. Hear also what happened in this region.
ramayan::1240.translation_literal: श्रूयतां (let it be heard) / राम (Rama) / शक्रस्य (of Indra) / कथाम् (story) / कथयतः (being told) / शुभाम् (auspicious) / अस्मिन् (in this) / देशे (region) / तु (indeed) / यत् (what) / वृत्तम् (happened) / तत् (that) / अपि (also) / शृणु (listen) / राघव (Raghava)
ramayan::1240.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1240.essence: The story begins by opening the past, not by rushing to the lesson.
ramayan::1240.simple_meaning: Visvamitra invites Rama to listen to a sacred tale about Indra and to hear the history of this place.
ramayan::1240.simple_insight: Some lessons arrive through stories before they arrive through explanation.
ramayan::1240.detailed_meaning: Visvamitra has begun explaining the ancient history of Vishala to Rama. He asks Rama to listen to Indra's story and to the events that once unfolded here, setting up the background for the larger tale that follows.
ramayan::1240.modern_relevance: A teacher leans in and says, 'Before I explain the rule, hear the story that made it necessary.' The lesson lands because the story comes first.
ramayan::1240.insight: It prepares the listener for a historical explanation, not a moral conclusion.

ramayan::1241.verse_sanskrit: पूर्वं कृतयुगे राम दिते: पुत्रा महाबला: । अदितेश्च महाभाग वीर्यवन्तस्सुधार्मिका: । । 14515 । ।
ramayan::1241.verse_hindi: O Blessed Rama in kritayuga, the sons of Diti were very strong and those of Aditi were spirited and righteous.
ramayan::1241.english_translation: O blessed Rama, in the Krita Yuga the sons of Diti were very powerful, and the sons of Aditi were noble, full of courage, and righteous.
ramayan::1241.translation_literal: पूर्वं (formerly/in the earlier age) / कृतयुगे (in the Krita Yuga) / राम (Rama) / दिते: (of Diti) / पुत्रा: (sons) / महाबला: (very powerful) / अदिते: (of Aditi) / च (and) / महाभाग (O fortunate one) / वीर्यवन्त: (endowed with valor) / सुदार्मिका: (highly righteous)
ramayan::1241.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::1241.essence: The conflict starts in an older order of power and virtue.
ramayan::1241.simple_meaning: Viswamitra describes an ancient age when the sons of Diti were mighty and the sons of Aditi were noble and righteous.
ramayan::1241.simple_insight: Some stories begin by showing the world before the conflict, so the real stakes can be understood.
ramayan::1241.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra is explaining an old cosmic history to Rama in the forest. He begins with the age before the present struggle, naming the powerful descendants of Diti and the righteous descendants of Aditi, setting up the origin of the conflict he is about to reveal.
ramayan::1241.modern_relevance: Before a family dispute, a workplace feud, or a long friendship turns bitter, there is usually an older pattern underneath it. Understanding that background changes how you hear the present crisis.
ramayan::1241.insight: It shifts attention from the immediate event to the deeper forces that shaped it.

ramayan::1242.verse_sanskrit: ततस्तेषां नरश्रेष्ठ बुद्धिरासीन्महात्मनाम् । अमरा अजराश्चैव कथं स्याम निरामया: । । 14516 । ।
ramayan::1242.verse_hindi: O Best among men a thought came to those illustrious ones, how can we be  free from old age, death and disease?
ramayan::1242.english_translation: Then a thought arose among those noble beings: how can we become immortal, ageless, and free from disease?
ramayan::1242.translation_literal: ततः (then) / तेषाम् (among them) / नरश्रेष्ठ (O best among men) / बुद्धिः (thought) / आसीत् (arose) / महात्मनाम् (of the noble ones) / अमराः (immortal) / अजराः (ageless) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / कथम् (how) / स्याम (may we become) / निरामयाः (free from disease)
ramayan::1242.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1242.essence: Even the radiant ones fear decay.
ramayan::1242.simple_meaning: The noble beings began wondering how they could escape old age, death, and illness.
ramayan::1242.simple_insight: Even the mighty are driven by the same fear of decline.
ramayan::1242.detailed_meaning: Indra's story has turned to the ancient struggle of the radiant beings. After hearing about the sons of Diti and Aditi, the narrator shows the noble ones thinking together about one desperate question: how to become free from aging, death, and disease.
ramayan::1242.modern_relevance: You scroll past another health headline, another anti-aging promise, another attempt to outrun decline. The fear is ancient: how do you stay untouched by time?
ramayan::1242.insight: It shifts attention from power itself to the fear underneath power.

ramayan::1243.verse_sanskrit: तेषां चिन्तयतां राम बुद्धिरासीन्महात्मनाम् । क्षीरोदमथनं कृत्वा रसं प्राप्स्याम तत्र वै । । 14517 । ।
ramayan::1243.verse_hindi: O Rama While the noble sons were reflecting over this matter an idea flashed across their minds to get nectar by churning the ocean of milk.
ramayan::1243.english_translation: O Rama, as the noble beings reflected, the thought arose: by churning the ocean of milk, we shall obtain the nectar there.
ramayan::1243.translation_literal: तेषाम् (of them) / चिन्तयताम् (while reflecting) / राम (O Rama) / बुद्धिः (an idea) / आसीत् (arose) / महात्मनाम् (of the noble beings) / क्षीरोद-मथनम् (churning of the ocean of milk) / कृत्वा (having done) / रसम् (nectar) / प्राप्स्याम (we shall obtain) / तत्र (there) / वै (indeed)
ramayan::1243.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1243.essence: A shared problem becomes solvable when clear thought finds the right method.
ramayan::1243.simple_meaning: As the noble beings thought it over, they came up with the plan to churn the ocean of milk and get nectar from it.
ramayan::1243.simple_insight: A life-changing solution can arrive after patient reflection, not frantic action.
ramayan::1243.detailed_meaning: The divine beings are still weighing how to escape old age, death, and disease. As they think together, the answer appears: churn the ocean of milk and obtain nectar. This verse is the moment of decision before the great undertaking begins.
ramayan::1243.modern_relevance: You sit with a hard problem long enough for a real solution to surface. The answer is not always force; sometimes it is a plan that comes only after deep collective thinking.
ramayan::1243.insight: It shifts the mind from helpless worry to strategic resolve.

ramayan::1244.verse_sanskrit: ततो निश्चित्य मथनं योक्त्रं कृत्वा च वासुकिम् । मन्थानं मन्दरं कृत्वा ममन्थुरमितौजस: । । 14518 । ।
ramayan::1244.verse_hindi: Thereupon, having decided to churn (the ocean mind) those very powerful ones, made Vasuki, (the great snake), as a rope and Mandara mountain as the churning rod.And started churning it.
ramayan::1244.english_translation: Thereupon, having decided to churn the ocean, those very powerful ones made Vasuki the rope and Mandara the churning rod, and began churning.
ramayan::1244.translation_literal: ततः (then) / निश्चित्य (having decided) / मथनम् (churning) / योक्त्रम् (rope) / कृत्वा (having made) / च (and) / वासुकिम् (Vasuki) / मन्थानम् (churning rod) / मन्दरम् (Mandara) / कृत्वा (having made) / ममन्थुः (they churned) / अमितौजसः (those of immeasurable power)
ramayan::1244.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1244.essence: Big goals become real only when you choose the method.
ramayan::1244.simple_meaning: They chose the plan, turned Vasuki into a rope and Mandara into the churning rod, and began the work.
ramayan::1244.simple_insight: Great tasks begin when you commit the right tools to the right aim.
ramayan::1244.detailed_meaning: The powerful gods and beings have already agreed to churn the ocean for nectar. Here, they set the method in motion: Vasuki becomes the rope, Mandara the rod, and the impossible undertaking begins to turn.
ramayan::1244.modern_relevance: You finally clear the table, gather the tools, and start the hard project instead of just talking about it.
ramayan::1244.insight: It shifts attention from wishing for a result to organizing the effort that makes it possible.

ramayan::1245.verse_sanskrit: अथ वर्षसहस्रेण योक्त्रसर्पशिरांसि च । वमन्त्यति विषं तत्र ददंशुर्दशनैश्शिला: । । 14519 । ।
ramayan::1245.verse_hindi: After a thousand years, the hoods of the snake made as rope vomitted venom and started biting the rocks of the Mandara mountain with their teeth.
ramayan::1245.english_translation: After a thousand years, the snake-ropes' hoods spat out poison, and their teeth bit the rocks of Mount Mandara.
ramayan::1245.translation_literal: अथ (then) / वर्षसहस्रेण (after a thousand years) / योक्त्रसर्पशिरांसि (the snake-hoods used as the rope) / च (and) / वमन्ति (spitting out) / अति (greatly) / विषं (poison) / तत्र (there) / ददंशुः (bit) / दशनैः (with teeth) / शिलाः (the rocks)
ramayan::1245.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1245.essence: Long effort can turn violent before it turns fruitful.
ramayan::1245.simple_meaning: The churning has gone on for a thousand years, and the snake used as the rope begins to spit poison and bite the mountain rocks.
ramayan::1245.simple_insight: Great work can turn bitter before it yields anything valuable.
ramayan::1245.detailed_meaning: The gods and demons are churning the ocean with Mount Mandara and Vasuki. After an immense stretch of effort, the strain shows: the serpent’s hoods spew poison and its teeth tear at the mountain. This is one step in the exhausting cosmic labor.
ramayan::1245.modern_relevance: You keep pushing through a project that has already taken everything out of you. At some point, the strain starts biting back, and the cost becomes impossible to ignore.
ramayan::1245.insight: It shows that even a grand effort can produce danger and damage before any reward appears.

ramayan::1246.verse_sanskrit: उत्पपाताग्निसङ्काशं हालाहलमहाविषम् । तेन दग्धं जगत्सर्वं सदेवासुरमानुषम् । । 14520 । ।
ramayan::1246.verse_hindi: Therefrom was produced halahala, virulent venom resembling fire.The entire universe  consisting of devatas, asuras and mortals was burnt down.
ramayan::1246.english_translation: There arose from it the terrible poison called halahala, blazing like fire. It scorched the entire universe, including the devas, asuras, and humans.
ramayan::1246.translation_literal: उत्पपात (arose) / अग्नि-सङ्काशम् (fire-like) / हालाहल-महाविषम् (the great poison halahala) / तेन (by that) / दग्धम् (burnt) / जगत्-सर्वम् (the whole world) / स-देव-असुर-मानुषम् (with devas, asuras, and humans)
ramayan::1246.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1246.essence: Powerful effort can unleash danger before it yields reward.
ramayan::1246.simple_meaning: A deadly poison came out of the churning and spread through everything, harming all beings equally.
ramayan::1246.simple_insight: Some forces hurt everyone without distinction, and no status can protect you from them.
ramayan::1246.detailed_meaning: The ocean has been churned for ages by devas and asuras using Mount Mandara and Vasuki. From that effort, halahala rises — a poison so fierce it burns all beings. This verse marks the crisis that forces the next divine intervention.
ramayan::1246.modern_relevance: A toxic leak spreads through the whole building, and no one can pretend it is someone else’s problem. Some damage is so wide that everyone must respond together.
ramayan::1246.insight: It shows how collective action can release danger that exceeds anyone’s control.

ramayan::1247.verse_sanskrit: अथ देवा महादेवं शङ्करं शरणार्थिन: । जग्मु: पशुपतिं रुद्रं त्राहि त्राहीति तुष्टुवु: । । 14521 । ।
ramayan::1247.verse_hindi: The devatas sought refuge in the great god Rudra who causes happiness, the Lord of all living beings. Save us, Save us, the cried.
ramayan::1247.english_translation: Then the devatas, seeking refuge, went to Mahadeva Shankara, Rudra, the Lord of beings, and praised him: "Save us, save us."
ramayan::1247.translation_literal: अथ (then) / देवा (the devatas) / महादेवं (to the great deity) / शङ्करं (Shankara) / शरणार्थिन: (seeking refuge) / जग्मु: (went) / पशुपतिं (to the Lord of beings) / रुद्रं (Rudra) / त्राहि (save) / त्राहीति (save, thus) / तुष्टुवु: (they praised)
ramayan::1247.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1247.essence: True refuge begins when power admits its limit.
ramayan::1247.simple_meaning: The devatas turned to Rudra for protection and pleaded for rescue.
ramayan::1247.simple_insight: Even the mighty have moments when they must ask for help.
ramayan::1247.detailed_meaning: The poison from the churning has spread through the worlds, and the devatas can no longer bear it. They rush to Rudra, calling him the Lord of beings, and cry out for protection. This verse marks their appeal before the divine response arrives.
ramayan::1247.modern_relevance: When everything you built starts to fail at once, pride drops away fast. In the middle of a crisis, you stop performing and start asking for help.
ramayan::1247.insight: It shifts the mind from self-reliance alone to rightful surrender in danger.

ramayan::1248.verse_sanskrit: एवमुक्तस्ततो देवैर्देवदेवेश्वर: प्रभु: । प्रादुरासीत्ततोऽत्रैव शङ्खचक्रधरो हरि: । । 14522 । ।
ramayan::1248.verse_hindi: Thereupon, Hari the Lord of celestial beings extolled by the devatas appeared bearing the conch and discus.
ramayan::1248.english_translation: Thereupon, Hari, the lord of the celestial beings, appeared before the devatas, bearing the conch and discus.
ramayan::1248.translation_literal: एवमुक्तः (thus spoken to) / ततः (then) / देवैः (by the devatas) / देवदेवेश्वरः (lord of the lords of the celestial beings) / प्रभुः (the powerful one) / प्रादुरासीत् (appeared) / ततः (then) / अत्रैव (here itself) / शङ्खचक्रधरः (bearer of the conch and discus) / हरिः (Hari)
ramayan::1248.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1248.essence: Help appears when the devatas can no longer carry the crisis alone.
ramayan::1248.simple_meaning: After the celestial beings prayed for help, Hari appeared before them with the conch and discus in hand.
ramayan::1248.simple_insight: When the crisis is beyond you, help can arrive in its own time.
ramayan::1248.detailed_meaning: The celestial beings have already sought refuge from the poison born of the churning. After their plea, Hari appears in radiant form with the conch and discus. It is a response scene, not the climax itself: the rescue begins, but the next verses explain what he will do.
ramayan::1248.modern_relevance: You hit a moment where your own effort has reached its limit, and you finally ask for help. The answer may not arrive as panic relief, but it can still arrive with force.
ramayan::1248.insight: It shifts the mind from self-reliance alone to timely refuge when power is insufficient.

ramayan::1249.verse_sanskrit: उवाचैनं स्मितं कृत्वा रुद्रं शूलभृतं हरि: । दैवतैर्मथ्यमाने तु यत्पूर्वं समुपस्थितम् । । 14523 । । त्वदीयंहि सुरश्रेष्ठ सुराणामग्रजोऽसि यत् । अग्रपूजामिमां मत्वा गृहाणेदं विषं प्रभो । । 14524 । ।
ramayan::1249.verse_hindi: Hari, smiling said to the tridentbearing Rudra O Chief of celestial beings you were born the earliest among the devatas. Therefore, while churning the ocean whichever is produced first shall be offered to you. Considering it the first offering, O Lord accept this venom.
ramayan::1249.english_translation: Hari, smiling, said to trident-bearing Rudra: "O chief of the radiant beings, you are the first-born among the devas. Therefore, while the ocean is being churned, whatever appears first should be offered to you. Considering it the first offering, O Lord, accept this venom."
ramayan::1249.translation_literal: उवाच (said) / एनं (to him) / स्मितं कृत्वा (having smiled) / रुद्रं (to Rudra) / शूलभृतं (the trident-bearer) / हरि: (Hari) / दैवतैः (by the devas) / मथ्यमाने (while being churned) / तु (indeed) / यत् (whatever) / पूर्वं (first) / समुपस्थितम् (appears) / त्वदीयम् (yours) / हि (indeed) / सुरश्रेष्ठ (O best of the devas) / सुराणाम् (of the devas) / अग्रजः (first-born) / असि (you are) / यत् (because) / अग्रपूजाम् (first offering) / इमाम् (this) / मत्वा (considering) / गृहाण (accept) / इदम् (this) / विषम् (venom) / प्रभो (O Lord)
ramayan::1249.speaker: Hari
ramayan::1249.essence: Even poison can be received as an act of honor.
ramayan::1249.simple_meaning: The divine speaker honors Rudra as the first-born among the radiant beings and asks him to accept the first thing that emerges from the ocean churn: the venom.
ramayan::1249.simple_insight: Respect can turn even poison into an offering.
ramayan::1249.detailed_meaning: The devas have prayed for rescue, and Hari appears to guide the crisis. As the ocean churns, the deadly venom rises first. Rather than panic, he frames it as Rudra's rightful first offering, showing reverence, order, and calm in a dangerous moment.
ramayan::1249.modern_relevance: A crisis hits before anyone is ready, and the first thing that surfaces is toxic. Instead of blame and chaos, you can still respond with dignity, order, and respect for who must carry the hardest part.
ramayan::1249.insight: It teaches you to meet danger with composure and to honor rightful role before reacting.

ramayan::1250.verse_sanskrit: इत्युक्त्वा च सुरश्रेष्ठस्तत्रैवान्तरधीयत । देवतानां भयं दृष्टवाश्रुत्वा वाक्यं तु शार्ङ्गिण: । हालाहलविषं घोरं स जग्राहामृतोपमम् । । 14525 । ।
ramayan::1250.verse_hindi: Visnu, the highest among the devatas having the spoken, vanished. Siva who had heard Visnus words and seen the fear of the gods received that  dreadful halahala
ramayan::1250.english_translation: Visnu, the highest among the devatas, having spoken, vanished. Shiva, seeing the fear of the gods and hearing Vishnu's words, took up the dreadful halahala poison, which was like nectar to him.
ramayan::1250.translation_literal: इत्युक्त्वा (having said thus) / च (and) / सुरश्रेष्ठः (the best among the gods) / तत्रैव (right there) / अन्तरधीयत (vanished) / देवतानाम् (of the gods) / भयम् (fear) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / अश्रुत्वा (having heard) / वाक्यम् (the words) / तु (but) / शार्ङ्गिणः (of the bow-bearing one) / हालाहलविषम् (halahala poison) / घोरम् (terrible) / सः (he) / जग्राह (took) / अमृतोपमम् (like nectar)
ramayan::1250.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1250.essence: He vanished after speaking; another took the poison without hesitation.
ramayan::1250.simple_meaning: Vishnu disappears after speaking, and Shiva calmly takes the deadly poison to protect the gods.
ramayan::1250.simple_insight: Real strength is taking on what others cannot bear.
ramayan::1250.detailed_meaning: The gods are being shaken by the churning of the ocean, and Vishnu appears to guide the moment. After speaking, he vanishes. Shiva sees the gods' fear, hears Vishnu, and accepts the poison himself, turning a deadly burden into something he can bear.
ramayan::1250.modern_relevance: A room goes quiet when the crisis lands on everyone at once. The person with the steadier heart steps forward and takes the hardest task without drama.
ramayan::1250.insight: It shows that leadership can mean absorbing danger so others can continue.

ramayan::1251.verse_sanskrit: देवान्विसृज्य देवेशो जगाम भगवान् हर: । ततो देवासुरास्सर्वे ममन्थू रघुनन्दन । । 14526 । ।
ramayan::1251.verse_hindi: Lord of the gods, venerable Siva went away to his abode leaving behind the devatas. O Descendant of Raghu then all the devatas and asuras resumed churning.
ramayan::1251.english_translation: Lord Shiva, the lord of the gods, departed to his own abode. Then, O Rama, all the gods and asuras resumed churning.
ramayan::1251.translation_literal: देवान् (the gods) / विसृज्य (having left) / देवेशः (lord of the gods) / जगाम (went) / भगवान् (venerable) / हरः (Shiva) / ततः (then) / देवासुराः (gods and asuras) / सर्वे (all) / ममन्थुः (churned) / रघुनन्दन (O descendant of Raghu)
ramayan::1251.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1251.essence: The work goes on after the moment of awe passes.
ramayan::1251.simple_meaning: Shiva leaves, and the gods and asuras continue churning the ocean.
ramayan::1251.simple_insight: Some tasks continue only after even the highest presence steps away.
ramayan::1251.detailed_meaning: After Shiva departs, the cosmic churning resumes. The gods and asuras keep working the mountain and ocean together, because the task is not finished and the larger drama of extracting amrita is still underway.
ramayan::1251.modern_relevance: A meeting ends, the senior person walks out, and the team keeps going because the hard part still remains. Some work only moves forward when everyone accepts the task is bigger than ego.
ramayan::1251.insight: It shifts attention from the figure at the center to the unfinished work itself.

ramayan::1252.verse_sanskrit: प्रविवेशाथ पातालं मन्थान: पर्वतोऽनघ । ततो देवास्सगन्धर्वास्तुष्टुवुर्मधुसूदनम् । । 14527 । ।
ramayan::1252.verse_hindi: O Sinless one after the mountain (Mandara) used as churning rod sank down to nether world (patala) the devatas along with the gandharvas invoked Visnu.
ramayan::1252.english_translation: O sinless one, after the churning mountain sank into the nether world, the gods and the gandharvas praised Vishnu.
ramayan::1252.translation_literal: प्रविवेश (entered) / अथ (then) / पातालं (the nether world) / मन्थानः (the churning mountain) / पर्वतः (mountain) / अनघ (sinless one) / ततः (then) / देवाः (the gods) / सगन्धर्वाः (along with the gandharvas) / तुष्टुवुः (praised) / मधुसूदनम् (Madhusudana, Vishnu)
ramayan::1252.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1252.essence: Even a cosmic task can sink without Vishnu's support.
ramayan::1252.simple_meaning: The mountain used for churning sank into the lower world, and the gods with the gandharvas praised Vishnu.
ramayan::1252.simple_insight: When the burden drops out of place, praise and appeal rise together.
ramayan::1252.detailed_meaning: The gods are churning the ocean with Mandara as the rod. The mountain sinks into the lower world, threatening the effort itself. In that crisis, the gods and gandharvas turn to Vishnu with praise before the next rescue is possible.
ramayan::1252.modern_relevance: You are halfway through a group task and the main tool fails. Before panic spreads, everyone looks for the one person who can steady the situation.
ramayan::1252.insight: It shows how collective effort can collapse without support, and how people instinctively turn to the power that can restore it.

ramayan::1253.verse_sanskrit: त्वं गति: सर्वभूतानां विशेषेण दिवौकसाम् । पालयास्मान्महाबाहो गिरिमुद्धर्तुमर्हसि । । 14528 । ।
ramayan::1253.verse_hindi: O mightyarmed Visnu you are the ultimate refuge for all living beings, specially for the devatas. Protect us, you (alone) are fit to lift up the Mandara mountain.
ramayan::1253.english_translation: O mighty-armed Vishnu, you are the refuge of all beings, especially the devas. Protect us; you alone are fit to lift the Mandara mountain.
ramayan::1253.translation_literal: त्वम् (you) / गतिः (refuge) / सर्वभूतानाम् (of all beings) / विशेषेण (especially) / दिवौकसाम् (of the devas) / पालय (protect) / अस्मान् (us) / महाबाहो (O mighty-armed one) / गिरिम् (the mountain) / उद्धर्तुम् (to lift up) / अर्हसि (you are fit)
ramayan::1253.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1253.essence: When your strength fails, refuge becomes the only real power.
ramayan::1253.simple_meaning: The devas pray to Vishnu for protection and ask him to lift the mountain that has sunk. They recognize him as the only power able to save the situation.
ramayan::1253.simple_insight: There is relief in knowing that real help exists when your own strength runs out.
ramayan::1253.detailed_meaning: The devas have begun the churning of the ocean, but the Mandara mountain has sunk into the underworld. Facing failure, they turn to Vishnu and ask him to protect them and lift it back up. The verse is their plea of total dependence.
ramayan::1253.modern_relevance: You have a problem that no amount of effort, planning, or cleverness can move. At some point, you have to admit what can only be held by something larger than you.
ramayan::1253.insight: It shifts the mind from self-reliance to rightful dependence on the supreme protector.

ramayan::1254.verse_sanskrit: इति श्रुत्वा हृषीकेश: कामठं रूपमास्थित: । पर्वतं पृष्ठत: कृत्वा शिश्ये तत्रोदधौ हरि: । । 14529 । ।
ramayan::1254.verse_hindi: Having heard these words, the controller of the sense organs, Visnu, assumed the form of a tortoise reclined in the ocean supporting the mountain on its back.
ramayan::1254.english_translation: Having heard these words, Vishnu, the controller of the senses, assumed the form of a tortoise and lay in the ocean, holding the mountain on his back.
ramayan::1254.translation_literal: इति (thus) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / हृषीकेशः (Hrishekesha, controller of the senses) / कामठं (tortoise-form) / रूपम् (form) / आस्थितः (having assumed) / पर्वतम् (the mountain) / पृष्ठतः (on the back) / कृत्वा (having made) / शिश्ये (lay down) / तत्र (there) / उदधौ (in the ocean) / हरिः (Vishnu)
ramayan::1254.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1254.essence: Great power can work from beneath, without needing to be seen.
ramayan::1254.simple_meaning: Vishnu takes the form of a tortoise and supports the mountain in the ocean so the churning can continue.
ramayan::1254.simple_insight: True support often looks humble, even hidden.
ramayan::1254.detailed_meaning: The gods have pleaded for help after the churning mountain sinks. Vishnu answers by taking a tortoise form and bearing the mountain from beneath the ocean, making the whole cosmic effort possible.
ramayan::1254.modern_relevance: When everyone is panicking over a project collapsing, the real rescue may be the person who quietly holds the weight no one can see.
ramayan::1254.insight: It shifts attention from visible action to the hidden support that makes action possible.

ramayan::1255.verse_sanskrit: पर्वताग्रे तु लोकात्मा हस्तेनाक्रम्य केशव: । देवानां मध्यत: स्थित्वा ममन्थ पुरुषोत्तम: । । 14530 । ।
ramayan::1255.verse_hindi: Visnu, the Supreme being, the soul of the universe standing amidst the devatas took hold of the peak of mountain with his hand and continued to churn the ocean.
ramayan::1255.english_translation: Visnu, the Supreme being, the soul of the universe, standing amid the devatas, took hold of the mountain peak with his hand and continued to churn the ocean.
ramayan::1255.translation_literal: पर्वताग्रे (at the mountain peak) / तु (then) / लोकात्मा (the soul of the universe) / हस्तेन (with the hand) / आक्रम्य (seizing, gripping) / केशवः (Keshava) / देवानाम् (of the devatas) / मध्यतः (in the midst) / स्थित्वा (having stood) / ममन्थ (churned) / पुरुषोत्तमः (the supreme being)
ramayan::1255.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1255.essence: The work succeeds because Vishnu holds the whole effort in place.
ramayan::1255.simple_meaning: Vishnu stands among the devatas, grips the mountain peak, and keeps churning the ocean.
ramayan::1255.simple_insight: Great work often continues because one steady hand refuses to let go.
ramayan::1255.detailed_meaning: The gods and the asuras are churning the ocean for what lies hidden within it. Vishnu stands at the center of the effort, holding the mountain steady with his hand so the work can continue. The verse shows his sustaining role in the cosmic task.
ramayan::1255.modern_relevance: A team project starts slipping apart because the main support failed. Everyone looks around, but one person quietly braces the structure and keeps the whole effort moving.
ramayan::1255.insight: It shifts attention from dramatic action to the quiet force that holds everything together.

ramayan::1256.verse_sanskrit: अथ वर्षसहस्रेण सदण्डस्सकमण्डलु: । पूर्वं धन्वन्तरिर्नाम अप्सराश्च सुवर्चस: । । 14531 । ।
ramayan::1256.verse_hindi: In this way thousand years rolled by. In the beginining came out Dhanvantari holding a staff and a water pot (carried by ascetics) and apsaras of high lustre.
ramayan::1256.english_translation: In this way, after a thousand years, Dhanvantari appeared first, carrying a staff and a water pot, along with radiant apsaras.
ramayan::1256.translation_literal: अथ (then) / वर्षसहस्रेण (by a thousand years) / सदण्डः (with a staff) / सकमण्डलुः (with a water pot) / पूर्वम् (first) / धन्वन्तरिः (Dhanvantari) / नाम (named) / अप्सराः (apsaras) / च (and) / सुवर्चसः (of great radiance)
ramayan::1256.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1256.essence: After immense effort, the first reward appears in unexpected form.
ramayan::1256.simple_meaning: After a thousand years of churning, Dhanvantari emerged first, carrying the marks of a sage, followed by radiant celestial women.
ramayan::1256.simple_insight: Great effort can bring forth gifts you did not expect.
ramayan::1256.detailed_meaning: The gods and demons are churning the ocean, waiting through an immense effort that has already reshaped the cosmos. After a thousand years, Dhanvantari rises first with sacred objects in hand, followed by radiant apsaras. The verse marks the first visible reward of the churning.
ramayan::1256.modern_relevance: You keep working on something for months, seeing nothing but strain and repetition. Then, suddenly, the first real result appears — not the one you predicted, but the one that proves the effort was alive.
ramayan::1256.insight: It shifts attention from the grind to the first signs of emergence.

ramayan::1257.verse_hindi: O Best among men excellent women emerged out of the essence produced by churning of waters. Therefore they are known as apsarasas.
ramayan::1257.english_translation: Excellent women arose from the essence produced by the churning of the waters. That is why they are called apsarasas.
ramayan::1257.translation_literal: अप्सु (in the waters) / निर्मथनात् (from churning) / एव (indeed) / रसाः (essences) / तस्मात् (from that) / वरस्त्रियः (excellent women) / उत्पेतुः (arose) / मनुजश्रेष्ठ (O best among men) / तस्मात् (therefore) / अप्सरसः (apsarasas) / अभवन् (became)
ramayan::1257.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1257.essence: What is churned under pressure can yield unexpected beauty.
ramayan::1257.simple_meaning: The churning of the waters produced radiant women, and that is the origin of the apsarasas.
ramayan::1257.simple_insight: Beauty can emerge from great disturbance.
ramayan::1257.detailed_meaning: The gods and the supreme being are churning the ocean to recover hidden treasures. As the work continues, Dhanvantari has already emerged, and this verse adds another marvel: the apsarasas, born from the essence of the waters themselves.
ramayan::1257.modern_relevance: A long project finally breaks open after months of pressure, and something unexpected and beautiful comes out of the strain. Not every difficult process yields only damage.
ramayan::1257.insight: It shifts attention from the effort itself to the unexpected gifts it can release.

ramayan::1258.verse_sanskrit: हतेषु तेषु पुत्रेषु दिति: परमदु:खिता । मारीचं काश्यपं राम भर्तारमिदमब्रवीत् । । 1461 । ।
ramayan::1258.verse_hindi: O Rama! afflicted with great grief when her sons were killed, Diti said to her husband Kasyapa, son of Maricha:
ramayan::1258.english_translation: O Rama! When her sons had been killed, Diti became deeply grief-stricken and spoke to her husband Kashyapa.
ramayan::1258.translation_literal: हतेषु (having been killed) / तेषु (those) / पुत्रेषु (sons) / दिति: (Diti) / परम-दु:खिता (deeply grief-stricken) / मारीचं (to Maricha/Kashyapa) / काश्यपं (Kashyapa) / राम (O Rama) / भर्तारम् (husband) / इदम् (this) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::1258.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1258.essence: Grief drives her straight to the one person who can hear it.
ramayan::1258.simple_meaning: Diti is overwhelmed by grief after her sons are killed, and she turns to her husband Kashyapa.
ramayan::1258.simple_insight: Loss can leave even the powerful speechless and desperate for someone to hear them.
ramayan::1258.detailed_meaning: The story shifts to the old cosmic feud between the children of Diti and the gods. After Diti’s sons are slain, she is crushed by grief and goes to Kashyapa, her husband, seeking a response to her suffering. The verse sets up her plea in the next line.
ramayan::1258.modern_relevance: You get the call no parent wants and everything narrows to one ache. Before you can think clearly, you need someone steady enough to hear you.
ramayan::1258.insight: It frames grief as a turning point that pushes a person toward counsel, not isolation.

ramayan::1259.verse_sanskrit: हतपुत्राऽस्मि भगवंस्तव पुत्रैर्महाबलै: । शक्रहन्तारमिच्छामि पुत्रं दीर्घतपोऽर्जितम् । । 1462 । ।
ramayan::1259.verse_hindi: O adorable one, your highly powerful sons, (devatas) have killed mine through extensive austerities. I am desirous of obtaining a (mighty) son capable of killing Indra.
ramayan::1259.english_translation: O adorable one, your highly powerful sons have killed mine. I want a son, earned through long austerity, who can defeat Indra.
ramayan::1259.translation_literal: हतपुत्रा (one whose sons have been killed) / अस्मि (I am) / भगवन् (O adorable one) / तव (your) / पुत्रैः (by sons) / महाबलैः (highly powerful) / शक्रहन्तारम् (Indra-killer) / इच्छामि (I desire) / पुत्रम् (a son) / दीर्घतपोऽर्जितम् (earned through long austerity)
ramayan::1259.speaker: Diti
ramayan::1259.essence: Grief asks for power that can strike back.
ramayan::1259.simple_meaning: Diti, grieving the loss of her sons, asks Kasyapa for a son powerful enough to defeat Indra, won through severe austerity.
ramayan::1259.simple_insight: Grief can harden into a wish for revenge when loss is not healed.
ramayan::1259.detailed_meaning: Diti, shattered after her sons are killed, turns to her husband Kasyapa with a fierce request: she wants a son who can defeat Indra. The verse begins the dangerous bargain that will shape the birth of a powerful enemy.
ramayan::1259.modern_relevance: After a humiliating loss, you may start wanting not healing but payback. Hurt can quietly turn into a plan.
ramayan::1259.insight: It shows how grief, if fed by anger, can become a desire to create force in the image of injury.

ramayan::1260.verse_sanskrit: साऽहं तपश्चरिष्यामि गर्भं मे दातुमर्हसि । ईश्वरं शक्रहन्तारं त्वमनुज्ञातुमर्हसि । । 1463 । ।
ramayan::1260.verse_hindi: I shall practise austerities. You ought to grant me a son who would be the supreme ruler of the world and capable of killing Indra. You can say yes (if you will).
ramayan::1260.english_translation: I shall practise austerities. You ought to grant me a son who would be the supreme ruler of the world and capable of killing Indra. You can say yes (if you will).
ramayan::1260.translation_literal: सा (that woman) / अहं (I) / तपः (austerities) / चरिष्यामि (shall practise) / गर्भम् (a son in the womb) / मे (to me) / दातुम् (to give) / अर्हसि (you ought) / ईश्वरम् (a supreme ruler) / शक्रहन्तारम् (killer of Indra) / त्वम् (you) / अनुज्ञातुम् (to grant) / अर्हसि (ought)
ramayan::1260.speaker: Diti
ramayan::1260.essence: A wounded wish becomes power when it is backed by tapas.
ramayan::1260.simple_meaning: Diti says she will do severe austerities and asks her husband to grant her a son powerful enough to defeat Indra.
ramayan::1260.simple_insight: Desire becomes sharper when it is backed by discipline.
ramayan::1260.detailed_meaning: Diti, grieving the loss of her sons, turns to Kasyapa and makes a fierce request: she will undertake austerities if he will give her a son strong enough to overthrow Indra. The moment reveals grief turning into determined ambition.
ramayan::1260.modern_relevance: After a brutal setback, you decide not to stay small. You train harder, commit longer, and aim at a result that would have seemed impossible yesterday.
ramayan::1260.insight: It shows how grief can harden into resolve and turn desire into disciplined pursuit.

ramayan::1261.verse_sanskrit: तस्यास्तद्वचनं श्रुत्वा मारीच: काश्यपस्तदा । प्रत्युवाच महातेजा दितिं परमदु:खिताम् । । 1464 । ।
ramayan::1261.verse_hindi: Then, Marichas son, exceedingly bright Kasyapa on hearing the words of Diti who was deeply grieved replied:
ramayan::1261.english_translation: Then Maricha, son of Kashyapa, the greatly radiant one, hearing Diti's words while she was deeply sorrowful, replied:
ramayan::1261.translation_literal: तस्याः (her) / तद्वचनं (that speech) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / मारीचः (Maricha) / काश्यपः (Kashyapa) / तदा (then) / प्रत्युवाच (replied) / महातेजाः (the greatly radiant one) / दितिम् (to Diti) / परमदुःखिताम् (deeply sorrowful)
ramayan::1261.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1261.essence: A reply is about to shape the fate of the whole exchange.
ramayan::1261.simple_meaning: Kashyapa hears Diti's grief and answers her. It is a transitional line, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::1261.simple_insight: Some verses only open the door; they do not carry the whole message.
ramayan::1261.detailed_meaning: Diti has just pleaded for a son who can kill Indra. Now Kashyapa, her husband, hears her sorrow and begins his reply. The verse simply sets up the exchange that will shape the next lines.
ramayan::1261.modern_relevance: Someone has just poured out a painful request, and the other person pauses before answering. The moment matters, but the real decision comes in the reply that follows.
ramayan::1261.insight: It marks the turning point where grief meets response, not resolution.

ramayan::1262.verse_sanskrit: एवं भवतु भद्रं ते शुचिर्भव तपोधने । जनयिष्यसि पुत्रं त्वं शक्रहन्तारमाहवे । । 1465 । ।
ramayan::1262.verse_hindi: O one vested with the wealth of austerities be it so. Prosperity to you Remain chaste, you will deliver a son who will kill Indra in the battle.
ramayan::1262.english_translation: O one rich in austerity, so be it. Blessings to you. Remain pure, and you will bear a son who will kill Indra in battle.
ramayan::1262.translation_literal: एवम् (so) / भवतु (let it be) / भद्रम् (good fortune) / ते (to you) / शुचिः (pure) / भव (be) / तपोधने (O treasure of austerity) / जनयिष्यसि (you will give birth) / पुत्रम् (a son) / त्वम् (you) / शक्रहन्तारम् (Indra-killer) / आहवे (in battle)
ramayan::1262.speaker: Kashyapa
ramayan::1262.essence: A granted wish can still carry the seed of conflict.
ramayan::1262.simple_meaning: Kashyapa agrees to Diti's request and tells her to remain pure through her austerity, promising that she will bear a son who can defeat Indra in battle.
ramayan::1262.simple_insight: Patient discipline can be turned toward even a dangerous wish.
ramayan::1262.detailed_meaning: Diti has asked Kashyapa for a son powerful enough to defeat Indra. After hearing her grief, Kashyapa consents, but only with strict conditions: she must remain pure and continue her austerity. This verse is part of that promise, not the full teaching.
ramayan::1262.modern_relevance: You want a result so badly that you accept hard conditions just to get it. The deeper question is whether the discipline shaping your wish is making it wiser or more dangerous.
ramayan::1262.insight: It shows how desire can borrow the language of discipline while still aiming at conquest.

ramayan::1263.verse_sanskrit: पूर्णे वर्षसहस्रे तु शुचिर्यदि भविष्यसि । पुत्रं त्रैलोक्यभर्तारं मत्तस्त्वं जनयिष्यसि । । 1466 । ।
ramayan::1263.verse_hindi: If you remain pure and clean, on completion of a thousand years you will give birth to a son through me who will be the lord of the three worlds.
ramayan::1263.english_translation: If you remain pure and clean, after a full thousand years you will bear a son through me who will be lord of the three worlds.
ramayan::1263.translation_literal: पूर्णे (completed) / वर्षसहस्रे (thousand years) / तु (indeed) / शुचिः (pure) / यदि (if) / भविष्यसि (you will become) / पुत्रम् (son) / त्रैलोक्यभर्तारम् (lord of the three worlds) / मत्तः (from me) / त्वम् (you) / जनयिष्यसि (will give birth)
ramayan::1263.speaker: Kashyapa
ramayan::1263.essence: Powerful outcomes arrive only after long restraint.
ramayan::1263.simple_meaning: Kashyapa tells Diti that if she stays pure for a thousand years, she will bear a son who will rule the three worlds.
ramayan::1263.simple_insight: Great power is promised only after long restraint and purity.
ramayan::1263.detailed_meaning: Kashyapa answers Diti after her grief and sets a severe condition: a thousand years of purity before conception. The promise is immense, but it comes only through disciplined restraint and patience, not impulse.
ramayan::1263.modern_relevance: You want the result now, but the thing you want may demand years of clean living first.
ramayan::1263.insight: It shifts desire into discipline by making the reward depend on sustained self-control.

ramayan::1264.verse_sanskrit: एवमुक्त्वा महातेजा: पाणिना स ममार्ज ताम् । समालभ्य ततस्स्वस्तीत्युक्त्वा स तपसे ययौ । । 1467 । ।
ramayan::1264.verse_hindi: Highly brilliant Kasyapa, having thus spoken, touched her gently with his palm, stroked her body and said, May good betide thee. Having said this, Kasyapa went away to perform austerities.
ramayan::1264.english_translation: Highly brilliant Kasyapa, having thus spoken, touched her gently with his palm, stroked her body and said, "May good betide thee." Having said this, Kasyapa went away to perform austerities.
ramayan::1264.translation_literal: एवमुक्त्वा (having thus spoken) / महातेजाः (highly brilliant) / पाणिना (with the hand) / सः (he) / ममार्ज (gently stroked) / ताम् (her) / समालभ्य (having touched gently) / ततः (then) / स्वस्ति (well-being) / इति (thus) / उक्त्वा (having said) / सः (he) / तपसे (for austerity) / ययौ (went)
ramayan::1264.speaker: Kasyapa
ramayan::1264.essence: A blessing is given, and the real test begins after it.
ramayan::1264.simple_meaning: Kasyapa blesses Diti, touches her gently, and leaves to continue his austerities. The verse is a transition, not a teaching.
ramayan::1264.simple_insight: Some moments matter only because they move the story forward.
ramayan::1264.detailed_meaning: Kasyapa has just granted Diti a boon under strict conditions. He blesses her, touches her gently, and departs to resume his austerities. The real consequence comes next, when Diti acts on the promise he has given.
ramayan::1264.modern_relevance: A conversation ends, and the next choice belongs to someone else. The important part is not the blessing itself, but what it sets in motion.
ramayan::1264.insight: It shifts attention from the spoken blessing to the consequences that follow it.

ramayan::1265.verse_sanskrit: गते तस्मिन्नरश्श्रेष्ठ दिति: परमहर्षिता । कुशप्लवनमासाद्य तपस्तेपे सुदारुणम् । । 1468 । ।
ramayan::1265.verse_hindi: O foremost among men after Kasyapa had left, Diti exceedingly delighted (at the prospect of having sons) reached Kushaplavana, and practised intense mortifications.
ramayan::1265.english_translation: After Kasyapa had left, Diti was filled with joy. She went to Kushaplavana and performed severe austerities.
ramayan::1265.translation_literal: गते (having gone) / तस्मिन् (he) / नरश्श्रेष्ठ (foremost among men) / दिति: (Diti) / परमहर्षिता (greatly delighted) / कुशप्लवनम् (Kushaplavana) / आसाद्य (having reached) / तपः (austerity) / तेपे (performed) / सुदारुणम् (very severe)
ramayan::1265.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1265.essence: Hope pushes Diti into severe discipline.
ramayan::1265.simple_meaning: Diti, happy after Kasyapa left, went to Kushaplavana and began very severe austerities.
ramayan::1265.simple_insight: Joy can turn into discipline when a long wish finally feels possible.
ramayan::1265.detailed_meaning: Kasyapa has just left after setting a condition for Diti. Filled with delight at the hope of a son, she goes to Kushaplavana and begins harsh austerities. The verse is a transition, showing her resolve before the next consequence unfolds.
ramayan::1265.modern_relevance: You finally get the message you were waiting for, and your whole body changes course. Hope can make endurance feel possible again.
ramayan::1265.insight: It shows how desire can harden into relentless effort once the mind locks onto a goal.

ramayan::1266.verse_sanskrit: तपस्तस्यां हि कुर्वन्त्यां परिचर्यां चकार ह । सहस्राक्षो नरश्श्रेष्ठ परया गुणसम्पदा । । 1469 । ।
ramayan::1266.verse_hindi: O foremost of men great treasure of virtues while she was practising austerities, the thousandeyed Indra  began to serve her.
ramayan::1266.english_translation: O foremost of men, while she was practising austerities, the thousand-eyed Indra began to serve her, full of excellent virtues.
ramayan::1266.translation_literal: तपस्तस्यां (while her austerity) / हि (indeed) / कुर्वन्त्यां (while doing) / परिचर्याम् (service) / चकार (did) / ह (indeed) / सहस्राक्षः (the thousand-eyed one) / नरश्श्रेष्ठ (O foremost of men) / परया (with supreme) / गुणसम्पदा (with a treasure of virtues)
ramayan::1266.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1266.essence: Steady austerity can make even power itself become service.
ramayan::1266.simple_meaning: Indra served Diti while she was doing severe austerities, showing respect to her spiritual power and virtue.
ramayan::1266.simple_insight: Quiet discipline can draw reverence even from the powerful.
ramayan::1266.detailed_meaning: Diti has begun intense austerities after Kasyapa leaves. In that atmosphere of disciplined effort, Indra himself starts attending to her needs. The verse is a supporting detail in the larger story of her tapas, not a separate teaching.
ramayan::1266.modern_relevance: You keep showing up for a hard practice no one notices. Then, unexpectedly, people who once ignored you start treating your effort with respect.
ramayan::1266.insight: It highlights how sustained austerity can command service and attention without demanding it.

ramayan::1267.verse_sanskrit: अग्निं कुशान् काष्ठमप: फलं मूलं तथैव च । न्यवेदयत्सहस्राक्षो यच्चान्यदपि काङ्क्षितम् । । 14610 । ।
ramayan::1267.verse_hindi: The thousandeyed Indra served her by providing fire, Kusha grass, sticks for burning,
ramayan::1267.english_translation: The thousand-eyed Indra provided her with fire, kuśa grass, sticks for burning, water, fruits, roots, and whatever else she desired.
ramayan::1267.translation_literal: अग्निं (fire) / कुशान् (kuśa grass) / काष्ठम् (sticks for burning) / अपः (water) / फलम् (fruit) / मूलम् (roots) / तथा एव च (and likewise) / न्यवेदयत् (offered/provided) / सहस्राक्षः (the thousand-eyed one) / यत् अन्यत् अपि (whatever else also) / काङ्क्षितम् (desired)
ramayan::1267.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1267.essence: Power becomes humble when it serves another's discipline.
ramayan::1267.simple_meaning: Indra served Diti by bringing everything needed for her austerities and daily ritual needs.
ramayan::1267.simple_insight: Quiet support can be a form of devotion, even from the most powerful.
ramayan::1267.detailed_meaning: Diti is deep in severe austerities, and Indra, the thousand-eyed one, has taken on the role of attendant. He brings her fire, grass, wood, water, fruits, roots, and anything else she asks for. The verse is a supporting detail showing his careful service.
ramayan::1267.modern_relevance: Someone is trying to focus on a hard practice, and another person quietly clears the room, brings water, and handles the small things. Real care often looks ordinary.
ramayan::1267.insight: It shifts attention from grand gestures to precise, supportive service.

ramayan::1268.verse_sanskrit: गात्रसंवहनश्चैव श्रमापनयनैस्तथा । शक्रस्सर्वेषु कालेषु दितिं परिचचार ह । । 14611 । ।
ramayan::1268.verse_hindi: Indra attended on Diti, stroking her limbs gently from time to time to help her regain their  suppleness and alleviate her fatigue.
ramayan::1268.english_translation: Indra attended on Diti, gently stroking her limbs from time to time and easing her fatigue at all times.
ramayan::1268.translation_literal: गात्रसंवहनः (massaging the limbs) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / श्रमापनयनैः (by removing fatigue) / तथा (and so) / शक्रः (Indra) / सर्वेषु (in all) / कालेषु (times) / दितिम् (Diti) / परिचचार (served, attended on) / ह (indeed)
ramayan::1268.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1268.essence: Real support is often quiet, repeated, and physical.
ramayan::1268.simple_meaning: Indra served Diti with care, massaging her body and relieving her tiredness whenever needed.
ramayan::1268.simple_insight: Care is shown in small, repeated acts that quietly support someone’s difficult effort.
ramayan::1268.detailed_meaning: Diti is deep in austerity, and Indra has taken on the role of a servant to help her complete it. He eases her fatigue with physical care, showing patient attendance rather than a dramatic speech or revelation.
ramayan::1268.modern_relevance: You notice someone worn down after days of strain and quietly bring water, a chair, or a hand on the shoulder. Support often looks ordinary.
ramayan::1268.insight: It shifts attention from grand help to steady, practical care.

ramayan::1269.verse_sanskrit: अथ वर्षसहस्रे तु दशोने रघुनन्दन । दिति: परमसम्प्रीता सहस्राक्षमथाब्रवीत् । । 14612 । ।
ramayan::1269.verse_hindi: O son of the Raghus ten years before completion of a thousand years. Diti, highly pleased with the services rendered by Indra, addressed him, saying:
ramayan::1269.english_translation: O son of the Raghus, ten years before the thousand years were complete, Diti, greatly pleased, then spoke to Indra.
ramayan::1269.translation_literal: अथ (then) / वर्षसहस्रे (in a thousand years) / तु (indeed) / दशोने (ten less) / रघुनन्दन (O delight of the Raghu line) / दिति: (Diti) / परमसम्प्रीता (greatly pleased) / सहस्राक्षम् (to the thousand-eyed one) / अथ (then) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::1269.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1269.essence: A long service reaches the moment that changes its meaning.
ramayan::1269.simple_meaning: After almost a thousand years, Diti, satisfied by Indra's service, spoke to him.
ramayan::1269.simple_insight: Some moments are only the turning point before a long consequence unfolds.
ramayan::1269.detailed_meaning: Indra has spent years serving Diti to win her trust and complete a dangerous vow. At the end of the long wait, she is pleased enough to speak. The verse simply marks the moment before she reveals the boon he has earned.
ramayan::1269.modern_relevance: You can pour years into earning a yes, then finally hear the words that change everything. The real turning point is often the sentence after the waiting.
ramayan::1269.insight: It marks the shift from patient service to the moment of reward.

ramayan::1270.verse_sanskrit: याचितेन सुरश्रेष्ठ तव पित्रा महात्मना । वरो वर्षसहस्रान्ते दत्तो मम सुतं प्रति । । 14613 । ।
ramayan::1270.verse_hindi: O best of the gods your illustrious father granted me a boon for a son I sought on completion of a thousand years (of penance).
ramayan::1270.english_translation: O best of the gods, your illustrious father granted me a boon for a son I sought on completion of a thousand years of penance.
