ramayan::1270.translation_literal: याचितेन (sought by request) / सुरश्रेष्ठ (best of the gods) / तव (your) / पित्रा (by father) / महात्मना (illustrious, great-souled) / वरो (boon) / वर्षसहस्रान्ते (at the end of a thousand years) / दत्तः (given) / मम (my) / सुतं (son) / प्रति (for, regarding)
ramayan::1270.speaker: Diti
ramayan::1270.essence: A promise made long ago is now coming due.
ramayan::1270.simple_meaning: Diti reminds Indra that his noble father once granted her a boon: after a thousand years of austerity, she would receive a son.
ramayan::1270.simple_insight: A long struggle can end in a promise that shapes everything after it.
ramayan::1270.detailed_meaning: Diti is speaking to Indra after serving him for years. She recalls the old bargain made by his father: after a thousand years of penance, she would be granted a son. This verse is part of that tense reminder, not the main revelation.
ramayan::1270.modern_relevance: You remember the promise someone made when the effort still felt endless. Now the deadline has arrived, and the words suddenly have weight.
ramayan::1270.insight: It keeps attention on the binding force of a boon and the consequences of past agreements.

ramayan::1271.verse_sanskrit: तपश्चरन्त्या वर्षाणि दश वीर्यवतां वर । अवशिष्टानि भद्रं ते भ्रातरं द्रक्ष्यसे तत: । । 14614 । ।
ramayan::1271.verse_hindi: O the best of the brave ten years is yet to go (for completion of austerities). You will  have a brother. May you prosper
ramayan::1271.english_translation: O best of the brave, ten years remain before the austerities are complete. You will see a brother then. May you prosper.
ramayan::1271.translation_literal: तपश्चरन्त्या (by one performing austerities) / वर्षाणि (years) / दश (ten) / वीर्यवतां वर (O best of the brave) / अवशिष्टानि (remain) / भद्रं ते (may good be to you) / भ्रातरं (a brother) / द्रक्ष्यसे (you will see) / तत: (then)
ramayan::1271.speaker: Diti
ramayan::1271.essence: The promised result is coming, but the waiting is still real.
ramayan::1271.simple_meaning: Ten years still remain before the austerities are finished, and then a brother will be born.
ramayan::1271.simple_insight: Some things cannot be rushed; they ripen in their own time.
ramayan::1271.detailed_meaning: Diti, pleased by the boon granted to her, tells Indra that the remaining ten years of austerity must still pass. Only then will the promised brother appear. The verse is a bridge in the conversation, not the main teaching.
ramayan::1271.modern_relevance: You want the answer now, but the process still has time left. The promise is real; it simply is not ready yet.
ramayan::1271.insight: It teaches you to respect the unfinished work instead of forcing a premature result.

ramayan::1272.verse_sanskrit: तमहं त्वत्कृते पुत्र समाधास्ये जयोत्सुकम् । त्रैलोक्यविजयं पुत्र सह भोक्ष्यसि विज्वर: । । 14615 । ।
ramayan::1272.verse_hindi: O Child Ill create in him eagerness victory. Together with him you will gain victory over the three worlds. Relieved of sorrows, enjoy youll with him.
ramayan::1272.english_translation: O child, I will place in him an eagerness for victory. Together with him, you will win the three worlds and enjoy them without grief.
ramayan::1272.translation_literal: तम् (that one) / अहम् (I) / त्वत्कृते (for your sake) / पुत्र (O child) / समाधास्ये (will place) / जयोत्सुकम् (eager for victory) / त्रैलोक्यविजयम् (conquering the three worlds) / पुत्र (O child) / सह (together with) / भोक्ष्यसि (you will enjoy) / विज्वरः (free from grief)
ramayan::1272.speaker: Diti
ramayan::1272.essence: She plans a future victory by shaping the child’s desire.
ramayan::1272.simple_meaning: Diti tells Indra that she will place a desire for victory in the future child, and that Indra will then enjoy victory over the three worlds with him.
ramayan::1272.simple_insight: A hidden intention can shape an entire future before anyone sees it.
ramayan::1272.detailed_meaning: Diti has already secured a boon for a son and is speaking to Indra about the child she will bear. She promises to shape him so he will seek victory, and imagines a future where Indra shares triumph through him. The verse is part of a larger, deceptive plan.
ramayan::1272.modern_relevance: A parent can quietly shape a child’s ambitions long before the child can name them. A hope planted today can become tomorrow’s drive.
ramayan::1272.insight: It shows how intention and influence can be used to steer another life from the inside.

ramayan::1273.verse_sanskrit: एवमुक्त्वा दितिश्शक्रं प्राप्ते मध्यं दिवाकरे । निद्रयाऽपहृता देवी पादौ कृत्वाऽथ शीर्षत: । । 14616 । ।
ramayan::1273.verse_hindi: After speaking thus to Indra, goddess Diti overpowered with sleep around midsday dropped off, her feet towards her head.
ramayan::1273.english_translation: After speaking thus to Indra, the goddess Diti, overpowered by sleep at midday, lay with her feet turned toward her head.
ramayan::1273.translation_literal: एवमुक्त्वा (having spoken thus) / दितिः (Diti) / शक्रम् (to Indra) / प्राप्ते (having reached) / मध्यं (midday) / दिवाकरे (at the sun) / निद्रया (by sleep) / अपहृता (overpowered) / देवी (the goddess) / पादौ (feet) / कृत्वा (having placed) / अथ (then) / शीर्षत: (toward the head)
ramayan::1273.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1273.essence: A careless moment can open the way for disaster.
ramayan::1273.simple_meaning: Diti falls asleep at midday right after speaking to Indra, and her body ends up in an inauspicious position.
ramayan::1273.simple_insight: A small lapse can carry huge consequences when desire is driving the moment.
ramayan::1273.detailed_meaning: Diti has just made a dangerous request that will shape the future of the gods and their enemies. Exhausted, she sleeps at midday with her feet turned toward her head. The scene matters because this careless moment opens the door to the next calamity.
ramayan::1273.modern_relevance: You finally stop at noon after pushing through a tense conversation, and your guard drops. One careless moment can change everything that follows.
ramayan::1273.insight: It shows how a single lapse in vigilance can undo a carefully held intention.

ramayan::1274.verse_sanskrit: दृष्ट्वा तामशुचिं शक्र: पादत: कृतमूर्धजाम् । शिरस्स्थाने कृतौ पादौ जहास च मुमोद च । । 14617 । ।
ramayan::1274.verse_hindi: Indra laughed. He rejoiced at the sight of her ominous posture of sleeping with her feet towards her head and her hair falling on her feet.
ramayan::1274.english_translation: Indra laughed. He rejoiced at the sight of her inauspicious posture, with her feet where her head should be and her hair falling toward her feet.
ramayan::1274.translation_literal: दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / ताम् (her) / अशुचिम् (impure, inauspicious) / शक्रः (Indra) / पादतः (from the feet) / कृतमूर्धजाम् (with hair made at the head/turned downward) / शिरस्स्थाने (in the place of the head) / कृतौ (placed) / पादौ (feet) / जहास (laughed) / च (and) / मुमोद (rejoiced) / च (and)
ramayan::1274.speaker: Indra
ramayan::1274.essence: The opening appears when vigilance slips.
ramayan::1274.simple_meaning: Indra sees Diti sleeping in a reversed, inauspicious posture and laughs with satisfaction.
ramayan::1274.simple_insight: A moment of weakness can become a turning point for someone watching.
ramayan::1274.detailed_meaning: Diti has just been tricked into falling asleep at midday, opening the way for Indra’s plan to stop the dangerous birth. Seeing her lying with her feet toward her head, Indra laughs because the trap has worked and the moment he needed has arrived.
ramayan::1274.modern_relevance: You finally catch the opening you were waiting for: the pause in someone's guard, the mistake in their timing, the one moment your plan can move.
ramayan::1274.insight: It shows a decisive advantage: watch for the exact moment when weakness creates opportunity.

ramayan::1275.verse_sanskrit: तस्याश्शरीरविवरं विवेश च पुरन्दर: । गर्भं च सप्तधा राम बिभेद परमात्मवान् । । 14618 । ।
ramayan::1275.verse_hindi: O Rama with great courage Indra entered her womb and severed her embryo into  seven pieces.
ramayan::1275.english_translation: Indra entered her body and, O Rama, split the embryo into seven parts.
ramayan::1275.translation_literal: तस्याः (her) / शरीर-विवरम् (body opening) / विवेश (entered) / च (and) / पुरन्दरः (Indra) / गर्भम् (embryo) / च (and) / सप्तधा (into seven parts) / राम (O Rama) / बिभेद (split) / परमात्मवान् (the mighty one)
ramayan::1275.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1275.essence: Indra destroys the embryo before Diti wakes.
ramayan::1275.simple_meaning: Indra enters Diti's body and divides the embryo into seven parts.
ramayan::1275.simple_insight: The verse is a plot step, not a teaching. It moves the story forward by showing the embryo being destroyed.
ramayan::1275.detailed_meaning: Diti has fallen asleep at midday after Indra spots the vulnerable posture she has taken. He slips into her body and cuts the embryo into seven pieces. The next verse shows the embryo crying out and waking her, so this line is only one step in the unfolding scene.
ramayan::1275.insight: It advances the action without offering a separate lesson.

ramayan::1276.verse_sanskrit: भिद्यमानस्ततो गर्भो वज्रेण शतपर्वणा । रुरोद सुस्वरं राम ततो दितिरबुध्यत । । 14619 । ।
ramayan::1276.verse_hindi: O Rama that embryo, being severed by Vajra having a hundred edges, cried at high pitch which awakened Diti.
ramayan::1276.english_translation: When the embryo was split by the hundred-edged thunderbolt, it cried out loudly, and Diti woke up.
ramayan::1276.translation_literal: भिद्यमानः (being split) / ततः (then) / गर्भः (the embryo) / वज्रेण (by the thunderbolt) / शतपर्वणा (with a hundred edges) / रुरोद (cried) / सुस्वरम् (loudly) / राम (O Rama) / ततः (then) / दिति: (Diti) / अबुध्यत (woke up)
ramayan::1276.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1276.essence: Violence inside the unseen still wakes the one it harms.
ramayan::1276.simple_meaning: The embryo was cut by Indra's thunderbolt and cried out loudly, waking Diti.
ramayan::1276.simple_insight: A hidden act can still be felt at once.
ramayan::1276.detailed_meaning: Indra has entered Diti's womb to destroy the embryo. The thunderbolt splits it, and the cry wakes Diti, showing that even a concealed act of force has an immediate, living consequence.
ramayan::1276.modern_relevance: You think the damage stayed hidden, but something in the room already felt it.
ramayan::1276.insight: It shows that force creates an instant response, even before the larger outcome is visible.

ramayan::1277.verse_sanskrit: मा रुदो मा रुदश्चेति गर्भं शक्रोऽभ्यभाषत । बिभेद च महातेजा रुदन्तमपि वासव: । । 14620 । ।
ramayan::1277.verse_hindi: Highly powerful Indra, even while saying to the crying embryo  Do not weep, Do not weep severed it.
ramayan::1277.english_translation: Highly powerful Indra, even while saying to the crying embryo, "Do not weep, do not weep," severed it.
ramayan::1277.translation_literal: मा रुदो (do not weep) / मा रुदश्चेति (saying, do not weep) / गर्भं (the embryo) / शक्रः (Indra) / अभ्यभाषत (spoke) / बिभेद (severed) / च (and) / महातेजाः (highly powerful) / रुदन्तम् (crying) / अपि (even) / वासवः (Indra)
ramayan::1277.speaker: Indra
ramayan::1277.essence: Gentle words do not make a violent act harmless.
ramayan::1277.simple_meaning: Indra tells the crying embryo not to cry, and still cuts it into pieces.
ramayan::1277.simple_insight: Power can speak gently and still act violently.
ramayan::1277.detailed_meaning: Indra has entered Diti's womb to destroy the unborn threat. The embryo cries out, but he continues anyway, speaking soothing words while using the thunderbolt. The verse is a grim action step in the larger story, not a teaching on its own.
ramayan::1277.modern_relevance: A harsh decision can wear a calm face. Someone may speak softly while still doing what hurts.
ramayan::1277.insight: It shows how cruelty can hide behind polite words and controlled tone.

ramayan::1278.verse_sanskrit: न हन्तव्यो न हन्तव्य इत्येवं दितिरब्रवीत् । निष्पपात ततश्शक्रो मातुर्वचनगौरवात् । । 14621 । ।
ramayan::1278.verse_hindi: Do not kill, Do not kill, said Diti. Subsequently Indra, in deference to the words of his mother, emerged out of the womb.
ramayan::1278.english_translation: Do not kill, do not kill, said Diti. Out of respect for his mother's words, Indra then emerged from the womb.
ramayan::1278.translation_literal: न हन्तव्यः (do not be killed) / न हन्तव्यः (do not be killed) / इति (thus) / एवम् (in this way) / दिति (Diti) / अब्रवीत् (said) / निष्पपात (came out) / ततः (then) / शक्रः (Indra) / मातुः (mother's) / वचनगौरवात् (out of respect for the words)
ramayan::1278.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1278.essence: A mother's plea can halt even the hand that was already raised.
ramayan::1278.simple_meaning: Diti begs for the embryo's life, and Indra stops because he honors his mother's words.
ramayan::1278.simple_insight: Even force yields when reverence enters the moment.
ramayan::1278.detailed_meaning: Indra has already struck the embryo in Diti's womb, and the crying child has awakened her. At her plea, he stops. The scene turns on one thing: a mother's words carry enough weight to halt even a god of thunder.
ramayan::1278.modern_relevance: A furious text is half-written, your reply is ready, and then you remember who is on the other side. Respect can interrupt violence before it becomes permanent.
ramayan::1278.insight: It shows how reverence can stop a destructive act before it hardens.

ramayan::1279.verse_sanskrit: प्राञ्जलिर्वज्रसहितो दितिं शक्रोऽभ्यभाषत । अशुचिर्देवि सुप्ताऽसि पादयो: कृतमूर्धजा । । 14622 । ।
ramayan::1279.verse_hindi: Armed with Vajra, Indra addressed Diti with folded palms, saying, O Devi you have slept,  with your head towards your feet and your hair falling on your feet.
ramayan::1279.english_translation: Armed with the thunderbolt, Indra addressed Diti with folded palms: "O Devi, you have slept with your head toward your feet, and your hair has fallen onto your feet."
ramayan::1279.translation_literal: प्राञ्जलिः (with folded palms) / वज्रसहितः (armed with the thunderbolt) / दितिम् (to Diti) / शक्रः (Indra) / अभ्यभाषत (spoke) / अशुचिः (impure) / देवि (O Devi) / सुप्ता असि (you have slept) / पादयोः (toward the feet) / कृतमूर्धजा (with the head placed)
ramayan::1279.speaker: Indra
ramayan::1279.essence: A small breach becomes the doorway for a larger ruin.
ramayan::1279.simple_meaning: Indra speaks respectfully to Diti after entering her womb, pointing out that she has violated ritual purity by sleeping in an inauspicious way.
ramayan::1279.simple_insight: A tiny lapse can become the opening through which a long consequence enters.
ramayan::1279.detailed_meaning: Diti has already been warned, and Indra has been waiting inside her womb to stop the birth of a threat to his rule. Before striking, he speaks to her with folded hands and points to the fault that made the opening possible.
ramayan::1279.modern_relevance: You ignore one small rule when you are tired, and later wonder how everything went sideways. The breach looked minor at the time; the consequences were not.
ramayan::1279.insight: It shows how one neglected boundary can create room for irreversible harm.

ramayan::1280.verse_sanskrit: तदन्तरमहं लब्ध्वा शक्रहन्तारमाहवे । अभिदं सप्तधा देवि तन्मे त्वं क्षन्तुमर्हसि । । 14623 । ।
ramayan::1280.verse_hindi: I have seized the opportunity and severed into seven pieces the foetus who would have been a slayer of Indra. O Devi shoudnt you forgive me?
ramayan::1280.english_translation: I seized the chance and cut the embryo that would have killed Indra into seven pieces, O Devi; should you not forgive me?
ramayan::1280.translation_literal: तदन्तरम् (that interval) / अहम् (I) / लब्ध्वा (having obtained) / शक्रहन्तारम् (Indra-slayer) / आहवे (in battle) / अभिदम् (I cut) / सप्तधा (into seven parts) / देवि (O Devi) / तत् (that) / मे (me) / त्वम् (you) / क्षन्तुम् (to forgive) / अर्हसि (should be able)
ramayan::1280.speaker: Indra
ramayan::1280.essence: A defensive act can still leave a moral wound.
ramayan::1280.simple_meaning: Indra explains that he took the chance and divided the threatening embryo into seven parts, then asks Diti to forgive him.
ramayan::1280.simple_insight: Some actions are done under pressure, but their consequences still remain.
ramayan::1280.detailed_meaning: Diti has been tricked into an inauspicious sleep, and Indra appears before her in remorseful triumph. He admits he split the threatening embryo into seven pieces to prevent his own death. The verse is a confession inside a larger divine deception.
ramayan::1280.modern_relevance: You act fast in a crisis, then have to live with what that speed destroyed. The explanation may soften it, but it does not erase the cost.
ramayan::1280.insight: It shows how victory and guilt can arrive together, even in the same breath.

ramayan::1281.verse_sanskrit: सप्तधातु कृते गर्भे दिति: परमदु:खिता । सहस्राक्षं दुराधर्षं वाक्यं सानुनयाऽब्रवीत् । । 1471 । ।
ramayan::1281.verse_hindi: Deeply distressed Diti, having come to know that the embryo had been severed into seven pieces, humbly spoke to the unassailable Indra.
ramayan::1281.english_translation: Deeply distressed Diti, having come to know that the embryo had been severed into seven pieces, humbly spoke to the unassailable Indra.
ramayan::1281.translation_literal: सप्तधा (into seven parts) / कृते (having been made) / गर्भे (in the embryo) / दिति: (Diti) / परमदु:खिता (deeply distressed) / सहस्राक्षं (to the thousand-eyed one) / दुराधर्षं (the unassailable one) / वाक्यं (speech) / सानुनय (humbly, with entreaty) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::1281.speaker: Diti
ramayan::1281.essence: Pain can make even accusation sound like a request.
ramayan::1281.simple_meaning: Diti is devastated when she learns the embryo has been cut into seven parts, and she speaks to Indra with humility.
ramayan::1281.simple_insight: Grief can soften even a powerful person into humility.
ramayan::1281.detailed_meaning: Diti has just learned that her embryo has been divided into seven pieces. Shocked and heartbroken, she turns to Indra, the unassailable thousand-eyed king, and speaks not with rage but with pleading humility. The passage is a step in the larger exchange, not its conclusion.
ramayan::1281.modern_relevance: You discover that something precious has been damaged beyond repair, and anger rises first. Then, somehow, you still have to speak carefully.
ramayan::1281.insight: It shows how distress can turn confrontation into a plea for understanding.

ramayan::1282.verse_sanskrit: ममापराधाद्गर्भोऽयं सप्तधा विफलीकृत: । नापराधोऽस्ति देवेश तवात्र बलसूदन । । 1472 । ।
ramayan::1282.verse_hindi: O Indra, Slayer of Balasura, because of my fault this embryo has been made into
ramayan::1282.english_translation: O Indra, Slayer of Balasura, because of my fault this embryo has been made into seven parts. No fault of yours exists here, O lord of the gods.
ramayan::1282.translation_literal: मम (my) / अपराधात् (because of fault) / गर्भः (embryo) / अयम् (this) / सप्तधा (into seven parts) / विफलीकृतः (made fruitless, ruined) / न (not) / अपराधः (fault) / अस्ति (exists) / देवेश (O lord of the gods) / तव (your) / अत्र (here) / बलसूदन (O slayer of Balasura)
ramayan::1282.speaker: Diti
ramayan::1282.essence: She absorbs the blame before asking for a way forward.
ramayan::1282.simple_meaning: Diti accepts blame for the embryo being split into seven parts and tells Indra he is not at fault.
ramayan::1282.simple_insight: Taking responsibility can soften anger and open the way to a new request.
ramayan::1282.detailed_meaning: Diti, grieving after her embryo has been divided sevenfold, speaks humbly to Indra. Instead of accusing him, she places the blame on herself and prepares to ask for a boon that will turn this loss into something meaningful.
ramayan::1282.modern_relevance: You make a mistake that affects everyone, and the first hard step is saying, clearly, that the fault is yours.
ramayan::1282.insight: It shifts the mind from blame to responsibility, making room for repair instead of conflict.

ramayan::1283.verse_sanskrit: प्रियं तु कर्तुमिच्छामि मम गर्भविपर्यये । मरुतां सप्तसप्तानां स्थानपाला भवन्त्विमे । । 1473 । ।
ramayan::1283.verse_hindi: This disaster to the embryo has happened contrary to expectations. Hence, I seek a favour from you. Let these seven pieces become seven guardians of marut regions (regions of the wind).
ramayan::1283.english_translation: I wish to do something pleasing. Let these seven pieces become the guardians of the seven regions of the winds.
ramayan::1283.translation_literal: प्रियम् (pleasing) / तु (indeed) / कर्तुम् (to do) / इच्छामि (I wish) / मम (my) / गर्भ-विपर्यये (in the change to the embryo) / मरुताम् (of the winds) / सप्त-सप्तानाम् (of the seven sevens) / स्थान-पालाḥ (guardians of the places) / भवन्तु (may become) / इमे (these)
ramayan::1283.speaker: Diti
ramayan::1283.essence: Broken things can still be given a sacred function.
ramayan::1283.simple_meaning: Diti asks Indra for a blessing: let the broken pieces of the embryo become guardians of the seven wind regions.
ramayan::1283.simple_insight: Even a painful loss can be turned toward a new role.
ramayan::1283.detailed_meaning: Diti has already admitted fault and accepted the damage done to her embryo. Instead of remaining in grief, she asks for a grace that transforms the seven pieces into guardians of the wind realms, turning tragedy into cosmic order.
ramayan::1283.modern_relevance: A plan falls apart after months of work, and you are left with pieces that no longer fit. This verse imagines asking for those broken parts to still serve a larger purpose.
ramayan::1283.insight: It shifts the mind from lamenting damage to seeking a constructive transformation.

ramayan::1284.verse_sanskrit: वातस्कन्धा: इमे सप्त चरन्तु दिवि पुत्रक । मारुता इति विख्याता दिव्यरूपा ममात्मजा: । । 1474 । ।
ramayan::1284.verse_hindi: O Son, all these seven are my sons of celestial beauty.They will become pesiding deities for Vata Skandha (divisions of wind) and let them be wellknown as maruts wandering in the universe.
ramayan::1284.english_translation: O son, let these seven move through the sky. They are my sons of radiant form, and they will be known as the Maruts.
ramayan::1284.translation_literal: वातस्कन्धा: (wind-divisions / divisions of wind) / इमे (these) / सप्त (seven) / चरन्तु (let them move) / दिवि (in the sky) / पुत्रक (O son) / मारुता: (Maruts) / इति (thus) / विख्याता: (well-known) / दिव्यरूपा: (of celestial form) / मम (my) / आत्मजा: (sons)
ramayan::1284.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1284.essence: What was broken is reimagined as a new form of power.
ramayan::1284.simple_meaning: The seven children are being assigned to move through the sky and become known as the Maruts, divine wind beings.
ramayan::1284.simple_insight: Some losses are transformed into a larger role instead of ending the story.
ramayan::1284.detailed_meaning: After the embryo is broken into seven, the divine mother asks for a new fate for them. She asks that these seven radiant sons become the Maruts, roaming the sky as wind powers. This verse is one step in that transformation, not the main teaching.
ramayan::1284.modern_relevance: A plan falls apart before it even begins, and you have to decide what it becomes now. Sometimes the answer is not repair, but reinvention.
ramayan::1284.insight: It shifts attention from what was lost to what can still be made of it.

ramayan::1285.verse_sanskrit: ब्रह्मलोकं चरत्वेक इन्द्रलोकं तथाऽपर: । दिवि वायुरिति ख्यातस्तृतीयोऽपि महायशा: । । 1475 । ।
ramayan::1285.verse_hindi: Among them, one will move about in Brahmaloka, another in Indraloka, and the third, well known as vayu will move around in the sky.
ramayan::1285.english_translation: Among them, one will move about in Brahmaloka, another in Indraloka, and the third, well known as Vayu, will move around in the sky.
ramayan::1285.translation_literal: ब्रह्मलोकम् (to Brahmaloka) / चरतु (let him move) / एकः (one) / इन्द्रलोकम् (to Indraloka) / तथा (likewise) / अपरः (another) / दिवि (in the sky) / वायुः इति (as Vayu) / ख्यातः (known) / तृतीयः अपि (the third also) / महायशाः (greatly renowned)
ramayan::1285.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1285.essence: Different natures belong in different realms of service.
ramayan::1285.simple_meaning: Three celestial sons are assigned different realms: one to Brahmaloka, one to Indraloka, and one to the sky as Vayu.
ramayan::1285.simple_insight: Great beings are given fitting places, each according to a larger order.
ramayan::1285.detailed_meaning: Brahma is speaking about the seven sons born from the disrupted pregnancy. He assigns them future stations among the celestial realms, naming one Brahmaloka, one Indraloka, and one Vayu. The verse is part of a larger blessing, not a complete teaching on its own.
ramayan::1285.modern_relevance: A parent mapping out different futures for children, each with a distinct strength, can feel this: not everyone is meant for the same role. Some are built for one arena, some for another.
ramayan::1285.insight: It frames difference as destiny of function, not as inequality.

ramayan::1286.verse_sanskrit: चत्वारस्तु सुरश्रेष्ठ दिशो वै तव शासनात् । सञ्चरिष्यन्तु भद्रं ते देवभूता ममात्मजा: । । 1476 । ।
ramayan::1286.verse_hindi: O best of devatas by your command the other four sons will remain celestial, and will range about in four directions.
ramayan::1286.english_translation: O best of the radiant beings, by your command the other four sons will remain celestial and roam in the four directions.
ramayan::1286.translation_literal: चत्वारः (four) / तु (indeed) / सुरश्रेष्ठ (O best of the radiant beings) / दिशः (the directions) / वै (indeed) / तव (your) / शासनात् (by command) / सञ्चरिष्यन्तु (will roam) / भद्रं ते (may good be to you) / देवभूताः (having become celestial beings) / ममात्मजाः (my sons)
ramayan::1286.speaker: Brahma
ramayan::1286.essence: Their place in the cosmos is assigned, not chosen.
ramayan::1286.simple_meaning: Four of the sons will remain in the celestial realm and move through the four directions by Brahma's command.
ramayan::1286.simple_insight: Some beings are assigned a vast, unseen role beyond ordinary life.
ramayan::1286.detailed_meaning: Brahma is distributing the sons of Diti into different cosmic functions. After naming the earlier three, he assigns the remaining four to roam the four directions as celestial beings. It is part of a larger account of their future roles, not a complete teaching on its own.
ramayan::1286.modern_relevance: A manager assigns team members to different regions in one long meeting, and you only hear one line of the rollout. The verse is that kind of detail: a placement inside a larger plan.
ramayan::1286.insight: It points to order in the cosmos, where each being has a designated sphere of movement.

ramayan::1287.verse_sanskrit: तस्यास्तद्वचनं श्रुत्वा सहस्राक्ष: पुरन्दर: । उवाच प्राञ्जलिर्वाक्यं दितिं बलनिषूदन: । । 1477 । ।
ramayan::1287.verse_hindi: The thousandeyed Indra, slayer of Bala, on hearing Ditis words, addressed her with folded palms, saying:
ramayan::1287.english_translation: Hearing her words, the thousand-eyed Indra, slayer of Bala, with folded palms said to Diti:
ramayan::1287.translation_literal: तस्याः (her) / तद्-वचनम् (that speech) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / सहस्र-अक्षः (thousand-eyed) / पुरन्दरः (Indra) / उवाच (said) / प्राञ्जलिः (with folded palms) / वाक्यम् (words) / दितिम् (to Diti) / बल-निषूदनः (slayer of Bala)
ramayan::1287.speaker: Indra
ramayan::1287.essence: Power bows before speech before it answers.
ramayan::1287.simple_meaning: Indra listens carefully to Diti and replies respectfully with folded hands.
ramayan::1287.simple_insight: Even a powerful figure can answer with humility when the moment calls for it.
ramayan::1287.detailed_meaning: Diti has spoken, and Indra—the thousand-eyed ruler of the heavens—responds not with force but with joined palms. This is a bridge verse in the exchange, showing his formal respect before he gives his answer in the next line.
ramayan::1287.modern_relevance: Someone challenges you in a meeting, and instead of snapping back, you pause and answer with calm respect.
ramayan::1287.insight: It shows that strength can include restraint, courtesy, and the willingness to listen before speaking.

ramayan::1288.verse_sanskrit: सर्वमेतद्यथोक्तं ते भविष्यति न संशय: । विचरिष्यन्ति भद्रं ते देवभूतास्तवात्मजा: । । 1478 । ।
ramayan::1288.verse_hindi: Everything will, no doubt, happen the way you said. Your sons will wander about as celestial beings. Prosperity to you.
ramayan::1288.english_translation: Everything will, no doubt, happen the way you said. Your sons will wander about as celestial beings. Prosperity to you.
ramayan::1288.translation_literal: सर्वम् (everything) / एतत् (this) / यथा उक्तम् (as said) / ते (to you) / भविष्यति (will be) / न (not) / संशयः (doubt) / विचरिष्यन्ति (will wander) / भद्रम् (prosperity) / ते (to you) / देवभूताः (celestial beings) / तव (your) / आत्मजाः (sons)
ramayan::1288.speaker: Indra
ramayan::1288.essence: A spoken promise becomes binding reality.
ramayan::1288.simple_meaning: Indra assures Diti that her wish will be fulfilled: her sons will become celestial beings and move freely in the higher realm.
ramayan::1288.simple_insight: A sincere request, once answered, can reshape an entire fate.
ramayan::1288.detailed_meaning: Diti has spoken with folded hands, and Indra responds with calm certainty. He agrees to her condition: her sons will become celestial beings and move in the higher realm. The verse seals the agreement before the final ascent.
ramayan::1288.modern_relevance: You wait for a hard conversation to end, and then the other person finally says, “Yes — that will happen.” The tension breaks, but only because a deeper bargain has already been accepted.
ramayan::1288.insight: It closes a promise that will soon be carried into action.

ramayan::1289.verse_sanskrit: एवं तौ निश्चयं कृत्वा मातापुत्रौ तपोवने । जग्मतुस्त्रिदिवं राम कृतार्थाविति नश्श्रुतम् । । 1479 । ।
ramayan::1289.verse_hindi: O Rama mother and sons having arrived at this conclusion in the tapovana  ascended to heaven with their desire fulfilled. This is what we have heard.
ramayan::1289.english_translation: O Rama, the mother and her sons, having reached this conclusion in the forest of austerities, ascended to heaven with their desire fulfilled. This is what we have heard.
ramayan::1289.translation_literal: एवम् (thus) / तौ (the two of them) / निश्चयम् (decision) / कृत्वा (having made) / मातापुत्रौ (the mother and the sons) / तपोवने (in the forest of austerities) / जग्मतुः (went) / त्रिदिवम् (to heaven) / राम (O Rama) / कृतार्थौ (having achieved their purpose) / इति (thus) / नः श्रुतम् (we have heard)
ramayan::1289.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1289.essence: The story ends with fulfilled purpose, not dramatic struggle.
ramayan::1289.simple_meaning: After agreeing on their course in the forest, the mother and her sons rose to a higher realm with their aim fulfilled.
ramayan::1289.simple_insight: Some endings come quietly, after the right choice has already been made.
ramayan::1289.detailed_meaning: Valmiki closes the Diti-Indra episode by saying that Diti and her sons reached a final decision in the forest of austerities and then went to the higher realm fulfilled. It is a compact narrative ending, not a teaching by itself.
ramayan::1289.modern_relevance: A long conversation ends, the decision is made, and everyone leaves the room changed. The real turning point was not the departure — it was the agreement reached before it.
ramayan::1289.insight: It completes the scene rather than teaching a new principle, so the focus stays on resolution and closure.

ramayan::1290.verse_sanskrit: एष देशस्स काकुत्स्थ महेन्द्राध्युषित: पुरा । दितिं यत्र तपस्सिद्धामेवं परिचचार स: । । 14710 । ।
ramayan::1290.verse_hindi: O Descendant of Kakustha (Rama) this is that country which was formerly inhabited by Indra. Here Indra  attended on Diti who achieved the fruit of her austerities.
ramayan::1290.english_translation: O Descendant of Kakustha, this is the country that was once inhabited by Indra. Here, Indra attended Diti, who had attained the fruit of her austerities.
ramayan::1290.translation_literal: एष (this) / देशः (country) / काकुत्स्थ (O descendant of Kakustha) / महेन्द्र-अध्युषितः (inhabited by Indra) / पुरा (formerly) / दितिम् (Diti) / यत्र (where) / तपः-सिद्धाम् (one perfected by austerity) / एवम् (thus) / परिचचार (attended upon) / सः (he)
ramayan::1290.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1290.essence: A place becomes sacred through what happened there.
ramayan::1290.simple_meaning: This place was once ruled by Indra, and it is remembered because Indra served Diti after her austerities bore fruit.
ramayan::1290.simple_insight: Some places carry memory. Their meaning comes from what was done there, not just what stands there now.
ramayan::1290.detailed_meaning: Rama is being shown a land tied to old cosmic memory. The speaker points out that Indra once dwelt here and served Diti after her tapas. The verse is a descriptive link in a larger account, not a teaching on its own.
ramayan::1290.modern_relevance: You walk into a room and feel its history before anyone speaks. Some places still carry the weight of what was endured, earned, or repaired there.
ramayan::1290.insight: It shifts attention from geography to the moral memory a place can hold.

ramayan::1291.verse_sanskrit: इक्ष्वाकोऽस्तु नरव्याघ्र पुत्र: परमधार्मिक: । । 14711 । । अलम्बुषायामुत्पन्नो विशाल इति विश्रुत: । तेन चासीदिह स्थाने विशालेति पुरी कृता । । 14712 । ।
ramayan::1291.verse_hindi: O Tiger among men (Rama) this highly virtuous and wellknown son named Vishala was born to Ikshvakus in Alambusa. Where, a city named Vishala was built.
ramayan::1291.english_translation: O Tiger among men, the highly virtuous and famous son of Ikshvaku, named Vishala, was born in Alambusa. A city called Vishala was built there.
ramayan::1291.translation_literal: इक्ष्वाकोः (of Ikshvaku) / अस्तु (was) / नरव्याघ्र (O tiger among men) / पुत्रः (son) / परमधार्मिकः (highly virtuous) / अलम्बुषायाम् (in Alambusa) / उत्पन्नः (born) / विशालः (Vishala) / इति (thus) / विश्रुतः (famous) / तेन (by him) / च (and) / आसीत् (was) / इह (here) / स्थाने (in this place) / विशाला (Vishala) / इति (thus) / पुरी (city) / कृता (made)
ramayan::1291.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1291.essence: A city can outlive the king who gave it its name.
ramayan::1291.simple_meaning: A king named Vishala was born in Alambusa, and a city named after him was founded there.
ramayan::1291.simple_insight: Some verses simply preserve lineage and place, showing how memory becomes geography.
ramayan::1291.detailed_meaning: Rama is being shown a sacred landscape tied to old kings and ancient memory. This verse identifies Vishala, a virtuous descendant of Ikshvaku, and explains how the city of Vishala received its name. It is background detail, not a teaching.
ramayan::1291.modern_relevance: You walk through a city whose name outlasted the people who gave it meaning. Most of history survives like that: as a signboard, a street, a story someone still repeats.
ramayan::1291.insight: It shifts attention from moral instruction to ancestral record and place-naming.

ramayan::1292.verse_sanskrit: विशालस्य सुतो राम हेमचन्द्रो महाबल: । सुचन्द्र इति विख्यात: हेमचन्द्रादनन्तर: । । 14713 । ।
ramayan::1292.verse_hindi: O Rama mighty Hemachandra was Vishalas son. Hemachandras successor was the celebrated Suchandra.
ramayan::1292.english_translation: O Rama, mighty Hemachandra was Vishala's son. Hemachandra's successor was the celebrated Suchandra.
ramayan::1292.translation_literal: विशालस्य (of Vishala) / सुतः (son) / राम (O Rama) / हेमचन्द्रः (Hemachandra) / महाबलः (mighty) / सुचन्द्रः (Suchandra) / इति (thus) / विख्यातः (celebrated) / हेमचन्द्रात् (after Hemachandra) / अनन्तरः (successor)
ramayan::1292.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1292.essence: A lineage is kept alive by remembering each name in order.
ramayan::1292.simple_meaning: This is a genealogical line naming Vishala, Hemachandra, and Suchandra in sequence.
ramayan::1292.simple_insight: Some verses simply preserve the chain of names that holds a lineage together.
ramayan::1292.detailed_meaning: The narration continues listing the ancient kings connected to this land. After Vishala comes Hemachandra, and after Hemachandra comes Suchandra. Nothing is argued here; the verse simply keeps the royal succession intact.
ramayan::1292.modern_relevance: You open an old family record and see names passing hand to hand across generations. The point is not drama — it is continuity.
ramayan::1292.insight: It reminds you that some passages exist to preserve memory, not to deliver a lesson.

ramayan::1293.verse_sanskrit: सुचन्द्रतनयो राम धूम्राश्व इति विश्रुत: । धूम्राश्वतनयश्चापि सञ्जयस्समपद्यत । । 14714 । ।
ramayan::1293.verse_hindi: O Rama son of Suchandra was Dhumraswa, wellknown Sanjaya was the son of Dhumraswa.
ramayan::1293.english_translation: O Rama, Suchandra's son was Dhumraswa, and Dhumraswa's son was the well-known Sanjaya.
ramayan::1293.translation_literal: सुचन्द्रतनयः (son of Suchandra) / राम (O Rama) / धूम्राश्वः (Dhumraswa) / इति (thus) / विश्रुतः (well-known) / धूम्राश्वतनयः (son of Dhumraswa) / च (and) / अपि (also) / सञ्जयः (Sanjaya) / समपद्यत (was born)
ramayan::1293.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1293.essence: A royal lineage is being listed, not a lesson being taught.
ramayan::1293.simple_meaning: This verse continues a royal family line, naming two more kings in sequence. It gives genealogy, not teaching or reflection.
ramayan::1293.simple_insight: Some verses simply place you in the lineage before the story moves on.
ramayan::1293.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is tracing the ancient solar dynasty for Rama. After naming Suchandra, he adds that Suchandra's son was Dhumraswa and Dhumraswa's son was Sanjaya. The verse serves the genealogy, not the plot.
ramayan::1293.insight: It shifts attention to ancestry rather than action, keeping the royal line intact.

ramayan::1294.verse_sanskrit: सञ्जयस्य सुतश्श्रीमान् सहदेव: प्रतापवान् । कुशाश्वस्सहदेवस्य पुत्र: परमधार्मिक: । । 14715 । ।
ramayan::1294.verse_hindi: Prosperous and powerful Sahadeva was Sanjayas son. Highly virtuous Kusaswa was Sahadevas son.
ramayan::1294.english_translation: Prosperous and powerful Sahadeva was Sanjaya's son. Highly virtuous Kusaswa was Sahadeva's son.
ramayan::1294.translation_literal: सञ्जयस्य (of Sanjaya) / सुतः (son) / श्रीमान् (prosperous, splendid) / सहदेवः (Sahadeva) / प्रतापवान् (powerful, radiant) / कुशाश्वः (Kusaswa) / सहदेवस्य (of Sahadeva) / पुत्रः (son) / परमधार्मिकः (highly virtuous)
ramayan::1294.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1294.essence: A royal line is being traced, not a lesson being taught.
ramayan::1294.simple_meaning: This is a genealogy line naming two descendants and describing them with honorific qualities.
ramayan::1294.simple_insight: It reminds you that lineage is remembered through both names and character.
ramayan::1294.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is listing the royal line in sequence: Sanjaya’s son Sahadeva, then Sahadeva’s son Kusaswa. The verse is part of a chain of ancestry, not a teaching moment, and it simply preserves the family line.
ramayan::1294.modern_relevance: A family tree gets read aloud at a reunion, and each name carries the weight of those who came before. This verse works the same way: it preserves continuity, not instruction.
ramayan::1294.insight: It shifts attention from doctrine to record, showing how epics preserve inheritance through names.

ramayan::1295.verse_sanskrit: कुशाश्वस्य महातेजा सोमदत्त: प्रतापवान् । सोमदत्तस्य पुत्रस्तु काकुत्स्थ इति विश्रुत: । । 14716 । ।
ramayan::1295.verse_hindi: Brilliant and powerful Somadatta was Kusaswas son. That Somadattas son was Kakutstha is wellknown.
ramayan::1295.english_translation: Brilliant and powerful Somadatta was Kusaswa's son. Somadatta's son was the well-known Kakutstha.
ramayan::1295.translation_literal: कुशाश्वस्य (of Kusashva) / महातेजा (very brilliant) / सोमदत्त: (Somadatta) / प्रतापवान् (powerful) / सोमदत्तस्य (of Somadatta) / पुत्रः (son) / तु (indeed) / काकुत्स्थः (Kakutstha) / इति (thus) / विश्रुतः (well-known)
ramayan::1295.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1295.essence: A royal name enters the lineage, not the argument.
ramayan::1295.simple_meaning: Somadatta is introduced as the son of Kusashva, and Kakutstha is named as Somadatta's son.
ramayan::1295.simple_insight: The verse simply preserves a family line, not a teaching.
ramayan::1295.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is tracing the solar dynasty's genealogy, naming Kusashva, Somadatta, and Kakutstha in sequence. No decision, emotion, or teaching is being argued here; the verse serves the larger royal lineage record.
ramayan::1295.insight: It keeps the ancestral line clear for the story that follows.

ramayan::1296.verse_sanskrit: तस्य पुत्रो महातेजा: सम्प्रत्येष पुरीमिमाम् । आवसत्यमरप्रख्यस्सुमतिर्नाम दुर्जय: । । 14717 । ।
ramayan::1296.verse_hindi: Son of Ikshvakus, Sumati comparable to devatas, invincible and exceedingly energetic is still ruling this city.
ramayan::1296.english_translation: Son of Ikshvaku, Sumati, comparable to the radiant beings, invincible and exceedingly energetic, still rules this city.
ramayan::1296.translation_literal: तस्य (his) / पुत्रः (son) / महातेजाः (greatly radiant) / सम्प्रति (still now) / एषः (this one) / पुरीम् (city) / इमाम् (this) / आवसति (dwells in, rules) / अमरप्रख्यः (like the radiant beings) / सुमतिः (Sumati) / नाम (named) / दुर्जयः (invincible)
ramayan::1296.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1296.essence: A noble line matters only if it still holds power with strength.
ramayan::1296.simple_meaning: Sumati, a powerful and invincible ruler descended from Ikshvaku, still governs this city.
ramayan::1296.simple_insight: Great lineage is shown by steady rule, not by loud claims.
ramayan::1296.detailed_meaning: The genealogy continues from Ikshvaku through Sahadeva, Kusashva, and Somadatta to Sumati, who still rules this city. The verse is part of a lineage list, preserving royal continuity rather than offering a teaching of its own.
ramayan::1296.modern_relevance: A family name can open doors, but it does not matter unless someone is still carrying the responsibility well today.
ramayan::1296.insight: It shifts attention from ancestry to the living duty of rule.

ramayan::1297.verse_sanskrit: इक्ष्वाकोस्तु प्रसादेन सर्वे वैशालिका नृपा: । दीर्घायुषो महात्मानो वीर्यवन्तस्सुधार्मिका: । । 14718 । ।
ramayan::1297.verse_hindi: By the grace of the Ikshvakus, all the kings of Vishala have been long lived and exalted, valiant and deeply religious.
ramayan::1297.english_translation: By the grace of the Ikshvakus, all the kings of Vishala have been long-lived, noble, valiant, and righteous.
ramayan::1297.translation_literal: इक्ष्वाकोः (of Ikshvaku) / तु (indeed) / प्रसादेन (by grace) / सर्वे (all) / वैशालिका (of Vishala) / नृपाः (kings) / दीर्घायुषः (long-lived) / महात्मानः (great-souled) / वीर्यवन्तः (valiant) / सुदार्मिकाः (deeply righteous)
ramayan::1297.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1297.essence: A noble lineage is measured by the character it leaves behind.
ramayan::1297.simple_meaning: The kings of Vishala are praised as long-lived, noble, brave, and righteous because of Ikshvaku's blessing.
ramayan::1297.simple_insight: Good rule is remembered as a blessing that outlives the ruler.
ramayan::1297.detailed_meaning: Valmiki pauses the story to describe Vishala's royal line. The city's kings are said to have inherited their strength and righteousness from Ikshvaku's grace, not from mere power. It is a genealogical praise, not a teaching.
ramayan::1297.modern_relevance: A family name still opens doors in some places, but character is what keeps them open. This verse remembers a line of rulers whose reputation came from how they lived.
ramayan::1297.insight: It frames leadership as inherited responsibility, not just inherited status.

ramayan::1298.verse_sanskrit: इहाद्य रजनीं राम सुखं वत्स्यामहे वयम् । श्व: प्रभाते नरश्रेष्ठ जनकं द्रष्टुमर्हसि । । 14719 । ।
ramayan::1298.verse_hindi: O Rama we shall spend the right happily here. O Best among men On the tomorrow we see Janaka.
ramayan::1298.english_translation: O Rama, we shall spend this night happily here. Tomorrow morning, best among men, you will see Janaka.
ramayan::1298.translation_literal: इह (here) / अद्य (today) / रजनीं (the night) / राम (Rama) / सुखं (happily) / वत्स्यामहे (we shall dwell/spend) / वयम् (we) / श्वः (tomorrow) / प्रभाते (at dawn) / नरश्रेष्ठ (best among men) / जनकं (Janaka) / द्रष्टुम् (to see) / अर्हसि (you are worthy/you should)
ramayan::1298.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1298.essence: Rest tonight; the next meeting comes at dawn.
ramayan::1298.simple_meaning: They plan to rest for the night and meet Janaka the next morning.
ramayan::1298.simple_insight: Not every important moment is dramatic; sometimes the path forward is simply to rest and continue tomorrow.
ramayan::1298.detailed_meaning: Rama has reached a new city, and the people around him speak with calm hospitality. The immediate concern is practical: spend the night here, then meet Janaka at dawn. It is a quiet pause before the next encounter in the larger journey.
ramayan::1298.modern_relevance: You arrive late in a new place, tired from travel, and someone says, “Sleep first. The meeting can wait until morning.” That small mercy can change the whole day.
ramayan::1298.insight: It shifts attention from urgency to timely rest before the next duty.

ramayan::1299.verse_sanskrit: सुमतिस्तु महातेजा विश्वामित्रमुपागतम् । श्रुत्वा नरवरश्रेष्ठ: प्रत्युद्गच्छन्महायशा: । । 14720 । ।
ramayan::1299.verse_hindi: Having heard of the arrival of Viswamitra the celebrated Sumati, most brilliant chief of kings proceeded (to receive him).
ramayan::1299.english_translation: Having heard of the arrival of Viswamitra, the celebrated Sumati, most brilliant chief of kings, went forth to receive him.
ramayan::1299.translation_literal: सुमतिः (Sumati) / तु (indeed) / महातेजाः (highly brilliant) / विश्वामित्रम् (Viswamitra) / उपागतम् (having arrived) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / नरवरश्रेष्ठः (best among kings) / प्रत्युद्गच्छत् (went forth to receive) / महायशाः (very famous)
ramayan::1299.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1299.essence: Honor begins when you go out to meet what deserves respect.
ramayan::1299.simple_meaning: Sumati hears that Viswamitra has arrived and immediately goes out to welcome him.
ramayan::1299.simple_insight: Respect is shown first by how quickly you rise to meet someone worthy.
ramayan::1299.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has arrived in Vishala, and the next verses show the formal welcome beginning. Sumati, praised for brilliance and fame, does not wait to be summoned. He goes out at once, marking the courtesy and rank of the meeting.
ramayan::1299.modern_relevance: You hear that someone important has arrived, and you do not keep them waiting in the lobby. You go meet them yourself.
ramayan::1299.insight: It highlights respectful initiative: honour is shown by moving toward the guest, not making the guest come to you.

ramayan::1300.verse_sanskrit: पूजां च परमां कृत्वा सोपाध्यायस्सबान्धव: । प्राञ्जलि: कुशलं पृष्ट्वा विश्वामित्रमथाब्रवीत् । । 14721 । ।
ramayan::1300.verse_hindi: Along with his spiritual preceptors and relatives he paid Viswamitra great respect,
ramayan::1300.english_translation: Then, with his teachers and relatives, he offered the highest honors. With folded hands, he greeted Vishvamitra and spoke kindly.
ramayan::1300.translation_literal: पूजां (honour) / च (and) / परमां (highest) / कृत्वा (having done) / सोपाध्यायः (with teachers) / सबान्धवः (with relatives) / प्राञ्जलिः (with folded hands) / कुशलं (after asking welfare) / पृष्ट्वा (having asked) / विश्वामित्रम् (to Vishvamitra) / अथ (then) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::1300.speaker: Sumati
ramayan::1300.essence: Honor is shown first in how you welcome someone.
ramayan::1300.simple_meaning: Sumati welcomes Vishvamitra with full respect, alongside his teachers and family, and greets him politely.
ramayan::1300.simple_insight: Respect is shown not only in words, but in how you receive someone.
ramayan::1300.detailed_meaning: Vishvamitra has arrived in Sumati’s kingdom, and the king comes out to receive him. He brings teachers and relatives, offers honor, folds his hands, and begins a courteous exchange. The scene is about formal welcome, not a teaching.
ramayan::1300.modern_relevance: You arrive at a home where everyone pauses before speaking. The host stands, greets you properly, and makes the room feel held before any conversation begins.
ramayan::1300.insight: It reminds you that dignity starts with the way you receive others.

ramayan::1301.verse_sanskrit: धन्योऽस्म्यनुगृहीतोऽस्मि यस्य मे विषयं मुनि: । सम्प्राप्तो दर्शनं चैव नास्ति धन्यतरो मम । । 14722 । ।
ramayan::1301.verse_hindi: O Sage no one is more blessed than me since you have favoured me with your arrival in my country.
ramayan::1301.english_translation: I am blessed. I am favoured, because the sage has come to my land and I have seen him; no one is more blessed than I.
ramayan::1301.translation_literal: धन्यः (blessed) / अस्मि (I am) / अनुगृहीतः (favoured) / अस्मि (I am) / यस्य (whose) / मे (my) / विषयम् (land/realm) / मुनिः (sage) / सम्प्राप्तः (has arrived) / दर्शनम् (sight/seeing) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / नास्ति (there is not) / धन्यतरः (more blessed) / मम (than me)
ramayan::1301.speaker: Sumati
ramayan::1301.essence: A noble guest makes the host feel blessed before speaking a word.
ramayan::1301.simple_meaning: The king welcomes Viswamitra with deep gratitude, saying that his land is blessed by the sage's arrival and by the chance to see him.
ramayan::1301.simple_insight: Meeting a worthy person can feel like a blessing before any words are spoken.
ramayan::1301.detailed_meaning: King Sumati has rushed out to receive Viswamitra with full honour. Standing before the sage, he says that the real blessing is not his own power or kingdom, but the sage's arrival and sight in his land.
ramayan::1301.modern_relevance: A respected teacher, elder, or mentor walks into your home, and the whole room changes. Before any advice is given, you already feel how rare the visit is.
ramayan::1301.insight: It shifts attention from status to reverence, showing that presence itself can be a gift.

ramayan::1302.verse_sanskrit: पृष्ट्वा तु कुशलं तत्र परस्परसमागमे । कथान्ते सुमतिर्वाक्यं व्याजहार महामुनिम् । । 1481 । ।
ramayan::1302.verse_hindi: Getting together they enquired one anothers health. And then Sumati spoke to the great ascetic (Viswamitra).
ramayan::1302.english_translation: After they had exchanged greetings and asked about each other's welfare, wise Sumati spoke to the great ascetic.
ramayan::1302.translation_literal: पृष्ट्वा (having asked) / तु (then) / कुशलं (welfare) / तत्र (there) / परस्परसमागमे (at the meeting with each other) / कथान्ते (at the end of the conversation) / सुमति: (Sumati) / वाक्यं (speech) / व्याजहार (uttered) / महामुनिम् (to the great sage)
ramayan::1302.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1302.essence: The meeting matters because it opens the way to speech.
ramayan::1302.simple_meaning: After the greetings, Sumati began speaking to Vishwamitra. The verse only marks the transition into the conversation.
ramayan::1302.simple_insight: Sometimes the important moment is simply the opening of a real conversation.
ramayan::1302.detailed_meaning: Sumati meets Vishwamitra after the respectful welcome already described in the previous verses. They exchange greetings and ask after each other's welfare. This line simply turns the scene toward speech, setting up the questions that follow about Rama and Lakshmana.
ramayan::1302.modern_relevance: You finally sit down with someone you respect, trade the polite first words, and only then does the real question begin.
ramayan::1302.insight: It shifts attention from the meeting itself to the conversation that will reveal what matters.

ramayan::1303.verse_sanskrit: इमौ कुमारौ भद्रं ते देवतुल्यपराक्रमौ । गजसिंहगती वीरौ शार्दूलवृषभोपमौ । । 1482 । । पद्मपत्रविशालाक्षौ खड्गतूणी धनुर्धरौ । अश्विनाविव रूपेण समुपस्थितयौवनौ । । 1483 । । यदृच्छयैव गां प्राप्तौ देवलोकादिवामरौ । कथं पद्भ्यामिह प्राप्तौ किमर्थं कस्य वा मुने । । 1484 । ।
ramayan::1303.verse_hindi: O Sage, wish you well Who are these two youths who seem to possess the  prowess of celestial beings. They walk with the gait of an elephant or a lion. They are courageous like tiger or a bull. Their large eyes are like lotuspetals. They are armed with scimitars, bows and quivers. They are young and handsome like Aswinikumaras dropped from heaven casually. Whose sons are they? How did they  come here on foot? With what purpose?
ramayan::1303.english_translation: O sage, may you be blessed. Who are these two youths whose prowess seems equal to celestial beings? They move with the gait of an elephant and a lion, brave like a tiger and a bull, with lotus-like eyes, swords, bows, and quivers. They are as beautiful as the twin Ashvins, just arrived from heaven. Whose sons are they? How did they come here on foot, and for what purpose?
ramayan::1303.translation_literal: इमौ (these two) / कुमारौ (youths, princes) / भद्रं ते (blessing to you) / देवतुल्यपराक्रमौ (with prowess equal to the divine) / गजसिंहगती (with elephant-and-lion gait) / वीरौ (brave ones) / शार्दूलवृषभोपमौ (comparable to tiger and bull) / पद्मपत्रविशालाक्षौ (with lotus-petal-wide eyes) / खड्गतूणीधनुर्धरौ (bearing sword, quiver, and bow) / अश्विनाविव (like the Ashvins) / रूपेण (by form) / समुपस्थितयौवनौ (arrived at youth) / यदृच्छया (by chance) / एव (indeed) / गाम् (land) / प्राप्तौ (having reached) / देवलोकात् (from the world of the divine) / इव (as if) / अमरौ (immortals) / कथम् (how) / पद्भ्याम् (by feet) / इह (here) / प्राप्तौ (have they reached) / किमर्थम् (for what purpose) / कस्य (whose) / वा (or) / मुने (sage)
ramayan::1303.speaker: Sumati
ramayan::1303.essence: Their appearance is so striking it turns curiosity into reverence.
ramayan::1303.simple_meaning: Sumati admires the two princes' extraordinary appearance and asks Viswamitra who they are, where they came from, and why they have arrived on foot.
ramayan::1303.simple_insight: Recognition begins with wonder: sometimes a person’s presence is so striking it demands a deeper story.
ramayan::1303.detailed_meaning: At Viswamitra’s arrival, Sumati sees Rama and Lakshmana for the first time. Their bearing, weapons, and beauty seem almost unearthly, so he pauses the conversation to ask who these boys are and why they have come to this place.
ramayan::1303.modern_relevance: You meet two quiet strangers in a train station, and something about them feels unmistakably significant. Before you know their names, you already know they carry a story.
ramayan::1303.insight: It trains attention to notice presence before explanation, and to ask who someone is before assuming.

ramayan::1304.verse_sanskrit: भूषयन्ताविमं देशं चन्द्रसूर्याविवाम्बरम् । परस्परस्य सदृशौ प्रमाणेङ्गितचेष्टितै: । । 1485 । । किमर्थं च मुनिश्रेष्ठ सम्प्राप्तौ दुर्गमे पथि । वरायुधधरौ वीरौ श्रोतुमिच्छामि तत्त्वत: । । 1486 । ।
ramayan::1304.verse_hindi: O Great ascetic they resemble each other in personality, expression and gestures. They adorn this land like Sun and moon in the sky holding excellent weapons. These heroes have trodden paths difficult to traverse. For what purpose have they come? I want to hear clearly.
ramayan::1304.english_translation: O great ascetic, they resemble each other in personality, expression, and gestures. They adorn this land like the sun and moon in the sky, holding excellent weapons. These heroes have taken paths difficult to traverse. For what purpose have they come? I want to hear clearly.
ramayan::1304.translation_literal: भूषयन्तौ (adorning) / इमम् (this) / देशम् (land) / चन्द्रसूर्यौ (the moon and the sun) / इव (like) / अम्बरम् (the sky) / परस्परस्य (of each other) / सदृशौ (similar) / प्रमाण-इङ्गित-चेष्टितैः (by stature, gestures, and movements) / किमर्थम् (for what purpose) / च (and) / मुनिश्रेष्ठ (O best among sages) / सम्प्राप्तौ (have arrived) / दुर्गमे (difficult) / पथि (on the path) / वरायुधधरौ (bearing excellent weapons) / वीरौ (the two heroes) / श्रोतुम् (to hear) / इच्छामि (I wish) / तत्त्वतः (truly, clearly)
ramayan::1304.speaker: Sumati
ramayan::1304.essence: Their presence is so striking that it demands an explanation.
ramayan::1304.simple_meaning: Sumati marvels at the two young warriors, comparing them to the sun and moon. He asks why they have come by such a hard route and wants the truth.
ramayan::1304.simple_insight: Curiosity can be reverent: sometimes you ask because you sense something important has arrived.
ramayan::1304.detailed_meaning: At Vishwamitra's hermitage, Sumati sees Rama and Lakshmana and is struck by their likeness, beauty, and weapons. He asks the sage why these extraordinary youths have come through such a dangerous path, opening the way for Vishwamitra's full account.
ramayan::1304.modern_relevance: You meet two strangers at the edge of a difficult journey and feel they carry more than they say. Before assumptions harden, you ask what brought them here.
ramayan::1304.insight: It shifts attention from appearance to purpose, inviting a truthful explanation before judgment.

ramayan::1305.verse_sanskrit: तस्य तद्वचनं श्रुत्वा यथावृत्तं न्यवेदयत् । सिद्धाश्रमनिवासं च राक्षसानां वधं तथा । । 1487 । ।
ramayan::1305.verse_hindi: On hearing his words, he (Viswamitra) related all about their stay at Siddhashrama and the slaying of rakshasas.
ramayan::1305.english_translation: On hearing his words, Viswamitra related the whole truth: their stay at Siddhashrama and the slaying of the rakshasas.
ramayan::1305.translation_literal: तस्य (his) / तत्-वचनम् (that speech) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / यथावृत्तम् (as it happened) / न्यवेदयत् (he reported) / सिद्धाश्रम-निवासम् (residence at Siddhashrama) / च (and) / राक्षसानाम् (of rakshasas) / वधम् (slaying) / तथा (and likewise)
ramayan::1305.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1305.essence: The answer shifts the scene from wonder to explanation.
ramayan::1305.simple_meaning: Viswamitra answers the king's question by recounting what happened at Siddhashrama and how the rakshasas were killed.
ramayan::1305.simple_insight: Some moments only move forward when the full story is finally told.
ramayan::1305.detailed_meaning: The two princes have just been noticed for their radiant bearing. Viswamitra now answers the king's inquiry by explaining who they are and what they have already done: lived at Siddhashrama and destroyed the rakshasas there. It is a report, not a teaching verse.
ramayan::1305.modern_relevance: A meeting pauses while someone finally gives the backstory everyone has been circling around. The room changes the moment the facts land and the real stakes become clear.
ramayan::1305.insight: It functions as narrative bridge, moving the scene from recognition to explanation.

ramayan::1306.verse_sanskrit: विश्वामित्रवचश्श्रुत्वा राजा परमहर्षित: । अतिथी परमौ प्राप्तौ पुत्रौ दशरथस्य तौ । । 1488 । । पूजयामास विधिवत्सत्कारार्हौ महाबलौ ।
ramayan::1306.verse_hindi: After hearing Viswamitra, the king (Sumati) got exceedingly delighted and extended
ramayan::1306.english_translation: After hearing Viswamitra, the king was exceedingly delighted and honoured the two sons of Dasharatha, who had arrived as the highest guests, with proper rites and hospitality, as they deserved.
ramayan::1306.translation_literal: विश्वामित्रवचः (Viswamitra's words) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / राजा (the king) / परमहर्षितः (greatly delighted) / अतिथी (guests) / परमौ (the highest) / प्राप्तौ (having arrived) / पुत्रौ (sons) / दशरथस्य (of Dasharatha) / तौ (those two) / पूजयामास (honoured) / विधिवत् (according to proper rites) / सत्कारार्हौ (worthy of hospitality) / महाबलौ (very powerful)
ramayan::1306.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1306.essence: True honour is shown in the way you receive worthy guests.
ramayan::1306.simple_meaning: The king is delighted to receive Rama and Lakshmana and treats them with full honour and hospitality.
ramayan::1306.simple_insight: Respect is shown not by words alone, but by how you receive people who arrive at your door.
ramayan::1306.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has explained who Rama and Lakshmana are and why they have come. Hearing this, King Sumati rejoices and receives the two sons of Dasharatha as honoured guests, giving them the formal welcome they deserve.
ramayan::1306.modern_relevance: Someone shows up at your home after a hard journey, tired and unknown to your family. You could be cautious, or you could meet them with full dignity. This verse chooses dignity first.
ramayan::1306.insight: It shifts attention from status to hospitality: power is revealed in how you welcome others.

ramayan::1307.verse_sanskrit: तत: परमसत्कारं सुमते: प्राप्य राघवौ । । 1489 । । उष्य तत्र निशामेकां जग्मतुर्मिथिलां तत: ।
ramayan::1307.verse_hindi: The descendants of Raghu (Rama and Lakshmana) having received great honour from Sumati, stayed there one night and thereafter set out for Mithila.
ramayan::1307.english_translation: Then, after receiving the highest hospitality from Sumati, Rama and Lakshmana stayed there for one night and then went on to Mithila.
ramayan::1307.translation_literal: तत: (then) / परमसत्कारं (great honour) / सुमते: (of Sumati) / प्राप्य (having received) / राघवौ (the two descendants of Raghu) / उष्य (having stayed) / तत्र (there) / निशाम् एकाम् (one night) / जग्मतुः (they went) / मिथिलां (to Mithila) / तत: (then)
ramayan::1307.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1307.essence: Hospitality is received, and the journey continues.
ramayan::1307.simple_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana were warmly received, spent one night there, and then continued on to Mithila.
ramayan::1307.simple_insight: Not every journey turns on a lesson; some verses simply carry the story forward.
ramayan::1307.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana are moving through King Janaka's country on the way to Mithila. Sumati honors them properly, they rest for a night, and then they continue onward. The verse marks a transition, not a teaching.
ramayan::1307.modern_relevance: You meet someone kindly, rest for a night, and move on to the next place. Some moments matter because they change nothing except the next step.
ramayan::1307.insight: It keeps the narrative moving without adding a new principle.

ramayan::1308.verse_sanskrit: तान् दृष्ट्वा मुनयस्सर्वे जनकस्य पुरीं शुभाम् । । 14810 । । साधु साध्विति शंसन्तो मिथिलां समपूजयन् ।
ramayan::1308.verse_hindi: All the ascetics, having seen that auspicious city of Janaka worshipfully admired Mithila saying, Excellent, Excellent
ramayan::1308.english_translation: All the ascetics, having seen the auspicious city of Janaka, praised Mithila with worshipful admiration, saying, 'Excellent, excellent.'
ramayan::1308.translation_literal: तान् (them) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / मुनयः (ascetics) / सर्वे (all) / जनकस्य (of Janaka) / पुरीम् (city) / शुभाम् (auspicious) / साधु साधु इति (excellent, excellent, thus) / शंसन्तः (praising) / मिथिलाम् (Mithila) / समपूजयन् (worshipfully honoured)
ramayan::1308.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1308.essence: Beauty and order can command reverence without saying a word.
ramayan::1308.simple_meaning: The sages see Mithila and praise its beauty with reverence.
ramayan::1308.simple_insight: Some places carry a quiet dignity that makes even the wise pause.
ramayan::1308.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana have arrived in Mithila for Janaka’s great gathering. As they enter the city, the gathered sages look on and marvel at its auspicious beauty, honouring it aloud. The line simply paints the sacred, orderly atmosphere before the next event unfolds.
ramayan::1308.modern_relevance: You step into a city that feels different the moment you arrive — calmer, cleaner, more held together. Before you can explain it, you already respect it.
ramayan::1308.insight: It frames the setting as worthy of reverence before the story moves on.

ramayan::1309.verse_sanskrit: मिथिलोपवने शून्यमाश्रमं दृश्य राघव: । । 14811 । । पुराणं निर्जनं रम्यं पप्रच्छ मुनिपुङ्गवम् ।
ramayan::1309.verse_hindi: At the sight of an old uninhabited, beautiful and desolate hermitage in a grove near Mithila, the descendant of the Raghus enquired of the foremost among the ascetics
ramayan::1309.english_translation: At the sight of an old, uninhabited, beautiful and desolate hermitage in a grove near Mithila, Rama asked the foremost among the ascetics.
ramayan::1309.translation_literal: मिथिलोपवने (in the grove near Mithila) / शून्यम् (empty) / आश्रमम् (hermitage) / दृश्य (seeing) / राघवः (Rama) / पुराणम् (old) / निर्जनम् (uninhabited) / रम्यम् (beautiful) / पप्रच्छ (asked) / मुनिपुङ्गवम् (the foremost among ascetics)
ramayan::1309.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1309.essence: He pauses before a silent place and asks its story.
ramayan::1309.simple_meaning: Rama sees a deserted but beautiful hermitage near Mithila and asks the sage about it.
ramayan::1309.simple_insight: Curiosity can be a form of respect. He notices what others might pass by.
ramayan::1309.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana have reached Mithila and are being shown the sights. Near the city, Rama notices a lonely old hermitage in a grove and asks the leading sage about its story. The verse sets up an explanation, not a teaching.
ramayan::1309.modern_relevance: You walk past a quiet building that feels abandoned, but something about it makes you stop and ask what happened there.
ramayan::1309.insight: It trains attention toward meaningful details and opens the door to understanding through questions.

ramayan::1310.verse_sanskrit: श्रीमदाश्रमसङ्काशं किन्न्विदं मुनिवर्जितम् । । 14812 । । ज्ञातुमिच्छामि भगवन् कस्यायं पूर्वमाश्रम: ।
ramayan::1310.verse_hindi: O Venerable one I wish to know why this auspicios looking hermitage was deserted by ascetics? To whom did this belong in the past.
ramayan::1310.english_translation: O Venerable one, I wish to know why this auspicious-looking hermitage was deserted by ascetics. To whom did it belong in the past?
ramayan::1310.translation_literal: श्रीमद् (auspicious, venerable) / आश्रम-सङ्काशम् (resembling a hermitage) / किम्-इदं (what is this) / मुनि-वर्जितम् (devoid of ascetics) / ज्ञातुम्-इच्छामि (I wish to know) / भगवन् (O venerable one) / कस्य (whose) / अयम् (this) / पूर्वम् (formerly) / आश्रमः (hermitage)
ramayan::1310.speaker: Rama
ramayan::1310.essence: A quiet place can carry a forgotten story.
ramayan::1310.simple_meaning: Rama asks Vishwamitra why the beautiful hermitage is empty and who lived there before.
ramayan::1310.simple_insight: Curiosity can open the next door before action begins.
ramayan::1310.detailed_meaning: Rama and the sages have reached a lovely but deserted hermitage near Mithila. Seeing its silence, Rama asks Vishwamitra about its former inhabitants and why it was abandoned. The question leads into the story that follows.
ramayan::1310.modern_relevance: You walk into a house that feels lived-in but empty, and you immediately want the story behind it. That instinct to ask before assuming keeps you humble.
ramayan::1310.insight: It shifts attention from appearance to origin, inviting inquiry before judgment.

ramayan::1311.verse_sanskrit: तच्छ्रुत्वा राघवेणोक्तं वाक्यं वाक्यविशारद: । । 14813 । । प्रत्युवाच महातेजा विश्वामित्रो महामुनि: ।
ramayan::1311.verse_hindi: Eloquent and brilliant Viswamitra, replied to the descendant of the Raghus saying:
ramayan::1311.english_translation: Hearing Rama's question, the eloquent and brilliant sage Vishwamitra replied.
ramayan::1311.translation_literal: तत् (that) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / राघवेण (by Rama) / उक्तं (spoken) / वाक्यं (speech) / वाक्यविशारदः (skilled in speech) / प्रत्युवाच (replied) / महातेजाः (very radiant) / विश्वामित्रः (Vishvamitra) / महामुनिः (great sage)
ramayan::1311.speaker: Vishvamitra
ramayan::1311.essence: The story begins when the sage answers the prince's question.
ramayan::1311.simple_meaning: Vishvamitra answers Rama's question about the deserted hermitage.
ramayan::1311.simple_insight: Some moments only open when someone finally answers with the full story.
ramayan::1311.detailed_meaning: Rama notices a beautiful hermitage near Mithila, empty of sages and life. He asks Vishvamitra why it stands deserted. This verse simply marks the sage's reply, leading into the hermitage's backstory.
ramayan::1311.modern_relevance: You ask why a place feels heavy before you know its history. Then someone finally names what happened there, and the silence makes sense.
ramayan::1311.insight: It shifts attention from the scene itself to the cause behind it.

ramayan::1312.verse_sanskrit: हन्त ते कथयिष्यामि श्रुणु तत्त्वेन राघव । । 14814 । । यस्येदमाश्रमपदं शप्तं कोपान्महात्मना ।
ramayan::1312.verse_hindi: O Descendant of the Raghus I shall tell all you about this hermitage cursed by the wrath of a great man.
ramayan::1312.english_translation: O descendant of the Raghus, I shall tell you the full truth: this hermitage was cursed in anger by a great man.
ramayan::1312.translation_literal: हन्त (well then) / ते (to you) / कथयिष्यामि (I shall tell) / श्रुणु (listen) / तत्त्वेन (in truth, fully) / राघव (O Raghava) / यस्य (whose) / इदम् (this) / आश्रमपदं (hermitage-place) / शप्तं (cursed) / कोपात् (from anger) / महात्मना (by a great-souled one)
ramayan::1312.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::1312.essence: A single curse can turn a sacred place into silence.
ramayan::1312.simple_meaning: Viswamitra begins explaining that the deserted hermitage was once cursed by an angry great sage.
ramayan::1312.simple_insight: Some places carry the weight of old anger long after the moment has passed.
ramayan::1312.detailed_meaning: Rama has asked why this beautiful hermitage stands empty. Viswamitra now answers, promising the full story: the place was once cursed by a great sage in anger. This verse opens the explanation, not the lesson itself.
ramayan::1312.modern_relevance: You walk into a room where everyone has gone quiet, but no one says why. Later, you learn one sharp moment changed everything. Some places still remember that moment.
ramayan::1312.insight: It sets up a story of cause and consequence, where one burst of anger reshapes an entire place.

ramayan::1313.verse_sanskrit: गौतमस्य नरश्रेष्ठ पूर्वमासीन्महात्मन: । । 14815 । । आश्रमो दिव्यसङ्काशस्सुरैरपि सुपूजित: ।
ramayan::1313.verse_hindi: O Best among men this hermitage resembling a celestial retreat and wellhonoured even by devatas  once belonged to illustrious Gautama.
ramayan::1313.english_translation: O best among men, this hermitage, shining like a celestial retreat and honored even by the devas, once belonged to the illustrious Gautama.
ramayan::1313.translation_literal: गौतमस्य (of Gautama) / नरश्रेष्ठ (O best among men) / पूर्वम् (formerly) / आसीत् (was) / महात्मनः (of the great-souled one) / आश्रमः (hermitage) / दिव्यसङ्काशः (resembling the divine) / सुरैः (by the devas) / अपि (even) / सुपूजितः (well honored)
ramayan::1313.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::1313.essence: A sacred place can still carry the ache of what happened there.
ramayan::1313.simple_meaning: Viswamitra tells Rama that this beautiful hermitage once belonged to the sage Gautama and was respected even by the devas.
ramayan::1313.simple_insight: Places can hold memory, holiness, and loss all at once.
ramayan::1313.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra is explaining the cursed hermitage to Rama before telling the full story of Ahalya. He identifies the place first: once radiant, once honored, once belonging to Gautama. The verse sets the emotional and moral stage for the tragedy that follows.
ramayan::1313.modern_relevance: You walk into a house after a family has broken apart. The rooms still look beautiful, but every corner carries a story of what was lost.
ramayan::1313.insight: It frames the setting as a wounded place whose beauty survives its history.

ramayan::1314.verse_sanskrit: स चेह तप आतिष्ठदहल्यासहित: पुरा । । 14816 । । वर्षपूगाननेकांश्च राजपुत्र महायश: ।
ramayan::1314.verse_hindi: O Highly renowned prince it was here in ancient times that Gautama in the company of Ahalya practised austerities for several years.
ramayan::1314.english_translation: O highly renowned prince, it was here in ancient times that Gautama, together with Ahalya, practised austerities for many years.
ramayan::1314.translation_literal: सः (he) / च (and) / इह (here) / तपः (austerity) / आतिष्ठत् (practised) / अहल्यासहितः (together with Ahalya) / पुरा (formerly, in ancient times) / वर्षपूगान् (years, long spans of years) / अनेकान् (many) / च (and) / राजपुत्र (O prince) / महायशः (highly renowned)
ramayan::1314.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1314.essence: A sacred place is made fragile by the lives that once sanctified it.
ramayan::1314.simple_meaning: Gautama and Ahalya lived here long ago and spent many years in austerity.
ramayan::1314.simple_insight: Some places carry the memory of long discipline before any tragedy enters them.
ramayan::1314.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing the old hermitage to Rama. Before the curse, this was a sacred place where Gautama and Ahalya lived in austerity for years. The verse is a setting detail, preparing the story of how that purity was later disturbed.
ramayan::1314.modern_relevance: You enter a house and feel the residue of years lived there — the routines, vows, and silences still seem to remain. Some places remember discipline before they remember damage.
ramayan::1314.insight: It anchors the scene in a world of prior devotion, so the coming violation lands harder.

ramayan::1315.verse_sanskrit: तस्यान्तरं विदित्वा तु सहस्राक्षश्शचीपति: । । 14817 । । मुनिवेषधरोऽहल्यामिदं वचनमब्रवीत् ।
ramayan::1315.verse_hindi: The thousandeyed Indra, consort of Sachi, having found an opportunity (during the absence of the ascetic), assumed the guise of the ascetic (Gautama) and said to Ahalya:
ramayan::1315.english_translation: The thousand-eyed Indra, consort of Sachi, having found an opportunity, assumed the guise of the ascetic and said to Ahalya:
ramayan::1315.translation_literal: तस्य (of that) / अन्तरं (opportunity, gap) / विदित्वा (having known) / तु (indeed) / सहस्राक्षः (the thousand-eyed one) / शचीपतिḥ (Sachi's consort) / मुनिवेषधारः (wearing the guise of an ascetic) / अहल्याम् (to Ahalya) / इदम् (this) / वचनम् (speech) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::1315.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1315.essence: Deception works best when it wears the right face.
ramayan::1315.simple_meaning: Indra notices Gautama is absent, disguises himself as a sage, and approaches Ahalya.
ramayan::1315.simple_insight: A hidden intention often begins by borrowing the appearance of innocence.
ramayan::1315.detailed_meaning: At Gautama’s hermitage, Ahalya is alone. Indra sees the opening left by Gautama’s absence, puts on an ascetic’s dress, and steps toward her. The verse sets up the deception that will follow.
ramayan::1315.modern_relevance: Someone messages you from an account that looks familiar, using the right tone and profile picture. The danger is not force; it is the borrowed shape of trust.
ramayan::1315.insight: It trains you to notice how wrongdoing often enters through disguise, timing, and imitation.

ramayan::1316.verse_sanskrit: ऋतुकालं प्रतीक्षन्ते नार्थिनस्सुसमाहिते । 14818सङ्गमं त्वहमिच्छामि त्वया सह सुमध्यमे । ।
ramayan::1316.verse_hindi: O most beautiful one those overtaken by passion would not await the completion of the menstrual period (favourable for copulation). O woman of fine waist I desire union with you.
ramayan::1316.english_translation: O beautiful one, those driven by desire do not wait for the proper time. I want union with you.
ramayan::1316.translation_literal: ऋतुकालम् (proper time / fertile period) / प्रतीक्षन्ते (wait for) / न (not) / अर्थिनः (those who desire) / सुसमाहिते (O well-composed one) / सङ्गमम् (union) / तु (but) / अहम् (I) / इच्छामि (desire) / त्वया सह (with you) / सुमध्यमे (O woman of fine waist)
ramayan::1316.speaker: Indra
ramayan::1316.essence: Desire ignores what should be waited for.
ramayan::1316.simple_meaning: Indra, disguised as a sage, speaks to Ahalya with lust and asks for union immediately, ignoring proper timing and restraint.
ramayan::1316.simple_insight: Desire can make a person abandon restraint and speak only for appetite.
ramayan::1316.detailed_meaning: Gautama is away performing austerities with Ahalya. Seizing the moment, Indra comes disguised as a sage and speaks to her with sexual intent. The verse marks the exact moment temptation enters the sacred hermitage.
ramayan::1316.modern_relevance: A private message arrives when someone is alone and vulnerable, dressed up as charm but carrying pressure. The danger is not only the request — it is the disguise.
ramayan::1316.insight: It exposes how craving overrides timing, reverence, and self-control.

ramayan::1317.verse_sanskrit: मुनिवेषं सहस्राक्षं विज्ञाय रघुनन्दन । 14819मतिं चकार दुर्मेधा देवराजकुतूहलात् । ।
ramayan::1317.verse_hindi: O Delight of the Raghus the evilintentioned Ahalya, inclined towards the king of the
ramayan::1317.english_translation: Recognizing the thousand-eyed one in the ascetic's disguise, the foolish Ahalya, driven by curiosity about the lord of the gods, made up her mind.
ramayan::1317.translation_literal: मुनिवेषम् (the ascetic's disguise) / सहस्राक्षम् (the thousand-eyed one) / विज्ञाय (having recognized) / रघुनन्दन (O delight of the Raghu line) / मतिम् (resolve) / चकार (made) / दुर्मेधा (foolish-minded) / देवराजकुतूहलात् (from curiosity about the king of the gods)
ramayan::1317.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1317.essence: Knowing better does not stop a reckless choice.
ramayan::1317.simple_meaning: Ahalya realizes the disguised Indra is standing before her, and curiosity leads her into a harmful choice.
ramayan::1317.simple_insight: Curiosity without discernment can open the door to ruin.
ramayan::1317.detailed_meaning: In Vishvamitra's hermitage, Indra has arrived in the guise of a sage. Ahalya recognizes him, yet her mind turns toward him anyway, moved by fascination with the king of the gods. This verse marks the moment her choice hardens.
ramayan::1317.modern_relevance: You know exactly who is texting you, and you know the message is trouble. The pull is not confusion — it's the thrill of looking anyway.
ramayan::1317.insight: It warns that recognition alone is not enough; you still have to govern desire and curiosity.

ramayan::1318.verse_sanskrit: अथाब्रवीत् नरश्रेष्ठ कृतार्थेनान्तरात्मना । 14820 । । कृतार्थाऽस्मि सुरश्रेष्ठ गच्छ शीघ्रमित: प्रभो । आत्मानं मां च देवेश सर्वदा रक्ष गौतमात् । 14821 । ।
ramayan::1318.verse_hindi: O Foremost of men with her hearts desire fulfilled, Ahalya said: O Chief of the
ramayan::1318.english_translation: Then Ahalya said to the foremost of men, her purpose fulfilled: “I am fulfilled, O chief of the radiant beings. O lord of the radiant beings, leave quickly from here. Protect me and yourself always from Gautama.”
ramayan::1318.translation_literal: अथ (then) / अब्रवीत् (said) / नरश्रेष्ठ (foremost of men) / कृतार्थेन (with fulfilled purpose) / अन्तरात्मना (with inner being) / कृतार्था (fulfilled) / अस्मि (I am) / सुरश्रेष्ठ (O chief of the radiant beings) / गच्छ (go) / शीघ्रम् (quickly) / इतः (from here) / प्रभो (O lord) / आत्मानम् (yourself) / माम् (me) / च (and) / देवेश (O lord of the radiant beings) / सर्वदा (always) / रक्ष (protect) / गौतमात् (from Gautama)
ramayan::1318.speaker: Ahalya
ramayan::1318.essence: Fulfillment here is brief; fear arrives immediately after.
ramayan::1318.simple_meaning: Ahalya tells Indra she feels fulfilled and asks him to leave quickly and protect both of them from Gautama.
ramayan::1318.simple_insight: A brief moment of desire turns into fear of consequences.
