ramayan::1506.verse_sanskrit: विश्वामित्रोऽपि तच्छ्रुत्वा ह्रिया किञ्चिदवाङ्मुख: । दु:खेन महताऽऽविष्टस्समन्युरिदमब्रवीत् । । 1577 । ।
ramayan::1506.verse_hindi: On hearing this Viswamitra hanging down his face a little with shame and anger and grief said:
ramayan::1506.english_translation: On hearing this, Vishvamitra lowered his face slightly in shame, and filled with great sorrow and anger, he spoke:
ramayan::1506.translation_literal: विश्वामित्रः (Vishvamitra) / अपि (also) / तत् (that) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / ह्रिया (with shame) / किञ्चित् (a little) / अवाङ्मुखः (face lowered) / दुःखेन (with grief) / महता (great) / आविष्टः (overcome) / समन्युः (angry) / इदम् (this) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::1506.speaker: Vishvamitra
ramayan::1506.essence: Recognition can hurt when it falls short of what you have earned.
ramayan::1506.simple_meaning: Vishvamitra hears the words, feels humiliated and angry, and begins to answer.
ramayan::1506.simple_insight: Even a great seeker can feel wounded when recognition falls short.
ramayan::1506.detailed_meaning: Brahma has just left after acknowledging Vishvamitra's austerity in a limited way. Vishvamitra lowers his face, shaken by shame, grief, and anger. The verse is a turning point into his protest in the next line, not a complete teaching by itself.
ramayan::1506.modern_relevance: You did years of hard work, and the title still sounds smaller than what you earned. The sting is real before the reply comes.
ramayan::1506.insight: It shows the emotional cost of being seen incompletely and sets up the complaint that follows.

ramayan::1507.verse_sanskrit: तपश्च सुमहत्तप्तं राजर्षिरिति मां विदु: । देवास्सर्षिगणास्सर्वे नास्ति मन्ये तप:फलम् । । 1578 । ।
ramayan::1507.verse_hindi: I have performed intense austerities. Yet rishis and devatas have recognised me only as a rajarshi. I think my penance has yielded fruit.
ramayan::1507.english_translation: I have performed intense austerities. Yet sages and radiant beings know me only as a royal sage. I think my austerity has borne fruit.
ramayan::1507.translation_literal: तपः (austerity) / च (and) / सुमहत् (very great) / तप्तम् (performed) / राजर्षिः (royal sage) / इति (thus) / माम् (me) / विदुः (know) / देवाः (the radiant beings) / सर्षिगणाः (with the groups of sages) / सर्वे (all) / न (not) / अस्ति (there is) / मन्ये (I think) / तपःफलम् (fruit of austerity)
ramayan::1507.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::1507.essence: Severe effort matters when the world still sees you as unfinished.
ramayan::1507.simple_meaning: Viswamitra says he has done severe austerity, and the result is that even the sages and radiant beings now recognise him as a royal sage.
ramayan::1507.simple_insight: Real effort changes who you become, even before anyone else fully understands it.
ramayan::1507.detailed_meaning: After Brahma departs, Viswamitra stands ashamed and angry. He has practiced severe austerity, yet the highest beings still call him only a royal sage. That sting pushes him to continue until his inner rank matches his outer effort.
ramayan::1507.modern_relevance: You spent years becoming good at something, but people still see you as the old version of yourself. The gap hurts — and it can also become fuel.
ramayan::1507.insight: It shifts the mind from craving approval to trusting sustained practice.

ramayan::1508.verse_sanskrit: इति निश्चित्य मनसा भूय एव महातपा: । तपश्चकार काकुत्स्थ परमं परमात्मवान् । । 1579 । ।
ramayan::1508.verse_hindi: O Descendant of Kakustha (Rama) this celebrated intellectual having decided in his mind once again performed greater austerities.
ramayan::1508.english_translation: Having resolved this in his mind, the great ascetic performed even greater austerities, O descendant of Kakustha.
ramayan::1508.translation_literal: इति (thus) / निश्चित्य (having decided) / मनसा (in the mind) / भूयः (again) / एव (indeed) / महातपाः (the greatly austere one) / तपः (austerities) / चकार (performed) / काकुत्स्थ (O descendant of Kakustha) / परमं (highest) / परमात्मवान् (the highly self-possessed one)
ramayan::1508.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1508.simple_meaning: After deciding firmly, the great ascetic returned to even more intense austerity.
ramayan::1508.simple_insight: Real resolve shows up as renewed effort, not wounded pride.
ramayan::1508.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has just felt stung that his austerity earned him only the title of rajarshi. Instead of stopping, he turns that hurt into stricter practice and resumes deeper penance before Trisanku enters the story.
ramayan::1508.modern_relevance: You felt overlooked after months of work, but you did not quit. You tightened your focus and kept going, letting discipline answer disappointment.
ramayan::1508.insight: It shifts you from reacting to criticism to strengthening your practice.

ramayan::1509.verse_sanskrit: एतस्मिन्नेव काले तु सत्यवादी जितेन्द्रिय: । त्रिशङ्कुरिति विख्यात इक्ष्वाकुकुलवर्धन: । । 15710 । ।
ramayan::1509.verse_hindi: At this time there lived a celebrated king, renowned in the Ikshvakus race, named Trisanku, who was truthful and self restrained.
ramayan::1509.english_translation: At that time lived a celebrated king of the Ikshvaku line named Trishanku, who was truthful and self-restrained.
ramayan::1509.translation_literal: एतस्मिन् (at this) / एव (indeed) / काले (time) / तु (but) / सत्यवादी (truth-speaking) / जितेन्द्रियः (self-controlled) / त्रिशङ्कुः (Trishanku) / इति (thus) / विख्यातः (well-known) / इक्ष्वाकुकुलवर्धनः (enhancer of the Ikshvaku line)
ramayan::1509.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1509.essence: A respected king is introduced before the desire that will test him.
ramayan::1509.simple_meaning: A king named Trishanku is introduced as truthful and self-controlled.
ramayan::1509.simple_insight: Some stories begin by showing the character’s stature before the trouble starts.
ramayan::1509.detailed_meaning: Valmiki introduces Trishanku, a respected king of the Ikshvaku line, before the real conflict begins. The next verse will show the desire that drives the episode, but here the focus is simply on who he is: a disciplined, honorable ruler.
ramayan::1509.modern_relevance: Before the request, the crisis, or the mistake, there is always a person with a reputation. This verse pauses there and lets you see the man before the event.
ramayan::1509.insight: It shifts attention from the coming action to the character that makes the action meaningful.

ramayan::1510.verse_sanskrit: तस्य बुद्धिस्समुत्पन्ना यजेयमिति राघव । गच्छेयं स्वशरीरेण देवानां परमां गतिम् । । 15711 । ।
ramayan::1510.verse_hindi: O Son of the Raghus (Rama) a thought arose in his mind to enter heaven with his physical body by performing a sacrifice.
ramayan::1510.english_translation: A thought arose in his mind: I will perform a sacrifice and reach the highest state of the radiant beings in my own body.
ramayan::1510.translation_literal: तस्य (of him) / बुद्धिः (thought) / समुत्पन्ना (arose) / यजेयम् (I will sacrifice) / इति (thus) / राघव (O descendant of Raghu) / गच्छेयम् (I may go) / स्वशरीरेण (with his own body) / देवानाम् (of the radiant beings) / परमाम् (highest) / गतिम् (state / destination) /
ramayan::1510.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1510.essence: A wish can be so large it immediately collides with what is possible.
ramayan::1510.simple_meaning: Trishanku decides he wants to reach the highest realm in his own body by performing a sacrifice.
ramayan::1510.simple_insight: Ambition can push a person to ask for what even tradition refuses.
ramayan::1510.detailed_meaning: Trishanku, a king of the Ikshvaku line, forms an impossible wish: he wants to ascend to the highest realm without leaving his body. This verse is the moment the desire appears, before Vasishta rejects it.
ramayan::1510.modern_relevance: Someone wants a shortcut that breaks the rules: the promotion, the transformation, the result — but without the cost. The wish itself is the story here.
ramayan::1510.insight: It shows how desire can overreach reality before anyone else even responds.

ramayan::1511.verse_sanskrit: स वसिष्ठं समाहूय कथयामास चिन्तितम् । अशक्यमिति चाप्युक्तो वसिष्ठेन महात्मना । । 15712 । ।
ramayan::1511.verse_hindi: Summoning Vasishta he (Trisahnku) communicated his intention, but the great Vasishta said it was not possible.
ramayan::1511.english_translation: He summoned Vasishta and told him what he had decided, but the great Vasishta said it was impossible.
ramayan::1511.translation_literal: स (he) / वसिष्ठं (Vasishta) / समाहूय (having summoned) / कथयामास (told) / चिन्तितम् (what was thought / decided) / अशक्यमिति (it is impossible, thus) / च (and) / अपि (also) / उक्तो (said) / वसिष्ठेन (by Vasishta) / महात्मना (the great-souled one)
ramayan::1511.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1511.essence: A wish can be sincere and still remain impossible.
ramayan::1511.simple_meaning: Trisanku shares his plan with Vasishta, but Vasishta refuses it as impossible.
ramayan::1511.simple_insight: Some desires meet a boundary you cannot force through.
ramayan::1511.detailed_meaning: King Trisanku has already formed the impossible wish to ascend in his body. He calls Vasishta, hoping the teacher will make it happen, but Vasishta rejects the request. The passage turns on that refusal.
ramayan::1511.modern_relevance: You finally say the thing out loud to someone wiser, hoping they’ll make it workable. They don’t. The disappointment is sharp, but the boundary is real.
ramayan::1511.insight: It shows the moment a private ambition meets a clear refusal, forcing the seeker to look elsewhere.

ramayan::1512.verse_sanskrit: प्रत्याख्यातो वसिष्ठेन स ययौदक्षिणां दिशम् । ततस्तत्कर्मसिद्ध्यर्थं पुत्रां स्तस्य गतो नृप: । । 15713 । ।
ramayan::1512.verse_hindi: Refused by Vasishta, the king went south in order to fulfil his purpose and approached Vasishtas sons.
ramayan::1512.english_translation: Refused by Vasishta, the king went south to fulfil his purpose and approached Vasishta's sons.
ramayan::1512.translation_literal: प्रत्याख्यातो (refused) / वसिष्ठेन (by Vasishta) / सः (he) / ययौ (went) / दक्षिणाम् दिशम् (to the southern direction) / ततः (then) / तत्-कर्म-सिद्ध्यर्थम् (for the success of that task) / पुत्रान् (sons) / तस्य (of him) / गतः (went) / नृपः (the king)
ramayan::1512.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1512.essence: Refusal does not end desire; it often sends it searching elsewhere.
ramayan::1512.simple_meaning: After Vasishta refused him, the king turned south and went to Vasishta's sons to complete his plan.
ramayan::1512.simple_insight: A blocked path can push desire into a worse direction.
ramayan::1512.detailed_meaning: Trishanku has already been told his plan is impossible. Instead of letting the refusal end the matter, he turns away and seeks Vasishta's sons in the south, hoping they will do what their teacher would not.
ramayan::1512.modern_relevance: You hear a firm no, then start looking for someone easier to persuade. The refusal did not end the craving; it only changed its route.
ramayan::1512.insight: It shows how stubborn wanting can keep searching for a workaround after clear refusal.

ramayan::1513.verse_sanskrit: वासिष्ठा दीर्घतपसस्तपो यत्र हि तेपिरे । त्रिशंङ्कुस्सुमहातेजा श्शतं परमभास्वरम् । । 15714 । । वसिष्ठपुत्रान् ददृशे तप्यमानान् यशस्विन: ।
ramayan::1513.verse_hindi: Most brilliant Trisanku approached the sons of Vasishta in the place where they  had been performing austerities for a long time. There he saw the famous, exceedingly effulgent sons of Vasishta one hundred in number practising penance.
ramayan::1513.english_translation: Most brilliant Trisanku approached the sons of Vasishta in the place where they had been performing austerities for a long time. There he saw the famous, exceedingly effulgent sons of Vasishta, one hundred in number, practising penance.
ramayan::1513.translation_literal: वासिष्ठा (of Vasishta) / दीर्घतपसः (of long austerities) / तपः (austerities) / यत्र (where) / हि (indeed) / तेपिरे (they practised) / त्रिशंङ्कुः (Trisanku) / सुमहातेजाः (highly radiant) / श्शतम् (a hundred) / परमभास्वरम् (exceedingly effulgent) / वसिष्ठपुत्रान् (the sons of Vasishta) / ददृशे (saw) / तप्यमानान् (practising penance) / यशस्विनः (the famous ones)
ramayan::1513.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1513.essence: The seeker enters a world shaped by long discipline.
ramayan::1513.simple_meaning: Trisanku goes to the sons of Vasishta, who are deep in penance, and sees their brilliance and discipline.
ramayan::1513.simple_insight: Some doors open only after you meet disciplined people where they live their practice.
ramayan::1513.detailed_meaning: Trisanku has been refused by Vasishta and now turns to Vasishta's sons. He reaches their hermitage and sees a hundred renowned ascetics absorbed in austerity. The scene sets up his next appeal, not a teaching yet.
ramayan::1513.modern_relevance: You walk into a quiet retreat where people have been waking before dawn for years. Their calm is not an accident — it is the visible shape of long practice.
ramayan::1513.insight: It prepares the next exchange by showing the ascetics' authority and Trisanku's desperation.

ramayan::1514.verse_sanskrit: सोऽभिगम्य महात्मनस्सर्वानेव गुरोस्सुतान् । । 15715 । । अभिवाद्यानुपूर्व्येण ह्रिया किञ्चिदवाङ्मुख: । अब्रवीत्सुमहाभगान्सर्वानेव कृताञ्जलि: । । 15716 । ।
ramayan::1514.verse_hindi: The king, having approached all the illustrious sons of his spiritual guide, paid obeisance to them in order of seniority. Bowing down his face in humility and with folded palms, he addressed all those distinguished sons of Vasishta saying:
ramayan::1514.english_translation: The king, having approached all the illustrious sons of his spiritual guide, paid obeisance to them in order of seniority. Bowing down his face in humility and with folded palms, he addressed all those distinguished sons of Vasishta saying:
ramayan::1514.translation_literal: सः (he) / अभिगम्य (having approached) / महात्मनः (great-souled) / सर्वान् एव (all indeed) / गुरोः सुतान् (the teacher's sons) / अभिवाद्य (having saluted) / अनुपूर्व्येण (in order) / ह्रिया (with modesty) / किञ्चित् (slightly) / अवाङ्मुखः (face lowered) / अब्रवीत् (spoke) / सुमहाभगान् (highly fortunate ones) / सर्वान् एव (all indeed) / कृताञ्जलिः (with folded palms)
ramayan::1514.speaker: Trisanku
ramayan::1514.essence: He lowers himself before asking for help.
ramayan::1514.simple_meaning: The king approaches Vasishta's sons respectfully, bows in order, and speaks to them with humility and folded hands.
ramayan::1514.simple_insight: Respect opens the door when pride would only close it.
ramayan::1514.detailed_meaning: Trisanku has been refused by Vasishta and now turns to Vasishta's sons. Before asking for help, he bows properly, lowers his face, and addresses them with formal respect. The scene sets up his plea for refuge in the next verse.
ramayan::1514.modern_relevance: You walk into a room after being turned down once already. Pride would harden you, but humility gives you another chance to be heard.
ramayan::1514.insight: It shows that even a desperate request begins with honor and restraint.

ramayan::1515.verse_sanskrit: शरणं व: प्रपद्येऽहं शरण्यान् शरणागत: । प्रत्याख्यातोऽस्मि भद्रं वो वसिष्ठेन महात्मना । । 15717 । ।
ramayan::1515.verse_hindi: O protectors of those who seek refuge in you, protect me. Wish you well. I have been refused by the great Vasishta.
ramayan::1515.english_translation: O protectors of those who seek refuge in you, protect me. Wish you well. I have been refused by the great Vasishta.
ramayan::1515.translation_literal: शरणं (refuge) / वः (to you) / प्रपद्ये (I seek) / अहम् (I) / शरण्यान् (protectors of those who seek refuge) / शरणागतः (having come for refuge) / प्रत्याख्यातः (refused) / अस्मि (I am) / भद्रम् (well-being) / वः (to you) / वसिष्ठेन (by Vasishta) / महात्मना (the great-souled one)
ramayan::1515.speaker: Trisanku
ramayan::1515.essence: Refuge becomes real only when pride has already been wounded.
ramayan::1515.simple_meaning: Trisanku humbly asks Vasishta's sons for protection after being rejected by Vasishta himself.
ramayan::1515.simple_insight: There is strength in asking plainly for help after humiliation.
ramayan::1515.detailed_meaning: Trisanku has already been turned away by Vasishta. Now he approaches Vasishta's sons, bows to them in order, and asks them to protect him. The verse captures the exact moment where wounded pride gives way to humble surrender.
ramayan::1515.modern_relevance: You send the apology text after being ignored, then sit with the sting before trying again. Pride wants to vanish. Humility keeps speaking.
ramayan::1515.insight: It shifts the mind from defending status to seeking rightful help.

ramayan::1516.verse_sanskrit: यष्टुकामो महायज्ञं तदनुज्ञातुमर्हथ । गुरुपुत्रानहं सर्वान्नमस्कृत्य प्रसादये । । 15718 । ।
ramayan::1516.verse_hindi: I wish to perform a great sacrifice. You are worthy enough to tender your consent. I pay homage to all the sons of my spiritual guide oblige.
ramayan::1516.english_translation: I wish to perform a great sacrifice. You are worthy enough to grant your consent. I bow to all the sons of my teacher and ask for your favor.
ramayan::1516.translation_literal: यष्टुकामः (wishing to perform a sacrifice) / महायज्ञम् (a great sacrifice) / तत् (that) / अनुज्ञातुम् (to grant permission) / अर्हथ (you are worthy) / गुरुपुत्रान् (the sons of the teacher) / अहम् (I) / सर्वान् (all) / नमस्कृत्य (having bowed) / प्रसादये (I ask for favor)
ramayan::1516.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1516.essence: Humility can carry a serious request farther than force.
ramayan::1516.simple_meaning: He wants to perform a great sacrifice and asks the sons of his teacher for their permission with full respect.
ramayan::1516.simple_insight: Respect does not weaken your request; it gives it dignity.
ramayan::1516.detailed_meaning: King Janaka has already been turned away by Vasishta, so he turns to the teacher's sons instead. He does not demand, even in urgency. He bows, asks permission, and places his need inside reverence.
ramayan::1516.modern_relevance: You need help, but the room is full of people who could say no. Instead of pushing harder, you lower your voice, name the request clearly, and let respect do some of the work.
ramayan::1516.insight: It teaches you to seek what you need without entitlement, keeping dignity on both sides.

ramayan::1517.verse_sanskrit: शिरसा प्रणतो याचे ब्राह्मणान् तपसि स्थितान् । ते मां भवन्तस्सिद्ध्यर्थं याजयन्तु समाहिता: । । 15719 । । सशरीरो यथाऽहं हि देवलोकमवाप्नुयाम् ।
ramayan::1517.verse_hindi: You, brahmins are established in austerity. I bow to you. I beg all of you to direct me with composed minds to direct me in order to attain heaven in physical form.
ramayan::1517.english_translation: You, brahmins are established in austerity. I bow to you. I beg all of you to guide me with composed minds so I may attain heaven in my own body.
ramayan::1517.translation_literal: शिरसा (with the head) / प्रणतः (bowed down) / याचे (I beg) / ब्राह्मणान् (the brahmins) / तपसि (in austerity) / स्थितान् (established) / ते (they) / माम् (me) / भवन्तः (you all) / सिद्ध्यर्थम् (for success) / याजयन्तु (may cause to perform the sacrifice) / समाहिताः (with composed minds) / सशरीरः (with the body) / यथा (so that) / अहम् (I) / हि (indeed) / देवलोकम् (the realm of the radiant beings) / अवाप्नुयाम् (may attain)
ramayan::1517.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1517.essence: Humility can do what pride cannot: unlock the help that makes success possible.
ramayan::1517.simple_meaning: He bows to the learned brahmins and asks them to help him perform the rite correctly so he can reach the higher realm while still alive.
ramayan::1517.simple_insight: There is strength in asking wisely and bowing before what you cannot do alone.
ramayan::1517.detailed_meaning: A rejected king stands before the sons of his teacher and the brahmins learned in austerity. He has been refused by Vasishta, yet he still wants to complete the sacrifice. So he lowers himself and asks for their composed help.
ramayan::1517.modern_relevance: You have tried everything you know, and the problem is still bigger than your pride. The breakthrough comes when you stop performing competence and ask the people who truly know.
ramayan::1517.insight: It shifts you from self-reliance as identity to humility as a practical path to success.

ramayan::1518.verse_sanskrit: प्रत्याख्यातो वसिष्ठेन गतिमन्यां तपोधना: । । 15720 । । गुरुपुत्रानृते सर्वान्नाहं पश्यामि काञ्चन ।
ramayan::1518.verse_hindi: O Ascetocs after having been rejected by Vasishta. I do not see any way other than the sons of my spiritual guide to help me achieve my purpose.
ramayan::1518.english_translation: O ascetics, after being rejected by Vasishta, I see no other way except the sons of my teacher.
ramayan::1518.translation_literal: प्रत्याख्यातो (rejected) / वसिष्ठेन (by Vasishta) / गतिम् (way, resort) / अन्याम् (other) / तपोधनाः (O ascetics, rich in austerity) / गुरुपुत्रान् (the sons of the teacher) / ऋते (except) / सर्वान् (all) / न (not) / अहम् (I) / पश्यामि (see) / काञ्चन (at all)
ramayan::1518.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1518.essence: When pride fails, the right guide becomes the only path.
ramayan::1518.simple_meaning: After Vasishta refuses him, he sees no alternative except the teacher's sons. The verse shows complete dependence on the guru's lineage.
ramayan::1518.simple_insight: Real humility begins when pride stops pretending you can do everything alone.
ramayan::1518.detailed_meaning: King Sagara has failed to secure the sacrifice through Vasishta. Standing before ascetics, he admits there is no other help left except the sons of his teacher. The moment turns urgency into surrender to rightful authority.
ramayan::1518.modern_relevance: You have asked three people and heard no. The deadline is still there, and the only person who can help is the one you almost avoided calling.
ramayan::1518.insight: It shifts the mind from self-reliance to rightful dependence on the teacher's line.

ramayan::1519.verse_sanskrit: इक्ष्वाकूणां हि सर्वेषां पुरोधा: परमा गति: । । 15721 । । पुरोधसस्तु विद्वांसस्तारयन्ति सदा नृपान् । तस्मादनन्तरं सर्वे भवन्तो दैवतं मम । । 15722 । ।
ramayan::1519.verse_hindi: For all the descendants of Ikshvakus the spiritual preceptor is the supreme resort for  salvation. Learned spiritual preceptors have always liberated kings. Hence you are all gods to me only next to Vasishta.
ramayan::1519.english_translation: For all the descendants of Ikshvaku, the teacher is the highest refuge. Learned teachers have always carried kings across. Therefore, after Vasishta, all of you are divine to me.
ramayan::1519.translation_literal: इक्ष्वाकूणां (of the Ikshvakus) / हि (indeed) / सर्वेषां (of all) / पुरोधा: (the family priest/teacher) / परमा (highest) / गति: (refuge, resort) / पुरोधसः (of teachers) / तु (indeed) / विद्वांसः (the learned) / तारयन्ति (carry across, save) / सदा (always) / नृपान् (kings) / तस्मात् (therefore) / अनन्तरम् (next, after) / सर्वे (all) / भवन्तः (you all) / दैवतं (divine beings) / मम (to me)
ramayan::1519.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1519.essence: Real guidance can carry you farther than force ever will.
ramayan::1519.simple_meaning: The teacher is the safest guide for a ruler, and a wise teacher can carry people across confusion. After Vasishta, these sages are treated with deep reverence.
ramayan::1519.simple_insight: You do not have to navigate every crisis alone; wise guidance can be the difference between confusion and passage.
ramayan::1519.detailed_meaning: Trisanku has been rejected by Vasishta and is pleading with Vasishta’s sons and other sages for help. In his desperation, he says the teacher is the highest refuge for Ikshvaku kings, because learned teachers have always carried rulers across danger. So he bows to them as sacred authority.
ramayan::1519.modern_relevance: You are stuck in a problem that your own effort has not solved, and the person who could help has more experience than you do. Humility becomes practical when you finally ask the right guide.
ramayan::1519.insight: It shifts you from self-reliance in panic to reverent trust in qualified guidance.

ramayan::1520.verse_sanskrit: ततस्त्रिशङ्कोर्वचनं श्रुत्वा क्रोधसमन्वितम् । ऋषिपुत्रशतं राम राजानमिदमब्रवीत् । । 1581 । ।
ramayan::1520.verse_hindi: O Rama to these words of king Trisanku, the hundred sons of the sage angrily reacted:
ramayan::1520.english_translation: Then, hearing Trisanku's words, the hundred sons of the sage, full of anger, said this to the king.
ramayan::1520.translation_literal: ततः (then) / त्रिशङ्कोः (of Trisanku) / वचनम् (words) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / क्रोध-समन्वितम् (accompanied by anger) / ऋषि-पुत्र-शतम् (hundred sons of the sage) / राम (O Rama) / राजानम् (to the king) / इदम् (this) / अब्रवीत् (said)
ramayan::1520.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1520.essence: The next refusal is already forming before the answer is spoken.
ramayan::1520.simple_meaning: After hearing Trisanku's request, the sage's hundred sons answered in anger.
ramayan::1520.simple_insight: A request can fail not because it is impossible, but because it violates the people you ask.
ramayan::1520.detailed_meaning: Trisanku has already been rejected by Vasishta and now turns elsewhere for help. The hundred sons of the sage hear his words and respond with anger, setting up the next refusal in this chain of appeals.
ramayan::1520.modern_relevance: You ask the second person after the first has already said no, hoping the answer will change. Sometimes the real issue is not the request — it is the boundary you keep trying to cross.
ramayan::1520.insight: It shows how a plea can trigger resistance when it ignores rightful limits.

ramayan::1521.verse_sanskrit: प्रत्याख्यातो हि दुर्बुद्धे गुरुणा सत्यवादिना । तं कथं समतिक्रम्य शाखान्तरमुपेयिवान् । । 1582 । ।
ramayan::1521.verse_hindi: O Evilminded one having been refused by the Guru true to his word, how could you bypass him and approach us who are mere off shoots (of the main).
ramayan::1521.english_translation: O evil-minded one, having been refused by the Guru who speaks the truth, how could you bypass him and approach us, who are only offshoots of the main line?
ramayan::1521.translation_literal: प्रत्याख्यातः (refused) / हि (indeed) / दुर्बुद्धे (evil-minded one) / गुरुणा (by the Guru) / सत्यवादिना (by the truth-speaking one) / तं (that) / कथम् (how) / समतिक्रम्य (having bypassed) / शाखान्तरम् (another branch / offshoot) / उपेयिवान् (did you approach)
ramayan::1521.speaker: Rishiputra
ramayan::1521.essence: A refusal from the source cannot be undone by asking around it.
ramayan::1521.simple_meaning: The sages' sons rebuke Trishanku for trying to go around his first teacher and seek help from a lesser branch after being refused.
ramayan::1521.simple_insight: Not every refusal is a door to be worked around; some boundaries deserve respect.
ramayan::1521.detailed_meaning: Trishanku has already been turned away by his guru, Vashistha. Angry, he turns to the sons of the sage instead. They stop him at once, saying he cannot bypass the one true authority and come to them as a shortcut.
ramayan::1521.modern_relevance: You get a no from the person who actually owns the decision, then try to reach their assistant, colleague, or manager to reopen it. The verse warns against treating hierarchy like an obstacle course.
ramayan::1521.insight: It teaches you to honour rightful order instead of seeking a side door after rejection.

ramayan::1522.verse_sanskrit: इक्ष्वाकूणां हि सर्वेषां पुरोधा: परमो गुरु: । न चातिक्रमितुं शक्यं वचनं सत्यवादिन: । । 1583 । ।
ramayan::1522.verse_hindi: For all the kings of the Ikshvakus race, their chief priest is their Guru. It is not possible
ramayan::1522.english_translation: For all the kings of the Ikshvaku line, the chief priest is their highest Guru. The word of one who speaks truth cannot be crossed.
ramayan::1522.translation_literal: इक्ष्वाकूणां (of the Ikshvakus) / हि (indeed) / सर्वेषां (of all) / पुरोधाः (the chief priest) / परमा (highest) / गुरु: (teacher) / न (not) / च (and) / अतिक्रमितुम् (to overstep) / शक्यम् (possible) / वचनम् (word) / सत्यवादिनः (of the truth-speaking one)
ramayan::1522.speaker: Rishiputra
ramayan::1522.essence: A truthful teacher's refusal is not something you can simply bypass.
ramayan::1522.simple_meaning: Among the Ikshvaku kings, the chief priest is the highest teacher, and his truthful word cannot be ignored or overruled.
ramayan::1522.simple_insight: There is strength in respecting guidance that comes from integrity, even when it blocks what you want.
ramayan::1522.detailed_meaning: Trisanku has pressed his demand, and the sages' sons answer with anger. They remind him that among the Ikshvakus, Vasishta is not just a priest but the highest authority, and his truthful refusal cannot be crossed.
ramayan::1522.modern_relevance: You push back against a mentor's boundary because you want a different answer. But the person who has earned trust by telling the truth is not there to be negotiated with.
ramayan::1522.insight: It shifts you from arguing for permission to respecting the limits set by truthful guidance.

ramayan::1523.verse_sanskrit: अशक्यमिति चोवाच वसिष्ठो भगवानृषि: । तं वयं वै समाहर्तुं क्रतुं शक्ता:कथं तव । । 1584 । ।
ramayan::1523.verse_hindi: When an adorable sage like Vasishta has already said, it is not possible, how can we help you conduct such a sacrifice?
ramayan::1523.english_translation: When the revered sage Vasishta has already said that it is impossible, how can we undertake that sacrifice for you?
ramayan::1523.translation_literal: अशक्यम् (impossible) / इति (thus) / च (and) / उवाच (said) / वसिष्ठः (Vasishta) / भगवान् (revered) / ऋषिः (sage) / तम् (that) / वयम् (we) / वै (indeed) / समाहर्तुम् (to undertake) / क्रतुम् (sacrifice) / शक्ताः (able) / कथम् (how) / तव (for you)
ramayan::1523.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1523.essence: A wise refusal cannot be bypassed by insistence.
ramayan::1523.simple_meaning: Vasishta has already refused, so the priests say they cannot go against his judgment and perform the sacrifice.
ramayan::1523.simple_insight: Respecting a clear refusal protects both dignity and order.
ramayan::1523.detailed_meaning: The priests are speaking after Vasishta has rejected the request. In the court of the Ikshvakus, a guru's word is binding. They are not just declining a ritual; they are defending the authority of truth-speaking wisdom.
ramayan::1523.modern_relevance: You keep trying to reopen a decision after the expert has already said no. The clean move is not pressure — it is respect for the boundary that was set.
ramayan::1523.insight: It shifts you from persuasion at any cost to honoring a clear limit.

ramayan::1524.verse_sanskrit: बालिशस्त्वं नरश्रेष्ठ गम्यतां स्वपुरं पुन: । याजने भगवाञ्छक्तस्त्रैलोक्यस्यापि पार्थिव । । 1585 । । अवमानं च तत्कर्तुं तस्य शक्ष्यामहे कथम् ।
ramayan::1524.verse_hindi: O Best one among men you are childish. Return to your capital. O Monarch the most venerable Vasishta is capable of conducting sacrifices performed by anybody in the three worlds. How can we dishonour him?
ramayan::1524.english_translation: O best among men, you are childish. Return to your own capital. The venerable Vasishta is able to conduct sacrifices in all three worlds. How can we dishonour him?
ramayan::1524.translation_literal: बालिशः (childish) / त्वम् (you) / नरश्रेष्ठ (O best among men) / गम्यताम् (let it be gone; return) / स्वपुरम् (to your own city) / पुनः (again) / याजने (in sacrifice-conducting) / भगवन् (venerable one) / शक्तः (capable) / त्रैलोक्यस्य (of the three worlds) / अपि (even) / पार्थिव (O king) / अवमानम् (dishonour) / च (and) / तत् (that) / कर्तुम् (to do) / तस्य (of him) / शक्ष्यामहे (shall we be able) / कथम् (how)
ramayan::1524.speaker: Vasishta
ramayan::1524.essence: You cannot build your goal by insulting the one who already deserves the role.
ramayan::1524.simple_meaning: Vasishta refuses the king's request and says the king should go home. A capable priest should not be insulted by being bypassed.
ramayan::1524.simple_insight: Real respect means not using someone else's worth as a tool for your own wish.
ramayan::1524.detailed_meaning: A king has come asking sages to perform a sacrifice that their own teacher Vasishta could do. The sages bristle at the insult. Vasishta speaks sharply: the king should return home, because asking them to step over their revered teacher is dishonour.
ramayan::1524.modern_relevance: You ask a senior colleague to redo work that your mentor already approved, and suddenly the room goes cold. The issue is not only the task — it's the disrespect hidden inside the request.
ramayan::1524.insight: It teaches you to see when a request becomes a slight, and to protect rightful honour without hesitation.

ramayan::1525.verse_sanskrit: तेषां तद्वचनं श्रुत्वा क्रोधपर्याकुलाक्षरम् । । 1586 । । स राजा पुनरेवैतानिदं वचनमब्रवीत् ।
ramayan::1525.verse_hindi: Having heard the confused words uttered by the sages in a state of anger, the king said again:
ramayan::1525.english_translation: Having heard the sages' angry, confused words, the king spoke again:
ramayan::1525.translation_literal: तेषाम् (their) / तत्-वचनम् (that speech) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / क्रोध-पर्याकुल-अक्षरम् (words agitated by anger) / सः (he) / राजा (the king) / पुनः एव (again) / एतानि (these) / इदम् (this) / वचनम् (speech) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::1525.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1525.essence: The king heard their anger and answered once more.
ramayan::1525.simple_meaning: After hearing the sages speak in anger and confusion, the king answered them again.
ramayan::1525.simple_insight: A tense exchange is still unfolding; the real meaning comes in the next line.
ramayan::1525.detailed_meaning: King Janaka is in the middle of a difficult exchange with the sages. They have just rejected his request, and their anger has sharpened the moment. This verse only marks that he heard them and replied again, so it serves the argument rather than completing it.
ramayan::1525.modern_relevance: A room goes quiet after a blunt refusal, and you realize the conversation is not over yet. This is the breath before the next reply.
ramayan::1525.insight: It marks a pause in the argument, not the lesson itself.

ramayan::1526.verse_sanskrit: प्रत्याख्यातोऽस्मि गुरुणा गुरुपुत्रैस्तथैव च । । 1587 । । अन्यां गतिं गमिष्यामि स्वस्ति वोऽस्तु तपोधना: ।
ramayan::1526.verse_hindi: O Men endowed with the wealth of asceticism I was rejected by my guru and now by his sons. I shall seek another way. Farewell to you.
ramayan::1526.english_translation: O men endowed with the wealth of asceticism, I was rejected by my guru and now by his sons. I shall seek another way. Farewell to you.
ramayan::1526.translation_literal: प्रत्याख्यातः (rejected) / अस्मि (I am) / गुरुणा (by the guru) / गुरु-पुत्रैः (by the guru's sons) / तथा एव च (and likewise) / अन्याम् (another) / गतिम् (way) / गमिष्यामि (I shall go) / स्वस्ति (farewell / may all be well) / वः (to you) / अस्तु (be) / तपोधनाḥ (you who are rich in asceticism)
ramayan::1526.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1526.essence: Rejected at every door, he leaves without begging.
ramayan::1526.simple_meaning: The king says he has been turned away by his teacher and then by the teacher's sons, so he will leave and find another way forward.
ramayan::1526.simple_insight: Rejection can become a turning point instead of an end.
ramayan::1526.detailed_meaning: A king comes to the forest sages seeking help, but they answer him with anger and refusal. He has already been turned away by his teacher, and now by the teacher's sons too. This verse captures the moment he chooses to leave rather than force his way in.
ramayan::1526.modern_relevance: You ask for guidance and get shut out twice. At some point, dignity means stepping back, naming the rejection, and finding a different path.
ramayan::1526.insight: It shifts you from pressing against refusal to choosing a new course with composure.

ramayan::1527.verse_sanskrit: ऋषिपुत्रास्तु तच्छ्रुत्वा वाक्यं घोराभिसंहितम् । । 1588 । । शेपु: परमसङ्कृद्धाश्चण्डालत्वं गमिष्यसि ।
ramayan::1527.verse_hindi: Having seen his fierce intent, the saints sons were infuriated. They cursed him saying, Be a Chandala
ramayan::1527.english_translation: Having heard his fierce intent, the sages' sons became terribly enraged and cursed him: "You will become a Chandala."
ramayan::1527.translation_literal: ऋषिपुत्राः (the sages' sons) / तु (indeed) / तत् (that) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / वाक्यम् (the speech) / घोराभिसंहितम् (filled with fierce intent) / शेपुः (cursed) / परमसङ्कृद्धाः (utterly enraged) / चण्डालत्वम् (state of a Chandala) / गमिष्यसि (you will become)
ramayan::1527.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1527.essence: Anger turns a dispute into a curse.
ramayan::1527.simple_meaning: The sages' sons hear the king's harsh reply, lose their temper, and curse him to become a Chandala.
ramayan::1527.simple_insight: A single burst of anger can turn a disagreement into a life-changing curse.
ramayan::1527.detailed_meaning: After being rejected by his teacher and the teacher's sons, the king answers with defiance. The sages' sons hear the threat in his words, flare with rage, and pronounce a curse that will drag him into a degraded state.
ramayan::1527.modern_relevance: A heated text thread can turn one sharp sentence into a lasting rupture. What you say in anger can reshape the whole relationship.
ramayan::1527.insight: It shows how quickly wounded pride can escalate into irreversible consequences.

ramayan::1528.verse_sanskrit: एवमुक्त्वा महात्मनो विविशुस्ते स्वमाश्रमम् । । 1589 । । अथ रात्र्यां व्यतीतायां राजा चण्डालतां गत: ।
ramayan::1528.verse_hindi: With this the highsouled sons of Vasishta entered their hermitage. And one night after the king became a Chandala (a lowcaste man).
ramayan::1528.english_translation: With this, the great-souled sons entered their own hermitage. Then, after the night had passed, the king became a Chandala.
ramayan::1528.translation_literal: एवम् (thus) / उक्त्वा (having spoken) / महात्मनः (of the great-souled ones) / विविशुः (entered) / ते (they) / स्वम् (their own) / आश्रमम् (hermitage) / अथ (then) / रात्र्याम् (in the night) / व्यतीतायाम् (having passed) / राजा (the king) / चण्डालताम् (the state of a Chandala) / गतः (became)
ramayan::1528.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1528.essence: The curse takes effect after the speakers are gone.
ramayan::1528.simple_meaning: After the sages returned to their hermitage, the king spent the night and was transformed into a Chandala.
ramayan::1528.simple_insight: Some words and actions carry consequences that arrive after the moment has passed.
ramayan::1528.detailed_meaning: Vasishta’s sons have just cursed the king in anger and gone back to their hermitage. The verse then marks the grim result: by the next night, the king has fallen into the cursed state of a Chandala. It is a transition, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::1528.modern_relevance: You leave a conversation thinking it was over, then wake up to the damage it set in motion. Some choices keep working long after the room has emptied.
ramayan::1528.insight: It shows consequence unfolding after speech, not in the heat of the moment.

ramayan::1529.verse_sanskrit: नीलवस्त्रधरो नील: पुरुषो ध्वस्तमूर्धज: । । 15810 । । चित्यमाल्यानुलेपश्च आयसाभरणोऽभवत् ।
ramayan::1529.verse_hindi: The king was tranformed into a darkcomplexioned dirty man with dishevelled hair. His body was besmeared with ashes and on his robes lay wreath collected from the cemetery. He had on him dark (soiled) clothes, and ornaments made of iron.
ramayan::1529.english_translation: The king became a dark, dishevelled man, with ashes on his body, cemetery garlands on his clothes, and iron ornaments.
ramayan::1529.translation_literal: नीलवस्त्रधरः (wearing dark clothes) / नीलः (dark) / पुरुषः (man) / ध्वस्तमूर्धजः (with dishevelled hair) / चित्यमाल्यानुलेपः (with cemetery garlands and ash-smeared body) / च आयसाभरणः (and with iron ornaments) / अभवत् (became)
ramayan::1529.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1529.essence: Royal status can vanish before anyone has time to object.
ramayan::1529.simple_meaning: The king was transformed into a frightening outcast figure, marked by ashes, dark clothes, loose hair, and iron ornaments.
ramayan::1529.simple_insight: A curse can strip away status in a single moment.
ramayan::1529.detailed_meaning: Vasishta's sons have just cursed the king, and the change takes hold immediately. His royal form is gone, replaced by the appearance of a Chandala, so the next verse can show how quickly courtly respect collapses.
ramayan::1529.modern_relevance: One harsh sentence in a room can change how everyone sees you. The room stays the same, but your place in it can vanish at once.
ramayan::1529.insight: It shows the visible social cost of a curse: identity, dignity, and belonging can all be overturned together.

ramayan::1530.verse_sanskrit: तं दृष्टवा मन्त्रिणस्सर्वे त्यज्य चण्डालरूपिणम् । । 15811 । । प्राद्रवन् सहिता राम पौरा येऽस्यानुगामिन: ।
ramayan::1530.verse_hindi: O Rama seeing him in the form of a chandala, all his counsellors, inhabitants of the city including his followers fled away.
ramayan::1530.english_translation: O Rama, seeing him in the form of a chandala, all his counsellors and the city people who followed him fled away together.
ramayan::1530.translation_literal: तम् (him) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / मन्त्रिणः (the counsellors) / सर्वे (all) / त्यज्य (abandoning) / चण्डालरूपिणम् (the one in the form of a chandala) / प्राद्रवन् (ran away) / सहिताः (together) / राम (O Rama) / पौरा (the city people) / ये (who) / अस्य (his) / अनुगामिनः (followers)
ramayan::1530.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1530.essence: Status can vanish in a single glance.
ramayan::1530.simple_meaning: The king’s own people saw his changed appearance and ran away from him in fear.
ramayan::1530.simple_insight: Fear can erase loyalty in an instant, leaving even power utterly alone.
ramayan::1530.detailed_meaning: After the king is transformed into a chandala-like figure, his counsellors, citizens, and followers cannot bear to look at him. They flee together, and the scene shows how completely his status has collapsed before the next turn in the story.
ramayan::1530.modern_relevance: You can feel the room change when people realize your situation has fallen apart. The same crowd that stood near you a moment ago can vanish first.
ramayan::1530.insight: It shows how quickly social support disappears when appearance and status are stripped away.

ramayan::1531.verse_sanskrit: एको हि राजा काकुत्स्थ जगाम परमात्मवान् । । 15812 । । दह्यमानो दिवारात्रं विश्वामित्रं तपोनिधिम् ।
ramayan::1531.verse_hindi: O Descendant of Kakustha wandering alone burning with distress night and day the king went to Viswamitra who was rich in asceticism.
ramayan::1531.english_translation: O descendant of Kakustha, the king, burning with distress day and night, went alone to Viswamitra, the treasure of ascetic power.
ramayan::1531.translation_literal: एकः (alone) / हि (indeed) / राजा (the king) / काकुत्स्थ (O descendant of Kakustha) / जगाम (went) / परमात्मवान् (endowed with great self-control) / दह्यमानः (being burned) / दिवारात्रम् (day and night) / विश्वामित्रम् (to Viswamitra) / तपोनिधिम् (treasure of ascetic power)
ramayan::1531.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1531.essence: Even a king must walk alone when suffering leaves no other choice.
ramayan::1531.simple_meaning: The king, overwhelmed by grief, went alone to Viswamitra for help.
ramayan::1531.simple_insight: When distress becomes unbearable, even a king must seek guidance.
ramayan::1531.detailed_meaning: Dasharatha is broken by the spell that has stripped away his dignity and turned him into an outcast figure. Alone and burning with shame, he goes to Viswamitra, the sage whose ascetic power can still alter events. The verse is a bridge into that encounter.
ramayan::1531.modern_relevance: You hit a point where pride stops helping and you finally call the one person who can steady the situation.
ramayan::1531.insight: It shifts the mind from self-protection to seeking the right help at the right time.

ramayan::1532.verse_sanskrit: विश्वामित्रस्तु तं दृष्ट्वा राजानं विफलीकृतम् । चण्डालरूपिणं राम मुनि: कारुण्यमागत: । । 15813 । ।
ramayan::1532.verse_hindi: O Rama on seeing the king reduced to a useless a chandala, sage Viswamitra was touched with pity.
ramayan::1532.english_translation: O Rama, seeing the king reduced to a useless chandala form, sage Viswamitra was moved to pity.
ramayan::1532.translation_literal: विश्वामित्रः (Viswamitra) / तु (indeed) / तम् (him) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / राजानम् (the king) / विफलीकृतम् (rendered helpless) / चण्डालरूपिणम् (in chandala form) / राम (O Rama) / मुनिः (the sage) / कारुण्यम् (pity) / आगत: (became moved)
ramayan::1532.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1532.essence: Compassion begins when you look past someone’s ruined appearance.
ramayan::1532.simple_meaning: Viswamitra sees the king transformed into a degraded, helpless form and feels compassion for him.
ramayan::1532.simple_insight: Pity can open the heart even when a person looks beyond help.
ramayan::1532.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has approached the distressed king who has been made to appear like a chandala. The sight is so extreme that the king seems helpless and unrecognisable. Instead of turning away, the sage feels compassion, preparing to speak.
ramayan::1532.modern_relevance: You meet someone after a collapse — unshaven, ashamed, barely holding themselves together. The first choice is not judgment. It is whether you can still see the person.
ramayan::1532.insight: It shifts attention from outward degradation to the human being still present beneath it.

ramayan::1533.verse_sanskrit: कारुण्यात्स महातेजा वाक्यं परमधार्मिक: । इदं जगाद भद्रं ते राजानं घोररूपिणम् । । 15814 । ।
ramayan::1533.verse_hindi: Exceedingly energetic and deeply pious, he looked at the king who was frightful in appearance and addressed him with compassion saying, welfare to you.
ramayan::1533.english_translation: Exceedingly energetic and deeply pious, he looked at the king who was frightful in appearance and addressed him with compassion saying, welfare to you.
ramayan::1533.translation_literal: कारुण्यात् (out of compassion) / सः (he) / महातेजाः (exceedingly radiant, powerful) / वाक्यम् (speech) / परमधार्मिकः (most righteous) / इदम् (this) / जगाद (said) / भद्रम् ते (welfare to you) / राजानम् (to the king) / घोररूपिणम् (having a frightening form)
ramayan::1533.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1533.essence: Compassion lets you speak gently to what distress has made unrecognizable.
ramayan::1533.simple_meaning: Moved by compassion, Vishwamitra speaks kindly to the king despite his frightening appearance.
ramayan::1533.simple_insight: Compassion can stay steady even when someone looks broken, cursed, or unrecognizable.
ramayan::1533.detailed_meaning: Rama has just reached the forest with Vishwamitra. The king is now disfigured by a curse and looks terrible to behold. Vishwamitra, moved by compassion, still greets him with kindness before asking what has happened.
ramayan::1533.modern_relevance: You meet someone after a collapse, and their face, voice, or posture tells you how much they have lost. The first honest response is not judgment but steadiness.
ramayan::1533.insight: It trains you to answer suffering with composure and humane speech instead of recoil.

ramayan::1534.verse_sanskrit: किमागमनकार्यं ते राजपुत्र महाबल । अयोध्याधिपते वीर शापाच्चण्डालतां गत: । । 15815 । ।
ramayan::1534.verse_hindi: O Mighty prince what brings your here, for you are the heroic lord of Ayodhya? Whose curse turned you into a chandala?
ramayan::1534.english_translation: O mighty prince, what brings you here, heroic lord of Ayodhya? Whose curse has turned you into a chandala?
ramayan::1534.translation_literal: किमागमनकार्यं (what is the purpose of your coming) / ते (your) / राजपुत्र (O prince) / महाबल (mighty one) / अयोध्याधिपते (lord of Ayodhya) / वीर (heroic one) / शापात् (by curse) / चण्डालतां (the state of a chandala) / गतः (gone)
ramayan::1534.speaker: Vishvamitra
ramayan::1534.essence: Respect survives even when status has collapsed.
ramayan::1534.simple_meaning: Vishvamitra asks the cursed king why he has come and who cursed him into this degraded state.
ramayan::1534.simple_insight: A fallen person can still be addressed with respect and curiosity.
ramayan::1534.detailed_meaning: Vishvamitra has just seen a king reduced by a curse to the appearance of a chandala. Moved by pity, he speaks to him gently, asking why he has come and what curse has brought him so low.
ramayan::1534.modern_relevance: You meet someone at their lowest and still choose dignity over disgust. The first question is not judgment, but understanding.
ramayan::1534.insight: It trains you to meet suffering with respectful attention before you try to fix it.

ramayan::1535.verse_sanskrit: अथ तद्वाक्यमाज्ञाय राजा चण्डालतां गत: । अब्रवीत्प्राञ्जलिर्वाक्यं वाक्यज्ञो वाक्यकोविदम् । । 15816 । ।
ramayan::1535.verse_hindi: In response to his words the king,  who had fallen into the state of a chandala yet proficient in expression, spoke to one (Viswamitra) expert in speech, with folded hands.
ramayan::1535.english_translation: In response to his words, the king who had fallen into the state of a chandala spoke with folded hands to the master of speech, who was skilled in speech.
ramayan::1535.translation_literal: अथ (then) / तद्-वाक्यम् (that speech) / आज्ञाय (having understood) / राजा (the king) / चण्डालताम् (the state of a chandala) / गतः (having gone) / अब्रवीत् (spoke) / प्राञ्जलिः (with folded hands) / वाक्यं (speech) / वाक्यज्ञः (knower of speech) / वाक्यकोविदम् (skilled in speech)
ramayan::1535.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1535.essence: Humiliation does not have to destroy your dignity.
ramayan::1535.simple_meaning: The king, now reduced to the lowest condition, answers respectfully with folded hands to the sage who questioned him.
ramayan::1535.simple_insight: Even in humiliation, dignity can remain in the way you speak.
ramayan::1535.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has just asked a fallen king how he came to this state. The king, though degraded and stripped of status, answers carefully and respectfully. This verse is the opening of his explanation, not the explanation itself.
ramayan::1535.modern_relevance: After being corrected in front of everyone, you still choose your words carefully instead of lashing out. That restraint changes the whole exchange.
ramayan::1535.insight: It shifts the mind from defending status to speaking with composure.

ramayan::1536.verse_sanskrit: प्रत्याख्यातोऽस्मि गुरुणा गुरुपुत्रैस्तथैव च । अनवाप्यैव तं कामं मया प्राप्तो विपर्यय: । । 15817 । ।
ramayan::1536.verse_hindi: Rejected by my guru and his sons, what I achieved was disaster and what I could not was the fulfilment of my wish.
ramayan::1536.english_translation: Rejected by my guru and his sons, what I achieved was disaster and what I could not was the fulfilment of my wish.
ramayan::1536.translation_literal: प्रत्याख्यातोऽस्मि (I have been rejected) / गुरुणा (by the teacher) / गुरु-पुत्रैः (by the teacher's sons) / तथा एव च (and likewise) / अनवाप्य एव (without obtaining) / तं (that) / कामम् (desired aim) / मया (by me) / प्राप्तः (obtained) / विपर्ययः (disaster / reversal)
ramayan::1536.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1536.essence: What he chased became the source of his ruin.
ramayan::1536.simple_meaning: He says he was turned away by his teacher and the teacher's sons. He got the opposite of what he wanted: failure instead of success.
ramayan::1536.simple_insight: Sometimes pursuit itself becomes the loss, even before the goal is missed.
ramayan::1536.detailed_meaning: A king in cursed disguise stands before a sage and admits the ruin of his life. He was refused by the very teacher he sought, and the wish he chased ended in reversal. The verse marks his recognition that desire has led him into the opposite of fulfilment.
ramayan::1536.modern_relevance: You pushed for the promotion, the approval, the one outcome you thought would fix everything. Instead, you got the fallout and the hollow feeling that the chase itself broke something.
ramayan::1536.insight: It shifts attention from craving success to seeing how desire can produce its own undoing.

ramayan::1537.verse_sanskrit: सशरीरो दिवं यायामिति मे सौम्यदर्शनम् । मया चेष्टं क्रतुशतं तच्च नाऽवाप्यते फलम् । । 15818 । ।
ramayan::1537.verse_hindi: O Gentle sage it is my intention to enter heaven with my physical body. I performed a hundred sacrifices but  did not reap its fruit.
ramayan::1537.english_translation: O gentle sage, my intention is to enter heaven with my physical body. I performed a hundred sacrifices, yet I did not receive their fruit.
ramayan::1537.translation_literal: सशरीरः (with the body) / दिवम् (to heaven) / यायाम् (I may go) / इति (thus) / मे (my) / सौम्यदर्शनम् (gentle-looking sage) / मया (by me) / चेष्टम् (performed) / क्रतुशतम् (hundred sacrifices) / तत् (that) / च (and) / न (not) / अवाप्यते (is obtained) / फलम् (fruit/result)
ramayan::1537.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1537.essence: Even a lifetime of merit can end in unanswered longing.
ramayan::1537.simple_meaning: The speaker says he wants to reach heaven while still alive, but even after a hundred sacrifices, he has not gained that result.
ramayan::1537.simple_insight: Even great effort can leave you face to face with disappointment, and that truth can become the start of deeper humility.
ramayan::1537.detailed_meaning: The king, rejected by his teacher and the teacher's sons, turns to a gentle sage with a painful confession: despite a lifetime of ritual merit, his goal has not been fulfilled. He is trying to understand why his spiritual effort has failed.
ramayan::1537.modern_relevance: You did the training, sent the applications, kept the promise, and still got nothing back. The ache of unrewarded effort is ancient, and it can open a harder honesty.
ramayan::1537.insight: It shifts you from expecting guaranteed payoff to facing the limits of ritual and effort with honesty.

ramayan::1538.verse_sanskrit: अनृतं नोक्तपूर्वं मे न च वक्ष्ये कदाचन । कृच्छ्रेष्वपि गत स्सौम्य क्षत्रधर्मेण ते शपे । । 15819 । ।
ramayan::1538.verse_hindi: O Gentle sage I have never told a lie in spite of troubled circumstances, I shall never dabble in falsehood. I swear upon it by kshatriya morality .
ramayan::1538.english_translation: Gentle sage, I have never spoken a lie, and I never will. Even in hardship, I swear by kshatriya duty.
ramayan::1538.translation_literal: अनृतं (falsehood) / न (not) / उक्तपूर्वं (spoken before) / मे (by me) / न (not) / च (and) / वक्ष्ये (I will speak) / कदाचन (ever) / कृच्छ्रेष्वपि (even in hardships) / गतः (gone) / सौम्य (gentle one) / क्षत्रधर्मेण (by kshatriya duty) / ते (to you) / शपे (I swear)
ramayan::1538.speaker: Rama
ramayan::1538.essence: Hardship does not excuse falsehood; it proves whether your word is real.
ramayan::1538.simple_meaning: Rama says he has never lied and never will, even in hardship. He swears to this as a matter of warrior duty.
ramayan::1538.simple_insight: Integrity is strongest when pressure is highest.
ramayan::1538.detailed_meaning: Rama is speaking to a gentle sage after lamenting the collapse of his hopes. He answers by grounding himself in one thing that cannot be taken away: his truthfulness. Even in suffering, he will not break his word.
ramayan::1538.modern_relevance: You are cornered in a conversation and tempted to soften the truth just to escape. This verse reminds you that pressure is exactly where character becomes visible.
ramayan::1538.insight: It shifts the mind from protecting comfort to protecting credibility.

ramayan::1539.verse_sanskrit: यज्ञैर्बहुविधैरिष्टं प्रजा धर्मेण पालिता: । । 15820 । । गुरवश्च महात्मान श्शीलवृत्तेन तोषिता: ।
ramayan::1539.verse_hindi: I have performed various sacirifices and ruled over my people guided by the law of righteousness. I have pleased eminent elders with my conduct and character.
ramayan::1539.english_translation: I have performed many kinds of sacrifices, ruled my people according to righteousness, and pleased great elders through my conduct and character.
ramayan::1539.translation_literal: यज्ञैः (by sacrifices) / बहुविधैः (of many kinds) / इष्टम् (performed) / प्रजा (the people) / धर्मेण (by righteousness) / पालिताः (protected, ruled) / गुरवः (the elders, teachers) / च (and) / महात्मानः (great-souled ones) / शीलवृत्तेन (by conduct and character) / तोषिताः (satisfied, pleased)
ramayan::1539.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1539.essence: Your conduct is the proof of your righteousness.
ramayan::1539.simple_meaning: A ruler says he has done sacrifices, governed justly, and earned the respect of noble elders through his conduct.
ramayan::1539.simple_insight: A good life is measured by how faithfully you carry responsibility, not by praise alone.
ramayan::1539.detailed_meaning: In the later Ayodhya dialogue, a king is defending the life he has lived: ritual duty, just rule, and disciplined conduct. He is not boasting; he is showing the moral record that should make his request worthy of acceptance.
ramayan::1539.modern_relevance: You look back after years of carrying a family, a team, or a company, and wonder why the people who benefited most still question your integrity.
ramayan::1539.insight: It shifts attention from claims to lived consistency: what you have repeatedly done becomes your moral evidence.

ramayan::1540.verse_sanskrit: धर्मे प्रयतमानस्य यज्ञं चाहर्तुमिच्छत: । । 15821 । । परितोषं न गच्छन्ति गुरवो मुनिपुङ्गव ।
ramayan::1540.verse_hindi: O Preeminent among sages I endeavour to do my duty. I intend to perform a sacrifice. My gurus do not appreciate this.
ramayan::1540.english_translation: O foremost among sages, though I am trying to do my duty and wish to perform a sacrifice, my teachers are not pleased.
ramayan::1540.translation_literal: धर्मे (in duty) / प्रयतमानस्य (of one striving) / यज्ञं (sacrifice) / च (and) / आहर्तुम् (to perform) / इच्छतः (of one wishing) / परितोषं (satisfaction) / न (not) / गच्छन्ति (they go) / गुरवः (the teachers) / मुनिपुङ्गव (O foremost among sages)
ramayan::1540.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1540.essence: Right action can still leave you without praise.
ramayan::1540.simple_meaning: A person may be trying to do the right thing and still not receive approval from respected teachers.
ramayan::1540.simple_insight: Doing what is right does not always feel rewarded in the moment.
ramayan::1540.detailed_meaning: A king has already defended his truth and his sacrifices. Now he tells a sage that, even while he tries to uphold duty and prepare a sacrifice, his teachers remain dissatisfied. The verse sits inside a larger argument about whether human effort can truly secure the right result.
ramayan::1540.modern_relevance: You spent weeks doing everything by the book, and the mentor still frowned. The work may be clean even when the response is not.
ramayan::1540.insight: It shifts attention from seeking approval to staying faithful to duty itself.

ramayan::1541.verse_sanskrit: दैवमेव परं मन्ये पौरुषं तु निरर्थकम् । । 15822 । । दैवेनाक्रम्यते सर्वं दैवं हि परमा गति: ।
ramayan::1541.verse_hindi: I consider destiny to be allpowerful. The effort of a man goes in vain. Everything is controlled by destiny. It is the supreme resort.
ramayan::1541.english_translation: I consider destiny to be all-powerful. Human effort is futile. Everything is overpowered by destiny; destiny is the highest refuge.
ramayan::1541.translation_literal: दैवम् (destiny) / एव (indeed) / परम् (supreme) / मन्ये (I consider) / पौरुषम् (human effort) / तु (but) / निरर्थकम् (without result) / दैवेन (by destiny) / आक्रम्यते (is overpowered) / सर्वम् (everything) / दैवम् (destiny) / हि (indeed) / परमा (highest) / गति: (refuge)
ramayan::1541.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1541.essence: He calls effort futile because he cannot bear the weight of consequence.
ramayan::1541.simple_meaning: Ravana says that human effort cannot beat destiny. He sees destiny as the force that decides everything and the highest refuge.
ramayan::1541.simple_insight: It can feel humbling when control slips from your hands and you realise not everything responds to willpower.
ramayan::1541.detailed_meaning: Ravana, pressed by consequences after rejecting counsel, speaks as a mind cornered by its own choices. He claims that effort is useless because destiny overrides everything, revealing both despair and self-justification in the same breath.
ramayan::1541.modern_relevance: You prepared for weeks, but the deal collapsed anyway. The mind reaches for a bigger explanation when effort fails — sometimes as wisdom, sometimes as a way to avoid responsibility.
ramayan::1541.insight: It shifts the mind from total control to the possibility that outcomes exceed personal effort.

ramayan::1542.verse_sanskrit: तस्य मे परमार्तस्य प्रसादमभिकाङ्क्षत: । । 15823 । । कर्तुमर्हसि भद्रं ते दैवोपहतकर्मण: ।
ramayan::1542.verse_hindi: My merits have been destroyed by destiny. Deeply afflicted, I crave a favour from you. You are fit to grant it. Wish you well
ramayan::1542.english_translation: You should grant me this favor. I am deeply afflicted, and destiny has ruined my efforts.
ramayan::1542.translation_literal: तस्य (of that) / मे (my) / परम-आर्तस्य (deeply afflicted) / प्रसादम् (favor, grace) / अभिकाङ्क्षत: (desiring, longing for) / कर्तुम्-अर्हसि (you are fit to do, you should grant) / भद्रम् ते (welfare to you) / दैव-उपहत-कर्मण: (of one whose actions have been struck down by destiny)
ramayan::1542.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1542.essence: When effort breaks, humility becomes the only door left.
ramayan::1542.simple_meaning: The speaker asks someone to grant a favor, saying he is crushed by fate and has no strength left to succeed on his own.
ramayan::1542.simple_insight: Sometimes the bravest move is to admit you cannot carry it alone.
ramayan::1542.detailed_meaning: A desperate speaker, already convinced that fate has defeated his efforts, turns to another person for help. This line is not the whole appeal but part of a larger plea for rescue, showing how helpless he feels before the next request for refuge.
ramayan::1542.modern_relevance: You have exhausted every option, and the problem still stands in front of you. At some point, pride gives way to the honest request: please help me.
ramayan::1542.insight: It shifts the mind from self-reliance to humble appeal when effort has failed.

ramayan::1543.verse_sanskrit: नान्यां गतिं गमिष्यामि नान्यश्शरणमस्ति मे । । 15824 । । दैवं पुरुषकारेण निवर्तयितुमर्हसि । ।
ramayan::1543.verse_hindi: I will not take refuge in anybody. There is no other protector for me. You are capable of averting my reverses in fate with human effort.
ramayan::1543.english_translation: I will not seek any other refuge. There is no other protector for me. You are capable of averting fate's blows through human effort.
ramayan::1543.translation_literal: नान्यां (no other) / गतिं (refuge, resort) / गमिष्यामि (I will go, I will seek) / नान्यश्शरणम् (no other shelter) / अस्ति (there is) / मे (for me) / दैवम् (fate, destiny) / पुरुषकारेण (through human effort) / निवर्तयितुम् (to turn back, avert) / अर्हसि (you are able, you should be able)
ramayan::1543.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1543.essence: True surrender asks for help where effort can still change the outcome.
ramayan::1543.simple_meaning: There is no other place to seek help. The speaker asks the listener to use human effort to reverse what fate has done.
ramayan::1543.simple_insight: When everything else fails, humility can still ask for help without giving up.
ramayan::1543.detailed_meaning: A king crushed by misfortune admits that no other refuge remains. He turns to another person and asks for active help, not pity, believing human effort can still push back what fate has done. The verse marks a desperate but clear surrender.
ramayan::1543.modern_relevance: You’ve exhausted every workaround, and the problem is still there. At some point, pride stops helping and you ask the one person who may still be able to move things.
ramayan::1543.insight: It shifts you from isolated struggle to honest dependence on the right help.

ramayan::1544.verse_sanskrit: उक्तवाक्यं तु राजानं कृपया कुशिकात्मज: । अब्रवीन्मधुरं वाक्यं साक्षाच्चण्डालरूपिणम् । । 1591 । ।
ramayan::1544.verse_hindi: What the king said was proved by his chandala form which the son of Kushika (Viswamitra) heard and out of compassion spoke these sweet words:
ramayan::1544.english_translation: Seeing the king in the form of a chandala, the son of Kushika, moved by compassion, spoke these gentle words.
ramayan::1544.translation_literal: उक्तवाक्यं (having spoken these words) / तु (indeed) / राजानं (the king) / कृपया (with compassion) / कुशिकात्मजः (the son of Kushika) / अब्रवीत् (spoke) / मधुरं (sweet) / वाक्यं (words) / साक्षात् (directly) / चण्डालरूपिणम् (in the form of a chandala)
ramayan::1544.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1544.essence: Compassion speaks softly to a person stripped of status.
ramayan::1544.simple_meaning: Viswamitra sees the king in a lowly disguise and responds with kind, gentle words.
ramayan::1544.simple_insight: Compassion can meet shame without flinching.
ramayan::1544.detailed_meaning: In the forest, Viswamitra stands before King Harishchandra, who has been reduced to a chandala-like state by his vow and suffering. Seeing the depth of the king's distress, Viswamitra answers not with judgment, but with tenderness.
ramayan::1544.modern_relevance: You meet someone after they have been humiliated, and you can either look away or speak gently. This verse chooses gentleness first.
ramayan::1544.insight: It shifts your response from social ranking to human suffering.

ramayan::1545.verse_sanskrit: ऐक्ष्वाक स्वागतं वत्स जानामि त्वां सुधार्मिकम् । शरणं ते भविष्यामि मा भैषीर्नृपपुङ्गव । । 1592 । ।
ramayan::1545.verse_hindi: O Descendant of Ikshvakus, O child, welcome. I know you as highly righteous. O eminent among kings fear not. I offer you refuge.
ramayan::1545.english_translation: O descendant of Ikshvaku, welcome, child. I know you as highly righteous. O foremost among kings, do not fear. I will be your refuge.
ramayan::1545.translation_literal: ऐक्ष्वाक (descendant of Ikshvaku) / स्वागतं (welcome) / वत्स (child) / जानामि (I know) / त्वां (you) / सुधार्मिकम् (highly righteous) / शरणं (refuge) / ते (for you) / भविष्यामि (I will be) / मा (do not) / भैषीः (fear) / नृपपुङ्गव (foremost among kings)
ramayan::1545.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::1545.essence: True refuge begins when someone sees your worth and removes your fear.
ramayan::1545.simple_meaning: Viswamitra welcomes Rama warmly, recognizes his righteousness, and promises protection. The meeting begins not with demand, but with trust and shelter.
ramayan::1545.simple_insight: Being seen clearly can feel like safety.
ramayan::1545.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has just heard the king's plea and now turns toward Rama with recognition instead of suspicion. He welcomes him as a righteous prince, reassures him, and offers himself as protector before asking for help with the sacrifice.
ramayan::1545.modern_relevance: You walk into a room already bracing for judgment, and someone says, 'I know who you are, and you're safe here.' That changes everything before the conversation even starts.
ramayan::1545.insight: It shifts the relationship from uncertainty to trust before any task begins.

ramayan::1546.verse_sanskrit: अहमामन्त्रये सर्वान्महर्षीन्पुण्यकर्मण: । यज्ञसाह्यकरान् राजन् ततो यक्ष्यसि निर्वृत: । । 1593 । ।
ramayan::1546.verse_hindi: O king I shall invite pious maharshis to assist you in the sacrifice which you will be able to perform with great relief.
ramayan::1546.english_translation: O king, I shall invite all the holy sages who can assist in the sacrifice, and then you will perform it with ease.
ramayan::1546.translation_literal: अहम् (I) / आमन्त्रये (shall invite) / सर्वान् (all) / महर्षीन् (great sages) / पुण्यकर्मणः (of holy deeds) / यज्ञसाह्यकरान् (those who help in the sacrifice) / राजन् (O king) / ततः (then) / यक्ष्यसि (you will perform the sacrifice) / निर्वृतः (with ease / relieved)
ramayan::1546.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::1546.essence: The right support makes a demanding duty possible.
ramayan::1546.simple_meaning: Viswamitra tells the king he will call the holy sages who can help with the sacrifice, so the ritual can proceed smoothly.
ramayan::1546.simple_insight: Right help turns a hard task into a bearable one.
ramayan::1546.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has just calmed the king and accepted his request. He now explains the next step: he will gather the sages needed for the rite, so the sacrifice can be completed without strain. The verse moves the scene from reassurance to practical preparation.
ramayan::1546.modern_relevance: You finally said yes to the project, and now the real work is assembling the right people. Relief comes not from doing everything alone, but from knowing who must be called in.
ramayan::1546.insight: It shifts attention from anxiety to coordination: the task becomes possible once the needed support is gathered.

ramayan::1547.verse_sanskrit: गुरुशापकृतं रूपं यदिदं त्वयि वर्तते । अनेन सह रूपेण सशरीरो गमिष्यसि । । 1594 । ।
ramayan::1547.verse_hindi: With the present physical body disfigured by the curse of your spiritual preceptor, you shall go to heaven.
ramayan::1547.english_translation: With the present physical body disfigured by the curse of your spiritual preceptor, you shall go to heaven.
ramayan::1547.translation_literal: गुरु-शाप-कृतम् (made by the teacher's curse) / रूपम् (form) / यत् (which) / इदम् (this) / त्वयि (in you) / वर्तते (remains) / अनेन (with this) / सह (along with) / रूपेण (form) / सशरीरः (with the body) / गमिष्यसि (you will go)
ramayan::1547.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1547.essence: A damaged body does not cancel a higher ascent.
ramayan::1547.simple_meaning: A curse has altered your body, but it does not block your higher destination. Even in this form, you will still attain a higher realm.
ramayan::1547.simple_insight: A painful mark does not cancel your worth or your future.
ramayan::1547.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra is speaking to King Trishanku after the sacrifice has been interrupted by a curse. He explains that the king's altered body will not prevent him from reaching a higher realm, setting up the extraordinary promise that follows.
ramayan::1547.modern_relevance: You walk into a room carrying an illness, a breakup, or a mistake everyone can see. The damage is real, but it does not get the final word about where your life can still go.
ramayan::1547.insight: It shifts attention from visible damage to the larger arc of a person's life.

ramayan::1548.verse_sanskrit: हस्तप्राप्तमहं मन्ये स्वर्गं तव नराधिप । यस्त्वं कौशिकमागम्य शरण्यं शरणागत: । । 1595 । ।
ramayan::1548.verse_hindi: O King since you have taken refuge in Viswamitra who is the protector of those who resort to him, I think heaven is already within your reach.
ramayan::1548.english_translation: O King, since you have taken refuge in Viswamitra, the protector of those who seek shelter, I think heaven is already within your reach.
ramayan::1548.translation_literal: हस्तप्राप्तम् (within reach) / अहम् (I) / मन्ये (think) / स्वर्गम् (heaven) / तव (your) / नराधिप (O king) / यत् (since) / त्वम् (you) / कौशिकम् (to Kaushika/Viswamitra) / आगम्य (having come) / शरण्यम् (the refuge-giver) / शरणागतः (having taken refuge)
ramayan::1548.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1548.essence: True refuge makes the highest good feel near.
ramayan::1548.simple_meaning: Taking shelter with a worthy protector brings you very close to the highest reward.
ramayan::1548.simple_insight: There is relief in being held by something greater than your own strength.
ramayan::1548.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra speaks to King Trishanku after accepting his plea. The king has come in surrender to a protector who can guide him beyond his fear and limitation. The verse turns that act of refuge into a promise of ascent.
ramayan::1548.modern_relevance: You finally ask for help after trying to carry everything alone. The relief is immediate: once you stop defending your pride, support can actually reach you.
ramayan::1548.insight: It shifts the mind from self-reliance as identity to surrender as access.

ramayan::1549.verse_sanskrit: एवमुक्त्वा महातेजा: पुत्रान् परमधार्मिकान् । व्यादिदेश महाप्राज्ञान् यज्ञसम्भारकारणात् । । 1596 । ।
ramayan::1549.verse_hindi: Most brilliant Viswamitra having thus spoken, ordered his deeply religious and highly
ramayan::1549.english_translation: Having spoken thus, the mighty sage ordered his highly wise sons to prepare the sacrificial materials.
ramayan::1549.translation_literal: एवमुक्त्वा (having spoken thus) / महातेजा: (the mighty-bright one) / पुत्रान् (sons) / परमधार्मिकान् (most righteous) / व्यादिदेश (ordered) / महाप्राज्ञान् (highly wise) / यज्ञसम्भारकारणात् (for the sake of sacrificial preparations)
ramayan::1549.speaker: Vishwamitra
ramayan::1549.essence: Spiritual purpose still depends on disciplined preparation.
ramayan::1549.simple_meaning: Vishwamitra gives instructions to his sons to arrange the items needed for the sacrifice.
ramayan::1549.simple_insight: Great rituals begin with clear, practical instruction.
ramayan::1549.detailed_meaning: Vishwamitra has just welcomed Rama and heard the signs that his refuge will succeed. Now he turns from blessing to action, instructing his righteous, intelligent sons to gather what the sacrifice needs. The verse is a bridge into the ritual preparations.
ramayan::1549.modern_relevance: You’ve decided to do something important, and now the real work starts: calling the right people, gathering what’s needed, and making it happen.
ramayan::1549.insight: It shifts attention from intention to execution, showing that sacred work still needs organized preparation.

ramayan::1550.verse_sanskrit: सर्वान् शिष्यान् समाहूय वाक्यमेतदुवाच ह । सर्वानृषिगणान्वत्सा आनयध्वं ममाज्ञया । सशिष्यसुहृदश्चैव सर्त्विज स्सबहुश्रुतान् । । 1597 । ।
ramayan::1550.verse_hindi: He summoned all his disciples, and said, Children bring here hosts of rishis along with their disciples and friends, officiating priests and persons wellversed in the Srutis. This is my order.
ramayan::1550.english_translation: He summoned all his disciples and said, "Children, bring here all the rishis, along with their disciples and friends, the officiating priests, and those well versed in the Vedas. This is my order."
ramayan::1550.translation_literal: सर्वान् (all) / शिष्यान् (disciples) / समाहूय (having summoned) / वाक्यम् (speech) / एतत् (this) / उवाच (said) / ह (indeed) / सर्वान् (all) / ऋषिगणान् (groups of rishis) / वत्सा (children) / आनयध्वम् (bring) / मम (my) / आज्ञया (by order) / सशिष्यसुहृदः (with disciples and friends) / चैव (and also) / सर्त्विजः (with officiating priests) / सबहुश्रुतान् (and those well versed in sacred learning)
ramayan::1550.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::1550.essence: A serious undertaking starts with gathering the right people.
ramayan::1550.simple_meaning: Viswamitra calls his disciples and instructs them to bring the rishis, priests, learned scholars, and their companions for the sacrifice.
ramayan::1550.simple_insight: Great work begins by gathering the right people, not by rushing ahead alone.
ramayan::1550.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has just welcomed Rama and Lakshmana and is preparing a major sacrifice. He now turns to his disciples and gives practical instructions to assemble the sages, priests, and learned guests needed for the ritual. The verse is a logistical step, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::1550.modern_relevance: You can't host something serious by improvising at the last minute. Before the work starts, the right people, roles, and support have to be gathered.
ramayan::1550.insight: It emphasizes preparation and coordination before a sacred or difficult task begins.

ramayan::1551.verse_hindi: If any one should speak with disrespect in response to my order, you may report the matter to me in full.
ramayan::1551.english_translation: If anyone speaks disrespectfully in response to my order, report everything to me exactly as it was, without omitting anything.
ramayan::1551.translation_literal: यद् (if) / अन्यः (another) / वचनम् (speech) / ब्रूयात् (should speak) / मद्वाक्यबलचोदितः (impelled by the force of my command) / तत् (that) / सर्वम् (all) / अखिलेन (completely) / उक्तम् (spoken) / मम (to me) / आख्येयम् (should be reported) / अनादृतम् (without neglect)
ramayan::1551.speaker: Visvamitra
ramayan::1551.essence: Authority stays clean only when nothing is hidden from it.
ramayan::1551.simple_meaning: Visvamitra wants complete honesty. If anyone responds to his command with disrespect, he should be told the whole thing exactly as it happened.
ramayan::1551.simple_insight: Clear authority depends on clear reporting, not convenient editing.
ramayan::1551.detailed_meaning: Visvamitra has gathered his disciples to arrange the sacrificial preparations. Before they scatter, he makes one thing plain: if anyone resists or speaks badly, he wants the full account. Precision and obedience matter in this sacred task.
ramayan::1551.modern_relevance: You asked a teammate to handle something delicate, and later hear only a cleaned-up version of the conflict. Real trust survives only when the whole story comes back, not the edited one.
ramayan::1551.insight: It teaches you to value exact reporting over social smoothing when responsibility is at stake.

ramayan::1552.verse_sanskrit: तस्य तद्वचनं श्रुत्वा दिशो जग्मुस्तदाज्ञया । आजग्मुरथ देशेभ्य स्सर्वेभ्यो ब्रह्मवादिन: । । 1599 । ।
ramayan::1552.verse_hindi: At his command the disciples set out in different directions. And as a result, expounders of the vedas began arriving from various countries.
ramayan::1552.english_translation: At his command the disciples set out in different directions. Then expounders of the Vedas arrived from every country.
ramayan::1552.translation_literal: तस्य (his) / तद्वचनं (that command) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / दिशः (directions) / जग्मुः (went) / तदाज्ञया (by his order) / आजग्मुः (came) / अथ (then) / देशेभ्यः (from countries) / सर्वेभ्यः (from all) / ब्रह्मवादिनः (expounders of the Vedas)
ramayan::1552.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1552.essence: Clear authority turns speech into immediate movement.
ramayan::1552.simple_meaning: The disciples obeyed at once and spread out in every direction. Soon, learned Vedic scholars began arriving from many lands.
ramayan::1552.simple_insight: When a teacher speaks clearly, action follows without delay.
ramayan::1552.detailed_meaning: A sage has given an order to gather respected Vedic scholars. His disciples immediately fan out across the land, and the response begins to come in from distant regions. The verse shows the smooth obedience and reach of the sage's influence.
ramayan::1552.modern_relevance: You send a message to organize something important, and people start moving before you finish your coffee. Clear direction turns scattered effort into real momentum.
ramayan::1552.insight: It shows how decisive instruction can mobilize people across wide distances.

ramayan::1553.verse_sanskrit: ते च शिष्या: समागम्य मुनिं ज्वलिततेजसम् । ऊचुश्चवचनं सर्वे सर्वेषां ब्रह्मवादिनाम् । । 15910 । ।
ramayan::1553.verse_hindi: All the disciples on their return, communicated to the sage shining in splendour what the expounders of the vedas had said.
ramayan::1553.english_translation: All the disciples on their return, communicated to the sage shining in splendour what the expounders of the Vedas had said.
