ramayan::1600.translation_literal: पशुः (the sacrificial animal) / अद्य (today) / हृतः (stolen away) / राजन् (O king) / प्रणष्टः (lost) / तव (your) / दुर्नयात् (because of bad rule / misrule) / अरक्षितारम् (one who does not protect) / राजानम् (a king) / घ्नन्ति (destroy) / दोषाः (faults) / नरेश्वर (O lord of men)
ramayan::1600.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1600.essence: Power without protection becomes its own punishment.
ramayan::1600.simple_meaning: A ruler who fails to protect what is entrusted to him brings trouble on himself. The loss of the animal is being blamed on weak protection.
ramayan::1600.simple_insight: Responsibility is measured by what you can safeguard, not by what you meant to do.
ramayan::1600.detailed_meaning: Ambarisha’s sacrifice has been interrupted because Indra has taken the sacrificial animal. The priest turns to the king and says the loss happened through his poor protection. In this moment, kingship is judged by guardianship.
ramayan::1600.modern_relevance: You left a child, a team, or a promise unguarded, and the damage followed fast. The verse lands on that painful truth: authority without protection becomes blame.
ramayan::1600.insight: It shifts leadership from status to accountability: if you are responsible, you must also protect.

ramayan::1601.verse_sanskrit: प्रायश्चित्तं महद्ध्येतन्नरं वा पुरुषर्षभ । आनयस्व पशुं शीघ्रं यावत्कर्म प्रवर्तते । । 1618 । ।
ramayan::1601.verse_hindi: O Best of men you must pay a big price for this. Bring either the beast or a man immediately so that the sacrifice can be completed.
ramayan::1601.english_translation: O Best of men, you must pay a great penance for this. Bring either the beast or a man immediately so the sacrifice can be completed.
ramayan::1601.translation_literal: प्रायश्चित्तम् (atonement) / महत् (great) / हि (indeed) / एतत् (this) / नरम् (man) / वा (or) / पुरुषर्षभ (best of men) / आनयस्व (bring) / पशुम् (beast) / शीघ्रम् (quickly) / यावत् (until) / कर्म (ritual) / प्रवर्तते (proceeds)
ramayan::1601.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1601.essence: A broken ritual demands immediate, costly repair.
ramayan::1601.simple_meaning: A priest demands immediate atonement after a ritual animal is lost. He says the sacrifice can continue only if the king brings back the animal or provides a human substitute.
ramayan::1601.simple_insight: Some mistakes demand an immediate, costly response before anything can proceed.
ramayan::1601.detailed_meaning: A sacrifice has gone wrong: Indra has taken the animal, and the priests blame the king’s failure to protect it. Now the high priest demands urgent atonement and orders the king to bring back either the missing beast or a human substitute so the ritual can continue.
ramayan::1601.modern_relevance: A critical system fails right before launch, and everyone turns to you for a fix. The pressure is not about comfort anymore — it is about whether the whole effort can still be saved.
ramayan::1601.insight: It shifts attention from blame to urgent repair before the larger work collapses.

ramayan::1602.verse_sanskrit: उपाध्यायवचश्श्रुत्वा स राजा पुरुषर्षभ । अन्वियेष महाबुद्धि: पशुं गोभिस्सहस्रश: । । 1619 । ।
ramayan::1602.verse_hindi: O Best of men (Rama) hearing the words of the high priest, the highly intellectual king searched for a human victim in exchange for thousands of cows.
ramayan::1602.english_translation: Hearing the priest's words, the wise king searched for a human substitute, offering thousands of cows in exchange.
ramayan::1602.translation_literal: उपाध्याय-वचः (the priest's words) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / सः (he) / राजा (the king) / पुरुष-ऋषभ (best of men) / अन्वियेष (searched for) / महा-बुद्धिः (highly intelligent) / पशुम् (a victim) / गोभिः-सहस्रशः (by thousands of cows)
ramayan::1602.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1602.essence: Desperation turns a king into a searcher.
ramayan::1602.simple_meaning: The king, after hearing the priest, looked for someone to replace the missing sacrifice, even offering great wealth.
ramayan::1602.simple_insight: A crisis can force desperate choices when a ritual promise has been broken.
ramayan::1602.detailed_meaning: A sacrificial ritual has been disrupted, and the priest demands a replacement before the ceremony can continue. The king, now under pressure and desperate to preserve the rite, searches widely for a substitute and offers enormous wealth to secure one.
ramayan::1602.modern_relevance: You discover a mistake too late and start offering anything to fix it. The panic is real, but so is the cost of trying to patch a broken promise.
ramayan::1602.insight: It shows how fear of consequences can push a ruler into frantic, compromised action.

ramayan::1603.verse_sanskrit: देशान् जनपदांस्तां स्तान्नगराणि वनानि च । आश्रमाणि च पुण्यानि मार्गमाणो महीपति: । । 16110 । । स पुत्रसहितं तात सभार्यं रघुनन्दन । भृगुतुंदे समासीनमृचीकं सन्ददर्श ह । । 16111 । ।
ramayan::1603.verse_hindi: O Dear Rama, the delight of Raghu clan the king scoured countries, villages, cities, forests, sacred hermitages till he saw sage Richika in the Bhrigutunda mountain sitting with his sons and wie.
ramayan::1603.english_translation: Searching through countries, towns, cities, forests, and sacred hermitages, the king finally saw Richika seated with his sons and wife on Bhrigutunda.
ramayan::1603.translation_literal: देशान् (countries) / जनपदान् (districts) / तान् (those) / स्तान् (those) / नगराणि (cities) / वनानि (forests) / च (and) / आश्रमाणि (hermitages) / च (and) / पुण्यानि (sacred) / मार्गमाणः (searching) / महीपतिः (the king) / स (he) / पुत्र-सहितम् (with sons) / तात (O dear one) / स-भार्यम् (with wife) / रघुनन्दन (delight of Raghu's line) / भृगुतुंडे (on Bhrigutunda) / समासीनम् (seated) / ऋचीकम् (Richika) / सन्ददर्श (saw)
ramayan::1603.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1603.essence: Need can drive a king to search every corner of the world.
ramayan::1603.simple_meaning: The king searched everywhere until he found the sage Richika seated with his family.
ramayan::1603.simple_insight: Searching can become devotion when the need is urgent enough.
ramayan::1603.detailed_meaning: A king has been told he must find a human being for a sacrificial purpose. He searches through lands, towns, forests, and hermitages until he reaches Bhrigutunda and sees sage Richika seated with his family.
ramayan::1603.modern_relevance: You keep checking one more street, one more contact, one more place because the problem will not wait. The search itself becomes the burden.
ramayan::1603.insight: It shows the relentless sweep of a search driven by necessity, not curiosity.

ramayan::1604.verse_sanskrit: तमुवाच महातेजा: प्रणम्याभिप्रसाद्य च । ब्रह्मर्षिं तपसा दीप्तं राजर्षिरमितप्रभ: । । 16112 । । पृष्ट्वा सर्वत्र कुशलमृचीकं तमिदं वच: ।
ramayan::1604.verse_hindi: The most brilliant king(Ambarisha) bowing to sage Richika, a brahmarshi who looked extremely resplendent with penance, propitiated him, enquired about the welfare of all and finally said:
ramayan::1604.english_translation: The brilliant king bowed to the sage Richika, propitiated him, asked after everyone's welfare, and then spoke these words.
ramayan::1604.translation_literal: तम् (to him) / उवाच (spoke) / महातेजाः (the highly brilliant one) / प्रणम्य (bowing) / अभिप्रसाद्य (having propitiated) / च (and) / ब्रह्मर्षिम् (to the brahmarshi) / तपसा (by penance) / दीप्तम् (radiant) / राजर्षिः (the royal sage) / अमितप्रभः (of boundless splendour) / पृष्ट्वा (having asked) / सर्वत्र (everywhere) / कुशलम् (welfare) / ऋचीकम् (Richika) / तम् (that) / इदम् (this) / वचः (speech)
ramayan::1604.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1604.essence: Humility comes before the request that changes everything.
ramayan::1604.simple_meaning: King Ambarisha approaches the sage with humility, honors him, asks about his wellbeing, and begins to speak.
ramayan::1604.simple_insight: Respect opens the door before any serious request is made.
ramayan::1604.detailed_meaning: King Ambarisha comes before the radiant sage Richika with folded hands and careful courtesy. He first asks after the sage's welfare, because the request he is about to make is grave and depends on reverence, not force.
ramayan::1604.modern_relevance: Before asking for a favour that could change someone's life, you soften your voice, bow your head, and make sure the other person feels seen first.
ramayan::1604.insight: It shows that difficult requests should begin with humility and care.

ramayan::1605.verse_sanskrit: गवां शतसहस्रेण विक्रीणीषे सुतं यदि । । 16113 । । पशोरर्थे महाभाग कृतकृत्योऽस्मि भार्गव ।
ramayan::1605.verse_hindi: O Fortunate descendent of the Bhrigu race if your son is sold as a sacrificial animal in exchange for a hundred thousand cows, my purpose will be answered.
ramayan::1605.english_translation: O fortunate descendant of Bhrigu, if your son is sold as a sacrificial animal in exchange for a hundred thousand cows, my purpose will be fulfilled.
ramayan::1605.translation_literal: गवां (of cows) / शतसहस्रेण (by a hundred thousand) / विक्रीणीषे (you sell) / सुतम् (son) / यदि (if) / पशोः (for an animal) / अर्थे (for the sake) / महाभाग (O fortunate one) / कृतकृत्यः (having accomplished my purpose) / अस्मि (I am) / भार्गव (O descendant of Bhrigu)
ramayan::1605.speaker: Ambarisha
ramayan::1605.essence: Need has become so sharp that a child is treated like payment.
ramayan::1605.simple_meaning: King Ambarisha tells Sage Richika that he will consider his task complete if the sage sells his son as a sacrificial animal for a huge payment.
ramayan::1605.simple_insight: A desperate demand can turn another person's child into a bargaining chip.
ramayan::1605.detailed_meaning: King Ambarisha has searched the land for a sacrificial animal and found none. Standing before the sage Richika, he presses for a terrible solution: one son in exchange for wealth. The verse is part of a tense bargaining sequence, not a self-contained teaching.
ramayan::1605.modern_relevance: A landlord says he’ll extend the deadline only if you hand over something you should never have to give up. Power can make cruelty sound practical.
ramayan::1605.insight: It shows how urgency can distort judgment and reduce a human life to a transaction.

ramayan::1606.verse_sanskrit: सर्वे परिसृता देशा याज्ञीयं न लभे पशुम् । । 16114 । । दातुमर्हसि मूल्येन सुतमेकमितो मम । 4
ramayan::1606.verse_hindi: I have roamed all countries but could not final the sacrificial animal. Shouldnt you spare one of your sons for a price?
ramayan::1606.english_translation: I have searched every land but have not found a fit sacrificial animal. Please give me one of your sons in exchange for a price.
ramayan::1606.translation_literal: सर्वे (all) / परिसृता (searched through) / देशा (lands) / याज्ञीयं (fit for sacrifice) / न (not) / लभे (I find) / पशुम् (animal) / दातुमर्हसि (you should give) / मूल्येन (for a price) / सुतम् (son) / एकम् (one) / इतः (from here) / मम (to me)
ramayan::1606.speaker: Ambarisha
ramayan::1606.essence: A formal request can hide an unbearable price.
ramayan::1606.simple_meaning: Ambarisha says he has searched everywhere for a sacrificial animal and asks for one son in exchange for payment.
ramayan::1606.simple_insight: Some demands sound lawful and still carry a terrible cost.
ramayan::1606.detailed_meaning: King Ambarisha has come to the sage Richika with a ritual problem: he needs a sacrificial animal and cannot find one anywhere. He presses the sage to sell him a son, turning a sacred request into a morally loaded bargain.
ramayan::1606.modern_relevance: A request can arrive dressed as procedure, paperwork, and fairness while asking for something you can never casually give. The pressure is real because the language sounds reasonable.
ramayan::1606.insight: It shows how duty can be twisted into a demand that ignores human cost.

ramayan::1607.verse_sanskrit: एवमुक्तो महातेजा ऋचीकस्त्वब्रवीद्वच: । । 16115 । । नाहं ज्येष्ठं नरश्रेष्ठ विक्रीणीयां कथञ्चन ।
ramayan::1607.verse_hindi: Thus addressed the exceedingly brilliant Richika said, O Best among men in no way shall I sell my first born.
ramayan::1607.english_translation: Thus addressed, the exceedingly brilliant Richika said, O best among men, I will never sell my eldest son.
ramayan::1607.translation_literal: एवमुक्तः (thus addressed) / महातेजाः (exceedingly brilliant) / ऋचीकः (Richika) / तु (indeed) / अब्रवीत् (said) / वचः (words) / न (not) / अहम् (I) / ज्येष्ठम् (eldest) / नरश्रेष्ठ (best among men) / विक्रीणीयाम् (would sell) / कथञ्चन (in any way)
ramayan::1607.speaker: Richika
ramayan::1607.essence: He will not turn his firstborn into a bargain.
ramayan::1607.simple_meaning: Richika refuses to sell his eldest son, no matter what the offer is.
ramayan::1607.simple_insight: Some lines cannot be crossed, even for a great reward.
ramayan::1607.detailed_meaning: A father is being pressed to give up a son for sacrifice. Richika answers at once: the firstborn is not for sale. The verse is part of a bargaining scene, not a teaching moment on its own.
ramayan::1607.modern_relevance: Someone offers you money to do something that feels wrong, and the pressure is intense. This is the moment you decide whether anything in you is not for sale.
ramayan::1607.insight: It draws a hard boundary around what love and duty will not trade away.

ramayan::1608.verse_sanskrit: ऋचीकस्य वचश्श्रुत्वा तेषां माता महात्मनाम् । । 16116 । । उवाच नरशार्दूलमम्बरीषं तपस्विनी ।
ramayan::1608.verse_hindi: Having heard Richika, the miserable mother of great sons, addressed Ambarisha, the foremost of men, saying:
ramayan::1608.english_translation: Having heard Richika, the ascetic mother of great sons spoke to Ambarisha, the best of men.
ramayan::1608.translation_literal: ऋचीकस्य (of Richika) / वचः (words) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / तेषाम् (of those) / माता (mother) / महात्मनाम् (of the great-souled ones) / उवाच (spoke) / नरशार्दूलम् (to the tiger among men) / अम्बरीषम् (Ambarisha) / तपस्विनी (the ascetic woman)
ramayan::1608.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1608.essence: The refusal is heard, and the conversation turns to the mother.
ramayan::1608.simple_meaning: Richika's wife, an ascetic mother, heard his refusal and turned to Ambarisha to continue the exchange.
ramayan::1608.simple_insight: The verse moves the scene forward; the real issue is still being negotiated.
ramayan::1608.detailed_meaning: Richika has just refused to sell his eldest son, and the bargaining is not over. His wife, a disciplined ascetic and mother of the boys, now speaks directly to King Ambarisha. The verse is a bridge in the argument, not its conclusion.
ramayan::1608.modern_relevance: A tense family conversation pauses for one person to step in and answer. The pressure is real, but the decision is still unfolding.
ramayan::1608.insight: It shifts attention from Richika's refusal to the next response in the negotiation.

ramayan::1609.verse_sanskrit: अविक्रेयं सुतं ज्येष्ठं भगवानाह भार्गव: । । 16117 । । ममापि दयितं विद्धि कनिष्ठं शुनकं नृप । तस्मात्कनीयसं पुत्रं न दास्ये तव पार्थिव । । 16118 । ।
ramayan::1609.verse_hindi: Venerable descendant of the Bhrugus (sage Richika) said that the eldest son cannot be sold. O King the youngest son, Sunaka, is my beloved son. You know, O King for that reason I will not give my yougest son.
ramayan::1609.english_translation: The venerable descendant of the Bhrigu line said the eldest son cannot be sold. O king, know that my youngest son, Sunaka, is my beloved child too; therefore, I will not give you my younger son.
ramayan::1609.translation_literal: अविक्रेयम् (not to be sold) / सुतम् (son) / ज्येष्ठम् (eldest) / भगवान् (venerable one) / आह (said) / भार्गवः (descendant of Bhrigu) / मम (my) / अपि (also) / दयितम् (beloved) / विद्धि (know) / कनिष्ठम् (younger) / शुनकम् (Sunaka) / नृप (O king) / तस्मात् (therefore) / कनीयसम् (younger) / पुत्रम् (son) / न (not) / दास्ये (I will give) / तव (to you) / पार्थिव (O king)
ramayan::1609.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1609.essence: What is beloved cannot be priced or surrendered casually.
ramayan::1609.simple_meaning: A father refuses to part with either of his sons: the eldest cannot be sold, and the youngest is beloved too.
ramayan::1609.simple_insight: Love does not become negotiable just because someone asks for it.
ramayan::1609.detailed_meaning: Richika is being pressed to give up one of his sons, but the mother steps in and draws a firm line. She names both children as beloved and refuses the bargain, turning the exchange into a moral statement about family love and what cannot be traded.
ramayan::1609.modern_relevance: Someone asks you to compromise on what matters most, and you feel the pressure to make it easy. This verse reminds you that some bonds are not for bargaining.
ramayan::1609.insight: It shifts the mind from treating people as exchangeable to seeing them as irreplaceable.

ramayan::1610.verse_sanskrit: प्रायेण हि नरश्रेष्ठ ज्येष्ठा: पितृषु वल्लभा: । मातृ़णां तु कनीयांसस्तस्माद्रक्षे कनीयसम् । । 16119 । ।
ramayan::1610.verse_hindi: O Best among men generally, the eldest sons are the favourites of their fathers, the youngest their mothers: For that reason, I shall keep my youngest son.
ramayan::1610.english_translation: O best among men, fathers generally favor their eldest sons, while mothers favor their youngest; therefore, I shall protect my youngest son.
ramayan::1610.translation_literal: प्रायेण (generally) / हि (indeed) / नरश्रेष्ठ (O best among men) / ज्येष्ठाः (eldest) / पितृषु (to fathers) / वल्लभाः (dear ones) / मातृणां (of mothers) / तु (but) / कनीयांसः (youngest) / तस्मात् (therefore) / रक्षे (I shall protect) / कनीयसम् (the youngest)
ramayan::1610.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1610.essence: Affection becomes duty when the youngest needs shielding.
ramayan::1610.simple_meaning: Mothers usually feel closest to the youngest child, so this mother says she will keep her youngest son with her.
ramayan::1610.simple_insight: Love often shows itself as protection for the one most exposed.
ramayan::1610.detailed_meaning: A mother is speaking in a tense exchange about whether her sons can be given away. She appeals to a common family pattern: fathers tend to favor the eldest, mothers the youngest. On that basis, she claims the youngest son as hers to protect.
ramayan::1610.modern_relevance: When a family decision leaves one child quieter, smaller, or easier to overlook, someone has to notice. This verse reminds you that care often means protecting the one who cannot argue for themselves.
ramayan::1610.insight: It shifts attention toward the child or person who is most vulnerable and most in need of protection.

ramayan::1611.verse_sanskrit: उक्तवाक्ये मुनौ तस्मिन् मुनिपत्न्यां तथैव च । शुनश्शेफस्स्वयं राम मध्यमो वाक्यमब्रवीत् । । 16120 । ।
ramayan::1611.verse_hindi: O Rama the sage and his wife having spoken thus, their middle son Sunassepha said on his own:
ramayan::1611.english_translation: O Rama, when the sage and his wife had spoken thus, Sunassepha, their middle son, spoke up on his own:
ramayan::1611.translation_literal: उक्तवाक्ये (when the words had been spoken) / मुनौ (by the sage) / तस्मिन् (in that one) / मुनिपत्न्यां (and by the sage's wife) / तथैव (likewise) / च (and) / शुनश्शेफः (Sunassepha) / स्वयं (himself) / राम (O Rama) / मध्यमः (the middle one) / वाक्यम् (words) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::1611.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1611.essence: The decisive voice now comes from the one being discussed.
ramayan::1611.simple_meaning: After the sage and his wife finished speaking, their middle son Sunassepha spoke for himself.
ramayan::1611.simple_insight: Sometimes the turning point is simply the moment someone finally speaks for themselves.
ramayan::1611.detailed_meaning: The sage and his wife have just argued over which son can be given away. In that tense silence, Sunassepha, the middle son, steps forward and speaks for himself. The scene is moving toward a painful family decision.
ramayan::1611.modern_relevance: A room goes quiet after two parents debate your future without asking you. Then you finally say what you want, and the whole conversation changes.
ramayan::1611.insight: It shifts attention from the parents' argument to the child's own agency.

ramayan::1612.verse_sanskrit: पिता ज्येष्ठमविक्रेयं माता चाह कनीयसम् । विक्रीतं मध्यमं मन्ये राजन् पुत्रं नयस्व माम् । । 16121 । ।
ramayan::1612.verse_hindi: O King my father says his eldest son cannot be sold, mother says that her  youngest son cannot be spared. From this I think middle son is already sold away. Therefore, take me
ramayan::1612.english_translation: O King, my father says his eldest son cannot be sold, and my mother says her youngest son cannot be spared. So I think the middle son is already sold. Therefore, take me.
ramayan::1612.translation_literal: पिता (father) / ज्येष्ठम् (eldest) / अविक्रेयम् (not to be sold) / माता (mother) / च (and) / अह (says) / कनीयसम् (youngest) / विक्रीतम् (sold) / मध्यमम् (middle one) / मन्ये (I think) / राजन् (O king) / पुत्रम् (son) / नयस्व (take) / माम् (me)
ramayan::1612.speaker: Sunassepha
ramayan::1612.essence: He volunteers himself where others are shielded.
ramayan::1612.simple_meaning: Sunassepha offers himself for purchase, saying the eldest and youngest sons are protected by their parents, so the middle son is the one to be given away.
ramayan::1612.simple_insight: He turns family logic into sacrifice, making himself the one who can be surrendered.
ramayan::1612.detailed_meaning: The sage and his wife have explained how parents usually favour the eldest and youngest sons. Hearing that, Sunassepha steps forward and offers himself instead of the protected children. The moment matters because his words begin the exchange that will save him.
ramayan::1612.modern_relevance: In a room where everyone is protecting their own place, someone quietly says, 'Take me instead.' That kind of self-offering changes the whole scene.
ramayan::1612.insight: It shifts attention from who is protected to who is willing to bear the cost.

ramayan::1613.verse_sanskrit: गवां शतसहस्रेण शुनश्शेफं नरेश्वर: । गृहीत्वा परमप्रीतो जगाम रघुनन्दन । । 16122 । ।
ramayan::1613.verse_hindi: O Delight of the Raghus (Rama) having purchased Sunassepha for a hundred thousands of cows the king refurned immensely pleased.
ramayan::1613.english_translation: The king, greatly pleased, took Sunassepha after paying a hundred thousand cows and departed.
ramayan::1613.translation_literal: गवां (of cows) / शतसहस्रेण (by a hundred thousand) / शुनश्शेफं (Sunassepha) / नरेश्वर: (the king) / गृहीत्वा (having taken) / परमप्रीतो (greatly pleased) / जगाम (departed) / रघुनन्दन (O delight of the Raghu line)
ramayan::1613.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1613.essence: Power can turn a person into an object and still call it satisfaction.
ramayan::1613.simple_meaning: The king paid a huge price, took the boy, and left feeling satisfied.
ramayan::1613.simple_insight: A life can be transferred like property when power is unchecked.
ramayan::1613.detailed_meaning: After the sage and his wife speak, Sunassepha offers himself as the one to be sold. The king accepts him in exchange for a vast payment and leaves pleased. The verse records the transaction, not a teaching.
ramayan::1613.modern_relevance: A powerful person signs the papers, pays the fee, and walks away satisfied while someone else pays the human cost.
ramayan::1613.insight: It shows how easily moral blindness can hide inside a successful deal.

ramayan::1614.verse_sanskrit: शुनश्शेफं नरश्रेष्ठ गृहीत्वा तु महायशा: । व्यश्राम्यत् पुष्करे राजा मध्याह्ने रघुनन्दन । । 1621 । ।
ramayan::1614.verse_hindi: O Foremost of men, O Delight of the Raghus (Rama) the illustrious king (Ambarisha) took Sunassepha with him. (On the way) at Pushkara he took some rest at noon.
ramayan::1614.english_translation: O foremost of men, O delight of the Raghus, the illustrious king took Sunassepha with him. At Pushkara, at noon, he rested.
ramayan::1614.translation_literal: शुनश्शेफं (Sunassepha) / नरश्रेष्ठ (O foremost of men) / गृहीत्वा (having taken) / तु (indeed) / महायशाः (the greatly renowned one) / व्यश्राम्यत् (rested) / पुष्करे (at Pushkara) / राजा (the king) / मध्याह्ने (at noon) / रघुनन्दन (O delight of the Raghu clan)
ramayan::1614.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1614.essence: A brief stop on the road keeps the rescue moving.
ramayan::1614.simple_meaning: King Ambarisha took Sunassepha with him and stopped to rest at Pushkara at midday.
ramayan::1614.simple_insight: A journey pauses, but the larger rescue is still unfolding.
ramayan::1614.detailed_meaning: King Ambarisha has already agreed to take Sunassepha away. On the road, he pauses at Pushkara in the heat of noon. The verse simply marks the moment before Sunassepha will meet his uncle and the next turn of the story begins.
ramayan::1614.modern_relevance: You finally get the child into the car after a long appointment, and everyone goes quiet at the first red light. The important thing is still happening, even in the pause.
ramayan::1614.insight: It keeps the focus on movement in the story, not on a completed teaching.

ramayan::1615.verse_sanskrit: तस्य विश्रममाणस्य शुनश्शेफो महायशा: । पुष्करक्षेत्रमागम्य विश्वामित्रं ददर्श ह । । 1622 । । तप्यन्तमृषिभिस्सार्धं मातुलं परमातुर: ।
ramayan::1615.verse_hindi: While the king was resting at Pushkara, the famous Sunassepha, very much distressed, happened to see his maternal uncle Viswamitra in the company of other sages performing austerities.
ramayan::1615.english_translation: While the king was resting at Pushkara, the famous Sunassepha, deeply distressed, came upon his maternal uncle Viswamitra, who was performing austerities with other sages.
ramayan::1615.translation_literal: तस्य (his) / विश्रममाणस्य (while resting) / शुनश्शेफः (Sunassepha) / महायशाः (the very famous one) / पुष्कर-क्षेत्रम् (to the sacred place Pushkara) / आगम्य (having come) / विश्वामित्रम् (Viswamitra) / ददर्श (saw) / ह (indeed) / तप्यन्तम् (practising austerities) / ऋषिभिः (with sages) / सार्धम् (together with) / मातुलम् (maternal uncle) / परम-आतुरः (utterly distressed)
ramayan::1615.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1615.essence: A weary search reaches its turning point in a sudden meeting.
ramayan::1615.simple_meaning: Sunassepha, exhausted and distressed, arrives at Pushkara and sees his maternal uncle Viswamitra among the sages.
ramayan::1615.simple_insight: Sometimes a single unexpected sight changes the direction of a life.
ramayan::1615.detailed_meaning: At Pushkara, King Ambarisha pauses on the journey after taking Sunassepha with him. In that pause, the boy—hungry, tired, and desperate—spots his maternal uncle Viswamitra absorbed in austerity with other sages. The meeting sets up the next turning point.
ramayan::1615.modern_relevance: You are drained, half-lost, and then you spot the one person who might change everything. A chance meeting can arrive exactly when you can no longer carry the burden alone.
ramayan::1615.insight: It shifts attention from the journey itself to the decisive encounter that interrupts it.

ramayan::1616.verse_sanskrit: विवर्णवदनो दीनस्तृष्णया च श्रमेण च । । 1623 । । पपाताङ्के मुनेराशु वाक्यं चेदमुवाच ह ।
ramayan::1616.verse_hindi: With his face discoloured due to thirst and fatigue, he (Sunassepha) immediately fell into the sages lap in a pitiable condition and said:
ramayan::1616.english_translation: With his face discoloured due to thirst and fatigue, he immediately fell into the sage's lap and said:
ramayan::1616.translation_literal: विवर्णवदनो (with a pale/discoloured face) / दीनः (wretched, pitiable) / तृष्णया (with thirst) / च (and) / श्रमेण (with fatigue) / च (and) / पपात (fell) / अङ्के (into the lap) / मुनेः (of the sage) / आशु (quickly) / वाक्यम् (speech) / च (and) / इदम् (this) / उवाच (said) / ह (indeed)
ramayan::1616.speaker: Sunassepha
ramayan::1616.essence: Exhaustion can speak before the mouth does.
ramayan::1616.simple_meaning: Sunassepha, exhausted and thirsty, rushes to the sage and begins speaking. This is the moment before he asks for protection.
ramayan::1616.simple_insight: Desperation can strip away pride and leave only the need to be heard.
ramayan::1616.detailed_meaning: Sunassepha, weak from thirst and fatigue, reaches his maternal uncle Vishvamitra at Pushkara and collapses at his feet. This verse is the emotional setup for his plea for rescue, not the plea itself.
ramayan::1616.modern_relevance: You arrive at someone’s door after holding yourself together all day. Before you can explain everything, your body gives you away.
ramayan::1616.insight: It shows a breaking point before speech, where suffering becomes visible before it becomes words.

ramayan::1617.verse_sanskrit: न मेऽस्ति माता न पिता ज्ञातयो बान्धवा: कुत: । । 1624 । । त्रातुमर्हसि मां सौम्य धर्मेण मुनिपुङ्गव ।
ramayan::1617.verse_hindi: O Noble man O Preeminent among ascetics I have no mother nor father nor friends nor relatives. You should protect me according to dharma.
ramayan::1617.english_translation: O noble one, O foremost among ascetics, I have no mother, no father, no relatives, no kin. Please protect me according to dharma.
ramayan::1617.translation_literal: न मेऽस्ति (I do not have) / माता (mother) / न पिता (nor father) / ज्ञातयः (relatives) / बान्धवाः (kin) / कुतः (how then) / त्रातुमर्हसि (you should protect) / माम् (me) / सौम्य (noble one) / धर्मेण (according to dharma) / मुनिपुङ्गव (foremost among ascetics)
ramayan::1617.speaker: Sunassepha
ramayan::1617.essence: Even without family, you can still ask dharma to stand with you.
ramayan::1617.simple_meaning: Sunassepha says he has no family left and asks the sage to protect him justly.
ramayan::1617.simple_insight: Even when support disappears, a person can still appeal to what is right.
ramayan::1617.detailed_meaning: Sunassepha, exhausted and desperate, falls at Vishvamitra's feet at Pushkara. He has no parents, no relatives, and no one to defend him. In that helplessness, he asks for protection through dharma itself.
ramayan::1617.modern_relevance: You are alone in a hospital corridor, your phone dead, no family answering, and the system keeps asking for someone to sign. This verse speaks to the dignity of asking for rightful care when you have no one else.
ramayan::1617.insight: It shifts the mind from social belonging to moral entitlement: even the unprotected can claim just treatment.

ramayan::1618.verse_sanskrit: त्राता त्वं हि मुनिश्रेष्ठ सर्वेषां त्वं हि भावन: । । 1625 । । राजा च कृतकार्यस्स्यादहं दीर्घायुरव्यय: । स्वर्गलोकमुपाश्नीयां तपस्तप्त्वाह्यनुत्तमम् । । 1626 । ।
ramayan::1618.verse_hindi: O Best among ascetics you are the protecor of everybody. You are promoter of others welfare. May the king fulfil his purpose. May I live long and become immortal and attain heaven after performing great penance. May I enjoy heaven.
ramayan::1618.english_translation: O best among ascetics, you are the protector of everyone and the giver of welfare. May the king fulfil his purpose. May I live long and become immortal, and attain heaven after performing the highest penance.
ramayan::1618.translation_literal: त्राता (protector) / त्वं (you) / हि (indeed) / मुनिश्रेष्ठ (best among ascetics) / सर्वेषाम् (of all) / त्वं (you) / हि (indeed) / भावनः (giver of welfare) / राजा (the king) / च (and) / कृतकार्यः (one who has accomplished his task) / स्यात् (may become) / अहम् (I) / दीर्घायुः (long-lived) / अव्ययः (undecaying) / स्वर्गलोकम् (the world of heaven) / उपाश्नीयाम् (may enjoy) / तपः (penance) / तप्त्वा (having performed) / हि (indeed) / अनुत्तमम् (the highest)
ramayan::1618.speaker: Sunassepha
ramayan::1618.essence: When all human support is gone, refuge becomes the only sane prayer.
ramayan::1618.simple_meaning: Sunassepha praises the sage as a universal protector and asks for a long life, freedom from decay, and the reward of his penance.
ramayan::1618.simple_insight: Even in fear, you can ask for protection without losing dignity.
ramayan::1618.detailed_meaning: Sunassepha, desperate and alone, has fallen at the sage's feet after saying he has no family to save him. Now he turns to the sage as his only shelter, praising him as a protector of all and pleading for life, endurance, and the fruit of his austerity.
ramayan::1618.modern_relevance: You are standing in a hospital corridor, trying to sound calm while your hands shake. In that moment, asking for protection is not weakness — it is the bravest thing you can do.
ramayan::1618.insight: It shifts the mind from self-reliance under threat to openly seeking refuge and rightful help.

ramayan::1619.verse_sanskrit: त्वं मे नाथो ह्यनाथस्य भव भव्येन चेतसा । पितेव पुत्रं धर्मात्मं स्त्रातुमर्हसि किल्बिषात् । । 1627 । ।
ramayan::1619.verse_hindi: O Virtuous one with a kind heart protect this orphan. Like a father who protects his son, save me from this peril.
ramayan::1619.english_translation: O virtuous one with a kind heart, protect this orphan. Like a father protecting his son, save me from this peril.
ramayan::1619.translation_literal: त्वं (you) / मे (my) / नाथः (protector) / हि (indeed) / अनाथस्य (of the orphan) / भव (become) / भव्येन (with noble) / चेतसा (mind) / पितेव (like a father) / पुत्रम् (a son) / धर्मात्मन् (virtuous one) / त्रातुम् (to save) / अर्हसि (you should) / किल्बिषात् (from peril)
ramayan::1619.speaker: Sunassepha
ramayan::1619.essence: True strength answers helplessness with fatherly care.
ramayan::1619.simple_meaning: A helpless child asks a righteous man to protect him with fatherly care and rescue him from danger.
ramayan::1619.simple_insight: There is deep relief in being met with kindness when you have nowhere else to turn.
ramayan::1619.detailed_meaning: Sunassepha, abandoned and afraid, turns to Viswamitra with no family left to defend him. He does not argue theology or status — he asks for protection, appealing to the oldest human bond: a father shielding a child.
ramayan::1619.modern_relevance: You are standing in a hospital corridor, holding your phone with shaking hands, and you need someone steady to answer. This verse speaks to the raw dignity of asking for care without shame.
ramayan::1619.insight: It shifts the mind from self-protection to sheltering the vulnerable with steady compassion.

ramayan::1620.verse_sanskrit: तस्य तद्वचनं श्रुत्वा विश्वामित्रो महातपा: । सान्त्वयित्वा बहुविधं पुत्रानिदमुवाच ह । । 1628 । ।
ramayan::1620.verse_hindi: Having heard Sunassepha, mighty ascetic Viswamitra consoled him in many ways and said to his sons:
ramayan::1620.english_translation: Having heard Sunassepha, the great ascetic Vishvamitra consoled him in many ways and then said to his sons:
ramayan::1620.translation_literal: तस्य (his) / तत्-वचनम् (that speech) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / विश्वामित्रः (Vishvamitra) / महातपाः (great ascetic) / सान्त्वयित्वा (having consoled) / बहुविधम् (in many ways) / पुत्रान् (to his sons) / इदम् (this) / उवाच (said) / ह (indeed)
ramayan::1620.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1620.essence: Compassion comes first; instruction follows only after fear is soothed.
ramayan::1620.simple_meaning: Vishvamitra hears Sunassepha’s plea, comforts him, and turns to address his sons.
ramayan::1620.simple_insight: A hard truth often begins with compassion, not force.
ramayan::1620.detailed_meaning: Sunassepha has pleaded for protection. Vishvamitra listens, calms him, and then speaks to his own sons. The verse is a bridge into the teaching that follows, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::1620.modern_relevance: A child tells you something frightening, and before you explain or correct, you steady them first. The next words matter more because the fear has already been held.
ramayan::1620.insight: It shifts attention from the plea itself to the compassionate response that prepares for instruction.

ramayan::1621.verse_sanskrit: यत्कृते पितर: पुत्रान् जनयन्ति शुभार्थिन: । परलोकहितार्थाय तस्य कालोऽयमागत: । । 1629 । ।
ramayan::1621.verse_hindi: यत्कृते पितर: पुत्रान् जनयन्ति शुभार्थिन: । परलोकहितार्थाय तस्य कालोऽयमागत: । । 1629 । ।
ramayan::1621.english_translation: The time has come for the one for whom virtuous fathers beget sons, seeking blessings for the next world.
ramayan::1621.translation_literal: यत्कृते (for whom) / पितरः (fathers) / पुत्रान् (sons) / जनयन्ति (beget) / शुभार्थिनः (seeking auspicious good) / परलोकहितार्थाय (for the welfare of the next world) / तस्य (for that one) / कालः (time) / अयम् (this) / आगत: (has come)
ramayan::1621.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::1621.essence: The promise behind care is tested when sacrifice is finally required.
ramayan::1621.simple_meaning: Parents raise children hoping for blessing beyond this life. Viswamitra says that moment has now arrived for this boy.
ramayan::1621.simple_insight: What you raise and protect may one day be asked of you in return.
ramayan::1621.detailed_meaning: Sunassepha has begged for protection, and Viswamitra turns to his sons with a grave appeal. He reminds them that fathers bring forth sons hoping for lasting merit, and says that the hour has come to prove that purpose.
ramayan::1621.modern_relevance: You spend years teaching, feeding, and shielding someone — then one day they need you to keep your word in a harder way than before. The real test of care is whether it survives the moment of cost.
ramayan::1621.insight: It shifts duty from sentiment to action: love must become a concrete sacrifice when the moment arrives.

ramayan::1622.verse_sanskrit: अयं मुनिसुतो बालो मत्तश्शरणमिच्छति । अस्य जीवितमात्रेण प्रियं कुरुत पुत्रका: । । 16210 । ।
ramayan::1622.verse_hindi: O sons of the sage this young boy has sought my protection. O Sons you may grant him his desire by merely offering your life.
ramayan::1622.english_translation: This young son of a sage seeks my protection. My sons, grant him what he wants by giving up your lives.
ramayan::1622.translation_literal: अयं (this) / मुनिसुतः (son of a sage) / बालः (young boy) / मत्तः (from me) / शरणम् (protection/refuge) / इच्छति (desires) / अस्य (his) / जीवितमात्रेण (by life alone) / प्रियम् (what is dear/desired) / कुरुत (do) / पुत्रकाः (sons)
ramayan::1622.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::1622.essence: Refuge becomes real only when you are willing to pay for it.
ramayan::1622.simple_meaning: A young boy asks for protection, and the sage asks his sons to honour that request even at the cost of their lives.
ramayan::1622.simple_insight: True refuge is proved by sacrifice, not by words.
ramayan::1622.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has taken in Sunassepha, a terrified boy with nowhere else to go. Turning to his own sons, he asks them to honour the boy's plea for protection, even if it costs them their lives. The moment tests what refuge really means.
ramayan::1622.modern_relevance: A frightened child shows up at your door, and everyone looks at you to decide whether safety is real or just a slogan. The verse asks what you are willing to spend to keep your promise.
ramayan::1622.insight: It shifts duty from sentiment to action: protection is only real when it costs something.

ramayan::1623.verse_sanskrit: सर्वे सुकृतकर्माणस्सर्वे धर्मपरायणा: । पशुभूता नरेन्द्रस्य तृप्तिमग्ने: प्रयच्छत । । 16211 । ।
ramayan::1623.verse_hindi: Engaged in the observance of righteousness, all of you have done virtuous deeds. By becoming sacrificial animals for the king, you may satisfy Agni.
ramayan::1623.english_translation: All of you are virtuous and devoted to righteousness. By becoming sacrificial animals for the king, you may satisfy Agni.
ramayan::1623.translation_literal: सर्वे (all) / सुकृतकर्माणः (those whose actions are virtuous) / सर्वे (all) / धर्मपरायणाः (devoted to righteousness) / पशुभूताः (having become sacrificial animals) / नरेन्द्रस्य (of the king) / तृप्तिम् (satisfaction) / अग्नेः (of Agni) / प्रयच्छत (grant)
ramayan::1623.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1623.essence: A holy purpose can still demand a terrible price.
ramayan::1623.simple_meaning: The speaker praises the boys as righteous and asks them to offer themselves as sacrificial animals so the fire ritual can be completed.
ramayan::1623.simple_insight: A ritual demand can turn praise into a cruel request.
ramayan::1623.detailed_meaning: A sage is trying to protect his vow and his sacrifice. He addresses the king's sons as virtuous and asks them to stand in for the missing offering, so Agni can be satisfied and the rite can continue.
ramayan::1623.modern_relevance: A room goes quiet when someone asks you to sacrifice more than you expected. The request may sound noble, but the cost is real.
ramayan::1623.insight: It shows how duty, ritual, and urgency can pressure people into surrendering far too much.

ramayan::1624.verse_sanskrit: नाथवांश्च शुनश्शेफो यज्ञश्चाविघ्नितो भवेत् । देवतास्तर्पिताश्चस्युर्मम चापि कृतं वच: । । 16212 । ।
ramayan::1624.verse_hindi: Then Sunassepha will be protected. The kings sacrifice will continue without hindrance. The gods will be gratified. My words also will come true.
ramayan::1624.english_translation: Then Sunassepha will be protected. The sacrifice will continue without hindrance. The deities will be satisfied. My word will also come true.
ramayan::1624.translation_literal: नाथवांश्च (protected) / शुनश्शेफः (Sunassepha) / यज्ञः (sacrifice) / च (and) / अविघ्नितः (without hindrance) / भवेत् (may be) / देवताः (the deities) / तर्पिताः (gratified) / च (and) / स्युः (may be) / मम (my) / च (also) / अपि (indeed) / कृतम् (fulfilled) / वचः (word)
ramayan::1624.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1624.essence: A true promise protects life without breaking the larger duty.
ramayan::1624.simple_meaning: The boy should be protected, the sacrifice should proceed without interruption, the deities should be satisfied, and the speaker's promise should be fulfilled.
ramayan::1624.simple_insight: Real integrity holds people, ritual, and speech together.
ramayan::1624.detailed_meaning: In Vishvamitra's sacrifice, a young boy has sought protection and the ritual is at risk of being disrupted. The speaker offers a solution that preserves the boy's life, keeps the ceremony intact, and proves that his own word can be trusted.
ramayan::1624.modern_relevance: You promised to handle the crisis without derailing the whole project. One careful decision can protect a person, preserve the process, and keep your word intact.
ramayan::1624.insight: It teaches you to solve conflict without sacrificing either compassion or commitment.

ramayan::1625.verse_sanskrit: मुनेस्तु वचनं श्रुत्वा मधुच्छन्दादय स्सुता: । साभिमानं नरश्रेष्ठ सलीलमिदमब्रुवन् । । 16213 । ।
ramayan::1625.verse_hindi: O Best of men (Rama) in response to the words of the sage Madhuchanda and others said thus in a casual way with selfesteem.
ramayan::1625.english_translation: Hearing the sage's words, the sons of Madhuchhanda and the others spoke to the best of men with a casual confidence.
ramayan::1625.translation_literal: मुनेः (of the sage) / तु (indeed) / वचनं (words) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / मधुच्छन्दादयः (Madhuchhanda and others) / सुताः (sons) / साभिमानं (with confidence / pride) / नरश्रेष्ठ (O best of men) / सलीलम् (casually) / इदम् (this) / अब्रुवन् (they spoke)
ramayan::1625.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1625.essence: Confidence can be the first sign of opposition.
ramayan::1625.simple_meaning: After hearing the sage, the sons replied to Rama with confidence and a casual tone.
ramayan::1625.simple_insight: A calm voice can still carry firm resistance.
ramayan::1625.detailed_meaning: Madhuchhanda and the other sons have just heard a proposal that protects one life by offering another. Turning to Rama, they answer without fear or softness. Their reply begins the objection that will challenge the whole sacrifice.
ramayan::1625.modern_relevance: A room goes quiet after a difficult proposal, and then someone finally speaks up. The tone may be calm, but the refusal is real.
ramayan::1625.insight: It marks the start of a moral challenge, not a settled teaching.

ramayan::1626.verse_sanskrit: कथमात्मसुतान् हित्वा त्रायसेऽन्यसुतं विभो । अकार्यमिव पश्याम श्श्वमांस इव भोजने । । 16214 । ।
ramayan::1626.verse_hindi: O Lord protecting others son by abandoning one own is like partaking the flesh of a dog. We consider it a prohibited act.
ramayan::1626.english_translation: How can you abandon your own sons and protect another man's son, O mighty one? We consider that an improper act, like eating dog meat.
ramayan::1626.translation_literal: कथम् (how) / आत्मसुतान् (one's own sons) / हित्वा (having abandoned) / त्रायसे (you protect) / अन्यसुतम् (another's son) / विभो (O mighty one) / अकार्यम् (improper act) / इव (like) / पश्यामः (we consider) / श्वमांसः (dog meat) / इव (like) / भोजने (in eating)
ramayan::1626.speaker: Madhuchhanda and others
ramayan::1626.essence: A noble rescue can still be wrong if it abandons your own children.
ramayan::1626.simple_meaning: The sons of Viswamitra object that he should not protect another boy while leaving his own children unprotected. They see that choice as morally wrong and disgusting.
ramayan::1626.simple_insight: Even a noble rescue can feel wrong if it violates the people closest to you.
ramayan::1626.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has asked Dasharatha for Rama and Lakshmana to protect his sacrifice and help save Sunassepha. His sons, hearing this, protest that their father should not sacrifice his own children for another man's son. Their anger reveals the human cost behind a righteous request.
ramayan::1626.modern_relevance: You volunteer for someone else's emergency while your own family waits for you at home. The praise feels hollow if the people who depend on you pay the price.
ramayan::1626.insight: It forces you to weigh public virtue against immediate family responsibility, and to see when rescue becomes neglect.

ramayan::1627.verse_sanskrit: तेषां तद्वचनं श्रुत्वा पुत्राणां मुनिपुङ्गव: । क्रोधसंरक्तनयनो व्याहर्तुमुपचक्रमे । । 16215 । ।
ramayan::1627.verse_hindi: On hearing the words of his sons Viswamitra, the eminent ascetic, eyes reddened with anger began to speak:
ramayan::1627.english_translation: On hearing his sons' words, the great sage Viswamitra, his eyes reddened with anger, began to speak.
ramayan::1627.translation_literal: तेषां (their) / तद्वचनं (that speech) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / पुत्राणां (of the sons) / मुनिपुङ्गवः (the foremost among sages) / क्रोधसंरक्तनयनो (with eyes reddened by anger) / व्याहर्तुम् (to speak) / उपचक्रमे (began)
ramayan::1627.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1627.essence: Respect lost in speech becomes anger in an instant.
ramayan::1627.simple_meaning: Viswamitra hears the princes' words and, angered by their insult, prepares to answer.
ramayan::1627.simple_insight: A single disrespectful reply can turn a calm exchange into a sharp confrontation.
ramayan::1627.detailed_meaning: Rama's sons have just spoken harshly to Viswamitra, refusing his request. The sage, normally composed, is visibly angered and starts to respond. This verse simply marks the moment before his rebuke begins.
ramayan::1627.modern_relevance: You are mid-conversation when the tone changes. One sharp sentence lands badly, and the room tightens before anyone even finishes speaking.
ramayan::1627.insight: It marks the shift from polite exchange to conflict, setting up the sage's rebuke.

ramayan::1628.verse_sanskrit: निस्साध्वसमिदं प्रोक्तं धर्मादपि विगर्हितम् । अतिक्रम्य तु मद्वाक्यं दारुणं रोमहर्षणम् । । 16216 । ।
ramayan::1628.verse_hindi: (You have) not only trangressed my words but also (you are) censurable according to dharma. You have uttered such audacious and dreadrul words causing the hair to stand on end.
ramayan::1628.english_translation: You have not only transgressed my words, but also spoken in a way condemned by dharma. You have uttered words so bold and dreadful that they make the hair stand on end.
ramayan::1628.translation_literal: निस्साध्वसम् (not fearless / not proper) / इदम् (this) / प्रोक्तम् (spoken) / धर्मात् (by dharma) / अपि (even) / विगर्हितम् (condemned) / अतिक्रम्य (having overstepped) / तु (but) / मद्वाक्यम् (my words) / दारुणम् (terrible) / रोमहर्षणम् (hair-raising)
ramayan::1628.speaker: Vishvamitra
ramayan::1628.essence: Crossing a moral boundary in speech invites a severe response.
ramayan::1628.simple_meaning: Vishvamitra rebukes the sons for crossing a clear boundary. Their words are not just rude; they are against dharma and deeply offensive.
ramayan::1628.simple_insight: Some speech does more than offend — it breaks the order that keeps trust possible.
ramayan::1628.detailed_meaning: Vishvamitra has asked for help, and his sons refuse with a cruel insult. Now he answers them in anger, naming their words as both disrespectful and against dharma. This verse begins the punishment that follows.
ramayan::1628.modern_relevance: You finally speak up in a room where everyone has been joking at someone else's expense. The line was crossed long before anyone raised a voice.
ramayan::1628.insight: It teaches you to see that words can violate duty, not just etiquette.

ramayan::1629.verse_sanskrit: श्वमांसभोजिनस्सर्वे वासिष्ठा इव जातिषु । पूर्णं वर्षसहस्रं तु पृथिव्यामनुवत्स्यथ । । 16217 । ।
ramayan::1629.verse_hindi: All of you shall live on earth for a thousand years, like the sons of Vasishta feeding on the flesh of dogs.
ramayan::1629.english_translation: All of you shall live on earth for a thousand years, like the sons of Vasishta feeding on the flesh of dogs.
ramayan::1629.translation_literal: श्वमांसभोजिनः (dog-meat eaters) / सर्वे (all) / वासिष्ठाः (sons of Vasishta) / इव (like) / जातिषु (among lineages) / पूर्णम् (full) / वर्षसहस्रम् (thousand years) / तु (indeed) / पृथिव्याम् (on earth) / अनुवत्स्यथ (you will live)
ramayan::1629.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::1629.essence: Anger here becomes a sentence, not just a feeling.
ramayan::1629.simple_meaning: Viswamitra curses the boys to live on earth for a thousand years, comparing them to a degraded lineage.
ramayan::1629.simple_insight: Words spoken in anger can become a lasting wound.
ramayan::1629.detailed_meaning: After the boys insult his authority, Viswamitra's anger hardens into a curse. He condemns them to remain on earth for a thousand years, and this verse is part of that punishment rather than a self-contained teaching.
ramayan::1629.modern_relevance: A sharp message sent in anger can keep echoing long after the argument ends. The damage often outlives the moment that caused it.
ramayan::1629.insight: It shows how wrath turns speech into punishment and turns a conflict into a long consequence.

ramayan::1630.verse_sanskrit: कृत्वा शापसमायुक्तान् पुत्रान् मुनिवरस्तथा । शुनश्शेफमुवाचार्तं कृत्वा रक्षां निरामयम् । । 16218 । ।
ramayan::1630.verse_hindi: Viswamitra the best of ascetics, thus cursed his sons. Sunassepha, (now) was filled with distress. To relieve him of his pain he said:
ramayan::1630.english_translation: The best of sages cursed his sons, and then, seeing Sunassepha in distress, he spoke to him words that brought relief.
ramayan::1630.translation_literal: कृत्वा (having done) / शापसमायुक्तान् (endowed with a curse) / पुत्रान् (sons) / मुनिवरः (the best of sages) / तथा (thus) / शुनश्शेफम् (Sunassepha) / उवाच (spoke) / आर्तम् (the distressed one) / कृत्वा (having made) / रक्षाम् (protection) / निरामयम् (free from pain)
ramayan::1630.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1630.essence: Mercy begins where the curse leaves off.
ramayan::1630.simple_meaning: Visvamitra’s sons are cursed, and then he turns to the distressed Sunassepha and speaks to ease his suffering.
ramayan::1630.simple_insight: Even a harsh correction can be followed by mercy.
ramayan::1630.detailed_meaning: Visvamitra has just spoken a terrible curse against his sons. In the next breath, the scene shifts to Sunassepha, who is suffering under the weight of that situation. This verse is a bridge, showing the sage’s move from judgment to relief.
ramayan::1630.modern_relevance: A tense conversation has already gone too far, and then you notice the person across from you is shaken. The next words matter more than the anger that came before.
ramayan::1630.insight: It shifts attention from punishment to the need to reduce suffering once the damage is done.

ramayan::1631.verse_hindi: Bedaubing your person with red sandal paste and adorned with red garlands, you will
ramayan::1631.english_translation: Adorned with red garlands and red sandal paste, approach the sacred sacrificial post and invoke Agni with words.
ramayan::1631.translation_literal: पवित्रपाशैः (with sacred cords) / आसक्तः (adorned) / रक्तमाल्यानुलेपनः (with red garlands and anointing) / वैष्णवम् (sacred, belonging to Vishnu) / यूपम् (sacrificial post) / आसाद्य (having approached) / वाग्भिः (with words) / अग्निम् (Agni, fire) / उदाहर (invoke)
ramayan::1631.speaker: Vishwamitra
ramayan::1631.essence: Ritual begins with preparation, then the right words.
ramayan::1631.simple_meaning: The sage instructs the boy to dress for the ritual, go to the sacrificial post, and call upon the fire with sacred words.
ramayan::1631.simple_insight: Preparation matters before any sacred act begins.
ramayan::1631.detailed_meaning: Vishwamitra has brought Sunahsepha into a ritual meant to break a curse and save him from ruin. This verse gives the next step: the boy must be ritually prepared, approach the sacrificial post, and recite the invocation that will carry the rite forward.
ramayan::1631.modern_relevance: Before a difficult ceremony, interview, or performance, you often need the outer preparation first: clothes, posture, breath, and words. The mind settles when the body knows what to do next.
ramayan::1631.insight: It shifts attention from fear to ritual action, showing that the next right step can steady the mind.

ramayan::1632.verse_sanskrit: इमे तु गाथे द्वे दिव्ये गायेथा मुनिपुत्रक । अम्बरीषस्य यज्ञेऽस्मिंस्तत स्सिद्धिमवाप्स्यसि । । 16220 । ।
ramayan::1632.verse_hindi: O Son of sage chant thse two sacred mantras in the sacrifice of Ambarisha.There after you will achieve success (long life).
ramayan::1632.english_translation: O son of the sage, chant these two sacred verses in Ambarisha's sacrifice. After that, you will achieve success and long life.
ramayan::1632.translation_literal: इमे (these) / तु (indeed) / गाथे (verses) / द्वे (two) / दिव्ये (sacred) / गायेथा (you should chant) / मुनिपुत्रक (O son of the sage) / अम्बरीषस्य (of Ambarisha) / यज्ञे (in the sacrifice) / अस्मिन् (in this) / ततः (then) / सिद्धिम् (success) / अवाप्स्यसि (you will attain)
ramayan::1632.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1632.essence: A threatened life is saved by following exact instruction.
ramayan::1632.simple_meaning: Sunahshepa is told to recite two sacred verses during Ambarisha's sacrifice. If he does, he will gain success and live.
ramayan::1632.simple_insight: Even in danger, the right words can become a way through.
ramayan::1632.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has placed Sunahshepa into a sacrificial rite as the price of rescue. Now the boy is instructed to recite two sacred verses in Ambarisha's yajna, with the promise that this will save him and grant him a future.
ramayan::1632.modern_relevance: You are handed a script in the middle of a crisis and told to trust it. The pressure is real, but so is the path forward.
ramayan::1632.insight: It shifts attention from fear to precise action under pressure.

ramayan::1633.verse_sanskrit: शुनश्शेफो गृहीत्वा ते द्वे गाथे सुसमाहित: । त्वरया राजसिंहं तमम्बरीषमुवाच ह । । 16221 । ।
ramayan::1633.verse_hindi: Sunassepha memorized the two verses with concentration of mind and hastened towards Amabarisha, a lion among kings. And said:
ramayan::1633.english_translation: Sunassepha, having firmly memorized the two verses, quickly approached that lion among kings, Ambarisha, and spoke.
ramayan::1633.translation_literal: शुनश्शेफः (Sunassepha) / गृहीत्वा (having taken) / ते (those) / द्वे (two) / गाथे (verses) / सुसमाहितः (with concentrated mind) / त्वरया (quickly) / राजसिंहम् (lion among kings) / तम् (that) / अम्बरीषम् (Ambarisha) / उवाच (spoke) / ह (indeed)
ramayan::1633.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1633.essence: Readiness is what lets the moment happen at all.
ramayan::1633.simple_meaning: Sunassepha quickly memorized the two verses and went to Ambarisha to speak them.
ramayan::1633.simple_insight: Preparation matters before a crucial moment arrives.
ramayan::1633.detailed_meaning: In the middle of a sacrificial sequence, the sage's son Sunassepha has just been given two sacred verses to recite. He commits them to memory at once and hurries toward King Ambarisha, because the ritual cannot wait.
ramayan::1633.modern_relevance: You rehearse the speech one last time and walk into the room before your nerves catch up. The moment rewards readiness, not hesitation.
ramayan::1633.insight: It shifts attention from the ceremony itself to the discipline of arriving prepared.

ramayan::1634.verse_sanskrit: राजसिंह महासत्त्व शीघ्रं गच्छावहे सद: । निर्वर्तयस्व राजेन्द्र दीक्षां च समुपाविश । । 16222 । ।
ramayan::1634.verse_hindi: Endowed with great strength, you are a lion among kings. We shall go to the sacrificial assembly without delay. O Indra among monarchs, take up initiatory rites
ramayan::1634.english_translation: Endowed with great strength, you are a lion among kings. We shall go to the sacrificial assembly without delay. O Indra among monarchs, take up initiatory rites.
ramayan::1634.translation_literal: राजसिंह (lion among kings) / महासत्त्व (of great strength) / शीघ्रम् (quickly) / गच्छावहे (let us go) / सदः (to the sacrificial assembly) / निर्वर्तयस्व (complete/perform) / राजेन्द्र (O best of kings) / दीक्षाम् (initiatory rites) / च (and) / समुपाविश (enter/take up)
ramayan::1634.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1634.essence: The moment demands readiness, not delay.
ramayan::1634.simple_meaning: A sage’s son urges the king to go at once to the sacrifice and begin the required rites.
ramayan::1634.simple_insight: Some moments ask for immediate action, not hesitation.
ramayan::1634.detailed_meaning: The sage’s son has just given Sunahshepa the sacred verses. Now he turns to King Ambarisha with urgency, calling him a lion among kings and telling him to come at once and begin the initiation needed for the sacrifice. It is a practical instruction, not a teaching verse.
ramayan::1634.modern_relevance: A trainer calls your name and the room is already waiting. There is no time for second-guessing now — you either step in and begin, or you stay outside.
ramayan::1634.insight: It shifts attention from reflection to immediate preparation for the task at hand.

ramayan::1635.verse_sanskrit: तद्वाक्यमृषिपुत्रस्य श्रुत्वा हर्षसमुत्सुक: । जगाम नृपति श्शीघ्रं यज्ञवाटमतन्द्रित: । । 16223 । ।
ramayan::1635.verse_hindi: At the words of the sages son, the king, eager with delight hastened towards the sacrificial ground.
ramayan::1635.english_translation: At the words of the sages son, the king, eager with delight, hastened towards the sacrificial ground.
ramayan::1635.translation_literal: तद्-वाक्यम् (that speech) / ऋषि-पुत्रस्य (of the sage's son) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / हर्ष-समुत्सुकः (eager with delight) / जगाम (went) / नृपतिः (the king) / शीघ्रम् (quickly) / यज्ञ-वाटम् (to the sacrificial ground) / अतन्द्रितः (without slacking)
ramayan::1635.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1635.essence: The king stops hesitating and moves the story forward.
ramayan::1635.simple_meaning: The king quickly goes to the sacrificial ground after hearing the sage's son speak.
ramayan::1635.simple_insight: A single reply can move a whole situation forward.
ramayan::1635.detailed_meaning: Sunassepha has just spoken to the king with courage and precision. Hearing him, the king moves quickly and without hesitation toward the sacrificial ground, setting the next ritual step in motion. This is a transition verse, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::1635.modern_relevance: A tense meeting ends, and one clear sentence changes the mood. The room shifts because someone finally acts instead of circling the issue.
ramayan::1635.insight: It marks the moment when hearing turns into action.

ramayan::1636.verse_sanskrit: सदस्यानुमते राजा पवित्रकृतलक्षणम् । पशुं रक्ताम्बरं कृत्वा यूपे तं समबन्धयत् । । 16224 । ।
ramayan::1636.verse_hindi: With the consent of the officiating priests the king invested Sunasepha with the sacred symbols with Kusa grass, dressed him in red apparel and tied him to the sacrificial post as a sacrificial animal.
ramayan::1636.english_translation: With the consent of the officiating priests, the king dressed Sunasepha in sacred grass and red cloth, then tied him to the sacrificial post as the victim.
ramayan::1636.translation_literal: सदस्यानुमते (with the consent of the priests) / राजा (the king) / पवित्रकृतलक्षणम् (marked with sacred signs) / पशुम् (the victim) / रक्ताम्बरम् (in red cloth) / कृत्वा (having made) / यूपे (to the sacrificial post) / तम् (him) / समबन्धयत् (bound)
ramayan::1636.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1636.essence: Consent does not cleanse a cruel act.
ramayan::1636.simple_meaning: The king prepares Sunasepha for sacrifice and binds him to the post after the priests agree.
ramayan::1636.simple_insight: Ritual can become cruel when authority stops asking what is right.
ramayan::1636.detailed_meaning: At the sacrificial ground, the king follows the priests' consent and turns Sunasepha into the intended victim. The scene is not about teaching but about the grim mechanics of a rite already set in motion.
ramayan::1636.modern_relevance: A committee signs off on a decision that hurts someone, and everyone feels relieved it was “approved.” The harm becomes easier to carry when it has paperwork.
ramayan::1636.insight: It shows how group approval can hide moral responsibility.

ramayan::1637.verse_sanskrit: सबद्धो वाग्भिरग्य्राभिरभितुष्टाव वै सुरौ । इन्द्रमिन्द्रानुजं चैव यथावन्मुनिपुत्रक: । । 16225 । ।
ramayan::1637.verse_hindi: Thus bound, the son of the sage praised the two devatas, Indra and Upendra with moving words.
ramayan::1637.english_translation: Thus bound, the son of the sage praised the two radiant beings, Indra and Upendra, with fitting words.
ramayan::1637.translation_literal: सबद्धो (thus bound) / वाग्भिः (with words) / अग्र्याभिः (excellent, foremost) / अभितुष्टाव (praised) / वै (indeed) / सुरौ (the two radiant beings) / इन्द्रम् (Indra) / इन्द्रानुजम् (Indra's younger brother, Upendra) / च (and) / एव (also) / यथावत् (properly, fittingly) / मुनिपुत्रकः (the son of the sage)
ramayan::1637.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1637.essence: Helplessness does not silence the one who can still praise.
ramayan::1637.simple_meaning: Bound to the sacrificial post, Sunasepha praised Indra and Upendra with beautiful words.
ramayan::1637.simple_insight: Even in helplessness, speech can become prayer and force change.
ramayan::1637.detailed_meaning: Sunasepha has been tied to the sacrificial post after the king's rush to complete the rite. In that desperate moment, the sage's son turns his fear into a hymn and praises Indra and Upendra with fitting words.
ramayan::1637.modern_relevance: You can be trapped in a situation you never chose and still choose your response. Even when your body is pinned by circumstance, your voice can remain free.
ramayan::1637.insight: It shifts attention from physical power to the dignity of response under pressure.

ramayan::1638.verse_sanskrit: तत: प्रीत स्सहस्राक्षो रहस्यस्तुतितर्पित: । दीर्घमायुस्तदा प्रादाच्छुनश्शेफाय राघव । । 16226 । ।
ramayan::1638.verse_hindi: O Descendant of Raghu (Rama) Indra, gratified with the secret hymn granted Sunassepha long life.
ramayan::1638.english_translation: Then Indra, pleased by the secret hymn, granted Sunassepha long life.
ramayan::1638.translation_literal: तत: (then) / प्रीत (pleased) / सहस्राक्षो (the thousand-eyed one, Indra) / रहस्य-स्तुति-तर्पित: (satisfied by the secret hymn) / दीर्घम् (long) / आयुः (life) / तदा (then) / प्रादात् (gave) / शुनश्शेफाय (to Sunassepha) / राघव (O descendant of Raghu)
ramayan::1638.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1638.essence: Hidden praise wins back a life.
ramayan::1638.simple_meaning: Indra, satisfied by Sunassepha’s hidden prayer, gave him a long life.
ramayan::1638.simple_insight: A sincere plea can open a door when every human door has closed.
ramayan::1638.detailed_meaning: Sunassepha has been bound for sacrifice and has just praised Indra and Upendra with secret hymns. The gods are moved, and Indra grants him long life. The verse completes the rescue, showing that devotion and prayer can break a deadly ritual.
ramayan::1638.modern_relevance: You’ve reached the point where no argument will help, only a deeper plea. In that helpless moment, a quiet, sincere appeal can still change everything.
ramayan::1638.insight: It shifts the mind from helplessness to the possibility that devotion can alter a sealed situation.

ramayan::1639.verse_sanskrit: स च राजा नरश्रेष्ठ यज्ञस्य च समाप्तवान् । फलं बहुगुणं राम सहस्राक्षप्रसादजम् । । 16227 । ।
ramayan::1639.verse_hindi: O Foremost of men O Rama the king also obtained from the sacrifics innumerable rewards by the grace of Indra several times greater than expected.
ramayan::1639.english_translation: O Rama, that king completed the sacrifice and received many times the expected reward through the grace of Indra.
ramayan::1639.translation_literal: स (he) / च (also) / राजा (the king) / नरश्रेष्ठ (O foremost of men) / यज्ञस्य (of the sacrifice) / च (and) / समाप्तवान् (completed) / फलम् (fruit/reward) / बहुगुणम् (many-fold) / राम (O Rama) / सहस्राक्षप्रसादजम् (born of Indra's grace)
ramayan::1639.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1639.essence: The sacrifice ended well because grace made the result greater than effort alone.
ramayan::1639.simple_meaning: The king finished the sacrifice and gained a much greater reward than expected through Indra's favor.
ramayan::1639.simple_insight: Right effort can open results larger than you planned for.
ramayan::1639.detailed_meaning: The sacrifice has just been completed after Sunashepha's hymn to Indra and Upendra. Now the king receives the sacrifice's full fruit, and that fruit comes amplified by Indra's grace. The verse closes the ritual outcome, not a teaching.
ramayan::1639.modern_relevance: You finish something difficult and only later see how much it changed things. The reward lands after the work is done, and it is bigger than you expected.
ramayan::1639.insight: It shows how completion and grace can together multiply the result of sincere action.

ramayan::1640.verse_sanskrit: विश्वामित्रो ऽपि धर्मात्मा भूयस्तेपे महातपा: । पुष्करेषु नरश्रेष्ठ दशवर्षशतानि च । । 16228 । ।
ramayan::1640.verse_hindi: O Best among men the righteous and mighty ascetic Viswamitra also continued his austerities at Pushkara for a thousand years.
ramayan::1640.english_translation: O Best among men, the righteous and mighty ascetic Viswamitra also continued his austerities at Pushkara for a thousand years.
ramayan::1640.translation_literal: विश्वामित्रः (Viswamitra) / अपि (also) / धर्मात्मा (righteous in nature) / भूयः (again, further) / तेपे (performed austerities) / महातपाः (great ascetic) / पुष्करेषु (at Pushkara) / नरश्रेष्ठ (O best among men) / दशवर्षशतानि (ten hundred years) / च (and)
ramayan::1640.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1640.essence: Enduring practice can remake even a former king.
ramayan::1640.simple_meaning: Viswamitra did not stop his austerities. He kept practicing for a thousand years at Pushkara.
ramayan::1640.simple_insight: Great change often comes from staying with the practice long after excitement fades.
ramayan::1640.detailed_meaning: After Indra grants long life to Sunassepha, the story turns back to Viswamitra. The king-turned-ascetic remains in Pushkara, grinding through austerity for a thousand years, showing that transformation in this epic is earned through relentless self-training.
ramayan::1640.modern_relevance: You keep showing up to the same hard practice when no one applauds and nothing seems to move. That is how character is built when shortcuts fail.
ramayan::1640.insight: It shifts attention from quick results to sustained self-mastery.

ramayan::1641.verse_sanskrit: पूर्णे वर्षसहस्रे तु व्रतस्नातं महामुनिम् । अभ्यागच्छन् सुरास्सर्वे तप: फलचिकीर्षव: । । 1631 । ।
ramayan::1641.verse_hindi: All the gods wanted to bestow the fruits of austerties on the mighty ascetic (Viswamitra). They approached him after a thousand years of penace and his final ritual bath.
ramayan::1641.english_translation: After a thousand years, the gods came to the great ascetic, who had completed his vow and bath, seeking to grant the fruit of his austerities.
ramayan::1641.translation_literal: पूर्णे (completed) / वर्षसहस्रे (in a thousand years) / तु (indeed) / व्रतस्नातं (one who has bathed after the vow) / महामुनिम् (great ascetic) / अभ्यागच्छन् (approached) / सुराः (the gods) / सर्वे (all) / तपःफलचिकीर्षवः (desiring to bestow the fruit of austerity)
ramayan::1641.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1641.essence: A thousand years of discipline can make even the gods come near.
ramayan::1641.simple_meaning: After a thousand years of severe discipline, the gods came to Viswamitra, ready to give him the fruit of his austerities.
ramayan::1641.simple_insight: Steady effort can change your standing so completely that even the highest powers respond.
ramayan::1641.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has finished a thousand years of fierce austerity and his ritual bath. The gods themselves come toward him, ready to acknowledge what his discipline has earned. This verse is the threshold before Brahma speaks and names the transformation.
ramayan::1641.modern_relevance: You finish a long season of discipline and suddenly the room feels different. People who once ignored your effort now notice the person you've become.
ramayan::1641.insight: It shifts attention from achievement as an event to transformation as earned character.

ramayan::1642.verse_sanskrit: अब्रवीत्सुमहातेजा ब्रह्मा सुरुचिरं वच: । ऋषिस्त्वमसि भद्रं ते स्वार्जितै: कर्मभिश्शुभै: । । 1632 । ।
ramayan::1642.verse_hindi: Exceedingly effulgent Brahma spoke to him, You have become a rishi through the selfearned sacred deeds. Fare you well.
ramayan::1642.english_translation: Exceedingly effulgent Brahma spoke to him, 'You have become a rishi through your own sacred deeds. Fare you well.'
ramayan::1642.translation_literal: अब्रवीत् (spoke) / सुमहातेजा (exceedingly effulgent) / ब्रह्मा (Brahma) / सुरुचिरं (beautifully) / वचः (words) / ऋषिः (a rishi) / त्वम् (you) / असि (are) / भद्रम् (well-being) / ते (to you) / स्वार्जितैः (self-earned) / कर्मभिः (by deeds) / शुभैः (auspicious)
ramayan::1642.speaker: Brahma
ramayan::1642.essence: Your own disciplined deeds can transform who you are.
ramayan::1642.simple_meaning: Brahma tells Viswamitra that his own noble actions have made him a rishi. Spiritual stature is earned through disciplined effort, not granted by status.
ramayan::1642.simple_insight: Real respect comes from what you repeatedly do, not from what you claim to be.
ramayan::1642.detailed_meaning: After a thousand years of austerity at Pushkara, the gods come to Viswamitra expecting to grant the fruit of his tapas. Brahma instead names the deeper result: Viswamitra has already become a rishi through his own purified actions.
ramayan::1642.modern_relevance: You finish years of work, and no one gives you the title you hoped for. Then the truth lands: the title was never the point — the person you became was.
ramayan::1642.insight: It shifts the mind from waiting for recognition to seeing character as self-made through action.

ramayan::1643.verse_sanskrit: तमेवमुक्त्वा देवेशस्त्रिदिवं पुनरभ्यगात् । विश्वामित्रो महातेजा भूयस्तेपे महत्तप: । । 1633 । ।
ramayan::1643.verse_hindi: Brahma, the lord of the gods, having said this returned to heaven. The brilliant Viswamitra continues his austerities.
ramayan::1643.english_translation: Brahma, the lord of the gods, having said this returned to heaven. The brilliant Viswamitra continues his austerities.
ramayan::1643.translation_literal: तमेवम् (thus) / उक्त्वा (having said) / देवेशः (lord of the gods) / त्रिदिवम् (to heaven) / पुनः (again) / अभ्यगात् (returned) / विश्वामित्रः (Viswamitra) / महातेजाः (brilliant) / भूयः (again) / तेपे (performed austerities) / महत् (great) / तपः (austerity)
ramayan::1643.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1643.essence: Recognition is not the end; the discipline continues.
ramayan::1643.simple_meaning: Brahma leaves after blessing Viswamitra, and Viswamitra keeps doing severe austerities.
ramayan::1643.simple_insight: True resolve does not relax after praise.
ramayan::1643.detailed_meaning: Brahma has just acknowledged Viswamitra's hard-won spiritual stature and returned to heaven. The story does not pause there: Viswamitra stays where he is and continues his severe austerities, showing that one blessing is not the end of his effort.
ramayan::1643.modern_relevance: You finally get the recognition you wanted, then the work still waits for you the next morning. Praise does not finish the discipline that earned it.
ramayan::1643.insight: It shifts attention from receiving approval to continuing the practice that made approval possible.

ramayan::1644.verse_sanskrit: तत: कालेन महता मेनका परमाऽप्सरा: । पुष्करेषु नरश्रेष्ठ स्नातुं समुपचक्रमे । । 1634 । ।
ramayan::1644.verse_hindi: O Foremost of men after a long lapse of time a chief nymph called Menaka came to bathe at Pushkara.
ramayan::1644.english_translation: After a long lapse of time, O foremost of men, Menaka, the chief nymph, approached Pushkara to bathe.
ramayan::1644.translation_literal: तत: (then) / कालेन (by time, after time) / महता (great, long) / मेनका (Menaka) / परमाऽप्सरा: (the foremost celestial nymph) / पुष्करेषु (at Pushkara) / नरश्रेष्ठ (O foremost of men) / स्नातुं (to bathe) / समुपचक्रमे (approached, began to come)
ramayan::1644.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1644.essence: Stillness can be broken by a single beautiful interruption.
ramayan::1644.simple_meaning: After a long time, Menaka arrives at Pushkara to bathe.
ramayan::1644.simple_insight: A quiet arrival can still change the course of a life.
ramayan::1644.detailed_meaning: Viswamitra has just been declared a rishi and returned to fierce austerity. After a long interval, Menaka, a celestial nymph, comes to the sacred bathing place at Pushkara. The verse sets up the moment before temptation enters his discipline.
ramayan::1644.modern_relevance: You are finally back in your rhythm, and then one small distraction walks in. It may look ordinary, but it can test everything you've built.
ramayan::1644.insight: It prepares the reader for how discipline can be interrupted by desire.

ramayan::1645.verse_sanskrit: तां ददर्श महातेजा मेनकां कुशिकात्मज: । रूपेणाप्रतिमां तत्र विद्युतं जलदे यथा । । 1635 । ।
ramayan::1645.verse_hindi: There the most brilliant son of Kusika Viswamitra saw Menaka whose beauty was incomparable. She looked like lightning in the clouds.
ramayan::1645.english_translation: There the brilliant son of Kusika, Viswamitra, saw Menaka. Her beauty was unmatched, like lightning in rain clouds.
ramayan::1645.translation_literal: ताम् (her) / ददर्श (saw) / महातेजाः (the brilliant one) / मेनकाम् (Menaka) / कुशिकात्मजः (son of Kusika) / रूपेण (in beauty) / अप्रतिमाम् (unmatched) / तत्र (there) / विद्युतम् (lightning) / जलदे (in clouds) / यथा (like)
ramayan::1645.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1645.essence: Beauty enters, and a long discipline is about to be tested.
ramayan::1645.simple_meaning: Viswamitra sees Menaka for the first time and is struck by her unmatched beauty.
ramayan::1645.simple_insight: Attraction can arrive suddenly and seize even the disciplined mind.
ramayan::1645.detailed_meaning: Menaka has just come to the sacred bathing place, and Viswamitra is still deep in austerity. In that instant, the sage sees her extraordinary beauty. The verse is a setup for the temptation that will test his resolve in the next line.
ramayan::1645.insight: It shows how a single sight can interrupt years of discipline.

ramayan::1646.verse_sanskrit: दृष्ट्वा कन्दर्पवशगो मुनिस्तामिदमब्रवीत् । अप्सरस्स्वागतं तेऽस्तु वस चेह ममाश्रमे । । 1636 । । अनुगृह्णीष्व भद्रं ते मदनेन सुमोहितम् ।
ramayan::1646.verse_hindi: On seeing her (Menaka) Viswamitra came under the influence of the god of love (fell in love with her). He said, O Apsara welcome to my hermitage stay here. I am infatuated with you: Oblige me. Wish you well.
ramayan::1646.english_translation: Seeing her, the sage was overcome by desire. He said, “Welcome, Apsara. Stay here in my hermitage. Be kind to me, who has been bewildered by love.”
ramayan::1646.translation_literal: दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / कन्दर्पवशगः (subdued by desire) / मुनिः (the sage) / ताम् (her) / इदम् (this) / अब्रवीत् (said) / अप्सरः (O apsara) / स्वागतम् (welcome) / ते (to you) / अस्तु (may it be) / वस (stay) / इह (here) / मम (my) / आश्रमे (in the hermitage) / अनुगृह्णीष्व (show kindness) / भद्रम् (auspiciousness) / ते (to you) / मदनेन (by love/desire) / सुमोहितम् (deeply bewildered)
ramayan::1646.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::1646.essence: Desire can undo years of discipline in one breath.
ramayan::1646.simple_meaning: Viswamitra sees Menaka and immediately loses his composure. He invites her to stay in his hermitage, speaking as a man overcome by desire rather than as a disciplined sage.
ramayan::1646.simple_insight: Even great discipline can crack in a single moment of attraction.
ramayan::1646.detailed_meaning: Menaka appears at Pushkara, and Viswamitra, the austere sage, is struck by her beauty. Instead of remaining steady, he speaks with desire and invites her to stay. This is a turning point showing how fragile his tapas still is.
ramayan::1646.modern_relevance: You meant to keep your boundary, then one message, one glance, one smile changes your tone. The mind can betray years of discipline in seconds.
ramayan::1646.insight: It shows how unchecked desire can interrupt even long spiritual practice and turn speech into self-betrayal.

ramayan::1647.verse_sanskrit: इत्युक्ता सा वरारोहा तत्र वासमथाकरोत् । । 1637 । । तस्यां वसन्त्यां वर्षाणि पञ्च पञ्च च राघव । विश्वामित्राश्रमे राम सुखेन व्यतिचक्रमु: । । 1638 । ।
ramayan::1647.verse_hindi: O Descendant of Raghu while that woman of an exalted race lived in the hermitage of Viswamitra, ten years rolled by happily.
ramayan::1647.english_translation: O descendant of Raghu, while that woman of noble form lived there, ten years passed happily in Vishvamitra's hermitage.
ramayan::1647.translation_literal: इत्युक्ता (thus spoken to) / सा (she) / वरारोहा (woman of noble form) / तत्र (there) / वासम् (residence) / अथ (then) / अकरोत् (made, took up) । तस्याम् (in that) / वसन्त्याम् (while living) / वर्षाणि (years) / पञ्च (five) / पञ्च (five) / च (and) / राघव (O descendant of Raghu) / विश्वामित्राश्रमे (in Vishvamitra's hermitage) / राम (O Rama) / सुखेन (happily) / व्यतिचक्रमुः (passed by, elapsed)
ramayan::1647.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1647.essence: A brief lapse can quietly consume years.
ramayan::1647.simple_meaning: Menaka stayed in Vishvamitra's hermitage, and ten years passed there in ease and happiness.
ramayan::1647.simple_insight: Some choices seem brief, but they can quietly reshape years.
ramayan::1647.detailed_meaning: Menaka has entered Vishvamitra's hermitage after his moment of weakness. The verse does not explain the fallout yet; it only shows time quietly slipping by while she remains there. The stillness of this delay prepares the grief and self-reproach that follow.
ramayan::1647.modern_relevance: You think one distraction will cost you an hour, and suddenly a whole season is gone. Time rarely announces its theft while it is happening.
ramayan::1647.insight: It shows how delay can deepen consequences before anyone fully notices.

ramayan::1648.verse_sanskrit: अथ काले गते तस्मिन्विश्वामित्रो महामुनि: । सव्रीड इव सम्वृत्तश्चिन्ताशोकपरायण: । । 1639 । ।
ramayan::1648.verse_hindi: As the period passed, Viswamitra the mighty ascetic was filled with grief, anxiety and
