ramayan::1839.modern_relevance: A family tree on an old document, a surname repeated across generations, a name your grandparents still remember — this verse is about continuity rather than argument.

ramayan::1840.verse_sanskrit: अम्बरीषस्य पुत्रोऽभून्नहुष: पृथिवीपति: । नहुषस्य ययातिस्तु नाभागस्तु ययातिज: । । 17042 । ।
ramayan::1840.verse_hindi: King Nahusha was the son of  Ambarisha. To Nahusha was born Yayati whose son was Nabhaga.
ramayan::1840.english_translation: King Nahusha was the son of Ambarisha. To Nahusha was born Yayati, whose son was Nabhaga.
ramayan::1840.translation_literal: अम्बरीषस्य (of Ambarisha) / पुत्रः (son) / अभूत् (was born) / नहुषः (Nahusha) / पृथिवीपतिḥ (king of the earth) / नहुषस्य (of Nahusha) / ययातिः (Yayati) / तु (and) / नाभागः (Nabhaga) / तु (and) / ययातिजः (born of Yayati)
ramayan::1840.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1840.essence: A king’s greatness is carried forward through his descendants.
ramayan::1840.simple_meaning: This is a royal genealogy: Ambarisha’s line continues through Nahusha, Yayati, and Nabhaga.
ramayan::1840.simple_insight: Some verses simply place a person inside a larger line of descent.
ramayan::1840.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is tracing the solar dynasty before Rama’s birth. This verse names the kings between Ambarisha and Nabhaga, preparing the family line that will soon lead to Dasaratha, Rama, and Lakshmana.
ramayan::1840.modern_relevance: You sometimes need to know where a story comes from before the main moment arrives. This verse is the quiet bridge that connects generations.
ramayan::1840.insight: It shifts attention from drama to lineage, showing how epic lives are rooted in inheritance.

ramayan::1841.verse_sanskrit: नाभागस्य बभूवाज: अजाद्दशरथोऽभवत् । अस्माद्दशरथाज्जातौ भ्रातरौ रामलक्ष्मणौ । । 17043 । ।
ramayan::1841.verse_hindi: Nabhagas son was Aja. Aja was the father of Dasaratha and Dasaratha, the father of  Rama and Lakshmana.
ramayan::1841.english_translation: Nabhaga's son was Aja. Aja was the father of Dasaratha, and Dasaratha was the father of Rama and Lakshmana.
ramayan::1841.translation_literal: नाभागस्य (of Nabhaga) / बभूव (was born) / अज: (Aja) / अजात् (from Aja) / दशरथः (Dasaratha) / अभवत् (became) / अस्मात् (from this one) / दशरथात् (from Dasaratha) / जातौ (were born) / भ्रातरौ (the two brothers) / रामलक्ष्मणौ (Rama and Lakshmana)
ramayan::1841.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1841.essence: Rama enters the story through a royal line already carrying its own weight.
ramayan::1841.simple_meaning: This is a genealogy line: Nabhaga's son was Aja, Aja's son was Dasaratha, and Dasaratha's sons were Rama and Lakshmana.
ramayan::1841.simple_insight: Lineage matters here because it places Rama inside a long royal family chain.
ramayan::1841.detailed_meaning: Vasishta is tracing Dasharatha's royal line for Janaka, moving through ancestors one by one. This verse simply names the link from Nabhaga to Aja to Dasaratha to Rama and Lakshmana, grounding Rama's story in an established dynasty.
ramayan::1841.modern_relevance: A family tree is being explained at a wedding or formal introduction, and you suddenly realise how much a name carries. Some people arrive as individuals; others arrive with generations standing behind them.
ramayan::1841.insight: It shifts attention from the hero alone to the inherited line that shaped his place in the story.

ramayan::1842.verse_sanskrit: एवं ब्रुवाणं जनक: प्रत्युवाच कृताञ्जलि: । श्रोतुमर्हसि भद्रं ते कुलं न: परिकीर्तितम् । । 1711 । ।
ramayan::1842.verse_hindi: Vasishta having thus described (the genealogy of Dasaratha) Janaka with folded hands rejoined, Be blessed. Let me relate the genealogy  of my race. Listen.
ramayan::1842.english_translation: Janaka, with folded hands, replied: "May you be blessed. Listen, and I will tell you the lineage of my race."
ramayan::1842.translation_literal: एवम् (thus) / ब्रुवाणम् (speaking) / जनकः (Janaka) / प्रत्युवाच (replied) / कृताञ्जलिः (with folded hands) / श्रोतुम् (to hear) / अर्हसि (you are worthy) / भद्रम् (blessing) / ते (to you) / कुलम् (lineage) / नः (our) / परिकीर्तितम् (be narrated)
ramayan::1842.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1842.essence: Respectful speech can turn a formal exchange into shared ground.
ramayan::1842.simple_meaning: Janaka respectfully answers the sage and asks him to listen while he describes his own family line.
ramayan::1842.simple_insight: Respect can open the way for truth to be shared.
ramayan::1842.detailed_meaning: Vasishta has just traced Dasaratha’s ancestry. Janaka stands before him with folded hands, answering not with argument but with courtesy. He now invites the sage to hear the lineage of his own house, keeping the marriage discussion formal and honour-bound.
ramayan::1842.modern_relevance: At a family meeting, someone shares their side of a difficult story, and you answer with respect instead of defensiveness. That calm courtesy keeps the conversation open.
ramayan::1842.insight: It shows how humility and order can guide even a formal exchange.

ramayan::1843.verse_sanskrit: प्रदाने हि मुनिश्रेष्ठ कुलं निरवशेषत: । वक्तव्यं कुलजातेन तन्निबोध महामुने । । 1712 । ।
ramayan::1843.verse_hindi: O Great sage O Best of ascetics while one offers his daughter (in marriage), one born in a noble family should describe his genealogy in full. Listen.
ramayan::1843.english_translation: O Great sage, O best of ascetics, while giving a daughter in marriage, a noble family should fully recount its lineage. Listen.
ramayan::1843.translation_literal: प्रदाने (in giving) / हि (indeed) / मुनिश्रेष्ठ (O best of ascetics) / कुलं (the lineage) / निरवशेषत: (without remainder, fully) / वक्तव्यम् (should be spoken) / कुलजातेन (by one born in a noble family) / तत् (that) / निबोध (listen, understand) / महामुने (O great sage)
ramayan::1843.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1843.essence: A noble marriage begins with full honesty about lineage.
ramayan::1843.simple_meaning: Janaka says that when a noble family arranges a marriage, it should openly and completely state its lineage.
ramayan::1843.simple_insight: Respect is shown through honesty and clarity, especially when families join through marriage.
ramayan::1843.detailed_meaning: Janaka is speaking to Vasishta after hearing the lineage of Rama and Lakshmana. He replies that a bride's family should answer with equal fullness, naming its own ancestry before the marriage discussion continues.
ramayan::1843.modern_relevance: A family meeting before an engagement turns tense because no one wants to say the hard things out loud. This verse asks for full honesty before a bond is formed.
ramayan::1843.insight: It shifts marriage from private sentiment to public accountability and clear family identity.

ramayan::1844.verse_sanskrit: राजाऽभूत् त्रिषु लोकेषु विश्रुत स्स्वेन कर्मणा । निमि: परमधर्मात्मा सर्वसत्त्ववतां वर: । । 1713 । ।
ramayan::1844.verse_hindi: There was a great man of religion king Nimi, strongest of men and wellknown in the three worlds by his own acts.
ramayan::1844.english_translation: King Nimi was famous in all three worlds through his own deeds. He was supremely righteous and the best of all living beings.
ramayan::1844.translation_literal: राजाऽभूत् (there was a king) / त्रिषु लोकेषु (in the three worlds) / विश्रुतः (well-known) / स्वेन (by his own) / कर्मणा (deeds) / निमिः (Nimi) / परमधर्मात्मा (supremely righteous in nature) / सर्वसत्त्ववताम् (of all living beings) / वरः (best)
ramayan::1844.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1844.essence: Reputation worth keeping is built by your own conduct.
ramayan::1844.simple_meaning: King Nimi was widely known because of his own actions. He was praised as deeply righteous and श्रेष्ठ among all beings.
ramayan::1844.simple_insight: Goodness becomes lasting when it is earned through action, not inherited reputation.
ramayan::1844.detailed_meaning: Janaka is tracing the royal lineage before a marriage alliance. He names King Nimi, not for spectacle, but to show the noble standard from which this family descends. The verse supports the genealogy, adding honor to the line before moving on to Nimi's son.
ramayan::1844.modern_relevance: A family name may open the door, but your conduct is what keeps it open. People remember the colleague, parent, or leader whose actions made the name trustworthy.
ramayan::1844.insight: It shifts respect from inherited status to character proven in action.

ramayan::1845.verse_sanskrit: तस्य पुत्रोमिथिर्नाम मिथिला येन निर्मिता । प्रथमो जनको नाम जनकादप्युदावसु: । । 1714 । ।
ramayan::1845.verse_hindi: Nimi begot a son named Mithi who constructed Mithila. He was the first Janaka whose son was Udavasu.
ramayan::1845.english_translation: Nimi begot a son named Mithi who constructed Mithila. He was the first Janaka whose son was Udavasu.
ramayan::1845.translation_literal: तस्य (his) / पुत्रः (son) / मिथिः (Mithi) / नाम (named) / मिथिला (Mithila) / येन (by whom) / निर्मिता (built) / प्रथमो (first) / जनकः (Janaka) / नाम (named) / जनकात् (from Janaka) / अपि (even) / उदावसुḥ (Udavasu)
ramayan::1845.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1845.essence: A future queen’s world is being built one ancestor at a time.
ramayan::1845.simple_meaning: Mithi, Nimi’s son, founded Mithila and became the first ruler called Janaka. The verse is part of a lineage list.
ramayan::1845.simple_insight: Some verses simply preserve the chain of ancestry that makes the larger story possible.
ramayan::1845.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is tracing the royal line of Mithila before Sita’s story begins. Nimi’s son Mithi is named as the founder of Mithila, and the verse places the first Janaka in that ancestry, setting up the family line that will matter later.
ramayan::1845.modern_relevance: A family tree on a phone screen, a surname on a marriage form, a grandfather’s name repeated at a funeral — identity often rests on the line that came before you.
ramayan::1845.insight: It shifts attention from dramatic action to lineage, showing how epics anchor later events in inherited history.

ramayan::1846.verse_sanskrit: उदावसोस्तु धर्मात्मा जातो वै नन्दिवर्धन: । नन्दिवर्धनपुत्रस्तु सुकेतुर्नाम नामत: । । 1715 । ।
ramayan::1846.verse_hindi: Virtuous Nandivardhana was the son of Udavasu whose son was Suketu.
ramayan::1846.english_translation: Virtuous Nandivardhana was the son of Udavasu, and Suketu was Nandivardhana's son.
ramayan::1846.translation_literal: उदावसोः (of Udavasu) / तु (indeed) / धर्मात्मा (virtuous) / जातः (was born) / वै (indeed) / नन्दिवर्धनः (Nandivardhana) / नन्दिवर्धनपुत्रः (son of Nandivardhana) / तु (indeed) / सुकेतुः (Suketu) / नामतः (by name)
ramayan::1846.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1846.essence: A royal line is being listed, one generation at a time.
ramayan::1846.simple_meaning: Nandivardhana was born to Udavasu, and Suketu was born to Nandivardhana.
ramayan::1846.simple_insight: The verse simply continues a royal lineage, linking one generation to the next.
ramayan::1846.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is tracing the ancestral line of Mithila's kings: Nimi, Mithi, Janaka, Udavasu, Nandivardhana, and Suketu. The verse adds another name to the chain, keeping the genealogy moving forward toward the later kings.
ramayan::1846.modern_relevance: A family tree on paper, a grandfather naming his grandson, a record kept so the line is not lost. The verse is part of a long memory, not a personal turning point.
ramayan::1846.insight: It teaches you to read the passage as genealogy, not guidance.

ramayan::1847.verse_sanskrit: सुकेतोरपि धर्मात्मा देवरातो महाबल: । देवरातस्य राजर्षेर्बृहद्रथ इति स्मृत: । । 1716 । ।
ramayan::1847.verse_hindi: Suketus son was the righteous and powerful Devarata, father of Brihadradha.
ramayan::1847.english_translation: Suketu's son was the righteous and powerful Devarata, father of Brihadradha.
ramayan::1847.translation_literal: सुकेतोः (of Suketu) / अपि (also) / धर्मात्मा (righteous) / देवरातः (Devarata) / महाबलः (powerful) / देवरातस्य (of Devarata) / राजर्षेः (of the royal sage) / बृहद्रथः (Brihadradha) / इति (thus) / स्मृतः (remembered as)
ramayan::1847.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1847.essence: A royal line is being listed, one name at a time.
ramayan::1847.simple_meaning: Devarata, the righteous and powerful son of Suketu, was remembered as the father of Brihadradha.
ramayan::1847.simple_insight: No teaching is being given here; the verse simply continues a royal genealogy.
ramayan::1847.detailed_meaning: The Ramayana pauses its main story to trace the lineage of Mithila’s kings. After naming Suketu, it identifies his son Devarata and notes that Devarata became the father of Brihadradha. The passage is setting up ancestral background, not making a philosophical point.
ramayan::1847.insight: It records family succession, not a moral instruction.

ramayan::1848.verse_sanskrit: बृहद्रथस्य शूरोऽभून्महावीर: प्रतापवान् । महावीरस्य धृतिमान् सुधृतिस्सत्यविक्रम: । । 1717 । ।
ramayan::1848.verse_hindi: Brihadradhas son was the heroic and powerful Mahavira, father of Sudhruti, who was armed with courage and the power of truth.
ramayan::1848.english_translation: Brihadradha's son was the heroic and powerful Mahavira, father of Sudhruti, who was armed with courage and the power of truth.
ramayan::1848.translation_literal: बृहद्रथस्य (of Brihadradha) / शूरः (heroic) / अभूत् (was) / महावीरः (greatly valiant) / प्रतापवान् (powerful, radiant) / महावीरस्य (of Mahavira) / धृतिमान् (steadfast) / सुधृतिः (Sudhruti) / सत्यविक्रमः (whose valor is rooted in truth)
ramayan::1848.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1848.essence: A royal line is being recorded, not a teaching being given.
ramayan::1848.simple_meaning: This is a genealogy line: it lists kings and their sons, praising their valor and steadiness.
ramayan::1848.simple_insight: Lineage can carry a family’s reputation, but it is still just a record of names and qualities.
ramayan::1848.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is tracing the royal line of Brihadradha through Mahavira to Sudhruti. The verse is part of a long ancestry list, adding noble qualities to each name rather than delivering a teaching or a turning point.
ramayan::1848.modern_relevance: You hear a family name and the stories attached to it, but the moment is still just a roll call. Some passages build history rather than challenge your choices.
ramayan::1848.insight: It helps you read this as background genealogy, not a standalone lesson.

ramayan::1849.verse_sanskrit: सुधृतेरपि धर्मात्मा दृष्टकेतुस्सुधार्मिक: । दृष्टकेतोस्तु राजर्षेर्हर्यश्व इति विश्रुत: । । 1718 । ।
ramayan::1849.verse_hindi: To Sudhruti was born the righteous Drishtaketu, committed to dharma. Rajarshi Drishtaketu was father to the wellknown Haryasva.
ramayan::1849.english_translation: To Sudhruti was born the righteous Drishtaketu, committed to dharma. Rajarshi Drishtaketu was father to the wellknown Haryasva.
ramayan::1849.translation_literal: सुधृतेः (of Sudhruti) / अपि (also) / धर्मात्मा (righteous in nature) / दृष्टकेतुः (Drishtaketu) / सुदार्मिकः (very devoted to dharma) / दृष्टकेतोः (of Drishtaketu) / तु (and) / राजर्षेः (of the royal sage) / हर्यश्वः (Haryasva) / इति (thus) / विश्रुतः (well known)
ramayan::1849.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1849.essence: A royal line is being carefully carried forward.
ramayan::1849.simple_meaning: This line continues a royal genealogy, naming Drishtaketu as Sudhruti's son and Haryasva as Drishtaketu's son.
ramayan::1849.simple_insight: Some verses simply preserve lineage, carrying the memory of a family forward.
ramayan::1849.detailed_meaning: The text is listing kings in sequence, moving from Sudhruti to Drishtaketu to Haryasva. Nothing is being argued or taught here; the verse simply keeps the ancestral chain intact as the genealogy continues.
ramayan::1849.modern_relevance: A family tree on old paper, a grandfather's name repeated at a funeral, a child asking who came before them — this verse is about preserving continuity, not making a point.
ramayan::1849.insight: It keeps attention on lineage and succession rather than interpretation.

ramayan::1850.verse_sanskrit: हर्यश्वस्य मरु: पुत्रो मरो: पुत्र: प्रतिन्धक: । प्रतिंधकस्य धर्मात्मा राजा कीर्तिरथस्सुत: । । 1719 । ।
ramayan::1850.verse_hindi: Haryasvas son was Maru, father of Pratindhaka. Pratindhakas son was the righteous king Kirtiratha.
ramayan::1850.english_translation: Haryashva's son was Maru, Maru's son was Pratindhaka, and Pratindhaka's righteous son was King Kirtiratha.
ramayan::1850.translation_literal: हर्यश्वस्य (of Haryashva) / मरु: (Maru) / पुत्रो (son) / मरो: (of Maru) / पुत्र: (son) / प्रतिन्धक: (Pratindhaka) / प्रतिंधकस्य (of Pratindhaka) / धर्मात्मा (righteous) / राजा (king) / कीर्तिरथस्सुत: (son Kirtiratha)
ramayan::1850.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1850.essence: A royal line is preserved by naming each successor.
ramayan::1850.simple_meaning: This is a genealogy line: Haryashva, Maru, Pratindhaka, and then King Kirtiratha. It records family succession, not a teaching.
ramayan::1850.simple_insight: Some verses simply preserve lineage, showing where a king comes from.
ramayan::1850.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is listing the royal line of ancestors and descendants, moving from Haryashva to Maru to Pratindhaka to Kirtiratha. The verse exists to preserve the chain of succession, not to make a moral argument or emotional point.
ramayan::1850.modern_relevance: A family tree on a document, a name repeated across generations, a record kept so the line is not lost — this verse is about remembering who came before.
ramayan::1850.insight: It shifts attention from meaning to lineage, showing continuity through names.

ramayan::1851.verse_sanskrit: पुत्र: कीर्तिरथस्यापि देवमीढ इति स्मृत: । देवमीढस्य विबुधो विबुधस्य महीध्रक: । । 17110 । ।
ramayan::1851.verse_hindi: The son of Kirtiratha was known as Devamidha. His son was Vibudha, father of Mahidhraka.
ramayan::1851.english_translation: The son of Kirtiratha was known as Devamidha. His son was Vibudha, father of Mahidhraka.
ramayan::1851.translation_literal: पुत्रः (son) / कीर्तिरथस्य (of Kirtiratha) / अपि (also) / देवमीढः (Devamidha) / इति (thus) / स्मृतः (known as) / देवमीढस्य (of Devamidha) / विबुधः (Vibudha) / विबुधस्य (of Vibudha) / महीध्रकः (Mahidhraka)
ramayan::1851.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1851.essence: A dynasty continues through remembered names.
ramayan::1851.simple_meaning: This is a genealogy entry: Kirtiratha's son was Devamidha, whose son was Vibudha, who fathered Mahidhraka.
ramayan::1851.simple_insight: Lineage is being recorded, not a teaching being given.
ramayan::1851.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is listing the descendants of Kirtiratha in sequence. Devamidha, Vibudha, and Mahidhraka are named only to preserve the royal line. The verse supports the genealogy around it rather than offering a standalone reflection.
ramayan::1851.modern_relevance: A family tree spreadsheet gets updated with one more name: son, grandson, great-grandson. The verse preserves continuity, not a lesson to apply.
ramayan::1851.insight: It keeps the royal lineage intact by naming each generation in order.

ramayan::1852.verse_sanskrit: महीध्रकसुतो राजा कीर्तिरातो महाबल: । कीर्तिरातस्य राजर्षेर्महारोमा व्यजायत । । 17111 । ।
ramayan::1852.verse_hindi: Mighty king Kirtirata was the son of Mahidhraka. He was a Rajarshi, father of Maharoma.
ramayan::1852.english_translation: Mighty king Kirtirata was the son of Mahidhraka. He was a Rajarshi, father of Maharoma.
ramayan::1852.translation_literal: महीध्रकसुतः (son of Mahidhraka) / राजा (king) / कीर्तिरातः (Kirtirata) / महाबलः (mighty) / कीर्तिरातस्य (of Kirtirata) / राजर्षेः (of the king-sage) / महारोमा (Maharoma) / व्यजायत (was born)
ramayan::1852.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1852.essence: A royal line is being recorded, not a lesson taught.
ramayan::1852.simple_meaning: This is a lineage note: Kirtirata, a powerful king and king-sage, was born to Mahidhraka and became the father of Maharoma.
ramayan::1852.simple_insight: Some verses simply preserve the chain of a royal family, keeping memory alive across generations.
ramayan::1852.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is tracing a royal genealogy, naming one king after another in an unbroken line. Kirtirata is identified as Mahidhraka's son and Maharoma's father, but no teaching or dramatic turn appears here.
ramayan::1852.modern_relevance: A family tree in an old record, a name passed down, a place in history quietly fixed before anyone argues about meaning.
ramayan::1852.insight: It teaches you to read this as continuity, not instruction.

ramayan::1853.verse_sanskrit: महारोम्णस्तु धर्मात्मा स्वर्णरोमा व्यजायत । स्वर्णरोम्णस्तु राजर्षेर्ह्रस्वरोमा व्यजायत । । 17112 । ।
ramayan::1853.verse_hindi: To Maharomas was born the virtuous Swarnaroma. Swarnaromas son was Hrasvaroma.
ramayan::1853.english_translation: To Maharomas was born the virtuous Swarnaroma. Swarnaroma's son was Hrasvaroma.
ramayan::1853.translation_literal: महारोम्णस्तु (to Maharoma) / धर्मात्मा (virtuous) / स्वर्णरोमा (Swarnaroma) / व्यजायत (was born) / स्वर्णरोम्णस्तु (to Swarnaroma's) / राजर्षेः (of the king-sage) / ह्रस्वरोमा (Hrasvaroma) / व्यजायत (was born)
ramayan::1853.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1853.essence: A royal line is being carefully traced, name by name.
ramayan::1853.simple_meaning: This is a genealogy verse: it lists the next two kings in a lineage, without adding teaching or reflection.
ramayan::1853.simple_insight: It gives the family line, not a lesson.
ramayan::1853.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is tracing the royal ancestry of a line of kings, naming Maharoma, Swarnaroma, and Hrasvaroma in sequence. The verse serves as a bridge in the genealogy, preparing for the next identification of the speaker's own lineage.
ramayan::1853.modern_relevance: You may not remember every name in a family history, but each link still matters. Some moments simply place you in a line that came before you.
ramayan::1853.insight: It shifts attention from meaning-making to continuity: who came before whom.

ramayan::1854.verse_sanskrit: तस्य पुत्रद्वयं जज्ञे धर्मज्ञस्य महात्मन: । ज्येष्ठोऽहमनुजो भ्राता मम वीर: कुशध्वज: । । 17113 । ।
ramayan::1854.verse_hindi: Hrasvaroma, was a religious king. He was a great soul. Of his two sons. I am the
ramayan::1854.english_translation: Of that righteous, great-souled king, two sons were born: I am the elder, and my brave brother is Kushadhvaja.
ramayan::1854.translation_literal: तस्य (of that) / पुत्रद्वयं (a pair of sons) / जज्ञे (were born) / धर्मज्ञस्य (of the righteous one) / महात्मनः (of the great-souled one) / ज्येष्ठः (the elder) / अहम् (I) / अनुजः (younger) / भ्राता (brother) / मम (my) / वीरः (brave) / कुशध्वजः (Kushadhvaja)
ramayan::1854.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1854.essence: The verse simply fixes family order before the story continues.
ramayan::1854.simple_meaning: A righteous king had two sons. The speaker is the elder brother, and Kushadhvaja is the younger, brave brother.
ramayan::1854.simple_insight: Family identity and rank are being established before the story moves on.
ramayan::1854.detailed_meaning: The verse belongs to a genealogy, not a teaching. It identifies Hrasvaroma's two sons and lets the speaker place himself as the elder brother of brave Kushadhvaja. The next verse uses that detail to explain inheritance and retirement.
ramayan::1854.modern_relevance: In a family introduction before a wedding or legal dispute, the details matter: who is elder, who is younger, and who carries responsibility next.
ramayan::1854.insight: It frames the speaker's position in the family so the next action makes sense.

ramayan::1855.verse_sanskrit: मां तु ज्येष्ठं पिता राज्ये सोऽभिषिच्य नराधिप: । कुशध्वजं समावेश्य भारं मयि वनं गत: । । 17114 । ।
ramayan::1855.verse_hindi: My father king Hrasvaroma crowned me king, entrusted Kusadhwaja to my care and retired to the forest.
ramayan::1855.english_translation: My father, King Hrasvaroma, crowned me king, entrusted Kusadhwaja to my care, and retired to the forest.
ramayan::1855.translation_literal: माम् (me) / तु (indeed) / ज्येष्ठम् (the elder one) / पिता (father) / राज्ये (in the kingdom) / सः (he) / अभिषिच्य (having anointed) / नराधिपः (the ruler of men) / कुशध्वजम् (Kusadhwaja) / समावेश्य (having placed, entrusted) / भारम् (burden/care) / मयि (on me) / वनम् (to the forest) / गतः (went)
ramayan::1855.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1855.essence: Kingship here means carrying another life, not enjoying power.
ramayan::1855.simple_meaning: His father made him king, placed his younger brother under his care, and then left for the forest.
ramayan::1855.simple_insight: Some responsibilities arrive already tied to grief. You carry them because love leaves them with you.
ramayan::1855.detailed_meaning: The speaker is describing his family line: an elder son crowned to rule, a younger brother placed in his care, and a father who chose the forest. The verse is part of a longer account of lineage, not a complete teaching by itself.
ramayan::1855.modern_relevance: You get the call that your parent is stepping back, and suddenly your sibling, your home, and the whole family rhythm are now your responsibility.
ramayan::1855.insight: It frames authority as a burden of care, not a prize.

ramayan::1856.verse_sanskrit: वृद्धे पितरि स्वर्याते धर्मेण धुरमावहम् । भ्रातरं देवसङ्काशं स्नेहात्पश्यन् कुशध्वजम् । । 17115 । ।
ramayan::1856.verse_hindi: After my aged father attained heaven, I looked after my brother Kusadhwaja, who resembles the celestials, affectionately and ruled the kingdom with righteousness.
ramayan::1856.english_translation: After my aged father attained heaven, I looked after my brother Kusadhwaja, who resembles the celestials, affectionately and ruled the kingdom with righteousness.
ramayan::1856.translation_literal: वृद्धे (when aged) / पितरि (father) / स्वर्याते (having gone to heaven) / धर्मेण (by righteousness) / धुरम् (the burden) / आवहम् (I bore) / भ्रातरम् (brother) / देवसङ्काशम् (celestial-like) / स्नेहात् (out of affection) / पश्यन् (seeing) / कुशध्वजम् (Kusadhwaja)
ramayan::1856.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1856.essence: You can bear the burden of rule without losing tenderness.
ramayan::1856.simple_meaning: He ruled after his father died, carrying the burden of the kingdom while caring for his brother with affection.
ramayan::1856.simple_insight: Responsibility does not have to make you hard or distant.
ramayan::1856.detailed_meaning: Hrasvaroma's father has died, and the kingdom has passed into his hands. He is not only governing justly; he is also protecting and loving his brother Kusadhwaja. The verse shows rule as care, not mere power.
ramayan::1856.modern_relevance: You are handling bills, family calls, and a tired parent’s medical paperwork all in one week. The pressure is real, but it does not have to turn you cold toward the people you are carrying.
ramayan::1856.insight: It teaches you to hold authority with affection, not as a license to become stern.

ramayan::1857.verse_sanskrit: कस्य चित्त्वथकालस्य साङ्काश्यादगमत्पुरात् । सुधन्वा वीर्यवान्राजा मिथिलामवरोधक: । । 17116 । ।
ramayan::1857.verse_hindi: A little later a powerful king named Sudhanva from the city of Sankasya beseiged Mithila.
ramayan::1857.english_translation: A little later a powerful king named Sudhanva from the city of Sankasya besieged Mithila.
ramayan::1857.translation_literal: कस्य चित्तु (then after some time) / अथकालस्य (at a certain time) / साङ्काश्यात् (from Sankasya) / अगमत् (came) / पुरात् (from the city) / सुधन्वा (Sudhanva) / वीर्यवान् (mighty) / राजा (king) / मिथिलाम् (to Mithila) / अवरोधकः (besieger)
ramayan::1857.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1857.essence: A siege arrives, and the next test begins.
ramayan::1857.simple_meaning: King Sudhanva came from Sankasya and laid siege to Mithila.
ramayan::1857.simple_insight: A new threat arrives, and the story’s pressure tightens.
ramayan::1857.detailed_meaning: After describing Janaka’s care for his kingdom and brother, the poem shifts to a new crisis: Sudhanva, a powerful king from Sankasya, marches against Mithila. This is the setup for the bow challenge that follows.
ramayan::1857.modern_relevance: A calm day at work changes when a difficult demand lands on your desk. The next problem does not wait for you to feel ready.
ramayan::1857.insight: It sets up the challenge that will test Mithila’s strength and Janaka’s response.

ramayan::1858.verse_sanskrit: स च मे प्रेषयामास शैवं धनुरनुत्तमम् । सीता कन्या च पद्माक्षी मह्यं वै दीयतामिति । । 17117 । ।
ramayan::1858.verse_hindi: He (Sudhanva) sent me a message: give me the great bow of Siva and the lotuseyed maiden Sita.
ramayan::1858.english_translation: He, Sudhanva, sent me a message: give me the great bow of Shiva and the lotus-eyed maiden Sita.
ramayan::1858.translation_literal: स (he) / च (and) / मे (to me) / प्रेषयामास (sent) / शैवम् (of Shiva) / धनुः (bow) / अनुत्तमम् (unsurpassed) / सीता (Sita) / कन्या (maiden) / च (and) / पद्माक्षी (lotus-eyed) / मह्यम् (to me) / वै (indeed) / दीयताम् (be given)
ramayan::1858.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1858.simple_meaning: Sudhanva demanded two things from Rama: the bow of Shiva and Sita herself.
ramayan::1858.simple_insight: A demand can reveal arrogance more clearly than a battle ever could.
ramayan::1858.detailed_meaning: Sudhanva has already marched on Mithila and now sends an outrageous message to Rama: hand over Shiva's great bow and Sita. The verse sets up the insult before the refusal and the fight that follow.
ramayan::1858.modern_relevance: Someone asks for what was never theirs to claim: your work, your partner, your dignity. The request itself tells you exactly what kind of person stands before you.
ramayan::1858.insight: It frames the coming conflict as a challenge to honor, not just strength.

ramayan::1859.verse_sanskrit: तस्याप्रदानाद्ब्रह्मर्षे युद्धमासीन्मया सह । स हतोऽभिमुखो राजा सुधन्वा तु मया रणे । । 17118 । ।
ramayan::1859.verse_hindi: O Brahmarshi when I refused, a great conflict broke out between him and me. In the encounter king Sudhanva was killed by me.
ramayan::1859.english_translation: O Brahmarshi, when I refused, a great conflict broke out between him and me. In the encounter, king Sudhanva was killed by me.
ramayan::1859.translation_literal: तस्य (of that) / अप्रदानात् (from not giving) / ब्रह्मर्षे (O Brahmarshi) / युद्धम् (battle) / आसीत् (was) / मया सह (with me) / सः (he) / हतः (killed) / अभिमुखः (facing me) / राजा (king) / सुधन्वा (Sudhanva) / तु (indeed) / मया (by me) / रणे (in battle)
ramayan::1859.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1859.essence: Pride turns a demand into a battle.
ramayan::1859.simple_meaning: Because I would not hand it over, Sudhanva and I fought. He came at me in battle and I killed him.
ramayan::1859.simple_insight: A refusal can turn quickly into violence when pride is involved.
ramayan::1859.detailed_meaning: In Mithila, Sudhanva has demanded Shiva's bow and Sita herself. This verse continues the account of that confrontation: the refusal led to battle, and the king fell before the speaker. It is a factual link in the larger story.
ramayan::1859.modern_relevance: A negotiation at work turns sharp the moment someone hears no. What began as a request becomes a clash because neither side can bend.
ramayan::1859.insight: It shows how a single refusal can escalate into irreversible conflict.

ramayan::1860.verse_sanskrit: निहत्य तं मुनिश्रेष्ठ सुधन्वानं नराधिपम् । साङ्काश्ये भ्रातरं वीरमभ्यषिञ्चं कुशध्वजम् । । 17119 । ।
ramayan::1860.verse_hindi: O Best of ascetics having killed king Sudhanva, I have crowned my heroic brother Kusadhwaja in Sankasya.
ramayan::1860.english_translation: O best of ascetics, after killing king Sudhanva, I crowned my heroic brother Kushadhwaja in Sankasya.
ramayan::1860.translation_literal: निहत्य (having killed) / तम् (him) / मुनिश्रेष्ठ (O best of ascetics) / सुधन्वानम् (Sudhanva) / नराधिपम् (king) / साङ्काश्ये (in Sankasya) / भ्रातरम् (brother) / वीरम् (heroic) / अभ्यषिञ्चम् (I crowned) / कुशध्वजम् (Kushadhwaja)
ramayan::1860.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1860.essence: Victory matters less than how you restore order afterward.
ramayan::1860.simple_meaning: After defeating Sudhanva, the speaker installed his brother Kushadhwaja as ruler in Sankasya.
ramayan::1860.simple_insight: Power is not just won; it is handed on with order.
ramayan::1860.detailed_meaning: In Vasishta’s presence, Janaka continues the story of the bow contest. Sudhanva has been killed, and the kingdom is not left in chaos. Janaka says he crowned his brave brother Kushadhwaja in Sankasya, showing the stability of his house before the marriage negotiations continue.
ramayan::1860.modern_relevance: A family business changes hands after a sudden loss, and everyone watches for disorder. The real test is whether the transition is clean, not just whether someone new takes charge.
ramayan::1860.insight: It frames authority as something that must be settled responsibly, not left hanging after conflict.

ramayan::1861.verse_sanskrit: कनीयानेष मे भ्राता अहं ज्येष्ठो महामुने । ददामि परमप्रीतो वध्वौ ते मुनिपुङ्गव । । 17120 । । सीतां रामाय भद्रं ते ऊर्मिला लक्ष्मणाय च ।
ramayan::1861.verse_hindi: O Great ascetic (Vasishta), this one is my youger brother and I am the elder one. O preeminent among ascetics with immense pleasure I am giving these maidens, Sita to Rama and Urmila to Lakshmana. Be blessed
ramayan::1861.english_translation: O great ascetic, this one is my younger brother and I am the elder one. With great joy, O best of sages, I give these brides to you: Sita to Rama and Urmila to Lakshmana. Be blessed.
ramayan::1861.translation_literal: कनीयान् (younger) / एषः (this one) / मे (my) / भ्राता (brother) / अहम् (I) / ज्येष्ठः (elder) / महामुने (O great ascetic) / ददामि (I give) / परमप्रीतः (greatly pleased) / वध्वौ (two brides) / ते (to you) / मुनिपुङ्गव (O best of sages) / सीताम् (Sita) / रामाय (to Rama) / भद्रं ते (blessings to you) / ऊर्मिलाम् (Urmila) / लक्ष्मणाय (to Lakshmana) / च (and)
ramayan::1861.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1861.essence: Joyful giving can be the highest form of recognition.
ramayan::1861.simple_meaning: Janaka joyfully gives Sita to Rama and Urmila to Lakshmana, while explaining that he is the elder brother and this is his younger one.
ramayan::1861.simple_insight: Some gifts are not transactions; they are acts of recognition and trust.
ramayan::1861.detailed_meaning: At Janaka's court in Mithila, the wedding alliance is being sealed after Rama has won Sita in the contest. Janaka speaks to Vasishta with public joy, naming the brothers and formally giving the two brides. The verse is part of the ceremonial exchange, not the main teaching.
ramayan::1861.modern_relevance: A family meeting turns quiet when everyone knows a life is changing forever. In that moment, the words are not just formalities — they are the public shape of a bond already felt.
ramayan::1861.insight: It frames marriage as a deliberate act of honouring kinship, not merely matching two people.

ramayan::1862.verse_sanskrit: वीर्यशुल्कां मम सुतां सीतां सुरसुतोपमाम् । । 17121 । । द्वितीयामूर्मिलां चैव त्रिर्ददामि न संशय: ।
ramayan::1862.verse_hindi: I offer my daughter Sita, who looks like a celestial maiden as reward for (Ramas) prowess and my second daughter Urmila (to Lakshmana). I proclaim it three times so that there is no doubt about it.
ramayan::1862.english_translation: I offer my daughter Sita, who looks like a celestial maiden as reward for Rama's prowess, and my second daughter Urmila as well. I declare it three times so there is no doubt about it.
ramayan::1862.translation_literal: वीर्य-शुल्काम् (as the price of valor) / मम (my) / सुताम् (daughter) / सीताम् (Sita) / सुर-सुत-उपमाम् (resembling a celestial maiden) / द्वितीयाम् (the second) / ऊर्मिलाम् (Urmila) / च एव (and also) / त्रिः (three times) / ददामि (I give) / न (not) / संशयः (doubt)
ramayan::1862.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1862.essence: A promise becomes real when you state it without hesitation.
ramayan::1862.simple_meaning: Janaka formally and repeatedly offers Sita and Urmila in marriage, making the promise unmistakable and final.
ramayan::1862.simple_insight: A clear promise creates trust because it leaves no room for hesitation.
ramayan::1862.detailed_meaning: In Janaka's court, after Rama has won Sita's hand by breaking Shiva's bow, the king seals the marriage offer for both daughters. He repeats it three times so everyone hears the commitment as final and unquestionable.
ramayan::1862.modern_relevance: You tell someone yes, then keep softening it with texts and explanations. Real commitment sounds different: clean, repeated, and unambiguous.
ramayan::1862.insight: It teaches you to make commitments plainly, so your words carry weight and can be trusted.

ramayan::1863.verse_sanskrit: ददामि परमप्रीतो वध्वौ ते रघुनन्दन । । 17122 । । रामलक्ष्मणयो राजन् गोदानं कारयस्व ह । पितृकार्यं च भद्रं ते ततो वैवाहिकं कुरु । । 17123 । ।
ramayan::1863.verse_hindi: O Delight of the Raghus (King Dasaratha), I offer these brides with immense pleasure to Rama and Lakshmana. You may perform the rites for your forefathers by gift of cows. Prosperity to you. Thereafter you may perform the marriage.
ramayan::1863.english_translation: O Delight of the Raghus, I offer these brides to Rama and Lakshmana with great joy. Let the cow-gift rites for your ancestors be performed, and then let the marriage rites be completed.
ramayan::1863.translation_literal: ददामि (I offer) / परमप्रीतः (greatly pleased) / वध्वौ (the two brides) / ते (to you) / रघुनन्दन (O delight of the Raghu dynasty) / रामलक्ष्मणयोः (for Rama and Lakshmana) / राजन् (O king) / गोदानम् (gift of cows) / कारयस्व (have performed) / ह (indeed) / पितृकार्यं (ancestral rites) / च (and) / भद्रम् ते (prosperity to you) / ततः (then) / वैवाहिकम् (marriage rites) / कुरु (do/perform)
ramayan::1863.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1863.essence: Joy and ritual prepare the way for the wedding.
ramayan::1863.simple_meaning: Janaka joyfully offers Sita and Urmila to Rama and Lakshmana, and asks Dasharatha to complete the ancestral rites and then the marriage ceremony.
ramayan::1863.simple_insight: A marriage begins with honour, ritual, and mutual goodwill.
ramayan::1863.detailed_meaning: In Mithila, Janaka has already accepted Rama's worth and is now formally giving both daughters to the Raghu princes. He asks Dasharatha to complete the cow-gift and forefather rites before the wedding proceeds, turning a royal alliance into a sacred, orderly union.
ramayan::1863.insight: It shows marriage as a public act of blessing, duty, and sequence, not just private feeling.

ramayan::1864.verse_sanskrit: मखा ह्यद्य महाबाहो तृतीये दिवसे प्रभो । फल्गुन्यामुत्तरे राजंस्तस्मिन्वैवाहिकं कुरु । । 17124 । । रामलक्ष्मणयो राजन् दानं कार्यं सुखोदयम् । ।
ramayan::1864.verse_hindi: Today the star Makha is on the ascendant. O King perform the marriage on the, third day from today under UttaraPhalguni star. Gifts may be given for the happiness of Rama and Lakshmana.
ramayan::1864.english_translation: Today the star Makha is on the ascendant. O King, perform the marriage on the third day from today under Uttara Phalguni. Gifts may be given for the happiness of Rama and Lakshmana.
ramayan::1864.translation_literal: मखा (Makha star) / हि (indeed) / अद्य (today) / महाबाहो (O mighty-armed one) / तृतीये (on the third) / दिवसे (day) / प्रभो (O lord) / फल्गुन्याम् (under Phalguni) / उत्तरे (Uttara) / राजन् (O king) / तस्मिन् (on that) / वैवाहिकम् (marriage rite) / कुरु (do) / रामलक्ष्मणयोः (for Rama and Lakshmana) / राजन् (O king) / दानम् (gifts) / कार्यम् (to be done) / सुखोदयम् (bringing happiness)
ramayan::1864.speaker: Vasistha
ramayan::1864.essence: A promise becomes real only when the rite is fixed and carried out.
ramayan::1864.simple_meaning: The marriage should be fixed for the third day, under the right star, with gifts arranged for Rama and Lakshmana.
ramayan::1864.simple_insight: Good timing matters, and so does preparing the celebration with care.
ramayan::1864.detailed_meaning: Janaka has accepted the match. Now the priestly details matter: the auspicious day, the star, the gifts, the formal marriage rites. This is the practical step that turns a royal promise into a wedding.
ramayan::1864.modern_relevance: You’ve agreed to something important, and now the calendar, the details, and the preparations all have to line up.
ramayan::1864.insight: It shifts attention from excitement to execution: choose the right moment and complete the formalities well.

ramayan::1865.verse_sanskrit: तमुक्तवन्तं वैदेहं विश्वामित्रो महामुनि: । उवाच वचनं वीरं वसिष्ठसहितो नृपम् । । 1721 । ।
ramayan::1865.verse_hindi: When Janaka the valiant king of Videha thus spoke (on the genealogy of his family) the mighty ascetic Viswamitra accompanied by Vasishta said to Janaka:
ramayan::1865.english_translation: When the valiant king of Videha had spoken, the mighty sage Vishwamitra, accompanied by Vasishta, said to Janaka:
ramayan::1865.translation_literal: तमुक्तवन्तं (having spoken thus) / वैदेहम् (the king of Videha) / विश्वामित्रः (Vishwamitra) / महामुनिः (the great sage) / उवाच (said) / वचनम् (speech) / वीरम् (valiant) / वसिष्ठसहितः (accompanied by Vasishta) / नृपम् (to the king)
ramayan::1865.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1865.essence: The conversation turns from Janaka to the sages.
ramayan::1865.simple_meaning: After Janaka finished speaking, Vishwamitra and Vasishta replied to him.
ramayan::1865.simple_insight: Some moments only move the story forward; they do not carry a teaching on their own.
ramayan::1865.detailed_meaning: Janaka has just spoken about his royal line and the marriage arrangements. Now Vishwamitra, with Vasishta beside him, answers him. The verse simply marks the turn in the conversation before the sages praise the two royal families.
ramayan::1865.modern_relevance: A meeting pauses after one person finishes speaking, and everyone turns to the next voice. Some lines are only the hinge between one important moment and the next.
ramayan::1865.insight: It marks a transition in the dialogue, not the teaching itself.

ramayan::1866.verse_sanskrit: अचिन्त्यान्यप्रमेयानि कुलानि नरपुङ्गव । इक्ष्वाकूणां विदेहानां नैषां तुल्योऽस्ति कश्चन । । 1722 । ।
ramayan::1866.verse_hindi: O Preeminent among men the glory of the two races of Ikshvakus as also of Videhas is in comprehensible and immeasurable. There is none equal to these kings of the Ikshvakus and Videhas.
ramayan::1866.english_translation: O foremost among men, the lineages of the Ikshvakus and the Videhas are beyond thought and measure. No one is equal to these royal houses.
ramayan::1866.translation_literal: अचिन्त्यानि (beyond thought) / अप्रमेयानि (immeasurable) / कुलानि (lineages) / नरपुङ्गव (foremost among men) / इक्ष्वाकूणाम् (of the Ikshvakus) / विदेहानाम् (of the Videhas) / न (not) / एषाम् (of these) / तुल्यः (equal) / अस्ति (is) / कश्चन (anyone)
ramayan::1866.speaker: Viswamitra
ramayan::1866.essence: Two great houses are being matched because neither stands below the other.
ramayan::1866.simple_meaning: The royal families of Ikshvaku and Videha are so great that no one can match them.
ramayan::1866.simple_insight: Some lineages carry a weight that everyone in the room can feel.
ramayan::1866.detailed_meaning: At Janaka’s court, Vishwamitra is arranging a marriage that will join two celebrated royal houses. He praises the unmatched standing of the Ikshvakus and the Videhas, setting the stage for why this union is worthy of Rama and Sita.
ramayan::1866.modern_relevance: At a family gathering where two respected families are discussing a marriage, everyone can feel the unspoken standard in the room. Some unions are not casual; they are framed by legacy, character, and responsibility.
ramayan::1866.insight: It frames the coming marriage as a union of equals, not a mere arrangement.

ramayan::1867.verse_sanskrit: सदृशो धर्मसम्बन्ध: सदृशो रूपसम्पदा । रामलक्ष्मणयो राजन् सीता चोर्मिलया सह । । 1723 । ।
ramayan::1867.verse_hindi: O King it is a perfect match between Sita and Rama and Urmila and Lakshmana. In respect of piety and beauty  the match is perfect.
ramayan::1867.english_translation: O King, the match is perfect between Rama and Lakshmana with Sita and Urmila. In virtue and beauty, the pairing is complete.
ramayan::1867.translation_literal: सदृशो (matching) / धर्मसम्बन्धः (bond in righteousness) / सदृशः (matching) / रूपसम्पदा (in beauty and form) / रामलक्ष्मणयोः (of Rama and Lakshmana) / राजन् (O king) / सीता (Sita) / च (and) / ऊर्मिलया (with Urmila) / सह (together)
ramayan::1867.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1867.essence: The right match joins beauty with shared virtue.
ramayan::1867.simple_meaning: The two brothers and the two sisters are perfectly matched in virtue and beauty.
ramayan::1867.simple_insight: Right union feels balanced, not forced.
ramayan::1867.detailed_meaning: At Janaka’s court, Viswamitra has just praised the two royal lineages. Janaka now points to the two marriages: Rama with Sita, Lakshmana with Urmila. He is not speaking of romance alone, but of a fitting union of character, virtue, and appearance.
ramayan::1867.modern_relevance: At a wedding where everyone is smiling for photos, you can still feel whether the pairing is truly aligned. Some bonds look good; others fit the whole life. This verse points to the second kind.
ramayan::1867.insight: It shifts attention from attraction alone to character-level compatibility.

ramayan::1868.verse_sanskrit: वक्तव्यं च नरश्रेष्ठ श्रूयतां वचनं मम । भ्राता यवीयान् धर्मज्ञ एष राजा कुशध्वज: । । 1724 । ।
ramayan::1868.verse_hindi: O Best of men my words deserve to be heard. This younger brother king Kusadhwaja is knower of righteousness.
ramayan::1868.english_translation: O best of men, hear my words. This younger brother, King Kusadhwaja, is a knower of righteousness.
ramayan::1868.translation_literal: वक्तव्यं (to be spoken) / च (and) / नरश्रेष्ठ (O best of men) / श्रूयताम् (let it be heard) / वचनं (word) / मम (my) / भ्राता (brother) / यवीयान् (younger) / धर्मज्ञः (knower of righteousness) / एषः (this) / राजा (king) / कुशध्वजः (Kusadhwaja)
ramayan::1868.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1868.essence: Worth begins with righteousness, not status.
ramayan::1868.simple_meaning: The speaker asks the listener to hear his words and introduces King Kusadhwaja as a younger brother who understands righteousness.
ramayan::1868.simple_insight: Respect for character matters before any proposal can succeed.
ramayan::1868.detailed_meaning: At Janaka’s court, the match for Rama and Lakshmana is being discussed. The speaker introduces Kusadhwaja, not with power or wealth first, but as a younger brother and a king who knows righteousness, preparing the ground for a worthy alliance.
ramayan::1868.modern_relevance: Before a family meeting about marriage, someone quietly says, “He’s a good man.” That single line carries more weight than status, money, or polish.
ramayan::1868.insight: It shifts attention from rank to moral fitness when judging a person.

ramayan::1869.verse_sanskrit: अस्य धर्मात्मनो राजन् रूपेणाप्रतिमं भुवि । सुताद्वयं नरश्रेष्ठ पत्न्यर्थं वरयामहे । । 1725 । ।
ramayan::1869.verse_hindi: O King, O Eminent among men we seek the hands of this virtuous kings two daughters, unrivalled in beauty, on earth, as consorts.
ramayan::1869.english_translation: O King, O Eminent among men, we seek the hands of this virtuous king's two daughters, unrivalled in beauty on earth, as consorts.
ramayan::1869.translation_literal: अस्य (of this) / धर्मात्मनो (virtuous, righteous-souled) / राजन् (O king) / रूपेण (in beauty) / अप्रतिमं (unrivalled) / भुवि (on earth) / सुताद्वयं (two daughters) / नरश्रेष्ठ (O best among men) / पत्न्यर्थं (for the sake of wives) / वरयामहे (we seek / choose)
ramayan::1869.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1869.essence: The proposal joins two noble houses through a match worthy of both.
ramayan::1869.simple_meaning: They ask the king for his two beautiful daughters as brides for the two princes.
ramayan::1869.simple_insight: A marriage proposal can be a turning point for an entire kingdom.
ramayan::1869.detailed_meaning: In Mithila, King Janaka is being approached with a formal proposal. The match is not random: Rama and Lakshmana are being paired with Sita and Urmila, and the speaker stresses the daughters' unmatched beauty and the king's righteousness.
ramayan::1869.modern_relevance: A family meeting turns serious when everyone realises this is not just about affection, but about the future two lives will build together.
ramayan::1869.insight: It frames marriage as a fitting union of character, not just attraction.

ramayan::1870.verse_sanskrit: भरतस्य कुमारस्य शत्रुघ्नस्य च धीमत: । वरयामस्सुते राजन् तयोरर्थे महात्मनो: । । 1726 । ।
ramayan::1870.verse_hindi: O king we choose your brothers daughters for the great souls: the young Bharata and the sagacious Satrughna.
ramayan::1870.english_translation: O king, we seek your daughters for the great-souled Bharata and the wise Shatrughna.
ramayan::1870.translation_literal: भरतस्य (of Bharata) / कुमारस्य (of the young prince) / शत्रुघ्नस्य (of Shatrughna) / च (and) / धीमतः (of the wise one) / वरयामः (we seek in marriage) / सुते (the two daughters) / राजन् (O king) / तयोः अर्थे (for those two) / महात्मनोः (of the great-souled ones)
ramayan::1870.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1870.essence: Two more royal matches are being formally placed before the king.
ramayan::1870.simple_meaning: The king is being asked to give his daughters in marriage to Bharata and Shatrughna, the younger sons of Dasharatha.
ramayan::1870.simple_insight: A marriage proposal can carry the weight of alliance, honor, and future duty.
ramayan::1870.detailed_meaning: In Mithila, the proposal is widening from Rama and Lakshmana to Dasharatha’s other two sons. Janaka’s side names Bharata and Shatrughna as worthy matches, continuing the formal exchange before the royal marriages are fixed.
ramayan::1870.modern_relevance: At a family meeting, names are being exchanged, alliances quietly taking shape, and everyone knows the next words will shape two households.
ramayan::1870.insight: It frames marriage as a public bond between families, not just a private choice.

ramayan::1871.verse_hindi: Bestowed with youth and beauty, these sons of Dasaratha resemble kings in defending the worlds and gods in valour.
ramayan::1871.english_translation: These are the sons of Dasaratha, radiant with youth and beauty, and mighty like guardians of the worlds and divine beings.
ramayan::1871.translation_literal: पुत्रा (sons) / दशरथस्य (of Dasaratha) / इमे (these) / रूपयौवनशालिनः (endowed with beauty and youth) / लोकपालोपमाः (like guardians of the worlds) / सर्वे (all) / देवतुल्यपराक्रमाः (having valor equal to divine beings)
ramayan::1871.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1871.essence: Their appearance and valor make the alliance fitting.
ramayan::1871.simple_meaning: Janaka's visitors praise Rama, Lakshmana, Bharata, and Shatrughna as handsome, youthful, and extraordinarily brave sons of Dasaratha.
ramayan::1871.simple_insight: Greatness can be seen before it is proven.
ramayan::1871.detailed_meaning: Janaka's court is weighing the marriage alliance. After the earlier proposal, the envoys now praise Dasaratha's four sons: their beauty, youth, and unmatched courage. It is admiration that supports the negotiation, not a teaching in itself.
ramayan::1871.modern_relevance: A parent hears strangers describe your child as capable, graceful, and strong. The words matter because they signal not just appearance, but the kind of life ahead.
ramayan::1871.insight: It adds honor to the match by presenting the princes as worthy in both form and force.

ramayan::1872.verse_sanskrit: उभयोरपि राजेन्द्र सम्बन्धेनानुबध्यताम् । इक्ष्वाको: कुलमव्यग्रं भवत:पुण्यकर्मण: । । 1728 । ।
ramayan::1872.verse_hindi: O King of kings (Janaka) the bond between your race with its pious deeds and the Ikshvakus  may be strenghthened by this alliance.
ramayan::1872.english_translation: O King of kings, let the bond between your line of pious deeds and the Ikshvaku line be strengthened through this alliance.
ramayan::1872.translation_literal: उभयोः (of both) / अपि (also) / राजेन्द्र (O king of kings) / सम्बन्धेन (by relationship) / अनुबध्यताम् (let it be bound together, strengthened) / इक्ष्वाकोः (of the Ikshvaku line) / कुलम् (lineage) / अव्यग्रम् (untroubled, steady) / भवतः (of your) / पुण्य-कर्मणः (of one with pious deeds)
ramayan::1872.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1872.essence: A good alliance strengthens both sides, not just the couple.
ramayan::1872.simple_meaning: The speaker asks that the marriage join two noble families and strengthen their shared bond.
ramayan::1872.simple_insight: Some unions are not just personal; they can steady whole families and traditions.
ramayan::1872.detailed_meaning: At Janaka’s court, the marriage negotiations for Rama and his brothers are moving toward completion. The speaker asks that the alliance do more than unite two households: let it strengthen the bond between Janaka’s righteous line and the Ikshvaku line.
ramayan::1872.modern_relevance: A family dinner turns into a careful conversation about a marriage, a business partnership, or a shared future. Everyone knows this is bigger than two people — the decision will tie together two worlds.
ramayan::1872.insight: It shifts attention from private gain to the long-term quality of the bond being formed.

ramayan::1873.verse_sanskrit: विश्वामित्रवच श्शृत्वा वसिष्ठस्य मते तदा । जनक: प्रांजलिर्वाक्यमुवाच मुनिपुङ्गवौ । । 1729 । ।
ramayan::1873.verse_hindi: Having heard the words of Viswamitra which echoed the wish of Vasishta, Janaka replied to the eminent ascetics with folded palms.
ramayan::1873.english_translation: Having heard the words of Viswamitra which echoed the wish of Vasishta, Janaka replied to the eminent ascetics with folded palms.
ramayan::1873.translation_literal: विश्वामित्रवचः (the words of Vishwamitra) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / वसिष्ठस्य (of Vasishta) / मते (in the wish) / तदा (then) / जनकः (Janaka) / प्राञ्जलिः (with folded palms) / वाक्यम् (speech) / उवाच (spoke) / मुनिपुङ्गवौ (to the eminent ascetics)
ramayan::1873.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1873.essence: Respectful listening can carry a decision forward.
ramayan::1873.simple_meaning: Janaka hears the sages' proposal and responds respectfully with folded hands.
ramayan::1873.simple_insight: Respect can open the door before agreement does.
ramayan::1873.detailed_meaning: In Mithila, the marriage alliance between Rama and Sita is being arranged. Janaka hears Vishwamitra speak in the spirit of Vasishta's approval and answers the two great sages with folded palms. The verse is a courteous transition, not the main decision itself.
ramayan::1873.modern_relevance: You hear a proposal that carries weight beyond the room. Before you answer, you pause, respect the people speaking, and let the moment settle.
ramayan::1873.insight: It shows that dignity begins with how you receive a serious request.

ramayan::1874.verse_sanskrit: कुलं धन्यमिदं मन्ये येषां नो मुनिपुङ्गवौ । सदृशं कुलसम्बन्धं यदाज्ञापयथ: स्वयम् । । 17210 । ।
ramayan::1874.verse_hindi: Since both of you, eminent ascetics, recomended this befitting alliance of the two races on your own, I regard my race as blessed.
ramayan::1874.english_translation: Since both of you, eminent ascetics, recommended this fitting alliance of the two races on your own, I regard my race as blessed.
ramayan::1874.translation_literal: कुलं (race/family line) / धन्यम् (blessed) / इदम् (this) / मन्ये (I consider) / येषाम् (whose) / नः (our) / मुनिपुङ्गवौ (two eminent ascetics) / सदृशम् (fitting) / कुलसम्बन्धम् (family alliance) / यत् (which) / आज्ञापयथः (you two command/recommend) / स्वयम् (yourself/your own accord)
ramayan::1874.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1874.essence: A marriage becomes blessed when the right people freely endorse it.
ramayan::1874.simple_meaning: Janaka says his family is blessed because the two sages themselves have recommended the match between the two royal houses.
ramayan::1874.simple_insight: A wise blessing can turn a marriage into something larger than a contract.
ramayan::1874.detailed_meaning: At Janaka’s court, Vishvamitra and Vasishta have just endorsed the alliance between Rama’s line and Janaka’s house. Hearing their agreement, Janaka responds with folded hands, treating the match as a blessing on both families.
ramayan::1874.modern_relevance: When two families meet over a marriage and everyone is quietly searching for signs of fit, a respected elder’s approval can settle the room.
ramayan::1874.insight: It frames marriage as a union sanctified by wise consent, not mere arrangement.

ramayan::1875.verse_sanskrit: एवं भवतु भद्रं व: कुशध्वजसुते इमे । पत्न्यौ भजेतां सहितौ शत्रुघ्नभरतावुभौ । । 17211 । ।
ramayan::1875.verse_hindi: Let it be so, Be blessed Let these two daughters of Kusadhwaja (Mandavi and Srutakirti) be the wives of Satrughna and Bharata respectively and serve them.
ramayan::1875.english_translation: So let it be, may all be well with you. Let these two daughters of Kusadhwaja, Mandavi and Srutakirti, become the wives of Bharata and Shatrughna and live with them.
ramayan::1875.translation_literal: एवम् (so) / भवतु (let it be) / भद्रम् (well-being) / वः (to you) / कुशध्वजसुते (the two daughters of Kusadhwaja) / इमे (these) / पत्न्यौ (two wives) / भजेताम् (may they serve / live with) / सहितौ (together) / शत्रुघ्नभरतौ (Shatrughna and Bharata) / उभौ (both)
ramayan::1875.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1875.simple_meaning: Janaka agrees that Mandavi and Srutakirti should marry Bharata and Shatrughna. It is a formal acceptance of the alliance between the two royal families.
ramayan::1875.simple_insight: Some blessings are also commitments. A family bond becomes real the moment it is spoken aloud.
ramayan::1875.detailed_meaning: Janaka has heard the sages' approval and now gives his consent. In the royal court, the marriage alliance is fixed: the daughters of Kusadhwaja will join Bharata and Shatrughna. This is the moment the agreement becomes public and binding.
ramayan::1875.modern_relevance: You can feel a conversation turn irreversible when the final yes is spoken. A family dinner, a business deal, a wedding plan — one clear consent changes everything.
ramayan::1875.insight: It turns private agreement into public commitment, making the alliance real and binding.

ramayan::1876.verse_sanskrit: एकाह्ना राजपुत्रीणां चतसृणां महामुने । पाणीन् गृह्णन्तु चत्वारो राजपुत्रा महाबला: । । 17212 । ।
ramayan::1876.verse_hindi: O Great ascetic let the valiant four princes take the hands of four princesses on the same day.
ramayan::1876.english_translation: O great ascetic, let the four mighty princes take the hands of the four princesses on the same day.
ramayan::1876.translation_literal: एकाह्ना (on the same day) / राजपुत्रीणां (of the princesses) / चतसृणां (of the four) / महामुने (O great ascetic) / पाणीन् (hands) / गृह्णन्तु (let them take) / चत्वारः (four) / राजपुत्राः (princes) / महाबलाः (mighty)
ramayan::1876.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1876.essence: The alliance is ready; now it must be sealed at once.
ramayan::1876.simple_meaning: Janaka asks that all four princes marry all four princesses on the same day.
ramayan::1876.simple_insight: A long-awaited match is ready to be sealed without delay.
ramayan::1876.detailed_meaning: At Janaka’s court, Vishwamitra and the sages have approved the alliance. Janaka now asks that Rama, Lakshmana, Bharata, and Shatrughna all wed Sita, Urmila, Mandavi, and Shrutakirti together, making the royal union complete in one decisive moment.
ramayan::1876.modern_relevance: A family group chat finally settles the wedding date after months of waiting. Everyone who matters has agreed, and now the only thing left is to make the commitment real.
ramayan::1876.insight: It shifts the mind from hesitation to formal commitment.

ramayan::1877.verse_sanskrit: उत्तरे दिवसे ब्रह्मन् फल्गुनीभ्यां मनीषिण: । वैवाहिकं प्रशंसन्ति भगो यत्र प्रजापति: । । 17213 । ।
ramayan::1877.verse_hindi: The wise, O Brahmin think the marriage is favourable when Bhaga is Prajapati on the succeeding day of the ascent of the two stars. (that is, when poorva is followed by uttara phalguni).
ramayan::1877.english_translation: The wise, O Brahmin, consider marriage auspicious on the next day after the rise of the two Phalguni stars, when Bhaga is the presiding force of Prajapati.
ramayan::1877.translation_literal: उत्तरे (later / succeeding) / दिवसे (on the day) / ब्रह्मन् (O Brahmin) / फल्गुनीभ्यां (from the two Phalguni stars) / मनीषिणः (the wise) / वैवाहिकं (marriage-related / auspicious for marriage) / प्रशंसन्ति (praise / consider auspicious) / भगः (Bhaga) / यत्र (where / when) / प्रजापतिः (Prajapati)
ramayan::1877.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1877.essence: The marriage is being placed within an auspicious cosmic order.
ramayan::1877.simple_meaning: Janaka is speaking about an auspicious marriage timing based on the stars.
ramayan::1877.simple_insight: Even sacred occasions were guided by careful timing and shared understanding.
ramayan::1877.detailed_meaning: Janaka is in the middle of arranging the four royal marriages with the sages' approval. Before the ceremony moves forward, he refers to the proper astrological day, showing that the union is being set within formal, auspicious order.
ramayan::1877.modern_relevance: You do not rush a moment that will reshape two families. Before the ceremony, the date itself must feel right.
ramayan::1877.insight: It shows how important transitions were marked by order, timing, and collective assent.

ramayan::1878.verse_sanskrit: एवमुक्त्वा वचस्सौम्यं प्रत्युत्थाय कृताञ्जलि: । उभौ मुनिवरौ राजा जनको वाक्यमब्रवीत् । । 17214 । ।
ramayan::1878.verse_hindi: King Janaka, having spoken these pleasing words, stood up and with folded hands  addressing both the great ascetics:
ramayan::1878.english_translation: Having spoken these gentle words, King Janaka rose and, with folded hands, addressed both great sages.
ramayan::1878.translation_literal: एवमुक्त्वा (having spoken thus) / वचस्सौम्यं (gentle words) / प्रत्युत्थाय (having risen) / कृताञ्जलि: (with folded hands) / उभौ (both) / मुनिवरौ (great sages) / राजा जनकः (King Janaka) / वाक्यम् (speech) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::1878.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1878.essence: Humility begins when power bows before wisdom.
ramayan::1878.simple_meaning: Janaka rises respectfully, folds his hands, and speaks to the two sages after offering kind words.
ramayan::1878.simple_insight: Respect is shown in posture as much as in speech.
ramayan::1878.detailed_meaning: Janaka has just received the sages' guidance on the marriage timing. Instead of remaining seated as a king might, he rises, folds his hands, and turns toward both ascetics with humility. The verse sets up his grateful response in the next line.
ramayan::1878.modern_relevance: You’ve just heard advice that matters, and you stop talking long enough to stand up and listen properly.
ramayan::1878.insight: It models gratitude through body language, not just words.

ramayan::1879.verse_sanskrit: परो धर्म: कृतो मह्यं शिष्योऽस्मिभवतो सदा । इमान्यासनमुख्यानि आसातां मुनिपुङ्गवौ । । 17215 । ।
ramayan::1879.verse_hindi: You have earned me a great religious merit. I shall be always your disciple O Eminent ascestics, occupy these important seats.
ramayan::1879.english_translation: You have earned me great merit. I will always be your disciple, eminent sages. Please sit on these honoured seats.
ramayan::1879.translation_literal: परः (great) / धर्मः (merit, righteousness) / कृतः (done, earned) / मह्यम् (for me) / शिष्यः (disciple) / अस्मि (I am) / भवतः (of you) / सदा (always) / इमानि (these) / आसन-मुख्यानि (chief seats) / आसाताम् (may they be seated) / मुनि-पुङ्गवौ (O eminent sages)
ramayan::1879.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1879.essence: Real honour begins when ego gives way to reverence.
ramayan::1879.simple_meaning: Janaka bows to the two sages, calls himself their disciple, and asks them to sit on the best seats.
ramayan::1879.simple_insight: Respect deepens when pride steps aside first.
ramayan::1879.detailed_meaning: Janaka has welcomed the two sages with honour and now rises with folded hands. He openly places himself below them, calling himself their disciple and offering them the best seats. The verse continues the formal, reverent reception before the marriage discussion.
ramayan::1879.modern_relevance: You meet someone who knows more than you do, and your first move is not to perform. You listen, lower yourself, and make room for their wisdom.
ramayan::1879.insight: It teaches you to honour true learning through humility, not just words.

ramayan::1880.verse_sanskrit: यथा दशरथस्येयं तथाऽयोध्या पुरी मम । प्रभुत्वे नास्ति सन्देहो यथार्हं कर्तुमर्हथ । । 17216 । ।
ramayan::1880.verse_hindi: Dasaratha has right on the city of Ayodhya as much as I have on this. This right is unquestionable. So do whatever you think right.
ramayan::1880.english_translation: Dasaratha has as much right to this city of Ayodhya as I do. There is no doubt about it. So please do whatever you think is proper.
ramayan::1880.translation_literal: यथा (as) / दशरथस्य (of Dasharatha) / इयम् (this) / तथा (so) / अयोध्या पुरी (the city of Ayodhya) / मम (of mine) / प्रभुत्वे (in authority) / न अस्ति (there is not) / सन्देहः (doubt) / यथार्हम् (as proper) / कर्तुम् (to do) / अर्हथ (you ought)
ramayan::1880.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1880.essence: Real authority begins by admitting what is not yours.
ramayan::1880.simple_meaning: Janaka says Ayodhya belongs to Dasharatha, not to him, and asks the sages to act as they see fit.
ramayan::1880.simple_insight: Clear boundaries can carry respect, not conflict.
ramayan::1880.detailed_meaning: Janaka is hosting two great sages and speaking with royal humility. He openly says Ayodhya is Dasharatha's city, not his, and invites the elders to decide the matter properly. The moment shows courtesy, clarity, and restraint.
ramayan::1880.modern_relevance: You are negotiating over a family property, and everyone is quietly testing ownership. Janaka's move is simple: name what is true, drop the ego, and let the right decision stand.
ramayan::1880.insight: It teaches you to acknowledge rightful ownership instead of turning every shared matter into a contest.

ramayan::1881.verse_sanskrit: तथा ब्रुवति वैदेहे जनके रघुनन्दन: । राजा दशरथो हृष्ट: प्रत्युवाच महीपतिम् । । 17217 । ।
ramayan::1881.verse_hindi: To the words of Janaka, king of Videha, king Dasaratha, the descendant of Raghu cheerfully replied:
ramayan::1881.english_translation: As Janaka of Videha spoke, the joyful king Dasharatha replied to the ruler.
ramayan::1881.translation_literal: तथा (thus) / ब्रुवति (speaking) / वैदेहे (to Janaka of Videha) / जनके (Janaka) / रघुनन्दनः (Raghunanda, Dasharatha) / राजा (king) / दशरथः (Dasharatha) / हृष्टः (delighted) / प्रत्युवाच (replied) / महीपतिम् (to the ruler)
ramayan::1881.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1881.essence: Joyful reply turns a formal exchange into shared trust.
ramayan::1881.simple_meaning: Dasharatha responds happily to Janaka after Janaka’s words.
ramayan::1881.simple_insight: A respectful exchange can carry the weight of a turning moment.
ramayan::1881.detailed_meaning: In Mithila, Janaka has just spoken about the marriage arrangement and the rights of Ayodhya and Mithila. Dasharatha answers with delight, showing relief and approval before the dialogue moves on to praise both princes and their kingdoms.
ramayan::1881.modern_relevance: A tense family conversation finally softens when someone answers with warmth instead of defensiveness. That small shift can open the whole room.
ramayan::1881.insight: It marks a pause in negotiation where goodwill replaces strain.

ramayan::1882.verse_sanskrit: युवामसङ्ख्येयगुणौ भ्रातरौ मिथिलेश्वरौ । ऋषयो राजसङ्घाश्च भवद्भ्यामभिपूजिता: । । 17218 । ।
ramayan::1882.verse_hindi: You both brothers are lords of Mithila. You possess countless virtues. You pay regards to  many rishis and hosts of kings.
ramayan::1882.english_translation: You are both the twin lords of Mithila, endowed with countless virtues. Rishis and hosts of kings honour you both.
ramayan::1882.translation_literal: युवाम् (you two) / असङ्ख्येय-गुणौ (possessing countless virtues) / भ्रातरौ (the two brothers) / मिथिलेश्वरौ (the lords of Mithila) / ऋषयः (rishis) / राज-सङ्घाः च (and hosts of kings) / भवद्भ्याम् (by you two) / अभिपूजिताः (honoured, reverenced)
ramayan::1882.speaker: Dasaratha
ramayan::1882.essence: Real merit draws honour before it asks for it.
ramayan::1882.simple_meaning: Dasaratha praises the two brothers as noble rulers of Mithila, rich in virtues and respected by sages and kings.
ramayan::1882.simple_insight: Respect grows naturally where character is already visible.
ramayan::1882.detailed_meaning: After Janaka speaks, Dasaratha responds with warm approval. He praises the two Mithila princes, their many virtues, and the honour they already receive from sages and kings. The verse is part of a courteous exchange, not a separate teaching.
ramayan::1882.modern_relevance: At a family gathering, someone introduces two people who have quietly earned everyone’s respect. The praise feels deserved because their conduct has already spoken for them.
ramayan::1882.insight: It shows how true worth is recognised through conduct, not claims.

ramayan::1883.verse_sanskrit: स्वस्ति प्राप्नुहि भद्रं ते गमिष्यामि स्वमालयम् । श्राद्धकर्माणि सर्वाणि विधास्यामीति चाब्रवीत् । । 17219 । ।
ramayan::1883.verse_hindi: Be safe. Be blessed. Let me retire to the camp. I have to perform the rites offerings to the forefathers.
ramayan::1883.english_translation: Be safe. Be blessed. Let me return to my camp. I must perform the rites for the ancestors.
ramayan::1883.translation_literal: स्वस्ति (may you be well) / प्राप्नुहि (obtain) / भद्रम् (auspiciousness) / ते (to you) / गमिष्यामि (I will go) / स्वम् (own) / आलयम् (dwelling, camp) / श्राद्ध-कर्माणि (ancestral rites) / सर्वाणि (all) / विधास्यामि (I will perform) / इति (thus) / च (and) / अब्रवीत् (said)
ramayan::1883.speaker: Dasaratha
ramayan::1883.essence: Courtesy does not cancel the duties waiting after the conversation ends.
ramayan::1883.simple_meaning: Dasharatha politely takes leave, blesses Janaka, and says he must return to his camp to perform ancestral rites.
ramayan::1883.simple_insight: Even kings pause for duty before the next step.
ramayan::1883.detailed_meaning: After Janaka and Dasharatha exchange honors, Dasharatha ends the meeting respectfully. He blesses Janaka, then says he will return to his own camp because the ancestral rites still await him. The verse simply marks the formal close of the exchange.
ramayan::1883.modern_relevance: You finish a long visit, smile at the host, and still have one more responsibility waiting at home. Grace includes leaving at the right time.
ramayan::1883.insight: It shows that respect and obligation can coexist in the same clean departure.

ramayan::1884.verse_sanskrit: तमापृष्ट्वा नरपतिं राजा दशरथस्तदा । मुनीन्द्रौ तौ पुरस्कृत्य जगामाशु महायशा: । । 17220 । ।
ramayan::1884.verse_hindi: Then renowned king Dasaratha, took leave of the two great ascetics. Then the rowned king Dasaratha took have of the king (Janaka) immediately following the two great ascetics.
ramayan::1884.english_translation: Then the renowned king Dasharatha took leave of the two great ascetics and quickly departed, with them leading the way.
ramayan::1884.translation_literal: तम् (him) / आपृष्ट्वा (having taken leave) / नरपतिम् (of the king) / राजा (the king) / दशरथः (Dasharatha) / तदा (then) / मुनीन्द्रौ (the two great ascetics) / तौ (those two) / पुरस्कृत्य (placing in front, leading) / जगाम (went) / आशु (quickly) / महायशाः (the greatly renowned one)
ramayan::1884.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1884.essence: Respectful departure leads straight into duty.
ramayan::1884.simple_meaning: Dasharatha respectfully takes leave of Janaka and departs right away, following the two great sages.
ramayan::1884.simple_insight: Even kings move on when the moment has ended.
ramayan::1884.detailed_meaning: After the meeting with Janaka and the sages, Dasharatha does not linger. He offers respect, follows the elders, and leaves at once. The verse simply moves the scene forward toward the ancestral rites he must now perform.
ramayan::1884.modern_relevance: You finish the meeting, say goodbye properly, and leave without dragging the moment out. Some duties begin only after the conversation ends.
ramayan::1884.insight: It shifts attention from the exchange itself to the next required action.

ramayan::1885.verse_sanskrit: स गत्वा निलयं राजा श्राद्धं कृत्वा विधानत: । प्रभाते काल्यमुत्थाय चक्रे गोदानमुत्तमम् । । 17221 । ।
ramayan::1885.verse_hindi: The king (Dasaratha) reached the abode, performed the sharaddha ceremony in accordance with the scriptures. Next day at dawn at appropriate time he gifted away cows (a ceremony performed by initiating the bridegrooms into the marriage.)
ramayan::1885.english_translation: The king returned home, performed the funeral rites properly, and at dawn gave away auspicious cows.
ramayan::1885.translation_literal: स (he) / गत्वा (having gone) / निलयं (to the abode) / राजा (the king) / श्राद्धं (funeral rites) / कृत्वा (having done) / विधानत: (according to proper procedure) / प्रभाते (at dawn) / काल्यं (at the proper time) / उत्थाय (having risen) / चक्रे (did) / गोदानम् (cow-gift) / उत्तमम् (excellent)
ramayan::1885.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1885.essence: Grief does not cancel duty; it sharpens it.
ramayan::1885.simple_meaning: Dasaratha returned home, completed the funeral rites correctly, and then rose early to give away cows as a ritual gift.
ramayan::1885.simple_insight: Even grief is met with order here: duty continues, step by step.
ramayan::1885.detailed_meaning: After leaving the sages, Dasaratha returns to his residence and performs the prescribed rites for the ancestors. At dawn he rises again and completes the cow-gift ceremony, showing the king still bound by ritual duty even in a sorrowful moment.
ramayan::1885.modern_relevance: You barely slept after the funeral, but the next morning still demanded paperwork, calls, and arrangements. Some duties do not pause for grief.
ramayan::1885.insight: It shows how ritual obligation continues even after loss, without letting emotion dissolve responsibility.

ramayan::1886.verse_sanskrit: गवां शतसहस्राणि ब्राह्मणेभ्यो नराधिप: । एकैकशो ददौ राजा पुत्रानुद्दिश्य धर्मत: । । 17222 । ।
ramayan::1886.verse_hindi: For the welfare of each of his sons the king (Dasaratha) religiously gave away a hundred thousand cows to brahmins.
ramayan::1886.english_translation: For the welfare of each of his sons, the king gave away a hundred thousand cows to the brahmins, acting according to dharma.
ramayan::1886.translation_literal: गवां (of cows) / शतसहस्राणि (hundred-thousands) / ब्राह्मणेभ्यः (to the brahmins) / नराधिपः (the king) / एकैकशः (for each one individually) / ददौ (gave) / राजा (the king) / पुत्रानुद्दिश्य (for the sake of his sons) / धर्मतः (according to dharma)
ramayan::1886.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1886.essence: His love takes the form of ritual giving.
ramayan::1886.simple_meaning: Dasaratha gives lavish gifts to brahmins for each of his sons, following ritual duty.
ramayan::1886.simple_insight: Love can become offering, not just sentiment.
ramayan::1886.detailed_meaning: After completing the rites at home, King Dasaratha gives immense gifts to brahmins for each of his sons. The verse is part of a ritual sequence, showing royal generosity and paternal concern rather than a separate teaching.
ramayan::1886.modern_relevance: After your child’s exam, you quietly pay for the teacher’s help and a meal for the family. Care often shows up as what you give, not what you say.
ramayan::1886.insight: It shows how a parent can turn affection into concrete generosity.

ramayan::1887.verse_sanskrit: सुवर्णश्रुङ्गा स्सम्पन्ना स्सवत्सा: कांस्यदोहना: । गवां शतसहस्राणि चत्वारि पुरुषर्षभ: । । 17223 । । वित्तमन्यच्च सुबहुद्विजेभ्यो रघुनन्दन: । ददौ गोदानमुद्दिश्य पुत्राणां पुत्रवत्सल: । । 17224 । ।
ramayan::1887.verse_hindi: Great among men and affectionate towards his children, (king Dasaratha), the delight of the Raghus donated in the name of his sons donates to the brahmins four hundred thousand cows. They were capable of abundance of milk. Their horns were plaited with gold. They were accompanied by calves. With them were given away bellmetal vessels for keeping milk and innumerable valuables.
ramayan::1887.english_translation: Great among men and affectionate towards his children, king Dasaratha, the delight of the Raghus, donated four hundred thousand cows to the brahmins in the name of his sons. The cows were rich in milk, had horns plated with gold, and came with calves. Along with them, he gave bellmetal vessels for storing milk and many other valuables.
ramayan::1887.translation_literal: सुवर्णश्रुङ्गा: (with golden horns) / सम्पन्ना: (well-endowed) / सवत्सा: (with calves) / कांस्यदोहना: (with bellmetal milk-vessels) / गवां शतसहस्राणि (hundred-thousands of cows) / चत्वारि (four) / पुरुषर्षभ: (bull among men) / वित्तम् (wealth) / अन्यत् (other) / च (and) / सुबहु (very much) / द्विजेभ्य: (to brahmins) / रघुनन्दन: (delight of the Raghus) / ददौ (gave) / गोदानम् (cow-gift) / उद्दिश्य (for the sake of) / पुत्राणाम् (of sons) / पुत्रवत्सल: (fond of his children)
ramayan::1887.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1887.essence: His affection becomes visible through extravagant giving.
ramayan::1887.simple_meaning: Dasaratha gives immense wealth and four hundred thousand cows to brahmins, dedicating the gift to his sons.
ramayan::1887.simple_insight: Love can take the form of costly giving, not just feeling.
ramayan::1887.detailed_meaning: After performing the funeral rites, Dasaratha rises at dawn and gives away vast wealth for the sake of his sons. The scene is not a teaching but a royal act of generosity, showing a father trying to secure blessing through sacrifice.
ramayan::1887.modern_relevance: You pay for a child’s school trip, a medical bill, a future you may never see. The love is real because it costs you something now.
ramayan::1887.insight: It shows love as concrete support: giving resources now to honor and protect the next generation.

ramayan::1888.verse_sanskrit: स सुतै: कृतगोदानैर्वृतस्तु नृपतिस्तदा । लोकपालैरिवाभाति वृत: स्सौम्य: प्रजापति: । । 17225 । ।
ramayan::1888.verse_hindi: With his sons for whose sake cows have been given away the cheerful king looked like  shining Prajapati surrrounded by the guardians of the world.
ramayan::1888.english_translation: Surrounded by his sons, for whom the cows had been gifted, the cheerful king shone like Prajapati surrounded by the guardians of the world.
ramayan::1888.translation_literal: स (that) / सुतैः (with sons) / कृतगोदानैः (by the performed cow-gifts) / वृतः (surrounded) / तु (indeed) / नृपतिः (the king) / तदा (then) / लोकपालैः (by the guardians of the world) / इव (like) / आभाति (shone) / वृतः (surrounded) / सौम्यः (cheerful/gentle) / प्रजापतिः (Prajapati)
ramayan::1888.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1888.essence: A king's generosity can make his family look almost cosmic.
ramayan::1888.simple_meaning: Dasaratha stood with his sons after giving away cows for them, and he looked radiant and honored, like a cosmic ruler surrounded by protectors.
ramayan::1888.simple_insight: A generous act can make a family feel larger than life.
ramayan::1888.detailed_meaning: Dasaratha has just completed grand gifts of cows in his sons' names. The court sees him standing among his sons, bright and satisfied, like Prajapati ringed by the guardians of the world. It is a ceremonial image, not a teaching verse.
ramayan::1888.modern_relevance: A father at a school prize ceremony beams while his children stand beside him. The moment matters less for the applause than for the quiet pride of having provided well.
ramayan::1888.insight: It shifts attention from doctrine to scene: a king's generosity is shown through public splendor.
