ramayan::1889.verse_sanskrit: यस्मिंस्तु दिवसे राजा चक्रे गोदानमुत्तमम् । तस्मिं स्तु दिवसे शूरो युधाजित्समुपेयिवान् । । 1731 । ।
ramayan::1889.verse_hindi: The day the king (Dasaratha) made a gift of the best (available) cows the heroic Yudhajit arrived.
ramayan::1889.english_translation: The day the king (Dasaratha) made a gift of the best cows, the heroic Yudhajit arrived.
ramayan::1889.translation_literal: यस्मिन् (on which) / तु (indeed) / दिवसे (day) / राजा (king) / चक्रे (made) / गोदानम् (gift of cows) / उत्तमम् (best) / तस्मिन् (on that) / तु (indeed) / दिवसे (day) / शूरः (heroic) / युधाजित् (Yudhajit) / समुपेयिवान् (having arrived)
ramayan::1889.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1889.essence: A royal gift ceremony and a visitor's arrival happen at the same time.
ramayan::1889.simple_meaning: On the very day Dasaratha made a grand gift of cows, Yudhajit arrived at his court.
ramayan::1889.simple_insight: It is a scene-setting detail, marking the timing of Yudhajit's arrival.
ramayan::1889.detailed_meaning: Dasaratha is in the middle of a royal gift ceremony, surrounded by the wealth and dignity of his court. On that same day, Yudhajit, the brave son of the Kekaya king and Bharata's maternal uncle, arrives to meet him. The verse simply sets the moment for the next exchange.
ramayan::1889.modern_relevance: You are in the middle of a family celebration when an important visitor arrives unannounced. The moment matters because it shifts the whole conversation, not because it teaches a lesson.
ramayan::1889.insight: It anchors the next event in a specific moment, without adding a moral claim.

ramayan::1890.verse_sanskrit: पुत्र: केकयराजस्य साक्षाद्भरतमातुल: । दृष्ट्वा पृष्ट्वा च कुशलं राजानमिदमब्रवीत् । । 1732 । ।
ramayan::1890.verse_hindi: Yudhajit, son of king Kekaya, Bharatas own maternal uncle met the king (Dasaratha) and enquiring about his wellbeing said:
ramayan::1890.english_translation: Yudhajit, son of King Kekaya and Bharata's own maternal uncle, met the king, asked after his welfare, and said this:
ramayan::1890.translation_literal: पुत्रः (son) / केकयराजस्य (of the king of Kekaya) / साक्षात् (directly) / भरतमातुलः (Bharata's maternal uncle) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / पृष्ट्वा (having asked) / च (and) / कुशलम् (welfare) / राजानम् (the king) / इदम् (this) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::1890.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1890.essence: A polite arrival opens the door to the next turn in the story.
ramayan::1890.simple_meaning: Yudhajit, Bharata's maternal uncle, arrives at Dasaratha's court and greets the king politely.
ramayan::1890.simple_insight: Sometimes the story turns on a simple arrival before anyone has said the real thing.
ramayan::1890.detailed_meaning: At Dasaratha's court, Yudhajit arrives as a messenger from Kekaya and first asks about the king's health. The scene is still in its opening movement; this verse only sets up the conversation that follows.
ramayan::1890.modern_relevance: Someone walks into a room with a careful smile, asking how you are before bringing the reason they came. The real turning point is still one sentence away.
ramayan::1890.insight: It marks a formal entrance and prepares the ground for the message that follows.

ramayan::1891.verse_sanskrit: केकयाधिपती राजा स्नेहात् कुशलमब्रवीत् । येषां कुशलकामोऽसि तेषां सम्प्रत्यनामयम् । । 1733 । ।
ramayan::1891.verse_hindi: My father, king of Kekaya affectionately enquires about your welfare. And they whose
ramayan::1891.english_translation: The king of Kekaya sends affectionate greetings and asks after your well-being; those whose welfare you wish is now secure.
ramayan::1891.translation_literal: केकयाधिपती (the lord of Kekaya) / राजा (king) / स्नेहात् (out of affection) / कुशलम् (well-being) / अब्रवीत् (said) / येषाम् (of whom) / कुशलकामः (wishing welfare) / असि (you are) / तेषाम् (of them) / सम्प्रति (now) / अनामयम् (free from illness / well)
ramayan::1891.speaker: Yudhajit
ramayan::1891.essence: Courtesy comes first; the real purpose follows after trust is softened.
ramayan::1891.simple_meaning: Yudhajit reports that the Kekaya king sends warm greetings and asks about Dasharatha's health.
ramayan::1891.simple_insight: A formal visit begins with care, not business.
ramayan::1891.detailed_meaning: Yudhajit has arrived in Ayodhya as Bharata’s maternal uncle. Before stating his real purpose, he first conveys his father’s affectionate inquiry after Dasharatha’s welfare. The verse is part of a courteous exchange, not the main point of the scene.
ramayan::1891.modern_relevance: You open a difficult conversation by checking on the other person's health first. That small courtesy changes the whole tone before any request is made.
ramayan::1891.insight: It shows how respect and goodwill prepare the ground before a serious message.

ramayan::1892.verse_sanskrit: स्वस्रीयं मम राजेन्द्र द्रष्टुकामो महीपति: । तदर्थमुपयातोऽहमयोध्यां रघुनन्दन । । 1734 । ।
ramayan::1892.verse_hindi: The king of Kekaya, O Indra among kings, O Joy of the Raghus, desires to see my  sisterss son and on that account I went to Ayodhya.
ramayan::1892.english_translation: The king of Kekaya, O best among kings, O delight of the Raghu line, wishes to see his sister's son. For that reason I have come to Ayodhya.
ramayan::1892.translation_literal: स्वस्रीयम् (sister's son) / मम (my) / राजेन्द्र (O best among kings) / द्रष्टुकामः (wishing to see) / महीपतिः (the king) / तदर्थम् (for that reason) / उपयातः (has come) / अहम् (I) / अयोध्याम् (to Ayodhya) / रघुनन्दन (O delight of the Raghu line)
ramayan::1892.speaker: Yudhajit
ramayan::1892.essence: The visit begins as an act of family affection, not politics.
ramayan::1892.simple_meaning: Yudhajit explains that he came to Ayodhya because the king of Kekaya wants to see his sister's son.
ramayan::1892.simple_insight: Sometimes a journey begins with family affection, not duty or drama.
ramayan::1892.detailed_meaning: Yudhajit, Bharata's maternal uncle, is speaking to Dasharatha in Ayodhya. He explains that his king came out of affection, wanting to see his sister's son, and sent him ahead. It is a courteous opening, not the main event.
ramayan::1892.modern_relevance: A relative shows up at your door with a simple reason that is really about love: someone older wants to see the child the family has been talking about.
ramayan::1892.insight: It frames the meeting as family-driven, preparing for the larger purpose that follows.

ramayan::1893.verse_sanskrit: श्रुत्वा त्वहमयोध्यायां विवाहार्थं तवात्मजान् । मिथिलामुपयातांस्तु त्वया सह महीपते । । 1735 । । त्वरयाभ्युपयातोऽहं द्रष्टुकाम स्स्वसुस्सुतम् ।
ramayan::1893.verse_hindi: O King having heard in Ayodhya that you have arrived in Mithila along with your sons for their marriage I came here speedily with a desire to see my sisters son .
ramayan::1893.english_translation: O King, having heard in Ayodhya that you had come to Mithila with your sons for their marriages, I hurried here, eager to see my sister's son.
ramayan::1893.translation_literal: श्रुत्वा (having heard) / त्वहम् (I) / अयोध्यायाम् (in Ayodhya) / विवाहार्थम् (for the purpose of marriage) / तव (your) / आत्मजान् (sons) / मिथिलाम् (to Mithila) / उपयातान् (having come) / तु (indeed) / त्वया सह (with you) / महीपते (O king) / त्वरया (quickly) / अभ्युपयातः (come near) / अहम् (I) / द्रष्टुकामः (desiring to see) / स्वसुः (of my sister) / सुतम् (son)
ramayan::1893.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1893.simple_meaning: He says he came quickly after hearing that Dasaratha had arrived in Mithila with his sons for the weddings, because he wanted to see his nephew.
ramayan::1893.simple_insight: Family affection can pull you across distance before duty even speaks.
ramayan::1893.detailed_meaning: King Janaka is welcoming Dasaratha, who has come to Mithila with Rama and Lakshmana for the marriage of the princesses. Janaka explains that he hurried over from Ayodhya out of affection for his sister's son, setting a warm, familial tone before the formal reception.
ramayan::1893.modern_relevance: You hear your sister's son is in town for a major family event, and you drop everything to see him before the day gets busy.
ramayan::1893.insight: It highlights how affection can move someone faster than obligation.

ramayan::1894.verse_sanskrit: अथ राजा दशरथ: प्रियातिथिमुपस्थितम् । । 1736 । । दृष्ट्वा परमसत्कारै: पूजार्हं समपूजयत् ।
ramayan::1894.verse_hindi: King Dasaratha, then accorded a warm welcome to the honoured guest.
ramayan::1894.english_translation: Then King Dasharatha, seeing the honoured guest who had arrived, welcomed him with great hospitality and full respect.
ramayan::1894.translation_literal: अथ (then) / राजा दशरथः (King Dasharatha) / प्रियातिथिम् (the dear guest) / उपस्थितम् (who had arrived) / दृष्ट्वा (seeing) / परमसत्कारैः (with great hospitality) / पूजार्हम् (one worthy of honour) / समपूजयत् (welcomed and honoured fully)
ramayan::1894.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1894.essence: True respect is visible in how you receive a guest.
ramayan::1894.simple_meaning: Dasharatha greets an honoured visitor with full respect and generous hospitality.
ramayan::1894.simple_insight: Respect is shown first in how you receive another person.
ramayan::1894.detailed_meaning: Dasharatha sees the guest who has come to Ayodhya and receives him with the highest honour. The scene is still part of the marriage visit and sets the tone for the evening before the deeper events begin.
ramayan::1894.modern_relevance: A guest arrives after a long drive, and you put the phone down, offer water, and make them feel expected. Small acts of welcome reveal the size of a heart.
ramayan::1894.insight: It shifts attention from status to hospitality, showing honour through action rather than words.

ramayan::1895.verse_sanskrit: ततस्तामुषितो रात्रिं सह पुत्रैर्महात्मभि: । । 1737 । । प्रभाते पुनरुत्थाय कृत्वा कर्माणि कर्मवित् । ऋषींस्तदा पुरस्कृत्य यज्ञवाटमुपागमत् । । 1738 । ।
ramayan::1895.verse_hindi: With the night spent with his virtuous sons, he who knew his duties got up at dawn and performed his daily devotionas and reached the sacrificial place following the  rishis.
ramayan::1895.english_translation: With the night spent with his virtuous sons, he who knew his duties rose at dawn, performed his rites, and then went to the sacrificial ground with the sages.
ramayan::1895.translation_literal: ततस्तामुषितो (then having spent that) / रात्रिं (night) / सह पुत्रैः (with sons) / महात्मभिः (with noble-minded) / प्रभाते (at dawn) / पुनरुत्थाय (rising again) / कृत्वा (having done) / कर्माणि (acts / rites) / कर्मवित् (knower of duties) / ऋषीन् (the sages) / तदा (then) / पुरस्कृत्य (placing in front) / यज्ञवाटम् (to the sacrificial enclosure) / उपागमत् (he approached)
ramayan::1895.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1895.essence: A ruler’s day begins with duty before ceremony.
ramayan::1895.simple_meaning: Dasharatha spent the night with his sons, rose at dawn, completed his morning rites, and went with the sages to the sacrificial area.
ramayan::1895.simple_insight: Ordinary discipline becomes sacred when every step is done with care.
ramayan::1895.detailed_meaning: Dasaratha has welcomed his guest and now follows the rhythm of an ordered royal morning. He spends the night with his noble sons, rises at dawn, performs the required rites, and goes with the sages toward the sacrifice. It is a calm setup before the marriage events begin.
ramayan::1895.modern_relevance: You wake before the house does, wash, pray, and get moving before the day's noise starts. Small acts done faithfully can steady everything that follows.
ramayan::1895.insight: It shows how disciplined routine prepares the mind for larger responsibilities.

ramayan::1896.verse_sanskrit: युक्ते मुहूर्ते विजये सर्वाभरणभूषितै: । भ्रातृभिस्सहितो राम: कृतकौतुकमंगल: । । 1739 । । वसिष्ठं पुरत: कृत्वा महर्षीनपरानपि । पितु स्समीपमाश्रित्य तस्थौ भ्रातृभिरावृत: । । 17310 । ।
ramayan::1896.verse_hindi: With the necessary auspicious rites preparatory to marriage performed at an auspicious moment, Vijaya, and keeping Vasishta and other maharshis in the forefront,  Rama accompanied by his brothers adorned with ornaments of every kind came into his  fathers presence.
ramayan::1896.english_translation: At the proper auspicious moment, Rama, adorned with every ornament and accompanied by his brothers, performed the marriage rites, placed Vasishta and the other great sages in front, and stood by his father surrounded by his brothers.
ramayan::1896.translation_literal: युक्ते (at the proper) / मुहूर्ते (at the auspicious moment) / विजये (Vijaya) / सर्वाभरणभूषितैः (adorned with all ornaments) / भ्रातृभिः (with brothers) / सहितः (accompanied) / रामः (Rama) / कृतकौतुकमंगलः (having performed the marriage rites and auspicious ceremonies) / वसिष्ठम् (Vasishta) / पुरतः (in front) / कृत्वा (having placed) / महर्षीन् (the great sages) / अपरान् अपि (and others also) / पितुः (of father) / समीपम् (near) / आश्रित्य (having approached) / तस्थौ (stood) / भ्रातृभिः (by brothers) / आवृतः (surrounded)
ramayan::1896.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1896.essence: Preparation and respect come before the great turning point.
ramayan::1896.simple_meaning: Rama arrives for the wedding ceremony with his brothers, fully adorned, and stands respectfully before his father with the sages ahead of him.
ramayan::1896.simple_insight: Some moments are about showing up with full respect, not making a statement.
ramayan::1896.detailed_meaning: The wedding ceremony is underway in Janaka’s court. Rama comes forward with Lakshmana and his brothers, dressed in ornaments, while Vasishta and the sages are placed first. The verse simply frames the ceremonial arrival before the formal exchange begins.
ramayan::1896.modern_relevance: You walk into the hall before the ceremony starts, dressed properly, with the people who guided you standing ahead. The moment is not about display; it is about order, respect, and readiness.
ramayan::1896.insight: It teaches you to honour the setting, the elders, and the rite before your own place in it.

ramayan::1897.verse_sanskrit: वसिष्ठो भगवानेत्य वैदेहमिदमब्रवीत् । राजा दशरथो राजन् कृतकौतुकमङ्गलै: । । 17311 । । पुत्रैर्नरवर श्रेष्ठ दातारमभिकाङ्क्षते ।
ramayan::1897.verse_hindi: Adorable Vasishta approached king Janaka and said, O King, of Videha king Dasaratha, the best of men with his sons having performed the auspicious rites preparatory to marriage is awaiting the bestower of the brides.
ramayan::1897.english_translation: Vasishta approached King Janaka and said, "O King of Videha, King Dasharatha, the best of men, has come with his sons after completing the auspicious marriage rites and is waiting for the bride-giver."
ramayan::1897.translation_literal: वसिष्ठः (Vasishta) / भगवन् (revered one) / एति (approaches) / वैदेहम् (to the king of Videha) / इदम् (this) / अब्रवीत् (said) / राजा (king) / दशरथः (Dasharatha) / राजन् (O king) / कृतकौतुकमङ्गलैः (with the marriage auspicious rites completed) / पुत्रैः (with sons) / नरवरश्रेष्ठ (best of men) / दातारम् (the giver) / अभिकाङ्क्षते (desires / awaits)
ramayan::1897.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1897.essence: The marriage ceremony advances when the giver is expected.
ramayan::1897.simple_meaning: Vasishta tells Janaka that Dasharatha has arrived with his sons after the marriage rites and is waiting for the bride-giver.
ramayan::1897.simple_insight: Big moments often begin with simple announcements and formalities.
ramayan::1897.detailed_meaning: At Janaka’s court, Vasishta steps forward as the marriage preparations are complete. He announces that Dasharatha has arrived with Rama and his brothers, ready for the next formal step. The verse simply moves the ceremony forward.
ramayan::1897.modern_relevance: A hall goes quiet while someone makes the formal announcement that the guests have arrived. The whole room shifts, but nothing deep is being argued yet — the ceremony is just moving to its next step.
ramayan::1897.insight: It keeps the scene moving by marking the transition from preparation to exchange.

ramayan::1898.verse_sanskrit: दातृप्रतिग्रहीतृभ्यां सर्वार्था: प्रभवन्ति हि । । 17312 । । स्वधर्मं प्रतिपद्यस्व कृत्वा वैवाह्यमुत्तमम् ।
ramayan::1898.verse_hindi: The giver and the receiver, indeed, attain all ends. Fulfil  your own duty by performing the auspicious marriage.
ramayan::1898.english_translation: The giver and the receiver, indeed, attain all ends. Fulfil your own duty by performing the auspicious marriage.
ramayan::1898.translation_literal: दातृ (giver) / प्रतिग्रहीतृभ्यां (for the receiver and giver) / सर्वार्थाः (all aims) / प्रभवन्ति (arise, become possible) / हि (indeed) / स्वधर्मम् (one's own duty) / प्रतिपद्यस्व (undertake, fulfil) / कृत्वा (having done) / वैवाह्यम् (marriage-related) / उत्तमम् (excellent, auspicious)
ramayan::1898.speaker: Vasishta
ramayan::1898.essence: Giving and receiving only matter when you finish your own duty.
ramayan::1898.simple_meaning: When both sides give and receive rightly, every purpose can be fulfilled. Janaka is told to complete the marriage by doing his own duty.
ramayan::1898.simple_insight: Right action creates completion on both sides, not just for the one who acts.
ramayan::1898.detailed_meaning: Vasishta has come to Janaka with Rama and his brothers after the wedding preparations. In this formal moment, he reminds the king that when giving and receiving are done properly, all aims are served — now Janaka must complete his own duty by finalising the auspicious marriage.
ramayan::1898.modern_relevance: You’ve done the introductions, the messages, the careful planning, and the family has agreed. The last step is not hesitation — it’s fulfilling the responsibility that belongs to you.
ramayan::1898.insight: It shifts attention from ceremony as display to ceremony as responsibility completed well.

ramayan::1899.verse_sanskrit: इत्युक्त: परमोदारो वसिष्ठेन महात्मना । । 17313 । । प्रत्युवाच महातेजा वाक्यं परमधर्मवित् ।
ramayan::1899.verse_hindi: Thus addressed by the great self Vasishta, Janaka, the exceedingly generous, highly lustrous, eminent in ethics replied.
ramayan::1899.english_translation: Thus addressed by the great self Vasishta, Janaka, the exceedingly generous, highly lustrous, eminent in ethics replied.
ramayan::1899.translation_literal: इत्युक्तः (thus addressed) / परम-उदारः (exceedingly generous) / वसिष्ठेन (by Vasishta) / महात्मना (by the great self) / प्रत्युवाच (replied) / महा-तेजाः (highly lustrous) / वाक्यम् (speech) / परम-धर्म-विद् (eminent in ethics)
ramayan::1899.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1899.essence: Janaka is about to answer; the argument has not landed yet.
ramayan::1899.simple_meaning: Janaka responds after Vasishta speaks to him, and the verse simply marks the start of his reply.
ramayan::1899.simple_insight: A reply is about to begin, but the teaching has not arrived yet.
ramayan::1899.detailed_meaning: In Janaka’s court, Vasishta has just urged him toward the marriage arrangement. This verse only introduces Janaka’s response; it does not yet reveal the substance of his answer, so it functions as a bridge in the scene.
ramayan::1899.modern_relevance: You can feel the pause before someone answers a serious question. The real meaning comes in the reply that follows, not in the fact that they were addressed.
ramayan::1899.insight: It marks a transition from prompting to response, not a complete teaching.

ramayan::1900.verse_sanskrit: कस्स्थित: प्रतिहारो मे कस्याज्ञा सम्प्रतीक्ष्यते । । 17314 । । स्वगृहे को विचारोऽस्ति यथा राज्यमिदं तव ।
ramayan::1900.verse_hindi: Did any guard prevent you? Whose command are you waiting for? Why do you hesitate to enter into your own house? This kingdom is like your kingdom.
ramayan::1900.english_translation: Who stood as your guard? Whose command are you waiting for? Why hesitate to enter your own house? This kingdom is like your own.
ramayan::1900.translation_literal: कस्स्थित: (who stood as) / प्रतिहारो (guard) / मे (my) / कस्य (whose) / आज्ञा (command) / सम्प्रतीक्ष्यते (is being awaited) / स्वगृहे (in your own house) / को (what) / विचारोऽस्ति (is hesitation) / यथा (as) / राज्यम् (kingdom) / इदम् (this) / तव (your)
ramayan::1900.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1900.essence: What is already granted does not need permission.
ramayan::1900.simple_meaning: Janaka tells Vishvamitra that there is no guard, no order to wait for, and no reason to hesitate. He is welcome to enter freely, as if the place were his own.
ramayan::1900.simple_insight: Sometimes dignity means removing the last excuse for hesitation.
ramayan::1900.detailed_meaning: After the marriage rites, Janaka speaks to Vishvamitra with royal generosity. He says no guard blocks the way and no command is needed. The moment matters because hospitality itself becomes a test of honour.
ramayan::1900.modern_relevance: You keep waiting for permission to start the conversation, send the email, or walk into the room. But the door is open, and the delay is only inside you.
ramayan::1900.insight: It shifts you from self-conscious delay to confident, rightful action.

ramayan::1901.verse_sanskrit: कृतकौतुकसर्वस्वा वेदिमूलमुपागता: । । 17315 । । मम कन्या मुनिश्रेष्ठ दीप्ता वह्नेरिवार्चिष: ।
ramayan::1901.verse_hindi: O Best of ascetics my daughters have performed all the rites relating to marriage. They (now) stand at the foot of the altar shining like the bright flames of fire.
ramayan::1901.english_translation: O best of ascetics, my daughters have completed all the marriage rites. They now stand at the foot of the altar, shining like the bright flames of fire.
ramayan::1901.translation_literal: कृतकौतुकसर्वस्वा (having completed all marriage rites) / वेदिमूलमुपागता: (having come to the foot of the altar) / मम (my) / कन्या (daughters) / मुनिश्रेष्ठ (O best of ascetics) / दीप्ता (shining) / वह्नेरिव (like fire's) / अर्चिष: (flames)
ramayan::1901.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1901.essence: The ceremony is ready; only the final step remains.
ramayan::1901.simple_meaning: Janaka says his daughters have completed the marriage preparations and are standing ready at the altar, radiant and prepared for the ceremony.
ramayan::1901.simple_insight: Some moments are sacred because everyone has arrived ready.
ramayan::1901.detailed_meaning: Janaka speaks to Vishwamitra after the marriage rites are complete. Sita and her sisters stand before the altar, glowing with ceremonial readiness. This verse is part of the formal invitation to proceed, not a teaching in itself.
ramayan::1901.modern_relevance: You have done all the preparation, and everyone is waiting for the next step. The room is ready; the moment has come to begin.
ramayan::1901.insight: It marks the transition from preparation to action, with no more delay.

ramayan::1902.verse_sanskrit: सज्जोऽहं त्वत्प्रतीक्षोऽस्मि वेद्यामस्यां प्रतिष्ठित: । । 17316 । । अविघ्नं कुरुतां राजा किमर्थमवलम्बते ।
ramayan::1902.verse_hindi: Ready at the altar, I have been awaiting you, O King Without hindrance proceed Why delay?.
ramayan::1902.english_translation: I am ready and waiting for you at this altar. Let the king proceed without delay. Why does he hesitate?
ramayan::1902.translation_literal: सज्जोऽहम् (I am ready) / त्वत्प्रतीक्षः (waiting for you) / अस्मि (I am) / वेद्याम् (on the altar) / अस्याम् (this) / प्रतिष्ठितः (placed) / अविघ्नम् (without hindrance) / कुरुताम् (let him do) / राजा (the king) / किमर्थम् (why) / अवलम्बते (does he delay / hesitate)
ramayan::1902.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1902.essence: The moment is ready; hesitation is the only barrier.
ramayan::1902.simple_meaning: Janaka says he is already standing at the marriage altar, ready for the ceremony to begin, and asks why the king is still delaying.
ramayan::1902.simple_insight: Readiness can be wasted by hesitation at the very moment action should begin.
ramayan::1902.detailed_meaning: Janaka is at the marriage pavilion with Sita prepared for the rite. Seeing Dasharatha still outside, he urges him to come forward at once so the ceremony can proceed without obstruction. The verse simply pushes the scene into motion.
ramayan::1902.modern_relevance: You have everything set for the conversation, the meeting, the decision — and someone is still hovering at the door. Sometimes the only thing left is to step in.
ramayan::1902.insight: It shifts attention from preparation to completion: once the moment is ready, delay becomes the real obstacle.

ramayan::1903.verse_sanskrit: तद्वाक्यं जनकेनोक्तं श्रुत्वा दशरथस्तदा । प्रवेशयामास सुतान् सर्वानृषिगणानपि । । 17317 । ।
ramayan::1903.verse_hindi: At the words of Janaka, Dasaratha brought his sons along with the hosts of ascetics and entered the marriage pavilion.
ramayan::1903.english_translation: At Janaka's words, Dasharatha then brought in all his sons and the assembly of sages, and entered the marriage pavilion.
ramayan::1903.translation_literal: तद्वाक्यं (that speech) / जनकेन (by Janaka) / उक्तं (spoken) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / दशरथः (Dasharatha) / तदा (then) / प्रवेशयामास (caused to enter) / सुतान् (his sons) / सर्वान् (all) / ऋषिगणान् (groups of sages) / अपि (also)
ramayan::1903.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1903.essence: The wedding begins when the king finally steps inside.
ramayan::1903.simple_meaning: Dasharatha heard Janaka's invitation and brought his sons and the sages into the marriage pavilion.
ramayan::1903.simple_insight: The moment moves forward through ceremony, not argument.
ramayan::1903.detailed_meaning: Janaka has invited the king of Ayodhya to proceed with the wedding rites. Dasharatha responds by entering the pavilion with all his sons and the gathered sages. The verse simply advances the scene toward Rama and Sita's marriage.
ramayan::1903.modern_relevance: A host calls everyone forward, and the room shifts from waiting to action. Some moments are not about decision anymore — only about stepping into what has already been arranged.
ramayan::1903.insight: It shifts attention from debate to the next required step.

ramayan::1904.verse_sanskrit: ततो राजा विदेहानां वसिष्ठमिदमब्रवीत् । । 17318 । । कारयस्व ऋषे सर्वमृषिभि: सह धार्मिक । रामस्य लोकरामस्य क्रियां वैवाहिकीं विभो । । 17319 । ।
ramayan::1904.verse_hindi: Thereafter the king of the Videhas to Vasishta, O Adherent of righteousness, O Lord O Maharshi perform with the rishis the marriage ceremony of Rama who causes delight to the three worlds.
ramayan::1904.english_translation: Thereafter the king of the Videhas said to Vasishta, "O righteous sage, O lord, perform the marriage rites of Rama, the delight of the three worlds, together with the sages."
ramayan::1904.translation_literal: ततः (thereafter) / राजा (king) / विदेहानाम् (of the Videhas) / वसिष्ठम् (to Vasishta) / इदम् (this) / अब्रवीत् (said) / कारयस्व (cause to be performed) / ऋषे (O sage) / सर्वम् (all) / ऋभिभिः (with the sages) / सह (together) / धार्मिक (righteous one) / रामस्य (of Rama) / लोकरामस्य (of the delight of the worlds) / क्रियाम् (rite) / वैवाहिकीम् (marriage) / विभो (O lord)
ramayan::1904.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1904.essence: The ceremony begins when the right authority gives the word.
ramayan::1904.simple_meaning: Janaka asks Vasishta to conduct Rama’s wedding rites with the assembled sages.
ramayan::1904.simple_insight: Some moments are made sacred by careful order, not by excitement.
ramayan::1904.detailed_meaning: In Janaka’s marriage pavilion, the formal waiting is over. He turns to Vasishta, the priestly authority, and asks him to begin Rama’s wedding rites with the gathered sages. The scene moves from preparation into sacred action.
ramayan::1904.modern_relevance: You have done the planning, gathered the people, and cleared the space. Now the moment only becomes real when someone begins the rite.
ramayan::1904.insight: It shifts attention from anticipation to the exact action that completes a solemn occasion.

ramayan::1905.verse_sanskrit: तथेत्युक्त्वा तु जनकं वसिष्ठो भगवानृषि: । विश्वामित्रं पुरस्कृत्य शतानन्दं च धार्मिकम् । । 17320 । । प्रपामध्ये तु विधिवत्वेदिं कृत्वा महातपा: । अलञ्चकार तां वेदिं गन्धपुष्पै स्समन्तत: । । 17321 । । सुवर्णपालिकाभिश्च छिद्रकुम्भैश्च साङ्कुरै: । अङ्कुराढ्यैश्शरावैश्च धूपपात्रै स्सधूपकै: । । 17322 । । शङ्खपात्रै स्स्रुवै स्स्रुग्भि: पात्रैरर्घ्याभिपूरितै: । लाजपूर्णैश्च पात्रीभिरक्षतैरभिसंस्कृतै: । । 17323 । ।
ramayan::1905.verse_hindi: Venerable and renowned ascetic Vasishta said Be it so.And with Viswamitra and virtuous Satananda in the forefront, an altar was duly improvised in the centre of the sacrificial pavilion. He adorned the altar on all sides  with fragrant flowers, golden ladles, waterpots with holes filled with sprouts, earthen vessels with sprouts, holders of burning fragrant incense conchshaped vessels, sacrificial ladles, bowls filled with with water for arghya and other purposes, vessels with roasted paddy and grains of rice.
ramayan::1905.english_translation: Venerable Vasishta said, "So be it." With Viswamitra and the righteous Satananda in front, the great ascetic duly prepared an altar in the center of the sacrificial pavilion. He adorned it all around with fragrant flowers, golden ladles, perforated water vessels filled with sprouts, earthen bowls with sprouts, incense holders with fragrant smoke, conch-shaped vessels, sacrificial ladles, bowls filled with arghya water, vessels filled with roasted grains, and bowls of sacred rice.
ramayan::1905.translation_literal: तथेत्युक्त्वा (having said "so be it") / तु (indeed) / जनकं (to Janaka) / वसिष्ठः (Vasishta) / भगवान् (venerable) / ऋषिः (sage) / विश्वामित्रं (Viswamitra) / पुरस्कृत्य (placing in front) / शतानन्दं (Satananda) / च (and) / धार्मिकम् (righteous) / प्रपामध्ये (in the center of the pavilion) / तु (indeed) / विधिवत् (according to ritual) / वेदिम् (altar) / कृत्वा (having made) / महातपाः (great ascetic) / अलञ्चकार (adorned) / ताम् (that) / वेदीम् (altar) / गन्धपुष्पैः (with fragrance and flowers) / समन्ततः (all around) / सुवर्णपालिकाभिः (with golden ladles) / च (and) / छिद्रकुम्भैः (with perforated vessels) / च (and) / साङ्कुरैः (with sprouts) / अङ्कुराढ्यैः (filled with sprouts) / शरावैः (with bowls) / च (and) / धूपपात्रैः (with incense vessels) / सधूपकैः (with fragrant smoke) / शङ्खपात्रैः (with conch-shaped vessels) / स्रुवैः (with ladles) / स्रुग्भिः (with sacrificial spoons) / पात्रैः (with vessels) / अर्घ्याभिपूरितैः (filled with arghya) / लाजपूर्णैः (filled with roasted grains) / च (and) / पात्रीभिः (with bowls) / अक्षतैः (with unbroken rice) / अभिसंस्कृतैः (prepared)
ramayan::1905.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1905.essence: Ritual begins by making the space worthy.
ramayan::1905.simple_meaning: Vasishta agrees and prepares the sacrificial altar with ritual items, flowers, incense, water, grains, and sacred vessels.
ramayan::1905.simple_insight: Sacred action begins with careful preparation, not haste.
ramayan::1905.detailed_meaning: Janaka has asked for Rama’s marriage rites to be performed. Vasishta, with Viswamitra and Satananda beside him, quietly arranges the altar in the sacrificial pavilion, surrounding it with ritual objects. The verse is scene-setting before the ceremony begins.
ramayan::1905.modern_relevance: You arrive early to set the room before the ceremony, the meeting, or the farewell. The care you put into the space already shapes what can happen there.
ramayan::1905.insight: It shifts attention from the event itself to the disciplined preparation that makes the event possible.

ramayan::1906.verse_sanskrit: दर्भैस्समैस्समास्तीर्य विधिवन्मन्त्रपूर्वकम् । अग्निमादाय वेद्यां तु विधिमन्त्रपुरस्कृतम् । । 17324 । । जुहावाग्नौ महातेजा वसिष्ठो भगवानृषि: ।
ramayan::1906.verse_hindi: Brilliant and worshipful rishi Vasishta chanted, mantras according to tradition, put the darbha grass of equal proportions around the altar, placed the fire on the altar, recited
ramayan::1906.english_translation: Brilliant and worshipful Vasishta, following the proper ritual and mantras, spread equal darbha grass around the altar, placed the fire on the altar, and offered the oblation into the fire.
ramayan::1906.translation_literal: दर्भैः (with darbha grass) / समैः (equal) / समास्तीर्य (having spread around) / विधिवत् (according to ritual) / मन्त्रपूर्वकम् (with mantras first) / अग्निम् (the fire) / आदाय (having taken) / वेद्याम् (on the altar) / तु (then) / विधिमन्त्रपुरस्कृतम् (preceded by ritual mantras) / जुहाव (he offered into the fire) / अग्नौ (into the fire) / महातेजाः (the brilliant one) / वसिष्ठः (Vasishta) / भगवान् (worshipful) / ऋषिः (sage)
ramayan::1906.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1906.essence: Right action begins by preparing the ground correctly.
ramayan::1906.simple_meaning: Vasishta performs the wedding ritual exactly as prescribed, preparing the altar and offering into the sacred fire.
ramayan::1906.simple_insight: Some moments matter because they are done exactly right.
ramayan::1906.detailed_meaning: Janaka has agreed to begin Sita and Rama’s wedding rites. Vasishta steps forward, lays the ritual grass, prepares the altar, and performs the fire offering. The verse is careful, ceremonial setup rather than the emotional peak.
ramayan::1906.modern_relevance: You set the room, check the list, light the candle, and begin properly because the moment deserves respect.
ramayan::1906.insight: It shifts attention from ceremony as decoration to ceremony as exact preparation.

ramayan::1907.verse_sanskrit: ततस्सीतां समानीय सर्वाभरणभूषिताम् । । 17325 । । समक्षमग्ने स्संस्थाप्य राघवाभिमुखे तदा । अब्रवीज्जनको राजा कौसल्यानन्दवर्धनम् । । 17326 । ।
ramayan::1907.verse_hindi: Thereafter king Janaka brought Sita adorned with various ornaments and placed her in the presence of Agni in front of Rama, the enhancer of the joy of Kausalya. And said:
ramayan::1907.english_translation: Thereafter king Janaka brought Sita, adorned with various ornaments, and placed her before Agni, facing Rama, the delight of Kausalya. Then Janaka said:
ramayan::1907.translation_literal: ततस् (thereafter) / सीताम् (Sita) / समानीय (having brought) / सर्वाभरणभूषिताम् (adorned with all ornaments) / समक्षम् (in front) / अग्नेः (of Agni) / संस्थाप्य (having placed) / राघवाभिमुखे (facing Rama) / तदा (then) / अब्रवीत् (said) / जनकः (Janaka) / राजा (king) / कौसल्यानन्दवर्धनम् (the enhancer of Kausalya's joy)
ramayan::1907.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1907.essence: The ceremony pauses at the edge of a life-changing vow.
ramayan::1907.simple_meaning: Janaka brings Sita forward in full ceremonial form and places her before the sacred fire and Rama, just before speaking the marriage words.
ramayan::1907.simple_insight: Some moments matter because they prepare the heart for a life-changing promise.
ramayan::1907.detailed_meaning: The marriage ritual has reached its decisive moment. Janaka brings Sita forward, richly adorned, and positions her before the sacred fire and in front of Rama. He is about to speak the words that unite them, so this verse serves as the formal lead-in.
ramayan::1907.modern_relevance: You pause before the room goes quiet and the next sentence changes everything. The setup matters because what follows cannot be taken back.
ramayan::1907.insight: It shows the ceremony reaching its threshold, where preparation gives way to binding words.

ramayan::1908.verse_sanskrit: इयं सीता मम सुता सहधर्मचरी तव । प्रतीच्छ चैनां भद्रं ते पाणिं गृह्णीष्व पाणिना । । 17327 । ।
ramayan::1908.verse_hindi: This my daughter Sita will be your partner in performing her rightful duty. Accept her. Farewell. Take her hand into your own.
ramayan::1908.english_translation: This is my daughter Sita, your partner in rightful duty. Accept her. May all be well with you. Take her hand in yours.
ramayan::1908.translation_literal: इयम् (this) / सीता (Sita) / मम (my) / सुता (daughter) / सहधर्मचरी (partner in rightful duty) / तव (your) / प्रतीच्छ (accept) / चैनाम् (her) / भद्रम् (well-being) / ते (to you) / पाणिम् (hand) / गृह्णीष्व (take) / पाणिना (with hand)
ramayan::1908.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1908.essence: True partnership means sharing the burden of dharma.
ramayan::1908.simple_meaning: Janaka gives Sita to Rama and asks him to accept her as a partner in life and duty.
ramayan::1908.simple_insight: Love is not only feeling; it is shared responsibility.
ramayan::1908.detailed_meaning: At the end of Sita's swayamvara, Janaka stands before Rama and formally gives his daughter in marriage. This is the decisive moment when public ritual becomes lifelong commitment, binding Sita and Rama as partners in dharma.
ramayan::1908.modern_relevance: You are not just choosing someone you love; you are choosing someone who will share the weight of your life. A real partnership is a joined duty, not a private feeling.
ramayan::1908.insight: It reframes marriage as mutual obligation and shared purpose, not possession.

ramayan::1909.verse_sanskrit: पतिव्रता महाभागा छायेवानुगता सदा । इत्युक्त्वा प्राक्षिपद्राजा मन्त्रपूतं जलं तदा । । 17328 । ।
ramayan::1909.verse_hindi: By being a devoted wife this highly fortunate Sita would always follow you like a shadow. Thus spoken, he sprinkled the water sanctified with mantras (on them).
ramayan::1909.english_translation: By being a devoted wife, this highly fortunate Sita would always follow you like a shadow. Thus spoken, the king then sprinkled water sanctified with mantras over them.
ramayan::1909.translation_literal: पतिव्रता (devoted wife) / महाभागा (highly fortunate) / छायेव (like a shadow) / अनुगता (following) / सदा (always) / इति (thus) / उक्त्वा (having spoken) / प्राक्षिपत् (sprinkled) / राजा (the king) / मन्त्रपूतम् (sanctified with mantras) / जलम् (water) / तदा (then)
ramayan::1909.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1909.essence: True devotion stays close without needing to be asked.
ramayan::1909.simple_meaning: Janaka blesses Sita as a devoted wife who will stay with Rama constantly, then completes the marriage rite with sanctified water.
ramayan::1909.simple_insight: Real devotion is steady presence, not dramatic display.
ramayan::1909.detailed_meaning: Janaka has just given Sita to Rama in marriage. Before sealing the rite, he praises her as a wife who will follow her husband faithfully, like a shadow that never leaves the body. Then he performs the sacred water offering.
ramayan::1909.modern_relevance: You know the difference between a relationship that looks good and one that stays loyal when life gets hard. This verse honors the kind of commitment that keeps pace with every season.
ramayan::1909.insight: It shifts attention from romance as excitement to devotion as reliable accompaniment.

ramayan::1910.verse_sanskrit: साधु साध्विति देवाना मृषीणां वदतां तदा । देवदुन्दुभिर्निर्घोष: पुष्पवर्षो महानभूत् । । 17329 । ।
ramayan::1910.verse_hindi: Then gods and sages exclaimed: well, well. Celestial kettledrums were sounded and there was a steady rain of flowers.
ramayan::1910.english_translation: Then the gods and sages exclaimed, “Well done, well done.” Celestial kettledrums sounded, and a great shower of flowers fell.
ramayan::1910.translation_literal: साधु साधु (well done, well done) / इति (thus) / देवाना (of the gods) / मृषीणां (of the sages) / वदतां (speaking) / तदा (then) / देवदुन्दुभिः (celestial kettledrums) / निर्घोषः (resounding sound) / पुष्पवर्षः (shower of flowers) / महान् (great) / अभूत् (became)
ramayan::1910.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1910.essence: Right action can draw celebration from the whole world.
ramayan::1910.simple_meaning: The heavens celebrate Janaka's gift of Sita with praise, music, and flowers.
ramayan::1910.simple_insight: A righteous act can feel so complete that even the world seems to applaud.
ramayan::1910.detailed_meaning: Janaka has just given Sita to Rama after the marriage pact. In that sacred pause, gods and sages approve aloud, celestial drums thunder, and flowers rain down. The verse is a celebration of the union, not a new teaching.
ramayan::1910.modern_relevance: At a wedding, the room goes quiet for a second after the vows, and then everyone breaks into smiles and applause. Some moments feel blessed before anyone says a word.
ramayan::1910.insight: It marks public, cosmic approval of a marriage grounded in dharma.

ramayan::1911.verse_sanskrit: एवं दत्त्वा तदा सीतां मन्त्रोदकपुरस्कृताम् । अब्रवीज्जनको राजा हर्षेणाभिपरिप्लुत: । । 17330 । ।
ramayan::1911.verse_hindi: Then king Janaka sprinkled on Sita waters sanctified by mantras, and immersed in delight said:
ramayan::1911.english_translation: Then king Janaka sprinkled on Sita waters sanctified by mantras, and, overflowing with joy, said:
ramayan::1911.translation_literal: एवम् (thus) / दत्त्वा (having given) / तदा (then) / सीताम् (Sita) / मन्त्र-उदक-पुरस्कृताम् (preceded by sanctified water) / अब्रवीत् (said) / जनकः (Janaka) / राजा (the king) / हर्षेण (with joy) / अभिपरिप्लुतः (overwhelmed)
ramayan::1911.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1911.essence: A father blesses the daughter he is letting go.
ramayan::1911.simple_meaning: Janaka formally gives Sita away in marriage, using sacred water and speaking with great joy.
ramayan::1911.simple_insight: A solemn blessing can also be a moment of deep joy.
ramayan::1911.detailed_meaning: Janaka has just praised Sita's steadfastness and the gods have responded with approval. Now he completes the marriage rite by pouring sanctified water over her and, overwhelmed with joy, prepares to give her to Rama's side.
ramayan::1911.modern_relevance: A parent finishes a wedding ritual with trembling hands and a full heart. The formal act is small; the love and release behind it are immense.
ramayan::1911.insight: It shows how sacred duty and personal joy can meet in one act.

ramayan::1912.verse_sanskrit: लक्ष्मणागच्छ भद्रं ते ऊर्मिलामुद्यतां मया । प्रतीच्छ पाणिं गृह्णीष्व माभूत्कालस्य पर्यय: । । 17331 । ।
ramayan::1912.verse_hindi: Lakshmana come and accept my daughter. Urmila ready to be bestowed upon you
ramayan::1912.english_translation: Lakshmana, come and accept my daughter. I have prepared Urmila for you; take her hand, and let no time pass.
ramayan::1912.translation_literal: लक्ष्मण (Lakshmana) / आगच्छ (come) / भद्रं ते (may good be to you) / ऊर्मिलाम् (Urmila) / उद्यताम् (made ready) / मया (by me) / प्रतीच्छ (accept) / पाणिं (hand) / गृह्णीष्व (take) / मा (do not) / अभूत् (let there be) / कालस्य (of time) / पर्ययः (delay)
ramayan::1912.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1912.essence: Janaka formally offers Urmila to Lakshmana.
ramayan::1912.simple_meaning: Janaka invites Lakshmana to accept Urmila as his bride and asks him not to delay the marriage.
ramayan::1912.simple_insight: Some moments ask for immediate acceptance, not hesitation.
ramayan::1912.detailed_meaning: Janaka has just given Sita to Rama in a grand ceremony. Still glowing with joy, he turns to Lakshmana and offers Urmila as well. The verse is a formal wedding invitation, not a teaching.
ramayan::1912.modern_relevance: At a wedding, everyone is waiting while the next ritual begins and the families look to the next pair. The verse simply moves the ceremony forward.
ramayan::1912.insight: It shifts attention from meaning to sequence: the marriage is being completed step by step.

ramayan::1913.verse_sanskrit: तमेवमुक्त्वा जनको भरतं चाभ्यभाषत । गृहाण पाणिं माण्डव्या: पाणिना रघुनन्दन । । 17332 । ।
ramayan::1913.verse_hindi: Janaka, having spoken thus to Lakshmana addressed Bharata: O Descendant of the Raghus hold Mandavis hand in your own.
ramayan::1913.english_translation: Having spoken thus, Janaka addressed Bharata: "O descendant of the Raghus, take Mandavi's hand in your own."
ramayan::1913.translation_literal: तम् (him) / एवम् (thus) / उक्त्वा (having spoken) / जनकः (Janaka) / भरतम् (to Bharata) / च (and) / अभ्यभाषत (addressed) / गृहाण (take) / पाणिम् (hand) / माण्डव्याः (of Mandavi) / पाणिना (with hand) / रघुनन्दन (O descendant of the Raghus)
ramayan::1913.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1913.essence: Marriage here is not romance alone; it is solemn agreement made before everyone.
ramayan::1913.simple_meaning: Janaka turns from Lakshmana to Bharata and asks him to take Mandavi's hand in marriage.
ramayan::1913.simple_insight: A wedding moves forward through clear, public consent.
ramayan::1913.detailed_meaning: Janaka has already blessed Sita and Urmila, and now he continues the marriage arrangements by speaking to Bharata. In the same ceremonial moment, he invites Bharata to accept Mandavi, making the royal alliances complete.
ramayan::1913.modern_relevance: At a family gathering, one blessing finishes and the next begins. The moment stays simple: say the names, join the hands, and let commitment become public.
ramayan::1913.insight: It shows how sacred commitments are made openly, with clarity and order.

ramayan::1914.verse_sanskrit: शत्रुघ्नं चापि धर्मात्मा अब्रवीज्जनकेश्वर: । श्रुतकीर्त्या महाबाहो पाणिं गृह्णीष्व पाणिना । । 17333 । ।
ramayan::1914.verse_hindi: The righteous king Janaka, said again: O Mightyarmed Satrughna take the hands of Srutakirti.
ramayan::1914.english_translation: The righteous king Janaka said to Shatrughna: O mighty-armed one, take Srutakirti's hand in your hand.
ramayan::1914.translation_literal: शत्रुघ्नं (to Shatrughna) / च (also) / अपि (indeed) / धर्मात्मा (righteous-souled) / अब्रवीत् (said) / जनकेश्वरः (king Janaka) / श्रुतकीर्त्या (of Srutakirti) / महाबाहो (O mighty-armed one) / पाणिं (hand) / गृह्णीष्व (take) / पाणिना (with hand)
ramayan::1914.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1914.essence: The final matching of hands completes the royal wedding.
ramayan::1914.simple_meaning: Janaka asks Shatrughna to take Srutakirti's hand in marriage.
ramayan::1914.simple_insight: A sacred family bond is being completed with formal grace.
ramayan::1914.detailed_meaning: Janaka has already offered Sita, Urmila, and Mandavi. Now he turns to Shatrughna and gives Srutakirti in marriage too. The scene is the closing movement of a royal wedding sequence, where each brother receives his bride in turn.
ramayan::1914.modern_relevance: At a wedding where every relative is waiting for the next name to be called, the last blessing lands with quiet finality. The ceremony is complete because each promise has been honoured in order.
ramayan::1914.insight: It closes the marriage sequence by matching the last brother with his bride.

ramayan::1915.verse_sanskrit: सर्वे भवन्तस्सौम्याश्च सर्वे सुचरितव्रता: । पत्नीभिस्सन्तु काकुत्स्था माभूत्कालस्य पर्यय: । । 17334 । ।
ramayan::1915.verse_hindi: O Descendants of Kakustha (Rama, Lakshmana, Bharata and Satrughna) you all are gentle. You possess sound character. You are true to your vows. Live with your wives. Let there be no delay.
ramayan::1915.english_translation: O descendants of Kakustha, you are all gentle, and all steadfast in your vows. Live with your wives. Let there be no delay.
ramayan::1915.translation_literal: सर्वे (all) / भवन्तः (you all) / सौम्याः (gentle) / च (and) / सर्वे (all) / सुचरितव्रताः (steadfast in good conduct and vows) / पत्नीभिः (with wives) / सन्तु (let there be) / काकुत्स्थाः (descendants of Kakustha) / मा (not) / अभूत् (let there be) / कालस्य (of time) / पर्ययः (delay)
ramayan::1915.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1915.essence: Once character and consent are settled, delay only weakens what is already right.
ramayan::1915.simple_meaning: Janaka blesses the four princes, praising their character and urging the marriages to proceed without delay.
ramayan::1915.simple_insight: A rightful union should not be held back once character and consent are in place.
ramayan::1915.detailed_meaning: Janaka has already invited the four princes to marry his daughters. After naming the pairings, he blesses Rama, Lakshmana, Bharata, and Shatrughna as gentle and steadfast, then asks that the marriages happen at once. It is the final formal step before the hands are joined.
ramayan::1915.modern_relevance: A family gathering has already agreed on the match, the elders have spoken, and everyone is waiting for the formal moment. This verse carries the relief of a clean decision finally becoming action.
ramayan::1915.insight: It shifts attention from hesitation to completion when the right bond is already clear.

ramayan::1916.verse_sanskrit: जनकस्य वच श्शृत्वा पाणीन् पाणिभिरास्पृशन् । चत्वारस्ते चतसृ़णां वसिष्ठस्य मते स्थिता: । । 17335 । ।
ramayan::1916.verse_hindi: At the words of Janaka the four princes took the hands of the four sisters with their own with the consent of Vasishta .
ramayan::1916.english_translation: At Janaka's words, the four princes took the hands of the four sisters, in Vasishta's presence.
ramayan::1916.translation_literal: जनकस्य (of Janaka) / वचः (words) / श्रृत्वा (having heard) / पाणीन् (hands) / पाणिभिः (with hands) / आस्पृशन् (touched) / चत्वारः (the four) / ते (they) / चतसृणाम् (of the four) / वसिष्ठस्य (of Vasishta) / मते (in the view/presence) / स्थिताः (stood)
ramayan::1916.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1916.essence: A spoken agreement becomes real the moment hands meet.
ramayan::1916.simple_meaning: At Janaka's command, the four princes joined hands with the four sisters, and Vasishta approved the match.
ramayan::1916.simple_insight: Some moments are simple and irreversible: a promise becomes a bond the whole room can witness.
ramayan::1916.detailed_meaning: In Janaka's court, after the grooming of the alliances is complete, the four princes and four sisters join hands. Vasishta's approval seals what has already been accepted by everyone present: the marriages are now formally joined.
ramayan::1916.modern_relevance: You watch two families go quiet as the signatures are finally placed. What felt uncertain a minute ago becomes real in one small, irreversible gesture.
ramayan::1916.insight: It marks the moment a public agreement becomes a binding commitment.

ramayan::1917.verse_sanskrit: अग्निं प्रदक्षिणीकृत्य वेदिं राजानमेव च । ऋषींश्चैव महात्मानस्सभार्या रघुसत्तमा: । । 17336 । । यथोक्तेन तदा चक्रुर्विवाहं विधिपूर्वकम् ।
ramayan::1917.verse_hindi: The great, noble princes of the race of Raghu, accompanied by their wives circumambulated the altar of the sacred fire. King Janaka and the sages in obedience
ramayan::1917.english_translation: The great, noble princes of the Raghu line, together with their wives, circumambulated the sacred fire altar, the king, and the sages, and then performed the marriage exactly as prescribed.
ramayan::1917.translation_literal: अग्निं (the fire) / प्रदक्षिणीकृत्य (having circumambulated) / वेदिं (the altar) / राजानम् (the king) / एव (indeed) / च (and) / ऋषीन् (the sages) / च (and) / एव (also) / महात्मानः (the noble ones) / सभार्याः (together with their wives) / रघुसत्तमाः (the best of the Raghu line) / यथोक्तेन (as said) / तदा (then) / चक्रुः (they performed) / विवाहम् (the marriage) / विधिपूर्वकम् (according to ritual)
ramayan::1917.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1917.essence: The union becomes complete only when it is sealed in ritual.
ramayan::1917.simple_meaning: The wedding is completed with ritual precision. The princes, their brides, King Janaka, and the sages all take part in the sacred ceremony.
ramayan::1917.simple_insight: Some moments matter because they are carried out with full reverence, not haste.
ramayan::1917.detailed_meaning: After Janaka gives his blessing, the four princes and the four brides complete the marriage rites around the sacred fire. King Janaka and the sages stand by as witnesses. The verse simply closes the ceremony before the shower of flowers.
ramayan::1917.modern_relevance: A wedding hall falls quiet as the final ritual begins. Everyone who mattered is present, and the moment becomes real not through excitement, but through exactness.
ramayan::1917.insight: It shifts attention from the romance of the match to the weight of the rite.

ramayan::1918.verse_hindi: While the descendants of Kakustha (Rama, Lakshmana, Bharata and Satrughna) held
ramayan::1918.english_translation: A brilliant shower of flowers fell from the sky as the descendants of Kakutstha held the delicate hands.
ramayan::1918.translation_literal: काकुत्स्थैः (by the descendants of Kakutstha) / च (and) / गृहीतेषु (when held) / ललितेषु (delicate) / च (and) / पाणिषु (hands) / पुष्पवृष्टिः (shower of flowers) / महती (great) / आसीत् (was) / अन्तरिक्षात् (from the sky) / सुभास्वरा (brightly shining)
ramayan::1918.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1918.essence: The wedding is sealed by a sign of joy from above.
ramayan::1918.simple_meaning: As the princes held the brides' hands, flowers rained down from the sky in celebration.
ramayan::1918.simple_insight: Some moments feel so complete that the world seems to bless them.
ramayan::1918.detailed_meaning: Rama, Lakshmana, Bharata, and Shatrughna have just taken their brides' hands in marriage. The sacred ritual is complete, and the sky answers with a shower of brilliant flowers. It is a brief, celebratory bridge in the wedding scene.
ramayan::1918.modern_relevance: At a wedding reception, the room goes quiet for a second when the couple stands together and everyone feels it at once. Some beginnings seem to carry their own blessing.
ramayan::1918.insight: It marks the marriage as an auspicious, publicly honoured turning point in the story.

ramayan::1919.verse_sanskrit: अथ रात्र्यां व्यतीतायां विश्वामित्रो महामुनिः । आपृष्ट्वा तौ च राजानौ जगामोत्तरपर्वतम् । । 1741 । । आशीर्भि: पूरयित्वा च कुमारांश्च सराघवान् ।
ramayan::1919.verse_hindi: Night over, the great ascetic Viswamitra, profusely blessed the princes born in the race of Raghu, took leave of the two kings and set out towards the northern (Himalayas) mountains.
ramayan::1919.english_translation: When night had passed, the great sage Vishvamitra blessed the princes of Raghu, took leave of the two kings, and departed for the northern mountains.
ramayan::1919.translation_literal: अथ (then) / रात्र्यां (in the night) / व्यतीतायां (having passed) / विश्वामित्रः (Vishvamitra) / महामुनिः (great ascetic) / आपृष्ट्वा (having taken leave) / तौ (those two) / च (and) / राजानौ (kings) / जगाम (went) / उत्तरपर्वतम् (to the northern mountain) / आशीर्भिः (with blessings) / पूरयित्वा (having filled) / च (and) / कुमारान् (the princes) / सराघवान् (with Raghu's descendants)
ramayan::1919.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1919.essence: Blessing complete, the teacher leaves and the story moves on.
ramayan::1919.simple_meaning: After the wedding night, Vishvamitra blesses the princes, says goodbye to the kings, and leaves for the northern mountains.
ramayan::1919.simple_insight: Some moments are only a turning of the road, but they still matter.
ramayan::1919.detailed_meaning: The wedding is over, and the sacred gathering at Mithila begins to dissolve. Vishvamitra, who brought Rama and Lakshmana here, gives his blessings, takes leave of Dasharatha and Janaka, and heads back toward the Himalayas. The verse simply marks that departure.
ramayan::1919.modern_relevance: You stay a little longer after the ceremony ends, exchanging final blessings before everyone drifts back to their own lives.
ramayan::1919.insight: It marks the close of one sacred chapter and the quiet beginning of the next.

ramayan::1920.verse_sanskrit: विश्वामित्रे गते राजा वैदेहं मिथिलाधिपम् । आपृष्ट्वाऽथ जगामाशु राजा दशरथ: पुरीम् । । 1742 । ।
ramayan::1920.verse_hindi: With the departure of Viswamitra, king Dasaratha who was the source of happiness to his subjects took leave of Janaka, king of Mithila and speedily set out for the city of Ayodhya.
ramayan::1920.english_translation: With Viswamitra gone, king Dasaratha, after taking leave of Janaka, the lord of Mithila, quickly departed for Ayodhya.
ramayan::1920.translation_literal: विश्वामित्रे (when Viswamitra) / गते (having gone) / राजा (the king) / वैदेहम् (to Janaka of Videha) / मिथिलाधिपम् (lord of Mithila) / आपृष्ट्वा (having taken leave) / अथ (then) / जगाम (went) / आशु (quickly) / राजा (king) / दशरथः (Dasaratha) / पुरीम् (to the city)
ramayan::1920.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1920.essence: The journey ends, and the court turns home.
ramayan::1920.simple_meaning: After Viswamitra left, Dasaratha said farewell to Janaka and hurried back to Ayodhya.
ramayan::1920.simple_insight: Sometimes the important thing is simply to leave well and return to what waits for you.
ramayan::1920.detailed_meaning: The meeting in Mithila is over. Viswamitra has departed, Dasaratha has taken leave of Janaka, and the royal party turns back toward Ayodhya. The verse moves the story onward; it records departure, not teaching.
ramayan::1920.modern_relevance: The wedding is over, the guests are gone, and you are packing the car in silence. The moment matters less for what was said than for the respectful way everyone leaves.
ramayan::1920.insight: It marks the transition from a sacred visit back to ordinary duty and travel.

ramayan::1921.verse_sanskrit: गच्छन्तं तं तु राजानमन्वगच्छन्नराधिप: । । 1743 । । अथ राजा विदेहानां ददौ कन्याधनं बहु ।
ramayan::1921.verse_hindi: King Janaka, lord of the Videhas, gave plenty of gifts to his daughters and followed king Dasaratha for some distance on his journey to Ayodhya.
ramayan::1921.english_translation: King Janaka, lord of the Videhas, gave plenty of gifts to his daughters and followed king Dasaratha for some distance on his journey to Ayodhya.
ramayan::1921.translation_literal: गच्छन्तम् (going) / तम् (him) / तु (indeed) / राजानम् (the king) / अन्वगच्छन् (followed) / नराधिपः (the ruler of men) / अथ (then) / राजा (the king) / विदेहानाम् (of the Videhas) / ददौ (gave) / कन्याधनम् (bride-gift) / बहु (much)
ramayan::1921.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1921.essence: Honor can be carried in gifts and in the distance you walk with someone.
ramayan::1921.simple_meaning: Janaka sends Rama's father off with honor, walking part of the way and giving generous bride-gifts to his daughters.
ramayan::1921.simple_insight: Respect is shown not just in words, but in how you send someone onward.
ramayan::1921.detailed_meaning: After the wedding in Mithila, Janaka escorts Dasaratha as he prepares to return to Ayodhya. He also gives rich gifts as bride-price for Sita and her sisters. The verse is a ceremonial detail, not a teaching.
ramayan::1921.modern_relevance: You leave a wedding with trunks packed, blessings exchanged, and someone walking you to the gate because the moment deserves it. This is that kind of honor.
ramayan::1921.insight: It shifts attention from the gift itself to the dignity of the farewell.

ramayan::1922.verse_sanskrit: गवां शतसहस्राणि बहूनि मिथिलेश्वर: । कम्बलानां च मुख्यानां क्षौमकोट्यंबराणि च । । 1744 । । हस्त्यश्वरथपादातं दिव्यरूपं स्वलङ्कृतम् । ददौ कन्यापिता तासां दासीदासमनुत्तमम् । । 1745 । ।
ramayan::1922.verse_hindi: The king of Mithila and father of the brides gave a hundred thousand cows, excellent woollen carpets, crores of silk garments, four divisions of elephants, horses, chariots and infantry and welldecorated, excellent male and  maidservants shining in celestial
ramayan::1922.english_translation: The king of Mithila and father of the brides gave a hundred thousand cows, excellent woollen carpets, crores of silk garments, elephants, horses, chariots, foot soldiers, and beautifully adorned male and female servants of excellent quality.
ramayan::1922.translation_literal: गवां (of cows) / शतसहस्राणि (hundred-thousands) / बहूनि (many) / मिथिलेश्वरः (the lord of Mithila) / कम्बलानाम् (of woollen carpets) / च (and) / मुख्यानाम् (excellent) / क्षौमकोट्यंबराणि (crores of silk garments) / च (and) / हस्त्यश्वरथपादातम् (elephants-horses-chariots-foot soldiers) / दिव्यरूपम् (divine-looking) / स्वलङ्कृतम् (well-adorned) / ददौ (gave) / कन्यापिता (father of the brides) / तासाम् (of them) / दासीदासम् (female and male servants) / अनुत्तमम् (unsurpassed)
ramayan::1922.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1922.essence: Janaka marks the marriage with lavish honour, not mere ceremony.
ramayan::1922.simple_meaning: Janaka sends lavish wedding gifts with Sita and her sisters: cattle, cloth, vehicles, servants, and riches beyond measure.
ramayan::1922.simple_insight: Great occasions are marked by generosity that honors everyone involved.
ramayan::1922.detailed_meaning: After Viswamitra departs, Dasaratha leaves Mithila, and Janaka follows him partway. This verse lists the immense gifts Janaka sends with his daughters, showing the scale of the wedding and the pride, joy, and honour surrounding the alliance.
ramayan::1922.modern_relevance: A family wedding fills the house, and the gifts keep piling up until everyone laughs at the excess. The real message is not the luxury — it is the care behind it.
ramayan::1922.insight: It turns a royal marriage into a public act of honour and abundance.

ramayan::1923.verse_sanskrit: हिरण्यस्य सुवर्णस्य मुक्तानां विद्रुमस्य च । । 1746 । । ददौ परमसंहृष्ट: कन्याधनमनुत्तमम् ।
ramayan::1923.verse_hindi: Immensely delighted, he gave his excellent daughters gold, pearls and corals.
ramayan::1923.english_translation: Immensely delighted, he gave his excellent daughters gold, pearls, and corals.
ramayan::1923.translation_literal: हिरण्यस्य (of gold) / सुवर्णस्य (of fine gold) / मुक्तानां (of pearls) / विद्रुमस्य (of corals) / च (and) / ददौ (gave) / परमसंहृष्टः (greatly delighted) / कन्याधनम् (bride-gift) / अनुत्तमम् (excellent)
ramayan::1923.speaker: Janaka
ramayan::1923.essence: Janaka’s joy becomes generosity as he sends his daughters away.
ramayan::1923.simple_meaning: Janaka joyfully gives rich bridal gifts of gold, pearls, and coral to his daughters.
ramayan::1923.simple_insight: Love can show itself as generous blessing, not just words.
ramayan::1923.detailed_meaning: After the marriage of Sita and her sisters, Janaka, king of Mithila, sends the departing royal party away with abundant gifts. This verse is part of the ceremonial exchange, not a teaching moment.
ramayan::1923.modern_relevance: A wedding ends and the parents quietly pack the car with gifts, cash, and blessings. The moment is about care, not philosophy.
ramayan::1923.insight: It shows a father sending his daughters forward with dignity and abundance.

ramayan::1924.verse_sanskrit: दत्त्वा बहु धनं राजा समनुज्ञाप्य पार्थिवम् । । 1747 । । प्रविवेश स्वनिलयं मिथिलां मिथिलेश्वर: ।
ramayan::1924.verse_hindi: The Lord of Mithila bestowed a lot of wealth on his daughters and with the consent of the king (Dasaratha) reentered his residence in Mithila.
ramayan::1924.english_translation: Having given much wealth and obtained the king's consent, the Lord of Mithila entered his own home in Mithila.
ramayan::1924.translation_literal: दत्त्वा (having given) / बहु (much) / धनं (wealth) / राजा (the king) / समनुज्ञाप्य (having obtained consent) / पार्थिवम् (the king) / प्रविवेश (entered) / स्वनिलयं (his own residence) / मिथिलां (Mithila) / मिथिलेश्वरः (the Lord of Mithila)
ramayan::1924.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1924.essence: Completion matters too: even celebration ends by returning home.
ramayan::1924.simple_meaning: After giving generous gifts and receiving the king's permission, the ruler of Mithila returned to his own palace.
ramayan::1924.simple_insight: Some moments are complete only when everyone has been honored and released.
ramayan::1924.detailed_meaning: Janaka has finished the wedding gifts and formalities. With Dasharatha's consent secured, the Lord of Mithila returns to his residence, while the larger royal procession is still about to move on. It is a quiet transition after a grand public ceremony.
ramayan::1924.modern_relevance: The guests have finally left after a wedding, and the house is full of folded chairs and spent flowers. The big moment is over; now comes the clean return to ordinary life.
ramayan::1924.insight: It marks the close of one royal duty before the next procession begins.

ramayan::1925.verse_sanskrit: राजाऽप्ययोध्याधिपतिस्सह पुत्रैर्महात्मभि: । ऋषीन् सर्वान् पुरस्कृत्य जगाम सबलानुग: । । 1748 । ।
ramayan::1925.verse_hindi: King Dasaratha of Ayodhya also left along with his great sons preceded by the sages and followed by the army.
ramayan::1925.english_translation: King Dasaratha of Ayodhya also left along with his great sons, preceded by the sages and followed by the army.
ramayan::1925.translation_literal: राजा (king) / अपि (also) / अयोध्याधिपतिः (lord of Ayodhya) / सह (along with) / पुत्रैः (with sons) / महात्मभिः (great-souled) / ऋषीन् (the sages) / सर्वान् (all) / पुरस्कृत्य (placing in front) / जगाम (went) / स बलानुगः (with the army following)
ramayan::1925.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1925.essence: A royal return is marked by reverence, not just movement.
ramayan::1925.simple_meaning: Dasaratha leaves with his sons, the sages ahead of him, and his army behind him.
ramayan::1925.simple_insight: The journey matters less than the order of respect and duty around it.
ramayan::1925.detailed_meaning: Dasaratha, king of Ayodhya, departs from Mithila with Rama, Lakshmana, and his other sons. The sages walk in front, the army follows behind. It is a formal royal return after the wedding, not a teaching verse.
ramayan::1925.modern_relevance: A family leaves a wedding with elders guiding the way and relatives trailing behind in cars. The movement itself is ordinary; the respect shown in who leads and who follows is what gives it meaning.
ramayan::1925.insight: It shifts attention from travel itself to the social order carried within it.

ramayan::1926.verse_sanskrit: गच्छन्तं तं नरव्याघ्रं सर्षिसङ्घं सराघवम् । । 1749 । । घोरा: स्म पक्षिणो वाचो व्याहरन्ति ततस्तत: ।
ramayan::1926.verse_hindi: While this tiger among men Dasaratha, was returning with the hosts of sages and his sons, he observed here and there frightening birds making disagreeable sounds.
ramayan::1926.english_translation: While that tiger among men, Dasaratha, was returning with the sages and Rama, frightening birds kept crying out on every side.
ramayan::1926.translation_literal: गच्छन्तम् (going) / तम् (that) / नरव्याघ्रम् (tiger among men) / सर्षिसङ्घम् (with the group of sages) / सराघवम् (with Rama) / घोराः (frightening) / स्म (indeed) / पक्षिणः (birds) / वाचः (sounds) / व्याहरन्ति (were uttering) / ततस्ततः (from here and there)
ramayan::1926.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1926.essence: Even a joyful return can be shadowed by signs of coming loss.
ramayan::1926.simple_meaning: As Dasaratha returned with Rama and the sages, birds cried out ominously from all directions.
ramayan::1926.simple_insight: Sometimes the world seems to warn you before sorrow arrives.
ramayan::1926.detailed_meaning: Dasaratha is leaving Mithila after the wedding events, surrounded by sages and his sons. As he travels back, the landscape itself turns uneasy: birds cry out in harsh, unsettling ways. The verse sets up an ominous mood before the next sign is noticed.
ramayan::1926.modern_relevance: You leave a celebration and something in the air feels wrong — a phone call, a silence, a sudden unease you cannot explain. Some moments carry warning before the mind can name it.
ramayan::1926.insight: It builds suspense and signals that the journey is shadowed by coming trouble.

ramayan::1927.verse_sanskrit: भौमाश्चैव मृगा स्सर्वे गच्छन्ति स्म प्रदक्षिणम् । । 17410 । । तान् दृष्ट्वा राजशार्दूलो वसिष्ठं पर्यपृच्छत ।
ramayan::1927.verse_hindi: Seeing the beasts on the way rushing to the right the tiger among men, enquired of Vasishta:
ramayan::1927.english_translation: Seeing the beasts on the way rushing to the right, the tiger among men asked Vasishta:
ramayan::1927.translation_literal: भौमान् (earthly) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / मृगाः (beasts) / सर्वे (all) / गच्छन्ति (go) / स्म (indeed) / प्रदक्षिणम् (to the right) / तान् (those) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / राजशार्दूलः (tiger among kings) / वसिष्ठम् (Vasishta) / पर्यपृच्छत (asked)
ramayan::1927.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1927.essence: An uncertain mind turns a passing sign into a question.
ramayan::1927.simple_meaning: Dasaratha sees the animals moving to his right and asks Vasishta what it means.
ramayan::1927.simple_insight: A small sign can stir a king’s mind when he senses something important ahead.
ramayan::1927.detailed_meaning: Dasaratha is travelling with Rama, his sons, the sages, and the army. He notices the animals moving on the right side of the road and turns to Vasishta for an explanation. The verse sets up a question about omens, not a teaching yet.
ramayan::1927.modern_relevance: You notice a strange pattern in the middle of an ordinary day and suddenly feel unsettled. Before you know it, you are asking someone wiser what it means.
ramayan::1927.insight: It shifts attention from the event itself to the mind’s search for signs and meaning.

ramayan::1928.verse_sanskrit: असौम्या: पक्षिणो घोरा मृगाश्चापि प्रदक्षिणा: । । 17411 । । किमिदं हृदयोत्कम्पि मनो मम विषीदति ।
ramayan::1928.verse_hindi: While the frightening birds are inauspicious, the deer on the right are favourables Why is this? My heart beats. My mind is depressed.
ramayan::1928.english_translation: The birds are frightening, but the deer on the right are auspicious. Why is this? My heart is trembling; my mind is sinking.
ramayan::1928.translation_literal: असौम्याः (unpleasant, inauspicious) / पक्षिणः (birds) / घोराः (terrifying) / मृगाः (deer) / च (and) / अपि (also) / प्रदक्षिणाः (to the right, auspiciously circling) / किम् (what) / इदम् (this) / हृदय-उत्कम्पि (heart-shaking) / मनः (mind) / मम (my) / विषीदति (sinks, grieves)
ramayan::1928.speaker: Dasharatha
ramayan::1928.essence: Mixed signs can disturb the heart before the truth is known.
ramayan::1928.simple_meaning: Dasaratha sees mixed omens and feels uneasy. The signs around him seem to pull in opposite directions, and his heart grows troubled.
ramayan::1928.simple_insight: Even a king can feel shaken when the world seems to warn him.
ramayan::1928.detailed_meaning: Dasaratha is travelling with sages and his sons when he notices birds and deer behaving as omens. He turns to Vasishta, troubled by the contradiction between fear and hope. This verse captures the moment before the meaning is explained.
ramayan::1928.modern_relevance: You read the message twice because the tone feels off. One part of you says stop; another says it means nothing. That split, before certainty arrives, is this verse.
ramayan::1928.insight: It shows how uncertainty can unsettle the mind before any event has even happened.

ramayan::1929.verse_sanskrit: राज्ञो दशरथस्यैतच्छ्रुत्वा वाक्यं महानृषि: । । 17412 । । उवाच मधुरां वाणीं श्रूयतामस्य यत्फलम् ।
ramayan::1929.verse_hindi: To these words of king Dasaratha the great ascetic Vasishta replied in a gentle voice, I shall tell you the consequences Listen.
ramayan::1929.english_translation: To these words of King Dasaratha, the great ascetic Vasishta replied in a gentle voice: "Listen, I will tell you what they mean."
ramayan::1929.translation_literal: राज्ञः (of the king) / दशरथस्य (of Dasaratha) / एतत् (this) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / वाक्यम् (speech/words) / महानृषिः (the great ascetic) / उवाच (said) / मधुराम् (sweet/gentle) / वाणीम् (voice/speech) / श्रूयताम् (let it be heard) / अस्य (of this) / यत् (what) / फलम् (result/meaning) ।
ramayan::1929.speaker: Vasishta
ramayan::1929.essence: Fear eases when someone can name what is happening.
ramayan::1929.simple_meaning: Vasishta calmly tells Dasaratha that he will explain the meaning of the signs and their result.
ramayan::1929.simple_insight: A clear answer can steady a frightened mind.
ramayan::1929.detailed_meaning: Dasaratha is shaken by ominous signs in the world around him and turns to Vasishta for guidance. The royal teacher answers gently, promising to explain what these signs mean before fear takes over the court.
ramayan::1929.modern_relevance: You notice a string of bad signs and start spiralling. Then someone steadier speaks slowly and says, "Let me explain what this actually means."
ramayan::1929.insight: It shifts panic into patient listening before judgment.

ramayan::1930.verse_sanskrit: उपस्थितं भयं घोरं दिव्यं पक्षिमुखाच्च्युतम् । । 17413 । । मृगा: प्रशमयन्त्येते सन्तापस्त्यज्यतामयम् ।
ramayan::1930.verse_hindi: The dreadful cries from the mouths of birds foretell an event of celestial nature likely to befall but the movements other of deer indicate restoration of peace. Therefore do not grieve.
ramayan::1930.english_translation: The dreadful signs from birds point to a terrible event from above, but these deer point to peace returning. So let go of your grief.
ramayan::1930.translation_literal: उपस्थितम् (arrived/present) / भयम् (fear) / घोरम् (terrible) / दिव्यम् (celestial) / पक्षि-मुखात् (from the mouths of birds) / च्युतम् (fallen/uttered) / मृगाः (deer) / प्रशमयन्ति (calm/soothe) / एते (these) / सन्तापः (grief) / त्यज्यताम् (let be abandoned) / अयम् (this)
ramayan::1930.speaker: Vasishta
ramayan::1930.essence: Fear shrinks when you read the whole field, not one sign.
ramayan::1930.simple_meaning: Vasishta explains that the bird signs point to danger, but the deer signs point to peace returning. Dasaratha should stop grieving and calm himself.
ramayan::1930.simple_insight: You do not have to let fear interpret everything.
ramayan::1930.detailed_meaning: King Dasaratha is shaken by omens before Rama's exile begins. Vasishta, the royal teacher, reads the signs differently: some point to danger, others to relief. He tries to steady the king before panic takes over.
ramayan::1930.modern_relevance: You see one alarming message and your mind starts building a disaster out of it. Before the spiral hardens, someone wise reminds you to read the whole picture, not just the loudest sign.
ramayan::1930.insight: It shifts the mind from panic to measured interpretation before reacting.

ramayan::1931.verse_sanskrit: तेषां संवदतां तत्र वायु: प्रादुर्बभूव ह । । 17414 । । कम्पयन् पृथिवीं सर्वां पातयंश्च द्रुमांच्छुभान् ।
ramayan::1931.verse_hindi: While they were conversing, a storm blew, shaking the earth and felling down beautiful trees.
ramayan::1931.english_translation: While they were conversing, a storm arose, shaking the whole earth and felling beautiful trees.
ramayan::1931.translation_literal: तेषां (of them) / संवदतां (while speaking together) / तत्र (there) / वायुḥ (the wind) / प्रादुर्बभूव (arose) / ह (indeed) / कम्पयन् (shaking) / पृथिवीं (the earth) / सर्वां (entire) / पातयन् (causing to fall) / च (and) / द्रुमान् (trees) / शुभान् (beautiful)
ramayan::1931.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1931.essence: Nature itself interrupts to warn that something grave is near.
ramayan::1931.simple_meaning: As the conversation continued, a violent wind suddenly rose, shaking the ground and toppling the trees.
ramayan::1931.simple_insight: Some moments announce themselves before they arrive.
ramayan::1931.detailed_meaning: Vasishta has just begun explaining the omen to Dasharatha. As the discussion continues, the wind itself answers: the earth trembles and the trees fall. The scene is not teaching a principle yet; it is the first visible sign of the approaching disturbance.
ramayan::1931.modern_relevance: You are mid-conversation when the room changes — a slammed door, a sudden silence, a message that makes everyone look up. Before anyone speaks, you already know something bigger has entered.
ramayan::1931.insight: It frames the moment as an omen, not a lesson, and keeps attention on the unfolding event.

ramayan::1932.verse_sanskrit: तमसा संवृतस्सूर्य स्सर्वा न प्रबभुर्दिश । । 17415 । । भस्मना चावृतं सर्वं संमूढमिव तद्बलम् ।
ramayan::1932.verse_hindi: The Sun was wrapped in dark. The quarters were devoid of brightness. The entire army was covered with ashes, as if they fainted.
ramayan::1932.english_translation: The sun was covered by darkness. The directions lost all brightness. The whole army was covered in ash, as if it had fallen unconscious.
ramayan::1932.translation_literal: तमसा (by darkness) / संवृतः (covered) / सूर्यः (the sun) / सर्वा (all) / न (not) / प्रबभुः (shone) / दिशः (the directions) / भस्मना (with ash) / च (and) / आवृतम् (covered) / सर्वम् (all) / संमूढम् इव (as if bewildered) / तत् बलम् (that army)
ramayan::1932.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1932.essence: Darkness and ash make the whole army seem defeated before the fight begins.
ramayan::1932.simple_meaning: Darkness hides the sun, the directions lose their light, and the army looks stunned and covered in ash.
ramayan::1932.simple_insight: A sudden change can drain all confidence from a whole crowd.
ramayan::1932.detailed_meaning: The scene turns ominous in the middle of the battlefield. A storm has risen, the sun is blotted out, and dust and ash cover the army. Valmiki is showing the shock spreading through everyone before the next moment of the episode.
ramayan::1932.modern_relevance: A room goes silent after one bad email lands on the screen. The light feels gone, and everyone waits, stunned, for what comes next.
ramayan::1932.insight: It shifts attention from action to atmosphere, showing how fear can spread before anyone speaks.

ramayan::1933.verse_sanskrit: वसिष्ठश्चर्षयश्चान्ये राजा च ससुतस्तदा । । 17416 । । संसज्ञा इव तत्रासन् सर्वमन्यद्विचेतनम् ।
ramayan::1933.verse_hindi: At that time Vasishta and other saints, the king and his sons held their senses under control. All others lost their consciousness.
ramayan::1933.english_translation: At that time Vasishta and the other sages, along with the king and his sons, remained fully conscious. Everyone else lost awareness.
ramayan::1933.translation_literal: वसिष्ठः (Vasishta) / च (and) / ऋषयः (sages) / च (and) / अन्ये (others) / राजा (the king) / च (and) / ससुतः (with his sons) / तदा (then) / संसज्ञाः (fully conscious) / इव (as if) / तत्र (there) / आसन् (were) / सर्वम् (all) / अन्यत् (the others) / विचेतनम् (unconscious)
ramayan::1933.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1933.essence: Steadiness reveals itself when everyone else loses control.
ramayan::1933.simple_meaning: Vasishta, the king, and the princes stayed aware, while everyone else fainted or lost consciousness.
ramayan::1933.simple_insight: Some people stay steady in the middle of shock while everything around them collapses.
ramayan::1933.detailed_meaning: A violent darkness has spread over the scene, shaking the army into confusion. In that moment, only Vasishta, the king, and the princes remain composed. The verse marks the contrast between inner steadiness and mass disorientation.
ramayan::1933.modern_relevance: In a crowded train station after a sudden announcement, everyone panics and starts moving at once. A few people stay clear-headed, checking what is real before they react.
ramayan::1933.insight: It highlights the difference between calm awareness and collective panic.

ramayan::1934.verse_sanskrit: तस्मिंस्तमसि घोरे तु भस्मच्छन्नेव सा चमू: । । 17417 । । ददर्श भीमसङ्काशं जटामण्डलधारिणम् । भार्गवं जामदग्न्यं तं राजराजविमर्दिनम् । । 17418 । । कैलासमिव दुर्धर्षं कालाग्निमिव दुस्सहम् । ज्वलंतमिव तेजोभिर्दुर्निरीक्ष्यं पृथग्जनै: । । 17419 । । स्कन्धे चासज्य परशुं धनुर्विद्युद्गणोपमम् । प्रगृह्य शरमुख्यं च त्रिपुरघ्नं यथा शिवम् । । 17420 । ।
ramayan::1934.verse_hindi: In that dreadful darkness while the army looked as if covered with ashes, king Dasaratha encountered the repressor of kings, descendant of Bhrugu and son of Jamadagni with a terrible crown of matted hair, inaccessible like Kailasa mountain and unendurable like the fire at the time of dissolution. The laymen gazing at his blazing energy,hanging an axe on his shoulder and holding a bow in his hand which flashed like lighning and the principal arrow he looked like Siva at the time of slaying of
ramayan::1934.english_translation: In that dreadful darkness, with the army covered as if in ashes, King Dasharatha saw the terrible Bhargava, Jamadagni's son, with matted hair, as hard to approach as Kailasa and as unbearable as the fire of dissolution. Blazing with energy, he stood with an axe on his shoulder and a bow in his hand, like Shiva with the weapon that destroys Tripura.
