ramayan::1934.translation_literal: तस्मिन् (in that) / तमसि (in darkness) / घोरे (terrible) / तु (indeed) / भस्मच्छन्ना इव (as if covered with ashes) / सा (that) / चमूः (army) / ददर्श (saw) / भीमसङ्काशम् (fearsome-looking) / जटामण्डलधारिणम् (wearing a crown of matted hair) / भार्गवम् (the Bhargava) / जामदग्न्यम् (son of Jamadagni) / तम् (that one) / राजराजविमर्दिनम् (repressor of kings) / कैलासम् इव (like Kailasa) / दुर्धर्षम् (hard to approach) / कालाग्निम् इव (like the fire of dissolution) / दुस्सहम् (unbearable) / ज्वलन्तम् इव (as if blazing) / तेजोभिः (with radiance) / दुर्निरीक्ष्यम् (hard to look at) / पृथग्जनैः (by ordinary people) / स्कन्धे (on the shoulder) / च (and) / आसज्य (hanging) / परशुम् (axe) / धनुः (bow) / विद्युद्गणोपमम् (like a cluster of lightning) / प्रगृह्य (holding) / शरमुख्यम् (chief arrow) / च (and) / त्रिपुरघ्नम् (Tripura-destroying) / यथा (like) / शिवम् (Shiva)
ramayan::1934.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1934.essence: A room can turn into judgment the moment power walks in.
ramayan::1934.simple_meaning: Dasharatha sees Parasurama in a terrifying form, blazing with power and carrying weapons like a force no ordinary person can face.
ramayan::1934.simple_insight: Some confrontations announce themselves before a word is spoken.
ramayan::1934.detailed_meaning: The wedding hall has become a crisis. Darkness, ash, and stunned silence fill the scene after Rama has broken Shiva's bow. Now Dasharatha sees Parasurama enter like a living catastrophe: a sage-warrior whose presence alone can shake a kingdom.
ramayan::1934.modern_relevance: You walk into a room and feel the temperature change before anyone speaks. Some people carry that kind of force, and everyone knows the moment they arrive.
ramayan::1934.insight: It frames the next exchange as a clash with overwhelming power, not a normal conversation.

ramayan::1935.verse_sanskrit: तं दृष्ट्वा भीमसङ्काशं ज्वलन्तमिव पावकम् । वसिष्ठप्रमुखा विप्रा जपहोमपरायणा: । । 17421 । । सङ्गता मुनयस्सर्वे सञ्जजल्पुरथो मिथ: ।
ramayan::1935.verse_hindi: At the sight of the fearful appearance of Parasurama looking like flaming fire, Vasishta and all other saints who were in the habit of chanting mantras and offering oblations to the fire whispered among themselves:
ramayan::1935.english_translation: At the sight of the fearful appearance of Parasurama looking like flaming fire, Vasishta and all other saints who were in the habit of chanting mantras and offering oblations to the fire whispered among themselves.
ramayan::1935.translation_literal: तम् (him) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / भीम-सङ्काशम् (fearful-looking) / ज्वलन्तम् इव (like blazing) / पावकम् (fire) / वसिष्ठ-प्रमुखाः (led by Vasishta) / विप्राः (brahmins) / जप-होम-परायणाः (devoted to chanting and fire-offering) / सङ्गताः (assembled) / मुनयः (sages) / सर्वे (all) / सञ्जजल्पुः (whispered) / अथो (then) / मिथः (among themselves)
ramayan::1935.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1935.essence: Fear can spread before a single word is spoken.
ramayan::1935.simple_meaning: The sages saw Parashurama's fierce form and began speaking quietly among themselves.
ramayan::1935.simple_insight: Some moments are so charged that even the wise fall into hushed uncertainty.
ramayan::1935.detailed_meaning: In the tense meeting after Rama's bow is broken, Parashurama appears in a blazing, terrifying form. Vasishta and the gathered sages, normally steady in ritual and mantra, are shaken into private whispers. The verse sets up the fear before the next challenge is spoken aloud.
ramayan::1935.modern_relevance: A room goes silent when someone powerful walks in and the atmosphere changes instantly. Even people who usually stay composed can feel the tension before a single word is said.
ramayan::1935.insight: It shows how presence alone can unsettle a whole group before any argument begins.

ramayan::1936.verse_sanskrit: कच्चित्पितृवधामर्षी क्षत्रं नोत्सादयिष्यति । । 17422 । । पूर्वं क्षत्रवधं कृत्वा गतमन्युर्गतज्वर: । क्षत्रस्योत्सादनं भूयो न खल्वस्य चिकीर्षितम् । । 17423 । ।
ramayan::1936.verse_hindi: Enraged at the slaughter of his father (by Kartaveeryarjuna), is he intent upon  exterminating the kshatriya race? Having slaughtered the kshatriyas, in the past he was freed from anger and grief. Is he again desirous of annihilating the kshatriyas?
ramayan::1936.english_translation: Enraged at the slaughter of his father, is he intent on exterminating the kshatriya race? He once destroyed the kshatriyas, then his anger and grief were gone. Surely he does not wish to do that again.
ramayan::1936.translation_literal: कच्चित् (whether) / पितृवधामर्षी (angered by the killing of his father) / क्षत्रम् (the kshatriya class) / नोत्सादयिष्यति (will not destroy) / पूर्वम् (before) / क्षत्रवधम् (the killing of kshatriyas) / कृत्वा (having done) / गतमन्युः (freed from anger) / गतज्वरः (freed from grief) / क्षत्रस्य (of the kshatriyas) / उत्सादनम् (destruction) / भूयः (again) / न (not) / खलु (indeed) / अस्य (of him) / चिकीर्षितम् (desired)
ramayan::1936.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1936.essence: Unhealed grief can return as a second round of violence.
ramayan::1936.simple_meaning: The sages wonder whether Parashurama, still furious over his father's death, will wipe out the warrior class again. They recall that he once did so and then calmed down.
ramayan::1936.simple_insight: A wound can become a weapon when grief is left unchecked.
ramayan::1936.detailed_meaning: Dasaratha has just seen Parashurama in the dark, terrifying and blazing with force. The sages around him quietly ask whether this Brahmin-warrior, once driven by his father's murder to destroy kshatriyas, is about to repeat that violence now.
ramayan::1936.modern_relevance: A furious text thread, a family grievance, a memory that still burns — and suddenly you want to make the whole world pay for one injury. The verse shows how old pain can try to become new destruction.
ramayan::1936.insight: It shifts attention from the immediate threat to the deeper danger of unresolved rage.

ramayan::1937.verse_sanskrit: एवमुक्त्वाऽर्घ्यमादाय भार्गवं भीमदर्शनम् । ऋषयो राम रामेति वचो मधुरमब्रुवन् । । 17424 । ।
ramayan::1937.verse_hindi: The saints having thus talked amongst themselves, offered arghya to the son of Bhargava, of dreadful appearance and addressed him in soothing words: O Rama O Rama.
ramayan::1937.english_translation: The saints, after speaking among themselves, offered respectful water to the fearsome Bhargava and gently said, "Rama, Rama."
ramayan::1937.translation_literal: एवमुक्त्वा (having thus spoken) / अर्घ्यम् (respectful offering of water) / आदाय (having taken) / भार्गवम् (to the Bhargava) / भीमदर्शनम् (fearsome in appearance) / ऋषयः (the sages) / राम राम इति ("Rama, Rama") / वचः (words) / मधुरम् (sweetly) / अब्रुवन् (spoke)
ramayan::1937.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1937.essence: Respect can cool anger before words do.
ramayan::1937.simple_meaning: The sages calm the tense moment by honoring Parasurama and speaking to him gently.
ramayan::1937.simple_insight: Respect can soften even a dangerous encounter.
ramayan::1937.detailed_meaning: Parasurama has appeared before Rama, blazing with anger over the destruction of the warrior class. The assembled sages step in, offer him respectful water, and address him with soothing words, trying to steady the meeting before the next exchange.
ramayan::1937.modern_relevance: A room goes silent after a sharp accusation, and someone lowers the temperature with a respectful gesture and a calm voice.
ramayan::1937.insight: It shows how courtesy can hold a volatile moment together long enough for reason to enter.

ramayan::1938.verse_sanskrit: प्रतिगृह्य तु तां पूजामृषिदत्तां प्रतापवान् । रामं दाशरथिं रामो जामदग्न्योऽभ्यभाषत । । 17425 । ।
ramayan::1938.verse_hindi: Valiant Parasurama, son of Jamadagni, having accepted the homage offered by the saints addressed Rama, son of Dasaratha and said:
ramayan::1938.english_translation: Valiant Parasurama, son of Jamadagni, having accepted the homage offered by the saints addressed Rama, son of Dasaratha and said:
ramayan::1938.translation_literal: प्रतिगृह्य (having accepted) / तु (then) / तां (that) / पूजाम् (homage) / ऋषिदत्ताम् (offered by the sages) / प्रतापवान् (the valiant one) / रामम् (to Rama) / दाशरथिम् (son of Dasaratha) / रामः (Rama) / जामदग्न्यः (Jamadagnya, Parasurama) / अभ्यभाषत (spoke to)
ramayan::1938.speaker: Parasurama
ramayan::1938.essence: Respect comes first, even before a clash of wills.
ramayan::1938.simple_meaning: Parasurama accepts the sages’ respect and then speaks directly to Rama.
ramayan::1938.simple_insight: Even tense encounters begin with formal respect before the real challenge is spoken.
ramayan::1938.detailed_meaning: The sages have just honored Parasurama after his fierce arrival. He receives their homage, then turns to Rama, son of Dasaratha. This verse simply opens the next exchange, leading into the challenge between two great warriors.
ramayan::1938.modern_relevance: A difficult conversation often starts with a small act of courtesy before anyone says the hard thing. That pause can change the whole tone.
ramayan::1938.insight: It shows a confrontation that still follows ritual respect before conflict.

ramayan::1939.verse_sanskrit: राम दाशरथे राम वीर्यं ते श्रूयतेऽद्भुतम् । धनुषो भेदनं चैव निखिलेन मया श्रुतम् । । 1751 । ।
ramayan::1939.verse_hindi: O Rama, Rama, son of Dasaratha I have heard in full of your marvellous prowess and your feat in breaking the bow of Siva.
ramayan::1939.english_translation: O Rama, son of Dasaratha, I have heard in full of your marvellous prowess and your feat in breaking the bow of Siva.
ramayan::1939.translation_literal: राम (Rama) / दाशरथे (son of Dasaratha) / राम (Rama) / वीर्यम् (prowess) / ते (your) / श्रूयते (is heard) / अद्भुतम् (marvellous) / धनुषः (of the bow) / भेदनम् (breaking) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / निखिलेन (in full) / मया (by me) / श्रुतम् (heard)
ramayan::1939.speaker: Parasurama
ramayan::1939.essence: Your deed speaks before you do.
ramayan::1939.simple_meaning: Parashurama tells Rama that he has already heard of Rama's great strength and the astonishing breaking of Shiva's bow.
ramayan::1939.simple_insight: Even a proud challenger must first acknowledge real strength.
ramayan::1939.detailed_meaning: Parashurama has just accepted the saints' welcome and now turns to Rama, the prince of Ayodhya. Before testing him, he openly recognises Rama's reputation: the bow has been broken, and that feat has reached him completely.
ramayan::1939.modern_relevance: Someone walks into the room already knowing what you did last year, before you say a word. Your reputation enters first, and it shapes everything that follows.
ramayan::1939.insight: It shows how public deeds create a reputation that precedes direct confrontation.

ramayan::1940.verse_sanskrit: तदद्भुतमचिन्त्यं च भेदनं धनुषस्त्वया । तच्छ्रुत्वाऽहमनुप्राप्तो धनुर्गृह्यापरं शुभम् । । 1752 । ।
ramayan::1940.verse_hindi: The fact that you have broken Sivas bow is an astonishing act. It is beyond imagination. Having heard it I have come here with another auspicious bow.
ramayan::1940.english_translation: The fact that you have broken Shiva's bow is astonishing and beyond imagination. Hearing that, I have come here with another auspicious bow.
ramayan::1940.translation_literal: तत् (that) / अद्भुतम् (astonishing) / अचिन्त्यम् (unthinkable) / च (and) / भेदनम् (breaking) / धनुषः (of the bow) / त्वया (by you) / तत् (that) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / अहम् (I) / अनुप्राप्तः (have come) / धनुः (bow) / गृह्य (taking) / अपरम् (another) / शुभम् (auspicious)
ramayan::1940.speaker: Parasurama
ramayan::1940.essence: Great strength only invites a harder test.
ramayan::1940.simple_meaning: Parashurama acknowledges Rama's feat and says he has brought another sacred bow for Rama to test.
ramayan::1940.simple_insight: Recognition comes before the next challenge.
ramayan::1940.detailed_meaning: Parashurama has just heard that Rama broke Shiva's bow at Janaka's court. Struck by the feat, he arrives carrying another powerful bow and prepares to test Rama's strength in front of everyone.
ramayan::1940.modern_relevance: Someone finally notices the hard thing you did, and instead of praise alone, they bring the next test.
ramayan::1940.insight: It frames achievement as a threshold, not an ending.

ramayan::1941.verse_sanskrit: तदिदं घोरसङ्काशं जामदग्न्यं महद्धनु: । पूरयस्व शरेणैव स्वबलं दर्शयस्व च । । 1753 । ।
ramayan::1941.verse_hindi: This mighty, dreadful bow was obtained through Jamadagni. You may display your prowess by fixing on it an arrow.
ramayan::1941.english_translation: This mighty, dreadful bow was obtained through Jamadagni. You may display your prowess by fixing on it an arrow.
ramayan::1941.translation_literal: तदिदं (this) / घोरसङ्काशं (fearsome-looking) / जामदग्न्यं (Jamadagnya's) / महद्धनुः (great bow) / पूरयस्व (fill it / string it) / शरेण (with an arrow) / एव (only) / स्वबलं (your own strength) / दर्शयस्व (show) / च (and)
ramayan::1941.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1941.essence: Strength is shown by meeting the test, not by talking about it.
ramayan::1941.simple_meaning: Janaka presents Rama with the great bow and asks him to show his strength by stringing it with an arrow.
ramayan::1941.simple_insight: Real strength does not need to boast; it proves itself in the moment of action.
ramayan::1941.detailed_meaning: In Mithila, after hearing of Rama's feat, Janaka brings out the great bow once owned by Jamadagni. This is the test before Sita's swayamvara: not a speech, but a physical proof of worth.
ramayan::1941.modern_relevance: A room goes quiet when someone finally asks, “Can you actually do it?” No speech matters then — only whether your hands can meet the moment.
ramayan::1941.insight: It shifts value from claims and reputation to direct demonstration under pressure.

ramayan::1942.verse_sanskrit: तदहं ते बलं दृष्ट्वा धनुषोऽस्य प्रपूरणे । द्वन्द्वयुद्धं प्रदास्यामि वीर्यश्लाघ्यस्य राघव । । 1754 । ।
ramayan::1942.verse_hindi: O Rama after witnessing your strength in stretching and stringing this bow, I shall engage you in a duel acclaiming your prowess.
ramayan::1942.english_translation: O Rama, after witnessing your strength in bending and stringing this bow, I shall engage you in a duel, praising your prowess.
ramayan::1942.translation_literal: तद् (then) / अहम् (I) / ते (your) / बलम् (strength) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / धनुषः (of the bow) / अस्य (this) / प्रपूरणे (in filling/stringing) / द्वन्द्वयुद्धम् (duel) / प्रदास्यामि (shall give/offer) / वीर्यश्लाघ्यस्य (of the one praised for valor) / राघव (Rama)
ramayan::1942.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1942.essence: Strength is acknowledged only by meeting strength head-on.
ramayan::1942.simple_meaning: The speaker says that if Rama can string the bow, he will fight him in single combat and praise his strength.
ramayan::1942.simple_insight: Real challenge often comes after the first proof of skill.
ramayan::1942.detailed_meaning: In Janaka’s court, the huge bow of Shiva has been brought out as the test for Rama. The speaker raises the stakes: if Rama can string it, he will acknowledge that strength and meet him in single combat. The moment is still part of the challenge, not the answer.
ramayan::1942.modern_relevance: You finally prove yourself in front of everyone, and the next test appears immediately. Earned respect often comes with a harder round.
ramayan::1942.insight: It frames victory as only the opening to the next contest.

ramayan::1943.verse_sanskrit: तस्य तद्वचनं श्रुत्वा राजा दशरथस्तदा । विषण्णवदनो दीन: प्राञ्जलिर्वाक्यमब्रवीत् । । 1755 । ।
ramayan::1943.verse_hindi: When king Dasaratha heard these words, his face fell. He humbly pleaded with him his hands folded:
ramayan::1943.english_translation: When king Dasaratha heard these words, his face fell. He humbly pleaded with him, hands folded:
ramayan::1943.translation_literal: तस्य (his) / तद्वचनं (that speech) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / राजा (the king) / दशरथः (Dasharatha) / तदा (then) / विषण्णवदनः (with a fallen face) / दीनः (dejected) / प्राञ्जलिः (with folded hands) / वाक्यम् (words) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::1943.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1943.essence: Power gives way when the moment turns dangerous.
ramayan::1943.simple_meaning: Dasharatha is shaken by the words he hears and responds with humility, folding his hands to plead.
ramayan::1943.simple_insight: Pride drops away when the truth becomes too heavy to resist.
ramayan::1943.detailed_meaning: At the bow contest in Mithila, Rama has just been challenged to prove his strength. The challenge lands hard on Dasharatha, who suddenly sees the cost of the moment. His face falls, and he pleads rather than commands.
ramayan::1943.modern_relevance: You hear a sentence that makes your stomach drop — and suddenly all your certainty is gone. The body knows before the mind does that something has changed.
ramayan::1943.insight: It shows how pressure can strip away status and leave only urgent humility.

ramayan::1944.verse_sanskrit: क्षत्ररोषात्प्रशान्तस्त्वं ब्राह्मणश्च महायशा: । बालानां मम पुत्राणामभयं दातुमर्हसि । । 1756 । ।
ramayan::1944.verse_hindi: You are a brahmana, highly renowned and withdrawn from anger against kshatriyas. It behoves of you to give assurance of security to my sons who are young.
ramayan::1944.english_translation: You are a brahmana, highly renowned and withdrawn from anger against kshatriyas. It behoves of you to give assurance of security to my sons who are young.
ramayan::1944.translation_literal: क्षत्ररोषात् (from anger against kshatriyas) / प्रशान्तः (calmed, withdrawn) / त्वम् (you) / ब्राह्मणः (a brahmana) / च (and) / महायशाः (highly renowned) / बालानाम् (of the young) / मम (my) / पुत्राणाम् (of sons) / अभयम् (fearlessness, security) / दातुम् (to give) / अर्हसि (you ought)
ramayan::1944.speaker: Dasharatha
ramayan::1944.essence: True strength proves itself by protecting the helpless.
ramayan::1944.simple_meaning: Dasharatha appeals to the warrior's own honour: as a calm, famous brahmana, he should protect the king's young sons instead of threatening them.
ramayan::1944.simple_insight: Real strength feels safest when it shields the vulnerable.
ramayan::1944.detailed_meaning: Dasharatha, shaken by the stranger's challenge, folds his hands and speaks carefully. He reminds Parashurama that a famous brahmana should not turn anger toward children, and asks for safety for his sons. The plea exposes how little room remains before violence.
ramayan::1944.modern_relevance: A parent standing at a school gate hears a heated adult voice rise over a child’s head. In that moment, status matters less than restraint. The strongest person in the room is the one who makes the child feel safe.
ramayan::1944.insight: It shifts power from dominance to protection, and asks you to measure strength by how safely others can stand near you.

ramayan::1945.verse_sanskrit: भार्गवाणां कुले जात: स्वाध्यायव्रतशालिनाम् । सहास्राक्षे प्रतिज्ञाय शस्त्रं निक्षिप्तवानसि । । 1757 । ।
ramayan::1945.verse_hindi: Born in the family of (saint) Bhrigu versed in the study of the Vedas and  observance of vows. You have promised in the name of  the thousandeyed Indra to renounce the arms.
ramayan::1945.english_translation: Born in the family of Bhrigu, devoted to Vedic study and vows, you promised before Indra and laid down your weapons.
ramayan::1945.translation_literal: भार्गवाणाम् (of the descendants of Bhrigu) / कुले (in the family) / जातः (born) / स्वाध्यायव्रतशालिनाम् (of those adorned with study and vows) / सहस्राक्षे (before the thousand-eyed one, Indra) / प्रतिज्ञाय (having promised) / शस्त्रम् (weapon) / निक्षिप्तवानसि (you have laid down)
ramayan::1945.speaker: Dasharatha
ramayan::1945.essence: Your own vow is the strongest limit on your next action.
ramayan::1945.simple_meaning: Dasharatha reminds Parashurama that he was born in a noble line, bound by study and vows, and had already vowed to give up weapons.
ramayan::1945.simple_insight: A promise becomes heavier when everyone knows your own code should have kept you from breaking it.
ramayan::1945.detailed_meaning: Dasaratha is pleading for his sons' safety after Parashurama has arrived in fury. He appeals to Parashurama's lineage, his vows, and the public promise he once made to renounce weapons. The verse is one step in a desperate argument, not the full teaching itself.
ramayan::1945.modern_relevance: A senior leader who once promised restraint now stands at the edge of breaking it. Everyone in the room knows the earlier vow, and that makes the pressure sharper, not softer.
ramayan::1945.insight: It shifts the focus from raw power to the weight of a vow already spoken.

ramayan::1946.verse_sanskrit: स त्वं धर्मपरो भूत्वा काश्यपाय वसुन्धराम् । दत्त्वा वनमुपागम्य महेन्द्रकृतकेतन: । । 1758 । ।
ramayan::1946.verse_hindi: By adhering to righteousness in life and having conferred the earth upon Kasyapa, you retired to the forest and made your residence on the Mahendra mountain.
ramayan::1946.english_translation: By adhering to righteousness in life and having conferred the earth upon Kasyapa, you retired to the forest and made your residence on the Mahendra mountain.
ramayan::1946.translation_literal: स (you) / त्वं (you) / धर्मपरः (devoted to righteousness) / भूत्वा (having become) / काश्यपाय (to Kasyapa) / वसुन्धराम् (the earth) / दत्त्वा (having given) / वनम् (to the forest) / उपागम्य (having gone) / महेन्द्रकृतकेतनः (one whose dwelling was made on Mahendra)
ramayan::1946.speaker: Ravana
ramayan::1946.essence: Your greatest power may be the life you once laid down.
ramayan::1946.simple_meaning: Ravana is reminding the sage of his former righteousness, his gift of the earth to Kasyapa, and his forest dwelling on Mahendra mountain.
ramayan::1946.simple_insight: A life of power can still be remembered for restraint and renunciation.
ramayan::1946.detailed_meaning: Ravana is speaking to the sage in a tense exchange, trying to disarm him by recalling his ancient greatness and disciplined life. He points to a past of righteousness, gift-giving, and forest dwelling before the argument turns darker in the next line.
ramayan::1946.modern_relevance: Someone can be defined by the choices they made before fame, anger, or ambition took over. The old version of you still matters.
ramayan::1946.insight: It frames authority as something earned through restraint, not force.

ramayan::1947.verse_sanskrit: मम सर्वविनाशाय सम्प्राप्तस्त्वं महामुने । न चैकस्मिन् हते रामे सर्वे जीवामहे वयम् । । 1759 । ।
ramayan::1947.verse_hindi: O Great ascetic today you have arrived evidently for the total destruction of our family.
ramayan::1947.english_translation: O great ascetic, you have come here for the complete destruction of my family. If Rama is killed, none of us will remain alive.
ramayan::1947.translation_literal: मम (my) / सर्वविनाशाय (for total destruction) / सम्प्राप्तः (arrived) / त्वम् (you) / महामुने (O great ascetic) / न (not) / च (and) / एकस्मिन् (in one) / हते (being slain) / रामे (Rama) / सर्वे (all) / जीवामहे (we live) / वयम् (we)
ramayan::1947.speaker: Dasharatha
ramayan::1947.essence: He sees one death as the collapse of his whole world.
ramayan::1947.simple_meaning: Dasharatha sees the sage's demand as a threat to his family’s survival, saying that if Rama dies, no one in the house will live.
ramayan::1947.simple_insight: A single demand can feel like the end of an entire family line.
ramayan::1947.detailed_meaning: King Dasharatha is cornered by Jamadagni's son, who has come demanding Rama's punishment. The king, already shaken by the loss this could bring, sees the request as nothing less than the ruin of his lineage.
ramayan::1947.modern_relevance: A parent hears one phone call and feels the whole house tilt. One mistake, one demand, one impossible choice can suddenly feel like it threatens everything you love.
ramayan::1947.insight: It shows how fear compresses the future into one unbearable loss.

ramayan::1948.verse_sanskrit: ब्रुवत्येवं दशरथे जामदग्न्य: प्रतापवान् । अनादृत्यैव तद्वाक्यं राममेवाभ्यभाषत । । 17510 । ।
ramayan::1948.verse_hindi: Disregarding these words of Dasaratha, the valiant son of Jamadagni said to Rama.
ramayan::1948.english_translation: Disregarding Dasaratha's words, the valiant son of Jamadagni spoke only to Rama.
ramayan::1948.translation_literal: ब्रुवति (while speaking) / एवम् (thus) / दशरथे (to Dasaratha) / जामदग्न्यः (the son of Jamadagni) / प्रतापवान् (the valiant) / अनादृत्य (disregarding) / एव (indeed) / तत्-वाक्यम् (that speech) / रामम् (to Rama) / एव (only) / अभ्यभाषत (spoke)
ramayan::1948.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1948.essence: The plea is ignored; the real challenge is aimed at Rama.
ramayan::1948.simple_meaning: Parashurama ignores Dasaratha's plea and turns his attention to Rama instead.
ramayan::1948.simple_insight: Some moments leave no room for negotiation; the real confrontation begins when words stop mattering.
ramayan::1948.detailed_meaning: Dasaratha has already pleaded, fearing the collapse of his house. But Parashurama, the fierce son of Jamadagni, refuses to engage with him and speaks only to Rama. The scene tightens around a direct challenge.
ramayan::1948.modern_relevance: You can feel a room change when one person stops answering the louder voice and addresses the one who must decide.
ramayan::1948.insight: It shifts attention from public pleading to the one person who can actually respond.

ramayan::1949.verse_sanskrit: इमे द्वे धनुषी श्रेष्ठे दिव्ये लोकाभिविश्रुते । दृढे बलवती मुख्ये सुकृते विश्वकर्मणा । । 17511 । ।
ramayan::1949.verse_hindi: These two excellent celestial bows are wellknown throughout the worlds. They are stout and strong. They are the best of all, wellmade by Visvakarma.
ramayan::1949.english_translation: These two excellent celestial bows are well known throughout the worlds. They are stout and strong, the finest, made by Vishvakarma.
ramayan::1949.translation_literal: इमे (these) / द्वे (two) / धनुषी (bows) / श्रेष्ठे (excellent) / दिव्ये (celestial) / लोकाभिविश्रुते (well known in the worlds) / दृढे (firm) / बलवती (strong) / मुख्ये (foremost) / सुकृते (well made) / विश्वकर्मणा (by Vishvakarma)
ramayan::1949.speaker: Jamadagnya
ramayan::1949.essence: Even the weapons announce that this is no ordinary contest.
ramayan::1949.simple_meaning: These are two famous, powerful bows made by Vishvakarma.
ramayan::1949.simple_insight: Power can be real, ancient, and still just part of a larger test.
ramayan::1949.detailed_meaning: Jamadagnya is speaking before Dasaratha and Rama, pointing out the two legendary bows brought out for the trial. He is building the case for the task ahead, showing that these are no ordinary weapons but world-famous objects of immense force.
ramayan::1949.modern_relevance: You walk into a room and the challenge is already on the table. Before anyone speaks of skill, the tools and the stakes are laid bare.
ramayan::1949.insight: It sets up the scale of the coming test by naming the bows as extraordinary and formidable.

ramayan::1950.verse_sanskrit: अतिसृष्टं सुरैरेकं त्र्यम्बकाय युयुत्सवे । त्रिपुरघ्नं नरश्रेष्ठ भग्नं काकुत्स्थ यत्त्वया । । 17512 । ।
ramayan::1950.verse_hindi: O Best among men O Descendant of Kakustha one of these broken by you, was given by the gods to the threeeyed Siva, who, wishing to fight the demon Tripura with this bow, destroyed him.
ramayan::1950.english_translation: O best among men, O descendant of Kakustha, one of these bows was given by the gods to the three-eyed Shiva, who, wishing to fight Tripura with it, destroyed that demon.
ramayan::1950.translation_literal: अतिसृष्टम् (given away) / सुरैः (by the gods) / एकम् (one) / त्र्यम्बकाय (to the three-eyed Shiva) / युयुत्सवे (desiring to fight) / त्रिपुरघ्नम् (the destroyer of Tripura) / नरश्रेष्ठ (O best among men) / भग्नम् (broken) / काकुत्स्थ (O descendant of Kakustha) / यत् (which) / त्वया (by you)
ramayan::1950.speaker: Jamadagnya
ramayan::1950.essence: Rama has already broken a bow that even Shiva once wielded.
ramayan::1950.simple_meaning: One of the two great bows was given by the gods to Shiva, who used it to destroy Tripura. Rama has already broken that bow.
ramayan::1950.simple_insight: The bow is not just an object; it carries the weight of victories no ordinary hand could match.
ramayan::1950.detailed_meaning: Jamadagnya is explaining the first bow to Dasaratha and Rama. He points to the one Rama has already broken and reminds them of its divine history: it once belonged to Shiva in the war against Tripura. The scene is building toward a test of Rama's strength.
ramayan::1950.modern_relevance: You sometimes meet an obstacle that carries a reputation bigger than its size. Everyone treats it like an impossible thing, until your own hands prove otherwise.
ramayan::1950.insight: It shifts attention from the object’s legend to the fact that you already met it and prevailed.

ramayan::1951.verse_sanskrit: इदं द्वितीयं दुर्धर्षं विष्णोर्दत्तं सुरोत्तमै: । तदिदं वैष्णवं राम धनु: परमभास्वरम् । समानसारं काकुत्स्थ रौद्रेण धनुषा त्विदम् । । 17513 । ।
ramayan::1951.verse_hindi: This second bow which is unassailable was given by chief of the celestials to Visnu. O Rama born in the race of Kakutstha this highly radiant bow of Visnu is as strong as the bow of Siva.
ramayan::1951.english_translation: This second bow, which is unassailable, was given by the chief of the celestials to Vishnu. O Rama of the Kakutstha line, this radiant bow of Vishnu is as strong as the bow of Shiva.
ramayan::1951.translation_literal: इदम् (this) / द्वितीयम् (second) / दुर्धर्षम् (unassailable) / विष्णोः (of Vishnu) / दत्तम् (given) / सुरोत्तमैः (by the chief of the celestials) / तत् (that) / इदम् (this) / वैष्णवम् (belonging to Vishnu) / राम (Rama) / धनुः (bow) / परमभास्वरम् (highly radiant) / समानसारम् (of equal strength) / काकुत्स्थ (O descendant of Kakutstha) / रौद्रेण (with that of Shiva) / धनुषा (with the bow) / तु (indeed) / इदम् (this)
ramayan::1951.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1951.essence: Rama stands before a test that matches divine force with divine force.
ramayan::1951.simple_meaning: The bow Rama is about to handle is Vishnu's own, radiant and unmatched, equal in strength to Shiva's bow.
ramayan::1951.simple_insight: Some challenges are not ordinary tests; they carry the weight of the highest powers.
ramayan::1951.detailed_meaning: In Janaka's court, the two famous bows are being identified before Rama's trial. One had belonged to Shiva; this one came from Vishnu himself. The verse builds the sacred scale of the contest, preparing for the moment Rama must prove himself.
ramayan::1951.modern_relevance: You open a file and realize the decision in front of you is bigger than the meeting. The room is quiet, but the stakes are ancient: this is a test of whether you can meet what truly matters.
ramayan::1951.insight: It frames the coming act as a measure of worth, not mere display.

ramayan::1952.verse_sanskrit: तदा तु देवतास्सर्वा: पृच्छन्ति स्म पितामहम् । शितिकण्ठस्य विष्णोश्च बलाबलनिरीक्षया । । 17514 । ।
ramayan::1952.verse_hindi: Then all the gods in order to ascertain the strength and weakness of Siva and Visnu enquired of the Grandsire, Brahma:
ramayan::1952.english_translation: Then all the gods asked the Grandsire Brahma to determine the strength and weakness of Shiva and Vishnu.
ramayan::1952.translation_literal: तदा (then) / तु (indeed) / देवतास्सर्वा: (all the gods) / पृच्छन्ति स्म (asked) / पितामहम् (the Grandsire) / शितिकण्ठस्य (of the blue-throated one, Shiva) / विष्णोश्च (and of Vishnu) / बलाबलनिरीक्षया (for the observation of strength and weakness)
ramayan::1952.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1952.essence: The gods pause to measure powers before the next move.
ramayan::1952.simple_meaning: The gods asked Brahma to judge the strength of Shiva and Vishnu.
ramayan::1952.simple_insight: Great powers are not always obvious at first glance.
ramayan::1952.detailed_meaning: The gods are preparing to understand the two great powers involved in the bow episode. They approach Brahma not for worship, but for discernment, wanting to know how Shiva and Vishnu compare before the next divine step unfolds.
ramayan::1952.modern_relevance: Before a major decision, people often ask the wrong question first: who is stronger, who will win, who has more power. The deeper issue is understanding what is actually at stake.
ramayan::1952.insight: It frames the scene as a search for comparison before action, not as a teaching in itself.

ramayan::1953.verse_sanskrit: अभिप्रायं तु विज्ञाय देवतानां पितामह: । विरोधं जनयामास तयो स्सत्यवतां वर: । । 17515 । ।
ramayan::1953.verse_hindi: Foremost among the truthful, Grandsire Brahma come to know the intention of the
ramayan::1953.english_translation: Foremost among the truthful, the Grandsire learned the intention of the gods and created conflict between the two.
ramayan::1953.translation_literal: अभिप्रायम् (intention) / तु (indeed) / विज्ञाय (having known) / देवतानाम् (of the gods) / पितामहः (the Grandsire) / विरोधम् (conflict) / जनयामास (caused to arise) / तयोः (of those two) / सत्यवताम् (among the truthful) / वरः (the foremost)
ramayan::1953.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1953.essence: Brahma turns hidden intention into open conflict.
ramayan::1953.simple_meaning: Brahma understood what the gods wanted and set Shiva and Vishnu against each other.
ramayan::1953.simple_insight: Sometimes a larger purpose begins by creating tension, not by avoiding it.
ramayan::1953.detailed_meaning: The gods approach Brahma to judge the power of Shiva and Vishnu. Brahma sees their hidden intention and stirs up conflict between the two, setting the stage for the terrifying contest that follows.
ramayan::1953.modern_relevance: A team meeting looks calm until someone quietly frames the real issue and the room changes. Sometimes the truth is not to smooth things over, but to reveal what is actually being tested.
ramayan::1953.insight: It shows how a hidden motive can be exposed and turned into a decisive test.

ramayan::1954.verse_sanskrit: विरोधे च महद्युद्धमभवद्रोमहर्षणम् । शितिकण्ठस्य विष्णोश्च परस्परजिगीषुणो: । । 17516 । ।
ramayan::1954.verse_hindi: In that thrilling fight between Siva and Visnu, each desirous of victory over the other, a ferocious battle took place causing ones hair to stand on end.
ramayan::1954.english_translation: In that thrilling fight between Siva and Visnu, each desirous of victory over the other, a ferocious battle took place causing one's hair to stand on end.
ramayan::1954.translation_literal: विरोधे (in the conflict) / च (and) / महत्-युद्धम् (great battle) / अभवत् (there was) / रोम-हर्षणम् (hair-raising) / शितिकण्ठस्य (of Siva) / विष्णोः (and of Visnu) / च (and) / परस्पर-जिगीषुणोः (of the two desirous of defeating each other)
ramayan::1954.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1954.essence: Two immense powers meet as rivals, and the air itself trembles.
ramayan::1954.simple_meaning: Siva and Vishnu fought a terrifying battle, each trying to defeat the other.
ramayan::1954.simple_insight: Even cosmic powers can clash when pride and rivalry take over.
ramayan::1954.detailed_meaning: Brahma has stirred conflict between the gods, and now Siva and Vishnu face each other in a battle so fierce it shakes the scene itself. The verse is not a teaching but a vivid combat detail leading into the next exchange.
ramayan::1954.insight: It sets up a clash driven by mutual challenge, not harmony.

ramayan::1955.verse_sanskrit: तदा तु जृम्भितं शैवं धनुर्भीमपराक्रमम् । हुङ्कारेण महादेव स्तम्भितोऽथ त्रिलोचन: । । 17517 । ।
ramayan::1955.verse_hindi: Then, with the Humkara produced by Visnu, Sivas bow of dreadful prowess was stretched, which struck the threeeyed Mahadeva motionless.
ramayan::1955.english_translation: Then, with the Humkara produced by Vishnu, Shiva's bow of dreadful prowess was stretched, and the three-eyed Mahadeva stood motionless.
ramayan::1955.translation_literal: तदा (then) / तु (indeed) / जृम्भितं (stretched) / शैवं (of Shiva) / धनुः (bow) / भीम-पराक्रमम् (of dreadful prowess) / हुङ्कारेण (with a humkara) / महादेवः (Mahadeva) / स्तम्भितः (made motionless) / अथ (then) / त्रिलोचनः (the three-eyed one)
ramayan::1955.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1955.essence: A single surge of force can freeze overwhelming power.
ramayan::1955.simple_meaning: Vishnu's force makes Shiva's mighty bow stretch, and Shiva stands unmoving before that power.
ramayan::1955.simple_insight: Some moments are pure force: even the great can be checked in an instant.
ramayan::1955.detailed_meaning: Brahma has stirred conflict among the gods, and now Shiva and Vishnu face each other in a terrifying contest. In this verse, Vishnu's humkara is enough to stretch Shiva's formidable bow and still the three-eyed Mahadeva, showing the scale of the divine clash.
ramayan::1955.modern_relevance: Two strong personalities collide in a room, and the whole atmosphere freezes. One sharp word, one decisive presence, and everyone feels who has the upper hand.
ramayan::1955.insight: It frames power as something that can halt even the mighty without a prolonged struggle.

ramayan::1956.verse_sanskrit: देवैस्तदा समागम्य सर्षिसघै स्सचारणै: । याचितौ प्रशमं तत्र जग्मतुस्तौ सुरोत्तमौ । । 17518 । ।
ramayan::1956.verse_hindi: Then hosts of sages, charanas and the gods assembled there and beseeched both of them, the preeminent among the gods to keep peace.
ramayan::1956.english_translation: Then the gods, together with hosts of sages and celestial singers, gathered there and begged those two supreme beings to make peace.
ramayan::1956.translation_literal: देवैः (by the gods) / तदा (then) / समागम्य (having assembled) / सर्षिसङ्घैः (with hosts of sages) / सचारणैः (with celestial singers) / याचितौ (begged) / प्रशमम् (peace) / तत्र (there) / जग्मतुः (they went) / तौ (those two) / सुरोत्तमौ (the two supreme among the gods)
ramayan::1956.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1956.essence: Even the strongest powers must yield to peace.
ramayan::1956.simple_meaning: The gods and sages gathered and asked the two great beings to stop fighting and make peace.
ramayan::1956.simple_insight: Even cosmic conflict ends when wiser voices call for peace.
ramayan::1956.detailed_meaning: After Shiva and Vishnu clash in a terrifying contest of power, the gods, sages, and celestial singers gather at the scene. Seeing the danger, they plead with both supreme beings to end the struggle.
ramayan::1956.modern_relevance: A family argument has gone too far, and everyone in the room can feel it. Sometimes the bravest move is not winning, but stopping the spiral before it burns everything.
ramayan::1956.insight: It shifts attention from victory to restraint when power has already gone too far.

ramayan::1957.verse_sanskrit: जृम्भितं तद्धनुर्द्रृष्ट्वा शैवं विष्णुपराक्रमै: । अधिकं मेनिरे विष्णुं देवा स्सर्षिगणास्तदा । । 17519 । ।
ramayan::1957.verse_hindi: Now that the bow of Siva was made inert by Visnus prowess, hosts of sages and  gods acknowlged Visnu as superior.
ramayan::1957.english_translation: Now that the bow of Shiva was rendered inert by Vishnu's power, the gods and hosts of sages regarded Vishnu as greater.
ramayan::1957.translation_literal: जृम्भितं (rendered inert) / तत् (that) / धनुः (bow) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / शैवं (of Shiva) / विष्णु-पराक्रमैः (by Vishnu's prowess) / अधिकम् (greater) / मेनिरे (considered) / विष्णुम् (Vishnu) / देवाः (the gods) / सर्षिगणाः (with the hosts of sages) / तदा (then)
ramayan::1957.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1957.essence: Power becomes undeniable when it can move what no one else can.
ramayan::1957.simple_meaning: Seeing Shiva's bow subdued, the gods and sages recognized Vishnu's greater power.
ramayan::1957.simple_insight: Real strength does not argue for itself; it becomes obvious when tested.
ramayan::1957.detailed_meaning: At Janaka's court, Shiva's great bow has just yielded to Vishnu's force through Rama. The gods and sages watching the contest understand what they have seen: this is no ordinary feat, and Vishnu's power is beyond comparison.
ramayan::1957.modern_relevance: You watch someone stay calm under pressure while everyone else panics. No speech changes the room as much as that steadiness does. Real authority is recognized after it is shown.
ramayan::1957.insight: It shifts the mind from claims of greatness to visible proof of power.

ramayan::1958.verse_sanskrit: धनू रुद्रस्तु सङ्कृद्धो विदेहेषु महायशा: । देवरातस्य राजर्षेर्ददौ हस्ते ससायकम् । । 17520 । ।
ramayan::1958.verse_hindi: Glorious Siva, enraged at this, placed the bow together with the arrow in the hands of Rajarshi Devarata in the country of Videha.
ramayan::1958.english_translation: Glorious Shiva, enraged at this, placed the bow together with the arrow in the hands of Rajarshi Devarata in the country of Videha.
ramayan::1958.translation_literal: धनू (the bow) / रुद्रः (Rudra) / तु (but) / सङ्कृद्धः (enraged) / विदेहेषु (in Videha) / महायशाः (the greatly famed one) / देवरातस्य (of Devarata) / राजर्षेः (of the royal sage) / ददौ (gave) / हस्ते (into the hand) / ससायकम् (together with the arrow)
ramayan::1958.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1958.essence: The bow is handed over, and the test moves toward Rama.
ramayan::1958.simple_meaning: Shiva, angered, gave the bow and arrow to King Devarata of Videha.
ramayan::1958.simple_insight: A sacred weapon changes hands, setting the next great trial in motion.
ramayan::1958.detailed_meaning: The gods have just acknowledged Vishnu's greater power over Shiva's bow. In response, Shiva hands the bow and arrow to King Devarata in Videha. This is the bridge between divine contest and Rama's coming trial.
ramayan::1958.modern_relevance: A challenge lands in your hands just after someone else has proven themselves stronger. What follows is no longer abstract — now you must meet it directly.
ramayan::1958.insight: It shifts attention from divine comparison to the human moment of receiving responsibility.

ramayan::1959.verse_sanskrit: इदं च वैष्णवं राम धनु: परपुरञ्जयम् । ऋचीके भार्गवे प्रादाद्विष्णु: स न्यासमुत्तमम् । । 17521 । ।
ramayan::1959.verse_hindi: This bow of Visnu, O Rama capable of conquering hostile cities, was given in trust to Richika belonging to the race of Bhrigu.
ramayan::1959.english_translation: This bow of Vishnu, O Rama, conqueror of hostile cities, was entrusted to Richika of the Bhrigu line.
ramayan::1959.translation_literal: इदं (this) / च (and) / वैष्णवं (belonging to Vishnu) / राम (O Rama) / धनु: (bow) / परपुरञ्जयम् (conqueror of hostile cities) / ऋचीके (to Richika) / भार्गवे (to the Bhrigu-born) / प्रादाद् (gave) / विष्णु: (Vishnu) / सः (he) / न्यासम् (entrusted object) / उत्तमम् (excellent)
ramayan::1959.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1959.essence: True power is revealed by who is trusted to hold it.
ramayan::1959.simple_meaning: Vishnu's bow, famed for conquering enemies, was once entrusted to Richika of the Bhrigu line.
ramayan::1959.simple_insight: Power is not only possessed; it is also entrusted, carried, and handed on with care.
ramayan::1959.detailed_meaning: In the midst of the bow's origin story, the speaker traces its sacred lineage back to Vishnu and the Bhrigu sage Richika. The point is not battle, but rightful custody: this is a weapon of immense force, passed on as a solemn trust before it reaches later hands.
ramayan::1959.modern_relevance: A family heirloom, a company password, or a signed legal document can carry more weight than force. Some things are powerful because they were entrusted, not seized.
ramayan::1959.insight: It shifts attention from ownership to stewardship: what matters most may be what you are trusted to carry.

ramayan::1960.verse_sanskrit: ऋचीकस्तु महातेजा: पुत्रस्याप्रतिकर्मण: । पितुर्मम ददौ दिव्यं जमदग्नेर्महात्मन: । । 17522 । ।
ramayan::1960.verse_hindi: Brilliant Ruchika gave this bow to his son, the great Jamadagni, my father, a man of unrivalled valour.
ramayan::1960.english_translation: Brilliant Ruchika gave this divine bow to my father, the great Jamadagni, a man of unmatched valour.
ramayan::1960.translation_literal: ऋचीकः (Ruchika) / तु (indeed) / महातेजाः (very radiant, brilliant) / पुत्रस्य (to his son) / अप्रतिकर्मणः (of one without equal in action, unrivalled) / पितुः (to the father) / मम (my) / ददौ (gave) / दिव्यम् (divine) / जमदग्नेः (of Jamadagni) / महात्मनः (of the great-souled one)
ramayan::1960.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1960.essence: The bow matters because of the lineage behind it.
ramayan::1960.simple_meaning: Ruchika gave the divine bow to Jamadagni, Rama's father, and the verse simply traces the bow's lineage.
ramayan::1960.simple_insight: Some objects carry a history that matters more than their shape.
ramayan::1960.detailed_meaning: In this exchange, the speaker explains how a powerful divine bow passed from Vishnu to Ruchika and then to Jamadagni. It is not the main teaching yet, but a link in the chain that establishes the bow's sacred origin before the story turns to its tragic use.
ramayan::1960.modern_relevance: You inherit things with a backstory: a family name, an old promise, a tool, a wound. What looks ordinary now may be carrying the weight of everyone who held it before you.
ramayan::1960.insight: It shifts attention from the object itself to the responsibility and history attached to it.

ramayan::1961.verse_sanskrit: न्यस्तशस्त्रे पितरि मे तपोबलसमन्विते । अर्जुनो विदधे मृत्युं प्राकृतां बुद्धिमास्थित: । । 17523 । ।
ramayan::1961.verse_hindi: My father equipped with ascetic energy renounced the weapon and was killed by Kartaveeryarjuna in a vulgar manner.
ramayan::1961.english_translation: My father, endowed with ascetic power, had laid down his weapon; Arjuna killed him by taking a base-minded course.
ramayan::1961.translation_literal: न्यस्तशस्त्रे (having laid down the weapon) / पितरि (in the father) / मे (of me) / तपोबलसमन्विते (endowed with ascetic power) / अर्जुनो (Arjuna) / विदधे (inflicted) / मृत्युं (death) / प्राकृतां (base, vulgar) / बुद्धिमास्थितः (having taken that mindset)
ramayan::1961.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1961.essence: A harmless man was killed by a mind too crude to respect restraint.
ramayan::1961.simple_meaning: Parasurama says his father was a powerful ascetic who had put down his weapon, yet Arjuna killed him through dishonourable thinking.
ramayan::1961.simple_insight: Some losses are made worse by the kind of mind that caused them.
ramayan::1961.detailed_meaning: Parasurama is speaking of the murder of his father Jamadagni. The father had renounced violence and stood in ascetic strength, yet Kartaviryarjuna killed him anyway. The verse is part of Parasurama's rising grief and rage before he vows revenge.
ramayan::1961.modern_relevance: You finally lower your guard, and someone uses that moment against you. The pain is not only in the loss — it is in the ugliness of how it happened.
ramayan::1961.insight: It frames violence as a moral failure of the attacker, not weakness in the victim.

ramayan::1962.verse_sanskrit: वधमप्रतिरूपं तु पितु श्शृत्वा सुदारुणम् । क्षत्रमुत्सादयन्रोषाज्जातं जातमनेकश: । । 17524 । । पृथिवीं चाखिलां प्राप्य काश्यपाय महात्मने । यज्ञस्यान्ते तदा राम दक्षिणां पुण्यकर्मणे । दत्त्वा महेन्द्रनिलयस्तपोबलसमन्वित: । । 17525 । ।
ramayan::1962.verse_hindi: O Rama Having heard the slaying of my father incomparable in extreme ruthlessness,
ramayan::1962.english_translation: Having heard of the unbearable and dreadful killing of my father, I destroyed the Kshatriyas again and again in anger. Then, after conquering the whole earth, I gave it as a gift to the noble Kashyapa at the end of the sacrifice, O Rama, and came here from the abode of Indra with the strength of austerity.
ramayan::1962.translation_literal: वधम् (killing) / अप्रतिरूपम् (unbearable, unmatched) / तु (but) / पितुः (of father) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / सुदारुणम् (very dreadful) / क्षत्रम् (the Kshatriyas) / उत्सादयन् (destroying) / रोषात् (from anger) / जातं जातम् (again and again, those born) / अनेकशः (many times) / पृथिवीम् (the earth) / च (and) / अखिलाम् (entire) / प्राप्य (having obtained) / काश्यपाय (to Kashyapa) / महात्मने (to the noble one) / यज्ञस्य अन्ते (at the end of the sacrifice) / तदा (then) / राम (O Rama) / दक्षिणाम् (as gift, fee) / पुण्यकर्मणे (to the meritorious one) / दत्त्वा (having given) / महेन्द्रनिलयः (the one dwelling in Mahendra's abode) / तपोबलसमन्वितः (endowed with the power of austerity)
ramayan::1962.speaker: Parasurama
ramayan::1962.essence: A wound turned into revenge can still leave you carrying the wound.
ramayan::1962.simple_meaning: Parashurama says he heard of his father's brutal killing, wiped out Kshatriyas in rage, conquered the earth, and then gave it away as a sacrificial gift before coming here.
ramayan::1962.simple_insight: Rage can make revenge feel endless, yet still leave the heart unsatisfied.
ramayan::1962.detailed_meaning: Parashurama stands before Rama after the broken bow. He explains the wound that shaped him: his father's murder drove him to destroy kings across the earth, then renounce his conquest as sacrificial gift. This is the burden he brings into the confrontation.
ramayan::1962.modern_relevance: You replay one betrayal until it becomes a whole identity. You start calling the revenge 'justice,' but the hurt keeps speaking through every move.
ramayan::1962.insight: It shows how grievance can harden into a lifelong mission and still remain unresolved inside.

ramayan::1963.verse_sanskrit: अद्यतूत्तमवीर्येण त्वया राम महाबल । श्रुतवान् धनुषो भेदं ततोऽहं द्रुतमागत: । । 17526 । ।
ramayan::1963.verse_hindi: O Mighty Rama when I heard that you have broken the bow with your extraordinary prowess, I have come here quickly.
ramayan::1963.english_translation: O mighty Rama, when I heard that you had broken the bow with extraordinary prowess, I came here quickly.
ramayan::1963.translation_literal: अद्य (today) / तु (indeed) / उत्तमवीर्येण (with extraordinary prowess) / त्वया (by you) / राम (Rama) / महाबल (mighty one) / श्रुतवान् (having heard) / धनुषः (of the bow) / भेदम् (breaking) / ततः (then) / अहम् (I) / द्रुतम् (quickly) / आगतः (came)
ramayan::1963.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1963.essence: His arrival is triggered by Rama’s feat, not by conversation.
ramayan::1963.simple_meaning: The speaker says he came quickly after hearing that Rama had broken the bow with great strength.
ramayan::1963.simple_insight: Great deeds travel fast; reputation can bring the next encounter before words do.
ramayan::1963.detailed_meaning: In the court of Mithila, the bow has already been broken and the contest is turning toward Sita’s marriage. The speaker arrives on hearing Rama’s feat, setting up the next exchange in which the bow’s origin and the kshatriya duty attached to it are revealed.
ramayan::1963.modern_relevance: You hear one remarkable thing about someone, and suddenly the room changes. A single act of strength or skill can draw the next challenge straight to your door.
ramayan::1963.insight: It shifts attention from the feat itself to the social force that feat creates.

ramayan::1964.verse_sanskrit: तदिदं वैष्णवं राम पितृपैतामहं महत् । क्षत्रधर्मं पुरस्कृत्य गृह्णीष्व धनुरुत्तमम् । । 17527 । ।
ramayan::1964.verse_hindi: Respect the duties of a kshatriya, O Rama Take hold of this great, uncommon bow of Visnu inherited by me from my father and forefathers.
ramayan::1964.english_translation: Respect the duties of a kshatriya, O Rama. Take hold of this great bow of Vishnu, inherited from my father and forefathers.
ramayan::1964.translation_literal: तत् (that) / इदं (this) / वैष्णवं (of Vishnu) / राम (O Rama) / पितृ-पैतामहम् (ancestral, from father and forefathers) / महत् (great) / क्षत्र-धर्मम् (kshatriya duty) / पुरस्कृत्य (placing first) / गृह्णीष्व (take hold of) / धनुः-उत्तमम् (best bow)
ramayan::1964.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1964.essence: Winning once is not enough; duty still asks for more.
ramayan::1964.simple_meaning: Rama is told to honour his warrior duty and take up the great ancestral bow.
ramayan::1964.simple_insight: Your role asks something of you before your pride does.
ramayan::1964.detailed_meaning: In the swayamvara hall, after Rama has already broken the bow, the next challenger steps forward with a harder test. He reminds Rama that a kshatriya must meet honour with action, then offers the great ancestral bow to see whether Rama can go further.
ramayan::1964.modern_relevance: Someone hands you the harder version of a task after you thought the first one was enough. The moment asks whether you can stay steady, accept your role, and meet the challenge without shrinking.
ramayan::1964.insight: It shifts attention from victory already won to the next obligation in front of you.

ramayan::1965.verse_sanskrit: योजयस्व धनुश्श्रेष्ठे शरं परपुरञ्जयम् । यदि शक्नोषि काकुत्स्थ द्वन्द्वं दास्यामि ते तत: । । 17528 । ।
ramayan::1965.verse_hindi: O Descendant of Kakustha this best bow is capable of conquering enemy cities. Fix an arrow. If it is possible for you to do so, then I shall engage you in a duel.
ramayan::1965.english_translation: O Descendant of Kakustha, this best of bows can conquer enemy cities. Fix an arrow. If you can, then I will fight you in a duel.
ramayan::1965.translation_literal: योजयस्व (fix) / धनुश्श्रेष्ठे (best bow) / शरं (arrow) / परपुरञ्जयम् (conquering enemy cities) / यदि (if) / शक्नोषि (you are able) / काकुत्स्थ (O descendant of Kakustha) / द्वन्द्वं (duel) / दास्यामि (I will give) / ते (to you) / ततः (then)
ramayan::1965.speaker: Parasurama
ramayan::1965.essence: Strength is no longer claimed; it must be proved in front of everyone.
ramayan::1965.simple_meaning: Parasurama challenges Rama to string the bow, fit an arrow, and face him in single combat if he can do it.
ramayan::1965.simple_insight: Power is being tested openly, with no room for excuses.
ramayan::1965.detailed_meaning: Parasurama has arrived after Rama breaks Shiva's bow. He hands over his own mighty bow and dares Rama to string it and prove himself in combat. The scene is a contest of force and honour, not a teaching moment.
ramayan::1965.modern_relevance: Someone hands you a task that looks impossible and waits to see whether you will shrink back. The pressure is public, immediate, and absolute.
ramayan::1965.insight: It shows a direct test of strength, where words stop and action must answer.

ramayan::1966.verse_sanskrit: श्रुत्वा तज्जामदग्न्यस्य वाक्यं दाशरथिस्तदा । गौरवाद्यंन्त्रितकथ: पितू राममथाब्रवीत् । । 1761 । ।
ramayan::1966.verse_hindi: Hearing the words of the son of Jamadagni (Parasurama), Rama, the son of Dasaratha, avoiding further conversation out of respect for his father intercepted Parasurama saying:
ramayan::1966.english_translation: Hearing the words of the son of Jamadagni, Rama, restrained by respect, then spoke to Parasurama.
ramayan::1966.translation_literal: श्रुत्वा (having heard) / तद् (that) / जामदग्न्यस्य (of Jamadagni's son) / वाक्यम् (speech) / दाशरथिः (Dasaratha's son) / तदा (then) / गौरवात् (out of respect) / आत्म-यन्त्रित-कथः (speech restrained by self-control) / पितुः (for father) / रामः (Rama) / अथ (then) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::1966.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1966.essence: Respect and self-control shape even a moment of confrontation.
ramayan::1966.simple_meaning: Rama hears Parasurama and answers only after holding himself back out of respect. He does not rush into argument.
ramayan::1966.simple_insight: Restraint can be stronger than a quick reply.
ramayan::1966.detailed_meaning: Parasurama has challenged Rama after the bow is lifted. Before the exchange can turn into open conflict, Rama pauses, measures his words, and answers with restraint. The moment shows his control under pressure.
ramayan::1966.modern_relevance: Someone corners you in front of others, and your first impulse is to fire back. You pause instead, because not every challenge deserves your full heat.
ramayan::1966.insight: It teaches you to answer pressure without losing self-command.

ramayan::1967.verse_sanskrit: श्रुतवानस्मि यत्कर्म कृतवानसि भार्गव । अनुरुंध्यामहे ब्रह्मन् पितुरानृण्यमास्थितम् । । 1762 । ।
ramayan::1967.verse_hindi: O Descendant of Bhrigu I have listened to the (marvellous) acts you have performed. O Brahman I commend you for discharging your duty in repaying the debt to your father.
ramayan::1967.english_translation: O Descendant of Bhrigu, I have heard of the great deeds you have done. O Brahman, I honour your resolve in repaying your father's debt.
ramayan::1967.translation_literal: श्रुतवान् (have heard) / अस्मि (I am) / यत् (which) / कर्म (deeds) / कृतवान् (done) / असि (you are) / भार्गव (O Bhargava) / अनुरुंध्यामहे (we honour/approve) / ब्रह्मन् (O Brahman) / पितुर् (of father) / अनृण्यम् (freedom from debt) / आस्थितम् (having taken up)
ramayan::1967.speaker: Rama
ramayan::1967.essence: Respect can survive even when two duties collide.
ramayan::1967.simple_meaning: Rama acknowledges Parasurama's deeds and respects his choice to repay his father's debt.
ramayan::1967.simple_insight: Respect can remain even in a confrontation; honouring duty does not require hostility.
ramayan::1967.detailed_meaning: Rama stands before Parasurama after the bow challenge. Instead of answering with anger, he speaks with measured respect, recognising the older sage-warrior's harsh vow to repay his father's debt. The moment softens the clash, even as the duel is about to begin.
ramayan::1967.modern_relevance: You can disagree with someone’s path and still recognise the weight of what drove them there. Sometimes the most mature response is respect before resistance.
ramayan::1967.insight: It shows how to acknowledge another person's duty without surrendering your own position.

ramayan::1968.verse_sanskrit: वीर्यहीनमिवाशक्तं क्षत्रधर्मेण भार्गव । अवजानासि मे तेज: पश्य मेऽद्य पराक्रमम् । । 1763 । ।
ramayan::1968.verse_hindi: You underrate me O Bhargava as though I am devoid of valour and incompetent to perform the duties of a Kshatriya. Now witness my energy and valour.
ramayan::1968.english_translation: You underrate me, O Bhargava, as though I am powerless in the duty of a warrior. Now witness my energy and valor.
ramayan::1968.translation_literal: वीर्यहीनमिव (as if devoid of valor) / अशक्तम् (powerless) / क्षत्रधर्मेण (by the duty of a warrior) / भार्गव (O Bhargava) / अवजानासि (you are underrating) / मे (my) / तेजः (energy) / पश्य (see) / मे (my) / अद्य (now) / पराक्रमम् (valor)
ramayan::1968.speaker: Rama
ramayan::1968.essence: Real strength does not beg to be believed; it appears when tested.
ramayan::1968.simple_meaning: Rama rejects Parasurama's dismissal and declares that he is fully capable of meeting a warrior's duty. He calls for his strength to be seen now.
ramayan::1968.simple_insight: Self-respect can be quiet until it must become action.
ramayan::1968.detailed_meaning: Rama has already answered Parasurama calmly, but the challenge still hangs in the air. Now he speaks with controlled anger: he refuses to be treated as weak and calls on Parasurama to see his force. The moment turns words into combat.
ramayan::1968.modern_relevance: At the moment someone assumes you will fold, you feel the heat rise in your chest. This verse is that instant when you stop shrinking and let your capability speak.
ramayan::1968.insight: It shifts you from being judged by others to meeting the challenge directly.

ramayan::1969.verse_sanskrit: इत्युक्त्वा राघव: क्रुद्धो भार्गवस्य शरासनम् । शरं च प्रतिजग्राह हस्ताल्लघुपराक्रम: । । 1764 । ।
ramayan::1969.verse_hindi: Having spoken thus, the enraged Rama, gifted with quick vigour, seized the bow and arrow from Parasuramas hands.
ramayan::1969.english_translation: Having spoken thus, the enraged Rama, gifted with quick vigour, seized the bow and arrow from Parasurama's hands.
ramayan::1969.translation_literal: इत्युक्त्वा (having spoken thus) / राघवः (Rama) / क्रुद्धः (enraged) / भार्गवस्य (of Bhargava / Parasurama) / शरासनम् (bow) / शरम् (arrow) / च (and) / प्रतिजग्राह (seized) / हस्तात् (from the hand) / लघुपराक्रमः (one of swift prowess)
ramayan::1969.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1969.essence: Rama answers doubt with immediate action, not more words.
ramayan::1969.simple_meaning: Rama, angered by Parasurama's challenge, quickly took the bow and arrow from his hands.
ramayan::1969.simple_insight: Some moments leave no room for debate. You either answer the challenge or yield to it.
ramayan::1969.detailed_meaning: Parasurama has insulted Rama's strength and demanded proof. Rama, no longer patient, takes the weapon from his hands. The scene turns from verbal challenge to direct contest in a single motion.
ramayan::1969.modern_relevance: Someone questions your capability in front of others, and the room goes quiet. You stop explaining and simply show what you can do.
ramayan::1969.insight: It shifts the moment from argument to action.

ramayan::1970.verse_sanskrit: आरोप्य स धनू राम श्शरं सज्यं चकार ह । जामदग्न्यं ततो रामं राम: क्रुद्धोऽब्रवीद्वच: । । 1765 । ।
ramayan::1970.verse_hindi: Infuriated Rama bent the bow stretched it, fixed the arrow and addressed Parasurama, the son of Jamadagni:
ramayan::1970.english_translation: Infuriated Rama bent the bow, strung it, and then spoke to Parasurama, the son of Jamadagni.
ramayan::1970.translation_literal: आरोप्य (having placed on) / स (he) / धनू (the bow) / रामः (Rama) / शरम् (the arrow) / सज्यम् (strung) / चकार (made) / ह (indeed) / जामदग्न्यम् (to the son of Jamadagni) / ततः (then) / रामम् (Rama) / रामः (Rama) / क्रुद्धः (angry) / अब्रवीत् (spoke) / वचः (words)
ramayan::1970.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1970.essence: Strength is proven first in action, then in speech.
ramayan::1970.simple_meaning: Rama strings the bow and prepares to answer Parasurama with words and force.
ramayan::1970.simple_insight: Some moments leave no room for hesitation. The body acts before the speech lands.
ramayan::1970.detailed_meaning: Rama has just taken Parasurama's bow and proved his strength. Now, still burning with anger, he strings the weapon and turns to answer the warrior sage. The scene is a final test of force, pride, and restraint.
ramayan::1970.modern_relevance: You finally get the chance to speak back after being underestimated. Your hands are steady before your mouth is.
ramayan::1970.insight: It shows the instant when power becomes action, not argument.

ramayan::1971.verse_sanskrit: ब्राह्मणोऽसीति पूज्यो मे विश्वामित्रकृतेन च । तस्माच्छक्तो न ते राम मोक्तुं प्राणहरं शरम् । । 1766 । ।
ramayan::1971.verse_hindi: You are a brahmin, O Parasurama. You are also related to Viswamitra. Hence you are worthy of homage. I cannot, therefore, release this against you to take your life.
ramayan::1971.english_translation: You are a brahmin, O Parasurama. You are also related to Viswamitra. Hence you are worthy of homage. I cannot, therefore, release this against you to take your life.
ramayan::1971.translation_literal: ब्राह्मणः (a brahmin) / असि (you are) / इति (thus) / पूज्यः (worthy of reverence) / मे (to me) / विश्वामित्र-कृतेन (through Viswamitra) / च (and) / तस्मात् (therefore) / शक्तः (able) / न (not) / ते (for you) / राम (O Rama) / मोक्तुम् (to release) / प्राण-हरम् (life-taking) / शरम् (arrow)
ramayan::1971.speaker: Rama
ramayan::1971.essence: Power is not complete until it knows whom it will not destroy.
ramayan::1971.simple_meaning: Even in a fight, Rama refuses to use a fatal weapon against someone he must respect.
ramayan::1971.simple_insight: Strength becomes noble when it knows where not to strike.
ramayan::1971.detailed_meaning: Rama has just seized and drawn the weapon against Parasurama. But before the final blow, he names the old warrior's standing as a brahmin and his link to Viswamitra. The conflict turns from rage to restraint.
ramayan::1971.modern_relevance: You finally have the perfect reply typed out, and it would wound. Then you remember who this person is to you, and you choose restraint over victory.
ramayan::1971.insight: It teaches you to let reverence limit force, even when you are fully capable of winning.

ramayan::1972.verse_sanskrit: इमां पादगतिं राम तपोबलसमार्जिताम् । लोकानप्रतिमान्वा ते हनिष्यामि यदिच्छसि । । 1767 । ।
ramayan::1972.verse_hindi: I shall destroy your mobility, O Parasurama or the higher worlds earned through your matchless asceteic energy. Tell me which one you choose.
ramayan::1972.english_translation: I shall destroy your mobility, O Parasurama, or the higher worlds earned through your unmatched ascetic power. Tell me which one you choose.
ramayan::1972.translation_literal: इमाम् (this) / पादगतिम् (movement of the feet, mobility) / राम (O Rama) / तपोबलसमार्जिताम् (earned through ascetic power) / लोकान् (worlds) / अप्रतिमान् (matchless) / वा (or) / ते (your) / हनिष्यामि (I shall destroy) / यत् इच्छसि (whichever you wish)
ramayan::1972.speaker: Rama
ramayan::1972.essence: Rama forces a final choice: keep your power, or keep your pride.
ramayan::1972.simple_meaning: Rama confronts Parasurama and says he will either stop him from moving or destroy the rewards of his severe austerities, forcing him to choose.
ramayan::1972.simple_insight: Some confrontations leave no middle path: you must answer for what you are trying to protect.
ramayan::1972.detailed_meaning: After Parasurama challenges him, Rama answers without backing down. He offers two outcomes: lose the power to move forward, or lose the fruits of the ascetic strength Parasurama has earned. The moment is a hard test of force and resolve.
ramayan::1972.modern_relevance: A hard conversation reaches the point where you can no longer dodge the real issue. You either protect your position or lose what you built by standing your ground.
ramayan::1972.insight: It shifts the mind from hesitation to decisive confrontation when a boundary has to be enforced.

ramayan::1973.verse_sanskrit: न ह्ययं वैष्णवो दिव्य श्शर: परपुरञ्जय: । मोघ: पतति वीर्येण बलदर्पविनाशनः । । 1768 । ।
ramayan::1973.verse_hindi: On conquering the hostile cities and destroying the pride and strength of the enemy
ramayan::1973.english_translation: This divine, Vaishnava arrow does not fail. It conquers enemy cities and destroys the pride of strength.
ramayan::1973.translation_literal: न हि (indeed not) / अयम् (this) / वैष्णवः (Vaishnava) / दिव्यः (divine) / शरः (arrow) / परपुरञ्जयः (conquering enemy-cities) / मोघः (failing in vain) / पतति (falls) / वीर्येण (by power/valour) / बलदर्पविनाशनः (destroyer of strength-pride)
ramayan::1973.speaker: Rama
ramayan::1973.essence: Right force does not miss its mark.
ramayan::1973.simple_meaning: Rama says this divine arrow cannot fail. It will strike down the enemy and crush arrogant strength.
ramayan::1973.simple_insight: Some force is meant to end pride, not just win a fight.
ramayan::1973.detailed_meaning: Parashurama has challenged Rama after the bow contest. Rama answers with calm certainty, naming the arrow as divine and undefeatable. The moment is not just about combat; it is about ending a proud warrior's last resistance.
ramayan::1973.modern_relevance: You finally speak after someone has tried to intimidate you for too long. The answer is steady, not loud: what is true does not need to boast.
ramayan::1973.insight: It shifts attention from fear of opposition to certainty in rightful action.

ramayan::1974.verse_sanskrit: वरायुधधरं रामं द्रष्टुं सर्षिगणा स्सुरा: । पितामहं पुरस्कृत्य समेतास्तत्र सङ्घश: । । 1769 । । गन्धर्वाप्सरसश्चैव सिद्धचारणकिन्नरा: । यक्षराक्षसनागाश्च तद्द्रष्टुं महदद्भुतम् । । 17610 । ।
ramayan::1974.verse_hindi: The gods with the Grandsire, Brahma in the forefront, accompanied by sages in groups assembled there to see Rama holding that mighty bow. Gandharvas, apsaras, siddhas, charanas, kinnaras, yakshas, rakshsas and nagas also came there to witness that great wonder.
ramayan::1974.english_translation: The gods, with Brahma in front, gathered in groups to see Rama holding the mighty bow. Gandharvas, apsaras, siddhas, charanas, kinnaras, yakshas, rakshasas, and nagas also came to witness that great wonder.
ramayan::1974.translation_literal: वरायुधधरम् (holding the best weapon) / रामम् (Rama) / द्रष्टुम् (to see) / सर्षिगणाः (with groups of sages) / सुराः (the gods) / पितामहम् (with the Grandsire) / पुरस्कृत्य (placing in front) / समेताः (assembled) / तत्र (there) / सङ्घशः (in groups) / गन्धर्वाप्सरसः (Gandharvas and apsaras) / चैव (and also) / सिद्धचारणकिन्नराः (siddhas, charanas, and kinnaras) / यक्षराक्षसनागाः (yakshas, rakshasas, and nagas) / च (and) / तद् (that) / द्रष्टुम् (to see) / महत् अद्भुतम् (the great wonder)
ramayan::1974.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1974.essence: The bow turns Rama into a wonder that draws all beings to watch.
ramayan::1974.simple_meaning: All kinds of celestial and mythical beings gather to watch Rama with the great bow. It is a scene of awe, not instruction.
ramayan::1974.simple_insight: Some moments are so overwhelming that even the highest beings come to witness them.
ramayan::1974.detailed_meaning: After Rama has taken up the great bow, the scene draws every order of being to the same place. Brahma leads the gods, and sages, celestial singers, nymphs, perfected beings, and serpent-beings all gather. The verse heightens the wonder of the moment before the final clash with Parasurama.
ramayan::1974.modern_relevance: A crowd falls silent when someone walks onstage and changes the room without speaking. This verse is that kind of pause — a moment too large for ordinary attention.
ramayan::1974.insight: It frames the event as a public marvel, not a private exchange, raising the scale before the confrontation.

ramayan::1975.verse_sanskrit: जडीकृते तदाऽलोके रामे वरधनुर्धरे । निर्वीर्यो जामदग्न्योऽसौ रामो राममुदैक्षत । । । 17611 । ।
ramayan::1975.verse_hindi: Then when Rama stretched the great bow, the world became motionless. The son of Jamadagni, Parasurama, bereft of prowess gazed at him with astonishment.
ramayan::1975.english_translation: Then when Rama stretched the great bow, the world became motionless. The son of Jamadagni, Parasurama, bereft of prowess gazed at him with astonishment.
ramayan::1975.translation_literal: जडीकृते (when made motionless) / तदा (then) / अलोके (the world) / रामे (in Rama) / वरधनुर्धरे (the holder of the great bow) / निर्वीर्यः (deprived of prowess) / जामदग्न्यः (the son of Jamadagni) / असौ (that one) / रामः (Rama) / रामम् (at Rama) / उदैक्षत (looked up)
ramayan::1975.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1975.essence: Rama's strength leaves the challenger speechless before a fight begins.
ramayan::1975.simple_meaning: Rama lifts the great bow, and the whole scene falls still. Parasurama, once fierce, stands powerless and stares in amazement.
ramayan::1975.simple_insight: Power can end a conflict without another blow.
ramayan::1975.detailed_meaning: At the bow of Shiva, Rama proves his strength before the gathered kings. Parasurama, the warrior-sage who came to test him, suddenly loses his force. The verse captures the instant before the old challenger yields.
ramayan::1975.modern_relevance: You walk into the room expecting a showdown, but one calm action ends it before words can harden into battle.
ramayan::1975.insight: It shows how overwhelming presence can silence resistance before force is used.

ramayan::1976.verse_sanskrit: तेजोभिहतवीर्यत्वाज्जामदग्न्यो जडीकृत: । रामं कमलपत्राक्षं मन्दं मन्दमुवाच ह । । 17612 । ।
ramayan::1976.verse_hindi: His energy subdued by Ramas prowess, the paralysed, Parasurama, son of Jamadagni spoke in gentle words to him whose eyes resembled the lotus petals:
ramayan::1976.english_translation: His energy subdued by Rama's prowess, the paralysed Parasurama, son of Jamadagni, spoke in gentle words to him whose eyes resembled lotus petals.
ramayan::1976.translation_literal: तेजोभिः (by prowess/energy) / हतवीर्यत्वात् (because his strength was struck down) / जामदग्न्यः (the son of Jamadagni) / जडीकृतः (made motionless) / रामम् (to Rama) / कमलपत्राक्षम् (lotus-petaled-eyed) / मन्दम् मन्दम् (very gently) / उवाच (spoke) / ह (indeed)
ramayan::1976.speaker: Parasurama
ramayan::1976.essence: Pride falls silent when it meets a power it cannot answer.
ramayan::1976.simple_meaning: Parasurama, overwhelmed by Rama's power, can only speak softly to him.
ramayan::1976.simple_insight: Even a fierce pride can be silenced by a greater force.
ramayan::1976.detailed_meaning: After Rama strings the great bow, Parasurama's force collapses. The once-formidable son of Jamadagni stands stunned before Rama and begins to speak gently, marking the turning point from challenge to surrender in the bow contest.
ramayan::1976.modern_relevance: A person who came in ready to argue suddenly goes quiet when the facts land. The room changes the moment strength meets a greater strength.
ramayan::1976.insight: It shows how confrontation can dissolve once a deeper force has already won.

ramayan::1977.verse_sanskrit: काश्यपाय मया दत्ता यदा पूर्वं वसुन्धरा । विषये मे न वस्तव्यमिति मां काश्यपोऽब्रवीत् । । 17613 । ।
ramayan::1977.verse_hindi: When I gave this entire earth to Kasyapa, he said to me, you shall not live in my country.
ramayan::1977.english_translation: When I gave the whole earth to Kasyapa long ago, Kasyapa told me, 'You must not live in my land.'
ramayan::1977.translation_literal: काश्यपाय (to Kasyapa) / मया (by me) / दत्ता (given) / यदा (when) / पूर्वं (long ago) / वसुन्धरा (the earth) / विषये (in the land) / मे (of me) / न (not) / वस्तव्यम् (to be lived) / इति (thus) / मां (me) / काश्यपः (Kasyapa) / अब्रवीत् (said)
ramayan::1977.speaker: Parasurama
ramayan::1977.essence: A past promise still decides what you may do now.
ramayan::1977.simple_meaning: Parasurama recalls that after giving the earth to Kasyapa, he was told he could not stay in that land.
ramayan::1977.simple_insight: A promise can still bind you long after the moment has passed.
ramayan::1977.detailed_meaning: Rama has just broken Parasurama's pride. Now the warrior-sage explains why he must step aside: long ago, after gifting the earth to Kasyapa, he accepted a vow that forbade him from living there. The verse prepares his withdrawal.
ramayan::1977.modern_relevance: You made a promise years ago, and it still reaches into your life today. The old commitment is why you cannot simply do what feels convenient now.
ramayan::1977.insight: It shifts attention from personal impulse to the binding force of an old vow.

ramayan::1978.verse_sanskrit: सोऽहं गुरुवच: कुर्वन् पृथिव्यां न वसे निशाम् । कृता प्रतिज्ञा काकुत्स्थ कृता भू: काश्यपस्य हि । । 17614 । ।
ramayan::1978.verse_hindi: O Descendant of Kakustha having gifted this earth to Kasyapa, I promised him that I would not live here, during night time. For the earth belongs to him.
ramayan::1978.english_translation: O descendant of Kakustha, having given this earth to Kasyapa, I made a promise that I would not live here at night. The earth belongs to Kasyapa, indeed.
ramayan::1978.translation_literal: सः (he) / अहम् (I) / गुरु-वचः (teacher's word) / कुर्वन् (doing, keeping) / पृथिव्याम् (on the earth) / न (not) / वसे (I live) / निशाम् (at night) / कृता (made) / प्रतिज्ञा (promise) / काकुत्स्थ (O descendant of Kakustha) / कृता (made) / भूः (earth) / काश्यपस्य (of Kasyapa) / हि (indeed)
ramayan::1978.speaker: Parasurama
ramayan::1978.essence: A true promise still binds you after the moment has passed.
ramayan::1978.simple_meaning: Parashurama says he is bound by a promise: after giving the earth to Kasyapa, he will not stay on it at night.
ramayan::1978.simple_insight: Keeping your word can matter more than keeping your comfort.
ramayan::1978.detailed_meaning: After Rama breaks Parashurama's bow, the wounded ascetic explains why he must leave. He once gave the earth to Kasyapa and vowed not to remain on it at night. Even in defeat, he will not abandon his promise.
ramayan::1978.modern_relevance: You promised something before you knew the cost. Now the cost is real, but the promise still stands in front of you.
ramayan::1978.insight: It shifts the mind from convenience to vow: what you said matters even when it becomes inconvenient.

ramayan::1979.verse_sanskrit: तदिमां त्वं गतिं वीर हन्तुं नार्हसि राघव । मनोजवं गमिष्यामि महेन्द्रं पर्वतोत्तमम् । । 17615 । ।
ramayan::1979.verse_hindi: For this, you should not destroy my mobility, O valiant son of the Raghus. I shall go to Mahendra, the best of mountains, with the speed of mind.
ramayan::1979.english_translation: For this, you should not destroy my mobility, O valiant son of the Raghus. I shall go to Mahendra, the best of mountains, with the speed of mind.
ramayan::1979.translation_literal: तद् (therefore/for this) / इमाम् (this) / त्वम् (you) / गतिम् (movement/power of going) / वीर (O valiant one) / हन्तुम् (to destroy) / नार्हसि (you do not deserve/should not) / राघव (O descendant of Raghu) / मनोजवम् (mind-speed) / गमिष्यामि (I shall go) / महेन्द्रम् (to Mahendra) / पर्वतोत्तमम् (best of mountains)
ramayan::1979.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1979.essence: What has fulfilled its time should not be forced to stay.
ramayan::1979.simple_meaning: The speaker asks Rama not to stop his power to move and says he will go to Mahendra mountain at the speed of thought.
ramayan::1979.simple_insight: Some beings cannot be held down; their nature is to move on.
ramayan::1979.detailed_meaning: A powerful being is speaking to Rama after explaining why he must leave this place. He asks Rama not to block his movement, then says he will depart for Mahendra mountain with effortless speed. The verse is a transition in an ongoing exchange, not a complete teaching.
ramayan::1979.modern_relevance: A friend is packing to leave after a hard conversation, already halfway out the door. You can feel that some departures are not rejection — they are simply the next movement of a life already in motion.
ramayan::1979.insight: It shifts attention from resistance to the inevitability of release and movement.

ramayan::1980.verse_sanskrit: लोकास्त्वप्रतिमा राम निर्जितास्तपसा मया । जहि तान् शरमुख्येन मा भूत्कालस्य पर्यय: । । 17616 । ।
ramayan::1980.verse_hindi: Strike with the, principal arrow the unrivalled worlds conquered by my asceticism. Do not delay, O Rama
ramayan::1980.english_translation: Strike with the chief arrow the incomparable worlds I have won through ascetic power. Do not delay, Rama.
ramayan::1980.translation_literal: लोकाः (worlds) / तु (indeed) / अप्रतिमा (incomparable) / राम (Rama) / निर्जिताः (conquered) / तपसा (by ascetic power) / मया (by me) / जहि (strike down) / तान् (those) / शरमुख्येन (with the chief arrow) / मा (do not) / भूत् (be) / कालस्य (of time) / पर्ययः (delay)
ramayan::1980.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1980.essence: Even the highest attainments must be released to what comes next.
ramayan::1980.simple_meaning: The speaker asks Rama to end it quickly with his best arrow. Even the worlds gained through great discipline are not permanent.
ramayan::1980.simple_insight: There is relief in seeing that even the highest achievements cannot be held forever.
ramayan::1980.detailed_meaning: A sage who has earned vast worlds through severe tapas stands before Rama and asks for release. He does not cling to his achievement. Instead, he points to the limits of all attained states and urges Rama to act without delay.
ramayan::1980.modern_relevance: You finally get the promotion, the title, the proof that you made it — and still, it cannot stay fixed in your hands. The verse cuts through that illusion before time does.
ramayan::1980.insight: It shifts attention from possession to impermanence, reminding you that even earned attainments are temporary.

ramayan::1981.verse_sanskrit: अक्षय्यं मधुहन्तारं जानामि त्वां सुरेश्वरम् । धनुषोऽस्य परामर्शात् स्वस्ति तेऽस्तु परंतप । । 17617 । ।
ramayan::1981.verse_hindi: By the fact that you have stretched this bow, I have come to know that you are Visnu, Lord of the gods, slayer of Madhu, O Imperishable one O Tormentor of enemies Fare well.
