ramayan::1981.english_translation: By the fact that you have stretched this bow, I have come to know that you are Vishnu, Lord of the gods, slayer of Madhu, O Imperishable One. Fare well, O scorcher of foes.
ramayan::1981.translation_literal: अक्षय्यं (imperishable) / मधुहन्तारं (slayer of Madhu) / जानामि (I know) / त्वां (you) / सुरेश्वरम् (Lord of the gods) / धनुषः (of the bow) / अस्य (this) / परामर्शात् (by the touching/stretching) / स्वस्ति (farewell / may it be well) / ते (to you) / अस्तु (let there be) / परंतप (O scorcher of foes)
ramayan::1981.speaker: Brahma
ramayan::1981.essence: The bow reveals the divine identity already present.
ramayan::1981.simple_meaning: Brahma recognizes Rama's divine identity the moment he handles the bow. The act is enough to reveal that this is Vishnu himself.
ramayan::1981.simple_insight: Recognition comes from direct contact, not argument.
ramayan::1981.detailed_meaning: Brahma has come with the gods to witness Rama's victory. After urging him to act, he now sees the bow in Rama's hands and understands who stands before him. The moment turns from request to revelation.
ramayan::1981.modern_relevance: Someone finally sees your competence when you handle the hard task without flinching. No speech changes their mind — the way you meet the challenge does.
ramayan::1981.insight: It shifts understanding from labels to evidence of capability.

ramayan::1982.verse_hindi: All your deeds are incomparable. You are unassailable in combat. All these hosts of gods have assembled here and are looking at you.
ramayan::1982.english_translation: All your deeds are incomparable. You are unassailable in combat. All these hosts of gods have assembled here and are looking at you.
ramayan::1982.translation_literal: एते (these) / सुरगणाः (hosts of gods) / सर्वे (all) / निरीक्षन्ते (are looking at) / समागताः (assembled) / त्वाम् (at you) / अप्रतिमकर्माणम् (one whose deeds are incomparable) / अप्रतिद्वन्द्वम् (without a rival) / आहवे (in battle)
ramayan::1982.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::1982.essence: Your greatness is confirmed by what cannot stand against you.
ramayan::1982.simple_meaning: The speaker says Rama’s actions are unmatched, his strength in battle cannot be resisted, and the gathered gods are watching him.
ramayan::1982.simple_insight: There is awe in being seen for what you truly are.
ramayan::1982.detailed_meaning: In the heavenly assembly after Rama stretches the bow, the gods gather and recognise what is happening before them. The speaker praises Rama as unmatched in action and unbeatable in combat, marking this as a revelation of his true stature.
ramayan::1982.modern_relevance: When everyone in the room goes quiet because they can feel something decisive has just happened, recognition arrives before applause. You don't need to announce your worth when reality has already done it.
ramayan::1982.insight: It shifts attention from self-display to being fully seen in the truth of your actions.

ramayan::1983.verse_sanskrit: न चेयं मम काकुत्स्थ व्रीडा भवितुमर्हति । त्वया त्रैलोक्यनाथेन यदहं विमुखीकृत: । । 17619 । ।
ramayan::1983.verse_hindi: I have been defeated by you, O Descendant of Kakustha lord of the three worlds. Therefore, it is not right for me to feel ashamed.
ramayan::1983.english_translation: I have been defeated by you, O descendant of Kakustha, lord of the three worlds. Therefore, it is not right for me to feel ashamed.
ramayan::1983.translation_literal: न / not / च / and / इयम् (this) / मम (my) / काकुत्स्थ (O descendant of Kakustha) / व्रीडा (shame) / भवितुम् (to become) / अर्हति (is fit) / त्वया (by you) / त्रैलोक्यनाथेन (by the lord of the three worlds) / यत् (because) / अहम् (I) / विमुखीकृतः (defeated, turned back) ।
ramayan::1983.speaker: Ravana
ramayan::1983.essence: Real defeat can strip away false shame.
ramayan::1983.simple_meaning: Ravana admits Rama has defeated him and says that, in such a defeat, shame has no place.
ramayan::1983.simple_insight: Even a fallen pride can recognize the truth and stop pretending.
ramayan::1983.detailed_meaning: Ravana has just realized Rama is no ordinary warrior but the lord of the three worlds. Faced with that truth, he drops the posture of wounded pride and admits defeat. The moment turns the battle into recognition.
ramayan::1983.modern_relevance: You lose the argument, the deal, or the match — and the harder part is not the loss but the pride around it. Sometimes dignity begins the moment you stop defending the indefensible.
ramayan::1983.insight: It shifts the mind from protecting ego to acknowledging reality cleanly.

ramayan::1984.verse_sanskrit: शरमप्रतिमं राम मोक्तुमर्हसि सुव्रत । शरमोक्षे गमिष्यामि महेन्द्रं पर्वतोत्तमम् । । 17620 । ।
ramayan::1984.verse_hindi: You are faithful to vows O Rama This arrow has no equal in prowess. It behoves of you to release it against me. After its release I shall go to the excellent Mahendra  mountain.
ramayan::1984.english_translation: You are faithful to vows, Rama. This arrow is unmatched in power. You should release it against me. After it is released, I will go to the great mountain Mahendra.
ramayan::1984.translation_literal: शरम् (arrow) / अप्रतिमम् (unmatched) / राम (Rama) / मोक्तुम् (to release) / अर्हसि (you should) / सुव्रत (of good vows) / शरमोक्षे (after the arrow is released) / गमिष्यामि (I will go) / महेन्द्रम् (Mahendra) / पर्वतोत्तमम् (the best of mountains)
ramayan::1984.speaker: Parasurama
ramayan::1984.essence: The challenge ends when the final weapon is finally named.
ramayan::1984.simple_meaning: Parasurama challenges Rama to use the unmatched arrow against him, and says he will then depart to Mahendra mountain.
ramayan::1984.simple_insight: Some confrontations end only when both sides accept what must happen.
ramayan::1984.detailed_meaning: Parasurama, having already acknowledged Rama's greatness, now offers the final test. He asks Rama to release the unmatched arrow at him, promising to withdraw to Mahendra afterward. The moment is a dramatic handover, not a teaching.
ramayan::1984.modern_relevance: A tense conversation reaches its limit, and both people know words are over. One final action will settle what pride and challenge have been circling.
ramayan::1984.insight: It marks the point where argument gives way to decisive action.

ramayan::1985.verse_sanskrit: तथा ब्रुवति रामे तु जामदग्नये प्रतापवान् । रामो दाशरथि श्श्रीमान् चिक्षेप शरमुत्तमम् । । 17621 । ।
ramayan::1985.verse_hindi: Thus spoke  Parasurama, son of Jamadagni to Rama, the valiant son of Dasaratha who (then) discharged the principal arrow.
ramayan::1985.english_translation: Thus spoke Parasurama, son of Jamadagni, to Rama, the valiant son of Dasaratha, who then discharged the supreme arrow.
ramayan::1985.translation_literal: तथा (thus) / ब्रुवति (speaking) / रामे (to Rama) / तु (indeed) / जामदग्नये (to the son of Jamadagni) / प्रतापवान् (the valiant one) / रामः (Rama) / दाशरथिः (son of Dasaratha) / श्रीमान् (splendid) / चिक्षेप (discharged) / शरम् (arrow) / उत्तमम् (supreme)
ramayan::1985.speaker: Parasurama
ramayan::1985.essence: Rama answers challenge with a single, final act.
ramayan::1985.simple_meaning: Parasurama speaks, and Rama answers by releasing his supreme arrow.
ramayan::1985.simple_insight: Some confrontations end only when action finally answers words.
ramayan::1985.detailed_meaning: Parasurama has challenged Rama and demanded that he prove himself. After the exchange, Rama, son of Dasaratha, releases the decisive arrow. The moment is a turning point, but it is still part of the unfolding confrontation, not a teaching on its own.
ramayan::1985.modern_relevance: A tense conversation reaches the point where words are no longer enough. Someone has to act, and the next move will decide everything.
ramayan::1985.insight: It shifts attention from verbal challenge to decisive response under pressure.

ramayan::1986.verse_sanskrit: स हतान् दृश्य रामेण स्वांल्लोकांस्तपसार्जितान् । जामदग्न्यो जगामाशु महेन्द्रं पर्वतोत्तमम् । । 17622 । ।
ramayan::1986.verse_hindi: Having witnessed the destruction of those regions earned by him through asceticism, the son of Jamadagni left for the best of mountains Mahendra.
ramayan::1986.english_translation: Having witnessed the destruction of those regions earned by him through asceticism, the son of Jamadagni left for the best of mountains Mahendra.
ramayan::1986.translation_literal: स (he) / हतान् (destroyed) / दृश्य (having seen) / रामेण (by Rama) / स्वान् लोकान् (his own realms) / तपसा (through asceticism) / अर्जितान् (earned) / जामदग्न्यः (the son of Jamadagni) / जगाम (went) / आशु (quickly) / महेन्द्रम् (to Mahendra) / पर्वतोत्तमम् (best of mountains)
ramayan::1986.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1986.essence: Recognition ends the struggle before words do.
ramayan::1986.simple_meaning: Parasurama sees that Rama has destroyed the worlds he earned through austerity, and he quickly departs for Mount Mahendra.
ramayan::1986.simple_insight: Some losses end a confrontation instantly. Pride falls away when reality becomes undeniable.
ramayan::1986.detailed_meaning: After Rama’s arrow strips away Parasurama’s hard-won power, the warrior-sage sees the ruin of the realms he earned by austerity. There is nothing left to contest. He turns away and leaves for Mahendra, ending the clash.
ramayan::1986.modern_relevance: You rehearse your argument, then one clear fact lands and the whole fight goes quiet. The moment of recognition can end what pride was trying to continue.
ramayan::1986.insight: It shifts attention from winning the exchange to recognising when resistance has already been broken.

ramayan::1987.verse_sanskrit: ततो वितिमिरास्सर्वा दिशश्चोपदिशस्तथा । सुरा स्सर्षिगणा रामं प्रशशंसुरुदायुधम् । । 17623 । ।
ramayan::1987.verse_hindi: Thereafter all the quarters including the intermediaries were cleared of darkness. Hosts of sages and gods extolled Rama when he wielded the bow.
ramayan::1987.english_translation: Thereafter all the quarters, including the intermediary directions, became free of darkness. Hosts of sages and gods praised Rama as he stood armed with the bow.
ramayan::1987.translation_literal: ततः (thereafter) / वितिमिराः (free of darkness) / सर्वाः (all) / दिशः (directions) / च (and) / उपदिशः (intermediate directions) / तथा (also) / सुराः (gods) / सर्षिगणाः (with hosts of sages) / रामम् (Rama) / प्रशशंसुः (praised) / उदायुधम् (with uplifted weapon/bow)
ramayan::1987.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1987.essence: Right action clears the air before anyone speaks again.
ramayan::1987.simple_meaning: After Parasurama's defeat, the sky and all directions cleared, and sages and radiant beings praised Rama.
ramayan::1987.simple_insight: A decisive act can restore order so fully that even the world seems to breathe again.
ramayan::1987.detailed_meaning: Parasurama has just confronted Rama and been overcome. In the immediate aftermath, the darkness lifts from every direction, and sages along with radiant beings praise Rama holding his bow. The verse marks the release of tension, not a new teaching.
ramayan::1987.modern_relevance: After the tense meeting ends, everyone in the room finally exhales. The argument is over, the air clears, and people can see who held steady under pressure.
ramayan::1987.insight: It shifts attention from conflict itself to the calm that follows rightful action.

ramayan::1988.verse_sanskrit: रामं दाशरथिं रामो जामदग्न्य: प्रशस्य च । तत: प्रदक्षिणी कृत्य जगामात्मगतिं प्रभु: । । 17624 । ।
ramayan::1988.verse_hindi: Parasurama, the competent son of Jamadagni, having praised Rama, the son of
ramayan::1988.english_translation: Having praised Rama, the son of Dasaratha, Parasurama circumambulated him and then departed for his own abode.
ramayan::1988.translation_literal: रामम् (Rama) / दाशरथिम् (son of Dasaratha) / रामः (Parasurama) / जामदग्न्यः (son of Jamadagni) / प्रशस्य (having praised) / च (and) / ततः (then) / प्रदक्षिणी-कृत्य (having circumambulated) / जगाम (went) / आत्म-गतिम् (to his own abode) / प्रभुः (the mighty one)
ramayan::1988.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1988.essence: Power becomes complete when even an opponent bows and leaves.
ramayan::1988.simple_meaning: Parasurama praises Rama, circles him respectfully, and leaves. The confrontation ends without further conflict.
ramayan::1988.simple_insight: Sometimes the strongest ending is to step back with respect.
ramayan::1988.detailed_meaning: After Rama's display of power, the fierce Parasurama is stripped of his challenge. He praises Rama, walks around him in reverence, and withdraws to his own realm. The scene closes the crisis, not with victory talk, but with recognition.
ramayan::1988.modern_relevance: A tense argument ends when the other person finally sees your point and stops pushing. No speech follows. Just a quiet shift, a nod, and the room breathes again.
ramayan::1988.insight: It shows that true strength can end conflict by earning respect, not by prolonging force.

ramayan::1989.verse_sanskrit: गते रामे प्रशान्तात्मा रामो दाशरथिर्धनु: । वरुणायाप्रमेयाय ददौ हस्ते ससायकम् । । 1771 । ।
ramayan::1989.verse_hindi: When Parasurama departed, Rama, son of Dasaratha with a serene mind gave the bow along with the arrow to Varuna of immeasurable strength.
ramayan::1989.english_translation: When Parasurama departed, Rama, son of Dasaratha, with a serene mind gave the bow along with the arrow to Varuna of immeasurable strength.
ramayan::1989.translation_literal: गते (having departed) / रामे (when Rama) / प्रशान्तात्मा (with a serene mind) / रामः (Rama) / दाशरथिः (son of Dasaratha) / धनुः (the bow) / वरुणाय (to Varuna) / अप्रमेयाय (to the immeasurable one) / ददौ (gave) / हस्ते (into the hand) / ससायकम् (together with the arrow)
ramayan::1989.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1989.essence: Victory ends in restraint, not possession.
ramayan::1989.simple_meaning: After Parasurama left, Rama calmly handed over the bow and arrow to Varuna.
ramayan::1989.simple_insight: When the confrontation ends, the right action is simply to release what was borrowed.
ramayan::1989.detailed_meaning: Parasurama has just tested Rama and withdrawn. The tension breaks at once: Rama, still composed, returns the divine bow and arrow to Varuna. The moment closes one ordeal and prepares for the next exchange with his father and the sages.
ramayan::1989.modern_relevance: The argument is over, the room has gone quiet, and you finally hand back the thing that kept everyone tense. Not every victory needs to be held onto.
ramayan::1989.insight: It shifts attention from triumph to release, showing that composure includes giving things back cleanly.

ramayan::1990.verse_sanskrit: अभिवाद्य ततो रामो वसिष्ठप्रमुखानृषीन् । पितरं विह्वलं दृष्ट्वा प्रोवाच रघुनन्दन: । । 1772 । ।
ramayan::1990.verse_hindi: Thereafter Rama the descendant of the Raghus, paid obeisance to Vasishta and other rishis, and looked at his father who appeared agitated said:
ramayan::1990.english_translation: Thereafter Rama, descendant of the Raghus, bowed to Vasishta and the other sages, and seeing his father distraught, spoke.
ramayan::1990.translation_literal: अभिवाद्य (having bowed) / ततः (then) / रामः (Rama) / वसिष्ठ-प्रमुखान् (led by Vasishta) / ऋषीन् (sages) / पितरम् (his father) / विह्वलम् (agitated) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / प्रोवाच (spoke) / रघुनन्दनः (the delight of the Raghu line)
ramayan::1990.speaker: Rama
ramayan::1990.essence: Victory is complete only when humility follows it.
ramayan::1990.simple_meaning: Rama bows to the sages and then speaks to his upset father.
ramayan::1990.simple_insight: Respect comes first, even in a moment of triumph.
ramayan::1990.detailed_meaning: After Parasurama leaves, Rama first honors Vasishta and the gathered sages. Only then does he turn to Dasharatha, who is visibly shaken by the crisis that has just passed. The verse is a bridge from confrontation to resolution.
ramayan::1990.modern_relevance: You finish a tense family argument and, before anything else, you acknowledge the elder who held the room together.
ramayan::1990.insight: It shows that composure includes courtesy, even after danger has passed.

ramayan::1991.verse_sanskrit: जामदग्न्यो गतो राम: प्रयातु चतुरङ्गिणी । अयोध्याभिमुखी सेना त्वया नाथेन पालिता । । 1773 । ।
ramayan::1991.verse_hindi: Parasurama, son of Jamadagni, has gone. Let the four divisions of the army of  which you are the commander proceed towards Ayodhya.
ramayan::1991.english_translation: Parasurama, son of Jamadagni, has gone. Let the fourfold army, led by you, proceed toward Ayodhya.
ramayan::1991.translation_literal: जामदग्न्यः (son of Jamadagni) / गतः (has gone) / रामः (Parasurama) / प्रयातु (let proceed) / चतुरङ्गिणी (fourfold) / अयोध्याभिमुखी (facing Ayodhya) / सेना (army) / त्वया (by you) / नाथेन (by the commander/lord) / पालिता (protected/led)
ramayan::1991.speaker: Rama
ramayan::1991.essence: The threat is over; now the journey can continue.
ramayan::1991.simple_meaning: Parasurama has left, and the army can now move on toward Ayodhya under your command.
ramayan::1991.simple_insight: The crisis has passed, and movement can resume.
ramayan::1991.detailed_meaning: After Rama's encounter with Parasurama, the tension breaks. With the danger gone, Rama turns back to the practical task before him: the army that has been waiting can now continue toward Ayodhya under its leader's protection.
ramayan::1991.modern_relevance: The tense meeting is over, and everyone is still waiting for your signal. Once the hard moment passes, the practical next step matters most.
ramayan::1991.insight: It shifts attention from dramatic confrontation to orderly continuation.

ramayan::1992.verse_sanskrit: सन्दिशस्व महाराज सेनां त्वच्छासने स्थिताम् । शासनं काङ्क्षते सेना चातकालिर्जलं यथा । । 1774 । ।
ramayan::1992.verse_hindi: The army which is under your command O King is awaiting your orders like the chatakas awaiting water. Direct them (to proceed).
ramayan::1992.english_translation: The army under your command, O King, is waiting for your orders like chatakas waiting for rain. Give the command to move.
ramayan::1992.translation_literal: सन्दिशस्व (give the order) / महाराज (O great king) / सेनां (the army) / त्वच्छासने (under your command) / स्थिताम् (standing) / शासनं (command) / काङ्क्षते (desires/waits for) / सेना (the army) / चातकालिर् (like the chataka bird) / जलं (water) / यथा (as)
ramayan::1992.speaker: Rama
ramayan::1992.essence: A waiting force becomes effective only when command arrives.
ramayan::1992.simple_meaning: Rama is told to give the order, because the army is ready and waiting for him to command it forward.
ramayan::1992.simple_insight: Readiness still needs a clear command before action can begin.
ramayan::1992.detailed_meaning: After Parasurama has departed, Rama stands before the assembled forces. The commander tells him the army is already under his control and only awaits his word, like a bird thirsting for rain. This is a bridge verse, not a teaching.
ramayan::1992.modern_relevance: A team is waiting in the conference room, laptops open, eyes on you. The plan is ready, but nothing moves until you speak.
ramayan::1992.insight: It highlights the moment where preparation becomes action through one decisive order.

ramayan::1993.verse_sanskrit: रामस्य वचनं श्रुत्वा राजा दशरथ स्सुतम् । बाहुभ्यां सम्परिष्वज्य मूर्ध्नि चाघ्राय राघवम् । । 1775 । । गतो राम इति श्रुत्वा हृष्ट: प्रमुदितो नृप: । पुनर्जातं तदा मेने पुत्रमात्मानमेव च । । 1776 । ।
ramayan::1993.verse_hindi: On hearing the words Parasurama has departed from Rama, king Dasaratha embraced him and kissed his forehead. The king, immensely happy, felt he and his son were reborn.
ramayan::1993.english_translation: On hearing that Parasurama had gone from Rama, king Dasharatha embraced his son and kissed his forehead. Overjoyed, he felt reborn, along with his son.
ramayan::1993.translation_literal: रामस्य (of Rama) / वचनं (the words) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / राजा (the king) / दशरथः (Dasharatha) / सुतम् (his son) / बाहुभ्याम् (with both arms) / सम्परिष्वज्य (having embraced) / मूर्ध्नि (on the head) / च (and) / आघ्राय (having kissed) / राघवम् (Raghava) / गतो (gone) / रामः (Rama) / इति (thus) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / हृष्टः (delighted) / प्रमुदितः (overjoyed) / नृपः (the king) / पुनर्जातम् (reborn) / तदा (then) / मेने (considered) / पुत्रम् (his son) / आत्मानम् (himself) / एव (indeed) / च (and)
ramayan::1993.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1993.essence: When danger ends, love feels newly alive.
ramayan::1993.simple_meaning: Dasharatha is overwhelmed with relief when he hears that the crisis has passed. He embraces Rama and feels as if both of them have been given back to life.
ramayan::1993.simple_insight: Some relief is so deep it feels like being born again.
ramayan::1993.detailed_meaning: Parasurama has just withdrawn from the confrontation, and the danger hanging over Rama is gone. Dasharatha rushes to his son, holds him close, and kisses his forehead. The moment is pure release after fear.
ramayan::1993.modern_relevance: You finally get the message that the worst has passed. Your whole body softens before you can even think, because relief can feel like coming back to life.
ramayan::1993.insight: It shows how fear can make safety feel like rebirth, not just comfort.

ramayan::1994.verse_sanskrit: चोदयामास तां सेनां जगामाशु तत: पुरीम् । पताकाध्वजिनीं रम्यां तूर्योद्घुष्टनिनादिताम् । । 1777 । । सिक्तराज पथां रम्यां प्रकीर्णकुसुमोत्कराम् । राजप्रवेशसुमुखै: पौरैर्मङ्गलवादिभि: । । 1778 । । सम्पूर्णां प्राविशद्राजा जनौघैस्समलङ्कृताम् ।
ramayan::1994.verse_hindi: Thereafter, king Dasaratha directed his army to proceed speedily in advance. When he    reached the city of Ayodhya it looked welldecorated with flags and banners. It  resounded with trumpets. The royal highways were sprinkiled with water and strewn with flowers. It was filled with groups of people. Awaiting with delight the arrival of  the king the citizens produced merry sounds with musical instruments.
ramayan::1994.english_translation: Thereafter, king Dasaratha directed his army to move ahead quickly. When he reached Ayodhya, the city was beautifully adorned with flags and banners, echoed with trumpets, and lined with water-sprinkled, flower-strewn roads. The delighted citizens welcomed him with music as he entered the city filled with crowds.
ramayan::1994.translation_literal: चोदयामास (he directed) / ताम् (that) / सेनाम् (army) / जगाम (went) / आशु (quickly) / ततः (then) / पुरीम् (to the city) / पताकाध्वजिनीम् (with flags and banners) / रम्याम् (beautiful) / तूर्योद्घुष्टनिनादिताम् (resounding with trumpets) / सिक्तराजपथाम् (with sprinkled royal roads) / रम्याम् (beautiful) / प्रकीर्णकुसुमोत्कराम् (strewn with heaps of flowers) / राजप्रवेशसुमुखैः (with auspicious citizens for the king's entry) / पौरैः (by citizens) / मङ्गलवादिभिः (speaking auspicious words) / सम्पूर्णाम् (filled) / प्राविशत् (entered) / राजा (the king) / जनौघैः (with crowds of people) / समलङ्कृताम् (adorned)
ramayan::1994.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1994.essence: Ayodhya welcomes its king with full celebration.
ramayan::1994.simple_meaning: Dasaratha returns to Ayodhya in triumph. The city is decorated, the roads are prepared, and the people welcome him with joy and celebration.
ramayan::1994.simple_insight: Sometimes a homecoming is felt by everyone in the city, not just the person returning.
ramayan::1994.detailed_meaning: After the encounter with Paraśurama, Dasaratha turns back toward Ayodhya. The army moves ahead, the streets are prepared, and the whole city rises to greet its king. This is a scene of public relief and royal arrival, not a teaching moment.
ramayan::1994.insight: It records a ceremonial return, not a moral instruction.

ramayan::1995.verse_sanskrit: पौरै: प्रत्युद्गतो दूरं द्विजैश्च पुरवासिभि: । पुत्रैरनुगत श्श्रीमान् श्रीमद्भिश्च महायशा: । । 1779 । । प्रविवेश गृहं राजा हिमवत्सदृशं पुनः ।
ramayan::1995.verse_hindi: Prosperous king Dasaratha of great fame followed by his elegant sons entered the city of Ayodhya while the citizens and brahmins came forward from a long distance to welcome him who reentered his palace looking like the Himalayan moutain.
ramayan::1995.english_translation: Prosperous king Dasaratha of great fame, followed by his elegant sons, entered Ayodhya. The citizens and brahmins came forward from far away to welcome him, and he reentered his palace looking like the Himalayan mountain.
ramayan::1995.translation_literal: पौरैः (by the citizens) / प्रत्युद्गतः (welcomed in advance) / दूरम् (from far away) / द्विजैः (by the brahmins) / च (and) / पुरवासिभिः (by the city-dwellers) / पुत्रैः (by the sons) / अनुगतः (followed) / श्रीमान् (the prosperous one) / श्रीमद्भिः (by the splendid ones) / च (and) / महायशाः (the very famous one) / प्रविवेश (entered) / गृहम् (the house/palace) / राजा (the king) / हिमवत्सदृशम् (like Mount Himalaya) / पुनः (again)
ramayan::1995.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1995.essence: A victorious return can still feel like a mountain moving home.
ramayan::1995.simple_meaning: Dasaratha returns to Ayodhya in honour, welcomed by the people and priests, with his sons beside him.
ramayan::1995.simple_insight: A homecoming can still feel vast and solemn, even when it is joyful.
ramayan::1995.detailed_meaning: Dasaratha has returned to Ayodhya after the tense events outside the city. Citizens, brahmins, and townspeople come out to greet him from a distance, while his sons accompany him. The verse simply paints the royal homecoming before the household scene begins.
ramayan::1995.modern_relevance: You walk back into your house after a long, hard day, and everyone is already waiting at the door. The relief is real, but so is the weight you bring with you.
ramayan::1995.insight: It shifts attention from action to atmosphere, showing how a public return can carry private gravity.

ramayan::1996.verse_sanskrit: ननन्द सजनो राजा गृहे कामै स्सुपूजित: । । 17710 । । कौसल्या च सुमित्रा च कैकेयी च सुमध्यमा । वधूप्रतिग्रहे युक्ता याश्चान्या राजयोषित: । । 17711 । ।
ramayan::1996.verse_hindi: The king and his kith and kin were received with honour in a pleasing manner. Kausalya, Sumitra and Kaikeyi of slender waist and other women attending on the king were busy in receiving the new brides.
ramayan::1996.english_translation: The king and his kith and kin were received with honour in a pleasing manner. Kausalya, Sumitra and Kaikeyi of slender waist and other women attending on the king were busy in receiving the new brides.
ramayan::1996.translation_literal: ननन्द (rejoiced) / सजनः (with kinsmen) / राजा (the king) / गृहे (in the house) / कामैः (with delights) / स्सुपूजितः (well-honoured) / कौसल्या (Kausalya) / च (and) / सुमित्रा (Sumitra) / च (and) / कैकेयी (Kaikeyi) / च (and) / सुमध्यमा (of slender waist) / वधूप्रतिग्रहे (in receiving the brides) / युक्ताः (engaged) / याश्चान्या (and other) / राजयोषितः (women of the king)
ramayan::1996.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1996.essence: The household turns to welcome the brides.
ramayan::1996.simple_meaning: Dasaratha returns home joyfully, and the queens prepare to welcome the new brides with honour.
ramayan::1996.simple_insight: Some moments are only about welcome, not wisdom.
ramayan::1996.detailed_meaning: Dasaratha has come back to Ayodhya with Rama and Lakshmana after the wedding. The palace is alive with celebration, and Kausalya, Sumitra, Kaikeyi, and the other royal women are occupied with receiving the brides. This is a scene of household joy, not a teaching verse.
ramayan::1996.modern_relevance: You come home after a long, important day, and everyone is already moving around the kitchen, making space, arranging clothes, welcoming the people who matter.
ramayan::1996.insight: It simply marks the arrival of a joyful family moment before the next event unfolds.

ramayan::1997.verse_sanskrit: ततस्सीतां महाभागामूर्मिलां च यशस्विनीम् । कुशध्वजसुते चोभे जगृहुर्नृपपत्नय: । । 17712 । ।
ramayan::1997.verse_hindi: Thereafter the queens received the highly fortunate Sita, Urmila of high fame and both the daughters of Kusadhwaja, Mandavi and Srutakirti.
ramayan::1997.english_translation: Thereafter the queens received the highly fortunate Sita, Urmila of high fame and both the daughters of Kusadhwaja, Mandavi and Srutakirti.
ramayan::1997.translation_literal: ततस् (thereafter) / सीताम् (Sita) / महाभागाम् (highly fortunate) / ऊर्मिलाम् (Urmila) / च (and) / यशस्विनीम् (famous, renowned) / कुशध्वजसुते (the daughters of Kushadhwaja) / च (and) / उभे (both) / जगृहु: (received) / नृपपत्नय: (the queens)
ramayan::1997.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1997.simple_meaning: The queens welcomed Sita, Urmila, Mandavi, and Shrutakirti with honour.
ramayan::1997.simple_insight: Some moments are simple: love is shown by how people receive one another.
ramayan::1997.detailed_meaning: Rama has returned to Ayodhya after exile, and the household is gathered in celebration. In this quiet domestic moment, the queens receive the four brides with honour, marking their entry into the royal family before the rituals continue.
ramayan::1997.modern_relevance: When your family gathers around a new marriage, the real welcome is not the ceremony — it is how gently everyone makes room for the new people in the house.
ramayan::1997.insight: It shifts attention from spectacle to hospitality, showing that belonging is created by respectful reception.

ramayan::1998.verse_sanskrit: मङ्गलालम्भनैश्चापि शोभिता: क्षौमवासस: । देवतायतनान्याशु सर्वास्ता: प्रत्यपूजयन् । । 17713 । ।
ramayan::1998.verse_hindi: With auspicious aricles in their hands, all the new brides who shone in silken apparels
ramayan::1998.english_translation: With auspicious articles in their hands, all the new brides, shining in silk garments, worshipped the household deities.
ramayan::1998.translation_literal: मङ्गलालम्भनैः (with auspicious articles) / च (and) अपि (also) / शोभिताḥ (shining) / क्षौमवाससः (wearing silk garments) / देवतायतनानि (the shrines of the deities) / आशु (quickly) / सर्वाः (all) / ताः (those) / प्रत्यपूजयन् (worshipped in return)
ramayan::1998.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1998.essence: New beginnings are made stable by reverence.
ramayan::1998.simple_meaning: The brides, dressed in silk and carrying auspicious items, first honored the household shrines as they entered their new home.
ramayan::1998.simple_insight: A new beginning feels steadier when you begin with respect, not entitlement.
ramayan::1998.detailed_meaning: Sita, Urmila, and the other princesses have just been welcomed into their husbands' homes. Before anything else, they honor the household deities. The moment is ceremonial, showing the grace and discipline expected as they enter a new life.
ramayan::1998.modern_relevance: Before the first dinner in a new apartment, you pause to light a lamp, clean the corner, and set things in order. The beginning feels different when you treat it with reverence.
ramayan::1998.insight: It shifts attention from personal arrival to respectful entry into a shared home.

ramayan::1999.verse_sanskrit: अभिवाद्याभिवाद्यांश्च सर्वा राजसुतास्तदा । स्वं स्वं गृहमथासाद्य कुबेरभवनोपमम् । । 17714 । । गोभिर्धनैश्च धान्यैश्च तर्पयित्वा द्विजोत्तमान् । रेमिरे मुदिता: सर्वा भर्तृभि: सहिता रह: । । 17715 । ।
ramayan::1999.verse_hindi: Then all the princesses paid obeisance to those worthy of worship and entered their residence that resembled the palace of Kubera.Thereafter pleased with gifting  cows, riches and corn to brahmins and satisfying them they joined their husbands and enjoyed themselves in privacy
ramayan::1999.english_translation: Then all the princesses paid obeisance to those worthy of worship and entered their residence that resembled the palace of Kubera. Thereafter, pleased, they gave cows, riches, and grain to the best of the learned men, satisfied them, and then enjoyed private time with their husbands.
ramayan::1999.translation_literal: अभिवाद्याभिवाद्यांश्च (having repeatedly saluted) / सर्वा (all) / राजसुतास्तदा (the princesses then) / स्वं स्वं (their own respective) / गृहम् (house) / अथ (then) / आसाद्य (having reached) / कुबेरभवनोपमम् (resembling Kubera's palace) / गोभिः (with cows) / धनैः (with wealth) / च (and) / धान्यैः (with grain) / च (and) / तर्पयित्वा (having satisfied) / द्विजोत्तमान् (the best of the twice-born) / रेमिरे (they rejoiced) / मुदिता: (delighted) / सर्वा: (all) / भर्तृभि: (with their husbands) / सहिता: (together) / रह: (in private)
ramayan::1999.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::1999.essence: Private joy comes after honoring what is worthy.
ramayan::1999.simple_meaning: The princesses return home, honor the learned, give gifts, and spend happy private time with their husbands.
ramayan::1999.simple_insight: Joy feels complete when gratitude, generosity, and homecoming all arrive together.
ramayan::1999.detailed_meaning: The wedding celebrations have ended. The princesses return to homes like Kubera's palace, first honoring the learned men with gifts of cows, wealth, and grain. Only then do they settle into married life, with the ceremony giving way to private joy.
ramayan::1999.modern_relevance: After the last guest leaves and the house is finally quiet, you notice the day meant more than the photos. The real celebration was the respect, the giving, and the return to home.
ramayan::1999.insight: It links celebration with gratitude and generosity before private enjoyment.

ramayan::2000.verse_sanskrit: कुमाराश्च महात्मानो वीर्येणाप्रतिमा भुवि । कृतदारा: कृतास्त्राश्च सधना: ससुहृज्जना: । । 17716 । । शुश्रूषमाणा: पितरं वर्तयन्ति नरर्षभा: ।
ramayan::2000.verse_hindi: All the princes who were best of men, great souls, incomparable in prowess on earth, capable of the use of weapons and endowed with wealth moved about with friends, serving their father and following his commands.
ramayan::2000.english_translation: All the princes who were best of men, great souls, incomparable in prowess on earth, capable of the use of weapons and endowed with wealth moved about with friends, serving their father and following his commands.
ramayan::2000.translation_literal: कुमाराः (princes) / च (and) / महात्मानः (great-souled) / वीर्येण (in prowess) / अप्रतिमाः (incomparable) / भुवि (on earth) / कृतदाराः (having wives) / कृतास्त्राः (trained in weapons) / च (and) / सधनाः (wealthy) / ससुहृज्जनाः (with friends) / शुश्रूषमाणाः (serving) / पितरम् (their father) / वर्तयन्ति (move about) / नरर्षभाः (best of men)
ramayan::2000.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::2000.essence: Power means little if you do not still serve the one who raised you.
ramayan::2000.simple_meaning: The royal sons are grown, skilled, wealthy, and surrounded by friends. Even so, they stay close to their father and serve his wishes.
ramayan::2000.simple_insight: Real strength still bows to love and duty at home.
ramayan::2000.detailed_meaning: At Ayodhya, Dasaratha's sons are no longer children. They are married, armed, wealthy, admired, and capable in every way. Yet they remain in their father's orbit, serving him with care. The verse sets up the family tension before Bharata is called.
ramayan::2000.modern_relevance: You may be capable, established, and admired, yet still choose to show up for the parent who raised you. That quiet loyalty says more than achievement ever could.
ramayan::2000.insight: It shifts attention from status to filial service as the measure of maturity.

ramayan::7001.verse_hindi: It was chosen by prosperous wives of gods as a reosrt. Hosts of gods and demons were wandering, there in the hope of tasting nectar.
ramayan::7001.english_translation: It was frequented by the wives of the gods, radiant and prosperous, and was roamed by hosts of gods and demons who came seeking nectar.
ramayan::7001.translation_literal: सेवितं (frequented by) / देवपन्तीभिः (by the wives of gods) / श्रीमतीभिः (by the prosperous, radiant ones) / श्रिया आवृतम् (covered with splendour) / देवदानवसङ्घैः (by hosts of gods and demons) / च (and) / चरितम् (roamed) / त्व अमृताशिभिः (by those seeking nectar)
ramayan::7001.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7001.essence: A radiant place draws even rivals into the same longing.
ramayan::7001.simple_meaning: The place is described as a dazzling heavenly region visited by divine wives and crowded with gods and demons searching for nectar.
ramayan::7001.simple_insight: Some places feel so abundant that even rival beings are drawn to them.
ramayan::7001.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is still describing the same wondrous region. It is so radiant that the wives of the gods dwell there, and both gods and demons wander through it, drawn by the hope of nectar. The verse adds texture, not a new teaching.
ramayan::7001.modern_relevance: You walk into a place so beautiful that everyone seems to want a piece of it. The scene matters less for advice than for atmosphere.
ramayan::7001.insight: It keeps the reader inside the landscape, building wonder through detail rather than argument.

ramayan::7002.verse_sanskrit: हंसक्रौञ्चप्लवाकीर्णं सारसैस्सम्प्रणादितम् । वैढूर्यप्रस्तरं रम्यं स्निग्धं सागरतेजसा । । 33518 । ।
ramayan::7002.verse_hindi: (It was ) full of small floats, flocks of swans, kraunchas, sarasas cackling in the ponds, with great joy. It had stretches of vaidurya stones on the shore and shone with the radiance of the sea
ramayan::7002.english_translation: It was full of swans, kraunchas, and sarasa birds calling joyfully. Its shore was strewn with vaidurya stones, and it shone with the sea's radiance.
ramayan::7002.translation_literal: हंस (swans) / क्रौञ्च (krauncha birds) / प्लव (small floats or waterbirds) / आकीर्णं (filled with) / सारसैः (with sarasa birds) / सम्प्रणादितम् (resounding joyfully) / वैढूर्यप्रस्तरम् (with vaidurya stones) / रम्यं (beautiful) / स्निग्धं (glossy, smooth) / सागरतेजसा (with the radiance of the sea)
ramayan::7002.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7002.essence: Beauty here is part of the world itself, not decoration added later.
ramayan::7002.simple_meaning: The verse paints a beautiful seashore filled with birds, shining stones, and the sea's glow.
ramayan::7002.simple_insight: Some places feel alive before anyone even speaks.
ramayan::7002.detailed_meaning: Ravana is moving through Lanka, and Valmiki pauses the action to show its beauty. Birds call across the water, shining stones line the shore, and the sea gives the city its glow. The verse is scenery, not a teaching.
ramayan::7002.modern_relevance: You step onto a shoreline at dusk and the whole place seems to hum — birds calling, water flashing, stone reflecting light.
ramayan::7002.insight: It trains the eye to notice atmosphere before plot.

ramayan::7003.verse_sanskrit: पाण्डुराणि विशालानि दिव्यमाल्ययुतानि च । तूर्यगीताभिजुष्टानि विमानानि समन्ततः । । 33519 । । तपसा जितलोकानां कामगान्यभिसम्पतन् । गन्धर्वाप्सरसश्चैव ददर्श धनदानुजः । । 33520 । ।
ramayan::7003.verse_hindi: Speeding along, the brother of Kubera (Ravana) saw palewhite, spacious aerial chariots on all sides controlled by those who had conquered the higher worlds by their penances. These chariots, decked with heavenly garlands, and ringing with divine music could fly where one desired. He saw gandharvas and apsaras as well.
ramayan::7003.english_translation: Speeding along, Ravana saw pale-white, spacious aerial chariots on all sides, decked with heavenly garlands and filled with divine music. He saw gandharvas and apsaras as well.
ramayan::7003.translation_literal: पाण्डुराणि (pale-white) / विशालानि (spacious) / दिव्यमाल्ययुतानि (endowed with heavenly garlands) / च (and) / तूर्यगीताभिजुष्टानि (filled with instrumental music and song) / विमानानि (aerial chariots) / समन्ततः (on all sides) / तपसा (by penance) / जितलोकानां (of those who had conquered the higher worlds) / कामगान् (flying as desired) / अभिसम्पतन् (speeding toward) / गन्धर्वाप्सरसः (gandharvas and apsaras) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / ददर्श (he saw) / धनदानुजः (the brother of Kubera)
ramayan::7003.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7003.essence: Beauty here is earned by discipline, not borrowed from fantasy.
ramayan::7003.simple_meaning: Ravana sees a heavenly region filled with flying chariots, music, celestial beings, and the signs of great penance.
ramayan::7003.simple_insight: Some realms are built by discipline, not desire.
ramayan::7003.detailed_meaning: Ravana is moving through a wondrous aerial landscape and notices the rewards of beings who conquered higher worlds through penance. The verse is part of a larger scenic description, not a teaching moment by itself.
ramayan::7003.modern_relevance: You scroll past glossy images of lives that look effortless, but behind some of them are years of discipline you never saw.
ramayan::7003.insight: It shifts attention from surface beauty to the hidden effort that created it.

ramayan::7004.verse_sanskrit: निर्यासरसमूलानां चन्दनानां सहस्रशः । वनानि पश्यन्सौम्यानि घ्राणतृप्तिकराणि च । । 33521 । ।
ramayan::7004.verse_hindi: He saw thousands of tree trunks with finesmelling resins and sandalwood trees.
ramayan::7004.english_translation: He saw thousands of sandalwood forests, with trunks rich in fragrant resin, soothing to the senses.
ramayan::7004.translation_literal: निर्यास-रस-मूलानाम् (of resin-rich roots/trunks) / चन्दनानाम् (of sandalwoods) / सहस्रशः (in thousands) / वनानि (forests) / पश्यन् (seeing) / सौम्यानि (pleasant) / घ्राण-तृप्ति-कराणि (giving satisfaction to the nose) / च (and)
ramayan::7004.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7004.essence: The journey pauses to linger on fragrance and abundance.
ramayan::7004.simple_meaning: Ravana sees many fragrant sandalwood forests, rich with resin and pleasing to the senses.
ramayan::7004.simple_insight: The verse simply paints the richness of the landscape; it is part of the scene, not a teaching.
ramayan::7004.detailed_meaning: Ravana continues flying through a wondrous region and notices countless sandalwood groves, their trunks full of fragrant resin. The verse adds sensory detail to the journey, building the beauty of the setting rather than making a moral point.
ramayan::7004.insight: It slows the scene down and lets the reader feel the world Ravana is passing through.

ramayan::7005.verse_sanskrit: अगरूणां च मुख्यानां वनान्युपवनानि च । तक्कोलानां च जात्यानां फलानां च सुगन्धिनाम् । । 33522 । ।
ramayan::7005.verse_hindi: (He saw) very fine aguru trees in the forest as well as pleasuregroves of takkola fruits, fragrant  trees of a fine variety and fragrant nutmegs.
ramayan::7005.english_translation: He saw very fine aguru trees in the forest, along with pleasure groves of takkola fruits, fragrant trees of a fine variety, and fragrant nutmegs.
ramayan::7005.translation_literal: अगरूणाम् (of aguru trees) / च (and) / मुख्यानाम् (of the finest) / वनान्युपवनानि (forests and pleasure groves) / च (and) / तक्कोलानाम् (of takkola fruits) / च (and) / जात्यानाम् (of a fine variety) / फलानाम् (of fruits) / च (and) / सुगन्धिनाम् (fragrant)
ramayan::7005.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7005.essence: The journey continues through a world of fragrance and abundance.
ramayan::7005.simple_meaning: He sees forests and groves filled with fragrant trees and fruits, rich with pleasant scents.
ramayan::7005.simple_insight: The scene is lush and overflowing, making the journey feel almost dreamlike.
ramayan::7005.detailed_meaning: Ravana's flight carries him over regions crowded with beauty and abundance. Instead of a teaching or turning point, this verse simply adds another layer to the landscape: fragrant trees, groves, and sweet-smelling fruits passing beneath him.
ramayan::7005.insight: It extends the visual panorama, keeping the focus on what Ravana passes over rather than on reflection.

ramayan::7006.verse_sanskrit: पुष्पाणि च तमालस्य गुल्मानि मरिचस्य च । मुक्तानां च समूहानि शुष्यमाणानि तीरतः । । 33523 । ।
ramayan::7006.verse_hindi: (He saw) tamala flowers in bloom, pepper shrubs in clusters and hoards of pearls kept for drying on the shores.
ramayan::7006.english_translation: (He saw) tamala flowers in bloom, pepper shrubs in clusters and hoards of pearls kept for drying on the shores.
ramayan::7006.translation_literal: पुष्पाणि (flowers) / च (and) / तमालस्य (of tamala) / गुल्मानि (shrubs/clusters) / मरिचस्य (of pepper) / च (and) / मुक्तानां (of pearls) / च (and) / समूहानि (heaps/collections) / शुष्यमाणानि (being dried) / तीरतः (from the shore)
ramayan::7006.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7006.essence: The shore itself is crowded with wealth and fragrance.
ramayan::7006.simple_meaning: Hanuman sees more natural riches and valuable goods along the shore, including flowers, pepper shrubs, and pearls drying nearby.
ramayan::7006.simple_insight: The scene keeps widening, showing a land overflowing with abundance and wealth.
ramayan::7006.detailed_meaning: Hanuman is moving through Lanka’s surroundings and taking in its astonishing abundance. The verse is part of a flowing list of sights—fragrant plants, stored pearls, and coastal wealth—meant to build the sense of a rich, powerful city, not to deliver a separate teaching.
ramayan::7006.insight: It continues the visual inventory of Lanka’s wealth, adding to the sense of opulence and scale.

ramayan::7007.verse_sanskrit: शङ्खानां प्रसरं चैव प्रवालनिचयं तथा । काञ्चनानि च शैलानि राजतानि च सर्वशः । । 33524 । ।
ramayan::7007.verse_hindi: He saw stretches of conches, heaps of corals and mounds of gold and silver too.
ramayan::7007.english_translation: He saw stretches of conches, heaps of corals, and mounds of gold and silver too.
ramayan::7007.translation_literal: शङ्खानाम् (of conches) / प्रसरम् (stretch, spread) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / प्रवालनिचयम् (heap of corals) / तथा (and so) / काञ्चनानि (golden) / च (and) / शैलानि (mountains) / राजतानि (silver) / च (and) / सर्वशः (everywhere, in all directions)
ramayan::7007.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7007.essence: The verse simply deepens the scenery with wealth and beauty.
ramayan::7007.simple_meaning: The scene is filled with conches, corals, gold, and silver spread everywhere.
ramayan::7007.simple_insight: The passage builds a vivid world of abundance, not a lesson to act on.
ramayan::7007.detailed_meaning: As the journey continues, the traveler passes through a lavish landscape crowded with precious and beautiful things. This line is part of a descriptive chain, not a teaching or turning point, so it supports the larger scene rather than standing alone.
ramayan::7007.insight: It adds visual richness to the journey without changing the story's direction.

ramayan::7008.verse_sanskrit: प्रस्रवाणि मनोज्ञानि प्रसन्नानि ह्रदानि च । धनधान्योपपन्नानि स्त्रीरत्नैश्शोभितानि च । । 33525 । । हस्त्यश्वरथगाढानि नगराण्यवलोकयन् ।
ramayan::7008.verse_hindi: He went watching fascinating waterfalls, pleasing ponds, cities filled with wealth and grain, looking splendid with beautiful women and full of elephants, horses and chariots.
ramayan::7008.english_translation: He went watching fascinating waterfalls, pleasing ponds, cities filled with wealth and grain, looking splendid with beautiful women and full of elephants, horses and chariots.
ramayan::7008.translation_literal: प्रस्रवाणि (waterfalls) / मनोज्ञानि (fascinating) / प्रसन्नानि (pleasing) / ह्रदानि (ponds) / च (and) / धनधान्योपपन्नानि (endowed with wealth and grain) / स्त्रीरत्नैः (with women of jewel-like beauty) / शोभितानि (adorned) / च (and) / हस्त्यश्वरथगाढानि (crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots) / नगराणि (cities) / अवलोकयन् (while looking)
ramayan::7008.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7008.essence: Abundance becomes visible before any explanation is needed.
ramayan::7008.simple_meaning: He looks over a land rich in water, wealth, grain, people, and royal splendor.
ramayan::7008.simple_insight: Some places feel alive with abundance before a single word is spoken.
ramayan::7008.detailed_meaning: As the journey continues, the observer sees waterfalls, ponds, prosperous cities, and crowded streets filled with animals, vehicles, and people. The verse builds the landscape’s richness piece by piece, preparing for the larger vision that follows.
ramayan::7008.modern_relevance: You drive past a city glowing at dusk, with traffic, lights, and homes packed close together. The scene itself tells you how much human effort has gone into making it thrive.
ramayan::7008.insight: It shifts attention from a place’s surface beauty to the living abundance beneath it.

ramayan::7009.verse_sanskrit: तं समं सर्वतस्निग्धं मृदुसंस्पर्शमारुतम् । अनूपं सिन्धुराजस्य ददर्श त्रिदिवोपमम् । । 33526 । ।
ramayan::7009.verse_hindi: It was a veritable heaven with the plain land flooded with the backwaters of the sea and gentle breeze blowing.
ramayan::7009.english_translation: It was a level land, soft on all sides, touched by a gentle breeze, a shore-like place of the sea king, like a region of the higher realm.
ramayan::7009.translation_literal: तम् (that) / समम् (level) / सर्वतस्निग्धम् (soft on all sides) / मृदुसंस्पर्शमारुतम् (with gentle-touch breeze) / अनूपम् (marshy shoreland) / सिन्धुराजस्य (of the sea king) / ददर्श (he saw) / त्रिदिवोपमम् (like the higher realm)
ramayan::7009.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7009.essence: The land itself feels like a calm threshold before the next turning.
ramayan::7009.simple_meaning: Rama saw a flat, pleasant stretch of land near the sea, made beautiful by soft winds and a heavenly look.
ramayan::7009.simple_insight: Some places feel calm before anything has even happened.
ramayan::7009.detailed_meaning: Rama is moving through the landscape near the sea. After forests, waters, and rich settlements, he sees a broad, gentle shoreland that feels almost otherworldly. It is a scene-setting detail, preparing for what comes next.
ramayan::7009.modern_relevance: You step out of a crowded train and feel the salt wind on your face. For a moment, the noise drops away and the world feels spacious again.
ramayan::7009.insight: It shifts attention from action to atmosphere, letting the setting carry the emotional weight.

ramayan::7010.verse_hindi: He saw a banyan tree with its branches spread on all sides measuring a hundred
ramayan::7010.english_translation: There he saw a banyan tree, cloud-dark in color, surrounded by sages. Its branches stretched in all directions for a hundred yojanas.
ramayan::7010.translation_literal: तत्र (there) / अपश्यत् (he saw) / सः (he) / मेघाभम् (cloud-like in hue) / न्यग्रोधम् (banyan tree) / ऋषिभिः (by sages) / वृतम् (surrounded) / समन्तात् (on all sides) / यस्य (whose) / ताः (those) / शाखाः (branches) / शतयोजनम् (a hundred yojanas) / आयताः (extended)
ramayan::7010.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7010.essence: A vast, sacred landscape is being revealed, not interpreted.
ramayan::7010.simple_meaning: He sees a vast banyan tree surrounded by sages, with branches stretching an immense distance in every direction.
ramayan::7010.simple_insight: Some places feel larger than nature itself, as if they hold memory, wonder, and sacred presence all at once.
ramayan::7010.detailed_meaning: The scene is still unfolding in a wondrous landscape of lakes, rivers, and sea-washed plains. Here Rama or the traveler notices a gigantic banyan tree ringed by sages, its branches stretching impossibly far. The verse is descriptive, not reflective.
ramayan::7010.modern_relevance: You turn a corner on a road trip and stop at a tree older than your family name. For a moment, scale itself feels holy.
ramayan::7010.insight: It trains attention on setting and scale before the story’s next turn.

ramayan::7011.verse_sanskrit: यस्य हस्तिनमादाय महाकायं च कच्छपम् । । 33528 । । भक्षार्थं गरुडश्शाखामाजगाम महाबलः ।
ramayan::7011.verse_hindi: In the past, the mighty Garuda brought an elephant and a huge tortoise and sat on a branch of this tree to feed on them.
ramayan::7011.english_translation: In the past, the mighty Garuda brought an elephant and a huge tortoise and sat on a branch of this tree to feed on them.
ramayan::7011.translation_literal: यस्य (whose) / हस्तिनम् (an elephant) / आदाय (having taken) / महाकायम् (huge-bodied) / च (and) / कच्छपम् (a tortoise) / भक्षार्थम् (for food) / गरुडः (Garuda) / शाखाम् (to a branch) / आजगाम (came) / महाबलः (mighty)
ramayan::7011.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7011.essence: The tree is so vast it holds a legend in its branches.
ramayan::7011.simple_meaning: Garuda once came here with an elephant and a giant tortoise and used the branch as a place to eat them.
ramayan::7011.simple_insight: The verse adds scale and wonder, not a teaching — it makes the tree feel ancient and immense.
ramayan::7011.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing a vast banyan tree by recalling its impossible history. A mighty bird once landed on its branch carrying an elephant and a tortoise for food. The verse builds the tree's grandeur, preparing for the branch to break.
ramayan::7011.insight: It sets the scene through mythic scale, showing the tree can bear even legendary weight.

ramayan::7012.verse_sanskrit: तस्य तां सहसा शाखां भारेण पतगोत्तमः । । 33529 । । सुपर्णः पर्णबहुलां बभञ्ज च महाबलः ।
ramayan::7012.verse_hindi: Due to the weight of this best of birds, the mighty Garuda, the leafy branch at once broke down.
ramayan::7012.english_translation: Due to the weight of this best of birds, the mighty Garuda, the leafy branch at once broke down.
ramayan::7012.translation_literal: तस्य (of that) / तां (that) / सहसा (suddenly) / शाखां (branch) / भारेण (by weight) / पतगोत्तमः (best of birds) / सुपर्णः (Garuda) / पर्णबहुलां (full of leaves) / बभञ्ज (broke) / च (and) / महाबलः (mighty)
ramayan::7012.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7012.essence: His weight alone was enough to break the branch.
ramayan::7012.simple_meaning: Garuda's weight was so great that the leafy branch broke at once.
ramayan::7012.simple_insight: Great force can break even what seems sturdy.
ramayan::7012.detailed_meaning: Garuda has settled on the vast banyan tree described in the previous verses. When he lands with his full weight, the leafy branch gives way and snaps. The verse is part of a scene-setting chain that leads into the sages gathered below.
ramayan::7012.modern_relevance: A crowded subway seat gives way when someone heavy sits down too fast. The moment is simple: strength has consequences, even when nothing meant to break.
ramayan::7012.insight: It adds physical momentum to the scene, showing Garuda's power before the sages appear below.

ramayan::7013.verse_sanskrit: तत्र वैखानसा माषा वालखिल्या मरीचिपाः । । 33530 । । अजा बभूवुर्धूम्राश्च सङ्गताः परमर्षयः ।
ramayan::7013.verse_hindi: Gathered together under the great tree were great sages like vaikhanasas, mashas, marichipas, valakhilyas, ajas and dhumras.
ramayan::7013.english_translation: There were gathered there the great sages Vaikhanasas, Mashas, Marichipas, Valakhilyas, Ajas, and Dhumras.
ramayan::7013.translation_literal: तत्र (there) / वैखानसाः (Vaikhanasas) / माषाः (Mashas) / वालखिल्याः (Valakhilyas) / मरीचिपाः (Marichipas) / अजाः (Ajas) / बभूवुः (were present) / धूम्राः (Dhumras) / च (and) / सङ्गताः (assembled) / परमर्षयः (great sages)
ramayan::7013.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7013.essence: The scene widens before the real danger begins.
ramayan::7013.simple_meaning: Many great sages were gathered beneath the tree. The verse simply names them as part of the scene.
ramayan::7013.simple_insight: Some moments matter only because they set up what comes next.
ramayan::7013.detailed_meaning: Garuda has broken a huge branch while feeding on an ancient tree. Before the next action unfolds, Valmiki pauses to show that many revered sages were present there, making the scene morally charged and dangerous.
ramayan::7013.modern_relevance: A crowd gathers around a fallen branch after a storm, and everyone suddenly remembers who was standing underneath. The real story is not the tree — it is who was in harm's way.
ramayan::7013.insight: It frames the next event as a matter of danger to innocent bystanders, not just brute force.

ramayan::7014.verse_sanskrit: तेषां दयार्थं गरुडस्तां शाखां शतयोजनाम् । । 33531 । । जगामादाय वेगेन तौ चोभौ गजकच्छपौ ।
ramayan::7014.verse_hindi: Out of compassion for the (endangered) seers Garuda carried away that hundredyojanalong branch along with the elephant and the tortoise with great speed.
ramayan::7014.english_translation: Out of compassion for the endangered sages, Garuda quickly carried away that hundred-yojana branch along with the elephant and the tortoise.
ramayan::7014.translation_literal: तेषाम् (for them) / दयार्थम् (out of compassion) / गरुडः (Garuda) / ताम् (that) / शाखाम् (branch) / शतयोजनाम् (hundred yojanas long) / जगामादाय (carried away, taking) / वेगेन (swiftly) / तौ (those two) / च (and) / उभौ (both) / गजकच्छपौ (the elephant and the tortoise)
ramayan::7014.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7014.essence: He sees danger and removes it before anyone is harmed.
ramayan::7014.simple_meaning: Garuda, feeling for the sages, swiftly carried off the huge branch along with the elephant and the tortoise.
ramayan::7014.simple_insight: Compassion can move faster than fear.
ramayan::7014.detailed_meaning: A giant branch has broken under Garuda's weight, and the sages beneath are in danger. To protect them, Garuda lifts away the branch and the two trapped beings with sudden speed. The verse is a rescue detail, not the main teaching.
ramayan::7014.modern_relevance: You notice the branch is about to collapse over people on the trail, and you move first, not after debating who should. Relief often begins with quick, protective action.
ramayan::7014.insight: It shows compassion as immediate intervention, not sentiment.

ramayan::7015.verse_sanskrit: एकपादेन धर्मात्मा भक्षयित्वा तदामिषम् । । 33532 । । निषादविषयं हत्वा शाखया पतगोत्तमः । प्रहर्षमतुलं लेभे मोक्षयित्वा महामुनीन् । । 33533 । ।
ramayan::7015.verse_hindi: Righteous Garuda, the best among the birds, stood on one foot and ate the flesh (of elephant and tortoise) and  with the branch of the tree, destroyed the settlement of the demons. Over the destruction of the demons and deliverance of the great seers he felt immeasurable happiness.
ramayan::7015.english_translation: Righteous Garuda, the best among the birds, stood on one foot and ate the flesh, then used the branch to destroy the settlement of the lower beings. Freed from the great seers, he felt immeasurable joy.
ramayan::7015.translation_literal: एकपादेन (on one foot) / धर्मात्मा (righteous one) / भक्षयित्वा (having eaten) / तदामिषम् (that flesh) / निषादविषयं (the settlement of the nisadas) / हत्वा (having destroyed) / शाखया (with the branch) / पतगोत्तमः (best among birds) / प्रहर्षम् (joy) / अतुलम् (immeasurable) / लेभे (obtained) / मोक्षयित्वा (having freed) / महामुनीन् (great sages)
ramayan::7015.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7015.essence: Rescue and destruction can come from the same fearless act.
ramayan::7015.simple_meaning: Garuda destroys the hostile settlement, frees the trapped sages, and feels great joy after doing it.
ramayan::7015.simple_insight: Right action can bring a clean, unmistakable joy.
ramayan::7015.detailed_meaning: Garuda has just carried away the branch to save the sages from danger. In the same swift act, he crushes the hostile settlement and releases the great seers. This verse marks the surge of satisfaction that follows a decisive rescue.
ramayan::7015.modern_relevance: You finally step in when others are trapped, and the whole situation shifts. The relief you feel comes from having acted cleanly, not from being praised.
ramayan::7015.insight: It shows that protecting the vulnerable and removing harm can be one single act.

ramayan::7016.verse_sanskrit: स तेनैव प्रहर्षेण द्विगुणीकृतविक्रमः । अमृतानयनार्थं वै चकार मतिमान्मतिम् । । 33534 । ।
ramayan::7016.verse_hindi: Quite happy, his energy redoubled, wise Garuda made up his mind to obtain nectar.
ramayan::7016.english_translation: Quite happy, his energy redoubled, wise Garuda made up his mind to obtain nectar.
ramayan::7016.translation_literal: सः (he) / तेनैव (by that very) / प्रहर्षेण (with delight) / द्विगुणीकृतविक्रमः (whose prowess was doubled) / अमृतानयनार्थं (for the purpose of bringing nectar) / वै (indeed) / चकार (made) / मतिमान् (the wise one) / मतिम् (the resolve)
ramayan::7016.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7016.essence: Victory can become the fuel for a harder task.
ramayan::7016.simple_meaning: Garuda, now energized by success, decided to go after the nectar too.
ramayan::7016.simple_insight: Success can sharpen courage and push you toward the next impossible task.
ramayan::7016.detailed_meaning: Garuda has just acted with speed and force, freeing himself from the earlier struggle. Flush with triumph, he immediately turns his attention to the nectar hidden in the divine realm. The verse is a transition in the action, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::7016.modern_relevance: You finish one hard thing and suddenly feel ready for the bigger one. That surge can become your next breakthrough if you aim it well.
ramayan::7016.insight: It shifts attention from the victory already won to the resolve needed for the next challenge.

ramayan::7017.verse_sanskrit: अयोजालानि निर्मथ्य भित्वा रत्नमयं गृहम् । महेन्द्रभवनाद्गुप्तमाजहारामृतं ततः । । 33535 । ।
ramayan::7017.verse_hindi: Twisting and twirling the grills of the window, he broke open the room made of gems and quietly carried away the nectar from Indras mansion.
ramayan::7017.english_translation: Twisting and twirling the grills of the window, he broke open the room made of gems and quietly carried away the nectar from Indra's mansion.
ramayan::7017.translation_literal: अयोजालानि (iron grills) / निर्मथ्य (twisting apart) / भित्वा (breaking) / रत्नमयम् (made of gems) / गृहम् (house/room) / महेन्द्रभवनात् (from Indra's mansion) / गुप्तम् (secretly) / आजहार (carried away) / अमृतम् (nectar) / ततः (then)
ramayan::7017.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7017.essence: He reaches the guarded prize and takes it in one clean breach.
ramayan::7017.simple_meaning: Garuda broke into Indra's jeweled chamber and stole the nectar in secret.
ramayan::7017.simple_insight: Great desire can make even a guarded treasure feel vulnerable.
ramayan::7017.detailed_meaning: Garuda has already overcome the guardians and built up the force for his mission. Now he reaches Indra's palace, tears through the jeweled enclosure, and takes the nectar unseen. The verse is a step in the larger sequence, not a teaching on its own.
ramayan::7017.modern_relevance: You finally get access to the locked file, the sealed room, the protected account — and one decisive move changes everything.
ramayan::7017.insight: It shifts attention from the obstacle to the force that can break through it.

ramayan::7018.verse_sanskrit: तं महर्षिगणैर्जुष्टं सुपर्णकृतलक्षणम् । नाम्ना सुभद्रं न्यग्रोधं ददर्श धनदानुजः । । 33536 । ।
ramayan::7018.verse_hindi: Ravana, the younger brother of Kubera, beheld that banyan tree called Subhadram ,which was a favoured resort of the sages bearing the ensignia of Garuda.
ramayan::7018.english_translation: Ravana, the younger brother of Kubera, beheld that banyan tree called Subhadra, a favoured resort of the sages and marked with the sign of Garuda.
ramayan::7018.translation_literal: तं (that) / महर्षिगणैः (by groups of great sages) / जुष्टं (frequented, loved) / सुपर्णकृतलक्षणम् (marked with the sign made by Garuda) / नाम्ना (by name) / सुभद्रं (Subhadra) / न्यग्रोधं (banyan tree) / ददर्श (saw) / धनदानुजः (the younger brother of Kubera)
ramayan::7018.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7018.essence: A single tree can hold reverence, memory, and omen at once.
ramayan::7018.simple_meaning: Ravana sees a banyan tree called Subhadra, known as a place where sages gather and marked by Garuda's sign.
ramayan::7018.simple_insight: A place can carry memory, sanctity, and warning all at once.
ramayan::7018.detailed_meaning: Ravana, already deep inside his strange, secret journey, comes upon a banyan tree revered by sages and marked with Garuda's sign. The verse simply pauses the action to name what he sees before he moves on.
ramayan::7018.modern_relevance: You turn a corner on a quiet road and notice a tree with offerings at its base. Some places feel ordinary until you learn what has happened there.
ramayan::7018.insight: It keeps the scene moving while reminding you that sacred places can stand in the middle of danger.

ramayan::7019.verse_sanskrit: तं तु गत्वा परं पारं समुद्रस्य नदीपतेः । ददर्शाश्रममेकान्ते रम्ये पुण्ये वनान्तरे । । 33537 । ।
ramayan::7019.verse_hindi: Ravana crossed over to the other side of the sea, the lord of rivers, and beheld a hermitage in a beautiful, secluded, sacred  place in the middle of the forest.
ramayan::7019.english_translation: Ravana crossed to the far shore of the sea and saw a hermitage in a beautiful, secluded, sacred forest.
ramayan::7019.translation_literal: तं (that) / तु (indeed) / गत्वा (having gone) / परं (farther) / पारं (to the farther shore) / समुद्रस्य (of the sea) / नदीपतेः (of the lord of rivers) / ददर्श (he saw) / आश्रमम् (hermitage) / एकान्ते (in seclusion) / रम्ये (beautiful) / पुण्ये (sacred) / वनान्तरे (in the midst of the forest)
ramayan::7019.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7019.essence: Obsession can carry you across impossible distances.
ramayan::7019.simple_meaning: Ravana reaches the far side of the sea and finds a secluded hermitage deep in the forest.
ramayan::7019.simple_insight: Even the most hidden places can be reached when obsession keeps moving.
ramayan::7019.detailed_meaning: Ravana has crossed the ocean and entered a remote forest. In the silence beyond the sea, he spots a sacred hermitage before meeting the figure he is truly seeking. The verse mainly sets the scene for the encounter that follows.
ramayan::7019.modern_relevance: You keep pushing through one more tab, one more road, one more door, until you reach the quiet place you were determined to find.
ramayan::7019.insight: It shifts attention from the journey itself to the hidden destination it is leading toward.

ramayan::7020.verse_sanskrit: तत्र कृष्णाजिनधरं जटावल्कलधारिणम् । ददर्श नियताहारं मारीचं नाम राक्षसाम् । । 33538 । ।
ramayan::7020.verse_hindi: There he saw a demon Maricha, by name, clad in dark deerskin and bark ,with matted hair and living on restricted food.
ramayan::7020.english_translation: There he saw a demon named Maricha, clad in dark deerskin and bark, with matted hair and living on restricted food.
ramayan::7020.translation_literal: तत्र (there) / कृष्णाजिनधरम् (wearing dark deerskin) / जटावल्कलधारिणम् (wearing matted hair and bark) / ददर्श (saw) / नियताहारम् (with restricted food) / मारीचम् (Maricha) / नाम (by name) / राक्षसाम् (the demon)
ramayan::7020.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7020.essence: Outward restraint can hide the same old nature.
ramayan::7020.simple_meaning: Ravana sees Maricha living like an ascetic, though he is a demon by nature.
ramayan::7020.simple_insight: Appearances can be deceptive; restraint does not always mean transformation.
ramayan::7020.detailed_meaning: Ravana has crossed the sea and reached a lonely hermitage. There he finds Maricha, once a fierce demon, now dressed like a forest ascetic and living on simple food. The scene prepares the meeting that follows, rather than delivering a teaching of its own.
ramayan::7020.modern_relevance: You meet someone who looks disciplined, humble, even harmless — but their outward calm may only be a costume.
ramayan::7020.insight: It reminds you to look beyond surface discipline and notice the deeper character underneath.

ramayan::7021.verse_sanskrit: स रावणस्समागम्य विधिवत्तेन रक्षसा । मारीचेनार्चितो राजा सर्वकामैरमानुषैः । । 33539 । ।
ramayan::7021.verse_hindi: When king Ravana reached there, Maricha received him  in accordance with tradition  and made worshipful offering to the king, fulfilling all his superhuman desires.
ramayan::7021.english_translation: When king Ravana reached there, Maricha received him in accordance with tradition and made worshipful offering to the king, fulfilling all his superhuman desires.
ramayan::7021.translation_literal: सः (he) / रावणः (Ravana) / समागम्य (having arrived) / विधिवत् (according to proper custom) / तेन (by that) / रक्षसा (by the demon) / मारीचेन (by Maricha) / अर्चितः (honoured, worshipped) / राजा (the king) / सर्वकामैः (with all desires) / अमानुषैः (superhuman, beyond human) / (was served)
ramayan::7021.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7021.essence: Respect can be used to serve another person's darkness.
ramayan::7021.simple_meaning: Maricha welcomed Ravana properly and served him everything he wanted, beyond ordinary human luxury.
ramayan::7021.simple_insight: Power can still be received with ritual respect, even when it is morally dark.
ramayan::7021.detailed_meaning: Ravana has crossed the sea and reached Maricha's hermitage. Maricha, once a fierce enemy and now living as an ascetic, receives him with full ceremonial honour and offers him whatever extraordinary comforts he can command. The verse sets up their dangerous conversation.
ramayan::7021.modern_relevance: You walk into a room where everyone knows the visitor is trouble, yet the host still smiles, serves tea, and plays along. Courtesy can hide complicity.
ramayan::7021.insight: It shows how hospitality can become a mask for alliance and hidden intent.

ramayan::7022.verse_sanskrit: तं स्वयं पूजयित्वा तु भोजनेनोदकेन च । अर्थोपहितया वाचा मारीचो वाक्यमब्रवीत् । । 33540 । ।
ramayan::7022.verse_hindi: Maricha extended his hospitality with appropriate food and water and said with meaningful words:
ramayan::7022.english_translation: Maricha first honoured him with food and water, then spoke to him in carefully chosen words.
ramayan::7022.translation_literal: तम् (him) / स्वयम् (personally) / पूजयित्वा (having honoured) / तु (indeed) / भोजनेन (with food) / उदकेन (with water) / च (and) / अर्थोपहितया (with meaningful) / वाचा (with speech) / मारीचः (Maricha) / वाक्यम् (words) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::7022.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7022.essence: Proper hospitality comes before hard speech.
ramayan::7022.simple_meaning: Maricha welcomed Ravana properly, offering food and water before speaking to him.
ramayan::7022.simple_insight: Courtesy can open the door to difficult conversation.
ramayan::7022.detailed_meaning: Ravana has come to Maricha's place in the forest. Maricha receives him with ritual hospitality, gives him food and water, and only then begins to speak. The verse is a bridge into their private exchange, not the exchange itself.
ramayan::7022.modern_relevance: A difficult conversation lands better when you begin with basic care instead of urgency. Even tension softens when someone feels properly received first.
ramayan::7022.insight: It shows how respect can prepare the ground before any serious talk begins.

ramayan::7023.verse_sanskrit: कच्चित्सुकुशलं राजन्लङ्कायां राक्षसेश्वर । केनार्थेन पुनस्त्वं वै तूर्णमेवमिहागतः । । 33541 । ।
ramayan::7023.verse_hindi: O king  O lord of the demons  hope all is well in Lanka. What brings you here again so soon ?
ramayan::7023.english_translation: O king, O lord of the demons, is all well in Lanka? What brings you here again so soon?
ramayan::7023.translation_literal: कच्चित् (whether?/is it) / सुकुशलं (well and safe) / राजन् (O king) / लङ्कायाम् (in Lanka) / राक्षसेश्वर (O lord of the demons) / केनार्थेन (for what purpose) / पुनः (again) / त्वम् (you) / वै (indeed) / तूर्णम् (quickly) / एवम् (thus) / इह (here) / आगतः (have come)
ramayan::7023.speaker: Maricha
ramayan::7023.essence: Polite questions can hide a larger trouble waiting to speak.
ramayan::7023.simple_meaning: Maricha greets Ravana politely and asks why he has come so quickly this time.
ramayan::7023.simple_insight: Not every meeting carries a lesson; some verses simply move the story forward.
ramayan::7023.detailed_meaning: Maricha has just welcomed Ravana with food and water. Now he speaks as a careful host, asking whether Lanka is safe and why the king of the demons has come in such haste. The verse sets up Ravana's reply.
ramayan::7023.modern_relevance: A friend shows up at your door unannounced, and you can tell something is off before they even sit down. This is the pause before the real reason comes out.
ramayan::7023.insight: It frames the scene as a courteous opening, not a teaching.

ramayan::7024.verse_sanskrit: एवमुक्तो महातेजा मारीचेन स रावणः । ततः पश्चादिदं वाक्यमब्रवीद्वाक्यकोविदः । । 33542 । ।
ramayan::7024.verse_hindi: Thus addressed by Maricha, the effulgent, eloquent Ravana replied with these words:
ramayan::7024.english_translation: Thus addressed by Maricha, the effulgent, eloquent Ravana replied with these words.
ramayan::7024.translation_literal: एवमुक्तः (thus addressed) / महातेजाः (greatly effulgent) / मारीचेन (by Maricha) / सः (he) / रावणः (Ravana) / ततः पश्चात् (then afterward) / इदम् (this) / वाक्यम् (speech) / अब्रवीत् (spoke) / वाक्य-कोविदः (skilled in speech)
ramayan::7024.speaker: Ravana
ramayan::7024.essence: Ravana is about to answer; this verse only turns the conversation forward.
ramayan::7024.simple_meaning: Maricha speaks to Ravana, and Ravana answers. The verse only marks the start of his reply.
ramayan::7024.simple_insight: Some lines only open the door to a response; they are not the response itself.
ramayan::7024.detailed_meaning: In Lanka, Maricha receives Ravana with careful hospitality and then asks why he has come so suddenly. This verse simply marks Ravana’s turn to speak next; the real exchange begins in the following lines.
ramayan::7024.modern_relevance: A meeting pauses for a breath after a hard question. Everyone waits for the answer, but this line only tells you the answer is coming.
ramayan::7024.insight: It shifts attention from the setup to the substance that follows.

ramayan::7025.verse_sanskrit: मारीच श्रूयातां तात वचनं मम भाषतः । आर्तोऽस्मि मम चार्तस्य भवान्हि परमा गतिः । । 3361 । ।
ramayan::7025.verse_hindi: O dear Maricha hear my words. I am distressed and you are my ultimate refuge.
ramayan::7025.english_translation: O dear Maricha, hear my words. I am distressed, and you are my ultimate refuge.
ramayan::7025.translation_literal: मारीच (Maricha) / श्रूयाताम् (let it be heard) / तात (dear one) / वचनम् (words) / मम (my) / भाषतः (while speaking) / आर्तः (distressed) / अस्मि (I am) / मम (my) / आर्तस्य (of the distressed one) / भवान् (you) / हि (indeed) / परमा (highest) / गतिः (refuge)
ramayan::7025.speaker: Ravana
ramayan::7025.essence: Powerful people still reach for refuge when pressure breaks their pride.
ramayan::7025.simple_meaning: Ravana tells Maricha that he is distressed and depends on Maricha for help.
ramayan::7025.simple_insight: Pride can crack in a single honest sentence.
ramayan::7025.detailed_meaning: Ravana has gone to Maricha because his own plans are tightening around him. Before he explains the full scheme, he first lowers himself and asks for help, revealing how urgent and unstable his situation has become.
ramayan::7025.modern_relevance: You finally call the one person you swore you did not need. The first honest sentence is often the one that opens the door to help.
ramayan::7025.insight: It shows that even the powerful must sometimes admit dependence before they can move forward.

ramayan::7026.verse_sanskrit: जानीषे त्वं जनस्थाने यथा भ्राता खरो मम । दूषणश्च महाबाहु स्वसा शूर्पणखा च मे । । 3362 । । त्रिशिराश्च महातेजा राक्षसः पिशिताशनः । अन्ये च बहवश्शूरा लब्धलक्षा निशाचराः । । 3363 । । वसत्नि मन्नियोगेन नित्यवासं च राक्षसाः । बाधमाना महारण्ये मुनीन्वै धर्मचारिणः । । 3364 । ।
ramayan::7026.verse_hindi: You know that my brothers, Khara and Dusana, the strongarmed heroes, my sister Surpanakha and  the mighty cannibal Trisira, and many other heroic demons successful in hitting their targets are bonafide residents. They have been harassing the followers of righteous path (the sages) at my behest.
ramayan::7026.english_translation: You know that my brother Khara, the strong-armed Dushana, my sister Surpanakha, the mighty man-eater Trishira, and many other brave night-roamers live in Janasthana by my command, troubling the sages who live by dharma.
ramayan::7026.translation_literal: जानीषे (you know) / त्वं (you) / जनस्थाने (in Janasthana) / यथा (how) / भ्राता (brother) / खरो (Khara) / मम (my) / दूषणः (Dushana) / च (and) / महाबाहु (strong-armed) / स्वसा (sister) / शूर्पणखा (Surpanakha) / च (and) / मे (my) / त्रिशिराः (Trishira) / च (and) / महातेजाः (mighty) / राक्षसः (night-roamer) / पिशिताशनः (man-eater) / अन्ये (others) / च (and) / बहवः (many) / शूराः (brave) / लब्धलक्षाः (successful at hitting targets) / निशाचराः (night-roamers) / वसन्ति (live) / मन्नियोगेन (by my command) / नित्यवासम् (permanent residence) / च (and) / राक्षसाः (night-roamers) / बाधमानाः (harassing) / महारण्ये (in the great forest) / मुनीन् (sages) / वै (indeed) / धर्मचारिणः (those who follow dharma)
ramayan::7026.speaker: Ravana
ramayan::7026.essence: Control without restraint becomes organized cruelty.
ramayan::7026.simple_meaning: Ravana reminds Maricha that his powerful relatives and many other demons are stationed in Janasthana under his command, and they are harassing the sages there.
ramayan::7026.simple_insight: Power used for harassment only deepens the rot already inside it.
ramayan::7026.detailed_meaning: Ravana is confiding in Maricha after admitting distress. He lists the forces under his control in Janasthana—Khara, Dushana, Surpanakha, Trishira, and many others—to show the scale of his reach. But the verse also exposes the moral decay of that power: they are being used against forest sages.
ramayan::7026.modern_relevance: A manager forwards a cruel task to a whole team and calls it strategy. The bigger the machine becomes, the easier it is to hide harm inside it.
ramayan::7026.insight: It shifts attention from raw power to the moral use of power.

ramayan::7027.verse_sanskrit: चतुर्दश सहस्राणि रक्षसां भीमकर्मणाम् । शूराणां लब्धलक्षाणां खरचित्तानुवर्तिनाम् । । 3365 । ।
ramayan::7027.verse_hindi: These fourteen thousand heroes, perpetrators of terrible deeds, skilled in hitting the targets had been acting according to the direction of Khara.
ramayan::7027.english_translation: These fourteen thousand heroes, perpetrators of terrible deeds, skilled in hitting the targets, had been acting according to Khara's command.
ramayan::7027.translation_literal: चतुर्दश (fourteen) / सहस्राणि (thousands) / रक्षसाम् (of the rakshasas) / भीमकर्मणाम् (of terrible deeds) / शूराणाम् (of the brave) / लब्धलक्षाणाम् (skilled in finding targets) / खरचित्तानुवर्तिनाम् (following Khara's will)
ramayan::7027.speaker: Ravana
ramayan::7027.essence: A huge army still moves at one man’s command.
ramayan::7027.simple_meaning: Ravana is describing the size and nature of Khara's force: fourteen thousand fierce warriors who obey Khara and are dangerous in battle.
ramayan::7027.simple_insight: Power can look impressive and still be only a tool of someone else's will.
ramayan::7027.detailed_meaning: Ravana is listing the strength of the forces stationed in Janasthana to persuade Maricha. He wants Maricha to see that Khara commands a vast, violent army. The verse is background detail, not a teaching on its own.
ramayan::7027.modern_relevance: A manager forwards you into a project by saying, “My whole team is behind this.” The numbers sound huge, but they only show how much force is being gathered, not whether the cause is wise.
ramayan::7027.insight: It frames the coming conflict as a clash with an organised force, not a lone enemy.

ramayan::7028.verse_sanskrit: ते त्विदानीं जनस्थाने वसमाना महाबलाः । सङ्गताः परमायत्ता रामेण सह संयुगे । । 3366 । । नानाप्रहरणोपेताः खरप्रमुखराक्षसाः ।
ramayan::7028.verse_hindi: These mighty demons, living in Janasthana, eqipped with different kinds of weapons, supported and led by Khara, met Rama in an encounter.
ramayan::7028.english_translation: These mighty demons, living in Janasthana, equipped with different kinds of weapons, supported and led by Khara, met Rama in an encounter.
