ramayan::7316.english_translation: Who are you, golden-hued and clad in yellow silk, wearing an auspicious garland of lotuses like a lotus pool?
ramayan::7316.translation_literal: का (who) / त्वं (you) / काञ्चनवर्णाभे (golden-hued) / पीतकौशेयवासिनि (clad in yellow silk) / कमलानाम् (of lotuses) / शुभाम् (auspicious) / मालाम् (garland) / पद्मिनी (lotus pool) / इव (like) / हि (indeed) / बिभ्रती (wearing, bearing)
ramayan::7316.speaker: Ravana
ramayan::7316.essence: He sees beauty, but his wanting already begins to distort it.
ramayan::7316.simple_meaning: Ravana is struck by Sita's beauty and asks who she is, describing her golden complexion, yellow silk, and lotus garland.
ramayan::7316.simple_insight: Sometimes beauty is so striking it leaves even arrogance searching for words.
ramayan::7316.detailed_meaning: In the Ashoka grove of Lanka, Ravana stands before the captive Sita and tries to name what he sees. Her beauty overwhelms him, but his question is still part of his attempt to claim and possess her.
ramayan::7316.modern_relevance: You meet someone whose presence stops your usual script. Even then, the real test is whether you see clearly or only desire to possess.
ramayan::7316.insight: It shows how desire can turn perception into pursuit, even when admiration begins the encounter.

ramayan::7317.verse_sanskrit: ह्रीः कीर्तिः श्रीश्शुभा लक्ष्मीरप्सरा वा शुभानने । । 34616 । । भूतिर्वा त्वं वरारोहे रतिर्वा स्वैरचारिणी ।
ramayan::7317.verse_hindi: O lady with a beautiful face, with lovely thighs, are you hri, shyness personified? Are you the auspicious lovely Lakshmi, the  goddess of wealth? Are you the goddess of fame? Are you an apsara? Are you Bhuti, the goddess of fortune? Or are you Rati, the goddess of love moving at your free will ?
ramayan::7317.english_translation: O lady with a beautiful face, with lovely thighs, are you Shyness herself, or Lakshmi, or Fame, or an apsara? Are you Fortune, or Rati, moving freely at will?
ramayan::7317.translation_literal: ह्रीः (shyness) / कीर्तिः (fame) / श्रीः (beauty, prosperity) / शुभा (auspicious) / लक्ष्मीः (Lakshmi) / अप्सरा (apsara) / वा (or) / शुभानने (O beautiful-faced one) / भूतिः (fortune, prosperity) / वा (or) / त्वं (you) / वरारोहे (O best-thighed one) / रतिः (Rati) (love) / वा (or) / स्वैरचारिणी (moving freely at will)
ramayan::7317.speaker: Ravana
ramayan::7317.essence: Desire makes him see a woman as many imagined forms at once.
ramayan::7317.simple_meaning: Ravana, struck by Sita's beauty, wonders if she is a goddess of beauty, fame, fortune, shyness, or love.
ramayan::7317.simple_insight: Attraction can blur the line between admiration and projection.
ramayan::7317.detailed_meaning: In Lanka, Ravana keeps questioning the radiant woman he has seized. Her beauty overwhelms him so completely that he cannot place her among ordinary women. The verse is part of his dazzled, possessive attempt to name what he sees.
ramayan::7317.modern_relevance: You meet someone so striking that your mind starts inventing stories about them before you know them.
ramayan::7317.insight: It shows how desire can turn a real person into a fantasy.

ramayan::7318.verse_sanskrit: समाश्शिखरिणस्स्निग्धाः पाण्डुरा दशनास्तव । । 34617 । । विशाले विमले नेत्रे रक्तान्ते कृष्णतारके ।
ramayan::7318.verse_hindi: Your teeth are even and pointed, white and beautiful.Your eyes are large and clear and sparkling with dark pupils with a red tinge at the corner.
ramayan::7318.english_translation: Your teeth are even and pointed, white and beautiful. Your eyes are large and clear, with dark pupils and a red tint at the corners.
ramayan::7318.translation_literal: समाः (even) / शिखरिणः (pointed) / स्निग्धाः (smooth, glossy) / पाण्डुराः (white) / दशनाः (teeth) / तव (your) / विशाले (large) / विमले (clear, pure) / नेत्रे (eyes) / रक्तान्ते (red at the edge) / कृष्णतारके (with dark pupils)
ramayan::7318.speaker: Hanuman
ramayan::7318.essence: The verse lingers on Sita's features, building a full portrait through careful detail.
ramayan::7318.simple_meaning: Hanuman continues describing Sita's beauty, focusing on her teeth and eyes.
ramayan::7318.simple_insight: Sometimes a single detail carries the whole feeling of presence.
ramayan::7318.detailed_meaning: In Lanka, Hanuman is hidden in the ashoka grove and carefully taking in every feature of the woman he has found. This line is part of his close, reverent examination of Sita, not a teaching on its own.
ramayan::7318.modern_relevance: You notice the exact curve of a smile or the steadiness in someone's eyes before you can explain why it matters.
ramayan::7318.insight: It trains attention to see beauty through precise, respectful observation.

ramayan::7319.verse_sanskrit: विशालं जघनं पीनमूरू करिकरोपमौ । । 34618 । । एतावुपचितौ वृत्तौ संहतौ सम्प्रवल्गितौ । पीनोन्नतमुखौ कान्तौ स्निग्धौ तालफलोपमौ । । 34619 । । मणिप्रवेकाभरणौ रुचिरौ ते पयोधरौ ।
ramayan::7319.verse_hindi: Your big hips are stout and strong, Your smooth thighs are like the trunk of an elephant, your breasts adorned with gems, are round and robust like palm fruits and drooping with heaviness with projected stiff nipples, shining and delightful, adding beauty.
ramayan::7319.english_translation: Your hips are broad and full, and your thighs are like the trunk of an elephant. Your rounded, firm breasts are beautiful, smooth, and adorned with jewels, like ripe palm fruits.
ramayan::7319.translation_literal: विशालम् (broad) / जघनम् (hips) / पीनम् (full, stout) / ऊरू (thighs) / करिकर-उपमौ (like elephant trunks) / एतौ (these two) / उपचितौ (well-developed) / वृत्तौ (rounded) / संहतौ (firmly joined) / सम्प्रवल्गितौ (well-formed) / पीन-उन्नत-मुखौ (full and raised at the top) / कान्तौ (beautiful) / स्निग्धौ (smooth) / तालफल-उपमौ (like palm fruits) / मणि-प्रवेक-अभरणौ (adorned with finest jewels) / रुचिरौ (lovely) / ते (your) / पयोधरौ (breasts)
ramayan::7319.speaker: Ravana
ramayan::7319.essence: Desire here speaks in admiration, but it is already trying to possess.
ramayan::7319.simple_meaning: Ravana is describing a woman's body in admiring detail, praising her hips, thighs, and breasts as beautiful and full.
ramayan::7319.simple_insight: Attraction can make the mind linger on details and lose its balance.
ramayan::7319.detailed_meaning: In Lanka, Ravana keeps pressing his desire toward Sita through praise and persuasion. This verse is part of his sensual description of her body, not a teaching moment. It shows his fixation growing more explicit as he tries to overwhelm her resistance.
ramayan::7319.modern_relevance: A compliment that starts respectful and turns possessive can feel like pressure in disguise. You can hear when admiration is no longer seeing you, but claiming you.
ramayan::7319.insight: It reveals how desire can become objectifying language, reducing a person to features.

ramayan::7320.verse_sanskrit: चारुस्मिते चारुदति चारुनेत्रे विलासिनि । । 34620 । । मनो हरसि मे कान्ते नदी कूलमिवाम्भसा । करान्तमितमध्यासि सुकेशी संहतस्तनी । । 34621 । ।
ramayan::7320.verse_hindi: O lady with an elegant smile, beautiful teeth, lovely  eyes you are enticing.Your slender waist can be compassed by my fist.Your hair is beautiful and your large breasts are rubbing against each other.You are capturing my mind  just as the flow of water in a river  touches its banks.
ramayan::7320.english_translation: O lady with an elegant smile, beautiful teeth, and lovely eyes, you are enchanting. Your slender waist can be held in a fist. Your beautiful hair and full breasts are captivating my mind just as water touches a riverbank.
ramayan::7320.translation_literal: चारु-स्मिते (with an elegant smile) / चारु-दति (with beautiful teeth) / चारु-नेत्रे (with lovely eyes) / विलासिनि (delightful woman) / मनः (mind) / हरसि (you steal) / मे (my) / कान्ते (beloved woman) / नदी-कूलम् (riverbank) / इव (like) / अम्भसा (by water) / कर-अन्त-मितम् (measured by the hand) / अध्यासि (you sit/are placed) / सुकेशी (with beautiful hair) / संहत-स्तनी (with full breasts)
ramayan::7320.speaker: Ravana
ramayan::7320.essence: Desire makes even beauty feel like something to take.
ramayan::7320.simple_meaning: Ravana is openly praising a woman's beauty, saying her features overwhelm his mind and stir desire.
ramayan::7320.simple_insight: Unchecked desire narrows the mind until beauty becomes possession.
ramayan::7320.detailed_meaning: In Lanka, Ravana is describing Sita's beauty in consuming detail, turning admiration into craving. The verse is not teaching restraint; it reveals the intensity of his fixation and the way desire grips his mind before it becomes action.
ramayan::7320.modern_relevance: You keep staring at a photo, then a profile, then another glance, and the wanting only grows. This is what fixation sounds like before it turns into obsession.
ramayan::7320.insight: It shows how quickly admiration can slide into possessive craving.

ramayan::7321.verse_sanskrit: नैव देवी न गन्धर्वी न यक्षी न च किन्नरी । नैवंरूपा मया नारी दृष्टपूर्वा महीतले । । 34622 । ।
ramayan::7321.verse_hindi: O beautiful lady I have not seen such a beauty earlier either among goddesses or among gandharavis, or yakshis or even among kinneris.
ramayan::7321.english_translation: I have never seen such a woman on earth before — not among goddesses, gandharvas, yakshas, or kinnaras.
ramayan::7321.translation_literal: नैव (not at all) / देवी (goddess) / न (not) / गन्धर्वी (gandharvi) / न (not) / यक्षी (yakshi) / न (not) / च (and) / किन्नरी (kinnari) / नैवंरूपा (of such form) / मया (by me) / नारी (woman) / दृष्टपूर्वा (seen before) / महीतले (on the surface of the earth)
ramayan::7321.speaker: Ravana
ramayan::7321.essence: A captivated mind starts ranking beauty instead of seeing a person.
ramayan::7321.simple_meaning: Ravana says he has never seen a woman like this before, not even among the most radiant beings he can imagine.
ramayan::7321.simple_insight: Desire narrows the mind until beauty feels like a conquest.
ramayan::7321.detailed_meaning: Ravana is speaking in the Ashoka grove after seeing Sita. He is overwhelmed by her beauty and compares her to celestial beings, trying to name what makes her unlike anyone he has seen. The verse is part of his attempt to possess what he cannot understand.
ramayan::7321.modern_relevance: You see someone and your mind starts racing ahead of your character. Attraction can make even a brilliant person speak like a collector.
ramayan::7321.insight: It shows how craving turns perception into possession-seeking.

ramayan::7322.verse_sanskrit: रूपमग्र्यं च लोकेषु सौकुमार्यं वयश्चते । इह वासश्च कान्तारे चित्तमुन्मादयन्ति मे । । 34623 । ।
ramayan::7322.verse_hindi: You are the most beautiful among women in the world. With all your tenderness and youth you are living in this forlorn forest. This maddens my heart.
ramayan::7322.english_translation: You are the most beautiful among women in the world. With all your tenderness and youth you are living in this forlorn forest. This maddens my heart.
ramayan::7322.translation_literal: रूपम् (beauty) / अग्र्यम् (foremost) / च (and) / लोकेषु (among the worlds) / सौकुमार्यम् (delicacy) / वयः (youth) / च (and) / ते (your) । इह (here) / वासः (dwelling) / च (and) / कान्तारे (in the forest) / चित्तम् (mind) / उन्मादयन्ति (madden) / मे (my) ।
ramayan::7322.speaker: Ravana
ramayan::7322.essence: Beauty without restraint becomes a force that distorts the mind.
ramayan::7322.simple_meaning: Ravana is overwhelmed by Sita's beauty, youth, and the shock of seeing her in the forest. His desire intensifies because he sees her in a place of danger and isolation.
ramayan::7322.simple_insight: Desire grows stronger when the mind turns beauty into possession.
ramayan::7322.detailed_meaning: In the forest, Ravana sees Sita and cannot contain his fascination. He praises her beauty and youth, but the praise is already turning into obsession. This line is part of his seductive approach before he tries to press her into leaving.
ramayan::7322.modern_relevance: You see someone vulnerable and your admiration starts to blur into wanting. The moment you stop respecting their boundary, attraction becomes harm.
ramayan::7322.insight: It exposes how quickly admiration can become entitlement when restraint is missing.

ramayan::7323.verse_sanskrit: सा प्रतिक्राम भद्रं ते नैवं वस्तुमिहार्हसि । राक्षसानामयं वासो घोराणां कामरूपिणाम् । । 34624 । ।
ramayan::7323.verse_hindi: It is not safe for a lady like you to reside here. Move out at once. This is only fit for the dwelling of horrible demons who can change their form at will.
ramayan::7323.english_translation: Move back, noble lady. You should not stay here. This is the dwelling of terrible shape-shifting demons.
ramayan::7323.translation_literal: सा (she) / प्रतिक्राम (move back) / भद्रम् (noble one) / ते (to you) / नैव (not at all) / वस्तुम् (to stay) / इह (here) / अर्हसि (you are fit) / राक्षसानाम् (of demons) / अयम् (this) / वासः (dwelling) / घोराणाम् (terrible) / कामरूपिणाम् (shape-shifting)
ramayan::7323.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::7323.essence: Beauty does not make a dangerous place safe.
ramayan::7323.simple_meaning: The speaker warns Sita that this place is no fit home for her. It is a dangerous place full of shape-shifting demons.
ramayan::7323.simple_insight: Some places are wrong for you, no matter how carefully you enter them.
ramayan::7323.detailed_meaning: In the forest, a man speaks to Sita after admiring her beauty. He immediately warns her to step away, because this land belongs to terrifying beings who can change form. The verse is part of a larger attempt to lure or alarm her, not a complete teaching on its own.
ramayan::7323.modern_relevance: A stranger’s message looks gentle at first, then the warning signs appear. You feel it in your body before you can explain it: this room, this chat, this offer is not safe for you.
ramayan::7323.insight: It sharpens discernment about environments that invite harm, even when they arrive wrapped in praise.

ramayan::7324.verse_sanskrit: प्रासादाग्राणि रम्याणि नगरोपवनानि च । सम्पन्नानि सुगन्धीनि युक्तान्याचरितुं त्वया । । 34625 । ।
ramayan::7324.verse_hindi: You deserve to stroll in the terraces of palaces, in beautiful, luxurious and fragrant city gardens.
ramayan::7324.english_translation: You deserve to stroll in the terraces of palaces, in beautiful, luxurious and fragrant city gardens.
ramayan::7324.translation_literal: प्रासादाग्राणि (the upper terraces of palaces) / रम्याणि (beautiful) / नगरोपवनानि (city gardens) / च (and) / सम्पन्नानि (well-provided) / सुगन्धीनि (fragrant) / युक्तानि (fit) / आचरितुं (to walk about) / त्वया (by you)
ramayan::7324.speaker: Ravana
ramayan::7324.essence: Luxury is offered here as bait, not blessing.
ramayan::7324.simple_meaning: He says she belongs in rich palace terraces and fragrant city gardens, not in the forest where she is held.
ramayan::7324.simple_insight: Even in captivity, dignity can be spoken to with reverence.
ramayan::7324.detailed_meaning: Ravana is trying to persuade Sita in the Ashoka grove. After praising her beauty and rejecting the forest as her place, he describes the comfort and elegance she should enjoy. This verse supports his larger attempt to tempt her away from Rama.
ramayan::7324.modern_relevance: Someone tries to flatter you into forgetting the cost of their offer. The setting sounds luxurious, but the real message is pressure dressed as care.
ramayan::7324.insight: It sharpens the contrast between genuine honor and manipulative praise.

ramayan::7325.verse_sanskrit: वरं माल्यं वरं भोज्यं वरं वस्त्रं च शोभने । भर्तारं च वरं मन्ये त्वद्युक्तमसितेक्षणे । । 34626 । ।
ramayan::7325.verse_hindi: O beautiful, blackeyed lady, I think you deserve the best of garlands, best of food,
ramayan::7325.english_translation: O beautiful, black-eyed lady, I think you deserve the best garlands, the best food, the best clothes, and a worthy husband.
ramayan::7325.translation_literal: वरम् (best) / माल्यम् (garland) / वरम् (best) / भोज्यम् (food) / वरम् (best) / वस्त्रम् (clothing) / च (and) / शोभने (O beautiful one) / भर्तारम् (husband) / च (and) / वरम् (excellent) / मन्ये (I consider) / त्वद्युक्तम् (fit for you) / असितेक्षणे (O black-eyed one)
ramayan::7325.speaker: Ravana
ramayan::7325.simple_meaning: Ravana tells Sita that she deserves only the finest things, including an excellent husband.
ramayan::7325.simple_insight: Even praise can be a form of pressure when it tries to bend your will.
ramayan::7325.detailed_meaning: In Lanka, Ravana tries to soften Sita with flattery after warning her that this place is no home for her. He lists the finest garlands, food, clothes, and then a worthy husband, revealing his attempt to persuade her without force.
ramayan::7325.modern_relevance: Someone compliments your taste, your worth, your standards — and then quietly uses that praise to steer your decision. The pressure is gentler, but the aim is the same.
ramayan::7325.insight: It shows how desire can disguise itself as admiration and persuasion.

ramayan::7326.verse_sanskrit: का त्वं भवसि रुद्राणां मरुतां वा वरानने । वसूनां वा वरावोहे देवता प्रतिभासि मे । । 34627 । ।
ramayan::7326.verse_hindi: O best of women O lady with beautiful buttocks  can you be one  of the Rudras or Maruts or Vasus? To me, you appear like a goddess.
ramayan::7326.english_translation: O best of women, can you be one of the Rudras, Maruts, or Vasus? To me, you appear like a goddess.
ramayan::7326.translation_literal: का (who) / त्वं (you) / भवसि (are) / रुद्राणां (of the Rudras) / मरुतां (of the Maruts) / वा (or) / वरानने (O beautiful-faced one) / वसूनां (of the Vasus) / वा (or) / वरावोहे (O best-breasted one) / देवता (a divine being) / प्रतिभासि (appear) / मे (to me)
ramayan::7326.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::7326.essence: Her presence is so noble it seems beyond the human world.
ramayan::7326.simple_meaning: Hanuman is startled by Sita’s radiance and asks whether she is a radiant being from the heavenly classes, not an ordinary woman.
ramayan::7326.simple_insight: True dignity can be so complete that it feels almost unreal.
ramayan::7326.detailed_meaning: Hanuman has reached the Ashoka grove in Lanka and finally sees Sita, sitting among enemies and sorrow. Her presence overwhelms him so completely that he wonders whether she belongs to one of the radiant classes of beings rather than to the human world.
ramayan::7326.modern_relevance: You meet someone in the middle of hardship, and their composure is so striking it stops you cold. Their presence feels larger than the room they’re in.
ramayan::7326.insight: It frames Sita’s suffering as untouched dignity, not weakness.

ramayan::7327.verse_sanskrit: नेह गच्छन्ति गन्धर्वा न देवा न च किन्नराः । राक्षसानामयं वासः कथं नु त्वमिहागता । । 34628 । ।
ramayan::7327.verse_hindi: Neither gandharvas, nor kinnaras, nor gods move here. This is only a dwelling place for the demons. How did you come here ?
ramayan::7327.english_translation: Neither gandharvas, nor kinnaras, nor gods move here. This is only a dwelling place for the demons. How did you come here?
ramayan::7327.translation_literal: न इह (not here) / गच्छन्ति (go) / गन्धर्वाः (gandharvas) / न (nor) / देवाः (gods) / न च (and not) / किन्नराः (kinnaras) / राक्षसानाम् (of demons) / अयम् (this) / वासः (dwelling place) / कथम् नु (how indeed) / त्वम् (you) / इह (here) / आगता (come)
ramayan::7327.speaker: Ravana
ramayan::7327.essence: Her presence makes the darkness of the place impossible to ignore.
ramayan::7327.simple_meaning: Ravana is startled that a woman has entered a place no celestial being visits, a city ruled by demons. He cannot understand how she arrived there.
ramayan::7327.simple_insight: Even power can be shaken by what it cannot explain.
ramayan::7327.detailed_meaning: In Lanka, Ravana is speaking to Sita after finding her in captivity. He lists the kinds of beings who do not come to this place, then admits his own astonishment: how did she reach a city meant only for demons? The verse is part of his questioning, not a complete teaching.
ramayan::7327.modern_relevance: You meet someone whose calm presence does not belong in the room's ugliness. For a moment, even the harshest place feels exposed.
ramayan::7327.insight: It shows how innocence or dignity can feel startling inside a corrupt environment.

ramayan::7328.verse_sanskrit: इह शाखामृगास्सिंहा द्वीपिव्याघ्रमृगास्तथा । ऋक्षास्तरक्षवः कङ्काः कथं तेभ्यो न बिभ्यसि । । 34629 । ।
ramayan::7328.verse_hindi: There are monkeys, lions, panthers, tigers, hyenas, bears, kanka birds and other wild animals here. How is it that you are not afraid of them?
ramayan::7328.english_translation: There are monkeys, lions, panthers, tigers, hyenas, bears, kanka birds, and other wild animals here. How is it that you are not afraid of them?
ramayan::7328.translation_literal: इह (here) / शाखामृगाः (tree-dwelling beasts, monkeys) / सिंहाः (lions) / द्वीपि-व्याघ्र-मृगाः (panthers-tigers-beasts) / तथा (and so forth) / ऋक्षाः (bears) / तरक्षवः (hyenas) / कङ्काः (kanka birds) / कथम् (how) / तेभ्यः (from them) / न (not) / बिभ्यसि (you are afraid)
ramayan::7328.speaker: Ravana
ramayan::7328.essence: Fear loses its grip when inner steadiness is stronger than the surroundings.
ramayan::7328.simple_meaning: Ravana keeps asking why the woman is not frightened by the wild animals around her. He is probing her impossible calm in a dangerous place.
ramayan::7328.simple_insight: Composure can be its own kind of power.
ramayan::7328.detailed_meaning: In Lanka, Ravana stands before a woman who should be terrified by the forest-like dangers around her. Instead, she remains steady. His question reveals both the danger of the place and the shock of seeing fear fail to control her.
ramayan::7328.modern_relevance: You walk into a chaotic room and expect fear to show on someone's face. Instead, they stay steady, and their calm unsettles everyone else.
ramayan::7328.insight: It highlights a presence so steady that danger no longer dominates the scene.

ramayan::7329.verse_sanskrit: मदान्वितानां घोराणां कुञ्जराणां तरस्विनाम् । कथमेका महारण्ये न बिभेषि वरानने । । 34630 । ।
ramayan::7329.verse_hindi: O Charming lady how is it that although alone you are not afraid of the dreadful, swift, powerful wild animals like elephants in rut ?
ramayan::7329.english_translation: O charming lady, how is it that, though alone, you do not fear the dreadful, swift, powerful wild elephants in the great forest?
ramayan::7329.translation_literal: मदान्वितानाम् (of those possessed by rut) / घोराणाम् (of the dreadful) / कुञ्जराणाम् (of elephants) / तरस्विनाम् (of the swift, powerful ones) / कथम् (how) / एका (alone) / महारण्ये (in the great forest) / न बिभेषि (you do not fear) / वरानने (O charming-faced one)
ramayan::7329.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7329.essence: Her calm in a deadly forest makes her presence feel extraordinary.
ramayan::7329.simple_meaning: A lone woman in a dangerous forest is being asked why she shows no fear, even of charging wild elephants.
ramayan::7329.simple_insight: Sometimes courage is so visible that it becomes its own mystery.
ramayan::7329.detailed_meaning: In the Dandaka forest, strange beauty has appeared where only danger usually lives. A speaker, startled by Sita's presence, asks why she does not tremble before the forest's fiercest creatures. The question is part of a larger exchange to identify who she is and why she is there.
ramayan::7329.modern_relevance: You walk home alone after dark, and every sound feels louder than it should. Then you notice someone moving with complete calm, as if fear has not entered their body.
ramayan::7329.insight: It frames fearlessness as something that can be noticed before it is explained.

ramayan::7330.verse_sanskrit: कासि कस्य कुतश्चित्त्वं किं निमित्तं च दण्डकान् । एका चरसि कल्याणि घोरान्राक्षससेवितान् । । 34631 । ।
ramayan::7330.verse_hindi: Who are you, O auspicious lady ? Who are your people? Why are you here? From where have you come? For what reason are you going about alone in this fierce Dandaka tract, inhabited by demons?
ramayan::7330.english_translation: Who are you, O auspicious lady? Who are your people? Why are you here? From where have you come? For what reason are you moving alone in this fierce Dandaka tract, inhabited by demons?
ramayan::7330.translation_literal: का (who) / असि (are you) / कस्य (whose) / कुतश्चित् (from where) / त्वं (you) / किम् (what) / निमित्तम् (reason) / च (and) / दण्डकान् (Dandaka forests) / एका (alone) / चरसि (you roam) / कल्याणि (O auspicious one) / घोरान् (fierce) / राक्षस-सेवितान् (inhabited by demons)
ramayan::7330.speaker: Ravana
ramayan::7330.essence: Polite questions can hide predatory intent.
ramayan::7330.simple_meaning: A stranger questions a lone woman in a dangerous forest, asking who she is, where she came from, and why she is there by herself.
ramayan::7330.simple_insight: Not every question is innocent; danger often begins with polite curiosity.
ramayan::7330.detailed_meaning: In the Dandaka forest, Ravana has approached Sita in disguise and begins probing her identity. This verse is part of his calculated attempt to draw her into conversation before revealing his true intent.
ramayan::7330.modern_relevance: A stranger keeps asking where you live, who sent you, and why you're alone. The questions sound polite, but your body already knows something is wrong.
ramayan::7330.insight: It shows how manipulation often starts with curiosity that is really a trap.

ramayan::7331.verse_sanskrit: इति प्रशस्ता वैदेही रावणेन दुरात्मना । द्विजातिवेशेण हि तं दृष्ट्वा रावणमागतम् । । 34632 । । सर्वैरतिथिसत्कारैः पूजयामास मैथिली ।
ramayan::7331.verse_hindi: Seeing Ravana, a villain in the guise of a brahmin praising her, Sita, the princess of
ramayan::7331.english_translation: Seeing Ravana, a wicked man disguised as a brahmin, Sita of Mithila honoured him with every hospitality.
ramayan::7331.translation_literal: इति (thus) / प्रशस्ता (praised) / वैदेही (Sita, daughter of Videha) / रावणेन (by Ravana) / दुरात्मना (evil-minded one) / द्विजातिवेशेण (with the guise of a twice-born man, a brahmin) / हि (indeed) / तं (him) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / रावणम् (Ravana) / आगतम् (arrived) / सर्वैः (with all) / अतिथिसत्कारैः (hospitalities to a guest) / पूजयामास (honoured) / मैथिली (Maithili, Sita)
ramayan::7331.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7331.essence: She answers deception with the dignity of a true host.
ramayan::7331.simple_meaning: Sita sees Ravana disguised as a brahmin and treats him like an honoured guest, offering full hospitality.
ramayan::7331.simple_insight: True character shows in how you treat someone before you know their intent.
ramayan::7331.detailed_meaning: In the forest, Ravana approaches Sita in disguise and flatters her with polite words. She does not yet know the danger. Seeing only a guest, she responds with the hospitality expected of a noble house, even as the trap closes around her.
ramayan::7331.modern_relevance: A stranger at your door says all the right things, and you still choose courtesy. That grace can be beautiful, even when the other person is hiding harm.
ramayan::7331.insight: It shows how dignity and hospitality can remain intact even under threat, before the danger is fully revealed.

ramayan::7332.verse_sanskrit: उपनीयासनं पूर्वं पाद्येनाभिनिमन्त्र्य च । । 34633 । । अब्रवीत्सिद्धमित्येव तदा तं सौम्यदर्शनम् ।
ramayan::7332.verse_hindi: She offered the handsome guest a seat first and then water for washing his feet with, and then invited him for food.
ramayan::7332.english_translation: She first offered him a seat, then water for washing his feet, and then invited him to eat.
ramayan::7332.translation_literal: उपनीय (having brought) / आसनं (a seat) / पूर्वं (first) / पाद्येन (with water for the feet) / अभिनिमन्त्र्य (having invited) / च (and) / अब्रवीत् (spoke) / सिद्धम् (prepared) / इति (thus) / एव (indeed) / तदा (then) / तम् (him) / सौम्यदर्शनम् (of pleasing appearance)
ramayan::7332.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7332.essence: Courtesy can be weaponized when discernment is absent.
ramayan::7332.simple_meaning: Sita treated the disguised visitor like an honored guest, giving him a seat, water, and food.
ramayan::7332.simple_insight: Good manners can be noble, but they can also leave you open to harm.
ramayan::7332.detailed_meaning: In the forest, Sita receives Ravana, disguised as a brahmin, with full hospitality. She cannot yet see the danger behind the courteous appearance, so she follows righteous custom and honors the guest before her.
ramayan::7332.modern_relevance: Someone arrives at your door sounding polished, respectful, and harmless. You want to be gracious, but grace without discernment can become a wound.
ramayan::7332.insight: It shows how courtesy, without suspicion, can be exploited by deception.

ramayan::7333.verse_sanskrit: द्विजातिवेषेण समीक्ष्य मैथिली समागतं पात्रकुसुम्भधारिणम् । अशक्यमुद्वेष्टुमपायदर्शनम् न्यमन्त्रयद्ब्राह्मणवत्तदाङ्गना । । 34634 । ।
ramayan::7333.verse_hindi: Sita, being a lady, was unable to doubt him since he came in the guise of a brahmin, holding a bottlegourd and a begging bowl. Without knowing his illintention she invited him in, mistaking him for a brahmin.
ramayan::7333.english_translation: Sita, seeing him arrive in the guise of a brahmin, holding a bottle-gourd and a begging bowl, invited him as a brahmin woman would.
ramayan::7333.translation_literal: द्विजातिवेषेण (in the guise of a twice-born) / समीक्ष्य (seeing) / मैथिली (Maithili, Sita) / समागतं (arrived) / पात्रकुसुम्भधारिणम् (holding a bowl and bottle-gourd) / अशक्यम् (impossible) / उद्वेष्टुम् (to distrust) / अपायदर्शनम् (one whose danger was not seen) / न्यमन्त्रयत् (invited) / ब्राह्मणवत् (like a brahmin) / तत् (that) / आङ्गना (woman)
ramayan::7333.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7333.essence: False holiness can disarm even careful trust.
ramayan::7333.simple_meaning: Sita treated the disguised Ravana as an honoured guest and invited him in, because his false appearance hid his danger.
ramayan::7333.simple_insight: Trust can be generous and still be exploited by deception.
ramayan::7333.detailed_meaning: In the forest hut, Sita sees Ravana disguised as a holy visitor carrying a bowl and bottle-gourd. His appearance blocks suspicion, and she receives him with the respect due to a guest. The verse shows the tragic ease with which innocence can be deceived.
ramayan::7333.modern_relevance: You open the door to someone who looks harmless, speaks politely, and carries all the right signs. By the time your instincts wake up, the damage may already be in motion.
ramayan::7333.insight: It teaches you to notice how appearances can silence caution before danger is named.

ramayan::7334.verse_sanskrit: इयं बृसी ब्राह्मण काममास्यतामिदं च पाद्यं प्रतिगृह्यतामिति । इदं च सिद्धं वनजातमुत्तमं त्वदर्थमव्यग्रमिहोपभुज्यताम् । । 34635 । ।
ramayan::7334.verse_hindi: O brahmin, here is the seat for you. Feel free to sit. Here is water to wash your feet with. This is the best of food for you collected from the forest. Please partake this without hesitation.
ramayan::7334.english_translation: O brahmin, here is a seat for you. Feel free to sit. Here is water to wash your feet with. This is the best of food for you, gathered from the forest. Please partake of it without hesitation.
ramayan::7334.translation_literal: इयम् (this) / बृसी (seat) / ब्राह्मण (O brahmin) / कामम् (as you wish) / आस्यताम् (may you sit) / इदम् (this) / च (and) / पाद्यम् (water for feet-washing) / प्रतिगृह्यताम् (may it be accepted) / इदम् (this) / च (and) / सिद्धम् (prepared) / वनजातम् (forest-grown food) / उत्तमम् (excellent) / त्वदर्थम् (for you) / अव्यग्रम् (without hesitation) / इह (here) / उपभुज्यताम् (may it be enjoyed)
ramayan::7334.speaker: Sita
ramayan::7334.essence: Hospitality can be pure even when danger is already near.
ramayan::7334.simple_meaning: Sita welcomes the disguised visitor with full hospitality, offering him a seat, water for his feet, and forest food without suspicion.
ramayan::7334.simple_insight: Kindness can be complete even before you know who is standing before you.
ramayan::7334.detailed_meaning: In the forest, Sita receives a stranger who appears to be a brahmin and treats him with proper honour. She offers a seat, water for his feet, and food. The tenderness of her welcome makes the coming betrayal even more tragic.
ramayan::7334.modern_relevance: Someone knocks on your door looking harmless, and you still choose courtesy before certainty. That instinct to welcome with dignity is what makes trust human.
ramayan::7334.insight: It shows how respectful conduct can exist even in danger, before suspicion has taken hold.

ramayan::7335.verse_sanskrit: निमन्त्र्यमाणः प्रतिपूर्णभाषिणीं नरेन्द्रपत्नीं प्रसमीक्ष्य मैथिलीम् । प्रसह्य तस्याहरणे धृतं मनः समर्पयत्स्वात्मवधाय रावणः । । 34636 । ।
ramayan::7335.verse_hindi: Ravana was observing the princess from Mithila, wife of a king inviting him  and speaking to him in cordial manner. Looking at her, he resolved to  abduct her forcibly, inviting his own death.
ramayan::7335.english_translation: Ravana, seeing Mithila's princess, the king's wife, speaking to him respectfully, fixed his mind on seizing her by force, even though it meant his own death.
ramayan::7335.translation_literal: निमन्त्र्यमाणः (being invited) / नरेन्द्रपत्नीम् (the king's wife) / प्रसमीक्ष्य (having carefully seen) / मैथिलीम् (Mithila's princess) / प्रसह्य (by force) / तस्याहरणे (in her abduction) / धृतम् (fixed) / मनः (mind) / समर्पयत् (he set) / स्वात्मवधाय (for his own death) / रावणः (Ravana)
ramayan::7335.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7335.essence: He turns welcome into violence and walks straight toward his own end.
ramayan::7335.simple_meaning: Ravana sees Sita treating him as a guest, and that very courtesy becomes the moment he chooses violence and seals his own ruin.
ramayan::7335.simple_insight: A respectful welcome can still meet a mind bent on harm.
ramayan::7335.detailed_meaning: In the forest, Sita offers a guest's welcome to the disguised Ravana. Instead of restraint, he studies her carefully and decides to seize her by force. The verse marks the exact instant his desire hardens into the act that will destroy him.
ramayan::7335.modern_relevance: Someone is polite to you in a tense conversation, and you still decide to push past every boundary. The damage begins the moment you choose force over restraint.
ramayan::7335.insight: It shows how desire can turn hospitality into danger and push a person toward self-destruction.

ramayan::7336.verse_sanskrit: ततः सुवेषं मृगयागतं पतिं प्रतीक्षमाणा सहलक्ष्मणं तदा । विवीक्षमाणा हरितं ददर्श तन्महद्वनं नैव तु रामलक्ष्णौ । । 34637 । ।
ramayan::7336.verse_hindi: Sita looked out for the beautiful figure of Rama who had gone to hunt the deer along with Lakshmana. Waiting eagerly for her husband, she only saw the vast stretch of green forest  but not Rama and Lakshmana.
ramayan::7336.english_translation: Sita looked out for the beautiful figure of Rama who had gone to hunt the deer with Lakshmana. Waiting eagerly for her husband, she saw only the green forest, not Rama and Lakshmana.
ramayan::7336.translation_literal: ततः (then) / सुवेषम् (beautifully dressed) / मृगयागतम् (gone hunting) / पतिम् (husband) / प्रतीक्षमाणा (waiting for) / सहलक्ष्मणम् (with Lakshmana) / तदा (then) / विवीक्षमाणा (looking intently) / हरितम् (green) / ददर्श (she saw) / तत् (that) / महत् (great) / वनम् (forest) / नैव (not at all) / तु (but) / रामलक्ष्मणौ (Rama and Lakshmana)
ramayan::7336.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7336.essence: She waits in hope, but the forest answers with emptiness.
ramayan::7336.simple_meaning: Sita waits for Rama and Lakshmana to return from the hunt, but all she can see is the forest.
ramayan::7336.simple_insight: Waiting can make every empty minute feel larger.
ramayan::7336.detailed_meaning: In the forest, Sita stands at the edge of the trees, watching for Rama and Lakshmana to return from hunting. Her gaze keeps searching, but the path stays empty. The verse slows the moment so the coming danger feels close.
ramayan::7336.modern_relevance: You keep checking the road after someone said they were on their way. The silence stretches, and every passing minute turns into a worry you can feel in your chest.
ramayan::7336.insight: It trains attention to the ache of waiting and the vulnerability of separation.

ramayan::7337.verse_sanskrit: रावणेन तु वैदेही तदा पृष्टा जिहीर्षता । परिव्राजकरूपेण शशंसात्मानमात्मना । । 3471 । ।
ramayan::7337.verse_hindi: Then Ravana in the guise of a mendicant with crooked intention to abduct her, asked Vaidehi to tell him about herself.
ramayan::7337.english_translation: Then Ravana, disguised as a mendicant and intent on abducting her, asked Vaidehi to tell him about herself.
ramayan::7337.translation_literal: रावणेन (by Ravana) / तु (indeed) / वैदेही (Vaidehi) / तदा (then) / पृष्टा (asked) / जिहीर्षता (desiring to abduct) / परिव्राजकरूपेण (in the form of a mendicant) / शशंस (told) / आत्मानम् (herself) / आत्मना (by herself)
ramayan::7337.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7337.simple_meaning: Ravana comes in disguise and asks Sita to reveal who she is.
ramayan::7337.simple_insight: A false appearance can hide a dangerous intent.
ramayan::7337.detailed_meaning: In the forest, Ravana approaches Sita disguised as a mendicant, hiding his plan to abduct her. He questions her under the cover of respectability, setting the stage for Sita's careful response in the next verse.
ramayan::7337.modern_relevance: A stranger arrives sounding polite, asking personal questions that feel slightly off. The danger is not loud at first; it wears a harmless face.
ramayan::7337.insight: It teaches you to notice when courtesy is being used as cover for harm.

ramayan::7338.verse_sanskrit: ब्राह्मणश्चातिथिश्चायमनुक्तो हि शपेत माम् । इति ध्यात्वा मुहूर्तं तु सीता वचनमब्रवीत् । । 3472 । ।
ramayan::7338.verse_hindi: He is a brahmin and also a guest. If unanswered he may curse me. Thinking this Sita thought for a moment and said:
ramayan::7338.english_translation: He is a brahmin and also a guest. If unanswered, he may curse me. Thinking for a moment, Sita then spoke:
ramayan::7338.translation_literal: ब्राह्मणः (a brahmin) / च (and) / अतिथिः (a guest) / च (and) / अयम् (this one) / अनुक्तः (not spoken to / unanswered) / हि (indeed) / शपेत (may curse) / माम् (me) / इति (thus) / ध्यात्वा (having thought) / मुहूर्तम् (for a moment) / तु (then) / सीता (Sita) / वचनम् (words) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::7338.speaker: Sita
ramayan::7338.essence: Courtesy can delay speech even in danger.
ramayan::7338.simple_meaning: Sita pauses because she sees a brahmin-guest before her and fears the harm of refusing him. Her restraint comes from duty and caution, not trust.
ramayan::7338.simple_insight: A brief pause can be wisdom when a single wrong response could cause harm.
ramayan::7338.detailed_meaning: In the forest, Ravana stands before Sita disguised as a mendicant. She does not yet know his true intent. Seeing a brahmin and guest, she hesitates, worried that silence might invite a curse. That pause leads into her reply.
ramayan::7338.modern_relevance: Someone knocks at your door with a polite voice, and you feel the pressure to respond carefully. Sita’s pause shows how quickly courtesy, fear, and judgment can all meet in one moment.
ramayan::7338.insight: It teaches you to pause before speaking when respect, risk, and uncertainty collide.

ramayan::7339.verse_sanskrit: दुहिता जनकस्याहं मैथिलस्य महात्मनः । सीता नाम्नास्मि भद्रं ते रामभार्या द्विजोत्तम । । 3473 । ।
ramayan::7339.verse_hindi: O best of brahmins be pleased to know I am Sita by name, daughter of the great Janaka, king of Mithila and wife of Rama.
ramayan::7339.english_translation: O best of brahmins, be pleased to know I am Sita by name, daughter of the great Janaka of Mithila, and wife of Rama.
ramayan::7339.translation_literal: दुहिता (daughter) / जनकस्य (of Janaka) / अहम् (I am) / मैथिलस्य (of the king of Mithila) / महात्मनः (of the great-souled) / सीता (Sita) / नाम्ना (by name) / अस्मि (I am) / भद्रम् (well-being) / ते (to you) / रामभार्या (Rama's wife) / द्विजोत्तम (best of brahmins)
ramayan::7339.speaker: Sita
ramayan::7339.essence: She answers with grace, even while danger is closing in.
ramayan::7339.simple_meaning: Sita identifies herself politely to the disguised Ravana: she is Janaka’s daughter and Rama’s wife.
ramayan::7339.simple_insight: Even under pressure, she answers with dignity and clarity.
ramayan::7339.detailed_meaning: In the Ashoka grove, Ravana questions Sita while disguised as a mendicant. She answers carefully, naming her father, her homeland, and her husband. The verse is a small but crucial part of the encounter, not the full teaching.
ramayan::7339.modern_relevance: A stranger asks a personal question you would rather avoid. You answer cleanly, without panic, and without giving away more than you must.
ramayan::7339.insight: It shows how to hold your identity firmly when someone tries to unsettle you.

ramayan::7340.verse_sanskrit: उषित्वा द्वादश समा इक्ष्वाकुणां निवेशने । भुञ्जाना मानुषान्भोगान्सर्वकामसमृद्धिनी । । 3474 । ।
ramayan::7340.verse_hindi: I lived in the house of the Ikshvakus for twelve years and enjoyed all kinds of pleasures meant for mortals.
ramayan::7340.english_translation: I lived in the house of the Ikshvakus for twelve years and enjoyed all kinds of pleasures meant for mortals.
ramayan::7340.translation_literal: उषित्वा (having lived) / द्वादश (twelve) / समा (years) / इक्ष्वाकुणां (of the Ikshvakus) / निवेशने (in the house) / भुञ्जाना (enjoying) / मानुषान् (human) / भोगान् (pleasures) / सर्वकामसमृद्धिनी (abundantly endowed with all desires)
ramayan::7340.speaker: Sita
ramayan::7340.essence: Past abundance can become sharp pain when love is absent.
ramayan::7340.simple_meaning: Sita says she lived in the Ikshvaku palace for twelve years, surrounded by every kind of human comfort and pleasure.
ramayan::7340.simple_insight: Even a life filled with comfort can be remembered as a time of loss.
ramayan::7340.detailed_meaning: Sita is speaking to the brahmin visitor in Lanka, explaining who she is and where she came from. Before describing her present suffering, she recalls the twelve years she spent in Ayodhya with Rama, when she knew royal comfort and fullness.
ramayan::7340.modern_relevance: You can have every comfort a home can offer and still feel the ache of what has been taken from you. Memory can turn abundance into proof of loss.
ramayan::7340.insight: It shifts the mind from counting comfort to noticing what made that comfort meaningful.

ramayan::7341.verse_sanskrit: ततस्त्रयोदशे वर्षे राजामन्त्रयत प्रभुः । अभिषेचयितुं रामं समेतो राजमन्त्रिभिः । । 3475 । ।
ramayan::7341.verse_hindi: In the thirteenth year, the king and lord Dasaratha consulted other kings and ministers to consecrate Rama.
ramayan::7341.english_translation: In the thirteenth year, the king and lord Dasaratha consulted other kings and ministers to consecrate Rama.
ramayan::7341.translation_literal: ततस् (then) / त्रयोदशे (in the thirteenth) / वर्षे (year) / राजा (the king) / अमन्त्रयत (consulted) / प्रभुः (the lord) / अभिषेचयितुम् (to consecrate) / रामम् (Rama) / समेतः (together with) / राजमन्त्रिभिः (with kings and ministers)
ramayan::7341.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7341.essence: A crowning is prepared just before fate interrupts.
ramayan::7341.simple_meaning: Dasaratha gathered his ministers and allies to prepare Rama's consecration in the thirteenth year.
ramayan::7341.simple_insight: A long-awaited honor is finally within reach, but the moment is still fragile.
ramayan::7341.detailed_meaning: After twelve years in the royal household, the plan to crown Rama finally moves forward. Dasaratha consults his ministers and allied rulers, setting the stage for a public consecration. The next verse shows how quickly that hope will be broken.
ramayan::7341.modern_relevance: The promotion email is drafted, the celebration is nearly set, and then one unexpected call changes everything. Some moments are only a breath away from becoming permanent.
ramayan::7341.insight: It shows how quickly a secure future can be overturned before it is even announced.

ramayan::7342.verse_sanskrit: तस्मिन्सम्भ्रियमाणे तु राघवस्याभिषेचने । कैकेयी नाम भर्तारमार्या सा याचते वरम् । । 3476 । ।
ramayan::7342.verse_hindi: Arrangements for consecration were on when queen Kaikeyi sought a boon from the king.
ramayan::7342.english_translation: As the consecration of Rama was being arranged, noble Kaikeyi asked the king for a boon.
ramayan::7342.translation_literal: तस्मिन् (at that time) / सम्भ्रियमाणे (being arranged) / तु (indeed) / राघवस्य (of Rama) / अभिषेचने (for the consecration) / कैकेयी (Kaikeyi) / नाम (named) / भर्तारम् (from her husband) / आर्या (noble lady) / सा (she) / याचते (asks) / वरम् (a boon)
ramayan::7342.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7342.essence: One request can overturn a kingdom’s next day.
ramayan::7342.simple_meaning: Just as Rama's consecration was being prepared, Kaikeyi asked Dasharatha for a boon she had been promised earlier.
ramayan::7342.simple_insight: A single request, made at the worst moment, can change an entire life.
ramayan::7342.detailed_meaning: The ministers have begun preparing Rama's consecration in Ayodhya. In that same charged moment, Kaikeyi steps forward and asks Dasharatha for a boon. The verse is the hinge before the exile, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::7342.modern_relevance: You are halfway through planning something joyful when one old promise suddenly returns and changes everything.
ramayan::7342.insight: It marks the instant when a private promise collides with a public future.

ramayan::7343.verse_sanskrit: प्रतिगृह्य तु कैकेयी श्वशुरं सुकृतेन मे । मम प्रव्राजनं भर्तुर्भरतस्याभिषेचनम् । । 3477 । । द्वावयाचत भर्तारं सत्यसन्धं नृपोत्तमम् ।
ramayan::7343.verse_hindi: For the fulfilment of the promise made to Kaikeyi earlier by my truthful fatherin law, who, to my good luck, was the best of kings, she asked for two boons. One was banishment of my husband and second, consecration of Bharata.
ramayan::7343.english_translation: Taking advantage of the boon earlier granted to Kaikeyi by my truthful father-in-law, who was the best of kings, she asked her husband for two boons: the exile of my husband and the consecration of Bharata.
ramayan::7343.translation_literal: प्रतिगृह्य (having received) / तु (indeed) / कैकेयी (Kaikeyi) / श्वशुरम् (father-in-law) / सुकृतेन (by good fortune) / मे (my) / मम (my) / प्रव्राजनम् (banishment/exile) / भर्तुः (of the husband) / भरतस्य (of Bharata) / अभिषेचनम् (consecration) / द्वौ (two) / अयाचत (asked for) / भर्तारम् (from her husband) / सत्यसन्धम् (truth-bound) / नृपोत्तमम् (best of kings)
ramayan::7343.speaker: Kaikeyi
ramayan::7343.essence: A forgotten promise can overturn everything you were preparing to celebrate.
ramayan::7343.simple_meaning: Kaikeyi used an old promise to demand two things: Rama's exile and Bharata's coronation.
ramayan::7343.simple_insight: A single request can overturn an entire life when it is backed by a binding promise.
ramayan::7343.detailed_meaning: The coronation of Rama is being prepared in Ayodhya. Kaikeyi steps into the fragile moment and invokes a boon Dasharatha once gave her. With that claim, she demands Rama's exile and Bharata's installation, setting the exile in motion.
ramayan::7343.modern_relevance: You think a conversation is settled, and then someone names a promise you forgot you made. One sentence later, the whole future has changed.
ramayan::7343.insight: It shows how a neglected vow can become the hinge on which an entire household turns.

ramayan::7344.verse_sanskrit: नाद्य भोक्ष्ये न च स्वप्स्ये न पास्येच कथञ्चन । । 3478 । । एष मे जीवितस्यान्तो रामो यद्यभिषिच्यते ।
ramayan::7344.verse_hindi: I shall not eat, or sleep or even drink if Rama is consecrated and I shall put an end to my life itself (said Kaikeyi).
ramayan::7344.english_translation: I shall not eat, or sleep, or even drink in any way. If Rama is consecrated, this will be the end of my life.
ramayan::7344.translation_literal: न अद्य (not today) / भोक्ष्ये (I will eat) / न च (and not) / स्वप्स्ये (I will sleep) / न (not) / पास्ये (I will drink) / च (and) / कथञ्चन (in any way) / एषः (this) / मे (of my) / जीवितस्य (of life) / अन्तः (end) / रामः (Rama) / यदि (if) / अभिषिच्यते (is consecrated)
ramayan::7344.speaker: Kaikeyi
ramayan::7344.essence: Fear of losing status turns into a threat against life itself.
ramayan::7344.simple_meaning: Kaikeyi says she will stop eating, sleeping, and drinking if Rama is crowned. She treats his consecration as the end of her own life.
ramayan::7344.simple_insight: Unchecked fear can harden into a desperate ultimatum.
ramayan::7344.detailed_meaning: At the moment Rama’s consecration is being prepared, Kaikeyi turns from queen to force of obstruction. She tells the king that if Rama is installed, she will refuse food, sleep, and water, making her demand impossible to ignore.
ramayan::7344.modern_relevance: A family conversation turns into a threat: 'If you do this, I’ll never speak again.' The hurt may be real, but fear can quickly become a weapon.
ramayan::7344.insight: It shows how attachment can distort speech into coercion and make private pain control everyone else.

ramayan::7345.verse_sanskrit: इति ब्रुवाणां कैकेयीं श्वशुरो मे स मानदः । । 3479 । । अयाचतार्थैरन्वर्थैर्न च याञ्चां चकार सा ।
ramayan::7345.verse_hindi: The king, my fatherinlaw, who respected her offered riches. Which she did not accept.
ramayan::7345.english_translation: The king, my father-in-law, who respected her, offered riches. She did not accept them.
ramayan::7345.translation_literal: इति (thus) / ब्रुवाणाम् (speaking) / कैकेयीम् (to Kaikeyi) / श्वशुरः (father-in-law) / मे (my) / सः (that) / मानदः (honour-giving one) / अयाचत (asked, offered) / अर्थैः (with riches) / अन्वर्थैः (appropriate, fitting) / न (not) / च (and) / याञ्चाम् (request) / चकार (made) / सा (she)
ramayan::7345.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7345.essence: She rejected gifts because her demand had already taken over.
ramayan::7345.simple_meaning: Dasharatha offered Kaikeyi fitting gifts and riches, but she refused to accept them.
ramayan::7345.simple_insight: Refusing what is offered can be a form of control, not simplicity.
ramayan::7345.detailed_meaning: Kaikeyi is speaking after demanding Rama's exile and Bharata's coronation. She recalls how Dasharatha, her honoured father-in-law, tried to satisfy her with wealth, but she would not be moved. The verse shows her fixed will, not a passing complaint.
ramayan::7345.modern_relevance: Someone offers you a raise, a favor, or an apology, but you already know what you want. The conversation is no longer about generosity — it's about leverage.
ramayan::7345.insight: It shows how desire can harden into refusal, making compromise impossible.

ramayan::7346.verse_sanskrit: मम भर्तामहातेजा वयसा पञ्चविंशकः । । 34710 । । अष्टादश हि वर्षाणि मम जन्मनि गण्यते ।
ramayan::7346.verse_hindi: My husband who was very bold was twentyfive years and I had completed eighteen years since my birth.
ramayan::7346.english_translation: My husband, who was very bold, was twenty-five years old, and I had completed eighteen years since my birth.
ramayan::7346.translation_literal: मम (my) / भर्ता (husband) / महातेजाः (very bold, very radiant) / वयसा (by age) / पञ्चविंशकः (twenty-five years old) / अष्टादश (eighteen) / हि (indeed) / वर्षाणि (years) / मम (my) / जन्मनि (at birth / since birth) / गण्यते (is counted)
ramayan::7346.speaker: Kaikeyi
ramayan::7346.essence: Old marriage years now serve a bitter argument.
ramayan::7346.simple_meaning: Kaikeyi states the ages of herself and her husband, Dasharatha, as part of her explanation to justify her position.
ramayan::7346.simple_insight: Some wounds begin with a single remembered fact that changes how everything feels.
ramayan::7346.detailed_meaning: Kaikeyi is speaking in the palace after demanding the boons that will send Rama into exile. She recalls that Dasharatha was twenty-five and she was eighteen when they were joined, grounding her argument in the long history of their marriage before she presses her demand further.
ramayan::7346.modern_relevance: You can hear the chill in a conversation when someone starts counting years, debts, and old promises instead of speaking from the heart.
ramayan::7346.insight: It frames the conflict as one rooted in memory, age, and marital history, not just a sudden quarrel.

ramayan::7347.verse_sanskrit: रामेति प्रथितो लोके गुणवान्सत्यवान्शुचिः । । 34711 । । विशालाक्षो महाबाहुस्सर्वभूतहिते रतः ।
ramayan::7347.verse_hindi: My husband known in the world as Rama is largeeyed, longarmed, virtuous, truthful, pure and is always engaged in the welfare of all beings.
ramayan::7347.english_translation: My husband, known in the world as Rama, is large-eyed, long-armed, virtuous, truthful, pure, and always devoted to the welfare of all beings.
ramayan::7347.translation_literal: रामेति (as Rama) / प्रथितः (famous) / लोके (in the world) / गुणवान् (endowed with virtues) / सत्यवान् (truthful) / शुचिः (pure) / विशालाक्षः (large-eyed) / महाबाहुः (long-armed) / सर्वभूतहिते (in the welfare of all beings) / रतः (delighted, devoted)
ramayan::7347.speaker: Kaikeyi
ramayan::7347.essence: Public greatness is built from truth, purity, and care for all.
ramayan::7347.simple_meaning: Kaikeyi describes Rama as a man known for virtue, truth, purity, and care for every being.
ramayan::7347.simple_insight: There is dignity in being known for what you protect, not what you take.
ramayan::7347.detailed_meaning: Kaikeyi is recalling Rama’s character in the middle of a painful family crisis. Before the exile is fully revealed, she names the qualities everyone already knows: Rama’s truthfulness, purity, and concern for all beings. The praise makes the coming betrayal feel sharper.
ramayan::7347.modern_relevance: You hear your name in a room where people are deciding your future. What they remember about you is not your status, but whether you were truthful, clean in motive, and good to others.
ramayan::7347.insight: It shifts attention from personal gain to conduct that benefits others.

ramayan::7348.verse_sanskrit: कामार्तस्तु महातेजाः पिता दशरथस्स्वयम् । । 34712 । । कैकेय्याः प्रियकामार्थं तं रामं नाभ्यषेचयत् ।
ramayan::7348.verse_hindi: The brilliant king, Dasaratha, father of Rama, overcome by passion,  did not consecrate Rama in order to please Kaikeyi.
ramayan::7348.english_translation: The brilliant king Dasharatha, overcome by desire, did not consecrate Rama in order to please Kaikeyi.
ramayan::7348.translation_literal: कामार्तः (overcome by desire) / तु (but) / महातेजाः (the brilliant one) / पिता (father) / दशरथः (Dasharatha) / स्वयं (himself) / कैकेय्याः (of Kaikeyi) / प्रियकामार्थं (for the sake of pleasing) / तम् (that) / रामम् (Rama) / न (not) / अभ्यषेचयत् (consecrated)
ramayan::7348.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7348.essence: A ruler lost his clarity, and a kingdom paid for it.
ramayan::7348.simple_meaning: Dasharatha was pulled by desire and chose Kaikeyi's pleasure over Rama's coronation.
ramayan::7348.simple_insight: Unchecked wanting can make even a noble person betray what matters most.
ramayan::7348.detailed_meaning: Rama is about to be crowned, and the entire kingdom is poised for that moment. But Dasharatha, weakened by desire and bound by Kaikeyi's influence, withholds the consecration. This single failure sets the exile in motion.
ramayan::7348.modern_relevance: You were ready to make the right call, then one person’s approval started to matter too much. A private craving can overturn a decision everyone else was counting on.
ramayan::7348.insight: It shows how desire can override duty and derail an entire course of action.

ramayan::7349.verse_sanskrit: अभिषेकाय तु पितुस्समीपं राममागतम् । । 34713 । । कैकेयी मम भर्तारमित्युवाच धृतं वचः ।
ramayan::7349.verse_hindi: When my husband Rama approached his father for the consecration she said these unhesitating words:
ramayan::7349.english_translation: When Rama came near his father for the consecration, Kaikeyi spoke these firm words: "My husband..."
ramayan::7349.translation_literal: अभिषेकाय (for consecration) / तु (but) / पितुः (of the father) / समीपम् (near) / रामम् (Rama) / आगतम् (having come) / कैकेयी (Kaikeyi) / मम (my) / भर्तारम् (husband) / इति (thus) / उवाच (said) / धृतम् (firm) / वचः (speech)
ramayan::7349.speaker: Kaikeyi
ramayan::7349.essence: One firm sentence can overturn a king’s plan.
ramayan::7349.simple_meaning: As Rama came to his father for the coronation, Kaikeyi spoke firmly, beginning to assert her claim over what should happen next.
ramayan::7349.simple_insight: A single firm statement can redirect an entire life.
ramayan::7349.detailed_meaning: Rama has come to Dasaratha expecting the consecration. Kaikeyi steps in with a hard, settled voice, preparing to invoke the promise that will send Rama away and place Bharata on the throne.
ramayan::7349.modern_relevance: You walk into a room expecting good news, and someone calmly changes the whole future with one prepared sentence.
ramayan::7349.insight: It shows how a decisive claim, once spoken, can override hope and set a new course.

ramayan::7350.verse_sanskrit: तव पित्रा समाज्ञप्तं ममेदं शृणु राघव । । 34714 । । भरताय प्रदातव्यमिदं राज्यमकण्टकम् ।
ramayan::7350.verse_hindi: O Rama, listen, your father has ordered that this kingdom be bestowed on Bharata without any obstacles.
ramayan::7350.english_translation: O Rama, listen, your father has ordered that this kingdom be bestowed on Bharata without any obstacles.
ramayan::7350.translation_literal: तव (your) / पित्रा (by father) / समाज्ञप्तं (ordered) / मम (my) / इदं (this) / शृणु (listen) / राघव (Rama) / भरताय (to Bharata) / प्रदातव्यम् (to be given) / इदम् (this) / राज्यम् (kingdom) / अकण्टकम् (without obstacles)
ramayan::7350.speaker: Kaikeyi
ramayan::7350.essence: The throne is redirected, and Rama’s life is about to break open.
ramayan::7350.simple_meaning: Kaikeyi tells Rama that his father has ordered the kingdom to be given to Bharata.
ramayan::7350.simple_insight: A single command can overturn an entire life.
ramayan::7350.detailed_meaning: In Ayodhya, Rama has come expecting consecration. Kaikeyi, speaking with fixed resolve, tells him that Dasharatha has ordered the kingdom given to Bharata instead. This is the blow that turns celebration into exile.
ramayan::7350.modern_relevance: You walk into a meeting expecting recognition, and instead hear the plan has changed without you. The ground shifts because someone else’s decision now defines your next move.
ramayan::7350.insight: It shows how quickly duty can become loss when authority is used against expectation.

ramayan::7351.verse_sanskrit: त्वया हि खलु वस्तव्यं नव वर्षाणि पञ्च च । । 34715 । । वने प्रव्रज काकुत्स्थ पितरं मोचयानृतान् ।
ramayan::7351.verse_hindi: O Rama of the Kakutstha dynasty, you should live in the forest for fourteen years and save your father from falsehood.
ramayan::7351.english_translation: O Rama of the Kakutstha dynasty, you should live in the forest for fourteen years and save your father from falsehood.
ramayan::7351.translation_literal: त्वया (by you) / हि (indeed) / खलु (certainly) / वस्तव्यम् (must be lived) / नव (nine) / वर्षाणि (years) / पञ्च (five) / च (and) / वने (in the forest) / प्रव्रज (go forth) / काकुत्स्थ (O descendant of Kakutstha) / पितरम् (father) / मोचयानृतान् (freeing from untruth)
ramayan::7351.speaker: Kaikeyi
ramayan::7351.essence: Dharma can demand that you lose what was meant for you.
ramayan::7351.simple_meaning: Rama is told to go into the forest for fourteen years so his father’s promise is not broken.
ramayan::7351.simple_insight: Sometimes honour means accepting a loss you did not choose.
ramayan::7351.detailed_meaning: Kaikeyi has just demanded that Rama be denied the throne and sent away. The demand is not random cruelty; it is framed as the price of keeping Dasharatha free from falsehood. Rama’s exile begins here.
ramayan::7351.modern_relevance: You’re asked to step aside so someone else can keep a promise they made before you arrived. The unfairness is obvious. The harder question is whether you can still act with dignity.
ramayan::7351.insight: It shifts attention from personal loss to the cost of keeping a binding promise.

ramayan::7352.verse_sanskrit: तथेत्युक्त्वा च तां रामः कैकेयीमकुतोभयः । । 34716 । । चकार तद्वचस्तस्या मम भर्ता दृढव्रतः ।
ramayan::7352.verse_hindi: My husband Rama, a man of fearlessness and firm resolution, said to Kaikeyi Be it so and carried out her words.
ramayan::7352.english_translation: Saying, "So be it," Rama, fearless and firm in vow, carried out Kaikeyi's words.
ramayan::7352.translation_literal: तथा (so) / इति (thus) / उक्त्वा (having said) / च (and) / तां (to her) / रामः (Rama) / कैकेयीम् (to Kaikeyi) / अकुतोभयः (fearless) / चकार (did, carried out) / तत्-वचः (that word) / तस्याः (her) / मम (my) / भर्ता (husband) / दृढ-व्रतः (firm in vow)
ramayan::7352.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7352.essence: Rama proves courage by obeying a vow that wounds him.
ramayan::7352.simple_meaning: Rama agrees to Kaikeyi's demand and immediately carries it out, even though it will send him into exile.
ramayan::7352.simple_insight: There is strength in keeping a promise even when it hurts.
ramayan::7352.detailed_meaning: Kaikeyi has just demanded Rama's exile and Bharata's coronation. Rama does not argue or hesitate. He answers calmly, then acts at once. This is the moment his fearlessness and loyalty become visible.
ramayan::7352.modern_relevance: You promised something before you knew the full cost. The cost arrived anyway, and now your character is measured by whether you still keep your word.
ramayan::7352.insight: It shifts the mind from self-protection to unwavering responsibility.

ramayan::7353.verse_sanskrit: दद्यान्न प्रतिगृह्णीयात्सत्यं ब्रूयान्न चानृतम् । । 34717 । । एतद्ब्राह्मण रामस्य ध्रृवं व्रतमनुत्तमम् ।
ramayan::7353.verse_hindi: O brahmin this is his firm resolve and his great vow: One should give and never take one should speak the truth and nothing but he truth.
ramayan::7353.english_translation: O brahmin, this is his firm resolve and his great vow: one should give and never take; one should speak the truth and never speak falsely.
ramayan::7353.translation_literal: दद्यान् (should give) / न (not) / प्रतिगृह्णीयात् (should receive) / सत्यम् (truth) / ब्रूयात् (should speak) / न (not) / च (and) / अनृतम् (untruth) / एतत् (this) / ब्राह्मण (O brahmin) / रामस्य (of Rama) / ध्रुवम् (firm) / व्रतम् (vow) / अनुत्तमम् (supreme)
ramayan::7353.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7353.essence: Rama's greatness rests on giving freely and never leaving truth.
ramayan::7353.simple_meaning: Rama's lifelong vow was simple and strict: give without grasping, and speak only what is true.
ramayan::7353.simple_insight: Integrity becomes easier when your rules are clear and few.
ramayan::7353.detailed_meaning: After Kaikeyi forces Rama into exile, the poem pauses to name the standard that defines him. Rama's greatness is not power but restraint: he gives, he refuses greed, and he never abandons truth.
ramayan::7353.modern_relevance: You are tempted to bend the truth to keep a job, save face, or protect an image. This verse asks whether your character can survive that bargain.
ramayan::7353.insight: It turns virtue into a daily discipline: generosity without grasping, honesty without exception.

ramayan::7354.verse_sanskrit: तस्य भ्राता तु द्वैमात्रो लक्ष्मणो नाम वीर्यवान् । । 34718 । । रामस्य पुरुषव्याघ्रस्सहायस्समरेरिहा ।
ramayan::7354.verse_hindi: Son to the second mother of Rama, his mighty halfbrother, by name, Lakshmana, a tiger among men and a  slayer of enemies in battle is a companion to him.
ramayan::7354.english_translation: Lakshmana, Rama's valiant half-brother by the second mother, a tiger among men and a warrior who helps in battle, is his companion.
ramayan::7354.translation_literal: तस्य (his) / भ्राता (brother) / तु (indeed) / द्वैमात्रः (born of the second mother) / लक्ष्मणः (Lakshmana) / नाम (by name) / वीर्यवान् (mighty) / रामस्य (of Rama) / पुरुषव्याघ्रः (tiger among men) / सहायः (helper/companion) / समरे (in battle) / इह (here)
ramayan::7354.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7354.essence: True companionship shows up before the battle starts.
ramayan::7354.simple_meaning: Lakshmana is Rama's younger half-brother, strong, brave, and always at his side in battle.
ramayan::7354.simple_insight: Some loyalties are not spoken first; they are proven by standing beside someone when danger comes.
ramayan::7354.detailed_meaning: Valmiki pauses the story to identify Lakshmana before the exile fully unfolds. He is Rama's younger half-brother, born of another mother, but already marked as a fierce companion in battle. The verse sets up the bond that will make exile bearable.
ramayan::7354.modern_relevance: When everything is shifting and one person still says, 'I'm coming with you,' that loyalty changes the whole journey.
ramayan::7354.insight: It highlights the kind of support that does not wait to be asked and does not disappear under pressure.

ramayan::7355.verse_sanskrit: स भ्राता लक्ष्मणो नाम धर्मचारी दृढव्रतः । । 34719 । । अन्वगच्छद्दनुष्पाणिः प्रव्रजन्तं मया सह ।
ramayan::7355.verse_hindi: Lakshmana, his brother, is righteous and steadfast. Bow in hand, he followed Rama along with me, into exile.
ramayan::7355.english_translation: Lakshmana, his brother, is righteous and steadfast. Bow in hand, he followed Rama along with me, into exile.
ramayan::7355.translation_literal: सः (he) / भ्राता (brother) / लक्ष्मणः (Lakshmana) / नाम (by name) / धर्मचारी (righteous in conduct) / दृढव्रतः (firm in vow) / अन्वगच्छत् (followed) / धनुष्पाणिः (with bow in hand) / प्रव्रजन्तम् (the one going into exile) / मया सह (with me)
ramayan::7355.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7355.essence: Loyalty becomes real when you follow into hardship.
ramayan::7355.simple_meaning: Lakshmana is described as righteous, resolute, and loyal. He followed Rama into exile with his bow in hand.
ramayan::7355.simple_insight: True loyalty shows up as action, not admiration.
ramayan::7355.detailed_meaning: Valmiki pauses in the exile narrative to describe Lakshmana’s character. He is not just Rama’s brother; he is the one who chose to follow him into the forest armed and unwavering. The verse builds the moral weight of that companionship.
ramayan::7355.modern_relevance: Someone packs a bag at dawn and leaves with you for a hard move, a hospital stay, or a life you didn't plan. Lakshmana is that kind of presence: steady, armed with resolve, and already beside you.
ramayan::7355.insight: It shifts attention from words of support to the cost of standing with someone.

ramayan::7356.verse_sanskrit: जटी तापसरूपेण मया सह सहानुजः । । 34720 । । प्रविष्टो दण्डकारण्यं धर्मनित्यो जितेन्द्रियः ।
ramayan::7356.verse_hindi: Rama who is ever righteous and selfcontrolled entered the Dandaka forest with matted locks, his brother and me.
ramayan::7356.english_translation: Rama, ever righteous and self-controlled, entered the Dandaka forest with matted hair, along with me and his younger brother.
ramayan::7356.translation_literal: जटी (matted-haired) / तापसरूपेण (in the form of an ascetic) / मया सह (with me) / सहानुजः (along with his younger brother) / प्रविष्टः (entered) / दण्डकारण्यं (the Dandaka forest) / धर्मनित्यः (ever righteous) / जितेन्द्रियः (one who has conquered the senses)
ramayan::7356.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7356.essence: Exile changed his clothes, not his conduct.
ramayan::7356.simple_meaning: Rama entered the forest as an ascetic, with Lakshmana and Valmiki, while remaining righteous and self-controlled.
ramayan::7356.simple_insight: Even in exile, he carries dignity, restraint, and purpose.
ramayan::7356.detailed_meaning: Valmiki is describing the three exiles after the loss of the kingdom: Rama, Lakshmana, and he himself entered the Dandaka forest. The line emphasizes Rama's ascetic appearance and steady self-mastery, setting the moral tone for their life in the wilderness.
ramayan::7356.modern_relevance: You leave behind comfort, status, and familiar routines, but still choose to show up with dignity. The setting changes; your conduct does not.
ramayan::7356.insight: It shifts attention from outward loss to inner discipline under pressure.

ramayan::7357.verse_sanskrit: ते वयं प्रच्युता राज्यात्कैकेय्यास्तु कृते त्रयः । । 34721 । । विचरामो द्विजश्रेष्ठ वनं गम्भीरमोजसा ।
ramayan::7357.verse_hindi: O best of brahmins three of us have been wandering with courage in the deep forest, dislodged from  the kingdom on account of  Kaikeyi.
ramayan::7357.english_translation: O best of brahmins, the three of us have been wandering bravely through the deep forest, driven from the kingdom because of Kaikeyi.
ramayan::7357.translation_literal: ते (these) / वयं (we) / प्रच्युता (displaced) / राज्यात् (from the kingdom) / कैकेय्याः (of Kaikeyi) / तु (indeed) / कृते (because of) / त्रयः (three) / विचरामः (we wander) / द्विजश्रेष्ठ (O best of brahmins) / वनम् (forest) / गम्भीरम् (deep) / ओजसा (with courage)
ramayan::7357.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7357.essence: Exile has begun, but courage keeps them moving.
ramayan::7357.simple_meaning: Rama, Lakshmana, and Sita are living in the forest because Kaikeyi's demand forced them out of the kingdom. They keep moving through the deep woods with courage.
ramayan::7357.simple_insight: Even exile can be met with steadiness when you refuse to collapse inside.
ramayan::7357.detailed_meaning: Rama, Lakshmana, and Sita have already left Ayodhya and entered the Dandaka forest. Speaking to the sage, they describe themselves as three exiles, pushed out by Kaikeyi’s choice, yet still moving forward with courage. The verse deepens the cost of Rama’s promise.
ramayan::7357.modern_relevance: You pack your life into one car because a decision you didn’t make has changed everything. Even then, you keep moving, because panic won’t carry you anywhere.
ramayan::7357.insight: It shifts attention from loss to composure under forced change.

ramayan::7358.verse_sanskrit: समाश्वस मुहूर्तं तु शक्यं वस्तुमिह त्वया । । 34722 । । आगमिष्यति मे भर्ता वन्यमादाय पुष्कलम् । रुरून्गोधा न्वराहांश्च हत्वाऽदायाऽमिषान्बहून् । । 34723 । ।
ramayan::7358.verse_hindi: Rest here awhile. My husband will return with plenty of meat of many kinds from the forest, killing deer, alligators and wild boars.
ramayan::7358.english_translation: Rest here for a while. My husband will return with plenty of forest food, having killed deer, boars, and alligators, and brought back meat in abundance.
ramayan::7358.translation_literal: समाश्वस (rest/be reassured) / मुहूर्तं (for a moment) / तु (indeed) / शक्यम् (possible) / वस्तुम् (to stay) / इह (here) / त्वया (by you) / आगमिष्यति (will return) / मे (my) / भर्ता (husband) / वन्यम् (forest food) / आदाय (having brought) / पुष्कलम् (abundant) / रुरून् (deer) / गोधान् (alligators) / वराहान् (boars) / च (and) / हत्वा (having killed) / आदाय (having brought) / आमिषान् (meat) / बहून् (many)
ramayan::7358.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::7358.essence: She speaks from ordinary trust, not from doubt or fear.
ramayan::7358.simple_meaning: She tells the visitor to wait a little, saying her husband will soon return from the forest with plenty of meat.
ramayan::7358.simple_insight: A simple promise can reveal complete trust in another person's return.
ramayan::7358.detailed_meaning: In the Dandaka forest, a woman speaks to a wandering brahmin with easy confidence. She believes her husband is out hunting and will soon come back with food. The line is part of a longer exchange, not a teaching on its own.
ramayan::7358.modern_relevance: You tell a guest to wait by the door, certain the person you love will be back with dinner soon.
ramayan::7358.insight: It serves as a small scene-setting reply, not a standalone teaching.

ramayan::7359.verse_sanskrit: स त्वं नाम च गोत्रञ्च कुलं चाचक्ष्व तत्त्वतः । एकश्च दण्डकारण्ये किमर्थं चरसि द्विज । । 34724 । ।
ramayan::7359.verse_hindi: O brahmin, tell me your name, your gotra and your pedigree. And the purpose for which you are going about all alone in this Dandaka forest
ramayan::7359.english_translation: O brahmin, tell me your name, your gotra, your lineage, and the purpose for which you are wandering alone in this Dandaka forest.
ramayan::7359.translation_literal: स (that) / त्वं (you) / नाम (name) / च (and) / गोत्रम् (gotra, clan) / च (and) / कुलम् (lineage) / च (and) / आचक्ष्व (tell) / तत्त्वतः (truly) / एकः (alone) / च (and) / दण्डकारण्ये (in Dandaka forest) / किमर्थम् (for what purpose) / चरसि (you roam) / द्विज (brahmin)
ramayan::7359.speaker: Sita
ramayan::7359.essence: Trust is not the same as giving away your guard.
ramayan::7359.simple_meaning: Sita asks the stranger to identify himself fully and explain why he is alone in the forest.
ramayan::7359.simple_insight: Careful questions can be the first protection when something feels off.
ramayan::7359.detailed_meaning: In the Dandaka forest, Sita speaks to the disguised Ravana as if he were a harmless brahmin. Before trusting him, she asks for his name, family line, and reason for being alone. The moment is part of Ravana's deception, not a teaching verse.
ramayan::7359.modern_relevance: A stranger starts asking personal questions too quickly, and your instincts tighten. Before you reveal anything, you want to know who is standing in front of you.
ramayan::7359.insight: It models cautious discernment: verify identity and intent before opening yourself further.

ramayan::7360.verse_sanskrit: एवं बृवन्त्यां सीतायां रामपत्न्यां महाबलः । प्रत्युवाचोत्तरं तीव्रं रावणो राक्षसाधिपः । । 34725 । ।
ramayan::7360.verse_hindi: To these words of Sita, Ramas wife, Ravana, the powerful king of demons, replied  sharp:
ramayan::7360.english_translation: When Sita, Rama's wife, was speaking thus, the mighty Ravana, lord of the demons, answered sharply.
ramayan::7360.translation_literal: एवं (thus) / बृवन्त्यां (while speaking) / सीतायां (to Sita) / रामपत्न्यां (Rama's wife) / महाबलः (mighty) / प्रत्युवाच (replied) / उत्तरं (in reply) / तीव्रं (sharp) / रावणः (Ravana) / राक्षसाधिपः (lord of the demons)
ramayan::7360.speaker: Ravana
ramayan::7360.essence: The answer matters less than the hardness behind it.
ramayan::7360.simple_meaning: Ravana cuts in sharply when Sita questions him.
ramayan::7360.simple_insight: A tense conversation is about to turn into a revealing confrontation.
ramayan::7360.detailed_meaning: In the forest, Sita has asked the stranger who he is and why he wanders alone. Ravana, hiding his true intent, answers with force. This verse is only the turn in the conversation, not the teaching itself.
ramayan::7360.modern_relevance: Someone asks a simple question, and the other person answers too quickly, too sharply. The reaction itself tells you something is being concealed.
ramayan::7360.insight: It marks the shift from polite inquiry to dangerous self-revelation.

ramayan::7361.verse_sanskrit: येन वित्रासिता लोकास्सदेवासुरपन्नगाः । अहं तु रावणो नाम सीते रक्षोगणेश्वरः । । 34726 । ।
ramayan::7361.verse_hindi: O Sita I am called Ravana, the lord of demons by whom all the worlds of demons,
ramayan::7361.english_translation: I am Ravana, lord of the host of rakshasas, the one by whom all the worlds, including the gods, asuras, and serpents, have been terrorized.
ramayan::7361.translation_literal: येन (by whom) / वित्रासिताः (terrified) / लोकाः (worlds) / स-देव-असुर-पन्नगाः (together with gods, asuras, and serpents) / अहम् (I) / तु (indeed) / रावणः (Ravana) / नाम (by name) / सीते (O Sita) / रक्षः-गण-ईश्वरः (lord of the host of rakshasas)
ramayan::7361.speaker: Ravana
ramayan::7361.essence: Power that needs applause is already insecure.
ramayan::7361.simple_meaning: Ravana identifies himself to Sita with a boast: he is the ruler whose power has frightened every realm, including divine and serpent beings.
ramayan::7361.simple_insight: Pride can sound like power, but it often reveals fear underneath.
ramayan::7361.detailed_meaning: In the Ashoka grove, Sita asks the stranger who he is and why he has come alone. Ravana answers with raw arrogance, naming himself as the terror of every realm. He is not teaching; he is trying to overwhelm her before revealing his desire.
ramayan::7361.modern_relevance: Someone walks into a room talking like they own it, listing achievements and influence before anyone has asked. The volume is meant to win the moment before the truth is even spoken.
ramayan::7361.insight: It exposes how self-importance tries to dominate a conversation before real dialogue can begin.

ramayan::7362.verse_sanskrit: त्वां तु काञ्चनवर्णाभां दृष्ट्वा कौशेयवासिनीम् । रतिं स्वकेषु दारेषु नाधिगच्छाम्यनिन्दिते । । 34727 । ।
ramayan::7362.verse_hindi: O flawless beauty of golden complexion seeing you clad in silk, I am not inclined to show any interest in my own wives.
ramayan::7362.english_translation: O flawless beauty of golden complexion, seeing you clad in silk, I am not inclined to show any interest in my own wives.
ramayan::7362.translation_literal: त्वाम् (you) / तु (but) / काञ्चनवर्णाभाम् (golden-complexioned) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / कौशेयवासिनीम् (wearing silk garments) / रतिम् (delight/interest) / स्वकेषु (in my own) / दारेषु (wives) / न (not) / अधिगच्छामि (I obtain/find) / अनिन्दिते (O blameless one)
ramayan::7362.speaker: Ravana
ramayan::7362.essence: Beauty becomes a weapon when desire ignores consent.
ramayan::7362.simple_meaning: Ravana says Sita’s beauty has made him lose interest in his other wives. He is flattering her while trying to seduce her.
ramayan::7362.simple_insight: Charm can hide predation. Flattery is not respect when it is used to cross a boundary.
ramayan::7362.detailed_meaning: In Lanka, Ravana keeps pressing Sita after revealing his identity and power. Instead of backing off, he uses praise and desire to pressure her, claiming her beauty has eclipsed his own wives. The scene shows his arrogance, entitlement, and moral blindness.
ramayan::7362.modern_relevance: Someone compliments you so intensely that it starts to feel like pressure, not appreciation. The words are polished, but the boundary underneath is being tested.
ramayan::7362.insight: It teaches you to hear desire and manipulation separately, and to protect your boundary even when the language is flattering.

ramayan::7363.verse_sanskrit: बह्वीनामुत्तमस्त्रीणामाहृतानामितस्ततः । सर्वासामेव भद्रं ते ममाग्रमहिषी भव । । 34728 । ।
ramayan::7363.verse_hindi: You will be the chief queen among the best of women I have won in wars. Be blessed.
ramayan::7363.english_translation: You will be the chief queen among the best of women I have won in wars. Be blessed.
ramayan::7363.translation_literal: बह्वीनाम् (of many) / उत्तमस्त्रीणाम् (of the finest women) / आहृतानाम् (brought) / इतस्ततः (from here and there) / सर्वासाम् (of all) / एव (indeed) / भद्रम् ते (good fortune to you) / मम (my) / अग्रमहिषी (chief queen) / भव (become)
ramayan::7363.speaker: Ravana
ramayan::7363.essence: His offer is not love; it is conquest wearing ornament.
ramayan::7363.simple_meaning: Ravana boasts that Sita should become his chief queen, above all the women he has taken from many places.
ramayan::7363.simple_insight: Power that treats people as trophies always reveals its own corruption.
ramayan::7363.detailed_meaning: In Lanka, Ravana stands before Sita and tries to overwhelm her with rank, wealth, and possession. He offers her the place of chief queen among the women he has seized, turning desire into a command. The verse is part of his coercive attempt to break her resolve.
ramayan::7363.modern_relevance: Someone with status tries to flatter you into accepting what you never asked for. The praise is only a mask for control.
ramayan::7363.insight: It exposes how ego turns attraction into ownership and dignity into bargaining.
