ramayan::7844.english_translation: O noble prince, give up grief. Take courage. Show enthusiasm to search and find Sita. Enthusiastic people will not sink in even the hardest tasks.
ramayan::7844.translation_literal: शोकं (grief) / विमुञ्च (give up) / आर्य (noble one) / धृतिं (courage, steadiness) / भजस्व (take, embrace) / सोत्साहता (with enthusiasm) / च (and) / अस्तु (let there be) / विमार्गणे (in searching out) / अस्याः (of her) / उत्साहवन्तः (enthusiastic) / हि (indeed) / नराः (people) / न (not) / लोके (in the world) / सीदन्ति (sink, despair) / कर्मसु (in actions) / अतिदुष्करेषु (in very difficult)
ramayan::7844.speaker: Lakshmana
ramayan::7844.essence: Courage keeps you moving when the task feels impossible.
ramayan::7844.simple_meaning: Lakshmana urges Rama to stop grieving, gather courage, and search for Sita with energy. People who stay enthusiastic do not collapse when the task is difficult.
ramayan::7844.simple_insight: Grief can wait; the next step still belongs to you.
ramayan::7844.detailed_meaning: Rama has just broken down searching for Sita. Lakshmana, steady and brave, interrupts the sorrow with practical resolve: stop sinking, keep moving, and search. This is the moment he tries to turn pain into action.
ramayan::7844.modern_relevance: You stare at a missing-person poster, a failed application, or a text that never came back. The ache is real, but the next step still asks for energy, not collapse.
ramayan::7844.insight: It shifts you from emotional paralysis to purposeful searching.

ramayan::7845.verse_sanskrit: इतीव सौमित्रिमुदग्रपौरुषं ब्रुवन्तमार्तो रघुवंशवर्धनः । न चिन्तयामास धृतिं विमुक्तवान्पुनश्च दुःखं महदभ्युपागमत् । । 36320 । ।
ramayan::7845.verse_hindi: Rama who carries on the (glorious) progeny of the Raghu dynasty, did not (however) consider seriously the words of Lakshmana, a man of great prowess. Forsaking his courage he was once again overtaken by deep sorrow.
ramayan::7845.english_translation: Rama, the glory of Raghu's line, did not fully take Lakshmana's words to heart. He let go of courage and was overtaken once more by deep sorrow.
ramayan::7845.translation_literal: इतीव (thus) / सौमित्रिम् (to Lakshmana) / उदग्र-पौरुषम् (of great prowess) / ब्रुवन्तम् (speaking) / आर्तः (grieved) / रघुवंश-वर्धनः (the increaser of the Raghu line) / न (not) / चिन्तयामास (considered deeply) / धृतिम् (courage) / विमुक्तवान् (having let go) / पुनः (again) / च (and) / दुःखम् (sorrow) / महत् (great) / अभ्युपागमत् (he was overtaken by)
ramayan::7845.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7845.essence: Grief can drown even clear counsel before courage returns.
ramayan::7845.simple_meaning: Rama hears Lakshmana, but grief still overwhelms him. His courage slips, and sorrow returns.
ramayan::7845.simple_insight: Even the strongest resolve can collapse when grief is still raw.
ramayan::7845.detailed_meaning: In the forest, Lakshmana urges Rama to steady himself and search for Sita. Rama is called the pride of Raghu's line, yet in this moment he cannot hold on to courage. The verse shows how sorrow can briefly defeat even the noblest will.
ramayan::7845.modern_relevance: You know what to do, and someone you trust is saying it clearly — but your chest is still tight, and the old panic comes back anyway.
ramayan::7845.insight: It shows that guidance alone is not always enough; the mind in grief may need time before it can act.

ramayan::7846.verse_sanskrit: स दीनो दीनया वाचा लक्ष्मणं वाक्यमब्रवीत् । शीघ्रं लक्ष्मण जानीहि गत्वा गोदावरीं नदीम् । । 3641 । । अपि गोदावरीं सीता पद्मान्यानयितुं गता ।
ramayan::7846.verse_hindi: Rama in dejection said these pitiable words to Lakshmana,O Lakashmana, go swiftly to the river Godavari and find out if Sita has gone there to get lotuses.
ramayan::7846.english_translation: Rama, overcome with sorrow, said to Lakshmana, “Go quickly and check the Godavari river. Perhaps Sita has gone there to gather lotuses.”
ramayan::7846.translation_literal: स (he) / दीनः (dejected) / दीनया (with pitiable) / वाचा (with speech) / लक्ष्मणम् (to Lakshmana) / वाक्यम् (words) / अब्रवीत् (spoke) / शीघ्रम् (quickly) / लक्ष्मण (Lakshmana) / जानीहि (find out) / गत्वा (having gone) / गोदावरीम् (the Godavari) / नदीम् (river) / अपि (perhaps) / गोदावरीम् (to the Godavari) / सीता (Sita) / पद्मानि (lotuses) / आनयितुम् (to bring) / गता (gone)
ramayan::7846.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7846.essence: Desperation turns even a king into someone searching for one small, ordinary clue.
ramayan::7846.simple_meaning: In panic and grief, Rama asks Lakshmana to go to the Godavari and see whether Sita went there for lotuses.
ramayan::7846.simple_insight: Fear makes the mind leap to the smallest hope.
ramayan::7846.detailed_meaning: After Sita disappears near the forest river, Rama is shaken enough to search for any possible clue. He sends Lakshmana to the Godavari, wondering whether she simply went to gather lotuses. It is a desperate, uncertain moment before the real search begins.
ramayan::7846.modern_relevance: You notice a loved one is missing from the room, and your mind grabs at the most ordinary explanation first. Grief always searches for a harmless answer before it accepts the wound.
ramayan::7846.insight: It shows how shock makes the mind cling to a hopeful possibility before facing loss.

ramayan::7847.verse_sanskrit: एवमुक्तस्तु रामेण लक्ष्मणः परवीरहा । । 3642 । । नदीं गोदावरीं रम्यां जगाम लघुविक्रमः ।
ramayan::7847.verse_hindi: Lakshmana, destroyer of enemywarriors, went to the beautiful river Godavari with quick steps following the instruction of Rama.
ramayan::7847.english_translation: Lakshmana, destroyer of enemy warriors, went with quick steps to the beautiful river Godavari, following Rama's instruction.
ramayan::7847.translation_literal: एवमुक्तस्तु (thus spoken to) / रामेण (by Rama) / लक्ष्मणः (Lakshmana) / परवीरहा (slayer of enemy heroes) / नदीं (to the river) / गोदावरीं (Godavari) / रम्यां (beautiful) / जगाम (went) / लघुविक्रमः (of swift stride)
ramayan::7847.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7847.essence: Loyalty becomes visible the moment you move without hesitation.
ramayan::7847.simple_meaning: Lakshmana immediately obeys Rama and goes to the Godavari river to search.
ramayan::7847.simple_insight: Loyalty can be quiet and immediate: you hear, you move, you help.
ramayan::7847.detailed_meaning: Rama has just learned that Sita may be missing near the Godavari. He sends Lakshmana at once, and Lakshmana goes quickly, ready to search every riverbank. The verse simply shows obedience in motion.
ramayan::7847.modern_relevance: Your friend calls in panic and you do not debate, delay, or overthink. You get up, grab your keys, and go.
ramayan::7847.insight: It shows how support becomes real only when instruction turns into action.

ramayan::7848.verse_sanskrit: तां लक्ष्मणस्तीर्थवती विचित्वा राममब्रवीत् । । 3643 । । नैनां पश्यामि तीर्थेषु क्रोशतो न शृणोति मे ।
ramayan::7848.verse_hindi: Searching for Sita at the landings of river Godavari, Lakshmana said to Rama, I am unable to find her at these landings.No one responds to my call.
ramayan::7848.english_translation: Searching the river landings, Lakshmana said to Rama, “I cannot see her at the crossings. No one answers when I call.”
ramayan::7848.translation_literal: तां (her) / लक्ष्मणः (Lakshmana) / तीर्थवती (with landings or crossings) / विचित्वा (having searched) / रामम् (to Rama) / अब्रवीत् (said) / न (not) / एनाम् (her) / पश्यामि (I see) / तीर्थेषु (at the crossings) / क्रोशतः (calling out) / न (not) / शृणोति (hears) / मे (my)
ramayan::7848.speaker: Lakshmana
ramayan::7848.essence: The search itself becomes the first proof of loss.
ramayan::7848.simple_meaning: Lakshmana searches the river crossings for Sita and tells Rama that he cannot find her and no one answers his calls.
ramayan::7848.simple_insight: Some losses give no reply at all, only silence.
ramayan::7848.detailed_meaning: Lakshmana has rushed to the Godavari after Rama’s anxious order. He searches the river landings for Sita and returns empty-handed, telling Rama that she is nowhere to be seen and no one answers his cries. The search itself becomes the first sign of disaster.
ramayan::7848.modern_relevance: You call a friend’s name in a crowded station, then again at the platform edge, and get only noise back. That empty silence is its own answer.
ramayan::7848.insight: It shifts the mind from searching for reassurance to facing absence directly.

ramayan::7849.verse_sanskrit: कं नु वा देशमापन्ना वैदेही क्लेशनाशिनी । । 3644 । । न ह्यहं वेद तं देशं यत्र सा जनकात्मजा ।
ramayan::7849.verse_hindi: Where could Vaidehi, destroyer of sorrow, go? I wonder. I am unable to trace the spot where the daughter of Janaka could be found.
ramayan::7849.english_translation: Where could Vaidehi, destroyer of sorrow, have gone? I do not know the place where Janaka's daughter could be found.
ramayan::7849.translation_literal: कं (where) / नु (indeed) / वा (or) / देशम् (place) / आपन्ना (gone to) / वैदेही (Vaidehi) / क्लेशनाशिनी (destroyer of sorrow) / न (not) / हि (indeed) / अहम् (I) / वेद (know) / तम् (that) / देशम् (place) / यत्र (where) / सा (she) / जनकात्मजा (Janaka's daughter)
ramayan::7849.speaker: Lakshmana
ramayan::7849.essence: Searching is hardest when even the searcher has no map.
ramayan::7849.simple_meaning: Lakshmana cannot find Sita and wonders where she could have gone. He admits he does not know the place where she might be found.
ramayan::7849.simple_insight: Even fierce loyalty can be shaken by helpless searching.
ramayan::7849.detailed_meaning: Lakshmana has searched the riverbanks near Godavari and still found no trace of Sita. Standing before Rama, he admits defeat: he does not know where Janaka's daughter has gone. The line deepens the panic before Rama's own desperate search.
ramayan::7849.modern_relevance: You have checked every room, every message, every place they might be. Still nothing. The helplessness of not knowing where to look is its own grief.
ramayan::7849.insight: It captures the moment when searching turns into raw uncertainty and the mind can no longer hold a plan.

ramayan::7850.verse_sanskrit: लक्ष्मणस्य वचश्श्रुत्वा दीनस्सन्तापमोहितः । । 3645 । । रामस्समभिचक्राम स्वयं गोदावरीं नदीम् । स तामुपस्थितो रामः क्व सीतेत्येवमब्रवीत् । । 3646 । ।
ramayan::7850.verse_hindi: Overwhelmed with grief on hearing Lakshmanas words, Rama himself went to river Godavari, and shouted, where are you, Sita?
ramayan::7850.english_translation: Overwhelmed with grief on hearing Lakshmana's words, Rama himself went to the Godavari River, and cried out, 'Where are you, Sita?'
ramayan::7850.translation_literal: लक्ष्मणस्य (Lakshmana's) / वचः (words) / श्रुत्वा (having heard) / दीनः (grief-stricken) / सन्तापमोहितः (bewildered by anguish) / रामः (Rama) / समभिचक्राम (went toward) / स्वयं (himself) / गोदावरीं नदीम् (the Godavari River) / सः (he) / ताम् (her) / उपस्थितः (having approached) / रामः (Rama) / क्व (where) / सीता (Sita) / इति (thus) / एवम् (so) / अब्रवीत् (said)
ramayan::7850.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7850.essence: Grief drives him to search in person, not stand apart.
ramayan::7850.simple_meaning: Rama hears Lakshmana's report, is overcome with grief, and goes to the river himself, calling out for Sita.
ramayan::7850.simple_insight: Love makes even the strongest person search with his own voice.
ramayan::7850.detailed_meaning: Lakshmana has just reported that he cannot find Sita anywhere along the river landings. Hearing this, Rama is shaken by grief and confusion. He goes himself to the Godavari, searching and calling out for Sita, showing how urgently the loss has struck him.
ramayan::7850.modern_relevance: You get the text that says she is not answering, and you still go look yourself. Some losses are too real to outsource.
ramayan::7850.insight: It shifts the moment from hearing bad news to personally entering the search.

ramayan::7851.verse_sanskrit: भूतानि राक्षसेन्द्रेण वधार्हेण हृतामिति । न तां शशंसू रामाय तथा गोदावरी नदि । । 3647 । ।
ramayan::7851.verse_hindi: Like the elements of Nature, river Godavari did not disclose Rama that Sita had been abducted by the king of demons who deserved death.
ramayan::7851.english_translation: Like the forces of nature, the Godavari did not tell Rama that Sita had been taken by the king of demons who deserved death.
ramayan::7851.translation_literal: भूतानि (the beings / forces of nature) / राक्षसेन्द्रेण (by the king of demons) / वधार्हेण (worthy of death) / हृतामिति (that she had been taken) / न (not) / तां (that) / शशंसू (revealed / told) / रामाय (to Rama) / तथा (thus) / गोदावरी (Godavari) / नदि (river)
ramayan::7851.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7851.essence: Even the river withholds the answer he most needs.
ramayan::7851.simple_meaning: The river stayed silent and did not tell Rama where Sita had gone.
ramayan::7851.simple_insight: Even nature offers no answer when grief is asking.
ramayan::7851.detailed_meaning: Rama stands on the bank of the Godavari, desperate and shaken, searching for Sita after her abduction. He asks the river for help, but the river gives no answer. The silence deepens his helplessness.
ramayan::7851.modern_relevance: You replay the last place you saw someone, hoping the room itself will explain what happened. It never does.
ramayan::7851.insight: It shows how grief can search every detail for a clue and still find only silence.

ramayan::7852.verse_sanskrit: ततः प्रचोदिता भूतैश्शंसास्मैतां प्रियामिति । न तु साभ्यवदतसितां पृष्टा रामेण शोचता । । 3648 । ।
ramayan::7852.verse_hindi: River Godavari (although) prompted by creatures (of Nature) to tell him about his beloved did not respond to brooding Rama.
ramayan::7852.english_translation: River Godavari, though urged by the creatures around her to tell Rama about his beloved, did not answer the grieving Rama when he asked.
ramayan::7852.translation_literal: ततः (then) / प्रचोदिता (prompted) / भूतैः (by beings) / शंस (tell) / अस्मै (to him) / ताम् (that) / प्रियम् (beloved one) / इति (thus) / न तु (but not) / सा (she) / अभ्यवदत् (spoke) / सीताम् (Sita) / पृष्टा (asked) / रामेण (by Rama) / शोचता (grieving) ।
ramayan::7852.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7852.essence: Even nature withholds comfort when loss is still unfolding.
ramayan::7852.simple_meaning: Even when Rama asks directly, the river stays silent and gives him no answer about Sita.
ramayan::7852.simple_insight: Some grief receives no reply. The world may stay silent even when your heart is breaking.
ramayan::7852.detailed_meaning: After Lakshmana’s words, Rama rushes to the Godavari, desperate for any sign of Sita. He asks the river itself. But this is only a passing moment in the search: the river does not reveal what has happened, keeping the sorrow alive.
ramayan::7852.modern_relevance: You keep checking your phone after the message that changed everything, hoping for one clarifying reply. Sometimes the silence is all you get.
ramayan::7852.insight: It shows grief meeting silence, and the search continuing without comfort or confirmation.

ramayan::7853.verse_sanskrit: रावणस्य तु तद्रूपं कर्माणि च दुरात्मनः । ध्यात्वा भयात्तु वैदेहीं सा नदी न शशंस ताम् । । 3649 । ।
ramayan::7853.verse_hindi: Remembering the evilminded Ravanas appearance and action, the river revealed nothing about Vaidehi out of fear.
ramayan::7853.english_translation: Remembering Ravana's form and the deeds of that evil-minded one, the river revealed nothing about Vaidehi out of fear.
ramayan::7853.translation_literal: रावणस्य (of Ravana) / तु (indeed) / तत्-रूपम् (that form) / कर्माणि (deeds) / च (and) / दुरात्मनः (of the evil-minded one) / ध्यात्वा (remembering) / भयात् (out of fear) / तु (indeed) / वैदेहीम् (about Vaidehi) / सा नदी (that river) / न (not) / शशंस (revealed) / ताम् (that)
ramayan::7853.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7853.essence: Fear can make even a witness go silent.
ramayan::7853.simple_meaning: The river stayed silent because it feared Ravana and remembered his violent nature.
ramayan::7853.simple_insight: Fear can silence even what might otherwise help.
ramayan::7853.detailed_meaning: Hanuman has reached the river near the place where Sita is being sought, but the search is still blocked. The river, remembering Ravana's terrifying power and cruelty, refuses to reveal anything about Vaidehi. This keeps the search moving through frustration and fear.
ramayan::7853.modern_relevance: You know something important, but the person asking has a reputation for retaliation. Even a small truth feels dangerous to say, so you stay silent.
ramayan::7853.insight: It shows how fear can prevent the truth from being spoken, even when someone is suffering.

ramayan::7854.verse_sanskrit: निराशस्तु तया नद्या सीताया दर्शने कृतः । उवाच रामस्सौमित्रिं सीतादर्शनकर्शितः । । 36410 । ।
ramayan::7854.verse_hindi: Disappointed by the river and emaciated by not being able to see Sita, Rama said to Lakshmana :
ramayan::7854.english_translation: Disappointed by the river and weakened by longing to see Sita, Rama said to Lakshmana:
ramayan::7854.translation_literal: निराशः (disappointed) / तया (by that) / नद्या (river) / सीताया (of Sita) / दर्शने (in seeing) / कृतः (made) / उवाच (said) / रामः (Rama) / सौमित्रिम् (to Lakshmana) / सीतादर्शनकर्शितः (worn down by seeing Sita not possible)
ramayan::7854.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7854.essence: Absence itself can exhaust the heart.
ramayan::7854.simple_meaning: Rama cannot find Sita and feels drained by the search. He turns to Lakshmana and speaks from that exhaustion.
ramayan::7854.simple_insight: Even a steady heart can wear thin when longing meets silence.
ramayan::7854.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana search the Godavari for any sign of Sita. The river gives nothing back, and Rama’s hope turns to strain. This verse sets up his words to Lakshmana in the next line, so it serves as a bridge rather than a full teaching.
ramayan::7854.modern_relevance: You keep checking your phone for one message that never comes. The silence itself starts to change your posture, your breath, your whole day.
ramayan::7854.insight: It shows how unreturned longing can drain even the strongest resolve.

ramayan::7855.verse_sanskrit: एषा गोदावरी सौम्य किंचिन्न प्रति भाषते । किं नु लक्ष्मण वक्ष्यामि समेत्य जनकं वचः । । 36411 । । मातरं चैव वैदेह्या विना तामहमप्रियम् ।
ramayan::7855.verse_hindi: O handsome Lakshmana this Godavari does not at all respond. How can I go to Janaka and my mother without Sita and break this unhappy news?
ramayan::7855.english_translation: O gentle Lakshmana, this Godavari gives no answer. How can I go to Janaka and to my mother without Sita, and bring them this bitter news?
ramayan::7855.translation_literal: एषा (this) / गोदावरी (Godavari) / सौम्य (gentle one) / किंचिन्न (not at all) / प्रति भाषते (speaks back) । / किं (how) / नु (indeed) / लक्ष्मण (Lakshmana) / वक्ष्यामि (shall I say) / समेत्य (having met) / जनकं (Janaka) / वचः (words) । / मातरं (mother) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / वैदेह्या (of Sita) / विना (without) / ताम् (that) / अहम् (I) / अप्रियम् (unpleasant) ।
ramayan::7855.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7855.essence: Even a prince can be stranded by the news he must carry.
ramayan::7855.simple_meaning: Rama stands before the Godavari, unable to get an answer, and feels the pain of having to return to Janaka and his mother without Sita.
ramayan::7855.simple_insight: Some losses are so heavy that even speaking about them feels unbearable.
ramayan::7855.detailed_meaning: Rama has reached the Godavari after searching for Sita. The river gives no help, and his grief turns toward a harder thought: he must face Janaka and his own mother without her. The verse catches the weight of news he cannot bear to deliver.
ramayan::7855.modern_relevance: You stare at your phone after the hospital call, knowing you have to explain the worst part to your family. The words exist, but your chest refuses to make room for them.
ramayan::7855.insight: It shifts grief from private pain to the burden of having to tell others.

ramayan::7856.verse_sanskrit: या मे राज्यविहीनस्य वने वन्येन जीवतः । । 36412 । । सर्वं व्यपनयेच्छोकं वैदेही क्व नु सा गता ।
ramayan::7856.verse_hindi: Where could have gone that Vaidehi, who  removed all my sorrows and sufferings when I lost my kingdom and survived on food available in the forest?
ramayan::7856.english_translation: Where could Vaidehi have gone, she who removed all my sorrow when I had lost my kingdom and was living in the forest on wild food?
ramayan::7856.translation_literal: या (where) / मे (my) / राज्यविहीनस्य (of one without a kingdom) / वने (in the forest) / वन्येन (with forest-food) / जीवतः (living) / सर्वं (all) / व्यपनयेच्छोकं (removed sorrow) / वैदेही (Vaidehi) / क्व (where) / नु (indeed) / सा (she) / गता (gone)
ramayan::7856.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7856.essence: You only feel exile fully after the one who softened it disappears.
ramayan::7856.simple_meaning: Rama grieves Sita’s disappearance. He remembers that she made exile bearable, and now he does not know where she has gone.
ramayan::7856.simple_insight: When the one who helped you endure is gone, the loss feels deeper than the hardship itself.
ramayan::7856.detailed_meaning: Rama is in the forest with Lakshmana, cut off from his kingdom and from Sita. He looks back on how her presence made exile bearable, and the pain of losing her now overwhelms every other sorrow.
ramayan::7856.modern_relevance: You were surviving a hard season because one person made it lighter. Then they stopped answering, and the whole weight came back at once.
ramayan::7856.insight: It shifts attention from the hardship itself to the person whose presence transformed that hardship.

ramayan::7857.verse_sanskrit: ज्ञातिपक्षविहीनस्य राजपुत्रीमपश्यतः । । 36413 । । मन्ये दीर्घा भविष्यन्ति रात्रयो मम जाग्रतः ।
ramayan::7857.verse_hindi: Away from relatives and away from the princess, I keep awake during nights which seem too long.
ramayan::7857.english_translation: Away from my relatives and unable to see the princess, I think my nights will be very long while I stay awake.
ramayan::7857.translation_literal: ज्ञातिपक्षविहीनस्य (of one bereft of relatives) / राजपुत्रीम् (the princess) / अपश्यतः (not seeing) / मन्ये (I think) / दीर्घाः (long) / भविष्यन्ति (will be) / रात्रयः (nights) / मम (my) / जाग्रतः (while staying awake)
ramayan::7857.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7857.essence: Separation turns a single night into a long vigil.
ramayan::7857.simple_meaning: Separated from his family and unable to see Sita, Rama feels that his sleepless nights will drag on endlessly.
ramayan::7857.simple_insight: Love can make time feel unbearable when the person you long for is gone.
ramayan::7857.detailed_meaning: Rama stands by the Godavari after losing Sita. Lakshmana is with him, but comfort is not enough. Cut off from family and from the princess he cannot find, he says the nights ahead will be painfully long.
ramayan::7857.modern_relevance: You keep checking your phone at 1:13 a.m., hoping for one message that would change the whole night. When the person you miss is absent, time itself starts to ache.
ramayan::7857.insight: It shifts attention from action to the inner cost of separation: longing changes how time is experienced.

ramayan::7858.verse_sanskrit: गोदावरीं जनस्थानमिमं प्रस्रवणं गिरिम् । । 36414 । । सर्वाण्यनुगमिष्यामि यदि सीता हि दृश्यते ।
ramayan::7858.verse_hindi: I will roam about the river Godavari, Janasthana and this mount Prasravana till I find Sita.
ramayan::7858.english_translation: I will search the Godavari, Janasthana, and this Mount Prasravana, and follow every path until I find Sita.
ramayan::7858.translation_literal: गोदावरीं (the Godavari) / जनस्थानम् (Janasthana) / इमम् (this) / प्रस्रवणम् (Prasravana) / गिरिम् (mountain) / सर्वाणि (all) / अनुगमिष्यामि (I will follow) / यदि (if) / सीता (Sita) / हि (indeed) / दृश्यते (is seen)
ramayan::7858.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7858.essence: Loss drives him to search every place without rest.
ramayan::7858.simple_meaning: Rama says he will search every place nearby until he finds Sita.
ramayan::7858.simple_insight: Love becomes relentless when someone you cherish is missing.
ramayan::7858.detailed_meaning: Rama stands in the forest after Sita's disappearance, speaking to Lakshmana with urgent resolve. He names the river, the hunting grounds, and the mountain around him, promising to search every path until he sees her again.
ramayan::7858.modern_relevance: You’ve checked the apartment, the parking lot, and the last place you saw her. You keep going because stopping feels impossible.
ramayan::7858.insight: It shifts grief into action: keep searching, keep moving, keep looking.

ramayan::7859.verse_sanskrit: एते मृगा महावीर्य मामीक्षन्ते मुहुर्मुहुः । । 36415 । । वक्तुकामा इव हि मे इङ्गितान्युपलक्षये ।
ramayan::7859.verse_hindi: O mighty Lakshmana these deer are looking at me again and again indicating that they wish to tell me something.
ramayan::7859.english_translation: O mighty Lakshmana, these deer are looking at me again and again, as if they want to tell me something.
ramayan::7859.translation_literal: एते (these) / मृगाḥ (deer) / महावीर्य (O mighty one) / माम् (at me) / ईक्षन्ते (are looking) / मुहुः मुहुः (again and again) / वक्तु-कामाḥ (wishing to speak) / इव (as if) / हि (indeed) / मे (to me) / इङ्गितानि (signs, hints) / उपलक्षये (I notice, I perceive)
ramayan::7859.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7859.essence: Longing makes the world feel like it is speaking back.
ramayan::7859.simple_meaning: Rama notices deer staring at him and thinks they may be trying to signal something.
ramayan::7859.simple_insight: Grief can make you read meaning into every sign around you.
ramayan::7859.detailed_meaning: Rama is searching the forest for Sita, and every sight feels charged with meaning. He tells Lakshmana that the deer keep looking at him as if they know something. The line deepens his anxious search, but the next verse carries the real question.
ramayan::7859.modern_relevance: You keep rereading a text, a glance, a silence, hoping it means something. When you are desperate, even a small sign feels loaded.
ramayan::7859.insight: It shows a mind so strained by longing that it starts treating ordinary details as messages.

ramayan::7860.verse_sanskrit: तांस्तु दृष्ट्वा नरव्याघ्रो राघवः प्रत्युवाच ह । । 36416 । । क्व सीतेति निरीक्षन्वै बाष्पसंरुद्धया दृशा ।
ramayan::7860.verse_hindi: With his vision blurred by tears, Rama, the best among men, looked at them and asked them Where is Sita?
ramayan::7860.english_translation: Seeing them, Rama, the best among men, answered with eyes choked by tears, asking, "Where is Sita?"
ramayan::7860.translation_literal: तान् (them) / तु (indeed) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / नरव्याघ्रः (tiger among men) / राघवः (Raghava) / प्रत्युवाच (answered) / ह (indeed) / क्व (where) / सीता (Sita) / इति (thus) / निरीक्षन् (looking) / वै (indeed) / बाष्प-संरुद्धया (by tears choked) / दृशा (with sight)
ramayan::7860.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7860.essence: Grief turns even a clue into a cry for the missing beloved.
ramayan::7860.simple_meaning: Rama sees the deer, but grief overwhelms him. He can only ask where Sita is, because everything else has narrowed to that one loss.
ramayan::7860.simple_insight: When love is missing, even the world feels like a question.
ramayan::7860.detailed_meaning: In the forest near Godavari, Rama keeps searching for Sita with Lakshmana beside him. The deer seem to signal something, and Rama turns to them through tears, asking where Sita is. This moment shows how completely her absence has overtaken him.
ramayan::7860.modern_relevance: You spot something that might help, but your mind is still fixed on the person who is missing. Even clues can feel like grief when love has become a wound.
ramayan::7860.insight: It shows how longing can narrow attention until every sign is read through loss.

ramayan::7861.verse_sanskrit: एवमुक्ता नरेन्द्रेण ते मृगास्सहसोत्थिताः । । 36417 । । दक्षिणाभिमुखास्सर्वे दर्शयन्तो नभस्थलम् । मैथिली ह्रियमाणा सा दिशं यामन्वपद्यत । । 36418 । । तेन मार्गेण धावन्तो निरीक्षन्ते नराधिपम् ।
ramayan::7861.verse_hindi: Thus asked by the prince, all the deer got up suddenly, and pointed towards the southern sky, the direction in which the princess from Mithila was carried off. Looking at the Lord of men (Rama), they started running in that direction.
ramayan::7861.english_translation: Thus asked by the prince, all the deer got up suddenly and pointed toward the southern sky, the direction in which the princess from Mithila had been carried off. Looking at Rama, they ran in that direction.
ramayan::7861.translation_literal: एवमुक्ता (thus spoken to) / नरेन्द्रेण (by the lord of men) / ते (those) / मृगाः (deer) / सहसा (suddenly) / उत्थिताः (rose up) / दक्षिणाभिमुखाः (facing southward) / सर्वे (all) / दर्शयन्तः (showing) / नभस्थलम् (the sky) / मैथिली (the princess of Mithila) / ह्रियमाणा (being carried away) / सा (she) / दिशम् (direction) / याम् (which) / अन्वपद्यत (had taken) / तेन मार्गेण (by that path) / धावन्तः (running) / निरीक्षन्ते (they looked at) / नराधिपम् (the lord of men)
ramayan::7861.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7861.essence: A clue can matter more than a speech.
ramayan::7861.simple_meaning: The deer suddenly rise, point south, and run that way, showing Rama the path Sita was taken.
ramayan::7861.simple_insight: Even small signs can guide you when you are desperate to find what matters.
ramayan::7861.detailed_meaning: In the forest, Rama has asked the deer what they know about Sita's disappearance. The animals answer not with speech but with movement: they rise, point south, and run toward the direction of her abduction. It is a clue, not a teaching.
ramayan::7861.modern_relevance: You replay the last message, the last location, the last clue, trying to reconstruct what happened. In panic, even tiny signs feel like lifelines.
ramayan::7861.insight: It shows how the search for answers can begin with careful attention to the smallest clue.

ramayan::7862.verse_sanskrit: येन मार्गं च भूमिं च निरीक्षन्ते स्म ते मृगाः । । 36419 । । पुनश्च मार्गमिच्छन्ति लक्ष्मणेनोपलक्षिताः ।
ramayan::7862.verse_hindi: Even Lakshmana marked that the deer were showing and looking at the path lying in that direction.
ramayan::7862.english_translation: Even Lakshmana saw that the deer were pointing out the path and the ground in that direction.
ramayan::7862.translation_literal: येन (by which) / मार्गं (path) / च (and) / भूमिं (ground) / च (and) / निरीक्षन्ते स्म (they were looking at) / ते (those) / मृगाः (deer) / पुनश्च (again) / मार्गम् (path) / इच्छन्ति (they want) / लक्ष्मणेन (by Lakshmana) / उपलक्षिताः (noticed, observed)
ramayan::7862.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7862.essence: Silent signs can carry the whole message.
ramayan::7862.simple_meaning: Lakshmana notices that the deer are silently indicating a direction by looking toward the path and the ground.
ramayan::7862.simple_insight: Careful observation can reveal meaning where words are absent.
ramayan::7862.detailed_meaning: Rama has just asked where Sita is, and the deer respond by pointing south. Lakshmana sees more than movement: he reads their silent signs and understands they are guiding the brothers toward the route Sita was taken.
ramayan::7862.modern_relevance: You catch the smallest shift in someone's eyes and realize they are trying to tell you something without words.
ramayan::7862.insight: It trains attention to read gesture, direction, and implication instead of waiting only for speech.

ramayan::7863.verse_sanskrit: तेषां वचनसर्वस्वं लक्षयामास चेङ्गितम् । । 36420 । । उवाच लक्ष्मणो ज्येष्ठं धीमान्भ्रातरमार्तवत् ।
ramayan::7863.verse_hindi: Observing intelligently their indications and understanding the meaning of their message, Lakshmana said to his distressed elder brother:
ramayan::7863.english_translation: Observing intelligently their indications and understanding the meaning of their message, Lakshmana said to his distressed elder brother:
ramayan::7863.translation_literal: तेषां (their) / वचनसर्वस्वं (the full meaning of the message) / लक्षयामास (he observed, understood) / च (and) / ईङ्गितम् (indications, gestures) / उवाच (said) / लक्ष्मणः (Lakshmana) / ज्येष्ठम् (to the elder one) / धीमान् (wise) / भ्रातरम् (brother) / आर्तवत् (in distress)
ramayan::7863.speaker: Lakshmana
ramayan::7863.essence: Careful attention can turn a gesture into guidance.
ramayan::7863.simple_meaning: Lakshmana carefully reads the deer’s signs and speaks to his troubled elder brother.
ramayan::7863.simple_insight: Sometimes the next right move begins with noticing what others are trying to show you.
ramayan::7863.detailed_meaning: In the forest, the deer’s sudden gestures are not random. Lakshmana sees the direction they are pointing and understands their warning. He turns to Rama, who is already distressed, and prepares to respond to the clue before them.
ramayan::7863.modern_relevance: You are staring at a confusing email thread, and one small line finally reveals what everyone has been circling around. Clear attention can turn noise into action.
ramayan::7863.insight: It trains you to read signs carefully before deciding what to do next.

ramayan::7864.verse_sanskrit: क्व सितेति त्वया पृष्टा यथेमे सहसोत्थिताः । । 36421 । । दर्शयन्ति क्षितिं चैव दक्षिणां च दिशं मृगाः । साधु गच्छावहे देव दिशमेतां हि नैऋतिम् । । 36422 । । यदि स्यादागमः कश्चिदार्या वा साऽथ लक्ष्यते ।
ramayan::7864.verse_hindi: O lord these deer are indicating the land on the southern side.Therefore it will be proper for both of us to proceed in the southwestern direction. Maybe we will get some clue or find that noble Sita.
ramayan::7864.english_translation: O lord, these deer are pointing to the southern land. It will be proper for both of us to go toward the southwest. Perhaps we will find some clue, or noble Sita herself.
ramayan::7864.translation_literal: क्व (where) / सिता इति (Sita, thus) / त्वया (by you) / पृष्टा (asked) / यथा (as) / इमे (these) / सहसा (suddenly) / उत्थिताः (stood up) / दर्शयन्ति (indicate) / क्षितिम् (the earth/land) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / दक्षिणाम् (southern) / च (and) / दिशम् (direction) / मृगाः (deer) / साधु (properly) / गच्छावहे (let us go) / देव (lord) / दिशम् (direction) / एताम् (this) / हि (indeed) / नैऋतिम् (southwestern) / यदि (if) / स्यात् (there is) / आगमः (arrival/clue) / कश्चिद् (some) / आर्या (noble woman) / वा (or) / सा (she) / अथ (then) / लक्ष्यते (is seen/marked)
ramayan::7864.speaker: Lakshmana
ramayan::7864.essence: A small clue can turn grief into a search.
ramayan::7864.simple_meaning: Lakshmana reads the deer’s movement as a clue and tells Rama to head southwest, hoping to find Sita or some trace of her.
ramayan::7864.simple_insight: Even desperate searching needs a direction. Hope becomes practical when you follow the smallest clue.
ramayan::7864.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana are searching for Sita in the forest. Lakshmana notices that the deer’s behavior points toward the southern side and urges Rama to turn southwest. The verse is a tactical step in the search, not the emotional peak.
ramayan::7864.modern_relevance: You replay the last message, the map pin, the half-remembered detail. In a crisis, you stop guessing and follow the clearest clue you have.
ramayan::7864.insight: It shifts the mind from panic to guided action: read the signs, choose a direction, keep moving.

ramayan::7865.verse_sanskrit: बाढमित्येव काकुत्स्थः प्रस्थितो दक्षिणां दिशम् । । 36423 । । लक्ष्मणानुगतश्शीमन्वीक्षमाणो वसुन्धराम् ।
ramayan::7865.verse_hindi: Handsome Rama said, yesand started in southern direction, carefully looking at the ground, followed by Lakshmana.
ramayan::7865.english_translation: Handsome Rama said, “Yes,” and set out toward the south, carefully watching the ground, with Lakshmana following him.
ramayan::7865.translation_literal: बाढम् (yes) / इति एव (thus indeed) / काकुत्स्थः (Rama) / प्रस्थितः (set out) / दक्षिणाम् दिशम् (toward the southern direction) / लक्ष्मण-अनुगतः (followed by Lakshmana) / शीमान् (handsome, noble) / वीक्षमाणः (looking) / वसुन्धराम् (the ground, earth)
ramayan::7865.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7865.essence: Read the sign, then move without hesitation.
ramayan::7865.simple_meaning: Rama agrees at once and heads south with Lakshmana, watching the ground as they go.
ramayan::7865.simple_insight: Sometimes the next right step is simple: agree, move, and stay alert.
ramayan::7865.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana are already following signs in the forest. Lakshmana points them south, and Rama immediately accepts the direction. They move together, alert and careful, as the search continues through the wild.
ramayan::7865.modern_relevance: You get a text, a clue, a nudge, and the day changes direction. The wise response is not drama — it is immediate, careful movement.
ramayan::7865.insight: It teaches you to respond quickly to good guidance without losing attention.

ramayan::7866.verse_sanskrit: एवं सम्भाषमाणौ तावन्योन्यं भ्रातरावुभौ । । 36424 । । वसुन्धरायां पतितं पुष्पमार्गमपश्यताम् ।
ramayan::7866.verse_hindi: Talking with each other, the two brothers took the path on earth strewn with flowers.
ramayan::7866.english_translation: While the two brothers were speaking to each other, they saw a path of flowers fallen on the earth.
ramayan::7866.translation_literal: एवं (thus) / सम्भाषमाणौ (speaking with each other) / तौ (those two) / अन्योन्यम् (to one another) / भ्रातरौ (the two brothers) / उभौ (both) / वसुन्धरायाम् (on the earth) / पतितम् (fallen) / पुष्पमार्गम् (path of flowers) / अपश्यताम् (saw)
ramayan::7866.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7866.essence: A small trail on the ground signals that something has already changed.
ramayan::7866.simple_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana keep talking as they notice a trail of flowers on the ground.
ramayan::7866.simple_insight: Small signs can matter when you are moving through uncertainty.
ramayan::7866.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana are walking together when they notice a strange trail of flowers on the ground. The verse is a quiet bridge into the next moment, where Rama will react to the sign and infer what has happened.
ramayan::7866.modern_relevance: You are walking with someone and notice a detail that changes everything — a dropped item, a broken seal, a trail left behind.
ramayan::7866.insight: It slows the scene and prepares the mind to read signs before the next revelation.

ramayan::7867.verse_sanskrit: तां पुष्पवृष्टिं पतितां दृष्ट्वा रामो महीतले । । 36425 । । उवाच लक्ष्मणं वीरो दुःखितो दुःखितं वचः ।
ramayan::7867.verse_hindi: Seeing showers of flowers fallen on the ground, valiant Rama sadly said these words to sorrowful Lakshmana:
ramayan::7867.english_translation: Seeing the shower of flowers fallen on the ground, valiant Rama sadly spoke these words to grief-stricken Lakshmana.
ramayan::7867.translation_literal: ताम् (that) / पुष्पवृष्टिम् (shower of flowers) / पतिताम् (fallen) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / रामः (Rama) / महीतले (on the earth) / उवाच (spoke) / लक्ष्मणम् (to Lakshmana) / वीरः (the valiant one) / दुःखितः (grieved) / दुःखितम् (to the grief-stricken one) / वचः (words)
ramayan::7867.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7867.essence: A small trace can reopen a wound faster than words.
ramayan::7867.simple_meaning: Rama sees the flowers on the ground and, heartbroken, speaks to Lakshmana. The scene is a clue that Sita has passed this way.
ramayan::7867.simple_insight: Grief sharpens attention; even fallen flowers can carry a message.
ramayan::7867.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana are following a flower-strewn path in the forest. Rama notices the fallen blossoms and immediately understands they are linked to Sita. His sorrow rises before the next verse explains why.
ramayan::7867.modern_relevance: You spot a scarf on the curb and suddenly know who was here. Small things can carry the weight of someone you miss.
ramayan::7867.insight: It trains you to read signs of loss carefully instead of rushing past them.

ramayan::7868.verse_sanskrit: अभिजानामि पुष्पाणि तानीमानीह लक्ष्मण । । 36426 । । पिनद्धानि हि वैदेह्या मया दत्तानि कानने ।
ramayan::7868.verse_hindi: O Lakshmana, here are the same flowers I had given Vaidehi to wear in the forest. I can recognize them.
ramayan::7868.english_translation: O Lakshmana, here are the same flowers I had given Vaidehi to wear in the forest. I can recognize them.
ramayan::7868.translation_literal: अभिजानामि (I recognize) / पुष्पाणि (the flowers) / तानि (those) / इमानि (these) / इह (here) / लक्ष्मण (Lakshmana) / पिनद्धानि (worn) / हि (indeed) / वैदेह्या (by Vaidehi) / मया (by me) / दत्तानि (given) / कानने (in the forest)
ramayan::7868.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7868.essence: A forgotten flower becomes proof of a love now wounded.
ramayan::7868.simple_meaning: Rama recognizes the flowers he once gave Sita to wear in the forest. Seeing them on the ground deepens his grief and confirms her presence here.
ramayan::7868.simple_insight: A small sign can carry a whole love story.
ramayan::7868.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana are following a trail of fallen flowers in the forest. Rama sees them and realizes they are the same flowers he had given Sita to wear. The sight turns a clue into painful certainty.
ramayan::7868.modern_relevance: You find the scarf, note, or receipt someone left behind, and the whole memory comes rushing back. A tiny object can reopen a bond you thought you had contained.
ramayan::7868.insight: It trains you to notice how grief often begins with recognition, not explanation.

ramayan::7869.verse_sanskrit: मन्ये सूर्यश्च वायुश्च मेदिनी च यशस्विनी । । 36427 । । अभिरक्षन्ति पुष्पाणि प्रकुर्वन्तो मम प्रियम् ।
ramayan::7869.verse_hindi: I think the Sun, the wind  and the famed earth have done me a favour by preserving these flowers.
ramayan::7869.english_translation: I think the Sun, the wind, and the famed earth have preserved these flowers for my sake.
ramayan::7869.translation_literal: मन्ये (I think) / सूर्यः (the Sun) / च (and) / वायुः (the wind) / च (and) / मेदिनी (the earth) / च (and) / यशस्विनी (the famed) / अभिरक्षन्ति (are preserving) / पुष्पाणि (the flowers) / प्रकुर्वन्तो (doing) / मम (my) / प्रियम् (favour)
ramayan::7869.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7869.essence: Love makes even the elements seem like keepers of memory.
ramayan::7869.simple_meaning: Rama feels that the sun, wind, and earth have protected the flowers he once gave Sita.
ramayan::7869.simple_insight: Even small signs of love can feel sacred when grief has sharpened your attention.
ramayan::7869.detailed_meaning: Rama has found the flowers he had once given Sita in the forest. Seeing them still preserved on the ground, he speaks to Lakshmana with painful tenderness, imagining that the sun, wind, and earth themselves protected them.
ramayan::7869.modern_relevance: You find a pressed flower in an old book and suddenly the whole past returns. Grief makes even ordinary things feel like they were kept alive for you.
ramayan::7869.insight: It trains the mind to read memory through signs, not explanations.

ramayan::7870.verse_sanskrit: एवमुक्त्वा महाबाहुं लक्ष्मणं पुरुषर्षभः । । 36428 । । उवाच रामो धर्मात्मा गिरिं प्रस्रवणाकुलम् ।
ramayan::7870.verse_hindi: Rigteous Rama, the best among men, having said these words to the longarmed Lakshmana, asked mount Prasravana, full of streams:
ramayan::7870.english_translation: Having spoken thus to Lakshmana, the righteous Rama, best among men, addressed the mountain Prasravana crowded with streams.
ramayan::7870.translation_literal: एवमुक्त्वा (having spoken thus) / महाबाहुं (to the long-armed) / लक्ष्मणं (Lakshmana) / पुरुषर्षभः (best among men) / उवाच (spoke) / रामो (Rama) / धर्मात्मा (righteous in nature) / गिरिं (to the mountain) / प्रस्रवणाकुलम् (crowded with streams)
ramayan::7870.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7870.essence: Grief makes the world feel capable of answering.
ramayan::7870.simple_meaning: Rama turns from Lakshmana and speaks to the mountain by the stream, continuing his search for Sita.
ramayan::7870.simple_insight: Grief can make even a mountain feel like a witness.
ramayan::7870.detailed_meaning: In the forest, Rama has just recognized Sita's flowers and feels her nearness and absence at once. He turns from Lakshmana and addresses Mount Prasravana itself, preparing to ask whether the mountain has seen Sita in this lonely place.
ramayan::7870.modern_relevance: You stand in a place that should feel ordinary, but one missing person changes everything. Suddenly you are speaking to the room, the road, the silence — as if they might answer.
ramayan::7870.insight: It shows how longing searches everywhere, even for witnesses that cannot reply.

ramayan::7871.verse_sanskrit: कच्चित् क्षितिभृतां नाथ दृष्टा सर्वाङ्गसुन्दरी । । 36429 । । रामा रम्ये वनोद्देशे मया विरहिता त्वया ।
ramayan::7871.verse_hindi: O king of the mountains have you seen a lady with beautiful limbs separated from me in this forest tract ?
ramayan::7871.english_translation: O king of the mountains, have you seen a lady with beautiful limbs, separated from me in this forest tract?
ramayan::7871.translation_literal: कच्चित् (whether) / क्षितिभृतां (of mountains) / नाथ (lord) / दृष्टा (seen) / सर्वाङ्गसुन्दरी (beautiful in every limb) / रामा (the lady) / रम्ये (lovely) / वनोद्देशे (in the forest tract) / मया (by me) / विरहिता (separated) / त्वया (by you)
ramayan::7871.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7871.essence: Loss makes you ask the world what it has seen.
ramayan::7871.simple_meaning: Rama asks a mountain whether it has seen Sita, the beautiful woman who has been separated from him in the forest.
ramayan::7871.simple_insight: Separation makes even the landscape feel like a witness to your loss.
ramayan::7871.detailed_meaning: Rama has reached Mount Prasravana with Lakshmana after searching the forest for Sita. Seeing the mountain, he speaks to it as if it could answer, asking whether it has seen her anywhere nearby. The verse is part of his urgent search, not a complete teaching on its own.
ramayan::7871.modern_relevance: You have retraced every street after someone vanished from your life, asking the world itself for a sign. Grief makes even stone feel like it should remember.
ramayan::7871.insight: It shows how longing narrows the mind until every place becomes a possible witness.

ramayan::7872.verse_sanskrit: क्रुद्धोऽब्रवीद्गिरिं तत्र सिंहः क्षुद्रमृगं यथा । । 36430 । । तां हेमवर्णां हेमाभां सीतां दर्शय पर्वत । यावत्सानूनि सर्वाणि न ते विध्वंसयाम्यहम् । । 36431 । ।
ramayan::7872.verse_hindi: Like a lion aiming at a petty animal, angry Rama  said, O Mountain before I destroy  all your slopes show me that goldenhued Sita with lustre like gold.
ramayan::7872.english_translation: Like a lion confronting a small beast, Rama angrily said to the mountain, "Show me that golden-hued Sita, radiant like gold. Before I destroy all your slopes, do not hide her from me."
ramayan::7872.translation_literal: क्रुद्धः (angry) / अब्रवीत् (said) / गिरिम् (to the mountain) / तत्र (there) / सिंहः (lion) / क्षुद्रमृगम् (small beast) / यथा (like) / ताम् (that) / हेमवर्णाम् (golden-hued) / हेमाभाम् (golden-radiant) / सीताम् (Sita) / दर्शय (show) / पर्वत (O mountain) / यावत् (before) / सानूनि (slopes) / सर्वाणि (all) / ते (your) / विध्वंसयामि (I destroy) / अहम् (I)
ramayan::7872.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7872.essence: Desperate love turns into a threat when it finds no answer.
ramayan::7872.simple_meaning: Rama speaks to the mountain in anger, demanding that it reveal Sita before he tears the mountain apart.
ramayan::7872.simple_insight: Love can make even restraint sound like a threat.
ramayan::7872.detailed_meaning: Rama stands on Prasravana with Lakshmana and calls to the mountain after asking whether it has seen Sita. When the mountain gives no answer, his grief turns fierce. This is not a teaching verse, but a flash of desperate, wounded urgency.
ramayan::7872.modern_relevance: You’ve asked the same question too many times and still have no answer. Frustration starts sounding like force when fear is underneath it.
ramayan::7872.insight: It shows how grief can harden into anger when longing meets silence.

ramayan::7873.verse_sanskrit: एवमुक्तस्तु रामेण पर्वतो मैथिलीं प्रति । शंसन्निव ततस्सीतां नादर्शयत राघवे । । 36432 । ।
ramayan::7873.verse_hindi: Thus addressed by Rama, the mountain echoed as if it was telling about Sita but did not show her to Rama.
ramayan::7873.english_translation: Thus addressed by Rama, the mountain echoed as if it was telling about Sita but did not show her to Rama.
ramayan::7873.translation_literal: एवम् (thus) / उक्तः (addressed) / तु (but) / रामेण (by Rama) / पर्वतः (the mountain) / मैथिलीं (about Maithili) / प्रति (toward) / शंसन् (telling) / इव (as if) / ततः (then) / सीताम् (Sita) / न (not) / अदर्शयत् (showed) / राघवे (to Rama)
ramayan::7873.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7873.essence: A hint of hope is not the same as seeing what you seek.
ramayan::7873.simple_meaning: The mountain seemed to hint at Sita's presence, but it did not reveal her to Rama.
ramayan::7873.simple_insight: Sometimes even a sign is not yet an answer.
ramayan::7873.detailed_meaning: Rama has reached the mountain and demanded news of Sita. The peak seems to answer, almost as if it knows her whereabouts, but it still withholds her from him. The search continues unresolved.
ramayan::7873.modern_relevance: You keep asking for one clear sign, but life gives you only a hint and then stays silent.
ramayan::7873.insight: It keeps the search moving by showing that partial clues are not the same as fulfillment.

ramayan::7874.verse_sanskrit: ततो दाशरथी राम उवाच च शिलोच्चयम् । मम बाणाग्निनिर्दग्धो भस्मीभूतो भविष्यसि । । 36433 । । असेव्यः सततं चैव निस्तृणद्रुमपल्लवः ।
ramayan::7874.verse_hindi: Rama, Dasarathas son said to the mountain, The fire of my arrows will reduce you to ashes.You will have no grass, no tree, no twig. You will be unfit to be served any more.
ramayan::7874.english_translation: Rama, Dasaratha's son, said to the mountain: "The fire of my arrows will reduce you to ashes. You will be left without grass, trees, or twigs, and no longer fit to be approached."
ramayan::7874.translation_literal: ततः (then) / दाशरथी (Dasaratha's son) / रामः (Rama) / उवाच (said) / च (and) / शिलोच्चयम् (to the mountain) / मम (my) / बाणाग्नि-निर्दग्धः (burned by the fire of arrows) / भस्मीभूतः (reduced to ashes) / भविष्यसि (you will become) / असेव्यः (not to be approached) / सततम् (always) / च (and) / एव (indeed) / निस्तृण-द्रुम-पल्लवः (without grass, trees, and leaves)
ramayan::7874.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7874.essence: Grief pushes him from plea into fury when silence continues.
ramayan::7874.simple_meaning: Rama threatens the mountain with destruction if it keeps hiding Sita. He says his arrows will burn it to ashes and strip it bare.
ramayan::7874.simple_insight: Anger can make even the impossible feel immediate.
ramayan::7874.detailed_meaning: Rama has already demanded that the mountain reveal Sita. When it stays silent, his grief turns fierce. He threatens to burn it down, showing how urgently he wants answers and how close despair is to rage.
ramayan::7874.modern_relevance: You keep refreshing your phone because someone important has gone silent. The longer the silence lasts, the more your mind turns sharp, urgent, and destructive.
ramayan::7874.insight: It shows how unanswered grief can harden into threat and force.

ramayan::7875.verse_sanskrit: इमां वा सरितं चाद्य शोषयिष्यामि लक्ष्मण । । 36434 । । यदि नाख्याति मे सीतामार्यां चन्द्रनिभाननाम् ।
ramayan::7875.verse_hindi: O Lakshmana if this river does not tell me about that noble Sita with countenance like the moon, I will drain it dry right now.
ramayan::7875.english_translation: O Lakshmana, if this river does not tell me about noble Sita, whose face is like the moon, I will drain it dry right now.
ramayan::7875.translation_literal: इमां (this) / वा (or) / सरितं (river) / च (and) / अद्य (today / right now) / शोषयिष्यामि (I will dry up) / लक्ष्मण (Lakshmana) / यदि (if) / न (not) / आख्याति (tells) / मे (to me) / सीताम् (Sita) / आर्याम् (noble) / चन्द्रनिभाननाम् (moon-like-faced)
ramayan::7875.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7875.essence: When love is threatened, even the world must answer.
ramayan::7875.simple_meaning: Rama says he will dry up the river if it does not reveal where Sita is. His grief has become fierce urgency.
ramayan::7875.simple_insight: Love can make searching feel absolute, not optional.
ramayan::7875.detailed_meaning: Rama has just been denied a sign of Sita by the mountain and is now speaking to the river beside him. In his anguish, he threatens even nature itself, showing how total his urgency has become.
ramayan::7875.modern_relevance: You are scrolling through missed calls, then checking the parking lot, then calling one more time because someone you love still hasn't answered. That desperate, narrowing focus is Rama's state here.
ramayan::7875.insight: It turns grief into relentless search, not passive waiting.

ramayan::7876.verse_sanskrit: एवं स रुषितो रामो दिधक्षन्निव चक्षुषा । । 36435 । । ददर्श भूमौ निष्क्रान्तं राक्षसस्य पदं महत् । त्रस्ताया रामकाङ्क्षिण्याः प्रधावन्त्या इतस्ततः । । 36436 । । राक्षसेनानुवृत्ताया मैथिल्याश्च पदान्यथ ।
ramayan::7876.verse_hindi: While Rama was angry with his eyes burning, he saw on the ground as he advanced large footprints of a demon and then the footprints of Maithili which signified as if chased by the demon, she was frightened and was running hither and thither, longing to see Rama.
ramayan::7876.english_translation: While Rama was furious, as if his eyes burned with fire, he saw on the ground the large footprints of a demon and the footprints of Maithili, who had been running here and there in fear, longing for Rama.
ramayan::7876.translation_literal: एवम् (thus) / सः (he) / रुषितः (angry) / रामः (Rama) / दिधक्षन् (wanting to burn) / इव (as if) / चक्षुषा (with eyes) / ददर्श (saw) / भूमौ (on the ground) / निष्क्रान्तम् (gone out / departed) / राक्षसस्य (of a demon) / पदम् (footprint) / महत् (great) / त्रस्तायाः (of the frightened one) / रामकाङ्क्षिण्याः (longing for Rama) / प्रधावन्त्याः (of her running) / इतस्ततः (hither and thither) / राक्षसेन (by the demon) / अनुवृत्तायाः (of the one followed) / मैथिल्याः (of Maithili) / च (and) / पदानि (footprints)
ramayan::7876.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7876.essence: Grief becomes sharper when the ground itself tells the story.
ramayan::7876.simple_meaning: Rama sees signs that Sita was chased and terrified. The footprints on the ground show her fear and the demon's pursuit.
ramayan::7876.simple_insight: Fear leaves traces, and love learns to read them.
ramayan::7876.detailed_meaning: Rama has reached the place where Sita vanished. Still burning with anger, he studies the ground and finds the footprints of a demon and of Sita running in terror. The discovery deepens the crisis, but it is only a clue, not the verse's full teaching.
ramayan::7876.modern_relevance: You arrive at the empty parking lot after the argument and notice the signs first: the dropped phone, the hurried steps, the silence. The mind starts reconstructing what happened before anyone speaks.
ramayan::7876.insight: It shifts attention from panic to close observation of evidence.

ramayan::7877.verse_sanskrit: स समीक्ष्य परिक्रान्तं सीताया राक्षसस्य च । । 36437 । । भग्नं धनुश्च तूणी च विकीर्णं बहुधा रथम् । सम्भ्रान्तहृदयो रामश्शशंस भ्रातरंप्रियम् । । 36438 । ।
ramayan::7877.verse_hindi: Bewildered to see the broken bow and quiver and many splinters of the chariot scattered all over, Rama said to his loving brother Lakshmana:
ramayan::7877.english_translation: Seeing Sita's trail, the broken bow and quiver, and the chariot shattered into pieces, Rama, his heart shaken, spoke to his dear brother Lakshmana.
ramayan::7877.translation_literal: स (he) / समीक्ष्य (having देखा) / परिक्रान्तं (traced around / examined) / सीतायाः (of Sita) / राक्षसस्य (of the demon) / च (and) / भग्नं (broken) / धनुः (bow) / च (and) / तूणी (quiver) / च (and) / विकीर्णं (scattered) / बहुधा (in many pieces) / रथम् (chariot) / सम्भ्रान्तहृदयः (with a bewildered heart) / रामः (Rama) / शशंस (spoke / told) / भ्रातरम् (to his brother) / प्रियम् (dear)
ramayan::7877.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7877.essence: The signs of loss arrive before the truth does.
ramayan::7877.simple_meaning: Rama sees signs of a violent struggle and realizes something terrible has happened to Sita.
ramayan::7877.simple_insight: Clues can strike harder than words when fear is already awake.
ramayan::7877.detailed_meaning: Rama has followed Sita's trail and now finds the broken remains of a fight: a shattered bow, a scattered quiver, and a ruined chariot. The evidence tells him that Ravana has taken her, and the sight shakes him before he even speaks to Lakshmana.
ramayan::7877.modern_relevance: You open the door and see the chair knocked over, the glass broken, the phone gone silent. Before anyone explains, your body already knows something is wrong.
ramayan::7877.insight: It shows how the mind reads physical evidence before the full story is known.

ramayan::7878.verse_sanskrit: पश्य लक्ष्मण वैदेह्याशशीर्णाः कनकबिन्दवः । भूषणानां हि सौमित्रे माल्यानि विविधानि च । । 36439 । ।
ramayan::7878.verse_hindi: O Saumitri  see the many broken bits of gold ornaments and garlands.
ramayan::7878.english_translation: Look, Lakshmana: the golden drops from Vaidehi's ornaments and the garlands have broken apart.
ramayan::7878.translation_literal: पश्य (look) / लक्ष्मण (Lakshmana) / वैदेह्याः (of Vaidehi) / शीर्णाः (broken) / कनकबिन्दवः (golden drops) / भूषणानाम् (of ornaments) / हि (indeed) / सौमित्रे (O Saumitri) / माल्यानि (garlands) / विविधानि (various) / च (and)
ramayan::7878.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7878.essence: Small traces can reveal a catastrophe before words do.
ramayan::7878.simple_meaning: Rama points out broken pieces of Sita's ornaments and scattered garlands on the ground, signs that something violent has happened.
ramayan::7878.simple_insight: Clues matter when grief is still forming. The mind can read loss before it can bear it.
ramayan::7878.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana are searching the forest after Sita's disappearance. Rama sees broken gold ornaments and torn garlands on the ground and calls Lakshmana's attention to them. The verse is a clue in the investigation, not the emotional conclusion.
ramayan::7878.modern_relevance: You notice a dropped earring, a torn strap, a phone left behind. Small signs can tell you something went wrong before anyone says a word.
ramayan::7878.insight: It trains the mind to read evidence carefully in a crisis instead of jumping to fantasy.

ramayan::7879.verse_sanskrit: तप्तबिन्दुनिकाशैश्च चित्रैः क्षतजबिन्दुभिः । आवृतं पश्य सौमित्रे सर्वतो धरणीतलम् । 36440 । ।
ramayan::7879.verse_hindi: See, O Lakshmana, the patches of blood looking like drops of shining gold spread all over the ground.
ramayan::7879.english_translation: See, O Lakshmana, the ground is covered everywhere with bright patches of blood, like drops of shining gold.
ramayan::7879.translation_literal: तप्तबिन्दुनिकाशैः (like shining drops) / च (and) / चित्रैः (variegated) / क्षतजबिन्दुभिः (with drops of blood) / आवृतम् (covered) / पश्य (see) / सौमित्रे (O Saumitri) / सर्वतः (everywhere) / धरणीतलम् (the ground)
ramayan::7879.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7879.essence: The ground itself becomes a clue to loss.
ramayan::7879.simple_meaning: Rama points to the blood-stained ground and tells Lakshmana that something violent has happened nearby.
ramayan::7879.simple_insight: A single sign can tell you something terrible has already happened.
ramayan::7879.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana are searching the broken battlefield after Sita's abduction. Rama notices the scattered ornaments, shattered chariot, and now the blood on the ground. He is reading the scene like evidence, trying to understand what happened to Sita.
ramayan::7879.modern_relevance: You walk into a room and see the overturned chair, the dropped phone, the sudden silence. Before anyone speaks, the signs already tell you something has gone wrong.
ramayan::7879.insight: It trains you to notice evidence before jumping to comfort.

ramayan::7880.verse_sanskrit: मन्ये लक्ष्मण वैदेही राक्षसैः कामरूपिभिः । भित्वाभित्वा विभक्ता वा भक्षिता वा भविष्यति । । 36441 । ।
ramayan::7880.verse_hindi: O Lakshmana, Vaidehi might have been cut into pieces, and eaten up by the demons who can assume any form at their free will.
ramayan::7880.english_translation: O Lakshmana, I think Vaidehi may have been cut apart or eaten by the demons who can change form at will.
ramayan::7880.translation_literal: मन्ये (I think) / लक्ष्मण (O Lakshmana) / वैदेही (Vaidehi) / राक्षसैः (by the demons) / कामरूपिभिः (who can assume any form) / भित्वा-भित्वा (having cut apart) / विभक्ता (divided) / वा (or) / भक्षिता (eaten) / वा (or) / भविष्यति (may have been)
ramayan::7880.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7880.essence: Fear makes the mind invent a tragedy before truth is known.
ramayan::7880.simple_meaning: Rama fears that Sita may have been torn apart or eaten by shape-shifting demons.
ramayan::7880.simple_insight: Grief often fills in the worst possible answer before there is proof.
ramayan::7880.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana stand in the forest, staring at broken ornaments, scattered flowers, and blood on the ground. Rama's mind races ahead of evidence, imagining the worst fate for Sita. This is not a teaching verse; it is the raw edge of panic.
ramayan::7880.modern_relevance: You find a dropped earring, a missed call, and an empty room. Your mind writes the worst story before facts arrive.
ramayan::7880.insight: It shows how fear turns clues into certainty and pushes the mind into catastrophe.

ramayan::7881.verse_sanskrit: तस्या निमित्तं वैदेह्या द्वयोर्विवदमानयोः । बभूव युद्धं सौमित्रे घोरं राक्षसयोरिह । । 36442 । ।
ramayan::7881.verse_hindi: O Lakshmana, two demons might have fought a dreadful duel at this place contesting with each other for the sake of Vaidehi.
ramayan::7881.english_translation: O Lakshmana, two demons might have fought a dreadful duel at this place contesting with each other for the sake of Vaidehi.
ramayan::7881.translation_literal: तस्या (for her) / निमित्तं (for the sake of) / वैदेह्या (of Vaidehi) / द्वयोः (of two) / विवदमानयोः (contending) / बभूव (there was) / युद्धं (battle) / सौमित्रे (O son of Sumitra) / घोरं (terrible) / राक्षसयोः (of two demons) / इह (here)
ramayan::7881.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7881.essence: The mind in panic writes the darkest explanation first.
ramayan::7881.simple_meaning: Rama thinks Sita may have been seized and fought over by two demons here, leaving signs of a violent struggle.
ramayan::7881.simple_insight: Fear makes every clue feel like a wound.
ramayan::7881.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana have reached a bloodstained spot in the forest after Sita's disappearance. Seeing the signs of struggle, Rama imagines a brutal fight between demons over her fate. The verse deepens the search, not the teaching.
ramayan::7881.modern_relevance: You find your friend's phone on the floor, cracked and silent, and your mind fills the gap with the worst story first.
ramayan::7881.insight: It shows how grief turns fragments into a full catastrophe before facts arrive.

ramayan::7882.verse_sanskrit: मुक्तामणिमयं चेदं तपनीयविभूषितम् । धरण्यां पतितं सौम्य कस्य भग्नं महद्धनुः । । 36443 । ।
ramayan::7882.verse_hindi: O handsome Lakshmana whose is this huge bow embedded with pearls and gems and adorned with gold fallen on the ground?
ramayan::7882.english_translation: O handsome Lakshmana, whose huge bow, inlaid with pearls and gems and adorned with gold, has fallen on the ground?
ramayan::7882.translation_literal: मुक्तामणिमयम् (made of pearls and gems) / च (and) / इदम् (this) / तपनीयविभूषितम् (adorned with gold) / धरण्याम् (on the ground) / पतितम् (fallen) / सौम्य (O gentle one) / कस्य (whose) / भग्नम् (broken) / महत् (great) / धनुः (bow)
ramayan::7882.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7882.essence: A broken bow reveals that violence happened here.
ramayan::7882.simple_meaning: A broken, jeweled bow lies on the ground, and the speaker asks whose it is.
ramayan::7882.simple_insight: The scene is pointing to a hidden clash, not a random object.
ramayan::7882.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana are tracking the signs left behind in the forest after Sita's abduction. They find a shattered, richly decorated bow on the ground and realize a powerful struggle has taken place here.
ramayan::7882.modern_relevance: You walk into a room after a fight and notice one broken object that changes everything. The clue is small, but the story behind it is huge.
ramayan::7882.insight: It trains you to read evidence carefully before jumping to conclusions.

ramayan::7883.verse_sanskrit: तरुणादित्यसङ्काशं वैडूर्यगुलिकाचितम् । विशीर्णं पतितं भूमौ कवचं कस्य काञ्चनम् । । 36444 । ।
ramayan::7883.verse_hindi: Whose is this shield of gold studded with Vaidurya, broken and strewn all over the ground, shining like the morning Sun?
ramayan::7883.english_translation: Whose is this shield of gold studded with Vaidurya, broken and strewn all over the ground, shining like the morning Sun?
ramayan::7883.translation_literal: तरुणादित्यसङ्काशम् (resembling the young sun) / वैडूर्यगुलिकाचितम् (covered with Vaidurya beads) / विशीर्णम् (broken apart) / पतितम् (fallen) / भूमौ (on the ground) / कवचम् (shield) / कस्य (whose) / काञ्चनम् (golden)
ramayan::7883.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7883.essence: A fallen warrior is first known by the broken things around him.
ramayan::7883.simple_meaning: A golden shield, decorated with gems, lies broken on the ground. The speaker is asking whose shield it is.
ramayan::7883.simple_insight: Sometimes the battlefield answers before the people do.
ramayan::7883.detailed_meaning: Lakshmana and the others are scanning the battlefield after the clash. Broken weapons and royal ornaments lie scattered in the dust. This verse is part of a chain of questions identifying the fallen warrior whose gear is now visible.
ramayan::7883.modern_relevance: You walk into a room after a fight has already ended. A cracked watch, a torn jacket, a dropped phone — the objects tell you something serious happened before anyone speaks.
ramayan::7883.insight: It shifts attention from the person to the evidence left behind.

ramayan::7884.verse_sanskrit: छत्रं शतशलाकं च दिव्यमाल्योपशोभितम् । भग्नदण्डमिदं कस्य भूमौ सम्यङ्निपातितम् । । 36445 । ।
ramayan::7884.verse_hindi: Whose parasol is this with a hundred spokes, festooned with wonderful flowers thrown down on the ground with broken staff ?
ramayan::7884.english_translation: Whose parasol is this with a hundred spokes, festooned with wonderful flowers, thrown down on the ground with its staff broken?
ramayan::7884.translation_literal: छत्रम् (parasol) / शतशलाकम् (with a hundred spokes) / च (and) / दिव्यमाल्योपशोभितम् (adorned with divine flowers) / भग्नदण्डम् (with broken staff) / इदम् (this) / कस्य (whose) / भूमौ (on the ground) / सम्यक् (fully) / निपातितम् (thrown down)
ramayan::7884.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7884.essence: A broken emblem reveals that someone powerful has already fallen.
ramayan::7884.simple_meaning: A royal parasol, once beautiful and intact, now lies broken on the ground. The speaker is asking whose fallen emblem it is.
ramayan::7884.simple_insight: Power leaves visible traces when a great warrior falls.
ramayan::7884.detailed_meaning: On the battlefield, Lakshmana and the others are examining the wreckage left behind after fierce combat. They see a shattered parasol, a sign of a fallen king or commander, and ask whose royal standard has been brought low.
ramayan::7884.modern_relevance: You can tell a lot from what is left on the floor after the argument, the meeting, or the crash. The symbols of control often break first.
ramayan::7884.insight: It trains you to read consequences through the fallen marks of status and defeat.

ramayan::7885.verse_sanskrit: काञ्चनोरश्छदा श्चेमे पिशाचवदनाः खराः । भीमरूपा महाकायाः कस्य वा निहता रणे । । 36446 । ।
ramayan::7885.verse_hindi: Whose are these donkeys, with golden chestcoverings, with the devils face, fierceful and huge and slain in the encounter ?
ramayan::7885.english_translation: Whose are these donkeys, with golden chest-coverings, with faces like devils, fierce and huge, slain in battle?
ramayan::7885.translation_literal: काञ्चनोरश्छदाः (with golden chest-coverings) / च (and) / इमे (these) / पिशाचवदनाः (devil-faced) / खराः (donkeys) / भीमरूपाः (terrible in form) / महाकायाः (huge-bodied) / कस्य (whose) / वा (indeed) / निहताः (slain) / रणे (in battle)
ramayan::7885.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7885.essence: Even the terrifying become only broken remains after battle.
ramayan::7885.simple_meaning: The speaker is pointing out fallen enemy donkeys, armored in gold and looking monstrous, and asking whose they were.
ramayan::7885.simple_insight: It captures the shock of seeing power reduced to wreckage.
ramayan::7885.detailed_meaning: After the battle, the scene is littered with ruined equipment and dead mounts. Someone surveys the field and asks whose huge, fearsome donkeys, covered in gold, have been killed in combat. The verse is part of a larger inventory of battlefield remnants.
ramayan::7885.modern_relevance: You walk past a wrecked car after the crash is over and notice the details only then: the polish, the damage, the sudden absence of life.
ramayan::7885.insight: It trains attention on the aftermath of violence, not the glory of it.

ramayan::7886.verse_sanskrit: दीप्तपावकसङ्काशो द्युतिमान्समरध्वजः । अपविद्धश्च भग्नश्च कस्य साङ्ग्रामिको रथः । । 36447 । ।
ramayan::7886.verse_hindi: Whose war chariot with a battle flag is this, shining like burning fire, turned upside down and broken?
ramayan::7886.english_translation: Whose war chariot with a battle flag is this, shining like burning fire, turned upside down and broken?
ramayan::7886.translation_literal: दीप्त-पावक-सङ्काशः (resembling blazing fire) / द्युतिमान् (radiant) / समर-ध्वजः (battle-flag) / अपविद्धः (thrown down) / च (and) / भग्नः (broken) / कस्य (whose) / साङ्ग्रामिकः (warlike) / रथः (chariot)
ramayan::7886.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7886.essence: A once-bright war chariot lies shattered on the ground.
ramayan::7886.simple_meaning: The speaker is pointing to a shattered war chariot and asking whose it was.
ramayan::7886.simple_insight: A battlefield can be read through its broken symbols before the full story is even told.
ramayan::7886.detailed_meaning: On the battlefield, the speaker sees a radiant chariot with its flag, now overturned and broken, among other ruined war gear. The verse is part of a sequence of identification questions, not a teaching in itself.
ramayan::7886.insight: It serves as a battlefield detail that advances the scene by identifying the aftermath of combat.

ramayan::7887.verse_sanskrit: रथाक्षमात्रा विशिखास्तपनीयविभूषणाः । कस्येमेऽभिहता बाणाः प्रकीर्णा घोरकर्मणः । । 36448 । ।
ramayan::7887.verse_hindi: Whose are these pointless arrows of the size of a chariot axle adorned with bright gold destroyed and scattered ? Who is he that has performed such terrible deeds?
ramayan::7887.english_translation: Whose are these arrows, as large as a chariot axle, adorned with bright gold, struck down and scattered? Who has done such terrible deeds?
ramayan::7887.translation_literal: रथाक्षमात्राः (as large as a chariot axle) / विशिखाः (arrows) / तपनीयविभूषणाः (adorned with bright gold) / कस्य (whose) / इमे (these) / अभिहताः (struck down) / बाणाः (arrows) / प्रकीर्णाः (scattered) / घोरकर्मणः (of the one who has done terrible deeds)
ramayan::7887.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7887.essence: The wreckage itself reveals the force behind it.
ramayan::7887.simple_meaning: The speaker points to a battlefield wreckage of shattered, gold-adorned arrows and asks who could have done such brutal work.
ramayan::7887.simple_insight: Violence leaves a visible trail, even when the fighter is unseen.
ramayan::7887.detailed_meaning: Lakshmana and the others are moving through the ruined battlefield, seeing broken chariots, slain horses, and scattered weapons. This verse is part of that grim survey: the speaker is identifying the scale of the fight by the wreckage left behind.
ramayan::7887.modern_relevance: You walk into a room after the argument is over: the chair is broken, messages are deleted, and nobody wants to say who started it.
ramayan::7887.insight: It trains attention on consequences first, not blame or story.

ramayan::7888.verse_sanskrit: शरावरौ शरैः पूर्णौ विध्वस्तौ पश्य लक्ष्मण । प्रतोदाभीशुहस्तो वै कस्यायं सारथिर्हतः । । 36449 । ।
ramayan::7888.verse_hindi: O Lakshmana  look at these two quivers filled with arrows and lying shattered.  The charioteer is holding a whip and reins in his hands and is lying dead. To whom do they belong?
ramayan::7888.english_translation: O Lakshmana, look at these two quivers filled with arrows and lying shattered. The charioteer, whip and reins in hand, lies dead. To whom do they belong?
ramayan::7888.translation_literal: शरावरौ (two quivers) / शरैः (with arrows) / पूर्णौ (filled) / विध्वस्तौ (shattered) / पश्य (look) / लक्ष्मण (Lakshmana) / प्रतोदाभीशुहस्तो (whip-and-reins-in-hand) / वै (indeed) / कस्य (whose) / अयम् (this) / सारथिः (charioteer) / हतः (killed)
ramayan::7888.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7888.essence: Battle leaves only damage, and the dead do not answer ownership.
ramayan::7888.simple_meaning: The verse points out a ruined war chariot, shattered quivers, and a dead charioteer, asking whose they are.
ramayan::7888.simple_insight: It shows how quickly battle strips power down to broken bodies and scattered weapons.
ramayan::7888.detailed_meaning: On the battlefield, the speaker draws Lakshmana's attention to the wreckage of a chariot: broken quivers, arrows everywhere, and the charioteer dead with whip and reins still in hand. The verse is part of a larger battlefield description, not a teaching on its own.
ramayan::7888.modern_relevance: You walk past the aftermath after a fight has already ended: a dropped phone, a torn bag, someone silent on the floor. The damage tells the story before anyone speaks.
ramayan::7888.insight: It trains you to read consequences directly, without romanticising conflict.

ramayan::7889.verse_sanskrit: कस्येमौ पुरुषव्याघ्र शयाते निहतौ युधि । चामरग्राहिणौ सौम्य सोष्णीषमणिकुण्डलौ । । 36450 । ।
ramayan::7889.verse_hindi: O best among men, O handsome Lakshmana see these carriers of fans with head dress and earrings studded with gems lying slain in the combat. Whose are they ?
ramayan::7889.english_translation: O best among men, O handsome Lakshmana, see these fan-bearers lying slain in battle, wearing headgear and gem-studded earrings. Whose are they?
ramayan::7889.translation_literal: कस्य (whose) / इमौ (these two) / पुरुषव्याघ्र (best among men) / शयाते (are lying) / निहतौ (slain) / युधि (in battle) / चामरग्राहिणौ (fan-bearers) / सौम्य (O handsome one) / सोष्णीषमणिकुण्डलौ (with headgear and gem-studded earrings)
ramayan::7889.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7889.essence: The dead attendants are clues to an unseen enemy.
ramayan::7889.simple_meaning: Rama points out two slain attendants in the battlefield and asks Lakshmana whose servants they were.
ramayan::7889.simple_insight: Some moments in conflict are only signs of a larger story unfolding around them.
ramayan::7889.detailed_meaning: On the battlefield, Rama and Lakshmana notice shattered chariots, broken weapons, and now two dead attendants with fans, headgear, and jeweled earrings. Rama is tracing the trail of an enemy through the wreckage, using these details to identify who has fallen nearby.
ramayan::7889.modern_relevance: You notice the small things after the damage is already done: a dropped badge, a torn sleeve, a broken phone. They tell you someone important was here.
ramayan::7889.insight: It trains attention to read battlefield clues before the full picture is revealed.

ramayan::7890.verse_sanskrit: पदवीपुरुषस्यैषा व्यक्तं कस्यापि रक्षसः । वैरं शतगुणं पश्य ममेदं जीवितान्तकम् । । 36451 । ।
ramayan::7890.verse_hindi: This indeed is the path the man or the demon has traversed. My enmity with him now has become hundredfold. This will end only with the extermination of his life.
ramayan::7890.english_translation: This indeed is the path the man or the demon has taken. My enmity with him has now become a hundredfold. It will end only with his death.
ramayan::7890.translation_literal: पदवी (path/track) / पुरुषस्य (of the man) / एषा (this) / व्यक्तम् (clearly) / कस्य अपि (of someone) / रक्षसः (of the demon) / वैरम् (enmity) / शतगुणम् (hundredfold) / पश्य (see) / मम (my) / इदम् (this) / जीवितान्तकम् (ending life)
ramayan::7890.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::7890.essence: Hatred turns evidence into a demand for destruction.
ramayan::7890.simple_meaning: The track shows that some man or demon passed here, and the speaker’s hatred has now become total. He believes only the enemy’s death can end it.
ramayan::7890.simple_insight: Rage narrows the mind until only destruction seems possible.
ramayan::7890.detailed_meaning: In the forest after the battle signs are found, the speaker studies broken chariots, fallen attendants, and the trail left behind. Seeing the enemy’s path, he turns grief into fury and concludes that nothing short of death will settle the matter.
ramayan::7890.modern_relevance: You see a shattered phone, a missed call, and one clue that sends your mind spiraling. Suddenly the whole story becomes revenge instead of understanding.
ramayan::7890.insight: It shows how quickly pain can harden into absolute hostility.

ramayan::7891.verse_sanskrit: सुघोरहृदयैस्सौम्य राक्षसैः कामरूपिभिः । हृता मृता वा सीता सा भक्षिता वा तपस्विनी । । 36452 । । नधर्मस्त्रायते सीतां ह्रियमाणां महावने ।
ramayan::7891.verse_hindi: O handsome one, those demons can change their form at will and are of dreadful nature. Have they abducted or devoured or killed her in this great forest. Even her righteousness could not protect the helpless Sita.
ramayan::7891.english_translation: O handsome one, those demons can change their form at will and are of dreadful nature. Have they abducted or devoured or killed her in this great forest? Even her righteousness could not protect the helpless Sita.
ramayan::7891.translation_literal: सुघोरहृदयैः (with dreadful hearts) / सौम्य (O gentle one) / राक्षसैः (by demons) / कामरूपिभिः (who can change form at will) / हृता (abducted) / मृता (dead) / वा (or) / सीता (Sita) / सा (she) / भक्षिता (devoured) / वा (or) / तपस्विनी (the ascetic woman) / न (not) / धर्मः (righteousness) / त्रायते (protects) / सीताम् (Sita) / ह्रियमाणाम् (while being carried off) / महावने (in the great forest)
ramayan::7891.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7891.essence: Goodness does not always prevent loss.
ramayan::7891.simple_meaning: Rama fears that Sita has been abducted, killed, or eaten by shape-shifting demons in the forest. He says even her righteousness could not protect her.
ramayan::7891.simple_insight: Sometimes doing everything right still does not stop tragedy.
ramayan::7891.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana are searching the forest after finding signs of violence. Seeing the trail, Rama imagines the worst: Sita may have been seized, killed, or eaten by demons. His grief turns into the bitter recognition that virtue does not always prevent suffering.
ramayan::7891.modern_relevance: You did everything carefully, and harm still found its way in. A hard lesson lands when control fails and goodness does not guarantee safety.
ramayan::7891.insight: It shifts the mind from moral certainty to humility before suffering.

ramayan::7892.verse_sanskrit: भक्षितायां हि वैदेह्यां हृतायामपि लक्ष्मण । । 36453 । । के हि लोके प्रियं कर्तुं शक्तास्सौम्य ममेश्वराः ।
ramayan::7892.verse_hindi: If Sita has been devoured or kidnapped, none in this world or even gods could do anything to make me happy, O handsome Lakshmana
