ramayan::7937.modern_relevance: You get a brutal email, then sit in the car for ten minutes before going inside. The facts are bad, but you do not have to let panic write the whole story.
ramayan::7937.insight: It shifts you from emotional collapse to clear observation before you decide what to do.

ramayan::7938.verse_sanskrit: तत्त्वतो हि नरश्रेष्ठ बुद्ध्या समनुचिन्तय । बुध्द्या युक्ता महाप्राज्ञा विजानन्ति शुभाशुभे । । 36615 । ।
ramayan::7938.verse_hindi: O best among men  judge the facts rightly with your intellect. The wise apply their minds and know what is right and what is wrong.
ramayan::7938.english_translation: O best among men, judge the facts rightly with your intellect. The wise apply their minds and know what is right and what is wrong.
ramayan::7938.translation_literal: तत्त्वतः (in truth) / हि (indeed) / नरश्रेष्ठ (O best among men) / बुद्ध्या (with the intellect) / समनुचिन्तय (reflect thoroughly) / बुद्ध्या (with the intellect) / युक्ताः (endowed) / महाप्राज्ञाः (the greatly wise) / विजानन्ति (know) / शुभाशुभे (the good and the bad)
ramayan::7938.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7938.essence: Right action begins with seeing the situation clearly.
ramayan::7938.simple_meaning: Rama is told to think carefully and judge reality with clear understanding. Wise people use their intellect to tell right from wrong.
ramayan::7938.simple_insight: Clarity can be stronger than emotion when you need to choose well.
ramayan::7938.detailed_meaning: Rama is being urged to stop being swept away by grief and look at the situation with clear judgment. The speaker says that truly wise people use discernment to see what is good and what is harmful, even in painful circumstances.
ramayan::7938.modern_relevance: You are staring at a message that could change everything, and your first reaction wants to run wild. This verse asks you to slow down, think cleanly, and let discernment speak before panic does.
ramayan::7938.insight: It shifts decision-making from emotional reaction to careful discrimination.

ramayan::7939.verse_sanskrit: अदृष्टगुणदोषाणामध्रुवाणां तु कर्मणाम् । नान्तरेण क्रियां तेषां फलमिष्टं प्रवर्तते । । 36616 । ।
ramayan::7939.verse_hindi: Good results are not expected from the actions of persons who cannot distinguish between their virtues and vices, from those who are unstable in their deeds.
ramayan::7939.english_translation: Good results do not arise from actions that are unstable and whose virtues and faults are not seen clearly, unless those actions are guided by wise effort.
ramayan::7939.translation_literal: अदृष्ट (not seen) / गुण-दोषाणाम् (of virtues and faults) / अध्रुवाणाम् (unstable) / तु (but) / कर्मणाम् (of actions) / न (not) / अन्तरेण (without) / क्रियाम् (right effort / action) / तेषाम् (of them) / फलम् (fruit, result) / इष्टम् (desired) / प्रवर्तते (arises, proceeds)
ramayan::7939.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::7939.essence: Unclear action rarely produces the result you wanted.
ramayan::7939.simple_meaning: Actions done without clear judgment, steadiness, and discernment do not lead to the desired result.
ramayan::7939.simple_insight: Confusion in action usually returns confusion. Clear seeing is what makes effort effective.
ramayan::7939.detailed_meaning: Rama is being advised in the middle of a hard moral argument. The speaker says that when a person cannot clearly see the good and bad in a situation, and acts without steadiness, the result will not be what is desired. It is a warning about confused action.
ramayan::7939.modern_relevance: You send the message while angry, then spend the next hour cleaning up the damage. The problem was never effort — it was acting before you could see clearly.
ramayan::7939.insight: It shifts you from impulsive doing to discerning action, where judgment comes before movement.

ramayan::7940.verse_sanskrit: त्वमेव हि पुरा राम मामेवं बहुशोऽन्वशाः । अनुशिष्याद्धि को नु त्वामपि साक्षाद्बृहस्पतिः । । 36617 । ।
ramayan::7940.verse_hindi: O Rama you yourself in the past have instructed me many times that way. Who can be your adviser in this matter ? You are indeed like Brihaspati.
ramayan::7940.english_translation: O Rama, you yourself have instructed me in this way many times before. Who could advise you in this matter, even if it were Brihaspati himself?
ramayan::7940.translation_literal: त्वमेव (you yourself) / हि (indeed) / पुरा (before, in the past) / राम (Rama) / माम् (me) / एवम् (thus) / बहुशः (many times) / अन्वशाः (you instructed) / अनुशिष्यात् (could advise, instruct) / हि (indeed) / कः (who) / नु (indeed) / त्वाम् (you) / अपि (even) / साक्षात् (directly) / बृहस्पतिः (Brihaspati)
ramayan::7940.speaker: Lakshmana
ramayan::7940.essence: True clarity needs no outside correction.
ramayan::7940.simple_meaning: Lakshmana reminds Rama that Rama has already taught him this wisdom many times, and that no adviser can really instruct Rama on such matters.
ramayan::7940.simple_insight: Sometimes the person you want to advise already sees more clearly than everyone else.
ramayan::7940.detailed_meaning: In the forest exile, Rama is grieving and thinking through what to do next. Lakshmana answers with respect and urgency: Rama has taught this wisdom before, and no one — not even Brihaspati — can outmatch his discernment.
ramayan::7940.modern_relevance: You are trying to explain a hard truth to someone who has already lived it better than you have. Sometimes the most honest response is not advice, but recognition.
ramayan::7940.insight: It shifts the mind from trying to instruct the wise to trusting their own discernment.

ramayan::7941.verse_sanskrit: बुद्धिश्च ते महाप्राज्ञ देवैरपि दुरन्वया । शोकेनाभिप्रसुप्तं ते ज्ञानं सम्बोधयाम्यहम् । । 36618 । ।
ramayan::7941.verse_hindi: Even gods cannot fathom your intellect. I am only trying to rouse your wisdom your sorrow has sent to sleep.
ramayan::7941.english_translation: Even the gods cannot fathom your intellect. I am only trying to rouse your wisdom, which sorrow has put to sleep.
ramayan::7941.translation_literal: बुद्धिः (intellect) / च (and) / ते (your) / महाप्राज्ञ (O very wise one) / देवैः (by the gods) / अपि (even) / दुरन्वया (hard to follow) / शोकेन (by sorrow) / अभिप्रसुप्तम् (fallen asleep) / ते (your) / ज्ञानम् (wisdom) / सम्बोधयामि (I am rousing) / अहम् (I)
ramayan::7941.speaker: Vibhishana
ramayan::7941.essence: Sorrow can put wisdom to sleep, but it cannot destroy it.
ramayan::7941.simple_meaning: Vibhishana tells Rama that his intelligence is beyond ordinary understanding, and that he is only trying to awaken Rama's buried judgment, which grief has dulled.
ramayan::7941.simple_insight: Grief can cloud your clearest thinking, but it does not destroy it.
ramayan::7941.detailed_meaning: In Lanka, Vibhishana is speaking to Rama at a moment of crisis. Rama's sorrow has slowed his judgment, and Vibhishana gently reminds him that his discernment is still intact. The next step is to restore clear action.
ramayan::7941.modern_relevance: You’ve been staring at the same message after bad news, knowing you’re smarter than this fog. Someone who cares about you may not need to fix you — only wake up the part of you that still sees clearly.
ramayan::7941.insight: It shifts you from identifying with grief to trusting that clear judgment can return.

ramayan::7942.verse_sanskrit: दिव्यं च मानुषं च त्वमात्मनश्च पराक्रमम् । इक्ष्वाकुवृषभावेक्ष्य यतस्व द्विषतां वधे । । 36619 । ।
ramayan::7942.verse_hindi: O bull among the Ikshvakus, weigh your divine and human prowess before you try to kill your enemies.
ramayan::7942.english_translation: O bull among the Ikshvakus, weigh your divine and human prowess before you try to kill your enemies.
ramayan::7942.translation_literal: दिव्यम् (divine) / च (and) / मानुषम् (human) / च (and) / त्वम् (you) / आत्मनः (of your own) / पराक्रमम् (prowess) / इक्ष्वाकुवृषभ (bull among the Ikshvakus) / अवेक्ष्य (having considered) / यतस्व (exert yourself) / द्विषताम् (of enemies) / वधे (in killing)
ramayan::7942.speaker: Lakshmana
ramayan::7942.essence: Power without clear seeing turns into waste.
ramayan::7942.simple_meaning: Before fighting, first understand the full range of your own power. Clear judgment should come before action.
ramayan::7942.simple_insight: You act better when you stop and assess what you truly have.
ramayan::7942.detailed_meaning: Lakshmana is trying to steady Rama, who is overwhelmed by grief and ready to lash out. He reminds Rama to judge both his human and extraordinary strength before rushing into revenge. The verse is part of a larger plea for clear-minded action.
ramayan::7942.modern_relevance: You are furious after a harsh message and want to fire back immediately. This verse asks you to pause, assess your real leverage, and choose the response that actually works.
ramayan::7942.insight: It shifts you from reactive anger to clear assessment before confrontation.

ramayan::7943.verse_sanskrit: किं तेन सर्वनाशेन कृतेन पुरुषर्षभ । तमेव त्वं रिपुं पापं विज्ञायोद्धर्तुमर्हसि । । 36620 । ।
ramayan::7943.verse_hindi: O best among men  where is the good in the destruction of all? Know your sinful enemy before you uproot him.
ramayan::7943.english_translation: O best among men, what good is there in total destruction? Know your wicked enemy first, then strike him down.
ramayan::7943.translation_literal: किं (what) / तेन (by that) / सर्वनाशेन (with total destruction) / कृतेन (done) / पुरुषर्षभ (O best among men) / तम् (that) / एव (indeed) / त्वम् (you) / रिपुम् (enemy) / पापम् (wicked) / विज्ञाय (having known) / उद्धर्तुम् (to uproot) / अर्हसि (you should)
ramayan::7943.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::7943.essence: Destruction without understanding only multiplies harm.
ramayan::7943.simple_meaning: Blind destruction is pointless. First understand the enemy clearly, then act against them.
ramayan::7943.simple_insight: Clear seeing protects you from turning force into waste.
ramayan::7943.detailed_meaning: Lakshmana is urging Rama not to let rage or grief turn into indiscriminate violence. The real task is to understand Ravana clearly and then remove only the source of harm, not everything around it.
ramayan::7943.modern_relevance: You want to fire off a furious text and wipe someone out in one reply. But once the damage spreads, you cannot take it back. First see who or what is actually causing the harm.
ramayan::7943.insight: It shifts you from reactive anger to precise judgment.

ramayan::7944.verse_sanskrit: पूर्वजोऽप्युक्तमात्रस्तु लक्ष्मणेन सुभाषितम् । सारग्राही महासारं प्रतिजग्राह राघवः । । 3671 । ।
ramayan::7944.verse_hindi: Even though Rama was elder, he could grasp the quintessence of the wise counsel only after Lakshmana had said it.
ramayan::7944.english_translation: Even though Rama was elder, he could grasp the quintessence of the wise counsel only after Lakshmana had said it.
ramayan::7944.translation_literal: पूर्वजः (elder) / अपि (even) / उक्तमात्रः (having been spoken) / तु (but) / लक्ष्मणेन (by Lakshmana) / सुभाषितम् (well-spoken counsel) / सारग्राही (grasping the essence) / महासारम् (the great essence) / प्रतिजग्राह (accepted, received) / राघवः (Rama)
ramayan::7944.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7944.essence: Age does not matter when clear counsel is finally heard.
ramayan::7944.simple_meaning: Rama, though older, accepted Lakshmana’s wise words and understood their deepest point.
ramayan::7944.simple_insight: Even wisdom can arrive through someone younger when pride is not in the way.
ramayan::7944.detailed_meaning: Lakshmana has just offered sharp counsel, and Rama is in the middle of weighing it. The verse shows that rank does not block understanding: Rama, though the elder, receives the best part of Lakshmana’s advice before answering with controlled anger.
ramayan::7944.modern_relevance: A younger teammate says the thing everyone older and louder missed. You pause, hear it fully, and let the right idea win over your ego.
ramayan::7944.insight: It shifts you from defending status to receiving truth wherever it appears.

ramayan::7945.verse_sanskrit: सन्निगृह्य महाबाहुः प्रवृत्तं कोपमात्मनः । अवष्टभ्य धनुश्चित्रं रामो लक्ष्मणमब्रवीत् । । 3672 । ।
ramayan::7945.verse_hindi: Restraining his anger, the longarmed Rama leaned over  his wonderful bow and spoke to Lakshmana:
ramayan::7945.english_translation: Restraining his anger, the long-armed Rama leaned on his splendid bow and spoke to Lakshmana:
ramayan::7945.translation_literal: सन्निगृह्य (having restrained) / महाबाहुः (the long-armed one) / प्रवृत्तं (arisen) / कोपम् (anger) / आत्मनः (of himself) / अवष्टभ्य (leaning on) / धनुः (bow) / चित्रम् (splendid) / रामः (Rama) / लक्ष्मणम् (to Lakshmana) / अब्रवीत् (spoke)
ramayan::7945.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7945.essence: He masters his anger before he speaks.
ramayan::7945.simple_meaning: Rama holds back his anger, steadies himself on his bow, and turns to Lakshmana to speak.
ramayan::7945.simple_insight: Even in grief, he does not let anger take over the moment.
ramayan::7945.detailed_meaning: After Lakshmana’s counsel, Rama gathers himself instead of erupting. He grips his bow, controls the surge of anger, and turns to his brother. The scene is still part of the search for Sita, so this line mainly shows his restraint before action.
ramayan::7945.modern_relevance: Your chest is tight, your jaw is set, and you still choose not to lash out. That pause can save the next hour.
ramayan::7945.insight: It shows emotional restraint before speech, turning raw anger into deliberate response.

ramayan::7946.verse_sanskrit: किं करिष्यावहे वत्स क्व वा गच्छाव लक्ष्मण । केनोपायेन गच्छेयं सीतामिति विचिन्तय । । 3673 । ।
ramayan::7946.verse_hindi: O dear Lakshmana, what shall we do? Where do we go ? Think of some means by which we can reach Sita.
ramayan::7946.english_translation: O dear Lakshmana, what shall we do? Where do we go? Think of some means by which we can reach Sita.
ramayan::7946.translation_literal: किम् (what) / करिष्यावहे (shall we do, we two) / वत्स (dear son) / क्व (where) / वा (or) / गच्छाव (shall we go, we two) / लक्ष्मण (Lakshmana) / केन (by what) / उपायेन (means) / गच्छेयम् (I may go / may reach) / सीताम् (to Sita) / इति (thus) / विचिन्तय (think over)
ramayan::7946.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7946.essence: Grief can make even a great man ask, 'How do I begin again?'
ramayan::7946.simple_meaning: Rama, shaken by grief, asks Lakshmana what they should do next and how they can find Sita.
ramayan::7946.simple_insight: Even the strongest person can pause and ask for help when love is at stake.
ramayan::7946.detailed_meaning: Rama has just restrained his anger and turned to Lakshmana in the forest. Sita is missing, and the search has become urgent. Instead of acting blindly, Rama asks for a way forward, showing grief, humility, and helplessness in one breath.
ramayan::7946.modern_relevance: You lose your phone, your plans collapse, and the one person you care about most is unreachable. In that moment, panic can narrow your mind; asking for a clear next step can open it again.
ramayan::7946.insight: It shifts the mind from emotional flooding to practical searching.

ramayan::7947.verse_sanskrit: तं तथा परितापार्तं लक्ष्मणो राममब्रवीत् । इदमेव जनस्थानं त्वमन्वेषितुमर्हसि । । 3674 । । राक्षसैर्बहुभिः कीर्णं नानाद्रुमलतायुतम् ।
ramayan::7947.verse_hindi: Lakshmana said to Rama, afflicted with grief, It is proper for you to (first) search in this Janasthana, covered with different kinds of trees and creepers, and teeming with demons.
ramayan::7947.english_translation: Lakshmana said to Rama, afflicted with grief, “You should search here in Janasthana first, a place crowded with many demons and covered with varied trees and creepers.”
ramayan::7947.translation_literal: तम् (to him) / तथा (thus) / परितापार्तम् (stricken with grief) / लक्ष्मणः (Lakshmana) / रामम् (to Rama) / अब्रवीत् (said) / इदम् एव (this itself) / जनस्थानम् (Janasthana) / त्वम् (you) / अन्वेषितुम् (to search) / अर्हसि (are fit / should) / राक्षसैः (by demons) / बहुभिः (many) / कीर्णम् (filled) / नाना-द्रुम-लतायुतम् (endowed with many trees and creepers)
ramayan::7947.speaker: Lakshmana
ramayan::7947.essence: Grief narrows the world; Lakshmana turns it back into a search.
ramayan::7947.simple_meaning: Lakshmana tells grief-stricken Rama to begin searching for Sita in Janasthana, a forest area full of demons, trees, and creepers.
ramayan::7947.simple_insight: Even in panic, the next step matters more than spiraling.
ramayan::7947.detailed_meaning: Rama has just stopped, overwhelmed by grief and urgency, asking Lakshmana where to go and how to find Sita. Lakshmana answers by naming the nearest dangerous region, Janasthana, and urging a practical search there first.
ramayan::7947.modern_relevance: You lose track of your phone in a crowded station, and your mind starts racing. Lakshmana’s answer is the antidote: stop widening the panic and search the nearest likely place first.
ramayan::7947.insight: It shifts the mind from helpless grief to immediate, focused searching.

ramayan::7948.verse_sanskrit: सन्तीह गिरिदुर्गाणि निर्दराः कन्दराणि च । । 3675 । । गुहाश्च विविधा घोरा नानामृगगणाकुलाः । आवासाः किन्नराणां च गन्धर्वभवनानि च । । 3676 । ।
ramayan::7948.verse_hindi: Here are difficult mountains, caves, valleys, dreadful caves full of different animals, dwellingplaces of kinneras and mansions of gandharvas.
ramayan::7948.english_translation: Here are difficult mountains, caves, valleys, dreadful caverns full of different animals, dwelling places of kinnaras, and mansions of gandharvas.
ramayan::7948.translation_literal: सन्ति (there are) / इह (here) / गिरिदुर्गाणि (mountain-forts, difficult mountains) / निर्दराः (without ravines, sheer) / कन्दराणि (caves, hollows) / च (and) / गुहाः (caves) / विविधाः (various) / घोराः (terrible) / नानामृगगणाकुलाः (crowded with many kinds of animals) / आवासाः (dwelling places) / किन्नराणाम् (of kinnaras) / च (and) / गन्धर्वभवनानि (mansions of gandharvas) / च (and)
ramayan::7948.speaker: Lakshmana
ramayan::7948.essence: Search widely when grief makes the world feel narrow.
ramayan::7948.simple_meaning: Lakshmana is pointing out the kinds of places where Sita might be hiding: mountains, caves, valleys, forests, and even the homes of other beings.
ramayan::7948.simple_insight: When someone is missing, your mind starts scanning every hidden place at once.
ramayan::7948.detailed_meaning: Rama is overwhelmed with grief and asks where to search for Sita. Lakshmana answers by listing the rugged, remote places around Janasthana — mountains, caves, valleys, and strange dwellings — to widen the search and steady Rama into action.
ramayan::7948.modern_relevance: You lose your keys, then your phone, then your calm. Suddenly every corner of the house looks possible, and you need someone beside you to think clearly.
ramayan::7948.insight: It shifts the mind from panic to practical searching by expanding the map of possible places.

ramayan::7949.verse_sanskrit: तानि युक्तो मया सार्धं त्वमन्वेषितुमर्हसि । त्वद्विधा बुद्धिसम्पन्ना महात्मानो नरर्षभ । । 3677 । । आपत्सु न प्रकम्पन्ते वायुवेगैरिवाचलाः ।
ramayan::7949.verse_hindi: Accompanied by me you should search for her in those spots. Great people endowed with wisdom do not destabilise in difficulties just as mountains are not shaken by the speed of the wind.
ramayan::7949.english_translation: Accompanied by me, you should search for her in those places. Great people endowed with wisdom do not waver in difficulties, just as mountains are not shaken by the force of the wind.
ramayan::7949.translation_literal: तानि (those places) / युक्तः (joined, accompanied) / मया (by me) / सार्धम् (together with) / त्वम् (you) / अन्वेषितुम् (to search) / अर्हसि (you ought) / त्वद्विधाः (those like you) / बुद्धिसम्पन्नाः (endowed with wisdom) / महात्मानः (great-souled, noble) / नरर्षभ (bull among men) / आपत्सु (in difficulties) / न (not) / प्रकम्पन्ते (waver) / वायुवेगैः (by the force of wind) / इव (like) / अचलाः (mountains)
ramayan::7949.speaker: Lakshmana
ramayan::7949.essence: Wisdom keeps you upright when hardship tries to shake you.
ramayan::7949.simple_meaning: Lakshmana urges Rama to search together and says wise people do not lose their steadiness in hardship.
ramayan::7949.simple_insight: Hard moments do not have to scatter you. Strength can look like staying steady and continuing the search.
ramayan::7949.detailed_meaning: Rama is grieving in the forest after Sita's disappearance, and Lakshmana answers his distress with resolve. He asks Rama to search the places together with him and reminds him that noble minds do not collapse under pressure.
ramayan::7949.modern_relevance: You are standing in a hospital corridor after bad news, trying to think clearly while your chest tightens. This is the moment to stay upright, keep moving, and let steadiness do its work.
ramayan::7949.insight: It shifts you from panic to composed action under pressure.

ramayan::7950.verse_sanskrit: इत्युक्तस्तद्वनं सर्वं विचचार सलक्ष्मणः । । 3678 । । क्रुद्धो रामश्शरं घोरं सन्धाय धनुषि क्षुरम् ।
ramayan::7950.verse_hindi: Thus advised, the angry Rama fixed a sharp arrow to his bow and roamed in the forest accompanied by Lakshmana.
ramayan::7950.english_translation: Thus advised, the angry Rama fixed a sharp arrow to his bow and roamed in the forest accompanied by Lakshmana.
ramayan::7950.translation_literal: इत्युक्तः (thus spoken to) / तद्वनं (that forest) / सर्वं (all) / विचचार (roamed) / सलक्ष्मणः (with Lakshmana) / क्रुद्धः (angry) / रामः (Rama) / शरं (arrow) / घोरं (terrible) / सन्धाय (having fitted) / धनुषि (on the bow) / क्षुरम् (sharp)
ramayan::7950.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7950.essence: Anger becomes motion when love is in danger.
ramayan::7950.simple_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana search the forest after the advice they received. Rama is angry and arms himself with a sharp arrow as they continue looking for Sita.
ramayan::7950.simple_insight: Grief can harden into action when love is threatened.
ramayan::7950.detailed_meaning: Rama has just been told to search the dangerous forest with Lakshmana. He responds not with speech but with movement, drawing a sharp arrow and roaming the woods in anger. This verse is the tense turn from instruction to pursuit, just before Jatayu appears.
ramayan::7950.modern_relevance: You get a message that something is wrong, and your whole body changes before your mind catches up. You stop scrolling, grab your keys, and go looking for answers.
ramayan::7950.insight: It shifts the mind from stunned feeling to immediate search and response.

ramayan::7951.verse_sanskrit: ततः पर्वतकूटाभं महाभागं द्विजोत्तमम् । । 3679 । । ददर्श पतितं भूमौ क्षतजार्द्रं जटायुषम् ।
ramayan::7951.verse_hindi: Then he saw the great Jatayu, a wonderful bird, looking like a mountain top, drenched in blood and fallen on the ground.
ramayan::7951.english_translation: Then he saw the great Jatayu, a wonderful bird, looking like a mountain peak, drenched in blood and fallen on the ground.
ramayan::7951.translation_literal: ततः (then) / पर्वतकूटाभम् (resembling a mountain peak) / महाभागम् (great-souled, noble) / द्विजोत्तमम् (best among the twice-born) / ददर्श (he saw) / पतितम् (fallen) / भूमौ (on the ground) / क्षतजार्द्रम् (wet with blood) / जटायुषम् (Jatayu)
ramayan::7951.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7951.essence: The search ends in a wounded witness.
ramayan::7951.simple_meaning: Rama comes upon Jatayu lying on the ground, wounded and covered in blood.
ramayan::7951.simple_insight: A search for hope turns suddenly into a sight of ruin.
ramayan::7951.detailed_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana are searching the forest after Sita's abduction. In the silence, Rama sees Jatayu, the noble bird, collapsed and bloodied on the ground. The sight is a grim turning point before he learns what happened to Sita.
ramayan::7951.modern_relevance: You follow a trail with rising hope, and then one detail tells you everything has gone wrong.
ramayan::7951.insight: It shifts the scene from searching to grieving, before the truth is even spoken.

ramayan::7952.verse_sanskrit: तं दृष्ट्वा गिरिशृङ्गाभं रामो लक्ष्मणमब्रवीत् । । 36710 । । अनेन सीता वैदेही भक्षिता नात्र संशयः ।
ramayan::7952.verse_hindi: On seeing Jatayu looking like the peak of a mountain, Rama said to Lakshmana, There is no doubt that this bird has devoured Vaidehi.
ramayan::7952.english_translation: On seeing Jatayu looking like the peak of a mountain, Rama said to Lakshmana, “There is no doubt that this bird has devoured Vaidehi.”
ramayan::7952.translation_literal: तं (him) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / गिरिशृङ्गाभं (resembling a mountain peak) / रामः (Rama) / लक्ष्मणम् (to Lakshmana) / अब्रवीत् (said) / अनेन (by this) / सीता (Sita) / वैदेही (daughter of Videha) / भक्षिता (devoured) / न (not) / अत्र (here) / संशयः (doubt)
ramayan::7952.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7952.essence: Shock can make the mind mistake appearance for fact.
ramayan::7952.simple_meaning: Rama looks at the bloodied Jatayu and wrongly assumes Sita has been eaten. He speaks in grief and shock, not with certainty.
ramayan::7952.simple_insight: Grief can turn a first glance into a false certainty.
ramayan::7952.detailed_meaning: In the forest, Rama and Lakshmana come upon the fallen Jatayu, huge and bloodied like a mountain peak. Rama, shaken by the search for Sita, instantly believes the bird must have devoured her. The verse captures his panic before the truth is known.
ramayan::7952.modern_relevance: You spot a shattered phone screen and jump to the worst conclusion before checking what really happened.
ramayan::7952.insight: It shows how fear can rush ahead of evidence and distort judgment.

ramayan::7953.verse_sanskrit: गृध्ररूपमिदं रक्षो व्यक्तं भवति कानने । । 36711 । । भक्षयित्वा विशालाक्षीमास्ते सीतां यथासुखम् । एनं वधिष्ये दीप्तास्यैर्घोरैर्बाणैरजिह्मगैः । । 36712 । ।
ramayan::7953.verse_hindi: This demon in the guise of a vulture has evidently eaten away the largeeyed Sita and is happily relaxing in the forest. With my terrific arrows with burning tips that can go straight I will kill him.
ramayan::7953.english_translation: This demon in the guise of a vulture has evidently eaten away the large-eyed Sita and is happily relaxing in the forest. With my terrific arrows with burning tips that can go straight I will kill him.
ramayan::7953.translation_literal: गृध्र-रूपम् (in vulture-form) / इदम् (this) / रक्षः (demon) / व्यक्तम् (clearly) / भवति (is) / कानने (in the forest) / भक्षयित्वा (having eaten) / विशालाक्षीम् (the large-eyed one) / आस्ते (is sitting) / सीताम् (Sita) / यथासुखम् (at ease) / एनम् (him) / वधिष्ये (I will kill) / दीप्त-आस्यैः (with flaming-tipped) / घोरैः (terrible) / बाणैः (arrows) / अजिह्मगैः (straight-going)
ramayan::7953.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7953.essence: Grief makes Rama mistake a wounded ally for Sita’s killer.
ramayan::7953.simple_meaning: Rama believes the vulture-like figure has eaten Sita, so he prepares to kill it with deadly arrows.
ramayan::7953.simple_insight: Grief can turn instantly into fury when you think someone you love has been taken.
ramayan::7953.detailed_meaning: Rama has found Jatayu fallen and bleeding in the forest. Seeing the bird in ruin, he assumes the worst about Sita’s fate and, in raw anguish, prepares to strike. This is a moment of misjudged grief before the truth is known.
ramayan::7953.modern_relevance: You see someone you trust collapsed and your mind fills the blank with the worst story. Before facts arrive, fear can already be reaching for blame.
ramayan::7953.insight: It shows how quickly pain can harden into retaliation when understanding is absent.

ramayan::7954.verse_sanskrit: इत्युक्त्वाभ्यपतद्गृध्रं सन्धाय धनुषि क्षुरम् । क्रुद्धो रामस्समुद्रान्तां कम्पयन्निव मेदिनीम् । । 36713 । ।
ramayan::7954.verse_hindi: Having siad so, Rama took his bow, fixed the sharp arrow, and aimed at the vulture. The seabound earth trembled.
ramayan::7954.english_translation: Having said so, Rama took his bow, fixed the sharp arrow, and aimed at the vulture. The seabound earth trembled.
ramayan::7954.translation_literal: इत्युक्त्वा (having said thus) / अभ्यपतत् (he rushed at) / गृध्रम् (the vulture) / सन्धाय (having fitted) / धनुषि (on the bow) / क्षुरम् (the sharp arrow) / क्रुद्धः (angry) / रामः (Rama) / समुद्रान्ताम् (to the edge of the sea) / कम्पयन् (shaking) / इव (as if) / मेदिनीम् (the earth)
ramayan::7954.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7954.essence: Raw grief can make even a noble person strike too fast.
ramayan::7954.simple_meaning: Rama, furious and convinced Sita has been eaten, raises his bow and rushes at the vulture.
ramayan::7954.simple_insight: A terrible mistake can come from love that has lost clarity.
ramayan::7954.detailed_meaning: In the forest, Rama sees Jatayu and believes the bird has devoured Sita. He draws his bow in rage and charges forward, ready to kill. The scene is still unfolding, so this verse is a violent reaction, not the lesson itself.
ramayan::7954.modern_relevance: You spot something alarming and move before checking the facts. In that first surge, anger feels like protection — and can make you wrong.
ramayan::7954.insight: It shows how grief can turn instantly into misdirected force before understanding catches up.

ramayan::7955.verse_sanskrit: तं दीनं दीनया वाचा सफेनं रुधिरं वमन् । अभ्यभाषत पक्षी तु रामं दशरथात्मजम् । । 36714 । ।
ramayan::7955.verse_hindi: But the vulture who was in a piteous state, vomitting foamy blood, spoke these words pathetically to Rama, son of Dasaratha:
ramayan::7955.english_translation: But the vulture, in a pitiful state and vomiting foamy blood, addressed Rama, son of Dasharatha.
ramayan::7955.translation_literal: तम् (that one) / दीनम् (wretched) / दीनया (with piteous) / वाचा (with speech) / सफेनम् (foamy) / रुधिरम् (blood) / वमन् (vomiting) / अभ्यभाषत (spoke) / पक्षी (the bird) / तु (indeed) / रामम् (to Rama) / दशरथात्मजम् (son of Dasharatha)
ramayan::7955.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7955.essence: A dying witness interrupts a fatal mistake.
ramayan::7955.simple_meaning: The vulture, badly wounded and bleeding, managed to speak to Rama.
ramayan::7955.simple_insight: Even in ruin, a true witness can still carry the truth.
ramayan::7955.detailed_meaning: Rama has just raised his bow against the bird he believes has taken Sita. Before the blow falls, the vulture, broken and bleeding, finds the strength to speak. This is the moment the attack turns into revelation.
ramayan::7955.modern_relevance: You assume the worst about someone who looks guilty. Then one cracked voice, speaking through pain, changes the whole story.
ramayan::7955.insight: It slows the mind before judgment and prepares it to hear a wounded truth.

ramayan::7956.verse_sanskrit: यामोषधिमिवायुष्मन्नन्वेषसि महावने । सा देवी मम च प्राणा रावणेनोभयं हृतम् । । 36715 । ।
ramayan::7956.verse_hindi: O Longlived one  she who you are searching in the forest like herbal medicine has been carried away by Ravana along with my life.
ramayan::7956.english_translation: O long-lived one, she whom you are searching for in the great forest, like a healing herb, has been carried away by Ravana along with my life.
ramayan::7956.translation_literal: या (that) / अमोषधिम् (healing herb) / इव (like) / आयुष्मन् (O long-lived one) / अन्वेषसि (you are searching for) / महावने (in the great forest) / सा (she) / देवी (lady) / मम (my) / च (and) / प्राणाः (life-breath) / रावणेन (by Ravana) / उभयम् (both) / हृतम् (taken away)
ramayan::7956.speaker: Jatayu
ramayan::7956.essence: The search is over, but the cost has already begun.
ramayan::7956.simple_meaning: Jatayu tells Rama that Sita has been taken by Ravana, and that the loss has cost him his life too.
ramayan::7956.simple_insight: Some truths arrive with such force that they feel like a death sentence.
ramayan::7956.detailed_meaning: In the forest after the abduction, the wounded Jatayu struggles to speak to Rama. He identifies Sita as the one Rama seeks and says Ravana has taken her, while the attack has also taken his own life.
ramayan::7956.modern_relevance: You finally find the person who saw what happened, and their voice is barely holding together. The answer comes, but it comes carrying grief.
ramayan::7956.insight: It turns a search into a confirmed loss, deepening the urgency and sorrow of the rescue.

ramayan::7957.verse_sanskrit: त्वया विरहिता देवी लक्ष्मणेन च राघव । ह्रियमाणा मया दृष्टा रावणेन बलीयसा । । 36716 । ।
ramayan::7957.verse_hindi: I have seen her snatched from you and from Lakshmana and carried off by powerful Ravana.
ramayan::7957.english_translation: I saw the divine lady snatched away from you and from Lakshmana by powerful Ravana.
ramayan::7957.translation_literal: त्वया (by you) / विरहिता (separated from) / देवी (the lady) / लक्ष्मणेन (by Lakshmana) / च (and) / राघव (Raghava) / ह्रियमाणा (being carried off) / मया (by me) / दृष्टा (seen) / रावणेन (by Ravana) / बलीयसा (by the powerful one)
ramayan::7957.speaker: Jatayu
ramayan::7957.essence: The witness to loss matters because it turns grief into action.
ramayan::7957.simple_meaning: Jatayu tells Rama that he saw Sita being forcibly taken away by Ravana while Rama and Lakshmana were absent.
ramayan::7957.simple_insight: Sometimes the worst truth is not that something is lost, but that you saw it happen and could not stop it.
ramayan::7957.detailed_meaning: Wounded and dying, Jatayu speaks to Rama after trying to resist Ravana. He confirms the terrible fact Rama needed to hear: Sita was seized and carried away while both brothers were away. This is a witness statement, not a teaching.
ramayan::7957.modern_relevance: You arrive too late and the scene is already over: the broken lock, the empty room, the message that says it happened while you were away.
ramayan::7957.insight: It gives Rama the missing fact he needs to begin the search and the fight.

ramayan::7958.verse_sanskrit: सीतामभ्यवपन्नोऽहं रावणश्च रणे मया । विध्वंसितरथश्चात्र पातितो धरणीतले । । 36717 । ।
ramayan::7958.verse_hindi: I descended down to protect Sita, and in the battle with Ravana his chariot destroyed fell down here on the ground.
ramayan::7958.english_translation: I came down to protect Sita, and in battle with Ravana his chariot was shattered and brought down to the ground here.
ramayan::7958.translation_literal: सीताम् (Sita) / अभ्यवपन्नः (came down to protect) / अहम् (I) / रावणः (Ravana) / च (and) / रणे (in battle) / मया (by me) / विध्वंसित-रथः (with shattered chariot) / च (and) / अत्र (here) / पातितः (brought down) / धरणी-तले (on the ground)
ramayan::7958.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::7958.essence: A fight is being reported, not interpreted.
ramayan::7958.simple_meaning: The speaker says he came to protect Sita, fought Ravana, and brought Ravana's chariot down to the ground.
ramayan::7958.simple_insight: The battle is being described step by step, not taught as a principle.
ramayan::7958.detailed_meaning: In the middle of the war, a witness describes what has just happened: the rescue of Sita and the destruction of Ravana's chariot in combat. The verse adds proof to the larger battle report, preparing for the next detail.
ramayan::7958.insight: It records battlefield aftermath, not a general lesson.

ramayan::7959.verse_sanskrit: एतदस्य धनुर्भग्नमेतदस्य शरावरम् । अयमस्य रथो राम भग्नसाङ्ग्रामिको मया । । 36718 । ।
ramayan::7959.verse_hindi: O Rama this is his broken bow, this is his quiver and this is his warchariot all devastated by me.
ramayan::7959.english_translation: O Rama, this is his broken bow, this is his quiver, and this is his war-chariot, all shattered by me.
ramayan::7959.translation_literal: एतत् (this) / अस्य (his) / धनुः (bow) / भग्नम् (broken) / एतत् (this) / अस्य (his) / शरावरम् (quiver) / अयम् (this) / अस्य (his) / रथः (chariot) / राम (Rama) / भग्न-साङ्ग्रामिकः (broken in battle) / मया (by me)
ramayan::7959.speaker: Jatayu
ramayan::7959.simple_meaning: Jatayu points out the broken bow, quiver, and chariot of Ravana, showing Rama that he fought to stop the abduction.
ramayan::7959.simple_insight: Even in defeat, a loyal act leaves a mark.
ramayan::7959.detailed_meaning: Jatayu lies wounded after trying to stop Ravana from carrying off Sita. Seeing Rama, he identifies the broken weapons and ruined chariot as proof of the battle he fought. The verse supports his account, not a complete teaching on its own.
ramayan::7959.modern_relevance: You arrive too late to stop what happened, but your effort still mattered. The evidence of your resistance is real, even if you could not win.
ramayan::7959.insight: It shifts attention from victory to the moral weight of resistance.

ramayan::7960.verse_sanskrit: अयं तु सारथिस्तस्य मत्पक्षनिहतो युधि । परिश्रान्तस्य मे पक्षौ छित्त्वा खड्गेन रावणः । । 36719 । । सीतामादाय वैदेहीमुत्पपात विहायसम् । रक्षसा निहतं पूर्वं न मां हन्तुं त्वमर्हसि । । 36720 । ।
ramayan::7960.verse_hindi: He is Ravanas charioteer slain by my wings in the battle.  As I was exhausted in the encounter Ravana clipped my wings,  took Sita, and flew into the sky. You need not kill me. I am already slain by the demon.
ramayan::7960.english_translation: He is Ravana's charioteer, slain by my wings in battle. As I grew exhausted in the fight, Ravana cut off my wings with his sword, took Sita, and flew into the sky. You need not kill me. I have already been slain by the demon.
ramayan::7960.translation_literal: अयम् (this) / तु (indeed) / सारथिः (charioteer) / तस्य (his) / मत्पक्षनिहतः (struck down by my wings) / युधि (in battle) / परिश्रान्तस्य (of the exhausted one) / मे (my) / पक्षौ (wings) / छित्त्वा (cutting off) / खड्गेन (with a sword) / रावणः (Ravana) / सीताम् (Sita) / आदाय (having taken) / वैदेहीम् (the daughter of Videha) / उत्पपात (flew up) / विहायसम् (into the sky) / रक्षसा (by the demon) / निहतम् (struck down) / पूर्वम् (already) / न (not) / माम् (me) / हन्तुम् (to kill) / त्वम् (you) / अर्हसि (are fit)
ramayan::7960.speaker: Jatayu
ramayan::7960.essence: Jatayu is already defeated, but his witness still matters.
ramayan::7960.simple_meaning: Jatayu explains that he fought Ravana, lost his wings, and was left dying after trying to stop Sita's abduction. He asks Rama not to kill him, because Ravana has already destroyed him.
ramayan::7960.simple_insight: Some injuries are deeper than death. He has already paid the price for trying to protect someone.
ramayan::7960.detailed_meaning: Jatayu lies wounded after fighting Ravana to stop Sita's abduction. He names the broken chariot, the severed wings, and the moment Ravana escaped with Sita. This is not a teaching verse but a dying witness giving Rama the truth.
ramayan::7960.insight: It completes the account of Sita's abduction and confirms Jatayu's sacrifice before he dies.

ramayan::7961.verse_sanskrit: रामस्तस्य तु विज्ञाय बाष्पपूर्णमुखस्तदा । द्विगुणीकृततापार्तस्सीतासक्तां प्रियां कथाम् । । 36721 । ।
ramayan::7961.verse_hindi: Having known from Jatayu the story of his beloved Sita, Rama was full of tears, his grief redoubled.
ramayan::7961.english_translation: Having learned from Jatayu the story of his beloved Sita, Rama was full of tears, and his grief doubled.
ramayan::7961.translation_literal: रामः (Rama) / तस्य (of that) / तु (indeed) / विज्ञाय (having known) / बाष्पपूर्णमुखः (with face full of tears) / तदा (then) / द्विगुणीकृत (made double) / तापार्तः (afflicted by grief) / सीतासक्ताम् (attached to Sita) / प्रियाम् (beloved) / कथाम् (story)
ramayan::7961.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7961.essence: Knowing the truth can make grief heavier, not lighter.
ramayan::7961.simple_meaning: Rama hears Jatayu's account of Sita and is overwhelmed by sorrow. The news makes his grief even deeper.
ramayan::7961.simple_insight: Some losses do not lessen with hearing the truth; they become more real and more painful.
ramayan::7961.detailed_meaning: Jatayu has just told Rama what happened to Sita and how he fought to stop Ravana. Rama now understands the full scale of the loss. The verse shows grief becoming sharper once the truth is known, just before Rama collapses in the next line.
ramayan::7961.modern_relevance: You finally get the full message after hours of silence, and the knot in your chest tightens instead of easing. Knowing the truth can hurt more than guessing.
ramayan::7961.insight: It shows how clear information can intensify grief rather than relieve it.

ramayan::7962.verse_sanskrit: गृध्रराजं परिष्वज्य परित्यज्य महद्धनुः । निपपातावशो भूमौ रुरोद सहलक्ष्मणः । । 36722 । ।
ramayan::7962.verse_hindi: Rama dropped the bow and embraced the king of birds. He fell down despondent on the ground and began crying along with Lakshmana.
ramayan::7962.english_translation: Rama dropped the bow and embraced the king of birds. He fell down helplessly on the ground and cried with Lakshmana.
ramayan::7962.translation_literal: गृध्रराजम् (the king of birds) / परिष्वज्य (having embraced) / परित्यज्य (having left aside) / महद्धनुः (the great bow) / निपपात (fell down) / अवशः (helpless) / भूमौ (on the ground) / रुरोद (wept) / सहलक्ष्मणः (together with Lakshmana)
ramayan::7962.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7962.essence: Grief can bring even the most resolute protector to the ground.
ramayan::7962.simple_meaning: Rama drops his bow, embraces Jatayu, and collapses in grief with Lakshmana beside him.
ramayan::7962.simple_insight: Even the strongest people can be undone by a loss they cannot fix.
ramayan::7962.detailed_meaning: After hearing Jatayu’s account of Sita’s abduction, Rama reaches the place where the wounded bird lies. The sight breaks his composure: he lays aside the bow, embraces the fallen ally, and collapses with Lakshmana in shared grief.
ramayan::7962.modern_relevance: You arrive too late to stop what happened, and the person who tried to help is lying hurt in front of you. The body knows before the mind does: this is grief, not strategy.
ramayan::7962.insight: It shifts the mind from heroic action to the cost of helpless witnessing.

ramayan::7963.verse_sanskrit: एकमेकायने दुर्गे निश्श्वसन्तं कथञ्चन । समीक्ष्य दुःखिततरो रामस्सौमित्रिमब्रवीत् । । 36723 । ।
ramayan::7963.verse_hindi: Rama saw Jatayu breathing with difficulty in that solitary, inaccessible place.Overcome by greater grief  he said to Lakshmana:
ramayan::7963.english_translation: Rama saw Jatayu breathing with difficulty in that lonely, hard-to-reach place, and, overcome by even greater grief, he spoke to Lakshmana.
ramayan::7963.translation_literal: एकमेकायने (in a solitary place) / दुर्गे (in a difficult-to-reach place) / निश्श्वसन्तं (breathing heavily) / कथञ्चन (with difficulty) / समीक्ष्य (having seen) / दुःखिततरो (more grieved) / रामः (Rama) / सौमित्रिम् (to Lakshmana) / अब्रवीत् (said)
ramayan::7963.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7963.essence: Grief deepens when you see the cost of loyalty lying before you.
ramayan::7963.simple_meaning: Rama finds Jatayu wounded and struggling to breathe in a lonely place. The sight deepens his grief, and he turns to Lakshmana to speak.
ramayan::7963.simple_insight: Some pain is so immediate that it leaves no room for composure.
ramayan::7963.detailed_meaning: In the forest, Rama comes upon Jatayu after the bird has tried to save Sita. The king of birds is dying in a hidden, difficult place. Rama's grief rises again at the sight, and he turns to Lakshmana before the next lament.
ramayan::7963.modern_relevance: You arrive at a hospital room and see someone who already gave everything trying to breathe. The shock is not just loss — it is seeing courage arrive too late.
ramayan::7963.insight: It shifts the mind from abstract sorrow to the raw reality of witnessing suffering up close.

ramayan::7964.verse_sanskrit: राज्यं भ्रष्टं वने वासस्सीता नष्टा हतो द्विजः । ईदृशीयं ममालक्ष्मीर्निर्दहेदपि पावकम् । । 36724 । ।
ramayan::7964.verse_hindi: I have been expelled from the kingdom. I am made to stay in the forest. I have lost Sita (my beloved wife). This bird (who was my wellwisher) has been slain. Such misfortune will burn even fire.
ramayan::7964.english_translation: I have been expelled from the kingdom. I am made to stay in the forest. I have lost Sita. This bird, who was my well-wisher, has been slain. Such misfortune would burn even fire.
ramayan::7964.translation_literal: राज्यम् (kingdom) / भ्रष्टम् (lost, fallen away) / वने (in the forest) / वासः (residence, stay) / सीता (Sita) / नष्टा (lost) / हतः (slain) / द्विजः (bird, twice-born) / ईदृशीम् (such) / इयम् (this) / मम (my) / अलक्ष्मीः (misfortune) / निर्दहेत् (would burn) / अपि (even) / पावकम् (fire)
ramayan::7964.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7964.essence: Loss can pile up until even strength feels fragile.
ramayan::7964.simple_meaning: Rama lists the blows that have fallen on him: exile, loss of Sita, and Jatayu's death. He says this level of misfortune could burn even fire.
ramayan::7964.simple_insight: Some grief is so heavy it feels larger than the world around it.
ramayan::7964.detailed_meaning: In the forest, Rama stands over the dying Jatayu after losing Sita and his kingdom. The losses come together at once: exile, separation, and the death of a loyal ally. His words gather that crushing moment into one lament.
ramayan::7964.modern_relevance: You get the call after the breakup, the layoff, and the family crisis all in the same week. At some point, the mind stops counting and only feels the weight.
ramayan::7964.insight: It gives language to grief that arrives in layers and overwhelms every attempt to stay composed.

ramayan::7965.verse_sanskrit: सम्पूर्णमपि चेदद्य प्रविशेयं महोदधिम् । सोऽपि नूनं ममालक्ष्म्या विशुष्येत्सरितांपतिः । । 36725 । ।
ramayan::7965.verse_hindi: Now if I enter even the great sea, the lord of the rivers filled with water, it will also dry up due to my misfortune.
ramayan::7965.english_translation: Now if I enter even the great sea, the lord of the rivers filled with water, it will also dry up due to my misfortune.
ramayan::7965.translation_literal: सम्पूर्णमपि (even though full) / चेद् (if) / अद्य (today) / प्रविशेयम् (I should enter) / महोदधिम् (the great ocean) / सः अपि (that also) / नूनम् (surely) / मम (my) / अलक्ष्म्या (by misfortune) / विशुष्येत् (would dry up) / सरिताम् पतिः (lord of rivers)
ramayan::7965.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7965.essence: Misfortune makes even abundance feel empty.
ramayan::7965.simple_meaning: Rama feels so crushed that he imagines his bad fortune could drain even the ocean dry.
ramayan::7965.simple_insight: Grief can make everything feel contaminated by failure.
ramayan::7965.detailed_meaning: Rama stands beside Jatayu, overwhelmed by loss. He has been exiled, Sita has vanished, and the wounded bird has just fallen. His despair spills into this image: even the full ocean would wither in his unlucky presence.
ramayan::7965.modern_relevance: You can be so shaken by one brutal day that even steady things feel fragile. In that state, your mind turns pain into a verdict on everything.
ramayan::7965.insight: It shows how grief distorts perception, making the world seem drained by your own bad fortune.

ramayan::7966.verse_sanskrit: नास्त्यभाग्यतरो लोके मत्तोऽस्मिन्सचराचरे । येनेयं महती प्राप्ता मया व्यसनवागुरा । । 36726 । ।
ramayan::7966.verse_hindi: In this world of the animate and the inanimate there is no one more unfortunate than me fallen into the trap of adversities.
ramayan::7966.english_translation: In all the moving and unmoving world, no one is more unfortunate than I, caught in this great net of misfortune.
ramayan::7966.translation_literal: नास्ति (there is not) / अभाग्यतरः (more unfortunate) / लोके (in the world) / मतः (than me) / अस्मिन् (in this) / सचराचरे (moving and unmoving) / येन (by whom) / इयम् (this) / महती (great) / प्राप्ता (obtained) / मया (by me) / व्यसनवागुरा (net of calamity)
ramayan::7966.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7966.essence: Pain can make the whole world feel like a trap.
ramayan::7966.simple_meaning: Rama says no one in the whole world is more unlucky than he is, because he feels trapped by a huge net of suffering.
ramayan::7966.simple_insight: Grief can make even a noble person feel singled out by fate.
ramayan::7966.detailed_meaning: Rama stands in the forest after losing his kingdom, his exile, and Sita. Jatayu lies fallen, and the next verse will name him as a friend of Dasharatha. Here Rama’s sorrow widens into a total sense of ruin.
ramayan::7966.modern_relevance: You watch one bad week turn into a story about your whole life. A breakup, a job loss, a family blow — and suddenly everything feels rigged against you.
ramayan::7966.insight: It names the way suffering narrows vision until pain feels universal and personal at once.

ramayan::7967.verse_sanskrit: अयं पितृवयस्यो मे गृध्रराजो जरान्वितः । शेते विनिहतो भूमौ मम भाग्यविपर्ययात् । । 36727 । ।
ramayan::7967.verse_hindi: This aged king of birds is my fathers friend. To my illluck, he is struck down and is lying on the ground.
ramayan::7967.english_translation: This aged king of birds is my father's friend. By my misfortune, he lies struck down on the ground.
ramayan::7967.translation_literal: अयं (this) / पितृवयस्यः (father's friend) / मे (my) / गृध्रराजः (king of birds) / जरान्वितः (endowed with old age) / शेते (lies) / विनिहतः (struck down) / भूमौ (on the ground) / मम (my) / भाग्यविपर्ययात् (because of my misfortune)
ramayan::7967.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7967.essence: He finds a loyal friend broken by the very crisis he is chasing.
ramayan::7967.simple_meaning: Rama sees Jatayu, his father's old friend, lying wounded on the ground and grieves that this has happened because of his own misfortune.
ramayan::7967.simple_insight: Grief gets sharper when you realise someone brave suffered for your sake.
ramayan::7967.detailed_meaning: After Sita's abduction, Rama and Lakshmana discover Jatayu, the aged king of birds and Dasaratha's friend, fallen and wounded on the earth. Rama's sorrow here is personal and immediate: the search has turned into a scene of loss, recognition, and helplessness.
ramayan::7967.modern_relevance: You arrive too late and find the person who tried to help you badly hurt. The shock is not only at the injury, but at the loyalty that paid the price.
ramayan::7967.insight: It shifts attention from the search itself to the human cost already paid.

ramayan::7968.verse_sanskrit: इत्येवमुक्त्वा बहुशो राघवस्सहलक्ष्मणः । जटायुषं च पस्पर्श पितृस्नेहं विदर्शयन् । । 36728 । ।
ramayan::7968.verse_hindi: Saying such words and showing filial affection, he caressed Jatayu repeatedly with Lakshmana.
ramayan::7968.english_translation: Saying this again and again, Rama and Lakshmana showed filial affection and gently touched Jatayu.
ramayan::7968.translation_literal: इत्येवम् (thus) / उक्त्वा (having said) / बहुशः (many times, repeatedly) / राघवः (Rama) / सहलक्ष्मणः (together with Lakshmana) / जटायुषम् (Jatayu) / च (and) / पस्पर्श (touched, caressed) / पितृस्नेहम् (filial affection) / विदर्शयन् (showing)
ramayan::7968.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7968.essence: Gratitude becomes physical when someone who protected you lies wounded.
ramayan::7968.simple_meaning: Rama and Lakshmana keep speaking with grief and then gently touch Jatayu, treating him with the love due to a father.
ramayan::7968.simple_insight: Love shows itself in small acts of tenderness, even in the middle of shock and loss.
ramayan::7968.detailed_meaning: After finding Jatayu fallen and wounded, Rama and Lakshmana stand over the bird who tried to save Sita. Rama speaks with anguish, then the two brothers touch him again and again with the respect and affection owed to a father’s friend. The moment deepens the sorrow before Jatayu speaks.
ramayan::7968.modern_relevance: You reach someone who protected your family and find him hurt on the ground. Before questions, before explanations, you kneel and touch his hand with gratitude.
ramayan::7968.insight: It shifts the mind from panic to reverent care, showing that grief can still be tender and orderly.

ramayan::7969.verse_sanskrit: निकृत्तपक्षं रुधिरावसिक्तं स गृध्रराजं परिरभ्य रामः । क्व मैथिली प्राणसमा ममेति विमुच्य वाचं निपपात भूमौ । । 36729 । ।
ramayan::7969.verse_hindi: Rama hugged the king of vultures with servered wings, drenched in blood and asking him where Sita who was as dear to him as his life was, he dropped him and fell down on the ground.
ramayan::7969.english_translation: Rama embraced the king of vultures, whose wings had been cut off and who was soaked in blood. Asking, "Where is Maithili, who is as dear to me as my own life?" he fell to the ground, overcome.
ramayan::7969.translation_literal: निकृत्तपक्षं (with cut wings) / रुधिरावसिक्तं (soaked in blood) / सः (he) / गृध्रराजं (the king of vultures) / परिरभ्य (embracing) / रामः (Rama) / क्व (where) / मैथिली (Maithili) / प्राणसमा (equal to life) / मम (to me) / इति (thus) / विमुच्य (releasing) / वाचं (speech) / निपपात (fell down) / भूमौ (on the ground)
ramayan::7969.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7969.essence: Grief hits hardest when love has nowhere to go.
ramayan::7969.simple_meaning: Rama holds the wounded vulture close, asks where Sita is, and collapses in grief.
ramayan::7969.simple_insight: Love can make even the strongest person break when someone precious is missing.
ramayan::7969.detailed_meaning: After finding Jatayu dying on the ground, Rama embraces the bird like a mourner embracing a fallen elder. The only question that matters is Sita. The answer is still unknown, and that uncertainty hits him so hard he collapses.
ramayan::7969.modern_relevance: You get the call that someone you love is missing, and the room goes silent. The body reacts before the mind can make sense of it.
ramayan::7969.insight: It shows how deep attachment turns a search into a wound, and a question into collapse.

ramayan::7970.verse_sanskrit: रामस्सम्प्रेक्ष्य तं गृध्रं भुवि रौद्रेण पातितम् । सौमित्रिं मित्रसम्पन्नमिदं वचनमब्रवीत् । । 3681 । ।
ramayan::7970.verse_hindi: Seeing the vulture lying on the ground thrown down by the fierce demon, Rama said to friendly Lakshmana:
ramayan::7970.english_translation: Seeing the vulture lying on the ground, thrown down by the fierce demon, Rama said to friendly Lakshmana:
ramayan::7970.translation_literal: रामः (Rama) / सम्प्रेक्ष्य (having seen clearly) / तम् (that) / गृध्रम् (vulture) / भुवि (on the ground) / रौद्रेण (by the fierce one) / पातितम् (thrown down) / सौमित्रिम् (to Lakshmana) / मित्रसम्पन्नम् (endowed with friendship) / इदम् (this) / वचनम् (speech) / अब्रवीत् (said)
ramayan::7970.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7970.essence: The sight of suffering stops him before words do.
ramayan::7970.simple_meaning: Rama sees the wounded vulture on the ground and turns to Lakshmana to speak.
ramayan::7970.simple_insight: Even in shock, he responds with care before he speaks.
ramayan::7970.detailed_meaning: After Jatayu is cut down in the forest, Rama reaches him and sees the bird fallen by a fierce enemy. He turns to Lakshmana, ready to speak in the middle of grief and urgency. This line sets up his lament in the next verse.
ramayan::7970.modern_relevance: You arrive too late and see someone hurt on the floor. Before the questions come, your voice has to find care first.
ramayan::7970.insight: It frames grief as immediate attention to the wounded before anything else.

ramayan::7971.verse_sanskrit: ममायं नूनमर्थेषु यतमानो विहङ्गमः । राक्षसेन हतस्संख्ये प्राणांस्त्यक्ष्यति दुस्त्यजान् । । 3682 । ।
ramayan::7971.verse_hindi: Struck down by the demon in the combat on my account this bird is going to give up his life which is indeed difficult.
ramayan::7971.english_translation: This bird, who was trying to help me, has been struck down by the demon in battle and will now give up his hard-to-surrender life.
ramayan::7971.translation_literal: मम (my) / अयम् (this) / नूनम् (surely) / अर्थेषु (in matters / for a purpose) / यतमानः (striving) / विहङ्गमः (bird) / राक्षसेन (by the demon) / हतः (struck) / संख्ये (in battle) / प्राणान् (life-breaths) / त्यक्ष्यति (will give up) / दुस्त्यजान् (hard to abandon)
ramayan::7971.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7971.essence: He sees a helper dying because he chose to stand in the way.
ramayan::7971.simple_meaning: Rama sees that Jatayu was struck down while trying to help him, and now the bird is dying.
ramayan::7971.simple_insight: Even loyal help can come at a terrible cost.
ramayan::7971.detailed_meaning: Rama has just reached the fallen vulture after Ravana's attack. Seeing Jatayu broken on the ground, he realises the bird fought for Sita and paid with his life. This line is Rama naming that sacrifice before the full exchange continues.
ramayan::7971.modern_relevance: You watch a friend step in for you and take the hit. The help was real, and so was the cost. Some loyalties leave a wound behind.
ramayan::7971.insight: It shifts attention from the battle itself to the price of protecting someone you love.

ramayan::7972.verse_sanskrit: अयमस्य शरीरेऽस्मिन्प्राणो लक्ष्मण विद्यते । तथा हि स्वरहीनोऽयं विक्लबस्समुदीक्ष्यते । । 3683 । ।
ramayan::7972.verse_hindi: O Lakshmana, it appears he is frightened and is experiencing excruciating pain in the body. His voice sounds faint, too.
ramayan::7972.english_translation: O Lakshmana, it appears he is frightened and is experiencing excruciating pain in the body. His voice sounds faint, too.
ramayan::7972.translation_literal: अयम् (this one) / अस्य (of him) / शरीरे (in the body) / अस्मिन् (in this) / प्राणः (breath, life) / विद्यते (is present) / तथा (thus) / हि (indeed) / स्वरहीनः (without voice) / अयम् (this one) / विक्लबः (distressed, frightened) / समुदीक्ष्यते (is seen)
ramayan::7972.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7972.essence: Pain can silence a body before it silences life.
ramayan::7972.simple_meaning: Jatayu is still alive, but he is badly hurt, frightened, and barely able to speak.
ramayan::7972.simple_insight: Even in collapse, a wounded being deserves notice, care, and patience.
ramayan::7972.detailed_meaning: Rama has found the fallen vulture after the battle with Ravana. Seeing Jatayu's broken condition, he speaks to Lakshmana with concern, not triumph. This verse is a close, compassionate observation before Rama asks what happened.
ramayan::7972.modern_relevance: You notice someone’s voice go thin after bad news, and you stop everything. Before questions, before plans, there is the simple act of seeing their pain clearly.
ramayan::7972.insight: It trains you to read suffering before words return, and to respond with care instead of haste.

ramayan::7973.verse_sanskrit: जटायो यदि शक्नोषि वाक्यं व्याहरितुं पुनः । सीतामाख्याहि भद्रं ते वधमाख्याहि चात्मनः । । 3684 । ।
ramayan::7973.verse_hindi: O Jatayu If you are still able to speak, tell me about Sita and about how you have been struck down.
ramayan::7973.english_translation: O Jatayu, if you are still able to speak, tell me about Sita and about how you have been struck down.
ramayan::7973.translation_literal: जटायो (O Jatayu) / यदि (if) / शक्नोषि (you are able) / वाक्यम् (speech) / व्याहरितुम् (to speak) / पुनः (again) / सीताम् (about Sita) / आख्याहि (tell) / भद्रम् (good fortune) / ते (to you) / वधम् (slaying / being struck down) / आख्याहि (tell) / च (and) / आत्मनः (of yourself)
ramayan::7973.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7973.essence: Grief turns instantly into a search for the missing truth.
ramayan::7973.simple_meaning: Rama asks the wounded Jatayu, if he can still speak, to tell him what happened to Sita and how he was struck down.
ramayan::7973.simple_insight: Even in shock, the first need is to know the truth.
ramayan::7973.detailed_meaning: Rama has found Jatayu dying after his battle with Ravana. He kneels beside the fallen bird and urgently asks for the only answers that matter: where Sita is, and what happened in the fight. The verse moves the search forward.
ramayan::7973.modern_relevance: You arrive after the accident and kneel beside someone who can barely speak. Before anything else, you need the facts: what happened, and who still needs help.
ramayan::7973.insight: It shifts attention from grief to urgent inquiry, so action can begin with clear information.

ramayan::7974.verse_sanskrit: किं निमित्तोऽहरत्सीतां रावणस्तस्य किं मया । अपराद्धं तु यं दृष्ट्वा रावणेन हृता प्रिया । । 3685 । ।
ramayan::7974.verse_hindi: Why did Ravana abduct Sita? What fault did he find with me so that he kidnapped my beloved ?
ramayan::7974.english_translation: Why did Ravana abduct Sita? What fault did he find with me so that he kidnapped my beloved?
ramayan::7974.translation_literal: किं (what) / निमित्तः (for what reason) / अहरत् (he carried away) / सीताम् (Sita) / रावणः (Ravana) / तस्य (of him) / किं (what) / मया (by me) / अपराद्धम् (fault was done) / तु (indeed) / यम् (which) / दृष्ट्वा (having seen) / रावणेन (by Ravana) / हृता (taken away) / प्रिया (beloved)
ramayan::7974.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7974.essence: Loss can make you search yourself for a fault that was never yours.
ramayan::7974.simple_meaning: Rama asks why Ravana took Sita and what fault he could possibly have committed to deserve it.
ramayan::7974.simple_insight: Love makes the loss feel personal, even when the reason is beyond your control.
ramayan::7974.detailed_meaning: Jatayu has just been found dying after trying to stop Ravana. Rama, shaken and desperate, asks the bird why Sita was taken and what mistake he himself made. The question reveals grief, disbelief, and the first wound of separation.
ramayan::7974.modern_relevance: You replay the moment someone left and keep asking what you did wrong. Sometimes the mind wants a reason more than the truth.
ramayan::7974.insight: It shows how grief turns into self-blame, even when the loss was caused by another person's choice.

ramayan::7975.verse_sanskrit: कथं तच्चन्द्रसङ्काशं मुखमासीन्मनोहरम् । सीतया कानि चोक्तानि तस्मिन्काले द्विजोत्तम । । 3686 । ।
ramayan::7975.verse_hindi: O best of birds how did her delightful, Moonlike face look when she was hijacked. What did she say at that time?
ramayan::7975.english_translation: O best of birds, how did her delightful, moonlike face look when she was seized? What did she say then?
ramayan::7975.translation_literal: कथं (how) / तत् (that) / चन्द्रसङ्काशम् (moon-like) / मुखम् (face) / आसीत् (was) / मनोहरम् (delightful) / सीतया (by Sita) / कानि (what) / च (and) / उक्तानि (spoken) / तस्मिन् काले (at that time) / द्विजोत्तम (O best of birds)
ramayan::7975.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7975.essence: Love after loss asks for every detail.
ramayan::7975.simple_meaning: Rama asks Jatayu how Sita looked when Ravana took her and what she said in that moment.
ramayan::7975.simple_insight: Grief wants details because love cannot bear the blank spaces.
ramayan::7975.detailed_meaning: Rama is questioning the wounded Jatayu after Sita’s abduction. He is desperate for any detail: her face, her words, the moment she was taken. The verse deepens his anguish, but it does not yet offer a teaching on its own.
ramayan::7975.modern_relevance: You replay the last message, the last look, the last sentence after someone is gone. The mind reaches for details because absence feels unbearable.
ramayan::7975.insight: It shows how loss turns the mind toward exact memory, searching for anything that can make the absence real.

ramayan::7976.verse_sanskrit: कथं वीर्यः कथं रूपः किं कर्मा स च राक्षसः । क्व चास्य भवनं तात ब्रूहि मे परिपृच्छतः । । 3687 । ।
ramayan::7976.verse_hindi: O father  how powerful is that demon ? How does he look?What work does he do? Where does he dwell? Do answer my questions?
ramayan::7976.english_translation: O father, how powerful is that demon? What does he look like? What work does he do? Where does he live? Please answer my questions.
ramayan::7976.translation_literal: कथं (how) / वीर्यः (powerful) / कथं (how) / रूपः (appearance) / किं (what) / कर्मा (deed or work) / सः (that) / राक्षसः (demon) / क्व (where) / च (and) / अस्य (his) / भवनम् (dwelling) / तात (father) / ब्रूहि (tell) / मे (to me) / परिपृच्छतः (of the one asking repeatedly)
ramayan::7976.speaker: Rama
ramayan::7976.essence: Grief looks for facts before it can move.
ramayan::7976.simple_meaning: Rama urgently asks Jatayu to describe Ravana’s strength, appearance, work, and home.
ramayan::7976.simple_insight: When loss is sudden, the mind reaches for details to make the enemy real.
ramayan::7976.detailed_meaning: Rama has just found Sita gone and is questioning Jatayu in anguish. Before grief can settle, he presses for every detail about the man who took her, trying to build a clear picture of the threat.
ramayan::7976.modern_relevance: You get a call saying someone you love has been taken or hurt. Before panic turns to action, you need facts: who, what, where, how strong, how close.
ramayan::7976.insight: It shifts the mind from raw shock to precise inquiry, so action can begin.

ramayan::7977.verse_sanskrit: तमुद्वीक्ष्याथ दीनात्मा विलपन्तमनन्तरम् । वाचातिसन्नया रामं जटायुरिदमब्रवीत् । । 3688 । ।
ramayan::7977.verse_hindi: Thereafter Jatayu, a piteous soul, looked up at Rama who was  crying incessantly and said this in a feeble voice:
ramayan::7977.english_translation: Thereafter Jatayu, a piteous soul, looked up at Rama who was crying incessantly and said this in a feeble voice:
ramayan::7977.translation_literal: तम् (him) / उद्वीक्ष्य (looking up) / अथ (thereafter) / दीनात्मा (a piteous soul) / विलपन्तम् (lamenting) / अनन्तरम् (continuously) / वाचा (with voice) / अति-सन्नया (very feeble) / रामम् (to Rama) / जटायुः (Jatayu) / इदम् (this) / अब्रवीत् (said)
ramayan::7977.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7977.essence: A dying witness still finds the strength to answer.
ramayan::7977.simple_meaning: Jatayu, badly wounded and weak, saw Rama grieving and spoke to him in a faint voice.
ramayan::7977.simple_insight: Even in collapse, the instinct to help and speak truth remains.
ramayan::7977.detailed_meaning: Jatayu lies grievously wounded after trying to stop Ravana. Rama is beside him, distraught and searching for Sita. In this moment, the bird gathers the last of his strength to answer, setting up the account of her abduction.
ramayan::7977.modern_relevance: You are shaken and exhausted, but someone still needs the truth from you. Even a weak voice can carry what matters most.
ramayan::7977.insight: It shifts attention from grief alone to the duty of speaking clearly in a crisis.

ramayan::7978.verse_sanskrit: हृता सा राक्षसेन्द्रेण रावणेन विहायसा । मायामास्थाय विपुलां वातदुर्दिनसङ्कुलाम् । । 3689 । ।
ramayan::7978.verse_hindi: Ravana, the lord of the demons created violent winds through terrific magic and whisked her away in the sky.
ramayan::7978.english_translation: Ravana, the lord of the demons, created violent winds through terrific magic and carried her away through the sky.
ramayan::7978.translation_literal: हृता (was carried off) / सा (she) / राक्षसेन्द्रेण (by the lord of demons) / रावणेन (by Ravana) / विहायसा (through the sky) / मायाम् (magic) / आस्थाय (having employed) / विपुलाम् (great) / वातदुर्दिनसङ्कुलाम् (filled with wind and storm)
ramayan::7978.speaker: Jatayu
ramayan::7978.essence: Power and deception can carry away what force cannot protect.
ramayan::7978.simple_meaning: Ravana abducted Sita by using powerful magic and flying through the sky.
ramayan::7978.simple_insight: The loss is sudden, violent, and beyond ordinary reach.
ramayan::7978.detailed_meaning: Jatayu, wounded and barely able to speak, is telling Rama what happened to Sita. He describes Ravana’s power and the terrifying way he took her away, setting up the full account of the abduction.
ramayan::7978.modern_relevance: A phone call comes in with the kind of news that changes the whole day. You do not get a neat explanation first — only the shock of something taken before you could stop it.
ramayan::7978.insight: It marks the abduction as a violent, overwhelming event rather than a simple disappearance.

ramayan::7979.verse_sanskrit: परिश्रान्तस्य मे तात पक्षौ छित्वा स राक्षसः । सीतामादाय वैदेहीं प्रयातो दक्षिणां दिशम् । । 36810 । ।
ramayan::7979.verse_hindi: O my child  when I was exhausted, that demon cut off my wings and carried Sita off in the southern direction.
ramayan::7979.english_translation: O my child, when I was exhausted, that demon cut off my wings and carried Sita off in the southern direction.
ramayan::7979.translation_literal: परिश्रान्तस्य (of the exhausted one) / मे (my) / तात (O child) / पक्षौ (wings) / छित्वा (having cut off) / सः (that) / राक्षसः (demon) / सीताम् (Sita) / आदाय (taking) / वैदेहीम् (the princess of Videha) / प्रयातः (departed) / दक्षिणाम् (southern) / दिशम् (direction)
ramayan::7979.speaker: Jatayu
ramayan::7979.essence: Exhaustion left him unable to stop the abduction.
ramayan::7979.simple_meaning: Jatayu tells Rama that Ravana cut off his wings while he was too exhausted to fight and then fled south with Sita.
ramayan::7979.simple_insight: Even brave resistance can end in injury when strength runs out.
ramayan::7979.detailed_meaning: Jatayu, wounded and barely able to speak, explains to Rama how Ravana overpowered him. He was exhausted, his wings were cut off, and Sita was taken away toward the south. This is not a teaching verse, but part of Jatayu's dying account.
ramayan::7979.modern_relevance: You give everything you have in one desperate moment, and still it is not enough to stop what is happening.
ramayan::7979.insight: It keeps the focus on the attack itself, showing the cost of Jatayu's failed defense.

ramayan::7980.verse_sanskrit: उपरुध्यन्ति मे प्राणा दृष्टिर्भ्रमति राघव । पश्यामि वृक्षान्सौवर्णानुशीरकृतमूर्धजान् । । 36811 । ।
ramayan::7980.verse_hindi: O scion of the Raghu race, I am gasping for breath. My eyes are reeling. I see root hair growing on the tops of golden trees.
ramayan::7980.english_translation: O scion of the Raghu race, I am gasping for breath. My eyes are reeling. I see root hair growing on the tops of golden trees.
ramayan::7980.translation_literal: उपरुध्यन्ति (are being obstructed) / मे (my) / प्राणा (breaths) / दृष्टिः (sight) / भ्रमति (is spinning) / राघव (O Raghava) / पश्यामि (I see) / वृक्षान् (trees) / सौवर्णान् (golden) / अनुशीरकृतमूर्धजान् (with root-hairs made on the tops)
ramayan::7980.speaker: Jatayu
ramayan::7980.essence: Heroic struggle can leave even truth hard to see.
ramayan::7980.simple_meaning: Jatayu is losing strength after the battle. He tells Rama that his breath is failing, his vision is spinning, and everything looks distorted.
ramayan::7980.simple_insight: Even a noble effort can leave you shattered before the truth is fully spoken.
ramayan::7980.detailed_meaning: Jatayu has been mortally wounded while trying to stop Ravana from carrying Sita away. In front of Rama, he can barely breathe or see clearly. This line captures the collapse of a heroic body at the edge of death.
ramayan::7980.modern_relevance: After a long fight, you sit in the parked car with your hands shaking, trying to explain what happened. Your body knows before your words do that you have reached the limit.
ramayan::7980.insight: It shows the cost of resistance and the fragility of perception under extreme strain.

ramayan::7981.verse_sanskrit: येन याति मुहूर्तेन सीतामादाय रावणः । विप्रणष्टं धनं क्षिप्रं तत्स्वामी प्रतिपद्यते । । 36812 । । विन्दो नाम मुहूर्तोऽयं स च काकुत्स्थ नाबुधत् ।
ramayan::7981.verse_hindi: The time Ravana kidnapped Sita is known as Vinda. The effect (of that time), is that her husband will regain his lost wealth. O scion of the Kakutstha race  he (Ravana )did not know it.
ramayan::7981.english_translation: The time Ravana kidnapped Sita is known as Vinda. The result of that moment is that her husband will quickly recover his lost wealth. O scion of the Kakutstha line, Ravana did not understand this.
ramayan::7981.translation_literal: येन (by which) / याति (goes) / मुहूर्तेन (in a moment) / सीतामादाय (having taken Sita) / रावणः (Ravana) / विप्रणष्टम् (lost) / धनम् (wealth) / क्षिप्रम् (quickly) / तत्स्वामी (its owner) / प्रतिपद्यते (regains) / विन्दो (Vinda) / नाम (named) / मुहूर्तः (moment) / अयम् (this) / सः (he) / च (and) / काकुत्स्थ (O Kakutstha) / न (not) / अबुधत् (understood)
ramayan::7981.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7981.essence: What seems like gain can be the first step toward ruin.
ramayan::7981.simple_meaning: Ravana's abduction of Sita is described as the moment that will lead to his own downfall and Rama's recovery of what was lost.
ramayan::7981.simple_insight: What looks like a victory can hide the seed of defeat.
ramayan::7981.detailed_meaning: After Jatayu describes Sita's abduction, he names the very moment of Ravana's success and says Ravana failed to understand its consequence. The theft of Sita is already tied to Ravana's destruction and Rama's restoration.
ramayan::7981.modern_relevance: You think you have won by taking what was never yours to keep. Days later, the same choice starts unraveling your life from the inside.
ramayan::7981.insight: It shifts attention from immediate gain to the hidden consequence already built into the act.

ramayan::7982.verse_sanskrit: त्वत्प्रियां जानकीं हृत्वा रावणो राक्षसेश्वरः । । 36813 । । झषवद्बडिशं गृह्य क्षिप्रमेव विनश्यति ।
ramayan::7982.verse_hindi: Ravana, king of the demons, will perish soon for running away with your beloved Janaki just like a fish carrying away a fishhook (which causes its destruction).
ramayan::7982.english_translation: Ravana, king of the demons, will perish soon for running away with your beloved Janaki, just like a fish carrying away a fishhook, which causes its own destruction.
ramayan::7982.translation_literal: त्वत्प्रियाम् (your beloved) / जानकीम् (Janaki) / हृत्वा (having seized) / रावणः (Ravana) / राक्षसेश्वरः (lord of the demons) / झषवत् (like a fish) / बडिशम् (fishhook) / गृह्य (taking) / क्षिप्रम् एव (very soon) / विनश्यति (will perish)
ramayan::7982.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7982.essence: Grabbing what is forbidden can be the start of your own collapse.
ramayan::7982.simple_meaning: Ravana will be destroyed by the very act of taking Sita, just as a fish is ruined by swallowing a hook.
ramayan::7982.simple_insight: What looks like a triumph can already contain the seed of ruin.
ramayan::7982.detailed_meaning: In the aftermath of Sita’s abduction, a speaker consoles Rama by explaining that Ravana has already trapped himself. The image is brutal and exact: the captor thinks he has gained something, but the act itself will bring his fall.
ramayan::7982.modern_relevance: You finally get what you wanted by crossing a line you knew was there. For a moment it feels like victory. Then you realise the line was the trap.
ramayan::7982.insight: It warns you that desire can become self-destruction when it ignores consequence.

ramayan::7983.verse_sanskrit: न च त्वया व्यथा कार्या जनकस्य सुतां प्रति । । 36814 । । वैदेह्या रंस्यसे क्षिप्रं हत्वा तं राक्षसं रणे ।
ramayan::7983.verse_hindi: You need not worry about Janakas daughter. You will soon enjoy the company of your beloved, Vaidehi after killing that demon.
ramayan::7983.english_translation: You need not worry about Janaka's daughter. You will soon enjoy Vaidehi's company after killing that demon in battle.
ramayan::7983.translation_literal: न / not / च / and / त्वया / by you / व्यथा / worry / कार्या / should be done / जनकस्य / of Janaka / सुतां / daughter / प्रति / regarding / वैदेह्या / with Vaidehi / रंस्यसे / you will enjoy / क्षिप्रं / soon / हत्वा / having killed / तं / that / राक्षसं / demon / रणे / in battle
ramayan::7983.speaker: Unknown
ramayan::7983.essence: Loss is not final when dharma still moves toward reunion.
ramayan::7983.simple_meaning: Rama is reassured that Sita will soon be regained after Ravana is killed in battle.
ramayan::7983.simple_insight: Even in loss, the bond is not broken; the separation is temporary.
ramayan::7983.detailed_meaning: Jatayu, dying after resisting Ravana, speaks to Rama with fierce clarity. He reassures him that Janaka's daughter will not remain lost forever: once Ravana falls in battle, Rama will be reunited with Sita.
ramayan::7983.modern_relevance: You are staring at a message that changes everything, and your mind keeps spiraling ahead. This verse steadies the panic: what has been lost is not beyond return.
ramayan::7983.insight: It shifts attention from immediate grief to the certainty of rightful restoration.

ramayan::7984.verse_sanskrit: असम्मूढस्य गृध्रस्य रामं प्रत्यनुभाषतः । । 36815 । । आस्यात्सुस्राव रुधिरं म्रियमाणस्य सामिषम् ।
ramayan::7984.verse_hindi: As he(Jatayu) was speaking to Rama with an alert mind even while dying, blood mixed with flesh started oozing from Jatayus mouth.
ramayan::7984.english_translation: As Jatayu spoke to Rama with an alert mind even while dying, blood mixed with flesh began to ooze from his mouth.
ramayan::7984.translation_literal: असम्मूढस्य (not bewildered) / गृध्रस्य (of the vulture) / रामं (to Rama) / प्रत्यनुभाषतः (speaking in reply) / आस्यात् (from the mouth) / सुस्राव (oozed) / रुधिरं (blood) / म्रियमाणस्य (of the dying one) / सामिषम् (mixed with flesh)
ramayan::7984.speaker: Valmiki
ramayan::7984.essence: Clear awareness can remain even as the body fails.
ramayan::7984.simple_meaning: Jatayu, still clear-minded as he died, spoke to Rama while blood and flesh flowed from his mouth.
ramayan::7984.simple_insight: Even at the edge of death, dignity can remain intact.
ramayan::7984.detailed_meaning: Rama has reached the dying Jatayu after the battle with Ravana. The wounded vulture is still lucid enough to answer him, but his body is collapsing. This verse lingers on the physical cost of his loyalty before he gives the final account.
ramayan::7984.modern_relevance: A person keeps speaking through tears in the emergency room, trying to give one last clear account before slipping away.
ramayan::7984.insight: It shows that courage is not loud; it can be the last clear words spoken through unbearable pain.

ramayan::7985.verse_sanskrit: पुत्रो विश्रवसस्साक्षाद्भ्राता वैश्रवणस्य च । । 36816 । । इत्युक्त्वा दुर्लभान्प्राणान्मुमोच पतगेश्वरः ।
ramayan::7985.verse_hindi: Ravana was Visravas son and Vaisravanas (Kuberas) brother, said Jatayu and gave up his rare life.
ramayan::7985.english_translation: Ravana was the son of Visravas and the brother of Kubera, said Jatayu, and the lord of birds gave up his rare life.
ramayan::7985.translation_literal: पुत्रः (son) / विश्रवसः (of Visravas) / साक्षात् (indeed) / भ्राता (brother) / वैश्रवणस्य (of Vaishravana/Kubera) / च (and) / इति (thus) / उक्त्वा (having said) / दुर्लभान् (rare) / प्राणान् (life-breaths) / मुमोच (released) / पतगेश्वरः (lord of birds)
ramayan::7985.speaker: Jatayu
ramayan::7985.essence: His last breath became a final act of help.
ramayan::7985.simple_meaning: Jatayu finishes identifying Ravana's lineage and dies after speaking. The verse marks the end of his last effort to help Rama.
ramayan::7985.simple_insight: Even in death, he gives Rama the final clue.
ramayan::7985.detailed_meaning: Jatayu, mortally wounded after resisting Ravana, uses his last breath to identify the abducter: Ravana is Visravas's son and Kubera's brother. Having spoken, the noble bird releases his life.
ramayan::7985.modern_relevance: Someone on the edge of collapse still finds the words that matter most. In that final minute, clarity becomes service.
ramayan::7985.insight: It shows that truth spoken at the end can still change everything.

ramayan::7986.verse_sanskrit: ब्रूहि ब्रूहीति रामस्य ब्रुवाणस्य कृताञ्जलेः । । 36817 । । त्वक्त्वा शरीरं गृध्रस्य जग्मुः प्राणा विहायसम् ।
ramayan::7986.verse_hindi: As Rama was saying to the vulture with folded palms Tell me, tell me( about Ravana) the life breath of the vulture soared into the sky leaving the body.
ramayan::7986.english_translation: As Rama was saying to the vulture, with folded palms, “Tell me, tell me,” the life breath of the vulture left the body and rose into the sky.
ramayan::7986.translation_literal: ब्रूहि (tell) / ब्रूहि (tell) / इति (thus) / रामस्य (of Rama) / ब्रुवाणस्य (while speaking) / कृताञ्जलेः (with folded palms) / त्वक्त्वा (having left) / शरीरं (the body) / गृध्रस्य (of the vulture) / जग्मुः (went) / प्राणा (the life breaths) / विहायसम् (into the sky)
